Resolve any mode you are unsure of with `hashcat --identify hashes.txt` or `hashcat --help | grep -i <keyword>` rather than trusting a note. The modes below are the ones you will actually hit.

| Hash type | Mode | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| NTLM | 1000 | NTDS dumps, SAM dumps, `--ntds` output. Extremely fast, so wordlist plus rules is nearly free. Use `--username` when the input is `user:rid:lm:nt:::`. |
| LM | 3000 | Only on ancient systems. Present as `aad3b435b51404eeaad3b435b51404ee` when empty, which means no LM hash was stored. |
| NetNTLMv1 (and with ESS/SSP) | 5500 | Responder and relay output. Cryptographically weak: with a known challenge it reduces to DES keys and is fully brute-forceable rather than guessable. |
| NetNTLMv2 | 5600 | The common Responder and poisoning output. Slower than NTLM but still fast. |
| NetNTLMv1 keyed by NT hash | 27000 | Official name `NetNTLMv1 / NetNTLMv1+ESS (NT)`. For validating an already-known NT hash against a captured response rather than guessing a password. |
| NetNTLMv2 keyed by NT hash | 27100 | Official name `NetNTLMv2 (NT)`. Same purpose for v2. Very useful for confirming which account a captured response belongs to when you already hold hashes. |
| Kerberos 5 TGS-REP etype 23 (RC4) | 13100 | Classic Kerberoast, `$krb5tgs$23$`. Fast. |
| Kerberos 5 TGS-REP etype 17 (AES128) | 19600 | `$krb5tgs$17$`. |
| Kerberos 5 TGS-REP etype 18 (AES256) | 19700 | `$krb5tgs$18$`. Roughly three orders of magnitude slower than 13100 because the AES string-to-key is PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA1 with 4096 iterations. This is the single most important number in modern Kerberoasting. |
| Kerberos 5 AS-REP etype 23 | 18200 | AS-REP roasting output, `$krb5asrep$23$`. |
| Kerberos 5 AS-REQ pre-auth etype 23 | 7500 | From captured pre-authentication, not from AS-REP roasting. Different artefact, commonly confused. |
| Kerberos 5 pre-auth etype 17 / 18 | 19800 / 19900 | AES pre-auth equivalents. |
| Kerberos 5 AS-REP etype 17 / 18 (AES) | 32100 / 32200 | Added well after the etype 23 mode, so an older note will claim AES AS-REP is unsupported. Same PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA1 cost as the AES TGS-REP modes. |
| Kerberos 5 TGS-REP / AS-REP etype 23 keyed by NT hash | 35300 / 35400 | The Kerberos equivalents of 27000 and 27100: confirm which account a ticket belongs to from a hash list rather than cracking a password. |
| Kerberos 5 etype 17 / 18 from the KDC database | 28800 / 28900 | Long-term keys out of an NTDS or KDC dump rather than off the wire. Note 28900 is a Kerberos mode, not the PostgreSQL one, which is 28600. |
| Domain Cached Credentials 2 (mscash2) | 2100 | Cached logons from `secretsdump` LSA output. PBKDF2 with 10240 iterations, so thousands of times slower than NTLM. Only worth attacking with a very targeted candidate set. |
| Domain Cached Credentials 1 (mscash) | 1100 | Legacy, fast, rare. |
| KeePass 1 and 2 | 13400 | Covers AES, Twofish and ChaCha20 variants, with or without a key file. Very slow by design. |
| DPAPI masterkey v1 / v2 | 15300 / 15900 | When you have a masterkey file but not the backup key and not the user's password. Variants exist for different context values. |
| WPA / WPA2 | 22000 | Replaced the old 2500 and 16800 modes. If a note says 2500, it is pre-2019. |
| IPMI2 RAKP HMAC-SHA1 | 7300 | BMC, iDRAC and iLO interfaces hand these out to unauthenticated requesters. High-value and frequently forgotten on internal engagements. |
| Cisco type 4 / type 5 / type 8 / type 9 | 5700 / 500 / 9200 / 9300 | Router and switch configs recovered from TFTP, backups or SNMP. Type 5 is cheap, type 8 and 9 are deliberately expensive. |
| Cisco PIX/ASA MD5 | 2400 / 2410 | Old but still found on ASAs. |
| IKE PSK MD5 / SHA1 | 5300 / 5400 | From an aggressive-mode VPN handshake. |
| MSSQL 2000 / 2005 / 2012+ | 131 / 132 / 1731 | From `sys.sql_logins`. |
| Linux shadow: descrypt / md5crypt / sha256crypt / sha512crypt / bcrypt | 1500 / 500 / 7400 / 1800 / 3200 | Note 500 is shared between md5crypt and Cisco type 5, because they are the same algorithm. |
| SSH and other private keys | 22911, 22921, 22931, 22941, 22951 | All named `RSA/DSA/EC/OpenSSH Private Keys`, distinguished by the cipher suffix in the hash line: `$0$`, `$6$`, `$1, $3$`, `$4$`, `$5$` respectively. `ssh2john` produces the line and the suffix tells you the mode. |
| Office 2013 and later | 9600 | Earlier Office versions have their own modes in the 94xx to 98xx range. |
| 7-Zip / RAR5 | 11600 / 13000 | Archive loot from shares. |
| JWT (HS256/384/512) | 16500 | From internal application traffic. |
| Ansible Vault | 16900 | Turns up in build and automation shares. |
| LUKS | 29511 to 29543 for LUKS v1, 34100 for LUKS v2 (Argon2) | The single mode 14600 still exists but is now labelled `LUKS v1 (legacy)`. The 295xx modes are split by hash and cipher, so `--identify` or `luks2hashcat` picks the exact one. |
| VeraCrypt | 29411 to 29483 | The old 137xx family is still present but labelled `(legacy)`. Numbering within the current family is hash by cipher-chain by XTS key size, with separate `+ boot-mode` variants. |
| BitLocker | 22100 | Not renumbered. |

Two mode-adjacent techniques worth knowing:

**NetNTLMv1 is not cracked, it is solved.** If you can force NTLMv1 with a fixed challenge, the response decomposes into DES operations over the NT hash, and the full keyspace is tractable. This is a deterministic recovery of the NT hash rather than a password guess, which means it works against a 30-character random machine account password. `ntlmv1-multi` handles the format conversion. The precondition is that the target permits NTLMv1 at all, which `LmCompatibilityLevel` on modern Windows usually prevents, so check before building the chain.

**Association attack, `-a 9`.** Feeds one candidate line per hash instead of the whole wordlist against every hash. This is how you test "username as password", "username plus year", or a known-password-reuse hypothesis across ten thousand NTDS hashes in seconds instead of running the cross product. It is the hashcat answer to what John's single-crack mode does.

#### Rules, and why rules beat a bigger wordlist

A rule file is a set of transformations applied to each candidate: capitalise, append digits, substitute characters, duplicate, truncate, reverse. `best64.rule` has 64 of them. `OneRuleToRuleThemAll` has roughly fifty thousand. Multiply a rule count by a wordlist size and you get the candidate count.

The reason this beats a bigger wordlist is architectural, not philosophical. On fast hashes hashcat applies rules **on the GPU**, generating candidates on the device. A larger wordlist has to be read from disk and pushed across PCIe, and on NTLM you will be I/O bound long before you are compute bound. So `rockyou.txt` at 14 million entries with a 50,000-rule file gives you roughly 7 x 10^11 human-shaped candidates at full device speed, whereas a 700GB wordlist gives you fewer, worse candidates at a fraction of the rate.

The other reason is candidate quality. A mask over eight lowercase characters and a rule-mangled dictionary can cover the same keyspace size, but real passwords cluster around dictionary words with predictable mangling. Rules go where the passwords are.

Practical rule set, roughly in the order you should run them:

| Rule file | Size | When |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `best64.rule` | 64 | First pass on anything. Seconds on fast hashes. Also the only rule file worth using on slow hashes. |
| `rockyou-30000.rule` | ~30k | Derived from real cracks. Good general second pass. |
| `d3ad0ne.rule`, `dive.rule`, `generated2.rule` | Large | Broader third pass on fast hashes. `dive.rule` is very large and only makes sense on NTLM-class speeds. |
| `OneRuleToRuleThemAll` / `OneRuleToRuleThemStill` | ~50k | The community consensus "one big rule file". The "Still" variant is a later re-optimisation. Excellent efficiency per rule. |
| Your own rules | Small | After a successful crack of an estate, extract the observed patterns into a tiny rule file. Estate-specific mangling is highly consistent, and a 20-rule file built from twenty cracked passwords will outperform a 50,000-rule generic file on the remainder. |

Rules stack: `-r rule1 -r rule2` applies the cross product, which explodes fast. Two 50,000-rule files is 2.5 billion transformations per candidate word and is almost never what you want.

On slow hashes (`2100`, `13400`, `19700`, `3200`) add `-S`. It switches to the slow-candidate code path where rules are applied on the host, which is correct when the hash itself is the bottleneck rather than candidate generation.

`--stdout` with a rule file and a small wordlist shows you exactly what candidates you are about to generate. Use it before committing GPU hours to a rule file you have not inspected.

#### Wordlist strategy

Work outward in three concentric rings.

**Ring one, the corpus lists.** `rockyou.txt` remains the correct first move because it is real, ordered roughly by frequency, and small enough to run with heavy rules instantly. Beyond it, the `weakpass` collections and the community lists on HashMob are the current maintained aggregations. Note that Hashes.org, which older notes point at, shut down in 2021 and its corpora were absorbed by the successor communities.

**The special case worth its own paragraph:** the Have I Been Pwned password corpus is published as NTLM hashes ordered by observed prevalence. For NTLM cracking specifically, running the ordered NTLM list is a direct hash-to-hash comparison with no candidate generation at all, which finds every previously-breached password in the estate almost instantly. Do this first on any NTDS dump. It is the highest-yield minute you will spend, and it produces a finding you can report ("N accounts use passwords present in public breach corpora") that is independent of whether you cracked anything else.

**Ring two, the organisation-specific list.** This is what separates a competent cracking pass from a lazy one, and it costs ten minutes. Build a list containing: the company name and its abbreviations, in every case variation; product and brand names; office locations and site codes; the local sports teams; the internal system names you harvested from DNS and from BloodHound CE computer objects; the words that appear in the estate's group and OU names; anything scraped from the public website with `cewl`; and the seasons, months and years. Then run it with a heavy rule file. Corporate passwords are overwhelmingly `<something local>` plus `<number>` plus `<punctuation>`, and the something-local is not in `rockyou.txt`.

**Ring three, generated candidates.** `maskprocessor` for pure pattern generation, `princeprocessor` for combining wordlist fragments into longer candidates (which is how you reach passphrases), `kwprocessor` for keyboard walks, and the `hashcat-utils` set (`combinator`, `expander`, `rli2`, `splitlen`) for list arithmetic. `rli2` in particular lets you subtract everything you have already tried from a new list so you do not repeat work.

Deduplicate aggressively. Running the same candidate twice across three overlapping lists is pure waste. Also keep a persistent found-password file across engagements, because password patterns repeat across the same industry and the same managed service provider.

#### Masks and keyspace

A mask is a positional character-set specification: `?l` lowercase, `?u` uppercase, `?d` digit, `?s` special, `?a` all printable, `?b` all bytes, plus up to four custom sets defined with `-1` through `-4`. Attack mode `-a 3`.

Masks are the right tool when you know the shape and not the content. Estate password policies produce shapes. `?u?l?l?l?l?l?d?d?d?d` is "capitalised word plus four digits", which is what a minimum-eight-character policy with complexity enabled actually generates. `--increment` with `--increment-min` and `--increment-max` walks lengths so you do not have to run each separately.

Hybrid modes are frequently better than either: `-a 6` appends a mask to each wordlist candidate, `-a 7` prepends one. `-a 6` with your organisation list and `?d?d?d?d` covers "CompanyName2025" for every company name variant and every year, which is a large fraction of real corporate passwords.

Keyspace arithmetic you should be able to do in your head:

| Keyspace | Size | At 100 GH/s (NTLM) | At 1 GH/s (13100) | At 5 MH/s (2100) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 8 chars, lower + digit (36^8) | 2.8 x 10^12 | ~28 seconds | ~47 minutes | ~6.5 days |
| 8 chars, mixed + digit (62^8) | 2.2 x 10^14 | ~37 minutes | ~2.5 days | ~1.4 years |
| 9 chars, mixed + digit (62^9) | 1.3 x 10^16 | ~1.6 days | ~5 months | infeasible |
| rockyou x 50k rules | 7 x 10^11 | ~7 seconds | ~12 minutes | ~1.6 days |
| 12 chars, full printable | 10^23 and up | infeasible | infeasible | infeasible |

Those device rates are order-of-magnitude illustrations, not benchmarks. Get your own with `hashcat -b -m 1000` and `-b -m 19700` on your actual hardware and write the numbers down, because the whole point of this table is that you can decide in advance whether an attack is worth starting.

Operational flags that matter: `--session <name>` so you can `--restore` after an interruption (the source got this right); `-o` for the output file; `--username` when the hash file contains user identifiers; `-w 3` or `-w 4` for workload profile on a dedicated cracking box; `--keyspace` to print the candidate count without cracking; `--status --status-timer` for machine-readable progress. Be careful with `-O`: the optimised kernels are substantially faster but cap candidate length, typically at 27 characters or fewer depending on mode, which silently excludes longer passwords. Use `-O` for the first fast pass and drop it for the long one.

For scale, hashcat's brain (`--brain-server` and `--brain-client`) deduplicates candidate work across multiple nodes, and Hashtopolis distributes tasks across a fleet. Rented GPU time is cheap and effective, with the obvious operational consideration that the hashes leave your infrastructure, which many engagement agreements prohibit outright.

#### When a hash is not worth cracking

This is the judgement call the source never mentions, and it is where operators waste the most time.

**Cryptographically hopeless targets.** Machine account passwords are 120 random characters and rotate every 30 days by default. gMSA and dMSA passwords are 240 bytes of random data. The `krbtgt` account, trust accounts, and Entra Connect (formerly Azure AD Connect) service accounts are all randomly generated. None of these will ever crack. If you want a machine account's secret, read it (`ReadGMSAPassword`, DCSync, LAPS) or recover it deterministically (NTLMv1 reduction, `UnPAC-the-hash`), do not queue it.

**Economically hopeless targets.** An etype 18 Kerberoast hash from a service account created in 2024 by an administrator using a password manager is not falling to any wordlist. Check the account's `pwdLastSet` and creation date: an account whose password was set once, recently, by automation is a different proposition from one set in 2016 by a human. Kerberoast everything, but queue selectively.

**Targets with no value.** Cracking is only worth the electricity if the resulting credential moves you. Before queueing a Kerberoast hash, check BloodHound CE: does the principal have a path to anything? A cracked password for a service account with no privileges, no local admin and no ACLs is a report line, not a foothold. Sort your queue by graph value, not by hash age.

**Targets where a non-cracking path exists.** This is the big one, and it is the defining shift from 2020 practice. Ask, before cracking: can I relay this authentication instead of cracking it? Can I write `msDS-KeyCredentialLink` and authenticate with a certificate, no password needed? Can I request a certificate and use `UnPAC-the-hash` to obtain the NT hash directly? Can I read the secret from LAPS, from a gMSA blob, from DPAPI with the domain backup key, from SCCM, from a backup product, or from a script on a share? In a modern estate the answer is yes far more often than the password is crackable, and every one of those paths is faster and quieter than a GPU run.

**Time-boxing.** Run the fast pass: HIBP NTLM list, rockyou with `best64`, rockyou with a large rule file, the organisation-specific list with a large rule file, and the policy-shaped masks. On NTLM that is under an hour. What falls, falls. What does not fall in the fast pass is very unlikely to fall in a week, and the correct response is to write it up as a password policy finding and go do something else. The exception is a single high-value hash with a clear path to domain compromise, which justifies as much hardware and as many custom rules as you can point at it.

### ProjectDiscovery and web-adjacent tooling on an internal engagement

The operator has this suite available, and the mistake is assuming it is only for external web assessment. Internal estates are full of web applications that nobody has patched, because nobody outside can reach them.

`pdtm` is the installer and updater for the suite, which saves you managing a dozen Go binaries by hand. The pieces that matter internally:

| Tool | Internal use |
| --- | --- |
| `naabu` | Fast port sweep across internal CIDRs, feeding a target list into `nmap` or `httpx`. |
| `dnsx` | Reverse-DNS sweep of internal ranges, which names the estate for you, and forward resolution of the hostnames you pull from certificates and LDAP. |
| `httpx` | Point it at every open port and get back status, title, technology fingerprint, TLS details and optionally a screenshot. This is the single highest-value ten minutes on an internal: it turns "eight thousand open ports" into "forty admin interfaces, twelve of which are printers and one of which is an unauthenticated Jenkins". |
| `tlsx` | Harvest common names and subject alternative names from every TLS service. Internal certificates leak internal hostnames, service names and sometimes entire naming conventions that DNS will not give you. |
| `nuclei` | Known-CVE and default-credential checking against the internal web estate. See the noise discussion below. |
| `katana` | Crawling an internal application once you have found something worth looking at. |
| `mapcidr` | Range arithmetic: expanding, splitting, excluding, deduplicating target lists. Unglamorous and constantly useful. |
| `cvemap` | Looking up whether the version `httpx` fingerprinted has anything exploitable. |
| `interactsh` | Out-of-band interaction detection for blind injection and SSRF. Needs the target to reach your listener, so on a segmented internal you self-host it inside the environment or it will report nothing and you will conclude wrongly. |
| `subfinder`, `uncover`, `asnmap`, `chaos` | External reconnaissance. Not applicable inside, except during scoping. |

`ffuf` is the content and parameter fuzzer. Internally it earns its place on the applications `httpx` found: discovering the `/admin` or `/actuator` or `/console` endpoint that the front page does not link to, enumerating virtual hosts on a shared internal reverse proxy by fuzzing the `Host` header, and brute-forcing parameters on an API with no documentation. Use auto-calibration to suppress soft-404 noise, filter or match on status code and size, and remember that internal applications frequently have no rate limiting at all, so the constraint is the application falling over rather than being blocked. `feroxbuster` is the reasonable alternative and recurses by default.

Where these fit in the workflow: they belong in the same phase as your port sweep, before you start on Active Directory, because they answer "what is on this network that will give me a credential or a shell without touching AD at all". The classic internal wins from this toolchain are default credentials on a management interface (iDRAC, iLO, IPMI, vCenter, switch web UIs, printers with LDAP credentials configured in them), unauthenticated Jenkins or Tomcat manager or JBoss, exposed Docker or Kubernetes APIs, unauthenticated Redis, Elasticsearch or MongoDB, Confluence and GitLab instances behind on patches, and Grafana or SonarQube with credentials in their configuration. Any of those is frequently a faster route to a domain credential than the entire AD chain, because internal applications are configured with service accounts that have far more privilege than they need.

On noise: nuclei with its default template set against an internal estate generates an enormous volume of requests, hits every WAF and IDS you have, and fills application logs. Constrain it. Filter by tag (`default-login`, `exposure`, `misconfig`), filter by severity, exclude the intrusive tags, rate limit it, and point it at the specific technologies `httpx` identified rather than firing everything at everything. A targeted nuclei run against forty identified applications is quiet and productive; an untargeted run against a /16 is a self-inflicted detection.

### Building and maintaining an operator toolbox

#### Structure it as a versioned tree

Keep tooling in one tree, under version control, with pinned versions. The specific layout matters less than the properties: you can reproduce it on a fresh VM in one command, you know which version of everything you used on a given engagement, and updates are deliberate rather than accidental.

```text
~/opt/
  src/          # cloned repositories, pinned to known-good commits
  bin/          # built or downloaded binaries on PATH
  windows/      # compiled Windows tooling, subdivided by framework target
  bofs/         # compiled BOF objects
  wordlists/    # corpora, rules, masks
  payloads/     # per-engagement build outputs, never reused across clients
```

Track `src/` as a manifest of repository plus commit rather than as submodules, because submodules make bisecting a broken update painful. Pin commits. A tool that worked last week and broke today is nearly always an upstream change, and being able to check out last week's commit while you finish the engagement is worth more than being current.

Python tooling gets isolated per tool. Impacket, certipy, bloodyAD, netexec and ldeep have overlapping and occasionally conflicting dependencies, and a single shared site-packages will break. Use `pipx` or `uv tool install` so each gets its own environment with its entry points on `PATH`. This also lets you keep two impacket versions when a script you need was removed or changed.

Distribution packages lag. Kali's impacket and netexec are usually months behind, and the features you want (a new coercion method, a new relay target, a fix for a protocol change) are in git. Install the critical tools from git and let the distribution provide the boring dependencies.

Keep engagement data out of the tooling tree entirely. Per-engagement directory with `scans/`, `loot/`, `notes/`, `payloads/`, and a hard rule that nothing generated for one client is ever reused for another, because payload reuse across clients is how a sample submitted by one organisation burns your infrastructure at the next.

#### Compiling Windows tooling for the target's runtime

Rubeus, Certify, SharpHound, Seatbelt, SharpDPAPI and the rest of the .NET ecosystem are source, not binaries. Which framework you target determines whether they run.

| Target framework | Where it is present |
| --- | --- |
| .NET Framework 3.5 | Not installed by default on Windows 10, Windows 11, or Server 2016 and later. It is an optional feature that is often absent. Only target this for genuinely legacy hosts. |
| .NET Framework 4.0 / 4.5 | The safe default. 4.x is an in-place upgrade family, so an assembly targeting 4.0 or 4.5 runs on any 4.6, 4.7 or 4.8 runtime. |
| .NET Framework 4.8 / 4.8.1 | Present on current Windows 10, Windows 11 and Server 2019/2022/2025. Targeting it works but gains you nothing over 4.5 unless you need a newer API. |
| .NET (Core) 6, 8 and later | Not present unless someone installed it. Requires either a matching runtime on the target or a self-contained publish, which produces tens of megabytes of files. Rarely the right choice for post-exploitation tooling. |

Practical rule: build the GhostPack family against 4.0 or 4.5 unless you have a specific reason otherwise, and keep a 3.5 build only for known-legacy targets. Verify what is on the target before you upload: the presence of framework version keys under `HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\NET Framework Setup\NDP` tells you what is installed, and the directories under `%WINDIR%\Microsoft.NET\Framework64` tell you the same thing from a file listing.

Building needs msbuild, which needs Visual Studio Build Tools, which needs Windows. Mono's msbuild can build some .NET Framework projects on Linux with the right reference assemblies, and it is worth trying, but it fails often enough on real projects that you will want the Windows VM anyway.

Native tooling is easier. BOFs and C loaders cross-compile from Linux with the MinGW-w64 toolchain (`x86_64-w64-mingw32-gcc`), and Go, Rust, Nim and Zig all cross-compile to Windows targets from Linux cleanly. Only the .NET Framework work genuinely needs Windows.

#### Why you rebuild instead of downloading release artefacts

There are public repositories of pre-compiled offensive .NET tooling. Every file in them has been submitted to every multi-scanner service thousands of times. They are hash-blocked, YARA-matched on their string tables, and in several cases specifically named in vendor detection documentation. Downloading `Rubeus.exe` from a releases page and uploading it to a target is equivalent to announcing yourself.

Rebuilding from source with even minimal changes moves you from "known-bad hash and known string set" to "unknown binary that still contains recognisable strings", which is a large improvement for very little work. The changes that matter:

Rename the assembly, the namespace, the project GUID and the output filename. The default namespace and assembly name are in signature rules. `InvisibilityCloak` automates exactly this renaming across a C# project, which is worth using because doing it by hand misses references.

Strip the obvious strings. Help text, banner art, exception messages and command names are all signature fodder, and much of it is dead weight in a tool you drive from a script. Cutting the unused commands out of a large tool both shrinks the signature surface and removes code paths you were never going to use.

Build in Release, without debug symbols, and do not ship the PDB.

Then measure rather than hope. `ThreatCheck` and `DefenderCheck` bisect a file against Defender's scanner and tell you the specific byte range that triggered, which lets you fix the actual signature instead of guessing. `AMSITrigger` does the equivalent for PowerShell content against AMSI. This loop, build, check, fix the identified bytes, rebuild, takes minutes and is the highest-value evasion work available because it addresses the cheap static detection layer directly.

Do not submit your builds to public multi-scanner services. Samples are shared with vendors, and a build you tested on Monday is a signature on Wednesday. Test locally against an offline scanner in a snapshot VM.

Understand the limit of all of this. Everything above defeats static signatures. It does nothing about behavioural detection, so a perfectly clean-scanning binary that opens a handle to LSASS, or loads the CLR into a process that has no business hosting it, or makes an unbacked-memory syscall, will still be caught. Note in particular that .NET Framework 4.8 added AMSI scanning of assemblies loaded from a byte array, which means in-memory `execute-assembly` style loading is scanned at load time, and the CLR load itself is an ETW event that mature EDR watches. That is why BOFs and native tooling have displaced `execute-assembly` for routine post-exploitation.

#### Keep a Windows build VM

You need one, and it should be a template you can restore, not a pet.

The build VM wants Visual Studio Build Tools with the .NET desktop workload and the framework targeting packs for 3.5 through 4.8, the Windows SDK for native work, and your tooling tree cloned. Keep it offline or on an isolated network segment. Snapshot it after setup so you can roll back when a build environment change breaks something.

Keep a second, separate VM as the detection test bed: a current Windows build with Defender enabled, cloud-delivered protection and sample submission both switched off, no network path to anywhere, and a snapshot to revert to after each test. This is where `ThreatCheck` runs and where you confirm a payload survives a scan. Cloud protection off is essential, because with it on you are testing against a service that learns from your test.

If you use a commercial C2, keep its artefact and loader customisation in version control alongside everything else, because a profile is as much a tool as a binary and an untracked profile change is an unreproducible engagement.

#### Maintenance cadence

Update deliberately, not continuously, and never mid-engagement. A sensible rhythm is to pull and rebuild the whole tree between engagements, run a smoke test against a lab domain, and record what changed. The lab domain matters: a functioning test AD with a domain controller, a member server, an AD CS role, a certificate template you have deliberately misconfigured, and an SCCM install if you can manage it, lets you verify that a tool still works before you find out on a client network. It also lets you answer "is this tool broken or is this estate hardened", which is the question you will be asking most often, and which is very difficult to answer from the client side of a firewall.



# Initial Access

## The gap this section fills

The rest of this document begins with you already inside. Network enumeration assumes an address on a routed segment. Active Directory enumeration assumes you can reach a domain controller. Lateral movement assumes a credential. Every one of those assumptions has to be paid for, and the source notes pay for none of them: their entire treatment of initial access is a single Metasploit module that pops a credential prompt at a user until they type something into it. That module is `post/windows/gather/phish_windows_credentials`, it requires you to already have a session, and it is therefore not initial access at all.

This section is about how the first foothold is actually obtained on a modern engagement, and about the fact that obtaining it is an engineering and campaign discipline rather than a single technique. It owns reconnaissance of the target organisation, the delivery channel, the human interaction, and the handoff into a position the rest of the document can use.

Boundaries, because several neighbouring sections own mechanics that appear here at campaign level. **Payload construction, loaders, obfuscation, container and delivery formats, and mark-of-the-web** belong to the Evasion and Payload Development section; this section decides *whether* you are delivering a payload and *how it travels*, not what is inside it. **Redirectors, domain fronting, listener design and C2 infrastructure** belong to the Command and Control section; this section hands the beacon over the moment it calls back. **Device code phishing, consent phishing, token structure and conditional access mechanics** belong to the Cloud and Modern Identity section; this section covers the campaign that drives them and the decision of which to run. **Internal password spraying** belongs to the Active Directory: Enumeration section, and **name-resolution poisoning and Responder** to the On-Path Attacks: The Modern Approach section; this section covers spraying an *externally exposed* authentication surface, which is a materially different problem. **Wireless** belongs to the On-Path and Traffic Attacks section; this section covers it only as one of several proximity routes.

Placeholders follow the document convention, with two additions used only here: `$PHISHDOMAIN` is a domain you control and are sending from, and `$ORG` is the target organisation's name as it appears in registration records.

## Framing the problem: choosing a route, not listing them

There are five routes to a first foothold. They are not a menu you work through in order; they are a decision, and the decision is driven more by the engagement than by the technology.

| Route | What you end up holding | Typical elapsed time | Typical blocker |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Exposed service exploitation | Code execution on a perimeter host, sometimes as root | Hours if a known-vulnerable appliance is exposed, otherwise weeks or never | A patched perimeter, which is now common |
| Valid credentials without exploitation | An identity, and whatever that identity can reach | Days, mostly spent pacing | MFA, conditional access, and the size of the password space |
| Social engineering | A credential, a session token, or code execution on a user endpoint | One to three weeks including infrastructure ageing | Deliverability, the mail security stack, and user reporting |
| Physical or proximity access | A network position, sometimes an unlocked workstation | One visit, plus reconnaissance | Network access control, and the fact that you have to be there |
| Supply chain or third party | Whatever the third party had | Weeks, and usually out of scope | Scope. Almost always scope |

**What determines which is appropriate.** Four inputs, in roughly descending order of how much they constrain you.

**The client's actual question.** This is the input operators most often skip and it dominates everything else. "Can someone get in from the internet" is a different question from "if someone gets in, what happens", which is a different question again from "does our detection and response work". If the client's real question is the second, then spending three weeks on a phishing campaign to earn a foothold you were going to be handed anyway is a waste of the engagement, and the right answer is an assumed-breach start with the foothold provisioned on day one. If the question is the third, the route matters enormously because the route is what generates the telemetry being tested. Ask which question you are answering before you choose a technique, and if the statement of work does not say, get it said.

**The scope.** Scope constrains the route more than skill does. A scope that lists three IP ranges and no people rules out social engineering entirely. A scope that says "the corporate estate" without listing assets means you have to establish the perimeter yourself and then get it confirmed, which is work before it is an attack. A scope that names a specific application is a web application test wearing a red team costume, and pretending otherwise wastes everyone's time.

**The rules of engagement.** Whether you may phish real staff, whether you may attempt exploitation against production during business hours, whether you may use credentials found in public breach data, whether you may enter a building, and whether social engineering may name real internal people as the sender. Each of these is a yes or no that removes or unlocks a route, and each of them needs to be written down rather than assumed. The ones most commonly assumed wrongly are breach data and impersonation of named internal staff.

**The time available.** Phishing is not a fast technique once you account for infrastructure. A domain that was registered last week is a domain that will be blocked, so a credible campaign needs its infrastructure standing weeks before the engagement window opens. If you are three days into a two-week test and you have not registered a domain yet, phishing is no longer available to you and you should stop planning around it. Exploitation is fast when it works and unbounded when it does not. Spraying is slow by construction because the pacing is dictated by lockout, not by your throughput.

### The honest answer is usually credentials

The most common real answer on a modern engagement is not exploitation. It is an identity: a valid credential, or a session token that stands in for one.

The reason is structural rather than fashionable. The externally exposed technical surface of a typical organisation has shrunk to a handful of managed appliances and a large number of SaaS tenancies, and both are patched by someone whose job is patching them. Meanwhile the number of identities has grown, every one of those identities is reachable from the internet by design because that is what SaaS means, and the credential quality distribution has not improved. One organisation of three thousand staff will contain someone whose password is the season and the year, someone whose password appeared in a breach corpus and was reused, and someone who will approve an authentication prompt they did not initiate. You only need one.

The second structural reason is that a credential lands you somewhere useful in a way an exploited edge device often does not. Code execution on a perimeter appliance gives you a position on a DMZ segment with a hardened, unfamiliar, frequently non-Windows operating system, no domain context, and often nothing to move to. A single valid user credential against the identity provider gives you mail, files, the internal directory, the intranet, the VPN, and a name to impersonate. In terms of what the rest of this document can use, the credential is worth more.

This has a consequence for how you spend reconnaissance effort. If credentials are the likely route, then **identity reconnaissance is the highest-value preparation you can do**, and it should get more of your time than port scanning. That inverts the habit most operators bring from a decade of network-first methodology.

### What each route unlocks, stated plainly

Be explicit with yourself about what a given foothold actually gives you, because which section of this document you turn to next depends entirely on it.

- **A valid cloud credential with MFA satisfied** gives you a token, mail, files, directory read, and often the ability to enrol a device. It gives you no code execution anywhere. Continue in the Cloud and Modern Identity section.
- **A valid credential that MFA blocks** gives you confirmation and a reporting finding, and very little else, unless you can find an application or protocol the policy does not cover.
- **A phished session cookie** gives you the authenticated session including the satisfied MFA claim, for as long as the cookie lives and the conditional access posture permits. Same continuation as above, with a shorter clock.
- **Code execution on a user endpoint** gives you a domain-joined position, a user token, local reconnaissance, and the entire internal half of this document. This is the richest foothold and the hardest to get.
- **Code execution on a perimeter appliance** gives you a network position and possibly credentials in configuration, and frequently nothing else without further work. Often the fastest route to a *network* position and the slowest to a *domain* position.
- **A network port in a meeting room** gives you layer 2 adjacency and everything the On-Path and Traffic Attacks section and the Active Directory: Enumeration section describe, subject to network access control.
- **A VPN credential** is the best of both: an identity that yields a routed internal position. Treat any exposed VPN portal as a priority target for exactly this reason.

## External reconnaissance and attack surface mapping

The objective of external reconnaissance is not a long list of hostnames. It is a **defensible model of the perimeter**: what the organisation exposes, which of it they know about, which of it they own, and which two or three items are worth your attention. A list of four thousand subdomains with no ownership determination and no prioritisation is a worse deliverable than a list of six, and it is a worse basis for an attack.

Work in this order, because each stage constrains the next: establish the organisation's identity in registration data, derive the domains and netblocks, expand to hosts, resolve and confirm liveness, fingerprint, and only then prioritise. Operators who start at "run subfinder against the domain in the scope document" routinely miss the acquisition whose netblock is the actual soft target.

### Passive versus active, and why the line matters

**Passive** reconnaissance sends no packets to infrastructure the target controls. You query third parties who already hold the data: registries, certificate transparency logs, DNS aggregators, internet-wide scan databases, search engines, code hosts, and the target's own records as republished by others. **Active** reconnaissance touches the target: DNS resolution against their authoritative nameservers, TCP connections, TLS handshakes, HTTP requests, port scans.

The line matters for two independent reasons and operators usually only think about one of them.

**Stealth.** Passive reconnaissance is invisible to the target. There is no log entry anywhere in their estate. Active reconnaissance is logged somewhere, and on a modern perimeter that somewhere is increasingly aggregated: a WAF, a CDN's bot management, an appliance's access log, cloud provider flow logs, and in some cases a managed detection service that alerts on scanning. You will not be caught by the port scan itself, because the internet background radiation of scanning is constant and nobody triages it. You may well be caught by a scan that correlates with something else you do later.

**Scope.** This is the reason that actually gets people into trouble. Passive reconnaissance against a hostname that turns out to belong to somebody else is a mistake with no consequence. Active reconnaissance against the same hostname is unauthorised activity against a third party, and the fact that a subdomain of the client's domain resolves to it does not make it theirs. Shared hosting, SaaS tenancies on shared infrastructure, CDN edge addresses, and marketing platforms all produce records that look like client assets and are not. **Do the ownership determination before you switch from passive to active, not after.**

Where common tools sit on the line, because several are ambiguous:

| Tool or action | Passive | Active | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `subfinder` | Yes | No | Passive by design. It queries third-party sources and does not resolve or connect |
| `amass enum` default | Mostly | Partly | Amass resolves what it finds by default, which is DNS traffic to the target's nameservers. Use its passive mode if you need a clean line |
| `amass enum -active` | No | Yes | Explicitly adds certificate grabbing and zone transfer attempts |
| Certificate transparency queries | Yes | No | You are querying a log operator, not the target |
| `crt.sh`, Censys, Shodan, FOFA lookups | Yes | No | Third-party data. Note that *your query* is visible to the operator, not the target |
| DNS resolution via a public resolver | Nearly | Marginally | The recursive resolver eventually queries the target's authoritative server, but not from your address and not attributable to you |
| DNS resolution direct to the target's NS | No | Yes | You are talking to their nameserver |
| `httpx`, `naabu`, `nmap`, `nuclei` | No | Yes | All of these connect |
| `tlsx` | No | Yes | It performs a TLS handshake with the target |
| GitHub and code search | Yes | No | Extremely high yield and completely invisible |

A practical rule: **complete the entire passive phase and the ownership determination before the first active packet.** It costs you nothing, it produces the scope conversation you need to have anyway, and it means your active phase is narrow and targeted rather than a broad sweep.

### Establishing the organisation's identity, and therefore its assets

Start from the corporate entity, not the domain, because the interesting assets are usually attached to a name you were not given.

**What it is.** Building the set of registered names, trading names, acquisitions, and subsidiaries associated with `$ORG`, and then finding the domains and netblocks registered to each.

**Why it works.** Registration data is deliberately public. Domain registrations, autonomous system and IP allocation records at the regional internet registries, and TLS certificates all carry organisational identity fields, and those fields are indexed. An acquisition made eighteen months ago is typically still running its own perimeter under its own name with its own patching cadence, connected to the parent by a VPN or a domain trust that nobody has reviewed. That is the highest-yield asset class in external reconnaissance and it is invisible if you only look at the domain in the scope document.

**Preconditions.** None beyond internet access.

**Commands.**

```bash
# Registration data for a known domain. RDAP is the current protocol; whois is the
# fallback and its output format varies by registry.
curl -s "https://rdap.org/domain/$DOMAIN" | jq
whois $DOMAIN

# IP allocation and organisation records. RDAP again, and it follows referrals
# between the regional registries.
curl -s "https://rdap.org/ip/$TARGET" | jq '.name, .handle, .remarks'

# ARIN's own search accepts an organisation name and returns netblocks
curl -s -H 'Accept: application/json' "https://whois.arin.net/rest/orgs;name=$ORG" | jq

# RIPE's search covers the European and Middle Eastern space
curl -s "https://rest.db.ripe.net/search.json?query-string=$ORG" | jq '.objects.object[].attributes'

# ASN to prefix expansion
whois -h whois.radb.net -- "-i origin AS64500" | grep -E '^route'
```

```bash
# ProjectDiscovery's ASN mapper resolves in several directions: org name, ASN,
# IP, or domain, and emits the prefixes.
asnmap -a AS64500
asnmap -d $DOMAIN
asnmap -org "$ORG"
```

**Verify it worked.** You should be able to state, for each netblock, which registry object attributes it to the client and whether the attribution is a direct allocation or an assignment from a provider. A prefix that RDAP attributes to a hosting company with a customer field naming the client is a different scoping conversation from a prefix the client holds directly.

**Detection and opsec.** None. These are third-party registry queries.

**Failure modes.** Registrar privacy services hide the registrant on most modern domain registrations, so domain-side pivoting on registrant identity mostly no longer works, which is why certificate transparency has become the primary discovery source. Historical registration data can still carry the pre-privacy details, and reverse-registrant search across historical snapshots is a commercial service rather than something you can do for free. Cloud-hosted assets have no netblock attribution at all: an application in a hyperscaler's address space attributes to the hyperscaler, so netblock enumeration systematically under-reports the modern perimeter and you must reach it through DNS and certificates instead.

**Common mistake.** Treating the netblock list as the perimeter. In an estate that has moved to cloud and SaaS, the registry-visible netblocks may cover the smaller and better-maintained half of the exposure. The DNS and certificate paths below are where the rest lives.

### Certificate transparency as a discovery source

**What it is.** Enumerating hostnames from the public append-only logs of issued TLS certificates.

**Why it works.** Certificate transparency was built to make certificate misissuance detectable, and browsers enforce it: Chrome and Safari will not accept a publicly trusted certificate that is not accompanied by signed certificate timestamps proving it was logged. The consequence, entirely intended by the design and entirely inconvenient for the certificate's owner, is that **every hostname anybody has ever obtained a publicly trusted certificate for is in a public, searchable, permanent log**. This is a fundamentally different data source from DNS brute force. Brute force finds names you can guess. Certificate transparency finds names nobody would guess, because it does not guess: it reads a list.

The specific classes of asset that leak this way and leak no other way:

- Internal-sounding hostnames that were given a public certificate for convenience. `jenkins-prod-uksouth`, `sccm-dp-02`, `vcenter-dr`, `sql-reporting-uat`. Nobody would brute-force these. They are sitting in the log.
- Names that were provisioned, certificated, and then never DNS-published or already decommissioned. These are historical intelligence about the naming convention even when they no longer resolve.
- Pre-production and staging environments, which are the classic soft target and are frequently named with an obvious pattern the log hands you.
- Acquisition and subsidiary domains, discovered by pivoting on the organisation field or on a shared certificate that covers names across several domains.
- The naming convention itself, which then makes your permutation-based brute force dramatically more effective.

**Preconditions.** None. Fully passive.

**Commands.**

```bash
# crt.sh HTTP interface. The JSON output is the one to script against. A single
# certificate carries many SANs, so name_value is newline-delimited WITHIN a
# field: split it before deduplicating or you will lose most of your results.
curl -s "https://crt.sh/?q=%25.$DOMAIN&output=json" \
  | jq -r '.[].name_value' | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]' \
  | sed 's/^\*\.//' | sort -u

# Certificate identity search. Do NOT filter expired certificates here: expired
# certificates are precisely where the historical internal-hostname leakage
# lives, and excluding them discards the most interesting part of the dataset.
curl -s "https://crt.sh/?identity=%25.$DOMAIN&output=json" | jq -r '.[].name_value' | sort -u

# Exact-match rather than substring, which cuts the noise dramatically on a
# common name. The doubled equals sign is correct and is the documented form.
curl -s "https://crt.sh/?q=$DOMAIN&match==&output=json" | jq -r '.[].name_value' | sort -u

# Common-name search
curl -s "https://crt.sh/?CN=%25.$DOMAIN&output=json" | jq -r '.[].name_value' | sort -u
```

Confirmed working query parameters on the HTTP interface are `q`, `identity`, `CN` and `match==`. <!-- VERIFY --> The organisation-subject parameter `O=`, and the `deduplicate=Y` and `id=` parameters that appear in circulating snippets, are not confirmed against a live response; test them before building a methodology on them.

**The PostgreSQL interface, and the trap that has invalidated most published snippets.** crt.sh exposes a read-only database directly, which is far faster than the HTTP interface for bulk work and is what the better tooling uses. Nearly every example query in circulation selects from a `certificate_identity` table. **That table no longer exists as a table.** It survives as a view purely so that schema introspection succeeds, which is exactly why the breakage is confusing: the object appears to be there, and then every `SELECT` against it raises an error stating that it has been superseded by a full-text search index. Use one of the two forms that work.

```bash
# Form one: full-text search against certificate_and_identities. This is what
# subfinder ships and it is the safe default.
psql -t -h crt.sh -p 5432 -U guest certwatch <<'SQL'
SELECT DISTINCT ci.NAME_VALUE
FROM certificate_and_identities ci
WHERE plainto_tsquery('certwatch', 'corp.example') @@ identities(ci.CERTIFICATE)
  AND ci.NAME_VALUE ILIKE '%corp.example%';
SQL

# Form two: reversed-token prefix match. identities() stores the domain
# backwards, so a suffix match becomes an indexable prefix match. Faster on
# large result sets, and the form to reach for when form one times out.
psql -t -h crt.sh -p 5432 -U guest certwatch <<'SQL'
SELECT DISTINCT ci.NAME_VALUE
FROM certificate_and_identities ci
WHERE ci.NAME_TYPE IN ('dNSName', 'commonName')
  AND reverse(lower(ci.NAME_VALUE)) LIKE reverse(lower('%.corp.example'));
SQL
```

**Pace this by connections, not by queries.** The service sits behind a connection pooler with a client-connection cap, so the failure mode is slot exhaustion rather than query throttling. Firing queries in parallel produces refusals across the board. Open **one** connection, reuse it for every query, and back off on connect rather than on statement.

```bash
# Certspotter's API covers the same logs with a different interface and
# different rate limiting, which matters because crt.sh throttles aggressively.
curl -s "https://api.certspotter.com/v1/issuances?domain=$DOMAIN&include_subdomains=true&expand=dns_names" \
  | jq -r '.[].dns_names[]' | sort -u
```

The unauthenticated Certspotter tier is tightly bounded and worth knowing before you script against it: on the order of 100 single-hostname queries and 10 full-domain queries per hour, with short-window caps of roughly 75 per minute and 5 per second. That makes it a precision instrument for a handful of domains rather than a bulk source, and it makes crt.sh or a self-hosted monitor the right choice for breadth.

```bash
# subfinder consumes certificate transparency among many other passive sources.
# It is the practical front end rather than something you replace with curl.
subfinder -d $DOMAIN -all -silent -o subs.txt

# Provider API keys go in the config file and materially change coverage.
# List the sources the build actually has, and check which are keyed.
subfinder -ls
subfinder -d $DOMAIN -s crtsh,certspotter -silent
```

**A coverage caveat that matters more than it sounds.** Do not assume a general-purpose enumeration tool gives you broad certificate transparency coverage. Amass version 5's certificate handling is, in practice, essentially crt.sh alone: there is no Certspotter or Censys plugin in its certificate source directory. Worse, its crt.sh plugin **hardcodes the exclude-expired filter**, so it systematically never sees expired certificates. That is the exact dataset containing pre-2016 internal hostnames, decommissioned staging environments, and the naming conventions of the previous generation of the estate. If you rely on amass for your certificate transparency coverage you will silently miss the most interesting half of it. Query crt.sh yourself without the filter, or use a tool that scans for expired certificates explicitly.

```bash
# tlsx works the other direction: given hosts, read the certificate and harvest
# the names in it. This finds siblings that CT alone missed because the
# certificate was issued by an internal CA, and it confirms what is live.
tlsx -l hosts.txt -san -cn -silent -resp-only | sort -u

# Certificate-based expansion across a netblock, which is how you find the
# vhost names behind an address you only know numerically. tlsx accepts ASN,
# CIDR, IP, host and URL input through the same -u/-host parameter.
tlsx -u $TARGETS -san -cn -silent -resp-only | sort -u
```

**Verify it worked.** You should have names that DNS brute force did not produce. If your certificate transparency output is a subset of your brute force output, either the organisation uses wildcard certificates exclusively or your query is wrong. Cross-check by searching for a name you already know is certificated.

**Detection and opsec.** Querying the logs is invisible to the target. Note the asymmetry, though: certificate transparency is also a *defensive* monitoring source, and a mature organisation subscribes to alerts on certificate issuance for names resembling theirs. If your phishing infrastructure obtains a Let's Encrypt certificate for a lookalike of the client's domain, that issuance appears in the same public log, and a defender running lookalike-domain monitoring will see it. This is a real and frequently overlooked way that phishing campaigns are burned before the first message is sent, and it is discussed again under domain selection below.

**Failure modes.** Wildcard certificates collapse the whole information gain: an organisation that issues `*.corp.example` learns nothing to the log about which hosts exist. Increasingly common and a genuine limitation. Internal certificate authorities do not log to public transparency logs at all, so anything issued from the enterprise PKI is invisible here, which is precisely the internal estate. Precertificates and final certificates both appear, so the same name shows up repeatedly and your deduplication needs to be by name rather than by log entry. Names in the log may be long dead; treat certificate transparency as a source of *candidate* names to be resolved, not as a live inventory. `crt.sh` rate limits and periodically returns partial results under load, so a single query returning few results is not evidence of a small footprint.

**Two ecosystem failure modes that silently return nothing, which is the worst kind.**

**The public certificate streaming firehose is a zombie.** The well-known hosted stream that most published monitoring recipes point at still completes the WebSocket upgrade cleanly, on both its root and domains-only paths, and then delivers **zero certificate frames**. The control plane is up and the data plane is empty. Because the connection succeeds, every naive health check passes and your monitor sits there reporting nothing while you believe it is working. A healthy firehose pushes many certificates per second, so **your liveness test must be "did I receive a frame within a few seconds", not "did the connection open".** Self-host the stream server, or use Certspotter's monitoring interface instead.

That is a specific instance of a general discipline worth carrying: **a 200 on a landing page, or a successful protocol handshake, is not evidence that a service works.** Verify data, not reachability. The same error underlies most of the stale tooling advice in this whole section.

**Direct log scraping now breaks on the newer log architecture.** The transparency ecosystem is migrating from the original append-only API to a static, tiled layout served as flat files. Tools that fetch entries with the classic entry-retrieval path against one of these newer logs receive a **redirect rather than log data**, and a scraper that does not follow or does not expect it simply produces empty output. There are now a substantial number of these tiled logs. Unless you specifically intend to consume raw logs, use an aggregator that has already dealt with this rather than scraping yourself.

### Subdomain and host discovery

Three mechanisms, and you need all three because they find disjoint sets.

**Passive aggregation** queries third parties who already know the names: certificate transparency, DNS aggregators, passive DNS, search engines, internet scan data. Highest yield per unit effort and completely invisible.

**Permutation and brute force** generates candidate names and resolves them. Finds the boring names that were never certificated and never linked. Its effectiveness is entirely a function of your wordlist and your permutation rules, and the best input to both is the naming convention you just learned from certificate transparency.

**Content-derived discovery** crawls what you already found and extracts names from HTML, JavaScript bundles, source maps, CSS, CSP headers, CORS policies, sitemaps, robots files, and API responses. Consistently underused and consistently productive, because a single-page application's bundle names every API host it talks to.

```bash
# Passive aggregation. Configure the provider keys; coverage without them is poor.
subfinder -d $DOMAIN -all -silent | anew subs.txt

# Amass, which correlates across sources into its own asset database rather
# than just emitting a list. The subcommands changed in v4, so check
# `amass -h` on the build you have rather than assuming v3 syntax.
amass enum -passive -d $DOMAIN -o amass-passive.txt
amass enum -active -d $DOMAIN -brute -o amass-active.txt
amass db -names -d $DOMAIN
```

```bash
# BBOT takes a different and often better approach: recursive, modular, and it
# chains discovery into scanning automatically. Module and flag names are the
# thing to check against the current version.
bbot -t $DOMAIN -p subdomain-enum
bbot -t $DOMAIN -p subdomain-enum -rf passive
bbot -t $DOMAIN -p subdomain-enum cloud-enum code-enum email-enum
bbot -t $DOMAIN -p kitchen-sink
```

```bash
# Permutation from a known-good set. alterx applies patterns to names you
# already have rather than brute-forcing a flat wordlist.
alterx -l subs.txt -enrich -silent | anew candidates.txt

# Resolve candidates at scale. Wildcard handling is the whole game here.
dnsx -l candidates.txt -r resolvers.txt -silent -a -resp -o resolved.txt

# puredns wraps massdns with wildcard detection and resolver validation, which
# is the part people get wrong when they drive massdns directly.
puredns bruteforce wordlist.txt $DOMAIN --resolvers resolvers.txt --write resolved.txt
puredns resolve candidates.txt --resolvers resolvers.txt --write resolved.txt
```

```bash
# Content-derived. katana crawls and can be told to stay in scope while still
# reporting out-of-scope hosts it saw referenced.
katana -u https://$TARGET -jc -kf all -d 3 -silent -o crawl.txt
grep -ohE '[a-z0-9._-]+\.'"$DOMAIN" crawl.txt | sort -u | anew subs.txt
```

**Verify it worked.** Compare the three sets. If permutation added nothing, your wordlist does not match the organisation's naming convention and you should rebuild it from the certificate transparency output. If crawling added nothing, you did not crawl the JavaScript.

**Detection and opsec.** Passive aggregation is invisible. Brute force resolution is a large volume of NXDOMAIN queries against the authoritative nameservers, which is visible in DNS query logging if anyone looks and is occasionally rate limited or blocked outright. Use a validated public resolver list rather than hitting the authoritative servers directly, both for speed and because it distributes the query source. Crawling is HTTP traffic to the target and appears in web logs and WAF telemetry.

**Failure modes.** Wildcard DNS records make brute force return a positive for every name you try, and if your tooling does not detect and strip that you will generate thousands of phantom hosts. Detect it explicitly by resolving a random name that cannot exist. Stale resolver lists cause both false negatives and, worse, false positives from resolvers that answer with hijack pages. Validate the resolver list before every campaign. CNAME chains into CDNs mean a resolving name tells you nothing about whether the client operates anything there. Rate limiting on the passive providers silently truncates results, so a suspiciously round number of results is a warning sign.

### Resolution, liveness and triage

The gap between "resolves" and "is a live service worth attention" is where most of the reduction from thousands of names to a handful of targets happens.

```bash
# Resolve, then probe. httpx is the standard triage step: it tells you what
# answered, on which port, with what title, status, technology, and length.
dnsx -l subs.txt -silent -a -resp-only | sort -u > ips.txt

httpx -l subs.txt -silent -status-code -title -tech-detect -web-server \
      -content-length -follow-redirects -o httpx.txt

# Screenshots turn a thousand-line file into something you can triage visually
# in a few minutes, which is the single highest-value time trade in this phase.
# -srd sets the output directory for stored responses and screenshots.
httpx -l subs.txt -ss -sr -srd recon-output -silent
```

```bash
# Port discovery, narrow first. The default top-100 is usually the right
# opening move against a large host list; a full sweep is for a short list.
naabu -l ips.txt -top-ports 100 -silent -o ports.txt
naabu -host $TARGET -p - -silent

# nmap for the detail once naabu has told you where to look. Do not run
# -A across a perimeter as an opening move.
nmap -sV -sC -p $(cut -d: -f2 ports.txt | sort -un | paste -sd,) -Pn -oA nmap-perimeter $TARGET
```

```bash
# CDN and cloud front-end detection. Knowing that an address is a CDN edge
# changes both the scope conversation and the value of scanning it.
cdncheck -i ips.txt -resp
```

**Triage order.** Once you have the httpx output, the prioritisation that consistently pays is: authentication portals first, then management interfaces, then anything with a version string in a banner or title, then anything that looks forgotten. Specifically, sort your list for VPN and remote access portals, single sign-on and federation endpoints, webmail, file transfer, and any hostname containing `dev`, `test`, `uat`, `staging`, `old`, `legacy`, `backup`, or a year. The forgotten-looking hosts are forgotten and therefore unpatched, and the authentication portals are both the highest-value exploitation targets and the surfaces you will spray later.

### Cloud and SaaS footprint

**What it is.** Enumerating the target's presence on shared cloud and SaaS platforms, where the asset is identified by a name in a provider's global namespace rather than by an address in a netblock the target owns.

**Why it works.** Object storage, tenanted SaaS, and platform-as-a-service all place customer resources at predictable hostnames in a global namespace. The namespace is global, so names are guessable; the existence or non-existence of a name is observable without authentication; and misconfiguration of access control on these resources is extremely common because the default is easy to change and the change is invisible. Separately, identity providers publish tenant configuration unauthenticated because client autodiscovery requires it, which turns the identity provider into a reconnaissance surface. That second point is the important one and it is covered in depth in the Cloud and Modern Identity section; what belongs here is the campaign-level use of it.

**Preconditions.** The organisation name, its domains, and a list of plausible prefixes and suffixes derived from them.

**Commands.**

```bash
# Multi-cloud storage and service name discovery across AWS, Azure and GCP
# namespaces. -kf takes a keyword file, -m a mutation wordlist, and -qs
# disables mutations and second-level scans when you want a fast first pass.
cloud_enum -kf keywords.txt -m mutations.txt -t 10 -f json -l cloudenum.json
cloud_enum -k $ORG -qs

# Object storage specifically, including permission checks on what is found.
# It covers several providers, not only AWS, selected with -provider.
s3scanner -bucket-file candidates.txt -provider aws -json
s3scanner -bucket "$ORG-backups" -enumerate
```

```bash
# Tenant confirmation and configuration from the identity provider. This is the
# single most informative unauthenticated request in a cloud engagement.
curl -s "https://login.microsoftonline.com/$DOMAIN/.well-known/openid-configuration" | jq -r '.issuer'
curl -s "https://login.microsoftonline.com/getuserrealm.srf?login=$USER@$DOMAIN&xml=1"
```

The hostname patterns worth building candidate lists against, because these are where the data is:

| Pattern | Platform | What lives there |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `<name>.s3.amazonaws.com`, `<name>.s3.<region>.amazonaws.com` | AWS S3 | Backups, static assets, exports, occasionally credentials |
| `<name>.blob.core.windows.net` | Azure Blob Storage | Same, plus deployment artefacts |
| `<name>.file.core.windows.net`, `<name>.table.core.windows.net` | Azure Storage | File shares and tables |
| `storage.googleapis.com/<name>` | Google Cloud Storage | Same |
| `<tenant>.sharepoint.com`, `<tenant>-my.sharepoint.com` | SharePoint and OneDrive | Documents, and the enumeration surface for usernames |
| `<tenant>.onmicrosoft.com` | Entra ID | The tenant's default domain, useful for spraying and for Teams targeting |
| `<name>.azurewebsites.net`, `<name>.azurefd.net` | Azure App Service, Front Door | Applications, often staging slots |
| `<name>.cloudfront.net`, `<name>.elb.amazonaws.com` | AWS CDN and load balancers | The front of an application whose origin may be reachable |
| `<name>.atlassian.net`, `<name>.slack.com`, `<name>.okta.com`, `<name>.zendesk.com` | SaaS tenancies | Identity, ticketing, chat. Each is an authentication surface and a pretext source |
| `<name>.firebaseio.com`, `<name>.web.app` | Firebase | Frequently world-readable databases |

**Verify it worked.** A confirmed tenant identifier, a confirmed federation state, and a list of storage names that returned something other than a generic not-found. For storage, distinguish clearly between "the name exists and is private", "the name exists and lists", and "the name does not exist"; the provider's error responses differ and the distinction is the finding.

**Detection and opsec.** Requests to the provider's global endpoints do not appear in the customer's logs unless they have enabled resource-level access logging, and even then a request to a non-existent name has no resource to log against. Identity provider metadata endpoints are hit constantly by legitimate clients and your query is indistinguishable. This whole subsection is effectively unobservable by the target, which is why it should be exhaustive.

**Failure modes.** Name guessing against a global namespace has a low hit rate and the hit rate is entirely a function of your candidate list, so invest there rather than in the tool. Providers rate limit aggressively on non-existent name lookups. Scope is the real hazard: a storage bucket named after the client may belong to a supplier, a former employee, or a company with a similar name, and reading its contents on that assumption is the kind of mistake that ends engagements. Confirm ownership from content before you report it and before you go further into it.

### Technology fingerprinting

**What it is.** Determining what software, version, and vendor sits behind each exposed service, well enough to decide whether a known vulnerability class applies.

**Why it works.** Servers volunteer a great deal. Response headers, cookie names, error page structure, URL path conventions, JavaScript bundle contents, favicon bytes, TLS handshake characteristics, and default file paths are all fingerprints, and most of them cannot be removed without breaking the product. Appliance vendors are especially generous here because their web front ends are distinctive and their version strings are frequently in a static asset path.

**Preconditions.** An HTTP or TLS service you can reach.

**Commands.**

```bash
# Header, cookie and wappalyzer-style fingerprinting in the triage pass.
httpx -l subs.txt -silent -tech-detect -title -status-code -web-server -jarm

# Deeper single-target fingerprinting.
whatweb -a 3 https://$TARGET

# Favicon hashing. Identical favicons across the internet identify a product
# reliably, and the hash is a search key in the scan databases.
httpx -u https://$TARGET -favicon -silent
```

```bash
# TLS-layer fingerprinting. JARM hashes the server's responses to a set of
# deliberately varied client hellos, which identifies the TLS stack and
# therefore very often the appliance or the C2 framework behind it.
tlsx -u $TARGET -jarm -silent
```

```bash
# Templated detection rather than exploitation. Restrict severity and tags on a
# production perimeter; a full template run is thousands of requests.
nuclei -l live.txt -tags tech,detect -severity info,low -silent -o nuclei-tech.txt
nuclei -l live.txt -tags cve -severity critical,high -rate-limit 20 -o nuclei-cve.txt
```

**Verify it worked.** For each priority target you should be able to name the product and either a version or a version range, and cite the evidence. "Citrix NetScaler, build string in `/vpn/js/rdx/core/lang/rdx_en.json.mobile`" is a finding. "Probably Citrix" is not. Where you cannot get a version from the front end, the version-independent behaviour of a specific vulnerability is sometimes the only way to distinguish, and that decision belongs in the safe-validation discussion below.

**Detection and opsec.** Fingerprinting is HTTP traffic and appears in access logs, WAF logs, and CDN bot analytics. Nuclei in particular is loud and its requests are signatured by several WAF vendors, so a full-template run against a monitored perimeter is a reasonable way to get your source address blocked and your activity noticed. If stealth matters, do the passive fingerprinting from scan databases first and reserve direct requests for the two or three hosts you actually care about.

**Failure modes.** CDNs and reverse proxies mask the origin entirely, so you fingerprint the CDN. WAFs return uniform responses that defeat error-page fingerprinting. Version strings are frequently wrong, either because the vendor did not update a static asset on patch or because the operator has a hotfix applied that does not change the banner. Never conclude "vulnerable" from a version string alone on a report; conclude "the exposed version is within the affected range" and say how you would confirm.

### Attack surface databases and internet-wide scan data

**What it is.** Querying third parties who have already scanned the internet, instead of scanning it yourself.

**Why it works.** Several organisations continuously scan the entire IPv4 space, capture banners and certificates, and index the results. That index is a passive reconnaissance source with two properties direct scanning does not have: it is invisible to the target, and it is historical, so it shows you what was exposed last month and has since been firewalled but not decommissioned.

**Commands.**

```bash
# uncover queries several of these engines through one interface and emits
# host:port, which feeds straight into httpx.
uncover -q "$ORG" -e shodan,censys,fofa,quake,netlas -silent
uncover -q 'ssl:"'"$DOMAIN"'"' -e shodan -silent | httpx -silent -title -tech-detect

# Shodan directly, for the filters uncover does not expose.
shodan search --fields ip_str,port,org,hostnames "ssl.cert.subject.CN:\"$DOMAIN\""
shodan search "org:\"$ORG\" http.title:\"login\""
shodan host $TARGET
```

The filters that consistently earn their keep, per platform. Confirm current syntax against the platform's own documentation, because all of these vendors revise their query languages.

| Platform | Query idiom | Use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Shodan | `ssl.cert.subject.CN:"example.com"` | Hosts serving a certificate for the domain, including ones DNS does not point at |
| Shodan | `ssl:"$ORG"` | Certificate organisation match, which finds assets across unrelated domains |
| Shodan | `http.favicon.hash:<hash>` | Every instance of a product worldwide, then filter to the target |
| Shodan | `org:"$ORG"`, `asn:AS64500` | Netblock-attributed assets |
| Shodan | `http.title:"..."`, `http.html:"..."` | Appliance login pages by their distinctive title or body text |
| Censys | `services.tls.certificates.leaf_data.subject.common_name: example.com` | The certificate path in the current Censys schema |
| Censys | `services.http.response.html_title: "..."` | Title search |
| FOFA | `cert="example.com"`, `domain="example.com"` | Certificate and domain search, strong coverage in Asia-Pacific |
| Netlas, ZoomEye, Fullhunt, LeakIX | Vendor-specific | Differing coverage and free-tier limits; worth cross-checking because none is complete |

**Verify it worked.** Cross-check at least one asset you found by direct scanning against the database, and at least one database result by direct probe. Discrepancies in both directions are normal and informative: a database result that no longer answers is historical exposure worth reporting, and a live service the databases missed is either recently deployed or on a non-standard port.

**Detection and opsec.** Invisible to the target. Note the reverse implication: **your own infrastructure is in these databases too.** Your redirector, your phishing host, and your C2 listener have been scanned, fingerprinted, JARM-hashed and indexed, generally within days of coming online. Defenders and threat intelligence vendors query these platforms for exactly that. The Command and Control section covers what to do about it; the point here is that the tool you use for reconnaissance is used against you.

**Failure modes.** Data staleness cuts both ways and there is no timestamp discipline you can rely on across platforms. Free tiers truncate results badly enough to produce a misleadingly small picture. Cloud-hosted assets attribute to the cloud provider in the `org` field, so organisation-based queries miss them entirely; certificate-based queries are the way in. And these platforms are themselves scanned-and-indexed by everyone including the target's threat intelligence provider, so a query is not a secret from the wider ecosystem even if it is from the client.

### Code, document and credential leakage

The highest-yield and lowest-effort part of external reconnaissance, and the one most likely to hand you a working credential before you have sent a single packet at the target.

**What it is.** Searching public code hosts, package registries, paste sites, document caches and CI logs for the organisation's secrets, internal hostnames, and configuration.

**Why it works.** Secrets get committed. They get committed by employees to personal repositories, by contractors to public ones, into container images published to registries, into front-end bundles served to every visitor, into CI logs, and into files that were shared with a link and indexed. Removing the secret from the current commit does not remove it from history, and forks and mirrors persist after deletion. Search is indexed and free.

**Commands.**

```bash
# Secret scanning across an organisation's public repositories, and across the
# full git history rather than the working tree.
trufflehog github --org=$ORG --results=verified
trufflehog github --org=$ORG --results=verified --exclude-archived
trufflehog git https://github.com/$ORG/repo --results=verified --json
trufflehog filesystem ./cloned --results=verified

# Issue and pull request comments are a separate and frequently productive
# surface, because secrets get pasted into discussions rather than committed.
trufflehog github --repo=https://github.com/$ORG/repo --issue-comments --pr-comments

gitleaks detect --source ./cloned --report-format json --report-path leaks.json
```

```bash
# Front-end bundles and source maps. Keys in JavaScript are extremely common
# and are served to anyone who loads the page.
katana -u https://$TARGET -jc -silent -em js -o js-urls.txt
# then retrieve and grep the bundles, and look for .map files alongside them
```

The manual searches that repay the time, run against GitHub code search and the equivalent on other hosts: the client's email domain, their internal domain suffix, their tenant identifier, their storage bucket names, their VPN hostname, and each of those combined with terms such as `password`, `apikey`, `token`, `BEGIN PRIVATE KEY`, `connectionstring`, `.env`, and `web.config`. Search employee names as repository owners too, because the leak is usually personal rather than corporate.

**Verify it worked.** A candidate secret is not a finding until you have established what it authenticates to and whether it is live. Validate it against the service it belongs to, once, with a single request, and record the result. Do not spray a discovered key against every service you can think of.

**Detection and opsec.** Code search is invisible to the target. Validating a discovered credential is not: it produces an authentication event in whatever the credential belongs to, and if the credential is dead it produces a failure event that may be alarmed. This is your first active step and it should be a deliberate one.
