Mail clients and browsers have very largely converged on rendering these as punycode precisely to defeat the technique, so the visual deception mostly does not survive to the user. Treat it as a curiosity rather than a tool.

**Reputation and categorisation checks before you commit.** Web filtering products categorise domains, and a domain in an unhelpful category, or an uncategorised one, is blocked in many enterprise configurations. Several vendors expose a lookup and a re-categorisation request form, and operators routinely use both: check where your domain sits, and if it is uncategorised or badly categorised, request a category consistent with your pretext. That request is a normal mechanism intended for site owners.

Check, at minimum, before you commit to a domain:

- Web filtering category with the major vendors whose products the target is likely to run, which your fingerprinting should have told you.
- Presence on the major reputation blocklists, for both the domain and the sending address.
- Certificate transparency history for the domain, which tells you what it was used for before.
- Passive DNS history, same reason.
- Whether the domain or its address range appears in a threat intelligence feed.

**Hosting the landing content on a trusted platform instead.** A structurally different approach that sidesteps the domain reputation problem entirely: host the content on a platform the target already trusts and cannot block. Document-sharing services, collaboration platforms, developer platforms, form builders, design tools, note-taking services, cloud storage and electronic signature services are all routinely used this way, because a link to a well-known software-as-a-service domain passes URL reputation checks, arrives with a valid certificate for a trusted name, and is frequently on an allow-list because the business uses it. Open redirects on genuinely trusted domains serve the same purpose: the link the user and the scanner see belongs to a reputable organisation, and the redirect is what takes them elsewhere.

The tradeoff is that you are operating inside somebody else's platform, subject to their abuse detection, their terms, and their ability to remove your content mid-campaign without notice. Have a fallback.

### The mail security stack you must survive

Assume the target runs a layered stack. Characterise it during reconnaissance, because each layer changes a specific decision.

**What you can learn about it from outside.** The MX records tell you who filters their mail, and that single lookup determines a large part of your approach.

```bash
# Who actually filters their mail. This is one lookup and it is the most
# informative thing you will learn about the mail path.
dig +short MX $DOMAIN

# Records pointing at a gateway vendor's hostnames mean a gateway in front of
# whatever the mailbox platform is. Records pointing directly at the mailbox
# platform mean its native protection is the whole stack.
```

**URL rewriting and time-of-click verification.** The dominant pattern: the gateway rewrites every link in inbound mail to point at its own service, so that when the user clicks, the service can evaluate the destination at that moment rather than relying on a judgement made at delivery.

Taking the Microsoft implementation as the detailed example, because it is the most commonly encountered and the best documented:

- Links are rewritten to a hostname under the service's own domain, with the data centre region in the label.
- **Scanning happens before delivery regardless of whether rewriting is enabled.** If rewriting is on, links are additionally scanned on click. If rewriting is off, the client calls the service's interface at click time for an extra check, in supported clients only.
- **URLs without an established reputation are detonated asynchronously in the background.** There is also an option to hold the message until scanning completes rather than delivering and scanning in parallel.
- Rewriting persists through manual forwards and replies, and applies per recipient.
- There are documented gaps, and they are the interesting part: it does not process links in mail-enabled public folders; it supports only HTTP, HTTPS and FTP; it does not protect URLs in rich-text-format messages; it **ignores messages signed with S/MIME**; and it no longer wraps links pointing at the vendor's own file-sharing services, although those are still processed. It also notes that using another service to wrap links first may prevent it from processing them at all.
- In the collaboration platform, links are checked at time of click but not rewritten.
- Click events are recorded and queryable in the hunting interface, which means the defender has a per-user click log.
- The "do not rewrite" list excludes URLs from rewriting during mail flow but they may still be blocked at click time, and the collaboration platform and web applications do not honour that list at all.

**What rewriting does to you, and how to respond.**

It **breaks unique-per-target URLs as a reliable identity signal**, because the rewriting service may fetch your URL itself. A per-recipient identifier in the link means the service's fetch registers as that recipient interacting, so your click data is polluted with automated fetches. Design your instrumentation to distinguish them, discussed below.

It **detonates your landing page in a sandbox**, from the service's own infrastructure, with an automated client. Which means your landing page will be visited by something that is not your target, before or at the moment your target visits. The standard responses are to serve benign content to anything that does not look like the intended human, and to keep the page inert until you want it live:

- **Gate on a human-interaction challenge.** A challenge-response widget placed in front of the content blocks nearly all automated analysis and looks entirely legitimate to a human. This is now the single most widely deployed evasion in this space, and it is the first thing to reach for.
- **Filter by source address and reputation.** Block data centre ranges, cloud provider ranges, known analysis infrastructure, and anonymising proxies.
- **Filter by user-agent.** Both allow-listing what you expect and blocking known automation. Evilginx exposes this per lure as a user-agent regular expression.
- **Geofence** to the countries your target population is actually in.
- **Delay activation.** Keep the lure pointed at benign content until the campaign window opens. Evilginx's `lures pause` does exactly this.
- **Serve a plausible real site to non-targets rather than an error.** A redirect to a genuine innocuous page is far less interesting to an analyst than a 403 or an obvious block page, and does not confirm that the URL is interesting.
- **Long random URL paths**, so that the URL is not guessable and enumeration of your infrastructure does not find live content.

**Attachment sandboxing.** The parallel control for files. Again using the well-documented implementation as the example:

- Attachments are opened in a virtual environment and observed, a process the vendor calls detonation. Typical completion is within fifteen minutes, sometimes longer.
- The action options are off, monitor, block, and dynamic delivery. **Dynamic delivery** delivers the message body immediately with a placeholder in place of the attachment, replacing it once scanning completes, which is designed to remove the delivery delay. Most documents can be previewed in a safe mode while scanning proceeds.
- **Attachments are identified by their true file type, not by the extension.** Renaming does not help.
- Password-protected attachments cannot be fully scanned unless the password is available, and the current behaviour is to quarantine them with a self-release path where the user supplies the password, at which point a just-in-time detonation runs before release. The historical technique of a password-protected archive with the password in the message body is therefore substantially closed on this platform: either the scanner extracts the password from the body, or the message is quarantined until someone supplies it. Note the documented gap: messages containing multiple password-protected attachments with *different* passwords, or a single archive containing items with different passwords, are not handled by that mechanism.
- Dynamic delivery has a list of scenarios where it cannot replace attachments, including public folders, messages moved out of the mailbox, and **S/MIME encrypted messages**.

**The practical conclusion about attachments.** On a well-configured modern mail platform, sending an executable payload as a mail attachment is the worst available option. The payload format and container discussion belongs to the Evasion and Payload Development section; the *campaign-level* decision that belongs here is that **you should generally not put the payload in the mail path at all.** Put a link in the mail and the payload behind the link, behind a human-interaction gate. That moves the payload out of reach of attachment sandboxing entirely, and it means the sandbox sees a link to a page that shows it something harmless.

**Other layers to expect.** Anti-phishing policies that model who normally emails whom and flag impersonation of internal and known external senders. Retroactive removal of messages already delivered, once a verdict changes, which means a message that arrived can be pulled out of the mailbox an hour later. First-contact safety tips and external-sender tags, which visually mark your message as from outside and are worth accounting for in the pretext rather than fighting. Behavioural analysis products that model normal communication patterns and score anomalies rather than matching signatures, which are markedly harder to evade than signature-based gateways because there is no signature to avoid.

**Macro blocking.** Office applications block macros by default in files originating from the internet, which closed the dominant delivery mechanism of the previous decade. The mechanism, and the container formats that strip the internet-origin marking, are covered in the Evasion and Payload Development section. The campaign-level point is that a macro-bearing document is no longer a viable primary delivery mechanism against a default-configured estate, and planning a campaign around one is planning around 2019.

### Three campaign types, three infrastructure shapes

Decide which of these you are running before you build anything, because they need different infrastructure and produce different outcomes. Mixing them produces a campaign that does neither well.

| | Credential and session capture | Payload delivery | Consent or authorisation flow |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Objective | A credential, or a session token | Code execution on an endpoint | An authorisation grant to an application you control |
| Infrastructure | A reverse proxy or a browser-in-the-middle host, a domain, a certificate | A hosting location for the payload, a delivery format, and C2 infrastructure behind it | An application registration in the target's identity platform, and a link |
| Domain requirement | Must look plausible in a browser address bar | Only needs to survive URL reputation. The address bar matters less | **None.** The link points at the genuine identity provider |
| Mail path exposure | A link. Low | Historically an attachment, now preferably a link. Higher | A link to a legitimate, trusted, correctly certificated domain. Minimal |
| Defeated by | Phishing-resistant authenticators | Endpoint detection, application control, macro and format restrictions | Restricting user consent, and blocking unverified publishers |
| Detection surface | Identity provider sign-in telemetry and risk detections | Endpoint telemetry, which is the richest of the three | Identity provider audit log, consent grant events |
| What you end up with | An identity. **Not** code execution | Code execution. **Not** necessarily an identity | Delegated access to data, scoped to whatever you asked for |
| Owning section | This section, with the cloud mechanics in Cloud and Modern Identity | Evasion and Payload Development for the format, Command and Control for the callback | Cloud and Modern Identity |

That last row but one is the one to internalise, and it is worth saying in the report: **adversary-in-the-middle gives you identity, not execution.** A captured session lets you read mail, browse files, enumerate the directory, and possibly register a device or grant consent. It does not give you a process on a workstation. If your engagement needs code execution on an endpoint, a credential campaign does not get you there and you need a deliberate bridge: a payload delivered through the access you gained, an application consent that yields something executable, or a second campaign.

The consent and authorisation route deserves a note here even though the Cloud and Modern Identity section owns it, because it has a property the other two do not: **the link points at the genuine identity provider, on its genuine domain, with its genuine certificate.** There is no lookalike domain, no certificate transparency alert, no URL reputation problem, and nothing for a mail gateway to detonate. The entire deception is in what the user is consenting to. From a pure deliverability standpoint it is the strongest of the three, which is why it is worth checking whether the target restricts user consent before you plan an elaborate proxying campaign.

### Tracking and instrumentation

**Why it matters.** Without instrumentation you cannot distinguish "the message did not arrive" from "it arrived and nobody clicked" from "everybody clicked and the landing page was broken", and those three have completely different responses. You also cannot write a report, because the report is largely a funnel.

**What to instrument, stage by stage.**

| Stage | How you know | Reliability |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Accepted by the receiving server | SMTP response code at handover | High. This is the one signal you can trust |
| Delivered to the inbox rather than junk | You mostly cannot tell | Low. Seed accounts are the only real answer |
| Opened | A tracking pixel | **Poor.** Image loading is blocked by default in many clients, and proxied in others |
| Clicked | A request to your link | Moderate. Polluted by security-service fetches |
| Landing page rendered by a human | Challenge-response completion, JavaScript execution, browser characteristics | Good, and this is the signal to build your funnel on |
| Credential submitted | Your capture | High |
| Session captured | Your framework's session list | High. But verify by replaying |
| Payload executed | C2 callback | High |
| Reported by the user | You do not see it. Ask the client afterwards | Requires the client's cooperation |

**Seed accounts are the highest-value piece of instrumentation and the most commonly omitted.** Include, in every campaign, a small number of mailboxes you control at the major providers, and, where the client will agree to it, a mailbox inside the target's own tenant. The internal seed is the only way to see what your message actually looked like after the target's stack finished with it: whether it landed in the inbox or the junk folder, whether the links were rewritten and to what, whether the attachment was replaced with a placeholder, whether an external-sender tag or safety tip was prepended, and how the whole thing renders in their client. Ask for it. It converts guesswork into observation and it costs the client nothing.

**Distinguishing humans from automated analysis.** Your click data is polluted by default, and if you do not separate the streams your report will overstate engagement. Signals that separate them, in rough order of usefulness:

- **Challenge-response completion.** The cleanest single discriminator available.
- **JavaScript execution and a plausible sequence of interactions**, rather than a single fetch of the top-level document.
- **Timing.** An automated fetch arrives within seconds of delivery, often before any human could have read the message. A human arrives minutes or hours later, in a pattern that follows the working day.
- **Source address characteristics.** Data centre and cloud ranges versus consumer or corporate egress. Note that a corporate target's egress may itself be a data centre range, so this is weaker than it looks.
- **User-agent coherence** with the rest of the request, and against the platform you expect.
- **Repeat visits from the same address with no session continuity**, which is a scanner pattern.

**Tooling.** Gophish remains the standard campaign manager despite being unmaintained: templates, target lists, per-recipient link generation, open and click tracking, and an API that other tooling integrates with. It has known default artefacts that defenders match on and that you must remove:

- An `X-Gophish-Contact` header in outbound mail, carrying the configured contact address, which leaks your operator address.
- An `X-Gophish-Signature` header on webhook calls.
- A recipient identifier in the click URL, by default the parameter name `rid`.
- A default administrative interface port and a default tracking-pixel path.

All four are single-line changes and every serious operator makes them. The recipient identifier is worth extra attention: it is a plaintext per-recipient value in the URL, so any security service that pre-fetches links marks that recipient as having clicked. That is precisely why the more recent integrations encrypt the lure parameters.

Evilginx has first-party integration with a Gophish fork, configured with `config gophish admin_url`, `config gophish api_key` and `config gophish insecure`, and verified with `config gophish test`. That reports lure clicks and session captures back into the campaign statistics, which gives you one funnel rather than two disconnected systems. The commercial build additionally offers submitting captured credentials as hashes rather than cleartext, which is a genuinely useful option for a client who does not want their staff's passwords in your tooling, and encryption of the custom lure parameters.

Out-of-band callback tokens are a cheap and useful supplementary signal: embed a uniquely named DNS or HTTP callback in your content and you get a record of anything that resolved or fetched it, including things that never reached your main infrastructure. Useful for detecting sandbox analysis specifically.

**What to record for the report.** Per recipient: sent, accepted, and the SMTP response. Per interaction: timestamp, source address, user-agent, and your human-or-automated classification with the reason. Per success: what you obtained and when. Aggregate: the funnel, with the automated fetches separated out. And separately, obtained from the client afterwards: how many people reported it, how quickly the first report came in, and what happened next. That last set is frequently the most valuable part of the whole exercise and you cannot collect it yourself.

## Pretext and campaign design

The pretext is the part of the campaign that decides whether the person acts, and it is the part operators put least effort into. A perfectly engineered delivery chain carrying "Dear User, your account will be suspended, click here" is a wasted week. This section treats pretext construction as a discipline with rules, because it has them.

### What makes a pretext work

Five properties. A pretext with all five works on almost anyone; a pretext missing one of them works on the inattentive; a pretext missing three does not work at all.

**It arrives from a plausible sender in a plausible context.** Not merely a plausible display name, but a plausible *relationship*: is this a person or system that would send this person this message? A message from the IT department to a member of staff is plausible. A message from the chief executive to a warehouse operative asking them to buy vouchers is not, which is why that campaign type has a low success rate despite its notoriety. Your personnel reconnaissance is what tells you which relationships exist.

**It asks for something the recipient has done before.** People comply with familiar processes almost automatically and scrutinise novel ones. "Sign in to review the document" is a thing they do twenty times a day. "Install this certificate by running the following command" is not. The more your request resembles the recipient's existing routine, the less thought it receives. This is the single most important property and it is the one that most distinguishes a good pretext from a bad one.

**It provides a reason.** Not urgency, a *reason*. A message that explains why this is happening now, in terms the recipient can situate in their own understanding of the organisation, is far more effective than one that simply demands action. "As part of the finance system migration announced last month" beats "immediate action required". Reasons come from reconnaissance: an announced merger, a system migration, an office move, a new supplier, a regulatory deadline, a published change to a policy.

**It is consistent in every detail with what it claims to be.** The right signature block, the right footer, the right tone, the right link format, the right level of formality, the right internal jargon, the right typography. Organisations have a house style and staff recognise deviations from it without being able to articulate what is wrong. Get their real emails if you can, from public sources, from a shared mailbox, from a support ticket, from a mailing list archive, and copy the format exactly.

**It makes the required action the path of least resistance.** One click, one obvious button, no decisions. Every additional step, every choice, every moment of confusion is an opportunity for the recipient to stop and think, and thinking is what you are trying to avoid.

**On urgency, which is the property people overuse.** Manufactured urgency does work, and it works by suppressing deliberation. It also fires every awareness-training alarm the organisation has installed, because "creates a sense of urgency" is on every phishing-awareness poster ever printed. Use mild, natural urgency of the kind real business correspondence contains: a deadline that exists for a stated reason, an end-of-day cutoff, a meeting tomorrow. Avoid the register of "URGENT: IMMEDIATE ACTION REQUIRED", which now reads as a training example.

**On authority.** Impersonating internal authority is effective and needs specific authorisation, because you are putting words in a real person's mouth and there are consequences for that person. Impersonating a *role* rather than a named individual is usually sufficient and much less fraught: "the IT service desk" rather than a named administrator. If you do want to name someone, agree it with the client in advance, name someone senior enough to be plausible and not so senior as to be scrutinised, and never impersonate the person who would be the escalation point for a report.

### Targeting: broad or precise

A real decision with a real tradeoff, and the right answer depends on the engagement's question.

**A broad campaign** goes to a large fraction of the workforce. Its advantage is arithmetic: with several hundred recipients you are near-certain to find someone who clicks, because you only need one. Its disadvantages compound. Volume is itself a detection signal, and a mail security stack that scores one message as borderline will score two hundred identical ones as a campaign. It generates multiple reports, and the first report burns the campaign for everyone. The pretext must be generic enough to fit everybody, which means it cannot be specific enough to be really convincing. And it touches many people, which increases the chance of hitting someone you should have excluded.

**A small precise campaign** goes to five or ten carefully chosen people with a pretext built for them specifically. Advantages: highly credible because it can reference things only relevant to those individuals, low volume so no campaign-level detection, few reporting opportunities, and a controllable blast radius. Disadvantages: the arithmetic works against you, so a single failure is the whole campaign, and it takes far more preparation per recipient.

**How to choose.** Ask what the engagement is testing.

- If the question is "can an attacker get in", a broad campaign maximises the probability of a yes and is the right answer.
- If the question is "would we detect and respond", a small precise campaign is the right answer, because a broad campaign tests the mail gateway and the reporting culture, not the detection and response capability. It also gives the defenders a fair test rather than an overwhelming one.
- If the question is "are our executives protected", the target set is chosen for you and it is small.
- If you are simulating a specific named adversary, match their observed targeting.

**A practical hybrid that works well.** Run a small, precise, well-built campaign first against a handful of well-chosen targets. If it succeeds, you have your foothold with minimal noise and you have preserved the option of a second wave. If it fails, escalate to a broader campaign, having learned something about the stack from the first attempt. Doing it the other way round burns the target population and the infrastructure.

**Whom to target.** The high-yield populations, and the reasons:

- **New starters.** Everything is unfamiliar, they have been told to expect setup instructions from strangers, they do not know the house style well enough to notice deviations, and they do not want to be the person who caused a problem in their first week. Consistently the most reliable population, and identifiable from professional network activity and from `pwdLastSet` clustering if you get directory visibility.
- **People whose job is to open attachments from strangers.** Recruitment, accounts payable, sales, customer support, procurement, press office, legal. Their job is literally to process unsolicited documents from unknown senders, and any awareness training that tells them not to is in direct conflict with their objectives.
- **Field staff, shift workers, and anyone who works from a mobile device.** Mobile clients show less detail, truncate sender addresses, make link inspection difficult, and are used in a hurry.
- **Anyone recently mentioned in public communications.** A person named in a press release about a new project is receiving unsolicited mail about that project already.
- **Technical staff, with a caveat.** They have the most valuable access and they are also the most likely to notice and report. High risk, high reward. A pretext that fits their world, a vendor security advisory, a code review request, a monitoring alert, works far better on them than a generic one, which will simply be reported.
- **Executive assistants.** Access to the executive's calendar and mail, high volume of legitimate external correspondence, and strong incentive to act quickly on anything that appears to come from their principal.

**Whom to exclude, and agree the list in advance.** People on leave, whose absence delays discovery and whose mail may be delegated. Anyone the client has flagged for welfare reasons. The security team, unless testing them is the point. Anyone whose role makes a false action genuinely dangerous, in clinical, safety-critical or financial-authorisation roles. And anyone recently disciplined over a security matter, which the client should tell you about and which is a genuine welfare concern.

### Timing

Timing is a real variable and it is cheap to get right.

**Time of day.** Early morning is the highest-yield window in most organisations: people are working through overnight mail, in volume, with less attention per message, and before the day's meetings have started. Immediately after lunch is a second, weaker peak. Late Friday afternoon is the classic choice for reducing scrutiny and it has a specific cost: if nobody triages it until Monday, your infrastructure has to survive the weekend and your foothold sits idle.

**Day of week.** Tuesday to Thursday for maximum engagement. Monday morning has volume but also higher alertness. Friday afternoon trades engagement for reduced response.

**Relative to real events.** This is where the leverage is. A message that arrives while the organisation is genuinely doing the thing your pretext refers to is far more effective than the same message at a random time. Look for: an announced system migration, a reorganisation, an acquisition, a results announcement, an office move, a new benefits provider, an audit, a regulatory deadline, a public incident, a major conference the staff are attending, or a holiday period when staffing is thin and processes are being bypassed. All of this is discoverable from public sources and it is the highest-value output of your reconnaissance for campaign design purposes.

**Relative to the security team.** Holiday periods, shift changes, and the aftermath of a real incident all reduce the attention available. Be careful with the last one: arriving in the middle of a genuine incident is both maximally effective and maximally likely to cause a serious deconfliction problem. If the client is dealing with something real, pause and ask.

**Relative to your own infrastructure.** Domain aged, certificate obtained well in advance, categorisation checked, seed accounts confirmed receiving, and the landing infrastructure tested end to end with a real browser from a real network. Do not send on the day you finish building.

### The pretexts that recur, and why

These recur because they work, and they work for structural reasons rather than accidental ones. The pattern to notice is that almost all of them describe a process the recipient already participates in.

| Pretext | Why it works | Typical objective |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A shared document requiring sign-in | The single most effective pretext in existence. Staff share and open documents constantly, the sign-in prompt is genuinely expected, and the flow is indistinguishable from the real one until the address bar | Credential and session capture |
| Voicemail, missed call, or fax notification | Automated, impersonal, and refers to a system the recipient half-remembers having. Low scrutiny because it appears machine-generated | Credential capture |
| Mailbox quota, mail migration, or password expiry | Refers to a real, familiar, recurring administrative process. Effective in inverse proportion to how modern the estate is | Credential capture |
| MFA re-enrolment or authenticator migration | Currently among the highest-yield pretexts, precisely because organisations genuinely are migrating authentication methods and telling staff to expect exactly this message | Credential capture, and enrolment of a method you control |
| Human resources: policy update, benefits, payroll, appraisal | Universally applicable, personally relevant, and mildly anxiety-inducing, which suppresses scrutiny. Payroll in particular gets attention | Credential capture, payload delivery |
| Invoice, purchase order, remittance advice, statement | Aimed at finance, whose job is to open exactly this. Works with an attachment because the recipient expects one | Payload delivery |
| A curriculum vitae or job application | Aimed at recruitment, whose job is to open unsolicited documents from strangers. The strongest attachment pretext that exists | Payload delivery |
| Delivery, customs or courier notification | Universally plausible, and the recipient often genuinely is expecting something | Credential capture |
| Legal notice, subpoena, complaint, regulatory correspondence | Alarming, urgent for a legitimate reason, and something the recipient will not want to ignore or delay | Payload delivery |
| An electronic signature request | Refers to a service the organisation almost certainly uses, arrives from a genuinely trusted domain if you host it there, and the whole point of the service is that you click through to a document | Credential capture, and hosting on a trusted platform |
| A calendar invitation or meeting join link | Arrives in the calendar rather than the inbox, is frequently processed by a different code path, and the recipient's habit is to click join without inspection | Credential capture |
| Reply to an existing thread, or a spoofed forward | If you have read access to a mailbox, replying inside a real thread removes almost every signal the recipient uses. The most effective pretext available and it requires a prior foothold | Anything. This is what you do with your *second* foothold |
| A vendor security advisory or patch notification | Aimed at technical staff in the register they actually read. Works on the population most other pretexts fail against | Payload delivery |
| Survey, training, or compliance module deadline | Mandatory, tedious, familiar, and clicked without thought precisely because it is tedious | Credential capture |
| A benefit or reward: bonus, voucher, gift, prize | Lower yield and higher reporting rate than the process-based pretexts, but it works on a distinct population that the others miss | Credential capture |

**The general principle behind the table.** Ordinary, procedural, slightly dull pretexts outperform dramatic ones. The best phishing message is one the recipient does not remember receiving, because it was indistinguishable from the forty other administrative messages they processed that morning. Operators consistently over-invest in cleverness and under-invest in mundanity.

**Writing the message.** Short. Shorter than you think. Three sentences and a link outperforms a well-crafted paragraph, because length invites reading and reading invites scrutiny. Match the house style exactly. Use the recipient's actual first name, in the form the organisation actually uses. Get the greeting and sign-off register right. Avoid the words that appear on awareness posters. And proofread it, because a spelling error in an otherwise plausible message is the single most commonly cited reason people report phishing.

## Other social channels

**The general point, and it is the most important thing in this section: email is the most defended channel in the organisation, and therefore often the wrong one.** Two decades of investment have gone into the mail path. There is a gateway, a sandbox, a link rewriter, a reputation system, a behavioural model, retroactive purge, an external-sender banner, a report button, and an awareness programme that has trained every member of staff to be suspicious of email specifically. Almost none of that exists on the other channels, and the trust model on several of them is materially more favourable to you.

So ask, deliberately, for every campaign: is email actually the best way to reach this person? Frequently it is not.

### Instant messaging and collaboration platforms

**What it is.** Delivering the pretext through the organisation's chat and collaboration platform, from an external tenant, a compromised internal account, or a guest identity.

**Why it works, and this is the important part.** Three independent reasons, and they compound.

**The filtering is a fraction of what mail gets.** There is generally no gateway, no attachment sandbox in the message path, no reputation system for senders, and where link protection exists it is a time-of-click check rather than the full pre-delivery scan, detonation and rewriting pipeline that mail receives. On the reference platform, links in chat are checked at click time and **are not rewritten**, which means the entire class of rewriting-derived detection and instrumentation pollution does not apply.

**The implicit trust is much higher.** Staff have been trained for twenty years to be suspicious of email. They have not been trained to be suspicious of the chat window, because the chat window is where their colleagues are. A message arriving in the same interface as a message from the person sitting next to them inherits some of that context. The interface presents a display name prominently and the underlying identity much less prominently, which is exactly the wrong way round for the recipient's purposes.

**The channel is designed for external collaboration and the default posture is permissive.** Collaboration platforms have to allow external parties in, because that is what they are for. The defaults have tightened over time but the pattern of a permissive default with an opt-in restriction persists, and organisations frequently have not opted in.

**Preconditions.** For the external-tenant route against Microsoft Teams: a business tenant of your own, an account in it with valid Teams and file-sharing licences, and the target organisation permitting external communication. For the compromised-account route: an existing foothold in the target tenant, which makes this a *second* foothold technique rather than an initial access one, and an extremely effective one.

**One precondition has changed and it will catch you out.** The standard approach used to be to spin up a free trial tenant for the sending account. That no longer works: users from trial-only tenants are now **blocked by default** from external communication, with no option for the *receiving* organisation to override it, and the tenant federation setting controlling this defaults to blocked. **You need a tenant with a paid subscription to send.** Budget for it, and provision it well before the engagement rather than discovering the problem on the day. The default for non-trial external domains, by contrast, remains permissive: allowing all external domains is still the default posture, which is why the technique works at all.

**Commands.** TeamsPhisher is the reference tool for the external route against Teams. Its mechanism is worth understanding rather than just invoking: it uploads the attachment to the sending account's own file-sharing site, then for each target verifies the user exists and can receive external messages, creates a thread, sends the message with a link to the file, and then removes the target from the thread. That last step is not incidental; the sequence of creating a group-style thread and then removing the target is what suppresses the external-sender warning interstitial that would otherwise give the recipient pause.

```bash
# Preview mode first, always. It resolves the friendly names your --personalize
# greeting will use and sends a test message to your own account so you can see
# exactly what the target will see.
python3 teamsphisher.py -u "sender@yourtenant.onmicrosoft.com" -p 'password' \
  -l targets.txt -a payload.zip -m message.txt --preview

# Live run
python3 teamsphisher.py -u "sender@yourtenant.onmicrosoft.com" -p 'password' \
  -l targets.txt -a payload.zip -m message.txt \
  --greeting "Good afternoon" --personalize --securelink --delay 5 --log
```

The flags that matter:

| Flag | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `-u`, `-p` | Sending account credentials in your own tenant |
| `-a` | The file to upload and link to |
| `-m` | A file containing the message text |
| `-e` / `-l` | A single target address, or a file of them one per line |
| `-s`, `--sharepoint` | Manually specify the file-sharing site name. Needed if your tenant uses a custom domain rather than the default |
| `--greeting` | Override the default greeting |
| `--personalize` | Attempt to resolve and use the target's first name |
| `--securelink` | Make the uploaded file viewable only by the individual recipient, which keeps it away from anyone investigating |
| `--preview` | Do not send. Resolve names and send a test to yourself |
| `--delay` | Seconds between targets, for rate limiting |
| `--nogreeting` | No built-in greeting; use only your message file |
| `--log` | Write output to a log file in the home directory |

You need to have signed in to the sending account's personal file-sharing site at least once before use, because the tool uploads there.

**Verify it worked.** The tool's own output confirms per-target enumeration and send. Actual verification is the callback or the credential capture. Use `--preview` and your own account as the target to confirm the rendering before you send to anyone real.

**Detection and opsec.** The sending tenant is entirely attributable to you, which is fine on an engagement and is why this technique is used mostly by red teams and by actors who do not care. Expect the file access to be logged in your own tenant, and expect the receiving organisation's audit log to record external messages and file access. `--securelink` restricts who can retrieve the file, which both protects the payload from analysis and reduces the audit trail available to a responder. Where the platform's link protection covers chat, links are checked at time of click, so a landing page with a human-interaction gate is still the right pattern.

**Failure modes.** The target organisation restricting external access, which is the correct mitigation and is increasingly the default. The specific interstitial-suppression behaviour the tool relies on has been changed by the vendor more than once, so the mechanism it uses today may not be the one that works tomorrow; treat the tool's behaviour as version-specific and test with `--preview` before every campaign. Licence requirements on the sending account. And the tool has not been updated for some time, so verify its behaviour against the current platform rather than assuming.

**The other platforms.** The same reasoning applies to every collaboration platform: the external-collaboration feature is the attack surface, the filtering is lighter than mail, and the trust is higher. Guest access to a shared channel or workspace, application and integration installation, and webhook-driven message injection are all worth enumerating. Where the organisation uses a chat platform with an app directory, a malicious or over-permissioned application is a route in its own right, and it lands in the same category as consent phishing.

**And the highest-value variant of all.** Once you have any foothold in the tenant, sending from a *genuine internal account* through the internal chat platform removes essentially every remaining signal. There is no external tag, no unfamiliar sender, no reputation question, no gateway, and the recipient's context is a message from a colleague. If your engagement objective is broad compromise rather than a single foothold, this is what you do with your first foothold, and it is far more effective than a second external campaign.

### Telephone and voice

**What it is.** Contacting the target by telephone to obtain information, a credential, an MFA approval, or an action.

**Why it works.** Real time, no artefact, no filter, and a strong social obligation to be helpful to a person who is speaking to you. There is no gateway between you and the recipient, no link for anything to rewrite, nothing to detonate, and no report button. The recipient cannot forward the call to security for analysis, cannot re-read it, and cannot show it to a colleague. They have to decide now, alone, under mild social pressure. That is a fundamentally more favourable position than any asynchronous channel offers.

**Where it is uniquely effective.** Three cases.

**Relaying an MFA number.** Covered under push fatigue above and it bears repeating here because voice is what makes it work. You trigger the authentication, then call and ask the person to read you the number on their screen. Number matching is designed to stop a user approving something they did not initiate; it does not stop a user cooperating with someone they believe is their service desk.

**Getting a credential reset or an MFA method re-enrolled.** Calling the service desk *as* a user, rather than calling a user as the service desk. This targets the identity verification process rather than the person, and identity verification at a service desk is frequently weak: a name, an employee number, a manager's name, a date of birth, all of which your reconnaissance has. A successful service desk social engineering call that results in a password reset or an authenticator re-enrolment yields access with no phishing infrastructure at all, and it is the technique most consistently under-tested on engagements.

**Warming a phishing message, or following one up.** A call that precedes the email establishes context and expectation. A call that follows it resolves the recipient's hesitation. Combining channels raises the success rate substantially over either alone.

**Preconditions.** A telephone number for the target, or the organisation's switchboard. Caller identification you control, which for practical purposes means a voice-over-IP service that permits setting the presented number. A pretext that survives real-time questioning, which is a much higher bar than one that survives being read.

**On synthetic voice, honestly.** Voice cloning from a short sample is now readily available, works well enough over a telephone connection to be convincing, and is genuinely used in criminal activity, most visibly in authorisation fraud where a finance staff member is called by what sounds like an executive. The relevant facts for an engagement:

- The sample requirement is small and public sources frequently provide it, from conference talks, earnings calls, podcasts, media interviews and social video.
- Telephone-quality audio is forgiving. The bandwidth limitations of a voice call hide many of the artefacts that would be obvious in high fidelity.
- Real-time conversational use is harder than a pre-recorded message, and latency and the handling of interruptions remain the weak points.
- **It requires specific authorisation and it is the most sensitive technique in this section.** You are creating a synthetic recording of a real, identifiable person, saying things they did not say, and using it to induce action. Get explicit written authorisation naming the individual whose voice is used, get that individual's own consent, restrict the recording's use to the engagement, and destroy it afterwards.
- Consider whether a *demonstration* is sufficient. On many engagements, showing the client that a convincing clone of their chief executive can be produced from public material in an afternoon achieves the reporting objective without deceiving any of their staff. That is frequently the better professional choice and it is worth offering.

<!-- VERIFY --> The current capability boundary for real-time conversational voice cloning moves quickly; assess the specific tooling available at the time of the engagement rather than relying on a general statement.

**Commands.** There is no meaningful tooling to list. What you need is a prepared script, a pretext that survives interruption, a plausible reason for the call, a named person to refer to, and a graceful exit if it goes wrong. Prepare the exit before the call, because you will need it.

**Verify it worked.** The information, the credential, the reset, or the approval. Record the call if the authorisation permits it and the jurisdiction allows it, because the recording is the evidence and the reconstruction from memory is not.

**Detection and opsec.** Almost nothing is logged unless the target organisation records calls, which many service desks do. The artefact is on the identity side: a password reset in the audit log, an MFA method registration, a successful authentication that followed a suspicious pattern. Those are the events a defender would find, not the call. Note that a service desk that follows its process correctly will log the verification it performed, which is exactly the record you want for the report.

**Failure modes.** A service desk that follows a callback procedure, which is the correct control and defeats the technique cleanly. A recipient who asks a question your pretext cannot survive. Being transferred to somebody more senior. Voice recognition of an accent inconsistent with the claimed identity. And the recipient simply hanging up, which happens and is fine.

**The engagement dimension.** Voice work is the most personally uncomfortable technique in this section, for both parties. You are lying to a person in real time and they will feel foolish afterwards. Bound it: agree the maximum number of attempts, agree which departments may be called, agree that you identify yourself immediately if the person becomes distressed, and agree what happens to any recording. Brief the client's point of contact so that they can reassure anyone who was called.

### Physical media

**What it is.** Leaving removable media, or delivering it by post, in the expectation that somebody will connect it.

**Why it works.** Curiosity, helpfulness, and the fact that a labelled device found in a car park presents itself as somebody's lost property. The mechanism that made this famous was autorun, which is long dead; the mechanisms that work now are quite different.

**The mechanisms that actually work now.**

**A device that presents itself as a keyboard.** A microcontroller in the form factor of a memory stick, a cable, or a charger, which enumerates as a human interface device and types a payload at machine speed. Nothing about it is removable storage, so removable-media policy does not apply, and the operating system trusts keyboards implicitly because it must. This is the primary mechanism and it is the reason physical media is still a viable technique.

**A file the user opens.** A conventionally formatted document or shortcut on ordinary storage, relying on the person opening it rather than on any automatic execution. Lower yield, no special hardware, and subject to the whole endpoint protection stack.

**A device that presents itself as a network adapter**, which can be used to influence the host's name resolution or routing. Overlaps with the on-path material.

**Delivery by post.** A branded package containing a device, with a plausible covering letter: a promotional item, a conference giveaway, a supplier sample, a hardware token, a wireless presentation device. Post is entirely unfiltered, arrives at a named individual, and carries the implicit credibility of a physical object with a printed label.

**Preconditions.** Physical access to a place the target's staff will be, or a postal address and a name. Authorisation, which must explicitly cover leaving devices in publicly accessible places and sending devices by post.

**Verify it worked.** A callback. Instrument the payload to report the hostname, username and device serial, because otherwise you cannot tell which of your devices was used or by whom, and "somebody plugged something in" is not a finding.

**Detection and opsec.** Endpoint telemetry will show the device enumeration, the process creation, and the network connection, which makes this a good technique for testing endpoint detection specifically. Some organisations block human-interface-device enumeration or require approval for new input devices, which is the correct mitigation and is worth checking for. Physical devices are recoverable evidence with your fingerprints and your infrastructure's address on them, so number them, log where each went, and retrieve what you can.

**Failure modes.** Nobody picks it up, which is the common outcome and is itself a finding worth reporting positively. Device control policy blocking enumeration. The payload being caught by endpoint protection, which is an evasion problem rather than a delivery problem. Keyboard layout mismatches mangling a typed payload, which is a real and frequently overlooked failure: a payload typed on the assumption of one keyboard layout produces garbage on another, so match the target's locale. And loss of devices, which are recoverable evidence.

### Codes in images, and channel-shifting generally

**What it is.** Embedding the link as a machine-readable code in an image rather than as text, so that the recipient scans it with a device that is not the one receiving the message.

**Why it works.** Two effects, and the second is the significant one.

**The link is not text in the message.** A mail gateway parsing the message for URLs finds none, so URL reputation, rewriting and detonation have nothing to act on. This is the effect people talk about and it is the weaker of the two, because the major gateways have added optical recognition of codes in images specifically to close it. Assume the code will be read.

**The link is followed on a different device.** This is the durable effect and it does not depend on any gateway weakness. The recipient reads the message on a managed corporate workstation with endpoint protection, a managed browser, a web proxy, and full telemetry. They then scan the code with their personal phone, which has none of that: no corporate proxy, no browser extension enforcing device identity, no endpoint agent, and no logging the organisation can see. **You have moved the interaction from the most instrumented device in the estate to the least.**

That reframing generalises well beyond codes in images, and it is the most useful way to think about channel selection. Every technique that shifts the interaction from a managed device to an unmanaged one buys you the same advantage: the code in the image, the message to a personal phone number, the message to a personal social account, the link that only works on mobile. If the organisation's controls are concentrated on the corporate endpoint, do not conduct the interaction on the corporate endpoint.

**Preconditions.** A pretext that plausibly requires scanning something: MFA enrolment, an authenticator migration, a parking or catering payment, a document access request, a conference or event check-in, a physical notice in a shared space.

**Verify it worked.** A request to your landing page from a mobile browser on a consumer network, which is a highly distinctive signature in your logs and confirms the channel shift worked as intended.

**Detection and opsec.** The organisation may see nothing at all, which is the point and is also the finding: an authentication from an unmanaged personal device is invisible to the endpoint side of their stack and visible only in the identity provider's logs. Where conditional access requires a compliant or managed device, this route fails at the identity provider rather than at the endpoint, which is exactly the control that should stop it and is worth reporting on either way.

**Failure modes.** Gateway optical recognition of the code, which is now common. Conditional access requiring a managed device, which is the correct mitigation. A recipient who has no reason to scan anything. And the practical one: a code that does not scan reliably from a screen, so test it from an actual phone photographing an actual monitor rather than from a clean image file.

## Exposed service exploitation

When it works, this is the fastest route to a foothold in this whole section: hours rather than weeks, no human interaction, no infrastructure ageing, no deliverability engineering. When it does not work, it consumes the engagement and produces nothing. The determining factor is almost never your skill; it is whether the target happens to expose something with a known, reliable, currently-unpatched flaw. Assess that early and honestly, and if the answer is no, redirect the effort into identity work rather than grinding on a patched perimeter.

Reference vulnerability *classes* rather than reciting identifiers, because the identifiers churn and the classes do not. Where specific chains are named below they are named as archetypes of a class, and the identifiers are given because they are useful for prioritisation and for report references.

### Why edge devices and remote access appliances are the perennial answer

**The observation.** Year after year, the initial access vector in real intrusions and the productive finding on real engagements is a virtual private network concentrator, a remote access gateway, a firewall management interface, a load balancer, or a file transfer appliance. Not a web application, not a mail server, not an operating system. This is not fashion; it is structural, and the reasons are worth understanding because they tell you where to look first.

**They are internet-facing by definition.** A remote access appliance whose purpose is to terminate connections from anywhere cannot be firewalled off. There is no compensating control available.

**They run bespoke, forked, and old code.** These are appliances: a vendor's proprietary management layer over a heavily modified operating system, frequently an old fork of a BSD or Linux base, with vendor-written network-facing code in memory-unsafe languages. The vendor's secure development maturity is not the same as a major operating system vendor's, and it shows in the vulnerability classes that keep appearing: buffer overflows, out-of-bounds reads, command injection through shell invocation, path traversal, and authentication logic that can be walked around.

**Compromise lands you inside.** This is the property that makes them uniquely valuable. A remote access appliance's job is to bridge the internet and the internal network. Code execution on it gives you a position that is already through the perimeter, frequently with routing to internal segments, and frequently with credentials or session material for users who authenticate through it.

**They cannot be patched without an outage.** Patching the device everybody uses to work remotely requires a maintenance window, and maintenance windows are scarce. The result is a systematically longer patch latency than for endpoints or servers, measured in weeks or months rather than days, on exactly the devices where exposure is highest.

**They rarely run endpoint detection.** You cannot install an agent on an appliance. Detection is limited to whatever the appliance logs, whatever the network sees, and whatever integrity checking the vendor provides, and appliance logging is frequently sparse, frequently local, and frequently not forwarded.

**They are often forgotten.** An appliance that works is invisible. Decommissioned units left powered and reachable, secondary units in a disaster recovery site, and units belonging to an acquired business are a recurring finding, and they are the least patched of all.

**Nobody owns them.** They sit between the network team, the security team and the vendor's support contract, and the practical consequence is that patch responsibility is ambiguous.

### The vulnerability classes, with archetypes

The classes recur across vendors. Learn the class and you will recognise the next one before it has a name.

**Memory disclosure yielding session material.** A read primitive in the request handling path returns adjacent memory, and that memory contains other users' session tokens. Devastating because it **bypasses multi-factor authentication entirely**: you are not authenticating, you are stealing a session that already authenticated. Requires no credentials and often leaves very little in the logs, because from the appliance's point of view a valid session token was presented.

Archetype: the Citrix NetScaler ADC and Gateway session token disclosure, CVE-2023-4966, described by the vendor as sensitive information disclosure when the device is configured as a gateway or authentication virtual server, categorised as an improper restriction of operations within the bounds of a memory buffer, and scored 9.4 by the vendor. Its successor CVE-2025-5777 is the same family: insufficient input validation leading to a memory overread on the same configurations, an out-of-bounds read combined with use of uninitialised resources and variables, scored 9.3 under the version 4 metric. Both are in the catalogue of known exploited vulnerabilities. A third in the same product family, CVE-2025-6543, is a memory overflow leading to unintended control flow, scored 9.2.

**Authentication bypass chained with authenticated command injection.** Two separate flaws, individually rated moderately, that compose into unauthenticated remote code execution. The class matters because it explains why vulnerability scores are a poor prioritisation input on appliances: an authentication bypass rated 8.2 and an authenticated command injection rated 9.1 combine into something worse than either.

Archetype: the Ivanti Connect Secure pairing of CVE-2023-46805, an authentication bypass in the web component allowing access to restricted resources by circumventing control checks, with CVE-2024-21887, a command injection in web components allowing an authenticated administrator to execute arbitrary commands. Chained, unauthenticated code execution. The same product line subsequently produced CVE-2024-21893, a server-side request forgery in the SAML component allowing access to restricted resources without authentication, and CVE-2025-0282, a stack-based buffer overflow allowing unauthenticated remote code execution, scored 9.0.

**Pre-authentication memory corruption in the VPN request path.** Classic, and the highest-risk class to actually exploit against production because failure means a crash.

Archetype: Fortinet FortiOS SSL-VPN. CVE-2023-27997 is a heap-based buffer overflow in SSL-VPN allowing a remote attacker to execute arbitrary code, scored 9.8. CVE-2024-21762 is an out-of-bounds write in the same product family allowing execution of unauthorised code, also 9.8. The same vendor's CVE-2024-55591 is an authentication bypass using an alternate path, allowing a remote attacker to gain super-administrator privileges through crafted requests to a websocket module, and CVE-2025-32756 is a stack-based buffer overflow spanning several of the vendor's product lines.

**Command injection through a parameter that reaches a shell.** The appliance takes a value from a request and interpolates it into a shell command or a filesystem path without sanitisation. Highly reliable to exploit, low crash risk, and therefore the class most suitable for careful validation against production.

Archetype: CVE-2024-3400 in the GlobalProtect feature of PAN-OS, described as command injection as a result of an arbitrary file creation vulnerability, enabling an unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary code with root privileges on the firewall, scored 10.0, with the vendor noting that the cloud, management-appliance and cloud-access variants of the product are not affected.

**Authentication bypass on a management interface.** The management interface should not be internet-facing at all, and frequently is. Archetype: CVE-2025-0108, an authentication bypass in the PAN-OS management web interface allowing an unauthenticated attacker with network access to bypass authentication and invoke certain scripts, categorised as missing authentication for a critical function and scored 8.8, with the vendor noting it does not itself give code execution but affects integrity.

**Unauthenticated access to an administrative function.** The most embarrassing class: a function that should require authentication does not check for it.

Archetypes: CVE-2023-20198 in the Cisco IOS XE web user interface, scored 10.0 and used as the initial access step in observed exploitation before a second flaw was used to escalate. CVE-2024-47575 in FortiManager, missing authentication for a critical function, scored 9.8. CVE-2024-27198 in JetBrains TeamCity, an authentication bypass allowing administrative actions, scored 9.8.

**Arbitrary file read.** Less dramatic than code execution and frequently just as effective, because the file you read is a configuration file containing credentials, a private key, or a session database. Archetype: CVE-2024-24919 in Check Point Security Gateways, information disclosure on gateways with remote access or mobile access enabled, scored 8.6.

**Deserialisation of untrusted data.** The dominant remote code execution class in managed application platforms, and the one that most often bypasses input validation entirely because the input is a serialised object rather than a string. Where the platform uses a cryptographic key to validate serialised state, leaking that key converts the platform's own state mechanism into a code execution primitive.

Archetype: CVE-2025-53770 in on-premises SharePoint Server, deserialisation of untrusted data allowing an unauthorised attacker to execute code over a network, scored 9.8, in the known exploited catalogue with active exploitation and a remediation due date of 21 July 2025. It is part of a chain that also involves CVE-2025-49706, improper authentication allowing spoofing, and CVE-2025-49704, code injection allowing an authorised attacker to execute code, together with CVE-2025-53771, a further improper authentication issue. The pattern to take from it: an authentication or spoofing weakness that gets you to an authenticated code path, plus a deserialisation primitive in that path.

**Improper authorisation allowing state reset.** Archetype: CVE-2023-22518 in Confluence Data Center and Server, an improper authorisation vulnerability allowing an unauthenticated attacker to reset the instance and create an administrator account, scored 9.8. Its predecessor CVE-2023-22515 allowed creation of unauthorised administrator accounts on publicly accessible instances, also 9.8. Both illustrate that "reset to a known state and create an administrator" is as good as code execution and is a distinct class from it.

**Hybrid identity trust abuse.** Newer and worth watching: a flaw not in a network-facing parser but in the trust relationship between an on-premises component and a cloud tenant. Archetype: CVE-2025-53786, an improper authentication issue arising from the guidance and configuration for hybrid Exchange deployments, scored 8.0. The class matters because the compromise crosses the boundary the organisation believed existed.

### Managed file transfer as its own class

**Why it deserves separate treatment.** Managed file transfer products combine every property you want in a target: internet-facing by design, holding the organisation's most sensitive data in bulk because that is their function, business-critical so patching is deferred, deployed by teams who are not security teams, and built on application stacks with long histories. The consequence has been a sustained run of mass-exploitation events against this product category, and it is the category where a single flaw most reliably yields data rather than merely access.

The archetypes, all confirmed and all in the known exploited catalogue:

| Product | Identifier | Class | Score |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Progress MOVEit Transfer | CVE-2023-34362 | SQL injection in the web application allowing an unauthenticated attacker to gain access to the database, and from there further impact | 9.8 |
| Cleo Harmony, VLTrader, LexiCom | CVE-2024-50623 | Unrestricted file upload and download leading to remote code execution | 9.8 |
| Cleo Harmony, VLTrader, LexiCom | CVE-2024-55956 | Unauthenticated import and execution of arbitrary shell commands by leveraging the default settings of an autorun directory | 9.8 |
| CrushFTP | CVE-2024-4040 | Server-side template injection allowing unauthenticated attackers to read files outside the sandbox, bypass authentication for administrative access, and execute code | 9.8 |
| CrushFTP | CVE-2025-31161 | Authentication bypass and takeover of the administrative account via a race condition in an S3-compatible authorisation method | 9.8 |

Note the recurring sub-patterns: default configuration doing something dangerous, template injection in a product that renders user-controllable content, and authentication logic with a race. Those are the things to look for in the next one.

### Exposed management interfaces

**The generic class, and it is the highest-yield thing to enumerate.** An administrative interface for anything, reachable from the internet, is a finding regardless of whether it has a named vulnerability, because the population of things that go wrong on an exposed management interface is large: default credentials, no authentication at all, an authentication bypass, a known exploit, or simply the fact that it is administrative and therefore a direct path to control.

What actually turns up on real perimeters, and each is worth a specific check:

- **Build and automation systems.** Continuous integration servers, artefact repositories, configuration management. Frequently reachable, frequently with weak authentication, and compromise yields both code execution and credentials to everything the pipeline touches. The CI/CD material in the Cloud and Modern Identity section covers this in depth.
- **Monitoring and observability.** Metrics, dashboards, log search, alerting. These aggregate information from the entire estate and frequently hold credentials for data sources, and read access alone is a substantial reconnaissance win.
- **Container and orchestration APIs.** Container daemon sockets and orchestration control planes exposed without authentication are a direct route to code execution on the host.
- **Databases and caches.** Databases and in-memory data stores exposed without authentication remain a real finding, more often in cloud deployments than on-premises.
- **Virtualisation and hypervisor management.** Management consoles and bare-metal hypervisor interfaces. Compromise here is compromise of everything running on the platform, and the virtualisation material in the Enterprise Infrastructure section covers what to do next.
- **Out-of-band management controllers.** Baseboard management controllers and their vendor-branded equivalents. Full pre-boot control of the host, a separate and usually ancient firmware stack, frequently default credentials, and almost never patched. The network-device material in the Enterprise Infrastructure section covers this territory.
- **Remote desktop and remote shell.** Direct exposure of remote desktop, virtual network computing, or remote management protocols. Where these are exposed, spraying against them is often the shortest path in the whole engagement.
- **Collaboration and knowledge platforms.** Wikis, issue trackers, code hosting. Both a target and an intelligence source: an internal wiki frequently contains architecture diagrams, runbooks, and credentials.
- **Enterprise management suites.** Network management, service desk, endpoint management, backup management. These have privileged agents on every host in the estate by design, which makes them the highest-value target class on any perimeter and the one where a single flaw yields the whole environment. The backup and storage material in the Enterprise Infrastructure section covers the backup case specifically.
- **Printers, cameras, building management, and other embedded devices.** Low value individually, and useful as a foothold on a segment nobody watches.

**Commands.** Discovery is the reconnaissance you already did; the specific step here is checking each one for the obvious failures.

```bash
# Templated checks for exposed panels, default credentials and missing
# authentication. Use tags to keep the request volume proportionate.
nuclei -l live.txt -tags panel,exposure,default-login,misconfig -severity medium,high,critical \
       -rate-limit 20 -o nuclei-panels.txt

# Screenshot everything, then triage visually. An exposed management interface
# is usually obvious at a glance and invisible in a text log.
httpx -l live.txt -ss -sr -srd recon-output -silent

# Non-HTTP services that answer without authentication
nmap -sV -Pn -p 2375,2376,6443,10250,5900,3389,5985,5986,623,161,9200,27017,6379 \
     --script=banner -oA mgmt-services $TARGETS
```

### Web application classes that lead to code execution or credential access

Full web application testing is a discipline in its own right and this document does not attempt it; what belongs here is which classes actually produce a *foothold* rather than a finding, because that is a much shorter list than the full catalogue of web vulnerabilities.

| Class | Why it yields a foothold | What to look for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pre-authentication SQL injection | Database access, credential hashes, and on several database engines a direct path to command execution | Unauthenticated search, login, and report parameters |
| Deserialisation | Direct code execution in the application's process | Serialised objects in cookies, view state, hidden fields, message queues, and any base64 blob that round-trips |
| Server-side template injection | Direct code execution | Anywhere user input reaches a template: error messages, name fields, email templates, document generation |
| Command injection | Direct code execution | Features that invoke external tools: conversion, imaging, network diagnostics, archive handling, printing |
| Arbitrary file upload | Code execution where the upload directory is served and executed | Upload features, and the interaction between extension checks and the web server's handler mapping |
| Path traversal to file read | Configuration files with credentials, private keys, session stores, source code | Any parameter naming a file, template, locale, theme, report or download |
| Server-side request forgery | Cloud instance metadata, and therefore cloud credentials. Also internal service access | URL parameters, webhook configuration, document fetchers, image proxies, PDF renderers. Check whether the environment enforces the hardened metadata service |
| XML external entity processing | File read and sometimes request forgery | Any XML or document-format upload, SAML endpoints, SOAP services |
| Authentication bypass via path normalisation or proxy confusion | Access to authenticated functionality | Disagreements between a reverse proxy and the application about what a path means. Encoded separators, semicolons, dot segments, double slashes |
| Token and assertion flaws | Authentication as any user | Unverified signatures, algorithm confusion, key confusion, missing audience checks. Especially on SAML and JWT paths |
| Exposed version control and configuration | Source code, credentials, internal hostnames | `.git`, `.svn`, `.env`, `.DS_Store`, editor backup files, archives named after the application |
| Secrets in front-end bundles | API keys, service credentials, internal endpoints | JavaScript bundles and their source maps. Consistently productive and consistently overlooked |
| Subdomain takeover | Control of a hostname in the target's own domain | Dangling records pointing at unclaimed third-party services. Consult the community-maintained catalogue of which services are claimable and how |

Two of these deserve extra comment for a campaign.

**Subdomain takeover is uniquely valuable to an initial access campaign** and not primarily as an exploitation finding. A hostname you control *inside the target's own domain* solves the domain reputation problem, the certificate transparency problem, and the plausibility problem in one move: your phishing link is on their domain, it has a valid certificate for their domain, and it passes URL reputation because their domain is reputable. That makes a takeover of a marketing subdomain worth considerably more to you than a low-severity finding on the main application. Note that claiming the dangling resource is registering something on a third-party platform and needs specific authorisation.

**Server-side request forgery reaching cloud instance metadata** is the standard route from a web application flaw to cloud credentials, and whether it works depends on whether the environment enforces the hardened, token-requiring version of the metadata service. Check the version in use, because it determines whether a simple request forgery is sufficient or whether you need a full request-forging primitive that can set headers.

### Validating an exploit safely against a production perimeter

This is the part that separates professional work from an outage. The technique is not the risk; the *validation* is.

**Establish a confidence ladder and climb it in order.** Do not start at the top.

1. **Version and configuration inference.** Fingerprint the product and version from banners, static asset paths, response characteristics and behaviour. Conclude "the exposed version is within the affected range". Zero risk. Frequently sufficient for the report.
2. **A safe, read-only, vendor-documented check.** Many advisories describe an observable that distinguishes vulnerable from patched without exercising the flaw. Nuclei templates are largely of this kind. Minimal risk.
3. **An out-of-band check.** For injection and request forgery classes, trigger an interaction with infrastructure you control rather than executing anything on the target. A DNS lookup or an HTTP request from the target proves the primitive without changing state. Low risk and high evidential value.
4. **Read-only exploitation.** Read a file, read a memory region, list a directory. Proves the flaw, changes nothing. This is the level at which most engagements should conclude on a production appliance.
5. **State-changing exploitation.** Write a file, create an account, execute a command. Real risk, needs a window and an agreement.
6. **Memory corruption.** Highest risk. A failed attempt against an appliance can crash the process, and on many appliances that means a device reboot and a loss of connectivity for every remote worker.

**Specific rules that prevent the specific accidents.**

**Do not fire memory corruption exploits at appliances during business hours.** The failure mode is not "the exploit did not work". It is "the device rebooted and four hundred remote staff lost their connection". If the class is memory corruption and the target is a remote access appliance, negotiate a window, tell the client exactly when, and have them watching.

**Reproduce in a lab before you touch production, whenever you can.** Vendor trial images and evaluation licences are widely available for exactly these products. An afternoon spent making the exploit reliable against a local instance of the same version converts an unbounded risk into a known one, and it tells you what the artefacts look like so you can describe them accurately in the report.

**Read the exploit code before you run it.** Public proof-of-concept code for high-profile perimeter vulnerabilities is a known vector for malicious code aimed at the people who run it. Assume any exploit you did not write is hostile until you have read it. Specific things to look for: outbound connections to addresses you did not configure, base64 or hex blobs that get executed, dependency installation from unexpected sources, obfuscated payloads, and shellcode you have not disassembled. Run it in an isolated environment the first time, on a host with nothing on it.

**Understand what the payload does before you send it.** A Metasploit module with a default payload will do something specific to the target. Know what. On an appliance, a payload that spawns a process in an unexpected way can destabilise the device even when the exploit itself is reliable.

**Check whether you are looking at a honeypot.** A deliberately vulnerable, deliberately exposed host is a real possibility on a mature target's perimeter and interacting with it hands the defender your tooling and your infrastructure.
