Greppable output exists for pipelines and is genuinely convenient, but it is a lossy summary. If you ran `-sV -sC` and only kept the `.gnmap`, you threw away the results. Always `-oA`, parse the `.gnmap` for target lists, and parse the `.xml` for anything you will put in a report. Writing output is also what makes `--resume` possible at all, and long sweeps do get interrupted.

#### Timing and performance

These are the flags that decide whether a scan finishes.

| Flag | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `-T0` to `-T5` | Timing templates: paranoid, sneaky, polite, normal, aggressive, insane. Each sets a bundle of the individual knobs below. `-T4` is equivalent to `--max-rtt-timeout 1250ms --min-rtt-timeout 100ms --initial-rtt-timeout 500ms --max-retries 6` plus a 10ms cap on TCP scan delay; `-T5` is `--max-rtt-timeout 300ms --min-rtt-timeout 50ms --initial-rtt-timeout 250ms --max-retries 2 --host-timeout 15m`. Note that neither caps UDP scan delay. |
| `--min-rate <pps>` | Send no slower than this many packets per second, overall |
| `--max-rate <pps>` | Send no faster than this |
| `--min-hostgroup <n>` | Scan at least this many hosts in parallel as one group |
| `--max-hostgroup <n>` | Cap on the same |
| `--min-parallelism <n>` | At least this many probes outstanding at once |
| `--max-parallelism <n>` | Cap on the same. `1` serialises entirely. |
| `--max-retries <n>` | Probe retransmissions per port. `-T4` sets 6, `-T5` sets 2. `0` disables retransmission entirely, which is fast and lossy. |
| `--host-timeout <t>` | Abandon a host after this long, however incomplete |
| `--initial-rtt-timeout <t>` | Starting guess for round trip time |
| `--min-rtt-timeout <t>` / `--max-rtt-timeout <t>` | Floor and ceiling on how long to wait for a reply |
| `--scan-delay <t>` | Minimum wait between probes to a host |
| `--max-scan-delay <t>` | Ceiling on the delay nmap will impose on itself when it detects rate limiting |
| `--defeat-rst-ratelimit` | Stop waiting for RSTs from hosts that rate-limit them. Faster, and will mark some closed ports as filtered. |
| `--defeat-icmp-ratelimit` | Stop waiting for rate-limited ICMP port-unreachable replies. Non-responsive UDP ports are labelled `closed\|filtered` instead of `open\|filtered`, so only ports that genuinely answer over UDP are called open. Much faster UDP, meaningfully less accurate. |
| `--randomize-hosts` | Shuffle target order rather than walking the range in sequence |

**`-T` templates versus `--min-rate` is the distinction people get wrong.** A `-T` template sets timeouts, retry counts, parallelism, and scan delay together; it describes *how patiently* nmap behaves. `--min-rate` sets a floor on transmit rate; it describes *how fast* packets leave. They interact, and `--min-rate` wins where they conflict, which is exactly the trap. `-T4 --min-rate 1280` tells nmap it must push at least 1,280 packets per second **even if it has concluded that the network is dropping them**. On a clean gigabit LAN that is fine and it is why the source's scans complete. Over a saturated site-to-site VPN, or through a firewall that rate-limits, it means nmap keeps hammering a link that cannot carry the traffic, loses replies, and reports closed or filtered ports that are actually open. A hard `--min-rate` buys you wall-clock time by spending accuracy, and unlike a `-T` template it will not back off when the evidence says it should.

So: use `--min-rate` when you know the path can take it, which on a flat internal LAN it usually can. Drop it and let `-T4` adapt when you are crossing a WAN, a VPN, or a pivot. Use `--max-rate` instead when the constraint is politeness or detection rather than speed.

**`--min-hostgroup` is what makes large ranges tractable.** Nmap scans in groups of hosts, and it does not report any host in a group until the whole group is done. The default group size starts small and grows, which for a single-port sweep across a /16 is disastrously inefficient: nmap spends its time waiting on RTT for a handful of hosts instead of keeping the pipe full. `--min-hostgroup 256` forces at least 256 hosts in flight, so the timeout for one silent host is amortised across 255 others. For a one-to-sixteen-port sweep across a large range, 256 to 1024 is right. The cost is latency in reporting: with `--min-hostgroup 1024` you see nothing until 1,024 hosts have finished, which is unhelpful if you wanted to start attacking early. That tension is why sweeps use large host groups and deep scans use small ones.

The general shape of the tradeoff:

| Situation | Settings |
| --- | --- |
| Flat internal LAN, few ports, huge range | `-T4 --min-hostgroup 512 --min-rate 2000 --max-retries 2 --host-timeout 15s` |
| Same, but you want early results to attack from | `-T4 --min-hostgroup 64 --min-rate 1000 --max-retries 2` |
| Across a VPN or WAN, lossy | `-T3 --min-hostgroup 64 --max-retries 4 --host-timeout 60s`, no `--min-rate` |
| Firewall is rate-limiting (nmap says so in `-v` output) | `-T3 --max-rate 300 --max-retries 3 --max-scan-delay 100ms` |
| Through a SOCKS pivot | `-sT -Pn -n -T4 --max-retries 1 --host-timeout 45s --max-parallelism 24` |
| Deep scan of a shortlist | `-T4 -p- --min-rate 500 --max-retries 3` per host, small host groups |
| Stealth matters | `-T2` or `-T1`, `--max-rate 20`, `--randomize-hosts`, one port at a time |
| Fragile OT or medical kit | `-sT --max-rate 10 --max-retries 1`, no `-sV`, no `-sC`, ask first |

Two diagnostics you should learn to read. When `-v` output says `Increasing send delay for 10.14.32.7 from 0 to 5 due to 11 out of 11 dropped probes`, nmap has detected loss and is backing off; if you have pinned `--min-rate` it cannot back off properly and your results are now suspect. When it says `Warning: 10.14.32.7 giving up on port because retransmission cap hit`, your `--max-retries` is too low for the path and you are losing open ports.

### Tier 1: liveness

**What it is.** Reduce a scoped address space to the addresses that have something behind them.

**Why the source's ping sweep misses most of a modern estate.** The source runs `nmap -sP -PE`, which is ICMP echo request and nothing else. On a 2010 network that was reasonable. Today:

- **Windows Firewall blocks inbound ICMPv4 echo by default** in the Domain, Private, and Public profiles. A domain-joined Windows workstation or server, out of the box, does not answer ping. Since Windows endpoints are the majority of most estates, an echo-only sweep can miss the majority of the estate.
- Host firewalls on Linux server builds are frequently configured the same way by baseline policy, and most hardening guides tell you to drop echo.
- Network ACLs commonly permit ICMP only between management ranges, so your foothold's source address is not one that gets answers.
- Cloud and virtual network security groups default to denying ICMP while permitting the service ports.
- Load balancers, NAT devices, and reverse proxies present a service on an address with no host that answers ICMP at all.

The rule to internalise: **"no response" is not "no host". It is "no information".** A liveness sweep produces a list of hosts that are definitely up. It does not produce a list of addresses that are definitely empty, and treating it as though it does is how you miss the domain controller.

There are three consequences. First, use several probe types, not one. Second, on the local segment use ARP, because ARP is authoritative. Third, and most importantly, **for the port-scanning tiers use `-Pn` and scan addresses regardless of whether they answered discovery.** A tier 2 sweep of 16 ports across a /16 is only sixteen times the cost of the ping sweep, and it finds every host whose firewall drops ICMP but allows SMB. On anything up to a /16, `-Pn` on the tier 2 sweep is simply the correct default, and the ping sweep becomes a cheap way to prioritise rather than a filter.

**ARP is different and you should trust it.** On your own broadcast domain, a host must answer ARP to receive IP traffic at all. There is no host firewall setting that suppresses ARP replies while leaving the host usable, because ARP is handled below the filtering layer. So on the local segment, ARP discovery is not a heuristic, it is ground truth, and it finds machines that drop every IP-layer probe you could send. Nmap does this automatically for local targets when privileged, which is why a `-sn` scan of your own subnet finds far more than a `-sn` scan of a remote one. It also means `-Pn` is pointless locally and `--disable-arp-ping` is usually a mistake.

**Preconditions.** Raw sockets for `-sS`, `-sn` with ARP, and any ICMP probe. A TCP connect scan and a `-sT` sweep are the unprivileged fallbacks. `--exclude` your own address, because scanning yourself wastes time and produces confusing results.

**Commands.**

```bash
mkdir -p nmap

# Local segment: ARP is authoritative. Nmap does this automatically for on-link targets.
sudo nmap -sn -n -v -e $IFACE $TARGETS -oA nmap/local-arp
sudo arp-scan -I $IFACE --localnet            # dedicated tool, also prints MAC vendors
sudo netdiscover -i $IFACE -r $TARGETS -P -N

# Remote ranges: multi-probe liveness, not echo alone
sudo nmap -sn -n -v --randomize-hosts \
  -PE -PP -PS445,443,3389,22,80,135 -PA80,443 -PU161,137 \
  --min-hostgroup 256 --min-rate 1280 --max-retries 2 --host-timeout 15s \
  --exclude $ATTACKER -iL $TARGETS -oA nmap/tier1-liveness

# Unprivileged fallback: TCP connect probes only
nmap -sn -n -v -PS445,443,3389,22,80 -iL $TARGETS -oA nmap/tier1-unpriv
```

`fping` is worth keeping around for the pure-ICMP case because it is faster than nmap at that one job and its output needs no parsing:

```bash
fping -a -q -g $TARGETS 2>/dev/null > alive-icmp.txt
```

The probe set in the tier 1 command is chosen deliberately. `-PE -PP` covers hosts that answer either ICMP type. `-PS445,443,3389,22,80,135` covers the overwhelming majority of live machines in a corporate estate: a Windows box answers on 445 or 135 or 3389, a Linux box on 22, anything with a management interface on 443. `-PA80,443` slips past stateless ACLs that filter SYN but pass ACK. `-PU161,137` catches network kit and Windows hosts that reply with an ICMP port unreachable, proving liveness even when every TCP port is filtered. On a domain network `-PU137` in particular finds Windows machines that are otherwise entirely silent.

**Verify it worked.**

```bash
awk -F'\t' '$2=="Status: Up" {split($1,a," "); print a[2]}' nmap/tier1-liveness.gnmap \
  | sort -u -t. -k1,1n -k2,2n -k3,3n -k4,4n > hosts-alive.txt
wc -l hosts-alive.txt
grep -c "^Host:" nmap/tier1-liveness.gnmap      # total addresses considered, sanity check
```

Sanity-check the number against reality. If a /22 that AD sites and subnets says is a user VLAN comes back with four live hosts, you have not found four hosts, you have found a filtering policy. Cross-check by running the tier 2 sweep with `-Pn` over the same range and comparing counts; a large discrepancy is the answer.

**Detection and opsec.** A liveness sweep touches every address in the range once or twice, which means a very high count of distinct destinations from one source in a short window. This is the classic **address scan** signature and it is what NDR platforms threshold on. It is more distinctive than a port sweep, because a port sweep at least resembles a scanner or vulnerability management appliance hitting a small set of hosts, whereas nothing benign walks an entire /16 saying hello. Vulnerability scanners do exactly this on a schedule though, which is why so many internal sweeps go unremarked: the estate already contains something that behaves identically. Find out whether it does, and from which source addresses, before deciding how careful to be.

**Failure modes.**

- **`You requested a scan type which requires root privileges.`** You asked for `-sS`, ICMP probes, or ARP without raw sockets. Use `-sT` and `-PS`, or fix the privileges.
- **Everything reports up.** You left `-Pn` on a `-sn` scan, or there is a device answering for the whole range. Check with `--reason`; if every host's reason is the same and the TTLs are identical, one box is answering for all of them.
- **Zero hosts up on a range you know is populated.** ICMP and your probe ports are all filtered. Skip tier 1 for that range and go straight to a `-Pn` tier 2 sweep.
- **Scan appears hung with no output.** `--min-hostgroup` is large and you are waiting for the first group to complete. Add `--stats-every 30s`, or lower the host group.

### Tiers 2 and 3: TCP port sweeps

#### What the source's port lists actually are

The source has three overlapping TCP lists with no explanation of any of them. They are worth dissecting, both because the reasoning is recoverable and because two of them contain outright errors that an operator would repeat.

**The small list:** `80,443,22,23,445,8080,8443,3389`. This one is good and its logic is sound: web, SSH, telnet, SMB, RDP. Eight ports that between them identify almost every machine a penetration tester wants to talk to, at eight probes per host. As a tier 2 list it holds up in 2040 with one glaring omission, which is WinRM on 5985 and 5986. On a modern Windows estate WinRM is the primary remote management path and is very often reachable when 3389 is not.

**The "Nessus discovery" list:** `139,135,445,80,22,515,23,21,6000,1025,25,111,1028,1029,79,497,548,5000,1917,53,161,49000,443,993,8080,2869,88,2222,3389`. This is heritage. It descends from the default port list of a Nessus TCP scanner from the era of Windows XP and Solaris, and it shows: 1025, 1028, and 1029 were the low ephemeral RPC ports Windows 2000 and XP used before the dynamic range moved to 49152 and above; 79 is finger; 497 is Retrospect backup; 1917 is an obsolete registered service; 2869 is the UPnP/SSDP HTTP endpoint of Windows XP-era networking; 548 is AFP, still alive on Macs but not the way you attack them; 6000 is X11, which is a genuinely great find but rare now; 515 is LPD printing, which is real but you would rather have 9100. Meanwhile it includes **161, an SNMP port, over TCP**, which is nearly always useless because SNMP is a UDP protocol and the TCP transport is not commonly enabled. That one port is the clearest tell that the list was copied rather than reasoned about.

**The "Nessus list minus the small list" variant:** `88,139,135,515,21,6000,1025,25,111,1028,1029,79,497,548,5000,1917,53,161,49000,993,8080,2869`. This is supposed to be the set difference so you can run it after the small sweep without duplicating work. It is wrong twice. It **still contains 8080**, which is in the small list, so it is not a set difference. And it **drops 2222**, which is in the full list and not in the small list, so it should have been kept. On top of that the full list is not a superset of the small list either, because the small list has 8443 and the full list does not. Three inconsistencies in a nine-line snippet, all of them invisible unless you sit down and diff the lists by hand.

**Common mistake.** Hand-maintaining set differences between port lists. It is fiddly, it silently breaks, and it saves almost nothing: re-scanning eight ports you have already done costs eight probes per host. If you genuinely want the difference, compute it rather than typing it:

```bash
SMALL="80,443,22,23,445,8080,8443,3389,5985,5986"
BROAD="21,22,23,25,53,80,88,111,135,139,389,443,445,464,515,548,636,993,1433,2049,2222,3268,3269,3306,3389,5432,5900,5985,5986,6000,6379,8000,8080,8443,9100,9200,9389,47001,49152"
comm -23 <(tr ',' '\n' <<<"$BROAD" | sort -n) <(tr ',' '\n' <<<"$SMALL" | sort -n) | paste -sd, -
```

#### Nmap's own answer: `--top-ports`

Nmap ships `nmap-services`, which carries an empirically measured open-frequency for every port. `--top-ports <n>` selects the N most frequently open ports, which is a far better default than any hand-written list, and `-F` is the top 100. Use it as your baseline.

But understand where the frequency data came from, because it changes how you use it. It is derived largely from internet-wide scanning, so it is weighted towards internet-exposed services and under-weights the ports that matter on an internal Windows network. Measured against the shipped `nmap-services` data, the TCP frequency ranks are:

| Port | Service | Rank in `nmap-services` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 445 | SMB | 9 |
| 8443 | HTTPS alt | 37 |
| 1433 | MSSQL | 42 |
| 49152 | Windows dynamic RPC | 43 |
| 88 | Kerberos | 57 |
| 389 | LDAP | 75 |
| 5432 | PostgreSQL | 84 |
| 636 | LDAPS | 143 |
| 3268 | AD Global Catalog | 187 |
| **5985** | **WinRM HTTP** | **430** |
| 5986 | WinRM HTTPS | 429 |
| 9200 | Elasticsearch | 732 |
| 6379 | Redis | 1683 |
| 2375 | Docker API, unauthenticated | 2903 |
| 6443 | Kubernetes API | 4867 |
| 47001 | Windows HTTPAPI / WinRM listener | 5484 |

So `--top-ports 100` misses WinRM, LDAPS, and the Global Catalog. `--top-ports 1000` misses Redis, Docker, Kubernetes, and 47001. The internet's idea of a common port is not your idea of an interesting port. The practical answer is `--top-ports` **plus** an explicit list of the internal ports you care about, which nmap merges for you:

```bash
nmap --top-ports 1000 -p 5985,5986,6379,2375,2376,6443,9200,9300,10250,47001,27017,11211,8009,15672,61616 ...
```

#### A clean tiered set of lists

```bash
# Tier 2: is this host worth a second look. 12 ports.
T2="22,80,135,139,443,445,1433,3389,5985,5986,8080,8443"

# Tier 2-DC: does this host look like a domain controller. Run across the whole range.
TDC="53,88,135,139,389,445,464,636,3268,3269,9389"

# Tier 3: broad service discovery. ~60 ports, live hosts only.
T3="21,22,23,25,53,80,88,110,111,135,139,143,389,443,445,464,465,515,548,587,623,636,873,993,995,1080,1099,1433,1521,1723,2049,2181,2222,2375,2376,3128,3268,3269,3306,3389,4786,5000,5432,5601,5672,5900,5985,5986,6000,6379,7001,8000,8009,8080,8081,8161,8443,8888,9000,9092,9100,9200,9389,10250,11211,15672,27017,47001,49152,61616"

# Tier 3b: nmap's own frequency data plus the internal ports it under-weights
# (use --top-ports 1000 with an explicit -p supplement)
```

What each tier 2 port buys you:

| Port | Service | Why it is in tier 2 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 22 | SSH | Linux, network kit, appliances. Key reuse and weak creds. |
| 80, 443 | HTTP(S) | The largest attack surface in any estate, and the fastest to triage |
| 135 | MSRPC endpoint mapper | Proves Windows. Feeds RPC enumeration and DCOM lateral movement. |
| 139, 445 | NetBIOS, SMB | The single most valuable internal port. Host and domain identification, shares, signing state, relay viability, and the path for most lateral movement. |
| 1433 | MSSQL | Links, `xp_cmdshell`, service account privilege, and it is everywhere |
| 3389 | RDP | Interactive access, certificate and NLA state, session harvesting |
| 5985, 5986 | WinRM | The modern remote management path. Frequently open where RDP is not. |
| 8080, 8443 | Alt HTTP(S) | Management consoles, CI, appliances, forgotten Tomcat |

**Commands.**

```bash
# Tier 2 across the whole scope, with -Pn so host firewalls cannot hide anything
sudo nmap -sS -Pn -n -v --open --reason --randomize-hosts \
  -p $T2 \
  --min-hostgroup 256 --min-rate 1280 --max-retries 2 --host-timeout 30s \
  --exclude $ATTACKER -iL $TARGETS -oA nmap/tier2-tcp

# Domain controller fingerprint sweep across the whole scope. Cheap, and it finds the
# machines that matter most.
sudo nmap -sS -Pn -n -v --open -p $TDC \
  --min-hostgroup 256 --min-rate 1280 --max-retries 2 \
  --exclude $ATTACKER -iL $TARGETS -oA nmap/tier2-dc

# Tier 3, live hosts only
sudo nmap -sS -Pn -n -v --open --reason -p $T3 \
  --min-hostgroup 64 --min-rate 1000 --max-retries 3 --host-timeout 120s \
  --exclude $ATTACKER -iL hosts-alive.txt -oA nmap/tier3-tcp

# Tier 3 alternative using nmap's frequency data plus the internal supplement
sudo nmap -sS -Pn -n -v --open --top-ports 1000 \
  -p 5985,5986,6379,2375,2376,6443,9200,10250,47001,27017,11211,8009,15672,61616 \
  --min-hostgroup 64 --min-rate 1000 \
  --exclude $ATTACKER -iL hosts-alive.txt -oA nmap/tier3-topports
```

**Tier 4: the deep scan.** Only on the shortlist, and only after tiers 2 and 3 have told you which hosts deserve it. Split it by service class, because the right follow-up for an SMB host is not the right follow-up for a web host.

```bash
# full TCP on the genuinely interesting hosts, in the background from early on
sudo nmap -sS -Pn -n -v --open -p- \
  --min-rate 800 --max-retries 3 \
  -iL shortlist.txt -oA nmap/tier4-allports

# version and default scripts on what tiers 2 and 3 actually found, per host
sudo nmap -sS -sV -sC -Pn -n -v --version-intensity 5 \
  -p $(awk -F'\t' '{print $2}' ports-per-host.tsv | sort -un | paste -sd, -) \
  -iL shortlist.txt -oA nmap/tier4-versions
```

Two things to keep straight about tier 4. `-p-` on a shortlist is where you find the interesting stuff, because non-standard ports are where administrators hide management interfaces and where developers leave debug listeners. And `-sV -sC` is the first point in the whole progression at which you are having real conversations with services, which means it is the first point at which application logs, failed authentications, and crashed embedded devices become your problem.

**Verify it worked.**

```bash
# host, port, proto, state, service from greppable output
awk -F'\t' '/\tPorts: / {
  split($1,h," "); ip=h[2];
  for (i=2; i<=NF; i++) if ($i ~ /^Ports: /) {
    p=substr($i,8); n=split(p,arr,", ");
    for (j=1; j<=n; j++) { split(arr[j],f,"/");
      if (f[2] ~ /^open/) print ip"\t"f[1]"\t"f[3]"\t"f[2]"\t"f[5] }
  }
}' nmap/tier2-tcp.gnmap | sort -u -t. -k1,1n -k2,2n -k3,3n > ports-per-host.tsv

# per-service target lists, which is what you actually attack from
awk -F'\t' '$2==445 {print $1}' ports-per-host.tsv | sort -u > smb.txt
awk -F'\t' '$2==3389 {print $1}' ports-per-host.tsv | sort -u > rdp.txt
awk -F'\t' '$2==5985 || $2==5986 {print $1}' ports-per-host.tsv | sort -u > winrm.txt
awk -F'\t' '$2==80 || $2==443 || $2==8080 || $2==8443 {print $1":"$2}' ports-per-host.tsv | sort -u > web.txt

# what is most common, to decide where to spend effort
cut -f2,5 ports-per-host.tsv | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -30
```

The cross-check that matters: `wc -l` of the tier 2 host list against `hosts-alive.txt` from tier 1. If tier 2 with `-Pn` found substantially more hosts than tier 1 found alive, tier 1 was being filtered and every conclusion you drew from it is suspect. That comparison is the single most useful number in the whole scanning phase and the source cheatsheet never computes it. It does concatenate the ping sweep and TCP sweep host lists, which is the right instinct:

```bash
cat hosts-alive.txt <(cut -f1 ports-per-host.tsv) | sort -u -t. -k1,1n -k2,2n -k3,3n -k4,4n > targets.txt
```

**Detection and opsec.** See the detection and opsec section below; the short version is that tier 2 across a whole range is a horizontal scan and is what NDR is built to spot, while tier 4 against a shortlist looks much more like normal administration.

**Failure modes.**

- **Every port on every host reports `filtered`.** A firewall is dropping rather than resetting. Confirm with `--reason` (`no-response` everywhere) and try `-PA`, a source port of 53 or 88 via `-g`, or accept that this path is blocked and pivot.
- **Every port on every host reports `open`.** Something is answering SYN for all addresses: a load balancer, a NAT device, a security appliance in transparent proxy mode, or an SYN-proxying firewall. Verify by completing a handshake and sending protocol data; if 445 and 22 and 3389 all speak the same nothing, they are all the same appliance. `-sT` plus `--reason` plus a `-sV` on a couple of ports settles it quickly.
- **Results differ between reruns.** You are losing packets. Lower `--min-rate` or drop it, raise `--max-retries`, and rerun the diff.
- **Scan finishes far too fast.** Check for a typo in `-p` or a `--host-timeout` so short that nmap gave up on everything. Nmap reports timed-out hosts in `-v` output; read it.
- **`Failed to resolve` on every line.** You forgot `-n` and the resolver is broken or unreachable.

### UDP scanning, honestly

The source has a UDP sweep with a literal `-pPORTS` placeholder and no guidance whatsoever. That is the honest reflection of how most people treat UDP: they know they should and they never do. It is worth doing, but only if you understand why it behaves the way it does, because otherwise you will run `-sU` against a /16 and it will still be going when the engagement ends.

**Why UDP scanning is slow and unreliable.** TCP gives you an unambiguous answer per probe: SYN/ACK means open, RST means closed. UDP has no handshake, so there is no positive acknowledgement of a closed port from the protocol itself. Nmap has to infer state from side channels:

| Response | State nmap reports |
| --- | --- |
| A UDP datagram back | `open` |
| ICMP type 3 code 3, port unreachable | `closed` |
| ICMP type 3, other codes (1, 2, 9, 10, 13) | `filtered` |
| Nothing at all, after retries | `open\|filtered` |

Two properties of that table cause all the pain. First, the only cheap negative signal is ICMP port unreachable, and **Linux rate-limits ICMP destination unreachable messages by default** (governed by `net.ipv4.icmp_ratelimit` and `net.ipv4.icmp_ratemask`) to roughly one per second. So scanning 1,000 UDP ports on one Linux host takes on the order of 1,000 seconds no matter how fast you send, because the host will not tell you about closed ports any faster than that. Nmap detects this and throttles itself accordingly, which is correct and is also why the scan takes seventeen minutes per host.

Second, an open UDP port only replies if your datagram looks like something the service understands. A DNS server ignores an empty datagram; it answers a DNS query. Nmap ships a payload database and sends protocol-appropriate probes for the ports it knows, which is why 53, 161, 137, 123, and 500 give reliable answers. For everything else it sends an empty datagram, the service ignores it, and you get `open|filtered`: **nmap could not distinguish an open port from a firewalled one.** That is not a bug and no scanner can do better without a protocol-specific probe.

This is where the source's `--reason` flag comes in, uncommented. `--reason` adds a column showing what decided each state, and on a UDP scan it is the difference between a useless and a useful result:

```text
PORT     STATE         SERVICE  REASON
53/udp   open          domain   udp-response ttl 127
123/udp  open          ntp      udp-response ttl 127
161/udp  open|filtered snmp     no-response
162/udp  open|filtered snmptrap no-response
500/udp  closed        isakmp   port-unreach ttl 127
```

Reading that: 53 and 123 genuinely answered. 500 is genuinely closed, and crucially **the fact that you got a port-unreach at all proves the host is up and not blanket-filtering UDP**, which retroactively upgrades those `no-response` results from "no information" to "probably filtered or probably a service that ignores empty datagrams". Without `--reason` you cannot make that distinction and every UDP result is equally worthless. Always use `--reason` on UDP scans.

**Which UDP ports are actually worth your time.** On an internal network, a short and well-chosen list:

| Port | Service | What it yields |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 53 | DNS | Internal name resolution, reverse zones, sometimes zone transfer, and the ADIDNS path |
| 67, 68 | DHCP | Subnet mask, gateway, DNS servers, domain name, and classless static routes describing the internal topology |
| 69 | TFTP | Unauthenticated read of network device configs, which contain credentials. Blind reads of predictable filenames still work. |
| 88 | Kerberos | Confirms a KDC. Combined with TCP 389 and 445 this is a DC. |
| 111 | rpcbind | Portmap dump, and the map of NFS exports |
| 123 | NTP | Host enumeration via `monlist` on unpatched ntpd, and clock skew which matters for Kerberos |
| 137 | NetBIOS name service | Hostname, domain, and service roles from a single query. **Works on Windows hosts that filter 445**, which makes it one of the highest-value UDP ports on a Windows estate. |
| 161 | SNMP | The best single UDP find internally. Full device config, interface list, ARP cache, routing table, running processes, installed software, and with a read-write community, config write and credential recovery. |
| 162 | SNMP trap | Indicates a management station worth attacking |
| 389 | CLDAP | Connectionless LDAP. A netlogon-style probe returns the domain name, forest name, DC name, and AD site without any credential. Excellent for identifying DCs and mapping site topology cheaply. |
| 500 | IKE / ISAKMP | VPN endpoint. Vendor fingerprint, and aggressive mode PSK hash recovery where it is enabled. |
| 623 | IPMI | Baseboard management controller. The RAKP authentication hash disclosure and cipher-zero authentication bypass are still live on real estates, and a BMC is a full out-of-band takeover of its host. |
| 1434 | MSSQL browser | Instance names and, critically, the **dynamic TCP port** of each named instance, which you cannot find with a TCP sweep of standard ports |
| 1900 | SSDP / UPnP | Device inventory, and on consumer-grade kit, port mapping you can abuse |
| 2049 | NFS | Exports, and frequently world-readable shares |
| 4500 | IPsec NAT-T | VPN endpoint behind NAT |
| 5353 | mDNS | Hostnames, service inventory, macOS and IoT discovery |
| 5355 | LLMNR | Confirms LLMNR is enabled, which is a prerequisite for name poisoning |
| 11211 | memcached | Unauthenticated cache dump, often containing session tokens |
| 17185 | VxWorks WDB debug agent | Unauthenticated memory read and write on embedded and OT devices |

**Commands.**

```bash
U_TOP="53,67,69,88,111,123,137,161,162,389,500,623,1434,1900,2049,4500,5353,5355,11211,17185"

# Sweep the high-value list across the whole scope. --reason is not optional here.
sudo nmap -sU -Pn -n -v --open --reason -p $U_TOP \
  --min-hostgroup 256 --min-rate 1280 --max-retries 2 --host-timeout 60s \
  --exclude $ATTACKER -iL $TARGETS -oA nmap/udp-sweep

# Faster and less accurate: non-responses become closed|filtered, so only ports that
# actually answer over UDP are reported open
sudo nmap -sU -Pn -n -v --open --reason --defeat-icmp-ratelimit -p $U_TOP \
  --min-hostgroup 512 --max-retries 1 --host-timeout 30s \
  -iL $TARGETS -oA nmap/udp-sweep-fast

# Confirm the ambiguous results with version detection on a tiny port set
sudo nmap -sU -sV -Pn -n -v --reason --version-intensity 3 \
  -p 161,53,123,137,623,1434 -iL hosts-alive.txt -oA nmap/udp-verify

# Targeted follow-up per service, which is where the value actually is
sudo nmap -sU -p161 --script snmp-info,snmp-sysdescr,snmp-interfaces,snmp-netstat -iL snmp.txt
sudo nmap -sU -p137 --script nbstat -iL $TARGETS
sudo nmap -sU -p623 --script ipmi-version,ipmi-cipher-zero -iL $TARGETS
sudo nmap -sU -p111 --script rpcinfo -iL $TARGETS
sudo nmap -sU -p500 --script ike-version -iL $TARGETS
sudo nmap -sU -p1900 --script upnp-info,broadcast-upnp-info -iL $TARGETS
sudo nmap -sU -p2049 -sV --script nfs-showmount -iL $TARGETS
ike-scan -M $TARGET                                  # then -A for aggressive mode
onesixtyone -c community.txt -i hosts-alive.txt      # SNMP community discovery at speed
```

Notice that the useful UDP work is almost all in the targeted follow-up, not the sweep. The sweep exists to produce `snmp.txt`. Twenty ports across a range is affordable; a thousand ports is not, and the marginal ports are not worth it.

**Verify it worked.** The `open|filtered` state is why the source's extraction is broken for UDP. `grep open/` matches the literal string `open/`, and in greppable output an ambiguous UDP port is written `161/open|filtered/udp//snmp///`. There is no `open/` in that, so **`grep open/` silently discards every ambiguous UDP result**, which on a UDP scan is most of the data you have. Match a prefix instead:

```bash
# includes both open and open|filtered
awk -F'\t' '/\tPorts: / {
  split($1,h," "); ip=h[2];
  for (i=2; i<=NF; i++) if ($i ~ /^Ports: /) {
    p=substr($i,8); n=split(p,arr,", ");
    for (j=1; j<=n; j++) { split(arr[j],f,"/");
      if (f[2] ~ /^open/) print ip"\t"f[1]"\t"f[3]"\t"f[2]"\t"f[5] }
  }
}' nmap/udp-sweep.gnmap > udp-results.tsv

awk -F'\t' '$4=="open"' udp-results.tsv                    # confirmed
awk -F'\t' '$4=="open|filtered"' udp-results.tsv | wc -l    # how much you cannot resolve
awk -F'\t' '$2==161 && $4 ~ /^open/ {print $1}' udp-results.tsv | sort -u > snmp.txt
```

**Detection and opsec.** UDP sweeps are quieter per host than TCP sweeps simply because they are slower, but the fanout pattern is the same and NDR thresholds on distinct destinations, not on protocol. SNMP probes with wrong community strings generate authentication failure traps on managed devices, which land in the network team's monitoring rather than the security team's, and network teams often notice things security teams do not. IKE probes are logged by every VPN concentrator. IPMI probes are logged by BMCs, which nobody reads. And `-sU -sV` against embedded or OT devices genuinely crashes them; UDP stacks on industrial kit are far less robust than TCP stacks, and a malformed probe to a PLC is an outage.

**Failure modes.**

- **Everything is `open|filtered`.** Either UDP is blocked in the path, or the host is silently dropping. Look for a single `closed` result anywhere on that host; one `port-unreach` proves the host answers and reclassifies everything else as meaningful.
- **The scan is projected to take days.** You gave `-sU` too many ports. Cut to the twenty-port list, or add `--defeat-icmp-ratelimit`, which stops nmap waiting for rate-limited port-unreachable replies and reports only genuinely answering ports as open.
- **`Warning: Servicescan failed to fill...`** Version detection on UDP is best-effort and frequently gives up. Not an error, just the limit of the technique.
- **Results change every run.** UDP is unreliable by design and probes get lost. Run it twice and take the union, which is legitimate rather than sloppy here.

### Fast scanners, and when they win

Nmap is accurate and stateful, which is exactly why it is slow: it tracks every probe, retransmits, adapts timing, and can tell you *why* a port is in a state. For the discovery phase you do not need any of that, you need a list of open ports. That is what the stateless scanners are for, and the standard modern pattern is **discover wide with a fast scanner, then characterise narrow with nmap**.

| Tool | Model | Strength | Weakness |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `nmap` | Stateful, adaptive | Accuracy, service and script detection, reasons, output fidelity | Slow at very large scale |
| `masscan` | Stateless SYN with its own TCP stack | Enormous ranges at very high rates | No real service detection, drops results under load, needs raw sockets |
| `naabu` | SYN when privileged, connect otherwise | Fast, clean nmap handoff, sane defaults, list-friendly | Discovery only, by design |
| `rustscan` | TCP connect, batched | Very fast per host, accurate because handshakes complete, integrated nmap handoff | Connect scan means it completes handshakes, so application logs see it; per-host rather than per-range strength |

#### masscan

Stateless means masscan does not keep per-probe state: it transmits at a fixed rate and records whatever comes back, using its own userland TCP stack rather than the kernel's. That is how it reaches rates nmap cannot. The consequence is that a lost reply is simply lost, so **masscan's accuracy is a function of rate**: at 1,000 packets per second on a LAN it agrees with nmap almost perfectly, at 100,000 across a WAN it will miss open ports and never tell you.

```bash
masscan -p1-65535,U:53,U:161 --rate 20000 \
  -iL $TARGETS --excludefile exclude.txt \
  --open-only -oL masscan-full.txt

# masscan -oL format: state proto port ip timestamp
awk '$1=="open" {print $4}' masscan-full.txt | sort -u -t. -k1,1n -k2,2n -k3,3n -k4,4n > masscan-hosts.txt
awk '$1=="open" && $2=="tcp" {print $3}' masscan-full.txt | sort -un | paste -sd, - > masscan-tcp-ports.txt

# hand off to nmap for the detail
sudo nmap -sS -sV -sC -Pn -n -v --open --reason \
  -p "$(cat masscan-tcp-ports.txt)" -iL masscan-hosts.txt \
  --min-rate 500 --max-retries 3 -oA nmap/stage2
```

Practical notes. `--rate` is a transmit rate, not a promise; if the NIC, the switch, or the path cannot carry it, masscan will not notice and you will get quiet false negatives, so start conservative and raise it while comparing against nmap on a sample. `--retries` adds retransmission and materially improves accuracy at the cost of proportionally more packets. `--wait` controls how long masscan listens after transmitting; the default is short and on a high-latency path you will lose the tail of your results, so raise it. Interrupting masscan writes a `paused.conf` which `--resume paused.conf` picks up. And `--excludefile` is not optional on a real engagement, because masscan at rate will happily flatten a printer or an OT device.

The `--banners` option grabs banners, which needs masscan to own the TCP conversation; because the host kernel would otherwise send a RST and kill it, masscan wants to use a source address the kernel does not answer for, plus a firewall rule to keep the kernel out of the way. It works, and it is still not a substitute for `-sV`.

#### naabu

naabu is the discovery-phase tool with the cleanest nmap integration, which makes it the natural front end for the two-stage pattern.

```bash
naabu -list $TARGETS -top-ports 1000 -rate 3000 -silent -o naabu-out.txt
naabu -list $TARGETS -p 22,80,135,139,443,445,1433,3389,5985,5986,8080,8443 -rate 5000 -o naabu-tier2.txt
naabu -list $TARGETS -top-ports 1000 -exclude-ports 9100,515,631 \
  -nmap-cli 'nmap -sV -sC --open --reason -oA nmap/naabu-stage2'
naabu -list $TARGETS -p - -rate 2000 -json -o naabu.json
```

`-scan-type s` is SYN and `-scan-type c` is connect; SYN is the default when privileged. `-nmap-cli` runs nmap over exactly the host and port pairs naabu found, which is the two-stage pattern in a single command. `-exclude-ports` is worth using to keep printers out of the scan.

#### rustscan

rustscan does batched TCP connect scans and then hands the open ports to nmap after `--`. Because handshakes complete, its results are accurate, and because it is a connect scan it works in places raw sockets do not.

```bash
rustscan -a $TARGET -r 1-65535 --ulimit 5000 -- -sV -sC --reason
rustscan -a $TARGETS -p 22,80,443,445,3389,5985 -g            # greppable
rustscan -a $TARGET --ulimit 5000 -t 1500 -b 2000 -- -A
```

The two knobs that decide whether rustscan is accurate are `--ulimit` and the timeout. Raise `--ulimit` and it goes faster; raise it too far relative to what the path can carry, or leave the timeout too low, and connections that would have succeeded time out and are recorded as closed. If rustscan and nmap disagree, raise the timeout before you believe rustscan.

#### Choosing

Use nmap alone up to about a /20 with a small port list; the speed difference is not worth the complexity. Use masscan or naabu when you have a /16 or larger, or when you need all 65,535 ports across more than a handful of hosts. Use rustscan when you want all ports on a specific host quickly, or when you cannot get raw sockets. And in every case validate: pick five hosts the fast scanner called empty and run nmap against them properly. If nmap finds ports the fast scanner missed, your rate is too high and every result you have is suspect.

### Scanning through a SOCKS proxy

**What it is.** After a pivot, your access to the internal network is a SOCKS proxy exposed by an implant or an SSH dynamic forward. Establishing that proxy in the first place, and the proxychains and layer 3 tunnelling detail, is covered in the Lateral Movement section. Scanning through it works, but almost everything in this section changes.

**Why SYN scanning cannot work through a proxy.** SOCKS is a session-layer protocol. Its entire vocabulary is "connect me to this host and port, and then relay bytes". There is no way to express "emit a bare SYN and describe the response", because the proxy's own kernel performs the handshake and the proxy only reports success or failure back to you. Raw packet construction is not available at any point, so:

- `-sS` is impossible. Every TCP scan through SOCKS is a connect scan, and you must say `-sT` explicitly since nmap defaults to `-sS` when privileged.
- `-sU` is effectively impossible. SOCKS5 defines a UDP ASSOCIATE command, but implant SOCKS servers usually do not implement it and `proxychains` does not proxy UDP at all.
- ICMP is impossible, so host discovery cannot work. `-Pn` is **mandatory**, not optional.
- `-O` and `--traceroute` are impossible; they need raw packets.
- `--min-rate`, `--max-rate`, and the RTT knobs become nearly meaningless, because your rate is set by the tunnel and the implant's sleep, not by anything nmap decides.

You also inherit a fundamentally different state model. Connect scan semantics are: connection established means open, connection refused means closed, timeout means filtered. The proxy usually collapses "refused" and "filtered" into a generic failure, so **through most SOCKS proxies you can distinguish open from not-open and nothing more.** Plan accordingly: scan for the small set of ports you intend to attack, and stop trying to characterise firewall behaviour.

**Preconditions.** A working SOCKS listener, and DNS handled deliberately. If the implant's SOCKS server cannot resolve names, or resolves them at your end, you will scan the wrong things. Use `-n` and IP addresses, and resolve names separately through a deliberate channel.

**Commands.**

```bash
# /etc/proxychains4.conf
#   strict_chain
#   proxy_dns          # comment out if you are resolving separately, which you should be
#   [ProxyList]
#   socks5 127.0.0.1 1080

proxychains4 -q nmap -sT -Pn -n -v --open \
  -p 22,80,135,139,443,445,1433,3389,5985,5986,8080,8443 \
  -T4 --max-retries 1 --host-timeout 45s --max-parallelism 24 \
  -iL internal-hosts.txt -oA nmap/pivot-tier2
```

The tuning above is not arbitrary. `--max-retries 1` because every retry is a full round trip over the C2 channel and retries are where proxied scans go to die. `--host-timeout 45s` to bound the damage from unreachable hosts. `--max-parallelism 24` because proxychains and most implant SOCKS servers fall over or start returning spurious failures when you open hundreds of simultaneous connections, and a broken proxy produces false negatives that look exactly like closed ports. If results look implausibly sparse, halve the parallelism and rerun.

Nmap does have a native `--proxies` option, but it is documented as incomplete and applies only to some scan types. `proxychains-ng` is the reliable route for nmap specifically.

**The better answer: get a real interface.** The right fix for all of the above is not to tune the proxy, it is to stop using one. `ligolo-ng` presents the remote network on a local TUN interface, so the kernel routes to it as a normal network. Once you have that, raw sockets work again, which means `-sS`, `-sU`, ICMP host discovery, and OS fingerprinting all come back, and nmap's timing logic works because it is measuring a real path rather than a proxy's behaviour. If you are going to do more than a handful of scans through a pivot, set this up first; it will save more time than any amount of flag tuning.

```bash
# on the operator host, once the ligolo-ng tunnel is established
sudo ip route add $TARGETS dev ligolo
sudo nmap -sS -Pn -n -v --open -p 22,80,135,139,443,445,1433,3389,5985,5986 \
  -T4 --max-retries 2 -iL internal-hosts.txt -oA nmap/pivot-syn
```

Other options and their limits. `ssh -D 1080` gives you a SOCKS5 proxy with the same constraints as any other. `chisel` gives you SOCKS over HTTP for restrictive egress, same constraints. `sshuttle` builds a transparent TCP-and-DNS tunnel via local packet filtering, which is more convenient than proxychains but still carries no UDP and no ICMP. Where the C2 framework provides its own port scanner running on the implant, that is often the fastest option for a quick look because it avoids the round trip entirely, at the cost of running scanning code inside a process EDR is watching. Cobalt Strike's `portscan` is the well-known example.

Whatever you use, keep the port list short and targeted. Through a pivot, a twelve-port tier 2 sweep across a /24 is a reasonable afternoon; `-p-` across a /24 is not going to happen.

**Detection and opsec.** Proxied scans are connect scans, so unlike a SYN scan they **complete handshakes and the target applications log them**. A tier 2 sweep across a /24 through a proxy produces a real connection and immediate teardown on every open port, which web servers, SSH daemons, and SQL servers all record. Additionally, all of that traffic originates from your pivot host, so from the defender's point of view one internal workstation suddenly started talking to 254 machines on twelve ports. That is a far stronger signal than an external scan, because internal workstation-to-workstation fanout has no benign explanation, and it is exactly the behaviour lateral movement detection is tuned for. Scan less, scan more precisely, and prefer targeting hosts you have a reason to target.

**Failure modes.**

- **Every port on every host reports closed or filtered.** The proxy is not actually forwarding. Test with a single known-open port using `curl --socks5-hostname` or `nc -X 5 -x 127.0.0.1:1080` before blaming the network.
- **Nmap warns it needs privileges.** You omitted `-sT`; it is trying to do a SYN scan. Add `-sT -Pn`.
- **Wildly inconsistent results between runs.** Parallelism is too high for the proxy, or the implant's sleep is long. Lower `--max-parallelism`, and set the implant's sleep to zero for the duration if the engagement permits it.
- **`proxychains` reports timeouts on everything after a while.** File descriptor exhaustion or a dead tunnel. Check the implant is still alive.
- **Hostnames resolve to the wrong thing.** `proxy_dns` is on and resolving through the chain, or off and resolving locally. Pick one deliberately, and prefer `-n` with IPs.

### Output handling

The source's extraction is `grep Up ... | cut -d' ' -f2` and `grep open/ ... | cut -d' ' -f2`, repeated five times. It works often enough to be dangerous. Collected, the problems are:

- **`grep Up` is an unanchored substring match.** It matches any line containing "Up", including resolved hostnames such as `backup01`, `supply-svr`, or `groupwise`. Without `-n` this silently injects down hosts into your target list.
- **`grep open/` misses `open|filtered`.** The greppable form is `161/open|filtered/udp//snmp///`, which contains no `open/`. On UDP scans, which is precisely where the source uses it, this discards the bulk of the results.
- **`cut -d' ' -f2` assumes the address is always the second space-delimited field**, which holds for `Host: 10.0.0.1 ()` and stops holding the moment the line format shifts or a hostname is present in an unexpected position.
- **Both patterns throw away the port.** You end up with a list of hosts that had something open, with no record of what, so the next tier cannot be targeted and you rescan blindly.
- **Nothing distinguishes the `Status:` lines from the `Ports:` lines**, so a scan that produced both can have its host list and its port list conflated.

Greppable output is one line per host, tab-delimited, with fields like `Host: `, `Status: `, `Ports: `, and `Ignored State: `. The per-port form within the `Ports:` field is `port/state/protocol/owner/service/rpc_info/version/`, comma-space separated. Parse on the tab and the slash, not on spaces:

```bash
# hosts up
awk -F'\t' '$2=="Status: Up" {split($1,a," "); print a[2]}' scan.gnmap

# all non-closed ports, as host/port/proto/state/service
awk -F'\t' '/\tPorts: / {
  split($1,h," "); ip=h[2];
  for (i=2; i<=NF; i++) if ($i ~ /^Ports: /) {
    p=substr($i,8); n=split(p,arr,", ");
    for (j=1; j<=n; j++) { split(arr[j],f,"/");
      if (f[2] ~ /^open/) print ip"\t"f[1]"\t"f[3]"\t"f[2]"\t"f[5] }
  }
}' scan.gnmap
```

For anything beyond target lists, parse the XML. It is the only output that retains NSE script results, version strings and their confidence, OS guesses, state reasons, and per-host timing. Greppable output has none of that, which means a `-sV -sC` scan whose XML you discarded has to be rerun.

```python
import xml.etree.ElementTree as ET

def parse(path: str) -> None:
    root = ET.parse(path).getroot()
    for host in root.iter("host"):
        if (status := host.find("status")) is None or status.get("state") != "up":
            continue
        addr = next(
            (a.get("addr") for a in host.iter("address") if a.get("addrtype") == "ipv4"),
            None,
        )
        names = [n.get("name") for n in host.iter("hostname")]
        for port in host.iter("port"):
            state = port.find("state")
            if state is None or not state.get("state", "").startswith("open"):
                continue
            svc = port.find("service")
            product = " ".join(
                filter(None, (svc.get("product"), svc.get("version"), svc.get("extrainfo")))
            ) if svc is not None else ""
            scripts = {s.get("id"): s.get("output") for s in port.iter("script")}
            print(
                f"{addr}\t{port.get('portid')}/{port.get('protocol')}\t"
                f"{state.get('state')}\t{state.get('reason')}\t"
                f"{svc.get('name') if svc is not None else ''}\t{product}\t"
                f"{','.join(names)}\t{';'.join(scripts)}"
            )

if __name__ == "__main__":
    import sys
    for p in sys.argv[1:]:
        parse(p)
```

Two shortcuts worth knowing. `-oX` output carries a stylesheet reference, so `xsltproc scan.xml -o scan.html` produces a browsable report with no extra tooling. And `nmap -oG -` writes greppable output to stdout, which is what you want when you are piping a scan straight into something else rather than keeping files:

```bash
sudo nmap -sn -n -oG - $TARGETS --exclude $ATTACKER \
  | awk '/Status: Up/{print $2}' > local-hosts.txt

xsltproc nmap/tier3-tcp.xml -o nmap/tier3-tcp.html
```

Merging results across scans is where the discipline pays off. Keep one `ports-per-host.tsv` accumulating from every scan you run, deduplicate it, and derive every per-service target list from it. That way a host found by masscan, a host found by the tier 2 nmap sweep, and a host found by the DC fingerprint sweep all end up in the same place, and you never scan the same thing twice because you lost the record.

```bash
cat nmap/*.gnmap | awk -F'\t' '/\tPorts: / {
  split($1,h," "); ip=h[2];
  for (i=2; i<=NF; i++) if ($i ~ /^Ports: /) {
    p=substr($i,8); n=split(p,arr,", ");
    for (j=1; j<=n; j++) { split(arr[j],f,"/");
      if (f[2] ~ /^open/) print ip"\t"f[1]"\t"f[3]"\t"f[2]"\t"f[5] }
  }
}' | sort -u > all-ports.tsv
```

### Detection and opsec

**What a SYN sweep looks like to the network.** Every flow monitor and NDR platform on the market builds a per-source-address model of behaviour, and the two features that matter are **distinct destination addresses** and **distinct destination ports**, counted over a rolling window. A tier 2 sweep maximises the first: one source touching every address in a range on a handful of ports. That is a horizontal or address scan, and it is the loudest thing in this section because nothing benign does it except a vulnerability scanner. A `-p-` scan against one host maximises the second: a vertical or port scan, which is loud in a different way but affects one destination and is much easier to lose in the noise.

In flow terms a SYN scan is a mass of flows with a single packet out and either nothing back or a single RST back, never establishing. Zeek records that as `S0` or `REJ` connection history, and that is the durable part of the statement. Be careful about the next step, because the folklore is out of date: **Zeek does not ship a scan detection policy.** There is no `policy/misc/scan.zeek` in a current distribution; the only scan-shaped script in the tree is a SumStats framework teaching example under `doc/`. Scan detection comes from a package installed through the Zeek package manager, or from the site's own SumStats script, which means the thresholds are whatever that package's author chose and whatever the site then tuned. So do not plan your pacing against a remembered default. If you have access to the deployment, read the loaded scripts and the actual threshold constants; if you do not, assume something in the region of tens of distinct destinations over a few minutes because that is the common shape, and understand that you are assuming. Commercial NDR does the same thing with more machine learning attached, and endpoint agents on the targets often report the inbound connection attempts too, so the same scan gets detected from both directions.

**Rate is the main detection variable.** Almost every scan detection is a threshold over a time window, so the same total number of probes spread over eight hours frequently does not trigger what the same probes in eight seconds does. That is the whole basis of stealthy scanning, and it is why `-T2`, `--max-rate`, and `--scan-delay` exist. It also means the correct stealth strategy is not "scan the same thing more slowly" but "scan much less". A slow, targeted scan of forty hosts on twelve ports beats a fast broad sweep on every axis: it is faster in wall-clock terms, it is under every threshold, and its results are more accurate.

Practical measures, roughly in order of value:

| Measure | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| Scan fewer hosts and fewer ports | The only one that reliably works. Derive targets from AD, DNS, and DHCP instead of sweeping. |
| `--randomize-hosts` | Removes the sequential-walk pattern, which is a trivially detectable signature |
| `--max-rate` and `-T2` / `-T1` | Stay under rate thresholds, at proportional cost in time |
| `--scan-delay` | Per-host pacing, which is what some detections actually measure |
| Split the scan across sources | Thresholds are usually per source address. Two footholds scanning half each halves each one's count. |
| Split the scan across time | One port across the whole range per hour, rather than twelve at once |
| `-g 53` or `-g 88` (source port) | Slips past stateless ACLs that permit by source port. Does nothing against stateful inspection or flow analytics. |
| `-D` decoys | Interleaves spoofed source addresses to obscure which is real. Does not reduce your own traffic, and burns credibility with the client if it triggers an incident. |
| `-sI` idle scan | Genuinely blind to the target, but needs a zombie with a globally incrementing IP ID, which modern operating systems do not provide. Effectively a museum piece. |
| Avoid `-sV`, `-sC`, and `-A` in sweeps | These complete handshakes and speak protocols, generating application-layer log entries and authentication failures |

**The `-sS` versus `-sT` opsec differential is real and worth using.** A SYN scan never completes the handshake, so the target application never sees a connection and logs nothing. The kernel and any host firewall see it, and an EDR agent with a network filter driver may see it, but the SSH daemon, the web server, and the SQL server do not. A connect scan completes and tears down, so every one of those services records a connection. If your scan is going through a SOCKS proxy you have no choice and you are generating application logs on every host you touch, which is another reason to keep proxied scans small.

**Ask, do not assume.** On a large number of internal engagements the honest answer is that nobody is watching. There is no NDR, the IDS is in monitor-only mode with default rules, the SIEM ingests domain controller logs and nothing else, and the vulnerability management appliance sweeps the entire estate every Tuesday so your scan is genuinely indistinguishable from business as usual. Under those conditions, spending three days on a slow scan to avoid detection that was never going to happen is the worst possible use of the engagement. Conversely, if the client has a mature SOC and the objective is to test detection, a fast sweep on day one ends the covert phase immediately.

So find out, and find out at the start. The specific questions worth asking, because they change what you do rather than just being nice to know: is there an NDR or IDS in the environment and is it in blocking or monitoring mode; does a vulnerability scanner sweep the estate, from which source addresses, and on what schedule; is this a detection test or an access test; is there any kit that must not be scanned, and can I have the list; will NAC or port security shut my switch port if I scan, and who do I call when it does. That last one is not theoretical; scan-triggered quarantine is common in NAC deployments and it will end your engagement's network access in the middle of a sweep. Better to know the number to ring.


## Service Enumeration

A port sweep produces a list of open sockets. That is not intelligence, it is a work queue. Service enumeration is the process of turning that queue into three things: an inventory of what the estate actually runs, a shortlist of hosts that will hand you a credential or a file without authentication, and a map of which authentication surfaces are misconfigured in a way you can abuse later. Almost every internal engagement is won or lost in this phase, because the difference between a two-hour path to Domain Admin and a two-day one is whether you noticed the backup console with default credentials on the third page of your httpx output.

The governing principle: **collect state, not vulnerabilities.** A scanner asks "is this host vulnerable". An operator asks "what does this host tell me about the estate, and what does it let me do without credentials". SMB signing status is not a vulnerability, it is a state flag that determines whether an entire attack class is available to you. LDAP RootDSE is not a finding, it is a free map of the forest. Collect the state first, correlate it, then decide where to spend effort.

### The triage table

This is the reference you will come back to. For each port: the service, what you extract, and why it matters. Ports are TCP unless marked UDP.

| Port | Service | Extract | Why you care |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 21 | FTP | Anonymous access, banner, writable root, directory listing | Anonymous read is common on appliances and build servers. Writable anonymous FTP on a web root is direct code execution |
| 22 | SSH | Version, host key, supported auth methods, key algorithms | Duplicate host keys across hosts means cloned images and shared keys. `keyboard-interactive` plus `password` means spraying is viable |
| 23 | Telnet | Banner, NTLM info if Windows, device model | Almost always a network device, printer, or IPMI console. Banner names the model, which names the default credentials |
| 25/587 | SMTP | Banner, `EHLO` capabilities, NTLM info, open relay, VRFY/EXPN | NTLM over SMTP leaks the domain and hostname unauthenticated. Open relay enables internal phishing from a trusted source |
| 53 | DNS | Zone transfer, SRV records, reverse PTR for the whole scope, version | Highest value per packet on any internal network. Names every host, locates every DC |
| 69 UDP | TFTP | Filename guessing for device configs | Router and switch configs, VoIP provisioning files. Configs contain credentials and SNMP strings |
| 79 | finger | User list | Legacy Unix. Free usernames |
| 80/443 | HTTP(S) | Title, status, technology, favicon hash, cert SANs, auth realm | Management interfaces with default credentials are the single most productive internal target class |
| 88 | Kerberos | Realm confirmation, user existence, pre-auth policy | Confirms an AD environment and gives you username validation and AS-REP roasting with no credentials |
| 110/143/993/995 | POP3/IMAP | Banner, NTLM info, `CAPABILITY` | Another unauthenticated NTLM domain leak. Mail servers are often the only externally reachable domain member |
| 111 | rpcbind | Program list, whether 100005 (mountd) is registered | Presence of mountd means NFS exports to enumerate |
| 123 UDP | NTP | Version, `monlist` on old daemons | `monlist` returns recently seen peers, which is free host discovery |
| 135 | MSRPC EPM | Endpoint map, interface UUIDs, bound ports, host name | Tells you which RPC services are exposed, which determines coercion and remote-execution options |
| 137 UDP | NetBIOS-NS | Machine name, workgroup or domain, logged-on user, MAC | Names a host and its domain in one UDP packet, works when SMB is locked down |
| 139/445 | SMB | Signing requirement, dialects, SMBv1, OS build, null and guest access, shares | The most important single scan on an internal network. See the SMB section |
| 161 UDP | SNMP | Community strings, sysDescr, interfaces, ARP and route tables, processes, config write | Network device configs, full topology, and frequently credentials. Very high hit rate, almost no logging |
| 389/636/3268/3269 | LDAP / LDAPS / GC | Anonymous bind, RootDSE, naming contexts, functional level, DC name, signing and channel binding policy | Fastest confirmation of an AD environment. Identifies domain, forest, and every DC |
| 427 | SLP | Service list | On ESXi this is the OpenSLP service. Also enumerates other appliances |
| 464 | kpasswd | Presence | Corroborates a KDC alongside 88 and 389 |
| 500/4500 UDP | IKE | Vendor ID, transform sets, aggressive mode | Aggressive mode with PSK yields an offline-crackable hash. Vendor ID names the firewall |
| 502 / 44818 / 47808 | Modbus / EtherNet-IP / BACnet | Device identity only | You are in OT. Read the fragile devices guidance before you touch anything here |
| 512/513/514 | rexec/rlogin/rsh | Banner | Trust-file based auth. Ancient Unix, occasionally still on tape libraries and jump hosts |
| 515 / 631 / 9100 | LPD / IPP / JetDirect | Model, firmware, SNMP string, address book | Printers hold LDAP bind credentials in their address book configuration. See printers below |
| 548 | AFP | Server info, shares | Mac fileservers and NAS. Frequently guest-readable |
| 623 UDP | IPMI | Version, cipher suites, RAKP hash disclosure | IPMI 2.0 hands out a crackable password hash to unauthenticated requesters. BMC access is out-of-band host takeover |
| 873 | rsync | Module list, whether modules require auth | Anonymous rsync modules are often whole-filesystem backups |
| 902 / 5988 / 5989 | VMware authd / CIM | Version | Confirms an ESXi host behind the web UI |
| 1099 / 4444 | Java RMI | Registry object list | RMI registry with a bound object is often deserialisation RCE |
| 1433 / 1434 UDP | MSSQL | Instance names, version, NTLM info, blank `sa` | Named instances on 1434 UDP reveal dynamic ports. `ms-sql-ntlm-info` leaks the domain unauthenticated |
| 1521 | Oracle TNS | Version, SID or service name | SID is a precondition for everything else against Oracle. Default credentials are legion |
| 1723 | PPTP | Presence | Legacy VPN, MS-CHAPv2 crackable |
| 2049 | NFS | Exports, export options, root squash setting | `no_root_squash` on a writable export is local privilege escalation and often lateral movement |
| 2181 / 2379 | ZooKeeper / etcd | Unauthenticated key dump | etcd on 2379 without auth is the entire Kubernetes cluster secret store |
| 2375 / 2376 | Docker API | `/version`, `/containers/json` | Unauthenticated 2375 is root on the host, trivially, via a privileged bind-mount container |
| 3000 | Grafana and friends | Version, login page | Default `admin/admin` is still endemic. Grafana holds datasource credentials |
| 3128 / 8080 | Proxy | Whether it will forward | An open internal proxy is a pivot and an egress path |
| 3260 | iSCSI | Target IQNs, whether CHAP is required | An unauthenticated iSCSI target is a raw disk image you can mount offline, including VM disks |
| 3306 | MySQL | Version, whether remote root is permitted, blank password | Older builds and appliance-embedded instances frequently allow `root` from anywhere |
| 3389 | RDP | NTLM info, NLA state, certificate CN | `rdp-ntlm-info` gives you DNS domain, NetBIOS name, and OS build with no credentials. NLA disabled means credential-free screenshotting |
| 4786 | Cisco Smart Install | Presence | Unauthenticated config read and write on affected switches |
| 5000 / 5001 | Various | Title | Synology DSM, Docker registry, and a dozen application defaults live here |
| 5060/5061 | SIP | Options response, extension enumeration | VoIP extensions and their weak digest passwords |
| 5432 | PostgreSQL | Version, whether `trust` auth is in `pg_hba` | `trust` for a non-local subnet means no password at all, and `COPY FROM PROGRAM` is command execution as the service account |
| 5601 | Kibana | Version, whether auth is enforced | Pre-8.0 Kibana is often anonymous, and its Elasticsearch backend holds indexed logs full of credentials |
| 5672 / 15672 | AMQP / RabbitMQ mgmt | Version, `guest/guest` | Management plugin with default guest gives message contents and often application credentials |
| 5900-5906 | VNC | Supported security types | Security type 1 is "None". A no-auth VNC console is an interactive session with no credential |
| 5985 / 5986 / 47001 | WinRM | Whether it answers, auth mechanisms | The primary post-credential execution path. Note 5986 for HTTPS, not 5956 |
| 6000-6010 | X11 | Whether access control is disabled | `xhost +` means keylogging and screen capture of a live desktop |
| 6379 | Redis | `INFO`, whether auth is required, protected-mode | Unauthenticated Redis is file write as the service account, which is RCE by several routes |
| 6443 / 10250 / 10255 | Kubernetes API / kubelet | Anonymous API access, `/pods`, `/runningpods` | Anonymous kubelet on 10250 with `--authorization-mode=AlwaysAllow` is exec into any pod on the node |
| 7001 | WebLogic | Version, console path | A long history of pre-auth deserialisation RCE. Console default credentials too |
| 8006 | Proxmox | Version | Hypervisor management. Root here is every VM's disk |
| 8009 | AJP | Presence | Tomcat AJP connector, file read and sometimes RCE if a listener is exposed |
| 8080 / 8443 / 8000 / 8888 | HTTP alternates | Same as 80/443 | Where management interfaces actually live. Never scan only 80 and 443 |
| 8086 | InfluxDB | Version, whether auth is enabled | Time-series data and an auth-bypass history |
| 8089 | Splunk mgmt | Version | Splunk REST API. Splunk credentials often reach everywhere because of universal forwarders |
| 8111 / 8153 | TeamCity / GoCD | Version | CI servers hold deployment credentials and run arbitrary build steps by design |
| 8140 | Puppet | Presence, CA | Configuration management is authority over every managed node |
| 8443 | Many | Title, cert | VMware, Fortinet, PRTG, Tomcat, and a hundred appliances |
| 8500 | Consul | Whether the HTTP API is open | Open Consul allows service registration and often script execution via health checks |
| 9000 | SonarQube, PHP-FPM, ClickHouse | Title, protocol | Disambiguate. PHP-FPM on 9000 reachable off-host is RCE |
| 9042 | Cassandra | Version, `cassandra/cassandra` | Default superuser is unchanged more often than not |
| 9090 / 9100 | Prometheus / node_exporter | Targets list, metrics | Prometheus has no auth by default and its targets list is a complete asset inventory of the monitored estate |
| 9200 / 9300 | Elasticsearch | `_cat/indices`, cluster name, version | Pre-8.0 clusters are usually anonymous. Indices contain logs, and logs contain credentials |
| 9392 / 9401 | Veeam | Version | Veeam holds credentials for every backed-up system, recoverable from its own database |
| 9418 | git daemon | Repository list | Anonymous git clone of internal source, including committed secrets |
| 10000 | Webmin, Backup Exec agent | Title, protocol | Disambiguate carefully. Both are high value |
| 11211 | memcached | `stats`, `stats items` | Cached session tokens and application data, no auth by design |
| 17988 / 17990 | HP iLO | Version | Corroborates iLO alongside the web UI |
| 27017 / 27018 | MongoDB | `listDatabases` without auth | Older deployments bind to all interfaces with no auth |
| 61616 | ActiveMQ | Version | Deserialisation and a recent history of pre-auth RCE |
| 49152+ | Dynamic RPC | Which interface is bound, via 135 | Resolve through the endpoint mapper rather than guessing |

### Service and version detection

**What it is.** Probing an open port to determine the application, version, and often the underlying OS, so that you can decide whether the port is interesting without manually connecting to it.

**Why it works.** Nmap's version detection has two stages. First it reads whatever the service volunteers on connect, which handles the large set of protocols that send a banner unprompted. If that does not produce a match, it walks a probe list, sending protocol-specific byte sequences and matching the responses against regular expressions in *nmap-service-probes*. Each probe is tagged with the ports it is normally relevant to and a rarity value from 1 to 9. `--version-intensity` sets the rarity ceiling, so intensity 2 sends only the most common probes and intensity 9 sends everything. This matters operationally because the probes are, by design, malformed or unexpected input to services that were not written to receive them, which is exactly the thing that crashes embedded network stacks.

The scripting engine is a separate layer that runs after version detection and uses its output to decide which scripts apply. `-sC` is precisely `--script=default`, nothing more, and the `default` category is a curated set chosen for usefulness rather than for safety. It is not a synonym for `safe`.

**Preconditions.** The port must be open and reachable. Version detection on a filtered port produces nothing but delay. Scripts that need credentials take them through NSE library arguments, not through their own flags.

#### NSE categories and whether to run them

| Category | Verdict | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `safe` | Run freely | Designed not to crash, exhaust, or exploit the target. Your default building block |
| `default` | Run, with care on fragile hosts | What `-sC` gives you. Overlaps `safe` heavily but is not a subset of it |
| `discovery` | Run | Actively queries services for topology and asset data. High value, low risk |
| `version` | Run | Extension of `-sV`, only runs when version detection does |
| `auth` | Run selectively | Tests anonymous and default access. Some members attempt logins, which touches lockout policy |
| `vuln` | Selectively, never blanket | Many members are safe checks, some are not. Read the script before running it against production |
| `intrusive` | Selectively | The category exists to say "this may bring something down or be logged loudly" |
| `brute` | Never blanket | Account lockout risk across a whole estate. Spray deliberately with a purpose-built tool instead |
| `dos` | Never on an engagement | It does what it says |
| `exploit` | Only against a chosen target | Not an enumeration tool |
| `fuzzer` | Never during enumeration | Slow, destructive, pointless at this stage |
| `malware` | Rarely | Looks for existing backdoors. Occasionally useful on a compromise assessment |
| `broadcast` | Locally only, deliberately | Sends broadcast and multicast traffic on your local segment. Genuinely useful for discovery, but noisy and it announces you |
| `external` | Understand before running | Sends data about the target to third parties. That is a data-handling decision, not a technical one |

The composite you want most of the time is an explicit intersection rather than a bare `-sC`:

```bash
# Broad, safe, useful. The workhorse.
nmap -sS -sV --version-intensity 5 -Pn -n -T4 -iL targets.txt \
  --script "default and safe" -oA nmap/services

# Everything nmap knows about SMB, minus the parts that log in
nmap -p139,445 -sV -iL smb-hosts.txt --script "smb* and not brute" -oA nmap/smb

# The unauthenticated NTLM information leak family, across every protocol that speaks it
nmap -sV -iL targets.txt --script "*-ntlm-info" -oA nmap/ntlm-info
```

#### Script arguments

NSE arguments come from shared libraries, so the same argument name works across every script that uses that library. The ones that matter:

| Argument | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `creds.global=user:pass` | Supplies credentials to every script that uses the `creds` library |
| `smbusername`, `smbpassword`, `smbdomain`, `smbhash` | SMB credentials for the whole `smb*` family |
| `unsafe=1` | Permits scripts to take actions that may crash the target. Deliberate, never casual |
| `newtargets` | Adds hosts discovered by scripts to the scan queue. Powerful and easy to lose control of |
| `max-newtargets=N` | Bounds the above |
| `http.useragent='...'` | Replaces the default nmap user agent, which is trivially signatured |
| `randomseed` | Reproducibility for anything that randomises |

```bash
nmap -p445 --script smb-enum-shares,smb-enum-users \
  --script-args 'smbusername=$USER,smbpassword=$PASS,smbdomain=$DOMAIN' $TARGET

# Long or reused argument sets belong in a file
nmap -iL targets.txt --script "default and safe" --script-args-file nse-args.txt
```

Use `nmap --script-help "<category or script>"` before running anything you have not read. It prints the description and the categories, and it is the fastest way to discover that a script you assumed was passive logs in.

#### Fragile devices

Some device classes fall over when probed. Printers, older BMCs (iLO 2 and 3, early iDRAC), VoIP handsets and call managers, UPS and PDU management cards, tape libraries, building management and OT controllers, medical devices, HSMs, and legacy embedded appliances. The failure is usually the version detection probes rather than the SYN scan, and the symptom ranges from a wedged management interface to a device that needs a physical power cycle.

Handle them by identity, not by guessing. A cheap first pass with no version detection lets you classify hosts, then you scan the robust majority aggressively and the fragile minority gently.

```bash
# Pass 1: banner-grab only, no probes, no scripts. Classify from what is volunteered.
nmap -sS -Pn -n -T3 -iL targets.txt --script banner -oA nmap/pass1

# Pass 2: fragile hosts, minimal probing, one connection at a time
nmap -sS -sV --version-light -Pn -n -T2 --max-parallelism 1 --max-retries 1 \
  --host-timeout 5m --scan-delay 100ms -iL fragile.txt -oA nmap/fragile
```

**Common mistake.** Running `nmap -A -T4` across an entire internal range because it is one flag. `-A` is `-sV -sC -O --traceroute`, applied indiscriminately, and it is the single most reliable way to knock a printer or a BMC offline and generate an incident ticket that ends your quiet phase early.

**Verify it worked.** Compare open-port counts between passes. A port that was open in the sweep and is now `filtered` or `closed` in the version scan usually means you crashed the service, not that the sweep was wrong. Re-probe that single port by hand with netcat or `openssl s_client` before concluding anything.

**Detection and opsec.** Version detection is the loudest thing in this whole phase. IDS rulesets ship nmap probe signatures, the default user agent is unmistakable, and the volume of short-lived connections from one source across many hosts is the classic scanning signature in NetFlow. Quieter alternatives: narrow the port set, drop to `--version-light`, spread the scan over time with `--scan-delay`, source from more than one internal host if you have them, and prefer protocol-native enumeration (LDAP, DNS, SMB negotiation) over probe-based fingerprinting, because those look like ordinary client behaviour.

**Failure modes.**

- All ports report `filtered` and the scan crawls: a host firewall or an inline IPS is dropping you. Confirm with a single-port scan from a different source.
- `Note: Host seems down` with `-Pn` absent: ICMP is blocked, which is normal internally. Always `-Pn` once you have already established the host exists.
- Version detection returns `tcpwrapped`: the connection was accepted and then closed before any data. Usually an inline device or TCP wrappers, and it means the port state is real but the service identity is unknown.
- Scripts silently do not run: version detection did not identify the service, so the port rule never matched. Force it with `--script` plus an explicit `-p`.

### The cross-protocol NTLM information leak

**What it is.** A family of services that will complete the first two legs of an NTLM handshake with an anonymous client and, in doing so, disclose the DNS domain name, NetBIOS domain and computer names, the DNS FQDN, and often the exact OS build number, with no credentials at all.

**Why it works.** NTLM's `CHALLENGE_MESSAGE` (type 2) is sent by the server before the client has proven anything. It carries a `TargetInfo` structure containing the NetBIOS and DNS names of the domain and computer, and, when `NTLMSSP_NEGOTIATE_VERSION` is negotiated, a `Version` field containing the major version, minor version, and build number of the server. Any protocol that wraps NTLM as an authentication mechanism inherits this leak: SMB, RDP with NLA, HTTP with Negotiate or NTLM authentication, SMTP, IMAP, POP3, MSSQL, telnet on Windows, and WinRM. That is why an unauthenticated scan can tell you a host is `FS01.corp.local`, domain `CORP`, build 20348.

This is the cheapest domain identification available and it works from a position with zero credentials.

```bash
nmap -sV -iL targets.txt --script "*-ntlm-info" -oA nmap/ntlm-info

# RDP alone, across the estate. Very high signal, very low noise.
nmap -p3389 -Pn -n --script rdp-ntlm-info -iL targets.txt -oA nmap/rdp-ntlm

# HTTP endpoints that offer Negotiate or NTLM. Path matters, so aim it.
nmap -p443 --script http-ntlm-info --script-args http-ntlm-info.root=/rpc/ $TARGET
nmap -p443 --script http-ntlm-info --script-args http-ntlm-info.root=/ews/ $TARGET
```

**Verify it worked.** You get a `DNS_Domain_Name` and `NetBIOS_Computer_Name` in the output. If you only get a product version, NTLM was offered but the target info block was empty, which some non-Windows implementations do.

**Detection and opsec.** Effectively invisible. You are performing the opening leg of a legitimate authentication attempt and then hanging up. No logon failure is recorded because no authentication was attempted. This is the enumeration you run when you cannot afford to be seen.

### SMB and NetBIOS

SMB is where an internal engagement is decided. It is the protocol that tells you the OS, the domain, the shares, the users, and, above all, whether relay is on the table.

#### Signing status: the single most important field you will collect

**What it is.** Every SMB server advertises, in its negotiate response, whether message signing is *enabled* (supported if the client asks) and whether it is *required* (mandatory, connection fails without it). You want the required flag, per host, across the entire estate.

**Why it matters.** NTLM relay works because NTLM authenticates a session but does not bind that session to the channel it arrived on. You coerce or capture an authentication from a victim account, forward the challenge and response to a different server, and that server authenticates you as the victim. SMB signing is what breaks this: signing keys are derived from the session key, which is derived from the account's NT hash.
