| High value marking | `highvalue` boolean property | Tiering and asset tags, surfaced as a tag list property |
| Owned marking | `owned` boolean property, set by hand-editing the DB | An asset tag applied through the UI or API |
| Custom queries | `customqueries.json` on the local filesystem | Saved queries stored server side, exposed over the API |
| Query language | Neo4j Cypher, read and write | openCypher, read-only |
| Multi-step prompted queries | Supported via `queryList` with `final: false` | Not supported |
| ADCS | Bolted on by community forks, modelled as `GPO` nodes | First-class node labels and composite edges |

#### Tiering and tagging replaced `highvalue`

Every legacy query containing `{highvalue:true}` or `n.highvalue = true` is dead. The property does not exist. CE replaced a single boolean with a tagging system: principals belong to asset groups or tiers, and the tag membership is exposed on the node as a list-valued property that you test with `CONTAINS`.

The form that has been stable across CE releases and that you will see in most current query sets is a `system_tags` property holding space-separated tags, with `admin_tier_0` for the Tier Zero set and `owned` for objects you control:

```cypher
// Tier Zero principals, preferred form on current CE: a node kind, not a property
MATCH (n:Tag_Tier_Zero) RETURN n

// Objects you have marked as owned
MATCH (n:Tag_Owned) RETURN n

// Legacy form, still honoured as a fallback on current builds
MATCH (n) WHERE n.system_tags CONTAINS 'admin_tier_0' RETURN n
MATCH (n) WHERE n.system_tags CONTAINS 'owned' RETURN n
```

Two mechanisms coexist and knowing which one your build uses saves real time. The older representation is a pair of string properties, `system_tags` for system-managed tags and `user_tags` for your own, with Tier Zero expressed as the substring `admin_tier_0` and owned as the substring `owned` inside `system_tags`. Note that `owned` is a value inside `system_tags`, not a property of its own.

The current representation is a **node kind**, which is to say a graph label rather than a property. Every privilege zone and label gets a kind named `Tag_` plus its name with spaces replaced by underscores, so the built-in Tier Zero zone is the kind `Tag_Tier_Zero` and the built-in Owned label is `Tag_Owned`. Matching on a kind is faster and cleaner than a substring test on a property, so prefer it. Current CE still falls back to the `system_tags` substring check when the kind is absent, which is why both forms work.

One CE-specific limitation to know before you plan around it: CE ships the default Tier Zero zone plus labels, and custom zones with additional tiers are an Enterprise feature. Do not write queries against `Tag_Tier_1` on a CE instance and conclude the estate is clean. If you want to see what tags actually exist, `CALL db.labels()` on a Neo4j-backed instance or the `/api/v2/asset-group-tags` endpoint will tell you, and reading it off the instance beats trusting any written reference including this one.

The practical difference is that Tier Zero is now **maintained for you**. CE seeds it with the objects that genuinely are domain-equivalent (Domain Admins, Enterprise Admins, Administrators, the domain object, the DC computer objects, Group Policy Creator Owners, the AdminSDHolder container, the CA and NTAuth objects, and so on). In legacy BloodHound `highvalue` was a thin hardcoded list and every operator hand-extended it. You should still extend the Tier Zero set with estate-specific assets: the ESXi service account, the backup service account, the Tier Zero jump host, the account that owns the EDR console. An attack path to the backup infrastructure is a full compromise even though no Microsoft-defined group is involved.

#### Edge additions and renames

CE both renamed edges and added a large number of new ones. The renames are mechanical, mostly capitalisation (`ManageCa` became `ManageCA`), but they silently break legacy queries because Cypher relationship types are case sensitive.

The additions are more interesting, because each one is a technique that legacy BloodHound could not represent at all:

| Edge | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `DCSync` | Composite edge computed during post-processing from `GetChanges` plus `GetChangesAll` (and `GetChangesInFilteredSet`). Legacy required you to compose the replication rights yourself. |
| `AddKeyCredentialLink` | Write access to `msDS-KeyCredentialLink`, that is, shadow credentials |
| `WriteSPN` | Write access to `servicePrincipalName`, enabling targeted Kerberoasting |
| `WriteAccountRestrictions` | Write to the account restrictions property set, which includes `msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity`, so RBCD |
| `SyncLAPSPassword` | Ability to read the LAPS password via directory replication rather than a direct attribute read |
| `DumpSMSAPassword` | Standalone managed service account password retrieval |
| `WriteGPLink` | Write access to `gPLink`, so the ability to link a controlled GPO to an OU |
| `ADCSESC1`, `ADCSESC3`, `ADCSESC4`, `ADCSESC6a`, `ADCSESC6b`, `ADCSESC9a`, `ADCSESC9b`, `ADCSESC10a`, `ADCSESC10b`, `ADCSESC13` | Composite certificate services escalation edges, computed during post-processing |
| `GoldenCert` | Control of a CA sufficient to forge certificates from its private key |
| `Enroll`, `AutoEnroll`, `EnrollOnBehalfOf`, `ManageCA`, `ManageCertificates`, `WritePKIEnrollmentFlag`, `WritePKINameFlag`, `DelegatedEnrollmentAgent` | The ADCS primitive edges the composites are built from |
| `PublishedTo`, `IssuedSignedBy`, `EnterpriseCAFor`, `RootCAFor`, `TrustedForNTAuth`, `HostsCAService` | ADCS structural edges |
| `CanAbuseUPNCertMapping`, `CanAbuseWeakCertBinding` | Certificate mapping weaknesses, relevant to the KB5014754 strong-mapping rollout |
| `ContainsIdentity`, `PropagatesACEsTo` | ACL inheritance and containment modelling, replacing the old habit of traversing `Contains` and hoping |

Two families are newer and worth knowing about specifically because they change how you read a graph.

**Trust edges.** Legacy modelled domain trusts with a single `TrustedBy` edge, which conveyed almost nothing. `TrustedBy` is **gone**: a CE migration split every existing one into `SameForestTrust` where the trust type was `ParentChild` and `CrossForestTrust` otherwise, and the string no longer exists anywhere in the schema. Alongside those two, CE adds edges for the abuse primitives that depend on trust configuration: `SpoofSIDHistory` where SID filtering is not enforced, `AbuseTGTDelegation` for TGT delegation across a trust with unconstrained delegation, and `HasTrustKeys` for possession of the trust key. The supporting properties on the trust are `trusttype`, `transitive`, `trustattributesinbound`, `trustattributesoutbound`, `spoofsidhistoryblocked` and `tgtdelegation`.

**Common mistake.** Carrying a `TrustedBy` query forward from an older cheat sheet. It will not error, it will silently return nothing, and you will conclude the estate has no trusts.

**Coercion and relay edges.** Recent CE releases model NTLM coercion and relay as graph edges, so a path can now legitimately route through "coerce authentication from this machine account and relay it to that LDAP or ADCS endpoint". This is a significant change: relay used to be entirely outside the graph and had to be reasoned about by hand. There are exactly four relay edges, `CoerceAndRelayNTLMToSMB`, `CoerceAndRelayNTLMToADCS`, `CoerceAndRelayNTLMToLDAP` and `CoerceAndRelayNTLMToLDAPS`, all of them post-processed rather than ingested, plus `CoerceToTGT` which is an ingest-time edge for Kerberos coercion. These edges depend on collected facts about signing and channel binding enforcement and on the WebClient service state, which means they depend on you having collected those facts.

The local group modelling is also more detailed than legacy fans expect. Machines now carry `ADLocalGroup` and `ADLocalUser` nodes, tied to the machine by `LocalToComputer`, with `MemberOfLocalGroup` expressing membership and `RemoteInteractiveLogonRight` expressing the RDP right. `DumpSMSAPassword` covers standalone managed service accounts on the host. The coarse edges still exist: `AdminTo`, `CanRDP`, `CanPSRemote` and `ExecuteDCOM` are all post-processed and derived from the `MemberOfLocalGroup` and `RemoteInteractiveLogonRight` digraphs, so old queries keep working and you get the fine-grained view as a bonus.

**Common mistake.** Writing `MATCH (g:LocalGroup)`. The Go schema names the constant `LocalGroup` but the label emitted into the graph is `ADLocalGroup`, and likewise `ADLocalUser`. The same trap exists for `WriteDACL`, which is written into the graph as `WriteDacl`.

#### Built-in pathfinding and pre-canned queries

A large fraction of the source's eighty-odd custom queries exist because legacy BloodHound's canned analysis was thin. CE ships a substantial pre-built query library in the Cypher tab, plus:

- **Pathfinding in the Explore tab.** Pick a source node and a target node and CE computes shortest paths across the traversable edge set. This subsumes every "shortest paths from owned to high value" query in the source. You do not need to hand-write the twenty-edge type filter list; CE knows which edges are traversable.
- **Per-node abuse information.** Select an edge or node and CE shows what the edge means, how to abuse it, how to detect the abuse, and references. This is the part the source notes were missing entirely: eighty queries that find things and zero words on what to do with a hit.
- **Tier Zero path exposure.** CE surfaces which principals have paths to Tier Zero without you asking, which is the single most useful default view in the product.

Write custom Cypher when you want something the UI cannot express: aggregation, counting, choke point analysis, estate-specific tag logic, or a query whose output you want to pipe into another tool. Do not write custom Cypher to re-implement pathfinding.

#### The API and ingest model

CE's API is the reason the tool became scriptable. Ingest is a three-call sequence: open an upload job, push one or more JSON or zip files into it, close the job. Closing the job is what triggers ingest and then post-processing.

```bash
# Authenticate and get a bearer token
curl -s -X POST "https://$BHHOST/api/v2/login" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"login_method":"secret","username":"'"$BHUSER"'","secret":"'"$BHPASS"'"}'

# Start an upload job, push files, close it
curl -s -X POST "https://$BHHOST/api/v2/file-upload/start" -H "Authorization: Bearer $JWT"
curl -s -X POST "https://$BHHOST/api/v2/file-upload/$JOBID" -H "Authorization: Bearer $JWT" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/zip' --data-binary @collection.zip
curl -s -X POST "https://$BHHOST/api/v2/file-upload/$JOBID/end" -H "Authorization: Bearer $JWT"

# Run Cypher and get JSON back
curl -s -X POST "https://$BHHOST/api/v2/graphs/cypher" -H "Authorization: Bearer $JWT" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"query":"MATCH (u:User) WHERE u.hasspn = true RETURN u.name","include_properties":true}'
```

Long-lived automation uses an API token rather than a JWT. The server issues a token ID and a token key, and each request carries three headers: `Authorization: bhesignature <token id>`, `RequestDate` holding an RFC3339 datetime, and `Signature` holding a base64 HMAC-SHA256 digest. Note that the `Authorization` header carries the token **ID**, not the key; the key never leaves your side.

The digest is a three-stage chain, each stage re-keying with the previous stage's output:

```python
digest = hmac.new(token_key.encode(), digestmod=hashlib.sha256)
digest.update(f"{method}{request_uri}".encode())        # 1: METHOD + URI, no delimiter
digest = hmac.new(digest.digest(), digestmod=hashlib.sha256)
digest.update(request_date[:13].encode())               # 2: RFC3339 truncated to the hour
digest = hmac.new(digest.digest(), digestmod=hashlib.sha256)
digest.update(body)                                     # 3: raw body bytes, nothing if empty
signature = base64.b64encode(digest.digest())
```

Three details cause almost all the failures. The method and URI are concatenated with **no** separator, giving strings like `GET/api/v2/self`. The URI is the raw request target including the query string, so `/api/v2/domains/x/details?skip=0&limit=0` is signed in full. And the date component is not a format string, it is a literal 13-character slice of the RFC3339 value, `YYYY-MM-DDTHH`, so everything below the hour is discarded and sub-second precision in the header is harmless. Requests are rejected if `RequestDate` is more than an hour either side of server time. For an empty body the third stage still runs, over zero bytes.

The point of all this is that you can drive the whole thing headlessly, which matters for two workflows: uploading collections from an operator relay as they land, and exporting query results into a report pipeline instead of screenshotting the browser.

The `bloodhound-cli` utility from the vendor manages the container stack. `install` bootstraps it, `up` and `down` start and stop it, `containers` gives you finer control (`up`, `down`, `start`, `stop`, `restart`, `build`), `logs <container>` tails one of `bloodhound`, `neo4j` or `postgres` with `-l` controlling how many lines, `check` validates the Docker environment, and `update` and `uninstall` do what they say.

The two you will actually need under pressure are the password ones, because the initial admin password is generated at first run and people lose it constantly. `bloodhound-cli config get default_password` **prints** the stored password without changing anything. `bloodhound-cli resetpwd` generates a new one, but it brings the stack down, recreates the default admin, and destroys that user's saved queries and settings in the process. Read before you reset.

Recent CE releases also expose a generic ingest schema for custom node and edge types, called **OpenGraph**, so you can push non-AD relationships into the same graph and path across them. That is how you model "this Jenkins job holds credentials for that service account" as an actual edge rather than a note in your findings document. The payload is a `graph` object holding `nodes` and `edges`, uploaded through the same `/api/v2/file-upload` endpoints SharpHound data goes through; the decoder distinguishes them by the presence of a `graph` key rather than the legacy `meta` and `data` keys.

```json
{
  "metadata": { "source_kind": "MySource" },
  "graph": {
    "nodes": [ { "id": "jenkins-job-42", "kinds": ["JenkinsJob"], "properties": { "name": "deploy-prod" } } ],
    "edges": [ { "kind": "HoldsCredentialFor",
                 "start": { "match_by": "id", "value": "jenkins-job-42" },
                 "end":   { "match_by": "property",
                            "property_matchers": [ { "key": "name", "operator": "equals", "value": "SVC_APP@CORP.LOCAL" } ] } } ]
  }
}
```

Constraints worth knowing before you build a pipeline against it: a node's `kinds` array is capped at three entries and the **first** one is the display kind that drives the icon; node `properties` must be flat, nested objects are rejected and `objectid` is explicitly prohibited; edge `kind` must match `^[A-Za-z0-9_]+$`; `match_by` accepts `id`, `property` or the deprecated `name`. Custom icons come from Font Awesome free-solid only, named without the `fa-` prefix.

The operational catch: full OpenGraph support requires the **PostgreSQL** graph backend, and current CE still defaults to Neo4j. Some of it works on Neo4j with functional and performance limitations, so if you are planning serious custom ingest, migrate the backend first with `bloodhound-cli pg`.

#### openCypher, and the fact that it is read-only

CE's Cypher endpoint accepts openCypher and **rejects mutating clauses**. `SET`, `CREATE`, `MERGE`, `DELETE`, `REMOVE`, and procedure calls are not available. This kills an entire genre of legacy query, including the two in the source labelled "(Warning: edits the DB)" that set `highvalue = true` on unconstrained delegation systems and on the top ten most-administered computers. The replacement is not a query, it is tagging: select the nodes and apply the Tier Zero or owned tag through the UI or the asset group API. This is strictly better, because tags are first-class, survive re-ingest, and are visible to everyone on the engagement rather than living in one operator's Neo4j.

The `{param}` parameter syntax in the source's cross-domain query is also dead twice over: Neo4j moved to `$param` years ago, and CE does not support the prompted multi-step query format that produced those parameters in the first place.

#### Post-processing, and why your first pathfind returns nothing

After ingest, CE runs an analysis pass that computes derived edges: `DCSync` from replication rights, the `ADCSESC*` composites from template and CA properties plus enrollment rights, ACL inheritance propagation, and cross-domain edge resolution. **Pathfinding before analysis completes is meaningless.** The UI shows analysis progress; wait for it. Operators regularly conclude an estate has no ADCS escalation path when what actually happened is that they queried the graph ninety seconds after upload. On a large estate the analysis pass can take considerably longer than the ingest.

### Collectors

#### SharpHound

**What it is.** The reference collector, a .NET binary that runs from a Windows context and enumerates the domain over LDAP plus a set of per-host remote protocols, writing BloodHound-format JSON into a zip.

**Why it works.** Almost everything SharpHound learns comes from the fact that **any authenticated domain principal can read the vast majority of the directory**. Group membership, ACLs on every object, `servicePrincipalName`, `userAccountControl`, `msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo`, `msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity`, GPO structure, OU containment, trust attributes, certificate template definitions in the configuration partition: all of it is readable by `Domain Users` by design, because AD is a directory and directories are for reading. There is no privilege escalation involved in mapping the estate. The privileged and noisy parts are the ones that leave LDAP and talk to individual hosts: session enumeration, local group enumeration, and registry reads.

**Preconditions.** A domain context (either a logged-on domain user, a runas-netonly token, or explicit LDAP credentials), TCP 389 or 636 to a domain controller, and working DNS resolution of the domain and of each target computer's FQDN. Per-host methods additionally need TCP 445 to each target. Certificate services and registry-based methods need reachability to the CA and DC hosts respectively.

**Commands.**

```powershell
# Full collection from a domain-joined context
.\SharpHound.exe --collectionmethods All --outputdirectory C:\Windows\Temp --zipfilename bh.zip

# LDAP-only, no host contact at all
.\SharpHound.exe --collectionmethods DCOnly --outputdirectory C:\Windows\Temp

# Explicit credentials, non-joined host or an alternate identity
.\SharpHound.exe --collectionmethods All --domain $DOMAIN --domaincontroller $DC `
  --ldapusername $USER --ldappassword $PASS

# LDAPS instead of cleartext LDAP
.\SharpHound.exe --collectionmethods DCOnly --domain $DOMAIN --domaincontroller $DC --secureldap

# Targeted: only the hosts you care about, throttled
.\SharpHound.exe --collectionmethods Session,LocalGroup --computerfile .\targets.txt `
  --throttle 1500 --jitter 30 --threads 5

# Session data over time
.\SharpHound.exe --collectionmethods Session --loop --loopduration 08:00:00 --loopinterval 00:20:00
```

Note that the PowerShell wrapper the source uses (`Import-Module SharpHound.ps1; Invoke-Bloodhound`) is a legacy artefact. Current SharpHound for CE is distributed as a binary and the CE web UI offers the matching collector for download, which is the version you want: collector and server version must agree, because the JSON schema is versioned and a mismatched collector produces a file the server refuses or misparses.

##### Collection methods, and what each one costs

This is the table the source never wrote, and it is the most useful thing on this page. "Noise" means detection surface, "cost" means wall clock time.

| Method | What it collects | Protocol | Privilege | Noise | Cost |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Group` | Domain group membership | LDAP to DC | Any domain user | Very low | Low |
| `ObjectProps` | All the object attributes the graph reasons over | LDAP to DC | Any domain user | Very low | Low to medium, large result set |
| `ACL` | DACLs on every object | LDAP to DC | Any domain user | Very low | Medium, this is the biggest LDAP payload |
| `Container` | OU and container structure, `gPLink` | LDAP to DC | Any domain user | Very low | Low |
| `Trusts` | Domain and forest trusts | LDAP to DC | Any domain user | Very low | Trivial |
| `GPOLocalGroup` | Local admin derived from Restricted Groups GPO settings | LDAP plus SMB read of SYSVOL | Any domain user | Low | Low |
| `CertServices` | Certificate templates, CAs, NTAuth and AIA stores | LDAP to the configuration partition | Any domain user | Very low | Low |
| `SPNTargets` | SPN-based abuse targets on kerberoastable accounts | LDAP to DC | Any domain user | Very low | Trivial |
| `LocalGroup` / `LocalAdmin` / `RDP` / `DCOM` / `PSRemote` | Local group membership on every computer | SAMR and remote registry over SMB, per host | Any domain user, unless `RestrictRemoteSam` is set | High, one connection to every host | High, scales with host count |
| `Session` | Who is logged on where | `NetSessionEnum` over SMB, per host | Any domain user on legacy, restricted by default on current Windows | **Highest** | High |
| `LoggedOn` | Who is logged on where, authoritatively | `NetWkstaUserEnum` and remote registry, per host | Local administrator on each target | Highest, and privileged | High |
| `UserRights` | Privileged rights assignments such as `SeEnableDelegationPrivilege` | LSA over SMB, per host | Elevated | High | High |
| `CARegistry` | CA registry configuration, needed for ESC6 and ESC7 reasoning | Remote registry on the CA | Local admin on the CA | Low volume, high privilege | Trivial |
| `DCRegistry` | DC registry configuration, certificate mapping and signing enforcement | Remote registry on DCs | Local admin on DCs | Low volume, high privilege | Trivial |
| `WebClientService` | Which hosts run WebClient, that is, are relay-coercible over HTTP | Per host probe | Any domain user | Medium | Medium |
| `DCOnly` | Everything obtainable from LDAP alone, no host contact | LDAP only | Any domain user | Very low | Low |
| `All` | Every method except `GPOLocalGroup` | Everything | Mixed | Highest | Highest |

**Session collection is the loud and privileged part.** Everything else is either a handful of paged LDAP searches against a domain controller or a small number of reads against specific infrastructure hosts. Session and local group collection are `O(computers)`: SharpHound opens an SMB connection to every computer object in the domain, in parallel, in a few minutes. On the wire that is one host initiating hundreds or thousands of TCP 445 connections in a tight window, which is a pattern no legitimate workstation ever produces. In the logs it is a 4624 logon type 3 followed by a 4634 on every single host in the estate, all from the same source, all within minutes.

It is also the part with the most defensive drift. `NetSessionEnum` used to be readable by any authenticated user; current Windows restricts the default permission on the `SrvsvcSessionInfo` registry security descriptor, and estates that applied the corresponding hardening guidance will return access denied. `RestrictRemoteSam` similarly kills SAMR-based local group enumeration. Both are commonly deployed now. Expect partial or empty session and local admin data in a hardened estate, and **do not read empty session data as "no admins are logged in anywhere"**.

##### Loop collection

Session data is a snapshot of a moving target. A single collection catches whoever happened to have a session at that instant, which on a workstation fleet is close to useless and on a server fleet is highly time-dependent: the Domain Admin who logs into the SQL box for twenty minutes on a Tuesday morning is the path you want, and you will not see them at 3am.

```powershell
.\SharpHound.exe --collectionmethods Session --loop --loopduration 12:00:00 --loopinterval 00:30:00
```

This runs session-only collection every thirty minutes for twelve hours, producing a separate JSON set each round. Ingest all of them: BloodHound accumulates the session edges, so the graph converges on "everyone who has been anywhere in the last twelve hours" rather than "everyone who was somewhere at 09:14". This is the single highest-value collection technique in the list and the source does not mention it.

The tradeoff is obvious and you should be explicit about it in your engagement plan. Loop session collection means you are producing that estate-wide TCP 445 fan-out pattern twenty-four times instead of once. If the engagement is testing detection, loop collection will get you caught, which is a valid outcome. If it is not, restrict `--computerfile` to servers and Tier Zero candidates and lengthen the interval.

##### All-methods versus targeted collection

`--collectionmethods All` is the right default when noise is not a constraint, because a missing collection method produces a **false negative that looks exactly like a clean result**. If you skip `CertServices` you will not see ADCS escalation and the graph will not tell you that it did not look.

Targeted collection is correct when noise is a constraint, and the sensible decomposition is in two passes:

```powershell
# Pass one: LDAP only. Complete structural picture, essentially undetectable.
.\SharpHound.exe --collectionmethods DCOnly,CertServices --outputdirectory .

# Pass two: after analysing pass one, touch only the hosts that matter.
.\SharpHound.exe --collectionmethods Session,LocalGroup --computerfile .\tier0-and-servers.txt --throttle 2000 --jitter 40
```

Pass one gives you every ACL, every group nesting, every delegation flag, every certificate template, every trust, and every kerberoastable account. That is the great majority of the graph's value. Pass two adds the session and local admin edges, but only against the small set of hosts that the pass one analysis identified as interesting: domain controllers, the CA, hosts where Tier Zero principals have `AdminTo`, servers holding SQL or backup SPNs.

**The LDAP-only stealth profile and what you give up.** `DCOnly` costs you `HasSession` (so no "where are the Domain Admins logged in" analysis, which is historically the most productive single query in the tool), locally-derived `AdminTo`, `CanRDP`, `CanPSRemote`, and `ExecuteDCOM` (you keep only what `GPOLocalGroup` can derive from Restricted Groups policy, which in a modern estate that manages local admin through LAPS and group nesting is often surprisingly complete), `UserRights`, and the registry-derived CA and DC configuration facts that ESC6, ESC7, and certificate mapping analysis depend on. What you keep is everything ACL-based, everything Kerberos-related, all delegation, all group structure, all GPO structure, all trusts, and the full certificate template definitions. In other words, **the stealth profile retains all of the ACL and Kerberos attack surface and loses the credential-locality attack surface**. That is a good trade in a monitored estate, and it is why the modern default is LDAP-first.

##### Verify it worked

Do not trust exit status. Check the artefacts:

```powershell
# Line-count the JSON inside the zip; each file should have a plausible count
Expand-Archive .\bh.zip -DestinationPath .\bh; Get-ChildItem .\bh | Select-Object Name,Length
```

Then check the graph, not the file. After ingest and analysis, confirm each collection concern actually landed:

```cypher
// Did ACL collection work? Zero ACL edges means it did not.
MATCH ()-[r]->() WHERE r.isacl = true RETURN count(r)

// Did session collection work?
MATCH ()-[r:HasSession]->() RETURN count(r)

// Did ADCS collection work?
MATCH (n:CertTemplate) RETURN count(n)

// How many computers did we actually reach for local group data?
MATCH (c:Computer) WHERE EXISTS { (c)<-[:AdminTo]-() } RETURN count(DISTINCT c)
```

SharpHound also writes a per-computer status log if you ask it to, which tells you which hosts refused, timed out, or returned access denied. That distinction matters enormously: "the host was offline" and "the host denied SAMR" and "the host returned an empty group" are three completely different conclusions and only the log separates them.

##### Failure modes

| Symptom | Cause |
| --- | --- |
| `LDAP connection failed` or immediate exit | No DNS resolution for the domain, or the specified DC is unreachable on 389/636. Kerberos in particular needs FQDNs and working reverse and forward DNS. |
| Collection completes in seconds with a tiny zip | Only LDAP ran; per-host methods were skipped because the port check failed or the computer set was empty |
| Every host returns access denied for sessions | `NetSessionEnum` permissions hardened, or you are running as a non-domain identity |
| Every host returns access denied for local groups | `RestrictRemoteSam` set, or SMB signing/negotiation failure |
| `Strong(er) authentication required` | LDAP signing and channel binding enforced on the DC; use `--secureldap` and a proper Kerberos or TLS-bound session |
| Collection hangs at high host counts | Port scan timeouts against a large offline population; reduce `--threads`, raise `--portscantimeout`, or supply a `--computerfile` of hosts you know are alive |
| Server rejects the upload | Collector and CE server schema version mismatch. Download the collector from the CE instance you are uploading to. |

#### bloodhound-python and the value of collecting from Linux

**What it is.** A pure-Python collector that speaks LDAP and SMB directly, so you can produce a full graph from a Linux implant or your own box with nothing but credentials and network reachability. No Windows host, no binary on disk in the estate, no .NET, no AMSI, no EDR looking at process behaviour on a domain-joined machine.

This is the single biggest opsec win available in collection and the source gets it right by accident ("great due to being able to collect from your attacking machine") without explaining why. The reason is that the entire detection surface moves. There is no process to be scanned, no in-memory .NET assembly, no unusual child process on a monitored endpoint. What remains is purely network-visible: LDAP searches and SMB connections from an IP address. If your relay is a device the estate expects to make LDAP queries, that is very little.

**Important version note.** The original `bloodhound-python` emits legacy-format JSON, which CE will not ingest. The CE-compatible collector is distributed separately and produces the current schema. Install the CE variant, not the one that first comes up:

```bash
pipx install bloodhound-ce
bloodhound-ce-python --help
```

The package is `bloodhound-ce` and the command it installs is `bloodhound-ce-python`. They are not interchangeable: `bloodhound-ce` is not a command and `bloodhound-ce-python` is not a package name. The two collectors live on different branches of the same repository, `master` for the legacy schema and `bloodhound-ce` for the current one, and the mainline `bloodhound` package never gained a CE output flag. Schema selection is by which package you installed, full stop.

**Common mistake.** `-c` on this tool is `--collectionmethod`, singular, unlike SharpHound's `--collectionmethods`. Also note there is no ADCS collection method here at all, so a graph collected this way will have no certificate services data and no ADCS edges. That absence looks identical to "no ADCS misconfigurations" and it is not the same thing.

**Commands.**

```bash
# Full collection with a password
bloodhound-ce-python -u "$USER" -p "$PASS" -d "$DOMAIN" -c All --zip -ns "$DC" -dc "$DC"

# Pass the hash
bloodhound-ce-python -u "$USER" --hashes ":$NTHASH" -d "$DOMAIN" -c All --zip -ns "$DC"

# Kerberos, from an existing ccache
export KRB5CCNAME=/tmp/user.ccache
bloodhound-ce-python -k --no-pass -u "$USER@$DOMAIN" -d "$DOMAIN" -c All --zip -dc "$DC"

# LDAP-only stealth profile
bloodhound-ce-python -u "$USER" -p "$PASS" -d "$DOMAIN" -c DCOnly --zip -ns "$DC"

# Use the global catalog for cross-domain resolution in a multi-domain forest
bloodhound-ce-python -u "$USER" -p "$PASS" -d "$DOMAIN" -c All --zip -ns "$DC" -gc "$DC"

# DNS over TCP, mandatory when tunnelling through a SOCKS proxy
bloodhound-ce-python -u "$USER" -p "$PASS" -d "$DOMAIN" -c DCOnly --zip -ns "$DC" --dns-tcp
```

Collection methods mirror SharpHound's names (`Group`, `LocalAdmin`, `Session`, `Trusts`, `ACL`, `ObjectProps`, `Container`, `RDP`, `DCOM`, `PSRemote`, `Default`, `DCOnly`, `All`), which is deliberate.

**Preconditions.** Credentials in some form, TCP 389 or 636 to a DC, and a nameserver that resolves the domain. The `-ns` flag exists because your Linux box's resolver almost certainly does not point at the domain's DNS, and without it every SPN and host lookup fails. If Kerberos is in play, the DC must be addressed by FQDN and time skew must be under five minutes.

**Failure modes.** `-c All` from Linux attempts session and local group enumeration over SMB against every computer, which is both slow and heavily dependent on SMB dialect and signing negotiation from a non-Windows stack. It is common for `DCOnly` to succeed perfectly and `All` to spend forty minutes producing almost no additional edges. Check whether you actually got session data before assuming there is none. The other classic is a partial ACL collection on a very large domain, where the LDAP paged search is interrupted and the resulting JSON is silently short.

#### rusthound-ce

**What it is.** A Rust reimplementation of the collector, statically linkable, fast, and notably good on large domains where the Python collector's memory use and single-threaded LDAP paging become the bottleneck. Same idea as bloodhound-python: LDAP-centric collection from a non-Windows host.

As with the Python collector there are two lineages. The original `rusthound` emits legacy-format output; `rusthound-ce` emits the CE schema. Use the CE build.

```bash
# Password auth, zip output
rusthound-ce -d "$DOMAIN" -u "$USER@$DOMAIN" -p "$PASS" -f "$DC" -z

# LDAPS
rusthound-ce -d "$DOMAIN" -u "$USER@$DOMAIN" -p "$PASS" -f "$DC" --ldaps -z

# Kerberos from a ccache
KRB5CCNAME=/tmp/user.ccache rusthound-ce -d "$DOMAIN" -f "$DC" -k -z

# Certificate services data is collected unconditionally, there is no flag for it
rusthound-ce -d "$DOMAIN" -u "$USER@$DOMAIN" -p "$PASS" -f "$DC" -z
```

`-f`/`--ldapfqdn` is the DC FQDN, `-i`/`--ldapip` is its address, and `-d`/`--domain` is the domain rather than the controller, which is a distinction the other collectors do not force on you. `-z`/`--zip` produces the archive, `-c`/`--collectionmethod` takes `All` or `DCOnly`, and `--ldap-filter`, `--ldaps`, `-k`/`--kerberos`, `-H`/`--hashes`, `-n`/`--name-server` and `--dns-tcp` behave as you would expect.

**Common mistake.** Passing `--adcs`. That flag belongs to the original RustHound, not RustHound-CE, where certificate templates, enterprise CAs, NT auth stores and issuance policies are always collected. On RustHound-CE it is a hard argument-parsing error, not a warning.

Its practical niche: a hundred-thousand-object domain where you want structural data quickly and reliably, and cross-compiling a single static binary onto a minimal Linux foothold with no Python runtime.

#### Collecting over ADWS instead of LDAP

Worth knowing because it changes the detection story completely. Active Directory Web Services listens on TCP 9389 on domain controllers and exposes essentially the same directory data over SOAP. It is the transport behind the `ActiveDirectory` PowerShell module's `-Server` behaviour in some configurations, and critically, **almost nobody monitors it**. Detection engineering, Defender for Identity signatures, and LDAP query inspection are all built around 389/636.

`SOAPHound` (a .NET collector) and `SoaPy` (a Python client for ADWS) collect directory data over ADWS and can produce BloodHound-compatible output. The typical SOAPHound flow builds a local cache of the directory first, then renders BloodHound JSON from the cache, which also means you can collect once and re-render without touching the DC again.

```text
soaphound --buildcache -c cache.json
soaphound --bhdump -c cache.json -o output/
soaphound --certdump -c cache.json -o output/
soaphound --dnsdump -c cache.json -o output/
```

The four dump modes are mutually exclusive and one is required. `-c`/`--cachefilename` and `-o`/`--outputdirectory` are as shown, and `--user`, `--password`, `--domain`, `--dc`, `-a`/`--autosplit` with `-t`/`--threshold`, `--nolaps`, `--showstats` and `--logfile` round out the set.

Two caveats, and the second one is a blocker rather than an inconvenience. ADWS collection is LDAP-equivalent in coverage, meaning it gives you the `DCOnly` picture and not session or local group data. And **SOAPHound emits legacy BloodHound 4.x JSON, not CE**: it hardcodes `version = 5` in its output where CE requires `6`, upstream development stopped in early 2024, and the active forks have not changed it either. Its ADCS data is emitted as GPO objects, which is not the CE ADCS model at all. So SOAPHound output needs conversion before CE will take it.

If you want the ADWS transport with CE-schema output, that is a different tool: `Soaphound.py` (`pipx install soaphound-py`, command `soaphound`) is a Python ADWS collector that emits `"version": 6` directly, with `-c` taking `Default` or `ADWSOnly`, a required `-dc`/`--domain-controller`, and `--zip`, `-op`/`--outputprefix`, `--cert-find` and `--trust-audit`.

#### Collection through netexec

`nxc` wraps the Python collector, which is convenient when you already have a credential loaded in your netexec workflow and do not want a second syntax:

```bash
nxc ldap "$DC" -u "$USER" -p "$PASS" --bloodhound --collection All --dns-server "$DC"
```

`--bloodhound` turns it on and `-c`/`--collection` takes a comma-separated, case-insensitive list from the same vocabulary as the Python collector: `Group`, `LocalAdmin`, `Session`, `Trusts`, `Default`, `DCOnly`, `DCOM`, `RDP`, `PSRemote`, `LoggedOn`, `Container`, `ObjectProps`, `ACL`, `ADCS`, `All`. `--dns-server` and `--dns-tcp` are global netexec options rather than LDAP-specific ones, so they work on every protocol.

netexec targets CE by default, depends on the `bloodhound-ce` package, and its ADCS collection is netexec's own implementation which errors out rather than falling back if it finds the legacy collector. There is one trap worth knowing: the CE-versus-legacy switch is read from `nxc.conf` with no fallback, so a hand-edited or stale config file that has lost its `[BloodHound-CE]` section silently reverts you to legacy output. If your ingest starts rejecting files after you touched the config, that is why.

It is the same collector underneath with the same tradeoffs. The value is workflow, not capability.

#### SilentHound and the LDAP dumpers

The source lists SilentHound under collectors. It is not a BloodHound collector: it does not emit graph JSON. It is an LDAP enumeration tool that writes flat text and CSV files (users, groups, hosts, descriptions, kerberoastable accounts) with a deliberately small query footprint. It belongs in the "operating without BloodHound" toolbox below, alongside `ldeep`, `bloodyAD`, and raw `ldapsearch`, not in the collector list. Filing it as a collector leads people to expect a graph and get a directory listing.

#### Collecting through a proxy after a pivot

You have a SOCKS proxy through a foothold and no interest in dropping a collector on the foothold itself. This works, with three specific traps.

```bash
# proxychains-ng config: quiet, strict, one SOCKS5 hop
# [ProxyList]
# socks5 127.0.0.1 1080

proxychains4 -q bloodhound-ce-python -u "$USER" -p "$PASS" -d "$DOMAIN" \
  -c DCOnly --zip -ns "$DC" --dns-tcp -dc "$DC" -w 4
```

**Trap one: DNS.** `proxychains` cannot proxy UDP, so name resolution silently fails or leaks to your local resolver. `--dns-tcp` forces DNS over TCP 53, which does go through the SOCKS tunnel. Without it you will see a collection that authenticates fine and then cannot resolve a single host. This single flag is the difference between working and not working and it is the most common proxied-collection failure.

**Trap two: concurrency.** A SOCKS tunnel over a C2 beacon has latency measured in whole seconds and a limited number of usable concurrent channels. Reduce worker counts hard (`-w 4` or lower). Default concurrency will saturate the tunnel, time out, and produce a partial collection that looks complete.

**Trap three: do not run `-c All` through a tunnel.** Session and local group collection means one SMB connection per computer object. Through a SOCKS proxy that is thousands of tunnelled TCP connections, which will take hours, destabilise your C2 channel, and probably still fail. Run `DCOnly` through the tunnel for the structural graph, and if you need session data, run a targeted `Session` collection from a host inside the estate against a short `--computerfile`.

If you have execution on a Windows foothold, running SharpHound there with `DCOnly` and exfiltrating the zip is usually cheaper and more reliable than proxying anything. LDAP-only collection produces a modest amount of data and a small number of connections.

#### Very large domains

Past roughly fifty thousand objects, collection and ingest both start to bite. The failures are distinct and have distinct fixes.

**Collection times out or never finishes.** Almost always the per-host portion. Diagnose by running `DCOnly` and seeing whether that completes; if it does, your problem is host contact, not LDAP. Fix by supplying an explicit `--computerfile` rather than letting the collector enumerate and probe every computer object, and by raising the port check timeout while reducing thread count so you are not opening ten thousand simultaneous sockets.

**LDAP results are truncated.** The DC's `MaxPageSize` and `MaxResultSetSize` administrative limits apply and a badly-behaved paged search can be cut off. Partition the collection by subtree instead of collecting the whole domain at once:

```powershell
# Collect one OU subtree at a time and ingest the results together
.\SharpHound.exe --collectionmethods DCOnly --distinguishedname "OU=EMEA,DC=corp,DC=local" --outputprefix emea
.\SharpHound.exe --collectionmethods DCOnly --distinguishedname "OU=AMER,DC=corp,DC=local" --outputprefix amer
```

**Common mistake.** `--searchbase`. That was the legacy SharpHound flag, along with `--ou`, and the CE collector replaced both with `--distinguishedname`. Flags and enum values are case-insensitive on the CE collector, so `--DistinguishedName` and `--CollectionMethods DCONLY` are both fine, but the *name* has genuinely changed. Do not trust the repository README either: it still documents `--secureldap` and a 500ms `--portchecktimeout` where the current source has `--forcesecureldap`, a separate `--ldapsslport`, and a 10000ms default. `src/Options.cs` in the collector's own repository is the only reliable reference.

Note also that `--searchforest` (`-s`) is a different thing entirely: it is a boolean that widens collection to every domain in the forest, not a search base.

You can also narrow with a raw LDAP filter (`--ldapfilter`) to collect, say, only servers, though be careful: a filter that excludes objects also excludes the ACLs on them, and you will not be told.

**Output is unmanageable or ingest fails.** The upload API accepts multiple files in one job, so split rather than shipping one enormous zip. Ingest and post-processing are the real bottleneck on big estates and both are memory-bound on Neo4j: raise the Neo4j heap and page cache in the container environment before concluding the data is bad. A stack with default 512MB heap will fail on a large forest in ways that look like corrupt input.

**Practical partitioning strategy.** Collect and ingest one domain at a time, in trust order, starting with the domain you have credentials in. Confirm each ingest and its analysis pass completed before starting the next. When you later add a second domain, cross-domain edges resolve during that domain's analysis pass, so paths that were invisible appear retroactively. That is expected and is a reason to re-run your pathfinding after every ingest rather than only at the start.

### Cypher, properly

The source dumps eighty queries with no explanation of the language, so a reader who hits a schema change or wants a variation is stuck. Cypher is small. Learn it once.

#### Patterns

A Cypher query is a pattern match over the graph. Nodes are parentheses, relationships are square brackets between dashes, and direction is an arrow.

```cypher
MATCH (u:User)-[:MemberOf]->(g:Group) RETURN u, g
```

`u` and `g` are **variables** you bind so you can refer to the matched thing later. `:User` and `:Group` are **labels**, the node's type. `:MemberOf` is the **relationship type**. The arrow direction is load-bearing: `(u)-[:MemberOf]->(g)` means u is a member of g, and reversing it finds nothing.

Properties can be matched inline or in a `WHERE`. These are equivalent:

```cypher
MATCH (u:User {hasspn: true}) RETURN u
MATCH (u:User) WHERE u.hasspn = true RETURN u
```

Prefer `WHERE`. Inline property maps only do equality, and the moment you need a comparison, a regex, or a list test you have to rewrite the query anyway.

Omit the label to match any node type, which is how you write queries that should apply to users, computers, and groups alike:

```cypher
MATCH (n) WHERE n.system_tags CONTAINS 'owned' RETURN n
```

Bind the relationship when you need to inspect it:

```cypher
MATCH (a)-[r]->(b) WHERE r.isacl = true RETURN a.name, type(r), b.name
```

`type(r)` returns the relationship type as a string, which is essential when you match on an unspecified relationship and then want to know what you found.

Bind the whole path when you want to visualise it. `p` is a path variable:

```cypher
MATCH p = (u:User)-[:MemberOf]->(g:Group) RETURN p
```

#### WHERE

Everything you would expect: `=`, `<>`, `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=`, `AND`, `OR`, `NOT`, `IN`, `IS NULL`, `IS NOT NULL`. Plus string predicates `STARTS WITH`, `ENDS WITH`, `CONTAINS`, and regex matching with `=~`.

```cypher
MATCH (g:Group)
WHERE g.objectid ENDS WITH '-512'
   OR g.objectid ENDS WITH '-519'
RETURN g.name
```

Two idioms you will use constantly. **RID matching**: well-known groups have fixed relative identifiers at the end of their SID, so `ENDS WITH '-512'` finds Domain Admins in any domain without knowing its name. **Case-insensitive name matching**: BloodHound stores `name` uppercased as `SAMACCOUNTNAME@DOMAIN.FQDN`, but do not rely on that, wrap it:

```cypher
MATCH (g:Group) WHERE toUpper(g.name) CONTAINS 'ADMIN' RETURN g.name
```

Useful RIDs:

| RID suffix | Group |
| --- | --- |
| `-512` | Domain Admins |
| `-513` | Domain Users |
| `-515` | Domain Computers |
| `-516` | Domain Controllers |
| `-517` | Cert Publishers |
| `-518` | Schema Admins |
| `-519` | Enterprise Admins |
| `-525` | Protected Users |
| `-526` | Key Admins |
| `-527` | Enterprise Key Admins |
| `S-1-5-32-544` | Built-in Administrators (local, not domain-suffixed) |

#### Variable-length relationships, and why queries hang

Group nesting and ACL chains are arbitrarily deep, so you need to traverse a repeated relationship. The syntax is `*min..max`:

```cypher
MATCH p = (u:User)-[:MemberOf*1..]->(g:Group) RETURN p
```

`*1..` means one or more hops, unbounded. `*1..5` means one to five. `*..5` means up to five. Bare `*` means unbounded in both directions of the range and is the same as `*1..`.

**Unbounded depth is what makes a query hang.** This is the most important thing in this section. The reason is not that the graph is large, it is that the number of *paths* grows combinatorially with depth even when the number of nodes does not. In a well-connected AD graph, a node's reachable set at depth 8 can be the entire domain, and the number of distinct paths to it can be in the billions. A query like this will run until something dies:

```cypher
// Do not run this
MATCH p = (a)-[*]->(b) RETURN p
```

The mitigations, in order of preference:

1. **Restrict the relationship types.** `-[:MemberOf|AdminTo|GenericAll*1..]->` prunes the branching factor enormously compared to `-[*1..]->`. An unrestricted traversal will happily route through structural edges like `Contains` that connect everything to everything.
2. **Use `shortestPath` or `allShortestPaths`** rather than enumerating all paths. These are breadth-first and terminate as soon as they find the shortest length.
3. **Bound the depth.** Five hops is a sensible working bound for exploratory queries. Real attack paths are usually two to five edges; if you need twelve you have found a curiosity, not a finding.
4. **Anchor both ends.** A pattern with a selective node on each end is dramatically cheaper than one with a free end. `(n {system_tags: ...})-[*1..5]->(m:Domain)` beats `(n)-[*1..5]->(m)`.

`MemberOf*1..` unbounded is the one exception where you can be relaxed, because group nesting is shallow and acyclic in practice. Everything else, bound it.

#### shortestPath versus allShortestPaths

Both take a single relationship pattern and do a breadth-first search. The difference is what they return when several paths tie for shortest.

`shortestPath` returns **one** path per source/target pair. `allShortestPaths` returns **every** path of the shortest length for that pair.

```cypher
// One route from each owned object to each Tier Zero object
MATCH p = shortestPath((s)-[:MemberOf|AdminTo|HasSession|GenericAll|GenericWrite|WriteDacl|WriteOwner|Owns|AddMember|ForceChangePassword|AllExtendedRights|AddKeyCredentialLink|WriteSPN|ReadLAPSPassword|ReadGMSAPassword|SyncLAPSPassword|CanRDP|CanPSRemote|ExecuteDCOM|SQLAdmin|AllowedToDelegate|AllowedToAct|AddAllowedToAct|WriteAccountRestrictions|DCSync|HasSIDHistory|Contains|GpLink|WriteGPLink*1..6]->(t))
WHERE s.system_tags CONTAINS 'owned'
  AND t.system_tags CONTAINS 'admin_tier_0'
  AND s <> t
RETURN p
```

Swap `shortestPath` for `allShortestPaths` and you get every tied route. That matters for two reasons in opposite directions. Offensively, `allShortestPaths` shows you alternatives: if the one route `shortestPath` chose runs through a host with an EDR agent you would rather not touch, there may be three others of equal length that do not. Defensively, `allShortestPaths` is what feeds choke point analysis, because a node appearing in many shortest paths is a high-leverage remediation.

The cost is output volume. `allShortestPaths` on a large estate with many owned nodes can return tens of thousands of paths and render as an unusable hairball. Start with `shortestPath` to establish that a route exists and how long it is, then switch to `allShortestPaths` on a narrowed source and target pair.

Both functions require that the pattern inside them be a single relationship pattern between two nodes. You cannot put a multi-segment pattern inside `shortestPath`. And note the `s <> t` guard: without it every node trivially reaches itself and the result is polluted.

#### RETURN: paths versus nodes

This determines whether you get a graph or a table, and choosing wrong is why so many of the source's queries are frustrating to use.

Returning a **path** gives you the graph view, with every intermediate node and edge rendered. This is what you want for anything you intend to look at and reason about.

Returning **nodes or scalars** gives you a table. This is what you want for inventory, counting, export, and anything you intend to feed into another tool.

```cypher
MATCH p = (u:User)-[:MemberOf*1..]->(g:Group)
WHERE g.objectid ENDS WITH '-512'
RETURN p                                    // graph view, shows the nesting

MATCH (u:User)-[:MemberOf*1..]->(g:Group)
WHERE g.objectid ENDS WITH '-512'
RETURN DISTINCT u.name AS effective_da      // table, exportable list
```

Several of the source's queries build a path and then return a bare node, which throws away the interesting part. The ESC2 and ESC3 queries do exactly this: they compute `allShortestPaths` and return `n`, so you learn that a vulnerable template exists but not how to reach it. `DISTINCT` matters on any query with a variable-length pattern, because multiple paths to the same node produce duplicate rows.

#### WITH, aggregation, collect, ordering, limiting

`WITH` is a pipeline stage. It passes results from one part of a query to the next and is where aggregation happens. Anything not carried forward in the `WITH` goes out of scope.

```cypher
// Count how many computers each user is admin to
MATCH (u:User)-[:AdminTo]->(c:Computer)
WITH u, count(DISTINCT c) AS boxes
WHERE boxes > 10
RETURN u.name, boxes
ORDER BY boxes DESC
LIMIT 20
```

Note that `WHERE` after `WITH` filters on the aggregate, which is how you express "having". This is the single most useful pattern for turning a graph into a prioritised list.

`collect()` builds a list, which lets you do set membership tests across the query:

```cypher
// Unconstrained delegation on anything that is not a domain controller
MATCH (dc:Computer)-[:MemberOf*1..]->(g:Group)
WHERE g.objectid ENDS WITH '-516'
WITH collect(dc.objectid) AS dcs
MATCH (c:Computer)
WHERE c.unconstraineddelegation = true AND NOT c.objectid IN dcs
RETURN c.name, c.operatingsystem
```

Comparing on `objectid` rather than `name` is deliberate: names collide across domains, SIDs do not.

Aggregation functions available: `count`, `collect`, `min`, `max`, `avg`, `sum`. Plus `size()` for list length, `length(p)` for path length in relationships, `nodes(p)` and `relationships(p)` to decompose a path, and `UNWIND` to explode a list back into rows.

#### Path predicates

`ALL`, `ANY`, `NONE`, and `SINGLE` let you filter on the contents of a path, which is how you express "reach this thing but not by cheating":

```cypher
// Control over a certificate template without merely having enrollment rights
MATCH p = allShortestPaths((s)-[*1..5]->(t:CertTemplate))
WHERE s.system_tags CONTAINS 'owned'
  AND s <> t
  AND NONE(r IN relationships(p) WHERE type(r) IN ['Enroll','AutoEnroll'])
RETURN p
```

`length(p)` sorts by hop count, which is how you find the easiest-looking routes first:

```cypher
MATCH p = shortestPath((s)-[:MemberOf|AdminTo|GenericAll|WriteDacl|Owns|WriteOwner|ForceChangePassword|AddMember*1..6]->(t))
WHERE s.system_tags CONTAINS 'owned' AND t.system_tags CONTAINS 'admin_tier_0' AND s <> t
RETURN p, length(p) AS hops
ORDER BY hops ASC
LIMIT 25
```

#### Dialect gotchas that will bite you

| Trap | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| `-[r:A\|:B]->` | The legacy leading-colon-per-type syntax is removed. Write `-[r:A\|B]->`. Several of the source's queries use the old form and will not parse. |
| `{param}` | Old parameter syntax, removed. Use `$param`, and note CE's Cypher tab has no prompted-parameter mechanism at all. |
| Rebinding a path variable | `MATCH p = (...) WITH ... MATCH p = (...)` errors with "variable already bound". The source's "Logged in Admins" query does exactly this. Use distinct names. |
| `OPTIONAL MATCH` as the first clause | Legal but almost never what you meant, and it makes every subsequent filter behave strangely. Lead with `MATCH`. |
| Case sensitivity | Labels, relationship types, and property names are all case sensitive. `ManageCa` is not `ManageCA`. |
| Write clauses | `SET`, `CREATE`, `MERGE`, `DELETE`, `REMOVE`, and `CALL` are rejected by CE. Use tagging instead. |
| Boolean literals | `TRUE`, `True`, and `true` all parse; property values are actual booleans, so `= 'true'` as a string never matches. |
| Missing versus false | `c.unconstraineddelegation = false` excludes nodes where the property is absent. If a collection method did not run, the property is null, not false. Use `coalesce(c.unconstraineddelegation, false) = false` when you mean "not delegating, including unknowns", and be aware which you want. |

### Corrected queries: the ones the source got wrong

Do not propagate these. Each one is a query an operator would plausibly copy and then draw a false conclusion from.

#### Kerberoastable users with old passwords

The source:

```cypher
MATCH (u:User) WHERE n.hasspn=true AND WHERE u.pwdlastset < (datetime().epochseconds - (1825 * 86400)) and NOT u.pwdlastset IN [-1.0, 0.0] RETURN u
```

Two defects: a second `WHERE` in the middle of a predicate, which is a parse error, and a reference to `n` which is never bound. Corrected:

```cypher
MATCH (u:User)
WHERE u.hasspn = true
  AND u.pwdlastset < (datetime().epochseconds - (1825 * 86400))
  AND NOT u.pwdlastset IN [-1.0, 0.0]
RETURN u.name, u.pwdlastset, u.serviceprincipalnames
ORDER BY u.pwdlastset ASC
```

**What to do with a hit.** These are the highest-value Kerberoast targets in the estate. A service account password unchanged for five years predates any modern complexity policy and very often predates AES support, so you will get RC4-HMAC tickets that crack fast. Roast these first, before you touch anything else.

**Common mistake.** A `WHERE` clause takes one predicate expression. Chain conditions with `AND`, never a second `WHERE`. And if you rename the pattern variable, rename it everywhere; the mixed `n`/`u` here is the classic result of editing someone else's query.

#### Kerberoastable users and where they are admin

The source:

```cypher
OPTIONAL MATCH (u1:User) WHERE u1.hasspn=true OPTIONAL MATCH (u1)-[r:AdminTo]->(c:Computer) RETURN u
```

Returns undefined variable `u`, and uses `OPTIONAL MATCH` as a leading clause where a plain `MATCH` is meant. Corrected:

```cypher
MATCH p = (u:User)-[:AdminTo]->(c:Computer)
WHERE u.hasspn = true
RETURN p
```

If you want kerberoastable accounts including their nested-group-derived local admin:

```cypher
MATCH p = (u:User)-[:MemberOf|AdminTo*1..4]->(c:Computer)
WHERE u.hasspn = true
RETURN p
```

**What to do with a hit.** This is your crack-priority list. A kerberoastable account that is local admin somewhere converts a cracked password directly into code execution, which is materially better than a kerberoastable account with no privileges.

#### The inverted date comparisons

This is the most instructive error in the whole source and it appears twice.

```cypher
// Source, titled "Users logged in the last 90 days"
MATCH (u:User) WHERE u.lastlogon < (datetime().epochseconds - (90 * 86400)) and NOT u.lastlogon IN [-1.0, 0.0] RETURN u

// Source, titled "Users with passwords last set in the last 90 days"
MATCH (u:User) WHERE u.pwdlastset < (datetime().epochseconds - (90 * 86400)) and NOT u.pwdlastset IN [-1.0, 0.0] RETURN u
```

Both return the **exact opposite** of their title.

Work through it. BloodHound stores these timestamps as **Unix epoch seconds**, so a larger number is a more recent time. `datetime().epochseconds` is now. Subtracting `90 * 86400` gives the epoch value for the moment 90 days ago. So:

- `timestamp < (now - 90 days)` means the timestamp is *smaller*, therefore *older*, therefore the event happened **more than** 90 days ago.
- `timestamp > (now - 90 days)` means the timestamp is *larger*, therefore *more recent*, therefore the event happened **within** the last 90 days.

Corrected, both directions, because both are useful:

```cypher
// Users who HAVE logged on in the last 90 days: the live accounts
MATCH (u:User)
WHERE u.enabled = true
  AND u.lastlogon > (datetime().epochseconds - (90 * 86400))
  AND NOT u.lastlogon IN [-1.0, 0.0]
RETURN u.name, u.lastlogon
ORDER BY u.lastlogon DESC

// Users who have NOT logged on in 90 days but are still enabled: the stale accounts
MATCH (u:User)
WHERE u.enabled = true
  AND u.lastlogon < (datetime().epochseconds - (90 * 86400))
  AND NOT u.lastlogon IN [-1.0, 0.0]
RETURN u.name, u.lastlogon
ORDER BY u.lastlogon ASC

// Passwords changed within the last 90 days
MATCH (u:User)
WHERE u.pwdlastset > (datetime().epochseconds - (90 * 86400))
  AND NOT u.pwdlastset IN [-1.0, 0.0]
RETURN u.name, u.pwdlastset
ORDER BY u.pwdlastset DESC

// Passwords not changed in over a year: spray and roast candidates
MATCH (u:User)
WHERE u.enabled = true
  AND u.pwdlastset < (datetime().epochseconds - (365 * 86400))
  AND NOT u.pwdlastset IN [-1.0, 0.0]
RETURN u.name, u.pwdlastset, u.hasspn
ORDER BY u.pwdlastset ASC
```

**Common mistake.** Epoch arithmetic reads backwards from natural language. "In the last 90 days" feels like a small number so people reach for `<`, but epoch time counts *up* from 1970, so recent is *large*. The reliable trick: build the threshold value once, and read the comparison as a plain number line. `now` is the biggest number, `now - 90 days` is smaller, older is smaller still. If you want recent, you want the bigger side, which is `>`.

The `NOT u.lastlogon IN [-1.0, 0.0]` guard is also load-bearing rather than decorative. AD represents "never" as 0, and BloodHound uses `-1` for "not collected". Both are enormously less than any threshold you compute, so without the guard every never-logged-on and every uncollected account lands in your "stale" bucket and inflates the finding. Note also that `lastlogon` is not replicated between domain controllers, so a per-DC value is only as good as the DC you asked; `lastlogontimestamp` is replicated but is deliberately imprecise by up to about two weeks. For "is this account dormant", use `lastlogontimestamp`. For "did this specific DC see this account recently", use `lastlogon`.

#### The duplicate ESC9

The source's ADCS set contains two entries both named "Find Unsecured Certificate Templates (ESC9)". The first is a verbatim copy of the ESC1 query body (`Enrollee Supplies Subject` plus `Client Authentication`) and has nothing to do with ESC9. The second is the real one, testing for `NoSecurityExtension` in the enrollment flags. Delete the first. An operator running it gets ESC1 results, labels them ESC9 in the report, and looks foolish in the debrief.

On current CE none of that query set works anyway, for a more fundamental reason covered below: those queries model certificate templates as `GPO` nodes with a `type` property, which was a community fork's hack. CE has real `CertTemplate` and `EnterpriseCA` node labels.

#### Legacy relationship-type syntax

The source's "Non Admin Groups with High Value Privileges":

```cypher
MATCH p=(g:Group)-[r:Owns|:WriteDacl|:GenericAll|:WriteOwner|:ExecuteDCOM|:GenericWrite|:AllowedToDelegate|:ForceChangePassword]->(n:Computer) WHERE NOT g.name CONTAINS 'ADMIN' RETURN p
```

The `|:` form no longer parses, and `NOT g.name CONTAINS 'ADMIN'` depends on an assumption about stored case. Corrected:

```cypher
MATCH p = (g:Group)-[:Owns|WriteDacl|GenericAll|WriteOwner|ExecuteDCOM|GenericWrite|AllowedToDelegate|ForceChangePassword]->(c:Computer)
WHERE NOT toUpper(g.name) CONTAINS 'ADMIN'
  AND NOT g.system_tags CONTAINS 'admin_tier_0'
RETURN p
```

**Common mistake.** Filtering privileged groups out by name substring is a heuristic, not a control. Groups called `SVC-Deploy` or `Helpdesk-T2` are frequently more privileged than anything called Admin. Filter on the Tier Zero tag, and use the name filter only as an additional cosmetic pass.

#### Rebound path variable

The source's "Logged in Admins":

```cypher
MATCH p=(a:Computer)-[r:HasSession]->(b:User) WITH a,b,r MATCH p=shortestPath((b)-[:AdminTo|MemberOf*1..]->(a)) RETURN p
```

`p` is bound by the first `MATCH` and then rebound by the second, which is an error. Corrected:

```cypher
MATCH (c:Computer)-[:HasSession]->(u:User)
WITH c, u
MATCH p = shortestPath((u)-[:AdminTo|MemberOf*1..4]->(c))
RETURN p
```

**What to do with a hit.** This finds users with an active session on a host they administer, which means their credentials are sitting in LSASS on a box where they have the privilege to have logged in interactively. It is the classic credential-harvesting shopping list. Also note the depth bound added here: the unbounded original is slow on any real estate.

#### Also broken, briefly

- `MATCH p =(m:User)-[r:AZResetPassword|AZOwns|...|AZOwnsAZAvereContributor]->(n)` contains `AZOwnsAZAvereContributor`, which is two edge names concatenated by a missing pipe and matches nothing. It should be `AZOwns|AZAvereContributor`.
- `MATCH (n:User {domain: {result}}) MATCH (m:Computer {domain: {}})` uses removed parameter syntax and an empty parameter placeholder.
- `WHERE g.objectid =~ "(?i)S-1-5-.*-525"` for Protected Users works but is a fragile regex where `ENDS WITH '-525'` is clearer and faster.
- `WHERE toUpper(c.operatingsystem) CONTAINS '7'` for Windows 7 matches any OS string containing the digit 7. Substring matching on OS strings is unreliable in general; prefer `STARTS WITH` on a specific product string, and cross-check `operatingsystemversion`.
- The plaintext-password query set depends on `plaintext` and `plaintextpassword` properties that no collector produces. They were manually written into the Neo4j database, which CE's read-only Cypher endpoint no longer permits. The modern equivalent is to keep your cracked credentials in your own store and use them to drive the owned tag, not to invent node properties.

### A curated query library

Organised by what you are trying to do. Each query says what to do with a result. Written in CE dialect; if you are on legacy, substitute `{highvalue:true}` for the Tier Zero tag test and `{owned:true}` for the owned tag test, and revert the ADCS node labels to the `GPO`-with-`type` form.

Throughout, `$T0` stands for the Tier Zero predicate `n.system_tags CONTAINS 'admin_tier_0'` and `$OWNED` for `n.system_tags CONTAINS 'owned'`. Substitute the actual property name your instance uses.

#### Mapping the estate

Run these first. They tell you how big the problem is and where to spend the engagement.

```cypher
// Object census: is this a 500-object lab or a 200,000-object forest?
MATCH (n) RETURN labels(n) AS kind, count(*) AS total ORDER BY total DESC
```

Sanity-checks your collection and tells you immediately whether ADCS, GPO, and OU data landed.

```cypher
// Domains and forests in the graph
MATCH (d:Domain) RETURN d.name, d.functionallevel, d.objectid ORDER BY d.name
```

If the client said "one domain" and you see four, your scope conversation just changed.

```cypher
// Tier Zero inventory: what does the tool consider domain-equivalent here?
MATCH (n) WHERE n.system_tags CONTAINS 'admin_tier_0'
RETURN labels(n) AS kind, n.name ORDER BY kind, n.name
```

Read this list critically and extend it. If the backup service account, the vCenter account, or the EDR console account is not in it, add them. Paths to those assets are full compromises and the default seed list does not know your client's estate.

```cypher
// Unsupported and end-of-life operating systems still enabled
MATCH (c:Computer)
WHERE c.enabled = true AND c.operatingsystem IS NOT NULL
RETURN c.operatingsystem AS os, count(*) AS hosts
ORDER BY hosts DESC
```

Aggregate first, then drill into specific versions. A count by OS string is a report finding on its own and tells you which hosts will fall to old local exploits.

```cypher
// Privileged group membership, fully unrolled through nesting
MATCH p = (n)-[:MemberOf*1..]->(g:Group)
WHERE g.objectid ENDS WITH '-512' OR g.objectid ENDS WITH '-519' OR g.objectid ENDS WITH '-518'
RETURN p
```

The effective membership of Domain Admins, Enterprise Admins, and Schema Admins, including everything nested. This is almost always larger than the client believes. Return it as a path so you can show *how* each principal got there, which is what makes the finding actionable.

#### Finding footholds

You have a low-privilege credential or none at all. What is reachable?

```cypher
// What can Domain Users do? The single most productive query in the tool.
MATCH p = (g:Group)-[r]->(n)
WHERE g.objectid ENDS WITH '-513' AND r.isacl = true
RETURN p
```

Any ACL edge from Domain Users is effectively an anonymous-authenticated privilege. Every one of these is a finding and most are a foothold. Also check `-515` (Domain Computers) and the Authenticated Users and Everyone principals, which are modelled as their own nodes.

```cypher
// Where can Domain Users get a shell?
MATCH p = (g:Group)-[:CanRDP|CanPSRemote|ExecuteDCOM|AdminTo|SQLAdmin]->(c:Computer)
WHERE g.objectid ENDS WITH '-513'
RETURN p
```

Your initial execution options with nothing but a domain account. Prefer the servers in this list over the workstations: better data, more sessions, often weaker endpoint tooling.

```cypher
// Accounts with no password required, or with a password in a readable field
MATCH (u:User)
WHERE u.enabled = true
  AND (u.passwordnotreqd = true OR u.description =~ '(?i).*(pass|pwd|creds|secret).*')
RETURN u.name, u.passwordnotreqd, u.description
```

Description-field credentials are still real and still common, particularly on service and contractor accounts. `passwordnotreqd` accounts may authenticate with an empty password; test them.

```cypher
// Machines running the WebClient service: NTLM relay coercion targets over HTTP
MATCH (c:Computer) WHERE c.webclientrunning = true RETURN c.name, c.operatingsystem
```

WebDAV coercion produces HTTP authentication, which is relayable to LDAP and to ADCS web enrollment even where SMB signing blocks the SMB path. Requires the `WebClientService` collection method to have run.

#### Credential access

Where is credential material sitting, and who can read it?

```cypher
// Who can read LAPS-managed local administrator passwords
MATCH p = (n)-[:ReadLAPSPassword|SyncLAPSPassword]->(c:Computer)
RETURN p
```

Each hit is a direct route to local admin on that host with no exploitation required, just an attribute read. Check whether the reader set is wider than intended: LAPS read rights delegated at OU level to a broad helpdesk group is a very common finding.

```cypher
// Computers with no LAPS: shared local admin password candidates
MATCH (c:Computer) WHERE c.enabled = true AND coalesce(c.haslaps, false) = false
RETURN c.name, c.operatingsystem
```

Where LAPS is absent, one cracked or dumped local administrator hash may work estate-wide. Test it against this list with `nxc smb --local-auth` before assuming.

```cypher
// Group managed service accounts and who can retrieve their passwords
MATCH p = (n)-[:ReadGMSAPassword]->(u)
RETURN p
```

gMSA passwords are retrievable as an attribute by the principals listed in `msDS-GroupMSAMembership`. A gMSA is usually a service account with real privilege, so this is often a short path to something useful. Retrieve with `bloodyAD` or `nxc ldap --gmsa`.

```cypher
// DCSync rights: who can replicate secrets out of the domain
MATCH p = (n)-[:DCSync|GetChangesAll]->(d:Domain)
RETURN p
```

Anything here that is not a domain controller or a known replication service is domain compromise. This edge is computed during post-processing, so if it is empty, confirm analysis finished before believing it.

```cypher
// Shadow credential targets: write access to msDS-KeyCredentialLink
MATCH p = (s)-[:AddKeyCredentialLink]->(t)
WHERE s.system_tags CONTAINS 'owned'
RETURN p
```

The cleanest privilege escalation primitive in modern AD: add a key credential, request a PKINIT TGT as the target, extract the NT hash from the PAC, remove the key credential. Requires a functioning ADCS or at least the KDC's certificate infrastructure. Abuse with `certipy shadow auto` or `pywhisker`.

#### Kerberos abuse

```cypher
// Kerberoastable accounts, ranked by whether they are worth cracking
MATCH (u:User)
WHERE u.hasspn = true AND u.enabled = true AND NOT u.objectid ENDS WITH '-502'
OPTIONAL MATCH (u)-[:MemberOf*1..]->(g:Group) WHERE g.system_tags CONTAINS 'admin_tier_0'
WITH u, count(g) AS t0groups
RETURN u.name, u.pwdlastset, u.serviceprincipalnames, t0groups, u.supportedencryptiontypes
ORDER BY t0groups DESC, u.pwdlastset ASC
```

Excluding the `-502` RID drops KRBTGT, which always has an SPN and is never roastable in any useful sense. Sort by Tier Zero membership then by password age: a privileged account with an ancient password is where you start. `supportedencryptiontypes` tells you whether you will get an RC4 ticket (fast to crack) or AES-only (much slower). Roast with `impacket-GetUserSPNs` or `nxc ldap --kerberoasting`.

```cypher
// AS-REP roastable accounts: Kerberos pre-authentication not required
MATCH (u:User) WHERE u.dontreqpreauth = true AND u.enabled = true
RETURN u.name, u.pwdlastset, u.admincount
```

These require no credentials at all to attack, so they are your first move with nothing but a username list. Harvest with `impacket-GetNPUsers` or `nxc ldap --asreproast`.

```cypher
// Accounts you can force an SPN onto: targeted Kerberoasting
MATCH p = (s)-[:WriteSPN|GenericAll|GenericWrite]->(u:User)
WHERE s.system_tags CONTAINS 'owned' AND u.hasspn = false
RETURN p
```

Write an SPN to a user you control the object of, roast it, remove the SPN. This converts object write access into a crackable hash and works against accounts nobody thought were service accounts. Prefer targets with old passwords.

```cypher
// Accounts not protected against delegation abuse
MATCH (u:User)
WHERE u.admincount = true AND u.enabled = true
  AND coalesce(u.sensitive, false) = false
  AND NOT (u)-[:MemberOf*1..]->(:Group {objectid: 'S-1-5-21-...-525'})
RETURN u.name
```

Privileged accounts that are neither marked sensitive-and-cannot-be-delegated nor in Protected Users can be impersonated via delegation and are subject to weaker Kerberos protections. Each one is both a finding and a target.

**Common mistake.** Writing this with an `EXISTS { ... }` subquery. **BloodHound CE does not support `EXISTS { }`** and it never has. The Cypher grammar defines the rule but the parser explicitly rejects it, returning `oC_ExistentialSubquery rule is not supported`, which surfaces through the API as an unparseable-query error. This is a parser-level refusal, so it fails identically on the Neo4j and PostgreSQL backends. Use `NOT (pattern)` as above, or the `collect()` and `IN` pattern shown earlier.

The `exists(n.prop)` *function* form is a separate and messier case: it parses, then executes on Neo4j and fails on PostgreSQL with `unknown cypher function: exists`. Use `n.prop IS NOT NULL` instead, which is portable across both.

#### Delegation

```cypher
// Unconstrained delegation on non-domain-controllers
MATCH (dc:Computer)-[:MemberOf*1..]->(g:Group) WHERE g.objectid ENDS WITH '-516'
WITH collect(dc.objectid) AS dcs
MATCH (c:Computer)
WHERE c.unconstraineddelegation = true AND NOT c.objectid IN dcs AND c.enabled = true
RETURN c.name, c.operatingsystem
```

Compromise any of these, coerce a domain controller to authenticate to it, and you have a DC TGT in your cache. This is a two-step to domain compromise and one of the highest-severity findings you can report. Add every hit to your Tier Zero tag set immediately, because the graph should treat them as domain-equivalent even though AD does not.

```cypher
// Constrained delegation, with and without protocol transition
MATCH (n)
WHERE n.allowedtodelegate IS NOT NULL AND size(n.allowedtodelegate) > 0
RETURN n.name, labels(n) AS kind, n.trustedtoauth AS protocol_transition, n.allowedtodelegate
ORDER BY protocol_transition DESC
```

With protocol transition (`trustedtoauth` true, that is S4U2Self plus S4U2Proxy) you can impersonate any non-protected user to the listed services from the compromised account alone. Without it you need an existing forwardable ticket, which is a materially harder precondition. Read the `allowedtodelegate` list carefully: an SPN on a domain controller, or an SPN with a service class you can substitute (the classic being requesting a ticket for a different service class on the same host), turns a narrow delegation into a broad one.

```cypher
// Resource-based constrained delegation already configured
MATCH p = (s)-[:AllowedToAct]->(t) RETURN p
```

Existing RBCD relationships. Anything unexpected here is either a misconfiguration or someone else's persistence.

```cypher
// Where you can configure RBCD yourself
MATCH p = (s)-[:AddAllowedToAct|WriteAccountRestrictions|GenericAll|GenericWrite]->(c:Computer)
WHERE s.system_tags CONTAINS 'owned'
RETURN p
```

Write access to a computer's account restrictions means you can set RBCD from a principal you control to that computer and then S4U your way to local SYSTEM on it. Needs either a machine account you control or the ability to create one, so check the domain's `ms-DS-MachineAccountQuota`:

```cypher
MATCH (d:Domain) RETURN d.name, d.machineaccountquota
```

A non-zero quota means any domain user can create a computer account and therefore has the SPN-bearing principal that RBCD requires. Zero, which is now a common hardening step, means you need to find an existing account you control with an SPN, or use a shadow-credential-derived certificate instead.

#### ACL and object control

This is where the depth in a real estate lives, and where the graph earns its keep.

```cypher
// Every ACL-derived control edge from something you own
MATCH p = (s)-[r]->(t)
WHERE s.system_tags CONTAINS 'owned' AND r.isacl = true
RETURN p
```

Your immediate next moves, one hop out. Run this after every new compromise. `isacl` is the flag that separates "somebody granted this" from structural edges, which is exactly the distinction you care about when looking for a misconfiguration.

```cypher
// First-degree object control, ranked: who holds the most direct power
MATCH (s)-[r]->(t) WHERE r.isacl = true
WITH s, count(DISTINCT t) AS controlled
WHERE controlled > 5
RETURN s.name, labels(s) AS kind, controlled
ORDER BY controlled DESC LIMIT 25
```

The top of this list is where the estate's real administrative power sits, regardless of what the group names say. In the report, these are your privilege-consolidation findings. Offensively, compromising a node near the top of this list is worth far more than its group membership suggests.

```cypher
// Control delegated through group membership rather than held directly
MATCH (s)-[:MemberOf*1..]->(g:Group)-[r]->(t) WHERE r.isacl = true
WITH s, count(DISTINCT t) AS controlled
WHERE controlled > 5
RETURN s.name, controlled ORDER BY controlled DESC LIMIT 25
```

The same question but accounting for nesting, which is where the surprises are. A user with zero direct ACLs can hold control over hundreds of objects through three layers of group nesting, and nobody has ever audited that.

```cypher
// Non-privileged principals who can add members to groups
MATCH p = (s)-[:AddMember|AddSelf|GenericAll|GenericWrite|WriteDacl|WriteOwner|Owns]->(g:Group)
WHERE coalesce(s.admincount, false) = false
  AND NOT s.system_tags CONTAINS 'admin_tier_0'
RETURN p
```

Group write access is transitive privilege: whatever the group can do, the writer can do by joining it. Chase these into the group's own outbound edges. This is the mechanism behind the majority of multi-hop AD attack paths.

```cypher
// Password reset rights across the estate
MATCH p = (s)-[:ForceChangePassword]->(u:User)
WHERE NOT s.system_tags CONTAINS 'admin_tier_0'
RETURN p
```
