The vocabulary first, because it is used loosely everywhere.

| Term | What it actually is | What it means for you |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **AV** | Signature and heuristic scanning of files and memory, with a blocking verdict. Historically a minifilter plus a scan engine plus a definition set | Defeated by novelty. A file nobody has seen before has no signature |
| **NGAV** | AV plus a local machine learning classifier and cloud reputation lookups, still fundamentally a file and process verdict engine | Defeated less easily by novelty, because the classifier generalises. Still a point-in-time verdict |
| **EDR** | A telemetry sensor that records process, thread, image, registry, file, network and memory events, ships them to a backend, and applies detection logic there as well as locally | Not defeated by novelty at all. It does not care whether it has seen your binary. It cares what your binary did |
| **XDR** | The same backend correlating endpoint telemetry with identity, mail, cloud and network sources | Your endpoint tradecraft can be perfect and you still get caught by the sign-in that came from the wrong ASN |
| **MDR / SOC** | Humans, on a rota, reading the alerts the above generate | The actual adversary. Everything else is plumbing |

The single most important correction to the source's model: **EDR does not primarily work by hooking the Win32 API**. It hooks userland APIs as a convenience layer for argument inspection, and it is the layer every public bypass targets precisely because it is the layer you can reach. The telemetry that actually catches operators comes from the kernel, from ETW, and from correlation performed in a cloud backend minutes after the event, where you have no reach at all. Spend your effort accordingly.

## How a modern endpoint agent actually observes you

### Userland API hooking

**What it is.** The agent injects a DLL into every process it wants visibility into, usually at process creation, and rewrites the first few instructions of selected functions so that control transfers to its own code before the real function runs. This is an **inline hook** or **detour**: the original bytes are replaced with a `jmp` to a stub, the stub logs and inspects arguments, then jumps to a **trampoline** holding the relocated original instructions and continues into the real function.

**Why the hooks go where they go.** Every Windows userland operation eventually becomes a syscall, and on Windows almost every syscall stub lives in *ntdll.dll*. A syscall stub is short and predictable: move the syscall number into `eax`, move the stack pointer into `r10`, execute `syscall`, return. Hooking *ntdll* therefore gives near total coverage of interesting operations for the cost of a few dozen hooks, and it catches code that skips the higher level wrappers entirely. That is the reason the source's confused paragraph gestures at *ntdll*: it is the last piece of userland code before the kernel boundary, and hooking it is the cheapest broad-coverage choice available in userland.

Higher layer hooks still exist and are placed deliberately, because they see semantics that the syscall layer has already thrown away. *kernel32*/*kernelbase* `CreateProcessW` sees the full command line before it is marshalled into a `RTL_USER_PROCESS_PARAMETERS` structure. *ws2_32* and *wininet* see hostnames before DNS resolution. *advapi32* sees service and registry paths as strings. *amsi.dll* sees script content. A vendor picks a mix: a small number of high value semantic hooks up top, a broad set of choke point hooks in *ntdll*.

Two related userland techniques are not classic inline hooks but serve the same purpose and are worth knowing because they survive naive unhooking:

- **Instrumentation callbacks.** A process-wide callback registered through `NtSetInformationProcess` with `ProcessInstrumentationCallback` fires on kernel-to-user transitions, including syscall returns. It is not a patch in *ntdll*, so restoring *ntdll* from disk does not remove it, and it observes syscalls regardless of how they were issued.
- **Hardware breakpoint hooking.** Debug registers plus a vectored exception handler give hooks with no modified bytes at all. Nothing to detect by comparing memory to disk.

**Why this layer is inherently bypassable.** The hook lives in your own process, in memory your own thread can write, installed by code running at your own privilege level. There is no security boundary between your shellcode and the hook. You can restore the original bytes from a clean copy of the file, you can map a fresh clean copy and use its stubs, you can call the `syscall` instruction yourself and never touch the hooked stub, you can remove the hooking DLL's entry from the loader lists, or you can simply avoid the specific functions that are hooked. All of these work. None of them are clever any more. Treat userland hook evasion as table stakes, not as an achievement, and understand that clearing it only removes the *argument inspection* capability, not the event stream.

**The consequence for detection.** When you unhook or use direct syscalls, the agent loses the pre-call argument view. It does not lose the process create event, the thread create event, the image load event, the memory allocation event, or the handle open event, because those come from the kernel.

### Kernel callbacks: the durable telemetry

Windows exposes a documented set of kernel notification interfaces that a driver can register for. These are the backbone of every serious EDR, and they are not reachable from userland at all.

| Callback registration | Fires on | What the agent gets |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `PsSetCreateProcessNotifyRoutineEx` / `Ex2` | Process create and exit | Full image path, PID, parent PID, creating PID and TID (which is not always the parent), command line, token, and a **veto**: the `Ex` variant can return a failure status and prevent the process from starting |
| `PsSetCreateThreadNotifyRoutine` / `Ex` | Thread create and exit | Which process created a thread in which other process. Remote thread creation is visible here with no userland hook whatsoever |
| `PsSetLoadImageNotifyRoutine` / `Ex` | Every DLL, EXE and driver mapped as an image | Full path, base address, whether the image is signed, and the process it landed in. This is where "why is *clr.dll* loading into *notepad.exe*" comes from |
| `CmRegisterCallbackEx` | Registry operations, pre and post | Key path, value name, data, calling process. Can also veto or rewrite |
| `ObRegisterCallbacks` | Handle create and duplicate on process and thread objects | The requesting process, the target process, and the requested access mask. Crucially it can **strip bits from the granted access**, which is how agents make `PROCESS_VM_READ` on *lsass.exe* fail for everyone but themselves |
| `FltRegisterFilter` (minifilter) | File system operations at a chosen altitude | Create, read, write, rename, close, with the ability to block or to scan the buffer before it hits disk |
| WFP callout driver | Network connection establishment, and optionally payload | Five tuple plus the owning process, at the kernel level, before any userland proxy sees it |
| ETW consumer in a protected process | See below | The memory and injection primitives that used to require a hook |

Note what this list means in practice. Process ancestry, remote thread creation, module loads, handle acquisition and access masks, registry writes and network connections with process attribution are all available to the agent **without a single userland hook**. Every one of those is a primitive that offensive tooling depends on. This is the core architectural point and the source's model missed it entirely.

**Why you cannot reach it.** Patching kernel code is prevented by Kernel Patch Protection on the structures that matter, loading your own driver requires a valid signature accepted by the current code integrity policy, and the callback arrays themselves are protected. Removing kernel callbacks requires arbitrary kernel read and write, which in practice means either a stolen signing key or an exploitable signed driver. That is a very different class of operation from patching a byte in your own address space, and it is loud in its own right.

**Protected process light.** The agent's own service typically runs as PPL with the anti-malware signing level, granted through an **ELAM** driver registered at boot. A PPL process cannot be opened for write, cannot be debugged, and cannot have code injected into it by a normal administrator. `SeDebugPrivilege` does not help. Killing the agent from userland as local admin is, on a correctly configured product, simply not available.

### ETW, and the provider that changed everything

**Event Tracing for Windows** is the operating system's built in high volume tracing framework. Instrumented components act as **providers**, a trace **session** subscribes to providers with a keyword mask and level, and a **consumer** reads the buffers. Almost everything in Windows is instrumented, and security products consume the parts they care about rather than building their own equivalents.

The providers that matter to you:

| Provider | Content of interest |
| --- | --- |
| `Microsoft-Windows-Threat-Intelligence` | The important one. Kernel-sourced events for memory allocation and protection changes, remote memory writes and reads, section mapping, remote thread context manipulation, thread creation, driver load and more. Consumption requires the listening process to be PPL anti-malware, so you cannot subscribe to it and you cannot easily silence it. It gives an agent the exact primitives it used to get from userland hooks on `NtAllocateVirtualMemory`, `NtProtectVirtualMemory`, `NtWriteVirtualMemory`, `NtMapViewOfSection` and `NtSetContextThread`, but from the kernel side of the boundary |
| `Microsoft-Windows-Kernel-Process` | Process and thread and image events, an alternative source to the callbacks |
| `Microsoft-Windows-Kernel-Registry` | Registry operations |
| `Microsoft-Windows-Kernel-File` | File operations |
| `Microsoft-Windows-Kernel-Network` | TCP and UDP with process attribution |
| `Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell` | Script block logging (4104) and module/pipeline logging (4103), plus engine lifecycle |
| `Microsoft-Windows-DotNETRuntime` and its Rundown counterpart | Assembly loads, method JIT events, module names, and the **CLR threat intelligence** surface used to spot in-memory .NET |
| `Microsoft-Windows-DNS-Client` | Queries and responses per process, including names that never appear in network telemetry because they were answered from cache |
| `Microsoft-Windows-WMI-Activity` | WMI operation and consumer creation, the source of most WMI persistence detections |
| `Microsoft-Antimalware-Scan-Interface` | AMSI scan requests and results, including content the AMSI provider did not itself block |
| `Microsoft-Windows-Security-Auditing` | The audit log, including 4688 process creation with command line where enabled, 4624/4625 logons, 4672 special privileges |

**The threat intelligence provider specifically.** Before it existed, an agent that wanted to know you had allocated `RWX` memory in another process had to hook `NtProtectVirtualMemory` in userland. Now it does not. Direct syscalls, indirect syscalls and full unhooking all leave that event stream completely intact. Any material that tells you syscalls "bypass EDR" is describing a 2019 product. Syscalls bypass *userland hooks*. The kernel still emits the event, and the backend still correlates it.

**The managed code angle.** Loading a .NET assembly from memory produces CLR ETW events describing the assembly name, module, and JIT activity, and the CLR is instrumented specifically to make in-memory assembly loading visible. A process that never had a reason to host the CLR suddenly hosting it, and JIT-compiling an assembly with no on-disk backing, is a strong signal on its own. This is why "execute-assembly" style tradecraft moved towards spawning a sacrificial process that plausibly hosts managed code, and why it is still one of the noisier things a C2 can do.

### AMSI: what actually gets scanned, and when

The **Antimalware Scan Interface** is a plain COM-ish interface exported by *amsi.dll*: `AmsiInitialize` to get a context, `AmsiOpenSession` to correlate related scans, `AmsiScanBuffer` or `AmsiScanString` to submit content, `AmsiCloseSession` and `AmsiUninitialize` to tidy up. Registered providers live under `HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\AMSI\Providers` as COM CLSIDs, and Defender registers itself there. A provider returns a result; anything at or above the "detected" threshold causes the caller to refuse to run the content.

The important property is that AMSI sits at the point where content is *about to be interpreted*, not at the point where it arrived. Obfuscation therefore does not help by itself, because the interpreter deobfuscates for you and then submits the result.

| Consumer | What it submits, and when |
| --- | --- |
| PowerShell | Each script block immediately before compilation and execution, including blocks produced at runtime by `Invoke-Expression`, so every layer of self-decoding gets scanned as it is peeled |
| Windows Script Host | JScript and VBScript source before execution |
| Office VBA | Macro content and, for some operations, the arguments of high risk calls made at runtime |
| Excel 4.0 macros | Sheet content and formula execution |
| .NET runtime | The byte array handed to in-memory assembly load paths, since .NET Framework 4.8 and in .NET Core/5+ |
| WMI | Operation payloads for some providers |
| Third party consumers | Anything that chooses to call the interface, including some EDR agents scanning their own captured content |

What AMSI does **not** see: native code you allocated and jumped into, compiled binaries that never pass through a scripting host, PowerShell running under a language runtime that predates the interface, and anything where you supplied the interpreter yourself. That last point matters: a custom host that embeds the PowerShell automation engine still gets AMSI, because the scan happens inside the engine, but a reimplementation of the parts of PowerShell you need does not.

### The filesystem minifilter

File operations pass through a stack of filter drivers ordered by **altitude**. An anti-malware minifilter typically registers pre-operation callbacks on create and write and a post-operation callback on cleanup, giving it three natural scan points: when a file is opened, when its contents change, and when the last handle closes. Scanning on close is the common choice because it sees the finished file exactly once. Verdicts are cached against the file's identity and change journal state so that repeated opens are cheap, which is why the second execution of a file is faster than the first and why touching a file can trigger a rescan.

Consequences for tradecraft. Writing a payload to disk gets it scanned even if you never execute it. Writing it in pieces and assembling in place still triggers a scan on close of the final write. Writing to a path excluded from scanning skips the scan but is itself recorded as a policy-relevant event by any agent that audits exclusions. Alternate data streams are scanned. Mounted containers such as ISO and VHD images used to launder the mark of the web, and current Windows propagates the mark into files extracted from them, so that specific trick is closed.

### Network filtering and egress telemetry

The **Windows Filtering Platform** lets a callout driver see connection establishment with the owning process attributed, which means egress is never anonymous on an instrumented host. On top of that:

- Enterprise proxies log the full URL, the user, the process where the agent integrates, the user agent, and the response size. Uncategorised or newly registered domains are commonly blocked outright by category, before any content inspection.
- TLS interception is widespread on managed estates via an enterprise root. Where it is not, JA3 and JA4 style client fingerprints still identify the TLS stack, and a fingerprint that does not match any browser or any Microsoft component on a workstation is anomalous by itself.
- Beaconing analytics look at inter-arrival time distributions, request size regularity, and total session counts to a single destination. Jitter widens the distribution but does not remove the periodicity, and long haul low and slow traffic is caught by volume-over-time rather than by any single request.
- DNS telemetry from `Microsoft-Windows-DNS-Client` sees names resolved by a process even when a proxy handles the connection, and sees cache hits that never touch the wire.

### Aggregation, and where detection actually happens

The local sensor is largely a shipper. It applies a small set of local blocking rules and a local classifier for latency-sensitive verdicts, then batches everything else to a backend. That backend is where the expensive work happens: cross-process correlation, cross-host correlation, prevalence lookups, sequence models, and analyst-authored detection logic that is updated daily without touching the endpoint.

Three operational consequences that people consistently underestimate:

1. **Detection is asynchronous.** Your payload can run cleanly, your callback can establish, and the alert can fire four minutes later when the backend correlates two events that were individually unremarkable. Absence of an immediate block is not evidence of success.
2. **Telemetry is retained and re-queried.** When new detection logic ships, it is run against stored history. An operation that looked clean in week one can be reconstructed in week six. You cannot unsend telemetry.
3. **Prevalence is global.** The backend knows how many machines in the world have seen your binary's hash, your signer, and your domain. "Never seen before" is itself a feature, and on some products a sufficiently rare and sufficiently suspicious file is held and detonated before it is allowed to run at all.

### The architectural summary

| Layer | Reachable from userland? | What removing it costs the defender | What it still leaves them |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Userland inline hooks | Yes, trivially | Argument inspection, content scanning, some local blocking | Everything below |
| AMSI | Yes, in your own process | Script and managed content scanning in that process | The AMSI ETW provider still logged the scan requests, and tampering is detectable |
| ETW writes from your own process | Yes, in your own process | Managed runtime and PowerShell telemetry from that process | Kernel providers, other processes, and the fact that a normally chatty provider went silent |
| `Microsoft-Windows-Threat-Intelligence` | No | Nothing you can do about it without kernel code execution | Memory, injection and thread manipulation events |
| Kernel callbacks | No | Nothing you can do about it without kernel code execution | Process, thread, image, registry, handle, file and network events |
| Cloud correlation | No | Nothing at all | The entire analytic surface, retroactively |

Public tooling clusters entirely in the top three rows. Operations fail on the bottom three.

## The detection taxonomy, properly

### Static detection

Static detection reaches a verdict on content without running it. It is the oldest layer, the easiest to defeat, and the one that still catches the overwhelming majority of unmodified public tooling because most operators download a release binary and run it.

**Hashes.** Exact cryptographic hashes of the whole file are the crudest form and are defeated by changing one byte. The variants that survive trivial mutation are more interesting:

| Hash type | Computed over | Defeated by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| SHA256 / MD5 | Whole file | Any single byte change |
| Authenticode hash | The PE excluding the signature blob and checksum | Any content change, but stable across re-signing |
| Imphash | The ordered list of imported DLL and function names | Changing the import table, dynamic resolution, or link order |
| Rich header hash | The undocumented Rich header describing the toolchain and object counts | A different compiler, version, or build configuration. Very effective at clustering builds from one operator |
| Section hashes | Individual PE sections | Changing that section only, so a payload swap in `.data` leaves `.text` matching |
| Fuzzy hashes (ssdeep, TLSH) | Rolling or locality-sensitive digests, giving a similarity score | Substantial structural change, not recompilation with a new key |

**Byte patterns and YARA-style rules.** A rule is a set of strings or byte sequences plus a condition, often anchored to file type, section, or offset. Real rules for offensive tooling target the parts that authors do not think to change: format strings in error messages, unusual mutex or pipe names, embedded configuration structure, the specific ordering of API name strings, .NET type and method names in the metadata tables, and PDB paths left in by a debug build. The important insight is that **a signature is written against whatever is stable in the artefact**, and what is stable is usually the parts nobody thought were interesting. Bisecting a binary against a scanner to find the flagged bytes is a routine and highly informative exercise: run it and you will usually find the trigger is a single string you could have removed for free.

**Import and structural analysis.** A binary that imports `VirtualAllocEx`, `WriteProcessMemory` and `CreateRemoteThread` has announced its intent in the import table. Resolving those dynamically moves the strings into the binary, where they can be encrypted, which is why nearly all loader tooling hashes API names. But structural analysis catches more than imports: a `.text` section marked writable, a section named unusually or not at all, a large high-entropy section with no imports referencing it, an entry point outside `.text`, a stripped or nonsensical compile timestamp, no version resource on a file claiming to be a Microsoft component, an icon lifted from a known application with mismatched metadata, a manifest requesting elevation on something claiming to be a document handler, and a raw size to virtual size ratio characteristic of a packer.

**Entropy.** Compressed or encrypted data is close to uniformly random and measures near 8 bits per byte, while compiled code sits around 6 to 6.5 and text much lower. High whole-file entropy used to be a strong packer signal. It has weakened in both directions: legitimate software is full of compressed resources and signed installers, and payload authors long ago learned to reduce apparent entropy by encoding to a lower-entropy alphabet, by splitting the ciphertext across many sections, by interleaving it with benign padding, or by storing it as something that looks like a resource. Entropy is now a weak feature that contributes to a classifier score rather than a rule on its own.

**Signing and reputation as static inputs.** A valid signature from a well-known publisher on a file with global prevalence in the millions is functionally a pass. A valid signature from a certificate issued last week to a company with no history is worse than no signature, because it is a strong anomaly. Self-signed is a non-starter on estates that enforce it.

**Where this leaves you.** A genuinely novel binary is not the problem it once was. Producing a unique hash is free, producing a build that trips no static rule is a morning's work with a local scanner, and static-only products are not what stops operations in 2026. The corollary is that time spent on static evasion past the point where local scanning is clean is time wasted, because the next layer does not care what your file looks like.

### Dynamic and behavioural detection

This is where operations actually die. The agent is not asking "is this file bad", it is asking "is this *sequence of events* consistent with an attack". Each individual event is usually benign.

**Process ancestry.** Parent and child relationships are the highest signal-to-noise feature in endpoint security, because normal software has a very small and very stable set of ancestry patterns. A shell spawned by an Office application, a script host spawned by a mail client, `rundll32` spawned by a browser, a signed Microsoft utility spawned by a process running from a user-writable directory: none of these require any knowledge of your payload. This is also the reason parent process spoofing exists, and why it is only a partial answer (see below).

**Command line content.** This is now the single richest detection source in existence, and it is the thing that killed the easy era of living off the land. Full command lines are captured at process creation by the kernel callback, by `Microsoft-Windows-Kernel-Process`, and by security audit event 4688 where the "include command line" policy is enabled. Detection logic against command lines is mature and specific: encoded PowerShell arguments, download cradles, `-nop -w hidden -enc`, WMI process creation with a remote host, service creation pointing at `cmd`, LOLBins invoked with argument shapes they never have legitimately, base64 with a UTF-16LE signature, unusual casing and character insertion used to defeat naive string matching (which is itself now a signature), and suspiciously long command lines in general. Any technique whose distinguishing feature appears on a command line should be assumed detected.

**Process access and memory operations.** Opening a handle to another process is recorded with the requested access mask, via `ObRegisterCallbacks`. The interesting masks are few and well known: `PROCESS_VM_READ` plus `PROCESS_QUERY_INFORMATION` for credential theft, `PROCESS_VM_WRITE` plus `PROCESS_VM_OPERATION` plus `PROCESS_CREATE_THREAD` for injection, `PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS` for the lazy. The target matters enormously: any handle to *lsass.exe* with read access from a non-standard process is close to a guaranteed alert on a modern estate, regardless of what you do with the handle, and many agents strip the access bits so the operation fails outright. Memory allocation, protection changes, remote writes and remote reads are all reported by the threat intelligence provider from the kernel.

**Injection patterns.** The classical sequence of allocate, write, change protection to executable, create remote thread is detected as a sequence, not as any one step. The many variants are individually named and individually detected: APC queueing to an alertable thread, thread context hijacking with suspend and `SetThreadContext` and resume, section mapping into the remote process rather than writing to it, `SetWindowsHookEx` and other callback-based loading, process hollowing with its distinctive create-suspended then unmap then write then resume shape, and early bird APC on a suspended process. What they share is a cross-process memory or execution primitive, and that primitive is exactly what the kernel telemetry reports. Choosing a more obscure variant changes which named rule fires, not whether the underlying events are recorded.

**Module load anomalies.** Every image map is reported with its path and signature status. The productive queries write themselves: a DLL loaded from a user-writable path into a signed process, a DLL loaded by a process that has no reason to need it, *clr.dll* or *mscoree.dll* appearing in a process that is not a managed application, *amsi.dll* or *vaultcli.dll* or *cryptsp.dll* loading somewhere unusual, a known-good DLL name loading from the wrong directory (a search-order hijack), and any image whose backing file was deleted after mapping.

**Unbacked memory.** This is the most durable memory-level detection and the one that catches the most tooling. Memory in a Windows process is either **image-backed** (`MEM_IMAGE`, mapped from a PE on disk by the loader, with a corresponding entry in the loader lists), **file-backed** (`MEM_MAPPED`), or **private** (`MEM_PRIVATE`, committed by the process itself). Legitimate executable code lives in image-backed memory, with a small and well characterised set of exceptions: JIT compilers, some interpreters, and a handful of anti-cheat and DRM systems. Therefore private committed memory with an executable protection, containing something that looks like code, and not corresponding to any loaded module, is anomalous by construction. Scanners walk the VAD tree looking for exactly this, and then scan the contents. `RWX` is worse than `RX` because almost nothing legitimate needs it. A PE header sitting at the base of a private allocation is worse still. This is the finding behind essentially every "beacon detected in memory" alert.

**Thread start addresses.** Thread creation reports its start address. A thread whose start address falls outside any loaded module is either injected shellcode or something doing its own code generation. This single feature, cheap to compute and available from the kernel callback, defeats a large amount of naive injection, and it is why techniques that reuse an existing thread or start in a module and pivot afterwards exist.

**Call stack inspection.** The more capable agents walk the call stack at the moment of a sensitive operation, either in a userland hook or at an ETW event. What they look for: a return address in unbacked memory, which means the caller was shellcode; a stack that cannot be unwound because the frames are not consistent with any function table; a syscall issued from an address outside *ntdll*, which is the tell for a naive direct-syscall implementation; a suspiciously short stack; and stacks whose frames are present but whose sequence is impossible for the API being called. This is the layer that indirect syscalls and call stack spoofing exist to address, and it is where current offensive and defensive research is actually happening.

**Token manipulation.** Enabling `SeDebugPrivilege`, adjusting a token's privileges, duplicating a token, impersonating, and swapping a process's primary token are all observable, and the audit log records special privilege assignment. A process that enables debug privilege and then opens a handle to a system process is a two-event sequence with almost no benign explanation.

**Correlation into a sequence.** The point that ties the section together. Consider: a signed Microsoft binary starts from a user's Downloads directory (unremarkable), it makes an outbound TLS connection to a domain first seen this month (mildly interesting), it allocates private executable memory (interesting), a thread starts outside any module (suspicious), and shortly afterwards a handle is opened to *lsass.exe* (alert). Any one of the first four in isolation generates nothing. Together they are a graph the backend recognises. **Your opsec problem is not any single event, it is the shape of the sequence.** Evasion that removes one event from a five-event chain buys you very little; evasion that changes the shape of the whole chain buys you a lot.

### Reputation and prevalence

Reputation is a detection input in its own right and it is invisible to local testing.

- **File prevalence.** How many distinct machines globally have seen this hash, and for how long. A first-seen file is a candidate for cloud-delivered blocking or for a hold-and-detonate decision on products that do that.
- **Signer reputation.** The certificate's age, its issuance history, and the prevalence of other files signed by it. A stolen or newly purchased certificate has a thin history and its first use is noteworthy.
- **Mark of the web.** Files written by browsers, mail clients and archive tools carry a `Zone.Identifier` alternate data stream, and the presence of that mark changes behaviour throughout the OS: Office opens in Protected View, script hosts refuse or warn, SmartScreen prompts, and some ASR rules key on it directly.
- **Domain and infrastructure reputation.** Registration age, categorisation, hosting ASN, certificate issuance history, passive DNS. A freshly registered domain on a cheap VPS with a certificate issued this morning is a bad choice regardless of how good your payload is. Categorisation-based proxy blocking will stop your callback before any endpoint control is involved.
- **Path and name plausibility.** The combination of a path, a filename, and a signer either matches the global norm or it does not.

### Machine learning classifiers

Both local and cloud classifiers are real and they matter, but it is worth being precise about what they key on, because the mystique is unhelpful.

**Static models** consume a feature vector extracted from the file: PE header fields, section characteristics and entropies, the import and export tables, string statistics and n-grams over printable strings, resource types and sizes, byte histograms and byte n-grams, and for managed code the metadata tables. They are excellent at recognising "this looks like the family of things in my malicious training set" and they generalise across small changes, which is why recompiling a public tool with a new key often still trips them while a from-scratch implementation does not.

**Behavioural models** consume sequences: API call or event n-grams, the process tree shape, timing. These are harder to fool because the features are the things you actually need to do.

Practical properties worth internalising. Classifiers are sensitive to distribution: content that shifts the feature vector towards the benign population moves the score, which is the mechanism behind appending large amounts of benign-looking data, borrowing icons and version resources and manifests from real software, linking in real libraries so the import table looks ordinary, and avoiding the structural oddities listed under static detection. They are also probabilistic, which means a score just under the threshold on your test machine can be over it after a model update, with no action on your part. And they are usually one input into a combined verdict rather than a standalone gate, so tuning against a single product's classifier score is a fragile way to spend time.

### Attack surface reduction and application control: prevention, not detection

The distinction matters because these do not generate an alert for an analyst to triage and then ignore. They stop the operation.

| Control | Mechanism | Effect on tradecraft |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **WDAC / App Control for Business** | Kernel-enforced code integrity policy specifying which code may run, by publisher, hash, path or file attributes. Applies to user mode binaries, DLLs, scripts and drivers depending on policy options | The strongest single control you will meet. An allow-listed estate stops arbitrary binaries dead, forces you into signed and permitted code, and with script enforcement puts PowerShell into Constrained Language Mode |
| **AppLocker** | Older, userland-assisted policy over executables, DLLs, scripts, installers and packaged apps | Weaker enforcement boundary than WDAC and historically bypassable through gaps in rule collections and default rule paths, but a well-written policy is still a serious obstacle |
| **Smart App Control** | Cloud-backed allow policy on consumer and some managed Windows installs, keyed on signing and reputation | Unsigned and unknown binaries are blocked rather than warned about |
| **Constrained Language Mode** | PowerShell restricts type creation, .NET method invocation, `Add-Type` and COM object instantiation | Removes almost all offensive PowerShell in one step. Most in-memory PowerShell tooling depends on reflection and P/Invoke, both of which are gone |
| **ASR rules** | Defender-enforced behavioural blocks, each independently configurable to audit or block | Named rules block Office applications creating child processes, Office writing executable content, script hosts executing downloaded content, obfuscated scripts, executable content from mail and webmail, `WMI` and `PSExec` process creation, untrusted and unsigned processes from USB, credential stealing from *lsass.exe*, and abuse of vulnerable signed drivers. Each one deletes a whole family of technique |
| **LSA protection (RunAsPPL)** and **Credential Guard** | *lsass.exe* as a protected process, and secrets isolated in a VBS enclave | Direct memory access to credential material is off the table without a kernel primitive. Credential Guard additionally means the derived material you want is not in *lsass* memory at all |
| **HVCI** | Hypervisor-enforced code integrity for kernel mode, plus the vulnerable driver blocklist | Removes most of the bring-your-own-driver class |
| **Process mitigations** (ACG, CIG, dynamic code prohibition, binary signature policy) | Per-process policy preventing dynamic code generation or requiring Microsoft-signed images | Where enabled, injection into that process fails structurally rather than being detected |

If you are on an estate with WDAC in enforcement, LSA protection on, ASR rules in block mode and Credential Guard enabled, the correct response is not a better loader. It is to stop trying to run code you brought and to start looking at credentials, delegated access, misconfigured ACLs, and the many paths through a domain that never require a payload at all.

## A layered model of what you must defeat

Five layers, in the order your operation encounters them. The honest assessment of relative difficulty is the point of the table.

| Layer | What is examining you | Difficulty in 2026 | What public tooling does about it |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **1. Getting on disk** | Minifilter scan on write and close, static signatures, local and cloud classifier, reputation and prevalence, mark of the web, application control policy | **Low**, unless application control is enforced, in which case **very high** | Solved. Every crypter, packer, and obfuscator addresses this layer, and a local scanner tells you immediately whether you succeeded |
| **2. Getting into memory** | Memory scanning of private executable regions, PE header detection, unbacked memory enumeration, module load telemetry, AMSI for scripted and managed content | **Low to moderate** | Well covered. Encryption at rest, sleep obfuscation, module stomping and header stomping are all commodity |
| **3. Executing** | Thread start address, call stack at sensitive operations, userland hooks, ETW threat intelligence memory events, instrumentation callbacks | **Moderate**, and rising | Partially covered. Direct and indirect syscalls, unhooking and stack spoofing exist in public tooling but are frequently implemented in ways that are themselves signatured |
| **4. Behaving** | Kernel process, thread, image, registry, handle and network telemetry, command lines, ancestry, cross-event correlation in the cloud, analyst review | **High**, and mostly unaddressed by tooling | Barely covered. There is no library you can link that makes lateral movement look like normal administration. This is a tradecraft problem, not a code problem |
| **5. Persisting** | Autostart enumeration and baselining, service and task creation telemetry, WMI subscription telemetry, registry callbacks, scheduled sweeps of every known persistence location, and the fact that persistence is durable evidence sitting on disk | **High**, because a persistence artefact is permanent and gets found on the next hunt even if it was missed at creation | Poorly covered, and frequently the thing that ends an engagement retroactively |

**The conclusion the source's model could not reach:** almost all publicly available evasion tooling addresses layers one and two, some of it reaches into layer three, and essentially none of it helps with layers four and five. Yet layer four is where operations are detected in practice. An operator with a mediocre loader and excellent behavioural discipline will survive longer than one with a state-of-the-art loader who runs a domain-wide share enumeration from a workstation at eleven in the morning.

## Evasion strategy at the level of principle

Tooling churns every eighteen months. The principles do not. Each of the following has a mechanism and a current viability, and several of them are simply solved for the defender now.

### Do not do the detected thing

The strongest evasion is not doing the thing that is detected, and it is consistently the least used. Every technique has an equivalent that produces a different, less monitored event chain. You want credentials from *lsass*: you could open a handle to it, or you could find them in a share, a script, a config file, a `SYSVOL` policy, a backup, a browser vault, a DPAPI blob you can decrypt offline, or a Kerberos ticket you can request legitimately. You want code on a remote host: you could inject into a process, or you could use the administrative interface the estate already uses for software deployment, which produces telemetry indistinguishable from Tuesday afternoon. You want to enumerate the domain: you could run a collector that touches every host, or you could issue paced LDAP queries from a context that queries LDAP all day anyway.

This is the highest-leverage principle in the entire discipline and it requires no code. Before you reach for a bypass, ask which event the detection is actually keyed on and whether there is a route to the same objective that never emits it.

### Living off the land, and its diminishing returns

**Mechanism.** Use signed, present, trusted binaries to perform your operation, so that static and reputation layers pass trivially and application control policies that trust Microsoft signatures are satisfied. This was extraordinarily effective when telemetry was file-centric.

**Why it decayed.** Command line capture. The whole value of a LOLBin is that the binary is trusted; the whole problem is that *what you asked it to do* is on the command line, in clear text, captured at process creation by the kernel, and matched against mature detection logic. `certutil` decoding a base64 file, `mshta` fetching a remote script, `regsvr32` with a remote scriptlet, `rundll32` with a `javascript:` URL, `msbuild` compiling an inline task, `wmic` creating a process on a remote host: every one of these is a named detection in every product, and several are blocked outright by ASR rules. The technique did not stop working mechanically, it stopped being quiet.

**Current viability.** Situational. The value is now in *which* LOLBin, not in the fact of using one. A binary that is present on the estate and used routinely by the estate's own administrators, invoked with an argument shape that matches its normal use, is still excellent. A binary from a public LOLBAS-style list invoked in the canonical way from that list is a detection, not an evasion. The half-life of any published LOLBin technique is short and you should assume anything on a public list is signatured.

### In-memory execution, and its limits

**Mechanism.** Never write the payload to disk, so the minifilter and everything keyed on file identity never sees it. Download and decrypt into memory, or receive it over an existing C2 channel, and execute in place.

**Limits.** This defeats layer one and nothing else. Memory is scanned. Private executable allocations are enumerated. Thread start addresses are checked. The CLR reports in-memory assembly loads over ETW. AMSI scans the buffer handed to managed load paths. "Fileless" was a meaningful advantage in 2016 and is now the baseline expectation that every defensive product is built around. Treat in-memory execution as necessary and completely insufficient.

### Unhooking, direct syscalls and indirect syscalls

**Mechanisms, precisely.**

- **Unhooking** restores the original bytes of hooked functions, either from a fresh read of the file on disk, from a manually mapped clean copy, or from the copy in a suspended child process's untouched *ntdll* before the agent's DLL loads.
- **Direct syscalls** skip the *ntdll* stub entirely: your own code sets up the registers and executes the `syscall` instruction from your own memory.
- **Indirect syscalls** set up the registers in your own code but transfer control to the `syscall` instruction *inside* *ntdll*, past any hook at the function's entry, so that the instruction pointer at the moment of the transition is in a legitimate module.

**What they defeat.** Userland inline hooks, and therefore the argument inspection and userland-derived blocking that depends on them. That is genuinely useful and it is why these techniques persist.

**What they do not defeat, and this is the part that matters.** Every kernel callback. The entire `Microsoft-Windows-Threat-Intelligence` event stream, which reports the memory and thread operations you were trying to hide from the kernel side of the boundary. Process instrumentation callbacks, which fire on the return path regardless of how the syscall was issued. Hardware breakpoint hooks, which have no bytes to restore. Unbacked memory scanning. And in the case of naive direct syscalls, a call stack in which the `syscall` originated from private memory, which is a cleaner detection than the hook it was avoiding. Indirect syscalls address that specific artefact and are the reason the technique moved that way, but they do not touch anything in the kernel.

**Current viability.** Necessary hygiene, not an evasion strategy. Also note that the *implementations* are heavily signatured: the well-known syscall stub generators produce recognisable code patterns, recognisable syscall number resolution routines, and recognisable sorted-export-address tricks. Using a public implementation unmodified reintroduces a static detection to solve a dynamic problem.

### Blinding telemetry, and why tampering is a gift to the defender

**Mechanisms.** Patch the first instruction of `EtwEventWrite` in your own process to return immediately, killing managed and PowerShell ETW from that process. Patch `AmsiScanBuffer` to return a clean verdict. Unregister an AMSI provider's COM registration. Disable a trace session or reduce its keyword mask. Unload a minifilter. Stop or disable the agent's service. Remove definitions.

**Why this is a trap.** Tampering with a security control is one of the highest-fidelity detections available, because there is no benign explanation. Legitimate software does not patch `EtwEventWrite`. Nobody accidentally unregisters an AMSI provider. Every one of these actions is itself instrumented: the agent watches its own configuration, its own service state, its own driver, its own registry keys, and the integrity of the functions it hooked. Products implement self-protection specifically here, and the backend alerts on the *absence* of expected telemetry as well as on the tampering event. A host that suddenly stops reporting is investigated, and "the sensor went quiet at 14:02" is the easiest incident timeline a responder will ever be handed.

There is also a scope-integrity argument that has nothing to do with stealth: you have changed the security posture of a production machine, and you now have to remember to change it back, correctly, on every host you touched.

**Current viability.** In-process AMSI and ETW patching remains widely used because it is cheap and it works locally, but assume both are detected by any competent product and treat them as a noise cost you are accepting knowingly. Anything that touches the agent itself should be treated as a last resort with an accompanying entry in your activity log.

### Module stomping and memory characteristic management

**Mechanism.** Rather than allocating private executable memory, load a real DLL that the process plausibly needs, then overwrite the code section of that mapping with your payload. The memory remains `MEM_IMAGE`, it is attributed to a real module with a real path, the thread start address falls inside a legitimate module, and a naive scan for unbacked executable memory finds nothing. Related techniques manage memory characteristics more generally: keeping the payload `RW` and only flipping to `RX` around execution, removing or corrupting the PE header of a loaded image so header-based scanning fails, splitting the payload across allocations, and ensuring allocation sizes and protections match the surrounding process's normal profile.

**What it does not solve.** The stomped region's contents no longer match the file on disk, and comparing a mapped image's code section against its backing file is exactly what the memory integrity scanners do. A module loaded into a process with no functional reason for it is a module load anomaly. And the technique's public implementations have their own recognisable patterns.

**Current viability.** Genuinely useful, still one of the better answers to memory scanning, and defeated by the specific tools built to look for it. Understand the trade: you have exchanged "unbacked executable memory" for "modified image-backed memory", and which is quieter depends entirely on what the defender is looking for.

### Sleep obfuscation

**Mechanism.** An implant spends the overwhelming majority of its life idle, so the state of its memory *while idle* is what any periodic scan encounters. Sleep obfuscation encrypts the implant's own memory before sleeping and decrypts on wake, arranging for the decryption to happen through a mechanism that does not require the implant's code to be resident and executable during the sleep: timer queue callbacks, APCs chained to perform protect-encrypt-wait-decrypt-protect, or a separate thread driving the transitions. During the sleep the region is encrypted and typically not executable, so a content scan finds noise.

**Why it is needed.** Beacon memory at rest is scanned. Agents run periodic memory scans, they scan on trigger events, and responders run targeted memory scanners against suspect processes. Unencrypted implant memory sitting in a process for hours is the easiest possible detection, and it is how a great deal of tooling with otherwise decent loaders gets found.

**What it does not solve.** The transitions themselves are observable: repeated protection changes on the same region are a pattern, and the specific mechanism used to schedule them has its own signature. A thread whose stack unwinds into an encrypted or unbacked region during the sleep is anomalous. And the sleep interval itself contributes to beacon timing analysis on the network side. Sleep obfuscation is necessary for any implant expected to live for days, and it does not make the process ordinary.

### Parent process and command line spoofing

**PPID spoofing.** Creating a process with an explicit parent through the extended startup attribute list makes the new process's recorded parent a process of your choosing, which breaks ancestry-based detection logic that reads the parent field. It does **not** break the kernel process notification callback, which reports the *creating* process and thread separately from the parent, so an agent using that data sees the real originator. Ancestry-based hunting that joins on creator rather than parent is unaffected. Treat PPID spoofing as defeating a subset of rules, not the concept.

**Command line spoofing.** Create the process suspended with a benign command line, rewrite the command line in the target's PEB process parameters, then resume. Anything reading the command line after the fact, including much manual triage, sees the benign version. But the process creation callback and the kernel process ETW provider capture the command line at creation, before you patched it, so the agent already has the real one. The mismatch between the recorded creation-time command line and the current PEB contents is itself a detection.

**Blocking non-Microsoft DLLs.** The mitigation policy that prevents non-Microsoft-signed binaries loading into a child process stops the agent's userland hooking DLL from being injected into it. That removes userland hooks from the child and nothing else, and the request for that mitigation policy is visible in the process creation telemetry.

The pattern across all three is instructive: each defeats the *convenient* source of a piece of information while leaving the *authoritative* source intact.

### Blending with the host

The general principle that subsumes most of the above. Every host has a normal: which processes run, from which paths, with which parents, at which times of day, talking to which destinations, and how often. Detection is fundamentally the identification of things outside that normal. Therefore:

- Look at the host before you act on it. What runs here? Which management agents, which scripting is normal, which admin tooling is already present and used?
- Prefer the estate's own mechanisms to your own. If the estate deploys software with a specific product, using that product is less anomalous than anything you bring.
- Match times to the user's working pattern. Activity from a workstation at 03:00 is a detection on its own in many environments.
- Keep volume down. Enumeration is the loudest thing most operators do, and it is loud because of its rate and breadth rather than its content. Paced, targeted queries against the objects you actually need beat a full collection every time.
- Pick host and process context to fit the action. Domain enumeration from a server that administrators use is unremarkable; the same queries from a receptionist's laptop are not.
- Name and path plausibility, for files, services, tasks and pipes. A default pipe name from a public C2 framework is a signature. A random GUID is also a signature, because nothing legitimate uses one there.

### Honest scorecard

| Technique | Defeats | Current status |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Recompiling, obfuscating, packing | Static signatures and hashes | Solved for you. Cheap and effective, and irrelevant beyond layer one |
| Living off the land | Static and reputation layers, some application control | Largely solved for defenders. Command line telemetry gutted it |
| In-memory execution | On-disk scanning | Baseline expectation, not an advantage |
| Unhooking | Userland hooks | Works, detectable via integrity checks of the agent's own hooks, defeats nothing in the kernel |
| Direct syscalls | Userland hooks | Works, and introduces a call stack artefact. Public implementations are statically signatured |
| Indirect syscalls | Userland hooks, plus the direct-syscall stack artefact | Current practice. Still defeats nothing in the kernel |
| AMSI patching | Script and managed content scanning in your process | Works, well detected, and the public one-liners are the most signatured strings in the discipline |
| ETW patching in-process | Managed and PowerShell telemetry from your process | Works locally, high-fidelity detection when the agent checks, and silence is itself a signal |
| Module stomping | Unbacked memory detection | Effective, and specifically targeted by memory integrity scanners |
| Sleep obfuscation | Memory scanning at rest | Necessary for long-lived implants. Transitions and timing remain observable |
| PPID spoofing | Parent-field ancestry rules | Partial. Creator-based telemetry is unaffected |
| Command line spoofing | Post-hoc command line reads | Partial and self-incriminating. Creation-time capture is authoritative |
| Call stack spoofing | Stack-based checks at sensitive operations | Live research area, genuinely useful, and implementation-specific |
| Disabling or tampering with the agent | Everything, briefly | The loudest option available. Effectively a self-report |
| Behavioural blending | Correlation, hunting, analyst review | The one that actually works, requires no tooling, and is the least practised |

## AMSI specifically

### What it is and why it exists

AMSI closes the gap between "the file was clean" and "the interpreter was handed something else entirely". Script content can be encoded, encrypted, downloaded, assembled at runtime and passed through arbitrary layers of transformation, and none of that content ever needs to touch disk. AMSI puts the scan at the point of interpretation so that whatever the interpreter is about to execute, in its final deobfuscated form, is what gets scanned.

The corollary, which is the single most important thing to understand about it: **obfuscating your script does not evade AMSI**. Each layer of self-decoding produces a new script block, and each new script block is submitted before it runs. Obfuscation only helps to the extent that the *final* content does not match a signature. What defeats AMSI is either not going through an AMSI-instrumented interpreter, or interfering with the scan itself.

### Bypass categories, conceptually

There are four, and everything published is an instance of one of them.

**1. Memory patching.** Modify the code or data that implements scanning inside your own process. The classic targets are `AmsiScanBuffer`, patched at its entry to return a success status with a clean result; `AmsiOpenSession`, patched to fail so that the caller has no session; and the private static field in the PowerShell automation assembly that records whether AMSI initialisation failed, set to `true` so the engine stops trying to scan. All of these are same-process, same-privilege memory writes and they all work mechanically. All of them are detected by products that verify the integrity of those functions, and the ETW AMSI provider records the abrupt cessation of scan requests from a process that was previously producing them.

**2. Provider unregistration or hijack.** AMSI dispatches to COM providers registered in the registry. Removing or redirecting that registration, or hijacking the COM class it resolves to, means the scan happens but no provider answers. This requires write access to the relevant registry location, which for the machine-wide registration means administrative rights, and both the registry write and the resulting loss of provider participation are observable. Per-user COM hijack variants exist and are correspondingly noisier in registry telemetry.

**3. Forcing an initialisation failure.** If AMSI fails to initialise, the consumer proceeds without scanning, because failing closed would break the system. Anything that makes initialisation fail therefore disables scanning for that consumer: corrupting or redirecting the provider registration so no provider loads, arranging for a stub *amsi.dll* to be found first through search order, or setting the automation engine's initialisation-failed state directly. This category is attractive because it can be achieved without patching any code, and it is well understood by defenders for exactly that reason.

**4. Avoiding the interface entirely.** The cleanest option. AMSI is a property of the *consumer*, not of the operating system, so a consumer that does not call it is not scanned. Options include using a language runtime version that predates the interface where it is still present, using a scripting or execution path that is not instrumented, doing the work in native compiled code rather than script, or reimplementing the small part of the interpreter's functionality you actually need. Note carefully that a custom .NET host embedding the PowerShell automation engine does **not** avoid AMSI, because the scan is inside the engine you are embedding.

| Category | Requires | Detected by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Memory patching | Code execution in the target process | Function integrity checks, ETW AMSI provider going silent, memory scan of the patched region |
| Provider unregistration | Registry write, usually admin for machine-wide | Registry callbacks, agent self-protection, configuration audit |
| Forced init failure | Varies: registry write, DLL placement, or in-process reflection | The same telemetry as the mechanism used, plus loss of scan events |
| Avoiding the interface | Choosing a different execution path | Nothing AMSI-specific. Everything else in this document still applies |

### The obfuscated one-liner, as a teaching example

The source's era produced a famous PowerShell one-liner that reflects into the automation assembly, retrieves the non-public static field controlling AMSI initialisation state, and sets it to `true`. It is worth understanding and it is worth never typing. It is very probably the single most signatured string in offensive security: it is signatured by AMSI itself, by static script scanning, by script block logging detections, and by every commercial and open detection rule set in existence. Any variant you find on the internet has been in every vendor's corpus for years.

The reason to study it is the obfuscation pattern, which is entirely transferable to content that is not already burned.

```powershell
# Teaching example only. This exact shape is universally signatured.
# 1. Reflection to reach a non-public static member without naming it in a way a
#    simple string match would catch.
$a = [Ref].Assembly.GetType('System.Management.Automation.Amsi' + 'Utils')

# 2. The member name is split and reassembled at runtime, so the literal never
#    appears in the source text.
$f = $a.GetField('amsi' + 'Init' + 'Failed', 'NonPublic,Static')

# 3. The write itself is unremarkable: a static field set on a null instance.
$f.SetValue($null, $true)
```

Three separable ideas here.

**Reflection as an indirection layer.** `[Ref].Assembly` is a terse way to obtain a reference to the automation assembly by way of a type that happens to live in it, avoiding an explicit assembly name. `GetType` and `GetField` with the `NonPublic, Static` binding flags reach members the language would not otherwise let you touch. The general lesson is that .NET reflection turns compile-time symbol references, which are visible in the source text and in the assembly metadata, into runtime string lookups, which can be constructed however you like.

**String splitting and runtime reassembly.** A signature matching the literal `amsiInitFailed` does not match `'amsi' + 'Init' + 'Failed'`. This is the same idea as the source's `'miMi' + 'kaTZ'` note, and it is the most basic form of the technique. Its limits are important: the string exists in memory once assembled, the concatenation pattern is itself a signature (rules match on suspicious concatenation adjacent to reflection), and AMSI sees the script block, so if the *behaviour* of the block is signatured rather than a literal within it, splitting achieves nothing. Splitting defeats naive literal matching and nothing more.

**Why it fails now.** The bypass targets a specific field in a specific assembly, so the whole construct is a fixed shape. Detection does not need the literal string; it can match on the reflection call sequence, on the binding flags combined with an assembly lookup, on the script block hash, or on the resulting memory state. Understand the mechanism, apply the ideas to content the corpus has not seen, and do not paste the one-liner.

### Verifying AMSI state

Useful for confirming what you are dealing with rather than for evasion.

```powershell
# Is the interface present and answering in this process?
[Ref].Assembly.GetType('System.Management.Automation.AmsiUtils') -ne $null

# What language mode are you in? Constrained means reflection and P/Invoke are gone,
# which matters far more than AMSI does.
$ExecutionContext.SessionState.LanguageMode

# Which AMSI providers are registered on the machine?
Get-ChildItem 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\AMSI\Providers'

# Is script block logging on? If so, everything you run is in the event log
# regardless of whether AMSI scanned it.
Get-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\ScriptBlockLogging' -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
```

**Detection note.** Reading the AMSI provider registry key and the logging policy is itself an enumeration pattern that some rule sets flag, because normal scripts do not check whether they are being logged. If you are going to check, check once.

## Interfering with security products

### Correcting the source

The source's "Disabling Antivirus on Windows" section contains two commands and neither does what it claims.

```powershell
# WRONG, from the source. This is a read cmdlet. It accepts no such parameter
# and disables nothing. At best it errors, at worst it silently prints
# configuration while you believe you have disabled protection.
Get-MPPreference -DisableRealTimeMonitoring $true
```

**Common mistake.** `Get-MpPreference` reads Defender's configuration. `Set-MpPreference` writes it. The parameter is `-DisableRealtimeMonitoring`, and the correct form is below. Note also the capitalisation of the noun: the module uses `Mp`, not `MP`, and while PowerShell cmdlet resolution is case-insensitive, the source's spelling is a good indicator that the line was copied without ever being run.

```powershell
Set-MpPreference -DisableRealtimeMonitoring $true
```

The second command in the source is presented as an AV bypass and is nothing of the sort.

```bash
# Mislabelled in the source. This writes the Restricted Admin registry value under
# the LSA key, which governs Restricted Admin mode for RDP. It has no relationship
# to antivirus whatsoever.
nxc smb $TARGET -u $USER -p $PASS -x 'reg add HKLM\System\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa /t REG_DWORD /v DisableRestrictedAdmin /d 0x0 /f'
```

That registry write belongs with the RDP and pass-the-hash material in the "Lateral Movement" section, and setting the value to `0` enables Restricted Admin mode rather than disabling anything. It is included here only so that nobody carries the mislabelling forward. (`cme` in the original is also dead; the current tool is `netexec`, invoked as `nxc`.)

### Tamper protection

Every current endpoint product implements self-protection, and on Defender it is called **tamper protection**. When it is on, and it is on by default on managed estates and enforced through the management plane rather than locally:

- `Set-MpPreference` calls that weaken protection are refused, or accepted and then silently reverted.
- Registry edits under the Defender policy keys are blocked or reverted.
- The service cannot be stopped or disabled through the service control manager.
- Definitions cannot be removed.
- Changes are only reversible from the management console, not from the endpoint, which means a local administrator genuinely cannot turn it off.

Attempting these operations generates events whether or not they succeed. Defender's operational log records configuration changes and protection state changes, and a blocked tamper attempt is logged as such and is a near-perfect detection.

| Event source | ID | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Windows Defender operational log | 5001 | Real-time protection disabled |
| Windows Defender operational log | 5007 | Configuration changed, including exclusion additions, with the before and after values |
| Windows Defender operational log | 5010 | Anti-spyware scanning disabled |
| Windows Defender operational log | 5012 | Antivirus scanning disabled |
| Windows Defender operational log | 5013 | Tamper protection blocked a change to Microsoft Defender Antivirus |
| Windows Defender operational log | 1116 / 1117 | Malware detected / action taken |
| Security log | 4688 | The process creation that made the change, with the full command line |
| Security log | 7036 / 7040 (System log) | Service state or start type change |

Note especially event 5007: it records the configuration before and after, which means an exclusion you add is not merely detectable, it is documented in the log with its full path.

### Exclusion paths as the quieter alternative

**What it is.** Rather than turning protection off, add a path, process, extension or process-name exclusion so that your specific working directory is not scanned. Protection remains on everywhere else, the product reports itself as healthy, and the estate's compliance dashboards stay green.

**Why it works.** Exclusions are a supported feature that exists because real software breaks under real-time scanning. Database files, build directories and line-of-business applications all legitimately need them, so exclusions are common and their presence is not intrinsically anomalous.

**Preconditions.** Local administrator, and tamper protection either off or not covering the exclusion surface. Where Defender configuration is managed centrally, locally added exclusions may be overwritten at the next policy refresh.

```powershell
# Read the current exclusion set first. Existing exclusions tell you what the estate
# already tolerates, and adding to an existing excluded tree is quieter than
# creating a new exclusion.
Get-MpPreference | Select-Object -ExpandProperty ExclusionPath
Get-MpPreference | Select-Object -ExpandProperty ExclusionProcess
Get-MpPreference | Select-Object -ExpandProperty ExclusionExtension

# Add and remove. Add-MpPreference appends, Set-MpPreference replaces the whole list,
# which is a good way to destroy an estate's carefully curated exclusions by accident.
Add-MpPreference -ExclusionPath 'C:\path\to\dir'
Remove-MpPreference -ExclusionPath 'C:\path\to\dir'
```

**Verify it worked.** Re-read `Get-MpPreference` and confirm the path is present. Then confirm behaviourally: write a file that you know is detected into the excluded path and confirm it survives.

**Detection and opsec.** Exclusion additions are audited. Event 5007 records the change with the path. Management consoles surface the full exclusion inventory across the estate and mature teams review it, because attacker-added exclusions are a well known technique and exclusion inventory review is a standard hunt. Some products alert specifically on exclusion addition by a process that is not the management agent. Adding an exclusion for a broad path, a whole drive, or a common extension is far louder than adding a narrow one. Adding an exclusion and never removing it leaves a permanent artefact attributable to your engagement.

**Failure modes.**

- `Set-MpPreference : Operation failed with the following error: 0x800106ba` or a generic access denied indicates tamper protection or a managed policy is refusing the change.
- The command succeeds, `Get-MpPreference` shows the exclusion, and it disappears within minutes: central policy refresh has reverted it.
- The exclusion is present and your payload is still killed: another product is doing the killing, or the detection happened at a layer exclusions do not cover, since a path exclusion suppresses file scanning and not behavioural blocking or ASR rules.

### Removing definitions

Defender's command line utility can delete the signature set, which leaves the service running and reporting as enabled while having nothing to detect with until the next update.

```powershell
& "$env:ProgramFiles\Windows Defender\MpCmdRun.exe" -RemoveDefinitions -All
```

**Reality check.** Tamper protection blocks this. It is a heavily signatured command line. Definitions update automatically and frequently, so the window is short. And "the endpoint has no antivirus definitions" is a compliance alert in any managed estate. This is a well known technique precisely because it is well known.

### The service and driver level

Below the configuration surface, an agent is a set of services and drivers. Attacking them is loud and structurally constrained.

- **Service stop and disable.** On a protected product the service is PPL and refuses to stop; on others, tamper protection blocks the change. Setting a service's start type to disabled in the registry survives a reboot, which is exactly why service start type changes on security services are monitored. The change appears in registry telemetry and in the System log.
- **Minifilter unload.** Detaching a filter driver requires the driver to permit unloading, and security minifilters do not. A filter manager unload attempt is logged.
- **Safe mode.** Booting into safe mode starts a minimal driver set, historically excluding third party security drivers. Configuring a safe mode boot and rebooting is about as visible as an action on a workstation can be: the boot configuration change, the reboot, the gap in telemetry, and the user noticing.
- **Bring your own vulnerable driver.** Conceptually: obtain a driver that carries a valid signature accepted by the machine's code integrity policy but contains a flaw exposing an arbitrary kernel read, write or process termination primitive, load it as a kernel service, and use that primitive to remove the agent's kernel callbacks, clear its ETW registrations, or terminate its protected process from kernel context. This is the only reliable way to remove kernel-level telemetry and it is a genuine capability. It is also the most heavily instrumented single thing you can do on a Windows host. The defences are layered and largely default now: HVCI, the Microsoft vulnerable driver blocklist which is enabled by default on current Windows and updated regularly, driver signature enforcement, and detection logic that alerts on kernel service creation, on the loading of any driver on a known-vulnerable list, and on the loading of any driver never before seen on the estate. Creating a kernel service requires administrator plus load driver privilege, writes a service registry key, and produces a driver load event that a competent product treats as critical. Public catalogues of vulnerable drivers exist and are read by both sides, which means anything you find in one is on the blocklist.

### The operational judgement

Disabling security software is almost always the wrong move on a real engagement, for four separate reasons that compound.

1. **It is detected.** Tampering has no benign explanation, which makes it the highest-confidence class of alert a product can raise. You will trade a probabilistic detection for a certain one.
2. **It is destructive.** You have modified the security posture of a production system. If you are wrong about reversibility, or you lose the host before you clean up, you have left a machine less protected than you found it, and that is a finding against you.
3. **It is frequently reversible only by reboot or by the management console**, which means you cannot quietly put it back.
4. **It usually does not solve your problem.** The reason your payload died is more often a behavioural detection or an application control policy than a file scan, and turning off real-time monitoring addresses neither.

What to do instead, in order of preference:

- Work out which layer actually caught you before changing anything. A local scan verdict, an AMSI block, a process that starts and immediately dies, a callback that never arrives, and an alert four minutes later are five different problems with five different answers.
- Change your payload or your technique rather than the defender's configuration. This is almost always cheaper.
- Choose an approach that does not generate the detected event at all.
- If you genuinely need a scanning exception for a specific tool in a specific directory, prefer the narrowest possible exclusion, log it in your activity record with a timestamp, and remove it before you leave.
- If a client explicitly asks you to demonstrate tamper resistance, do it deliberately, on an agreed host, at an agreed time, with the response team informed, and treat the resulting alert as the deliverable rather than as a failure.

## Testing your tooling responsibly

### Build a lab that resembles the target

A build that is clean against a default Defender install on a workstation with no internet connectivity tells you almost nothing about a managed estate. The gap between those two is where most operational surprises live.

What a representative lab needs:

- **The same products, at the same versions.** Ask during scoping which endpoint products are deployed. If the client will tell you, that single answer is worth more than any amount of generic hardening work.
- **Cloud connectivity enabled**, at least for some tests. Cloud-delivered protection, block-at-first-sight and prevalence lookups are a large fraction of a modern product's efficacy and they are entirely absent from an offline VM. Test both states so you know which detections are local and which are cloud.
- **Realistic policy.** Tamper protection on, ASR rules in their real mode, application control policy applied, LSA protection and Credential Guard set as the estate sets them, PowerShell logging enabled. A product in its out-of-the-box state is a different product.
- **A domain**, because a great deal of behavioural detection keys on ancestry, on identity, and on the difference between a workstation and a server.
- **Telemetry visibility of your own.** Run Sysmon with a well-known configuration, capture the relevant ETW providers, and enable full audit policy including command line capture. The point is not to detect yourself, it is to *see what you emit*. Reading your own telemetry is the single most educational thing you can do with a lab, and it is the only way to develop intuition for layer four.
- **Memory inspection tooling.** Scanners that enumerate private executable memory, unbacked regions, modified image sections and suspicious thread start addresses will find your loader's memory artefacts long before a product does, and they tell you exactly which artefact to fix.

### Do not submit samples to multi-engine scanning services

This is the mistake that costs the most and is the easiest to avoid. Public multi-engine scanning services exist to feed the anti-malware industry. Submitting a file to one distributes it to participating vendors, who ingest it into their corpora, and a sample that trips any heuristic gets analysed and signatured. You will typically have days at most before your build is dead everywhere, and your file hash, the metadata, and often the file itself become permanently queryable by anyone including the client's own blue team and any threat intelligence vendor they subscribe to.

Second-order consequences that people forget:

- **Hash queries are also submissions of a sort.** Looking up a hash tells the service, and anyone watching its telemetry, that someone possesses that file. Defenders monitor for lookups of hashes associated with their estate.
- **Attribution and clustering.** A sequence of submissions from one account, with the same Rich header, the same PDB path fragment, the same builder artefacts, clusters your builds into a recognisable toolkit that then gets tracked as a unit. You have created a signature for yourself, not just for one payload.
- **Client-visible embarrassment.** A client's threat intelligence platform lighting up on the payload you uploaded three days before the engagement is a genuinely bad conversation.
- **Third party no-distribute scanners** advertise that they do not share samples. You are trusting an anonymous service, often one with criminal clientele, with your tooling. The threat model there is worse, not better.

### Scan locally instead

Local scanning gives you the verdict without the distribution. Defender's own command line utility scans a specific file on demand, which is the fastest way to answer "does this trip the on-box engine".

```powershell
# Scan a single file with the local engine. ScanType 3 is a custom scan of the
# specified path.
& "$env:ProgramFiles\Windows Defender\MpCmdRun.exe" -Scan -ScanType 3 -File 'C:\path\to\payload.exe'
```

Beyond a yes or no answer, the productive technique is **bisection**: repeatedly scan truncated or modified copies of the artefact to find the byte range that triggers the verdict.
