| Short-haul C2 | Interactive work: short sleeps, high volume, post-exploitation | High during use, because this is where the noisy actions happen. | Days to weeks, rotated |
| Long-haul C2 | Persistence check-in only: very long sleeps, minimal traffic | Lowest, because it does almost nothing. | The whole engagement |
| Exfiltration and loot | Bulk data transfer | High and volumetrically obvious. | Per-transfer |
| Management | Your own access to the estate: SSH, log aggregation, monitoring | Not target-facing at all. | The whole engagement |

Each tier gets its own domains, its own redirectors and, where the framework allows, its own listeners. The reason is simple: the actions that get you caught are concentrated in the delivery and short-haul tiers, and if your long-haul persistence beacons call back to the same domain as the process injection you did on Tuesday, then a single detection removes your access entirely.

The **long-haul and short-haul split** deserves stating explicitly because it is the most useful single piece of infrastructure design in this section. On every host where you establish persistence, run a long-haul implant with a sleep measured in hours or a day, on its own domain, on its own redirector, doing nothing but checking in. Do no post-exploitation from it. When you want to work, task it once to spawn a short-haul implant on a different listener and different infrastructure, do the work there, and let the short-haul implant die. If the short-haul channel is detected, and the noisy activity means it is the one that will be, the defender burns a domain and a redirector and kills an implant that was going to exit anyway. Your long-haul access, which has produced almost no telemetry, is untouched. Re-establish and continue.

The **tiered redirector model** extends the same logic. Multiple redirectors point at one team server; multiple domains point at each redirector where the framework supports a callback list. A defender who blocks one domain does not block the channel. A defender who identifies one redirector address does not identify the team server. When Cobalt Strike or a similar framework supports multiple hosts in a single listener's callback list, use it, because an implant that fails over to a second domain survives the first being blocked without any action from you.

#### Infrastructure opsec

The infrastructure is itself part of the operation and it leaks.

**Never reuse infrastructure across clients.** One domain, one VPS, one certificate serving two engagements links them permanently in passive DNS and scan history. If either is ever published, both are.

**Never allow direct access to management ports.** SSH restricted to your management addresses or reachable only over a VPN, key authentication only, no passwords. The team server's operator port on loopback only, reached through a forward. Any framework web UI on loopback only.

**Assume the host will be seized or subpoenaed.** Full disk encryption, no client data stored on target-facing hosts, loot pulled back to your own storage and removed from the infrastructure promptly, and no credentials on the redirectors beyond what they need to forward traffic. A redirector should hold nothing except a web server configuration.

**Segregate identities.** Registrar accounts, hosting accounts and payment methods dedicated to this work and not shared with anything that identifies you or your employer more than the engagement already does. Registration details and WHOIS data are indexed and searched.

**Log everything, centrally, off the target-facing hosts.** Access logs from the redirectors and the team server's own logs, shipped to a host that is not exposed. This gives you three things: evidence for the report, the ability to notice when your infrastructure is being probed, and the ability to tell your own traffic from someone else's. RedElk exists specifically for this and does the enrichment and alerting for you.

**Monitor for your own burn.** Watch for your domains appearing in threat feeds, your certificates being flagged, your redirector addresses being scanned from the target's address space (a very strong signal that the blue team has found you), and unusual requests to your listener URIs from addresses that are not your implants. A sandbox replaying your traffic from a security vendor's address range is an early warning that a payload has been submitted for analysis.

#### Infrastructure as code

Build the infrastructure with a repeatable definition rather than by hand. Provisioning with Terraform or equivalent and configuration with Ansible or equivalent gives you three things that matter operationally: you can rebuild a burned redirector in minutes instead of an afternoon, every redirector is configured identically so a filtering mistake does not exist on only one of them, and the definition is a record of what you built which feeds directly into the teardown checklist. Public projects exist that provide red team infrastructure modules for exactly this; whether you use one or write your own, the requirement is that no piece of your infrastructure exists only as a set of commands somebody ran once.

### Traffic shaping and blending

The governing principle, and the one most operators get wrong: **your traffic must resemble the target's normal traffic, not generic internet traffic.** A beautifully crafted profile imitating a popular social media API is worthless in an environment where that platform is blocked, and it is worse than worthless in an environment where nobody has ever used it, because "the only host in the estate that has ever talked to this service" is a stronger signal than a slightly odd user agent. Blending is a property of a pair, your traffic and their baseline, not a property of your profile in isolation.

That means reconnaissance of the egress path comes before profile design. What you want to know:

- Is there a proxy, and is it explicit (configured or PAC-discovered) or transparent?
- Does it authenticate, and with what?
- Does it inspect TLS, and if so does it install its own root CA on the endpoints?
- What URL categories are permitted, and is uncategorised traffic blocked or allowed?
- Can hosts resolve arbitrary external domains, or only through an internal resolver, and does that resolver recurse for unknown zones?
- What does the estate's outbound traffic actually consist of? Which SaaS platforms, which CDNs, which update services?
- What browsers and versions are deployed, so your user agent can match something that exists?

You get most of this from a single foothold: the proxy configuration in the registry or the PAC file, the installed browsers and their versions, the certificate store for an inspection CA, the local DNS configuration, and a few minutes of watching what the host does on its own.

#### Shaping the request

Once you know the environment, the profile is a specification of a plausible client-server conversation.

**User agent.** Match a real browser at a real version, on the platform the implant is actually running on. A Chrome-on-Windows user agent from a host with no Chrome installed is a mismatch an analyst catches, and a user agent naming a browser version that never existed is caught by automation. Note that modern Chromium user agents are deliberately frozen and reduced, so the string carries less information than it used to and a plausible one is easy to produce; the effort should go into matching what the estate deploys. If the implant uses the operating system's HTTP stack and inherits the system proxy, consider whether a non-browser user agent belonging to a legitimate updater or line-of-business application is more plausible than a browser one, particularly for a long-haul channel that checks in from a service context where no browser would be running.

**URIs.** Model them on a real application. The best source is a capture of a genuine transaction from software the target uses: a session status poll, a telemetry submission, an asset fetch with a content hash in the path. Real applications have structure. They have versioned API paths, they use consistent naming conventions, they fetch static assets with cache-busting hashes, and the same URI appears many times. A randomly generated path of the correct length has none of that structure and reads as random to a human analyst even though it defeats a signature.

**Method and direction.** Use GET for the poll and POST for the output, because that is what real applications do, and because a stream of large POST bodies with no corresponding GETs is odd. Watch the sizes: a poll with no work to do should be small in both directions, and a large response to a request that carries no meaningful input is a mismatch.

**Headers.** Consistency is what matters. Send the `Accept`, `Accept-Language` and `Accept-Encoding` headers that the browser you are impersonating would send, in the order it would send them. Do not send a `Cookie` on the first request to a host that has never set one. Do not send a `Referer` that does not correspond to a page you claim to have visited. If you encode metadata into a cookie, make the cookie name and format match something real, and make sure the server's responses set it plausibly. On the server side, make the response headers match the content you claim to be returning: a `Content-Type` of `application/javascript` and a body that is base64 with no JavaScript around it is an obvious mismatch, which is exactly why profile transforms let you wrap the payload in a `prepend` and `append` that make it look like the thing it claims to be.

**Protocol version.** Most implants speak HTTP/1.1. On a modern network where browsers negotiate HTTP/2 to essentially every major service, an HTTP/1.1 connection to a web-looking destination is a minor but real anomaly, and one that a defender comparing your session against the baseline can see. Where the framework supports HTTP/2 or HTTP/3, that is a genuine blending advantage rather than a novelty.

**TLS.** The certificate must be valid for the hostname and issued by a CA the host trusts. If the environment inspects TLS, your certificate is replaced by the proxy's and the proxy sees your plaintext, so assume everything inside the tunnel is inspected: your URIs, your headers and your payload sizes are all visible, and any payload transfer will be scanned. That does not break the channel, but it means the shaping work matters more, not less.

#### Sleep, jitter and scheduling

**Sleep** is your latency budget and your primary volume control. **Jitter** randomises it as a percentage, so a 3600 second sleep with 37 percent jitter produces intervals between roughly 2268 and 3600 seconds.

Jitter defeats naive periodicity detection, which looks for a low variance in inter-arrival times. It does not defeat a determined analysis, because a uniform random distribution over a fixed range is itself a distinctive distribution, and because the total number of connections to a single external destination over a week is anomalous regardless of their spacing. Use high jitter, always, and do not imagine it makes you invisible.

The bigger lever is **volume and duration**. Fewer, larger, less frequent transactions look more like normal software behaviour than a steady drip. And an implant that checks in continuously for two weeks including nights and weekends is doing something no user-context application does. Schedule around the target's working hours: a long-haul implant that only calls home during the local business day is dramatically less anomalous than one that beacons at 03:00 on a Sunday from a workstation whose user has never logged in at that hour. Most frameworks support some form of working-hours restriction and a kill date, and both should be set: the working hours to blend, the kill date so that any implant you lose track of dies by itself rather than becoming an incident for the client after you have gone home.

**Response padding** deals with a specific detection. If every idle poll produces a byte-for-byte identical response, that constant response size is a signature. Cobalt Strike's `data_jitter` appends a random amount of random data to server responses for exactly this reason, and other frameworks have equivalents. Set it.

#### Hosting believable content

The redirector should serve a real website on the same domain and the same port as your C2 URIs. When an analyst pastes your domain into a browser, and they will, they should get a working site consistent with the domain name and the category it is registered under, not a default web server page, not a blank 200, and not a redirect to an unrelated well-known site. Clone something plausible, or stand up a small legitimate-looking site with real content, and make sure the paths your profile does not use return sensible 404s from that site rather than from a bare server.

The same logic applies to everything an inquisitive person can reach: certificate details that look like a real organisation, a robots.txt, a favicon, security headers that a real site would set. None of it stops a determined investigation. All of it raises the cost of the first five minutes, and the first five minutes is often the whole triage budget.

#### Working within the constraints you find

Some concrete cases and what they force:

- **Authenticating proxy, no direct egress.** You need a transport that uses the host's HTTP stack so it inherits the proxy configuration and authenticates as the current user. Implants that open raw sockets will simply fail, and the failure mode is silence.
- **TLS inspection with an endpoint-installed CA.** Your certificate is irrelevant, the proxy sees everything, and your JA3 or JA4 fingerprint is the one the proxy presents upstream rather than yours. Focus entirely on the HTTP layer and on payload content.
- **Category allowlist only.** Nothing gets out unless it is in an approved category. Your domain must be categorised into one of them before you start, which means the domain work happens weeks in advance.
- **No external DNS.** Clients query an internal resolver only. DNS C2 still works if that resolver recurses, and the query arrives at your server from the resolver, not from the host.
- **Egress only from specific servers.** Workstations have no route out at all. This is what peer-to-peer transports are for: one implant on a host with egress, everything else linked internally.
- **Application allowlisting on the endpoint.** A separate problem from network shaping, but it constrains your delivery and execution choices upstream of any of this.

### Detecting C2 as a discipline

Understanding how C2 is detected is not defensive trivia, it is the thing that justifies every choice above. This section is the detection surface, organised by where the detection lives.

#### TLS fingerprinting

**What it is.** Identifying the software originating or terminating a TLS connection from the structure of its handshake rather than from its content.

**Why it works.** A TLS ClientHello contains an ordered list of supported cipher suites, an ordered list of extensions, the supported elliptic curves and the point formats. Those lists are determined by the TLS library and its configuration, not by the application logic, and they are remarkably stable and remarkably varied between libraries. Hashing them produces a fingerprint. **JA3** is the original MD5-based client fingerprint, with **JA3S** for the server response. **JA4** and its family (JA4S for the server, JA4H for HTTP, JA4X for certificates) are the current generation from FoxIO, designed to be human-readable, sortable and more resistant to trivial evasion than JA3. **JARM** is different in kind: it is an active scanning technique that sends a series of crafted hellos to a server and fingerprints the server's responses, so it identifies your team server from the outside without any traffic from your implants.

**What it means for you.** A Go implant using the standard library produces a Go fingerprint. A Python implant produces a Python fingerprint. Neither has ever been produced by a browser, so on a network where the baseline is browsers and a handful of known applications, your implant's fingerprint is unique in the estate on day one. Two mitigations exist. Use the operating system's own TLS stack, so your fingerprint is Schannel's and matches what Windows components already produce, which is why Cobalt Strike's use of WinINet is an underrated advantage. Or use a library that deliberately mimics a browser's hello, which in the Go world is what uTLS exists to do.

On the server side, scan your own infrastructure and know what it looks like. A default team server's JARM is published, tagged automatically by internet-wide scanning services, and searchable by anyone. Terminating TLS at a CDN or at a redirector with a standard web server configuration solves this, because the fingerprint the world sees belongs to the web server and not to the framework.

#### Beacon periodicity and flow analysis

**What it is.** Statistical analysis of connection metadata to find a pattern that indicates automated check-in rather than human-driven traffic.

**Why it works.** Human browsing is bursty and irregular. Automated check-in is not. Given a set of connection records between one internal host and one external destination, the analysis looks at the distribution of inter-arrival times, the consistency of bytes sent and bytes received per connection, the total number of connections, and the duration over which the pattern persists. Low variance in timing scores highly. Consistent small payload sizes score highly. A pattern that persists for days scores highly. Tools such as RITA compute exactly this from Zeek connection logs, and every commercial network detection product has an equivalent.

**What it means for you.** Jitter widens the timing distribution and reduces the timing component of the score. It does nothing about the other components. Long sleeps reduce the connection count. Working-hours restriction breaks the continuity. Response padding breaks the size consistency. Rotating destinations breaks the single-destination aggregation. Doing all of those together is what it takes, and even then a channel that runs for a fortnight is fundamentally visible to anyone who looks hard enough. The realistic goal is not to be invisible, it is to be far enough down a ranked list of anomalies that nobody gets to you.

#### Destination reputation and prevalence

**What it is.** Judging a destination by what is known about it and by how many hosts in the organisation have ever talked to it.

**Why it works.** This is the cheapest and most effective detection in the whole section, and it requires no packet inspection. A domain registered eleven days ago, in no category, that exactly one host in a ten thousand seat estate has ever resolved, is suspicious on those facts alone. Add passive DNS showing the domain has one A record pointing at a small hosting provider, and Certificate Transparency showing a single certificate issued a week ago, and the case is essentially made without ever looking at the traffic.

**What it means for you.** Everything in the domain and reputation subsection above. Age, categorisation, plausibility, reputable address space, and, where possible, a destination that other hosts in the estate genuinely do talk to.

#### Volumetric and timing analysis

Long connection durations, sustained sessions to a single destination, an upload-to-download ratio that inverts the normal browsing pattern, and sudden bursts of outbound data are all watched. Exfiltration is where most operations are caught volumetrically, because the traffic volume required to move real data is very hard to hide. Split large transfers, throttle them, spread them over time, and prefer to move a small amount of high-value data over a large amount of everything.

#### DNS tunnelling detection

The signals are specific and strong: query volume per registered domain, cardinality of unique subdomains under one parent, label length distribution, entropy of the label content, unusual record type mix with TXT and NULL over-represented, NXDOMAIN rate, and the ratio of bytes in queries to bytes in responses. Any DNS security product finds a default DNS C2 channel quickly. Treat DNS as an emergency channel or a very slow long-haul channel and never as a working one.

#### Host-based and process behaviour indicators

Network detection finds the channel; endpoint detection finds the implant. The signals that matter most:

- **Named pipes.** Sysmon event 17 (pipe created) and 18 (pipe connected) plus EDR equivalents. Default pipe names for every public framework are in detection content. Anomalous pipe names, and pipe connections between workstations, are both signals.
- **Process ancestry and command lines.** A `rundll32.exe` or `dllhost.exe` with no arguments, spawned by an unusual parent, immediately followed by network activity or by a remote thread, is the classic fork-and-run pattern. Office spawning a script host, a service host spawning a shell, a browser spawning `cmd`: all of it is watched.
- **Cross-process memory operations.** Sysmon event 8 records remote thread creation; EDR products additionally see `VirtualAllocEx`, `WriteProcessMemory` and the various thread-creation primitives through kernel callbacks, and correlate them. Injection into a sensitive process, above all `lsass.exe`, is universally alerted.
- **Memory region properties.** Executable memory not backed by a file on disk is the single most reliable indicator that something has been loaded reflectively. RWX regions are worse. A thread whose start address lies in unbacked memory is worse still.
- **Call stacks.** Modern EDR captures the call stack at the moment of a sensitive API call or syscall. A stack containing a frame in unbacked memory, or a stack that is impossibly short, or a return address that does not correspond to a call instruction, all indicate manipulated execution. This is why return address spoofing and call stack synthesis are now standard implant features rather than research curiosities.
- **CLR and script engine telemetry.** Loading the .NET runtime into a process that does not normally host it, AMSI scanning of loaded assemblies and scripts, and ETW events for assembly load and method JIT compilation. This is the specific reason a .NET implant is a bigger commitment than it looks.
- **Handle and token operations.** Duplicating tokens, opening handles to `lsass`, and manipulating impersonation are all instrumented.

#### Memory scanning of implants at rest

**What it is.** Periodically or reactively scanning process memory for the signature of a known implant, or for the structural anomalies that indicate any implant.

**Why it works.** An implant that spends 99 percent of its life asleep spends 99 percent of its life as decrypted, signature-able bytes in memory. Signature scanning finds known frameworks: public YARA rules exist for essentially every framework's implant, and tooling exists to locate and parse configuration structures directly out of a memory image. Cobalt Strike's configuration, obfuscated with a single-byte XOR, is extracted by public tooling in one command, and the same is broadly true across frameworks. Structural scanning finds unknown implants: tools in the mould of PE-sieve and Moneta enumerate memory regions looking for executable private memory, mismatches between a module on disk and its image in memory, and modified section headers, none of which depend on knowing what the implant is.

**The counter, and its counter.** **Sleep obfuscation** encrypts the implant's own memory before sleeping and decrypts it on waking, using a timer queue, an APC chain or a ROP sequence to perform the encryption, sleep and decryption without any of the implant's own code needing to be resident and executable during the sleep. Havoc ships this, the commercial frameworks ship it, and Cobalt Strike exposes it through the sleep mask kit. It genuinely defeats naive signature scanning at rest.

It is not the end of the story. The mechanism used to implement the sleep is itself detectable: an unusual timer queue entry, a thread waiting in an odd state, a stack pointing at unbacked memory during the sleep, an RW region of a suspicious size whose contents have high entropy and change between samples. Public tooling exists specifically to hunt sleeping, obfuscated implants on exactly those properties. The realistic position is that sleep obfuscation moves you from "trivially found by a memory scan" to "found by someone who is specifically looking for obfuscated sleepers", which is a large and worthwhile improvement and not invisibility.

#### The honest summary

**A default-configuration deployment of any well-known framework is detected by any competent security product.** Not "might be", not "risks being". Default certificates, default profiles, default pipe names, default sacrificial processes, default fingerprints and unmodified public implants are the best-covered detection content in the industry, because they are what the vendors have the most samples of and the most customer incidents from.

What actually determines whether you survive is the sum of the work described in this section: an implant whose memory does not look like a known implant, a loader you control, in-process execution rather than fork and run, a profile derived from the target's real traffic, a domain with age and category, infrastructure that does not answer scanners, sleep and scheduling that keeps your volume low, and the discipline to keep the noisy work on infrastructure you are willing to lose. None of those items is optional and none of them is sufficient alone.

### Operational discipline across a team

The framework and the infrastructure are half of it. The other half is process, and it is what separates an engagement that produces a useful report from one that produces an argument with the client.

#### Operator logging

Every framework worth using logs every operator action with a timestamp, an operator identity, the target it was directed at, and the output that came back. Cobalt Strike writes per-day, per-Beacon transcripts to disk alongside the collected screenshots, keystrokes and downloads. Sliver records tasking and output in its database and log directory. Mythic records everything in PostgreSQL with per-operator attribution and ATT&CK mapping and can forward to external systems. This is not bureaucracy, and there are four concrete reasons it exists:

- **Deconfliction.** When the client's security team asks whether the process injection on that host at 14:32 was you, you need to answer in minutes with evidence, not with a guess.
- **Reporting.** The log is the raw material for the attack narrative. Reconstructing a three-week engagement from memory produces a worse report and takes longer.
- **Your own sanity.** On a long operation with several operators you will need to know what has already been tried on a host, which credentials came from where, and what you changed.
- **The concurrent-intrusion case.** If a real intrusion happens during your engagement, and this does occur, your log is what separates your activity from theirs. Without it, everything gets attributed to you or, far worse, their activity gets dismissed as yours.

Practical requirements: unique operator identities and no shared accounts, synchronised clocks with an agreed timezone (use UTC and be explicit about it), logs backed up off the team server, and the whole set preserved until the report is delivered and accepted.

#### Deconfliction with the blue team

Agree the mechanics before the engagement starts, not when the first alert fires.

- A **named point of contact** on the client side with authority to answer deconfliction questions, and an out-of-band way to reach them that does not depend on the systems you are testing.
- A **declared source address list**: every address your traffic will originate from, provided up front or held in escrow depending on the engagement's rules. If the test is intended to exercise detection, the list is held by a trusted party and released on request rather than published to the whole security team.
- An agreed **response procedure**: if the client sees activity they cannot attribute, they ask, and you answer within an agreed window. If they suspect a real intrusion, the engagement pauses and you help them rule your activity in or out.
- A **stand-down procedure**: a single instruction that stops all activity, and a known-good way to deliver it to every operator quickly.
- An agreed position on **what happens when you are detected**. Detection is a result, not a failure. Record the time, record what you were doing, and find out afterwards what triggered it, because that is one of the most valuable findings the engagement can produce.

Do not let deconfliction requirements push you into naming your artefacts obviously. The answer is not a filename containing the word "pentest", it is an internal register that lets you identify your own artefacts instantly. Which brings us to the register.

#### The artefact register

Maintain, continuously and not retrospectively, a record of everything you have put into the environment. This is the document that makes teardown possible and that answers deconfliction questions. At minimum:

| Category | Record |
| --- | --- |
| Implants | Host, user context, process and PID, listener and infrastructure, sleep and kill date, time established, operator |
| Files written | Full path, host, filename, hash, purpose, time, whether removed |
| Persistence | Mechanism (service, scheduled task, run key, WMI subscription, COM hijack, startup item), exact name and location, host, time, removal command |
| Accounts and groups | Accounts created, groups modified, ACLs changed, on which object, by whom, when |
| Configuration changes | Registry values, policy changes, firewall rules, disabled protections, original value recorded so it can be restored |
| Credentials obtained | Account, type of material, source host and method, time |
| Forged tickets and certificates | What was forged, for which principal, validity window, what key material it depended on |
| Infrastructure | Every domain, redirector address, certificate, listener and profile, with dates |
| Delivery | Every phishing message sent, to whom, when, with what payload and hash |

Two rules make this work. Record it at the moment you do it, because reconstruction is unreliable. And record the removal step at the same time as the creation step, because that is when you know exactly what you did.

Set a **kill date** on every implant you build. It costs nothing and it means an implant you lose track of, on a host that was offline during teardown, expires by itself rather than sitting in the client's estate calling out to a domain you no longer own. A domain you no longer own that live implants still call is a genuine liability for the client, because anyone can register it.

#### End-of-engagement teardown

Work from the register, in reverse order of installation, and verify rather than assume.

**On the target estate.** Remove persistence first, because otherwise you kill an implant and it comes back. Then remove files, in-memory implants, created accounts and group memberships. Restore every configuration change to its recorded original value, including anything you disabled. Remove any tooling dropped to disk, and check the locations you used habitually. Kill remaining sessions.

**Things that need the client to act.** Some cleanup is not yours to do. Forged Kerberos tickets remain valid until the key material they rely on is changed, so if you obtained the KRBTGT hash, the client needs to reset that account's password, and it needs to be done twice with an appropriate interval to invalidate both current and previous keys. Any account whose credentials you obtained should be rotated. Any certificate template weakness you exploited, and any certificate you enrolled, needs handling by their PKI team, including revocation. Machine account passwords you reset, delegation you configured, ACLs you changed on objects you did not create: list them explicitly in the report with the remediation step, and confirm the client has actioned them rather than assuming.

**Verify.** Re-enumerate the hosts you touched and confirm the artefacts are gone. Query for the scheduled tasks, services and accounts by name. Check that the implants no longer check in. A teardown you have not verified is a teardown that has not happened.

**On your own infrastructure.** Export and archive the logs and loot you need for the report. Destroy the target-facing hosts rather than reusing them. Revoke certificates. Decide deliberately what happens to the domains: keeping them for the duration of any implant kill dates prevents someone else registering a domain that live implants are calling, and is often the responsible choice even though it costs a renewal. Then delete client data from your systems according to the engagement's data handling terms, and mean it, including from operator laptops, scratch directories and password managers.

**Hand over the indicators.** The deliverable that clients value most after the findings themselves is a complete indicator list: your domains, addresses, hashes, filenames, pipe names, account names, timestamps and techniques. It lets them tune detection against a known ground truth and it turns the engagement from a report into an improvement. It is also the final proof that your register was accurate.

### Comparison

Status assessments below reflect the state of each project as best I can establish it and are the kind of thing that changes; check the repository or vendor before committing to any of them.

| Framework | Implant technology | Licence | Transports | Extensibility model | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Cobalt Strike | C, x86 and x64 (Beacon) | Commercial, openly sold | HTTP, HTTPS, DNS, SMB pipe, TCP, External C2, foreign Metasploit | BOFs, kits (artifact, resource, sleep mask, process inject, UDRL, post-ex), Aggressor Script, malleable profiles | Actively developed; the reference product and the most heavily signatured defaults |
| Nighthawk | C | Commercial, vetted purchase | HTTP, HTTPS and others; evasion-oriented channel controls | Vendor SDK and in-implant opsec controls | Actively developed; restricted distribution keeps detection thin |
| Brute Ratel C4 | C (Badger) | Commercial, vetted purchase | HTTP, HTTPS, DNS over HTTPS, SMB, TCP, external | BOFs and vendor extension interface | Actively developed; permanently affected by the 2022 leak and subsequent criminal abuse |
| Outflank Security Tooling | C | Commercial, vetted purchase | HTTP, HTTPS and others | Vendor toolkit | Actively developed; procurement-gated |
| Sliver | Go | Open source (GPL) | mTLS, WireGuard, HTTP, HTTPS, DNS, named pipe and TCP pivots | Armory packages, aliases and extensions, BOF and COFF loading | Actively maintained; the default open source choice. See the Sliver material earlier in this section |
| Mythic | Per agent: C#, Go, Python, Rust and others | Open source (BSD) | Per profile: HTTP, configurable HTTP, websocket, dynamic HTTP, DNS, SMB, TCP, plus custom containers | Payload type containers, C2 profile containers, translation containers, browser scripts, GraphQL API | Actively maintained; the most architecturally flexible option |

# Cloud and Modern Identity

## Microsoft Entra ID and Azure

The source notes contain an empty `### Azure` heading and eight BloodHound queries. That is a fair reflection of where the industry's collective cheatsheet was in 2020 and a completely inadequate reflection of where the targets are now. Most organisations you will test are hybrid or cloud-first. On-premises domain compromise is increasingly a *means* to tenant compromise rather than the end of the engagement, and in a cloud-first tenant there may be no domain at all. This section is written from scratch and is deliberately the longest treatment of a single identity platform in this document. It covers Entra ID and Azure specifically; AWS, Google Cloud, CI/CD, source control and secrets discovery are covered by the AWS, Google Cloud and developer estate material later in this same Cloud and Modern Identity section.

Two framing points before any technique.

First, **Entra ID is not Active Directory**. It shares a marketing lineage and almost no technical DNA. If you carry over Active Directory instincts you will waste days looking for things that do not exist and miss the things that do.

Second, **the credential is the token**. Passwords are an input to token issuance and are frequently not even that, given passwordless and federated flows. Every meaningful attack in this section is either obtaining a token, extending the reach of a token you already have, or arranging to be able to mint tokens indefinitely. Once that clicks, the rest of the section is mostly detail.

### Naming, because Microsoft keeps changing it

| Current name | Previous names you will still see in tooling and logs |
| --- | --- |
| Microsoft Entra ID | Azure Active Directory, Azure AD, AAD |
| Microsoft Entra ID role | Azure AD role, directory role |
| Microsoft Graph | successor to Azure AD Graph (*graph.windows.net*, now retired) and the older MSOnline/provisioning API |
| Microsoft Graph PowerShell SDK | successor to the retired *AzureAD* and *MSOnline* PowerShell modules |
| Microsoft Entra Connect Sync | Azure AD Connect, DirSync, Azure AD Sync |
| Microsoft Entra Cloud Sync | Azure AD Connect cloud sync, Azure AD Connect cloud provisioning |
| Microsoft Entra Domain Services | Azure AD Domain Services, AAD DS |
| Microsoft Entra Private Access / Internet Access | parts of what was Azure AD Application Proxy and MCAS |
| Microsoft Entra Verified ID | Azure AD Verifiable Credentials |
| Microsoft Entra Permissions Management | CloudKnox |

Object names in the API, class names in tooling, and event names in logs lag the marketing renames by years. The Graph resource is still `/servicePrincipals`, the audit log still says "Azure AD", and AzureHound still emits `AZ`-prefixed node labels. Write findings in current names, read logs in old ones.

## The identity model

### Why Entra ID is a genuinely different system

Active Directory is a replicated LDAP directory with a Kerberos KDC bolted to it, running on domain controllers you own, on ports you can reach, speaking protocols you can attack directly. Entra ID is a multi-tenant SaaS identity provider you interact with exclusively over HTTPS REST APIs. The consequences are structural.

| Active Directory | Entra ID |
| --- | --- |
| Kerberos (88), NTLM, LDAP (389/636), SMB, DRSUAPI | OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect over 443, SAML and WS-Federation for legacy apps |
| Domain controllers you can enumerate, reach, and sometimes own | No controllers. Microsoft-operated global endpoints, principally *login.microsoftonline.com* and *graph.microsoft.com* |
| Security descriptors (DACLs) on every object, with granular per-attribute rights | Role-based model. Roles carry fixed permission sets. There is no per-attribute ACL you can rewrite |
| Group Policy pushes configuration and code to domain members | Intune (and Configuration Manager, co-managed) pushes configuration and code to enrolled devices |
| SIDs, `objectSid`, RIDs | GUIDs (`objectId` / `id`). Synced objects also carry an on-premises SID |
| Replication is an attack surface (DCSync) | No replication protocol is exposed to you |
| Password hashes are the currency (pass-the-hash, overpass-the-hash, tickets) | Tokens are the currency. NT hashes are worthless against cloud endpoints |
| Trusts between domains and forests | Cross-tenant access settings, B2B/B2C, federation |
| `nltest`, `net`, LDAP queries, SPN scanning | Microsoft Graph, ARM REST API, and the portals |

There is no equivalent of a DACL write primitive, so the huge Active Directory family of ACL-abuse attacks has no direct analogue. What replaces it is the application and service principal model, which is where almost all Entra privilege escalation lives. And there is no offline hash to crack, so credential attacks move to tokens, which cannot be cracked but can be stolen, replayed, and exchanged.

Practically: nothing in this section needs network position. It needs a token and internet access. Conversely, nothing in this section is invisible, because every call you make is a logged API request to Microsoft. See the detection section.

### Principal types

Getting these distinctions right matters more than usual because the escalation paths run between them.

**User.** A human identity or a human-shaped service identity. Three provenances that behave differently:

- **Cloud-only**, created in Entra ID. Managed entirely in the cloud.
- **Synchronised** (also "hybrid"), created on-premises and projected into the tenant by Entra Connect. Marked with `onPremisesSyncEnabled` set true. Most attributes, including the password when password hash sync is on, are authoritative on-premises. You generally cannot edit these attributes in the cloud; the sync engine overwrites them.
- **Guest** (B2B), an external identity from another tenant or a consumer account, with `userType` of `Guest`.

**Group.** Two kinds, and the difference is load-bearing:

- **Security group**, used for access assignment. Can be assigned membership statically or dynamically (a rule over attributes).
- **Microsoft 365 group**, which additionally carries a mailbox, SharePoint site, and Teams team. Members can often add themselves.

Orthogonal to that is **role-assignable** (`isAssignableToRole` set true). A group can only be granted an Entra role if it was created role-assignable, this cannot be changed afterwards, and role-assignable groups are themselves protected: only Privileged Role Administrator and Global Administrator can alter their membership or owners. This is a deliberate barrier against the "I have `Group.ReadWrite.All`, therefore I have Global Administrator" path. It is also frequently missed by people who assume all groups are equal.

Synchronised groups cannot be edited in the cloud, which means a synced group holding an Entra role is a *hybrid escalation path*: change membership on-premises, wait for the sync cycle, inherit the cloud role.

**Application registration** (`/applications` in Graph, "App registrations" in the portal). The *definition* of an application: its display name, its redirect URIs, the permissions it requests, its credentials, whether it is single or multi-tenant, and its `appId` (client ID). It lives in exactly one tenant, the **home tenant**. It is a template. It has no permissions of its own in any tenant.

**Service principal** (`/servicePrincipals`, "Enterprise applications" in the portal). The *instance* of an application in a specific tenant. This is the security principal that actually holds role assignments, permission grants, and group memberships. For a single-tenant app there is one application object and one service principal, both in the same tenant, and the portal blurs them together, which is why people confuse the two. For a multi-tenant app there is one application object in the publisher's tenant and one service principal in *every tenant that has consented to it*, including yours. Microsoft's own first-party applications appear in your tenant as service principals with no corresponding application object you control.

The critical asymmetry: **credentials live on the application object, permissions live on the service principal.** If you can write to the application object in its home tenant, you can add a credential and then authenticate as the service principal in every tenant where it exists, inheriting whatever permissions each tenant granted it. That is the single most reliable escalation and persistence primitive in Entra ID and it is covered in detail later.

Service principals also come in flavours: `Application` (backed by an app registration), `ManagedIdentity`, and `Legacy`. The `servicePrincipalType` attribute tells you which.

**Managed identity.** A service principal whose credential is managed by the platform and never exposed to you as a secret. Two forms:

- **System-assigned**, created with a specific Azure resource, lifecycle-bound to it, one-to-one, deleted with the resource.
- **User-assigned**, a standalone Azure resource you create, which can be attached to many compute resources simultaneously.

A managed identity is retrieved by code running on the resource, from a local endpoint, with no secret in the code. It is a normal service principal in the directory otherwise: it can hold Azure RBAC role assignments, Entra roles, and Graph application permissions. The user-assigned variant is an escalation gift, because "attach this identity to a resource I control" is a resource-plane operation that yields a directory-plane identity.

**Device.** A registered, joined, or hybrid-joined machine, with a device object in the directory holding a device ID and public keys. Devices matter because of conditional access (compliant/joined device requirements) and because of the primary refresh token.

**Administrative unit.** A container for scoping role assignments to a subset of users, groups, or devices. It is not an OU: it does not form a hierarchy that objects live inside exclusively, it does not affect GPO or anything like it, and objects can be in several AUs. It exists solely to scope role assignments. There is also a hardened variant, **restricted management administrative unit**, whose members can only be modified by admins with roles scoped to that AU, explicitly blocking tenant-wide admins. That is a defensive feature and also an excellent persistence primitive.

### The Azure resource hierarchy

Azure resources are a separate tree from the directory, anchored to it by tenant.

```text
Tenant (Entra ID directory)
  └── Root management group  (id == tenant id)
        └── Management group(s)      (nestable, up to 6 levels)
              └── Subscription
                    └── Resource group
                          └── Resource   (VM, storage account, key vault, ...)
                                └── Sub-resource (a blob container, a secret, ...)
```

Azure RBAC assignments inherit downwards and only downwards. An assignment at a management group applies to every subscription beneath it. An assignment at a resource group applies to every resource in it. There is no deny-by-default override for a broader allow, other than the explicit **deny assignment** mechanism, which is used by Azure Blueprints and managed applications and which you will rarely see.

Two things to note when enumerating. Subscriptions are not visible to a principal with no role assignment on them, so "I see no subscriptions" means "I have no assignments", not "there are none". And the root management group is often not visible even to Global Administrators until the elevation described below, which is the whole point of that elevation.

### The two authorisation systems

This is the single most common source of confusion, so be precise about it in reports.

| | Entra ID roles | Azure RBAC |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Governs | Directory objects: users, groups, applications, service principals, devices, roles, tenant settings | Azure resources: subscriptions, resource groups, VMs, storage, key vaults, and the management plane operations on them |
| Assignment scope | Tenant-wide, or scoped to an administrative unit, or scoped to a single application (for some roles) | Management group, subscription, resource group, or individual resource |
| Example roles | Global Administrator, User Administrator, Application Administrator, Privileged Role Administrator | Owner, Contributor, Reader, User Access Administrator, Virtual Machine Contributor, Key Vault Secrets User |
| API surface | Microsoft Graph, *graph.microsoft.com* | Azure Resource Manager, *management.azure.com* |
| Where you read it | `/roleManagement/directory/roleAssignments` in Graph, "Roles and administrators" in the portal | `Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments` in ARM, "Access control (IAM)" in the portal |
| Custom roles | Yes, Entra custom roles, limited permission set | Yes, custom role definitions with `actions`/`notActions`/`dataActions` |

They are separate. **Global Administrator gives you nothing on Azure resources by default, and Owner on every subscription gives you nothing in the directory.** An operator who reports "we obtained Global Administrator therefore we own the infrastructure" without demonstrating the elevation has skipped a step, and a client who understands the model will notice.

Some Entra roles do carry resource-adjacent power (for instance Intune-related roles governing device management, or the roles that manage the tenant's federation configuration), and some resource permissions reach the directory through managed identities, which is the reverse path. Both directions are covered below.

Note also **Privileged Identity Management** (PIM), which turns role assignments into *eligible* assignments requiring activation, optionally with approval, justification, MFA, and a time limit. PIM applies to both Entra roles and Azure RBAC. Operationally: a target with PIM may hold no active roles at the moment you enumerate, and the interesting finding is the *eligibility*, which lives in a different Graph path than active assignments. Tooling that only enumerates active assignments will under-report privilege in a mature tenant. BloodHound models this as a separate edge.

### The elevation path from directory to resources

A Global Administrator can grant themselves the **User Access Administrator** Azure RBAC role at the **root scope** (`/`), which is above every management group and therefore every subscription in the tenant. From User Access Administrator at root, they assign themselves Owner anywhere they like.

**What it is.** A single API call that converts tenant-level directory control into tenant-wide Azure resource control.

**Why it works.** The tenant owns the root management group. Microsoft provides a deliberate, documented mechanism for a Global Administrator to recover access to subscriptions whose owners have left, because otherwise an orphaned subscription would be unrecoverable. The mechanism is a self-service toggle, not an approval workflow.

**Preconditions.** Global Administrator in the tenant. (Historically some documentation implied other roles could do it; treat Global Administrator as the requirement.)

**Commands.**

```bash
# ARM REST, with a token whose audience is https://management.azure.com/
curl -s -X POST \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $ARM_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Length: 0" \
  "https://management.azure.com/providers/Microsoft.Authorization/elevateAccess?api-version=2016-07-01"
```

```powershell
# Az PowerShell / Azure CLI equivalents
az rest --method post --url "https://management.azure.com/providers/Microsoft.Authorization/elevateAccess?api-version=2016-07-01"
```

The portal equivalent is the "Access management for Azure resources" toggle on the Entra ID Properties blade.

**Verify it worked.** Enumerate subscriptions again. Before elevation, a Global Administrator with no assignments sees none. Afterwards, every subscription in the tenant is listed, and a role assignment for your principal exists at scope `/`.

```bash
az account list --refresh -o table
az role assignment list --scope "/" --include-inherited -o table
```

**Detection and opsec.** The elevation is logged in the Entra ID audit log as a directory-level action and creates a role assignment at root scope that is trivially auditable and monitored by any tenant with a competent detection programme. It is also *persistent until removed* and highly visible in a review, so it is a loud action. Prefer it when you need to demonstrate blast radius, and note in the report that the toggle is off by default and that the assignment should be removed after use. Removal is the `DELETE` on that role assignment, or the portal toggle.

**Failure modes.** A 403 means the token is not a Global Administrator's, or the token audience is wrong. A token for Graph will not work against ARM: you need an ARM-audience token, which is the single most common mistake in cloud tooling. If subscriptions still do not appear after success, refresh the token, because the assignment is not reflected in an already-issued token's evaluation cache in some clients.

The reverse direction (resource control yielding directory control) is not a single API call. It runs through managed identities and through compute that holds hybrid identity secrets, and it is covered under privilege escalation and the hybrid seam.

## Tokens are the credential

Everything else follows from this section. If you internalise one thing about attacking Entra ID, make it this: **you are not stealing passwords, you are stealing and manipulating bearer tokens, and a bearer token is a self-contained grant that the resource accepts without asking the identity provider anything.**

### The three token types

OpenID Connect on top of OAuth 2.0 produces three artefacts and they are not interchangeable.

| Token | Format | Audience | What it is for | Attacker value |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Access token** | JWT, signed by Entra ID, not encrypted, readable | A specific **resource** (Graph, ARM, Key Vault, a custom API) | Presented to that resource as `Authorization: Bearer`. Carries the identity and the granted scopes | Immediate but short-lived. Cannot be refreshed or exchanged |
| **Refresh token** | Opaque to you, encrypted by Entra ID, only Entra ID can read it | The **token endpoint** | Redeemed at */oauth2/v2.0/token* for new access tokens | The prize. Long-lived, and redeemable for tokens against *other* resources |
| **ID token** | JWT, signed, readable | The **client application** | Tells the client who signed in. Never sent to a resource API | Informational only. Useful for reading claims about the identity and the authentication context |

The most important row is the middle one. An access token is a 60-to-90-minute window against one resource. A refresh token is typically weeks of access, against potentially many resources, renewable, and it survives the user closing their laptop. When you have the choice, take the refresh token.

There is a fourth artefact that is not an OAuth token but functions as one: the **session cookie** on *login.microsoftonline.com* (the `ESTSAUTH` / `ESTSAUTHPERSISTENT` family). It represents the interactive browser session at the identity provider. Replay it into a browser and you can complete authorisation code flows for arbitrary applications without ever seeing the password or a second factor. This is what adversary-in-the-middle phishing kits harvest.

### What is inside an access token

Access tokens issued by Entra ID for Microsoft resources are JWTs: three base64url segments separated by dots, header, payload, signature. The payload is *not encrypted*. You read it by base64-decoding it. Do not use online JWT decoders on a real engagement token; decode locally.

```bash
# Decode the payload of a JWT held in $TOKEN
python3 -c 'import sys,base64,json; p=sys.argv[1].split(".")[1]; print(json.dumps(json.loads(base64.urlsafe_b64decode(p + "="*(-len(p)%4))),indent=2))' "$TOKEN"
```

```powershell
# PowerShell equivalent
$p = ($TOKEN -split '\.')[1].Replace('-','+').Replace('_','/')
while ($p.Length % 4) { $p += '=' }
[System.Text.Encoding]::UTF8.GetString([Convert]::FromBase64String($p)) | ConvertFrom-Json | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 5
```

The claims that matter operationally:

| Claim | Meaning and why you care |
| --- | --- |
| `aud` | The **audience**: which resource will accept this token. A Graph token presented to ARM is rejected. Checking `aud` first solves most "403 for no reason" problems |
| `iss` | Issuer, contains the tenant ID: `https://login.microsoftonline.com/{tenantId}/v2.0` (v2) or `https://sts.windows.net/{tenantId}/` (v1) |
| `tid` | Tenant ID |
| `oid` | Object ID of the principal in the directory. This is the stable identifier, use it, not the UPN |
| `sub` | Subject, pairwise per application. Not a directory identifier |
| `upn` / `unique_name` / `preferred_username` | The user's name. Present for users, absent for service principals |
| `appid` / `azp` | The client application that requested the token. Tells you *what* the user was using, and is the field defenders alert on when it is Azure CLI at 3am |
| `scp` | Delegated **scopes** granted, space-separated, for example `User.Read Mail.Read`. Present when acting on behalf of a user |
| `roles` | **Application permissions** (app roles) held. Present for client-credentials tokens, that is, a service principal acting as itself |
| `amr` | Authentication methods references, for example `pwd`, `mfa`, `rsa`, `hwk`, `fido`, `wia`, `ngcmfa`. **`mfa` present means multi-factor was satisfied when this token was minted** |
| `wids` | Well-known IDs: the role **template** GUIDs of tenant-wide Entra roles the principal holds, not the tenant-specific assignment object IDs. `62e90394-69f5-4237-9190-012177145e10` is Global Administrator. Microsoft's built-in roles reference is the lookup table for the rest |
| `iat`, `nbf`, `exp` | Issued at, not before, expires. Unix time |
| `acr` / `acrs` | Authentication context class, used by conditional access authentication context |
| `deviceid` | Device object ID, present when the token derives from a device-bound flow. Its presence is what satisfies "require compliant device" style policies |
| `xms_cc` | Client capabilities, notably `cp1`, indicating the client can handle claims challenges, which is what makes continuous access evaluation possible |
| `idtyp` | Present as `app` for application-only tokens. A cheap way to spot a service principal token |

Two operational reads. First, `scp` versus `roles` tells you instantly whether you hold a delegated token (acting as a user, limited to the intersection of the app's grants and the user's own rights) or an application token (acting as the app, with no user in the picture and no user-level restriction). Second, `amr` containing `mfa` is the claim you exploit: it is a statement that MFA already happened, and it travels with the token.

### Lifetimes, and why refresh tokens are the prize

| Artefact | Default lifetime | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Access token | 60 to 90 minutes, randomised within that window to avoid thundering herds | Not configurable downward in any supported way for most resources; the old configurable token lifetime policy for access tokens was retired |
| Access token, CAE-capable resource | Up to 28 hours | Longer *by design*, traded against near-real-time revocation. See below |
| Refresh token | Sliding, 90 days of inactivity in the general case, 24 hours for single-page applications and for email one-time-passcode flows | The split is by flow type, not by public versus confidential client, which is the usual misstatement. Each redemption issues a new refresh token and resets the clock, so an actively used refresh token effectively does not expire |
| Primary refresh token | 14 days, renewed automatically while the device is in use | Effectively indefinite on a live device |
| Browser session cookie | Governed by sign-in frequency and persistent-browser settings in conditional access | Default is a rolling session, not a hard expiry |
| Device code | About 15 minutes from issuance | The phishing window |
| SAML assertion from a federated IdP | Set by the IdP, commonly an hour | Irrelevant once exchanged for Entra tokens |

Refresh token lifetime is **no longer configurable** through the configurable token lifetime policy; Microsoft retired that and directs tenants to conditional access **sign-in frequency** instead. This matters when you write remediation advice: telling a client to shorten refresh token lifetime via CTL is out of date guidance. Sign-in frequency, and continuous access evaluation, are the current controls.

### Refresh token exchange and the family of client IDs

A refresh token is issued to a specific client (`appid`) for a specific set of scopes. When you redeem it, you may ask for scopes against a *different resource*, and Entra ID will issue an access token for that resource provided the client is authorised for it and consent exists. This is the mechanism behind "I had a Graph token and now I have an ARM token".

```bash
# Redeem a refresh token for an access token addressed to a different resource
curl -s -X POST "https://login.microsoftonline.com/$TENANT/oauth2/v2.0/token" \
  -d "client_id=$CLIENT_ID" \
  -d "grant_type=refresh_token" \
  -d "refresh_token=$REFRESH_TOKEN" \
  -d "scope=https://management.azure.com/.default offline_access"
```

The `.default` scope means "everything this client has already been granted for that resource", which avoids having to guess individual scope names. `offline_access` is what asks for a refresh token back.

Beyond changing resource, there is a stronger trick. Microsoft operates a set of first-party public clients that share a refresh token pool, marked by a **`foci`** value of `1` in the token response. A refresh token issued to one member of this **family of client IDs** can be redeemed *as a different family member*, by simply passing a different `client_id` in the redemption request. Because different first-party clients have different pre-consented permission sets and are treated differently by conditional access, this converts a token from a narrow client into a token from a broad one.

```bash
# Same refresh token, redeemed under a different family client_id
curl -s -X POST "https://login.microsoftonline.com/$TENANT/oauth2/v2.0/token" \
  -d "client_id=$OTHER_FAMILY_CLIENT_ID" \
  -d "grant_type=refresh_token" \
  -d "refresh_token=$REFRESH_TOKEN" \
  -d "scope=https://graph.microsoft.com/.default offline_access"
```

Widely documented first-party client IDs, useful because they are pre-consented in every tenant and raise no consent prompt:

| Client ID | Application name as Microsoft publishes it | In the FOCI family |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `04b07795-8ddb-461a-bbee-02f9e1bf7b46` | Microsoft Azure CLI | Yes |
| `1950a258-227b-4e31-a9cf-717495945fc2` | Microsoft Azure PowerShell | Yes |
| `d3590ed6-52b3-4102-aeff-aad2292ab01c` | Microsoft Office | Yes |
| `9ba1a5c7-f17a-4de9-a1f1-6178c8d51223` | Microsoft Intune Company Portal | Yes |
| `1fec8e78-bce4-4aaf-ab1b-5451cc387264` | Microsoft Teams | Yes |
| `1b730954-1685-4b74-9bfd-dac224a7b894` | Azure Active Directory PowerShell | **No** |
| `29d9ed98-a469-4536-ade2-f981bc1d605e` | Microsoft Authentication Broker | **No** |

**Common mistake.** Assuming every well-known first-party client ID is a FOCI family member. It is not. `1b730954-...` and `29d9ed98-...` are the two that catch people out, because they are the two most frequently pasted: the first because tooling has used it as a default client for years, the second because it is the client all PRT requests are made against and therefore the one you reach for on device and PRT work. Neither appears in the published FOCI client list, so a refresh token issued to a genuine FOCI client will not necessarily redeem under them, and a refresh token issued to *them* is not portable across the family. Being pre-consented with broad permissions is a different and independent property from being in the family; keep the two ideas separate. The current family membership list is maintained as a CSV in Secureworks' family-of-client-ids research repository and mirrored in AADInternals' source, and it grows, so check it rather than working from a five-entry memory.

If a redemption returns **AADSTS700016**, the client ID is not present in the tenant, which in practice means you have transcribed a GUID wrongly. Compare it character by character against Microsoft's own published first-party application ID list before assuming anything about the tenant.

Tooling that implements this: **ROADtools**, where `roadtx refreshtokento` is the idiomatic command for pure refresh-token redemption (`roadtx gettokens --refresh-token` also accepts one), with `-c`/`--client` and `-r`/`--resource` selecting client and resource. ROADtools is actively maintained. **TokenTactics** exposes a set of `Invoke-RefreshTo*` functions, one per target resource, and here the repository matters: the original `rvrsh3ll/TokenTactics` has been stale since late 2024, and the maintained line is **TokenTacticsV2** under `f-bader`, which keeps backwards-compatible aliases so the classic function names still work. Pull the original and you get the stale one, which is the trap.

Operationally, this is why "we found a low-privilege Azure CLI token in a CI log" is not a low-severity finding. The token is a refresh token for a family client, and it can become a Graph token, an ARM token, an Outlook token, and a SharePoint token, none of which trigger a new authentication event that conditional access will evaluate as an interactive sign-in.

### The primary refresh token

The **primary refresh token** (PRT) is the single most powerful credential on a Windows endpoint joined or registered to Entra ID, and it is why endpoint compromise so often equals cloud identity compromise.

**What it is.** A long-lived refresh token bound to *both* a user and a device, issued during device join or interactive sign-on, held by the Cloud Authentication Provider (`CloudAP`) plugin inside LSASS, with its associated session key protected by the TPM where one exists. It is what makes single sign-on to Microsoft 365 work from a joined machine without prompting.

**Why it is powerful.** Three reasons stacked. It is device-bound, so tokens derived from it carry a `deviceid` claim and satisfy conditional access policies that require a compliant or hybrid-joined device, which are precisely the policies designed to stop credential theft. It usually carries an `mfa` claim from the original join or sign-in, so it satisfies MFA requirements. And it is a refresh token, so it can be redeemed for access tokens against any resource the user can reach, and under any family client ID.

**Preconditions.** Code execution on the device. SYSTEM (or a token-manipulation path to it) for the direct LSASS extraction route; the user's own context is sufficient for the browser-cookie route.

**Mechanism of use.** You do not usually exfiltrate the PRT itself, because using it requires the session key, which is TPM-protected and non-exportable on modern hardware. Instead you ask the local machine to produce a **PRT cookie** (`x-ms-RefreshTokenCredential`), which is a signed JWT proving PRT possession, valid for a few minutes, and usable from anywhere. Getting one requires a nonce from Entra ID first.

```text
1. Request a nonce from https://login.microsoftonline.com/common/oauth2/token  (grant_type=srv_challenge)
2. Ask the local CloudAP/BrowserCore component to sign a PRT cookie over that nonce
3. Present the PRT cookie to the /authorize endpoint as a cookie
4. Receive an authorisation code, redeem it for a token pair off-host
```

Routes to step 2, in increasing order of privilege required and noise:

- **`BrowserCore.exe`** (the native messaging host used by Edge and Chrome for Windows SSO) will produce a PRT cookie for the logged-on user when spoken to over its stdio protocol, from the *user's own context*, no elevation. This is the quietest route. Implemented by ROADtools (`roadtx browserprtauth`, with `roadtx prt` and `roadtx prtenrich` alongside it, plus the ROADtoken helper) and by AADInternals's `Get-AADIntUserPRTToken`, which takes `-Method` of `BrowserCore`, `TokenProvider` or `CloudAP` and defaults to `BrowserCore`. Note that this cmdlet is in the **AADInternals-Endpoints** module, not the main one, and do not confuse it with `New-AADIntUserPRTToken` in the main module, which *constructs* a PRT cookie from a refresh token and session key you already hold rather than reading anything off the local machine.
- **`sekurlsa::cloudap`** in Mimikatz, as SYSTEM, dumps the CloudAP cache including the encrypted PRT and the key material context, followed by `dpapi::cloudapkd` to derive the session key. Requires SYSTEM and defeats nothing if Credential Guard is protecting the relevant secrets.
- **Device impersonation.** If you hold the device certificate and transport key (extractable from a non-TPM or software-key device), you can request a fresh PRT for a user whose credentials you have, from your own machine, producing device-compliant tokens off-host.
- **Registering your own device.** If policy allows a user to join or register devices (a common default), authenticate as that user, register a device you control, and you now legitimately hold a PRT and a compliant-device claim. This is the route that turns "we have one password and MFA" into "we bypass the compliant-device policy". `roadtx device` and AADInternals's `Join-AADIntDeviceToAzureAD` implement it. The latter takes `-AccessToken`, `-DeviceName`, `-DeviceType`, `-OSVersion`, and crucially `-JoinType` of `Join` or `Register`: registration is the lower-privilege operation and is what a default tenant permits every user to do, so try that first. `Join-AADIntOnPremDeviceToAzureAD` emulates a hybrid join through the sync API, and `Join-AADIntDeviceToIntune` enrols into Intune, which is the step that produces a *compliant* device rather than merely a registered one.

**Verify it worked.** Decode the resulting access token and confirm a `deviceid` claim and, where expected, `mfa` in `amr`. If `deviceid` is absent, the flow fell back to a non-device-bound path and will not satisfy device-based conditional access.

**Detection and opsec.** Entra ID sign-in logs record the client application, the device ID, and the authentication protocol, and Identity Protection has a specific "primary refresh token access attempt" style detection for local PRT theft attempts. On the endpoint, LSASS access for the Mimikatz route is the usual high-fidelity signal (Sysmon event ID 10, EDR handle-access telemetry); the `BrowserCore.exe` route is far quieter because it is a legitimate binary performing its normal function, and the giveaway is an unusual parent process. TPM-backed keys mean the extraction routes that dump secrets are increasingly unavailable, pushing operators toward the BrowserCore and device-registration routes.

**Failure modes.** A nonce mismatch produces an immediate rejection at `/authorize`. Credential Guard blocks the LSASS-dump route. A TPM-bound session key means the PRT blob you exfiltrated is unusable off-host, which manifests as a signature failure rather than an obvious error. If the device has been marked non-compliant or deleted, tokens derived from the PRT lose their compliance value even though the PRT still works.

### Conditional access, and when it is actually evaluated

**Conditional access** is the policy engine that sits in the token issuance path. A policy is an if-then: for these users, these applications ("target resources"), and these conditions (device platform, client app type, location, sign-in risk, user risk, authentication flow, device state, insider risk), require these controls (MFA, compliant device, hybrid-joined device, approved client app, app protection policy, password change, terms of use) or block.

The operationally decisive fact: **conditional access is evaluated at token issuance, not at token use.** Once a token exists, the resource accepts it on the strength of its signature and claims. The policy engine is not consulted again. Therefore a stolen token bypasses every conditional access control that was satisfied at issuance, including MFA, for the token's remaining lifetime and, if you have the refresh token, for far longer than that.

Additional structural properties you should be able to explain to a client:

- **There is no default deny.** Conditional access is an allowlist of policies, not a default posture. Any application, client type, or user combination not covered by a policy is unprotected. Enumerating the *gaps* is more productive than enumerating the policies.
- **Exclusions are the standard weakness.** Break-glass accounts, service accounts, "the CEO complained", specific applications that broke, specific named locations. Every exclusion is an attack path, and exclusions are exactly what an authenticated read of the policy set reveals.
- **Named and trusted locations** are IP-based. If a policy grants MFA exemption from the corporate egress range, then any code execution inside that range, or any proxy through it, inherits the exemption. Trusted-location exemptions are the most common reason MFA does not apply to an attack you expected it to block.
- **Report-only mode** means a policy that looks protective in an export is enforcing nothing. Always check the `state` field, which is `enabled`, `disabled`, or `enabledForReportingButNotEnforced`.
- **Legacy authentication** is the classic gap. Policies must explicitly block "other clients"/legacy authentication clients, and where Basic authentication remains enabled for a protocol, conditional access support for it is limited or absent.
- **Workload identities are not covered by ordinary policy.** Conditional access for service principals is a separate feature requiring an additional licence (Workload Identities Premium), so in most tenants a service principal's client-credentials sign-in is subject to no policy at all, from any IP, with no MFA concept. This is why service principal credential theft is so valuable.
- **Authentication flow conditions.** The condition is called **Authentication Flows**, and it currently targets exactly two flows: **device code flow** and **authentication transfer**. That is the mechanism a tenant uses to kill device code phishing outright. Where the condition is absent, or present but scoped to a subset of users, device code phishing is available. Because there are only two selectable flows, this is a quick thing to check and a quick thing to recommend.

**Continuous access evaluation** (CAE) changes the picture partially. For CAE-capable resources (the major Microsoft 365 workloads and Graph), the resource itself subscribes to critical events and can reject a token mid-lifetime, returning a **claims challenge** that forces the client back to the identity provider. The trade is a longer access token (up to 28 hours) for near-real-time revocation. Critical events include account disable or delete, password change or reset, an administrator explicitly revoking sessions, high user risk detected by Identity Protection, and conditional access policy changes.

The consequences for you are specific. Against a CAE-enabled resource, a stolen access token can be killed within minutes by a defender who disables the account or revokes sessions, so your access is no longer guaranteed for the full token lifetime. Against a non-CAE resource, a stolen access token remains valid until `exp` regardless of what the defender does, because nothing re-checks. And CAE only works with clients that advertise the `cp1` capability, so a hand-rolled client that does not advertise it gets the short, unrevocable token instead of the long, revocable one, which is often the outcome you prefer.

### Scopes, audiences, and permission models

Two permission models, and mixing them up produces most of the confusing 403s in cloud work.

**Delegated permissions** (scopes, the `scp` claim). The application acts *on behalf of a signed-in user*. Effective access is the **intersection** of what the application was granted and what the user can actually do. A delegated `User.ReadWrite.All` held by an app does not let a plain member rewrite every user, because the user cannot. Consent for delegated permissions can be given by the user themselves (subject to tenant consent settings) or by an administrator on behalf of everyone.

**Application permissions** (app roles, the `roles` claim). The application acts *as itself*, with no user. Effective access is exactly what was granted, tenant-wide, with no user-level ceiling. Application `User.ReadWrite.All` genuinely means every user in the tenant. Application permissions **always** require administrator consent. This asymmetry is why service principal compromise is so much more valuable than user compromise at the same nominal permission name.

**Audience.** `aud` names the resource. Common ones:

| Resource | `aud` / scope prefix |
| --- | --- |
| Microsoft Graph | `https://graph.microsoft.com` |
| Azure Resource Manager | `https://management.azure.com` (also `https://management.core.windows.net`) |
| Key Vault data plane | `https://vault.azure.net` |
| Azure Storage | `https://storage.azure.com` |
| Exchange Online / Outlook | `https://outlook.office365.com` |
| SharePoint / OneDrive | `https://<tenant>.sharepoint.com` |
| Azure SQL | `https://database.windows.net` |
| Azure AD Graph (retired) | `https://graph.windows.net` |

Getting a token for the wrong audience is the number one cause of a working credential appearing not to work. If a call returns 401 with a message about an invalid audience, decode the token and check `aud` before doing anything else.

### The operational summary of the token model

- A password gets you a token. A token is what you actually use. Optimise for tokens.
- Prefer refresh tokens over access tokens, PRTs over refresh tokens, and service principal credentials over all of them because they have no MFA and usually no conditional access.
- MFA is a property of the issuance event, recorded in `amr`, not a property of each API call. Steal a post-MFA artefact and MFA is behind you.
- Exchange tokens between resources and between family clients rather than re-authenticating, because re-authenticating re-invokes conditional access and generates an interactive sign-in event.
- The defender's counters that actually bite are phishing-resistant authentication, device binding, token binding where available, CAE, and short sign-in frequency. Not token lifetime tuning.

## Reconnaissance without credentials

Entra ID exposes a surprising amount of tenant configuration to completely unauthenticated requests, because federation and client autodiscovery require it. This is by design and Microsoft has repeatedly declined to change it. It is the cheapest phase of a cloud engagement and it should be complete before you send a single authentication attempt.

Be precise in the report about what is unauthenticated, because clients frequently assume otherwise. The table at the end of this subsection does that.

### Confirming a domain belongs to a tenant, and finding the tenant ID

**What it is.** Establishing that `$DOMAIN` is a verified domain of some Entra tenant, and obtaining that tenant's GUID.

**Why it works.** OpenID Connect requires an issuer to publish a discovery document at a well-known path so that clients can find its endpoints and signing keys without prior configuration. Entra ID serves that document per tenant, and it accepts a *domain name* as the tenant identifier in the path. The `issuer` field in the response contains the tenant GUID. No authentication is possible on a metadata endpoint by definition.

**Preconditions.** Internet access. Nothing else.

**Commands.**

```bash
# Tenant ID from a domain name. The issuer field carries the GUID.
curl -s "https://login.microsoftonline.com/$DOMAIN/.well-known/openid-configuration" | jq -r '.issuer, .token_endpoint, .authorization_endpoint'

# The v1 federation metadata document also carries the tenant ID and the signing certificates
```
